div.head: Commentary Notes
div.note:
1 Dramatis Personæ]
From Rowe (ed. 1709); there is no list in the quartos or folios. Most editors reproduce it with modifications of detail. Theobald (ed. 1733), followed by virtually all eds., adds Old Man, Tenant to Gloster and A Captain, employ’d by Edmund.

2 LEAR]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Leir, the sp. of the old play [The True Chronicle Historie of King Leir (1605)—hereafter called Leir; see ], of Raphael Holinshed [The Historie of Englande (1587); see ], and (as Leyr) of Spenser (F.Q.…[see ]) crops up occasionally in Q [256, 265, 269, 788] though Lear is the usual form, as it is invariably in F. The sp. is Leire in John Higgins’s portion of The Mirour for Magistrates (1574, rev. 1587—hereafter called Mirour) and Leir in William Warner’s Albions England (1586); see , . The sp. Leir derives from the the oldest literary source of the Lear story, Geoffrey of Monmouth’s 12th-c. Latin History of the Kings of Britain [Historia regum Britanni; see ]. Perrett (1904, pp. 158–9), after listing all variant spellings of the name in accounts of the Lear story: The substitution of ea for ei, ey, occurs before Shakespeare only in Henslowe’s Diary [fol. 9], where the performance of kinge leare (i.e. [Leir]) is recorded on Apr. 6, 1593–4. A contemporary ballad which seems influenced by the play (see ) uses the spelling Leare. Kökeritz (1959, p. 65): Shakespeare’s pronunciation was perhaps closer to lair than to modern leer. Foakes (ed. 1997): A spelling perhaps chosen to distinguish Shakespeare’s play from the old play of King Leir. For the possibility that Lear’s name was also Edgar, see n. 1031. Malone (ed. 1790): Geoffrey of Monmouth says, that Leir, who was the eldest son of Bladud [or Baldud], nobly governed his country for sixty years. According to that historian, he died about 800 years before the birth of Christ; see the next n. According to Geoffrey, Leir was the tenth king of Britain after its founding by Brute. Hamilton (1983, pp. 39–40), emphasizing James I’s links to Lear: In George Owen Harry, Genealogy of…James (1604, pp. 42–4), Leir and Regan become the most prominent descendants after Brutus’ sons, as they do also in William Warner’s Albions England, where Regan is not named.
Comment on supposed mythical backgrounds seems to begin with Davies (1809, pp. 400–1), who says that the legendary King Llyr, or Leirus…was unknown in Wales before the days of Geoffry, of Monmouth.…The tale was, originally, mythological; (p. 501): Llyr implies the sea, or the sea beach. This name has a constant reference to the rites of the Diluvian god. (Cf. DP n. 17 below.) Accordingly Yonge (1863; 1884, pp. 229–30): In Celtic, Lir, is the sea. He is also…a god in the elder Irish belief, and father of Manannán, the Erse Neptune. Afterwards, later ballads humanized Lear as an Irish or Welsh king. Elton (1882; 1890, pp. 279–80): Lir was [an] Ocean-god who was worshipped both in Ireland and Britain.…In the Welsh histories he appears as Lear. According to the version in Geoffrey of Monmouth’s history [see ]…King Lear built the town of Leicester…and his daughter Cordelia is represented as burying him in a vault under the River Sore. Rhys (1888, pp. 562–3): The story, as it reached the great dramatist, had confounded Llûd-a- with Llyr or Lear.…The father of Creid-a-ylad was Llûd-a-, the Celtic Jupiter. B. (1897, pp. 35–6): The Welsh legends…speak of two kings named Llyr, or Lear. The former of them, who is also called Llûdd Llaw Ereint, flourished about 3105 Anno Mundi; the other, Llyr Llediath, at a much later date.…He is confounded with the earlier Llyr,…the father of Cordelia, or…Creiddylad, citing several Welsh texts. Rhys (1901, p. 547 n.): There has been a good deal of confusion as to the name Llyr: thus for instance, the Welsh translations of Geoffrey of Monmouth make the Leir of his Latin into Llyr [the Welsh king].…As to the Leir of Geoffrey’s Latin, that name looks as if given its form on the strength of the legr- of Legraceaster, the Anglo-Saxon name of the town now called Leicester, of which William of Malmesbury (Gesta Pontificum, §176) says, Legrecestra…a Legra fluvio praeterfluente sic vocata. Professor [J. H.] Stevenson [however]…regards Legra as an old name of the Soar, and as surviving in that of the village of Leire, spelled Legre in Domesday. It seems to point back to a Legere or Ligere, which recalls Liger, the Loire. (Ibid., pp. 547–9): Probably the Welsh Llyr is…the Goidelic genitive Lir.…The nominative…was ler, sea. Craig (ed. 1901, pp. xxxv f.): Professor Rhys…writes to me: Although I know no trace of the story of King Lear in Welsh literature, I see no reason whatever for supposing that Geoffrey invented it, but I think rather that he found it in a Celtic story.…The Red Book of Jesus College calls Leir always Llyr, which is the Welsh for the Irish Lir,…but [Rhys goes on] this Llyr is nearly [clearly?] quite unconnected with Welsh literature, and is mixed up with Lludd Llawereint, the Welsh equivalent of the Irish king…Lludd or Nuada of the Silver Hand. Perrett (op. cit., pp. 3 ff.): The legend of Brutus was…unknown in Wales until in 796 Nennius transferred it to his compilation [Historia Britonum] from the Irish Liber de sex aetatibus mundi.…Without the founder there could have been no line of Brute, no Leir King of Britain. The creation of the dynasty lies outside the province of naive folk-lore, and must have been the work of a cleric who had read Nennius. Perrett (pp. 6–8) rejects Geoffrey’s claim that Brutus’s descendant Leir was the eponymous founder of Leicester (Leir-cestre, or Kairleir); rather, both Leir-cestre and the village of Leire were named from the river Legra or Leir(e), as the Soar was alternatively called, and where according to Geoffrey (see ) Cordeilla buried Leir. The association of king and town was in this case unusually happy, the two names being derivatives of the same root. Leir, Llyr means water.…The creation of Leicester by Leir, as of King Leir himself, is due only to Geoffrey’s associative ingenuity. The association of the king’s name with the mythical Llyr of Welsh mythology or Llud of Welsh legend comes later (ibid., p. 16): The Welsh translations of Geoffrey, which begin in the 12th century, recognise Leir as Llyr, a prominent name in Welsh national literature.…Llyr means the waves, the sea, or water, and like [Irish] Ler is held to be the name of a Celtic ocean-god. Bromwich (1961, p. 429): Geoffrey of Monmouth’s Leir appears to be derived from Legrecestra, the O.E. name for Leicester, where Leir was said to have been buried (see BD 217). The Bruts render this name by Llycacr, under the influence of the Llycacr of Welsh tradition. But beyond this there can be no connection between the two characters. Relating the Welsh Llyr to the Norse Hlér, Snorri’s name for Ægir, the Nordic Neptune, Markey (1982, pp. 58–9) reconstructs a Welsh succession myth in which a Welsh sea-god divides his realm among priests/kings (= Coronilla), warriors (= Ragan), and cultivators (= Cordeilla). Three other commentators imagine, in different ways, that Lear’s name is descriptive. Mackay (1884, p. 38): Leire signifies in Keltic, austere and pious. Ruggles (1895, p. 202): Suggesting lere, lore or wisdom…attained through sorrow and suffering. Fleissner (1974, p. 183): There may well be resonances of OE lære (empty)…awaiting spiritual fulfillment.

3–4 King…Burgundy]
This King of the Franks derives from Geoffrey (see ), whereas in later accounts he is called by the Greek name Aganippus; the Duke of Burgundy is Sh.’s invention; see n. 39. Both are anachronisms. France is a king (see 206) of the Gallic realm founded by the Franks and Merovingians in the 5th and 6th centuries A.D.; Burgundy is a duke (see 268), hence apparently not the leader of the 5th-c. Teutonic kingdom of Burgundy nor of the second kingdom (of Burgundy or Arles) created by the Treaty of Verdun in 843, but rather of the French duchy of Burgundy, created by Charles the Bald in 877. Both names postdate the reign of Lear, which according to Geoffrey (see ) falls between the time of the prophets Elias (Elijah; fl. c. 875–850 B.C.) and Elisha (fl. c. 850–800) and that of Isaiah and Hosea (both fl. from 740) before the founding of Rome. Elliston (ed. 1820, p. vi): Holinshed dates the events in the yeare of the world [i.e., Anno Mundi] 3105, at what time Ioas reigned in Iuda (see ). Edelman (1992, p. 152), without citation: The Jewish year of 3105…is c. 656 bc. Crook (ed. 1907, p. xl): According to the date given in the Reference Bible the wicked Joash reigned about 842 b.c., i.e. about 200 years before the foundation of Rome, and 1,000 years before the Roman conquest of Britain. His rule is now generally dated later, in the early years of the 8th c., until c. 786. John Stow’s A Summarie of Englyshe Chronicles (1565, fols. 11v–12r) begins Leire’s reign in 844 and Cordyla’s in 805. In Stephen Batman’s Doome warning all men to the Iudgmente (1581, p. 439) Cordilla raigned alone after his [Leyer’s] death 5. yeares, the yere of the worlde. 1358. [error for 3158] the year before Christ. 805. To be consistent with the dates above, his death must have been somewhat later, in the earlier 8th c. Perrett (1904, p. 20): A king of the Franks in Gallia some 1000 years before time is a remarkable anachronism, even for Geoffrey. He therefore speculates that Geoffrey had in mind the marriage of another rex Francorum with another disinherited younger sister, of Clovis with Clotilda, as related by Gregory of Tours [in Historia Francorum].…Both kings learn by report of the outcast princess’s beauty, and send ambassadors to ask her in marriage; after some hesitation the request is granted. The title King of France was usually changed in Sh.’s immediate sources: he is one of the twelue kings that ruled Gallia in Holinshed, Aggannip of Celtica in Spenser, the Gallian king in Warner and Leir; see , , , . Law (1924, pp. 40 ff.): In Geoffrey and some of his successors, France is identified with the central third of Caesar’s tripartite Gaul, Gallia Celtica, having a seat of government in or near Paris. Shakespeare’s Burgundy occupies its rival northern third, Belgia. Muir (ed. 1952, p. xxxv): Higgins [Mirour, 1574; see ], alone of the authors Shakespeare is likely to have read, speaks of the king of Fraunce; in the 1587 ed. [fol. 34v] he also appears as Prince of Fraunce. Kullmann (1987): Burgundy is the Netherlands, which in the 15th c. belonged to the dukedom of Burgundy and in the 16th c. was subordinated to the Spanish king as the Burgundian district (Reichskreis). Sh.’s contemporaries contrasted the Dutch and French national characters, as Sh. does here.

5 Cornwall]
In Geoffrey, the king gives his two elder daughters duobus ducibus cornubie uidelicet & albanie (ed. A. Griscom, 1929, p. 264; see ); the dux cornubiae, leader of Cornwall, is named Henuinus (see ). Perrett (1904, pp. 165–6) lists all later variations on his name; in accounts probably known by Sh. he is Hinnine…Prince of Camber and Cornwall (Mirour), Henninus the duke of Cornewall (Holinshed), the Cornish Prince (Warner), and king of Cambria (Spenser); see , , , . In Leir there are kings of Cornwall and Cambria; Morgan, Prince or King of Cambria (not Cornwall) is Ragan’s husband, and the otherwise unnamed King of Cornwall (not Albany) is Gonorill’s. Perrett (op. cit., pp. 162–4) shows how an ambiguity in Geoffrey resulted in confusion in many later accounts about which of Leir’s daughters married Cornwall. Among Sh.’s probable sources, only Higgins in Mirour gives the sisters their Shn. husbands. Verity (ed. 1897): In 1336 [1337: Burke’s Peerage] the earldom [of Cornwall] was raised to a duchy by Edward III. in favour of his son, the Black Prince, and of his heirs, eldest sons of the kings of England. Since that time the Prince of Wales has always been duke of Cornwall—as was Prince Henry when Sh. was writing Lr.: he had become Duke of Cornwall upon the accession of James I to the English throne in 1603. After his death in November 1612 the title passed to Prince Charles. Wells (ed. 2000): In terms of Sh.’s time, therefore, Cornwall would have had to be Lear’s son, not his son-in-law. Elton (1966, p. 293): Such titles, without necessarily being identified with their current holder, could serve…as symbolic abstractions, reminding audiences of the dangers of division as well as of James’s role against division. Wickham (1973, p. 36) believes that audience members would have made such identifications. Colie (1974, p. 191): Albany and Cornwall were imaginable titles in the English Renaissance; the earls of Cornwall had been both Plantagenets and Piers Gaveston; the kings of Scotland descended from a darkling Duke of Cornwall.

6 Albany]
On this name for Scotland see n. 5 below. Geoffrey’s dux albaniae, leader of Albania (see prev. n.), is named Maglaunus (see ). Perrett (1904, pp. 165–6) lists all later variations on his name; in Sh.’s immediate sources he is king of Albany (Mirour), Maglanus the duke of Albania (Holinshed), the Prince of Albanie (Warner), and as Maglan king of Scottes living in Albania (Spenser); see , , , . In Leir Gonorill marries the King of Cornwall; see prev. n. Sh.’s character is named simply Duke of Albany. Verity (ed. 1897): This title was created in 1398 and conferred by Robert III. of Scotland on his brother Robert, afterwards the celebrated Regent. Amongst those who have held it is Lord Darnley. He was made Duke of Albany a few days before his marriage with Mary Queen of Scots, and thenceforth the title was commonly a royal title held by some Prince of the Blood. In fact the title passed from Darnley to his son James Stuart, who held it 1567–87, and later passed to James’s second son Charles, who was created Duke of Albany at his baptism on 23 Dec. 1600 and so held the title when Sh. was writing Lr. Draper’s (1937, p. 182) erroneous belief that James held the title then vitiates his theory that the consistently good and virtuous character of Albany was intended as a compliment to Sh.’s king and patron. Wells (ed. 2000): Duke is the highest title of the aristocracy, ranking immediately below royalty.

7 Gloster]
Sh. gives this name to the character who in his source for the subplot, Sidney’s Arcadia (1590), is the unnamed, blind former king of Paphlagonia (2.10; see ). Because of the character’s proximity to and dealings with Cornwall and Regan in the course of the play, Sh. apparently wished him to be from one of the western dominions in Lear’s kingdom; see n. 875. Smith (1946, p. 170) suggests that he derives from Eldol dux [or consul] claudiocestrie of Saxon times in Geoffrey (6.16; ed. A. Griscom, 1929, pp. 378, 403]), the original of two characters, Earl of Gloster (father to Edwyn) and Edoll Earl of Chester, in the apocryphal play The Birth of Merlin. Crook (ed. 1907): A name of Roman origin, and could not have existed as a title in the days of Lear. Colie (1974, p. 191): A Plantagenet royal title until the fifteenth century and would again become a royal title. Throughout Q1 and nearly half the time in F the name is spelled Gloster; Q2 changes more than half of Q1’s occurrences to Glocester; F’s Glouster and less frequent Gloucester may reflect only Folio modernization (Hunter, ed. 1972). Blayney (1972, p. 189): The distinguishing mark of [Compositor] B in the Folio is not the -s/ces- variation but the inclusion of medial -u- in either form. Halio (ed. 1992): In dialogue, Glouster is Compositor B’s preferred spelling, Gloster Compositor E’s. Q[1] consistently uses Gloster, which reflects the proper pronunciation—and probably Sh.’s spelling. Wells (ed. 2000): There were earls of Gloucester from the twelfth century to the fourteenth, and dukes from 1385, but both titles were extinct in Shakespeare’s time.

8 Kent]
Sh.’s counterpart of the faithful counsellor Perillus in Leir; see . Malone (in Boswell, ed. 1821, 10:143) finds the origin of both characters in Geoffrey, where Leir’s train is reduced to a single attendant: see , and compare Holinshed, . Perrett (1904, pp. 203–5), after tracing Perillus’s origin in the character Eubulus in Sackville & Norton’s Gorboduc: So much Kent and Perillus have in common:—each is a counsellor who attempts to dissuade the king from his fatal purpose; excites his anger by interceding for the heroine; at Gon.’s court, suffers the first shock of her infidelity ([Leir 817–71; see ]); and is afterward a faithful attendant upon the king throughout his distress. But they are as little alike in temperament as their respective kings. Colie (1974, p. 191): The earls of Kent were local noblemen who had died out early in the sixteenth century; the title revived under Elizabeth in 1572. Bullough (1973, p. 271; cf. 1969, p. 49): Did Leir’s faithful companion become the Earl of Kent because Kent was [Brian] Annesley’s county?; see DP n. 17. Dutton (1986, p. 143): Lr. reflects James I’s wish to unify Britain; Kent’s name, with Albany’s and Cornwall’s, completes the traditional symbolism of England as the three-cornered island. Sh. may make the character earl of the southeastern province of Kent because of the play’s association with its principal town Dover and because of Kent’s ready access to news from just across the channel in France; see nn. 1242, 1638+1. On his alias Caius see n. 3249. Scragg (1992, p. 140 n.): Perhaps the title was suggested by the banished Earl of Kent in Marlowe’s Edward II. Wells (ed. 2000): Earls rank below dukes and marquises.

9–10 Edgar…Edmund]
These are the counterparts of the blind Paphlagonian king’s faithful and treacherous sons, Leonatus and the bastard Plexirtus, in Sidney’s Arcadia (2.10.1, 4; see , ). Their Saxon names are surprising among so many Celtic ones. Malone (ed. 1790): The names…were probably suggested by Holinshed, citing Historie (1587, 1:122—actually, Harrison’s Description): Edgar, the sonne of Edmund, brother of Athelstane. Musgrove (1956, pp. 294–5) thinks Sh. may have derived these names from William Camden’s account in Remaines (1605, p. 50) of their etymological significance—Edgar, blessed honor; Edmund, blessed peace— and (p. 90) of the two Anglo-Saxon kings: King Eadgar [959–75] was called the Peaceable…[the later] king Edmund for his Valour, Iron-side. Cf. Thomas Milles, Catalog of Kings (1610, pp. 19–20): Eadgar, son of Eadmund king of Wessex, was renowned for ruling a united Britain peacefully; on the contrary, his grandson Edmund Ironsides’s later defeat by the Danes resulted in a fatal division of the country. For such reasons King Edgar was often urged as a model for James I: see Flahiff (1974, pp. 230 ff.). Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 46): But an earlier Edmund, King of East Anglia 841–69, was perhaps better known as a hero, for his stand against a Viking army, and as a saint, who gave his name to Bury St Edmunds. (Ibid., p. 108 n.): Harry’s Genealogy of…James [1604]…mentions Edgar (42) and Edmund, Earl of Richmond (48), as ancestors of James. Musgrove also suggests (p. 296) a source in Richard Hakluyt’s Principall Navigations (1598, 1:6–9): Not far from [an] account of the saintliness of Edgar is another passage…briefly describing a murder plot in which Edmund Ironsides and his son Edmund, and yet another Edgar, are mentioned. Hard by appears the name Oswald, as one of Edgar’s bishops. The names of various earls of Kent and Gloster are also found in the early pages of Hakluyt and in Camden. Hamilton (1983, pp. 39 ff.): Other Edgars were ancestors of King James. Edgar Atheling, grandson of Edmund Ironsides, sole male issue of the Saxon line, and briefly king of England after Harold, later joined king Duncan’s son Malcolm III, king of Scotland after the death of Macbeth; Malcolm married Edgar Atheling’s sister Margaret, later St. Margaret of Scotland, and their son Edgar, who thus united Saxon and Scottish blood, succeeded him as king of Scotland after the Atheling helped him overthrow the usurper Donald Bane and his supporter Edmund, another of Malcolm’s sons. William Warner, Albions England (1589, pp. 101–2) and John Speed, The History of Great Britaine (1611, p. 384) note the significance of this marriage for uniting English and Scottish blood before the accession of James. The Scottish king Edgar’s sister Matilda later married Henry I, son of William the Conqueror, thus reintroducing Saxon blood to the English royal lineage as well. See further Burelbach (1987, pp. 133–4) and Perrello (1997), who attempts to draw further analogies with Edward Martyr, son of Edgar the Peaceable. Hunter (1845, 2:270), followed by Muir (1951, p. 12), Salingar (1983, p. 161), and Halio (ed. 1992), thinks the name Edmund may have been suggested by Sh.’s important source, Samuel Harsnett’s A Declaration of Egregious Popish Impostures (1603; see, e.g., p. 1): Mr. Peckham’s name being Edmund, and the principal actor being Father Edmunds. Similarly Bullough (1973, p. 301): In Harsnett, two important characters were Edmunds and [the Catholic martyr] Edmund Campion; but Edgar’s brother has no other connection with the tract. Harsnett gives Campion’s first name only once (p. 83), as Edmundus. Knight (1973, p. 55; cf. 1977, p. 177): Sh. was to immortalize Edmund [Lambert, John Shakespeare’s brother-in-law] as one who illegitimately stole the paternity of a brother by mortgage foreclosure, an idea repeated by Kornstein (1994, p. 221): The case could be described as an attempt by Edmund [Lambert] to steal his brother-in-law’s inheritance. Might this have played a role in Shakespeare’s choice of name? The similarities with Lambert are not very close, and those with Sh.’s younger brother Edmund nonexistent. The courts apparently upheld Lambert’s foreclosure; see Chambers (1930, 2:35–41). Fleissner (1991, pp. 168–9) speculates that the base-born son of Sh.’s brother was also named Edmund, and that Sh. had him in mind when writing the play; what documentary evidence exists indicates that he was named Edward and was born and died in 1607, well after the play had been performed.
Levin (1965, p. 78): The jingling juxtaposition of Edgar and Edmund emphasizes the polarity of the half-brothers. The name Edmund occurs in many contemporary plays, but Edgar only in A Knack to Know a Knave (1592). Munro (ed. 1957, 6:892): The actor playing…Edgar has more character changes than any other role in Shakespeare’s plays. Edgar sets off as himself, becomes an outlaw, is disguised as Poor Tom, is re-clad by an Old Man, helps Gloucester to the cliff, changes character to assist him after the fall, poses as a rustic and kills Oswald, appears in disguise to Albany, fights Edmund as an unknown knight-at-arms, and becomes himself once more to rule [in] the kingdom. In Q and F the character is named both Bastard (or Bast.) and Edmund. Stallybrass (2000, p. 125) speculates that Q1 had to print Edmund as Bastard because Okes was short of italic Es, and that (pp. 128–9) the name Edmund in the final act reflects his rise in power. In Q1 the form Edmund appears 33 times, and Edmond appears only at 3128 in Q1 and not at all in Q2. In F, Compositor E, who set the name 18 times, repeats the aberrant spelling Edmond at 3128 and uses it also in 351, perhaps influenced by Compositor B, who uses it in 10 of his 19 settings of the name. Stone (1980, p. 151 n.) supposes that Compositor B set 351 at the top of page qq3v and subsequently, to avoid crowding, transferred it and a few other lines back to the bottom of the previous page qq3, which was mostly set later by Compositor E. Although Edmund is the preponderant form in F by a ratio of 25:12, and the form in all likely sources and possible influences (see above), the recent Oxford (1986) and Cambridge (1992) editions of the F text normalize to the minority form Edmond. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 532) suppose that the F manuscript had Edmond in directions and prefixes, but its pattern of occurrence in F indicates rather the idiosyncratic spelling of F1 Compositor B, who generally treated his copy more freely than the less experienced Compositor E.

11 Curan]
The name is not found in any of the sources, or in any other Elizabethan play. Browne (1876, pp. 432–3): Curan…figures in the old romances as the son of a Danske king, who became a servant in the house of King Edel of Northumberland, in order to woo his daughter Argentile. He was better known as Havelock.…The story of Curan forms an episode in [William] Warner’s Albion’s England [Bk. 4, ch. 20, pp. 83–7], first printed in 1586. The work contained a version of the Lear story; see n. 676 and . Greg (1940, p. 434): No doubt one of Oswald’s fellows (he had come with some company [860]) to Regan’s house. Brooke (ed. 1947), rather: Curan seems to be a confidential agent of Gloucester who finds it worth his while to pass on to Edmund the information that he picks up. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 513): The name is an alternative early form of Currant. But this variant is not recorded in English before the 18th c., and the personal name was originally Danish. Kökeritz (1959, p. 46): The u pronounced as in but, not cure. Foakes (ed. 1997): It is unusual for a character with so small a role to be named by Shakespeare, who may have initially envisaged a larger part for him. The name could be a version of Ciaran; a noted sixth-century Irish abbot of this name was made a saint.

12 Doctor]
In F this character’s role is assumed by a Gentleman who has medical knowledge; see nn. 2349–50, 2744.

13 Fool]
Like the Fool in Timon, Lear’s jester has no proper name such as Touchstone, Feste, or Lavatch. Though Sh.’s jesters are occasionally addressed as Fool, as this one is at 628, 658, 1339, 1359, 1586, and 1727, there is no reason why eds. should, as they occasionally do, consider this appellation as his proper name; all third-person references to him call him the (a, my, his, etc.) Fool, not Fool. In Q1 his name is capitalized in stage directions (except in 1777) and lower-case within lines (except in 451 and 628); in F the name is always capitalized, as is the word used as a common noun (except in 698). Foakes (ed. 1997): Shakespeare’s most original addition to the story, and a role probably designed for Robert Armin, though it could have been doubled by the boy-actor playing Cordelia. This doubling is doubtful: see .

14 Steward]
This character is identified in stage directions and speech prefixes as Steward or Stew. in both Q and F except for Q1’s Oswald. and Osw. at 857+1 and 859; see also nn. 506, 507. He is addressed once by the name Oswald in Q and F at 857, and twice again in F’s additional lines at 833 and 848. Perrett (1904, pp. 205–10) shows that though in several accounts from Wace’s 12th-c. Roman de Brut onward disdain is shown to Lear by men, upstart courtiers, and Gonorill’s Parasites (Leir 759; see ), Sh.’s Steward is immediately modelled on Skalliger and (as Adee, ed. 1890, p. xlvi, first suggested) on the Messenger-Murderer of Leir: see nn. 519–20, 860, 862, 2426–7, 2851. Musgrove (1956, pp. 294, 296) notes that Camden (Remaines, 1605, p. 65) explains the etymology of the Saxon name—osvvold, Ger. House-ruler or Steward—and that Hakluyt (Principall Navigations, 1598, 1:8) names an Oswald, bishop to King Edgar, adding, Where else should Shakespeare have learnt that Oswald meant steward? Just conceivably…from Verstegan’s (or Rowlands’s) Restitution of Decayed Intelligence in Antiquities, published in Antwerp in 1605, which glosses Oswald [p. 266] in much the same way as Camden…though without using the word steward. No character named Oswald appears in previous Elizabethan plays; there is a nobleman by that name in the apocryphal Birth of Merlin (?1608), Merlin so names a martyred Saxon king in Spenser’s F.Q. 3.3.38–9, and the name appears in Geoffrey of Monmouth (ed. A. Griscom, 1929, pp. 525 ff.). Foakes (ed. 1997): Another Saxon name, recalling two British saints, the better known being the tenth-century St Oswald of Worcester, Archbishop of York. Sh.’s Oswald would probably not call saints to mind, however. Doubtful etymologies are offered by Withycombe (1973)—god of power—and Nathan (1986)—strong mouth.

15 Gonerill]
Gonorilla in Geoffrey (see ). Perrett (1904, p. 159) lists all the variant spellings in subsequent accounts; among Sh.’s probable sources she is Gonorilla in Holinshed, Gonerell in Mirour, and Gonorill in Warner, Spenser, and Leir; see , , , , . In a contemporary ballad apparently influenced by the play she is Gonorell (see ). In Sh.’s Qq she is Gonorill (exc. Gonoril at Q1 2014+22 and 2301) as in the old play, and in F1 she is always Gonerill. The preferred modern spelling Goneril, introduced by Capell (ed. 1768), has no authority; Colman (ed. 1982) and Halio (ed. 1992) have returned to F’s Gonerill. A number of commentators attempt Celtic etymologies. Yonge (1863; 1884, pp. 229–30): Possibly from Gwrvorwyn, man-maid, or virago, an epithet for Lyr’s two daughters; see n. 2. Moberly (ed. 1876): This name seems to be derived from Gwenar, the British form of Vener (Venus). Taylor (1883, p. 317), extrapolating from Lyr the ocean-god (see n. 2 above) and a song representing his daughters as blowing on a ship: Regan may be the black tempest, rack, Goneril the cold piercing winter blast (cf. gonair, the piercer,), and Cordelia the gentle wind or zephyr. Mackay (1884, p. 38): From Celtic gonach, sharp, keen, cruel, wounding. Markey (1982, p. 59): The form found in the Welsh Llyr legends, Coronilla contains the crown/horn word, Lat. corona, W corun. Jacobson (1980, p. 596), perhaps inevitably, followed by Adelman (1992, p. 109; cf. p. 298): Brings to mind gonorrhea, a Greek word used on a few occasions before 1606 by English writers, mainly pharmacists or satirists (OED; Williams, 1994), never by Sh. Burelbach (1987, p. 130) suspects puns on gonos, gonel, and gromwell, words never used by Sh.

16 Regan]
Perrett (1904, pp. 159–60): In Geoffrey, Regau or Regan (see ); in Spenser, Regan; in Mirour, Leir, and the contemporary ballad, Ragan; in Holinshed, Regan (also Ragaie, according to Perrett, p. 160; unattested); unnamed in Warner; see , , , , . In Sh. she is Rag. and Ragan. at 325 and 331 in Q1, otherwise Regan in Q1 and F. Ekeblad (1957, pp. 193–4) notes a minor character named Regan in Robert Greene’s Selimus (ca. 1592). Except for Leir, no other play has a Regan or Ragan; and Ragau in Jacob and Esau (1554) is male. Kökeritz (1959, pp. 3–4, 84) would pronounce the first syllable as in regal, not ray, in apparent contradiction of the common Ra- spelling. As they do for Goneril, commentators supply Celtic etymologies. Yonge (1863; 1884, pp. 229–30), wildly: Perhaps from Bronwen, or white bosom,…another daughter of Lyr. Moberly (ed. 1876): Regan is probably of the same origin as Rience in the Holy Grail; reian meaning in Cornish to give bounteously. Mackay (1884, p. 38): From [Celtic] righinn, hard, stubborn, unyielding, unbending. Henderson (1897, p. 352): Regan looks very like Riogan, a queen. Jacobson (1980, p. 596): Recalls rego and regina. Markey (1982, p. 59): Ragan contains the ruler/priest word, OIr. rí king : rígain queen. Ford (privately): I don’t know why Regan would have a name derived from Irish (rígan queen; noble lady) rather than Welsh. In George Owen Harry’s Genealogy of…James (1604, p. 42) James I is shown to be descended from Ragan 2. doghter of Leir and Henwyn Duk. of Cornwall. Burelbach (1987, p. 130) suspects puns on rig wanton, rigg dog, and riggon half-castrated animal, forms never used by Sh.

17 Cordelia]
Perrett (1904, p. 160): In Geoffrey and Holinshed [and once in Warner], Cordeilla (see , , ); in Mirour, Cordila, Cordile, or Cordell (see ); in Warner and Leir, Cordella (see , ); in Spenser, Cordeill once and twice Cordelia, the only such spelling in accounts before Lr. (see , ); in the contemporary ballad she is Cordela (see ). In Sh.’s Q1 and F she is always Cordelia. Hales (1876, p. 306) first noticed a contemporary of Sh. named Cordell Annesley, and Isham (1954, p. 150) found that her name was given as Cordelia when she was married to William Hervey or Harvey (St. Giles, Cripplegate, 5 Feb. 1607/8) and buried (St. Martin-in-the-Fields, 5 May 1636); on the possibility that Sh. had her in mind when creating Cordelia, see . Perrett (pp. 161–2) also notes another contemporary (d. 1631), daughter of William Fleetwood (d. 1594) and wife of Sir David Foulis, whose name (according to DNB) was Cordelia; a Cordele Fleetewood was baptized at St. Olave, Silver Street on 23 Aug. 1579 [this latter and the next are from an anonymous correspondent]. The church register also records the baptism of Cordelia Tailor on 1 Dec. 1605; this was Sh.’s local London parish. Wells (ed. 2000) notes Sh.’s practice of giving significant names—cf. Marina, Perdita, Miranda—in his late plays, and various etymologies for this one have been proposed. Ruskin (1862, p. 764): Heart-lady. Mackay (1884, p. 38): From [Celtic] cord, agreement, or to agree, or corr, excellent, and dileach, loving, affectionate. Davies (1809, p. 206): Creirddylad,…the daughter of Lludd Llaw Eraint…or of Llyr, the margin of the sea,…[is] Cordelia, the daughter of King Lear, and in British mythology our Proserpine (p. 401); see DP n. 2 above. Yonge (1863; 1884, p. 230), accepting this identification: in the Mabinogion, Creirdyddlydd remains with her father till the day of doom.…The Germans fancy Cordula is a diminutive of the Latin cor, a heart; others have wildly made it the feminine of Cordeleo, lion heart, and it has been confused with Delia, the epithet of Diana, from Delos, her birthplace. Levith (1976, p. 26; 1978, p. 57) repeats the latter etymologies. Rhys (1901, p. 547 n.): Cordelia is probably the Creurd-a-ilad of the Black Book [of Carmarthen; facs. J. Gwenogvryn Evans, (Oxford, 1888)], p. 49b, and the Creid-a-ylat of the Kulhwch story (the Oxford Mabinogion [ed. Ryhs & Evans (Oxford, 1887)], pp. 113, 134), and her father was Llûd-a- Llawereint (= Irish Nuada Airgetlám) and not Llyr; cf. DP n. 2 above. Perrett (op. cit., pp. 160–1) agrees, adding, The name Cordeilla probably took its shape through a play upon cor, heart, which recurs more than once, from Matthew Paris’s commota est corde illa [Chronica Majora, ed. Luard, p. 31] to Gallia’s deare Cordella, cordiall to my heart [Leir 709]. McAlindon (1991, p. 177): Titus Andronicus (an aged hero)…refers to his daughter as the cordial of mine age to glad my heart (1.1.166 [194]). Stauffer (1949, p. 201): The name might be one of those anagrams of the Elizabethan love-sonneteers for the Idea of the Heart. E. G. Withycombe, Oxford Dictionary of English Christian Names (3rd ed., 1977): It may be the same as Cordula, which appears in Welsh and Cornish calendars as the name of one of the companions of St. Ursula [4th c.], and is found in German as Kordula or Kordel. Jacobson (1980, p. 596): Connected…to Latin cor, but also to Greek dēlos (= clear, plain),…a lady clear in heart. Markey (1982, p. 59): Cordeilla, not to be identified with Creiddylad daughter of Llud Llawereint, contains the heart word, Lat. cor(d), Gk. kēr, OIr. cride, W craidd…which signified the seat of passion and affection, the root of fecundity. Ford (privately): Creiddylad (the correct form of the name) is unlikely to be the source of Cordelia, and I’d say that Latin heart is more to the point. Satin (1966, p. 446): Spenser, from whom Sh. got his spelling, may have selected this variant because Delia was a popular Renaissance anagram for ideal—as in the Delia sonnet sequence by Samuel Daniel; similarly Kinney (1976, p. 684), Anderson (1987, p. 7), and Foakes (ed. 1997); Wells (ed. 2000) finds the notion strained. Spenser varies between Cordeill and Cordelia to fit the meter. Fisher (1990, p. 89): Intimates heart…and bond (cord) and…healing effect of a cordial. Fleissner (1991, p. 44): A different anagram, cord (bond) and a lie, i.e. she broke her bond to Lear. But she never did. Hughes (1992, p. 273): Meaning coeur de Lear, heart of Lear. Unlikely: the different stress and vowel in Cordelia does not fit such an etymology.

18–19 Knights…Attendants]
Foakes (ed. 1997): In 1.4 Lear is attended by at least four knights.…In 2.2 the entry in F calls for a Gentleman (Knight in Q speech headings) to accompany Lear, and there are no more entries for knights after this point. Q confuses them with servants in 1.4, while F generally calls an attendant who speaks as Gentleman, several being required in the course of the action. On these variant names for the same character, typical of texts (such as Rom. Q2) deriving from an author’s drafts, see nn. 538 and 580, and on the reappearance of attendant characters in later scenes under the same or different names, see nn. 874 and 1615. A Captaine is specified in 5.3 (see 2939, 2969, 2981, 2981+1) and others at 3058+1 (cf. n. 2982) and 3239, in Q only (see n. 3208–10).

0.3 Historie]
F alters to Tragedie. The entrance for Q in the Stationers’ Register (26 Nov. 1607) for Nathaniel Butter and John Busby, like the Q title page which agrees with its wording closely, calls the play a historye. Blayney (1982, p. 83) thinks it likely that a handwritten title page was added to the MS as a trial layout for the printer. If so, Butter presumably created its content and might have invented its title by analogy with the earlier The True Chronicle History of King Leir (S.R. 14 May 1594; 1605). Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 90): Apparently Butter was anxious to challenge Leir by claiming simultaneously that the new play was like the old one, and superior to it because of its subplot, performance before James, and authorship by Sh. Greg (1940, p. 381): King Lear was popularly regarded as no less historical than, say, King John, and…Chronicle would be the natural description of a play dealing with either. Shakespeare did not…treat the story as history, and the folio editors rightly classed the piece among the tragedies.…Had Butter been better informed, I have little doubt that he would have called his play a tragedy rather than a true chronicle. Sternfeld (1963, p. 132): In the Folio…the histories treat of English kings, the tragedies of Greek, Roman, Italian, Danish, Scottish, and ancient British matters, as is the case in King Lear [and Cym.]. Taylor (1983, p. 451 n.): Q’s title prepares a surprise by not giving away Shakespeare’s drastic departure from all previous accounts. Wittreich (1984, p. 76): History, tragedy, and comedy are all acknowledged on the 1608 title page, comedy in the sullen and assumed humor of Tom of Bedlam, a phrase implying that Edgar represents a tragicomic pattern, citing Peck (1967). But humor means merely a mental disposition (OED, sb. 4–6), not comicality, a sense the word did not yet have (OED, 7). Wells (ed. 2000): History…could mean simply a narrative. Everett (1998, p. 215): If we don’t call King Lear a tragedy, it is hard to know what we do call a tragedy, or what we do call King Lear.

1 <Actus Primus. Scœna Prima.>]
The act-scene division absent from Q is supplied throughout in F. See .

1 <Scœna Prima>]
Eds. since Rowe (see textual n.) have generally located the opening scene in Lear’s Palace, a word found twice in the text (438, 755). Crook (ed. 1907): Probably at Leicester…built by King Leir, and first called Caerleir; but see DP n. 2. Like Thorndike (1948, pp. 119, 246), Brooke (ed. 1947) so locates the scene, noting that Leicester, Leir-cester, is the geographical center of England. Kittredge (ed. 1940): That town is not mentioned in the play; curiously, Leister is printed for Gloster at Q 1586. In Leir 418 (see ) the court is located in Troynouant, or London, the chief town in Britain (Perrett, 1904, p. 258). Greg (1940, pp. 431–2): The text gives no hint as to the situation of the royal palace.…It may have become [after the division of the kingdom] the residence of one of the king’s daughters: if so, it must be identified with Cornwall’s, for Lear certainly left it to go to Albany’s ([312–13]).…But in [sc. 2] Gloucester’s words, and…to night ([359]) do not…hint at any change of locality; so that it would appear possible, either that Lear was holding his court at Gloucester’s, or else that Gloucester, after the division of the kingdom, remained in possession or at least in charge of the royal palace.…Royal business was usually transacted in the morning, and the whole affair [of 1.1] would probably be over before dinner [the mid-day meal]. Thus there would be ample time for the king to leave the same evening in order to take up his residence with Goneril [citing 311–13].…It can be no great distance, since he would hardly propose riding far into the night.
Greg (1940, p. 300): The…scene certainly calls for a throne or chair of state, and possibly for a table on which the map could be spread out.…But there is no discovery of persons; Lear walks on.…Thus the inner stage [i.e., alcove] could be dispensed with, the throne being set in place before the play began and removed at the end of the scene. Leggatt (1992, p. 214): It is not certain that this property [chair] was flown; it could have been simply carried on and off. Adams (1948, p. 315), however: The rear stage curtains open upon a setting of great splendor: The Globe Company’s standard throne room set included a throne, dais with canopy, carpets…, and colorful tapestries. The inner stage is now not thought to have been spacious, and there is no textual authority for Adams’s details. Rosenberg (1972, pp. 33–9) reviews a history of stage-settings resembling Stonehenge, classic or Hebraic temples, medieval castles, Westminster, futuristic or expressionistic structures, etc. Foakes (ed. 1997): There may have been banners…with badges or emblems to mark the court as English. The time of the action is pre-English, however.
Goethe (1813–16; tr. R. S. Bourne, ed. Spingarn, 1921, p. 188): In this scene Lear seems so absurd that we are not able, in what follows, to ascribe to his daughters the entire guilt. Perrett (1904, pp. 156–7) shows how many later critics distort this remark to mean that Lear is already mad—see n. 3–10—or that the whole scene is absurd. Rosenberg (1972, p. 15): He was commenting on the acting version by Friedrich Ludwig Schroeder.…Cutting the scene suited Schroeder’s purposes [viz., to arouse pity] but, Goethe observed, it annulled the play. Coleridge (MS note, dated 1 Jan. 1813, in 1773 ed. of Sh.; ed. Raysor, 1960, 1:53): Lear’s was an old story, rooted in the popular faith—a thing taken for granted already, and consequently without the effects of improbability. Secondly, it is merely the canvas to the characters and passions, a mere occasion.…Let the first scene of Lear have been lost, and let it be only understood that a fond father had been duped by hypocritical professions of love and duty on the part of two daughters to disinherit a third, previously, and deservedly, more dear to him, and all the rest of the tragedy would retain its interest undiminished, and be perfectly intelligible. White (1880, pp. 114–15): The action in this whole scene, excepting that of Kent, is so unreasonable and unnatural as to be almost absurd.…But for this Shakespeare is not responsible, except in so far as he is made so by the choice of the story.…Lear’s purposed division of his kingdom, his behavior to his daughters and their behavior to him, and his consequent disinheritance of the youngest are a postulate which is not to be questioned. They are absurd, but without their absurdity there would have been no play.…With the disinheriting of Cordelia the absurdity stops short.…In this first scene is deployed the whole potentiality of the tragedy. The germ of every character, the spring of every dramatic motive developed during the whole five acts, is to be found there; and every personage of any importance is there, excepting the Fool and the legitimate Edgar. Bradley (1904, p. 151): The scene is not absurd, though it must be pronounced dramatically faulty in so far as it discloses the true position of affairs only to an attention more alert than can be expected in a theatrical audience or has been found in many critics of the play.…(p. 249) This scene acts effectively, and to imagination the story is not at all incredible. It is merely strange, like so many of the stories on which our romantic dramas are based. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 146): The scene…is a magnificent statement of a magnificent theme. It has a proper formality, and there is a certain megalithic grandeur about it, Lear dominating it, that we associate with Greek tragedy. Its probabilities are neither here nor there. A dramatist may postulate any situation he has the means to interpret, if he will abide by the logic of it after. Nicoll (1928, pp. 145, 154), remarking the crushing of Acts I and II of Leir into a single scene: This first scene is a failure. It is easily the most uninteresting long scene of the drama, and must strike any actor as an almost impossible scene to play satisfactorily.…To find an explanation for Lear’s decisions and demeanour in this first scene we need to know the subsequent development of the plot; by themselves they are perfectly unintelligible. Law (1958, p. 120): The violent rush of the opening scene makes it one of the most remarkable in all Shakespeare. At a single blow the scene provides exposition for both plot and subplot, disposes of the love-test and the selection of husbands for the three daughters,…adds the banishment of Kent to that of Cordelia…[and gives] a vivid portrayal of most of the important figures. Frost (1958, p. 583): Since the folk-tale was old and well known, All questions of motivation are bypassed at the outset, and we start with the naked myth.…As the earlier play King Leir surely demonstrates sufficiently, any conceivable rationalization is bound to be weak and inadequate. Goldberg (1974, p. 16): The air of folk-tale ceremony makes this first scene curiously ambiguous.…Explanations, causes, motives are apparently unnecessary at first.…Later, however,…it seems rather as if the characters may have been concealing them, even from themselves. Gardner (1967, pp. 1, 4): The action begins with a violent improbability, which the author does nothing to prepare for or mitigate.…No other of Shakespeare’s great tragedies opens with a great set scene. Kinney (1976, p. 677): Of all the major Shakespearean tragedies, only King Lear plunges us so rapidly and so persistently into the midst of its central issues. Reibetanz (1977, p. 19): Shakespeare has thoroughly removed the carefully placed hints about motivation that abound in his primary source, The History of King Leir. There, several reasons are given for Leir’s strange conduct: he is sad and distraught because his wife has just died, and he wants to resign the throne to live in devout contemplation; he is ignorant of the affairs and characters of his daughters, For fathers best do know to gouerne sonnes; he devises the love-test to trick Cordelia into marrying the suitor he favours.…[As in Beaumont & Fletcher and much Jacobean drama] this [scene’s] emphasis is highly theatrical: it concerns itself more with the immediate forcefulness of the dramatic situation than with tying the causal details of the situation into a realistic pattern, thus rendering the characters archetypal and enigmatic. Zak (1984, p. 118): Shakespeare took great care to keep Lear’s psyche cloaked,…as if our bewilderment…was a necessary first step to understanding him. Like Moulton (1885; 1893, p. 205), Bradley (op. cit., p. 53), Van Doren (1939; 1954, p. 204), so Bowers (1980, p. 14): What Shakespeare has done is to move up into the first scene of his play what is the turning-point of the total story.…Instead of the first half of the play being devoted to the rising action culminating in the kingdom’s division,…Shakespeare allows himself almost the full length of the play to work out the far-reaching and complex results of Lear’s tragic decision.

2 Kent]
See DP n. 8.

2 Gloster]
See DP n. 7. Rolfe (ed. 1880): In the 1st folio the name is here spelt Gloucester, but in many places in the play (as in Rich. III.) it is Gloster or Glouster, and the abbreviations used are Glo., Glou., Glost., etc. The 1st quarto has Gloster.

2 Bastard]
In Q1 Edmund is so designated in stage directions at 2, 334, 1752, 1967, 2059, and 2267, and in all speech prefixes he is Bast.; he is Edmund in stage directions at 1117, 2846, 2896, and 2937. F makes a few changes to Edmund and Edm. (2, 29, 32, 34, 487, 498, 1752, 1970) and a reverse change at 1117; on its changes to the spelling Edmond, see DP n. 9–10 and . Brown (ed. 1976): He may enter by a different door and stand waiting for his father; or he may enter with Gloucester, attendant on him like a servant.…He speaks only when directly addressed and then seems to have heard nothing of the foregoing talk. On whether or not he hears the succeeding talk, see n. 12–27.

3–36 I…comming]
Muir (ed. 1952): The opening dialogue introduces the underplot, and gives us a glimpse of Kent before his intervention at [128]. Brown (ed. 1976): Their brief exchange can give a sense of foreboding, or resignation, or simply of awaiting future clarification. The conversation, in prose, is a remarkably low-key prelude to the tragedy. Harbage (ed. 1958, p. 14): Its tone is casual, jocular, polite. Mack (1965, pp. 93–4): The atmosphere…[is] urbane, even relaxed.…We are momentarily lulled into…security. Vickers (1968, p. 351): The prose conversation…establishes a norm against which Lear’s powerful verse seems still more forceful. Reibetanz (1977, p. 19): The choric scene…actually leaves us off guard for both the ritualism and the vehemence of what follows. Foakes (ed. 1997): The scene [1.1] begins and ends with informal prose…framing the formal state ceremony.

3–10 I…moytie]
Johnson (ed. 1765): There is something of obscurity or inaccuracy in this preparatory scene. The King has already divided his kingdom, and yet when he enters he examines his daughters, to discover in what proportions he should divide it. Coleridge (MS notes, 1818–19, ed. Foakes, 1989, p. 95): The triple division is stated here as already determined, and in all its particulars, previously to the trial of professions.…These first 4 or 5 lines of the play…let us know that the trial is but a trick; and that the grossness of the old king’s rage is in part the natural result of a silly trick suddenly and most unexpectedly baffled and disappointed. Singer (ed. 1856): What can be plainer than that Lear has predetermined the division of his kingdom, and only alters it when Cordelia disappoints and vexes him? Hudson (ed. 1871): This speech…infers the trial of professions to be a sort of pet device with the old King, a thing that has no purpose but to gratify a childish whim. The opening forecasts Lear’s madness by indicating that dotage has already got the better of his reason and judgment. Verity (ed. 1897): The play begins with these remarks upon what seems to Lear’s friends a piece of waywardness and inconsistency. They strike a keynote. Bradley (1904, p. 281): The first lines tell us that Lear’s mind is beginning to fail with age. Formerly he had perceived how different were the characters of Albany and Cornwall, but now he seems either to have lost this perception or to be unwisely ignoring it.…Of course I do not mean that he is beginning to be insane, and still less that he is insane. The lines show only that Lear’s decision is unexpected, not that it is due to inconstancy or senility (his age is not yet given) or that an unequal division would have been wiser. See also n. 53–8. In the source-play Cambria and Cornwall discuss their expectations for a whole scene; see Leir 398–467 ().

4 affected]
Schmidt (1874): Love[d] (OED, Affect v.1 2a).

5 Duke of Albany]
See DP n. 6.

5 Albany]
Kemshead (ed. 1875): The old Celtic name for Scotland, and indeed for the whole island, was Albion, which probably means a land of mountains. A trace of this still exists in the name Clan Alpin. Rivet & Smith (1979, p. 248, s. v. Albion): In Irish and Gaelic up to the twelfth century, Alba…was the regular name for the region of Scotland north of the Forth, and some Irish writers use the name for the whole of Britain. Wright (ed. 1875) gives the prevailing Elizabethan understanding of the name Albany, quoting from Harrison’s Description of Britaine in Holinshed (1577, fol. 39v [1587, p. 116]): The third and last part of the Island he [Brute] allotted vnto Albanacte hys youngest sonne.…This later parcel at the first, toke the name of Albanactus, who called it Albania. But now a small portion onely [i.e., those parts of Scotland north of the Firths of Clyde and Forth] of the Region (beyng vnder the regiment of a Duke) reteyneth the sayd denomination, the reast beyng called Scotlande, of certayne Scottes that came ouer from Ireland to inhabite in those quarters. It is [i.e., was formerly] deuided from Loegres [England] also by the Humber, so that Albania as Brute left it, conteyned all the north part of the Island that is to be foũd beyond the aforesayd streame, vnto the point of Cathenesse. Cf. n. 42–3. Verity (ed. 1897): Cf. The Faerie Queene, II.10.14: But Albanact had all the Northrene part, Which of himselfe Albania he did call; and the pseudo-Shakespearian play Locrine [1595], where Albanact is one of the characters and addresses his warriors as Braue cavileres, princes of Albany [ed. Brooke, 2.3.1]. Camden, Remaines (1605, p. 41) defines Alban as White or High and notes that Saint Albans was the first British martyr.

5 Cornwell]
See DP n. 5. In Q the spelling is Cornwell here and at 37, 73, and 135, and Cornewell at 1970; otherwise it is spelled with an a (Cornwals, Cornwall, Cornewal, Cornewall), as it is throughout F. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 511) note that Shakespeare had an uncle by marriage called Cornwell [Cornell, Cornehill, Cornish]: see Mark Eccles, Shakespeare in Warwickshire (1961) [pp. 10, 21–2, 29]. The spelling Cornwell for the place appears elsewhere, e.g. Warner’s Albion’s England (1586, p. 57), and a character named Cornwell appears in the play Nobody and Somebody (ca. 1605). Wells (ed. 2000): An independent kingdom until it came under Anglo-Saxon rule in the tenth century.

6 vs]
Goggin (ed. 1910) and most eds.: I.e. Kent and Gloucester. Houghton (ed. 1957): Gloucester cannot use a royal plural. Weis (ed. 1993): The royal plural…was also used by other important personages, giving no evidence. Hunter (ed. 1972): Our people (perhaps an attempt to include Edmund in the conversation). But since Edmund has just returned after years of absence from court, did alwaies seeme can hardly apply to him. Bradley (1904, p. 447) imagines that Sh. might have omitted to write an intended scene in which Gloucester encourages Lear to divide the kingdom and Kent dissents. If it were so, there would be additional point in the Fool’s reference to the lord who counselled Lear to give away his land [669+1], and in Gloster’s reflection [1944]…(said, of course, not to the King but to Gloster and perhaps others of the council).…Who are the us [6] from whom Kent is excluded? I do not know, for there is no sign that Kent has been absent. But if Kent, in consequence of his opposition, had fallen out of favour and absented himself from the council, it would be clear. Perrett (1904, p. 175): The council-scene [comparing 669+1]…has evidently taken place before the opening of the play. In Geoffrey [see ] we have indeed a consilium procerum for the actual division, but the king does not take counsel over the intended division except in [Leir], where Sc. 1, modelled on I, ii of Gorboduc, reveals Leir in council with his nobles, whose proferred [sic] advice only serves to strengthen the king’s conviction that his own plan is best; see .

7 diuision]
Deighton (ed. 1891): I.e. which he was about to make. Crook (ed. 1907): Lear…has not yet divided his kingdom,…so that Gloucester is speaking either from rumour or from imagination. Goggin (ed. 1910): The division has been made before the play commences, and is known to Gloucester and Kent, if not to Burgundy and France as well (see [211–12]). Harrison (ed. 1937): There remains only the public and ceremonious ratification. Cf. n. 3–10.
The serpent of division was cause for alarm to an Elizabethan or Jacobean audience; cf. 1H4 3.1. Holloway (1961, p. 80): Time and again this kind of event occurs in contemporary drama (Gorboduc, The Misfortunes of Arthur, Selimus, Woodstock, Locrine are examples). Its status as decisively misguided or evil is not in doubt; and it is the established sign or first step in a movement which threatens chaos or actually brings it. Elton (1966, pp. 78–9): Such admonitions…as recur from Gorboduc (1562; reprinted in 1590 annexed to Lydgate’s Serpent of Division) to the utterances of Shakespeare’s royal patron would have been present in the playwright’s mind. Chalmers (1799, pp. 414–16): In Basilikon Doron, 1603 [STC 14350], p. 83, King James warned his son, In case it please God to prouide you all these three kingdoms, make your eldest sonne Isaac, leauing him all your kingdomes.…Otherwaies by deuiding your kingdomes, ye shall leaue the seede of diuision & discord…as befell to this Ile, by the diuision…to the three sonnes of Brutus, Locrine, Albanacte, and Camber. The poet knew also, that the King had strongly recommended to his first Parliament, the union of his two Kingdoms.…[Such circumstances] fixed the determination of Shakspeare, to write, dramatically, on the story of Lear. George Owen Harry (The Genealogy of…James, 1604, pp. 39–40), having traced James’s descent from Brutus through Ragan and Cornwall, stresses James’s unifying role as only the second King of Brittayne since the whole Ile [was] deuided into England, Scotland, and Wales. Wickham (1973, p. 35): James was often identified as the second Brute (prophesied by Merlin) who would return and reunite the kingdom, as he was by Samuel Daniel, Thomas Dekker, Anthony Munday, and (adds Wittreich, 1984, p. 24), William Herbert. Axton (1977, pp. 134–5): James hoped for a speedy ratification of his plan [to unify England and Scotland]; but the Commons…debated Union for five years.…James enlisted sympathetic polemicists.…The Bishop of Bristol [John Thornborough]…(echoing James) likens the division of the realm to the first sin committed in Paradise. Cf. n. 1968. Patterson (1984, pp. 65–9) surveys many tracts, pamphlets, and parliamentary speeches of 1604 supporting James’s plans for union, and political opposition to those plans. Idem (1989, p. 106), however: The play offered for inspection a disastrous representative of monarchy, and one who shared with the current monarch a striking number of characteristics. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 15), to the contrary: Lear behaves in a way precisely opposite to that James had recommended to his heir, and so is no fictional portrait of the king himself. Bullough (1973, p. 272): The divided land motif…recurs often in [Geoffrey’s] chronicle; for almost invariably the partition of the kingdom leads to war; he names, besides the sons of Brut and daughters of Leir, Mempricius and Malin, Belinus and Brennius, Margan and Cunedag, and Ferrex and Porrex. Foakes (op. cit., p. 12): The [Q1] title-page may also have reminded some readers of Locrine, published in 1595 as Newly set foorth, ouerseene and corrected, By W.S., a play that shows the civil strife and wars with Huns and Scythians that follow when Brutus divides his kingdom among his three sons…[and of] Robert Greene’s Selimus, published in 1594, a play about an early-sixteenth-century Emperor of Turkey and his three sons, the youngest of them, Selimus, rising to power by poisoning his father and murdering his brothers.…Gorboduc…an academic play about the strife that erupts when a pseudo-historical King of Britain divides his kingdom…includes among its cast a Duke of Cornwall and a Duke of Albany.
McElwaine (1911, p. 425), however, defends Lear’s action: For a king without an heir male to divide his kingdom between his three daughters would hardly have been a strange act. In default of sons, all the daughters of a feudal lord succeeded to the estate in equal shares. Lear, therefore, only anticipates the division of the estate on his death. But, by the common law, freeholds of inheritance were not generally devisable by will; they were assignable only by formal delivery of the possession thereof in the tenant’s lifetime. If Lear wishes Cordelia’s share to be a third more opulent than her sisters’, he must assign it to her during his life, for on his death she will only inherit equally with Goneril and Regan.…If we can find in this first scene the seeds whence madness springs, they are to be found rather in his departure from his scheme of partition. Joseph (ed. 1966): Equal division among heiresses was English law until 1925. With Cordelia married to a foreign ruler (and presumably abroad) civil war might soon develop. Indeed, once the whole land has been divided equally between Albany and Cornwall, they soon fall out.…Only the greater danger from France unites the British rulers. Battenhouse (1969, p. 279), recalling Joshua’s innocuous division of his lands (Josh. 11:23), asks whether not Lear’s plan itself but his mismanagement of it…is for Shakespeare the basic cause of the tragedy? Like Nevo (1972, p. 263), Rosenberg (1972, p. 41): The wiser men in Lear’s court, Gloster and Kent, have spoken calmly of the expected division, and will only object when Cordelia is disenfranchised. There are no implied directions to make what he does now seem unnatural in the theatre. Colie (1974, p. 197): Not only was there no rule against abdication,…in cases where a male heir lacked, was young, or was weak, political disruption could be expected…; it could be argued that in trying to secure assent to the division…Lear showed foresight of an unexpected sort.…But there is an interesting record of aristocratic division of wealth: consideration of daughters’ material prosperity often contributed to the financial difficulty of noble families, some of which collapsed at the centre because of generosity in dowries and jointure arrangements. By treating his kingdom as if it were simply his land, an estate, Lear threatened his land, his country, at its centre too.…[Perhaps] Shakespeare made his profoundest comment on kingly misapprehension of rule and on ancient modes of governing. Seltzer (1981, p. 170): In no line of King Lear is this particular bit of Lear’s foolishness mentioned even once. Shakespeare verbalizes potential dangers more powerfully than any other dramatist when he considers them necessary for development of his action. Turner (1988, p. 101): We may think Lear unwise to have divided his kingdom until we remember the results of Gloucester’s exclusive favouring of legitimacy and primogeniture. The society fractures along its own fault-lines. Berry (1993, pp. 75–6): The political problem is not which of these unappealing satraps to hand over power to. It is to set up a system which will survive Lear, while permitting him a guiding hand in late old age. That system will not be a unitary state. Rather, it will illustrate, and indeed dramatize, Lear’s propensity to divide and rule. The post-abdication outcome will be a dynamic tripartition, which is the political extension and reflection of Lear’s relations with his daughters (and sons-in-law).…[Cordelia] is to receive the most desirable portion of Britain, the South-East, together with a Continental alliance, probably France.…Cordelia holds all the cards. By continuing Lear’s balancing act, she can dominate Goneril/Albany and Regan/Cornwall, playing off one against the other.…If Cordelia should bear a child, that opens up the prospect of a future reunification of the Island under her issue. Over these agreeable political manoeuvres the elder statesman will preside.…I see no folly in this scheme. On the contrary, it appears to me that Lear has planned his retirement rather well. Levin (1994, p. 208): Lear’s division of the kingdom by the rule of gavelkind to defeat the law of primogeniture would explain the interest shown by the King of France, the insouciance with which Cordelia greets the loss of her gift, even the reason that Cordelia is so curt in her answers to Lear’s request for thanks. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 17): His distribution of his lands…, in contemporary terms, appears to have been illegal. Queen Elizabeth had sought advice from her counsel on whether she could dispose of property, and her counsel advised her that any property, whether it came by descent from royal ancestors or from other sources, had to be regarded as part of the royal estate, and not as owned by the monarch as an individual.…[It could be given away] only by an open letter of authorization formally conferring the title, written on parchment and with the great seal attached, as the law prescribed, citing Law Reports 1.148, a case studied by Ernst Kantorowicz in The King’s Two Bodies (Princeton, 1957), pp. 9–15 and 405–9. However, No character suggests that Lear’s actions might be illegal, and under James I, Robert Cecil, appointed Lord Treasurer in 1608, determined that Crown lands would have to be sold off to raise revenue. Lear was of course not subject to English law, the division of his kingdom is not exactly analogous to the alienation of a piece of his property, and perhaps his public ceremony before the whole court would seem as effective as an open letter of authorization. Leir divides his kingdom in all of the sources; the division is immediate in most, partial in Holinshed and Mirour (1587 version), and posthumous in Mirour (1574 version) and Warner (see , , ). On the question of the legality of abdication, see n. 43–6.

7 kingdomes]
Most eds. prefer F’s Kingdome, since the addition of terminal -s is a common error. Collier (ed. 1843) defends the Q plural: it refers to the separate dominions given [i.e., allotted, not yet deeded] by Lear to the Dukes. Delius (ed. 1854) thinks the Q reading a genitive, kingdom’s; but English does not use such a construction with inanimate nouns. Taylor & Warren (1983, p. vi) argue that kingdome means kingly power (OED, sb. 1) and that Q therefore refers to Lear’s division of powers; but the word in this sense of sovereignty…kingship is used only in the singular, and in any case Lear publicly divides our kingdome (43, 86, 190, all singular), and apportions territory shown on a map, not sovereignty in the abstract. Taylor and Warren further argue that in his source [Leir; see ] Leir’s sons-in-law were not Dukes but the sovereigns of neighbouring kingdoms, so that the division of Leir’s own kingdom amounted to a re-division of the boundaries of three kingdoms. The word moytie (see n. 10), however, clearly means the share of Lear’s own kingdom that each duke will receive, not the sum resulting from re-division, a term Gloucester does not use. Meyer (1994, p. 145): Q’s reading makes no sense as far as Lear’s purpose is concerned. In Leir (ll. 318, 456, 549, 651, 893, 2142; see , , , , , ) the king, Cordella, and the dukes always refer to the division of the kingdom singular, never plural.

8 values]
Schmidt (1875): Esteem[s] (OED, v. 4). Cf. 1222.

9 equalities]
Most eds. agree with Capell (1783, 1.2:140) that F’s qualities will appear a printer’s corruption…suiting less with the context. Werstine (1983, p. 286), however, notes that such literal errors are rare in the pages set by F Compositor B. Many concede with Steevens (ed. 1778) that either reading will do, and Foakes (ed. 1997) like a few others thinks that F makes better sense. Capell also thinks Q’s equalities gives the passage a superior numerousness, i.e. (apparently) better rhythm. The possible meanings for each term are:
(1)Equalities. Coleridge (MS notes, 1794–): Shares perfectly equal. Delius (ed. 1854): Divisions equal in size and worth (Ger.). Wright (ed. 1875): Equal conditions. Craig (ed. 1901): Shares. Wells (ed. 2000): Correspondences, i.e. (presumably) corresponding features of the territories. Schmidt (1879, p. 12) argues for a singular: Equality cannot be predicated of a part by itself, but only of the relationship of parts to each other; it is essentially a singular idea. We cannot say: the equalities of the three parts are perfect, but only: the equality, etc. (Ger.). Deighton (ed. 1891): This is logically true, but it is dangerous to say of Elizabethan English that a word could not have been employed in a sense different from that more logical modern usage, citing Steevens’s (op. cit.) quotation from Edmund Tilney’s The flower of friendshippe (1568, sig. B4): After this match made, and equalities considered. Perrett (1904, p. 150): Schmidt’s argument would apply as well to any abstract noun. But early modern English had a strong tendency to use abstracts in the plural, citing Franz [§196]. Hudson (ed. 1881): The portions are weighed out or arranged so equally, or in such equality. A proleptical mode of speech. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Elizabethan usage often pluralizes abstract names when two or more persons or things are in question, comparing worships (779) and sights (2474), adding, Disregard of the old idiom has led some editors to accept the Folio reading. Cf. 2550. Colie (1974, p. 198): His division of the kingdom was just. He divided the land into three rich parts, intending for his favourite child a third evidently not larger, but more opulent, than those assigned her sisters. Stone (1980, p. 213): Gloucester cannot be citing as evidence for Lear’s impartiality…that impartiality itself (qualities…). The evidence lies in the apportionment of the kingdom into exactly equal shares (equalities…).
(2)Qualities. Warburton (ed. 1747): The properties of the several divisions. Rolfe (ed. 1880): Values. Tovey (ed. 1896): The advantages and disadvantages of each division. MacCracken (ed. 1914): Positions of rank. Muir (ed. 1952): The mental and moral qualities of the dukes. Brown (ed. 1976): The nature of everything. Horsman (ed. 1973): That the quality of each duke is nicely balanced with that of the other is a point which is not in question. Perrett (1904, pp. 146–51): On Regan Lear bestows an ample third…no less in space…than that conferr’d on Goneril. How then could the third third, reserved for Cordelia, be more opulent than either of [the] other two, and represent the father’s largest bounty?…The thing is clearly impossible. Perrett therefore prefers F’s qualities, meaning commodities to be reaped, which might be equal despite differences in area among the three divisions. The same argument could support equalities—of value. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): The unmentioned third part designed for Cordelia is, as appears later [92; cf. n. 42–3], more opilent than the others.…[Capell’s] argument for [equalities], as having more numerousness, is based upon the idea that three parts instead of two are being discussed.…If it were here, as Schmidt supposes, a question of the relationship of three parts equal to one another, the idea would be one of triple equality, and equalities, as Capell says, would suit the context better. Since only two are in question, the Folio qualities (special traits giving each part value [OED, sb. 7]) suits it better.

9 weighed]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Balanced against one another. Craig (ed. 1901): Carefully considered and adjusted.

9 curiositie]
The word may refer here either to a kind or quality of behavior—Warburton (ed. 1747): Exactest scrutiny; Craig (ed. 1901): The most minute and scrupulous attention or examination (OED, sb. 1, 2)—or to a personal disposition—Steevens (ed. 1778): Scrupulousness or captiousness (OED, 4, 5). Here it seems to be the latter, a quality in the dukes. In Sh.’s only other uses of the word (see 338, 598–9, and Tim. 4.3.303 [1934]) it has a pejorative cast, but here it need be only neutral; Rann’s (ed. 1794) Capricious disposition and Brooke’s (ed. 1947) Whimsicality, frivolous reason would seem to imply a censure of both dukes that is neither clearly deserved nor relevant to a discussion of the King’s actions. Foakes (ed. 1997): Also the curiosity of Albany and Cornwall about their shares, and inquisitiveness on the part of others.

9–10 neither…eithers]
Eds. generally understand both pronouns to refer to the dukes, not to their shares.

10 make…moytie]
Rann (ed. 1794): Give one portion the preference to the other.

10 moytie]
Steevens (ed. 1773): The strict sense of the word moiety is half, one of two equal parts [OED, sb. 1]; but Shakespeare commonly uses it for any part or division [OED, 2]. Schmidt (1875): Sh. uses both meanings with about equal frequency, but here in the looser sense. Nonetheless Delius (ed. 1854), followed by a few others, prefers the former meaning: Gloster, since he speaks only of the two dukes, seems not altogether familiar with Lear’s plan, expecting the division exclusively between these two (Ger.). Cf. n. 41.

12–27 His…acknowledged]
Goggin (ed. 1910), following Coleridge (see ): The unblushing effrontery with which Gloucester speaks of Edmund’s illegitimacy, even before Edmund himself, is intended to show the influences which have been at work in moulding the character of Edmund and to explain the misfortunes which are later to befall Gloucester himself. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Coleridge did not perceive that [these lines] are spoken in a private conversation between Kent and Gloucester, and that Edmund stands in the background and hears nothing until he is called forward at 27. Wilson (ed. 1960): Some are doubtful whether the subject would be thought too delicate for discussion in Sh.’s day. But cf. blushed…brazed [13–14]. Vickers (1968, pp. 352–3): Gloucester’s balanced formal style is too courtly for Kent: I cannot conceive you, a verb which Gloucester complacently quibbles on, as he recalls the bastardy with an equally complacent antithesis: Sir…bed…[and] another brazen quibble [on fault].…Coleridge’s description of this word-play as most degrading and licentious levity…is too indignant, but the complacency of attitude shown by the quibbling is meant to be alienating. Gardner (ed. 1969): The audience would instinctively associate a bastard with the likelihood of treacherous villainy, and the conversation…exposes the roots of the social stigma which generated an illegitimate son’s perverse reactions. The scene prepares the ground for the subplot. Cf. Bacon, Of Envy (1625, p. 42): Bastards are Enuious: For he that cannot possibly mend his owne case, will doe what he can to impaire anothers. Elton (1966, pp. 132–3) quotes several contemporary statements on the defective status and natures of bastards. Jones (1975, p. 132): Gloucester’s half-embarrassed, half gloating ambivalence between the shame of his adultery and the remembered pleasure does have in it the seeds of Lear’s tremendous sway from exultation into horror at what he has come to see [in 4.6] as an all pervasive and ungovernable sexuality. The Sokols (2000, p. 29): Gloucester’s embarrassment and Kent’s attempt to be gracious does reflect a turnabout of social attitudes circa 1606. Not long before then, according to social historians [citing Lawrence Stone and others], many high born fathers did not blush to acknowledge their bastards openly, and with pride.

12 breeding…charge]
Deighton (ed. 1891), following Schmidt (1874): His bringing up has been at my expense (OED, Breeding vbl. sb. 3). But another meaning better introduces the rest of the speech: Hunter (ed. 1972): I might be held responsible for his birth (OED, 1). Weis (ed. 1993): Or, his personal behaviour (OED, 4). Joseph (ed. 1966), charge: Perhaps unconsciously, blame (OED, sb. 16; cf. 456). The Sokols (2003, pp. 23, 157): Although a bastard was legally filius nullius, the child of no one, and therefore incapable of inheriting land from either parent, under both canon and common law the father was obliged to support him.

14 braz’d]
Wright (ed. 1875): Hardened, made insensible. OED (ppl. a.): Fig. Brazened, rendered shameless. Kittredge (ed. 1940): As if plated with brass. Joseph (1964, p. 86): Hardened against shame by the fire of his blushes; or acquired a tanned complexion from their heat (Weis, ed. 1993). Cf. 1101, brazen fac’t. Cavell (1969, p. 276): Perhaps…soldered fast to it, a sense not attested in OED until 1677 and not again until 1835.

15 conceiue you]
Muir (ed. 1952): Kent uses the word in the sense of understand; Gloucester puns on it in his next speech. Van Dam [1935, p. 45] thinks the quibble is only possible if the word is used intransitively, and urges the omission of you. This improvement is not absolutely necessary. Greg (1949, p. 399; cf. 1946, p. 232), supporting Van Dam: Gloucester’s reply suggests that what Kent said was I cannot conceive—. Wilson (ed. 1960): Van Dam’s emendation would give a neater quibble in [16]; and you may be a common error [i.e., common to Q and F]. But Gloucester’s pun holds good even if you is understood as repeated in 16, where it would be an ethic dative (Horsman, ed. 1973).

16 fellowes]
OED (sb. 9): A familiar synonym for: Man, male person; (9a): With qualifying adj., as good,…old, young, etc. Cf. 550, 631, 705, 1098, 1130, 1158, 1316, 1572, 1961, 2226, 2534, 3250.

16 Could]
Warburton (MS notes, 1747–) suspects a quibble: Was a mistress of her trade; not attested in OED in a specifically sexual sense.

19 smell]
Heilman (1948, p. 15): Detect; but here is an early suggestion of an unhealthy world, comparing 642, 1343, 2170, 2549, 2570, 2576, 2621.

19 fault]
Muir (ed. 1952): Perhaps a quibble…: (a) misdeed, (b) loss of scent by hounds. Shakespeare often compares sin to a bad smell. Cf. Ham. [3.3.36 (2312)]. Lott (ed. 1974) compares 897, 1343, 2576. In certain expressions—cold fault, make out a fault, etc.—the word seems to mean virtually the scent itself (see OED, sb. 8). Weis (ed. 1993): Gloucester may mean Do you feel that I have gone astray? (lit. lost the trail). Hulme (1962, p. 112): Wordplay on a small flaw or crack and a sin, an act of intercourse; the latter sense is not supported by OED, and Williams (1994) provides only one possible pun on faulty, dated 1635. Like McCall (1977, p. 124), Ross (1978, p. 5) detects a pun on fart, citing Kökeritz (1953, p. 311, n. 2). Astington (1985, pp. 330 ff.), quoting several doubtful instances as parallels: female genitals and scent of sex, both indicating in Gloucester the darkness of sex-hatred, even a hint of hysteria. Williams provides two supporting exx., both only possible puns, in Marston, and does not cite this line. Though Rubinstein (1984) attributes the sense breach (pudendum), she quotes neither this line nor any other ex., yet is cited by Halio (ed. 1992) and Foakes (ed. 1997), the latter comparing 643 (stincke), 897 (smell out), 2570 (stench). Adelman (1992, p. 295): Pun on foutre as well; no supporting exx. appear in Williams or elsewhere.

20 issue]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Quibble, specified by Brown (ed. 1976): Result/child.

21 proper]
Malone (ed. 1790): Handsome (OED, a. 8). Delius (ed. 1854): Seemly, without fault (Ger.) (OED, 7). Chambers (ed. 1906) combines both senses: Fine. Brown (ed. 1976): Appropriate (to the fault).

22 by…Law]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Legitimately begotten.

22–3 some yeare]
Eccles (ed. 1792): About a year. See 339. On Sh.’s frequent use of some before a singular noun of time, see Abbott §21, Schmidt (1875), Franz §354. Cf. 3156. Wells (ed. 2000): Edgar’s seniority…indicates that Edmund was adulterously begotten.

23 no deerer]
Only Brown (ed. 1976) detects a quibble: More costly/more beloved. Ribner (1958, p. 48): Gloucester’s sentiment here (cf. 351–2) might seem commendable to a modern audience, but Gloucester is denying the laws of society.
