23–4 account]
Schmidt (1874): Estimation (OED, sb. 11). Regarding Theobald’s punctuation (see textual n.), Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 359) quotes D. Nichol Smith: A sentence constructed "though…yet…" is hardly colloquial. In Wilson (ed. 1960) Duthie withdraws his defense of F.

24 knaue]
Muir (ed. 1952): Fellow—not implying moral disapproval. Wilson (ed. 1960): Boy. See n. 573; cf. 622. Hunter (ed. 1972): The sense of villain…may be present by irony. Weis (ed. 1993): Rascal (jocularly affectionate); see n. 26.

24 something]
Abbott (§68): Used adverbially like somewhat (OED, adv. 2c). Cf. Franz §397.

24 sawcely]
Schmidt (1875): With impertinent boldness (OED, a.1 2). Cf. 1172, 1317. Deighton (ed. 1891): Impudently in not having been duly summoned.…The word knave, used here with an affectionate sense, but meaning also a servant, accounts for the words before he was sent for. Harbage (ed. 1958), additionally: Bawdily. OED (Saucy a.1 2b): Wanton, lascivious. In Shaks. as a term of serious condemnation; in modern examples only playful.

24 into]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 122): F’s to is perfectly possible, citing Cor. 5.3.124–5 (3479–80), thy Mothers wombe That brought thee to this world.

26 whoreson]
Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956): Bastard. Brown (ed. 1976): Young rogue. Brooke (ed. 1947): This and knaue are terms of bluff affection. Harbage (ed. 1958): But literally applicable. Foakes (ed. 1997): Both terms contemptuously evoke Edmund’s condition as inferior and a bastard.

32 My seruices]
Deighton (ed. 1891): I am your humble servant to command; a courteous form of expression to a superior. OED (Service1 sb. 9): In complimentary expressions: Respect, duty.…b. pl. in the same sense, quoting this l. Wells (ed. 2000): A bow or other gesture of respect is called for. Elton (1966, p. 286): In contrast to Kent’s true service, Edmund offers his services to almost everyone else.…He serves his father and his brother ([498]), both against their interests; he serves his proxy father, Cornwall, in his own interest; and, in another sense as well, he serves the lusts of Goneril and Regan. The importance of the concept of service to the play is discussed by Barish & Waingrow (1958), Mack (1965, pp. 103–44), and Strier (1988). Forms of the word and its cognates appear at 336, 498, 516, 535, 544, 553, 555, 562, 571, 617, 622, 1059, 1072, 1091, 1093, 1207, 1350, 1378, 1676, 1866, 2146, 2147, 2274, 2296, 2704.

33 I must]
Deighton (ed. 1891): I am bound, for your father’s sake.

33 sue]
Schmidt (1875): To beg, to intreat (OED, v. 22b).

34 study deseruing]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Endeavour to deserve the honour of being better known to you, or to deserve your love (Brown, ed. 1976). OED (Study v. 11): To aim at, seek to achieve. Jacobs (1975, p. 19) finds a debt to Thomas Kyd’s Spanish Tragedy 1.2.151, I shall studie to deserue this grace, though the use of study (n. or v.) + infin. is common in Sh.; cf. 302–3. Mahood (1992, p. 172): Edmund calculatingly expects material benefit, viz. protection and preferment. Halio (ed. 1992): The words carry an ominous implication—though perhaps only in retrospect.

35 out]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Abroad (OED, adv. 2). That Sh. intended us to know no more than this of Edmund’s whereabouts, occupation, or reasons for leaving home for nine years and for returning now has hardly discouraged speculation. Eccles (ed. 1792) imagines travel, or serving in the army; Coleridge (MS notes, 1818–19, ed. Foakes, 1989, p. 98), foreign education from boyhood to the present time; Hudson (ed. 1879), travelling abroad, or…pursuing his studies, or…some kind of foreign service. Gervinus (1849–50; tr. 1875, p. 632): Edmund’s father has kept him away from his house…[being] ashamed of him. Wright (ed. 1875): Edmund has been seeking his fortune abroad, there being no career for him at home in consequence of his illegitimate birth. Halio (ed. 1992): Renaissance nobles often sent their children to be brought up in other noblemen’s homes, sometimes in their own country, sometimes abroad. Foakes (ed. 1997): As Prince Henry, elder son of James I, was placed in the household of the Earl of Mar. Hunter (ed. 1972): His absence helps to explain the ignorance of Edmund’s nature shown both by his brother and by his father. Lott (ed. 1974): It is a reason for the villainy in Edmund’s character; he has not had long association with his father and brother. Pyle (1948, p. 453): Perhaps suggested by the parenthetical remark [in Sidney’s Arcadia 2.23.7; ed. Feuillerat, 1:300] that Plexirtus was called home by his father before he falsly got his kingdom.

35 nine yeares]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Therefore Gloster appears to introduce his son to Kent for the first time. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Why nine years? Probably to show that, since his breeding or training was finished, he had fully grown into manhood.

35–6 away…againe]
This is generally taken as a statement of Gloucester’s intent, but it could as well be Edmund’s. Muir (ed. 1952): Perhaps these words seal Gloucester’s doom.

35 shall]
Horsman (ed. 1973): Must, comparing 2964 and adding (p. 222), It suggests that Edmund has only this one opportunity to outwit his brother; but the word may imply only simple futurity or purpose. Cf. n. 40. On the ellipsis of the verb of motion see n. 312.

37–8 Sound…followers]
The gravity of the occasion naturally requires ceremony, lending pomp and dignity (Long, 1971, p. 164).

37 Sennet]
Dessen & Thomson (1999): A fanfare played within…frequently in the Shakespeare canon. Wright (ed. 1875): A particular set of notes on a trumpet or cornet which marked the entrance or exit of a procession, and is different from a flourish. Naylor (1896, p. 178): The notes of a sennet are unknown. Three times [in the Sh. canon] it marks the entrance or exit of a Parliament, three times is used in a Royal or quasi-royal procession, and the remaining [three] cases are royal, or near it.…[The occasional spellings Sonet and sonnet] seem to point to a derivation of the word from sonare.…But other forms…Synnet, Signet, Signate…may be proper derivatives of signum, and thus make this trumpet call a signal instead of a sounding. Craig (ed. 1901) cites the SDs in John Marston’s Antonio and Mellida 1.1 in which cornets sound a sennet before an entrance and a flourish after an entrance, upon a meeting, and after an exit. But in Dr. Faustus B 1012 a flourish precedes the sennet. Skeat (1901, p. 265): First of all, several trumpets would play a general flourish, then a single trumpet or cornet would play a signal-call, the sennet or signate. Cowling (1913, p. 47): A sennet is not a fanfare but a short piece of music. It lasted long enough for a stage-procession to file in, for a banquet to be laid, or…during a dumb-show. Manifold (1956, p. 28): Its instrumentation is always plural when given at all; and it is usually called upon to accompany a fairly lengthy bit of action on the stage. So Gardner (ed. 1969): A sennet needed two or three trumpets. OED accepts Skeat’s derivation from signet rather than Elson’s (1900, p. 324), Cowling’s, and Sternfeld’s (1963, p. 197) from sonnet or sonata. Long (1971, p. 164) finds it ominous that no flourish is sounded here for Lear, suggesting that his majesty is unstable, while one is sounded for the entrance of others at 202 (F only) and the exeunt at 291 (F only).

37 Enter one…Coronet]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 107) finds this direction too vague for a prompt-book; it is missing from F, which apparently derives from a playbook or a transcript of one. (Prompt-book is a 19th-c. term, reflecting contemporary, not Jacobean, use of the playbook to monitor performances.)

37 Coronet]
Pope’s added SD (see textual n. 147) implies that Lear gives his own crown. Delius (ed. 1854): Lear instead delivers to his sons-in-law, who remain dukes after this transaction, a smaller ducal crown. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905), more fancifully: Perhaps it was the coronet held by the lineal prince which Lear, having no male heir, now confers upon his sons-in-law to the exclusion of Cordelia from the succession. Perrett (1904, pp. 152–3): Now why should a coronet be borne in at the head of the procession, preceding the king himself? It cannot be a symbol of his majesty, for…this is but a coronet.…The explanation is that the coronet was intended for Cordelia.…[Its presence] gives Lear’s children an inkling of what his purpose is, supplying an additional motive for the elder daughters’ flattery, and adding a new beauty to Cordelia.…Again, from the point of view of the audience, the presence of the coronet excites curiosity as to what is to happen, gives point to darker purpose, and…[helps] prevent any suspicion that the king really means to measure the dowers by professions of love. So Neilson & Thorndike (ed. 1909): Apparently intended for Cordelia as emblem of her new realm; her sisters already wear coronets. Cf. [147]. Though there is not the slightest textual evidence for any part of this statement, the general idea has appeared plausible to Muir (ed. 1952), Wilson (ed. 1960), Fraser (ed. 1963), and others. Dove & Gamble (1969, pp. 312–17): Obviously it has nothing to do with Goneril or Regan, who have been made duchesses by their husbands; obviously it is not for France, who has a king’s crown, or Burgundy, who has his own ducal coronet. It clearly represents some British territorial rule, since it is later divided between Albany and Cornwall.…Since it would be absurd to give Cordelia British territory to rule if she were going off to be Queen of France or Duchess of Burgundy, it must be her prize for victory in the love test.…Lear wants her to stay with him in Britain as the prop of his old age, and with this in mind he offers her the glittering and totally unexpected bait of the opulent third of the kingdom.…Lear is the third suitor. Zak (1984, p. 189, n. 3): Dove and Gamble cannot logically argue that her replies to Lear are clipped becaue she realizes that to express her love would be to sacrifice herself to Lear. If his plan is a surprise, she cannot know that. Admittedly the fact that Cordelia must choose between her suitors and her father could be made clearer. If originally intended for Cordelia, the coronet would presumably have indicated that her power was to be ducal, comparable to that of her sisters and their husbands. Greg (1955, p. 384 n.): It is not, perhaps, characteristic of Shakespeare to look so far ahead in his directions, for the coronet is not called for till [147]. However, it is evident that he has clearly visualized the scene, and there is subtlety in the provision he makes. When Lear says to his Beloued Sonnes Cornwall and Albany This Coronet part betweene you, he is bidding them to share the executive office only; he retains on his own head the crown as symbol of The name, and all th’addition to a King. This touch is lost in F, in which, since no provision is made, we must suppose that Lear takes the coronet from his own head to part between the Dukes.
Other intended recipients have been proposed. On the assumption that Lear is a master politician arranging in advance for the ideal balance of power in Britain and France, Jaffa (1957) theorizes elaborately but on no textual evidence that the coronet is intended for Burgundy, whose marriage to Cordelia would subjoin his duchy to hers and allow Cordelia to remain in Britain, eventually to become its queen. It cannot be intended for France, since the princess’s marriage to that foreign king would have unbalanced the system of powers and would have given rise to French claims on the British throne and open the possibility that Britain would become an appendage to France. Shand (1987, p. 80): Probably intended for France [more probably] or Burgundy, whichever succeeds in gaining Cordelia’s hand.…It might very well be sufficiently similar to the coronets worn by Cornwall and Albany that the intention would be evident from its first appearance.…[It signifies] the dowry Cordelia brings with her, and…France’s new political and domestic status.…Lear’s intention here is comparable with what would have happened at the time of the royal wedding in 1554 if Mary I had been allowed to proceed with her plan to crown Philip (already King of Naples and Jerusalem, though not yet of Spain. Such a coronation,…though contentious, was not unthinkable.
That Lear’s coronet is not the symbol of the third, more opulent (92) intended for Cordelia, but the crown of Britain itself, has been suggested by Wright (ed. 1875) and others, assumed by Heilman (1948, p. 73), and argued by Williams (1971, pp. 99–100). One may doubt that in F Lear wears a coronet, from the 15th c. to modern times A small or inferior crown; spec. a crown denoting a dignity inferior to that of the sovereign, worn by the nobility, and varying in form according to rank (OED, sb. 1). Sh. consistently makes this distinction elsewhere: in 1H6 5.4.123–34 (2765–76) Charles is directed to swear allegiance to Henry’s Crowne while as viceroy, shadow of himselfe, he wear only a Coronet; and whereas we hear nine times of Julius Caesar’s crown, the waggish Casca only once calls it a coronet (JC 1.2.238 [341]) ironically to understate Caesar’s ambition. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 14): Shakespeare and his audience well knew the difference…: crowns typically had raised sides,…had between four and eight raised arches over the circlet, and were topped with an emblem symbolic of the power belonging to kings. Coronets…were circlets worn by princes and dukes. Wells (ed. 2000): Lear himself would wear the royal crown, and Albany and Cornwall would wear coronets, citing Gurr (1997, p. 165). When in 675–8 Lear’s Fool speaks of the king’s cleaving his golden crown and giving away both parts, he is speaking figuratively of the power symbolized by the crown; he need not be referring to the coronet of this scene, at which he was not apparently present. That Lear is bareheaded or crowned with weeds in the storm scenes does not prove that he gives his own crown away here, since even if he retained it he probably would not be wearing it when he returns from hunting in 1.4 or bursts out of Goneril’s house at the end of that scene. Bevington (ed. 1980): Perhaps a chaplet or garland.

37 Lear]
Rosenberg (1972, pp. 22–32) records how actors have characterized Lear upon his entrance as the archetypal titan; the hard, practicing monarch; the madman king; and the everyman-king. Cf. Brown (ed. 1976, p. 425), and Foakes (ed. 1997, pp. 23–9), who says of this entrance, It is proper that [Lear]…should make a processional entry…, sit on a throne, and wear royal robes and a crown. He is to conduct state business, in a formal ceremony publishing the division of the kingdom, and determining a husband for his youngest daughter (p. 13). Wells (ed. 2000): A ritualistic and hierarchical entry, probably through the central entrance.…Lear presumably sits center-stage.

37 Gonorill, Regan]
On the spelling, see DP n. 15. Rosenberg (1972, p. 49): They are gorgeously dressed [cf. 1569], Goneril is beautiful, and aware of her beauty [cf. 1109], and they are passionate women, with some humor, social grace, and the physical strength to ride long hours through the night and preside at battles.

38 Cordelia]
Rosenberg (1972, p. 57): Each polar extreme of Cordelia’s possibility has sometimes been seized by critics and actors as her identity. At one end she is the ultimate Christ figure, or, close by, enskyed and sainted by the powers vested in Bradley. At the nadir, she is sour and egotistic, self-willed, obstinate, sulky, proud, or a sweet milksop. In fact she moves between extremes, one somewhat short of Bradley’s canonization and the other touching the arrogance and ego-aggrandizement of her father. See . Horsman (ed. 1973): She will have to be as near to the audience as possible for the asides in lines [67] and [82–4], which separate her clearly from the others. Cf. n. 176.

38 followers]
Rosenberg (1972, p. 14), citing 1033–6, speculates that Edgar may be present as a mute member of Lear’s attendant knights. Foakes (ed. 1997): The Fool has been brought on stage at this point, as by Jonathan Miller in the BBC television version [1982]. Wells (ed. 2000) But his entry in 1.4 is so elaborately built up as to suggest that he has not been seen before.

39–309 Lear.…Cord.]
Verity (ed. 1897): With the entrance of the king the tone naturally changes, and conversational prose…gives place to verse.

39 Lear]
Granville-Barker (1927, p. 164 n.): In Reinhardt’s Berlin production of the play, he placed Lear for this first scene upon an exaggeratedly high throne and so suggested…isolation. Sprague (1944, p. 282): When the King himself first speaks, it used to be literally from the throne, where he was seated as early as Colman’s eighteenth century acting edition [1768; see ]. When, however, Shakespeare’s text [rather than Nahum Tate’s; see ] came to be used, a procession very often replaced the discovery [of a throned Lear]. Reynolds (1962, p. 86): There is no hint of a throne in the text, but one would be appropriate for Lear’s formal division of his kingdom; he considers the possibility of lowering it to the Globe stage for this scene only, and the difficulties of leaving it onstage throughout Act 1 during four scenes having different settings. But as Sprague indicates, Lear might well walk on and stand.

39 Attend]
Schmidt (1874): Wait on (OED, v. 7). Kemshead (ed. 1875): Escort hither (OED, v. 8). Only Lee (ed. 1908) understands a volitive subjunctive—Bid the lords attend upon us—to which Gloucester’s reply is not so apt. Harbage (1963, p. 400): It is fitting that his first words should be a command.

39 my]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 359): Perhaps Q anticipates this word in the next line.

39 Lords…Burgundy]
On the anachronism see DP n. 3–4. In practically every earlier version of the Lear story Cordelia is wooed by the King of Gallia or France. Perrett (1904, p. 214): In no earlier version except [Leir] does he conduct his suit in person, and only there [115–16; see ] is to be found a hint of rivals in her love. Tamblyn (1922, pp. 346–9): Why should Shakespeare have invented a Burgundy to stand thus in invidious contrast to [France] the old enemy of England?…Shakespeare intends not the Burgundy of Philip and Charles the Bold as a whole but the Imperial Circle of Burgundy of the sixteenth century, embracing the Netherlands and Franche Comté, all of which in 1605 had been for fifty years [since 1556] a possession of Spain. Holding these dominions, Philip II and Philip IV called themselves Duke of Burgundy.…In the back of his head, at least, Shakespeare had him [the King of Spain] identified with Burgundy. Baldwin (1922, p. 504): France and Spain were the candidates for the hand of the Princess Elizabeth [of England] as France and Burgundy are for that of Cordelia. Immediately after the accession of King James, Rosny, the French ambassador, proposed a marriage between Elizabeth and the Dauphin of France, a proposal that was supposed at the time to have met with high favor from King James. On the other hand, James was trying to dicker off Prince Henry and Princess Elizabeth to the King of Spain and the catholic interests.…Thus the marriage of Princess Elizabeth was a live issue 1603–6, within which period Lear was written, and the contestants were France and Spain. Law (1924, pp. 46–8; 1936, pp. 223–6): Sh.’s Burgundy is a composite of several 14th- and 15th-c. dukes of Burgundy with whom Sh. was familiar from the parts of Holinshed on which he had based his history plays; (pp. 226–7): The stories of rivalry with France, of courtship or marriage with the English royal house, and a series of broken promises to England might suggest the name of Burgundy for the dishonorable suitor. Berry (1993, p. 74): The French alliance is manifestly preferable. The Duchy of Burgundy was always land-locked [but see above].…France offers an inexpugnable base, with the eternal assurance of support for or intervention in British affairs, just as in the subsequent play. It would always have been France, in the competition for Cordelia’s hand. Burgundy was there to make it an auction.

39 Burgundy]
Walker (1854, p. 240): The pronunciation of Burgogne, a form found in F H5 5.2.7 (2994; cf. Bourgougne, 5.2.1.SD [2986] and Burgonie, 3.5.42 [1421]), would restore [metrical] harmony to this line and to 268 and 272. In F the forms Burgogne, Bourgougne (there is but one instance of each) and Burgonie appear only in the pages set by Compositor A; elsewhere in F and in Q Lr. the name is spelled with a d; in F all these forms are trisyllabic as a rule. But several times in this play the meter seems to imply that the last two syllables were unstressed and almost elided; cf. 213, 260, 268, 272, and n. 47. Smidt (1964, p. 153) thinks that Gloster is a speech prefix for 40, mistakenly added at the end of a metrically regular 39.

40 shall]
Abbott (§315): I shall sometimes means a mixture of I am bound to and I am sure to. Hence it is often used in the replies of inferiors to superiors. Cf. n. 2964. Kittredge (ed. 1940): A regular form of assent to a command. Shall was felt to be more respectful than will, since it denotes absolute futurity, without any suggestion that obedience is a matter of will.

40 Leige]
Chambers (ed. 1906): Feudal lord (OED, Liege adj. 1). White (ed. 1862): F’s Lord was caught from the line above. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 165): Or the playhouse manuscript [behind F] may have had the abbreviation L., and [the scribe who prepared printer’s copy from it] may have interpreted this as Lord. Greg (1949, p. 399): If the book had L. it undoubtedly stood for Lord. No one doubts the Q reading; as Duthie remarks, Lord sounds very tame after Lords in the previous line, and it is unlikely that the Q compositor would have expanded an L. in his copy to Leige.

40 Exit.]
F adds the needed SD; see 202–3. Modern eds. generally follow Capell (see textual n.) in making Edmund go off with his father, even though, as Koppel (1899, p. 14) says, he can have nothing to do with summoning the suitors. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 229): There is no authority for Edmund’s exit, and the producer is quite at liberty to let him stay and listen to the momentous proceedings. Horsman (ed. 1973): To see a legitimate heir deprived of her land…and to observe, and perhaps even to make a first impression upon, Goneril and Regan. Halio (1998, p. 105) also argues for his remaining. Cf. n. 202.

41–59 Meane…first?]
Capell (1783, 1.2:141) defends his eclectic conflation of Q and F versions of Lear’s speech: Neither were to be followed entirely: not the quarto, as wanting several lines quite essential, and having readings besides less eligible; not the folio, which has also it’s readings short [i.e., in quality] of quarto ones, in the speech’s end and beginning; that towards the end wanting something of the quarto’s simplicity, and that towards it’s beginning falling short of the other’s dignity. Doran (1931, pp. 61–3): The reference to France and Burgundy interrupts the course of thought, which is resumed with [53].…Line [45] is short, suggesting a textual disturbance of some kind. It may be that the phrase my daughters of line [53] once formed the last foot in line [45], and that the intervening lines were a later addition. Line [42] is also short. To [58]…Gonorill should perhaps be attached and the last line of the speech made into a half-line. The passage in the folio is regular throughout.…Line [42]…may be short in the quarto because the printer, carrying too much in his head, forgot the opening words, Giue me.…The lines addressed to Cornwall and Albany are logically in place…[and] must have been in the speech as it was first written. Moreover, they remedy the meter of line [45]. But they introduce a new metrical irregularity into line [50].…The fact that, if the lines preceding have been omitted from Q1 at all, this line has been patched proves that the omission is not a careless one due to printer or transcriber. Yet no reason for the omission is apparent. The passage is better with the lines than without them. It is at least as probable that they are additional to the folio, made to smooth out a passage which had been left faulty by a former revision. The lines in the folio cannot be considered part of the original passage on the basis of their furnishing necessary information. [All of its facts appear again in 4–10, 71, 73, 136, 145–6].…The folio passage shows some variations which do not appear to be printer’s substitutions.…Although the two parenthetical lines, [54 and 55], could have been accidentally lost from Q1, they may instead have been added to the folio…to emphasize by iteration the serious nature of Lear’s abdication. About this whole passage it is possible to argue both ways. But the fact that the lines which are only in the folio occur in a passage which shows evidences of revision is presumptive evidence of their being additional in that text. Brooke (ed. 1947): The speech casts doubt on the theory [see ] that the Quarto version of the play is a reconstruction, based upon an actor’s memory, shorthand notes, or both. The Quarto lacks seven lines that are in the Folio and makes four important verbal substitutions [in 43, 44, 45, and 58].…It has three metrically short lines, in addition to the last. Otherwise it is a pretty faithful parallel to the Folio, and as a dramatic unit the shortened [i.e., Q] speech holds together well. Taylor (1983, p. 96): F makes Lear’s crucial second speech…both much longer and more complex, intellectually and syntactically. As a result, Lear dominates the scene even more dramatically, marshalling his subjects and his thoughts with the same authority. In fact F here adds only 6 and a fraction pentameter lines to Lear’s more than 100 lines in the scene—which he dominates dramatically in both Q and F. Harbage (1963, pp. 400–1): The King speaks like a king, with masterful economy and decisiveness. The fine rounded periods…lend him an air of power and grandeur.

41 we]
Lott (ed. 1974): The royal we for I (OED, pron. 2); used throughout the speech.

41 darker]
The word is unusual and its precise meaning here hard to pin down. Warburton (ed. 1747) gives the general meaning more secret (OED, Dark a. 7, quoting this l. as its first ex. of this figurative sense). To some it has religious, political, or psychological overtones that anticipate the tragic outcome. Empson (1951, p. 127): We are directed to the idea of renunciation [i.e., of the world and of life] by his calling it a darker purpose; in the eyes of the world it would be a gloomy one. I think that an Elizabethan audience would naturally interpret the speech in religious terms. (There is another reference to the idea later in the scene: So be my grave my peace [133].) They would also think the purpose dark because they would feel a very practical disapproval for any plan to divide England and thereby risk civil war. Traversi (1952, p. 45): The adjective is carefully chosen as a first indication of the obscure, unrealized sources of the emotions which are soon to come to the surface in the form of uncontrolled passion. For Stetner & Goodman (1968, pp. 84 ff.), Blechner (1988, pp. 314 ff.), and other psycholanalytic critics, that hidden passion is incest. Parker (1991, pp. 140 ff.), following Dove & Gamble (1969): Lear’s darker (cunning, perplexing, deceptive) purpose is to win the hand of his own daughter and consequently defeat the rivals, keeping her filial love and her opulent land for the remainder of his life; despite Lear’s statements otherwise, he plans only a partial abdication. Edwards (ed. 1975): Graver, as contrasted with the happy business of the betrothal of Cordelia. Weis (ed. 1993): Ironically, unenlightened.
The comparative form darker has also raised mild disagreements about who in the court knew how much and when (cf. n. 7). Johnson (ed. 1765): That is, we have already made known in some measure our desire of parting the kingdom; we will now discover what has not been told before, the reasons by which we shall regulate the partition. Hudson (ed. 1871): Lear’s darker purpose probably is his secret plan for surprising his daughters into a rivalry of affection. So Bullough (1973, p. 340 n.), since that is the further mystery in Leir 144 (see ). Wright (ed. 1875): It is not clear that Gloucester knew anything of Lear’s intention to include Cordelia in the distribution of the kingdom. Darker purpose therefore means more secret design, with which Gloucester and Kent were not acquainted, though they were aware of the king’s general intention. Similarly Schmidt (ed. 1879) and Eidam (1880, p. 19; 1898, p. 30), adding that neither nobleman yet knows of Lear’s plan to resign his power, or else they would have mentioned it in their opening remarks. Dove & Gamble (1969, pp. 308, 310–11): No one, least of all Cordelia, had any suspicion that the kingdom was to be divided into three.…If Kent and Gloucester were supposed to know about a three-fold division of the kingdom,…in the forefront of their minds would have been Cordelia’s unequal portion rather than the equal portions of Albany and Cornwall. No reference is made to Cordelia, however. The dowry, known in advance to the suitors, may have been financial rather than territorial, since ceding a third of Britain to France would have been abhorrent to an English audience. Perrett (1904, p. 145 and n.), however: The king’s plan [of tripartite division] is known to his councillors, Kent and Gloucester, and to Cordelia’s suitors (cf. [211, 266]), but not in detail to Cordelia, or to her sisters and their husbands, who may be supposed to have been recently summoned from their ducal residences to Lear’s court; Kent and Glou.…enter together, discussing the intended division. If we choose, we may imagine that they have already commented on Cordelia’s share. (Ibid., p. 179): We may imagine that darker purpose means the same to Lear as to Kent, that is, the trick [to get Cordelia to declare her love—see n. 53–8]; which was therefore no sudden idea, but part of the plan pre-arranged by Lear before the opening of Sc. 1. Muir (ed. 1952): The councillors only know of Lear’s intention to divide the kingdom, and of the shares designed for Goneril and Regan. In Leir (133 ff.) the counsellor Skalliger announces Leir’s plans to marry his daughters and divide his kingdom as dowries, and then falsely confides a further mystery, the plan, recommended by Skalliger (Leir 37–42) but rejected by Leir, to reward the daughter most who professes most love. Since in Lr. the elder daughters are already married, Verity (ed. 1897) rejects reference to that plan here: More secret, i.e. than the question of Cordelia’s betrothal. He has just sent for France and Burgundy, and the object of his summoning them…might be readily surmised by the court; whereas his design of partitioning the kingdom has been communicated only to intimate counsellors like Gloucester and Kent. Weis (ed. 1993): Since Lear’s intentions to divide his kingdom, give away his powers, and arrange Cordelia’s marriage must have been already known, the phrase may indicate that Lear is ignorant of what his subjects do or do not know about his policies. But because of its own ignorance of the facts, the audience could not form such a judgment about Lear at this point. Wells (ed. 2000): Perhaps referring to his previously unannounced plan to add his unmarried daughter, Cordelia, to the married ones as recipients of his bounty. Verity’s explanation is adequate: having just summoned Cordelia’s two suitors for the obvious purpose of awarding her to one of them, Lear now turns to his darker (less obvious) plans for dividing the realm.

41 purposes]
Jackson (1983, p. 334): Lear is announcing his abdication, dealing with Cordelia’s suitors, apportioning the kingdom, and calling for protestations of love. These linked reasons are merged into one in F’s singular purpose. Van Dam (1935, p. 17): The addition or the omission of a final s is the most common of the misprints of the time.

42 The…diuided]
Though Capell (1783, 1.2:141) thinks the line is of four feet, the Q verse is defensible: it lacks two unaccented syllables, but the slight pause for stage action before know may substitute for one of them, and two strong stresses on map there sound suitably peremptory. F’s addition Giue me makes more regular meter, though its added that is often omitted (see textual nn.).

42 map there]
Deighton (ed. 1891): That is lying there. But it might have been borne by a follower (38). Koppel (1899, p. 6 n.): Gloster and Kent may have it with them when they enter discussing the division. Foakes (ed. 1997) prefers Kent, though in many productions an attendant carries it. Wells (ed. 2000): The mid-line pause allows for action (conveying the map). Perrett (1904, p. 144): A similar map…is used for the division discussed in [1H4 3.1.69 (1597)]. Also in the old Richard II [i.e., Woodstock; ed. A. P. Rossiter, 1946, 4.1.220]. Mahood (1992, p. 237): The same property map [as in 1H4] may have been used. Hutchings (2000, p. 82): In Marlowe’s 2 Tamburlaine (5.3.126) the tired ruler, dividing his empire between two sons, refers to a map. Foakes (ed. 1997, pp. 17–18): Shakespeare may well have had in mind contemporary maps such as those of Christopher Saxton [Atlas, 1579], which visibly represented forests, rivers, villages, and towns as if to display the value of the land; he provides an illustration. Gillies (1998, p. 33) finds the same suggestion in the opulent pastoralism of Lear’s reading of his own map. Holland (1997, p. 170): In the RSC production of 1993 the map papered the stage floor and in the last Acts was ripped and shredded.

42–3 know…kingdome]
Perrett (1904, pp. 148–9): The division must have resembled that in Ch. 21 of Holinshed, How Britaine at the first grew to be divided into three portions [see n. 5], where Harrison describes how Brute partitioned the island among his three sons Locrine, Camber, and Albanact: The original story [of Lear] does not expressly locate the daughters’ dowers, but the versions which do so naturally assume that the North [orig. Albanact’s portion] went with Gon., the West [Camber’s portion, Cambria, plus Cornwall] with Reg.; Cordelia was to have received Locrine’s portion, England or Lhoegria, in the south, which Harrison describes as the greatest and best region. Similarly Craig (ed. 1931): The division of Lear’s kingdom seems to be a traditional one; it appears also in 1 Henry IV, iii, i, 70 ff. [1600–7]. And in Gorboduc and Anthony Munday’s Triumphs (1606): see Axton (1977, pp. 136–7) See also n. 7. Berry (1993, p. 74): Cornwall is the western region, together with a portion of the heartland. Gloucester fits easily into the system, for the Earl of Gloucester is the Duke of Cornwall’s vassal [cf. 996].…There is no name for Cordelia’s portion, but it must be the South-East jut of the Island, together with its share of the heartland.…Kent’s regard for Cordelia is more than a purely personal sympathy. She would have been his regional overlord. Dover is the regional port. In Leir, Cambria and Cornwall possess their own kingdoms at the beginning of the play and flee to them when routed by Cordella and the Gallian King at the end (see , ); Lear’s kingdom, which for a while they divide between themselves, apparently comprises the rest of the island. Cf. n. 138.
Tilley K89, like Wittreich (1984, p. 390), detects behind Lear’s words the proverb Every kingdom divided soon falls and compares Matt. 12:25; Dent (1981) is dubious. Munro (ed. 1957): Hence intimating disaster to follow. See also n. 43–6.

43 first]
Warburton (ed. 1747): The first reason of his abdication was the love of his people, that they might be protected by such as were better able to discharge the trust; and his natural affection for his daughters, only the second. Idem (MS notes, 1747–79, Folger Libr.): First is used for principal. Jennens (ed. 1770) objects: He is so far from giving the love of his people as the first reason of his abdication, that he does not so much as hint at that, but his own ease is the reason he gives…and he gives no second reason at all. Jackson (1983, p. 334) thinks that Lear has several purposes in mind; see n. 41. Weis (ed. 1993): Q’s reading strikes a more hierarchical note (first: most important; first in sequence) better suited perhaps to the ceremonial political process. Wells (ed. 2000): Most pressing (OED v. 4d). Though Q makes some sense, most eds. have preferred F’s fast as a durior lectio peculiarly in Shakespeare’s manner (Staunton, ed. 1859). Anon. (MS notes [1754–65] in F2, Copy 21, Folger Libr.): Fixed (OED, a. 1). Cf. Schmidt (1874): Firm, confirmed. Joseph (ed. 1966) and Halio (ed. 1973): Pun on swift. Hunter (ed. 1972): Fast sorts oddly with shake in [44], giving the impression of the abdication as a charade rather than a necessity. Clayton (1983, p. 124): An authorial revision anticipating Lear’s characteristic firmness; cf. Jackson, loc. cit. If so, F’s variant makes no practical difference, since Lear is equally firm in Q without it; but F’s fast is at least as likely to be the original reading in the copy for Q. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 359): The Q compositor may have misread fast as frst and expanded this to first: or the a may actually have appeared to him to be ir. The latter is the more likely: in Hand D of the MS of Sir Thomas Moore (British Libr., Harleian MS 7368), possibly but not necessarily Sh.’s handwriting, are several instances of a indistinguishable from ir. Smidt (1964, p. 153): Because the line has an extra syllable in both texts, The word first or fast may have been meant for deletion and was possibly hard to make out in the manuscript.

43–6 intent…death]
Greg (1940, p. 388): Similarly in Leir 26–8 (see ) the king prepares to resigne these earthly cares, And thinke vpon the welfare of my soule. Empson (1951, p. 126): Which is quite specifically religious; but you might say that Shakespeare deliberately weakened this. Draper (1936, pp. 89, 92): Sh. shows the impossibility of evading the responsibility of rule; Lear’s abdication is foolish and tragically ruinous. Fraser (1962, p. 73): Lear’s abdication is a self-indulgent…charade and comparable to the slackening of fibre of Leir, torn ’Twixt childrens loue, and care of Common weale (Leir 203). In Leir 1–31, however, the king’s motives are also emotional and practical: he is grieving our (too late) deceast and dearest Queen and anxious, for the sake of his daughters, to replace their mothers good aduice and government with that of three princely mates who will be joined to them with equall dowry. Doran (1931, p. 46), anticipating Ribner (1951–2, pp. 64–6), finds a similarity with Sh.’s source for the Gloucester plot, Sidney’s Arcadia: The chief political lesson of the Arcadia, that of the central story of Basilius and his daughters, is that a king who retires from the active office of government will endanger his state. Fripp (1938, p. 659): Lear proceeds to do what is expressly forbidden in the Bible, and was regarded in Shakespeare’s time as the mark of weakness and dereliction of duty, like Carter (1905, p. 432) quoting Ecclus. 33:17–22, and noting that in Gorboduc 1.1 Sackville and Norton paraphrased this text to warn against the king’s similar action there. Ribner (1960, pp. 118–19): Lear’s resignation of his throne and division of his kingdom…were a violation of the king’s responsibility to God, and they could result only in the chaos on every level of creation which is the subject of the play. By his resignation of rule Lear disrupts the harmonious order of nature.…God’s order…decrees that the king rule for the good of his people until God relieves him of his responsibility by death. Shalvi (1967, p. 215): Lear commits an act of betrayal…divesting himself, most sinfully and criminally, of his divine duty. Axton (1977, pp. 31, 139): A king could not legally divide his realm.…[Edmund] Plowden [Reports, 1571] compares a monarch and a subject who have daughters and no son.…A king’s daughters could not receive a divided crown or crown lands: the crowne shall discende only to the eldeste & thother shall have no part of thinritance [sic] thereof.…Politically, Lear commits the original sin. Shakespeare, writing of it in the darkest hours of the Union debate, holds out no hope of forgiveness and no palliative for the inexorable punishment.
Lear’s abdication has its defenders, however. Empson (1951, p. 127): To abdicate for religious reasons, like Charles V., would [not] seriously be considered wicked as a breach of Hierarchy. However, abdication in favour of your children does get called unnatural in Gorboduc,…[and] to divide the kingdom would be considered much worse. Charles abdicated sovereignty of the Netherlands in 1555 and of Spain in 1556, to become a monk. Rosenberg (1972, p. 41): The abdication of Charles V was praised by Montaigne as his worthiest action; see . Howarth (1970, p. 170): It was praised by Spanish and English chroniclers as admirable and heroic. Moreover, Sh. had read the Book of Kings, in which David abdicates in favour of Solomon. Levin (1979, pp. 150–1): In his Defence of the Right of Kings (1616, p. 270) King James raises no objection to the idea that kings may renounce the right of royalty, and of their own accord give over the kingdom. From a hint in Howarth (ibid.), Levin adds, King David abdicated in favor of his son Solomon [1 Kings 1:48]…with the approval and assistance of Nathan the Prophet and Zadok the Priest,…which ushered in the golden age of Israel’s history. In any case, he concludes, the notion of unresignability of kingship…does not figure in the play. Farley-Hills (1990, p. 218): Stage abdications are not uncommon and generally approved (as in Middleton’s Phoenix and Hengist, King of Kent). See also n. 7.
That Lear does not mention his late queen (except at 1409–10) seems highly significant to feminist and psychoanalytic critics. Dundes (1976, p. 360): There is no Queen Lear—leaving the father available as a sexual object for his daughters, particularly Cordelia. Or, her absence displace[s] the nurturing female body (Greenblatt, 1982, p. 105), highlight[s] her psychological presence (Kahn, 1982, p. 37; cf. Erickson, 1985, p. 110), and seems initially to allow for a fantasy of male parthenogenesis but ends by releasing fantasies far more frightening than any merely literal mother could be (Adelman, 1992, p. 104). Earlier critics explain her absence differently. James (1951, p. 101): The play’s violent and outrageous beginning…cuts away from our imaginations any sense of the preceding life of Lear and his family.…The family begins here;…what has been in the past is nothing and nowhere. Gardner (1967, p. 5): We never hear anything in the course of the play of Lear’s wife, the mother of his daughters, of the wooing and marriage of Goneril and Regan, of the relations between Cordelia and her sisters before the play begins.…A Georgian poet, Gordon Bottomley, wrote a play called King Lear’s Wife, in which he portrayed Lear as an intolerable husband and motivated the cruelty of Goneril and Regan by showing them as daughters resenting their father’s treatment of their mother. Any such conception of circumstantial motives for their cruelty is wholly alien to Shakespeare’s conception and presentation. No suggestion is ever hazarded as to why they are as they are. It is enough that they simply are.

44 shake]
OED (v. 13): Trans. To dislodge or get rid of (something, a person’s hold, etc.) by shaking one’s body, limbs, clothes, etc. Const. from, off, quoting this l. Schmidt’s (1875) numerous exx. always have off or from. Possibly the next word in this line, all, might be a misreading of off: in Hand D of Sir Thomas More f occasionally resembles an l, and a/o misreadings are common. Although the resemblance is not so close between ff and ll, the Q compositor may have seen of (see the next n.) and interpreted it as al, spelling it all. A scribe preparing the promptbook from the same MS would have had to repeat the error.

44 of]
Delius (ed. 1854): A variant form of off (OED). Ridley (ed. 1935) and the Oxford eds. (1986 Q, 2000) adopt off. Jackson (1983, p. 333): Which gives a neat opposition with on in the next line.…Of as a spelling of off turns up in several Shakespearean good quartos. However, shake by itself may mean shake off or scatter (OED v. 14, 15; cf. 1816), and Sh.’s usual phrase is shake off from a thing or place; thus of here may mean simply belonging to. F’s from avoids three open vowels in of(f) our Age, and removes the ambiguity in of.

44 state]
F’s Age is generally preferred, and the ambiguous Q reading is seldom commented on. Rook, glossing Ridley’s (ed. 1935) text in Wolfit (ed. 1956): Majesty. Jackson (1983, p. 333): Not just Lear’s kingdom, rule, and status, but his physical condition, i.e., as an old man (Weis, ed. 1993). In its 12 occurrences in Q and F the word usually has a political reference, but at 1429 it refers to Lear’s health and at 1246, 1634, and 2914 it has other and ambiguous meanings. Since Q’s state can hardly be a misreading of Age, F’s Age must be a deliberate change, perhaps to remove obscurity or ambiguity and to make a more obvious connection with yonger in the next line, as Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 23) suggests. Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960, p. 133): A memorial anticipation by Q’s reporters of state at 55; but that line is not in Q, and may be a later addition in F. Jackson (op. cit., p. 334): Reminiscent of the seventh Age of Man described in AYL 2.7.163–6 (1142–5), making explicit what in Q was conveyed in the antitheses between yonger yeares and one sense of our state.

45 Confirming]
Except to Clayton (1983, p. 124), Jackson (1983, pp. 333–4), Weis (ed. 1993), and Wells (ed. 2000), confirming cares and business on the young makes strained sense at best, and F’s Conferring is almost universally preferred. Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960, p. 133), improbably: a memorial anticipation by the Q reporters of confirme (146), a hundred lines later. The idiom confirm on appears nowhere else in Sh. nor in exx. of confirm listed in OED, though confirm to, ratify a bestowal (OED, v. 2c) appears in 3H6 1.1.172 (193). Rather than confirming confirm, the recurrence of the same Q/F variant at 88 may mean only that conferring was ill written in both places. Deighton (ed. 1891) justifies F: To confer on or upon is generally used in regard to that which is an honour, privilege…and perhaps this is the sense here, the cares and business being of a kingly character. Taylor (1985, p. 179): F slightly alters the emphasis, from the legal and ceremonial confirmation of decisions already made…to the King’s act of donation. Foakes (ed. 1997): The words could be confused in secretary hand.

45 yonger yeares]
Both Q and F (yonger strengths) mean in effect the same. Crook (ed. 1907): Younger, and therefore stronger men. Strengths is an example of metonymy. Yeares is equally so, and the gloss applies to either reading. Since Q’s yeares can hardly be a misreading for F’s strengths, F deliberately substitutes a less predictable word, pointing a contrast with the physical weakness implied by F’s crawle. Kirschbaum (1945, p. 14): Q’s word is hackneyed, F’s precise. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 22) finds F’s phrase more Shakespearian and likes the obvious connection between strengths and Vnburthen’d, neither word found in Q. Smidt (1964, p. 153): Yonger yeares is more economical in that it implies the advanced age of Lear while allowing the quite appropriate word state to be used in the preceding line. Jackson (1983, p. 334): F makes the latent content of [Q’s] Confirming explicit by altering the semi-redundant yeares to strengths, this change prompting the change of while we Vnburthen’d crawle toward death, which elaborates the personal motive to the point where Lear presents his abdication as almost a renunciation of the world. Taylor (1985, p. 179): F implies…superior ability to govern. The F reading also avoids the jingle of repeated y’s and r’s. It has been almost always preferred and adopted.

45–50 while…now]
These F lines, whose presence creates a seven-foot verse line (50), are probably a later addition designed to make the exposition clearer, though Delius (1876, pp. 134–5) thinks them too essential to have been omitted from Q except by accident, as does Kermode (1994, p. 101), and Koppel (1877, p. 75) considers them one of only two passages omitted from Q. Thomas (1984, p. 507) cites as evidence the short line 45 and the misleading false apposition of yonger yeares with France and Burgundy. Stone (1980, pp. 66–7): [Line 50] is composed of the last half-line of the addition combined with an abbreviated version of what stands in Q as a complete line. This pattern strongly suggests interpolation.…The passage cannot have been accidentally omitted [from Q]…since the accident must have been accompanied by the deliberate expansion of the half-line…to exactly the length of a pentameter.…Whoever made [a supposed deliberate cut] must have given careful attention to expanding this half-line, while beginning the cut casually in mid-sentence, leaving a metrical gap.…Aside from the metrical deficiency [i.e., a short line 45], no manner of hiatus is noticeable in Q: the lines supplied in F are not essential. The F lines do audibly identify two major characters who in Q are not so identified until 135. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 224): The Folio’s stressed identification of Albany and Cornwall, France and Burgundy [90], seems deliberate and is certainly valuable. Moreover, the F lines provide a more explicit motive for Lear’s actions. So Taylor (1983, pp. 381–2): In Q, as in Shakespeare’s sources for the Lear story, Lear’s abdication is either an unexplained misjudgement or a given…; in F…abdication is…explicable and precedented. This overstates the case, however; in fact, in most of Sh.’s possible sources for the Lear story there is no abdication at all: in Holinshed, Higgins, and Warner, as in Geoffrey (see , , , ), the elder daughters seize power by rebellion, and only in Spenser (2.10.30.3) and Leir (552) does he resign his regiment (see , ). In all sources the king, conscious of his advancing years and lack of male issue, makes explicit his intent to provide for succession by marrying his daughters to princes who can rule his lands after his death or resignation. In Warner (see ) and Leir (31, 143, 319, 440, 2255; see , , , , ) his gift of land is specifically called a dowry; in Leir he is weary of The world and earthly cares (26–7; cf. 447) and knows that pale grym death doth wayt vpon my steps (228; see , , ). In Q Lr. the king’s motives are similar but are clarified only in a later speech (131 ff.). He is evidently feeling his yeares (45) and wants rest and nurcery (131–2), and hence wishes to resign or shake the cares and busines of our state (44); he also wishes to complete the marriages of his daughters by arranging a husband for Cordelia (50–53), and intends his gift of land to each as a dower (136). The lines added here to F repeat explicitly his wish to be Vnburthen’d of his cares and make an earlier announcement that he intends the gifts of land as Dowers. They also add the new motive that future strife may be preuented; only in Leir (47–8, 55, 68; see ) among Sh.’s possible sources is anxiety expressed about doubtful succession (47), future peace (48), and marriage alliances against forrayne hate (55). In Q the king’s wishes are mainly personal and familial; in F they are political as well. Clayton (1983, p. 125) finds the addition an improvement: The Folio version lays a strong foundation for the development of sympathy and admiration by providing Lear with a creditable, rational, and regal motive for his division of the kingdom. Halio (ed. 1992): In any event, Lear’s good intention does not succeed, citing the unsubstantiated rumors of division at 934–9 and 1628–30. Exaggerating Q/F differences, Massai (2000, p. 440) even asserts that in Q, Lear wishes to retain his power and expresses no wish to abdicate; but of course his declaration of intent to bestow all his territories and all…business of our state on younger men can only mean abdication. He repeats that intention again in both texts at 144–5, giving away sway, reuenue, execution and keeping in retirement only the honorific titles (additions; see n. 144) of royalty.

46 Vnburthen’d]
Roberts (1978, pp. 384–90): The play’s unusually large number of un- prefix words, especially in this scene and in 3.4, are a language of inversion,] that reflects Lear’s upheaval, from his unkinging in 1.1 to his unsettled wits and identification with unaccommodated man in 3.4. Thomson (1993, p. 82): Certainly the negating construction is in keeping with the overall impression of a chaotic world; but it also, like a double negative, reminds us of duality, conveying an idea and its opposite, thereby giving us greater ability than the characters to see the truth about them and their world.

46 crawle]
OED (v.1 3a): To move or progress very slowly, quoting this l. as its first ex. Deighton (ed. 1891): Drag out our few remaining days. Kittredge (ed. 1940): That Lear’s old age is not feeble (however he may express himself) is clear from the whole of Act i. He still goes a-hunting. Gardner (ed. 1969): The ring of ageing self-pity is real enough.

46 Our son of Cornwal]
Elsewhere Sh. uses this form of nomenclature only in R3 2.4.6 (1493) and 4.1.14 (2489) and 2H4 4.4.12 (2383). Rosenberg (1972, p. 48): Cornwall, old enough to see himself a father to Edmund [cf. 1994–5], might be an older husband to Regan, thus explaining her early exchange of oeillades with Edmund and Lear’s care in the first scene always to address Cornwall first, though (Kent thought) he more affected Albany.

46–7 son…Sonne]
Lott (ed. 1974): I.e. son-in-law (OED, sb. 1c). Cf. 146, 1290, 1320. Halio (ed. 1992): In the sources, none of the daughters has a husband until after the love contest; cf. Perrett (1904, p. 175) and n. 45–50.

47 Albany]
Abbott (§469): Polysyllabic names often receive but one accent at the end of the line. Cf. 82, 192, 213, 260, 268, 272, 956, 1643, 2907, 2961, 3203. Rosenberg (1972, pp. 47–8) argues that Albany, whom Edgar may regard as a young contemporary [cf. 3300], may be much more youthful than Cornwall (cf. n. 46): A very young Albany, married to the dominating Goneril, would fit the design of a naive character slow to comprehend evil and intrigue, at first hesitant to counteraction and never fully committed.

48 this houre]
Delius (ed. 1854): Modifies publish—publish now, to avoid future strife (Ger.). Deighton (ed. 1891): Without delaying the matter.

48 constant]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Seems a confirmation of fast intent [43]. Steevens (ed. 1778): Firm, determined (OED, a. 1). Hunter (ed. 1869) compares constant pleasure (2850). Hoeniger (ed. 1968): From the Latin certa voluntas.

49 seuerall]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Separate, and so particular (OED, a. 2, 8). Brooke (ed. 1947): Respective.

49 Dowers]
The usual legal meaning of dower was the husband’s gift of land to be made available to his widow, but it was sometimes used as here for dowry, the property given on marriage to the husband by a wife’s friends or family (the Sokols, 2000, p. 100). Sh. so uses it at 115, 136, 208, 223, 281 1505; Dowrie occurs at 264. Wilson (ed. 1960): Gon. and Reg. have been married only recently. In the sources they are not yet married: see n. 45–50. In F.Q. 2.10.27.5–6 and Leir 31 the king intends the dowers to be equall (see n. 41); here and in 85–8 Lear’s intent is less clear (Bullough, 1973, p. 338 n.). Skottowe (1824, p. 99): Holinshed, also, makes the disposal of the kingdom entirely a matter of uncertainty till the king had heard the answers of his daughters; but there the king’s intent is to choose a successor, not divide the kingdom: see .

50 May…Burgundy]
Jackson (1983, pp. 335–6): A consequence of the late insertion of TLN 4[5]–50 is the overloading, with fourteen syllables, of F’s line [50].…We have what appears to be an extrametrical afterthought. Though citing Abbott (see n. 47), Jackson notes that none of the thirty lines that he cites is as long as this line in F, and there is no other fourteen-syllable line in Lear. A half-hearted attempt at patching may be seen in F’s omission of Q’s two great, but the result seems still so oddly careless or inept that Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 22–3) is confident that Sh. could not have made the revision.

50 preuented]
Delius (ed. 1854): More than hinder; it means anticipate, forestall (Ger.) (OED, v. 1, 5). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Prevent in Shakespeare never loses the force of pre-, comparing 1938, 2158.

50 France and Burgundy]
On the anachronism see DP n. 3–4. Clarkes (1879, p. 755): Shakespeare occasionally uses the names of their countries as titles for sovereigns, giving exx. Jonson, Masque of Blackness 206–7, refers to the rite of stiling princes, after the names of their princedoms. Cf. Denmark and Norway in Ham., Egypt in Ant., Sicilia in WT, etc. In Leir 63 (see ) Cordella’s suitors are diuers Peeres.

50 Burgundy]
On the pronunciation see n. 39.

51 Great]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Of lofty rank [OED, a. 12]; not great, fierce [OED, a. 4], in their rivalry. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 23) finds the repetition of the word from 50 very clumsy and suspect. Perhaps, however, there is intentional play on powerful or eminent in 50, and either noble or fierce in 51.

52 amorous]
Deighton (ed. 1891): In order to win her love.

52 soiourne]
Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): In none of the Lear stories preceding Shakespeare’s is the King of France at court wooing Cordelia at the time of the love-test. Halio (ed. 1992): [The] rivalry for Cordelia’s hand is Shakespeare’s invention.

53 here]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Here and now.

53–8 tell…it]
Bradley (1904, pp. 249–50): The very first words of the drama, as Coleridge pointed out [see n. 3–10], tell us that the division of the kingdom is already settled in all its details, so that only the public announcement of it remains. Later we find that the lines of division have already been drawn on the map of Britain [see 42, 68], and again that Cordelia’s share, which is her dowry, is perfectly well known to Burgundy, if not to France [see 211, 266]. That then which is censured as absurd, the dependence of the division on the speeches of the daughters, was in Lear’s intention a mere form, devised as a childish scheme to gratify his love of absolute power and his hunger for assurance of devotion. And this scheme is perfectly in character. Herford (ed. 1899): Three distinct versions were current among the Elizabethans. According to the first (that of Geoffrey of Monmouth [see ] and the Mirror for Magistrates), Lear questions his daughters to ascertain which deserves the largest of the three prospective shares, thinking to guerdon most where favour most he found [Mirour, ed. 1587, fol. 34; see ]. According to the second (Spenser’s), three equal shares have already been arranged, and the questions aim merely at a formal test of the competency of the heirs to inherit them [see ]. In the third version (Holinshed’s), the questions are a mere disguise for the king’s partiality to Cordelia: he designs to bequeath the kingdom entire, and preferre hir whome he best loued, to the succession. Holinshed says as well that Leir wants to vnderstand the affections of his daughters towards him; see . Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): The Lear of Holinshed loved Cordeilla the youngest farre aboue the two elder [see ], and Shakespeare has made this special fondness, which does not appear in the other stories, underlie and explain the whole situation. His Lear has prearranged his largest bounty for her, because he loved her best and counted on having her love show up as the best.…Her father, in the Chronicle History [i.e., Leir], shows no preference. The proposition to make them eche a Ioynter more or lesse, As is their worth, to them that loue professe [37–38; see ] arises from Skalliger, a courtier, and the king does not agree. He says [39–41] his zeale is fixt to be vnpartiall and to give No more, nor lesse, but euen all alike. He adopts Skalliger’s suggestion, finally [78 ff.], as a stratagem, planning that when they ioyntly shall contend, Eche to exceed the other in their loue, he will then take Cordella, Euen as she doth protest she loues him the best, at the vantage, to make her grant him one request, To shew thou louest me as thy sisters doe, Accept a husband [i.e. a King of Brittany, to wit the rich King of Hibernia; 138–9, see ] whom my selfe will woo. Indeed part of Leir’s motive is To try which of daughters loues me best: Which till I know, I cannot be in rest; he does not assume, as Lear does, that it will prove to be Cordelia. It is Skalliger, not Leir, who says that whose answere pleaseth him the best, They shall haue most (154–5). In Geoffrey, Leir conducts a genuine trial to find out which daughter is deserving of the largest portion, ut sciat quae illarum maiore regni parte dignior esset (see above); in Higgins’s Mirour, where Cordila is not Leire’s favorite, and He thought to giue, where fauoure most he fande, he is not so clearly conducting a contest as seeking reassurance—all doubtes of duty to abande (see )—that his daughters love him and so deserve their portions at all; in Spenser (F.Q. 2.10.27–8) Leyr originally intends equal portions but then asks without clear motivation to hear which daughter loves him most (see ); in Warner no motive at all is given (see ).
Although in Sh. Lear has already decided which daughter loves him best and is to receive the largest portion, critics still think of the daughters’ public professions of love as a trial or contest. Consequently either Lear or Sh. (or both) is censured, or else elaborately defended. Ulrici (1839; tr. 1876, 1:443) offers a defense: The whole demand was but a freak of the imagination, which Lear did not mean to take into serious consideration.…The concealed motive of this freak, and its execution, was probably Lear’s wish,—by an open and public assurance of his daughters’ love and piety,—to convince himself that his abdication could be of no danger to himself, and that doubts about its propriety were unfounded. Idem (1867, p. 295): In Ludwig Devrient’s portrayal, Lear indulges this sudden impulse only to pass the time until France and Burgundy enter, and speaks of largest bountie with an ironical smile to imply its opposite and express his certainty that his daughters loved and respected him equally. Bucknill (1859, pp. 138–9; 1867, pp. 174–5), on the other hand: That the trial is a mere trick is unquestionable.…Does it not lead us to conclude that from the first the king’s mind is off its balance; that the partition of his kingdom, involving inevitable feuds and wars, is the first act of his developing insanity; and that the manner of its partition, the mock-trial of his daughters’ affections, and its tragical denouement, is the second, and but the second act of his madness? Similarly Kreyssig (1874, 2:113): Lear’s first words are those of a man who is not quite right in the head. Danby (1948, p. 175): Age has decayed Lear’s already infirm judgment and made him more liable to attacks of choler. Hoeniger (1992, p. 330): A typical medical diagnosis of Lear’s illness in Shakespeare’s time would identify it as acute hypochondriac melancholy developing into mania. Moreover, the example of Nebuchadnezzar (Dan. 2–4), whom Lear broadly resembles (citing Wittreich, 1984, p. 102) showed that uncontrolled passion [is] a sin leading to punishment in the form of madness (pp. 313–14). Perrett (1904, pp. 157–8): To believe with subtle denseness that Lear was insane from the beginning is to take all human interest from the play. Foakes (ed. 1997, pp. 59–60): One effect of his interaction with the Fool is to confirm that he is in his right mind. As long as Lear can participate in cross-talk with the Fool, he thinks he is sane, and so, I believe, does the audience. Perrett (p. 177), having said that the idea of the love-test as stratagem derives from Leir [77–87; see ]: In Sh., it is a trick to disguise Lear’s preference for Cordelia…, whom he confidently expects to show herself worthy of that largest bounty.…Yet the true inward motive…is to draw from the quiet, reserved, undemonstrative girl…the gratification of a warm and unrestricted expression in words of a love no less than his own. Archer (in Lee, ed. 1908, pp. xxiii–xxv): The necessity for dramatic compression would, of course, lead him [Sh.] to prefer the version which made King Lear’s transference of power immediate and complete; and the putting up of the kingdom to a sort of auction in which the princesses should outbid one another in effusiveness, was a touch of senility…that admirably accorded with his general design. But, having made King Lear conceive this plan, why should the poet at once proceed to show that the portions are predetermined, and the boasting-match an empty form…by openly assigning their portions to Goneril and Regan before Cordelia has spoken?…On the whole, I cannot but think that we have here one of those pieces of inexplicable incuriousness, not to say slovenliness, that we so often encounter in Shakespeare.…The truth is, no doubt, that Shakespeare felt it impossible to dissemble the fairy-tale element in the groundwork of his play…and thought it best to face the improbabilities and have done with them, as rapidly as possible. Frost (1958, pp. 577, 582–3): The ritual nature of the scene serves to free both actor and playwright from the demands of strict verisimilitude, suits the folkloristic nature of the story, and produces the effect of nightmarish inevitability. Elliott (1959, pp. 255–7): Lear tries to make the unusual division of the kingdom seem publicly justified by an elaborate ceremony. Jorgensen (1967, pp. 69–70, 95): It is ritualistic unreasonableness, including ceremonial denunciation, but has a motive: Lear is seeking some reassurance of identity, in what most old people need: love—the deepest and most certain evidence that they are wanted and needed. Dawson (1978, p. 138): Sh. did not intend a realism: It is a thoroughly emblematic scene of ritual and spectacle. Freeman (1993, p. 6), noting many financial metaphors in the scene, ascribes its curiously ritualistic character to its informing ceremony, the hearing, or audit, of state accounts. Bransom (1934, p. 15): The proposal was as sudden to Lear as it was to everybody else.…The motive had been at work in the unconscious part of his mind, and was simply a desire to have his self-love flattered. Whitaker (1941, p. 382): Sh. has asked us to accept Lear’s whim at its face value and has relied upon the character of the participants to motivate what follows. He makes the actions of the three sisters convincing, but he deprives us of the sympathy for Lear as a man and the respect for his position as a king and father that the subsequent action of the play demands. Stauffer (1949, p. 194): It is a kind of public game Lear has thought up to flatter himself.…The rules are that each tall compliment must exceed the last, and…Lear saves his joy Cordelia for the final sweet of the banquet. He does not disown Cordelia because he thinks she does not love him. He knows that she does. But she has humiliated him in public, and his feelings are deeply hurt. [He gets] even with her by humiliating her before her suitors. Bhattacharya (1981, pp. 14–16): The public justification of his decision is a stratagem to beguile the two elder daughters, since What the daughters may have to say is not material at all and will not change their pre-determined shares. Indeed, while they speak their end-stopt lines, stilted and stereotyped hyperboles, He should be enjoying the joke, but he should be contemptuously inattentive to this mockery of true ceremony. Downes (1988, pp. 246–7): The ambiguity of Lear’s illocutionary speech-act, which is both question and command, generates a network of paradox or inconsistencies. He exercises his power in renouncing it; his renunciation of kingly identity generates Lear’s passage through madness, or loss of self; and his identification of love with obedience entails both the hypocritical obedience of Goneril and Regan and the alienating (though loving) disobedience of Cordelia.
Since the performance that Lear requires of his daughters as part of the public formalities of his resignation is not a trial or contest, it need not be seen as a whimsical, selfish, or empty exercise designed to reassure him, or as a trick to disguise his partiality, but rather as a public demonstration of the rightness of his decisions: that is, he can expect Cordelia’s warmest professions of love to justify his decision to reward her the most generously. Her failure embarrasses him in seeming to be a public refutation of his judgment, hence the violence of his response. So Neilson & Hill (ed. 1942): He has envisaged the proclamation as an official act, duly witnessed, and as an opportunity for a public display of gratitude pleasing to his pride. It is apparent, too, that the portion reserved for Cordelia, his favorite daughter, is richer…than the territories allotted to her sisters…and that Lear’s preference for Cordelia, injudiciously stressed, has dictated this largest bounty and his expectations of a surpassing avowal of affection from her. When, therefore, Cordelia fails him, he is taken completely by surprise. His pride, both regal and paternal, is sharply wounded, he feels defied and publicly humiliated, and he breaks into a paroxysm of anger. Olson (1961, p. 201): If Lear is giving up his authority and still wants security and dignity, he can only trust to their love; and his insistence upon their public profession of it is an attempt to have it warranted and witnessed as a formal part of the compact of the delivery of property and power. Kinney (1976, p. 684): Cordelia refuses to honor ceremony and occasion. In doing so, she endangers the script which Lear has so carefully orchestrated and so undermines—by accident or design—the pacts just made between the king and his successors. Farley-Hills (1990, p. 192): The question was eminently sensible, but not the reaction to the answers. [King] James would almost certainly have approved the request, not only because it seems to echo Christ’s request [Luke 7:42]…but because James himself was obsessed with the need for declarations of love.…It is not only a mark of Lear’s affectionate nature that he should think love so important, but psychologically it is exactly what we would expect of an old man, until now all-powerful, giving himself into the power of his daughters. Who would not want reassurance at such a moment? Berry (1993, pp. 68–9): The public affirmation of love is an exercise that no power in the world disregards.…Asking for a token of love, clearly, is neither unreasonable nor wrong.…It is the form of Lear’s question that irritates…by its pretence that extent and quality of reward can be made immediately commensurate with the love-protestation.

54–5 (Since…State)]
F’s added lines, like 49–50, may be an attempt to reiterate and clarify Lear’s motives, though, as there, Delius (1876, p. 134) considers them too indispensable to have been omitted from Q except accidentally; Doran (1931, p. 60) admits the possibility. Jackson (1983, p. 336): F’s parenthetical spelling-out of the full political import of his abdication…further amplifies Q’s excessively condensed [44]. Hart (1942, pp. 146–7), however, considers them merely redundant for intelligent auditors and their absence from Q1 an improvement, and Richman (1986, p. 377) prefers in stage practice Q’s simpler and sparer sequence, in which Lear does not interrupt the question to his daughters. Smidt (1964, p. 153): F gives two somewhat contradictory motives, conferring power and publishing dowers; the Q omissions are the result of authorial revision in Q, not failure of memory and memorial anticipation, as Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 22–5) argues.

54 will]
Abbott (§319): Purpose. Crook (ed. 1907): The determinative future (OED, v.1 10). Cf. Franz §617.

54 diuest]
OED, 2: Fig. To strip (a person or thing) of possessions, rights, or attributes; 2b: Refl. To divest oneself of: to strip or dispossess oneself of; to put off, throw off, lay aside, abandon, rid oneself of, quoting this l. as its first ex. Though use of divest or devest as a legal term referring specifically to property or rights dates from the mid-16th c., Heilman (1948, p. 71), like many others, insists that the word here, as elsewhere in Sh., is part of a pattern of clothing imagery: This undressing for easy sleep is also a removal of armor against the arrows of fortune, and point[s] toward the clothes-tearing scene [1888–9] as a climax.

54 both]
Schmidt (1874), OED (adv. 1b), and Franz §589 give exx. of both used with more than two nouns.

54 Rule]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Duties of rule.

55 Interest of]
Glosses include the mental—thought of (Moberly, ed. 1876), interest in (Meiklejohn, ed. 1879; OED, sb. 7); the practical—management of (Crook, ed. 1907); and the economic—profit derived from (Lee, ed. 1908; OED, 10b); but the most common interpretation is legal—possession, property (Schmidt, 1874); title to, claim to (Goggin, ed. 1910; OED, 1a). Cf. 2H6 3.1.84 (1380), all your Interest in those Territories, and n. 91.

56 shall we say]
The verb governed by Which. Only Blake (2002, p. 315) makes the phrase an emphatic discourse marker meaning really.

57 largest]
Joseph (ed. 1966): Both biggest and most generous (OED, a. 1). Skottowe (1824, p. 100): In Leir the portions are equal (see nn. 41, 49) and are disposed of by lot (Leir 550; see ).

57 extend]
Joseph (ed. 1966): (i) Widen, make larger; (ii) proffer (OED, v. 6, 9).

58 Where…Gonorill]
Though the Q line makes perfect sense and, if the two first words are accented, passable meter, the hypermetrical F line (with the resultant short line 59) has been preferred (see textual n.). Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 24–5) confidently declares the Q line to be non-Shn., and the F line to be authorial in part because its added word Nature is a key word in this play. Seymour’s conjecture, adopted by Halio (ed. 1973; see textual n.), is attractive because it gives perfect sense and metrical regularity to both lines, but how Q could be a misreading of it is unclear. Halio (ed. 1992): F’s revision of Q is incomplete or incompletely transcribed. Probably Gonerill was erroneously or unnecessarily placed at the end of the previous line, producing a hypermetric line followed by a short one; Doran (1931, p. 61) favors that lineation.

58 merit…challenge it]
Schmidt (1875), challenge: Claim as due (OED, v. 5, 6); cf. 2782. In Q, it refers to bountie; by omitting it F’s Nature doth with merit challenge requires the verb to be absolute, the only instance recorded by the OED (5e), or else to mean contest (OED, 7). If challenge means (absolutely) claim, F’s Nature is generally taken to mean Natural filial affection (Steevens, ed. 1778) or paternal affection (Muir, ed. 1952)—see n. 441—and with merit is understood to mean joined with merit—either other merits (Steevens, ed. 1778), or personal excellence (Hudson, ed. 1871), or filial affection (Muir, ed. 1952). Thus two kinds of virtue (nature and merit) make a stronger claim for reward than either one. Tovey (ed. 1896): All the three sisters had a claim [by Nature] as Lear’s daughters. That daughter would deserve the most who loved him best [i.e. by merit of her affection]. Verity (ed. 1897): Where natural affection together with general merit makes the strongest claim to it. Wilson (ed. 1960): Lear implies that the most fulsome declaration of natural affection will be the most meritorious, and so most deserving of reward. Or rather, will demonstrate the degree of desert and so justify his apportionment, which is already decided; see n. 53–8. Crook (ed. 1907), somewhat differently: Where natural gifts and high merit each claim. Alternatively, Nature may be the only noun, if with merit is understood as an adverbial phrase meaning deservedly, an idea suggested by Furnivall (1874, p. 237), supported with many examples by Crosby (1879), and adopted by Hudson (ed. 1879) and others. Taking challenge to mean contest, Becket (1787, p. 36): Where nature and merit are contending for superiority. Similarly Hunter (ed. 1869): Where natural and actual affections vie with each other. Hudson (ed. 1871): Where filial love vies with individual worth, which has the higher claim to reward. Deighton (ed. 1891): Where natural instinct and merit vie with each other in claiming. Edwards (ed. 1975): Whose natural affection is as great as (challenges) her personal desert.

59 our…first]
Brown (ed. 1976): The half-line implies a hushed pause before Goneril replies. See n. 60.

59 eldest]
Rosenberg (1972, pp. 46–7), citing yong bones (1445; cf. brow of youth, 798), the fact that in the Renaissance marriage by women of all classes generally took place no later than the early twenties, and children were expected promptly, and the probability that to make any sense of the Edmund intrigue, Goneril and Regan must still be young enough for a passion that is taken for granted, argues that the three daughters (and Gloucester’s two sons) are all relatively young: A kind of vague early maturity in the children satisfies the conventional concept; but a character pattern coloring the children toward the younger—even very young—end of the spectrum could offer powerful support to the pervasive thematic contrasts of age versus youth, parent versus child, order versus revolt.

60–6, 74–81 Sir…you, Sir…loue]
Perrett (1904, p. 180–1): To Gon. and Reg. his open declaration that the kingdom has been divided [42–3], together with the coronet [37, F], plainly shows that they can hope to win no greater share directly by flattery.…Then why do Gon. and Reg. flatter? The two duchesses, who already wear coronets in their own right, know that this other coronet can only be intended for Cordelia, the last and least. They know then that this function…is planned for the glorification of their young sister. Therefore they flatter.…They frame their answers in such a way that it becomes impossible for Cordelia to say anything.…Everywhere [in previous versions of the story] before [Leir] they give flattery pure and simple, with the intention…of winning the best share. In [Leir 97–197; see ] a new motive occurs, the jealous sisters flatter in order their sister’s wreck to wage. In Sh. their motive for flattery is the same. Possibly; but though their jealousy is reiterated explicitly in Leir, it is not mentioned in Lr. Goneril and Regan act as if they believed they were in a contest with each other as well as with Cordelia, though perhaps they are with simple cynicism complying with what they perceive to be yet another of Lear’s whims (cf. 320–4). Harbage (ed. 1958, p. 22) and Mack (1965, pp. 57–8) find the situation reminiscent of the morality play, where the psychomachia of the central character is externalized by vices and flatterers on one side, virtues and truth-speakers on the other. Kinney (1976, pp. 681–2), more kindly: He will award his inheritance…to those daughters who demonstrate the capacity to rule through their capacity for the ritual of rule: their obedience to ceremony figures their respect for the royal prerogative as well as the family order.
