Brown (ed. 1976): Goneril and Regan can both speak as if their speeches have been prepared beforehand: parallel phrases, catalogues, steady yet varying rhythms, and the neatness with which both finish with love…all aid this impression. Hammond (1991, p. 101): Goneril and Regan adopt [Lear’s] rhetoric, forcing it to quote commonplaces about love so as to mask their own lack of true filial feeling, and to evade dispute.

60–6 Sir…you]
Malone (ed. 1790): From Holinshed; see . Greg (1940, p. 389): In Leir 256–7 (see ) Ragan contrasts her simple vtterance with the true intention of my heart. Goneril’s use of the familiar rhetorical trope of the inadequacy of language is paradoxical. While In Cordelia’s case, the declaration of the inadequacy of language happens to express a true state of feeling (Barton, 1971, p. 24), Dry (1973, pp. 13–14): It is the poor breath alone that serves to make Goneril rich; and Latham (1977, p. 164): The structure of the speech is highly rhetorical; six of its seven lines make a comparison.…Moreover, the whole passage displays the vice of periergia, a superfluity of words.

60 Sir]
The first line of Goneril’s speech, like that of Regan’s (74), begins with Sir and is hypermetrical. It has been variously adjusted: see textual nn. and , . Hypermetric Sir in Q is also dropped from F at 74, 221, and 1527, but is retained in seemingly analogous cases at 715, 1180, 1217, and 2989; hypermetric Come sir is dropped from F at 731 and 746. See n. 731. Speeches beginning with a hypermetrical Sir appear elsewhere in F: see, e.g., Shr. 4.4.1 (2181), JC 3.2.262 (1803), Oth. 1.1.120 (133), Ant. 2.2.74 (766), 2.6.75 (1271).
Moberly (ed. 1876): Here Sir possibly represents the time taken on the stage for a deep reverence, and might be lined separately. Bransom (1934, p. 17): A line to itself. There would then follow a long pause, which is needed for her to recover from the shock of surprise and to find words to answer so strange a demand. Without Sir Q’s line makes sufficiently regular meter, the first stress falling naturally on loue, as is required by F’s omission of do. Hogan (1962, p. 73): We can treat Sir as extrametrical—spoken while Goneril is moving forward to address her father—and print it as a separate line. Foakes (ed. 1997): It is possible that she kneels, and Regan after her; this would add visual point to…[1435 and 2810–12], especially if Cordelia…remains standing at [93], citing Bratton (ed. 1987, p. 65).

60 loue]
Hawkes (1959, pp. 180–1): Goneril and Regan (at 76) pun on love = appraise (OED, v.2 2), a sense Cordelia rejects (at 67). Hogan (1962, pp. 72–3): F’s omission of do may be one of many devices the F compositor uses here to make the long line fit his measure.

60 words]
F’s word means the same; Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 122) calls it a singular used collectively, citing OED (sb. 4; 3 is more apposite). Hogan (1962, p. 72): The supporting example from Jonson’s Poetaster, adduced by OED and Duthie, is worthless, since Jonson’s line reads words, not word. Delius (ed. 1854) compares more in word, then matter (1736), a line in a passage often thought to be spurious, as Furness (ed. 1880) notes. Though Furness finds the singular more truly Shakespearian, Muir (ed. 1952) points out the plural in the counterpart line in Leir—Which cannot be in windy words rehearst (239; see )—and like Walker (1953, p. 63), Evans (1961, p. 325) suggests that the compositor may have shortened the word: The F1 line is very crowded. So also Hogan: F was evidently struggling with his measure.

60 weild]
Rann (ed. 1794): Express (OED, v. 4d). Deighton (ed. 1891): Handle. Though in wield there is no inherent idea of weight…yet…matter here seems to mean not merely subject, but weighty subject. Doran (1931, p. 97): A common spelling…from the fourteenth to the eighteenth centuries, citing OED.

60 matter]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Either the substance, the great burden of her love, or simply the subject (OED, sb. 10). Foakes (ed. 1997): The relation between words, matter or meaning, and deeds comes under recurrent scrutiny, citing 76, 198, 258–60, 398, 1736, 2543–51.

61 Dearer]
Schmidt (ed. 1879): More dearly. Latham (1977, p. 165): The first of several words here reflecting Goneril’s mercenary nature.

61 eye-sight…libertie]
Page (ed. 1889): The whole expression is hyperbolical and confused. Schmidt (ed. 1879): Space is space in general, the realm of external appearances, the world; eyesight is the capacity to comprehend it; liberty the freedom to enjoy it (Ger.). Crook (ed. 1907): The power to see, a wide field of vision, and freedom to behold. Roti (1974): Goneril is envisioning her portion of the kingdom and freedom from her father’s authority. Eye-sight is usually taken to mean power of sight, and the comparison is proverbial (Dent, 1981, E249.1). Jones (1977, p. 12) compares Erasmus’s comment in his Adagia, Nam oculo nihil carius. Spilsbury & Marshall (ed. 1905), however, take the word to indicate extent: As far as the eye can see. Space, the vaguest of the three terms, is the most widely defined: the limits within which motion is possible (Wright, ed. 1875); the possession of space in which to move (Moberly, ed. 1876); ample range of movement, as opposed to confinement within limits (Tovey, ed. 1896); absolute, complete freedom (Craig, ed. 1901); unbounded space, including the whole world (Spilsbury & Marshall, ed. 1905); the external world (Brooke, ed. 1947); scope (for the exercise of liberty) (Harbage, ed. 1958); time, i.e. long life (Weis, ed. 1993). Some eds. distinguish carefully between the two latter terms, others combine them: Campbell (ed. 1964): Space means freedom from imprisonment; liberty means freedom of action; McCann (ed. 1964): Space: freedom to move about at will; liberty: personal freedom, freedom to think and speak as one would desire; Lee (ed. 1908): Fullest range of liberty. Wells (ed. 2000): Also domain or property (OED sb1 7c). Muir (ed. 1952): It may mean merely spacious liberty; Wilson (ed. 1960): Hendiadys. Horsman (ed. 1973): The form of the statement and F punctuation…seem to require three terms, precluding a hendiadys.

61 eye-sight]
Heilman (1948, pp. 58, 25): The words…introduce the sight pattern in the play; References, whether literal or figurative, to the act of seeing, to things seen (sights), to the conditions of seeing (darkness and light), and to the means of seeing (eyes) persist throughout the play. This sight pattern relentlessly brings into the play the problem of seeing, and what is implied is that the problem is one of insight, of the values which determine how one sees. Foakes (ed. 1997): Cf. 2064.

62 valued…rare]
Most eds. adopt F’s comma after valued, requiring that word to mean considered of worth or importance (OED, v. 4). Thus Deighton (ed. 1891): Prized, either for its richness or for its rarity. Craig (ed. 1901) first points out an alternative meaning: Estimated (OED, 1); with no comma, Q may be read estimated to be either rich or rare. Dent (1981, T145) compares the proverb That Thing which is rare is dear. Idem (1984, p. 789) compares L223, Liberty is worth more than gold.

63 No…life]
Herwegh (ed. 1869): Still more exaggerated in Leir [241; see ]: I thinke my life inferiour to my loue. Verity (ed. 1897): So in the similar story in the Gesta Romanorum the eldest daughter says I loue you as mych as myn owne lyfe [BL Addit. MS 9066, ed. S. Herrtage, 1879, p. 48]. Cf. too Holinshed’s account…[see ], and Spenser’s Faerie Queene, ii.10.28 [That she much more then her owne life him lou’d; see ]. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) add, In the Mirour, the replies of both sisters are made together: more Then they themselues did loue, or any worldly wight (see ). The comparison is proverbial: Dent (1981, L244.1).

63 with grace]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Attended with favour (OED, Grace sb. 7). Verity (ed. 1897): I.e. life endowed with…natural charm, attractiveness (OED, 1). Brooke (ed. 1947): Enhanced by grace. Latham (1977, p. 166): Any possible theological overtone [OED, 6b] is obscured by the two purely physical words following. Dent (1981, G394), however, compares the proverb The Grace of God is worth a fair.

63 health, beautie, honour]
Dent (1981, H288, F4, N22) compares the proverbs Health is a jewel (great riches), A fair Face is half a portion, and A good Name is better than riches.

64 a]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 359): Possibly a compositor’s error: The copy may have had as a.

64 friend]
Only van Dam (1935, pp. 55–6) defends Q: Apocopated form of friended = favoured. Weis (ed. 1993): As much as child ever loved, or father, <or> friend <ever loved>. Wells (ed. 2000): Friend could mean relative, or lover; but her love for her father is at issue. F also makes an elliptical sentence. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 52), citing common r/o and e/u errors: F’s found in Q’s MS may have been misread as frend. Moberly (ed. 1876): As much love as child ever gave or father received. Brown (ed. 1976): Experienced/discovered the true nature of. Bevington (ed. 1988): I.e., found himself to be loved. Foakes (ed. 1997): Met with.

65 poore]
Either insufficient (OED, a. 4) or deficient in quality or worth (OED, 5). Bevington (ed. 1980): Cheap (OED, 5). King (apud Halio, ed. 1992): Impoverished.

65 vnable]
Schmidt (1875): Weak, impotent (OED, a. 2b). Deighton (ed. 1891): Incapable…of adequate expression.

66 Beyond…much]
Eds. disagree whether so much refers to particular comparisons or to the attempt to make comparisons or measurements at all. Johnson (ed. 1765): I love you beyond limits, and cannot say it is so much. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Beyond all power of saying.…Here so much is used idiomatically, to signify an indefinite amount or quantity. Delius (ed. 1854) and Schmidt (ed. 1879) would put so much within quotes to indicate idiomatic use. Tovey (ed. 1896): A comparison, if adequate, would end, So much I love you; but Goneril says she can find no such comparison. Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Probably…accompanied by a wide opening out of the arms. Heath (1765, p. 314), Wright (ed. 1875), and Verity (ed. 1897): So much refers to the particular comparisons that Goneril has just made; cf. . Kittredge (ed. 1940): Beyond every kind of comparison that can be imagined.…Manner is the emphatic word. Manner may mean either kind or degree (OED, sb. 9, 10). Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Any manner of assigning quantity.

67, 82–4 What…silent, Then…tongue]
Perrett (1904, p. 279): Sh. copied Cordella’s asides in Leir 254 and 274; see .

67 What]
Interrogative pronoun. Only Blake (1992; 2002, p. 292) considers it an exclamation, O horror, a reading possible only in F.

67 doe]
Either Q’s reading or F’s speake is possible. Schmidt (1879, p. 12), followed by Furness (ed. 1880), Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 122), and others: With doe the following verbs loue and be must be infinitives (following an assumed shall). But after F’s speake they could equally well be parallel imperatives, Cordelia’s commands to herself. Werstine (privately) suggests a less symmetrical construction: What…speake? Loue, and be silent. Q’s doe has its strong defenders. Deighton (ed. 1891): When her turn comes to be questioned. Verity (ed. 1897): Speak hardly accords with love and be silent. Lee (ed. 1908): Speak…is scarcely in keeping with Cordelia’s mistrust of verbal professions. But Knight (ed. 1840), preferring F as usual: Doe is the feebler reading, which destroys the force of the answer. Munro (ed. 1957): Speake is preferable as the durior lectio, what shall I do being a common phrase.
The reason for the variant is unclear. Craig (ed. 1901): It is rather curious to have these rival readings…when the same two words come into the text later I’ll do it before I speak, [248]…and again leaves the history unspoke that it intends to do, [259–60]. Did Shakespeare first write do, and then, seeing that doing was Cordelia’s forte, speaking her difficulty, did he make her consider the more difficult point? Van Dam (1935, p. 56): Perhaps the adapter preferred speak because the word was used by Lear, at ll. [59, 73, and 96]. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 122): A scribe preparing copy for F may have decided that speake was required by the context since the point at issue is the daughters’ declarations. Ioppolo (1991, p. 169): The texts diverge here in the evolution of Cordelia’s character.…In the Quarto she decides to do nothing and in the Folio she decides to say nothing. Since in the dramatic context she can (and does) act only by speaking or not speaking, the choice of words makes no practical difference.

67 loue…silent]
Crook (ed. 1907): Cordelia at once gives the keynote of her character. Her love shows itself in deeds, not words. Tilley L165, Whom we love best to them we can say Least, also cites TGV 2.2.17–18 (585–6), I, so true loue should doe: it cannot speake, For truth hath better deeds, then words to grace it, which Wilson (ed. 1960) calls a perfect comment here. Harbage (1963, p. 401): The falsity of her sisters would be evident without Cordelia’s prompting asides; the protestations of love…are self-stigmatizing. Cavell (1969, p. 293): It is not that Goneril and Regan have taken the words out of her mouth, but that she cannot say them, because for her they are true.…She is not disgusted by her sister’s flattery (it’s nothing new); but heartbroken at hearing the words she wishes she were in a position to say. Berry (1993, p. 77): Though Cordelia has committed the grossest of solecisms [see n. 93], Shakespeare stills such thoughts as subversive to his immediate dramatic purpose…with the simplest of technical tricks, the aside.…The audience is bidden, not invited, to take Cordelia’s part. It is tampering with the jury.…The aside is a form of ingratiation that no other character in this scene is permitted to practise.

68–73, 85–8 Of…speake, To…Gonorill]
Brown (ed. 1976): Lear’s…precise legal phraseology, lengthening phrases, and (to Goneril) glowing evocations of natural riches, suggest public utterance rather than intimacy.

68 bounds]
Deighton (ed. 1891): The lands enclosed by these boundaries (possibly OED, sb.1 3). Verity (ed. 1897): Pointing to the map before him. See n. 42. Foakes (ed. 1997): Or draws on it, or tears part of it off and hands it to Goneril.

69 shady]
F’s shadowie means the same, and the difference, as Taylor (1983, p. 380) says, could result from…a copyist’s or compositor’s error. Elsewhere Sh. uses forms of both words in reference to trees: for shadowie Wright (ed. 1875) compares Lr. 2921 and TGV 5.4.2 (2123), and Craig (ed. 1901) AYL 4.1.217 (2122). Craig finds a parallel in North’s Plutarch, and Muir (ed. 1952) finds one for shady in Montaigne, but since the words are common alternatives, neither need derive from a specific source. Lott (ed. 1974): The forests are full of trees and therefore rich in timber.

69–70 and…Riuers]
Adee (facs. 1890, p. xxvii): Probably [in Q] this is a printer’s blundering omission due to the ductus literarum of the recurring and. So Doran (1931, p. 57): Lines 69–70 are constructed on the same pattern, each beginning With… and each having and after the caesural pause. It would have been easy for the printer’s eye to fall to the second half of line [70] after he had set the first half of line [69]. Stone (1980, p. 239): Against this it might be argued that the reviser’s additions…at the beginning of the play tend to be more frequent and fussy than they are elsewhere; hence this could be a genuine addition (Halio, ed. 1992, p. 277).

69 Champains]
Valpy (ed. 1833): Open plains (OED, sb. 1)

69 rich’d]
Steevens (ed. 1778): To rich is an absolute verb (OED, v.1), not an abbreviation of enrich. Rolfe (ed. 1880): Used by S. nowhere else. Although most editors follow Rowe in adding a comma (see textual n.), thus making rich’d refer to bounds, the F punctuation makes equally good sense if with is understood as repeated before wide skirted meades (70), thus making rich’d refer to Champains. So Brown (ed. 1976): Well-tilled.

70 plenteous]
Schmidt (1875): Abundant (OED, a. 2). Deighton (ed. 1891): Bringing plenty.

70 wide skirted]
Generally taken as a compound (see textual n.). Deighton (ed. 1891): Having broad borders, i.e. extensive (OED, Skirted pp. a. 2, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Tovey (ed. 1896): The champain country, on the other hand, is not broken up into separate fields.

70 meades]
Unlike champaigns, grasslands used specifically for cropping or pasture (OED, Meadow sb. 1). Foakes (ed. 1997): Presumably lying alongside rivers.

71 thee…thine]
McIntosh (1963, p. 54) takes the intimate pronouns to imply a relaxation of Lear’s formal manner because he is gratified by his daughter’s response; and so at 85. But Lear would naturally use thee/thou as father speaking to one of his daughters, and has not previously used singular you to any of them.

71 Lady]
Hudson (ed. 1871): The lord of a thing is…the owner of it, and lady is here used as the counterpart of lord in this sense.

71 Albaines]
Just possibly a dissyllable, but since the spelling occurs nowhere else in either text or in the sources, it probably results from transposition of letters, as van Dam (1935, p. 18) says.

71 issue]
On F’s issues Wilson (ed. 1960): The plur. suggests successive heirs. Presumably it may not mean multiple offspring of the same generation, as at Cym. 2.1.47 (883), since only the eldest son could be heir. Horsman (ed. 1973): The plural usage was common, citing OED (sb. 6): Descendants.

72 perpetuall]
Hunter (ed. 1972): This is no temporary division of the kingdom. From now on, Britain will cease to exist as an entity. The Sokols (2000, p. 257): Lear attempt[s] to set up a perpetual entail, although he fails to use precisely the right form of words (heirs of your body).

73 speake]
Hudson (ed. 1856): Probably the [F] omission was accidental, the word being necessary to the measure. Dyce (ed. 1857): Lear has concluded his address to Goneril with speak first; and he afterwards finished that to Cordelia with Speak. Perhaps, but the latter speake is absent from Q; see n. 92. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 123): In both cases where speake is omitted—F [73], Q [92]—there is metrical deficiency; but…Shakespeare often ends speeches with metrically incomplete lines. Werstine (1983, p. 283): Compositor B also omitted the last word of LLL 5.2.312 (2237). But there he had a full line, and the erroneous relining makes the case not exactly comparable.

74–81 Sir…loue]
Verity (ed. 1897): Observe the rhetorical, fanciful style (prize…worth, most…sense, felicitate). Assumed feeling naturally tries to disguise its unreality by fine-sounding phrases. Latham (1977, pp. 166–7): Regan’s speech is less formally rhetorical than Goneril’s, and it falls into two self-contradictory parts [dividing at 77].…Unlike Goneril’s measured, end-stopped lines, Regan’s tend to run on.…Goneril’s delivery must be powerful with the rhetorical framework clearly imposing itself upon the material; for Regan there is (apparently) the sense that she is borne along by the emotion which is not fully in her control as the lines swell out and run on.

74 Sir…is]
Without the introductory Sir, which may be read as a separate line (see n. 60), this line may be spoken as a rough pentameter. To Greg (1933, p. 253; 1942, p. 90), Q’s extra syllables suggest a report of an actor’s corrupt delivery. Van Dam (1935, p. 18): We have to pronounce I’m, o’th, and sistris, in which case (p. 58) the Q line is unexceptional. F makes the line more regular by omitting three syllables (Sir, same, is).

74 Sir]
White (ed. 1862): It is a delicate touch of keeping that Goneril and Regan should both render their yet not discrowned father this lip-service. She is of course speaking to the king on a formal occasion before the court.

74 selfe same]
F reduces to selfe, meaning same (OED, a. 1b). Both expressions are common in Sh. and occur in both Q and F: see Abbott §20, Schmidt (1875), Franz §318, and cf. 1218, 2347+35. Van Dam (1935, p. 94), finding selfsame Mettle in Tim. 4.3.179 (1799): This Q line…can not be lightly dismissed. Kermode (1994, p. 101), however, finds Q’s reading an erroneous vulgarisation.

74 mettall]
Schmidt (1875): Substance or material (OED, sb. 8). OED (1f): Fig.…The stuff of which a man is made, with reference to character: cf. Mettle. Tovey (ed. 1896): Metal and mettle are only two forms of the same word, gradually distinguished in sense, for convenience’ sake, mettle being now used exclusively for spirit or courage. Hunter (ed. 1972): Spirit. But the pun on metal is given strength by price [see n. 75] and worth in the following line…with the implication: My price can be measured in metal. Weis (ed. 1993): I.e., precious metal.

75 prize]
OED (v.1 1): To estimate the (relative) value of;…esteem, account as worth (so much). Hunter (ed. 1972) prints price, a related word derived from the same original prise, but it is a later form with more specialized meaning. Although a few modern commentators—e.g., Kittredge (ed. 1940), Harrison (ed. 1948)—take the verb to be an imperative to Lear, most consider it a declarative governed by I in l. 74. Muir (ed. 1952): Cf. Leir, 240: I prize my loue to you at such a rate; see . Gardner (ed. 1969): Following the idea of metal, however, the line has an acquisitive ring, and seems also to claim an assessment equal to Goneril’s.

75 me]
Crook (ed. 1907): Me, myself. The simple pronoun for the reflexive, as in [54, vs] above. Or possibly direct object of an imperative.

75 in…heart]
As punctuated in Q, the phrase modifies prize and could be either an asseveration like in truth or, as more usually taken, an indication of her special value. Thus Theobald (ed. 1733): Regan would say, that in the Truth of her Heart and Affection, she equals the worth of her Sister. The usual modern punctuation, putting F’s full stop after worth, makes the phrase modify find in l. 76. Tyrwhitt (in Steevens, ed. 1778): In my true heart I find. Deighton (ed. 1891): In examining my loyal heart. OED (Heart sb. 6): The seat of one’s inmost thoughts and secret feelings; one’s inmost being; the depths of the soul; the soul, the spirit; cf. def. 35. Cf. 111, 852, 1867, 2713, 3081. McAlindon (1991, pp. 175–182): Referred to about sixty times in the play, the heart is arguably its major image. To follow a selection of the principal passages in which it occurs is to come very close to an understanding of what the play is about and why it affects us so deeply.…[182] The heart is the central microcosm in the correspondent and contrarious universe of Lr. Cf. Kirsch (1990, pp. 8–9, 104–5).

76 names]
OED (v.1 6d): State, give particulars of, quoting this l. as its first ex.

76 deed]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Reality, as in the phrase in very deed (OED, sb. 5c). Moberly (ed. 1876): Exact character. Furness (ed. 1880) translates Delius’s (ed. 1854) gloss förmliche, rechtskräftige Erklärung as a formal, legal definition (OED, 4), but it may mean deposition, declaration. Crook (ed. 1907): Used in its legal sense of clear description and title. Eccles (ed. 1792) finds a sense of doing: That kind of agency by which my own love operates,—the same effects of which it is productive. Hunter (ed. 1972): (1) action; (2) legal instrument. Regan finds in her heart a document containing the very words that Gonerill has been using. Halio (ed. 1992): From which she can read her love. Brown (ed. 1976): What my love really does/promises.

77 came]
Q’s word may be an error, since the tense is inconsistent with names (76); F’s comes too regularizes meter.

77 short]
Moberly (ed. 1876): F’s too short means simply short. Hudson (ed. 1881): Short of me in this.

77 That]
Johnson (ed. 1765): That…is referred to find [76].…I find that she names…, that I profess. Capell (1783, 1.2:141): Or it must have the sense of—in that. Wright (ed. 1875), alternatively: For that. Abbott §284 and Franz §552 instance both meanings; cf. 182. Hunter (ed. 1869) suggests both in that and something like so that: Leaving for me to profess. Wells (ed. 2000) alone: To the extent that.

79 precious]
Delius (ed. 1854) refers this to joys, not square, and Deighton (ed. 1891) seems to paraphrase similarly: The most dearly prized enjoyments of sense. The syntax does not seem easily to yield such a meaning. Most commentators take the word in its usual sense of valuable, but a few relate it loosely to the general sense fastidious (OED, 3). Wright (ed. 1875): Delicately sensitive. Herford (ed. 1899): Exquisitely susceptible. Ridley (ed. 1935): Exacting. Harbage (ed. 1958): Precise.

79 square of sence]
The difficult word in this crux, square, has been given a wide spectrum of interpretations:
(1)Extent or area. Edwards (1748, p. 43) The full complement. Johnson (ed. 1765): Compass, comprehension. Verplanck (ed. 1847): As circle is now sometimes used. Lettsom (1853, p. 464): Compass, area. Caldecott (MS notes, 1813–33): Most antient Maps were divided into squares;…the idea, here transferred to sense. Brooke (ed. 1947): All the joys that manifest themselves through the various senses are thought of as laid out on an area or square of sensibility as on a map. White (ed. 1862): The entire domain. Hudson (ed. 1871): Fulness or wealth. Wright (ed. 1875): Part of my nature. Leo (1880, p. 56): Room, area, of feeling…the heart; Idem (1885, p. 109): Sphere, space, province of feeling…the heart. Garrett (1905, p. 284): Position upon the [chess] board. Herford (ed. 1899): Region of our sensible nature. Lee (ed. 1908): The most precious segment, the summit or acme. Houghton (ed. 1957): Piece. Stetner & Goodman (1968, p. 86): Sexual double entendre. So Horsman (ed. 1973): The most precious area of sense, i.e., the genitals.
(2)Measure. Halliwell (ed. 1865) cites (in support of a different meaning) The Passenger of Benvenuto (1612, p. 21): their owne interests, after which square they measure all things. Moberly (ed. 1876): Estimate, citing Tro. 5.2.132–3 (3128–9), to square the generall sex By Cressids rule. Schmidt (1879, p. 12): Guideline, norm (Ger.)—of sensible thought; hence, in the superlative, ideal pattern of good judgment (see below). Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905, p. 151): Shakespeare frequently uses square in the sense of measure, meaning, figuratively, what the carpenter’s square is used for mechanically, and he uses it so here, citing Ant. 2.3.6–7 (970–1), I haue not kept my square, but that to come Shall all be done by th’Rule. Chambers (ed. 1906): Measuring instrument. MacCracken (ed. 1914): The carpenter’s square is used here figuratively, as a rule or standard. So Kittredge (ed. 1940). Gardner (ed. 1969): Regan’s language is too contrived and effusive for simple carpentry. Phelps (ed. 1917): Test. Harbage (ed. 1958): Measurement. OED (sb. 2): Fig. A canon, criterion, or standard; a rule or guiding principle; a pattern or example. (Very common c 1550–1650). Colman (ed. 1982): A golden set-square was an emblem of temperance, citing no evidence; but see Spenser, F.Q. 2.1.58.1.
(3)Perfection, highest degree. Holt (1749, p. v): The utmost perfection…(alluding to the Pythagorean Tenet which held a Square to be the most perfect Figure). Schmidt (1879, p. 12): Choicest harmony (balance, symmetry) of reason (Ger.); see above. Tovey (ed. 1896): The idea of perfection, as derived from that of regularity and harmony of proportion, suggested by the mathematical figure and the carpenter’s rule. Craig (ed. 1901): Sense absolute, sense in its perfection, citing John Bodenham, Bel-vedere (1600; ed. 1875. p. 73), Councell and good aduise is wisdomes square, where square may instead mean measure. Goggin (ed. 1910): Geometrical figures were often used as emblems of perfection, e.g. the pentagon and the circle. OED does not support this usage. Hunter (ed. 1972): Senses, not out of square (unbalanced) but in their proper constitution. Edwards (ed. 1975): Properly proportioned feelings. Hankins (1978, p. 71): The word has an ethical content.…Right angles and straight (recta) lines become symbols of uprightness and rectitude.
(4)Scheme of four parts or sides. Warburton (1739, p. 196): The four nobler senses, viz. the sight, hearing, taste, smell. For a maid could not with decorum insinuate, that she knew of any pleasures, which the fifth afforded. Smith (apud Grey, 1754, 2:102): There were two squares referred to by Goneril [in 61–2 and 63].…The second square [grace, health, beautie, honour] is of the superlative kinds of joys…and Regan professes herself an enemy to three.…His dear Highness’ love [i.e., grace] is the only joy of the square which she values. Hunter (ed. 1869): The astrological square of the twelve houses.…The most precious square would thus denote one most abounding in good tokens or fortunes. Anderson (1927, p. 9) quotes Batman vppon Bartholome (1582, 3.7; cf. Wits Theater, 1599, pp. 37–8): The Philosopher…lykeneth the soule Sensibilis, to a quadrangle square, and foure cornered. Craig (ed. 1931): Reference to the psychological diagram of the mental powers in the form of a square whose sides are sense, appetite, motion, and judgment. Gardner (ed. 1969): The sensible soul which…included the vegetal soul and rational soul contained in it (saith Aristotle) as a triangle in a quadrangle, as Robert Burton pointed out in The Anatomy of Melancholy [1.1.2.5]. The sensible soul, or faculty, included the five senses, and common sense, imagination and memory, and its general organ in the brain, from which principally the sensible operations are derived. The qualification most precious suits this interpretation completely. Joseph (ed. 1966) cites J. B. Bamborough, The Little World of Man (1952, pp. 31 f.) for the idea of the square as symbol of the Sensible Soul. Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): Figurative for the human body or human life. See The Faerie Queene, II.ix.22, a quadrate was the base (the lower part of the soul, which works through sense). Halio (ed. 1992): In Pythagorean terms, the square is an emblem of the material world, or the world of sense, the physical universe.…Compare Leonardo’s famous drawing of the human figure inscribed within a square, citing S. K. Heninger, Touches of Sweet Harmony (1974, p. 111) and G. L. Hersey, Pythagorean Palaces (1976, pp. 88 ff.).
Most commentators now accept some version of (2). For emendations, see the textual nn. and . Collier (1852, p. 434; 1853, p. 449) thinks his Perkins Folio emendation to sphere exactly conveys Edwards’s meaning. Stetner & Goodman (1970): The most precious sphere of sense is the eye. Wilson (ed. 1960) adopts and defends Hanmer’s spirit, understood as life, essence: See Troil. 1.1.[58] [92]; 3.3.106 [1958+2], where spirit of sense = the essence of sensibility ([Onions, 1911]).…The word spirit or sprite might be misread square. Schmidt defines spirit of sense in Tro. as the most delicate faculty of perception, which if right would make good sense here. As for sense, most take it to mean sensation, though Hudson (ed. 1871) understands sensibility, or capacity of joy, Leo (1880, p. 439) sentiment of the heart, and Becket (1815, 1:126), Schmidt (1879, p. 12) reason, and Koppel (1899, p. 16) good sense, understanding; according to Schmidt, Regan’s love is so great that she will know nothing of all joys, which even a pattern of reason professes to be joys (Ger.). The line becomes sufficiently if not perfectly understandable if sense is emphatic: my father’s love is more valuable than all the joys of sense; cf. Verity below. In his Valediction Donne distinguishes between true love and that whose soul is sense.

79 possesses]
Generally preferred to F professes. Schmidt (1879, p. 12) defends F: Acknowledges to be joys (Ger.). Similarly Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Professes…in the sense of shows forth or attests. Verity (ed. 1897): The difference being all joys which the choicest estimate of sense actually has, i.e. feels, is capable of, and professes to feel. I think that professes strikes a wrong note, that Regan does not mean to doubt the reality of the joys of sense but to emphasise that she, unlike others, is an enemy to them because she knows the higher joy of loving and being loved by Lear. Goggin (ed. 1910): Professes…decidedly weakens the force of Regan’s protestation, unless we are to understand that she intends a stroke of irony and means merely I will profess as much as you like. Stetner & Goodman (1970): The word hypocritically suggests religious renunciation of earthly things. Weis (ed. 1993): F’s professes…may be intended to sound an appropriately mannered note by echoing profess at [77]. Though either word could have been a misreading for the other, the F reading can be more easily explained as such. White (ed. 1862): Caught from the second line above. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Probably a misprint due to profess in [77]. So Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 166), Muir (ed. 1952), Wilson (ed. 1960).

80–4 And…tongue]
Eds. universally link 80 metrically with 81 to form an eleven or twelve syllable line. It is just possible that 81 is a short line and that Cordelia’s aside is a discrete speech of two lines, dividing after I. See n. 85.

80–1 I…loue]
Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) point out similar extravagance in earlier versions of the story: aboue all Criatures of the worlde (Gesta Romanorum [BL Add. MS. 9066, ed. Herrtage, 1879, p. 49]), [Farre] aboue all other creatures of the world (Holinshed [see ]), greater loue to him profest Then all the world (Spenser [see ]). Similarly in Geoffrey (ed. Griscom, 1929, p. 263; see ), super omnes creaturas; in Higgins, more Then they themselues did loue, or any worldly wight; Warner, Her life inferior to her loue; see , . In Leir 241 this last sentiment is given to Gonorill; Ragan responds (268–72; see ) that if Lear wishes, she will reject all her suitors To ratify my loue before your eyes.

80 felicitate]
Capell (1783, 1.2:141): An affected expression, and before it a line that’s all affectation. The word does not appear elsewhere in Sh. OED quotes this as the sole example of its adjectival use, and does not record its use as a verb until 1628. Wright (ed. 1875): Made happy, giving other examples of participles formed on the model of the Latin participle in -atus. Cf. Walker (1860, 2:324 ff.), Abbott §342, Franz §159.

81 highnes]
Kittredge (1940): Objective genitive: the love that I feel for your Majesty.

82–4 Then…tongue]
Q’s line division is erroneous, and F’s, accepted by all eds., leaves 84 as a short line. Halio (ed. 1992): A short…line at the end of a speech is not unusual in Shakespeare’s mature drama, citing Wright (1988, pp. 116–42). Possibly both Q and F are wrong, and Cordelia’s aside was not intended to link metrically with Regan’s speech but to be discrete, a comment separated in form as well as content. Such is easily possible if it is divided after I. Q’s ampersand would not normally occur at the beginning of a line of verse; the manuscript’s and and Cordelia were abbreviated in order to fit the line into the shorter measure resulting from the compositor’s indenting his stick between this line and 96 (where the short measure forced a turnover); see .

82 poore Cord.]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Then is Cordelia most poor. Gardner (ed. 1969): Cordelia at first loses heart, thinking she must remain poor since she cannot match her sister’s protestations. Hunter (ed. 1972) adds, She feels the lack of gifts within her. Possibly Cordelia is playing on two senses of poor: unfortunate and impoverished (OED, a. 6, 1). Either way, she could mean that she will be poor in the future (because undowered by Lear) or that she is already poor; if the latter, she may refer to her poverty in rhetoric, or just possibly, with intentional irony, to her lack of a filial love so total as to surpass and exclude all other joys—the claim by her sisters that she mocks again in 106–110+1. On scansion see n. 47.

83 so]
Crook (ed. 1907): Really poor. Lee (ed. 1908): Poor in love; deficient (OED, 5). Gardner (ed. 1969): She then takes heart in the thought that Lear will recognize the true weight of her love, and grant her her share of the kingdom, conceding that a less forthright interpretation…will add sentiment to Cordelia. Cf. the prev. n.

84 more richer]
Wright (ed. 1875) thinks that F’s more ponderous has the appearance of being a player’s correction to avoid a piece of imaginary bad grammar [i.e., a double comparative], but Rolfe (ed. 1880) objects that it was not considered bad grammar at that time, and Brooke (ed. 1947) points to the very same phrase in Ham. 3.2.304 (2175–6). Abbott (§11): The inflections -er and -est,…lost some of their force, and sometimes received the addition of more, most, for the purpose of greater emphasis. Wells (ed. 2000): Much. Cf. Franz §217a, and 231, 237, 1177, 1225, 1258, 1386, 1718. Sh. often associates the words rich and golden with the words tongue, words, and speech. The Clarkes’ (ed. 1868) argument that richer is the antithesis to poore (82) has been decisive for many editors. Deighton (ed. 1891): Ponderous…is difficult to understand as antithetical to poor. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Assuredly a heavy tongue is not an expressive organ of speech, nor is ponderous love a felicitous phrase. Elsewhere Sh. uses ponderous twice literally (Ham. 1.4.50 [635], MM 3.2.276 [1761]) and once figuratively (WT 4.4.524 [2385]); OED (a. 1b) quotes this l. as its earliest ex. of figurative use, meaning heavy…unwieldy. The use of the word here has been defended. Schmidt (1879, p. 12): Sh. chose it in opposition to light (wanton, frivolous, fickle) love, as in the proverbial phrase light o’ love. But that usage generally refers to amatory rather than filial love, and Schmidt does not explain why Sh. might have been dissatisfied with richer. Bradley (1904, p. 319 n.) ventures to do so: Does it not sound…like the author’s improvement of a phrase that he thought a little flat? And, apart from that, is it not significant that it expresses the same idea of weight that appears in the phrase [I…mouth (97–8)]? Craig (ed. 1901): Perhaps this word is suggested by Regan’s self-metal, gold, but only the gold of words. Cordelia cannot produce golden words, cannot coin her heart in words, but her heart has love of a better and weightier metal. Wilson (ed. 1960): Ponderous itself suggests the balance used to distinguish false coins from genuine. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Perhaps Cordelia felt that her tongue was heavy and slow compared with the loose tongues of her sisters, and her heart heavy and slow, too, with the dismay of these glib professions, and yet weightier in honesty. She says the opposite, however: that her love is ponderous, more than her tongue. Her tongue, being light and weak, is unable (65) to wield the matter (60) of her weighty love for Lear. Cf. AYL 1.2.257 (424): What passion hangs these waights vpõ my toong? As Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 28–30) rightly says, ponderous is not a word likely to have occurred to a scribe preparing F copy, nor would such a scribe have erased a double comparative here and added one at 1718. Duthie’s theory that Q’s richer is an actor-reporter’s anticipation of 252 is scouted by Kirschbaum (1951, p. 170): Did the Elizabethan actors habitually contaminate their speeches with other actors’ speeches?

84 tongue]
Harrison (ed. 1948) and Foakes (ed. 1997) specify a metonym: Words.

85 To…euer]
Flatter (1948, p. 16): Lear, not hearing Cordelia’s aside, speaks a full line rather than complete her part-line. Cf. n. 80–4. But part-lines may be completed by speakers who do not hear them, e.g., 2371–3, 2674–6.

85 hereditarie]
If Rowe’s pointing is adopted (see textual n.), this word must be an adjective modifying third (86), and the line corresponds, as Deighton (ed. 1891) says, with to…perpetuall (71–2) in Goneril’s case. Wells (ed. 2000): By inheritance. Without the comma, as in Q and F, the line may also mean this, or hereditarie may conceivably be a noun meaning, as Ridley (ed. 1935) and Berry (1993, p. 71) say, heirs, though the usage is unattested in OED or elsewhere in Sh. Assuming it anyway, Berry argues, Regan has secured a better deal than Goneril. She has much wider terms in which to dispose of her inheritance, which become (p. 80) the claimed right to make Edmund Earl of Gloucester [Duke of Cornwall? he is named Earl of Gloucester by Cornwall in line 1987]. Goneril, however, assumes an equal right to Edmund (if Albany can be disposed of).

86 Remaine]
Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Imperative or optative. OED (v. 3b): To continue to belong to one, quoting this l. as its last ex.

86 ample]
Schmidt (1874): Large, copious (OED, a. 2, quoting 2347+12).

86 third]
Foakes (ed. 1997): The West Country and Wales. The Sokols (2000, p. 99): A third was the common law proportion of estates reserved to widows as dower. Lear’s odd gift giving hints toward an act of leaving his estate on death to three wives, as in a bizarre version of dower, not giving it in life to three daughters. See n. 49. But Lear’s intent is clearly to divest himself immediately, as he does.

87 validity]
Rann (ed. 1794): Value (OED, 4). Weis (ed. 1993): Also, Legal efficacy (OED, 1).

87 pleasure]
Moffatt (ed. 1889): By metonymy, for capacity of giving pleasure. Harbage (ed. 1958): Pleasing qualities.

88 confirm’d]
Except in the 18th-c. variorums F’s conferr’d has been generally preferred, the Q reading being considered a repetition of the error at 45 (see n.). The idiom to confirm a title or property on is not attested by OED or found in Sh. As Mason (1807, p. 591) says, We confer on a person, but we confirm to him. So OED (Confirm v. 2c), quoting 3H6 1.1.172 (193), Confirme the Crowne to me and to mine Heires. Jackson (1983, p. 344, n. 47) thinks it unlikely that the same mistake would have been made twice; but since the same Q compositor was probably reading from the same difficult MS (see ), one mistake may confirm the other.

88 but]
Jones (1995, p. 178): In F Shakespeare has punched a rhythmic hole in the first line of verse by cutting But, and thus creating poetic-dramatic time and space for the father to swivel his old body upon the throne and bend his full regard towards the youngest daughter. There is no hole; the line in F is metrically full.

89–91 our…you]
Hodge & Kress (1982, p. 154): The formal pronouns express power; the informal thy etc. in 111 ff. signify his anger and contempt…but also express accidentally the intimacy he really feels.

89 the…least]
The difference from the F variant, our last and least, can not be discussed without reference to the following lines (90–1) unique to F. The Q variant makes perfect sense in the Q context while the F variant does not, and the F variant makes perfect sense in the F context while the Q variant does not. On the face of it these facts suggest, as they did to White (ed. 1862), that if Q represents an earlier version, lines 90–1 may be a later addition (see n. 90–1) and the F variant here is an adjustment made to accommodate them. Moreover, the wish to include the additional F lines explains why editors have so often inclined to the F variant, since the Q variant does not fit with those lines. If 90–1 are not a later addition but were overlooked in the Q compositor’s copy, it is unlikely that the compositor, finding that he had set nonsense, changed this phrase rather than consult his copy in order to discover his omission of the ensuing lines. Greg (1933, p. 256; 1942, pp. 91–2), however, dismisses revision: Surely the loss of a line and a half has occasioned the [F] reconstruction; assuming (questionably) a text reported from performance, he attributes the loss to an actor’s failure of memory. Van Dam (1935, p. 53): Q represents prompt-book cutting to change F’s difficult poetry into clear language. No one else believes that Q derives from a playbook.
Rann (ed. 1794) compares JC 3.1.189 (1411), Though last, not least in loue, the only other echo in Sh. of the proverb Last but not least (Tilley L82); Furness (ed. 1880) records many contemporary instances; Steevens (ed. 1773) finds a remote and very doubtful parallel (in a speech addressed to a different character in a different context) in Leir 2657–8 (see ). The commonness of the phrase has been cited in arguments both that Sh. did and did not write the Q line. Dyce (ed. 1857) thinks F’s departure from the proverbial formula a flagrant error, and Staunton (ed. 1859), a misprint. Verity, in Irving & Marshall (ed. 1889): To take a proverbial saying and twist it round to mean something quite different while the sound is much the same, or reversing a well-worn maxim: nothing is gained by the artifice; the effect produced is one of simple incongruity. But White (op. cit.) sees gains: In the rewriting there was a happy change made from the commonplace of last not least to an allusion to the personal traits and family position of Cordelia. Furness (ed. 1880): If…last, not least, was a hackneyed phrase in Shakespeare’s time, it is all the more reason why it should not be used here. Its very opposition to the common use and wont makes it emphatic. Perrett (1904, p. 291) agrees, adducing the variant The Last; and the Least [viz. request] from Lyly’s 1598 petition to the Queen (ed. Bond, 1:71). So also Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 27): The double contrast with last and least isolates our Ioy, and, throwing greater emphasis upon it, makes it more effective. Sisson (1956, 2:230): The Q phrase is of some irrelevance to the trend of the speech though of somewhat sentimental appeal. Foakes (ed. 1997): Q, unlike F, offers an internal direction for Lear to embrace Cordelia; F diminishes her importance, adding a reminder that the main purpose of the occasion is to determine whom she will marry. But that would seem to magnify her importance.

89 last]
Wells (ed. 2000): Both last-born and last to be asked.

89 least]
In Q the word means lowest in…position (OED, adj. 2), in F it apparently means smallest (OED, 1), though other meanings are possible. Delius’s (ed. 1854) Youngest is redundant after last, though Bhattacharya (1980–1) finds alliterative reduplicative phrases not uncommon in English and in Sh. Deighton (ed. 1891): Little, citing little seeming substance in 216 (which does not clearly refer to Cordelia’s stature) and Lear’s ability to carry her at the end of the play. Wilson (ed. 1960): Latest born and least in precedence.…Prob. refers also to Cord.’s stature. Edwards (ed. 1975): Least in public importance. There is no reference to Cordelia’s height in the sources. Craik (1956, p. 11) finds in Stephen Batman’s The Doome warning all men to the Iudgmente (1581, p. 439) a reference to Cordilla the daughter of King Leyer, and least of all hir sisters, but the reference could be to either stature or status.

89 in our deere loue]
F’s to whose yong loue may be an adjustment to suit the new lines 90–1. Jackson (1983, p. 339): Q’s deere loue echoes Leir 286 (see ). But Sh. had used this formulaic phrase many times before.

90–1 The…interest]
Capell (1783, 1.2:142): Lear’s speech is improved in simplicity, tenderness, and it’s diction’s propriety without these lines. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxvii): They were probably omitted from Q because they seemed nonsensical; cf. n. 91. Doran (1931, p. 127): Since 90–2 are metrically regular in F, the changes are deliberate. Hart (1942, pp. 146–7) considers the lines redundant for intelligent auditors and their absence from Q1 an improvement. Greg (1933, p. 256; 1942, pp. 91–2): Omitted because of an actor’s failure of memory alone; see n. 89. Jackson (1983, p. 335): The F addition helpfully identifies…suitors twice. Ioppolo (1991, p. 170): Lear offers her his affection [our deere loue] in the Quarto and offers her affection to France and Burgundy in the Folio. But in both texts his affection for her is evident in his address—our ioy—and in both the French princes are Great ryuals in our youngest daughters loue.

90 Vines…Milke]
Wilson (ed. 1960): France and Burg. have presumably argued their cases by referring to the particular riches of their domains. Here those riches seem to stand by metonymy for their sovereigns; but see n. 91. Edwards (ed. 1975): This conveys a sense of richness rather than describes the agriculture. See the Song of Solomon, 5:1). Mahood (1992, p. 157): Lear has just indicated the tracts of land he has apportioned to Cornwall’s duchy in the south-west and to Albany’s in the north. There remains a portion more fertile than the moors and mountains of the other regions; one that Lear hopes, before he sets up his rest on Cordelia’s kind nursery, to see joined to the natural wealth of a great realm across the Narrow Seas.

90 Milke of Burgundie]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Put, I suppose, for—the pastures of Burgundy. Moberly (ed. 1876): In ascribing vines to France, and not to Burgundy, the poet may have thought of the pastoral countries of Southern Belgium as forming part of Burgundy (as they did till the death of Charles the Bold, 1477), otherwise we should not understand the distinction; as in the French Burgundy wine-growing was of very old standing. Law (1936, pp. 223–7): Why should Shakespeare allude to watrish Burgundy [283], and the milk of Burgundy as opposed to the vines of France, with an implication that the duchy was a low, flat, cattle-raising district instead of the vine-growing uplands close to Germany today?…The geographical references…[are] phrases applicable only in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries when the dukedom of Burgundy controlled lands in the low countries of Flanders, Artois, Brabant, and Hainault, which came near forming an independent kingdom. See DP n. 3–4, n. 39. Halio (ed. 1992): May signify a rich wine; compare Bristol milk; but this metaphorical slang name, dating from mid-17th c., refers only to sherry (OED, Milk sb. 5), a Spanish wine. Foakes (ed. 1997): Did Shakespeare intend to suggest something insipid about the character?

91 Striue]
Contend (OED, v. 3), not endeavor (OED, 9).

91 interest]
The sense of the F revision is hard to determine exactly. Either the two suitors or the riches of their lands striue to be interest to whose [i.e., Cordelia’s] yong loue. Most commentators follow Theobald (ed. 1733) and Steevens (ed. 1778) in taking interest as the past participle of interess (a verb not found elsewhere in Sh.), but a few take it to be the noun interest or even a shortened form of interested. The idiom interessed to is unattested in OED (though its exx. include one into and one whereunto); the usual idiom, interessed in, would not have required the change from Q’s in to F’s to. The awkward to apart, only two contemporary meanings of interess make any kind of sense: to be invested with, to have a right or share; to be admitted to a privilege (OED, v. 1, quoting this l.), and to be concerned, involved (OED, 2). The majority of editors favor the first, although Tovey (ed. 1896: to connect themselves closely), Craig (ed. 1901: closely connected, interested, concerned), and Muir (ed. 1952) elect the second. Taylor (1983, p. 433, n. 35): OED’s first ex. is from a passage in Holinshed that Sh. drew on for Mac. Schmidt (1874; ed. 1879), who finds neither interest nor interess as verbs in Sh., and Koppel (1899, pp. 18–19) and Kittredge (ed. 1940), take interest to be a noun meaning claim (OED, sb. 1), a sense common in Sh.; Kittredge glosses, Strive to be a claim; present their claims in rivalry. This meaning, claim, does not make easy sense if their refers to the suitors—they can more easily assert a claim than be one—but it makes passable sense if their refers to the countries’ riches, which as enticements to marriage might make a claim on Cordelia’s love. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) apparently also understand a noun: [Be?] of interest. Verity (ed. 1897), following a suggestion in Schmidt and Furness (ed. 1880), apparently understands a shortened form of interested: Having an interest in, implying allied to. No one seems to have suggested that interest could be a noun meaning advantage, benefit (OED, 2), a sense common in Sh.; thus the riches of the suitors compete to enrich Cordelia in marriage. Such a reading makes simple, straightforward sense and fits with the troublesome to in F line 89.

91 win]
Kirschbaum (1945, p. 15), assuming a priori that Q’s variants are usually corrupt: Q’s word vulgarizes Lear’s character. Wilson (ed. 1960): The gambling metaphor is significant. Both readings are forced: in Sh. the word commonly means to be victorious in a contest (OED, v.1 3) or simply to get, obtain (OED, 6). Although Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 30) considers Q’s word a weaker synonym of F’s draw, it may mean virtually the same: Schmidt (1874) defines the latter word as To win, to get, and OED (v. 45) as To take, receive, or obtain, quoting this l.; cf. 1773. Ioppolo (1991, p. 170), oddly: Draw (in speech?); but Lear is asking her to describe her love, not her dowry.

92 third, more opulent]
F’s spelling opilent does not appear elsewhere in F and is unattested in OED. Craig (ed. 1901, p. xxx): The most fertile and desirable third. Cf. n. 90. It might or might not be larger; see nn. 7, 9. Asserting without evidence that it is larger, Avery (1998, p. 52) finds in Lear’s display of the map a symbolic rhetoric publicizing the humiliation of Lear’s eldest daughters and his intent to retain psychological control over the women. Wickham (1973, p. 43): There is an obvious but unstated bonus…, and that is the capital city—Troynovant of the Brutus story, Leicester of the Leir story.…When Cordelia throws away her portion, it is England, and with it the capital city of an united Britain, which remains divided against itself until the return of a second Brutus [King James] to New Troy [London]. Perrett (1904, pp. 147–8) finds comic relief in the theory of Felsing (1879, p. 63) that Lear’s presence makes Cordelia’s third richer.

92 sisters]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Have drawn is elliptically understood. But it could as well be the pl. possessive sisters’.

92 speake]
Added in F, perhaps by analogy with 59 and Q 73, and evidently to make a full line of verse. Though it does not necessarily imply a momentary silence from Cordelia (see n. 73), and there is none in any source, critics speak of one, perhaps metaphorically. Freud (1913; 1925, 4:256) sees a silence symbolic of death, Dundes (1976, p. 362), of repressed incestuous desire (speech is sexual; dumbness…asexual), and Levenson (1972, p. 217) finds analogues to the silence of Christ before Herod in the medieval Passion plays, and to magical silences in folk tales. See the next n. Jones (1995, p. 178): Added to heighten attention—Lear’s, the court’s, ours—upon Cordelia and her reply.

93 Nothing]
Hunter (ed. 1972): I can say nothing designed to…opulent. I refuse to enter this charade. Coleridge (MS notes, 1818–19, ed. Foakes, 1989, p. 98): Something of disgust at the ruthless hypocrisy of her sisters, some little faulty admixture of pride and sullenness in Cordelia’s Nothing—well contrived to lessen the glaring absurdity of Lear—but the surest plan that of forcing away the attention from the nursery-tale the moment it has answered its purpose, that of supplying the canvas to paint on. Lloyd in Singer (ed. 1856, 9:524) defends Cordelia’s almost sullen and repulsive tone as the response, to Lear’s crudity of manners, of one whose speech was usually reserved and low and laconic, while conceding that Certain it is…that she took too little thought for the fact that her disinheriting was a greater misfortune to her father than to herself. Verity (ed. 1897): Her conduct is intelligible, if not tactful.…She will have no part in such hypocrisy. Again, strong, loving natures…do not talk about their feelings; they cannot heave the heart into the mouth, least of all in public and for a motive such as Lear had mentioned. Goggin (ed. 1910): Even had she wished, Cordelia could hardly have said more than had already been said by Goneril and Regan.…It is going too far, however, to say that she has some of Lear’s own obstinacy and imperiousness of character. Tactlessness is the worst fault that can be alleged against her. Like Wilson (ed. 1960, p. xxv)—In Cordelia there is nowhere any fault—Bhattacharya (1981, pp. 17–18, 25–6): Cordelia is exempted from even the most small fault (779) by 197 and 3299. Harbage (1963, p. 401): Cordelia is not asked to declare her love as love, but as a means of drawing A third more opulent…[and is asked] to mend her speech…lest it may mar her fortunes. She is revolting not against an attempt to breach her natural reticence but against a demand to participate in an auction. Furnivall (ed. 1908): Probably, as Prof. March suggests, Cordelia already lovd [sic] the King of France. Compare Rosalind’s What talk we of fathers…? [AYL 3.4.38–9 (1745–6)]. Fraser (1978–9, p. 8): Cordelia is speaking somehow humorously, lightly, to defuse the situation, as does Cordoylle in Wace’s Brut. Lear misunderstands, and the ploy fails. Goldberg (1985, p. 133), new-historically: Cordelia refuses to enter the sphere of speech because to speak is always a kind of betrayal, a violation of interiority. Berry (1993, p. 77): Has not Cordelia committed the grossest of solecisms? The opening scene is a great public spectacle, the division of the realm. It is theatre of monarchy. On such occasions the roles are determined, the individual compressed within the part. For the individual to assert self against the programming is, in this context, intolerable.
Harrison (ed. 1937; rev. 1949): In Lear Shakespeare very deliberately used the words Nothing and Nature in all their possible meanings, as a kind of knell which tolls insistently throughout the play. Rosenberg (1972, p. 69): Linked negative words spread through the language like a dark shadow: besides the thirty-odd nothings, no sounds one hundred fifty times, not almost three hundred times, neither, nor, none, ne’er, never another hundred. Against this, the rare affirmatives—yes less than ten times, yea and aye some twenty-five times—cast only a faint light. Colie (1966, pp. 463–81): The Renaissance was obsessed with nothing. Psychoanalytically, Shengold (1974, p. 119) finds nothing to mean castration and blindness, and Willbern (1980, pp. 245–7), licentiousness denied, organs deprived, female genitals, etc. Tayler (1990, pp. 17 ff.) finds throughout the play a quibbling connection between no and know, between negation and knowledge. Others focussing on the word nothing are Empson (1930, pp. 59–60), Heilman (1948, pp. 323–4 n.), and Burckhardt (1961, pp. 33–50; 1968, pp. 237–59). Rosinger (1968, pp. 495–6; 1988, p. 54), Gill (1984, p. 210), and Milward (1987, p. 160) seek a parallel in Christ’s refusal to answer his accusers in Matt. 27, Mark 14:56, 60–1, Luke 23:9, and John 19:9; but Cordelia does answer.

94–5 Lear.…Nothing.]
Delius (1876, p. 135): It is quite incredible that this cardinal point in the drama, on which everything turns, should have been only an afterthought of the poet. Naturally, all this must have been contained in the original text, and have been either wilfully or carelessly omitted by the compositor of the Quarto. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxvii): Perhaps the ductus literarum explains it, as Nothing occurs in the lines immediately preceding and following. The exchange may, as Adee says, be a delicate acting-touch, but it is hardly essential and could well be a later improvement, pace Delius. Van Dam (1935, p. 41): These three extra words [Nothing twice, speake] of F admirably serve to emphasize Cordelia’s answer, so that the audience cannot miss the point which is the key of the play. There is no doubt that they are new interpolations, and…that the F text will represent a theatrical revision of [Q1]. Richman (1986, p. 377): The repetition heightens the scene, laying dramatic emphasis on the king’s stunned incredulity and his daughter’s unshakeable firmness. Still, the sequence in Q continues that sense of spare directness which characterizes Q’s opening scene. Ioppolo (1991, p. 170), on F: Presenting a stronger confrontation. Halio (ed. 1992): The F additions…not only make Cordelia’s response emphatic, but provide the actor playing Lear with space for further reaction.

96 How]
OED (adv. 4), Ellipt. for…How say you? and used interjectionally, the mod. equivalent being What? or What! Here in Q the word expresses Lear’s stunned surprise at Cordelia’s answer, and might have been followed by a pause. Being extrametrical, it may have been intended to function as a separate line, somewhat like the introductory Sir beginning several Q lines: see n. 60. The addition of 94–5 in F makes it supererogatory, and editions from F onwards generally omit it, making 96 a regular verse line. Cf. 100, 1280. Greg (1933, p. 254; cf. 1942, pp. 90–1) considers it an actor’s transposition, recorded by a stenographer: The Quarto borrows How from [100] to prefix unmetrically [here]. Van Dam (1935, p. 96): How…is one of the most common expletives in the Shakespeare texts. Its commonness excludes any convincing evidence that…it is borrowed from [100]. On the generally discredited idea that Q represents a stenographic report of a performance, see .

96 nothing…nothing]
Douce (1807, 2:146) suggests a source in the classical philosophers’ rule nihil ex nihilo fit. See Epicurus, Ep. ad Hdt. 38, Lucretius, De Rer. Nat. 1.149–266. Baldwin (1944, 2:543): From Persius, Sat. 3.84. Kittredge (ed. 1940), Muir (eds. 1952 and rev. 1957), and Fleissner (1968, p. 144) cite contemporary uses of the proverb (see also Tilley N285), and Jorgensen (1954, pp. 208–9) and Elton (1966, pp. 179–90) discuss philosophical, religious, and literary treatments of the idea. Harrison (ed. 1937, rev. 1949) notes its ironic use here: Out of Cordelia’s nothing comes everything in the play. Jorgenson and Soellner (1968, pp. 65–6) argue for Lear’s moral obtuseness: Elizabethans knew that God had created the world and man’s soul from nothing. Fleissner (1962, p. 68 n.): The interpretation without a cause, there can be no effect,…is in complete accord with Christian principles. Elton (op. cit., pp. 179 ff.): Nothing, echoed throughout the play as an ironic refrain, is, in typically Shakespearean analogy, relevant to the individual, the family, the state, and the created universe.…(p. 180) Lear’s expression may…imply that the creation out of nothing which man is will result in nothing, or that man…strives self-destructively to return to his original state.…Cursing the world, Lear wishes it to be annihilated.…(p. 181) Yet nothing…has also a pointed religious irony in the play.…The doctrine ex nihilo. formulated at the Fourth Lateran Council of 1215…was fundamental to providence and other basic articles of faith.…(p. 188) In rejecting creation ex nihilo, Lear was a pious pagan but a skeptical Christian. But of course Lear is talking immediately of his and Cordelia’s human powers only, and Dent (1981) quotes the proverb’s use by Bishop Cranmer. Colie (1966, esp. pp. 219–51) reviews centuries of theological and philosophical discussion of paradoxes inherent in the concept of an existent nothing.

96 can]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 26) thinks F’s will preferable: Can is appropriate [at 663, Sh.’s only other direct use of the proverb] here, for Lear is stating a general truth; but at [96] it is will which is appropriate, for Lear is thinking of the immediate result of Cordelia’s words. Can is the more usual word in contemporary proverbial usage.

97 Vnhappie…am]
Deighton (ed. 1891): It is my unhappiness, misfortune, that.

97–8 I…mouth]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Either I am not ready at expressing by words what I feel at my heart; or else—those sentiments of tenderness and affection which profess to come from the heart, are not confined meerly to my mouth. Hudson (ed. 1871) compares Beaumont & Fletcher, The Maid’s Tragedy 1.1.111, My mouth is much too narrow for my heart. OED (Heart sb. 5): = mind, in the widest sense, including the functions of feeling, volition, and intellect, quoting Cor. 3.1.256–7 (1985–6), his Heart’s his Mouth: What his Brest forges, that his Tongue must vent. Cf. 392. Idem (54c): To wear one’s h. in one’s mouth, to have one’s h. at one’s tongue’s end: to be always ready to speak what is in one’s mind. There are proverbial echoes: see Tilley H331, H334. Greg (1940, p. 389) compares Leir 277–8 (see ), where Cordella says, I cannot paynt my duty forth in words, I hope my deeds shall make report for me. See n. 67. Noble (1935, p. 229) compares Ecclus. 21:26, The heart of fooles is in their mouth: but the mouth of the wise in is their heart; cf. Tilley H312, and M602, compared by Dent (1981). Colie (1974, p. 126) compares 1 John 3:18: My litle children, let vs not loue in worde, nether in tongue onely, but in dede & in trueth (Geneva). Patterson (1984, p. 72), topically: A reproach to James’s claim, in…1604, that his tongue should ever be the trew Messenger of his heart.

98–9 I…lesse]
Rolfe (ed. 1880) compares Holinshed (see ), I haue loued you euer, and will continuallie (while I liue) loue you as my naturall father.…so much as you haue, so much you are worth, and so much I loue you, and no more. Verity (ed. 1897) compares Leir 279–80 (see ): But looke what loue the child doth owe the father, The same to you I beare, my gracious Lord. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) add parallels in Gesta Romanorum, BL Addit. MS 9066 (ed. Herrtage, 1879, p. 49) and in Spenser (see ). Hudson & Black (ed. 1911) think that Higgins, Mirour, is the source for the harsh note in Cordelia’s speech; see . Hammond (1991, p. 101): Cordelia’s intervention is felt to be so disruptive partly because she does not quote her father; she does not allow his mode of speech to prescribe her part for her. She has her own voice, and it does not speak in commonplaces.

98 my…Maiestie]
To make the line scan, Abbott (§468) treats Maiestie as a dissyllable, as does Furness (ed. 1880), who also cites Walker (1854, p. 174). Adams in Irving & Marshall (ed. 1889): The middle syllable is rapidly and lightly pronounced, as in enemy, general. Cf. 140, 159. Alternatively, into my may be read without stress.

99 bond]
Eccles (ed. 1792): What I am bound to by duty. Rann (ed. 1794): As the ties…between child and parent require. Rolfe (ed. 1880) compares AWW 1.3.188 (518), my loue hath in’t a bond. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) compare Higgins, Mirour (rev. 1587, fol. 34r): For nature so doth binde and duty mee compell, | To loue you, as I ought my father, well. Danby (1949, pp. 129 ff., 178) stresses the importance of the word, meaning natural tie, a duty willingly accepted and carried out because it answers to right instinct. Stauffer (1949, p. 195): Here, expressed with more than the severity of Spartan and Stoic, is love, allegiance, responsibility, and faith. Her love is a duty, but it is willingly assumed; it is responsible enough to contemplate future allegiance to a husband, and strong enough to vent its present helplessness in the prim lecture of a schoolmistress. Cordelia’s bond is not the shackles of a slave, but the knitting of human brotherhood realized by her free spirit. Traversi (1952, p. 44): She introduces the central conception of the play. The bond to which she refers is, of course, far more than a legal obligation. Shakespeare’s choice of the family unit for the central theme of his tragedy is in itself significant, because it implies a relationship founded most immediately upon blood, involving the strongest and most obscure instincts of the personality.…The family…is a symbol of ordered living. Joseph (ed. 1966): Unfortunately for Cordelia, the phrase can also be taken…in a grudging, legal sense. Bradbrook (1957, pp. 142–3), improbably, finds reminiscences of the commercial bond in MV. Cf. 438, 983, 1462. Morris (1957, pp. 154–6): Cordelia deliberately insults Lear, mocking his own materialism. Ribner (ed. 1967): In larger terms…the bond of nature, that which links child to father as it links mankind to God, all being part of a great and harmonious cosmic order. Cf. 438, 983, 1462. Salingar (1986, pp. 96–7): The term has a fateful ambiguity; Cordelia tries to press home the sense of a covenant for mutual benefit, and reciprocal but not umlimited obligation, but Lear reacts to the implication of bondage, bond as a fetter of imprisonment. Turner (1988, p. 100): The feudal equivalent of the Roman pietas, a composition of nature and society, affection and duty, prudence and love, religion, custom, value, law and the sense of justice. The Sokols (2000, p. 39): Cordelia states truly that her obligation is sure, although Lear takes her to mean primarily that it is limited.…A proper appreciation of human bonds, what is owed, what is needed, and how much it is proper to demand, is crucially deficient in Lear’s kingdom and family, citing confusions of love and pelf in this episode and at 385.

100 Goe…to]
OED (Go v. 91b): Used in imp. to express disapprobation, remonstrance, protest, or derisive incredulity. Cf. Franz §454, and 621, 1759, 2550. Wells (ed. 2000): Come, come! F’s How, how means approx. the same: Craig (ed. 1901): Expressive of impatience and irritation; see n. 96. Greg (1940, p. 390) compares Leir 285 (see ), Why how now, Minion. F’s change of phrase allows Lear to address Cordelia by name, as he does his other daughters at 58 and 73. This addition is not needed by the audience, since she names herself at 67 and 82; perhaps in F it makes Lear seem sterner than in his earlier our ioy (88). Taylor (1985, pp. 181–2): Here and at 115 and 256 a pruning of the Quarto’s colloquialisms gives an impression of a more titanic Lear. Blake (1996, p. 163), however: It seems likely that the expression go to was regarded as a strong rebuke and [as] belong[ing] to a less formal register. Its omission from F here and at 256 make[s] his condemnation of her much weaker. Van Dam (1935, p. 59): Changed in F to correct the blank verse.

100–1 mend…mar]
Proverbial antithesis noted by OED (Mar v. 3b) and Dent (1981, M875.1). Rolfe (ed. 1880) compares Ven. 478, Luc. 578, Son. 103.10.

102–14 Good…true]
Verity (ed. 1897): Cordelia’s simple style is an intentional contrast to the florid speeches of Goneril and Regan. Orkin (1979, p. 64): The rhetorical symmetries and repetitions of isocolon, epistrophe, polyptoton, and anaphora emphasize the mutuality of a relationship that is shortly to be shattered.

102 Good my Lord]
Abbott (§13): The possessive Adjectives, when unemphatic, are sometimes transposed, being really combined with nouns (like the French monsieur, milord). Clarkes (1879, p. 421): An Italian idiom. Verity (ed. 1897): Perhaps to give emphasis to the adjective. Smith (ed. 1902): Occurs most commonly when the address begins a sentence. Cf. Franz §328, and 112, 128, 1715, 1778, 1782, 1785, 1803, 1934 (F), 1960, 2040, 2093, 2861.

103 begot]
Abbott (§343): Owing to the tendency to drop the inflection -en, the Elizabethan authors frequently used the curtailed forms of past participles…[or] the past tense for the participle. Cf. Franz §§167, 168, and 259, 420, 472, 615, 853, 1236, 1287, 1771, 2496, 2628, 2784, 2892, 3034, 3054. Sh. prefers begot to begotten 27:4.

103 loued]
Doran (1931, p. 51): F’s lou’d is an erroneous contraction.

104 returne]
Hoeniger (ed. 1968): (i) Observe in turn, or (ii) by way of return. Wells (ed. 2000): Pay back, citing OED v.1 21a).

104 those…as]
The earliest editor to comment, Eccles (ed. 1792) correctly takes those to mean such; cf. Franz §340. OED (As adv. [conj., and rel. pron.] 24): The antecedent such is also replaced by that, those, or entirely omitted, leaving as as an ordinary relative pronoun = That, who, which, quoting Rom. 2.1.35–6 (785–6). Schmidt (1874, As) gives other exx.; cf. 588. Alternate interpretations are more doubtful. Abbott §384, followed by Craig (ed. 1901) and Lee (ed. 1908): An ellipsis: Return those duties back as (they) are most fit (to be returned). Moberly (ed. 1876): Are is used by attraction to the word duties and the phrase means as is right fit.

104 right]
Schmidt (1875): Most. OED (adv. 5): Precisely, exactly, just, quite, altogether, to the full.

105 Obey…honour]
Supporting Malone (ed. 1790), Perrett (1904, pp. 123, 239) suspects the influence of Camden’s account (Remaines, 1605; see ) of the Wessex king Ina, which includes in it a passage from Gen. 2:24 similar in language; see n. 106–110+1. Carter (1905, p. 432) compares Eph. 5:23, 6:1–2. Baldwin (1943, pp. 174–5): [Richard] Savage and [Edgar I.] Fripp [Minutes and Accounts, 1921–9, 3:xxviii] think this is from the Catechism. It certainly echoes the fifth commandment in some form. The Little Catechism in commenting upon the duty to honour one’s father and mother rephrases as To looue, honor, & succor my Father and Mother.…[Dean Alexander Nowell’s Latin commentary] puts obey in the forefront as does Cordelia. Milward (1987, p. 160): Cf. Exod. 20:12, Deut. 5:16. Danby (1949, p. 130): Cordelia’s Obey you, love you,…honour you alludes to the marriage vow, which she devastatingly reminds her married sisters of in the lines immediately following. In the marriage service in the Book of Common Prayer (1559 ed.) the woman is asked, Wilt thou obey hym and serue hym, loue, honour, and kepe him, in sycknes and in health? And forsakynge al other, kepe the onely to him. Joseph (ed. 1966): The language echoes both the Marriage Service and Fourth Commandment; Cordelia points out that a daughter should most honour her father, and that once married she cannot love and obey him to the same extent. Rosenberg (1972, p. 58): She virtually offers Lear the marriage pledge…then halves it. Cordelia’s language may suggest that the loves due to father and husband are similar; but she is quick to point out that one cannot exclude the other as her sisters seem to promise. Critics who think that Lear’s love for Cordelia is incestuous speak of this scene as a failed marriage ritual or nullified wedding ceremony: see Barber (1980, pp. 197–8), Boose (1982, p. 333). Adelman (1992, p. 118): She seems willing to cuckold [her father] by choosing a husband in place of him.

105 most]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Above all men; not in contrast with the measure of her obedience and love. But it may be simply an intensive superlative. OED (adv. 1): In the greatest degree; to the greatest extent. So Moberly (ed. 1876): Most highly.

106–110+1 Why…all]
Steevens (ed. 1773): In a passage substituted in Mirour in 1587 (fol. 34), Cordelia promises To loue you as I ought my father, well. | Yet shortely I may chaunce, if Fortune will, | To finde in heart to beare another more good will. | Thus much I sayd of nuptiall loues that ment; in the 1574 ed. she says simply, We loue you chiefly for the goodes you haue (see ). Kittredge (ed. 1936, p. 1196; ed. 1940, p. xii): But this is a very natural reflection, i.e., not owing to any source, comparing Oth. 1.3.180–9 (527–36). Perrett (1904, p. 78): Polydore Vergil’s Anglicae Historiae (1st ed., Basel 1534, §55) first alludes to the love she will bear towards her future husband; (p. 124): the incident in Mirour (1587) was re-written with the help of P[olydore] V[ergil]. The English tr. An abridgement of the notable woorke of P. Vergile (1546; ed. Ellis, 1846) is faithful to the 1st ed. concerning Leir. Bishop Percy (in Steevens, ed. 1778, 9:349) identifies the story of Ina, king of the West Saxons, in William Camden’s Remaines (1605), as the source for Lr., and Malone (ed. 1790) thinks it the source for Cordelia’s reply here; others are skeptical; see . Bullough (1973, p. 274): Camden is using Polydore Vergil’s assertion that the good daughter would love her husband more than her father. That assertion is as follows: That shee didd allwayse carrie her father in her ies, and showlde doe while she lived, albeit afterward it mighte chaunce her to loove an other more ardentlie, meaninge therin her housbond; with the which aunswere (albeit it was sharpe and wittee) Leir was…angree (Polydore Vergil, English History, anon. tr. 1546; ed. Henry Ellis, 1846, p. 36). Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) improbably suspect that Camden’s story may borrow its phraseology from Lr., performed by 1606 but not published until 1608. Greg (1940, p. 389) compares Leir 269–70 (see ), only remotely similar. Milward (1987, p. 161): Cordelia recalls the ideal of marriage, as stated in [Gen. 2:24, Matt. 19:5, Eph. 5:31].
Smith (ed. 1902): The prevailing note of her character is simplicity and truth. Bradley (1904, p. 320–1): But truth is not the only good in the world, nor is the obligation to tell truth the only obligation. The matter here was to keep it inviolate, but also to preserve a father. And even if truth were the one and only obligation, to tell much less than truth is not to tell it. And Cordelia’s speech not only tells much less than truth about her love, it actually perverts the truth when it implies that to give love to a husband is to take it from a father. There surely never was a more unhappy speech. Kinney (1976, p. 679): Cordelia, given her turn at the proper place, insists on the language of reality rather than the language of pageantry, insists on a vocabulary borrowed from Kent and Gloucester rather than that provided by her father and sisters. Avery (1998, p. 53): In their questions, analysis, and logic…Cordelia’s sentences defy the grammar of ritual.

107, 110+1 all]
Wright (ed. 1875): Altogether (OED, adv. 2). Cf. Abbott §28, Franz §371, and 712.

107, 110+1 Happely]
Both this and F Happily are variant forms of Haply. OED (Haply adv.): By hap,…perchance. Halio (ed. 1992): F’s spelling…suggests a possible pun; Q’s spelling happely, a variant of happily, could do so as well. Weis (ed. 1993) suggests another: Appropriately (OED, Happily adv. 3). Stone (1980, p. 224): It cannot mean fortunately.

108 hand]
Weis (ed. 1993): In the formal clasping of hands at the marriage ceremony.

108 Must]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Is destined to. But it may mean simply will, or must perforce if he is to wed me.

108 plight]
Capell (1774, 1.1:51): Troth-plight. OED (sb.1 3): Pledge. Rolfe (ed. 1880): The only instance of the noun in this sense in S., though the verb…occurs several times. Weis (ed. 1993): Also suggests…her circumstances, good or bad.

109 halfe my loue]
Donnelly (1955, p. 153): This phrase produces Lear’s reaction—it is total, and therefore incestuous, love that he wants from her. Without arguing the therefore, one may ascribe Lear’s rage at least partly to Cordelia’s continued public defiance of his wishes and to the clear implication in this speech that her sisters’ professions, which have pleased him so much, must be specious.

109 care]
Crook (ed. 1907): I.e., care for him.

110+1 to…all]
Om. from F. Pope (ed. 1725) restored it, without which the sense was not compleat. Delius (ed. 1854): Possibly Sh. struck it as needless repetition of what had been said. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 166): Doubtless these words in Q are authentic. They complete the sense of the speech admirably. The F compositor has been guilty of a careless omission, due to eye-skip. Rosenberg (1972, p. 62): Only this one time [in this dialogue] does Cordelia allow herself a familiar word of relationship. Father. If the Quarto line is left out, the speech has a loaded sting aimed at sisters and brothers-in-law.…It could be aimed at marriage itself; it could be a cue of love for Lear…that he misses. Brown (ed. 1976): Incomplete verse-lines indicate silences. Taylor (1983, p. 87): By leaving the insult undefined, F implies a tougher, harsher Cordelia. Bevington (1987, p. 509): The F reading [is] strained, almost absurd and contradictory. Halio (ed. 1992): The omission…may have been the result of revision, eliminating a redundancy from lines [106–7] (and an irregular half-line).
