Foakes (1993, p. 185): F removes the scornful second line…but still Cordelia’s response remains…untender. Jones (1995, p. 171): Q end[s] strongly, with a punch line; F has lost Quarto’s clinching effect.

111 goes]
The general meaning is To take a specified course (OED, v. 5); more particularly, To act…in accordance or harmony with (OED, 5), and possibly Of…language…: To have a specified tenor (OED, 16, quoting Mac. 1.3.87 [190] as its first ex.). Deighton (ed. 1891): Are these the real feelings of your heart, not merely words? Brown (ed. 1976): Agrees.

111 this…heart]
The F inversion thy heart with this means virtually the same. Malone (ed. 1790): The change in F to the more common form was made from ignorance of his meaning and phraseology…in the playhouse copies after his retirement from the theatre. For heart see n. 75. King (apud Halio, ed. 1992), suspects a pun on Cordelia’s name, citing refs. to [Lear’s own] heart in 122 and 134; see DP.

112 good my]
F inverts. See n. 102. F makes the opposite inversion at 1934.

113 vntender]
OED (a. 1): Ungentle, unkind, quoting this l. as its first ex. Wells (ed. 2000): Shakespeare coined 93 latinate words beginning in un-, citing Garner (1982, pp. 165–6). Malone (ed. 1790) compares Ven. 187, young, and so vnkinde. Joseph (ed. 1966): Also stiff, unbending; unattested in OED; see next n. Gardner (ed. 1969): Pun on tender meaning young (OED, 4).

114 So…true]
Tennyson (apud H. Tennyson, 1897, 2:290) found this line one of three repartees in Shakespeare which always bring tears to my eyes from their simplicity. Granville-Barker (1927, pp. 188–9): Being young, she answers uncalculatingly with pride to his pride.…To miss this likeness between the two is to miss Shakespeare’s first important dramatic effect. Leech (1950, p. 63): We have a passage approaching stichomythia:…the employment of broken lines removes the appearance of a prepared device. Joseph (ed. 1966), true: (i) Not lying, faithful; (ii) straight, not twisting. Foakes (ed. 1997): Loyal, virtuous, and speaking the truth.

115–27 Well…daughter]
Dr. Bucknill (1859, p. 139): This speech shows that Lear’s mind is unbalanced from the beginning: It is madness or it is nothing. Not, indeed, raving, incoherent, formed mania, as it subsequently displays itself; but exaggerated passion, perverted affection, enfeebled judgment. Verity (ed. 1897) finds only wild impulsiveness that borders on insanity; Smith (ed. 1902), merely wounded vanity and anger; Goggin (ed. 1910), passion and lack of thought that increase with opposition, as his banishment of Kent shows. Johnson (1975, pp. 151–6): The less formal thous and thees in the speech show the doting father subconsciously unable to let go the daughter he is cursing. Perhaps similarly, Henry uses the same pronouns in condemning Scroop in H5 2.2.94 (723) ff., with whom he had formerly been close, a bedfellow (4.2.8; 635).

115 Well]
F’s omission makes somewhat more regular verse, though van Dam (1935, p. 59) finds the Q line faultless.

115 thy…dower]
Craig (ed. 1901) compares TGV 3.1.78 (1147), Then let her beauty be her wedding dowre. On the legal meaning of dower see n. 49. In claiming that Lear is violating the spirit of inheritance law, Hawley (1998, p. 68) seems to confuse dower and dowry.

116–18 Sunne…Heccat…orbs]
Capell (1783, 1.2:142): The oaths given to Lear…are admirable for their solemnity, and are taken from out the creed of his times as fables have given it:…so that as well his Hecate here, as his Apollo [see 172 and n.] and Jupiter [192] afterwards, are consonant to his imputed religion. Moberly (ed. 1876): The Druidical gods are, according to Cæsar (Bell. Gall. vi. 17), Apollo, Mars, Jove, and Minerva. Lear’s two oaths, by Apollo and Jupiter, are therefore historically accurate; so is his swearing by Night, as (c. 18) Galli se omnes ab Dite patre prognatos prædicant, and by Hecate, as a temple of Diana once occupied the place of the present St. Paul’s in London. (Palgrave’s Anglo-Saxons, p. 51). Perrett (1904, p. 248): To this list Harrison, in Holinshed (1577, pt. 1, ch. 8, fols. 8–8v; 1587, p. 1, ch. 9, 1:22) adds Dis, Saturn, Mercury, Diana, and Hercules as gods worshipped under Britain’s founder Brute. Kittredge (ed. 1940) quotes Ovid, Meta. 7.94–7, on the worship of Hecate, and Elton (1966, pp. 173–6) offers many possible Elizabethan sources for Sh.’s knowledge of pagan worship of classical gods and heavenly bodies. Kranz (1938, p. 37) compares the invocation of several gods in Seneca, Oed. 248 ff.

116–18 by…Sunne]
Horsman (ed. 1973) compares Leir 516 (see ): Vpon the radiant splendor of the Sunne—there descriptive, not an oath.

117 mistresse]
The Q reading makes poor sense, and F’s miseries is hardly better. Only Baldini (1966, 1:167) explains Q: The mistress (padrona) of Hecate can only be the moon. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905), as usual, defend F: Hecate, as goddess of night and death and the underworld, is acquainted with grief. Colman (ed. 1982), without explanation: F makes sense. Daniel (facs. 1885, p. xx): I suppose the scribe preparing the Qo. for the Fo. edition struck out the end of this word and inserted eries in the margin; perhaps the stroke of his pen included the t, or the printer thought it did, and so, instead of misteries, miseries got into the Fo. Doran (1931, p. 98): It is equally probable, however, that the word was badly written in the manuscript and that both the printer of Q1 and the [playbook’s] transcriber made of it what they could. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 360): Q’s mistresse might be either a mishearing or a misreading of misteries. The reading almost universally adopted is F2’s mysteries, a totally unauthorized guess by the F2 editor that makes a certain sense—secret rites (Kittredge, ed. 1940; OED, sb. 3)—but seems something of a non-sequitur, since Lear is naming a series of heavenly bodies—sun, moon, other orbs—and their powers. For that reason van Dam (1935, p. 50), arguing that Hecate’s secrets (or sorceries) converts this list to a strange potpourri and illogical medley, suggests the meaning [the moon’s] ministries, functions (OED, sb.2 1). No one has suggested mistiness, meaning dimness, obscurity (OED), which differs from mistress by only a minim or two and so could be easily misread, and which makes a clear contrast to radience. The word had been used since the 14th c., and though Sh. does not use it elsewhere, he several times associates mist and misty with night and darkness, as in misty night (Luc. 356) and vast obscuritie or mistie vale (Tit. 5.2.36; 2322). It is harder to imagine, however, how F’s miseries could be a misreading of the word, unless in MS it were spelt mistines.

117 Heccat]
Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): A triple deity—called Phœbë, or the Moon, in heaven; Diana on the earth; and Hecate or Proserpine in the under-world. Root (1903, p. 54): Her connection with witchcraft, though found in many Latin authors (notably Seneca, Medea), is perhaps to be traced to the incantation of Medea in Met. 7.1–293; cf. n. 973. Brower (1971, p. 385) compares in particular Jason’s invocation in Golding’s 1567 tr. of Met. 7.136–7, By triple Hecates holie rites, and by what other power So euer else had residence within that secret bower. Hunter (ed. 1972): Following…sun, and preceding the orbs, this may refer to Hecat—more properly Hecatè—as the moon; but mysteries suggests the Hecat who presides over witchcraft. Edwards (ed. 1975): Goddess of the world of spirits. The QF spelling indicates a dissyllable, as usual in Sh.

117 might]
All eds. accept F’s correction to night. Root (1903, p. 55): Sh. elsewhere us[es] the name Hecate as equivalent with Night, comparing Mac. 3.2.41 (1199) and MND 5.1.384 (2167). Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 511): Q could be defended—the mysteries and the might of Hecate—but the construction would be awkward; the proposed easy misreading produces more natural syntax and a more explicit contrast with the sun. Van Dam (1935, p. 50) does so defend Q (see prev. n.), emending to her might: At Hamlet iv,7,174 [3166] the F has the same misprint the for her.…A tautological misprint is possible too: The mistresse…the might. Weis (ed. 1993), forcing syntax: That power, through the astrological influence of the planets.

118 all]
In effect this word may modify orbs: the operation of sun, moon, and all the other orbs.

118 operation]
Delius (ed. 1854): The influence upon the life or death of mortals (Ger.), an astrological reference that Wright (ed. 1875) finds in keeping with the speech of Edmund [469 ff.] in the next scene. Craig (ed. 1901) cites Ant. 2.7.27 (1364), where the word means benign agency (OED, sb. 2).

118 orbs]
Tovey (ed. 1896): The planets. But sun and moon may be included. Hulme (1962, pp. 175–6): Associations with sight and wheels may…have conveyed a sense of order and of retribution consistent with the appearance of these images elsewhere in the play, citing 3130–6.

119 From]
Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): By or by means of. OED (prep. 10): Indicating a place or position where action or motion is originated; (11): Indicating a person as a more or less distant source of action. Cf. Franz §485. See next n.

119 whome]
Abbott (§264): Who is used of inanimate objects regarded as persons. Cf. Franz §335, and 385, 2347+14, +17. The heavenly orbs, one of them addressed as a goddess, are identified with their governing divinities.

120–269 Heere…firme]
Williamson (1963, pp. 56–8): Lear explodes in a rhetoric of a new quality.…The singular forms I, me, my appear and persist for the unrehearsed part of the scene…until Cordelia’s share of the kingdom has been redistributed, and Lear can proceed…as originally planned.

120 paternall]
OED’s first instance of the adjective. Cf. Leir 314 (see ): Call not me father.

120 care]
Care for her; cf. n. 109.

121 Propinquitie]
Schmidt (1875): Nearness of blood, kindred (OED, b). Sh.’s only use of the word. It is found in Harsnett’s Declaration (1603, p. 143). Deighton (ed. 1891) compares R2 1.1.119 (124), Such neighbour neerenes to our sacred bloud.

121 property]
Delius (ed. 1854): Blood-community. Schmidt (1875): Ownership (OED, sb. 1). Wright (ed. 1875): Identity. Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Literally, Ownness of blood. Tovey (ed. 1896): Lear disowns Cordelia. Some eds. treat the singular noun as a plural: Bald (ed. 1949): Rights pertaining to; Weis (ed. 1993): Distinguishing characteristics of blood-kinship. Foakes (ed. 1997): Rights of possession or disposal due by their blood relationship.

121 blood]
OED (sb. 8): Popularly treated as the typical part of the body which children inherit from their parents and ancestors; (9) Hence, Blood-relationship, and esp. parentage. Cf. 1515, 1923, 1947, 1993.

122 heart]
OED (sb. 10): The seat of love or affection. Cf. 134, 1875.

123 this]
Steevens (ed. 1773) and most eds.: This time. Cf. 2485. Quinn (ed. 1970), alternatively: (1) i.e., from my crown; or (2) i.e., from my heart. Foakes (ed. 1997): Or the map?

123 barbarous Scythyan]
Abbott (§468): Both dissyllables. The cruelty and barbarity of the tribes of southern Russia were proverbial. Wright (ed. 1875) cites Purchas, Pilgrimage (1614, p. 396), and Rolfe (ed. 1880), Tit. 1.1.131 (154), Was neuer Sythia halfe so barbarous. Wells (ed. 2000): In Marlowe’s Tamburlaine Scythians are twice called barbarous, citing Pt. 1 3.3.271, Pt. 2 3.4.19. Their cannibalism is referred to in Herodotus 4.18 and Montaigne (tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 1:223) (cited by Moberly, ed. 1876), Harrison’s Description, pt. 1, ch. 4 (in Holinshed, 1587, 1:5–6; cited by Perrett, 1904, p. 292), and elsewhere; see n. 124. Hankins (1978, p. 177) compares Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 7.5.2. Doloff (1994, p. 493): Sextus Empiricus’s Outlines of Pyrrhonism (tr. ca. 1591 lost) reports that Scythians cut their fathers’ throats when over the age of sixty. Halio (ed. 1992): According to Harrison [loc. cit.]…the ancient Scots were of mixed Scythian and Spanish blood—a fact that does not seem relevant here.

124 generation]
Though this word is often glossed as children (Capell, 1783, 1.2:142) or offspring (Wright, ed. 1875; OED, sb. 3, quoting this l.), its more probable meaning here is kind (Hudson, ed. 1879) or family (OED, 6), including forebears—senses making a slightly better parallel with the actual parent-child situation that Lear sees (Hunter, ed. 1972). Staunton (MS notes, 1864–74): Herodotus [4.18] relates that the Scythians eat their aged and impotent relatives.…Compare Byron’s Tragedy, by Chapman, Act IV [4.2.126, 132]…To teach…The Scythians to inter, not eate their Parents. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) quote an account from ch. 11 of The Fardle of Facions (1555) of the Scythians’ eating aged friendes…and kindesfolke. Salingar (1983, p. 166) suggests a source in Montaigne, who refers to cannibals eating their fathers; see . Craig (ed. 1901) points out that Sh. uses progeny to mean ancestors in Cor. 1.8.12 (737). Traversi (1952, p. 46): Pregnant with meaning for Lear’s own future. Joseph (ed. 1966): Lear is most likely to find what he detests most in the thought of those who eat their parents. Velz (1989, p. 179): Here is a context of family malice are the familicide and the cannibalism of Ovid [Meta. 1.144 ff., Lycaon], combined as in Titus. Some feminist critics specify feeding on a potential mother. Asp (1986, p. 195), followed by Callaghan (1989, p. 115): Lear devours his own grandchildren. Adelman (1992, p. 305): This image may be understood as derivative from Lear’s infantile desire to feed on Cordelia-as-mother.

124 Messes]
White (ed. 1883): Food (OED, sb. 1).

125 gorge]
OED (v. 2): Glut, quoting this l.

125 to my bosome]
Deighton (ed. 1891): To my heart. OED (sb. 6): Fig. The breast considered as the seat of thoughts and feelings. Cf. Heart. Cf. 297, 1069, 2413, 2859+2–+3, 2992. Wright (ed. 1875): The lack of these words in Q reliev[es] the construction at the expense of the metre. Certainly they are not necessary to the sense, and do not fit with two of the three participles, pittyed and relieued. Presumably they are added in F to make explicit what is already implied, that Lear’s predictions are not general but state his personal intentions. The meter would be passable without them if Q divided the line after bee. Wells (ed. 2000) thinks be as is elided, invoking Cercignani (1981, p. 291), who does not cite this ex.

126 neighbour’d]
OED (v. 6b): Placed near to, quoting this l. Crook (ed. 1907): Made welcome as neighbors are. Kittredge (ed. 1940): As closely hugged to my breast; as dearly loved. Weis (ed. 1993): Helped in time of need.

126 pittyed]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): I.e., as well (as much) pitied.

126 relieued]
Harrison (ed. 1948): Helped in distress (OED, v. 1).

127 sometime]
Schmidt (1875): Former (OED, a. 2f).

128 Good my Liege]
On the transposed adjective see n. 102.

129–30 Peace…wrath]
Hubler (1935, p. 434): The [Q1] compositor has set up the half line with which the speech begins and the following line as one line. Brown (ed. 1976): Peace, Kent! is followed by a silence in which no one onstage will move.

130 Dragon]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Lear would wear a helmet like Arthur’s [and his father, Uther Pendragon’s] with a [Welsh] dragon crest symbolizing Britain. Craig (ed. 1901): Possibly, but Shakespeare refers to the dragon often as the emblem of savage ferocity, citing Jn. 2.1.68 (362), R3 5.3.350 (3822), Cor. 4.7.23 (3114). Elliott (1959, p. 263): Suggests Satan, governing Lear by pride and wrath. Fraser (1962, p. 93): Like man in general, an ambiguous and manifold emblem: the chief of creatures and the sum of all ill. Elton (1966, p. 192 n.): Symbol of the king, borne by the Tudors Henry VIII and Elizabeth; he cites Henry Peacham, Minerva Britanna (1612, p. 30).

130 his]
Perhaps meaning its; see n. 727.

130 wrath]
Most commentators follow Capell (1783, 1.2:142): His wrath’s object, i.e. Cordelia. Rolfe (ed. 1880): By metonymy. But Koppel (1899, p. 19) understands literally the wrath that Lear is struggling with, and in support Dubislav (1916) cites Ham. 3.4.112 (2493), O step betweene her, and her fighting soule. Similarly Maxwell (apud Muir, ed. 1952): Lear’s wrath [is] an extension of his personality…his union with which must remain intact if he himself is to hold together, comparing 183–4. Joseph (ed. 1966): (i) Do not try to deprive the dragon of his anger; (ii) do not attempt to insert yourself between the dragon and the object of his anger. In each case there is the implication that whoever does so will himself become the target. Gardner (ed. 1969): Fulfilment of his wrath. Halio (ed. 1973): Perhaps simply a property of [the dragon’s] fierceness, not its object.

131–2 I…nurcery]
Bradley (1904, p. 250): Part of the absurdity of Lear’s plan is taken to be his idea of living with his three daughters in turn. But he never meant to do this. He meant to live with Cordelia, and with her alone. Wilson (ed. 1960): Her refusal to bid for her portion forces him to adopt the plan of living in turn with Gon. and Reg. The assumption that nursery involves Lear’s living with Cordelia opens difficult questions of whether she might live together with her husband on the continent or he with her in Britain, whether the intended husband is France or Burgundy or neither, and even whether Lear intends her to have a husband at all; see Lusardi & Schlueter (1991, pp. 24–31) and nn. 37 and 41. Perhaps inevitably, psychoanalytic critics find Lear’s remark evidence of his frustrated desire for his daughter both as object of sexual desire and as substitute mother; see, e.g., Holland (1966, p. 343), Chaplin (1969, p. 32), Boose (1982, p. 334), Kahn (1986, pp. 39–40). Though Foakes (ed. 1997, pp. 60–1) seems inclined to agree, he points out that Gloucester speaks as affectionately of Edgar (427+2), and that both parents react similarly, love for a favourite turning to hatred: It was proverbial that the greatest hate proceeds from the greatest love, citing Tilley H210. The play give no clue where Lear expects her to reside, married or disinherited.

131 lou’d her most]
Like Geoffrey, Holinshed records this preference, as Malone (ed. 1790) notes. See n. 53–8 and , .

131 set my rest]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Mak[e] a particular spot a resting place (OED, Rest sb.1 5: Place of resting or residing; residence, abode, citing Ham. 2.2.13 [1033]). The common phrase to set (up) one’s rest (Dent, 1981, R86.1) had several figurative meanings, including To take up one’s (permanent) abode (OED, sb2 7f, citing Lodge’s Rosalynde, source for AYL). But Cordelia’s kind nurcery can only figuratively be a place. Many have followed Hunter (ed. 1869): The rest [in primero] was the highest stake a person was able or disposed to venture [OED, sb.2 6]; and to set up one’s rest was to determine what one should stake. Wright (ed. 1875): Metaphorically,…to stake one’s all (OED, sb.2: To set one’s final hope or trust upon or in something). Tovey objects that Lear does not use the expression with any notion of hazard. Others follow Rolfe (ed. 1880) in finding a quibble on repose (OED, sb.1 3), citing Rom. 5.3.110 [2967], set vp my euerlasting rest (though there the meaning may be resting place). Craig (ed. 1901) provides examples of such a quibble in other authors. Similarly Kittredge (ed. 1940): To rely with confidence and to the full, with also a suggestion of the repose to which Lear looks forward. The phrase could also mean figuratively To be resolved or determined (OED, sb.2 7c, citing Err. 4.3.27 [1210] and MV 2.2.103 [665]) or To…settle upon,…to place one’s whole aim or end in, something (OED, sb.2 7d), senses quite possible though the former is somewhat redundant after thought. Thus Wilson (ed. 1960): Commit myself finally to.

132 kind]
In many of its appearances in the play this word adds to its usual meanings of benevolent, affectionate, generous, etc. the root meaning birth, origin, nature (OED, sb. 1–6) and so implies behavior that is natural by reason of kinship (OED, a. 1–3). Cf. 285, 825, 1324, 1852, 2560, 2780, and, for (un)kindness, 589, 599, 1413, 1671, 2347+43. Coursen (1976, pp. 270–2) shows the range of meanings in the play. Hunter (ed. 1972, p. 33): The family is (in this play and elsewhere) the model of the nation, and the nation the model of the kind or species: at each level survival depends on kindness.

132 nurcery]
Wright (ed. 1875): Nursing (OED, 1, quoting this l.); cf. Franz §670. Verity (ed. 1897): Tender care. Elliott (1959, p. 255): Gardening.…Lear is thinking of his land’s future. OED, 4, however, attests to the place but not the practice of gardening. Jorgensen (1967, p. 129): Lear wants…solicitous cherishing.…Cordelia had signified for him, not sexuality, but comfort. Like Novy (1984, p. 152), Dreher (1986, p. 65), and Kahn (1986, pp. 39–40), Adelman (1992, pp. 116–17): Lear would make his daughters his mothers, deliberately putting himself in the position of infantile need.…Imagining himself an infant sleeping at her breast, he revisions [death] as plenitude. Lear never expresses such imaginings, and an aged man may need a nurse’s care without being, or being thought, infantile. Wells (ed. 2000); Natural care, as from a mother. Though the primary meaning of the word refers to the care and upbringing of children, it could suggest other kinds of nurture, as in gardening and medicine. Cf. Nurse-keeper, A sick-nurse (OED, 1st ex. 1602).

132 hence…sight?]
Lear has been addressing Kent; many eds. think he now addresses Cordelia. The arguments for each are:
(1)Kent. Heath (1765, p. 315): In the next words Lear sends for France and Burgundy, in order to tender them his youngest daughter, who must therefore be present. Delius (ed. 1854): Lear addresses Kent directly but speaks of Cordelia before and after this in the third person. Dyce (ed. 1857): Lear repeats the order to Kent at 169. White (ed. 1862): Although Kent has merely broken in with Good, my liege, Lear is choleric and unreasonable enough to hound him from his presence upon such slight provocation. Hudson (ed. 1871): Perhaps…Lear anticipates remonstrance from Kent. Goggin (ed. 1910): Kent falls back, but comes forward again at [148].
(2)Cordelia. Jennens (ed. 1770): Cordelia, not Kent, has raised his fury to the highest pitch. Lear only gradually becomes enraged at Kent’s persistently repeated opposition, until he banishes him at 189. Malone (ed. 1790): Lear is capable of the quick transition or inconsistency of ordering Cordelia out and then calling in her suitors to face her. Wright (ed. 1875): After the king in reply to Kent’s interruption had justified his conduct he could scarcely order him from his sight. Rolfe (ed. 1880): Cordelia would perhaps be no more likely [than Kent at 170] to leave at the first impatient word of her father. Tovey (ed. 1896): Cordelia…remains…distressed and anxious, on the stage, while her father, who turns away from her, has time to forget that he had dismissed her. Verity (ed. 1897): Speaking of her [in 131–2] Lear might well look towards her, and so break out into a passing expression of disgust. Perrett (1904, p. 44): In Layamon’s Brut 3079 ff. the king passing sentence on his daughter gives a similar order yet continues to address her. Hunter (ed. 1972): She does not obey, and Lear accepts this.
Lear has been addressing Kent, and only surmise supports the claims that Lear is at the highest pitch of fury, and in rage dismisses Kent from the court or stage. Neither Kent nor Cordelia leaves the stage. The speech may mean simply Stand aside, Kent, out of my immediate line of sight; do not intrude here, in the business before me.
Uniquely, Koppel (1899, p. 21) imagines the remark directed at Albany and other courtiers who in the foreground step protectively beween Lear and Cordelia.

132 hence]
OED (adv. 2): Go hence, depart; but alternately, (Away) from here,…to a distance (adv. 1). Cf. 2684.

132 auoide]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Leave—not, keep out of (OED, v. 7). Either meaning is possible.

133 So…as]
Moberly (ed. 1876): May I rest in my grave only on condition [that]. Deighton (ed. 1891): May I find peace in my grave as surely as. Foakes (ed. 1997): May my rest in the grave be peaceful in as much as. Or possibly, Thus let my grave (rather than her nursery) be my peace (rest), since. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 163): The trend of the action is clearly foreshadowed.

133–4 giue…from]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Deprive someone of something. Though OED does not attest the phrase, see Give (v. 4), Assign…ownership, and From (prep. 6), Denoting removal,…privation. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Take away from and give to others. Edwards (ed. 1975): This curious phrase is a carry-over from Lear’s intention to give away his daughter in marriage. For heart see n. 122.

134 who stirres?]
Delius (ed. 1854): A threat to intimidate any chance opposition. Moberly (ed. 1876): The courtiers seem unwilling to obey. Furness (ed. 1880), more probably: The circle of courtiers are so horror-struck at Lear’s outburst of fury, and at Cordelia’s sudden and impending doom, that they stand motionless. Deighton (ed. 1891): What, does nobody stir? Frost (ed. 1909): Lear is so impetuous that he hardly gives time for his attendants to hear his orders before he browbeats them for not executing them. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Merely a form of impatient command:…be quick about it, somebody!

136 digest]
Rann (ed. 1794), figuratively: Possess, enjoy; supported by Schmidt (1874). Wright (ed. 1875): Incorporate. Coleridge (MS notes, 1808–19): Digerere, i.e. bear off between you, or blend into your former portions this third. The metaphor is taken from pharmacy. Brown (ed. 1976): Absorb. More literally, White (ed. 1862): Break it up, divide, dissolve; Frost (ed. 1909): L. digero, digestus, to carry asunder, dissolve (OED, v. 1). In Mirour, Cordila complains, Leire divided his kingdom between Albany and Cornwall, But nought at all, hee gaue of dowry mee; see .

136 this]
Foakes (ed. 1997), comparing these (68) and this (86): Lear may again point to or hand over part of the map; [F’s the] may be a casual slip.

137 pride]
Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956): Lear considers that Cordelia is too arrogant to offer adequate expressions of love.

137 she cals]
Bradley (1904, p. 321): As a matter of fact, Cordelia has said nothing about plainness.

137 plainnes]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Candour, outspoken honesty (OED, 2). Cf. 158, 1176. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Self-confidence. Muir & Danby (1950, p. 51): In Sidney’s Arcadia 1.4.2, 5 [Feuillerat, 1.26, 29], Basilius interprets Dametas’s rude simplicitie as simple plainnesse. Hulme (1962, p. 75) detects a proverbial echo, citing Tilley P384.

137 marrie her]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Get her a husband. Gardner (ed. 1969): Be her marriage dowry. Verity (ed. 1897): Since she will have no other dower. Horsman (ed. 1973): Give her, with a dowry, in marriage.

138 inuest]
OED (v. 5): To establish (a person) in the possession of any office, position, property, etc. Cf. n. 54. Wells (ed. 2000): The Q reading makes invest less metaphorical: wrap you in. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): In the preceding Lear stories, Lear’s abdication was forced upon him after having designated what his daughters’ dowries should be after his death, as Holinshed puts it (see ). Like Perrett (see n. 42–3), Draper (1937, pp. 181–2): In the final division, the two realms of Goneril and Regan must roughly have corresponded to England and to Scotland. The titles of the respective husbands bear this out, Cornwall and Albany. Cornwall in ancient times was more extensive than the modern shire; and…Cornwall’s capital is the city of Gloucester in the south-central section of the island. Albany then, apparently received the northern half of Britain;…he was already duke of ancient Albany, the region north of the Firths of Clyde and Forth. The exact division must remain speculative; if Cordelia’s intended portion was to the southeast (see n. 42–3), it could not easily be assimilated into the nothern and southern kingdoms that Draper imagines, but would fall entirely into the southern one.

138 in]
Craig (ed. 1901) prefers this to F with, for Shakespeare, though he has once the expression invest with [2H4 4.5.73 (2627)], uses invest in three times.

139 Preheminence]
Harrison (ed. 1948): Authority (OED, 1; The h in obs. spelling was inserted to avoid hiatus).

139 large]
Delius (ed. 1854): Resplendent, rich. Deighton (ed. 1891): Manifold. Lee (ed. 1908): Spacious. Tovey (ed. 1896): Ample. Schmidt (1874), most accurately: Great, considerable.

139 effects]
Delius (ed. 1854): Attributes. Verity (ed. 1897): Manifestations of power. OED (sb. 3): Sign, token. Cf. 1463. Wells (ed. 2000): Accompaniments.

140 troope with]
Delius (ed. 1854): Form its train. OED (v. 2b): To associate with, quoting Rom. 1.5.48 (621) and this l. as first exx. Hunter (ed. 1972): Also, all that results from.

140 Maiestie]
On the scansion see n. 98.

140 our selfe]
Royal we. Wright (ed. 1875) compares R2 1.4.42 (616), and Schmidt (1875) gives eight other such uses in Sh.

140 by…course]
OED (Course sb. 33b): By turns. The plan of monthly alternation is not found in the sources, though Perrett (1904, p. 188) finds analogues in other texts. In Leir 555 (see ) the king decides to soiorne with my sonne of Cornwall, who is chosen husband of Gonorill.

141 With reseruation]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Reserving to myself as a body-guard. Craig (ed. 1901): Drawn from the language of law, and means [with] a saving clause. OED (3): The action or fact of reserving…some right, power, privilege, etc.; a right, etc., thus reserved, quoting 1550.

141 hundred]
Hudson & Black (ed. 1911, p. xxvii): The only Elizabethan writer who revives the retinue incident…is Higgins in Mirour, where Leire keeps sixty Knights (in ed. 1587, fol. 35r; in 1574, threscore knightes & squires; see , and cf. 750) as in Geoffrey’s account (see ). Perrett (1904, pp. 186–9) explains that the number was reduced to forty in some intervening accounts owing to a common scribal confusion of .XL. and .LX., and adds, In Sh. alone Lear makes the reservation himself, and the number is rounded off to a hundred, a number not found in any source. In Malory a character who appears in the story of King Arthur and other tales, Sir Barraunte Le Apres, is called The King with the Hundred Knights, but there is no evidence that Sh. knew of him. Probably he simply chose a common round number; cf. 2356, centurie. On the knights’ squires see n. 750. Wells (ed. 2000): They are a hundred knights plus their servants, citing Sinden (1980).
The knights might serve Lear practically as servants, messengers, companions, guards during travel, etc., but they are also symbols of his identity and status. Heilman (1948, p. 316): The Holinshed account itself gives a clue as to how the retainers were to be understood. When Lear escapes to France, Cordelia sends him money to buy clothes and to reteine a certeine number of seruants that might attend vpon him in honorable wise, as apperteined to the estate which he had borne [see ]. Colie (1974, p. 199), citing Stone (1965): A great social figure would have had a household—witness Catherine of Aragon after her repudiation, or Mary Stuart in her detention—distinguished by a train of retainers. Retainers were not only a sign of an aristocrat’s prestige but a defence of his prerogatives.…One deep theme of this play is the meaning of deference to those who expected it as their due. The significance of King Lear would be greatly lessened if we could not understand what it meant to the king, to his children, to his nobles and servants, that men were deferred to according to their rank in society. From the point of view of the aristocratic ethos, there was nothing odd about Lear’s wanting to maintain the exhibition of his former greatness, even after he had delegated its great function to others. From the point of view of the new functionalism, equally, there was nothing peculiar about Goneril’s [cf. 843–8] and Regan’s [cf. 1533–8] attempts to cut down their father’s retinue: Elizabeth never allowed Mary Stuart a quota of armed servants. Delaney (1977, p. 433): The conflict reflects the long Tudor controversy over maintenance: the right of a peer to support an armed and uniformed (liveried) body of retainers, a practice which by Sh.’s time had become a token of an aristocrat’s devotion to an archaic style of conspicuous consumption. Farley-Hills (1990, p. 198): Lear’s wish to retain his hundred knights is modest. By abdicating he has not, of course, ceased to be of exalted rank. Gervase Markham, in a book published in 1598 [A Health to…Serving Men, sig D4v], is insistent on the obligation of the gentry to keep as large a retinue as their rank permits, both for the employment it affords and because an orderly society depends on a proper assertion of rank. Mahood (1992, p. 160), citing Stone, Colie, and Delany: A subject of almost startling topicality,…a paradigm of the crisis of the aristocracy between 1580 and 1620,…[when] many of its members were rapidly relinquishing their land and the revenue it had brought and, in consequence, their ability to support throngs of armed retainers: a process accelerated by the Tudor sovereigns’ mistrust of private armies, and by the changing attitudes on the part of the gentry towards the idea of liveried service in a noble household.…The arrival of such a riding household on a visit to another nobleman put an inevitable strain on both parties, and made high demands of the owner’s hospitality and of the guests’ hospitage. Butler (1992, pp. 1–2): Lear imposes…a silly and expensive routine, similar in its folly to King James’s creating 906 knights in the first four months of his reign (Stone, p. 74). Lear is not creating any new knights, but retaining present ones, and the expense of maintaining them and Lear is the one condition he imposes on his daughters when he deeds them each half a kingdom worth immeasurably more than that expense. They did accept the gift on those terms. Citing Boehrer (1990), Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 67): In 1608 another progress by James proved as unwelcome as rain in harvest, and the owners of great houses in its path moved their households to other parts of the country ([John] Nichols, [Progresses…of King James, 1828,] 1:517–24). Byrne (1960, p. 203): At Stratford in 1959, while Lear’s knights behaved impeccably, Goneril was a harassed lady of a great house, faced with the shattering aspects and inconveniences and housewife’s worry of a royal visitation.

142 sustayn’d]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Maintained. OED (v. 6): To furnish with the necessaries of life. Cf. 854, 1757.

142 shall]
Wright (ed. 1875): Ordinary future sense…with perhaps something of the idea of fixed intention.

142–3 abode Make]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Periphrasis for abide, comparing TGV 4.3.23 (1793).

143 onely]
Rolfe (ed. 1880) considers this a transposed adv., citing Abbott §420 and Shn. exx. Goggin (ed. 1910): Put at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis. More probably it is a conjunctive adv. in normal position. OED (conj. 1): With this…exception only; but, citing Wiv. 2.2.233 (990).

143 still]
Schmidt (1875): In future (no less than formerly; for ever (OED, adv. 4c). Cf. 170, 759, 2251. Brooke (ed. 1947) thinks F’s shall is possibly copied from…the line above. Wilson (ed. 1960): F.’s shall effectively throws all the emphasis on only.

143–4 retaine…King]
Lloyd (in Singer, ed. 1856): In a most important respect he contemplates no abdication at all. Houghton (ed. 1957): Lear wants the impossible—to have the honour and glory of power without its responsibilities; and in this desire lay part of the cause of his tragedy. But he is retaining only his honorific titles: see the next note. Perrett (1904, p. 183): There is no precedent for this [reservation of title] in the versions where the king dispossesses himself…but in Hol[inshed, 1577, fol. 39v; cf. n. 5]…Lear’s ancestor Brute…retained his title after dividing Britain between his three sons. Jones (1971, p. 165): It may be that [3H6 4.6.24–52 (2405–34)] furnished this detail.

144 additions]
The word is crucial, since it indicates how much of his kingship Lear wants to retain. OED (sb. 4): Something annexed [added] to a man’s name, to show his rank, occupation, or place of residence, or otherwise to distinguish him; style of address, quoting this l. Rushton (1858, p. 14): The description of an individual in a legal document, as esquire, gentleman, yeoman, &c. Except for its ordinary general meaning of something added, the word always means in Sh. a name or title, whether honorific or distinctive (e.g., H5 5.2.339 [3329], Cor. 1.5.65–6 [821]), identifying (e.g., Wiv. 2.2.298 [1049]), or descriptive (e.g., Tro. 1.2.20 [179]); at its furthest extension it means good name (Ham. 1.4.20 [621+4]). Cf. 1097, 3009, 3273. The Clarkes (ed. 1868) thus correctly understand the term: All the titles belonging to a king. Lear is asking to retain only his accustomed forms of address—the name King and such honorifics as your Majesty, Royall Lear (148), etc. which the other characters do in fact naturally continue to use throughout the play. The one exception, Oswald’s refusal to use such address at 609, causes Lear to erupt in rage. Watson (1960, p. 197): He wishes to retain the name and the title of king.…[Doubtless] the preservation of this symbol of high moral and social rank would have been considered by the Jacobean audience a matter of great importance. The pl. additions of Q fits well with the preceding all, but as Rolfe (ed. 1880) points out, F’s sing. addition can refer to a multiplicity of titles, as at 1097, 3273, and elsewhere in Sh. So Brown (ed. 1976), properly: Kingly title. So Nahum Tate (1681, p. 5) (pace Massai, 2000, p. 441) understands in rewriting the lines: The Name alone of King remain with me, Yours be the Execution and Revenues.
Commentators who understand the term to include other privileges of kingship—state and ceremonies (Rann, ed. 1794), outward honour (Schmidt, 1874), external observance (Furness, ed. 1880), perquisites (Porter & Clarke, ed. 1905), (other) belongings (van Dam, 1935, p. 19), prerogatives (Heilman, 1948, p. 71; Orgel, ed. 1999), precedence, honour, marks of distinction (Wilson, ed. 1960), trappings of kingship…superfluities of a mock king (Billington, 1991, p. 207), even his state (Draper, 1936, pp. 82, 85) and the crown (Jaffa, 1957, p. 412 n.)—misunderstand and exaggerate Lear’s demand, making him seem more vain, arbitrary, and unrealistic than he is at this point. Like Goneril, they see him trying to manage those authorities he has given away (522+1–+2); but additions are not authorities. Foakes (1993, p. 184) recapitulates two centuries of misinterpretation in print and on stage: This is not to crawl unburdened toward death, but rather to hold on to the privileges and lifestyle of a monarch without the responsibility which makes those privileges and lifestyle tolerable to others. Idem (ed. 1997, pp. 19–23): He is still perceived as King.…The burden of authority remains, and he is always the monarch. In fact, however, Foakes’s citations from the text show only that Lear’s family and friends continue to address him by the honorific titles that they might naturally have used even if he had not insisted upon them here as one of two conditions of his gift. Lear does, of course, remain every inch a king by birth, and demands the respect due to a parent or former monarch, but his sometimes peremptory behavior while sane is always occasioned by a perceived offense, not by a continual desire to hold on to royal privileges or authority. Colie (1974, p. 199) even extends the term to cover his retinue of a hundred armed knights, though they are a separate and prior provision, and Kermode (2000, p. 187) even understands (perhaps metaphorically) clothes, robes and furr’d gowns, even a coxcomb (the proper addition of the Fool). Fraser (1978–9, p. 3), psychoanalytically: He may still retain Parental power.

144 The sway]
Schmidt (1875): Rule, dominion (OED, sb. 6). Brooke (ed. 1947): These words, attached to line [144] in the Folio and prefixed to line [145] in the Quarto, belong metrically to neither. The Q line is preferable: it may be read as almost regular verse if of the is elided to o’th’.

145 reuenue]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Accented by S. on the first or second syllable, as suits the measure. Here on the second.

145 execution]
Schmidt (1874): Action, working (OED, sb. 3: The performance or fulfilment (of an office or function), quoting this l.). Colman (ed. 1982): Executive authority, powers; unattested by OED.

145 rest]
Elliptical for all the other business (Johnson, ed. 1765), offices (Clarkes, ed. 1868), or authority (Edwards, ed. 1975).

146 sonnes]
See n. 46–7.

147 Coronet]
See n. 37.

147 part]
Perrett (1904, p. 183): The action of handing over the coronet corresponds to the action of drawing lots in [Leir 550; see ], the source for the actual division of the whole land in Lr. Wilson (ed. 1960): The idea of dividing between Corn. and Alb. is absurd and obviously ad hoc. A few critics—e.g., Heilman (1948, p. 73), Elliott (1959, p. 262), Soellner (1984, pp. 287–8)—think that Lear bends, breaks, or tears the coronet in two; others believe that his statement is not to be taken literally. Davidson (1975, p. 75): Emblematic: the land, power, and glory symbolized by the coronet is to be divided. So Brown (ed. 1976). Still, something must be done onstage with the coronet as a physical property. Sprague (1944, p. 282): Booth…introduced the impressive, almost sacramental gesture of taking the crown from a Page and holding it above the heads of Goneril, Regan, Albany and Cornwall, who kneel in front of the throne. Darton (ed. 1928) includes the SD, The Attendant with the coronet offers it humbly to both Gon. and Reg. and they touch it graciously: he stands aside with it. Skillan (ed. 1967): cornwall and albany mount the rostrum and each grasps the coronet with one hand as a sign of possession. They then rise and return up l. lear then replaces the coronet on the cushion held by the noble standing on the l. of the throne. Rosenberg (1972, p. 67): Powerful Lears have torn it in two in an excess of anger, less powerful ones have tried to break it, and failed. Mikhoels split it with one blow of his sword. Shand (1987, p. 81): Perhaps Cornwall goes on to tip his violent hand, dividing the coronet himself. Perhaps he and Albany twist it out of shape. Perhaps they stand a moment, frozen by impossibility, before handing the coronet over to an attendant for future disposal. Or perhaps Lear himself avoids all this by simply handing the coronet to an attendant, and Cornwall and Albany both move to take it up, then stop, held off by its wholeness.…[Lear does not] yield up, and furthermore do violence against, his own royal crown. His dismissal or violation of a coronet emblematic of Cordelia’s dowry, of Cordelia herself, proceeds organically from his hurting wrath against her. Bevington (ed. 1988): Perhaps Lear gestures toward this coronet…, hands it to his sons-in-law, or actually attempts to divide it.

147 betwixt]
F prints the equivalent betweene here and at 1759; at 184 and 438 (’twixt) the reverse exchange occurs. F Compositor B may use the shorter form to fit at the end of the full line 438; the other three instances, set by Compositor E, probably reflect changes in F copy. Rolfe (ed. 1880): The same words are often interchanged in the quarto and folio texts of Richard III.

148–51 Royall…prayers]
Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 276): Kent’s respectful protest…[is] an instance of the figure parrhesia.

149–50 honor’d…followed]
Mahood (1992, p. 158): The echo of 105 makes plain that the Earl’s devotion to the King is of the same nature as Cordelia’s.

151 prayers]
Kemshead (ed. 1875): There is an allusion here to clergymen praying for their patrons in what was known as the bidding prayer, and probably also to the practice of…appealing to patron saints. Houghton (ed. 1957): This suggests Christian intecessory prayer as contrasted with the pagan gods involved by Lear above and…below.

152 The…shaft]
Granville-Barker (1927, p. 146) admires the strength of such single lines as…[this] with its hammering monosyllables. Most commentators understand the line as Lear’s warning to Kent to stand aside and not interfere further lest Lear loose the arrow of his wrath at him. Skillan (ed. 1967), however: His meaning is that kent is going to aim himself against lear who bids him shoot, i.e., to come straight to the point of his criticism. Similarly Hunter (ed. 1972) and Halio (ed. 1973; ed. 1992). Berryman (1946, p. 151) does not believe that a parallel in Purg. 25.17 suggests Sh.’s acquaintance with Dante. Miola (1992 p. 165): Lear’s metaphoric bow evokes Seneca, Hercules Furens 989 ff., 1300.

152 make from]
Hunter (ed. 1869) and most eds.: Go out of the way of. He and Meiklejohn (ed. 1879) give examples of make used to signify motion, such as make to or for, make away, make forth (OED, v. 35). The form here is unattested by OED, but is easily made and understood by analogy. Hunter (ed. 1972), however: Make from is unknown to dictionaries, but must give some sense like let go. But such a sense does not accord well with Kent’s next sentence; see n. 153.

153 fall]
The word may imply that Lear is standing above Kent; or the meaning may be figurative or analogous, as calamity, vengeance, or a sword or lash may be said to fall on a victim (OED, v. 1e, 4). Hoeniger (ed. 1968) and Brown (ed. 1976): Strike. In consequence of his misunderstanding (see n. 152), Skillan (ed. 1967): kent replies that he is not going to attack lear. But it is hard to imagine Kent letting his aim fall and as a consequence shooting himself in the heart, and hard to explain why he would call such a self-sacrifice unmannerly. Wells (ed. 2000): Perhaps indicating a change of tactic: that he will speak plainly—i.e. direct an arrow at Lear—even at risk to himself.

153 forke]
Wright (ed. 1875): The point of the arrow. Though Craig (ed. 1901) gives many contemporary examples to prove that the usual barbed head of an arrow (OED, sb. 9, quoting only this l.) is meant here, just as likely it is An arrowhead that, instead of a barb, has two points like a pitchfork (Kittredge, ed. 1940). Wright quotes from Ascham’s Toxophilus (1545, Bk. 2, fols. 19r–v) the descriptions of three kinds of arrowheads for warfare: the modern Englyshe heades having lytle barbes, another having two poyntes or barbes, lookyng backewarde…which surely we call in Englishe a brode arrowe head or a swalowe tayle, and one hauing ii. poyntes stretchyng forwarde, and this Englysh men do call a forkehead.

153 inuade]
Wright (ed. 1875): Penetrate. So OED (v. 2a), adding fig.…after the manner of an invader and quoting this l. and 1787 as its first exx.

154 the…vnmannerly]
Abbott (§458): Two extra syllables are sometimes allowed, if unemphatic, especially at the end of the line. To make the F line scan he accordingly elides the last two syllables; alternatively, one might elide of my. Cf. 243, 501, 749, 1242, 1436, 1533.

154 region]
OED (6b): A part…of the body, quoting this l. as its second ex., after Oth. 4.1.83 (2465).

155 when]
Now when. Kent is excusing his boldness as necessary. Only Lott (ed. 1974) understands a future meaning: He implies that this will never happen—but see 159.

155 is man]
Q2’s is mad is an obvious correction. Foakes (ed. 1997): Perhaps merely extremely foolish (OED, a. 2). Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 361): The Q[1] compositor may have been influenced by vnmannerly [154]…and/or man [155].…[Or it] may be a straightforward misreading of mad: n is found for d (and vice versa) elsewhere, citing Shn. exx.; cf. 1505. Only Stallybrass (2000, p. 124) finds man perfectly plausible as the source of puns on man and mannerly.

155 What…doe]
Capell (1783, 1.2:142): Spoke on seeing [his] master put his hand to his sword. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Manifestly a protest against Lear’s unwise action in giving his whole kingdom to Goneril and Regan.

155 thou]
Hunter (ed. 1972): The second-person singular, normally used to inferiors and intimates, is very extraordinary when applied to a king; Kent seems to be trying shock therapy in an attempt to bring Lear to his senses. But Kent continues to use it through 194, when all hope of therapy is past. Perhaps he considers himself an intimate on the basis of long and close service; cf. 149–51. So Lott (ed. 1974): He is speaking bluntly to an old friend. Hodge & Kress (1982, p. 145): Intimacy brought about through Kent’s loss of control.

155 ould man]
Harrison (ed. 1948): The phrase to a still-ruling king is grossly insulting. Muir (ed. 1952): Kent’s bluntness increases Lear’s rage. Mahood (1992, p. 158): In such a deference society [the phrase is F. M. L. Thompson’s] as that of England under James, the play’s original audience must have been profoundly outraged by Kent’s [words].…Even today’s audience asks itself if there is not something blameworthy in the candour of Cordelia and Kent, for we have not yet taken sides. Berry (1993, p. 80): Kent’s loss of temper, like Cordelia’s, is unpardonable: they have a duty to handle an elderly and splenetic monarch. But Foakes (ed. 1997) compares 1435. Strier (1988), pp. 113 ff.) defends Kent’s following behavior as virtuous, morally mandated disobedience.

156–9 think’st…folly]
Harrison (ed. 1948): One of many passages in Lear where the abstract [dutie, power, flatterie, honours, Maiestie] is strikingly and effectively used for the person. Wells (ed. 2000): The personified abstractions…suggest a morality play.

157 bowes]
OED (v.1 6): To become a thrall or subject.

157–8 when…bound]
Abbott (§501): Trimeter couplet. Moberly (ed. 1876): Alexandrine. Bayfield (1920, p. 126) would re-divide 156–8, ending power…bound.

158 plainnes]
See n. 137. Andresen (1974, pp. 157–8) compares the proverb Truth is plain (Tilley T593; cf. T575).

159 Maiestie]
On the scansion see n. 98.

159 stoops]
Schmidt (1875): Figuratively, = to bow down, to yield, to submit (OED, v.1 2). Brooke (ed. 1947): Preferable to the Folio’s falls. Wilson (ed. 1960), agreeing: Parallels bows in [157]. Duthie (ed. 1949): Falls makes good sense, but the similarity of sound between it and folly is unpleasing to some.…Stoops may have occurred in the middle of a group of words carried in [the F compositor’s] head as he set up his types, and he may have substituted falls through recollection of fall in line [153]—and perhaps the sound of folly was contributory to the error. Gold (1961, p. 141), finding stoops inconsistent with the character of Lear, defends F falls as indicating a fall of kings, and fall into sin, that is irreversible, despite Kent’s Reuerse (159), Checke (160), and Reuoke (178). Jackson (1983, pp. 337–8) develops Gold’s arguments further, claiming that, though Lear betrays senility in both texts, F represents a Shn. revision changing emphasis from Lear’s personal to his political malfeasance: Falls is the more appropriate verb in F; but in Q stoops, which suggests doddering old age…is better suited than falls would be to Lear’s error of judgement about Cordelia. Lear of course is not evidently doddering in either Q or F, and makes the same errors in both; and no motive for such a shift in emphasis is suggested.

159 Reuerse thy doome]
Whatever the reason for F’s change to reserue thy state, a majority of commentators and eds. think that the Q original makes better, and apparently clearer, sense. Doome must mean primarily judgement or decision…; a sentence (OED, sb. 2), with possibly, as Munro (ed. 1957) suggests, an implication of destiny (OED, 4), even Lear’s own fate (Weis, ed. 1993). F’s vaguer state has been taken to mean royalty (Delius, ed. 1854), dignity and power (Furness, ed. 1880), pomp (Brooke, ed. 1947), authority (Neilson & Thorndike, ed. 1909), honour (Sisson, ed. 1954), kingdom (Wilson, ed. 1960), status (Gardner, ed. 1969), and everything—rank, dignity, plenary power (Phelps, ed. 1917). Kirschbaum (1945, p. 17) notes Sh.’s previous use of reverse…doom in Tit. 3.1.24 (1160) and Rom. 3.3.59 (1861), and revoke…doom in 3H6 2.6.46 (1329); cf. TGV 3.1.224–5 (1292–3). Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 125–6) shows that in Leir’s reuerse Our censure [i.e., his decision to marry his daughters and divide his kingdom; Leir 505–6; see ] and Perillus’s ruthlesse doome [i.e., to disinherit Cordella; Leir 567; see ] the source-play contains the elements of Q’s Reuerse thy doome and not of F’s reserue thy state; and it contains the elements of Q’s Reuoke thy doome in line [178] against F’s reuoke thy guift. The Q reading is doubtless authentic. Commentators generally agree that it refers to Lear’s judgment on Cordelia, the subject that Kent continues to speak of in the following lines (161–4), and that the F reading apparently refers to surrendered attributes of royalty, which are not the context of Kent’s quarrel with the King (Stone, 1980, p. 214). Thirlby (MS notes, 1733–47): I prefer Qs reading. The other advice wd have been properer before. Verity (ed. 1897) and a few others think that Q may refer to both subjects; Sisson (1956, 2:230) denies the possibility. Furness (op. cit.) and some others partial to the F text in general argue that despite the context of the rest of Kent’s speech, which is concerned with Cordelia, uppermost in Kent’s mind is Lear’s safty, not mentioned explicitly until the end of his next speech (168). Goggin (ed. 1910) objects that in both Q and F Kent is clearly pleading for Cordelia, as [162–4] show, not arguing that Lear should reconsider his decision as to the partition and abdication, the time to protest against which had passed. So also Verity (op. cit.): In the conversation with Gloucester at the beginning Kent did not condemn the king’s purpose of abdication, nor did he make any protest till Lear cast off his sometime daughter. Doran (1931, pp. 54–5): The conclusion of Kent’s speech…appears to be a direct appeal for Cordelia, and to indicate that hideous rashnes refers to Lear’s banishment of her. In the folio, this phrase must refer to Lear’s abdication. But Lear would have surrendered his power even if…he had considered himself able to give Cordelia a third of his kingdom. Kent’s justification of her, therefore, does not follow logically upon, indeed is quite disconnected from, his denunciation of Lear’s rashness in surrendering his state. For this reason, I believe the quarto reading to be the original. Van Dam (1935, p. 47): [Kent’s] second argument is Lear’s safety which Furness holds to be only applicable to Kent’s advice of retaining his kingship, but, surely, it is just as applicable to the doom, for Lear had thought to set his rest on Cordelia’s kind nursery ([131–2]), and his safety was endangered when he had to rely on Goneril and Regan. If there is any passage which is obviously right in Q and wrong in F, it is here.
The change from Q to F has been variously explained. Johnson (ed. 1765) was inclined to think that Sh. changed a Q reading more apposite to the present occasion (the judgment of Cordelia) to the F reading which conduces more to the progress of the action (the future of Lear and his kingdom). Tovey (ed. 1896) takes the corresponding change in 178 from doome to guift as confirmation of intentional and, he thinks, authorial change here. See also Jackson (prev. n.). White (ed. 1862): Between reverse and reserve the difference is only the transposition of two letters; and that change once made by accident, the other would naturally follow by design. Duthie (op. cit.) questions White’s naturally: If faced with reserue thy doome the F proof-reader would in all probability have altered reserue to reuerse even without recourse to the copy. Doran (op. cit.): I believe…the folio a subsequent alteration made by Shakespeare to emphasize Lear’s political folly. Kirschbaum (1941, p. 150) finds F infinitely richer and more complex than Q, making Kent prescient of the whole tragedy to come. Stone (1980, p. 214) imagines a non-Shn. reviser wishing here and at 178 to alter, or elaborate, the motivation of Kent’s protest. It is difficult to imagine the reason for it, but the result is, in any case, unconvincing. Jones (1995, p. 227): The change is part of Sh.’s purging of romance elements in Q, in this case the doom, that romance and faery neighbour of the curse, the blessing, the riddle, the ukase, which [Leir and Q Lr.] share with the last plays. Most likely the change was intentional, whoever made it.

160 best consideration]
Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Consideration = reflection (OED, 2). Moberly (ed. 1876): That consideration which will be best, comparing AYL 1.3.41 (498), safest haste. Craig (ed. 1901): Best is sometimes used by Shakespeare as a mere phrase of courtesy, without a very distinct meaning [citing Cym. 1.1.156 (191), best advice]…Some, however, see here a reference to the saying, Second thoughts are best. Neither Tilley T247 nor Dent (1981) detects that proverb here. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): With most careful deliberation.

161 hideous]
OED (a. 2): Terrible, distressing, or revolting to the moral sense, quoting this l.

161 answere…iudgement]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Let my life be answerable for my judgement, or I will stake my life on my opinion. Cf. 517, 1224. Abbott (§364): Subjunctive used optatively or imperatively. Cf. Franz §637, and 1444.

163 low]
Verity (ed. 1897) compares 3236–7. Wilson (ed. 1960, p. xxiv): He is clearly comparing the subdued, almost whispered, tones of Cordelia’s reply to Lear with the brazen speeches of her sisters.

163 sound]
F’s plural, and according change of verb, seems to Doran (1931, p. 44) typical of many such indifferent variants introduced, she thinks, by a scribe or compositor.

164 Reuerbs]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Presumably a word of the poet’s own making, meaning…reverberates (OED, citing this l. as its first ex.). Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 53): Apocope, the omission of the last syllable of a word,…Shakespeare employs with great freedom. Wilson (ed. 1960): Poss.…quibble upon verb = word.

164 hollownes]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Making no [great] sound (OED, 3, citing this l.). Craig (ed. 1901): A play on…concavity [OED, 1]…and…insincerity [OED, 4], giving other Shn. examples. Deighton first detects the proverb Empty Vessels sound most (Tilley V36).

165 Kent…more]
Adee (ed. 1890, p. xlv), Perrett (1904, p. 204), and Lee (ed. 1909, p. xxxix) compare Leir 569 (see ), where Leir says to Perillus at this point, Vrge this no more, and if thou loue thy life.

166 held]
Craig (ed. 1901): Considered (OED, Hold v. 12).

166 pawne]
Steevens (ed. 1773): A thing of which I had the possession, not the property; and which was entrusted to me [as a pawn or pledge, ed. 1778] to be employed in waging war against your enemies (OED, sb.2 1). This loose meaning of loan or temporary possession makes sense and may be right, but in the strict sense pawn = pledge does not fit, since the giver of the pawn, not the receiver, is the one pledged to action. Hence the Clarkes (ed. 1868), A pledge to stake against; Hudson (ed. 1871), A thing to be impawned or put in pledge against your enemies; and Schmidt (1875), A stake hazarded in a wager. OED does not attest such a usage of the word, and Craig (ed. 1901) notes this line as the only instance in Shakespeare of its use in this sense. Muir (ed. 1952): But see [419, pawn downe my life] and Cym. I. vi. 194 (815), where pawn (vb.) is used in the sense of stake. Gardner (ed. 1969): The gage thrown down in a tournament. Though Furness (ed. 1880) scoffs at Capell’s (1783, 1.2:143) suggestion that the chess piece was meant, several have accepted it, if only as a concealed pun (Muir). Henley (in Reed, ed. 1785): That is,…the commonest of your subjects. Kemshead (ed. 1875): The pawn being the piece of lowest value. Garrett (1905, p. 284): It is the office of the pawn to keep the king from falling.

167 To…it]
Elze (1886, p. 36) makes a pentameter with en’mies.

167 wage]
An intransitive use such as that in 1502 does not seem possible here, and what Kent means by waging a pawn against enemies varies with the meaning of the object pawn (see n. 166). The context might suggest to use in conflict—as Muir (ed. 1952) says, The preposition against suggests…waging war—but nothing like that usage is attested in OED, an objection that applies to pawn = chessman. But a life, wager, or chessman might be wagered or ventured and lost—cf. lose in this line—so that either Schmidt’s (1875) To stake, to bet (OED, v. 6) or Moberly’s (ed. 1876) Venture (OED, 5: Risk the loss of) makes good sense.

167 nor feare]
Q makes perfect sense and a parallel construction with the previous line: I have never in the past held…nor do I now fear to lose. F’s awkward nere feare invites emendation. Sisson (1956, 2:230): The Folio reading is one more example of the frequent e:d misprint, and should stand with the obvious emendation feared (feard). Wilson (ed. 1960): The F collator prob. changed Q nor to nere but overlooked feare.

168 safty]
Most eds. tacitly assume the common meaning freedom from danger (OED, 1), and some credit Kent with the prescience to apprehend danger (see n. 159). But Deighton (ed. 1891): Well-being; his personal safety is not here in question, citing R2 1.1.32 (37), where no personal danger is referred to. Schmidt (1875) gives many Shn. exx. of safety = welfare, good fortune, success, though not this l.

168 motiue]
Muir (ed. 1952): Moving cause (OED, sb. 4). F drops the article the, perhaps to make more regular verse; van Dam (1935, p. 59) considers this to be miscorrection of a faultless line.

170 See better]
Page (ed. 1889): So as to distinguish real from false friends. Or less specifically, see without error. Hudson (ed. 1856): That you err not. Seronsy (1958): With more wisdom, more insight. Bullough (1973, p. 351 n.) compares Leir 577–8 (see ): Ah, who so blind, as they that will not see The neere approch of their owne misery?

171 still]
Ever; see n. 143. Joseph (ed. 1966): Also motionless.

171 blanke]
Most eds. begin with Hanmer’s (ed. 1743–4, 6:Gloss.) literal gloss, A white or mark to shoot at, but clearly Kent’s speech is figurative. OED (sb. 2): The white spot in the centre of a target; hence fig. anything aimed at, the range of such aim. Johnson (ed. 1765): See better, says Kent, and keep me always in your view. The speech might be simply an answer to 169: Keep me in your sight, and see no farther than me; but the question would still remain how Lear would then see better than he presently does. Kittredge (ed. 1940) thinks it is answered by implication: The mark at which thy eye directs itself in accurate sight; the counsellor to whom thou dost look for sound advice. Perhaps this means that Lear will show better judgment (clearer sight) by retaining a loyal friend like Kent rather than banishing him from his sight. Thus Seronsy (1958): [Loyal] Kent…will be the very center of Lear’s beam of wisdom—i.e., his looking to Kent will confirm Lear’s improved insight. Other proposals seem more problematic. Hudson (ed. 1856): Let me be the mark to direct your sight, that you err not; but a mark or target can direct sight only to itself. Deighton (ed. 1891), continuing the archery metaphor in 152: the true blank is that to which you still look for faithful service; the mark at which your thoughts aim; the reading requires that Kent’s me mean not himself but the abstraction faithful service. Craig (ed. 1901): Sh. might have had in mind Lyly’s Euphues and his England [ed. Bond, 2:166], the white, which shooteth not, but receiueth, being the patient, not the agent; but is Kent asking to be shot at? Milward (1987, p. 162) apparently thinks so: Kent implies that Lear, in aiming at him as his target…is really shooting at what is dearest to himself— and Kent invites him to do so. Frost (ed. 1909): Kent would rather see the shaft aimed at himself than at Cordelia; but Lear has threatened to shoot only Kent, not Cordelia. Elsewhere Sh. does use blank to mean line of fire (Oth. 3.4.128 [2284]) and a target in the line of direct, or level, aim (Jenkins, ed. Ham., 1982, 4.1.42 [2628+2]); here it might have OED’s second figurative meaning, range of fire, as it does in WT 2.3.5 (904) and in point-blanke (2H6 4.7.26 [2660]). Hale (1968, pp. 33–7): In Elizabethan gunnery manuals blank with only one exception means point-blank not target, and so refers to range of fire, i.e., the distance a bullet was believed to travel level before falling to earth. Therefore the line means, Let me still remain the one who represents a true and undeviating [i.e., level] line in your affection—a very free rendering. Similarly Hunter (ed. 1972): The direct line of sight, as of an arrow or gun directed truly, that is point-blank, at its target. So Colman (ed. 1982): True aim (i.e. helping you to see things straight; cf. point blank). Gardner (ed. 1969): Here, truth. Halio (ed. 1973): The image invoked is that of the eye itself, with blanke = pupil, or the main agent of sight.

172 Appollo]
See n. 116–18. Malone (ed. 1790): Bladud, Lear’s father, according to Geoffrey of Monmouth [ed. Griscom, p. 262], attempting to fly, fell on the temple of Apollo, and was killed. This circumstance our author must have noticed, both in Holinshed’s Chronicle [1577, p. 19; 1587, p. 12] and The Mirrour for Magistrates [1574, fol. 46r]. Idem, in Boswell (ed. 1821): Shakspeare learnt from hence that Apollo was worshipped by our British ancestors. Skottowe (1824, p. 131): The old play…most probably put Apollo, and Jupiter too, into Shakspear’s head, citing Leir 186; see . Like Greg (1940, p. 400), Muir (ed. 1952): Leir in Layamon’s The Brute also invokes Apollo. Crook (ed. 1907): Classical allusions [in this play] are very few. Lear, however, does not hesitate to call upon the Roman gods, of whom he mentions Apollo, Jupiter, and Cupid, while he calls Edgar both Theban and Athenian. Kent refers to the Roman goddess, Juno, calls himself by the Roman name, Caius, and mentions the Greek…Ajax; while Edgar speaks of the Roman emperor, Nero, who lived a thousand years later. Bullough (1973, p. 274): In William Harrison’s Description of England, printed in Holinshed (1577, pt. 1, ch. 8, fols. 7–11v; 1587, pt. 1, ch. 9, 1:19–29), Sh. would have learned of the changes in [the Britons’] religion from nature-worship to polytheism before the birth of Christ; cf. n. 116–18. Hunter (ed. 1972): An appropriate god to invoke at this point, as he was both the archer-god…and the sun-god (the god of clear seeing).

173–4 Now…vaine]
The line may be read as a pentameter if the first three syllables are elided without stress. The turnover of in vaine, caused here as at 194 by the Q compositor’s indenting his stick to a shorter measure on the bottom half of this page, suggests that the line appeared as one verse in the MS.

174 swearest]
Dyce (ed. 1864–7, Glossary): Swearest by. Abbott (§200): The preposition is omitted after some verbs which can easily be regarded as transitive. Cf. Franz §630, and 1155, 1761, 1765, 3144. Wright (ed. 1875): Adjurest. Shakespeare frequently uses the verb in a transitive sense, when it has a person for its object.…But in the sense of appealing to a deity by an oath it is not common. Crook (ed. 1907): Invokest (OED, v. 7, quoting this l. as its last ex.).

174 in vaine]
Wilson (ed. 1960): I.e. they will not hear you. Joseph (ed. 1966): Or Kent is not affected by his oath. Bradley (1904, p. 310 n.): Nor must we take Kent’s retort…for a sign of disbelief. He twice speaks of the gods in another manner ([196, 2002]), and he was accustomed to think of Lear in his prayers ([151]).

175 Vassall]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Literally servant, but here used as a term of abuse. OED (sb. 3): A base or abject person; a slave, quoting this l.

175 recreant]
The Q reading, like Vassall, may be a general term of abuse, or it may refer particularly, as Delius (ed. 1854) hinted, to Kent’s rebelliousness or even to his disobedience of Lear’s command (169). Tovey (ed. 1896): An apostate, one who has renounced his faith; afterwards, one who is a traitor to his liege lord, citing R2 1.1.144 (149), A recreant and most degenerate traitour. OED (sb. 2): One who breaks allegiance or faith; an apostate, deserter, villain, quoting Cor. 5.3.114 (3469). So in 181 F adds the word in this sense, as Lear insists on Kent’s allegeance. Here, whoever changed to the F Miscreant may, as Delius thought, have been referring to Kent’s apparent contempt towards the gods, since the word may mean A misbeliever, heretic,…infidel (OED, sb. 1). But see n. 174, and Deighton (ed. 1891): Here in the more general sense of worthless fellow (OED, 2: A vile wretch; a villain, rascal, quoting R2 1.1.39 [44], a traitour and a miscreant). The immediate cause of Lear’s rage is more likely to be Kent’s effrontery, possibly indicated by Q, than his religious attitudes, if they are what F refers to. Foakes (ed. 1997): F’s substitution was to avoid repetition in [181], where F adds the word. Greg (1942, p. 93), considering Q a reported text, thinks recreant here is an actor’s anticipation of 181.
Although neither Q nor F gives a SD here, editors and directors have done so (see textual n.); 177 seems to imply some threatening action by the king. Of Rowe’s SD (see textual n.) Sprague (1944, p. 283) says, Betterton’s business, we say—with a fair chance of being right. Later Lears were more violent. In their promptbooks: Kemble, attempt[s] to draw his sword…; Forrest lets his staff fall—in trying to unsheath; the younger J. W. Wallack Seizes his sword from Physician…; and Charles Kean <?seizes> a battleaxe from Lord/James—a supernumerary. Rosenberg (1972, p. 72): Dunn’s Lear held a knife at Kent’s throat. Salvini swept down from his throne, his sword half-drawn…; it was only his own self-control that finally stopped him.…and Redgrave’s old, old Lear, in his fury, could only fumble his great broadsword half out of its sheath. Warren (1985, p. 209): In Santa Cruz, 1982, Lear was unarmed and drew Cornwall’s sword. Bratton (ed. 1987): Macready and Irving had sword-bearers in the background, and seized their sheathed swords…; Edmund Kean…began to draw his sword, and was prevented by Albany and Cornwall, as was Phelps. J. P. Kemble had Albany and Gloucester perform the same office. Holland (1997, p. 41): In Nicholas Hytner’s RSC production of 1990, Lear hurled Kent to the floor…appalled by his [own] violence.

176 Alb. Cor.]
Honigmann (1976, p. 123), not citing this l.: Such [doubled] speech-prefixes are usually reserved for short replies or exclamations that any two persons might well make independently, and choric speech is then quite acceptable. He suggests other alternatives, however: In a realistic context where non-ritualistic lines are concerned it may be that there ought to be only one speaker, who indicates by a gesture that he speaks for both (p. 122). Here the double prefix may merely mean that both speakers act in concert, whoever speaks. Alternatively, Many All speeches could be divided between two or more consecutive…speakers (ibid.). Seymour (1805, 2:89) proposes Alb. Dear sir. | Corn. Forbear. Van Dam (1935, p. 41): F is apparently a revised Q text.…one remove further from Shakespeare’s original. For stage performance the insertion of [176]…enlivens and emphasizes the situation in a brilliant way. The interruption in F does suggest intervention, ranging from Capell’s (ed. 1768) interposing to Darton’s (ed. 1928) they put out hands to restrain him to stronger actions recorded by Sprague (1944, p. 283): Kemble [who omits this line], attempting to draw his sword, is withheld by Albany…& Gloster [standing beside him];…[restraining J. W. Wallack,] Alb R Corn L take hold of him and take the sword—he throws them off. Rosenberg (1972, p. 72): Samuel Phelps (1804–1878) was stayed so gently by his sons-in-law that it seemed he needed no staying. Urkowitz (1980, p. 32) quotes a promptbook of James B. Roberts’s New York production in 1858: Lear, seizing Axe from guard, Albany and Cornwall stop him, take Axe. He believes that in Q the king halts because Kent brazenly stands up to him, conceding (p. 33) that there is no hint in the text that the king…uses any kind of weapon at all. (Ibid., p. 82): Albany and Cornwall…move to assert their new power. They may only try deferentially (Deare Sir) to calm Lear, who remains in command for the rest of the scene. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxvii) thinks the line and its implied intervention a hindrance to the rapid action of the quarrel between Lear and Kent; Doran (1931, p. 60) thinks accidental omission from Q is possible; most eds., following F, include it. Cunnington (1910, p. 447): The added F line clashes with the do which begins Kent’s reply, so Doe is om. from F, pointing to F revision and suggesting that 176 is new matter, not a Q omission. The new line in F gives emphasis to Lear’s rash temper, but could be omitted without showing a gap. Foakes (op. cit., p. 185): The added line…heightens the violence of Lear and the peremptory nature of his behaviour.

176 Cor.]
Halio (ed. 1973) is the first to interpret this as an abbreviation for Cordelia, not Cornwall, as does Goldring (1983), who argues at length that it is an F revision of great weight to our understanding of Cordelia, Albany, Kent, and Lear. Ioppolo (1991, p. 171) finds the speech assignment highly unlikely: Albany and Cornwall enter together…so it would not be unusual for them to speak together. Foakes (1993, p. 253) points to F’s change of Glost. to Cor. at 204 and added reference to Cornwall and Albany in 46–7: All three changes go together,…identifying for the audience two important background characters who in Q remain silent and unnoticed. Idem (ed. 1997): And Cordelia was dismissed from Lear’s sight at [132]. There is no basis for the claim of Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 532) that on bibliographical grounds Cor. is likelier to be Cordelia. F Compositor E, who set this line, used this abbreviation as speech prefix for all of Cornwall’s speeches through 1144, halfway through page qq6v, on the last sheet of the quire to be set. (The one exception in 1025 was probably influenced by the SD directly above.) The next sheet to be set was rr3v:4, on which Compositor B had very likely already begun work. On both these pages B abbreviated to Corn. as he did for the rest of the play (exc. in 1975). Thereafter E, apparently influenced by his more experienced mate, did the same, perhaps at the urging of the proof-corrector, who read and made changes in qq6v. Whatever the cause for E’s change of practice after 1144, in this early line, 176, he would have abbreviated Cornwall to Cor., his consistent spelling for the first third of the play. F’s added line, the only speech given to either duke until Act 2, keeps them from being absolute mutes here. They have been discussed and treated as a pair throughout the scene, and at this point neither has more apparent motive to restrain Lear or defend Kent. After Lear, they are the two men of highest rank present, and are Lear’s sons-in-law and heirs; very possibly they stand on each side of the king, from whence they could restrain him. Cordelia certainly stands apart from them (see n. 38), facing him, and in any case is less likely than the two men to offer physical restraint, if such is offered.

177 Doe]
OED (Do v. 38): A word of…incitement = Go on! Skillan (ed. 1967): Perform your threat. Tovey (ed. 1896): Ironical encouragement, citing Tro. 2.1.42 (896–8). Though Wilson (ed. 1960) thinks it detracts from the dignity, Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 126) finds it effective, and Munro (ed. 1957) thinks it functions as linking up Kent’s statement with the previous speech, and is probably genuine. Its omission from F makes a more regular pentameter line. As a reply to Lear’s apparent assault, amidst onstage movement, it may have been intended as a separate line; cf. nn. 60, 74, 96, and see .

177 the]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 361): Q’s the may be a misreading [for F’s thy]: for e/y misreadings see Dover Wilson [1934, 1:112]. Idem, in Wilson (ed. 1960), to the contrary: The F comp. has prob. repeated thy from earlier in the line.

178 disease]
Like Koppel (1899, p. 24), Bradley (1904, p. 447): Goneril and Regan, comparing 1516. So Edwards (ed. 1975): Those who may kill you. Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956): Rashness. Wilson (ed. 1960): Flattery, comparing 157.

178 doome]
See n. 159. Of F’s guift Collier (ed. 1843) says, Perhaps…the gift made to Goneril and Regan, presumably of Cordelia’s portion.

179 whilst]
whil’st. Both spellings mean While. See n. 1717.

179 vent]
Schmidt (1875): Utter (OED, v. 5).

179 clamour]
Walker (1860, 1:156): Lamentation. More probably, Crook (ed. 1907): Violent speech. OED (sb. 1): Excited outcry of vehement appeal, complaint, or opposition. Patterson (1984, pp. 71–2), topically: We do not need to allegorize Kent into a figure for the reformist party in the Commons to recognize…a connection between his stand…and The Apology’s protest on 20 June 1604 defending free speech for the right and good of…country.

181 recreant]
See n. 175.

181 on thy allegeance]
Harrison (ed. 1937): The most solemn form of command.…To disobey was high treason. Wells (ed. 2000): It may cause Kent to kneel.

182 Since]
F’s more difficult That has been defended by White (ed. 1862) as more in keeping with the style of this play, by Schmidt (1879, p. 14) as more in the tone of suppressed passion which characterizes the speech (Ger.) and as leading more directly to 186, and by Brooke (ed. 1947) as the formal language of judicial sentence. It means the same as Q’s doubtless authorial Since: seeing that (White), because…for that (see n. 77; OED, conj. 2), inasmuch as (Meiklejohn, ed. 1879). Still, the construction is unusual: such that clauses seem normally to come after the main clause, not at the beginning of the sentence. Cf. nn. 981, 3099.

182 vs]
Brooke (ed. 1947): In changing from me (line [181]) to us, Lear marks his assumption of royal dignity and power. See nn. 41, 140.

182–5 Since…beare]
Skottowe (1824, p. 101) compares Leir 505–11; see .

182–4 vow…sentence]
On F’s plurals Wilson (ed. 1960), following Duthie (1949, p. 167): An audience will only be conscious of one vow, the terrible oath in ll. [115–26], and of one sentence, that at ll. [135–47], which decides the future of the kingdom. Q is also preferable on grounds of metre and style. F’s plurals must be credited to the comp. or scribe. Or press-corrector: see textual n. Musgrove (1957, pp. 170–1) reports in one copy the F variant sentences, (see ); Hinman (1963, 1:305; cf. 1961, p. 15) finds it the possible explanation of the F plural: The [proof-]reader simply called for the removal of the adventitious comma…[but] Compositor E misread the dele sign and added an s instead. Weis (ed. 1993), however: Corrected F uses the plural, because Kent questions both Lear’s decisions, to break up the kingdom, and his treatment of Cordelia.

183 durst]
Schmidt (1874): Preterite of dare (OED, A.4).

183 straied]
F’s strain’d is clearly right, though Johnson (ed. 1765) thinks straied could mean exorbitant…passing due bounds; Evans (1961, p. 325), erring; and Weis (ed. 1993), Sinfully out of control. Duthie (ed. 1949): A compositor may easily omit a single letter accidentally…[or] may have taken the n for an e. Rann (ed. 1794), strain’d: Excessive (OED, ppl. a. 3: Exerted…to an abnormal degree). Weis (op. cit.): Forced beyond its proper limits…unreasonable. Rolfe (ed. 1880) compares (220+1), This strained passion, and Muir (ed. 1952) gives other exx., but these more exactly mean forced (OED, 4, 5). Brown (ed. 1976), oddly: Deliberate.

184 betweene]
