On F’s betwixt see n. 147.

184 sentence]
F’s press-correction sentences, is rejected by most eds. (see textual n.) but defended by Musgrove (1957, pp. 170–1). Hinman (1963, 1:305): The correction is lamentably wrong. See n. 182–4.

184 powre]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Execution of the sentence. Edwards (1750, p. 156) and most others: Rather power to execute the sentence. Bevington (ed. 1992): Power to command and judge.

185 Which]
Despite Warburton (ed. 1747), this relative pronoun refers only to the crime of coming between (184); the crime of forcing a broken vow (182) is referred to by its own separate and parallel which clause (183).

185 nor…nor]
Wright (ed. 1875): For neither…nor (OED, conj.1 2b).

185 nature]
Page (ed. 1889): As a man. OED (sb. 2): The inherent and innate disposition or character of a person. Cf. 258, 500, 782, 906, 1057, 1149, 1173, 1218, 1455, 2303+1, 2764, 3201.

185 place]
Page (ed. 1889): Dignity as a sovereign. Deighton (ed. 1891): Position as king.

185 can beare]
Rann (ed. 1794): Without departure from…dignity.

186 made good]
Schmidt (1874) and Onions (1911) give many exx. of four meanings of make good in Sh.: prove to be blameless, prove to be true (OED, Good adj. 22c), perform, carry into effect (OED, 22b), and maintain (OED, 22d). Though they quote this line as an instance of the last, any of the meanings is possible here, as is one other: replace, restore (OED, 22f); cf. Horsman (ed. 1973): Repaired (after Kent’s attacks upon it). Conceivably one could also substitute in the first case other meanings of good, such as honourable, valid, in force, or adequate (OED, 3, 18, 19). The absolute construction is more usually referred to take (186) than to beare (185), and the meaning varies according to the inferred subject of made. Steevens (ed. 1773): Albany and Cornwall must have made good (i.e., temporarily restored) Lear’s power, yielding [him] the ability to dispense it in this instance. Halio (ed. 1973): This interpretation strains at technicalities. Delius (ed. 1854): Lear is mocking Kent’s expressed wish (159): You wish me to make good my power: well, I do so; and the first use I make of it is to banish you! (Ger.); so also Craig (ed. 1901). Similarly Gardner (ed. 1969): A cynical echo of [177–8]…—since I am restored in strength, here’s your fee. Halio (ed. 1992): Lear has not yet relinquished his kingship…as the subsequent dialogue with Burgundy and France…shows. Most eds., however, make Lear, or his action of rewarding Kent, the agent. Johnson (ed. 1765): The sentence of banishment shall establish, shall maintain, that power so executed; likewise Hudson (ed. 1879): Take thy reward in or by a demonstration of our power. Hunter (ed. 1972): Lear says that since Kent has interposed himself between sentence and power he will find no gap between these two in his case: the sentence and power will appear together. In similar interpretations the absolute participle is taken as equivalent to being thus made, potency being thus resumed (Capell, 1783, 1.2:143), a proof [i.e., proved] (Malone, ed. 1790), asserted (Halliwell, ed. 1865), re-established (Harrison, ed. 1937), and carried into effect (Kittredge, ed. 1940), backed up by [Albany and Cornwall] (Lott, ed. 1974). Others take the construction as equivalent to an if clause: if our power be properly vindicated (Kemshead, ed. 1875), if my power is to be a reality (Tovey, ed. 1896) or is to maintain itself (Ridley, ed. 1935) or is to be demonstrated as real (Harbage, ed. 1958). Two take it as stating a precondition, equivalent to since: our power not being lost (Verity, ed. 1897), our power being strong enough (Buck, ed. 1907). Henley (ed. 1903) refers it to beare: Which I can suffer neither as a man nor as a king, and keep my power. Q2’s unauthoritative emendation make has appealed to a few editors. Wright (ed. 1875), like Stone (1980, p. 203), takes the phrase as an imperative to Kent: establish our power by taking thy punishment as an acknowledgement of it; Crook (ed. 1907), as an adverbial clause modifying beare: if we would retain the power we hold. A few others understand make as parallel to beare: thus my power could not…excuse (Warburton, ed. 1747), defend, justify (Eccles, ed. 1792), bear us out in…the violation of an oath (Rann, ed. 1794). Conjectural emendations of Our to Nor or Or (see ) make explicit the supposed parallel. Muir (ed. 1952): The rhyme take—make is, however, ugly.

187–9 Foure…fift]
since the numbers are indifferent, and consistent with each other, there is no evident reason for F’s change to Fiue and sixt. Van Dam (1935, p. 104): If Q is right, the F printer may have misread the symbol 4 for 5, and the press-reader…may have miscorrected fift into sixt instead of changing Fiue into Foure. Brooke (ed. 1947): There is a similar inconsistency between nine and ten in Othello I.iii.279 [630]. The explanation may be that Shakespeare used Roman letters for numerals. In Elizabethan script v and x often had a preliminary stroke which could cause them to be read iv, ix. Presumably if the Q compositor misread V and set Four, he would consistently have made the easy misreading of sixt as fift. For an argument that F reflects Sh.’s revision, see n. 190. On the common use of the old -t ending for ordinals see Franz §236.

187 for prouision]
Schmidt (1875): Preparation (OED, sb. 2b: Esp.…supplying of necessaries for a household, an expedition). Cf. 1498.

188 diseases]
Malone (ed. 1790): The alteration [to F disasters]…was made by the editor, in consequence of his not knowing the meaning of the original word. Diseases, in old language, meant the slighter inconveniencies, troubles, or distresses of the world [OED, sb. 1].…The provision that Kent could make in five days, might in some measure guard him against the diseases of the world, but could not shield him from its disasters. To Steevens’s (ed. 1793) objection that five days may surely enable him in some degree to provide against the disasters (i.e. the calamities,) of the world, Malone (Boswell, ed. 1821) replies, The disasters or calamities of the world are…loss of health, or substance, or children, or friends.—No provision of five days could guard against these. Schmidt (1874), diseases: Trouble. Verplanck (ed. 1844) finds the phrases diseases of the world and disease in the world in Wyclif’s 1388 tr. of the Bible (John 16:33). Most eds. agree with Malone, though Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 61) and a few followers are suspicious of diseases because it echoes 178. Duthie argues that in Shakespeare’s day disasters could mean simply pieces of ill luck, misfortunes; but with its clear sense of astrological influence, it seems usually to have meant ruinous, sudden or great misfortune, calamity (OED, sb. 2).

189 to turne]
Eccles (ed. 1792): We allot thee to turn.

189 backe]
OED (sb. 24g): With turn…upon, Abandon, forsake, quoting this l. The phrase need not mean that Kent be out of the kingdom then, but that he start his journey into exile; see the next n. Lee (1909, p. xl): In the old play [i.e., Leir] Perillus is not punished for his protest by banishment. But he absents himself from the court and does not meet his old master again until his unfilial daughters have thrust the King from their doors. Jenkins (1987, p. 79): Sh. derived the banishment from Plutarch by way of his earlier tragedy Tim. 3.5, where the loyal Alcibiades’ banishment has many details of dialogue similar to Kent’s.

190 tenth]
Though Daniel’s (1870, p. 77) conjectural alteration to sen’th involves the change of only one letter and an apostrophe, there is no need for it or for Collier’s (ed. 1858) seventh, since tenth makes perfect sense and Q and F agree. Nor is there reason for Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 532) to declare the Q reading an evident error needing emendation to next; and their elaborate theory that Sh., hearing a rhyme, later corrected to sen’th, then adjusted to F’s Fiue and sixt (187–9) to form a series, but that F mistakenly reproduced Q’s tenth anyway, is dependent on the doubtful assumption that F was set from Q2 copy, not a MS. Several agree with Hudson (ed. 1879): As Mr. [Joseph] Crosby writes me, The King orders Kent on the sixth day to turn his hated back, and start; and, as we can hardly suppose the King’s palace, or Kent’s, to be on the edge of the kingdom, he gives him three days to get out of our dominions; so that on the tenth he shall have crossed the line. Since following is ambiguous—following today, or following the day Kent turns his back on the kingdom?—it is even possible that Lear is giving Kent ten days’ leeway, not three, as Sohmer (1999, §14) suggests. Wittreich (1984, p. 99) suggests an ironic prediction of the actual day of Kent’s death, but the chronology of the play is too indeterminate for certainty.

191 truncke]
OED (sb. 3): The body considered apart from the soul or life, quoting this l. Deighton (ed. 1891): Used contemptuously. Serpieri (1979, p. 1070): He is socially annihilated…nothing more than a piece of flesh.

191 dominions]
OED (sb. 2b): Territory…subject to a king or ruler.…Often in pl., quoting this l.

192 Iupiter]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Shakespeare makes his Lear too much a mythologist; he had Hecate and Apollo before. See nn. 116–18, 172. Delius (ed. 1854): Lear now…swears a weightier oath by a higher god (Ger.). Elton (1966, p. 178): Such underlining by repetition of Lear’s initial pagan devotion may be preparation for Lear’s subsequent crisis of faith. On the scansion see n. 47.

193 This…reuokt]
Verity (ed. 1897): Said with grim emphasis, in ironical allusion to Kent’s revoke thy doom [178]. So Granville-Barker (1927, p. 165), who would stress This.

194–201 Why…new]
Hales (1874, p. 26): The rhyme is necessary to mitigate the heat of the scene. Verity (ed. 1897): Its rhyme has much the same effect of formal leave-taking as the rhymed couplet which we get so often at the end of a scene.…Also it is designed to give a certain ring of epigram, each couplet being a terse, sententious summary of what is passing through Kent’s mind as he turns towards each of the persons addressed. Craig (ed. 1901): After the storm comes the equanimity of Kent’s rhymed lines. Harrison (ed. 1937): The rhyme…stiffens the speech and gives it a special prophetic or moral significance. Leech (1950, p. 63): The rhyme…takes away from the speaker the sense of actuality, prevents the too easy giving of our sympathy. Gardner (ed. 1969): It allows Kent to accept banishment with deliberate indifference, showing control and regularity of thought (Lott, ed. 1974) or weary detachment (Wells, ed. 2000). Hunter (ed. 1972): Kent’s couplets…mark the recession of the verse-level from immediate passion to sententious generality. Brown (ed. 1976): Couplets aid a general impression of speed and lightness. Cf. 279–86, 2943–6. Leggatt (1992, p. 188): As words are balanced against each other—friendship and banishment (freedom and banishment in the Folio), old and new—so Kent balances Cordelia, whom he trusts, against Goneril and Regan, whom he does not.…The whole first scene displays this fascination with antithesis: eloquence and silence, flattery and honesty, loyalty and treachery, gain and loss.

194 Why]
Though F omits, apparently as hypermetrical, Jennens (ed. 1770) justifies the word: It seems to express Kent’s blunt humour the more strongly; and the nicety of the measure is not worth insisting on. Q2 omits thus instead, and van Dam (1935, p. 59), who finds F’s line unspeakable, proposes to omit king. But the Q line makes a good enough pentameter if thee well is unaccented, as it must be anyway in F.

194 thee]
Abbott (§212): Instead of thou, Thee…follows imperatives which, being themselves emphatic, require an unemphatic pronoun. Cf. Franz §283, and 2480, 3210.

194 since]
Sh. uses since as a conjunction some 478 times, sith (F) only some 23; cf. Franz §559, and 1535. Wright (ed. 1875): The two particles appear to have been used indifferently by Shakespeare; that is, he did not use the former in a temporal sense, the latter in a logical or illative sense only. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 532): F’s line is crowded, sith thus is not very felicitous, and the need to insert thus immediately after might have given Compositor E the hint (consciously or not) to alter since to sith.

194 thus]
Verity (ed. 1897): So self-willed and despotic.

194 appeare]
Thomson (1983, p. 170): The word point[s] up Lear’s histrionics.

195 Friendship…here]
Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 217): Metastasis, the turning back of an objection.…Kent turns the sentence [of banishment] back upon the king. Wilson (ed. 1960, p. xxviii): The state of inversion of normal moral order is suggested by the pattern of Kent’s words. Schell (1983, p. 160): The kingdom has paradoxically become a place of exile. Foakes (ed. 1997): A constant theme of the Fool.

195 Friendship]
Jennens (ed. 1770): Friendship seems more properly opposed to banishment; for what is banishment, but the being driven away from our friends and countrymen? [F’s Freedome] may with greater propriety be opposed to slavery. But cf. AYL 1.3.138 (603), To libertie, and not to banishment. Since either reading will do, the reason for F’s change is not apparent. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 362) wonders if the Q compositor both misread freed as frend (he compares Pies/Pins at 1267) and made a guess at the illigible -ome. Schell (1983, p. 159): Freedom refers to both Kent’s candor, willingness to speak and act openly, and Lear’s integrity and generosity of spirit.

195 here]
Jacobson (1975): This world, in contrast to an unspoken…the other world…after death. But Kent has not been sentenced to death.

196 protection]
OED quotes F’s shelter as its first ex. for (sb. 1b): Something which affords a refuge from danger. Elton (1966, pp. 331–2) finds either reading an ironical commentary on hopes for the gods’ special providence.

197 rightly…iustly]
OED (Justly adv. 3): With good reason or truth. Cf. 1638+7. Since the F inversion of these two words hardly changes or improves meaning, the transposition may be due in either text to a compositor’s (or, particularly in F, a scribe’s; see ) holding the line in memory as he set (or wrote) it. Blayney (1982, p. 7): In F, iust was set for [Q] right in Tro. 1.3.164 (624) and R2 1.3.55 (352).

197 thinks, and hast]
Doran (1931, p. 22): The printer of Q2 evidently noticed that the second verb…was in the second person; since the third person seemed to be called for, he altered it to [hath].…The original error consisted in the [Q1] printer’s having dropped an e from thee [196; cf. 817, 2248] and in his having [accordingly] changed the first verb from the second to the third person. The folio reads [think’st, and hast].

198 large]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Ample. Deighton (ed. 1891): Extravagant, citing WT 4.4.147 (1963). Page (ed. 1889): Liberal. OED (a. 9): Pompous, imposing, assuming airs of grandeur, quoting this l. as its first ex.

198–9 deedes…wordes]
Carter (1905, p. 433) and Colie (1974, p. 126) compare John 3:18: Let vs not loue in worde…but in dede and in trueth. Milward (1987, p. 162): Which form as it were the motto of the play.

198 approue]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Prove the sincerity and truth of. Clarkes (1879, p. 510): Prove equal to. Hudson (ed. 1879): Make good. OED (v. 3): To demonstrate practically…make proof of. Cf. 1237, 1470.

199 effects]
Brooke (ed. 1947): (Actual) results, in antithesis to mere words. Cf. 436, 1463.

200 Princes]
Probably the daughters of Lear and their husbands. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Princesses (the word applied to either sex) (OED, sb. 1a, b).

201 shape…course]
The phrase is nautical (Falconer, 1965, p. 71). OED (v. 16d): To steer for, to a place. Also trans. and fig. Kent says figuratively that he will stay on his old course (direction, OED, sb. 12; way of acting, OED, 21) even when it takes him into, and while he is in, another country. Cf. 416, 527, 719, 865, 1245, 1369, 1991, 2849. Though Heron (1785, p. 305) interprets old as of an old man, and Lee (ed. 1908) in old age, both supported by OED (a. 2, quoting this l.), all others agree that it means former or customary (OED, 7). His course is variously specified as principles (Johnson, ed. 1765), temper and character (Moberly, ed. 1876), manner of life (Deighton, ed. 1891), way of speaking plain truth (Craig, ed. 1901), career (Lee, ed. 1908), self (Phelps, ed. 1917), [service] as a faithful and plain-spoken subject (Kittredge, ed. 1940), honesty (Harbage, ed. 1958), constan[cy] to lear (Skillan, ed. 1967). Phelps (ed. 1917): Kent will begin life again elsewhere. Wright (ed. 1875), following the conj. of As You Like It (see ), finds a pun on corse; Furness (ed. 1880) objects that such a pun would be uncalled for and that to shape a corse is unintelligible.

202 Enter]
F adds Flourish—A fanfare (of horns, trumpets, etc.), esp. to announce the approach of a person of distinction (OED, sb, 7a)—here and at 291, 1073, and 2982, and generally in Sh. (Naylor, 1896, p. 167). Manifold (1956, p. 26): There is little evidence of its having any particular tune.…Within the theatre it can be played on trumpets, or cornetts, or…on any other instrument.…If they were extemporized, it is likely that they were brief and simple.…Except where length is specially called for, there is no need for the Flourish to be more than the simplest two-note call. Though Urkowitz (1980, p. 38) imagines an undefined blending of movement in the Quarto, made clear by F’s added Exit. at 201, Kent’s adew, completing a couplet, indicates an exit, surely by a different stage door. Bratton (ed. 1987): Irving had Edmund re-enter here. See n. 40.

202 France and Burgundie]
Rosenberg (1972, p. 74) imagines Burgundy older, shrewder, more practical; France is easily seen as the young hero…[and] must have the quality of passion below the surface, citing 358, 1505. Foakes (ed. 1997): Banners, coats of arms, or other insignia probably establish these characters as foreigners in the English court, comparing Colours at 2349, 2845, 2918. Those later battlefield banners would not appear here, of course, and France and Burgundy are obviously foreigners even without insignia. Wells (ed. 2000): The suitors…would presumably make some form of obeisance to Lear.

204 Glost.]
To virtually all eds. since Theobald (ed. 1733) F’s Cor. seems erroneous; Doran (1931, p. 81) considers a reassignment to Cornwall insignificant. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 168): After what has passed [e.g., 120 ff.] it would of course be totally impossible to give line [204] to Cordelia. Cornwall [see 176]…might conceivably draw Lear’s attention to the approach of newcomers. But [as Theobald argued] it seems more natural that Gloucester, entering in attendance on France and Burgundy, should announce them to the king. The F speech-heading may be due to an aberration on the part of the compositor. Urkowitz (1980, p. 40): [If] France and Burgundy are waiting, then Cornwall’s speech could be a careful prodding of the dangerous king. Cf. also n. 176. Similarly Foakes (ed. 1997): The change in F may…allow Lear to see Kent off the stage before he notices Gloucester’s entry. There is no evidence that Lear fails to react to the flourish and entrance of his noble guests. Viswanathan (1990, p. 179), however: Lear is…in a muse after the exchanges with Cordelia and Kent. Halio (ed. 1992): Cordelia seems a more appropriate speaker [than Cornwall], since Burgundy and France are her suitors. Ioppolo (1991, p. 171): She probably would not formally announce her own suitors. The speech is of course for the benefit of the audience, identifying newcomers to the scene, and would be spoken as the entering parties approach the King. Foakes (op. cit.): Lear told Cordelia to avoid his sight at [132], and it would be inappropriate for her to put herself forward here. He may even look around for her, or even pull her forward to exhibit her to her suitors. There is no hint of such action in the lines.

204 Heers]
Abbott (§335): Inflection in -s preceding a plural subject. Cf. 1769, 1844, 1885, 2092. Verity (ed. 1897): Where the subject consists of two nouns (as here) the tendency is to attract the verb to the nearer; cf. Franz §679.

205–6 My…you]
The Q1 compositor may have read this as one verse line in his MS, since he abbreviated both Lord and Burgundie to fit it into the shorter measure he was using for most of this page (as is evident from the turnovers at 213–14 and 227).

206 first]
Bradley (1904, p. 258) speculates at length, as surely no audience ever has, why Lear addresses the Duke of Burgundy before the King of France, suggesting that the apparent choice in public here is a mere fiction because Cordelia’s marriage has been prearranged, or even (p. 446) that an explanation was cut when the play was shortened. Muir (ed. 1952) accepts an explanation that Bradley rejects: Lear does not wish to insult France by offering Cordelia’s hand without a dowry. Surely the main reason is dramatic effect: France will take Cordelia, as in the sources, but first Burgundy’s backpedaling wins sympathy for France and her.

206 addres]
Wright (ed. 1875): Direct our speech to, address ourselves to. OED (v. 8c) quotes this l. as its first ex. of this intransitive use.

206 a]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 192; withdrawn in Wilson, ed. 1960): The Q reading gives the passage more point than F’s this, emphasizing that Burgundy, a Duke, has had the temerity to set up as rival to a King. Muir (ed. 1952): But the same point would be made by stressing king. Horsman (ed. 1973): Perhaps the indefinite article shows…[such] emphasis.

207 hath]
Abbott §247: The relative…frequently takes a singular verb, though the antecedent be plural. Cf. Franz §155, and 262, 1070, 1574.

207 riuald]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Glossary): Been competitor for (OED, Rival v. 2, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Schmidt (ed. 1879): Used as a verb only here in Sh.

207 least]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Lowest [estimate] (OED, a. 5c, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Schmidt (ed. 1879): For at least, only here in Sh.

208 require]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Ask. Not so imperative as in modern usage, comparing 2986.

208 present]
Schmidt (1875): Immediate (OED, a. 5).

209 quest]
Steevens (ed. 1778): Expedition. The term originated from Romance. Becket (1787, p. 231): Request, solicitation. Rann (ed. 1794): Pursuit (OED, sb.1 4, quoting this l.). Perrett (1904, p. 111 n.) suspects an allusion to Jason’s quest, so called in MV 1.1.172 (181).

210 Royall]
F’s added Most regularizes meter, though Van Dam (1935, p. 60) thinks that the Q line is perfect and F’s a quasi-correction, if Royall is pronounced roy’l.

210 maiesty]
On the scansion see n. 98.

211 what]
F’s hath is elliptical, omitting the object (what, that which) of offered. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 127): Hath offered better suggests that Burgundy thinks that the offer is still open. He must think so in either text.

212 nor will]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Nor are you likely to. Wilson (ed. 1960): The query [see textual n.] may indicate an exclamation. Burg. is taken aback by ll. [207–9]—he does not know Cord. is out of favour. Halio (ed. 1992): A full stop…makes Burgundy’s reply sound too peremptory. Caught off guard by Lear’s question, the duke does not know what to make of it and responds with a query of his own.

212 tender]
Schmidt (1875): Offer (OED, v.1 1, 2).

213 Burgundie]
On the scansion see nn. 39, 47.

214 so]
Capell (1783, 1.2:143): Speaking indefinitely…—so and so, at such and such price. Eccles (ed. 1792): Worthy of that high dowry. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Elliptically punning on dear in the senses of affectionately valued and of high value. Wright (ed. 1875) prefers only the former of these, Kittredge (ed. 1940) the latter, as the next line shows. Derocquigny (1928, p. 460): Dear (i.e. affectionate, loving) to us…so (i.e. dear).

215 prise]
Schmidt (1875): Worth, value (OED, sb. 6).

216 little]
Depending on the interpretation of the following words, either small, slight (describing substance and indirectly Cordelia) or not much, hardly (modifying seeming).

216 seeming]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Beautiful (= seemly, unattested in OED, ppl. a.). Steevens (ed. 1773): Specious (unattested in OED, though see vbl. sb. 3, and Schmidt, 1875); so Kittredge (ed. 1940): Nothing genuine, not real. Wright (ed. 1875): In appearance (OED, ppl. a. 3). Horsman (ed. 1973): Manifesting, showing. Edwards (ed. 1975): Which seems small (in comparison with one-third of England). The word has been joined by a hyphen to make a compound with either little—that seems so slight and shallow (Moberly, ed. 1876), little and unimposing as she may seem (Meiklejohn, ed. 1879), refer[ring] ironically to Cordelia’s blunt professions of sincerity…with small speciousness,…all reality and no pretence (Craig, ed. 1901), mere physical presence…i.e., Cordelia without dower (Brooke, ed. 1947), whose value now seems little to the materialistic Burgundy (Hoeniger, ed. 1968), who is (1) inconsiderable (2) outspoken (Fraser, ed. 1963), who appears unpretentious but who is in fact monstrous (Quinn, ed. 1970)—or with substance—That little creature, who seems to be something real, but is in fact a mere vain semblance of reality. Seeming substance (not little) is emphatic. The phrase is practically a compound word and might be written seeming-substance (Kittredge); pretence sincerity (Wilson, ed. 1960, quoting Verity, ed. 1897): A kind of antithetic compound; little (a boy-actor) and worthless (substance as matter or reality, and as wealth) (Foakes, ed. 1997). Thus the phrase has been taken variously to disparage Cordelia’s beauty, stature, bearing, sincerity, candor, monetary worth, and genuineness. Mahood (1957, p. 43): At the simplest interpretation, Lear is saying: She is not much to look at, but because we know, or guess, how little seeming there is in Cordelia…, we feel the anticipatory irony of his words, an irony all the more sharp if Lear himself is being ironic and means: This genuine creature who refuses to flatter (Muir [ed. 1952]).

216 substãce]
Schmidt (ed. 1879): In Sh. the word expresses reality in opposition to appearance, called at various times shadow and seeming.…Perhaps seeming is to be taken as a gerund, and seeming substance is then a being whose reality is just appearance (Ger.). Clarkes (ed. 1868): That small scrap of womanhood, that mere morsel of humanity…without any of her former advantages as daughter to a king. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Her whole slight person, body and mind. Brooke (ed. 1947): mere physical presence. Harrison (ed. 1948): Creature,…body. Ribner (ed. 1967): Lear is implying that since the love she had always shown him was mere pretense, she is entirely a creature without substance. Brown (ed. 1976): Being/wealth.

217 it]
Mahood (1992, p. 158): Lear attempts to strip Cordelia even of her femininity in the contemptuous it.

217 with]
Deighton (ed. 1891): With nothing…except.

217 peec’st]
An aberrant, probably phonetic spelling, corrected in F’s piec’d. Possibly the compositor, carrying piec’d in his memory, erroneously set the homophone. But since the same anomaly occurs elsewhere in the play (cf. 1542) and in F texts of other plays set by various compositors, it may reflect copy: cf. pronounc’st (Tit. 3.1.50 [1186], Q and F), forc’st (Tit. 4.1.72 [1618], F), and sawc’st (Cor. 1.9.53 [808] and Cym. 4.2.50 [2310]). Hunter (ed. 1869): Eked out (OED, v. 6). Hudson (ed. 1871): Added to it. Weis (ed. 1993): Supplemented. Tovey (ed. 1896): A figure…from patching cloth [by Sh.’s day, patching in general]. Cf. 1999. Hunter (ed. 1972): Here used ironically.

218 fitly]
Schmidt (1874): With propriety,…well (OED, a. 1). Craig (ed. 1901): By its fitness.

218 like]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Suit (OED, v.1 1). Schmidt (1874): Please. Cf. 1164.

218 your grace]
Delius (ed. 1854): Meaning the duke. OED (Grace sb. 16b): A courtesy-title now only given to a duke, a duchess, or an archbishop. Formerly used in addressing a king or queen. Cf. 1060, 1220, 1405, 1475, 1904, 1920, 1951, 2881.

220 I…answer]
Crook (ed. 1907): I cannot tell how to answer.

221 Sir]
F’s omission makes a regular line. See n. 60.

221 infirmities]
Rann (ed. 1794): Imperfections, faults, defects (of character; OED, sb. 4). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Defects of fortune; disabilities (of strength; OED, 1). Joseph (ed. 1966): Invalidated claims to honours and possessions.

221 owes]
Steevens (ed. 1773): [Is] possessed of, owns (OED, v. 1). Cf. 650. Becket (1787, p. 72, n. 1): Cannot but acknowledge (OED 1c).

222 new adopted]
Delius (ed. 1854): I.e., she now has no father but Lear’s hatred (Ger.). Deighton (ed. 1891): Newly received into our hatred. Tovey (ed. 1896): An expression all the more forcible because ironical.

223 Couered]
Some meanings of the word—overlaid, enveloped, dressed, even (ironically) shielded—make a kind of sense. Thus Weis (ed. 1993): With my curse hanging over her, or, veiled with my curse. Eds., however, almost universally prefer F Dow’rd, which shares the bitter irony of adopted and is relevant to giving one’s daughter in marriage. OED (Dower v. 1): To give a dowry to, quoting this l. as its first ex. Kittredge (ed. 1940): With my curse as her sole dowry. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 363): It may be that the copy had douered: the first letter…illegible: and the compositor…guessed couered. Munro (ed. 1957): Q is doubtless a misreading of script: some forms of capitals D and C were similar.

223 stranger’d]
Dyce (ed. 1864–7, Glossary): Estranged, alienated (OED, Stranger v. 1, quoting only this l.). Cf. 122. Abbott §294 lists passive verbs in Lr. formed from adjectives and nouns: cf. Franz §662, and 1007, 1812, 2056+13, 2398, 2730; see also n. 1455.

224 Take…her]
Proverbial: Tilley T28, Take it or leave it.

226 election]
Craig (ed. 1901): Of a mate, in Cym. 1.2.28 (248). Keeton (1967, p. 46): Used in its legal sense—presumably free, deliberate choice (OED, 2). The Sokols (2000, p. 108) demur: If this is so, then seemingly Burgundy means that the legal doctrine of election does not properly apply forcing him to have either no hope of marrying Cordelia, or no hope of receiving a marriage portion. The reason would be because originally there had been no such condition made implicitly or explicitly on his courtship. If it is one,…a very strained legal allusion.

226 makes…vp]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Come[s] forward (OED, Make v.1 96n). Malone (ed. 1790): Comes…to a decision (Schmidt, 1875; OED, 96k <b>, quoting only this l.). Rann (ed. 1794): Is…determined (OED, 96l: Arrange). Clarkes (ed. 1868): The expression…is idiomatic and elliptical; conveying the effect of makes not up its mind. Tovey (ed. 1896): The verb active used intransitively for the passive.

226 conditions]
Provisions, terms of agreement (OED, sb. 1). Schmidt (1879, p. 14), troubled by the F preposition In, attempts unnecessarily to make conditions mean qualities (OED, 13), referring to the qualities of Cordelia enumerated in 221–3; but OED (1b) records in among alternatives to the usual on. Hunter (ed. 1972): When the condition of the lady is of the kind you describe; but the noun is plural in Q and F.

227 leaue her]
Cordella gives such advice to the Gallian King, Leir 691 (see ).

228 tell]
Hunter (ed. 1972): (1) report to; (2) count.

228 for]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): As for (OED, prep. 26). Cf. 2868+1, 3029, 3270.

229 your]
Page (ed. 1889): Objective genitive; the love (or friendship) of you, that which I give you. Deighton (ed. 1891): The love with which you have treated me.

229–30 such…To]
Abbott (§281): In relatival constructions, e.g. so…as,…one of the two can be omitted. Cf. 568, 1287–8, 1575–6, 1638+5–+6. Hudson (ed. 1879): The Poet omits as in such cases, when the verse is against it. Franz (§572, Anm. 1): Often before an infinitive.

229 stray]
Johnson (1755): Act of wandering (OED, sb. 4, quoting this l.). Moberly (ed. 1876): Go so much astray.

230 beseech]
Abbott (§399): When there can be no doubt what is the nominative, it is sometimes omitted. Franz (§306): Esp. first-person pronouns before beseech, prithee etc. Cf. 888, 1195, 1222–3, 1314, 1318, 1590, 1597, 1620, 2320, 2762, 2914–15, 2916, and n. 891.

231 auert]
Warburton (ed. 1747): To turn, simply. OED (v. 4): Trans. To turn away (the face, eyes, thoughts), quoting this l. Schmidt (ed. 1879): Not elsewhere in Sh.

231 a…way]
Craig (ed. 1901): In a worthier, better direction;…on a better person.

231 more worthier]
On the double comparative see n. 84.

232–3 nature…hers]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Lear seems to be denying Cordelia…kinship to the human species. Cf. 1128.

232 nature]
OED (sb. 11): The creative and regulative physical power which is conceived of as operating in the material world and as the immediate cause of all its phenomena; (11b): More or less definitely personified as a female being. Cf. 335, 434, 789, 1128, 2034, 2362. Bullough (1973, p. 302) compares Leir 896–905, 1264–74; see , .

235 she, that]
All admit that F’s whom is bad grammar, but some eds. excuse it, and Franz §334 gives other exx. Wilson (ed. 1960), who censures the same error in Tmp. 5.1.76 (2032) as compositor’s grammar, defends it here as conversational grammar. Werstine (1983, pp. 279–80): Lear is almost unique among the Folio tragedies in preferring who[m], where, and which to quarto copy that.…Doran [1931, p. 45] argued that the Folio variants are probably authorial, but did not explain why similar changes are not found in other Folio plays in which authorial revision is suspected—Troilus or Hamlet, for example.…The alterations to Quarto that [may be a] scribal sophistication. However, even these changes might be related to the increasing grammatical complexity of Shakespeare’s late style. On distinctions in Sh. between that, who, and which see Abbott §§258–9 and Franz §§335, 339; for F’s substitutions for Q’s pronouns cf. 259, 724, 733, 781, 816, 1146, 1316, 1350, 2654, 2911, 3188. Foakes (ed. 1997): Perhaps an error caught from [232].

235 euen but now]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Only a moment ago.

235 best]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Dearest. Muir (ed. 1952): Main object of love. F’s omission makes awkward verse or requires doubtful pronunciation; see the next n. Only Schmidt (1879, p. 14) finds the adjective implied in the noun and hence redundant. Duthie (ed. 1949): The F compositor presumably omitted it accidentally. Collier (ed. 1878), defending his emendation blest: The compositor caught best from [237].

235 obiect]
Delius (ed. 1854): Always in Sh. an object of sight (Ger.). Cf. 1268. Clarkes (1879, p. 572): Of affection. Page (ed. 1889): Of your thoughts, wishes. Tovey (ed. 1896): Of sympathy. Lee (ed. 1908): Of attraction. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Of your love and favour. Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 168–9): In Shakespeare, as to-day, the noun is always accented on the first syllable, the verb on the second.

236 argument]
Schmidt (1875): Theme, subject (OED, sb. 6). Cf. 936.

236 Balme]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Solace (OED, sb. 6).

237 most…most]
On the double superlatives see n. 84. Craig (ed. 1901): Cf. most best in Ham. 2.2.122 (1149). Collier (ed. 1843): More forcible than F. Wright (ed. 1875): F’s The…the patched the grammar. Duthie (ed. 1949): Memorial confusion in Q, anticipating 275–6. Foakes (ed. 1997): Altered perhaps [in F] so as not to anticipate [275–6]. Q does not anticipate, there being no double superlatives at 275–6; and single superlatives forty lines later would hardly have seemed a redundancy.

237 trice]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Instant (OED, sb.2, quoting this l.). The phrase in a trice is common: see Dent (1981, T517).

238 monstrous]
Schmidt (1875): Shocking, horrible in wickedness (OED, a. 6), with the root meaning unnatural (OED, 1a). Cf. 241, 427, 912, 1098, 2311+2, 3118. Dundes (1976, p. 361) compares Per. 5.3.86 (2342), monstrous lust; but France, far from imputing incest to Cordelia, is defending her from suspicion of any crime.

238 dismantell]
Delius (ed. 1854): Strip off (OED, v. 3, quoting this l. as the first of only two exx.). Lott (ed. 1974): Like a robe of honour.

239 foulds]
Brooke (ed. 1947): Lear’s love has been wrapped around Cordelia like a rich oriental garment, fold over fold. OED (sb.3) quotes this l. as its first ex. of fig. use.

240–1 such…That]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Shakespeare occasionally uses that for as in phrases where the word such occurs. So Abbott §279, Franz §340. Cf. 253–4, 1196–7.

241 monsters]
Theobald (ed. 1733): Makes a Monster, a Prodigy, of it (OED, v. 1, quoting only this l.). See n. 238 and cf. 2311+2 and Cor. 2.2.77 (1290).

241 or]
Most eds. take this to be the coordinating conjunction (OED, conj.2), but Johnson (ed. 1765) suggests the alternative that it is the subordinating conjunction meaning before (OED, conj.1 1b), requiring the alteration of F Fall to Falls and yielding the sense before your affection can be infected with hatred.

241 you]
F’s your has been almost universally preferred. Though Q makes sense, it seems to direct sharp criticism more directly and rudely at Lear: he is tainted, not simply his affections. Stone (1980, p. 214) would even make you the object of monsters: Lear’s misjudgment makes him monstrous. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 363): yor may have been misread as you. The same error appears in Q at [1480] and [1726]. In Hand D of Sir Thomas Moore the u and r are often very similar, and the spelling yor appears repeatedly. Werstine (privately): The spelling yor appears hundreds of times in MSS, e.g., 8 times in the MS play Tom a Lincolne.

241 for voucht]
A few have tried to make sense of the Q reading. Johnson (ed. 1765) takes for to mean in consequence of (OED, prep. 22): For having vouch’d affection which you did not feel. Likewise Jennens (ed. 1770), although he believes the real cause of the estrangement of Lear’s love…was the vouch’d affections of his three daughters.…Regan and Goneril had, by their superior art in coaxing, won all Lear’s love from Cordelia. Stone (1980, p. 214): Q is perfectly intelligible and correct. Weis (ed. 1993): The affections you asserted you felt for her have now discredited you. No one seems to have suggested that for might mean instead of, in place of (OED, 5), which makes at best difficult sense and suggests no motive as alternative to Cordelia’s offense: in place of former affection you [have] fallen into a new attitude of condemnation [attaint; see n. 242], or, in place of vouched affections, now tainted ones. Halio (ed. 1973) prints for without explanation, presumably considering it a variant spelling of fore. Most eds. adopt F’s fore-voucht (which may be Q’s meaning if you is an error for your). Capell (1783, 1.2:143–4): Fore-warranted, warranted afore to be true by many testimonies. Most agree with Wright (ed. 1875)—Formerly professed—in unambiguously making Lear the voucher. Malone, after initially (1783, p. 48) agreeing with Jennens, reluctantly concludes (ed. 1790) that Lear’s previous declarations, alluded to in 236, must be meant here, since, though the plural affections favours this interpretation, France had not heard the sisters’ professions in this scene.

242 Falne]
Most eds. understand the auxiliary must be as repeated from 240; F’s Fall requires an added must if F’s singular affection is its subject. Q’s past participle implies a taint already completed; F’s infinitive, a present or future taint. A majority of eds. prefer Q, which seems more natural in the context (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 169). Furness (ed. 1880): In F, The last syllable of Fallen was absorbed by the first syllable of into.

242 taint]
Almost the whole range of meanings of the word has been suggested. Jennens (ed. 1770): Corruption (OED, sb. C2) of Lear’s judgment. Davies (1783, 2:267): Censure (OED, C1: Discredit, dishonour, disgrace) for misplaced affection. Malone (ed. 1790): Decay (OED, C2) of Lear’s affections. Rann (ed. 1794), perhaps following Becket (1787, p. 321): Censure of insincerity. Delius (ed. 1854): Suspicion that his affections were ill-founded. Hudson (ed. 1881): For attaint or attainder…reproach or impeachment as fickle or false (OED, A3; see n. 241). Deighton (ed. 1891): Infect[ion] with some disease (OED, A2, C1b). Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): horribly to blame for having ever pretended to love Cordelia. Harbage (ed. 1958): With the implication that the affection, and the oath attesting it, were tainted in the first place. Mahood (1966, p. 159): This can be a discreetly oblique statement of what Kent has said bluntly: that if Lear questions Cordelia’s love for him he is out of his mind. But the lines are primarily directed at Cordelia (with whom we assume he has reached an understanding…) and the effect on her of France’s fleeting and simulated disquiet is to call forth an eloquent self-defence which at the same time makes plain her feelings for this much worthier lover.

242 which]
Seymour (1805, 2:91): Refers to…her offence. Boodle (1884, p. 216): Referred to the main statement, sure…monsters it. Brooke (ed. 1947): France…politicly omits to develop the second [alternative] (namely, that Lear is at fault) and returns to the first.

242 her]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Emphatic. Of the two alternatives France chooses the second, for the first is to him incredible.

243 reason…miracle]
Crook (ed. 1907): Reasoning…not supported by miracle. Maxwell (1950, pp. 142–3) considers the play’s references to miracles (cf. 1242, 2497) incidental, not systematic: they represent Shakespeare’s indifference to anachronism, even though at times in the pre-Christian world of the play (p. 147) a Christian outlook is both presupposed and expressed. Although in classical Latin miraculum meant simply a wonderful thing or event, critics often give it specific theological significance in Lr. Wilson (ed. 1960): Unless it was vouched for by divine revelation. Milward (1987, p. 163): The theological idea that miracles are needed to bring the reason of man to faith in God, citing John 20:30–1, 4:48. Muir (ed. 1952): Perhaps a reference to the controversy about natural religion, as in Montaigne,…[Bk.] iii. passim. Lott (ed. 1974): I.e., Christianity depending on reasoning rather than revelation. France’s hyperbole approaches very near to irony. Brown (ed. 1976): In the charged context, his unforced religious imagery can be quietly effective. Murphy (1984, p. 5): Like the exorcisms in Harsnett, the miraculous faith of the Papal Church was the diabolic foe of Anglican teaching that the miracles (i.e. of the New Testament and of the primitive church, the Age of the Apostles ending ca. 100 A.D.) have ceased, citing Reginald Scot, Archbishop Bancroft, John Walker, and John Deacon as well as Harsnett. Cf. n. 2497. On the scansion see n. 154.

244–5 Could…Maiestie]
If this is a verse line (see textual n.) it is hypermetric, containing fourteen syllables. Elze (1886, p. 36) reads in me. I as elided without accent, and Maiestie as a dissyllable (see n. 98). Quite possibly 244 is a short line and, if both I and yet are accented, 245 is the equivalent of a full one.

244 Could]
Wilson (ed. 1960): = the mod. meaning of F Should.

245 yet]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Emphatic: in spite of all you have said in denunciation of me, comparing 824, 2504, 3196.

246–55 If…liking]
Elton (1966, p. 80 n.): Cordelia’s attitude accords also with James’s, in warning against the flattery of monarchs, in Basilikon Doron (1603, pp. 16, 21). The idea was commonplace. In Leir 302 (see ) Cordella declares, My toung was neuer vsde to flattery. Greg (1940, p. 390) compares Cordell’s speech to Gallia in Leir 654–5 (see ): He lou’d me not…because I could not flatter him.

246 If for]
Jennens (ed. 1770) was the first to recognize that the phrase represented broken or elliptical speech, expressing (he thought) the modest fear and bashful diffidence of Cordelia, heightened by her concern under her present pitiable circumstances. Similarly Tovey (ed. 1896): The confusion is in keeping with Cordelia’s eagerness to clear herself in the eyes of the man she loves (to which Verity, ed. 1897, adds, though he had clearly shown that his belief in her was unshaken [242–4]). Similarly Goggin (ed. 1910): Her language throughout this short speech is involved and betokens great agitation. Lott (ed. 1974): Her sentence is complex because she wants to state her case fully. Steevens (ed. 1793) correctly glosses for as meaning because (OED, conj. 1), comparing 338; cf. 3104. The If clause has been variously completed: If it is for that [= because] (cf. Abbott §387); Seeing it is so that (Capell, 1783, 1.2:144); If I am to be deprived of your grace and favour (Eccles, ed. 1792); If this be my offense, that (Malone, ed. 1790); If you disown me (Ger.) (Delius, ed. 1854); If I must be treated thus (Moberly, ed. 1876); If I suffer, or you misjudge me because (Tovey, op. cit.); Even if you are enraged with me because (Muir, ed. 1952); Even if you reject me because (Gardner, ed. 1969). OED (If conj. 4): In pregnant senses: a. Even if, even though; though. Perrett (1904, p. 294) rejects Pope’s inserting for…I speake in a parenthesis: We get an assertion from Cordelia quite out of keeping with her character; but it is like what she says in 253–4.

246 want]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Have not (OED, v. 2).

247 To…entend]
An apparent alexandrine. Elze (1886, p. 37) attempts pentameter by reading -pose not, since without accent.

247 and…not]
Muir (ed. 1952): I.e. to do what I have promised. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): To act in accordance.

247–8 what…speake]
Greg (1940, p. 389) compares Leir 278 (see ): I hope my deeds shall make report for me.

247 well]
Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Virtuously—i.e., with good intentions. Weis (ed. 1993): Thoroughly. F’s will is an apparent misreading (also in 531) that few eds. follow; the future auxiliary is not needed, and meter would be better without it. Schmidt (ed. 1879), however, thinks it indicates customary action. Weis (op. cit.) considers it an obsolete form of well, but it is unattested by OED and does not occur in Sh.

247 entend]
Intend, mean to do (OED, Intend v. 18). Only Strutt (apud Seymour, 1805, 2:91): Conceive to be (OED, 13).

248 that]
The relative clause is the object of beseech (245).

248 you]
Though the body of the speech is addressed to Lear, Jennens (ed. 1770) would direct this to France, a switch in mid-sentence that Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 511) find awkward.

248 may know]
Stone (1980, p. 214): Subjunctive after beseech, citing Abbott §369, The Subjunctive after verbs of command and entreaty. Cf. Franz §647. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 363): Some editor of Q’s copy misunderstood Cordelia to be addressing France. Ingham (1967, p. 82): If an error, possibly a failure of a listener to distinguish the final k of make from the initial kn of knowne, which was still pronounced with a [k]. Weis (ed. 1993): May know would entail an awkward switch by Cordelia in mid-sentence from Lear to France. But may know makes perfect sense if addressed to Lear: Comprehend as fact or truth (OED, v. 10), To be cognizant, conscious, or aware of (a fact)…to understand (OED, 11). Wells & Taylor’s (ed. 1986, Q) emendation acknow (= OED, Know 3) is not necessary. Wells (ed. 2000): Jowett (privately) suggests emendation of Q’s you to hee, i.e. he—France—may know. F’s make knowne, addressed to Lear, must mean tell my suitors, since all else present (except Gloucester) know the cause of Lear’s displeasure. Ioppolo (1991, p. 171) sees different Cordelias in Q and F: in Q she appears to appeal to him to understand, in F she demands that he state publicly the reasons for her words; actually in both texts she says I…beseech. In Q Cordelia defends herself, in F she asks Lear to mitigate his condemnation; in either case the suitors are edified. In Leir 654–5 Cordella herself makes such an account to the Gallian King; see .

249 vicious blot]
OED (Blot sb. 2): A moral stain; a disgrace, fault, blemish. Hence the phrase may mean a stain of vice; cf. 3133, vicious place. But possibly vicious means reprehensible (OED, a. 3); cf. Ham. 1.4.24 [621+8], vicious mole of nature. The F comma after murder seems to put this phrase as first of a series of three faults named in this line; but the Q punctuation would allow it to be a general introductory catchall, particularized by the crimes—murther…dishonord step—that follow. If so, blot would have by metonymy to include the action causing the stain; so Harrison (ed. 1948): Vicious act which blots my honor.

249 murder]
This word has troubled many, on the two grounds that Cordelia could never contemplate that any body would suspect her of murder (Collier, 1852, p. 436), and that it accords not with the other charges she enumerates, being more drastic (Keightley, 1867, p. 322). Moberly (ed. 1876): The gradation vicious blot, murder, foulness, would not be happy. Furness (ed. 1880) declares Collier’s emendation nor other, adopted by several eds., as an emendatio certissima, restoring the rhythm, according with the ductus literarum, and offering no violence to the consistency of Cordelia’s character. Doran (1931, pp. 97–8) disagrees: If one grants that murther could be a misreading of nor other, then he must admit that or is an insertion by the printer of Q1. The reading of F could then have been a copy only of the reading in Q1. However, it is the folio, the later text, which has the spelling agreeing with the ductus literarum; Q1 spells murder. The emendation will not do, therefore, and the text will have to be accepted as it is. Hulme (1962, pp. 259–60) suggests mirder, amorous sporting; OED records the Scots verb mird but no noun. For other proposed emendations, see . The charges that murder is unacceptable are easily answered: if murder is the first instance of several vicious blots (see prev. n.), Cordelia is simply beginning with the worst that could be imagined of her. Lettsom (1853, p. 464): France has just before said—Sure…monsters it; that is…it can be nothing short of some crime of the deepest dye—and therefore murder does not seem to be so much out of place in the mouth of Cordelia. White (1880, p. 828): A touch of demure satire at the hyperbolical absurdity of Lear’s denunciation. Tovey (ed. 1896): Her words are impetuous, not studied. There is also much irony in her entreaty, and this is more effective the greater the contrast between her real offence and those of which, from Lear’s treatment of her, she might be supposed guilty. He has just called her a wretch…hers; and France and Burgundy, who did not witness the earlier scene, would naturally from this suppose that Cordelia had committed some dreadful crime. Craig (ed. 1901): Cordelia, with a touch of scorn, mentions the most extreme vices she can think of. With the plain speaking so characteristic of her, she says, I have not been discarded and so upbraided because I am a murderess, or a wanton. The Clarkes (ed. 1868) add a reminder of the era of the world in which the story took place…when the poisoning of one sister by the other, and the putting out the eyes of a man suspected to be a traitor…seem but a part of the savage procedure common to persons in power at that period.

249 foulnes]
The word has hardly evoked comment. Kittredge’s (ed. 1940) unchastity would make vncleane action redundant. More likely it means here any particularly abhorrent crime other than murder: disgusting wickedness, dishonesty,…violence (OED, sb. 2, 4). Cordelia’s catalogue moves from great to lesser crimes. Cf. OED (Foul a. 7): Morally or spiritually polluted; abominable, detestable, wicked, noting the common phrases foul fiend (used 8 times in this play) and foul thief (= the devil).

250 vncleane]
Delius (ed. 1854): The Biblical word for F’s vnchaste. OED (a. 1): Morally impure or defiled; unchaste. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Dissyllabic adjectives and participles are accented on the first syllable when they are followed by an accented word or syllable, comparing intire (263), vnprizd (284), and extreame (2462).

250 dishonord]
OED (ppl. a. d): Dishonourable, dishonouring, quoting this l. as its second ex., after MM 4.4.31 (2302). See n. 284.

250 step]
Lettsom (1853, p. 464): Cf. faux pas. Deighton (ed. 1891): Proceeding (OED, sb. 3, quoting this l.).

251 grace and fauour]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Synonyms. OED (Grace sb. 6): Favour…or its manifestation. See nn. 290, 298, 680, 1473.

252 euen]
Weis (ed. 1993): Simply.

252 for which]
Eccles (ed. 1792): For the want of which. Hudson (ed. 1871): For got repeated [before want] by mistake. Instead of the, presumably.

252 rich]
F’s richer makes superior sense; Q implies that Cordelia’s candor is her only enriching quality. Horsman, ed. 1973): Not to mention the jingle with for which. Possibly the Q compositor misread richer as riche, and modernized to rich.

253 still]
Furness (ed. 1880): Constantly (OED, adv. 3, 7b). Cf. 851–2, 1382, 1615, 1967, 2180. Tovey (ed. 1896) lists several Shn. compounds with the word.

253 soliciting]
OED (ppl. a.) quotes this l. as its first ex. OED (Solicit v. intr. 12): To make request or petition; to beg or intreat; possibly also the sense of allure, entice (OED 4, 5).

254 As]
On F’s That see n. 240–1.

254 I haue]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Pronounced I’ve.

255 lost]
Schmidt (1874, Lose): To ruin (OED, v.1 2b, To ruin in estimation, quoting this l. as its first ex.). For verbs in the causative see Franz §630. Kittredge (ed. 1940) compares Ant. 4.12.29 (2785). Joseph (ed. 1966): Or, less probably: removed me from. Wells (ed. 2000): Deprived me of (OED 3).

255 in]
Wright’s (ed. 1875) in respect of is more likely than his alternative in the amount of. Cf. Abbott §162, In the case of, about, Franz §505.

255 liking]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Cordelia uses the cold word liking instead of love. Muir (ed. 1952) adds, deliberately. Horsman (ed. 1973): Not always a colder word, comparing AYL 1.3.28 (485). Foakes (ed. 1997): Cf. 231.

256 Goe…to]
See n. 100. Collier (ed. 1843): The words are natural, but detrimental to the measure. Greg (1942, p. 91): They are an actor’s insertion, by trick of memory, from Q 100. F’s omission of them, however, results in an irregular line that later eds. have attempted to remedy (see textual n.). There is of course no reason why 255 and 257 may not be short lines and 256–7 Goe…borne be read as a pentameter, thou hadst being elided, as commonly, to thou’dst; cf. 2493 (Q thou hadst, F thou’dst). Wells (ed. 2000) would read 256–7 better…better as an alexandrine by further eliding to haue. F can make perfectly regular lines if 256 is ended with thou and 257 is begun with Had’st, as in most editions.

256–7 better…better]
Colie (1974, p. 128) compares Job 3:3.

258 no more]
F’s omission makes easier meter; but the Q line makes passable pentameter if Is it and more but are elided.

258 tardines]
Sh.’s only use of the word. Deighton (ed. 1891): Reticence. OED (a): Slowness of movement or action, quoting this l. as its first ex. Lott (ed. 1974): Holding-back.

258 in nature]
See n. 185.

259 That]
For F’s Which see n. 235.

259 historie]
Schmidt (1874): Communication of what is in the hearts of men. Muir (ed. 1952): Account. Perhaps a play on the word, since the history describes the future.

259 vnspoke]
On curtailed forms of participles see n. 103. Rolfe (ed. 1880): The only instance of the form in S. OED (ppl. a.) quotes only this l.

259 that]
Of what. On the common ellipsis of the preposition in a relative clause see OED (That relative pronoun 8).

260 to do]
Though Walker (1953, p. 7), assuming that Q prints a text reported by actors, suspects these words to be an actor’s metrically redundant interpolation lacking sense, in all likelihood they were in both the authorial MS behind Q and the theatrical MS behind F. Her reasoning—Cordelia’s fault has been her refusal to express the volume (history) of her love and not a refusal to say what she intended—is beside the point, since France is speaking generally, not about the preceding scene, which he did not witness. For the supposedly lacking sense, see the prev. n.

260 Burgundie]
On the scansion see nn. 39, 47.

261 what…to]
Craig (ed. 1901): How like you, comparing Shr. 4.3.17, 20, 23 (1995, 1998, 2001). Gardner (ed. 1969): Will you have. The idiom is still current. OED (v.1 2a): To declare…[an] opinion, or intention. Brooke (ed. 1947): to here means on the subject of.

261–3 Loue is…point]
Steevens (ed. 1773): His love wants something to mark its sincerity. Wright (ed. 1875) compares Son. 116, which Q’s Loue is recall[s] even more clearly than F’s metrical elision Loue’s (Horsman, ed. 1973).

262 respects]
Malone (ed. 1790): Prudential considerations. Capell (1783, 1.2:144): Of fortune, and such like. F’s regards means the same (Knight, ed. 1840, et al.). Wright (ed. 1875): Perhaps the change was made in consequence of the recurrence of the…word in [273]. Greg (1942, p. 93), considering Q a reported text, thinks that Q’s respects here is an actor’s anticipation of 273.

262–3 stãds Aloofe]
OED (Stand v. 83): To stand away at…some distance (from), quoting this l. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Have nothing to do with.…A plural subject often has a verb in the singular, especially when the noun has a more or less collective sense. See n. 207. Muir (ed. 1952): The line sounds better without the s.

263 intire]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Single. Verity (ed. 1897): The whole point to be thought of; practically…= essential. Deighton (ed. 1891): I.e. her true value as a woman, not the amount of dowry she brings. Horsman (ed. 1973): Unmixed. See n. 250. Lott (ed. 1974): Stressed on the first syllable.

264–9 She…sworne]
F’s correct relining is not indebted to Q2’s incorrect version, though the three words that F adds to 269 almost look like an attempt to fill out the incorrect Q2 line; cf. n. 268–9. Doran (1931, p. 29): Q2’s correction is only a partial one, indicating that the printer…is himself responsible for it.…[It] improves the last two lines…but it leaves the first two short.

264 and dowre]
Sargeaunt (1933, p. 921): Her self and her dower. Van Dam (1935, p. 56): Person and dower united, made one. Weis (ed. 1993): In her person Cordelia combines those virtues and endowments of character which are so valuable as to be a dowry in themselves. Most eds. prefer F’s a Dowrie, taking the line to mean Her virtues are riches enough (Deighton, ed. 1891). Muir (ed. 1952, p. xxxv): In Mirour He [Aganippus, King of France] deemde that vertue was of dowries all the best; see . Jones (1971, p. 177): Cf. AWW 2.3.144 (1045–6). Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 511) cite confusions of a and and in H8 2.4.175 (1541), Son. 129:11, and WT 1.2.104 (175); a and & were similar. Q has been defended by Jennens (ed. 1770), Collier (ed. 1843), and most forcefully by Ridley (ed. 1935): Q is quite intelligible and stronger: it is herself that I want, dowry or no dowry; but her perfections are such that they are dowry besides. So Stone (1980, p. 214): She is her own dowry, citing Abbott §20 on Sh.’s common use of self as a noun. Dowre was a common sp. of dower, not of dowrie. The Sokols (2000, p. 99): Here Dower…means dowry; on the legal distinction, see n. 49. Harbage (1963, p. 402): The perfection of compliments, from this urbane, fair-minded, and generous man.

265 Royall Leir]
White (ed. 1862) cites R3 3.7.[22] (2235) and Ant. 5.2.[37] (3243) to show that F’s Royal King is not a redundancy. Onions (1911), royal: Noble, majestic, generous, munificent. Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 61–2) compares 2643 and 3138.

266–7 giue…hand]
Foakes (ed. 1997): Burgundy takes her hand, and drops it again at 270. But Burgundy is speaking conditionally: If you give…I will take. Wells (ed. 2000): Alluding to the betrothal formality of handfasting.

268–9 Dutches…firme]
Collier (ed. 1843) retains the added F words although they seem to weaken the sense and clog the metre. Stone (1980, p. 62) agrees that they are intrusive. Jackson (1983, pp. 332–3), uniquely, defends their highlighting of Lear’s intransigence, his blend of firmness and infirmity. Elze (1886, p. 37) scans the line by shortening Burgundie (see n. 39) and contracting I haue and I am. Q lines 267–9, properly divided as in F, scan adequately without the F addition and somewhat clumsily with it. Brown (ed. 1976) thinks there are two half-lines, with a pause after each.

272 Peace…Burgundie]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): A formal good-bye. On the scansion see nn. 39, 47.

273–4 since…wife]
Law (1936, p. 222): Ungallant Burgundy attempts to lay all the blame on the lady.…Her retort is crushing. Virtually all critics contemn Burgundy, but Berry (1993, p. 80), uniquely: Burgundy, so apparently pusillanimous in his scene, has done well in staying clear of the British entanglement, and of Cordelia’s advanced sense of duty.

273 that]
Abbott (§287): Conjunctional affix. OED (conj. 7): Formerly added with a conjunctive force to various words that are now commonly used conjunctionally without it. Cf. Franz §546, and 339, 981, 1535, 2303+15, 2660, 2685, 3222.

273–4 respects Of fortune]
Generally preferred to F’s respect and Fortunes. In Q, respects means considerations as at 262. Schmidt (1879, p. 15): F might be a hendiadys meaning the same as Q. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Respect means esteem for Cordelia; her sudden loss of respect (they assert on no evidence) is the cause of France’s choler (358). Similarly, Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Respect = reputation. Wilson (ed. 1960), following Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 54) and Muir (ed. 1952): F means deferential esteem and material considerations. Harrison (ed. 1937): The F version, with both words singular, means my dowry. Stone (1980, p. 214): F comes close to nonsense. Since no one but Lear has shown any disrespect to Cordelia, and Q’s line reaffirms France’s charge in 262, Q is more probably right. Cordelia rightly mocks Burgundy for loving only her dowry, but she can hardly think, as in F, that her standing among her family and friends should be unimportant to him.

274 shall]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Here probably conveys the senses both of shall and will as we now use them.

275–86 Fairest…find]
Skottowe (1824, p. 121): In Holinshed Aganippus takes Cordeilla for her virtues without dower; see . Atkinson (1936) suggests that Sh. may have been indebted to Gerard Legh’s Accedens of Armory (1562) for France’s direct claiming of Cordelia. Lott (ed. 1974): The situation is paradoxical: a loved child no longer loved and a princess without inheritance. France…play[s] on its contrasts in his measured lines. Satin (1966, p. 474): In Leir 582–742 (see ), a highly romantic scene, reminiscent of the style of Thomas Dekker. Bullough (1973, p. 289): In Leir the Gallian King does not arrive in Britain until Cordella has been driven out, and he meets and woos her in his disguise as a pilgrim. Shakespeare avoids the mild humour and naive sentiment of this scene by having the French King take her publicly in full court.

275 rich…poore]
Noble (1935, p. 229) finds a parallel for the oxymoron in 2 Cor. 6:10: as poore, and yet making many rich: as hauing nothing, and yet possessing all thinges. Milward (1987, p. 163) and Shaheen (1987) add 2 Cor. 8:9: Our Lord Iesus Christ,…being riche, for your sakes became poore, that ye through his pouertie might be made riche.

277 ceaze vpon]
Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 122): No doubt an authorial spelling of seize. Deighton (ed. 1891): Eagerly appropriate (OED, v. 7, 9); perhaps with some older sense of legal claim to ownership. So Weis (ed. 1993): With overtones of the legal term seise, to put someone in legal possession of property or office (OED, 1). Cf. 1058. Brown (ed. 1976): He kneels, or kisses her, or gives some other token of his love. Or seizes her hand (Foakes).

278 Be it]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Either conditional—if it be—or a subjunctive used imperatively—let it be. Moberly (ed. 1876): It must surely be. Crook (ed. 1907): May I be.

278 lawfull]
Lott (ed. 1974): Perhaps he fears there may be some restraint on a suitor immediately following another.

279–86 Gods…find]
On the formal and epigrammatic effect of the rhyme, see n. 194–201. The couplets are variously explained and defended. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 146) sees them as loosening the tension after the hard-bitten 269. Armour (ed. 1930): France has been carried away gradually by his pity for the forsaken Cordelia, and intoxicated by her near presence. There is first a riot of antithesis and oxymoron; then he becomes lyrical, and his outburst is in rhyme. McCann (ed. 1964): By contrast, Lear’s [succeeding] lines [287–90] are not end-stopped. Reibetanz (1977, p. 32): The language of rhymed paradoxy shows that France is from another world than Lear’s dark one. Hunter (ed. 1972): The couplets indicate (as usual) a formalization of the attitudes involved. Brown (ed. 1976): Rhyme quickens the dialogue. Idem (ed. 1996): Showing France’s complete control over his choice. Lear also speaks in rhyme, but in short insistent phrases. The rhyme may suggest ceremony, as a king takes a queen. Foakes (ed. 1997): These rhyming couplets formally conclude the state business of the scene. Only Nicoll (1928, p. 156) dislikes them: The lines are, unfortunately, Sh.’s own, manifesting in their stiffness and mental rigidity the dramatist’s recognition of his own failure to make the scene live.

279 Gods, Gods!]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Not vocative; = O, the gods, the gods!—who have neglected Cordelia. So Hunter (ed. 1972): He loves her because the gods seem to have abandoned her. But surely this is a simple exclamation, = ye gods! France has immediate evidence of their—Lear’s and Burgundy’s—cold neglect; he cannot divine the gods’ feelings, nor is he likely to prefer his own to theirs.

279 from]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Because of (OED, prep. 14). More probably OED (7): Indicating a state, condition, etc. which is abandoned or which is changed for another.

279 couldst]
Abbott (§473): Est in superlatives is often pronounced st after dentals and liquids, not citing this l. Cf. Franz §722.

280 kindle]
OED (v.1 4): To be aroused…To become inflamed, ardent, or warm, in contrast to couldst.

280 inflam’d respect]
Crook (ed. 1907): Ardent love.…The word inflamed carries on the metaphor [of kindle]. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Passionate regard. Perrett (1904, p. 213) notes that in Geoffrey of Monmouth Aganippus is amore virginis inflammatus (ed. Griscom, 1919, p. 265); the metaphor is a commonplace. Foakes (ed. 1997): France echoes 273 but with a different meaning.

281 thy]
F corrects to my. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 365): Probably an accidental repetition of the first word in the line. Weis (ed. 1993) forces a sense from Q: Cast into what you see as the perilous uncertainties of fortune, i.e. Lear thought of Cordelia’s banishment as punitive. F’s reading is less complex: my chance means my lot.

281 throwne…chance]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Left to the chance of my accepting or rejecting her. Deighton (ed. 1891): With the idea, in chance, of good fortune, and perhaps, in thrown, of the throwing of dice. Craig (ed. 1901): Allotted to me. OED (Chance, sb. 3): (One’s) hap, fortune, luck, lot.

283 Dukes]
Sargeaunt (1909, p. 243), finding something ludicrous in the idea that France refers to [Burgundy] himself and his predecessors and successors, suspects a missing apostrophe. Idem (1933, p. 921): I take Dukes to be possessive case singular.…France means all the Duke’s possessions.…There is but one Duke of Burgundy. But France means the phrase to be ludicrous, sarcastically referring either to the whole line of Burgundian dukes or to all other such suitors as this duke.

283 watrish Burgundie]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Weak, spiritless (OED, a. 5: Containing excess of water.…Dilute, thin, poor…not firm or compact). Wright (ed. 1875): Used with a notion of contempt. See [watrish diet, Oth. 3.3.15 (1607)]. Burgundy was the best watered district of France. See Heyleyn (A little Description of the Great World, ed. 1633, p. 122): That which Queene Katharine was wont to say, that France had more rivers then all Europe beside; may in like manner be said of this Province in respect of France. Burgundy once included the Netherlands; see n. 39. Verity (ed. 1897): In reference to the wine Burgundy, though the sneer seems hardly appropriate to the wine. Armour (ed. 1930): [Referring] to the weakening of wine with water. Though OED records the watering of wine from the 14th c., it does not attest the use of Burgundy as the name of wine before the end of the 17th c. Craig (ed. 1931): Contemptuously, water being the symbol of fickleness.

284 vnprizd]
Abbott (§375): -ed is used for -able.…unprized by others, but precious [i.e., unprizeable, priceless] to me; cf. Franz §662, Smithers (1970, pp. 34–5), and 250, 410, 775, 819, 1510, 2370, 2456, 2724. So Wright (ed. 1875): Priceless (OED, ppl. a. 3, querying the meaning and quoting only this l.). Rolfe (ed. 1880): But the other sense [i.e., not valued, despised; so Schmidt, 1875] gives us an antithesis…instead of a mere repetition of epithets. Rolfe (ed. 1903): Used nowhere else by S.

285 vnkind]
On the ellipsis of subject and verb see Franz §563a. But who or what is unkind? If people at court, then the adjective here includes the combined senses of unnatural [OED, a. 4] and unaffectionate [OED, 6] (Clarkes, ed. 1868); also unlike kindred—see n. 132. In this case them would refer to only Burgundy and Lear (cf. their, 279), since theirs is the only unkindness to Cordelia that France or the audience has witnessed. Staunton (ed. 1859) suggests that the unkind one may be Cordelia: Unkinn’d, i.e.…forsaken by your kindred; in a later MS note (1860–74) he cites Ven. 204, She…died unkind, glossing deprived of kindred—but kind there means offspring (OED, sb. 11b). Lott (ed. 1974): Even though <they think you> unnaturally cruel, spoken ironically. Possibly the farewell is unkind, in the senses of unnatural or inappropriate (OED, a. 4; cf. Kind a. 1c, Proper, appropriate, fitting) or even Lacking in…kindly feeling (OED, 6), since Cordelia need not wish well people who have treated her badly. Though Sh. does not use the phrase kind farewell, see kinde commends (R2 3.1.38 [1350]) and kinde goodnight (Mac. 3.4.120 [1402]).

286 here…where]
Johnson (ed. 1765): These have the power of nouns (OED, Here adv. B, As sb. <nonce-uses>: = This place, quoting this l. as its first ex.; Where, adv. 14). Cf. Rom. 1.1.198 (206), hees some other where. See also Abbott §77.

287–90 Thou…benizon]
Q1’s mislining ruins the rhymes and, Hubler (1935, p. 430) argues, is evidence against Q’s being a reported text, since a reporter who was trying to line his verse properly would get the lining of the couplets correct. He ascribes the mislining to the compositor’s trying to conserve space, truncating 287 and turning over part of 291. Greg (1936, p. 177): There was ample room to divide the lines properly.…The natural inference is that the copy before the compositor was undivided. He believed…that the passage was intended for verse, but he was unable to recognize the lines correctly and even failed to notice the rime. Though Greg is technically right that there is enough room for For we at the end of 287, the compositor was setting a shorter measure with an indented stick for most of this page (hence the turnovers at 290–1 and 293–4), and may have erroneously made the verse line shorter than he needed to, in order to fit it readily within his narrowed margins. The copy may have been unclearly divided as well. See . Armour (ed. 1930): The rhyme is to mark Lear’s exit. Gardner (ed. 1969): The end of cool formality is marked with…the rhyming couplets.

289–90 therfore…benizon]
Delius (ed. 1854): Addressed not to the King of France but to Cordelia (Ger.). But possibly it is addressed to both. Lear’s therfore seems to mean because we have no such daughter as Cordelia, hence no reason to bid farewell with fatherly expressions of goodwill to either her or her fiancé. Though Goneril may expect the customary further complement of leaue taking betweene France and him (but see n. 327–8), Lear’s brusque dismissal and exit with noble Burgundy can only seem a snub to France, perhaps why he soon parts in choller (358).

290 grace]
See n. 251.

290 benizon?]
Schmidt (1874): Blessing (OED, sb. 2: esp. that of a father). The query is used in place of an exclamation mark, as commonly.

291–2 come…sisters]
Elze (1886, p. 37): A pentameter if -gũdy. Bid are elided and unaccented syllables. See n. 39.

291 Exit]
On F’s added Flourish see n. 202. Brown (ed. 1996): Trumpets and a formal, though hurried, processional exit extend this moment, allowing the audience time to observe how each person on stage reacts to the outcome of this scene. Foakes (ed. 1997): If Edmund has remained on stage…he would leave with the others here; see nn. 40, 202.

293–6 The…Father]
Greg (1936, p. 178): The quarto compositor…made the first words of Cordelia supply the end of a line begun by France. The division was thus upset at the start and he floundered on for another three lines before settling down to a normal metrical division.

293 The]
Most eds. retain the QF reading rather than emend to Rowe’s Ye, since the line makes good sense either as a vocative (the usual interpretation) or as an ironic appositive to your sisters (Porter & Clarke, ed. 1905). Steevens (ed. 1793): It [is] frequently impossible, in ancient MSS. to distinguish the one word [ye] from the customary abbreviation [ye] of the other [the]. Supporting The, Walker (1860, 3:276) compares JC 5.3.99 (2589), The last of all the Romans, far thee well, and 3H6 5.5.38 (3013), Take that, the likenesse of this Rayler here. Schmidt (ed. 1879) adds Cor. 1.6.6–7 (609–10), The Roman Gods, Leade their successes, and Per. 3.1.1 (1113), The God of this great Vast, rebuke these surges. White (ed. 1862), however, finds the original singularly awkward, if not senseless, and Simpson (1931, p. 447), colourless, reduc[ing] the text to flat commonplace.

293 iewels]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Who are naturally dear and precious to him. Harrison (ed. 1948): Whom my father values so highly. Wilson (ed. 1960): Term of endearment = darling, treasure, citing Oth. 1.3.195 (543) and TGV 4.4.47 (1867).

293 washt]
Wright (ed. 1875): That is, with tears. Schmidt (1875) and Rolfe (ed. 1880) give Shn. exx. of this usage. Phelps (ed. 1917): I do not think Cordelia is weeping. She means her eyes are clear. Ridley (ed. 1935): There is no reason why Cordelia should be tearful at leaving her sisters, though every reason why she should be at thus leaving her father. Both meanings are possible, as Brown (ed. 1976) and Halio (ed. 1992) note. Bratton (ed. 1987): Granville Barker’s instruction in 1940 was that Cordelia wept not out of self-pity, but for the kindness of France.

294 you what]
Walker (1860, 1:68–70) and Abbott §414 give many Shn. exx. of the redundant object. Franz (§304): It follows verbs of knowing, perceiving, and thinking. Cf. Idem (1935, p. 393): Here two clauses, I know you and I know what you are, are combined. Wright (ed. 1875) compares Mark 1:24, and Tovey (ed. 1896), Luke 4:31.

296 named]
Page (ed. 1889): By their true names. Lott (ed. 1974): Which would be too abusive.

296 vse]
Capell (1783, 1.2:144) prefers this to F’s Loue, since Love was not a thing to be thought of, from those sisters; but good usage might be asked and expected. Greg (1942, p. 93), however, imagining vse the substitution of an actor familiar with later events: She had yet no ground for supposing they would use the old man ill. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 55): The next line makes this clear.…Cordelia is in effect saying to Goneril and Regan, You have said that you love our father—do so.…The person responsible for the Q reading was thinking ahead to their later mistreatment. That person was probably Sh., preparing the audience. Besides, Cordelia has already heard a doubtful Kent exhort the sisters to match their large speeches and wordes of loue with suitable deedes (198–9), and her whole speech here shows the same doubt that they will do so; and vse fits well with duties (301) in Goneril’s reply.

297 professed]
Wright (ed. 1875): Which had made professions (OED, ppl. a. 2—sometimes with an implication of not real—quoting this l.). Clarkes (ed. 1868): Professing, or full of professions. Many eds. since Steevens (ed. 1778) have given the past participle the present, active meaning professing, perhaps unnecessarily.

297 bosoms]
See n. 125. Rolfe (ed. 1880): Love, comparing 2992. Tovey (ed. 1896): And care.

297 commit]
Brown (ed. 1976): Entrust/imprison.

298–9 But…place]
Brown (ed. 1996): Possibly spoken aside.

298 grace]
See n. 251. Deighton (ed. 1891): Such favour that he would listen to my words.

299 preferre]
Schmidt (1875): Recommend (OED, v. 4, but only things, not persons). Clarkes (ed. 1868): Promote (OED, 1). Joseph (ed. 1966): Also prefer for him; but such a meaning is not attested for prefer to. Foakes (ed. 1997): She already seems to be thinking of restoring Lear to the throne. But Cordelia’s statement is conditional—If I stood in his grace—and she could be thinking of sheltering Lear in France, as Cordella wishes to do in Leir 1281–3, 1817 (see , ). There is no reason to think that the better place is the very throne that Lear has chosen to renounce.

300 So]
Deighton (ed. 1891): With these words.

301–2 Gonorill…Regan]
The names are reversed in F. In Q the division of lines in the scene is more nearly equal, and Goneril consistently speaks first. Doran (1931, p. 176): The transposition…may have been done by either [Q or F] printer. Kirschbaum (1945, p. 19): It is really immaterial which of the two is given either speech. McLeod (1983, p. 166), however: The F inversion may be intentional, giving Regan consistently shorter speeches and Goneril more lines.

301 Prescribe]
Malone (ed. 1790): Used formerly without to subjoined (OED, v. 2).

301 vs]
McLeod (1983, p. 166): Possibly the royal us also favored by Regan at 313. But neither is speaking as a queen in either text, simply as spokesman for vs both, Cordelia having addressed them jointly.

301 duties]
F’s singular dutie means virtually the same, the duty of each. On the pluralizing of abstract nouns, see n. 9. Werstine (1983, p. 264): Particularly striking among Compositor E’s literal substitutions are his frequent deletions and additions of final -s.

302 study]
Schmidt (1875): Endeavour (OED, sb. 4). Cf. 34.

303 content]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Please. Much stronger than in modern usage (OED, v. 1b).

304 at…almes]
The construction is difficult though the general meaning is clear. Regan says mockingly that France received Cordelia without dowry when fortune was doling out petty charities, not bestowing bounteous awards (Kittredge, ed. 1940). The phrase is Shn.: in Oth. 3.4.122 (2276–7) Cassio may adopt some other course, To fortunes almes. In both instances Fortune’s alms may mean her charitable action or the material substance given (OED, sb. 1). The difficult word is at. There seems no lexical basis for glossing as one of the alms (Delius, ed. 1854) or to subsist on the alms (Moberly, ed. 1876). Wright’s (ed. 1875) Used with the price at which anything is valued (OED, prep. 27) yields a kind of sense: France received you at the value of mere alms. Sense can be made more easily. OED (25): Of relation to someone’s will or disposition: e.g. at his…mercy; thus Caldecott (MS notes, 1813–33), At the mercy of fortune, and Hunter (ed. 1869), At the charity of chance. So Joseph (ed. 1966): Given by Fortune as a matter of chance not desert. There is an implied contrast with what is given by Heaven, also not as a matter of desert, but of grace. Less likely is OED (24): Of conditioning circumstance: e.g. at…expense, charge: though Craig (ed. 1901) cites Pepys’s Diary (ed.
