Minors, 1879, 10:189), buried at the alms of the parish, and glosses i.e. at the expense of the parish, such a reading here takes the sting out of Regan’s taunt. One other possibility has been overlooked: OED (11): Determining the source from which anything comes, and at which we seek it: e.g. To…receive…at. Cf. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 511): The place where Fortune dispenses petty charity.

304 scanted]
Craig (ed. 1901): Begrudged, stinted (OED, v. 5). Cf. 1418, 1459, 1721.

305 are worth]
Theobald (ed. 1733): Deserve. Cf. 1320.

305 worth that…wanted]
In Q, Regan taunts Cordelia both for her new impoverishment and for having brought it on herself by disobeying Lear. OED (Want, v. 2): To fail to have, or get; (2e): To be deprived of, to lose. Regan says, You have deserved your lack or loss of value, i.e., the amount of your devaluation. Thus Rann (ed. 1794), on a hint from Malone (ed. 1790, 10:680): [You well deserve] the loss of dower, which you have missed of through your undutifulness. Though simple clarity has been sacrificed to alliteration and wordplay, Q’s reading is intelligible and is a logical conclusion to Regan’s insult. A more difficult interpretation, involving a shift in tone, would make the whole line a sarcasm: You certainly showed yourself worthy of having that dowry you lost! Weis (ed. 1993): You deserve the nothing that you appear to have desired, or, and you are utterly worthless, i.e. you are lacking in worth, and that is all you are worth. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 365): Q’s worth is repeated from earlier in the line. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 511) would change Q’s the worth to the worst: Cordelia has…asked for (wanted) the worst. But not even Regan can believe that Cordelia wanted to be disinherited and disowned. Wells (ed. 2000) glosses courted, not quite the same as wanted. F’s change of the second worth to want increases the wordplay, introduces much ambiguity, and has resulted in many conjectural emendations (see ). Theobald (ed. 1733) takes both wants to mean lack: You well deserve to meet with that Want of Love from your Husband, which you have profess’d to want for our Father; but on the evidence in this scene Regan can hardly predict that France will lack love for Cordelia. Steevens (ed. 1773): You are well worthy to deserve the want (i.e. poverty) which…you have wanted (i.e. solicited or desired to have). Tollet (in Steevens, ed. 1778): You are well deserving of the want of the dower that you are without. This apparent redundancy—Jennens (ed. 1770) calls it a kind of Hebraism, like seeding seed (Gen. 1:29)—is named by Wright (ed. 1875) a cognate accusative, and Schmidt (ed. 1879) gives several Shn. exx. such as wrong not that wrong (Err. 2.2.172 [566]) and loue…left vnlou’d (Ant. 3.6.52–3 [1806–7]). Rann (ed. 1794): [You] well deserve the state of want which you have so narrowly escaped. Wright (op. cit.): You…deserve the want of that affection [Lear’s] in which you yourself have been wanting. Tovey (1883, p. 426; ed. 1896): You well deserve the poverty from which you have been exempt hitherto. Weis (op. cit.): And you thoroughly deserve the lack of that which you have forgone. Modern eds. have continued all these permutations and combinations, want meaning deprivation of dowry, of inheritance, and/or of fatherly or marital affection, and wanted meaning lacked or sought. Both the Q and F texts are difficult; Malone and Tollet show that they may be interpreted as meaning the same. Colman (ed. 1982): Gonerill rhymes here (scanted/wanted) to imitate the pithiness of a proverb. Halio (ed. 1992): The alliteration and word-play (anadiplosis) emphasise Gonerill’s sarcasm.

306 Time shal vnfould]
For such proverbs as Time brings the truth to light, Truth is time’s daughter, etc., see Tilley T324, T338, T580, T591; cf. 3123. Fraser (1962, pp. 41–5), Elton (1966, p. 75 n.), Andresen (1974, pp. 155–8, 166) and Fabiny (1984) cite a wealth of contemporary treatments of the temporis filia veritas theme, and Iwasaki (1973) discusses its use in emblems. Collins (1903, p. 851) finds a version in Sophocles, Frag. 280. Carter (1905, p. 433) compares Job 28:11, Luke 8:17, Num. 32:23, 1 Cor. 3:13, and Prov. 28:13, and Milward (1987, p. 164), Matt. 19:26; in none of these is time the agent. Tayler (1990, p. 29) compares Matt. 10:26. Colman (ed. 1982): Cordelia caps Gonerill’s pseudo-proverb with one of her own. Hammond (1991, p. 100): Also in a sententious couplet. Fabiny (op. cit., pp. 236–9): The proverb establishes Cordelia as the most concentrated emblematic representative of Truth, Purity, and Innocence.

306 pleated]
This and F’s plighted are collateral forms of plaited and here mean the same, primarily folded (hence concealed [Halio, ed. 1992]) and secondarily interweaved (OED, Pleat v. 1, 2, quoting this l. as its first ex. of fig. use). F’s form may add a quibble on pledged (OED, ppl. a.1 1); so Hunter (ed. 1972): Swearing as the truth, things that are false. Johnson (in Steevens, ed. 1773): Complicated, involved. Hudson (ed. 1871): And so ma[d]e dark. Craig (ed. 1901): Figuratively, dissembling. Horsman (ed. 1973): Devious.

307 Who]
In Q, Who refers to people in general (Dyce, ed. 1865); in the different F line, it refers to Time (Mason, 1785, p. 340). In Q, a one-line proverb about Time is balanced by a pointed one-line application of it to people such as Goneril and Regan. In F, both lines describe Time’s action more generally and impersonally. There is some danger in the F line that Who will at first seem to mean whoever rather than refer to Time. Duthie (ed. 1949): The F version…sounds more awkward and stilted than that of Q; but the speech is a sententious one.

307 couers faults]
Henley (in Malone, ed. 1790), Wordsworth (1864, p. 162), and Noble (1935, p. 229) find an allusion to Prov. 28:13 (AV): He that covereth his sins, shall not prosper. Milward (1987, p. 165): Which may have suggested Cordelia’s ironical addition [308]. Muir (1986, p. 58): This chapter [Prov. 28] was appointed to be read on St Stephen’s Day [Hassel, 1979, p. 24]—the day on which King Lear was performed before James I. See . Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 532) prefer Mason’s emendation covert (see textual n.): The image of time covering faults is…eccentric (see n. 306). But time must cover them for a while until revealing them eventually; and cf. WT 4.1.2 (1581): Time that makes, and vnfolds error.

307 shame them]
In Q, shame is the subject and them the object of derides: Whoever covers faults, shame mocks them at last. The lack of agreement between the plural them and the singular antecedent Who has led to emendation to the plural Who cover and to Singer’s compound verb (see textual n.). But Elizabethan grammar allowed -s inflections on verbs after a plural subject (Abbott §333), as perhaps Who is here, or might consider whoever a group; and possibly them is intentionally put here to point to both sisters, as he would not. In F, with shame is adverbial and derides loses its object by ellipsis: [Time] who covers faults, at last [unfolds them and] derides [them] with shame (essentially Sisson’s [1956, 2:231] reading). Derides should be transitive, since the intransitive To laugh contemptuously (OED, v. 2) with shame makes no sense. In Q its object is apparently Who[ever], in F it is faults (Schmidt, ed. 1879). See .

308 Well…prosper]
Crook (ed. 1907): Spoken ironically. Or as a formal courtesy.

310–32 Sister…heate]
Verity (ed. 1897): Goneril is a stronger character than Regan, with more originality of mind and power of initiative. So here it is she who sees the trouble before them and proposes to meet it. Regan merely echoes her sister’s words, and would further think of the matter.…The interview between the sisters is of great importance (1) as foreshadowing their conduct towards Lear, (2) as confirming and illustrating the impression of his character which the earlier part of the scene has made.…At the same time, from the point of view of the play’s construction, it seems a little artificial to make them remain behind thus instead of leaving with Albany and Cornwall. Adams (1948, p. 316): Goneril and Regan move back to the study, i.e. to the Globe’s inner stage or alcove; but such movement is not necessary. Smith (ed. 1902): Note the change from verse to prose. We pass with it from the higher plane of passion to underhand scheming. Vickers (1968, p. 351): The brief prose conversation between Goneril and Regan is at once a sign that the ceremony and public usage is over and also a pointer to their dissimulation as they lay aside all pretence of respect to Lear. Horsman (ed. 1973): The scene ends as it began, with talk, knowing and confident, in prose. Rosenberg (1972, p. 82): Goneril and Regan now seem least evil. They face a practical problem, taking care of an old father, and they discuss this practically.…If no love is expressed for him, neither is hate: they are concerned for their own convenience. Later, they discover evil. Yet the lines reveal a mounting difference and competition between them, ominous of the fierce rivalry that will destroy [them]. Berry (1993, p. 72): Goneril and Regan are not close; the opening address, Sister, is cool and functional, and no first-name terms are exchanged, nor is the thou form.

310–12 Sister…night]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 365): In setting up prose as verse here F takes over an error from Q. Or from a common MS behind Q and the playbook.

311 neerely]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Closely, vitally. OED (adv. 3): Particularly, quoting this l.

312 will]
Abbott (§405): Purpose[s] motion (OED, v.1 18), as does shall, is, and must, without a verb of motion. Cf. Franz §621, and 35, 355, 521, 641, 839, 1600, 2400.

312 hence to night]
Eccles (ed. 1792): There is not, I think, throughout the play, the least hint given as to the particular part of the realm in which any scene lies, till we are introduced towards the conclusion into the neighborhood of Dover; nor are we informed whether it be intended that either of the sisters should make the palace of Lear her future residence. All we know is that he was to abide alternately with them in whatsoever part they held their court. Greg (1940, p. 432): Royal business was usually transacted in the morning, and the whole affair would probably be over before dinner. Thus there would be ample time for the king to leave the same evening in order to take up his residence with Goneril.…It can be no great distance, since he would hardly propose riding far into the night. Halio (ed. 1992): Lear has not actually stipulated with whom he will first reside…, but Regan rightly assumes that Gonerill, as the eldest daughter, will be first.

314–26 You…banishment]
Keats (1818; in Spurgeon, 1928, p. 50): How finely is the brief of Lear’s character sketched in this conference—from this point does Shakespeare spur him out to the mighty grapple—the seeded pride that hath to this maturity blowne up [Tro. 1.3.316–17 (782–3)] Shakespeare doth scatter abroad on the winds of Passion, where the germs take b<u>oyant root in stormy Air, suck lightning sap, and become voiced dragons—self-will and pride and wrath are taken at a rebound by his giant hand and mounted to the Clouds—there to remain and thunder eve<r>more.

314 changes]
Schmidt (1874): Caprice (OED, sb. 4b: Inconstancy, fickleness, quoting this l.).

315 not]
Most eds. agree with Dyce (ed. 1865) that this word dropt out of the folio by oversight and that the result is in defiance of common sense. Delius (ed. 1854) and Schmidt (ed. 1879) think that little means too little up to now; it will get worse (Ger.); but, as Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 169) points out, this contradicts the daughters’ complaints that Lear hath euer been full of changes from long ingrafted habit.

317 appeares]
The verb lacks a clear subject. Possibly there is an ellipsis of it; see Abbott §404, Franz §306. Alternatively, with…off may be loosely construed as a nominative.

317 grosse]
OED (a. 3): Obvious. Abbott (§1): Adjectives are freely used as adverbs; cf. Franz §368. Most eds., however, prefer F’s regular adverbial form grossely.

318 infirmitie…age]
Perhaps proverbial: Tilley A72, Old Age is full of infirmities; but since Tilley’s single ex. postdates the play, Dent (1981) is dubious.

319 slenderly]
OED (adv. 1): Scantily,…poorly.

319 knowne himselfe]
Seymour (1805, 2:93): Been in the full possession of his faculties. Crook (ed. 1907): Known his own mind. Plato’s widely known Apollonian proverb Nosce teipsum (see Tilley K175) carries the clear implication, know your own limits if you wish to be wise; cf. AYL 3.5.57 (1830). Foakes (ed. 1997): By understanding the relation, in Sir Philip Sidney’s words, between erected wit, or intelligence, and infected will, or the desires prompted by the senses. The phrase has been taken to anticipate Lear’s process of self-knowledge in the play: see Jenkins (1964), Jorgensen (1967), and many others, and see .

320–4 The…them]
Craig (ed. 1901) compares Leir 195: For he, you know, is alwayes in extremes; see .

320 of his time]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Part of his life (OED, sb. 7a). Cf. 383.

320 hath]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Probably the nominative is the best…time, but may be he, colloquially pronounced, and written a, and sometimes omitted altogether, especially before has or hath. See Abbott (§400): The omission of the nominative is…common with has; see also §402. Cf. Franz §306, and 1590.

321 rash]
Craig (ed. 1901): Hasty, hot-headed (OED, a. 2). Cf. 161, 1453.

322 ingrafted]
This and F’s ingraffed are variant forms of engrafted. OED (v. 2): Fig.…To implant…in the mind. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Firmly embedded in his nature. Muir & Danby (1950, p. 49): Possibly Sh. derived the word from Sidney’s Arcadia [2.10.2]; but Sh. had used the word several times before, e.g. Son. 37–8, JC 2.1.184 (818).

322 condition]
Malone (1783, p. 48): Qualities of mind. Delius (ed. 1854): Disposition (OED, sb. 11). Cf. 2347+34.

323 therwithal]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Together with them.

323 infirme]
OED (a. 2): Feeble, esp. through age, quoting this l. as its first ex. Cf. 1675.

324 cholericke]
OED (a. 3): Irascible, quoting this l. Gardner (ed. 1969): Choler was properly one of the four humours (with blood, melancholy, and phlegm) which made up the body’s complexion. An excess of choler, which caused ill-temper and anger, was thought to be commonplace in old age. Mahood (1992, p. 238): See [L.] Stone, Crisis [of the Aristocracy, 1965], p. 224, on the exessive irritability of men in the sixteenth century, which he puts down to bad diet. Hoeniger (1992, p. 318): There can be little doubt that Goneril uses choleric in the modern sense, well-established by Shakespeare’s time, of prone to anger rather than referring to his humoral condition. For by a tradition as old as Hippocrates, the prevailing humor of old age was thought to be black bile or melancholy, not choler, which was that of youth.

324 yeares]
OED (Year 5b): Pl. Old age.

325, 331 Rag., Ragan.]
On the spelling see DP n. 16.

325 vnconstant]
Schmidt (1875): Unsteady, fickle. Wright (ed. 1875): Irregular, uncertain, abrupt. Joseph (ed. 1966): Impatient; unattested in OED.

325 starts]
OED (sb.2 4a): A sudden and transient effort or display of energy, quoting this l. Cf. 1H4 3.2.125 (1945), start of spleene (OED 4d: A sudden fit of passion). Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): Ill-considered actions. Like Bucknill (1859, pp. 140–1) and Kellogg (1866, pp. 17–18), Hoeniger (1992, pp. 309 ff.) considers these starts to be evidence of a long ingrafted madness, particularly that habitual madness of anger which the stoics called brevis furor. The daughters, however, speak only of a former rashness and lack of self-knowledge; they refer to his vnconstant starts and vnruly waywardnes as recent developments due to the infirmity of age, now (in the present scene) appearing too grossly in his treatment of Cordelia and Kent.

325 like]
Wright (ed. 1875): Likely (OED, a. 9). Cf. 2287, 2843+9.

327–8 There…him]
Complement, so spelled from Q1 until Theobald’s ed. of 1757, has been until recently understood to mean Observance of ceremony…formal civility.…Now compliment (OED, sb. 8b, quoting this l.). But the statement may seem a non-sequitur amidst the sister’s scheming, and, as Nelson (1974, p. 194) remarks, neither sister has left the stage to learn that farewell ceremonies are going on. Shirley (1963, p.43) imagines that they may hear an offstage flourish of trumpets. Delius (ed. 1854): They are simply apprehensive that further conflict could arise during the further compliment of leave-taking (Ger.); similarly Wilson (ed. 1960): Prob. sarcastic; cf. [358]. Verity (ed. 1897): While Lear is thus engaged, she and Regan will confer. But complement may also mean That which completes or makes perfect (OED, 3). In addition to the exile of Kent, what completes the picture of Lear’s poore iudgement is his (perhaps predictable) further alienation of France. Hunter (ed. 1869): Goneril refers to the dissolution of amity between France and Britain. Ross (1978, pp. 25–6): Lear’s breaking with France complements his banishment of Kent. Nelson (op. cit.): Goneril’s reference is to the leave-taking which we have just witnessed on the stage, not to a formal ceremony. Foakes (ed. 1997): Burgundy’s name might rather be expected here. A matter of authorial inadvertence? Only if compliment rather than complement is understood. Cf. 358, 1505, 3187, and see the textual n. Dessen (1999, p. 55), compliment: (1) usually a noun or verb that requires some formal act of civility, courtesy, or respect but can mean (2) complement (the usual spelling), accoutrement.
This puzzling phrase, an apparent non-sequitur and inconsequence in the sisters’ conference, is susceptible of a simple explanation. They are attempting to justify further action against Lear on the grounds of his instability. They name the three instances of his rashness that they have just witnessed: his casting off of Cordelia; his banishment of Kent; and his further complement of insulting and dismissing France without ceremony, thus opening a breach between two countries. Gloucester repeats the catalogue in the next scene. Though only the sense completion is needed, conceivably both meanings of complement may apply: the compliment of Lear’s rude dismissal of France is the complement that rounds out their list of instances. As Nelson says, the sisters cannot know that there will be any further ceremonious leave-taking between Lear and France, and indeed such niceties seem unlikely. The hot-bloudied France (1505, F), we hear soon, in choller parted (358). Wells (loc. cit.) lists modern productions in which this difficult phrase has been cut.

328 hit]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Agree (OED, v. 17, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Rann (ed. 1794): Proceed upon one plan. Hudson (ed. 1871): Unite in the same plan or course of action (OED, 19: To direct one’s course…to strike out, in, in a particular direction). Clarkes (ed. 1868): Let us strike at the same time, let us act in concert. Hunter (ed. 1972): Aim together is also possible. Brown (ed. 1996): May…suggest physical force and cruelty. Craig (ed. 1901) compares Leir 1156, ile strike it sure (see ); there Ragan is talking alone, and means simply strike. Most eds. find F’s sit a feeble and erroneous substitution for a genuine reading; hit = agree being a new usage at the time, Q’s word is not likely to be a compositor’s error (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 170). Rather, F’s sit is likely to be a compositor’s lapse of aural memory (Stone, 1980, p. 215). A few defend F. Schmidt (1879, p. 15): To hold a session, to take counsel together (Ger.); but his instances, as Furness (ed. 1880) points out, refer to a judicial assembly or a session more or less formal and solemn, a meaning strained when applied to an agreement between sisters. Brooke (ed. 1947): That is, in order to continue this conversation. Horsman (ed. 1973): Take counsel. Weis (ed. 1993): Take up an agreed position. McLeod (1983, pp. 157 ff., 191 n. 11): The Q and F variants may be co-ordinate, each valid in its context. Variants so close in spelling or sound, however, may be suspected to be the result of misreading or a slip of aural memory of one of the words. McLeod proposes fit as a graphically and literarily defensible reading.

329 cary]
Schmidt (1874): To bear (OED, v. 28d). Eds. qualify: Is allowed (Crook, ed. 1907), Have any real (Harrison, ed. 1937), (Continue to) wield (Wilson, ed. 1960).

329 dispositions]
OED (Disposition sb. 7): Inclination (sometimes = desire, intention, purpose); state of mind or feeling.…In pl.…mental tendencies or qualities; hence nearly = sense 6. Thus for F’s singular disposition, OED (6): Tendency…of the mind…temperament. Dyce (ed. 1865): Either reading may stand, pointing out that Goneril uses both forms, plural at 733 and singular at 807, Q and F agreeing in both cases. Cf. 456, 733, 807, 1229, 1975, 2303. For F Compositor E’s omission of terminal -s, see n. 301.

329 as he beares]
Verity (ed. 1897), bear: To have (OED, v.1 7). Deighton (ed. 1891): In the same capricious manner as at present. Verity (ed. 1897): With his usual impulsiveness. Muir (ed. 1952): In the way we have just seen. Rolfe (ed. 1880): Snatching back his authority the moment his will is crossed. Weis (ed. 1993): With such moods as are innate in him.

330 last]
Empson (1951, p. 128): Seems to imply previous renunciations. Muir (ed. 1952): Recent (OED, a. 3).

330 surrender]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Of Cordelia’s portion. Adams, in Irving & Marshall (ed. 1889): Of the kingdom. Joseph (ed. 1966): Also giving way to passion.

330 offend]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Give us trouble instead of being a benefit.

331 on’t]
Means the same as F’s of it (OED, On prep. 22b). Cf. 669+10, 958, 1478, 2239, and n. 632.

332 doe]
Like Bransom (1934, p. 36), Kittredge (ed. 1940): Emphatic—in contrast with think. Foakes (ed. 1997): Their stated intent is good theatre, though nothing comes of it. But 522 may suggest at least some strategic agreement.

332 it’h heate]
Steevens (ed. 1773): We must strike while the iron is hot. The phrase is common: Dent (1981), citing Tilley I94. Less likely interpretations are Craig’s (ed. 1901) In one continuous effort, citing WT 1.2.96 (166), and Willson’s (1979) detection of a pun on lust. Weis (ed. 1993): Urgently.

333 <Scena Secunda>]
Goggin (ed. 1910): This Scene shows several marks of haste or carelessness in composition. Presumably it takes place on the day following Scene i., since Gloucester says that the King is gone to-night (i.e. last night [see n. 359]…). Yet how have Gloucester and Edmund reached Gloucester’s castle (where the scene is supposed to take place) after the King’s departure, unless we are to assume that they travelled all night for no apparent purpose? Again, why should Edgar be supposed to write to Edmund when they were living under the same roof and could see each other at any moment?…Again, where is Edmund’s lodging in which Edgar is to be concealed? If it were Edmund’s room in the castle, are we to asume that Edgar lies hidden there for a fortnight, perhaps more (see [811]), until the night Regan comes to the castle (II.i.)?…And why, if all three were residing under one roof, and that Gloucester’s castle, should Gloucester himself have any difficulty in finding Edgar? A further inconsistency appears in the fact that Edgar had seen Gloucester last night without Edmund’s knowledge, yet Edmund had been with Gloucester at the palace in Scene i., and must have travelled home with him. See nn. 811 and 926. Budd (ed. 1935) finds further improbabilities in the scene: It is, for instance, most unlikely that Edgar, had he been the cunning plotter that Edmund pretends, would have provided evidence against himself by committing his thoughts to writing.…Moreover, why should Edmund forge an incriminating letter when Gloucester does not know Edgar’s handwriting—a fact in itself improbable? Why, again, should not a man of Edgar’s honesty and courage tackle Gloucester at once on the accusation instead of lending colour to it by later taking to hiding and disguise?
Eccles (ed. 1792) moves this scene to the beginning of Act 2 (926) so that Edgar will not, improbably, wait in hiding for a fortnight (see 811) before Edmund takes further action to discredit him and Gloucester takes action to pursue him (993–5). As Furness (ed. 1880) notes, Eccles removes from his text the contradictory evidence in 358–61 that Sh. wanted 1.2 to follow 1.1 immediately.
Most eds. since Pope (see textual n.) locate the scene at Gloucester’s Castle, without authority, as Perrett (1904, p. 259) notes. Ringler (1981, p. 185): Castles were first brought to England by the Normans, while according to Holinshed King Lear died in 812 BC; see DP n. 3–4. There are two objections to the term castle. Gloucester’s dwelling during the play is always called a house (see 1588, 1755, 1971, 2342) and is described at 1588 as little. Hunter (1908, pp. 84–6) also notes the absence of any evidence that Gloucester and Edmund have travelled at all between the first and second scenes, and urges the greater likelihood that Gloucester’s agitation in 358–61 follows soon after his leaving the council chamber, not after a leisurely day’s travel back to his own house. In fact, Hunter argues, the best explanation for Gloucester’s ignorance of Edgar’s whereabouts (412), for Edgar’s opportune arrival (462), and for Edmund’s question about when Edgar last saw Gloucester is that all three persons have temporary and separate lodgings in different parts of the city where the Court has been held. Gloucester of course might still be troubled, at his own home, a day after the momentous events of the first scene. Adams (1948, p. 316), on no evidence: As long as the Edmund sub-plot runs parallel to the main plot, it is staged in five scenes, on the upper stage, which represents a room in the second floor of Gloucester’s Castle. Such extensive staging on an upper stage is now generally discredited. Cf. nn. 948, 1751, 1969, 2057. Reynolds (1951, p. 99) rejects this theory, which requires many scenes in the balcony with nobody on the stage below. Actually, I know of no such scenes in Elizabethan drama definitely placed above, where they would be more remote from the audience. Bratton (ed. 1987) records stage-settings showing a Tudor castle, pallisaded Saxon camp, Druid henge, or modern room.
Bradley (1909, pp. 238–40) argues that the place had better be left vague, as Sh. intended; if 1.2 occurs at court, as Hunter argues, and the scene enacted in 2.1 is expected to take place that same evening (426), then several absurdities ensue: by the time 2.1 occurs, a considerable interval has elapsed. Edmund, for some reason left totally unexplained, has failed to produce Edgar; and…not only have Gloucester and Edmund gone into the country, but Edgar has gone too. And he has gone to the same place!…Shakespeare, if he imagined any place at all for I, ii,…imagined the place of I, i. But it was not necessary to indicate a place, and he may have known that the spectators would not trouble their heads about the matter.…In II, i, on the other hand, it was necessary to have a definite place, for the plot requires that almost all the chief persons should meet at Gloucester’s house in the country. So he put Edgar in concealment in his father’s house, confident that the spectators would not ask the awkward question how and when he got there. Granville-Barker’s (1927, p. 149 n.) conjectures that for some economy in the working out of the sub-plot Sh. changed his mind about when the mock-duel of Edmund and Edgar would take place, without changing this very evening (426). Greg (1940, p. 432 and n.): But surely this would be an incredible piece of clumsiness on the part of an experienced dramatist; the locality must be the same in both [1.2 and 2.1], as this very euening and the call for light…torches (963–4) imply. Greg therefore believes that the two scenes happen at Gloucester’s house on the day after the events of 1.1; see nn. 359, 926. The assumption of Bradley and many others that a considerable interval has elapsed between 1.1 and 2.1 may depend on a misinterpretation of within a fortnight (see n. 811). It is possible that 1.1 ends at mid-day, and that on that same day Lear travels to Goneril’s and Gloucester returns to his house (see n. 312); that 1.2 takes place at Gloucester’s house on the morning of the next day; that 1.3, 1.4, and 1.5 occur at Goneril’s house before dinner (midday) of that same day; and that the false duel in 2.1 takes place during the evening of that same day, as Edmund promised it would, before the later arrival of Cornwall and Regan, who are seeking to avoid receiving Lear at their house. Greg (op. cit., p. 439), however, points out that certain other indications imply a longer though vaguer interval between 1.1 and 1.3: two daies (601; but see n.), pined away (603), Knights grow ryotous (513), great abatement (589), of late (597), and within a fortnight (811). He explains the discrepancy by a double stream of time flowing in the play, a rapid one for foreground events and a more leisurely one for events in the background. On theories about double time in this play, and their inconclusiveness, see Knowles (1999, pp. 44–5), and n. 1638+1.

335–56 Thou…Bastards]
In Q Edmund’s soliloquy is misprinted as prose. Doran (1931, p. 129) suspects that revisions in Sh.’s MS obscured the line divisions. Like Crane (1952, p. 162), Vickers (1968, p. 351): [Edmund] begins and ends in verse soliloquies frankly admitting his guile and cynicism to us, while his dissembling intrigue is conducted in prose. See nn. 358–446 and 447–61, and cf. 499–504. Foakes (ed. 1997): This scene inverts the arrangement [of 1.1], and is in prose, framed by two verse soliloquies.…[Edmund] is given a sympathetic prominence through direct address to the audience. Danby (1949, p. 32): No medieval devil ever bounced on to the stage with a more scandalous self-announcement. Bratton (ed. 1987): Edmund is clearly related to the Vice of the medieval stage, who was not only a boisterous source of mischief, but also a manager of events and mediator between audience and action…; thus he speaks in confiding soliloquy here. Findlay (1994, p. 225): Such conspiratorial confidence is characteristic of bastard villains who follow on the tradition of the Vice character. Brown (ed. 1996): A vein of humor in the soliloquy can be…indulged, in byplay with the audience, crude gestures, and caricature [of] different voices.
Warburton (ed. 1747): Sh. makes his bastard an Atheist. Steevens (apud Johnson, ed. 1765, 8:2K4v): Edmund only speaks of nature in opposition to custom, and not…to the existence of a God. Idem (ed. 1773): Edmund means only as he came not into the world as custom or law had prescribed, so he had nothing to do but to follow Nature and her laws, which make no difference between legitimacy and illegitimacy, between the eldest and the youngest. Idem (ed. 1778): Edmund concludes this very speech by an invocation to heaven [356]. Spilsbury & Marshall (ed. 1905): Edmund seeks to justify his villainy. He poses as the victim of society, which punishes him for his illegitimacy. Draper (1938, pp. 132–3): His initial soliloquy…gives the key-note of his character. Obviously, such sentiments were outrageous to Elizabethans, who regarded the laws of legitimacy and primogeniture as sacred.…With unspeakable impudence, he even calls on the gods to stand up for bastards. Brennan (1990, p. 188): A defiantly blasphemous inversion of…Heb. 12:8. Orgel (ed. 1999, p. xxxvi): Illegitimacy was a commonplace fact of Shakespeare’s England,…and though illegitimate children were barred from the line of succession and the inheritance of landed estates, no stigma was attached to the fact of bastardy itself. Noblemen freely acknowledged their illegitimate children, and often provided handsomely for them, and illegitimacy was no bar to social and political success: Elizabeth’s powerful minister the Earl of Leicester was illegitimate, as were, technically, both Elizabeth herself and…Queen Mary I. Edmund…loses nothing on account of it.…Even if he were not illegitimate, he would be entitled only to what his father chooses to give him: under the English law of primogeniture, the eldest son inherits the title, and the bulk of the estate. The Sokols (2000, pp. 27–9), however, show that the older tolerance for bastardy was fast disappearing in the early 17th c.: see n. 12–27. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Edmund’s soliloquy rings all the changes on the words natural and base and legitimate. He is a natural son—i.e., a bastard. The Elizabethans supposed the word bastard to be derived from the adjective base, though in fact the resemblance between the words is quite accidental. The substance of Edmund’s argument is that a younger son who is a bastard has as much natural right to be his father’s heir as an elder son who is legitimate, since the distinction is merely a matter of law (which is only codified custom) and not of nature. Armstrong (1949, p. 665) finds a possible source for Edmund’s epicurean atheism in Sidney’s Arcadia 3.10.4–5, in Cecropia’s debate with Pamela about various conceptions of nature. Muir (ed. 1952, p. lxii) finds the idea of two Natures in Montaigne [not cited]…and in Holland’s preface to his translation of Pliny [1601, π2v–4]. Traversi (1952, p. 48): The connection of rationalism with a disruptive force founded ultimately on the blood is as clear in Edmund as it was formerly in Iago. Elton (1966, pp. 126–7, 131 n.): This distinction between natural right and man-made law, between nature and convention,…emerges in the Renaissance with the rediscovery of nature itself, challenging tradition on all human levels. Here the relativistic skepticism is heard shattering the old absolutistic faith in the universality of God’s law; in place of the latter an Epicurean libertinism is erected.…In the early seventeenth century, custom, previously associated with natural law, began to be seen as a hindrance to the operation of nature and to be classed with mere opinion; thus nature was considered, as in some versions of modern psychology, to coincide with natural desires. Thus, within a century a major significance of that slippery word nature as natural law, or the absolute law of God, became metamorphosed to natural law, or the relative law of man. To this change Edmund, a confessed naturalist, gives voice; and as a libertine naturalist, despite his pagan devotions to the fertility goddess Natura, he would tend to be considered an atheist.…Edmund’s speech may be seen as a blasphemous parody of prayer.…Edmund’s form of address is thou; his services are due to Nature in the double sense of votary and lover. Skillan (ed. 1967): Being a creature of impulse, he will be ruled by it. Gardner (ed. 1969): With brisk irreverence Edmund throws out religion, custom, and civil order. Goldberg (1974, p. 74): The cheap, naturalistic commonplaces he flashes about are obviously self-fortifying rationalizations rather than a deeply pondered philosophy. Foakes (1993, p. 189): The ruling ideology…thought it an impiety monstrous, to confound God and Nature.…For it is God, that only disposeth of all things according to his own will.…It is Nature that can dispose of nothing, but according to the will of the matter wherein it worketh [Raleigh, History of the World, 1614, sig. E2v].

335–7 Thou…custome]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Nature, my, thy, My, I, and custom are emphatic. Booth (1994, pp. 44–6) half-seriously suggests that Thou Nature art plants an unconscious hint of the speech’s ensuing contrast of the natural and artificial.

335 Nature]
See nn. 232, 335–56. Mason (1785, p. 340): Edmond calls nature his goddess, for the same reason that we call a Bastard a natural son.—One, who according to the law of nature, is the child of his father, but according to those of civil society, is nullius filius. Hudson (ed. 1879, p. 22): Since his dimensions are so well compact, his mind so generous, and his shape so true, he prefers Nature as she made him to Nature as she has placed him; and freely employs the wit she has given, to compass the wealth she withheld. Thus our free-love philosopher appeals from convention to Nature; and, as usually happens in such cases, takes only so much of Nature as will serve his turn. For convention itself is a part of Nature; it being no less natural that men should grow up together in families and communities than that they should grow up severally as individuals. Bradley (1904, pp. 301–2): He is the product of Nature—of a natural appetite asserting itself against the social order; and he has no recognised place within this order. So he devotes himself to Nature, whose law is that of the stronger, and who does not recognise those moral obligations which exist only by convention.…Practically, his attitude is that of a professional criminal. Draper (1938, p. 133): In taking Nature for his goddess, Edmund renounces both religion and the laws of human society. Bald (1948, pp. 339, 342): Nature and its derivatives…occur more frequently in this than in any other play of Shakespeare, and most often with reference to the the relation of parent and child.…Edmund’s nature is an ironic echo of that invoked by the other characters.…His nature is a disruptive force, the antithesis of order and degree.…This conception of nature implies a savage primitivism. Heilman (1948, pp. 124–5): For Edmund, Nature…is vital force, the individual will, sexual vigor.…Edmund asserts his will against the order of the whole—the order implied by nature as it is used by practically every other character. Danby (1949, p. 32): Edmund worships a Goddess [The malignant Nature of Hobbes] of whom neither Hooker nor Bacon would approve. Houghton (ed. 1957): Possibly Nature…is the dominant idea of the play.…The word Nature occurs forty times in this play…while one-fifth of all Shakespeare’s uses of the word unnatural are in Lear. Harbage (ed. 1958): Edmund’s Nature is the material and mechanistic as distinct from the spiritual and heaven-ordained. Joseph (ed. 1966): Unregenerate nature conceived of as a goddess of all that is evil in the natural world since the Fall. For varied concepts of Nature see Arthur Lovejoy, Essays in the History of Ideas (Baltimore, 1945) and Knights (1959, pp. 84–91). Bald and Elton (see n. 335–56) discuss the contemporary background of freethought behind Edmund’s stance. Bullough (1973, p. 303 n.) quotes Samuel Butler’s character of an atheist: He draws a Map of Nature by his own Fancy, and bounds her how he pleases, without Regard to the Position of the Heavens, by which only her Latitude is to be understood, and without which all his Speculations are vain, idle, and confused.…He commits as great an Error in making Nature (which is nothing but the Order and Method by which all Causes and Effects in the World are governed) to be the first Cause, as if he should suppose the Laws, by which a Prince governs, to be the Prince himself (Characters, ed. A. R. Waller, 1908, pp. 112–13).

335 Goddesse]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Patroness of my fortunes.

335 thy law]
Verity (ed. 1897): As society is against him he is not responsible, he thinks, to its custom. Halio (ed. 1992): Nature’s as opposed to religion’s laws and those of society. Weis (ed. 1993): Used ironically, because in Edmund’s conception of nature there are no structuring laws, but only primitive instincts.

336 bound]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Edmund sees his relation to his goddess as a parody of the feudal service owed to a liege lord.

337 stand in]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Remain in (OED, Stand v. 15e: To be, to continue or remain in a specified state, position, etc. e.g. to stand in doubt, danger; cf. def. 38). Cf. 2054, 2056+3, 2182. Capell (1783, 1.2:145): Be exposed to (OED 52e, 53). Hunter (ed. 1869): Cf. Psa. 38:17, And I truly am set in the plague (Great Bible, 1539, tr. Vulgate Quoniam ego ad plagam paratus sum). Hulme (1962, p. 274): Insist upon, citing OED 72 and Tit. 4.4.105 (2099), a doubtful reading. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Be dependent on. Gardner (ed. 1969): Wait [for].

337 plague]
Steevens (ed. 1773), generally: A situation where I shall be plagued and tormented. Goggin (ed. 1910): From the primary meaning of a blow, stroke, wound (Lat. plaga) [OED, sb. 1], plague came to mean affliction, calamity, evil [OED, 2], and hence anything causing trouble or vexation. [OED, 2b]. Cf. 2234. Sh. uses the term colloquially in imprecations and exclamations (a plague on, what the plague) to mean pestilence, mischief (OED, 3d, citing Rom. 3.1.91 [1524], 1H4 2.2.39 [771]). Most eds. specify the nature of the trouble. Dodd (1752, 2:116–17): Oppression…punishment or scourge. Griffith (1775, p. 355): Tyranny. Capell (1783, 1.2:145): Vexation. Delius (ed. 1854): Curse. Halliwell (ed. 1865): The infectious rule of custom. Clarkes (ed. 1868): The social banishment awarded to those…smitten by…the plague. Kemshead (ed. 1875): Evil or injustice. White (ed. 1883): Toils, perplexity. Tovey (ed. 1896): The prejudices of society, which he compares to a virulent epidemic. Crook (ed. 1907): Buffets or blows. Lee (ed. 1908): Taint. Joseph (ed. 1966): Malignancy. Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): Trials. Horsman (ed. 1973): That nuisance custom. Staunton (ed. 1859): Possibly…place, or boundary, from plaga. See .

337 custome]
Here not simply tradition but its codificaton into laws concerning legitimacy and primogeniture. So Halio (ed. 1992): Usage with the force of law. Halliwell (ed. 1865): Custom concerning not merely his illegitimacy, but his juniority…that bids the younger son yield to the elder, a decree he determines wickedly to evade by becoming the only son. Muir (ed. 1952): Montaigne [tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 2:127] mentions that once some articles of their religion be made doubtfull and questionable, people will immediatly reject (as a tyrannicall yoke) all impressions they had in former times received by the authoritie of Lawes, or reverence of ancient custome—as Edmund repudiates custom. Salingar (1983, p. 143) cites passages (tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 1:105 [Of Custome], 3:117–18 (Upon Some Verses of Virgil), 3:340 [Of Experience]) in which Montaigne contrasts Custom with Nature. Elton (1966, p. 129) compares Malheureux’s complaint against the tyranny of national custom in Marston’s The Dutch Courtesan (1604), 2.1.77–81, a play much indebted to Montaigne. Mueller (1994, p. 216) compares Richard Gloucester’s first speech in The True Tragedy of Richard III (1594): Shall law bridle nature, or authoritie hinder inheritance? (353).

338 curiositie]
Steevens (ed. 1773): An over nice scrupulousness; see n. 9. Wright (ed. 1875): In favour of the elder born. Kittredge (ed. 1940): In defiance of nature and common sense. Muir’s (ed. 1952) gloss squeamishness, false delicacy, over-particularity or fastidiousness [OED, sb. 4a] seems to Salingar (1983, p. 165; 1986, p. 270) to underplay the sting. Theobald’s (ed. 1733) curtesie, as in AYL 1.1.46 (48), is rejected by Heath (1765, p. 318): [It is not] suitable to Edmund’s character to term that a curtesy, which he endeavors to expose as a folly, and by Steevens (ed. 1778): Orlando is not there inveighing against the law of primogeniture, but only against the unkind advantage his brother takes of it.…Edmund, on the contrary, is turning this law into ridicule and hence naturally uses a phrase of contempt. Tovey (ed. 1896): Edmund perhaps contemptuously changes the [legal] term courtesy of nations…[which] means a concession made by law to established custom (OED, sb. 3b, 4). Salingar (1983, p. 143; 1986, p. 122), following Taylor (1925, p. 59): Edmund probably owes his word, curiosity…to Florio; but many writers used the word, and Sh. often uses curious in similar senses. To make the line scan Walker (1854, p. 201) and Elze (1886, p. 37) would pronounce curious’ty.

338 depriue]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Disinherit. Wright (ed. 1875) cites Baret, Alvearie (1573): To cast his sonne out of his house, to…put him from the hope of succession or inheritance for some misdeede. To abastardise him. Craig (ed. 1901): Debar me, keep me out of my rights (OED, v. 3b, quoting only this l.), citing the prose Hystorie of Hamblet (1608, ch. 4; in Bullough, 7:106): rather then he would depriue himselfe by publishing the lasciuousnes of his mother. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Edmund is a younger son, so that even if he were legitimate, he could not inherit his father’s lands. Hunter (ed. 1972) finds also a more general sense: Reduce my powers.

339 for that]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Because. See nn. 246 and 273 and Franz §560.

339 mooneshines]
OED (sb. 1d): Transf. (jocular). A month. nonce-use, quoting this l. Brown (ed. 1976): Nothings.

340 lag]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Lagging behind, later than (OED a. 1, quoting this l.). See 22–3.

340–56 why…Bastards]
Proverbially, Bastards by chance are good, by nature bad (Tilley B104), but the vogue for paradox (see Vickers, 1968, pp. 305 ff.) produced arguments such as Thomas Milles’s in The Treasurie of Auncient and Modern Times (1613, pp. 723–5), Approouing, that the Bastard is more worthy to be esteemed, then he that is lawfully borne, or Legittimate. Milles’s paradox derived, perhaps by way of Anthony Munday, from Ortensio Lando’s (or Landi’s) Paradossi (1543, no. 18), as Rice (1932, p. 72) and Vickers (op. cit., pp. 311–12) have shown. Cf. n. 345–9. Hume (1909, pp. 23–4) identifies Juan Huarte’s Examen, tr. Richard Carew (1594, pp. 319–21), as another instance of the idea, Kittredge (ed. 1940) compares Webster’s Duchess of Malfi 4.1.41 and Devil’s Law Case 4.2.275–80, and Elton (1966, pp. 131–2 n.) cites many other parallels, among them Burton’s Anatomy of Melancholy 2.3.2, noted by Brownlee (1960, p. 275). Salingar (1986, pp. 123–4) adds Montaigne’s Upon Some Verses of Virgil.

340 why bastard?]
The question is elliptical, seeming to mean Why should I be called a bastard, a base one? rather than Why am I illegitimate? So Kittredge (ed. 1940): Why should he be rated as base—i.e., inferior, low, vile—when he is as good in mind and body as any legitimate son? Tovey (ed. 1896), however: He angrily recollects that his illegitimacy would be a bar, even if he were the elder brother.

340 base]
Craig (ed. 1901): The expression base son, for bastard, is to be met with in Sidney’s Arcadia, and in the chronicles of Holinshed and Hall; but bastard has apparently no etymological connection with the adjective, citing OED (sb. and a.).

341 dementions]
OED (Dimension sb. 4): Pl. Material parts, as of the human body. The sp. occurs in MV 3.1.60 (1271).

341 compact]
Schmidt (1874): Composed (OED Compacted ppl. a.1), citing several Shn. exx. Craig (ed. 1901): The word occurs in Leir 1212 (see ). See n. 863.

342 generous]
Schmidt (1874): Noble-minded, magnanimous (OED, a. 2, quoting LLL 5.2.629 [2582] as its first ex.).

342 true]
Schmidt (1875): Conformable to nature; not attested by OED until 1870. Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Of true proportions, well-shaped, citing Son. 62.6, No shape so true; cf. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Symmetrical. OED (a. 4b): Of the right kind, such as it should be, proper, quoting Son. 62. Joseph (ed. 1966): Straight (?OED 4d). Craig (ed. 1901), less probably: Truly a likeness of my father, followed by Muir (ed. 1952): Truly stamped. Perhaps there is a play on legitimate, lawful (OED, 4c).

343 honest]
Muir (ed. 1952): Chaste (OED, a. 3b).

343 madams]
Delius (ed. 1854): Used ironically.…Edgar’s mother is here to be understood (Ger.).

344–5 why…Base?]
If line 343 was intended to end at issue, the following question would be both a complete syntactic unit and (in Q) the first of several regular verse lines. Okes’s compositor mistakenly set the whole speech as prose, and whoever relined the F text may have wished to avoid a short line either in 343 or here. F’s addition of Base, Base? seems an imperfect attempt to eke out a full verse line; cf. the repetitions at 2645, 3280 (F). Doran (1931, p. 127): Possibly added by actors. Greg (1933, p. 255; 1942, p. 91), however: Q’s syncopated line (with…bastardie?) is due to an actor’s faulty memory. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Any word, if repeated over and over in a monotone, seems to lose its significance. Edmund plays this trick with base and legitimate, in order to prove that they are meaningless terms.

344–5 base bastardie]
Pierce (1979, pp. 7–8) takes F’s basenes Barstadie not as two appositives but as an ellipsis for Why do they brand bastardy with baseness? Empson (1967, pp. 97, 407–10): The F sp. reflects a Shn. pronunciation barstardy (unattested in OED). Maxwell (1967, pp. 257–8; 1968, p. 122): A pretty obvious metathetic misprint.

345–9 who…wake]
See n. 340–56 for contemporary statements of the idea. Thomas Milles, Treasurie (1613, pp. 723–4): Bastards are begot in more heat and vigour of loue…then the most part of our Legittimate Children, and are mostly ingenious, of sprightly iudgement, and commonly accompanied with beseeming corpulence of bodie, whereas many legitimate children, conceived without anie gayetie of heart, are dul of spirite, lame of disposition, and deformed in body. Huarte (tr. Carew, 1594, p. 321) provides the physiological explanation: Bastard children are ordinarily made of seed hote and dry: and from this temperature…spring courage, brauerie, and a good imagination; whereas married women produce dullards from their cold, moist wombs. Gardner (ed. 1969): Edmund’s point is…the accepted teaching of 17th century medicine. Robert Burton in The Anatomy of Melancholy [1.2.1.6] mentions husbands who pay their debt (as Paul calls it) to their wives remissly, by which means their children are weaklings, and many times idiots and fools. So Edmund’s justification of himself is…recognizably authoritative, and the audience must take his point, uncomfortable as it is.

345 lusty…nature]
Though some general sense can be found, strict interpretation is uncertain. Bald (ed. 1949), Muir (ed. 1952), Harbage (ed. 1958), and others gloss the phrase as if it read the stealth of natural lust, taking stealth to mean secrecy (OED, sb. 5) and lusty to imply lustful (OED, a. 4). Kittredge (ed. 1940) glosses lusty as Vigorous (OED, 5), a sense that suits stealth = furtive action (OED, 4, quoting this l.). In any case, of nature presumably means natural as opposed to lawful. OED (sb. 9): The inherent dominating power or impulse (in men or animals) by which action or character is determined, directed, or controlled; (14): State of nature:…(a) the moral state natural to man, as opposed to a state of grace; (b) the condition of man before the foundation of organized society; (c) an uncultivated or undomesticated condition. Brown (ed. 1976) alone detects the root sense stealth = plundering (OED, 1), allowing of nature to mean from nature. Foakes (ed. 1997): Edmund aligns himself with beasts…as against custom, morality, and order.

345 take]
The obvious meaning, understood by most eds., is derive or receive (OED, v. 31, 34). Halio (ed. 1992) and Weis (ed. 1993) suggest alternatively the sense require—require a greater and more vigorous mental constitution, demand a stronger effort—, but this sense (OED, 28) does not appear in Sh., or apparently elsewhere until the 19th c.

345 more composition]
Craig (ed. 1901): A fuller blending, mixture (OED, sb. 15, 19), comparing Jn. 1.1.88 (96), the large composition of the bastard Faulconbridge; but large there may mean general, not big or full-bodied. Edmund seems to imply that owing to the greater vigor of his begetting he is better knit, and so has more strength of constitution (Kittredge, ed. 1940). Though no recorded sense of constitution fits exactly, see formation…construction, the putting (of things) into proper position, constitution of body (OED, 2, 3, 16). Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Physical and mental components, i.e. completeness of a strong constitution. Horsman (ed. 1973): Proper combination or congruity of parts.

345 feirce quality]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): More energetic quality of body or mind (OED, Fierce a. 5; Quality sb. 2), comparing 967. Harrison (ed. 1948): Ferocity (OED, 1). Harbage (ed. 1958): Mettlesome, thoroughbred (OED, 2: High-spirited, brave, valiant).

347 stale dull lyed]
Most eds. accept F’s dull stale tyred, assuming lyed to be a misreading of tyred or tyrd (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 347). Stone (1980, p. 52): It would appear likelier that dull lyed was a phonetic mistake for dull-eyed…a vivid image. Dull-eyed occurs in MV 3.3.14 (1700) and Per. 1.2.2 (225).

347 bed]
Muir (ed. 1952): The marriage bed, its pleasure staled with custom and the body wearied with sexual intercourse (Partridge, 1947, p. 105).

348 the creating of]
F om. of, evidently to make more regular verse, but perhaps wrongly: see n. 349. Furness (ed. 1880): Although [creating] is a noun [OED, vbl. sb., quoting this l. as its first ex.], and therefore preceded by the, yet it is so far confused with the gerund as to be allowed the privilege of governing a direct object. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 511): Q presumably interpolated the grammatically expected preposition. (Blayney notes at least five instances of interpolated of in Okes’s setting of Shirley’s Relation of his Travels.) But of was not necessarily expected: see Franz §667. Abbott (§93): The substantival use of the verbal with the before it and of after it seems to have been regarded as colloquial—as perhaps here. Cf. n. 508, and 2359.

348 fops]
Schmidt (ed. 1879): Not dandies but dupes. OED (sb. 1): Fool. See 447, 681. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Weaklings. Lothian (1949, p. 56): So Edmund considers Edgar.

349 got…the]
The F line is metrically short; perhaps the previous line should be divided after tribe, Q’s of being retained.

349 got…wake]
Hunton (1892, p. 451) quotes from Brantôme’s Dames Galantes (pub. posth. 1666) the opinion of Aucuns…des philosophes contrasting gallants bastards with legitimate dullards qui se font dans un lict lourdement, fadement, pesamment, à loisir, et quasi à demy endormis (ed. Garnier, 1967, p. 94). Gardner (ed. 1969): Not only casually…but in the morning, when the…father’s blood was cold, lacking fierce quality. Cf. n. 340.

349 tweene]
OED (prep.): Aphetic form of atween, between.

349 a sleepe and wake]
Schmidt (1875), wake: The state…of being awake (OED, sb.1 1), comparing 1685 and 1H4 3.1.216 (1759), twixt wake and sleepe. If a is thus an article rather than a worn-down on (see OED, A prep.1 11), it applies to both nouns; conceivably, though, the phrase may be understood as asleep and ’wake. Dent (1981, A347.1): Between Asleep and awake is proverbial; cf. MND 4.1.147 (1672), Halfe sleepe, halfe waking.

349 the]
All eds. accept F’s then, assuming an overlooked tilde or macron over the e. Heilman (1948, p. 126): The announcement of his plan…is connected with the statement of his nature theory by the word then—precisely as if his scheme followed as a logical projection of the theory into action.

350 your]
Deighton (ed. 1891): To which you are heir.

351 is to]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Is equally felt towards. Moberly (ed. 1876): As Gloucester himself had said [23–4].

352 fine…Legitimate]
The F addition further emphasizes the sarcasm already present in my legitimate; without it the rest of the speech in Q may be divided to form full and regular verse lines.

352, 353 legitimate]
On the adjective used as noun and vocative see Franz §358.

353 letter]
Foakes (ed. 1997): Edmund may draw it from a pouch or pocket here or hold it as he comes on stage. Dessen & Thomson (1999): A widely used property and plot device cited in over 400 directions.

353 speede]
Schmidt (1875): Succeed (OED, v. 1). Cf. 2651. Joseph (ed. 1966): Also proceed swiftly.

354 inuention]
Schmidt (1874): Device (OED, sb. 6). Hunter (ed. 1972): Power of inventing (lies) (OED, 4: Inventiveness).

355 tooth’]
F’s to’th’ essentially agrees, and the reading is intelligible. Rowe (see textual n.) follows F but puts a dash after the next word; to apparently means go to (OED, To prep. 1c; Franz §530; Pittock, 1984, p. 209), and the punctuation is explained by Delius (ed. 1854): What he will inflict upon him he does not say; he is interrupted by the entrance of his father (Ger.). Caldecott (MS notes, 1813–33): Be up with, equal to. Nichols (1862, p. 9): Shall advance to, or take the place of, the legitimate. Perring (1885, p. 323): To has three possible meanings: shall stretch himself to the height of, shall reach unto, and put himself on a level with, the legitimate; shall hie him to, to do upon him [a] foul deed; shall attain unto legitimacy. Craig (ed. 1901): Shall come up to, or shall assail and get the better of:…fair sense, and…in the manner of Shakespeare. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): The Elizabethan gave shall by itself the value of a verb [Abbott §§405, 315],…i.e., shall attain, to’th’; see n. 312. So Clayton (1984, p. 208): Edmund the Base Shall to [= become]…Edmund the Legitimate. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 367): Conceivably, proceed against the legitimate [cf. n. 2319].…But…this does not make good sense in the context. It is absurd for Edmund to say if…thriue, I shall proceed against, act against, attack my legitimate brother. He is acting against him anyway. Wilson (ed. 1960) finds Sisson’s (1956, 2:231) explanation turn into the legitimate far-fetched. Honigmann (1965, p. 165) suspects too spelled as to: If…my invention thrive, Edmund the base shall [thrive] too. The legitimate! Foakes (ed. 1997): This reading leaves The legitimate…out of place. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 511): There may also be a pun on tooth (= bite).
Many emendations have been proposed (see textual n. and ). Most often adopted is top the, first proposed by Capell (see 1783, 1.2:146) and first published by Edwards (1750, pp. 138–9); Capell finds in it a fitting opposition to base…[and] it’s connection with grow, which has no natural introduction unless preceded by top. Malone (ed. 1790) and Dyce (ed. 1864–7, Glossary) show Sh.’s frequent use of the verb; cf. 3168+3. Greg (1928, p. 40): If the tail of the p were for any reason obscured, top would naturally be misread as too. Duthie (p. 368) compares Q out, F Pat at 463. Muir (ed. 1952): The context requires a word meaning overthrow or surpass.…Certainly an actor would find it easier to say with the right note of triumph. Hanmer (ed. 1743) defends toe th’: To come up to and be upon even ground with him. Johnson (ed. 1765) adopts this reading as meaning To kick him out or literally to supplant. Malone (ed. 1790): In Devonshire, as Sir Joshua Reynolds observes to me, to toe a thing up, is, to tear it up by the roots, in contrast to Edmund’s I grow. Tannenbaum (1941, p. 59), like Johnson: To spurn. Wells (ed. 2000): A noun as a verb. Pope’s (ed. 1725) be th’ is doubted by Edwards (loc. cit.): If he got the inheritance…that could not make him be the legitimate. Kellner (1925, §154): Pope’s be is borne out by the Elizabethan hand: to and be can hardly be told from one another. Brooke’s (ed. 1947) odd taw th’ (= tan the) has won no adherents.

355 grow]
Barry (1974, p. 162): The word has both a metaphorical (Edmund as plant) and a literal force.

356 now…Bastards]
Halliwell (ed. 1865): The gods appear rather to be derided than invoked. Elton (1966, p. 130): His libertine sensuality conjoined with his materialistic naturalism is blasphemously expressed in the invitation of potency.

356 stand vp for]
OED (Stand v. 103o): To defend, support, take the part of, champion, quoting this l. Heilman (1948, p. 314): Edmund puns on tumescence.

358–446 Kent…strange]
Vickers (1968, pp. 351, 354): Gloucester as a nervous and rather ludicrous old man is given prose, and is partly characterized by the brief repetitions and jumpy syntax of age. In F his first four lines are verse. Edmund naturally responds in prose, but see also n. 335–56. Brown (ed. 1976): Gloucester’s short phrases…show him to be anxious and ineffectual. Foakes (ed. 1997): Gloucester appears not to notice Edmund’s presence; it is as if he has just heard amazing news.

358–61 Kent…gadde]
In F Gloucester’s phrases end with question marks. Most eds. have interpreted these according to contemporary usage as equivalent to exclamation points; see textual nn. Halio (ed. 1992): But a querying or wondering tone seems more appropriate for Gloucester here.

358 in choller]
In anger (OED, sb.1 2); see n. 324. Craig (ed. 1901): In…I.i., there is no appearance of any choler in France; but see [327–8], where another interview is spoken of; this may have been described in a scene, afterwards struck out by Shakespeare or by the players; also see [1505], where the epithet hot-blooded is applied to France. The other interview may be imaginary—see n. 327–8—and the missing scene surely is; and hot-bloodied (1505 F) does not necessarily mean choleric. After Bransom (1934, p. 193), Greg (1940, p. 444) imagines further that France, incensed at some fresh insult to Cordelia, departed in a rage, determined to wrest by force her portion from…Albany and Cornwall. Mahood (1992, p. 159): Lear’s savage dismissal of Cordelia, causing her to weep for the first time in the scene, and the studied insult of his exit hand in hand with noble Burgundy may well beget an anger which is further fanned by her sisters’ contempt for his chosen queen, and which can be made clearly evident as he sweeps from the scene.

359 to night]
Daniel (1877–9, p. 216): Frequently used…in the sense of the night last past [OED, adv. 3: Perhaps only said in the morning], and Edmund, who here promises his father full satisfaction as to Edgar’s guilt, …this very evening [426], could not say this if the night of the day on which he is speaking were already come.…We must mark this scene as a separate day, the day following the opening scene. See n. 333. Verity (ed. 1897): Cf. MV 2.5.18 (855). Cf. 1363. Greg (1940, pp. 432–3): Edmund might keep his promise later the same evening if this scene were continuous with 1.1, but more probably it takes place on the following day; see nn. 333, 926.

359 subscribd]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Transferred. OED (v. 5): To sign away, yield up, quoting only this l. In support Malone (ed. 1790) compares 1673 and Tro. 4.5.105 (2667), neither close in meaning. Capell (1783, 1.2:146): Subscrib’d to his power’s contraction. Deighton (ed. 1891): Not that there was a deed which he literally signed, but that he made a formal transfer of his authority. Tovey (ed. 1896) defends cancelled (unattested) by an unhelpful reference to the obscure 2137. F’s Prescrib’d has a few adherents. Malone (MS notes, 1773–90, fol. 45): Ascertained—marked out his powers, the several particulars of it being enumerated & written down. Cf. Weis (ed. 1993): Instructed. Schmidt (1879, p. 16): Restricted, limited (OED, v. 4). Stone (1980, p. 215): But Lear has not retained limited power: he has surrendered it all.

360 confined]
Capell (1783, 1.2:146): Confin’d himself.

360 exhibition]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Allowance (OED, sb. 2). Collier (ed. 1843): Maintenance (OED, 1). Less probably, Crook (ed. 1907): Kingly pomp without the kingly power.

361–432 Edmund…withall]
Black (1962, pp. 255–6): Shakespeare’s third use of the suspicious father and the son who conceals a letter [cf. TGV 1.3.45–59 (347–61), R2 5.2.56–117 (2425–94)]…is combined with another [device] borrowed from Iago himself—that of the reluctant witness whose pretence of concealment causes his evidence to be accepted without question.

361 vpon the gadde]
Gad = goad. Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:27–8): A sharp-pointed Instrument to prick forward Oxen (OED, Gad sb.1 4, quoting only this l.; cf. Tit. 4.1.103 [1651]). OED (4b): Upon the gad: as if pricked with a gad; suddenly. (Cf. upon the spur of the moment.) Less probably, Johnson (ed. 1765): By the sudden stimulation of caprice, as cattle run madding when they are stung by the gadfly. Deighton (ed. 1891): Goaded by sudden impulse.

361 how now]
OED (How adv. 4b): Ellipt. for How is it now? Often used interjectionally. Cf. 467, 540, 579, 626, 634, 703, 857, 919, 1025, 1118, 2073, 2149, 2206.

361 what newes]
Brooke (ed. 1947): In Edmund’s letter.

362 So please]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Elliptical for if it so please; merely a courteous form of address.

363 earnestly]
Schmidt (1874): Eagerly,…urgently (OED, Earnest a. 1: Implying intensity of feeling). Joseph (ed. 1966): Determinedly; not attested.

363 put vp]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): To pocket up (OED, v. 53n).

366 Nothing]
Harrison (ed. 1937): Gloucester’s tragedy also begins with the word nothing. Cf. 93. Willbern (1980, p. 244): The letter is nothing, a hoax.

367 what needes]
Abbott (§297): The impersonal [verb] needs…often drops the s, as in Q2; F’s needed makes the tense consistent with were in 365.

367 terrible]
White (ed. 1862): In haste and terror; unattested by OED. Abbott (§3): Frightened, explaining, Adjectives…ending in ful, less, ble, and ive, have both an active and a passive meaning;…a fearful (pass.) coward, and a fearful (act.) danger. Cf. 825. Horsman (ed. 1973): May be merely intensive…= great haste.

367 dispatch]
Schmidt (1874): Getting rid of (OED, sb. 7, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Hunter (ed. 1972): Also, Haste (OED, 6b). Lott (ed. 1974): A possible play…[on] sending of letters.

368 qualitie]
Schmidt (1875): Nature (OED, sb. 8).

369 lets see]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Parental authority of the old fashion often seems tyrannical to us moderns, comparing R2 5.2.56 (2425) ff.

370 spectacles]
Page (ed. 1889): Not invented till the 13th century. The phrase is proverbial: Dent (1981), S733.1), To need no Spectacles. Brown (ed. 1996): As Gloucester’s joke indicates, the whole episode can be very funny…[or] nervy and unsettling. Wells (ed. 2000): It is not necessary to suppose that Gloucester actually uses spectacles, contra Teague (1991, p. 185).

371 Ba.]
See textual n. Greg (1940, p. 152): The addition of the speaker’s name…is obviously necessary and correct. The speech in [Q uncorr.] begins a fresh paragraph but is not indented.

371 pardon me]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Excuse me from showing it.

371 letter]
Bradley (1904, pp. 256–7) notes a gross improbability: No sort of reason is given why Edgar, who lives in the same house with Edmund, should write a letter to him instead of speaking; and…Gloster appears to be unacquainted with his son’s handwriting. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 204 n.): The likelihood…depends somewhat upon the large, loose organisation of a great nobleman’s household of that day, of which Shakespeare’s audience would know well enough. Thaler (1929, p. 61): Sh. answers these objections [in 499–502].…Why should these two stop to ask questions? Muir (ed. 1952, p. xlix): Edmund’s forged letter…might be regarded as a more plausible method of broaching conspiracy than by word of mouth because the writer could deny his handwriting, or pretend he was making an assay of his brother’s virtue. McNeal (1958, p. 44) improbably finds a source in Gonorill’s interception of her husband’s letters in Leir 991–8. Blayney (privately) points to a recent historical precedent, the Star-Chamber judgment of 11 Feb. 1585/6 against Thomas Lovelace for seeking to gain the goods and lands of his cousins Leonard and Richard by a counterfeit letter implicating them in treasonous plots against the queen (John Stow, A Summarie of the Chronicles, 1590, p. 725).

372 ore read]
Schmidt (1875): Peruse (OED, Over-read v. 1).

372 for]
See n. 228.

373–4 your liking]
Though the Q reading might be justified (Collier, ed. 1843), almost all eds. prefer F’s your ore-looking. Schmidt (1875), o’erlook: Peruse (OED, v. 3); cf. 2895. Fit for liking is somewhat redundant, and Q can be explained as a misreading of copy perhaps more easily than F. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 368): The copy may have had yor or loking. The compositor’s eye may have skipped over the second or, or he may have thought it an error in the copy. The o in loking may have been blind so that it looked like an i. Alternatively, the F compositor just possibly misread his MS copy’s liking as loking and unconsciously extended your to your ore to make sense. There is no practical difference between the phrases, and they are so similar graphically that one or the other is probably a misreading.

376 to detaine or giue]
Goggin (ed. 1910): By giving or by detaining.…The so-called gerundial (really dative) infinitive. Cf. 1387.

377 in part]
Delius (ed. 1854): Because he has only read part (Ger.).

378 too blame]
Abbott (§359): Infinitive active is often found where we use the passive—here, to be blamed. Cf. 2872. OED (Blame, v. 6): In the 16–17th c. the to was misunderstood as too, and blame taken as adj. = blameworthy, culpable, quoting Shn. exx. See also Franz §§455, 654, and cf. 1235.

381 essay]
Malone (ed. 1790): Either essay or assay may mean a trial. To assay not only signified to make trial of coin (Johnson, ed. 1765: a metallurgical term), but to taste before another (Steevens, ed. 1793: a term from royal tables). Wright (ed. 1875): The two words essay and assay are etymologically the same. OED (Assay sb. 1): The trying (of a person or thing) (= Essay sb. 1); (Assay sb. 12): Tasting the food or drink before giving it to an exalted personage (= Essay sb. 4); erroneously, (Assay sb. 11): Fig. A taste, a foretaste, quoting this l. and J. King, Jonah (1594), A taste and assay beforehand. Rolfe (ed. 1880): S. uses the word [essay] only twice [see Son. 110.8], having elsewhere assay. Cf. say, 3099. Muir (ed. 1952, p. 251): The word is too commonplace to derive from Montaigne. Salingar (1983, p. 132), however: Edmund is speaking, like Montaigne, about a literary composition. Though, as Salingar says (p. 164), One or two of the Essays are cast in the form of letters, there is no reason to think that Edmund considered this brief note such an essay, or as a literary exercise to try out or disclose (Edmund’s) moral quality or his own powers of intrigue. It is a part or means of his practises and busines (502).

381 tast]
Schmidt (1875): Trial (OED, sb.1 2: A trying, testing, quoting this l.).

382–9 This…Edgar]
Traversi (1952, p. 48): A rationalization of the opinions more passionately, instinctively, held by Regan and Goneril. Wilson (ed. 1960): This letter sets before us the main theme of the whole play.

382 policie…age]
Most eds. include F’s added and reuerence. Delius (1876, p. 135): On this reverence of old age depends the policy which forbids sons to inherit during their fathers’ life. Like Delius, Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 368): The words were omitted from Q by carelessness in the compositor, since This policie of age is of course nonsense. Not so Evans (ed. 1898), though he follows F: This…line of conduct with regard to age and this reverence for it; nor apparently Capell (1783, 1.2:146): Political regiment [connected with old age]…and the reverence establish’d by it. Equally possible meanings of Q are This cunning of the aged (see next n.) or This course of action adopted by the aged as advantageous or expedient (OED, 5). Most eds. follow Schmidt (ed. 1879) in considering the phrase a hendiadys equivalent to This policy, or custom, of reverencing age (Hudson, ed. 1879); cf. nn. 272–3, 865. Verity (ed. 1897), alternatively: Perhaps = politic reverence, the adjective having the notion cautious, not going too fast. Foakes (ed. 1997): Gloucester reads silently at first…[since] there is no antecedent for This policy. But This may be introductory, Referring to something which is mentioned immediately after or something now in vogue (OED, a. 1b, 1d).

382 policie]
Warburton (ed. 1747): That fathers shall keep all they have till they die. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Policy (which often means cunning or strategic art [OED, sb.1 3, 4b]) suggests that this order of society is a clever trick on the part of the aged. Taylor (1925, pp. 12–13), Henderson (1940, pp. 46–7), and Reyher (1947, pp. 511–12) cite passages from Montaigne’s Of the Affection of Fathers to Their Children recommending that aged fathers distribute their wealth to their children to avoid envy and malice; see . Sullivan (1925, pp. lxiv f.): Similar passages in Pettie’s 1581 tr. of Guazzo’s Civile Conversation (ed. 1925, 2:65–8) blame fathers for not so distributing their wealth. See n. 43–6 for biblical advice to the contrary. Foakes (ed. 1997): Lear, indeed, handed over the management of his revenue.

382 reuerence]
Generally taken to mean respect for or deference towards (OED, sb. 1) old age, and the of admits of that interpretation; but if policie and reuerence are in parallel, then both must refer to traits possessed by or characteristic of age. In this case Edmund could be resenting both age’s cunning and its condition or state of being respected or venerated (OED, 3, quoting from More’s Utopia, reuerence of the elders).

383 bitter]
In an unpublished note Whiter (apud Muir, ed. 1952) sees an association with tast 381 and relish 384.

383 best…times]
Cf. 320. Wright (ed. 1875): The best periods of our lives. Deighton (ed. 1891): I.e. youth.

383 fortunes]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Inheritances.

384 oldnes]
Schmidt (ed. 1879): Not elsewhere used in Sh.

384 relish]
OED (v.1 3): To enjoy, quoting this l. as its first ex.

384–5 idle…fond]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Synonyms: silly, though idle connotes useless (OED, a. 2) and fond, foolish, imbecile (OED, a. 2, 3). See 522+1, 820, 2814. Gardner (ed. 1969): I am coming to think our own needless and stupid submission really lies beneath this oppression. Foakes (ed. 1997) detects a reminder of Lear in 1.1.

385 who]
Wright (ed. 1875): The antecedent really being the persons implied in tyranny. Rolfe (ed. 1880): But the it shows that [tyranny] is grammatically and rhetorically neuter. See n. 119.

385 swaies]
Schmidt (1875): Rule[s] (OED, v. 9). Cf. 144.

386 suffered]
Wright (ed. 1875): Tolerated.

390 Hum]
See n. 1828.

390 slept…wakt]
Most eds. adopt F’s Sleepe but not wake to make Gloucester re-read the letter’s words exactly. The change can not have been intentional; Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 170) suggests that F’s wake is due to an e:d misreading of wakd. Wells (ed. 2000): I is stressed.

392 hart]
OED (Heart sb. 5): = Mind, in the widest sense, including the functions of feeling, volition, and intellect.

393 this to you]
Q has seemed to most eds. a more natural phrase than F’s you to this to describe the arrival of a letter, and more consistent with who brought it? There is no practical difference in meaning, and F’s phrase could easily be a simple metathesis. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 171) prefers it to Q as more pointed and idiomatic, citing OED (v. 45b): Come to = to get at, attain, get possession of.

395 throwne…casement]
Verity (ed. 1897) compares JC 2.1.36–8 (653–5). Brooke (ed. 1947): Where in turn it is borrowed from Plutarch’s life of Caesar.

396 closet]
Wright (ed. 1875): Private room (OED, sb. 1).

397 Caractar]
Schmidt (1874): Handwriting (OED, Character sb. 4c). Cf. 1009.

398 matter]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Subject matter (OED, sb.1 9, 11). Cf. 1736, 1985, 2441, 2616.

398–9 were…were]
Abbott (§368): Subjunctive in a subordinate sentence, followed by subjunctive by attraction. Cf. Franz §644, Anm. 2.

398 durst]
OED (Dare v.1 A.5): Past Subj. or Conditional durst (= would dare), though often…used indefinitely of present time. Cf. 1297, 2290, 2684.

399 that]
Wright (ed. 1875): The matter; expanded by Craig (ed. 1901): Seeing it is as it is, i.e. far from good.

399 faine]
Schmidt (1874): Gladly (OED, Fain adv. B). Cf. 559, 693.

401 his?]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 401): Gloucester naturally repeats his question (397) after Edmund’s evasive answer. Wilson (ed. 1960): F’s his. marks the point at which Glo. is convinced, though F may also be a question. Or Q an exclamation (Wells, ed. 2000).

402 heart]
Sincere intent. See OED (sb. 7, 39a). Cf. 418, 852.

404–8 Hath…reuenew]
Doran (1931, p. 46) finds this passage typical of the way the F printer introduced variants on colorless words: Hath/Has, heretofore/before, often/oft, declining/declin’d, his/the, the/his.

404 Hath…heretofore]
F’s indifferent Has is a modernization, and F’s indifferent before may be a scribal or compositorial simplification. Or they may both be the compositor’s use of short forms in a full line on a full page. So Hogan (1962, p. 78): The whole speech is so short that F hoped to get it into one line of print as Q had done before him.…F achieves his aim by shortening his customary Glou. and businesse—and, as I think, by replacing the authentic Hath by Has and heretofore by before.…Hath he is more Shakespearian.

404 soũded]
Deighton (ed. 1891): A figure from taking soundings in water (OED, Sound v.2 6).

405 often heard him]
F’s inversion to heard him oft is indifferent; the shorter oft may be due to a full line.

406 sons at]
Abbott (§381): The participle is sometimes implied in the case of a simple word, such as being. Cf. Franz §660.

406 perfit]
Schmidt (1875), perfect: Full, ripe (OED, a. 1c: Grown up). Q’s form occurs only thrice in F1 (H5 3.6.70, 75 [1517, 1522], R3 3.7.90 [2308]) and thrice in the good quartos (MND 1.2.96, 109 [356, 368], Per. 5.1.206 [2184]); F’s perfect is the norm.

407 declining]
OED (Decline v. 10): Fig. To fall off or fail in force, vigour, or vitality. F’s shorter declin’d may be due to a full line; it makes virtually no difference in meaning.

407–8 father…reuenew]
Muir (ed. 1952) cites contemporary arguments that fathers should not foolishly cling to power and possessions. See also n. 382.

407–8 his…the]
Q may be preferable to F’s inversion the…his, more pointedly hinting that Edgar is not merely generalizing but is referring in fact to his father.

407 ward]
Verity (ed. 1897): This describes the position in which Lear has placed himself. It seems intended to emphasise the parallelism between the main plot and the minor. Cf. 359–60. The term is legal, referring to the feudal lord’s right to control the property of an underage heir of a deceased tenant. The Sokols (2000, p. 404): By the second half of the sixteenth century wardship was regarded as an anachronistic feudal relic.

410 detested]
Wright (ed. 1875): Detestable. See n. 284.

411 sir]
F’s sirrah is surprising. Kittredge (ed. 1940): A form of sir; used in familiar address, as by parents to children or by masters to servants. Quinn (ed. 1970): Here used as an indication of intimacy. But McCann (ed. 1964) thinks it disrespectful: A mark of impatience in Gloucester. Skillan (ed. 1967): glo. is speaking with authority. OED (a. 1): Expressing contempt, reprimand, or assumption of authority. Elsewhere in the play it is used only towards servants or inferiors: see 574, 627, 645, 694, 1141, 1963, 2240.

411 I]
Wright (ed. 1875): The common way of printing ay. Only Weis (ed. 1993), alternatively: I understand his drift. Stone (1980, p. 52): F’s Ile is a sophistication. It would be very odd if Gloucester were telling Edmund to search for Edgar so that he, Gloucester, could arrest him: he surely means Edmund both to seek out Edgar and to seize him. Presumably Gloucester may deputize Edmund to make an arrest for him. Cf. 1049. Either reading will do; most eds. have followed F.

412 abhominable]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): The usual Elizabethan spelling…denotes the formerly accepted derivation from ab homine (cf. [LLL 5.1.24 (1762)]). Hence the word usually carried the meaning of unnatural or unfit for human society. OED: No other spelling occurs in the first folio of Shaks., which has the word [14] times.

413–21 I…danger]
Goggin (ed. 1910): Edmund’s object is to prevent a meeting between Edgar and Gloucester.…Hence his proposal that Gloucester should wait and have his suspicions confirmed later.
