Vickers (1968, p. 355): We can gauge the dissembling in [Edmund’s] style…in the insincerity of the images, in their artificial extended form, and in the formality of the language.

414 against]
OED (Indignation 2b) attests to the idiom, quoting this l.

415 this]
Virtually all eds. prefer F’s his. Wilson (1934, 1:112): An h:th error, comparing his/this confusions at LLL 5.2.566 (2518) and MV 4.1.30 (1935).

415 should]
Brooke (ed. 1947): More deferential than will or shall.

416 certaine]
Hudson (ed. 1879): Safe or sure. Deighton (ed. 1891): Direct…to your object. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Without the risk of making a mistake. Harrison (ed. 1948): Know[ing] where you are going.

416 course]
See n. 201.

416 where]
Abbott (§134): Used metaphorically as we now use whereas (OED, conj. 12b). Cf. Franz §554.

418 gap]
Craig (ed. 1901): Breach (OED, sb. 1; cf. 6, deficiency).

418 heart]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Whole principle (OED, sb. 2). Cf. 1684. Other connotations may apply as well: purpose, inclination (OED, 7), the innermost or central part (OED, 17), the solid central part (OED, 18, 19), vital, essential, or efficacious part (OED, 20).

419 pawn]
Schmidt (1875): To pledge. Craig (ed. 1901): Stake, echoing 166, ironically (Wilson (ed. 1960). OED (v.) gives both senses.

419 downe]
OED (adv. 12): Upon the table, quoting this l.

420 wrote]
On curtailed forms of participles see n. 103. Rolfe (ed. 1880): For the [past tense Sh.] has usually writ [but see 380], for the [participle] writ or written. As a participle, wrote appears elsewhere only at Ant. 3.5.11 (1735) and Cym. 3.5.2, 21 (1893, 1917).

420 feele]
OED (v. 4): Fig. To test…to sound…feelings or intentions, quoting this l.

420 affection]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Sentiments (OED, sb. 5: Disposition towards).

420 your honour]
Malone (ed. 1790): The usual mode of address to a lord in Shakspeare’s time. Lott (ed. 1974): To gain his ends, Edmund now speaks to his father with the greatest deference.

421 further]
Additional (OED, a. 2). Q makes excellent if not superior sense. F’s other could easily be a lapse of aural memory by a scribe or compositor.

421 pretence]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Purpose (OED, sb. 3). Cf. 599.

421 of danger]
Rann (ed. 1794): Of endangering your person.

423–4 I…this]
Granville-Barker (1927, p. 149 n.): But he never does. Shakespeare may have remembered…that he had lately used this none too fresh device in Othello.

424–5 aurigular]
OED (Auricular a. 2): Perceived by the ear, quoting this l. Sh. does not elsewhere use the word. Muir (ed. 1952): He might have known it from Brooke’s Romeus and Juliet, Florio’s tr. of Montaigne, or Harsnett’s Declaration (1603, p. 9). The unique spelling may be either an error or a reproduction of popular pronunciation (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 80). Lott (ed. 1974): Edmund’s pompous phraseology contributes to the deferential manner.

425 haue…satisfaction]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Be convinced one way or the other. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Have full information.

426 this…euening]
Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): This conference is not given. But it may be what happens at the beginning of 2.1. See n. 333.

427– monster.]
See n. 238. Many eds. replace the period with a dash (see textual n.), implying that 427+2 completes the sentence. The image is proverbial: Dent (1981), I66.1, Ingratitude is monstrous (a monster).

427+1–+3 Bast.…earth!]
Delius (1876, p. 141): Abridged by someone other than Sh.: Not only is Gloucester’s speech rendered incomplete…but the touching expression of paternal affection for his unjustly suspected son is ruthlessly struck out. Wilson (ed. 1960): F om., prob. accidentally. As usual Schmidt (1879, p. 18) defends F: since otherwise in the first two scenes, nor until 3.6, not a word of sympathy and warmth for his sons falls from the lips of Gloucester (Ger.) these lines are uncharacteristic and un-Shn. Similarly Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 60): Omitted perhaps because the idea of Gloucester loving Edgar tenderly and entirely seemed absurd or contradictory in relation to his previous fulminations. Bradley (1904, pp. 294–5 n.): Schmidt’s idea…is surely an entire mistake. See, not to speak of general impressions, [1946 ff.]. Foakes (op. cit., p. 314): The lines could be taken as showing that he is full of changes [said of Lear]. Taylor (1983, p. 88): The F cut reflects artistic sensitivity, forc[ing] an audience to attend to the unspoken mental processes of the character instead of making them explicit. But Gloucester’s thought processes have been made explicit in previous speeches. Halio (ed. 1992): Theatrical cuts this early in the text are rare, and the column that [Compositor] B was setting on signature qq3v shows signs of crowding later on. On the other hand, the lines are not indispensable…[and] may have been deleted by a reviser. Perhaps, if the cut is intentional, someone thought Gloucester’s expostulations were becoming tedious.

427+1 Nor…not]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Emphatic double negative. Cf. 616, 1741, 2590, 2822, 3257.

428 wind mee into]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Insinuate into…enable me to penetrate into his secret designs or purposes (OED, v.1 13b). Wright (ed. 1875): Gain his confidence in some circuitous way. Hudson (ed. 1871): Worm yourself into him. Muir (ed. 1952): Make cautious, indirect advances, as if according to Polonius’s instructions in Ham. 2.1.1–68 (890–964). As for mee, Abbott (§220): The old [ethical] Dative, where we should use for me; cf. Franz §294. Tovey (ed. 1896): Ethic (or emotional), expressing keen interest on the speaker’s part. Bevington (ed. 1988): Used colloquially.

428 frame]
Craig (ed. 1901): Fashion, manage (OED, v. 8).

428 your]
Though Q makes perfect sense, most eds. adopt F’s the, perhaps to avoid repeating your in successive lines.

429 after…wisedome]
Deighton (ed. 1891): In the way that seems wisest to you.

429–30 vnstate my selfe]
Heath (1765, p. 320): Give even my rank and fortune. So Steevens (ed. 1773), comparing Ant. 3.13.30 (2186), Vnstate his happinesse: Edgar has been represented as wishing to possess his father’s fortune, i.e. to unstate him; and therefore [i.e., continuing the same idea] his father says he would unstate himself. Davies (1783, 2:271): I would give all I am worth. OED (v. 1): To deprive of state, rank, or estate. Harrison (ed. 1937): As afterwards comes to pass. Idem (ed. 1948): One of many touches of bitter irony in this tragedy, for it is not until he has unstated himself that Gloucester does indeed learn the truth about his two sons. A different interpretation begun by Warburton (ed. 1747) and continued by Johnson (ed. 1765) is summarized by Capell (1783, 1.2:146): Lay aside…his parental state so as to free his judgment from his affections as a kind father or his resentments as an injur’d one.

430 due]
Schmidt (1874): Such as a thing ought to be,…perfect (OED, a. 6).

430 resolution]
Warburton (ed. 1747): That I may act as justice requires. Steevens (ed. 1773): To punish him. But most follow Mason (1785, p. 342)—to be certain of the fact—and Dyce (ed. 1864–7, Glossary): Conviction, assurance…certainty, freedom from doubt (OED, 13b, quoting this l.). Tovey (ed. 1896): The only place where [Sh.] uses the substantive resolution for certitude. Bransom (1934, p. 206): Contrary to what has so often been affirmed, namely, that Gloster was too easily taken in, he was as a matter of fact suspicious about the whole thing at first.

431 presently]
Dyce (ed. 1864–7, Glossary): Immediately (OED, adv. 3). Cf. 669+3, 1310, 1393, 2874+1.

431 conuey]
Johnson (ed. 1765): To manage artfully (OED, v. 12: with secrecy, privacy, or craft, quoting this l.).

432 as…meanes]
Deighton (ed. 1891): With all the dexterity that circumstances allow.

432 withall]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): With it; with the facts (OED, Withal adv. 2: Therewith). Franz (§536) improbably: At the same time (OED, 1b).

433–44 These…Graues]
Capell (1783, 1.2:146–7): The ensuing descant on what were then esteem’d natural prodigies, is one of the weaknesses [of Gloucester]; and serves admirably to give a requisite degree of the probable to this father’s credulity. Heilman (1948, p. 42): Significantly, this astrological habit of mind is shared by no one else in the play; but see 118–19, 1631, 2347+34. Gloucester’s belief in astrology and the significance of portents would not have marked him as unduly superstitious in Jacobean eyes. Virtually everyone believed in the power of the stars to influence the world, usually without having a clear notion of the extent of their influence. Astrologia naturalis, the study of the influence of heavenly bodies on tides, weather, plant life, and birth, growth, and decay (including qualities of human character and individual fortune), was a branch of physical study. The stars could exert influence in accordance with the will of God as part of general providence, and such influence was consistent with free will because inclina astra non necessitant or non cogunt. General acceptance of natural astrology in the 16th and 17th centuries is reflected in frequent allusions to it in Sh.’s plays. More controversial was astrologia judicialis, the theory and practice of prophecy, in which horoscopes were considered guides to life, and planetary conjunctions, comets, meteors, and solar and lunar eclipses were interpreted as omens to the state and its rulers. This study was both widely believed in and actively defended, and at the same time attacked as ineffective, fraudulent, or irreligious, the last in part because attempts to pry into the future raised suspicions of demonic collusion, as in magic or witchcraft. Gloucester’s belief in judicial astrology may therefore be somewhat more superstitious than the belief in natural astrology expressed by Lear (see 118–19, possibly 2958–9) and Kent (see 1631–2, 2347+34); but it would not have seemed extraordinary. Fleay (1879, p. 119): The Queen [Anne] had recently (October, 1604) been consulting astrologers and firmly believed in them. Joseph (ed. 1966, pp. 50–2): Gloucester is often mis-read as saying that the stars determine human actions. But in fact his words [433–4]…[do] not mean that they cause no good, but that they are signs of trouble in the future. A portent is not a cause, but a symptom, of what will happen,…warnings of divine wrath.…He is not mistaken when he declares, We…time [441–2].…In 1580…the Queen, her prelates, and trusted counsellors…accepted a terrifying earthquake as a portent of divine anger. The Privy Council ordained a weekly fast day;…the Bishop of London published an Order of Prayer upon Wednesdays and Fridays. Elton (1966, pp. 147–51), however: Gloucester shows such a degree of anxious subservience to astral influences as to represent pagan superstition, citing the arguments in the 1605 tr. of Le Loyer, A Treatise of Specters, dedicated to King James, himself an opponent of judicial astrology. Darby (1938, p. 256): The play’s examination of astrology, a topic missing from the sources, was introduced to compliment the king. The popularity of astrology, and the arguments pro and contra the judicial kind, have been widely discussed: see, e.g., Camden (1933); Allen (1941); Paul Kocher, Science and Religion in Elizabethan England (San Marino, 1953); Keith Thomas, Religion and the Decline of Magic (New York, 1971); and Bernard Capp, English Almanacs 1500–1800: Astrology and the Popular Press (Ithaca, N. Y., 1979). Concerning Sh.’s own beliefs, see n. 447–61.
Similarities have been discovered between this speech and Edward Gresham’s Strange feareful & true newes (1606) (by Harrison, 1933, pp. 856, 896); Himbert de Billy’s Certaine Wonderful Predictions (1604, sig. A5v) (by Parr, 1945, pp. 46–7); Florio’s tr. of Montaigne’s An Apologie of Raymond Sebond (by Muir, ed. 1952, p. 252; see below); prophecies about the end of the world in Matthew 24 and Mark 13 (by Noble, 1935, p. 229; Houghton, ed. 1957; Reibetanz, 1977, p. 26) and in Luke 21 and Revelation 16 (Holloway, 1961, p. 76); and other pamphlets claiming planetary influence (by, e.g., Porter & Clarke, ed. 1905, p. 163: Christopher Heydon, A Defence of Iudiciall Astrology, 1603; William Lilly, Englands Propheticall Merline, 1644). These parallels probably show only that the kinds of disasters foreseen and the apocalyptic language of the prophecies were commonplaces; Taylor (1941, p. 180) quotes several close analogues from the prognostications suppressed early in Elizabeth’s reign. Brown (ed. 1976): Gloucester…voic[es] anxieties that were operative in Shakespeare’s own day rather than in primitive Britain.…He thus introduced a totally familiar note of middle-aged, prudential, conservative, credulous, and defeatist opinion that the audience could relate immediately to their own experience. Idem (ed. 1996): In some productions he has entered consulting an almanac. Perrello (1997, pp. 11–12) speculates that Sh. remembered a comet that appeared at the disastrous death of King Edgar in 975 and the succession of his (possibly bastard) son Edward Martyr, but the analogies are both remote and inconsistent.
For theories that the phrase late eclipses alludes to solar and lunar eclipses of 1605, see .

434 wisedome of nature]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Natural philosophy. Furness (ed. 1880): Wisdom concerning nature, the knowledge of natural laws. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Scientific reasoning as to natural causes. See n. 232. Joseph (ed. 1966, pp. 51–3): Not an equivalent for scientific scepticism. He means simply that, although a natural scientific explanation of one kind or another can be put forward in ascribing the eclipses to normal physical causes, yet what has actually followed their appearance shows them to have been portents.…The New Science as represented by Francis Bacon did not contest this view. He declared that sound astrology involves predictions. Tovey (ed. 1896), followed by Craig (ed. 1901) and Goggin (ed. 1910), questionably: The reason of the natural man.

435 reason]
OED (v. 5b): To explain…by (or as by) reasoning, quoting this l. as its first ex. On F’s added it, see Abbott (§226): It is sometimes used indefinitely, as the object of a verb, without referring to anything previously mentioned, and seems to indicate a pre-existing object in the mind.…[Sometimes] = matters. Cf. Franz §295, and 520, 2241.

435 thus and thus]
OED (adv. 1e): Expressing minuteness or detail in the description, quoting this l. Craig (ed. 1901): Give various accounts of the cause. Verity (ed. 1897): Intended apparently as a rather contemptuous phrase, comparing Cym. 5.5.203 (3484).

435 nature]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Human nature. Deighton (ed. 1891): Mankind as part of the order of nature. OED (sb. 13): The material world, or its collective objects and phenomena, esp. those with which man is most directly in contact. Cf. 2478, 2577, 2648.

435 scourg’d]
Afflicted (OED, v. 2), not punished.

436 sequent]
OED (a. 2): That follows as a result or a logical conclusion, quoting this l.

436 effects]
Results, fulfilments; see n. 472. Moberly (ed. 1876) compares Tro. 1.3.94–101 (553–60). Elton (1966, p. 161): Despite Gloucester’s fearful over-belief [in portents],…his dire prognostication is ironically fulfilled; as in Macbeth, omens are not entirely repudiated as false but are linked, in dramatically ironical terms, to the disasters of those who involve themselves with such forewarnings. On the other hand, the confident and mocking Edmund…at the end attempts to violate his own individualistic determinism, Despite of his own nature ([3201]). Thus, near the start of the tragedy, the Renaissance dilemma is poised between two rival cosmic explanations: supernaturalism, in the astrological determinism of the aged earl; and its philosophical offspring, naturalism, in the materialist determination of his illegitimate son. Joseph (ed. 1966, pp. 52–3): Effects, here, has the sense, facts, actual occurrences.…Gloucester is already experiencing them.…The religious view held equally by Anglicans and Papists (and by adherents of other sects too) is found in Aquinas and goes still further back. It is that human beings are endowed with Free Will, but that they are nevertheless subject to the influence of the stars upon that part which is physical and not soul.…Whatever influence might be exerted by the stars on the body (which included the passions), the will was left free. Men were not determined, but inclined, towards a course of action; by the exercise of Free Will the inclination could be resisted. This view was held by Walter Raleigh and Francis Bacon, both convinced that Providence works through an interaction of Fortune and the Free Will of human beings; and one of the ways in which Fortune works for these men, is in the influence of the stars. To be a scientist was not necessarily to deny the influence of the stars. Cf. Fraser (1962, pp. 46–60), and n. 433–44. Gardner (ed. 1969): Robert Burton, quoting ancient authority, agreed that if we be ruled by reason, [the stars] have no power over us; but if we follow our own nature, and be led by sense, they do as much in us as brute beasts, and we are no better (The Anatomy of Melancholy [1.2.1.4]). Once more Shakespeare, with typical impartiality, gives Edmund the enlightened argument; the villain is seeing straight, and the self-righteous are questionable.

436–41 loue…Childe]
Vickers (1968, p. 356): The dramatic effect of this symmetry, coming as it does after much fluent, unpatterned conversation, is to make Gloucester’s reasoning seem over-careful, if not artificial, in its exact correspondences. Holloway (1961, p. 78): The Homily of 1574 Against Disobedient and Wilful Rebellion…clearly sees dissension between parents and children as the predictable counterpart of dissension in the body politic. Wells (ed. 2000) finds thematic parallels in Gorboduc, citing Mendonça (1960), and in Ovid, citing Bate (1993, p. 172).

436–41 fals off]
Schmidt (1874): Prove[s] faithless. OED (Fall v. 91f): To diminish, quoting this l. as its first ex. Horsman (ed. 1973): Revolts (OED, 91e). Muir (ed. 1952) finds a faint parallel in Mirour (rev. 1587, fol. 34v; not in 1574): Their former loue and friendship waxed cold. Sh., however, had used similar language before: cf. Ven. 387, affection…must be cool’d, Tim. 5.1.59 (2268), Friends falne off.

437 diuide]
OED (v. 14): Become separated…from…each other, quoting this l. Deighton (ed. 1891): Take up opposite sides in quarrels.

437–43 mutinies…disorders]
Brooke (ed. 1947), following Wright (ed. 1875): The lines depict the outburst of suspicion, fear, and brutality that followed the discovery of the Gunpowder Plot, 5 November 1605. See .

437 mutinies]
Verity (ed. 1897): An insurrection; not merely of soldiers, as now (OED, sb. 1). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Riots. Wilson (ed. 1960): Strife (OED, 2: Discord, contention).

438 Pallaces treason]
Doran (1931, p. 49): F’s in Pallaces, Treason; and adds words with or without which the sentence was grammatically good, and which may either have been omitted from Q or added by the printer [or a scribe] in F.

438 bond]
See n. 99.

438 betweene]
On F’s ’twixt see n. 147. Hogan (1962, p. 79): F, unable to fit betweene, replaced it by the (in this context) cacophonous ’twixt.

439–44 This…Graues]
Delius (1875–6, p. 135) improbably thinks that the compositor of Q thoughtlessly omitted this passage, which must have been in the original text because Edmund’s monologue, which follows,…is directly connected with it; but the idea of astrological influence is sufficiently present in Q’s lines to provoke Edmund’s remarks. Fleay (1879, p. 119), believing Q to be the version acted at court on 26 Dec. 1606, thinks this passage was carefully left out for that performance (and later restored in F) because In 1605…James was popularly supposed to be on any thing but good terms with Prince Henry. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxviii) objects that much the same matter appears in Q’s 473+1–+7, which would have been seen in that performance. Moriarty (1913, p. 462): The transfer of lines expressing belief in astrology from Edmund’s lips in Q (473+1–+6) to Gloucester’s in F (439–44) shows attention to motivation; on Edmund’s lips the lines merely moved Edgar to ridicule and were mere stage business, from Gloucester’s they show that what the eclipses portend are motivating forces, corroborating his new suspicions of Edgar. Since the lines are not identical, however, it is not necessary to insist that the quarto lines of Edmund’s speech inspired the folio lines given to Gloucester. Chambers (1930, 1:467), thinking Q a report of a theatrical version, suggests that the omission, if not an error, was directed by the censor for political and social criticism in the passage, though he does not specify what these are. Doran (1931, pp. 57–8), rejecting Fleay’s argument because it assumes a theory of the text which the evidence does not seem to warrant, namely, that Q1 and F represent collateral manuscripts, each one having been derived independently of the other from Shakespeare’s original version, proposes, It may be that the printer of Q1, having set the phrase betweene…father, remembered to have seen the word villaine in the sentence following; he glanced back at the manuscript to read the next sentence and his eye caught the second occurrence of villaine, some lines farther down. He did not notice what preceded, and therefore set the sentence beginning find…Edmund, unaware that he had omitted three sentences. Hart (1942, p. 147): These lines and 473+1–+6 were omitted from their respective texts because they both merely expand or elaborate what Gloucester says in 433–9. Stone (1980, pp. 239–40) doubts that the lines were in the Q MS: (a) The train of thought in Q is perfectly connected. There is a natural link between [bond…father] and [find…villaine]: it is clear that he had Edgar in mind. The additional lines in F merely make the connection more explicit.…(b)…The additional words [find out]…would have jogged [the Q compositor] into consciousness of error.…(c)…It is quite likely that, discovering [in 473+1–+6]…a vein he had just deliberately extended [here],…[the reviser] cancelled original matter rather than undo his own work. (d)…The word machination (line [442]) appears in the course of another addition ([2890])—and nowhere else in Shakespeare. Taylor (1983, pp. 84–5) dismisses censorship by arguments similar to Adee’s, that a censor would have objected to both this passage and 473+1–+7, and objects to Doran’s theory of eyeskip on some of Stone’s grounds. But he reverses order of F addition here and omission at 473+1–+6: Gloucester ruminates [in F] about what comes vnder the prediction, but in fact…the first reference to a prediction…comes almost forty lines later ([469–70]), immediately before Edmund’s omitted lines. It would therefore have been exceptionally easy for anyone excising Edmund’s later lines to turn back to Gloucester’s speech and, in the process of inserting a similar catalogue there, to include in it an offhand allusion which had not yet actually been explained. This claim that no prediction has yet been mentioned is too literal-minded: see n. 440. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 224) approves of the F addition here: Gloucester can hardly be shown too distracted. The added lines make explicit what is implied by portend no good to vs (433–4): having stated in general terms the bad effects that follow eclipses, Gloucester applies the generalization to the immediate present, seeing the partial fulfilment of it that has already occurred as an omen for even more disasters to come. The lines may have been added to fill out his train of thought. Foakes (ed. 1997): The lines add a specific comment on his own and on Lear’s situation and enlarg[e] the theme of order inverted, the world upside-down. Weis (ed. 1993): Q is more economical here than F, perhaps because it wishes to reserve some of this material for Edmund’s parody of it (not in F) at [473+1–+6].
Welsford (1935, p. 261): Recurrent throughout the play is the sense that the breaking of human ties, especially ties of close blood or plighted loyalty, is so abnormal and unnatural that it must be a symptom of some dread convulsion in the frame of things that must bring about the end of the world unless some Divine Power intervenes.

439, 444 villaine]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Edgar…by the very breath of treachery has become ignoble, a villain (villein) in the sense of peasant. Cf. n. 2152.

440 prediction]
Warburton (ed. 1747) suspected some topical reference. Tovey (ed. 1896): That, namely, to which Edgar refers [in 469].…Obviously an allusion to a contemporary publication known to some of the audience. But there were too many such publications for any one to be alluded to (see n. 433–44.). Gloucester is simply substantiating the truth of his own prediction in the immediately preceding lines: that since eclipses are forerunners of disasters, These late eclipses…portend no good to vs. Lear’s treatment of Cordelia and Edgar’s supposed treatment of Gloucester show the prediction to be already coming true. The there’s in 440 and 441 are emphatic. Hunter (ed. 1972): Also, the prediction of the end of the world in the New Testament…Mark 13:12–13. Milward (1987, p. 165) compares other such predictions in Joel 2:31, Acts 2:20, Matt. 24:29. See also the next n.

440–1 Son…Childe]
Verity (ed. 1897): Gloucester’s superstitiousness…is emphasised as showing why he does not require stronger evidence before believing in the guilt of his son.…He regards Edgar’s supposed treachery as one of the sequent effects of the disorders in the heavens, and therefore accountable. Goggin (ed. 1910): It is remarkable that Gloucester should show himself so clear-headed in regard to Lear’s treatment…of Cordelia…and yet fail to see that he himself is no less unjust to Edgar. But…he falls by his superstition. Noble (1935, p. 229) compares Mark 13:8–12, Mic. 7:6; Hunter (ed. 1972, p. 40) cites similarities of phrase in the Homily against Wilful Rebellion (Certain Sermons of Homilies, ed. 1817, p. 541), which he thinks may also derive from Mark; Shaheen (1987, p. 147) adds Matt. 10:21 and Luke 12:52–3, 21:16, and notes references to children mistreating parents in Leir 753–4, 761–2, and 767–8 (see ). Cf. n. 441–2. Joseph (ed. 1966, p. 52): There are no certain grounds for regarding Gloucester as old-fashioned or superstitious in his assumption that This villain…prediction. He is not saying that Edgar’s behaviour has been caused by the stars, or even by the eclipses, but simply that it is one of the actual occurrences which they portended. This does not mean, moreover, that by studying the portents it would have been possible to predict the behaviour of Edgar in particular, but that they predicted such things in general, of which he affords one particular example. Fleay (1879, p. 119): The phrase was carefully left out of Q before the court performance of 1606, because liable to misconstruction by the Court as alluding to strained relations between James and Prince Henry. Cf. n. 473+1–+6. There is of course no reason to think it was ever part of the text behind Q.

441 byas of Nature]
Wright (ed. 1875): Natural inclination (OED, Bias sb. 3). OED (Nature sb. 2b): The general inherent character or disposition of mankind—cf. 1384, 1566, 1700, 1780, 1851, 2056+1, 2648; (9e): Natural feeling or affection—cf. 58, 782, 906, 1462, 1972, 2162. Kemshead (ed. 1875) and many later eds. have found an allusion, common in Sh., to the game of bowls, in which a bowling piece with an intentionally uneven distribution of weight (bias) is able to run an oblique path (bias) (OED, 2). Tovey (ed. 1896) argues that such a connotation is not necessary, since bias was commonly used for anything oblique before [Sh.] began to write (OED, 1: An oblique or slanting line). More likely here is the connotation of OED 4: Set course,…ordinary way, found in the proverb To run against the Bias (Tilley B339). Joseph (ed. 1966): Veers away from the course. A metaphor taken from navigation.

441–2 We…time]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Shakspeare has here in mind the signs and calamities predicted in Matt. x. 21, Luke xxi. 16, 25, and other parts of Scripture. So, in the last scene of the play, Is this…horror? [3224–5]. Similarly Carter (1905, p. 433) cites Matt. 24 and Mark 13. Cf. n. 440–1. Verity (ed. 1897): He quotes unconsciously from Edgar’s supposed letter [383; cf. 320], and speaks as the typical old man (laudator temporis acti) whose lament is things are not now as they were in my day. On apocalyptic language in astrological prophecies, see n. 433; on Renaissance fear that the world would end soon, see ; and see n. 3224–5.

442 Machinations]
Schmidt (1875): Plotting[s] (OED, 1, quoting 2890, its only other use in Sh.). See nn. 437–43, 439–44. Salingar (1983, p. 161): Harsnett (Declaration, 1603, sig. A3v) accuses the Jesuits of treasonable machinations.

442 hollownesse]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Insincerity (OED, sb. 4: falseness). Cf. n. 164.

443 disquietly]
Delius (ed. 1854): Used causatively. OED: In a disquieting manner, quoting this l. as its first of two exx.

444 find out]
OED (Find, v. 20c): Discover the…true character of. Though the first ex. cited by OED is dated 1711, the phrase is used in this sense in AWW 3.6.93 (1826). Sh. usually omits the adv. (see OED, 8), as in 2549.

444 loose]
Schmidt (1874): Cause to be lost (OED, Lose v.1, citing this l.). Kittredge (ed. 1940): A backhanded promise to reward his detective work.

445 thee]
Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Dative. Furness (ed. 1880): Note the change to the more affectionate thee. Mazzon (1992, p. 132): Elsewhere Gloucester constantly addresses Edmund by the more formal you.

446 Kent]
Smith (ed. 1902): His reference to the injustice done to Kent gives point to the folly of his own credulity.

446 honest]
Virtually all eds. prefer F’s honesty. OED records honeste as a 16th-c. sp. of honesty. The Q compositor may have confused the words, or misread honestie as honeste and set honest. Schmidt (1874): Love of truth, upright conduct (OED, sb. 3d).

446 strange strange]
This is an idiomatic and effective exit-line for the troubled Gloucester; a number of eds. have preferred it to F’s terser ’Tis strange. Possibly F Compositor B shortened the phrase in order to place the Exit in the same line. So Hogan (1962, p. 79), adding that Q’s repetition is characteristic of Gloucester, as at 1029, 1035, 2509. The whole page (qq3v), set concurrently with its forme-mate (qq4), is extremely dense and crowded, lacking any lines of white space, and the space type before and period after the Exit have been omitted to make it fit.

447–61 This…bastardy]
Bishop Warburton (ed. 1747) approves of Sh.’s severe ridicule of the wretched, monstrous, impious, and Italian notion of judicial astrology, which seeks to deny free will and encourage moral irresponsibility. He further appreciates Sh.’s oblique and politic method of attack against an idea still held in some reverence in his day, namely by making its proponent Gloucester a Pagan fatalist and its attacker the villain and atheist. But astrology did not necessarily deny free will or personal responsibility: see n. 433–44. Whether the villain Edmund is also an atheist is another matter. Craig (1925, p. 104): The cynical rejection of the supernatural by Edmund must be set down to infidelity.…He denies the influence of the heavens, which must be meant to indicate his denial of religion. Fripp (1938, p. 665): Such a parody of the [Calvinist] doctrine of Necessity and Grace, under the guise of astrology, would sound blasphemous in 1606, and is hostile to the whole tenour of the drama, comparing 2347+34, 3136. Dick (1944, pp. 17–47) surveys the widespread satires of the quackeries of judicial astrology in popular literature and drama of the day, and Elton (1966, pp. 155–60), the many protests against attributing natural illnesses to supernatural causes, and one’s crimes and follies to destiny rather than to one’s own wicked desires. Since such arguments issue from characters as virtuous as Helena (AWW 1.1.216–19 [223–6]), they hardly imply atheism, but only such skepticism as that voiced by William Fulke in 1563, quoted by Taylor (1941, p. 180), or by Sir Thomas Browne in Vulgar Errors 1.11, quoted by Thaler (1929, p. 119), or by George Pettie in A Petite Pallace (1576; ed. 1908, 1:71), quoted by Reyher (1947, p. 508 n.). Edmund, however, seems to go further and reject any planetary influence on that I am. So Fraser (1962, pp. 24–5, 46–7): Edmund’s incredulity and self-sufficiency deny order and causality or agency beyond himself, including providence. Allen (1941, pp. 184–6) groups Edmund with D’Amville of The Atheist’s Tragedy and Byron of Chapman’s Byron’s Conspiracy as characters who do not believe in astrology: All of these opponents of astrology are not out-and-out villains, but they are all skeptics, all fellow realists. They are Marlowes, Harriots, and Warners.…The Renaissance…was both fearful and suspicious of them. Lafeu tells one all about these Edmunds and D’Amvilles…: They say miracles are past; and we have our philosophical persons, to make modern and familiar, things supernatural and causeless. Hence it is that we make trifles of terrors, ensconcing ourselves into seeming knowledge, when we should submit ourselves to an unknown fear [AWW 2.3.1–6 (893–7)]. The literary men of the Renaissance knew what happened to such people; eventually these freethinkers met bad ends. Tillyard (1943, p. 55): He is as sound as Raleigh [History 1.2.11] on the impiety…of imagining that God had constrained the mind and will of man to impious acts by any celestial inforcements. and he is justly the critic of his father’s superstitions. But he is…brazen in arrogating to himself a viciousness that would have triumphed over every stellar inducement to virtue.…We may be meant to look on Edmund as one of those superlatively vicious men whom the stars and their own wills have joined to produce. If this is so, there is dramatic irony in his denying the influence of the stars in words of wickedness that substantiate it in a sense quite other than he intended. Harrison (ed. 1937), on the tone: This second soliloquy of Edmund is in prose, the first [335–56] in verse, which contrasts the passion of the first with the cynicism of the second speech. Smith (1958, pp. 174–6) argues in Edmund’s defense that the repeated allusions here to lechery, adultery, bastardy, etc. add up to a justifiable criticism of Gloucester; but Coleridge (1833; ed. Foakes, 1989, p. 103) remarks on the use which Shakespeare always makes of his bold villains as vehicles for expressing opinions and conjectures of a nature too hazardous for a wise man to put forth directly as his own, or from any sustained character.
Whether Edmund’s viewpoint equals Sh.’s, as Wilson (1903, p. 4) asserts, has been much discussed. Fraser-Harris (1927) and Schark (1926) deny that Sh. believed in astrology, Clark (1929) asserts that he did. Camden (1933) is non-commital: the contradictory viewpoints throughout the plays are the characters’, not Sh.’s. Darby (1938): Sh. was flattering King James’s beliefs; see n. 433. Allen (op. cit., pp. 149, 165): Poets and dramatists seldom overleap the opinions of their age; seldom are they found in the ranks of the violent partisans; and indeed Sh. was more given to speaking about the stars and their services and disservices to men than most of his literary fellows. Bald (1948, p. 349): While he would have hesitated to deny that the stars could affect men’s lives, there is nothing to suggest that he had so much faith in their influence as to deny the freedom of the will. Free-will is of the essence of tragedy. After studying all the astrological references in the plays and poems, Sondheim (1938–9) concludes that Sh. believed in natural astrology but not that the stars controlled the destiny of individuals, rulers, or nations. He uses astrological references as rhetorical ornament, to express mood or atmosphere, to symbolize such abstract concepts as happiness and misfortune, fate and chance, or to allow his characters to affirm or negate the power of the stars over human destiny; but he was not deeply concerned with the subject, and his characters show no knowledge of astrology beyond the commonplaces available in any almanac. Cf. Stone (1953).
Vickers (1968, pp. 356–7): Edmund is now made…to express his scorn…in the same rhetorical symmetries as Gloucester.…The rhetorical structure of the speech, with its expanding size (length of phrase) and force (terminology), and its contemptuous repetition, gives the abuse a great channelled focus, so producing a double effect as Edmund both mocks the style and by this means attacks superstition more powerfully. Brown (ed. 1976): His prose has strong syntactical organization and a confident profusion of words, parallels, anthitheses, and variations.

447 excellent]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Surpassing (OED, adj. 1b: In bad or neutral sense.…supreme). Hunter (ed. 1972): Also splendid (from Edmund’s anti-human point of view). Foakes (ed. 1997): Used caustically.

447 foppery]
Schmidt (1874): Folly (OED, sb. 1). Cf. 348, 681. Only Ridley (ed. 1935): Affectation. Robertson (1897; 1909, p. 109): Montaigne, on stellar involvement, similarly derides this common foppery…that our owne interests disturbe heaven, and his infinite is moved at our least actions (tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 2:328).

448 sicke in Fortune]
Schmidt (1875), sick: Figuratively, distempered and corrupted or ailing (OED, a. 1); cf. 2685, the infection of his fortune. There is no need for Kittredge’s (ed. 1940) ingenious elaboration, Our fortune has had too much of our own foolish conduct—more than it can digest—and the result is misfortune.

448 surfeit]
OED (sb. 5): Sickness…arising from intemperance; also…from other causes. The construction is elliptical—(which sickness is) often the surfeit—but the apposition with the general idea in when…sicke is clear. The F plural surfets makes an inferior parallel, and defenders of F usually substitute a more remote substitute for sickness: evil consequences (Page, ed. 1889), misfortunes (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 132), etc. Doran (1933, p. 52 n.) traces the unusual sense, as well as Gloster’s faith in the astrological predictions and Edmund’s skepticism, to Montaigne’s Of Vanitie; see .

449 make guiltie]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Accuse as causing.

449 disasters]
OED (sb. 2): Misfortune, quoting this l. Rolfe (ed. 1880): An astrological term. Verity (ed. 1897): Conveying the notion ill-starred; Lat. negative prefix dis + astrum, a star. Lott (ed. 1974): Therefore ironical here.

450 the Starres]
Furness (ed. 1880), followed by Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 132), prefers F’s Starres because particular stars are referred to, not the stars in general. But if one’s particular stars are referred to, the usual formula is my stars or our stars, as in JC 1.2.140 (239). Edmund seems to be referring generally to the sun, moon, and all other heavenly bodies thought to influence life. OED (sb.1 3): In Astrology, used of the planets and zodiacal constellations. F’s omission of the article may be a simple accident, destroying the parallelism in Q.

450 by necessitie]
Schmidt (1879, p. 19): Usage is in favor of by, but on [F] is Shakespearian. On necessity occurs twice in close succession in LLL 1.1.[148, 154 (159, 165)]; by necessity is found nowhere else in Sh. Unfortunately for Schmidt, by necessity occurs in 3H6 3.3.68 (1802), and on necessity, which occurs twice in LLL only because one speaker playfully echoes or quotes the previous speaker’s words, is found nowhere else in Sh. Moreover, Schmidt’s list of exx. showing that Sh. has an unmistakable preference for the prepositions on and upon to express that which gives the motive or impulse to anything (Ger.) offers no statistical count and contains doubtful analogues. Here in Q five parallel phrases all begin with by; F’s change to on in one of them weakens the parallelism to no obvious advantage.

452 Trecherers]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 369): This form may be influenced by Adulterers in the next line. F’s Treachers seems to have been a somewhat more usual form, but OED records both, and Sh. never uses either again. It is not clear why the Q compositor should have substituted a longer and less common form; it is more likely that he found it in his copy, probably Sh.’s MS. The meaning is the same: A deceiver, a cheat;…sometimes, a traitor (OED).

452 spirituall]
Surprisingly no one attempts to defend the Q reading. Edmund might mean that the the influencing power is of the nature of a spirit or incorporeal supernatural essence; immaterial (OED, Spiritual a. 4). Since the word may also suggest the influence of God and his angels (Spirit sb. 3d, 6), Edmund might further be ironically mocking the notion of attributing evil to heauenly or diuine agency (if not alluding specifically to the belief that planetary influence could be directed by divine providence). Weis (ed. 1993) glosses of planetary influence without explaining how that would be spiritual. F’s Sphericall, which makes a good parallelism with planitary and a good enough one with heauenly, though none at all with diuine, is universally adopted. OED (a. 3: Of or pertaining to the celestial spheres—i.e., in which the planets moved) quotes this l. as its first ex. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 369) suggests a misreading—i/e, t/c. The [Q] compositor may have read sphericall as sphiritall. Or there may have been too many strokes, so that he thought he saw a u before the a.…In either case…he decided to ignore the h. Perhaps because this theory requires not one misreading but three or four, Taylor (1983, p. 453) suggests a misreading of the spelling spiricall. OED records spire in the 14th and 15th cents., spere in the 14th to 16th cents., and sperycall in the 16th c., but does not record spiricall. The possibility remains that spirituall is Sh.’s reading and that F represents a simplification of the durior lectio. Convinced of spiricall, Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 512) suggest a pun on spiracle: spirit as breath of God.

452 predominance]
Wright (ed. 1875): Powerful influence. Rolfe (ed. 1880) cites astrological uses of predominant in AWW 1.1.197 (203) and WT 1.2.202 (284).

453 of]
Wilson (ed. 1960): To.

454 influence]
Schmidt (1874): The power exerted by heavenly bodies on terrestrial or other celestial bodies (OED, sb. 2). Cf. 1182. Deighton (ed. 1891): The modern sense [OED, 4] being a relic of the astrological belief, as in Son. 78.10, LLL 5.2.859 (2820).

454 diuine]
Though sometimes glossed obliquely—celestial, planetary (MacCracken, ed. 1914), supernatural (Muir, ed. 1952)—the word means precisely proceeding from God (OED, a. 2). On planetary influence as an agent of providence, see n. 433–44 Edmund’s irony is sardonic in the extreme.

454–5 thrusting on]
Generally glossed as impulse (Hunter, ed. 1869) or incitement (Deighton, ed. 1891). Perhaps preferable is OED (Thrust v. 8c): To press, force, or impose the acceptance of (upon some one), citing TN 2.5.146 (1152). So Foakes (ed. 1997): Imposition, and Wells (ed. 2000), Compulsion. Only Joseph (ed. 1966) takes on to mean forward.

455 admirable]
Schmidt (1874): Deserving the highest praise, wonderful, delightful (OED, a. 1, 2).

455 whoremaster man]
OED (Whoremaster sb.): = Whoremonger…one who practises whoredom; a fornicator, lecher, quoting this l. as an ex. of attrib. use. Of Whore-master-man Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 192) says, F several times has supererogatory hyphens.…The compositor is doubtless to blame.

456 lay…to the charge]
OED (Charge sb. 16b): Phr. To lay to one’s charge: to impute to one as a fault, quoting this l. A few eds. insist on following F’s lay…on, though as Schmidt (ed. 1879) admits, on is contrary not only to present usage, but also to Shakespearian (Ger.). Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 170): F’s on may be an erroneous repetition of the on in line [455] or of that in (F) line [450].

456 gotish]
OED (a. 1b): Lascivious, lustful, citing this l. Dent (1981) compares Tilley G167, As lecherous as a Goat.

456 disposition]
See n. 329.

456 Starres]
Stars in general, consistently with 450. F’s a Starre is not consistent with the following two lines. See nn. 450, 460.

457 compounded]
Harbage (ed. 1958): (1) Came to terms [OED, v. 12] (2) created [OED, 4].

457–8 Dragons…maior]
Harbage (ed. 1958): Cited because of the suggestiveness of their names. Hunter (ed. 1972): Because of the associations with violence.

457–8 Dragons taile]
Some eds. erroneously understand the constellation Draco. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905), correctly: The Dragon’s Head, which indicated the northward node of the moon[’s orbit] when crossing the ecliptic [OED], and the Dragon’s taile, the southward node [OED, quoting this l.], were in the Elizabethan astrology important in the government of nativities; the Dragon’s Head being indicative of good, the tail of bad, as in Edmund’s case. Rusche (1969, p. 162): It detracted from a good horoscope and made a bad one worse, citing Ptolemy’s Tetrabiblos. Hunter (ed. 1972): Chaucer (A Treatise of the Astrolabe II.4) names the Tail of the Dragon among the wicked planets. Williams (1994), Dragon: Woman in her sexual capacity, quoting this l. Foakes (1997): With overtones of evil, as Satan was familiarly called the dragon.

458 Vrsa maior]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): The great bear; the constellation so called (OED, 2a, quoting this l.). Parr (1946, pp. 182, 184; 1953, pp. 81, 84), correcting Knobel (1916, 1:459): The constellation of Ursa Major exerted the combined influences of Mars and Venus.…An Elizabethan audience who [1953: which] perceived that Edmund was born under the rough and lecherous constellation of Ursa Major would have strongly suspected him sooner or later to compound with such women of the play as were available [1953: assailable]. Kitson (1996, p. 203) suspects a conscious irony: Since the constellation never sets in these latitudes, so this would apply to everyone, adding Bears were regarded as lecherous.

459 Fut]
Dyce (ed. 1857): Seems to be a misprint for Tut, rather than intended for Foot or ’Sfoot. Sh. uses Tut (sometimes Tut tut) 37 times and Fut nowhere else. Daniel (facs. 1885, p. xv n.) suggests the propriety of restoring to the text the oath Fut…which, without the slightest authority, is invariably changed to Tut in modern editions. Fut and Ud’s Fut are common forms of the oath Foot, God’s Foot, citing Marston’s What You Will [4.1.270]. OED (Fut): ?An instinctive exclamation; but cf. Foot; (Foot sb. 1b): In the oath or exclamation, Christ’s foot, later ’s foot or simply foot. Sh. uses the oath only once, Sfoote in Tro. 2.3.5 (1210) Q, F. Craig (ed. 1901) cites (inaccurately) six occurrences of the spelling Fut in Marston’s plays. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Pooh! nonsense!, unattested. Edwards (ed. 1975): Explosive sound of disgust. Following Partridge, 1947, p. 119), Colman (1974, p. 195), tentatively: Edmund’s expletive may be influenced by foutra, used in 2H4 5.3.99 (3119), footre, and 115 (3139), fowtre, not as interjections but in the form a foutre for. Idem (ed. 1982): May derive from French vb foutre, to fuck. F omits it, along with some other oaths printed in Q. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 170): Surely its absence from F is due to the purging away of profanity in accordance with the Act [to Restrain Abuses of Players] of [27 May] 1606. The purging could have been official censorship or self-censorship by the company. Taylor (1983, pp. 78–9) suspects that the cut was made for the court performance of 26 Dec. 1606, and takes the omission as evidence that Q was set from Sh.’s foul papers rather than from a reported text reflecting performance. He thinks the word could have been excised by Sh., his company, a censor, a scribe, an editor in Jaggard’s printing shop, or even a compositor. (See also ibid., p. 109.) Howard-Hill (1985, p. 168 n.): It would have been an easy matter to change the offensive Fut to Tut had Shakespeare, the players, or the Folio editors wished. The expletive Tut or variants are commonly associated with vice-like characters in Shakespeare and elsewhere.

460 that]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): What (OED, dem. pron. 7).

460 maidenlest]
Doran (1931, p. 98): Seems to be an error in all three texts, and must have appeared in the original manuscript. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 370): F takes over a mis-spelling from Q; but Wells & Taylor (1987) cite other words in Sh. and Dekker—stormest, easilest, busielest—omitting the i in the superlative. McCann (ed. 1964): Most innocent, benign. Or most mild and chaste, not rough and lecherous. Wells (ed. 2000): Also perhaps newest, noting a nova discovered by Kepler, shining brightly 1604–6.

460 starre]
Skillan (ed. 1967): Probably the constellation of Virgo, the Virgin, the emblem of purity, and referred to as a whole. Edmund may refer to none in particular; many constellations are named after maidens. Kitson (1996, p. 203), however: The planet Venus, the lesser benefic. Harbage (1963, p. 404): We must admit delight in that maidenliest star that might have twinkled at Edmund’s bastardizing.

461 my]
Objective genitive: of me.

461 bastardy]
OED (2): Begetting of bastards. Cf. JC 2.1.138 (769), guilty of a seuerall Bastardie. Q is clear and Shn.; F’s bastardizing, perhaps intended as an improvement, is a rarer word, not found elsewhere in Sh. OED (Bastardize v. 2): To beget bastard issue. Obs. rare., quoting only this l. Muir (ed. 1952) finds the word in Florio’s tr. of Montaigne (1603; ed. 1910, 1:46).

462 Enter Edgar]
In the left margin in Q1, apparently added to the page as an afterthought after the text was set. McKenzie (1973, p. 129): A marginal note proper, comparing 944 (n. 948) and 1595. Rosenberg (1972, p. 91): Edgar has been acted here—to emphasize what he will change from—as: naive, dreamily bookish, bewildered, submissive, uncertain, drunk, wenching, a fop.

463 Edgar;]
F omits. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 171): Unless we adopt the Q reading here there is no point in F’s Pat: he comes…. The Q Edgar; occurs at the beginning of a line close beside the marginal stage direction Enter Edgar, and this may have confused the F compositor. Presumably Duthie means that the compositor omitted the second Edgar as redundant; but he or a scribe may as well have thought it an erroneous speech prefix following the entrance and so deleted it. As for the punctuation, Q’s semicolon may be right, marking a pause, or may be a substitution for a question mark, indicating an exclamation. See the next n.

463 and out]
The lack of an antecedent for hee in F and the similarity in shape of Q out and F Pat: suggest corruption rather than revision. Similarly Q’s mine for F my Cue in 464 suggests that the Q MS may have had an earlier reference to a cue. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 512): Perhaps Q’s and out is a misreading for ons Q [ = cue] out: It seems…likely that mine itself is right, contrasting my cue (in the sense the role I must play: see OED, sb2 [4]) with Edgar’s cue (the name Edgar, which cues his entrance).…An earlier use of cue has been accidentally omitted. Eyeskip from ons to out would be easy enough. This is very plausible. Even more simply, the Q MS may have read Edgar; ons qu, [or Qu,; see F Wiv. 3.2.45 (1306), 3.3.37 (1381)] hee comes. Capital O, Q, and P are all similar in secretary hand, as are small p and q, and either of the latter might be mistaken for an o if drawn with an indistinct descender. A somewhat illegible Qu, or qu, might have been taken for out by the Q compositor, especially if he had already misread ons (= on’s, on his) as and, and taken for pat by the scribe preparing the playbook from the MS behind Q. (For the likelihood that Q and the original playbook both derive from Sh.’s rough draft, see .) For the expression come (up)on his cue Wells & Taylor (ibid.) cite R3 3.4.26 (1994), where F spells cue as Q. F’s Pat is generally glossed as in Rann (ed. 1794): Opportunely, in the nick of time (OED, 1). Ridley (ed. 1935) notices a possibly suspicious and certainly interesting circumstance, that F both here and in…[Ham. 3.3.73 (2350)] inserts a pat of which Q [reading but] knows nothing. Both lines were set by F Compositor B. F’s omission of ons/and can only be speculated upon. The word caused the Q compositor difficulty, and may have baffled a scribe preparing (earlier, from the same author’s MS; see ) a transcript for the playbook; someone may have struck out or underlined the second Edgar and seemed to include ons for deletion as well (see prev. n.); or the scribe read Qu, as Pat and, taking the capital to indicate the beginning of the sentence, overlooked or ignored the troublesome ons.

463 Catastrophe]
Warburton (ed. 1747): The natural winding up of the plot in the Comedy of the ancients…owing to the artful and yet natural introduction of the persons of the Drama into the scene, just in the nick of time (OED, 1). Wright (ed. 1875): Like the Deus ex machina which Horace warns against. Miola (1994, p. 188): The turn that resolves the plot. Edmund, a New Comedic intriguer, the architectus doli, is cheekily confident that the intrigue will work, in fact, has already worked.

463 old Comedy]
Usually taken to mean classical comedy generally; see prev. n. and Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Latin comedy, whose methods Shakespeare followed once, and outdid, in [Err.]. Miola (1994, p. 188): Not Aristophanes, but Plautus and Terence…New Comedy. Perrett (1904, p. 277) and McNeal (1958, p. 44): Sh. has Leir in mind. Only the Clarkes (ed. 1868): We think that the passage very likely includes allusion to the adage, Talk of the devil, and he instantly appears [Tilley D294].…There may have been some well-known morality or ancient dramatic show, where the devil…came in thus patly at the catastrophe of the piece. Spivack (1958, p. 67), cited by Wells (ed. 2000): In late morality plays, allegorical figures come in at the end to punish sinners. Halio (ed. 1973): Early Tudor plays often lacked adequate dramatic motivation; the Catastrophe…might arrive quite arbitrarily. Weis (ed. 1993): Edmund suggests that Edgar can always be relied on to act according to expectation.

464 mine]
If cue is part of 463 (see n.), mine means the same as F’s my Cue. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 370) attempts at length to show how the Q compositor could have misread my cu as myne; Blayney (apud Wells & Taylor, 1987, p. 512): He was simply bewildered by my Q, and gave up. If mine is right but unclear because of errors in Q and F 463, F’s substitution might have been inserted in the playbook to make Edmund’s train of thought clear to an audience. F’s Cue has been variously glossed. The primary meaning, the concluding word or words of one actor’s speech which serve as signal to another actor to enter or speak (OED, sb.2 1), adduced by Corney (1865), Wright (ed. 1875), and others, does not suit the context since Edgar has not spoken, though his entrance may serve as a sign…when to speak or act (OED, 2). Hunter’s (ed. 1869) The cue I am to take up from my father’s speech fits the figurative sense A hint or guiding suggestion how to act (OED, 2). Crook’s (ed. 1907) Line of action suits the sense The part assigned one to play…; the proper or politic course to take (OED, 3, quoting this l.). Perhaps most convenient to this context is OED (4): Humour, disposition…proper to any action.

464 villanous]
Possibly suitable for my villainous purposes, but more probably as a general term of opprobrium: see OED (a. 5): Detestable, quoting Wiv. 3.5.92 (1759), villanous smell. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Miserable (OED, 1c).

464 melancholy]
Brown (ed. 1976): That melancholy that was then a modish pose for young men. Muir (1951, p. 13): In Harsnett (1603) all the demoniacs are melancholy, esp. Marwood (p. 24; see ), and ch. 21 concerns men of a melancholick constitution (p. 131; see ).

464 sith]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 370) suggests an unconscious repetition of th from with two words earlier. Possibly a spelling variant reflecting pronunciation: OED (Sigh, v.) records the variant sithe, and sigh as a variant of sith, since. OED (Sithe, sb.2) gives only one ex. of the noun spelled sith. F’s sighe substitutes the more familiar form. Capell (1783, 1.2:147): Is the gamut [see n. 466] a sigh?…’Tis probable that Edmund contents himself with a serious posture and look, without sighing. At least the O (465) may be sighed. Hunter (ed. 1972): It is not clear why Tom o’Bedlam…should have a characteristic sigh—though he may well have whined. As Muir suggests, the sighing may have been usual rather than characteristic.

464–5 them of Bedlam]
Though Q makes sense, all eds. before 1986 follow F’s Tom, anticipating Edgar’s impersonation. Duthie (1949, p. 370): Probably an e/o misreading. The compositor, reading tem, may have introduced the h on his own responsibility. Or the copy may have had thom; or Thom (Stone, 1980, p. 178). OED (Tom sb. 7c): Tom o’ Bedlam, a madman, a deranged person discharged from Bedlam…and licensed to beg, quoting this l. as its first ex. See n. 1265, and cf. 2176+5. John Aubrey so uses the phrase Tom ô Bedlams in The Natural History of Wiltshire 2.4 (ed. Britton, p. 93; noted by Kittredge, ed. 1940). Jonson, in The Divell is an Asse 5.2.35, alludes to the popular song Thom. o’ Bet’lem; its musical settings are discussed by Simpson (1966, pp. 263–6, 710–13) and its various texts collected in Loving Mad Tom: Bedlamite Verses of the XVI and XVII Centuries, ed. Jack Lindsay (1927); see .

465 these eclipses]
Taylor (1983, p. 86), citing 472: Edmund is reading from a book in F. In both texts he says he read about eclipses this other day. Thomson (1988, p. 182): Why should this [469–70] even raise the possibility that he is reading [the prediction] again now? These may refer simply to things…familiarly known (OED, a. 1b).

465–6 diuisions]
Edmund begins to parody his father’s superstition, using Gloucester’s word diuide (437) here and in 473+2. Like Gloucester he may be referring to the divisions in Lear’s family as well as to the general kinds of estrangement that he details in 473+1–+5. Hunter (ed. 1869) suggests play on another meaning, the notes of the gamut having been also called divisions. So Moberly (ed. 1876). Like Naylor (1896, p. 36), Tovey (ed. 1896) wonders whether, ironically playing with the subject, he takes the word in its musical sense (modulations) also, and proceeds to illustrate it by humming a discord. Verity (ed. 1897) suspects a quibbling reference to its musical sense variation, citing Rom. 3.5.29–30 (2061–2), and the idea is elaborated by Elson (1900, p. 115). The interpretation is doubtful: division, as Sh. clearly knew (see 1H4 3.1.208 [1749]), means florid ornamentation in playing a stringed instrument, achieved by subdividing one long note into many rapid ones. Sadie (1980, 5:510): This was music intended to dazzle. That is not at all what Edmund is doing in speaking or singing the names of four notes of the gamut. Nonetheless Bevington (ed. 1992) thinks that the musical sense florid variations on a theme…prompt[s] Edmund’s singing. Hunter (ed. 1972): Counterpoint against plainsong; but Edmund cannot be singing counterpoint or descant. See the next n.

466 Fa…Me]
Capell (1783, 1.2:147) finds a very heap of impertinence: For is the gamut a sigh? or humming a mark of villanous melancholy, and serious consideration? The purpose of the added words in F is puzzling, as is their delivery. Expanding on a note in his General History of Music (1789, 3:344), Burney (in Malone, ed. 1790) says: Shakspeare…shews by the context that he was well acquainted with the property of these syllables in solmisation, which imply a series of sounds so unnatural, that ancient musicians prohibited their use. The monkish writers on musick say, mi contra fa est diabolus: the interval fa mi, including a tritonus, or sharp 4th, consisting of three tones without the intervention of a semitone, expressed in the modern scale by the letters F G A B, would form a musical phrase extremely disagreeable to the ear. Edmund, speaking of eclipses as portents and prodigies, compares the dislocation of events, the times being out of joint, to the unnatural and offensive sounds, fa sol la mi. Rann (ed. 1794): A series of harsh, inharmonious sounds, to which Edmund humorously compares the disorders portended by eclipses. Knight (ed. 1840): It is not…that Edmund compares the dislocation of events to the unnatural and offensive sounds,…but that in his affectation of humming the gamut as Edgar enters, he employs unnatural and offensive sounds.…They are a pretended accompaniment to his thoughts, but they are not an interpretation of them. Wright (ed. 1875): For this [i.e., Burney’s] note, Mr. Chappell assures me, there is not the slightest foundation. Edmund is merely singing to himself in order not to seem to observe Edgar’s approach. Furness (ed. 1880): Just as Mistress Quickly sings and downe, downe, adowne’a in [Wiv. 1.4.43 (436)], when Dr. Caius is approaching. Chappell, letter to Wright (27 July 1880): There should be no chord at all, because Edmund speaks of melody, not of harmony. Moberly (ed. 1876): The true explanation probably is that the sequence…(with mi descending) is like a deep sigh. White (1880, pp. 831–2): This succession of notes suggests a discord that must be resolved by the chord of the tonic. This resolution would have been implied if Edmund had gone on, as he naturally would have done, and sung fa, sol, la, mi, fa. But, beginning on the sub-dominant, he stops short of the tonic upon the leading note of the scale; and this when he has just said, These…divisions,—divisions being used in a double sense, that of distraction, and…of a rapid succession of notes. Idem (ed. 1883): Edmund sings merely to seem at ease; but S. has made him sing quite in keeping with the last part of his speech.…Moreover, his singing leads Edgar to ask him what serious contemplation he is in. Tovey (ed. 1896): Possibly nothing more than a stage direction to hum, put in this fashion by an ignorant and unmelodious printer. Elson (1900, p. 111: Sh. presented the worst possible interval in music…as prognostication of the discords to come. Halio (ed. 1992): Or [as] the sound of a Bedlamite? E. G. (1928, p. 440): Edmund evidently is about to say Father, but when he hears the sound of the first part of the word, his mischievous nature prompts him to supply, instead, the remaining syllables of the diabolical progression. Skillan (ed. 1967): At O (465) A big sigh as he turns facing oblique r., and then a somewhat exaggerated brooding on events. This is a rehearsal, which gives him great satisfaction, and he happily sings a few notes to himself. Battenhouse (1969, pp. 442–3): The tune signals that Edmund’s whole plot is a work of black magic. Anderson (1971–2, p. 278): The pun on musical divisions signs the sound of the spheres; the whole natural series is in eclipse.
So doubtful are these suppositions as to cause further doubt that the F addition is more than actor’s gag. The four notes of the gamut do not follow from the musical sense of diuisions (see prev. n.). The words may be spoken rather than sung (they are certainly not hummed). Although the tritone was considered a diabolic interval in medieval musical theory, by Sh.’s time it was an interval occasionally used in part singing and was part of the major-seventh chord. The four notes may form an ascending scale, or the last note may be below the first. If they form an ascending scale, they may span a tritone but be part of the regular scale. In the English, Lancashire, or four-note system of sol-fa, used in John Day’s Psalmes (1570), Thomas Morley’s Practical Music (1597), and all subsequent English books of musical instruction, fa, sol, la, mi were the syllables for notes four through seven of every major scale. Even if Sh.’s audience had heard four notes spanning a tritone, there is hardly reason to think that they would have associated them with divisions past, present, or future, or with Edmund’s diabolic character, or that Sh. expected them to do so. Edmund’s reference (if there is one) to Tom of Bedlam in 464–5 might suggest that Edmund is repeating a phrase from the popular song of that name (see ); but that sequence of notes does not occur in the song. Possibly Edmund is imitating the Vice of the old Comedy, who seems on occasion to have said or sung sol la mi fa sol; see n. 1879.
There may be two possibilities not hitherto suggested. The system of solmisation used until Sh.’s day, called Guidonian (Clarkes, 1879, p. 443) was originally invented by Guido of Arezzo, and in Renaissance books on musical theory was often illustrated by the Guidonian hand, a mnemonic device in which each syllable of the whole gamut is assigned to a different joint on the fingers of one hand. Sadie (1980, 17:458) illustrates a common or typical hand, in which the tips of the fingers from the fifth to the index represent fa sol la mi. Moreover, Morley, whose music Sh. may have used (e.g., in AYL 5.3), wrote in his influential Practical Music (1597, Annotations, fol. ¶3) that each of Guido’s syllables was associated with one of the planetary spheres to denote the tone of music that it emitted, fa sol la mi being associated with Jupiter, Mars, Sol, and Venus respectively. The mnemonic hand also had a long history of use for calendar computations (see Carol Berger, The Hand and the Art of Memory, Musica Disciplina 35 [1981], 105–11). It is possible that Edmund is counting on the fingers of one hand, perhaps even pretending to be absorbed in astrological calculations.

467 How now]
See n. 361.

469–70 this…day]
The other day; see Franz §316. Wright (ed. 1875): As in WT 5.2.129 (3138). Brown (ed. 1976): He takes up…an astrological almanac real or pretended.

470 should]
Deighton (ed. 1891) cites Abbott (§325): Was…(destined, likely) to, who does not quote this l.

471 busie]
Schmidt (1874): To employ, to keep engaged (OED, v. 1). Deighton (ed. 1891): Take the trouble to pay any attention to. Clarkes (ed. 1868): By these contemptuous inquiries put into the mouth of the sensible and worthy Edgar, our poet has emphasised his own opinion upon the astrological creed.

471 about]
F’s with is virtually indifferent; see OED (Busy, v. 1b). With busy or busied Sh. elsewhere uses about thrice and with twice.

472–473+5 I…what]
Vickers (1968, p. 358): With a doubly ironic effect Edmund, having parodied his father’s style, now imitates it seriously.…If it is not as symmetrical as Gloucester’s…his voice hardens the whole with his own contemptuous alliteration.…Edmund is extemporizing in his father’s style, a feat which increases our admiration for him (as it had for Iago) though with a sinister tinge.

472 effects]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Fulfilments of the prediction, comparing 2283. Cf. 436. OED (sb. 2a): Contemplated result.

472 writ]
The past tense fits a prediction already made and read, but F’s writes is acceptable. Taylor (1983, p. 86): F implies a property book. On Q’s curtailed form see n. 103.

472 succeed]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Follow; cf. 470. OED (v. 11): To turn out (…well or ill), quoting this l. Cf. 3157. Both meanings are pertinent: the predicted consequences are unhappy ones, and some have in fact begun to ensue unhappily. Johnson (ed. 1765): Edmund, with the common craft of fortune-tellers, mingles the past and future, and tells of the future only what he already foreknows by confederacy, or can attain by probable conjecture. Reibetanz (1974, p. 48): Every disaster that Edmund mentions actually comes about.

473 vnhappily]
OED (adv. 2): With evil fortune.

473+1–+6 as…Astronomicall]
For theories that F’s omission of the Q lines is due to censorship or substitution, see n. 439–44. Taylor (1983, pp. 81–5) questions censorship for topicality because the passage deals largely with hoary generalities; because the events most likely to cause concern if alluded to—vnnaturalnesse between James and Prince Henry (ca. 1610–12), the Midlands dearth of 1608, nuptial breaches rumored between Queen Anne and James early in his reign (1603–4) or between Lady Howard and the Earl of Essex in 1613—do not coincide in time; and because the censor needed to cut only ten words, not the whole catalogue. Taylor believes it was cut by Sh. because of its mocking tone and outdated topicality. Clare (1990, p. 134): But censors cut rather than prune.…[The] allusions…suggest matters more immediate than power struggles in pagan Britain.…It is probable that he decided to remove the whole speech so as to prevent the actors reviving any of its parts. Thirlby (MS notes, 1725–33): If Sh. afterwards struck it out,…it was not well done. Johnson (ed. 1765) restores the lines as something which naturally introduces the following dialogue. Capell (1783, 1.2:147) and Granville-Barker (1946, p. 224) suspect that the omission is authorial, since the F addition of 439–44 makes these lines somewhat redundant in matter. Hart (1942, p. 147), however, thinks each of these passages was omitted because redundant; see n. 439–44. Delius (1876, p. 141): A non-authorial abridgement that leaves Edmund’s speech incomplete: Edmund…must necessarily add, to gain his point, what this evil omen consists in, which is to instil anxiety into his brother’s mind. Schmidt (ed. 1879) improbably suspects that the lines are spurious because they contain six words not used elsewhere in Sh., one of them unnaturalness. Muir (ed. 1952): Of these menace (as a noun) and dissipation are to be found in Florio’s Montaigne [a probable source, and], malediction, astronomical and cohort were not uncommon. Besides, in earlier plays Sh. had used menace (verb), astronomy, and unnatural. The language is mannered because Edmund is being whimsical, esp. in the heavy alliteration of death, dearth, dissolutions, divisions, maledictions, diffidences, and dissipations. Sh. could just have heard unnaturalness in Volpone (1605–6), and could have remembered astronomical from Holinshed, Lyly, Sidney, or Holland’s Plutarch (1603), cohort from Caesar or Holland’s Livy (1600), and malediction from Sidney’s Arcadia or Plutarch. Halio (ed. 1992, p. 266): Folio lineation [i.e., 473 as a separate line]…suggests that a cut has been made. Foakes (ed. 1997): The effect is to tighten the dialogue and to avoid repetition of Gloucester’s superstitious anxieties.

473+1 as of]
Elliptical: such as the effects of.

473+1 vnnaturalnesse]
Behavior lacking in or contrary to natural filial or parental affection. OED (a. 3b): Devoid of natural feeling; acting at variance with the dictates of nature. Cf. 986, 1753, 1757.

473+2 amities]
Schmidt (1874): Friendship, pl. here and in Ham. 5.2.42 (3544).

473+2–+3 menaces…nobles]
Fleay (1879, p. 119): Possibly alluding to the Gunpowder Plot. But the phrase would include both more and less than that Plot, and therefore would not point clearly to it.

473+3–+4 diffidences]
Wright (ed. 1875): Distrust (OED, 1).

473+4 dissipation]
OED (1): Dispersing, quoting this l. Though Tovey (ed. 1896) takes this to mean troops scattered far and wide over the country to repress conspiracy or pursue conspirators, most eds. agree with Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Disbanding. Deighton (ed. 1891): Mutinous behaviour in troops. Wilson (ed. 1960): Melting away by desertion and disease—a common fate of military bands in Sh.’s day. See next n. and .

473+4 Cohorts]
The original meaning is A body of infantry in the Roman army (OED, sb. 1). Kittredge (ed. 1940): The word…fits the era of the play as Shakespeare seems to have imagined that era—the time of more or less Romanized Britain—though the fabulous Lear’s reign was long before that time, comparing centurie (2356). Most eds. follow Clarkes (ed. 1868): Large troops of soldiers (OED, 2), or Hunter (ed. 1869): Military attendants. The dispersion of Edmund’s military cohorts undoes him in 5.3. Kelcy (1932, p. 361): This predicts the dwindling of Lear’s train of knights. Lee (ed. 1908) and Harrison (ed. 1937) deny any military significance, but their sense persons united in…a common cause (OED, 3) is not attested before the 18th c.

473+4–+5 breaches]
OED (sb. 3): The breaking of…any legal or moral bond, quoting this l. Edmund is of course aware of his father’s nuptial breach, and will soon attempt to bring about another. Fleay (1879, p. 119) detects an allusion to Lady Frances Howard’s liaison with Robert Carr ca. 1610 and her annulment of marriage with the third earl of Essex in 1613. Cf. Taylor (1983, pp. 113–14, n. 22).

473+6 sectary]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Votary (OED, sb. 3, quoting this l.). The word recurs only in H8 5.2.105 (3119); it may derive, Henderson (1940, p. 48) suggests, from Montaigne (tr. Florio, 2:204, 208).

473+6 Astronomicall]
Evans (ed. 1898): The word astronomy originally included…astrology…; astrology, though as old as the 14th century [OED], does not occur in Shakespeare. Sondheim (1938–9, pp. 249–50 n.): A distinction [was] made between theoretical astronomy, which corresponded to modern astronomy, and practical or applied astronomy, which was further subdivided into astrology and the science of time-measurement.…Only in the seventeenth century was the present division made.

474 Come, come]
Moberly (ed. 1876): A truce to this light talk! Tovey (ed. 1896): Used with similar abruptness to change the subject in [Jn. 5.6.16 (2571)]. Kittredge (ed. 1940): A smiling protest against being regarded as sectary astronomical. Then Edmund becomes serious. Or perhaps the protest is against Edgar’s flippant skepticism, whereupon Edmund suggests that the predictions may be coming true even in Gloucester’s displeasure towards Edgar. The latter is the apparent train of thought in F, which omits these two words because they serve no purpose, Edgar’s intervening speech having been omitted.

475 Why]
F’s omission of this exclamation is such an unimportant change as to suggest oversight of printer or scribe.

476 Spake]
The archaic preterite, common in Sh. Cf. Franz §165, and 1868, 2389.

477 Two…together]
Schmidt (1875), together: Without intermission (OED, adv. 5). The Clarkes’ (ed. 1868) an idiom of indefinite time seems to be unattested.

478 in]
Alternative for on (OED, Term sb. 9); cf. Franz §502.

479 or]
F’s double negative nor is quite possible in Sh. (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 133).

479 countenance]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Behaviour, manner (OED, sb. 1), comparing 558.

481 Bethinke…selfe]
OED (v. refl. 8): Call to mind, recollect.

482 forbeare his presence]
Verity (ed. 1897): Gloucester will interpret Edgar’s avoidance of him as a sign of guilt: hence the advice. Bradley (1904, p. 257): Is it in character that Edgar should be persuaded without the slightest demur to avoid his father instead of confronting him and asking him the cause of his anger? Muir (ed. 1952): Edmund has made him believe that his life is in danger.

483 qualified]
Schmidt (1875): Moderate[d] (OED, v. 8).

484 rageth]
OED (v. 4b): To have…a high degree of intensity, quoting this l.

484 with]
Rann (ed. 1794): Even by.

484–5 mischiefe…parson]
Malone (apud Steevens, ed. 1778): Destruction. Capell (1783, 1.2:147): Harm. Joseph (ed. 1966), alternatively: The extra annoyance of your person being present.

485 allay]
Hudson (ed. 1879): Subside (OED, v. 10). On transitive verbs used intransitively see Abbott §293, Franz §629, and cf. 741, 753, 1502.

487–93 I…Edm.]
F’s added lines mainly reiterate the ideas in Edmund’s previous and following speech, though they give Edgar more time to become convinced, do explain (in case the audience wonders) where he will hide, and promise a later reconciliation as a motive for him to lie low now. None of this is strictly necessary. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxix): This long digression from Edmund’s stage business impedes the action, which naturally joins That’s my feare to the by-play where Edmund is no honest man, if there bee any good meaning towards his confiding brother. Cunnington (1910, p. 487): The lines are added to explain how it is that Edgar is supposed to have written to Edmund. They introduce…a lodging for Edmund that is other than Gloucester’s home.…Shakespeare’s original conception was that Edmund should be living…in Gloucester’s house. Moriarty (1913, p. 462): Edmund’s sending Edgar to his room allows him to control Edgar’s specific actions and prepares for 2.1. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 224) approves of part of the addition: The hiding away of Edgar from his father is a good point made. Doran (1931, p. 63): The different position of goe arm’d…is proof that the alteration…is a deliberate one. The [added] lines…do not contain information essential to the understanding of the plot. We need only know that Edgar gets himself out of the way of his father, and that Edmund keeps track of him until he has effected his plan. But the folio lines add definiteness to his whereabouts and are therefore desirable. Stone (1980, p. 240): Neither the invitation nor the promise is relevant to the plot, nor are they referred to again. They do, however, help to explain why Edgar…should later appear so conveniently.…If this were the motive for interpolating the lines, they must have been introduced as an afterthought, perhaps in the theater. Honigmann (1982, p. 149): F’s addition surely makes Edgar’s gullibility more acceptable, in so far as he believes Edmund’s story less instantaneously, and a feasible course of action is mapped out for him. Muir (1983, p. 106): The F version is manifestly a great improvement, but not a revision. The Q compositor’s…eyes skipped from That’s my fear, brother to brother, accidentally omitting the intervening passage. The Q passage, feeble as it is, can hardly be what Shakespeare ever wrote. The original was happily restored in F.

487, 493, 498 Bast., Edm., Bast.]
On the variant SP, see .

487–8 continent]
Valpy (ed. 1833): Temperate. Hudson (ed. 1879): In its old sense of self-restrained or subdued (OED, a. 1, quoting this l.). Harrison (ed. 1937), oddly: Which will keep you from rashness.

487–8 forbearance]
Deighton (ed. 1891) and most eds. understand a repetition of the sense in 482: Keep out of his way. OED (Forbear v. 4): To endure the absence or privation of…a person or thing. Craig (ed. 1901): For forbear in the sense of withdraw, see [Ant. 5.2.175 (3406), MM 4.1.22 (1793)]; but that meaning is at best implicit in these two cases. A few eds. make the word virtually synonymous with the preceding adjective: Neilson & Thorndike (ed. 1909): Continence (restraint); Harrison (ed. 1937): Patience (OED, sb. 2).

488–9 as I say]
Skillan (ed. 1967): This does not refer to a previous statement, but is an emphasis on what he now says.

489 lodging]
Greg (1940, p. 434): Perhaps a house adjoining the castle.…Since Edgar appears to have no difficulty in making his escape [2.1]…, [probably] he was not actually within the castle walls. Lott (ed. 1974): In a large castle-like building, wings containing the private apartments of the family could be very much apart from the main military area, and self-contained.

490 fitly]
OED (adv. 1b): At the fitting time, quoting this l. as its earliest ex. Deighton (ed. 1891): Conveniently…without risk.

490 ye]
Abbott (§236): The original distinction between ye (nominative) and you (objective) was disregarded by Elizabethan authors. Cf. Franz §288, and 821, 1120, 1157, 1542, 2469, 2693.

491 arm’d]
Skillan (ed. 1967): edg. has to be made to appear…violent.…edm. is making sure that his brother shall have a sword in order to provide the show of a fight at 961.

493 to the best]
