Deighton (ed. 1891): For the best; as is best for you. Crook (ed. 1907): To the best of my ability. OED (Best a. 10e) gives both meanings for the phrase. The first is preferable: Edmund is persuading Edgar, not praising himself.

493 goe arm’d]
Foakes (ed. 1997): It is likely that [487–93] were added in F, and this phrase omitted as repetitive; but some think the lines were cut from Q, and this phrase, by oversight, retained. See n. 487–93.

494 meaning]
OED (vbl. sb. 1): Intention, quoting this l.

495 faintly]
Hudson (ed. 1879): Qualifies told. Schmidt (1874): In a feeble…manner. Deighton (ed. 1891): Only in faint outline, not colouring the picture in its true horrors.

496 image and horror]
Wright (ed. 1875): The horror which an exact description of it would give.…Hendiadys. So Deighton (ed. 1891) and Wright (1981, p. 175): Horrible image, Wright adding, The horror of it is intensified by the hendiadys. Cf. 3225.

497 anon]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Shortly (OED, adv. 5). Less probably, Kemshead (ed. 1875): Immediately (OED, 4).

498 I doe]
To those who would emend (see textual n. and ), Jennens (ed. 1770): It is a proper answer already…I am your servant. Deighton (ed. 1891): Rest assured that your interests are safe in my hands.

499–504 A…fit]
On Edmund’s return to verse see n. 335–56.

499 credulous Father]
Perrett (1904, p. 282) finds Geoffrey of Monmouth’s credulus…pater [see ] a possible verbal influence; but the Latin refers to Leir, and cf. Luc. 1522, the credulous old Priam.

499 noble]
Moberly (ed. 1876) compares the villain’s cynical contempt for his victim’s moral superiority in AYL 1.1.165–71 (160–6) and Oth. 1.3.399–402 (745–7).

500–1 Whose…none]
Tilley T221: They that do no harm suspect none.

500 nature]
See n. 185.

501 honesty]
Schmidt (1874): Love of truth, upright conduct (OED, sb. 3d). On the scansion see n. 154.

502 practises]
Wright (ed. 1875): Plots, contrivances (OED, 6c). Cf. 1010, 1048, 1391, 3108.

502 ride easie]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Find it easy to guide. McCann (ed. 1964): Go easily (as the rider fits the horse’s back).

502 I…busines]
Eccles (ed. 1792): I perceive what course…to pursue.

503–4 Let…fit]
Crook (ed. 1907): Two lines of rime to end the scene.

503 Let…wit]
Elton (1966, p. 132, n. 40) cites Tilley B687, The younger Brother has the more wit, and contemporary statements about the younger brother’s resistance to primogeniture.

503 wit]
OED (sb. 5): Cleverness. Horsman (ed. 1973), questionably: Contrivance, stratagem, a rare sense (OED, 6c) not occurring elsewhere in Sh.

504 meete]
OED (a. 3): Suitable. Lee (ed. 1908): Fair game. Muir (ed. 1952): The end justifies the means.

504 fashion]
Schmidt (1874): Shape (OED, v. 3b, quoting this l.). Only Joseph (ed. 1966): If fashion is taken as a noun and fit as a verb,…that I can fit to the fashion.

504 fit]
Eccles (ed. 1792): I.e., To…my own purposes.

505 <Scena Tertia>]
Granville-Barker (1927, p. 144): The [first] two scenes together form a sort of double dramatic prologue; and they might, by modern custom, count as a first act, for after them falls the only clearly indicated time-division in the play. Daniel (1877–9, p. 216): After the last scene, an interval of something less than a fortnight…must now be supposed. But that is hardly certain; see n. 811. Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956): Some days later. Smith (ed. 1902): In the interval Goneril is fully instated in her new power, and has gained confidence in her ability to deprive Lear of the remnants of his authority. The time interval is at best indefinite; the passing of at least a few days seems suggested by by day and night (510), Knights grow ryotous (513), great abatement (589), of late (597, 733), pined away (603), and perhaps I had thought (716); cf. n. 333. Spilsbury & Marshall (ed. 1905): The interest of this scene lies in (1) That the Fool is the unconscious occasion for Goneril to interfere with Lear’s attendants. Lear strikes one of Goneril’s servants for chiding his Fool.…(2) In Goneril’s expressed intentions to goad Lear into ill-advised actions. She knows her power by now, and craftily devises that Lear should afford her occasions for the use of it. Quinn (ed. 1970): This scene is notable for its subtle suggestion of that social anarchy which is to be the outer circle of Lear’s descent into chaos.
Brooke (ed. 1947) conjecturally locates the scene: Albany was the old name of North Britain, above the Humber River. York, a very ancient city which was the military capital of Roman Britain, would be the natural residence of Goneril and her husband. It is a hundred miles north of Leicester (where Brooke locates Lear’s palace; see n. 1). Wherever Albany’s house is, Lear will have to be able to ride from it to Cornwall’s house and then onwards to Gloucester’s house in (apparently) a little more than a day; see nn. 333, 539, 1273.

506 Gentleman]
F identifies as Steward. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 107): The manuscript from which Q was printed could [not] itself have been used as a prompt-book. Wilson (ed. 1960): Sh. does not invent [the name Oswald] till Gon. has to call for him [in 833]. Later references suggest he is foppishly dressed (see [1089–92, 1128–31]), e.g. in Alb.’s cast-off garments. There is no textual evidence to support the last detail; and would Albany’s garments be foppish? Foakes (ed. 1997): An important official, as controller of Goneril’s household.

507 gentleman]
Page (ed. 1889): Attendant (on a person of rank). Despite the third-person allusion in his presence, the gentleman could be Oswald; in 1226 Regan refers to Goneril’s steward as her Gentleman (F; Gentlemen in Q). But it could as well refer to one of Oswald’s fellow seruants (520). Wells (ed. 2000): A steward would normally have had important responsibilities,…but the role was likely to be occupied by upstarts, citing Burnett (1997, p. 173).

508 of]
Abbott (§178): Of naturally followed a verbal noun. Cf. 973, 3168, after participial adjectives, and n. 348.

508 foole]
Verity (ed. 1897): It is significant…that the faithful Fool should be the immediate cause of the troubles that now close round his master. Empson (1951, p. 129): Rather than his shadowy train of deboshed knights. Lott (ed. 1974): The Fool must have made some caustic remark which offended Goneril’s attendant. See n. 505.

510 By…night]
F’s comma may suggest that these words are exclamatory, not adverbial as Whalley and Steevens (in Reed, ed. 1785) thought. Malone (ed. 1790, ad loc. and 10:680) supports Capell’s punctuation (see textual n.) by citing similar phrasing at Ham. 1.5.164 (861) and H8 1.2.213 (567). Kittredge (ed. 1940): King Lear also swears by day and night in [116–17], noting Thus Tate understood the passage. In his King Lear he reduces Goneril’s speech to By Day and Night this is insufferable, I will not bear it (1681, p. 10). But in Tate that speech refers to the present action of the tripping of Oswald, whereas here she may be generalizing. Most eds. agree with Clarkes (ed. 1868): Daily and nightly, constantly, perpetually; cf. OED (By, prep. 19b). Every hour, immediately afterwards in the same line, seems to confirm this interpretation. Perrett (1904, p. 207): In Leir 776–7 Gonorill daily endures quips and peremptory taunts…from my doting father; see .

511 flashes]
Wright (ed. 1875): Blazes, breaks out (OED, v.1 10, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Cf. Ham. 2.1.33 (925).

511 grosse]
Schmidt (1874): Enormous, unseemly, shocking (OED, a. 4). Joseph (ed. 1966): Obvious, crude (OED, 3).

511 crime]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Offence (OED, sb. 2). Cf. 2324. Harbage (1963, p. 405): Lear is no easy house-guest.…But there are details that warn us to suspend judgment—the slyness of her methods, the docile readiness of her man, and the rancor of her judgment in 522+2–+3.

512 ods]
Schmidt (1875): Quarrel, contention, discord (OED, sb. 3).

513 ryotous]
Goggin (ed. 1910) thinks that there is something to this claim, since Goneril repeats it at 715 and 750–5. But see n. 586–872. Halio (ed. 1992): A hundred knights and squires given to hunting and other sport would doubtless cause some problems, which Gonerill decides to exacerbate, forcing a confrontation. Cf. nn. 141, 1340–6, 1535. Bransom (1934): It is noteworthy that Goneril says nothing about these charges to her husband at the end of the scene when she is trying to justify her conduct. Colie (1974, p. 201): The playwright is careful to deny Goneril her claims to justification in this respect.…That Lear’s knights were troublesome, we have only Goneril’s authority; when we hear Regan linking Edgar and the knights [cf. 1033–4], an association clearly false, we must wonder about the knights’ behaviour altogether. So also Farley-Hills (1990, pp. 199–200). Mahood (1992, p. 162): There is nothing to indicate riotous behaviour in either the Quarto or the Folio version of [1.4], simply because the Knights are not on stage to riot. Hattaway (2000, p. 200), on Peter Brook’s 1962 production: Before Brook the knights were not much noticed. Brook had them overturn tables on stage. Yet Shakespeare’s company may have decided that, at court, this would be dangerous, given that King James’s favourite sport—like that of King Lear—was hunting. Boswell-Stone (1896, p. 4 n.): None of the sources…has aught to say about the dissensions between Lear’s knights and his sons-in-laws’ households. Cf. n. 539–40.

513 obrayds]
Common sp. variant of upbraid (OED, v.).

513 vs]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Note the transfer of the royal plural from Lear to Gonerill. But vs may simply refer to the household, the vs all of the previous line.

514 trifell]
Wright (ed. 1875): Trifling occasion.

514 hunting]
Craig (ed. 1901) notes that in Layamon’s Brut the king’s love and habit of hunting is referred to three times. Houghton (ed. 1957): This may somehow have reached Shakespeare’s notice. Elton (1966, p. 119 n.): Goneril and Regan are generally strangers to the feudal and nonutilitarian language of archery, hunting, and horsemanship, shared by Lear, Kent, and Edgar. Cf. James’s commitment to the institution of knighthood, the king notoriously increasing the number of knights, as well as to the sport of hunting, on account of which he enlarged stables and kennels; indeed, he was held to devote more time to the chase than to serious affairs of state. Farley-Hills (1990, p. 201), after quoting complaints about James’s dedication to the hunt: Shakespeare is concerned with reinforcing the kingly image, and in a way peculiarly acceptable to James, not criticizing his hero, for Lear is not neglecting state business. In the drama of the period it is neglect of the hunt by rulers that often suggests unmanliness and unfitness to govern.

516 come]
OED (v. 24): To become.

516 slacke]
Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Slow (OED, a. 4). OED (1): Negligent; (1b): Short of, quoting this l.

517 answere]
Answer for (OED, v. 6). Cf. 161, 1224.

518 heare]
Brown (ed. 1976): Perhaps Lear’s Horns [538, F].

519–23 Put…you]
Q’s prose seems intended for verse. Cf. 525–8. Doran (1931, p. 106): Apparent revision on the transcript [which became the playbook]…may account for the failure of the printer of the folio to set…verse, because (p. 129) the marginal additions were not clearly lined. But see .

519–20 Put…seruants]
Perrett (1904, p. 206): Cf. Leir 759–60: Gonorill sets her Parasites of purpose oft, In scoffing wise to offer him disgrace; see .

519 Put on]
Wright (ed. 1875): Assume (OED, v.1 46d). Cf. 1196.

519 wearie]
Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Such…as would naturally result from weariness. Craig (ed. 1901): Yawning, or with a look of sickness or disgust. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): The best possible stage direction for the right way of playing Oswald’s entrance [575].

520 fellow seruants]
Collier (ed. 1843): The quartos, needlessly and injuriously, as regards the verse, insert servants…; but the whole scene is there printed as prose. F reduces to Fellowes. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 371: It is conceivable that Q gives us the authentic reading, Shakespeare having written a long line here. [A scribe] may have emended the line on his own responsibility in order to achieve a pentameter: (he may have been influenced by [526]).

520 it]
See n. 435. The presumed referent is Lear’s behavior. Lott (ed. 1974), however: The negligence.

520 in question]
Moberly (ed. 1876): To argument. OED (Question, sb. 1c): In question, in dispute, in controversy;…So also with into and in = into, quoting the phrase come in question from Grafton’s Chronicle (1568). Whoever altered in to to in F may have preferred to after the verb of motion. Sh. does not elsewhere use either version of the phrase; he generally uses in question after verbs such as call, have, etc. Cf. 946, 2976.

521 dislike]
F’s distaste means the same (OED, v. 2). Sh. uses the Q word often; of the four other uses of the verb distaste, only Tro. 2.2.66 (1051) has a similar meaning.

521 let him to]
For omission of verbs of motion after auxiliary verbs, see n. 312.

522+1–+4 not…abusd]
F omits. Theobald (ed. 1733) restores the lines as they are fine in themselves, and very much in Character for Gonerill. Capell (1783, 1.2:148): Plainly an omission of negligence. Delius (1876, p. 141): A non-authorial cut that leaves the sense incomplete: Thus the unfortunate audience do not know in what respect Goneril’s mind is one with Regan’s. Deighton (ed. 1891): May have been rejected by Shakespeare when revising. Moriarty (1913, pp. 462–3): Here Goneril explains to Oswald her theory of governing her father, but F moves it to 1.4 (842–55) so that she may defend to Albany her actions toward her father. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 225), approving: The Folio omissions [here and at 527] save some repetition and show her to us terser and less familiar with her servant. Bransom (1934, p. 36 n.): I am strongly for omitting the lines, but I admit their obscurity and…bad taste…may be intentional to denote her uneasiness. Hart (1942, p. 147): The lines here and at 527 merely repeat in different words what Goneril has said earlier in the same scene. Wilson (ed. 1960): The kind of gnomic passage that tempted a prompter to cut. Doran (1933, p. 57): Originally, added deliberately to Q, and derived from Montaigne: In…Of the Affection of Fathers to their Children…he would have found the picture of an old man, always imperious and rough, now doubly tempestuous in spirit with the dotage of old age and unwilling to relinquish the care of his house to those who could better manage it; cf. n. 1426–30, and see . Taylor (1983, pp. 96–7): F’s cut is part of a deliberate retrenchment of anything which might too directly suggest senility, to reduce the danger of an audience finding Lear, on occasion, merely embarrassing. But Lear is not present to embarrass us. Foakes (1993, p. 186): The omission of these contemptuous lines [and of 527+1–+2]…puts the emphasis…entirely on the misbehaviour of Lear and his retinue as wronging her. Hardly entirely; in F Goneril is still collecting grievances, instigating her servants to make more trouble grow by their insolence, hoping to force a question, and conspiring with Regan to renounce the very filial responsibilities to Lear that were the conditions of their inheritance. Idem (ed. 1997): The omission of all four lines softens the character of Goneril here, by removing both her insulting words about her father, and her conscious plotting against him. But Goneril is still plotting (i’de…question), and is suborning her servants to insult her father. Lines 522+1–+2 may have been cut because they merely reiterate Goneril’s motives, explained more fully a short while before (314–30); lines 522+3–+4 may have been cut because of their obscurity.

522+1 ouerruld]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Controlled by his fancies.

522+1 idle]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Senseless, silly (OED, a. 2b). Meiklejohn (ed. 1879), Joseph (ed. 1966): Useless (OED, 2a).

522+1 manage]
Wright (ed. 1875): Wield (OED, v. 2).

522+2 authorities]
Verity (ed. 1897): The plural = attributes of authority, powers (OED, 1, 4).

522+2–+3 old…again]
Proverbial: Tilley M570, Old Men are twice children. Dent (1981) compares Tilley K132, An old Knave is no babe, which is not apposite. In Leir 181 Ragan says that Leir dotes, as if he were a child agayne, in 784 Gonorill refers to his doting doltish withered wit, and each calls him doterd (758) or dottard (1188); see , , , . Leir is called doting in Mirour (1574, fol. 50); see .

522+3 checkes]
Generally taken to mean a verbal check—reproof, reprimand, rebuke (OED, sb. 4)—in opposition to verbal flatteries. But some eds. understand a physical check (OED, 9): harsh treatment…to control their submission (Henley, in Steevens, ed. 1793), restraint…to keep them in the right path (Verity, ed. 1897), forbidding them power (Porter & Clarke, ed. 1905), punishments or restrictions (Lee, ed. 1908). Davies (1783, 2:272) may mean both: Managed with the same controul, and checked in the same manner.

522+3 as…abusd]
The suspicion of textual corruption has led to many attempts at emendation: see textual nn. and .

522+3 as]
The variety of glosses suggests more disagreement than in fact there is: in most, as is taken generally to mean similarly as, just as with—i.e., as parallel, as additional means, as alternative, or as substitution. Tollet (in Steevens, ed. 1778): [Just] as. Tyrwhitt (in Steevens, ed. 1778), and many others: As well as. Koppel (1899, p. 34): As earlier with. So Joseph (ed. 1966): The daughters have given Lear flatteries. Now they intend to administer rebukes. Seymour (1803, p. 47): Or. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Instead of, in lieu of. Goggin (ed. 1910): As well with (i.e. instead of). McCann (ed. 1964): That seem.

522+3 flatteries]
Occasionally extended beyond its usual meaning to indulgences (Warburton, ed. 1747; Rann, ed. 1794), coaxings and soothings (Capell, 1783, 1.2:148), appliances of persuasion (Henley, in Steevens, ed. 1793), caresse[s] (Seymour, 1803, p. 47), cajolements (Porter & Clarke, ed. 1905), pleasing deceptions (Dent, ed. 1927). Davies (1783, 2:272), by synecdoche: Gross flatterers…offensive from their want of discretion. Edwards (ed. 1975): She thinks Lear is behaving the worse because she and Regan have flattered him so much.

522+4 they…abusd]
When (as is usual) they is referred to old fooles, abusd is taken to mean deceived (Johnson, ed. 1765), the worse for (Capell, 1783, 1.2:148), misguided (Moberly, ed. 1876), misled…as to the true position of affairs (Lee, ed. 1908), deluded (Clarkes, ed. 1868), under a misapprehension (Bald, ed. 1949). See n. 1611. Caldecott (MS notes, 1813–33): I.e., abused by themselves. When they is referred to flatteries, abusd is glossed as abus’d by their [i.e., children’s] becoming more peevish and perverse (Warburton, ed. 1747), are made a bad use of (Tollet, in Steevens, ed. 1778) or thrown away (Caldecott, MS notes, 1813–33), making children the worse for them (Capell, 1783, 1.2:148), found only to increase their perverseness (Rann, ed. 1794), being felt by him [i.e., the king] (Halliwell, ed. 1865), found to feed their folly (Herford, ed. 1899), seen to have bad results (Edwards, ed. 1975). See n. 1226.

523–4 tell you…Very]
F’s omission of Very to make smoother meter may follow from its (relatively indifferent) change from tell you to haue said.

525–8 And…dinner]
Though the Q lines are set as prose, they, like 519–23, seem intended for verse. F’s omission of 527+1–+2 makes verse difficult in the remainder of the speech; there seems no other reason why Goneril should switch to prose there. F’s omission of very and goe in 527 suggests an attempt, either abandoned or overlooked, to make regular meter.

526 fellowes]
OED (Fellow sb. 1): Co-worker. Cf. 1645.

526–7 what…so]
Moberly (ed. 1876): The vixenish tone of Goneril makes the line defy scanning. Elze (1886, p. 37), however, scans it by eliding to o’t no without accent.

527+1–+2 I…speake]
Delius (1876, p. 141): A non-authorial cut of the weighty resolution that she would take an opportunity of telling her father her mind unreservedly. Schmidt (ed. 1879): Lines struck out in the Folio because they repeat the idea of [519–20]; but that they are the poet’s lines is clear from the meter, even though they are printed as prose in the Qq (Ger.). Cf. n. 522+1–+4. Although the sentence is somewhat redundant, F’s omission of it impairs the verse (see n. 525–8) and may be accidental. Werstine (1983, p. 284): Perhaps [Folio] Compositor E’s eye skipped from the I of I would directly to the word Ile that is printed [in Q2] beneath would, thereby missing the intervening line. (It may be significant that Q1 reads ile here, making the suggested error somewhat less probable if E had been working from that earlier quarto. If he were working from MS, the error could be a scribe’s, not his.

527+1 would]
Joseph (ed. 1966): Would like to,…want to.

527+2 occasions]
Schmidt (1875): Opportunit[ies] (OED, sb.1 1). Deighton (ed. 1891): An opportunity…of speaking out my mind. Greg (1940, p. 391) compares similar expressions of intent by both sisters in Leir 839–40 and 1155–6; see , .

527 straight]
Goggin (ed. 1910): Straightway, at once. Cf. 1311, 2014+4, 3244, 3253.

527 very]
Wright (ed. 1875): Exact. Munro (ed. 1957): Possibly omitted [from F] by scribe or compositor, but metrically needed. See n. 525–8. Maxwell (apud Wilson, ed. 1960): Eye-skip from my to ry.

529 <Scena Quarta.>]
Smith (ed. 1902): Hitherto [Lear] has appeared merely hasty, wayward, and imperious, but we now begin to see the better elements of his character. The pathos of his lot is emphasized by the solicitude of Kent and the significant utterances of the Fool, and he now wins our sympathy. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): This entire scene of the disguise and hiring of banished Kent, and the tripping up of Oswald, etc., is Shakespeare’s invention. Not entirely, perhaps. Lee (1909, p. xl): In Leir [868–73.] Perillus meets the outcast Leir and offers his companionship to the royal vagrant, who accepts it without recognising his old courtier; see . Skottowe (1824, p. 122): In the old play the king of France has a courtier, Mumford, attendant on him, in disguise, whose characteristics are coarse pleasantry, and blunt straight forward honesty. Hence the assigning of the same humour to Kent. Goggin (ed. 1910): A new character is introduced in the person of the Fool, whose function in the play is not as usual to make fun for the groundlings, but is essentially sad and tragic, namely to keep before the minds of Lear and of the audience the folly of the King. Armour (ed. ca. 1930): In this scene the loyalty of the banished courtier, Kent, to his king is in immediate contrast to the disloyalty of the favoured daughter, Goneril, to her father. Daniel (1877–9, p. 216): Time about mid-day, citing dinner in 528, 539, 572–3. Kittredge (ed. 1940): This scene is practically continuous with Scene iii. Cf. [514] with [539]. Adams (1948, p. 318): But Lear has written to Regan, and is now out of doors.

531–7 If…labour]
Dent (ed. 1927): The first seven lines explain Kent’s reappearance; the explanation is necessary if we are to understand what follows. Halio (ed. 1992): The Elizabethan convention of impenetrable disguise operates here and throughout the rest of the play. Foakes (ed. 1997): In performance, it is usually as a serving-man or a rough soldier. At [3249] he gives his new name as Caius, but it is never otherwise mentioned in the play. Buck (ed. 1907): Kent had after his banishment followed Cordelia into France. From there he has now returned in order to be near the king at the time when her expedition to restore her father reaches England. For this theory there is not the slightest evidence; it is presumably intended to explain Kent’s and Cordelia’s knowledge of each other’s plans: see 1242–7. Righter (1962, p. 185): For Kent and Edgar, the necessity for the adoption of disguise, of false identity, in order to remain oneself is one of the most painful paradoxes of King Lear.

531 as well]
Capell (1783, 1.2:149): As effectually as I have defac’d my person by a strange attire; cf. 2753–5. Steevens (ed. 1778): We must suppose that Kent advances looking on his disguise. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 371), on F’s erroneous will: The same substitution…occurs in F at [247]. F Compositor E set both lines. Horsman (ed. 1973): Here, it leaves the sentence incomplete, with if introducing…may carry.

531 other]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Than my natural ones.

531 accents]
Theobald (ed. 1733): Tone, and Utterance (OED, sb. 4). The plural may not rule out OED (3): The mode of utterance peculiar to an individual [or] locality. Crane (1952, p. 162): Throughout the scene he speaks prose…; prose lends a certain common quality to his native bluntness and thus contributes to the preservation of his incognito. Skillan (ed. 1967): The dialect adopted is that of the West country. But there is too little evidence to identify any one dialect. Rosenberg (1972, p. 96): In performance, usually a rustic brogue. Halio (ed. 1992): And a blunt, plainspoken manner.

532 defuse]
Q and F agree on the variant sp. of diffuse. Steevens (ed. 1773): To diffuse speech, signifies to disorder it, and so to disguise it (OED, v. 6, quoting only this l., but comparing Diffused, a. 1: Disordered, obscure). Dyce (1844, p. 223) cites Barclay’s Ship of Fooles (1570, fol. 53v), diffuse, vnknowen, harde and obscure, adding, Kent does not wish to render his speech difficult to be understood, but merely to disorder it, to disguise it. Tovey (ed. 1896): Disordered, hence wild and uncouth. There is no need for the several attempts to involve the meaning disperse, such as Theobald’s (ed. 1733) Spread…widely from what it used to be, or for Steevens’s (op. cit.) alternative to speak broad, with a clownish accent.

533 carry through]
OED (v. 55): Bring safely through difficulties, quoting this l. as its first ex.

533 full issue]
Crook (ed. 1907): Complete success in the purpose indicated in 535. Maclean (1960, p. 51): Presumably…service…and an active concern for Lear’s safety…[and perhaps] to further in this way an eventual recovery of position and respect (if not altogether power) by Lear.…Subsequently, in any event, Kent neither reiterates his purpose nor develops its implications; he refers more than once to some mysterious intent [532, 2757], but never clears that matter up.…Kent devotes himself primarily to shoring up ruin. Edwards (ed. 1975): The reconciliation of Lear and Cordelia.

534 raz’d]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Effaced (OED, v. 5). See n. 531. Moberly (ed. 1876): Erased (OED, 3). The word also means shaved (OED, 2), but suggestions by Harrison (ed. 1948), Muir (ed. 1952), and others of a quibble on that meaning ignore Oswald’s reference in 1136 to Kent’s gray beard.

534 likenes]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Appearance (OED, 2).

534 Kent]
Hunter (ed. 1972): In case the audience have not recognized his voice, he announces his identity.

535–7 if…labour]
Elton (1966, p. 292): Kent’s…soliloquy carries an analogical overtone of the Good Servant and the parable of the talents (Matt. 24:45–51, 25:15–30; Luke 12:42–6).

535 where]
Deighton (ed. 1891): In the presence of. Crook (ed. 1907): In the service of.

536 So…come,]
Capell (1783, 1.2:149): A wish…and parenthetical. Knight (ed. 1840): Predictive: So it may come that.

536 So]
Deighton (ed. 1891): In that way.

536 come]
Wright (ed. 1875): Come about, comparing 933.

537 full of labour]
The phrase appears again in TN 3.1.66 (1278); with F’s pl. labours, nowhere else. In Q, labour means pains (OED, sb. 5), Sh.’s most common meaning. F’s pl. means particular works or exertions (OED, 3); thus Capell (1783, 1.2:149): Ready for any hard services, and any number of them. Joseph (ed. 1966): Anxious to perform services; capable of all sorts of work. Sh.’s other ten instances of the plural are all preceded by a possessive or by a demonstrative pronoun, rather than occurring in phrases such as this. Though most eds. follow their F copy-text, Walker (1860, 1:255–6) and Ridley (ed. 1935) prefer Q here.

538 <Hornes within>]
F’s added SD is clearly theatrical in origin. Harrison (ed. 1948): Offstage. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Lear returns from hunting [514]. This is significant. He is hale and hearty, though eighty years of age [2815]. Wilson (ed. 1960): Lear so dressed w[oul]d at once engage King James’s interest with his passion for the chase. Wells (ed. 2000): Perhaps he wears hunting boots. Shirley (1963, p. 74): The change in fanfare [from 37 Sennet and 291 Flourish] goes hand-in-hand with the diminishing respect accorded the old man by his two daughters.

538 Enter Lear]
Taylor (1983, p. 404): Q, characteristically of a foul-paper text, often fails to supply necessary entrances and exits; in particular, on eight other occasions it calls only for the entrance of one or more main characters, omitting to mention others who clearly enter at the same time; see nn. 874, 970, 1024, 1117, 1273, 1403, 2058, 2744. F adds the vague and Attendants; one of the attendants is later specified to be a Knight (583 ff.). Hunter (ed. 1972): Some knights must be present if Gonerill’s image of Lear’s household is to make sense. Mahood (1992, p. 162): Five or six attendants would have been a reasonable stage retinue for a king. Lear, who is to be joined by his Fool and possibly in 1.5 by a Gentleman, perhaps comes in [here] with four Knights. One is immediately sent to see about dinner [540] and two others are dispatched in turn [573–4, 605] to find the Fool. The one who has had the brush with Oswald [577–8] is sent [604] to Goneril, whom we may think of as getting her own back by immediately cashiering him and forty-nine of his colleagues. But that may happen later: see n. 810.

539–40 Let…readie]
Crook (ed. 1907): Lear’s conduct bears out Goneril’s remark in [522+1–+2]. But Lear is apparently giving orders to his own attendants, not to Goneril’s servants; see n. 580. Mahood (1992, p. 161), however: The medieval regulations of the Harleian household…confirm that a guest of senior rank took over control of the house. This custom was still observed, during Shakespeare’s time, in the summer progress of the sovereign. There is thus nothing untoward in King Lear, in his daughter’s house, ordering dinner when he wants it. All the same, in life as in art, the situation could become fraught. And Goneril may not consider an abdicated ruler, now her dependent, to be a guest of senior rank. Foakes (ed. 1997): Lear’s prose here contrasts with his formal verse in the ceremonial opening scene, but he is just as peremptory. Duthie (ed. 1949): At line [580] etc. F gives speech-heading Knigh. Lear has reserved to himself a retinue of Knights, and it is presumably these (or some of them) who have been in attendance on him while he has been hunting. There is no basis for Meagher’s (1965, p. 98) supposition that the Attendant…, presumably wearing the livery of Goneril and Albany, does not respond to his command. Bratton (ed. 1987) records productions which added to this scene unruly behavior by the knights to support Goneril’s claims.

539 iot]
Schmidt (1874): The smallest quantity imaginable (OED, sb.1). Wright (ed. 1875): Here of time, as in TN 3.2.1 (1383).

539 dinner]
Weis (ed. 1993): The main meal of the day, eaten at this time in the middle of the day (OED, sb. 1). Lear leaves Goneril’s house at midday and apparently arrives at Gloucester’s house in the afternoon of the following day (see n. 1273).

540 how now]
see n. 361.

540 what]
Abbott (§254): What is often used…where we should use who, especially in the phrase what is he?; apparently with little sense of of what kind or quality, but possibly of what condition or rank. Cf. Franz §342, and 549, 1286, 1616, 1825, 1905, 1907, 2488, 2667, 3045, 3070, 3078, 3124.

540 thou]
Verity (ed. 1897): Ordinarily used in addressing inferiors, e.g. by a master to a servant, who replies by you: cf. Kent’s answers and the Knight’s [587–8]. Mulholland (1967, p. 42): The disguised Kent was himself addressed with 27 th[ou] and 3 you forms by Lear (sane), and 33 th and 5 you forms by his equals.

541 A man]
Hunter (ed. 1972): With a secondary sense of a servant. Kent abandons his initial verse in response to the King’s prose. Vickers (1968, p. 351), however: Kent as the good counsellor speaks verse, but adopts prose when he disguises his likeness and borrows other accents. See also nn. 1145–1216, 1185–9.

542, 544 professe]
Delius (ed. 1854): Lear uses this in the sense of trade or calling [OED, v. 5]. Kent replies in the sense of assertion [OED, v. 2] (Ger.).

544–8 I…fishe]
Traversi (1952, p. 51): Kent’s attitude corresponds, in the public sphere, to that of Cordelia in her interpretation of the duties of a daughter. Both are plain-speaking where matters of principle or judgment are concerned. Cordelia’s lack of the glib and oily art of flattering speech is fairly balanced by Kent’s pride in his ability to deliver a plain message bluntly. His confession of principles is indeed a summary of the virtues which find their highest expression in true loyalty; the determination to be consistent with his own nature (to…seeme), to show and expect fair-dealing (to…honest), to reflect more than to speak (to…little), above all, to cling to traditional sanctions of moral behaviour (to feare iudgement), are all qualities which the world around him…is busily engaged in inverting. Vickers (1968, p. 359): Kent’s mock-catechism, non-sequiturs, and other quizzical contradictions show the kind of riddling humour that in another play would be the mark of a clown. Murphy (1984, p. 177): His speech is in part a satiric jibe at the convention of Tom-tell-troth, Plain Richard, etc. These tend to be the stock dramatic conventions of the Protestant Reformed Englishman free from the lying hypocrisy and deceit of Rome, Italianate Englishmen, and duplicitous Jesuits.

544 no lesse]
Tovey(ed. 1896): Said with covert irony, Kent being greater than he seemed. Dent (1981) compares Tilley S214, Be what thou would Seem to be.

545 in trust]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Trust…with any business. Goggin (ed. 1910): In a place of trust. Either is possible. OED (sb. 5a): The condition of having confidence reposed in one, or of being entrusted with something; esp. in the phrase in trust. Cf. Oth. 2.3.126 (1238).

546 conuerse]
Johnson (ed. 1765): To keep company [OED, v. 2], not to discourse or talk. The latter, modern meaning, coming into use at the end of the 16th or beginning of the 17th c., is rare in Sh. if it exists at all; in given instances it is hard to distinguish from the related meaning to communicate or interchange ideas (OED, 4). Craig (ed. 1901): Accented on the first syllable.

546 wise]
Carter (1905, p. 434) and Shaheen (1987, p. 148) compare Ecclus. 9:17, Prov. 13:20.

546 sayes little]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Men who are no tattlers nor tale-bearers. Dent (1981, W799) detects the proverb Few words show men wise. Shaheen (1987, p. 148) compares Prov. 17:27–8.

547 feare iudgement]
Griffith (1775, p. 357): To respect the laws. Capell (1783, 1.2:149): Fear coming before a judge. Like Eccles (ed. 1792) many eds. find a reference to the Last Judgment or at least to divine judgment. Moberly (ed. 1876): The meaning is that he has a conscience. Noble (1935, pp. 229–30): Cf. Ps. i. 6: Therefore the ungodly shall not be able to stand in the judgment; Jer. viii. 7 G: my people knoweth not the iudgement of the Lord.…Kent means that he fears God. Kittredge (ed. 1940): God’s final judgment.…This might be construed to accord with the pagan religion of Lear’s time; but eat no fish [548] is a manifest anachronism. Muir (ed. 1952): By an earthly, or a heavenly, judge. Halio (ed. 1992): Kent may, however, simply be declaring his desire to serve well, fearing his master’s censure.

547 when…chuse]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): When it is not to be avoided. Otherwise or but is understood. Dent (1981, p. 265) attests to Sh.’s frequent use of the idiom.

548 eate no fishe]
Apparently jocular, and the incongruity of the phrase is enough to provoke laughter (Foakes, ed. 1997), but the point of the quip is not agreed on. The phrase has been taken to refer to Catholicism, sumptuary laws, weak diet, patriotism, bawdry, or nothing at all:
(1)Catholicism. Warburton (ed. 1747): In Queen Elizabeth’s time the Papists were esteemed, and with good reason, enemies to the government. Hence the proverbial phrase of, He’s an honest man and eats no fish; to signify he’s a friend to the Government and a Protestant. The eating fish, on a religious account, being then esteem’d such a badge of popery, that when it was enjoin’d for a season by act of parliament, for the encouragement of the fish-towns, it was thought necessary to declare the reason; hence it was called Cecil’s fast. To this disgraceful badge of popery Fletcher alludes in his Woman-Hater [4.2.247–9], who makes the courtezan say, when Lazarillo, in search of the Umbrano’s head, was seized at her house by the Intelligencers, for a traytor. Gentlemen, I am glad you have discover’d him, a should not have eaten under my roofe for twenty pounds; and surely I did not like him, when a cal’d for Fish. And Marston’s Dutch Courtezan [1.2.19–20]. I trust I am none of the wicked that eat fish o’Fridays. Of Warburton’s proverbial evidence Grey (1752, p. 24) says, I am apt to believe, it is a Proverb of your own making; and though Kittredge (ed. 1940) likewise asserts that this phrase became proverbial in the sense of to be a sound Protestant and loyal to the state, no such usage has been found. Blakeway (apud Boswell, ed. 1821): Not a badge of popery.…[According to] Walton, Life of Hooker…[Elizabeth] would never eat flesh in Lent without obtaining a licence from her little black husband <Archbishop Whitgift>. But Lent is a special, and small, part of the year, and several eds. agree with Tovey (ed. 1896) that in 1606 a hit at Catholics would have been timely: Papists were especially under a cloud just after the Gunpowder Plot.
(2)Sumptuary laws. Grey (loc. cit.): It is well known, that Fish Days were as strictly observed then by Protestants, as Papists; and in Lent, Dispensations were frequently granted to such Protestants, who upon Account of Sickness, or ill Health, could not eat Fish, to eat Flesh; as you may be informed…by Dr. Fuller, Mr. Strype, and several other Writers upon those Times. Singer (ed. 1826) cites a letter from Whitgift in 1596 enjoining the clergy of his diocess [sic] to attend to the observance of the fasts and fish days among their respective parishioners, and severely animadverting upon the refractory spirit which disposed them to eat flesh out of due season contrary to law. Staunton (ed. 1859): The Act to which Warburton refers was a Statute passed in the fifth year of Elizabeth, 1562, Cap. v. touching Politick Constitutions for the Maintenance of the Navy. Sect. xiv.-xxiii. The fifteenth section of this Act provides, that any person eating flesh on the usual fish-days, shall forfeit Three Pound for every time he or they shall offend; or else suffer three months close imprisonment without bail or mainprise. It is probable that the greatest objection to the Act was the order in Sect. xiv.:—That from the Feast of St. Michael the Archangel, in the Year of our Lord God 1564, every Wednesday in every week throughout the whole year, which heretofore hath not by the laws or customs of this realm been used and observed as a Fish-day—shall be hereafter observed and kept, as the Saturdays in every week be or ought to be. The penal part of this statute was mitigated in 1593, the thirty-fifth of Elizabeth, cap. vii. sect. xxii., to a forfeiture of twenty shillings or one month’s imprisonment. In the same Act it was provided, that all the Statutes recited in it should continue in force only until the end of the Parliament next ensuing, which met October 24th, 1597, and was dissolved February 9th, in the following year, when they were presumed to have expired. So late, however, as 1655, Izaak Walton, in the second edition of his Compleat Angler, refers to those very few that are left, that make conscience of the laws of the nation, and of keeping days of abstinence. Kemshead (ed. 1875): In the recoil from the involuntary asceticism beef and mutton reigned exclusively on all tables, and to detest fish in all shapes and forms had become a note of Protestantism, citing J. A. Froude, Hist. of Eng. 8:432–5 (1866). Clarkes (ed. 1868): Kent, in his just-assumed blunt fashion of speaking, means to infer that he is not very strict in the observance of abstinence and fast days. Moberly (ed. 1876): Neither by Roman Catholic rule, nor in obedience to Protestant acts for the maintenance of fisheries. Armour (ed. ca. 1930): Perhaps…Kent wishes merely to establish his character as a rather strange and original sort of fellow.
(3)Weak diet. Capell (1783, 1.2:149): The play…was not of [Queen Elizabeth’s] time.…[Kent] was a jolly fellow, and no lover of such meagre diet as fish. Craig (ed. 1901), paraphrasing Capell as meaning I am no weakling, quotes Falstaff’s contempt for the many fish meales that contribute to the pusillanimity of demure boyes, 2H4 4.3.90–2 (2326–8). Stewart (1948, p. 188): Since fish was the food of servants and underlings, Kent…knows that he will make a hit with Lear by this inconsequential ending, for it stamps him as a man of spirit and quality. Harbage (ed. 1958): Unmanly diet (?).
(4)Patriotism. Perrett (1904, p. 249): Possibly Kent means to declare himself a true Briton. For [John] Speed [History of Great Britaine (1611; 1623, p. 22)] quotes from Dio Nicaeus that the Britains did till no ground, neither eat fish.
(5)Bawdiness. Muir (ed. 1952), followed by Wilson (ed. 1960): From [Rom. 1.1.30 (33): Tis well thou art not fish], it seems possible that Kent’s meaning is indecent. But the apparent meaning there of membrum virile does not suit this context. Fraser (ed. 1963), followed by McCall (1977, p. 135): I use no prostitutes. Elton (1966, p. 290 n.): Cf. Barnabe Rich’s The Irish Hubbub (1617), p. 25, the whoremaster…Senex Fornicator, an old Fishmonger, and the old fishmonger Polonius [Ham. 2.2.174 (1210)]. Colman (1974, pp. 100, 194) is cautious of bawdy meanings of fishmonger and fish (= female), but Williams (1994) documents them; neither cites this l.
(6)Nothing. Lott (ed. 1974): Possibly…just inconsequential, a third, alliterative item in a series: fear—fight—fish.

549 What]
See n. 540. Brooke (ed. 1947): Lear repeats the question Kent has twice humorously evaded. Kent evades again.

550 fellow]
See n. 16.

550–1 as…king]
Rosenberg (1972, p. 97): A characteristic, provocative remark that must draw a special glance from Lear. Lott (ed. 1974): Kent already has some conception of the King’s sorry state. But Lear’s state is not observably sorry; the audience has not yet witnessed even faint neglect (597) towards him. Kent must refer only to Lear’s abdication: he is a king without a realm.

552–3 If…enough]
Tovey (ed. 1896): The first hint that Lear repents of having parted with his state. The neglect that he has noticed [547] has set him thinking. But Lear’s remark may be only a labored witticism without any hint of repentance: I certainly possess much less than a king usually does; if you possess proportionally as much less than a subject usually does, you’ll qualify for poor. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 128): Would have been uncomfortably pertinent to the financial difficulties which James soon encountered. They do not specify difficulties or dates.

552 be]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 134) defends F’s be’st by reference to 2H6 3.2.295 (2009), Ant. 1.5.59 (590), and Abbott (§298): Indicative…used subjunctively after if; cf. Franz §644.

552 for…for]
Franz (§482): In the quality of, in the capacity of, as (OED, prep. 19).

552 he is]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 171) and Munro (ed. 1957) agree that F’s hee’s is unauthorial and awkward. Duthie suggests a compositor’s error of aural memory or a scribe’s misreading of i as e; Munro, that the compositor contracted the words in order to justify the crowded line (which elides for a without space).

553–72 what…yet]
Elton (1966, p. 285 n.), citing contemporary parallels: Kent’s petition to serve Lear, as well as his intended master’s reply…, appears to follow a set form.

554 Seruice]
On the importance of this term and concept to the play see Barish & Waingrow (1958), Mack (1965, pp. 103–5), among others.

555 Who]
Abbott (§274): The inflection of who is frequently neglected. Cf. Franz §333, and 2347+8, 3206.

557 fellow]
OED (sb. 10a): The customary title of address to a servant or other person of humble station. Cf. 617, 1724, 1955, 2139, 2212, 2240, 2242, 2480, 3240.

558 countenance]
See n. 479. Only OED (sb. 4): The look…of a person’s face, quoting this l. Wells (ed. 2000): Or bearing. Donovan (privately) suggests a secondary meaning, patronage, citing Herford & Simpson’s note (9:453) on Jonson, Every Man Out 3.5.152.

559 faine]
See n. 399.

561 Authoritie]
Elton (1966, p.): As Shakespeare emphasizes James’s political wisdom in uniting instead of dividing, so his defense of service underlines his patron’s political concern, divine right and authority. Edwards (ed. 1975): Kent is not flattering, though Lear is flattered. Kent, who freely chooses the conditions of feudal service, acknowledges only the king as the source of authority. Brown (ed. 1996): Ingrained greatness or inherited power? Foakes (ed. 1997): A term Lear disowns at [2602]. At this point, however, he may still seem authoritative; see 329, 522+2.

562 canst]
Q2’s unauthoritative addition of thou, followed by F, is unnecessary. Abbott (§241): After a verb ending with the second person singular inflection, the thou is sometimes omitted in questions. Cf. Franz §306, and 667, 891, 1028, 1076, 1184, 1483, 1723, 1783, 2212, 2594. Q2 need not have influenced F here; the added thou may be explained as an unconscious insertion of a smoothing word by both printers (Doran, (1931, p. 114).

563 keepe…counsaile]
Rushton (1873, p. 72): Kent may mean, not I can keep counsel honestly or conscientiously, but I can keep counsel in honest things, as Psellus in Euphues [and his England] says:—As for keeping your counsayle, in things honest, it is no matter, & in causes unlawful, I will not meddle [ed. Bond, 2:110, italics added]. Eds. interpret in both ways. Kirschbaum (apud Muir, ed. 1952; rev. 1957, p. 257) cites Jonson’s Sejanus 1.1.23–4: There be two [flatterers], Know more, then honest councells. See n. 1146–53. But Kent is not speaking of offering flattery; keep counsel always means keep secrets or confidences (Schmidt, 1874, Counsel; OED, sb. 5d).

563 ride, run]
Dent (1981, R117.1): The pairing is proverbial: To Ride and run.

563–4 mar…it]
Delius (ed. 1854): A proof of his honesty (Ger.). Moberly (ed. 1876): Conversely, tell a plain tale without marring it, as implied in the next words. Tovey (ed. 1896): Kent makes himself out to be an honest blockhead, who can only deliver correctly what is sufficiently simple. Harrison (ed. 1937): He will have none of the fantastic talk of the typical courtier (such as Osric in Hamlet), which he mimics at [1180–3]. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Kent implies that he is too outspoken to be a skilful talker. Munro (ed. 1957): A common phrase, citing Tilley T38, A good Tale ill told is marred in the telling, which is not very apposite. Lott (ed. 1974): An old joke about servants was their inability to carry messages correctly, citing no exx.

564 curious]
Apparently a derogatory term, perhaps the opposite of plaine; but its meaning has been hard to give precisely. Delius (ed. 1854): Affected, mannered; cunning (Ger.) (OED, a. 7b?; 10b). Clarkes ed. 1868): Elaborate, complicated, involved, unsimple (OED, 8). Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): A carefully worked-out story [OED, 9], or, a story that needs care in the telling [OED, 13?, unattested before 1681]. Evans (ed. 1898): Literally made with care, so elaborate, accurate [OED, 11]; but…here perhaps means no more than what we call a good story. Craig (ed. 1901) quotes North’s Plutarch, Tiberius and Caius (ed. 1597, p. 865): Tiberius wordes…being very proper…where Caius wordes were full of finenesse and curiositie. Kelcy (1932, p. 361): A strange tale, that is, an account of a strange occurrence, Kent will mar by telling it bluntly, without trying to make an impression on his hearer (OED, 16, unattested before 1715). Brown (ed. 1976): Ingenious.

565 bluntly]
Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 98): In Leir, The King of Gallia’s companion, Mumford, boasts of his bluntness (386–9 [see ]), which could have suggested the style of speech the disguised Kent assumes, comparing 1171–2.

566 diligence]
Schmidt (1874): Assiduity in service. But OED (sb. 2): Speed, dispatch, haste, quoting this l.

568 so…to]
On the omission of as see n. 229–30.

568–9 Not…thing]
Verity (ed. 1897): Perhaps proverbial. No proverb has been found; cf. Tilley M696, To Marry young is too early, to marry old is too late. McCann (ed. 1964): He is young enough to have sex-interest,…not old enough to be foolishly affectionate for other reasons. Brown (ed. 1976), to the contrary: Neither not sexually nor being too old for sex. More probably, Kent will be guilty of neither the easy infatuation of youth nor the extreme dotage of old age, being of mature years. Wells (ed. 2000), however: Williams (Glossary [1998]) glosses sing as coit with.

569–70 on my backe]
OED (Back, sb. 23d): Weighing upon as a burden, quoting this l. as its first ex.

570 fortie eight]
Bradley (1904, p. 308) cites as evidence of Kent’s greater age ancient (1135), old fellow (1158), ancient [F]…reverent (1204), and too old (1206). Budd (ed. 1935): He is here deliberately pretending to be a dozen or so years younger than he actually is in order to improve his chances of obtaining employment. Fripp (1938, p. 665): He is nearer seventy. Brooke (ed. 1947), citing Baldwin (1927, p. 250): The age of Kent is not suggested by any of the sources, and it would fit with [John] Heminge’s at the time the play was produced. In fact, Baldwin thinks that Kent’s age is altered from the source, where his counterpart is as old as Leir. Faber (1964): He is in disguise. Elton (1966, p. 242), citing Renaissance opinions that advanced age begins from forty to forty-nine: In ambivalent fashion, Lear’s shadow, Kent, can function with his master;…Kent can also stand virile proxy against the villainous young, viz. Oswald. Hankins (1978, p. 62), numerologically: Kent is in his forty-ninth year…his grand climacteric [i.e., 7 x 7] if his life is goverened by sevens. Smidt (1990, p. 132): Kent in the first half of the play certainly gives the impression of having the vitality of youth, twice getting the better of Oswald. Mahood (1992, p. 238): John Russell Brown [privately; cf. ed. 1996] points out, however, that Kent’s claim to be forty-eight can be part of his act, and that Shakespeare probably sees him as Gloucester’s contemporary, who might well be expected to die soon. Cf. nn. 1135, 3300–1.
Bratton (ed. 1987): At this point Edmund Kean, J. P. Kemble, and W. C. Macready had Lear ask and Kent give his name, Caius. See n. 3249.

571 Follow…mee]
Brown (ed. 1976): Hiring an unknown man without a personal recommendation was very odd indeed, especially…in Jacobean times, comparing 32–4. Foakes (1993, p. 186): Lear has no sense of restraint as to the number of followers he can retain. But one is a small addition to a hundred, and Kent’s hire is a plot necessity.

571–2 if…dinner,]
Most eds. connect this clause with the following (see textual n.). Halio (ed. 1992): Lear’s capricious attitude is clearer with a full stop after dinner.

572 yet]
Capell (1783, 1.2:149): Loosely for—presently.

572–3 dinner, ho dinner]
Rosenberg (1972, p. 99): The first order may have been conspicuously ignored: Lear is perhaps already getting from Goneril’s servants the colder looks she decreed. But see n. 538: he seems to have given this order to his own attendants, not Goneril’s.

573 knaue]
Grey (1754, 2:106): A boy [OED, sb. 1], or man-servant [OED, 2]. Hudson (ed. 1871): A common term of familiar endearment (OED, 3c, quoting 626). Most eds. assume that knaue and foole refer to the same person. Cf. 626, 1727. The terms are commonly paired: so Dent (1981, F506.1), To be both Fool and knave, comparing 834, 1356–7, 1727. On the Fool’s age, see n. 626.

573 goe you]
Meagher (1965, p. 98): To another Attendant. See n. 538.

574 you]
Verity (ed. 1897), of F’s You you: Repetition of a pronoun is a sign of contempt, comparing 606. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 533): Might easily result from dittography.

574 sirra]
See n. 411.

575 Enter Steward]
See n. 519. Davies (1783, 2:273): He generally enters the stage in a careless disengaged manner, humming a tune, as if on purpose to give umbrage to the King by his neglect of him. Bratton (ed. 1987): The singing entrance is specified by Edmund Kean, J. P. Kemble, and Macready.

576 So…you]
Moberly (ed. 1876): To excuse me. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Literally, may it be pleasing to you. Wilson (ed. 1960): Excuse me; I’m busy. Aberbach (1979, p. 130) needlessly suspects a source in Job 29:16: I called my seruant, but he would not answer.

577 fellow]
OED (sb. 10c): Contemptuously. A person of no esteem or worth. Cf. 1170, 1218, 1316, 2534, 3025.

577–8 clat-pole]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Spelt also clotpole and clod-poll. A thick-skull, a blockhead [OED, 2]; a fellow with a head like a clod of earth. Though Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 372) suggests that the a may be a misreading of o, which is F’s sp. here and in Sh.’s two other uses, Clatpoles occurs in Tro. 2.1.117 (970). Sh. may have coined the word. Lott (ed. 1974): Lear tries to pretend to himself that Oswald has been too stupid to answer his question.

578 backe]
To the exit of Knight marked by modern eds. (see textual n.) the Oxford eds. (1986 Q, 2000) add an exit of Kent here and his re-entrance at 579. Bratton (ed. 1987): Tate had Kent pursue Oswald, and Macready and Irving also sent him off with the Knight.…Tate had Kent bring Oswald back…[as did] Garrick, J. P. Kemble, Edmund Kean, Macready, and Irving. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 512): If Kent is to speak [580] he must exit at some point. Blayney [MS ed. of Q1] has him leave after…there [577], with call…backe [577–8] addressed to a Gentleman, and referring to Kent, rather than Oswald. Since most eds. do not give 580 to Kent, his exit and return are not needed; see n.

579 asleepe]
Dent (1981, A347.2) doubtfully suggests a proverb, I think X is Asleep.

579 how now]
See n. 361.

579 mungrel]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Cur, wretched fellow; properly an animal of mixed breed, not true-bred. Cf. 1095.

580 Kent.]
F changes to Knigh., as do most eds., perhaps assuming Kent. to be a misreading. Kirschbaum (1945, p. 21): Ascription to Kent spoils Shakespeare’s intention in this scene, for in F Kent’s first action for his master is his sudden manhandling of the saucy steward.…This prompt and surprising defence…affects and pleases Lear. Maguire (1996, p. 86): One may as easily conclude the reverse, that Shakespeare, writing Q, gave line [580] to Kent with satisfactory effect but later decided to keep him silent until 616. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 84): Since Q heads lines [583, 586, 593, and 602] seruant. it is unlikely that Kent.…is a wrong expansion of Knt. for Knight. (Ibid., p. 83): These [seruant, Knight] are doubtless just different appellations for the same character. Since the abbreviations Knt. or Kt. do not occur anywhere in the whole Folio, nor in Q Lr., and Kni. occurs only in F H5 658, here the Q compositor would probably have had to expand K. or Knigh[t] rather than those abbreviations. More likely he misread se, as K, an easy confusion in many hands including Hand D in Thomas Moore; thus an abbrev. such as ser. or seru., both common throughout F, could here have been misread Kn. or Ken., r, u, and n being very similar. There is no apparent reason why both Kent and another of Lear’s servants should have followed Oswald and both should have reported on his behavior; dramatic economy requires only one person, as in F. Clearly seruant is not an alternate designation for Kent, since Kent has not been back at court long enough to observe the change of behavior of the generall dependants (590) or of the fool (603).
A single servant appears and speaks lines again in 1.5, 2.4, 3.1, 4.3, 4.4, 4.6, 4.7, and 5.3. In F he is designated Gentleman (except in 4.3, om. from F); in Q he is called seruant in 1.5, Knight in 2.4, Doctor in 4.4, and Gentleman otherwise. Perrett (1904, pp. 195–201) notes that Lear has a single attendant in none of his immediate sources, only in Geoffrey of Monmouth (see ), but argues that he is the same person throughout Shakespeare’s play. Rosenberg (1972, p. 101): In the theatre this knight is usually recognized from the I, i court scene as a particular personal attendant on Lear; he may play the role of Gentleman in the storm, and also join Lear in his brief resurgence at the end. Certainly the same actor could play the role of attendant in all of the scenes, but it is not certain that the attendant remains the same dramatic personage. In 1.5 he is Lear’s servant, one of his asses (908), but need not be the same as in 1.4. The Knight/Gentleman in 2.4 could well be the same Gentleman in 3.1 whom Kent recognizes and who knows the fool (1624); he is sent to Dover specifically in Q, more vaguely towards Cordelia in F, and is almost certainly the same who returns with reports of Cordelia in 4.3 (Q only). But the Gentleman in following scenes is probably a different person. In 4.4 and 4.7 in F he replaces Q’s Doctor, a member of Cordelia’s party not Lear’s; and the Gentleman who discovers Lear in 4.6, having been sent out by Cordelia (see 2632), is more likely to be one of her party than one of Lear’s knights who has found her camp and joined the search. The Gentleman in 5.3 could be Albany’s. On the reappearance of Knights, Gentlemen, and Messengers throughout the play, see nn. 874 and 1615.

580 daughter]
Wells & Taylor (p. 533), of F’s Daughters: A typical Compositor E error.

583 roundest]
Delius (ed. 1854): Bluntest, rudest (OED, Round a. 13).

586–600 My…into’t]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Lear’s Knights never show riotous or quarrelsome behaviour. They justify the King’s favourable testimony [795–9]. Goneril’s assertions to the contrary [513, 713–15, 750–5] are mere falsehood. Cf. [1609]. Mack (1965, p. 31) notes also Albany’s significant unawareness of what Goneril is complaining about later in this scene. Mahood (1992, pp. 161–2): If Lear’s Knights were the rabble that Goneril describes, this brief encounter would surely have exploded into violence. But the Knight’s sober and judicious comments show where the true fault lies. Foakes (ed. 1997): But the behaviour of Lear and Kent verges on the riotous in this scene—as Goneril soon exclaims (717–20). But Lear and Kent do not riot until provoked, and the fact remains that there is no support in the text for Goneril’s claim that the knights grow riotous. Cf. nn. 513, 751. Nonetheless, in performance the knights sometimes give support to Goneril’s claims by their riotous (and more dramatic) behavior.

587 ẽtertained]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Treated (OED, Entertain v. 8). Halio (ed. 1992): Although Gonerill has just given instructions to slight Lear [519]…Shakespeare conveys the illusion of a greater passage of time. But obviously the disrespect began before 519: see 507–8, 596–7.

588 that…as]
Abbott (§280): That [those, etc.]…used with as (in which way) used for which, quoting this l. See also n. 104, and cf. 808.

588 ceremonious affection]
Crook (ed. 1907): Loving attention to ceremonious duty. Harrison (ed. 1937): Manners, even between parents and children, were very formal. Neglect of courtesies to the ex-King shows of falling off of love. Hunter (ed. 1972): The affection due to a father and the ceremony appropriate to a king. Colie (1974, p. 201): Ceremonious affection is entirely absent from this house, as we know from Goneril’s planning with Oswald [516 ff.] to withhold deference from her father. Gradually we realize the symbolic importance of withholding the ceremony normally due a father and a king: Goneril seeks to destroy the old man’s sense of himself long before king-killing becomes part of the action. Cf. n. 141.

589 of kindnesse]
Delius (1876, p. 135): Without F’s necessary phrase, accidentally omitted from Q, one does not know what sort of abatement the knight means. Brooke (ed. 1947): Courtesy (OED, 4: Kind…action or conduct). More likely parallel with affection— Good will, favour, friendship (OED, 5)—though in 599 Lear characterizes neglect as vnkindnesse. See n. 132.

589 apeer’s]
Abbott (§244): The relative is frequently omitted.…In many cases the antecedent immediately precedes the verb to which the relative would be the subject. Cf. Franz §348, and 641, 1667, 1806, 1885, 1976, 2347+34.

590 generall]
OED (a. 1c): All collectively, quoting this l.

590 Duke]
Hunter (ed. 1972): In a court of law this would be found unreliable. Albany later (line [786]) is ignorant of the situation, and the rest of his conduct in the play confirms the truth of this ignorance. Th[is] speech…marks Shakespeare’s anxiety to emphasize the isolation of Lear.

590 also]
Jespersen (1929, p. 221): Sh. nearly always puts it in the mouth of vulgar or affected persons, citing this l. as a possible instance.

592 Ha!]
OED (int. 1): An exclamation expressing, according to the intonation, surprise, wonder, joy, suspicion, indignation, etc. Cf. 742, 823, 2543, 3235.

594 my dutie]
Metonymy, substituting adjunct for subject. Thus Deighton (ed. 1891): I in my duty.

596 remember’st]
Dyce (ed. 1864–7, Glossary): To remind (OED, v 7).

596–7 conception]
Schmidt (ed. 1879): Sh. uses only of ill thoughts, esp. of suspicion or jealousy (Ger.).

597 faint neglect]
Opinion is divided whether this means slight degree…of neglect (Hunter, ed. 1869), so faint that he has been doubtful whether it was intentional (Rolfe, ed. 1880), or neglectful deeds which are cold, without zeal, not forward to do one’s duty (Schmidt, 1874), dull, languid (Idem, ed. 1879), indolent (Kermode, in Evans, ed. 1974), halfhearted (Brown, ed. 1976). Recent eds. incline to the latter meaning; Wilson (ed. 1960), exceptionally, understands slight: As Lear, the self-deceiver, still sees it though the Knight (l. [589]) finds it great. Neither couldst neglect (279) nor wearie negligence (519) is an exact parallel, but they are suggestive. Goneril has urged colder looks (525), and Craig (ed. 1901) notes that in the old play Leir says of Gonorill, euery day her Kindnesse did grow cold (Leir 2262; see ). At 495 faintly means without vividness (OED, 4), a different sense though allied to in a weak, feeble, or languid manner (OED, 3). OED does not attest to the meaning hardly perceptible (Faint, a. 5) before 1660, nor to the adverbial counterpart before 1695 except for two questionable Shn. exx.

598 which]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Referring to his own conception [596–7].

598–9 I…vnkindnesse]
Hudson (ed. 1871): The passage is rather curious as discovering a sort of double consciousness in the old King. Smith (ed. 1902): We have here the first indication of Lear’s finer qualities. Though hasty in temper, he is at least generous. But cf. Wilson, n. 597. Greg (1940, p. 396) compares Leir 2263–4: Which [i.e., Gonorill’s unkindness] I with patience put up well ynough, And seemed not to see the things I saw; see .

598–9 ielous curiositie]
Steevens (ed. 1793): Punctilious jealousy, resulting from a scrupulous watchfulness of his own dignity. MacCracken (ed. 1914): Jealousy over trifles. Cf. nn. 9, 338.

599 very]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Actual (OED, a. 2).

599 pretence]
See n. 421.

599 purport]
Though Doran (1931, p. 85) prefers Q’s reading, editors generally adopt F’s purpose; see textual n.

599 vnkindnesse]
See nn. 132, 589. Urkowitz (1980, p. 83), however: Ingratitude, citing Thomas Elyot, The Governour (1531, fols. 162v f.).

600 wher’s…foole]
Verity (ed. 1897): These repeated demands after the Fool show how dear he is to his master and thus prepare us for the familiar tone which Lear allows him. They also excite interest in him.

601 this two]
Abbott (§87): A [and this were] frequently inserted before a numeral adjective, for the purpose of indicating that the objects enumerated are regarded collectively as one. Cf. Franz §316.

602–3 Since…away]
Steevens (ed. 1793): This is an endearing circumstance in the Fool’s character, and creates such an interest in his favour, as his wit alone might have failed to procure for him. Coleridge (MS notes, 1818–19, ed. Foakes, 1989, p. 99): The Fool [is] no comic buffoon to make the groundlings laugh, no forced condescencion on Shakespeare’s genius to the taste of his audiences. Accordingly, he is prepared for—brought into living connection with the pathos of the play, with the sufferings. Clarkes (ed. 1868): This speech serves to depict Cordelia’s power of attaching and endearing those around her. Cavell (1969, p. 287): His pining is directly due to his love for Lear and distress at Lear’s shame—the latter a hypothesis. Hunter (ed. 1972): The first description of the Fool characterizes him as delicate and sensitive. (Ibid., p. 11): But It is easy to sentimalize him; too much is often made of a supposed relationship with Cordelia.…[This passage] says no more than that the Fool feels keenly the pressures of the new world of Gonerill and Regan. Unlike Cordelia he has the destructive energy of innocence, comparing 834. Mahood (1992, p. 162): The suggestions of a closely knit family in the Knight’s use of the possessive, and his concern for the retainer whom Goneril’s servants merely chide ([507–8])…give the lie to Goneril’s account of him and his companions as riotous, insolent and deboshed.

602 into]
Schmidt (1874): Unto, to. Idem (ed. 1879): Very commonly used by Sh. before the names of countries (Ger.).

604 No…it]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Lear’s rejoinder serves to denote her old father’s already awakened consciousness that he had done her grievous injustice. Verity (ed. 1897): He cannot bear to hear her spoken of and have his loss brought home to him. Crook (ed. 1907): Lear is still angered at any reference to Cordelia.

604–5 goe you…goe you]
Meagher (1965, p. 98), improbably: These commands are not given to Lear’s knights but to household attendants who ignore them, and the entrances of the Fool and Goneril (624, 702) result from coincidence. See n. 538. Mahood (1992, p. 163): The Knight can reappear among the small number of soldiers who represent the Century [2356] that Cordelia sends out…to seek her father. It can even be he who, in 4.5 [i.e. 4.6], grasps the demented King in his arms [2630].…[In Q he] is with Lear when he arrives at Gloucester’s house in 2.4. His unremarkable remarks in the ensuing scene are, however, attributed in the later version [F] to a Gentleman, presumably the same…who appeared at [921].…Some directors…turn the Knight of 1.4 into a composite character who speaks all the lines given to a Gentleman in the second, third and fourth acts. Cf. n. 874.

605–6 you cal]
Schmidt (ed. 1879): Cal is an infinitive.

606–7 sir…sir?]
Not sirra; see n. 411. Lott (ed. 1974): Lear is using the term of address ironically.

607 who am I]
Weidhorn (1969, p. 307) finds a metaphysical validity to the question, since Oswald’s answer robs Lear of name and identity—an exaggeration, since all other characters continue to use his name and titles throughout the play. Dent (1981, W318.1): The question is possibly a proverb.

609 My…Father]
Verity (ed. 1897): Of course Lear expected The king; he had specifically retained the title [144]. Crook (ed. 1907): Oswald insinuates by this that Lear’s only title to honour is that he is Goneril’s father, and Lear quickly sees the intended insult. Watson (1960, p. 188): Her position is given preeminence over his…a monstrous personal insult. Burton (1973, p. 114): It is not only the content of Oswald’s reply but also its form (minor [i.e., verbless], no term of address) that infuriates Lear.

610 my Lords]
Wilson (ed. 1960): I.e. Alb.’s.

610 knaue]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Menial [OED, sb. 2]…(with quibble on scoundrel [see n. 451]). Cf. 1088, 1090, 1091, 1094, 1217, 1356–7.

612–13 I…me]
Though Oswald speaks prose in this scene, F sets this speech anomalously as two half-lines of verse, truncating you pardon me to your pardon apparently so that they may be read as a single line. The line is too long to be set without some kind of division or turning. Cf. 617–18. Deighton (ed. 1891): Said without any…penitence, but rather with a contemptuous courtesy. Cf. 593. Taylor (1985, p. 189): Sorry, you have the wrong chap,…[with] the imputation of mental incompetence.

612 this]
F’s these reflects a wish to be more literal, replacing a pronoun representing a mass noun with one representing a count noun (Blake, 1996, p. 161).

614 bandie]
Hanmer (ed. 1743–4, 6:Gloss.): A metaphor taken from striking the balls at Tennis. Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:5, Glossary): Retort, strike back. OED (v. 6b): To give and take (blows, words, reproaches, compliments, etc.); to exchange, quoting this l. Goggin (ed. 1910): I.e. try to outface. Cf. 1459. Joseph (ed. 1966): Eyes should be lowered in the presence of persons of higher rank.

615 struck]
On the short participle see n. 103. Of F’s strucken Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 134) says, There is no reason to doubt that it is Shakespearian, citing exx. from Abbott §344. Neither is there reason to think it is Sh.’s, since the form was common (OED). In F texts strucken occurs 4 times, strooken and stricken each twice, and stroken once. If Shn. usage can be inferred from F, given the wide variety of its printer’s copy, strook and struck are Sh.’s usual forms, occurring in F some 75 times; cf. 1442, 1625. Craig (ed. 1901), who like most eds. assumes that Lear has struck Oswald for his impudence, nonetheless oddly glosses stricken dumb with wonder. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 166): Lear’s striking Oswald for his insult is an outrage and reprovable impertinence. Watson (1960, pp. 188–9): On the contrary, given the immense prestige which attached to the position of a king, The Jacobean audience would consider Lear’s response to such an insult to his kingly position but mild. They would applaud Kent’s tripping Oswald.

616–21 Nor…wisedome]
Dent (ed. 1927): The clash between Kent and Oswald indicates that the conflict had really commenced: on the one side loyalty—disguised; on the other—sycophancy and disloyalty—unmasked.

616 Nor…neither]
On the double negative see n. 427+1.

616 tript]
Sprague (1944, p. 285) records how various producers have subjected Oswald to tripping, torturing, beating, and further indignity on his exit. Kent throws Oswald over to the King (Kemble), swings him roughly to C & then knocks his hat off (Forrest), pulls him on by the ears (Wallack), pursues Oswald with his Staff, till he is off the Stage (Kemble), crying Help! Help! (Forrest). Rosenberg (1972, p. 102): Often…to the laughter of Lear and his knights, who…may handle Oswald very roughly, toss him up, throw him out. Bratton (ed. 1987): Kent’s first chastisement of Oswald struck some eighteenth-century critics as unseemly, low pantomime. Garrick cut Kent’s driving Oswald off…; but Edmund Kean gradually broadened the scene. Gardner (1967, p. 8): The episode always arouses delighted laughter in the theatre and affords genuine relief to the audience’s feelings.

616 football player]
Moberly (ed. 1876), who was Assistant Master of Rugby, where the modern game of football was developed, notes stoutly, This noble game was then a somewhat vulgar recreation, practised by the London apprentices in Cheapside to the terror of respectable citizens. Verity (ed. 1897): Elizabethans did not rank it with more exclusive sports such as hawking and coursing, fencing and tennis. Marcia Vale, The Gentleman’s Recreations (1977, p. 112): It seemed…too violent and scrabbling for a gentleman, and it was unlikely to form part of a gentle upbringing. James, in Basilikon Doron [1599, p. 143], debars from the pursuits of a future king, al rumling violente exercises; as the foote-bal, meeter for laming nor making able the users thereof. Elyot [Gouernour, 1531, fol. 99v], speaking scornfully of foote balle, wherein is nothinge but beastly furie, and exstreme violence, considers it an activity which should be utterly abiected of al noble men. Base clearly means lowly rather than laid low and so is consistent with Kent’s later insults to Oswald in 2.2; still, the phrase is odd, since Oswald hardly seems given to physical violence. Davies (1783, 2:274): It refers to his tumbling down, like a football player who has missed a kick. Deighton (ed. 1891): Kent trips Oswald as one trips up an opponent at football. Herwegh (ed. 1869), followed by Muir (ed. 1952): The epithet follows from Lear’s bandy, since in football as in tennis a ball is hurled back to one’s opponent. Hulme (1962, pp. 73–4) detects the proverb All fellows at football, meaning Never stand upon place. Tilley F182 does not cite this l., and Dent (1981, p. 30) queries Hulme’s ascription. Hunter (ed. 1972): Oswald objects to being made a tennis-ball; Kent trips him up and says that football, a plebeian game, is more suitable for him than tennis, a royal and noble game.

617–18 I…thee]
F treats Lear’s speech as verse, setting it as two part-lines because there is not room for a full or turned line. Cf. 612–13.

618 thou…thee]
Mahood (1992, p. 161): The social bond betweeen lord and vassal…epitomised, evidently taking and to mean and accordingly. Thirlby (MS notes, 1733–47) takes thou seru’st to mean I make thee my servant.

619 differences]
Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Of rank—the difference between yourself and the king. Most eds. agree, but some find other kinds of differences. Caldecott (MS notes, 1813–33): Those rules or distinctions, that constitute propriety of behavior. Verity (ed. 1897): Between Lear as My lady’s father and Lear as king. Frost (ed. 1909): In your treatment of Lear and your mistress. Goggin (ed. 1910): Oswald had had the impudence to draw distinctions with regard to Lear and his daughter; Kent will now teach him to draw distinctions between the King and a low-born wretch like himself. Colman (ed. 1982) detects a quibble on deference to superiors, and Brown (ed. 1976) one on quarreling.

620 measure…length]
Deighton (ed. 1891): By lying his full length. OED (Measure, v. 2f): Fall prostrate, quoting MND 3.2.429 (1476) and this l. as its first two exx. Quinn (ed. 1970): If you want to see how big a man you are.

620 lubbers]
OED (sb. 4): A big, clumsy, stupid fellow, quoting this l.

621 goe too]
See n. 100. Whether it represents impatience (Wright, ed. 1875), protest (Kittredge, ed. 1940), derisive incredulity (Fraser, ed. 1963), or disgust (Lott, ed. 1974), or is as Deighton (ed. 1891) and Tovey (ed. 1896) suggest, possibly an exhortation meaning Get along with you, the phrase seems intended to prod Oswald to quicker action.

621 you haue]
Until recently eds. have preferred F’s inversion, usually as converted to a question by Theobald (see textual nn.). But Stone (1980, p. 215): Q has been needlessly altered: You know better: a piece of sardonic encouragement to the chastened Oswald. F’s version, framed as a question, is not impossible, but does not follow as naturally from the rest of the speech. Schmidt (ed. 1879), comparing instances of a superfluous you or thou after an imperative in 860, 875, 1439, 1759, 1765, 2065, and 2583: The F reading is an imperative, not a question. To Deighton (ed. 1891) it is a sarcasm: Ah, you are wise enough (are you?) to…be off. If a question, it may mean Are you in your senses, that you dare to be so familiar and outspoken in the presence of the king? (Craig, ed. 1901); Have you any common sense? If so, be off with you (Kittredge, ed. 1940); Are you going to be reasonable? (Joseph, ed. 1966); or possibly, Have you learned your lesson? Hunter (ed. 1972): The Steward hesitates.…Kent’s phrase means Surely you have more sense than to resist. Blayney (apud Wells & Taylor, 1987, p. 512): The phrase is conditional, requiring an initial If.

621 so]
F’s interjection is generally taken to mean That’s right! (Muir, ed. 1952). Hunter (ed. 1972): It marks the Steward’s wise acceptance of the situation and his exit.

622 knaue]
See nn. 24, 573.

623 earnest]
Earnest money (OED, sb.2), As token that he really takes Kent into his service (Delius, ed. 1854, Ger.). Though eds. beginning with Schmidt (ed. 1879) have noted Shn. puns elsewhere on the meaning seriousness (OED, sb.1 2), such a quibble would be without point here.

624 Enter Foole]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 372): Lear sends two people to fetch the Fool—at lines [573–4] and [605–6]. It is reasonable (though not necessary) to suppose that they both come back with him. We may perhaps imagine the third Knight meeting the first Knight and the Fool on their way to the King, and returning with them. Cf. n. 538. The Fool may of course enter alone; he seems to be unattended, since his entrance is unnoticed until he speaks. The knights would serve no purpose but to stand idly upstage for 200 lines before exiting again. Lear’s order to my people at 763 (apparently still not carried out by 785 or 803) could be made only to Kent and the Fool. Cf. n. 785. Rosenberg (1972, pp. 102–3): However he comes on—bouncing, dancing, crawling, strolling, singing, glooming—…this [is] one of the most dense, complex moments of confrontation in the play. He must enter in time to hear Lear’s last words, and possibly in time to see Kent’s service in tripping Oswald (Foakes, ed. 1997).

625 coxcombe]
Clearly the Fool’s cap, though descriptions differ, as did the cap itself. Minsheu (1617, s.v. cockes-combe): Naturall Idiots and Fooles…doe accustome themselues to weare in their Cappes, cocks feathers or a hat with a necke and heade of a cocke on the top and a bell thereon &c. Warburton (ed. 1747): On the top of the fool or jester’s cap was sewed a piece of red cloth, resembling the comb of a cock. Capell (1783, 1.2:14): This cap of his, long, pointed, and red. Douce (1807, 2:317–18): A hood resembling a monk’s cowl, which, at a very early period, it was certainly designed to imitate, covered the head entirely, and fell down over part of the breast and shoulders. It was sometimes decorated with asses ears, or else terminated in the neck and head of a cock, a fashion as old as the fourteenth century. It often had the comb or crest only of the animal, whence the term, illustrating these varieties in Pl. II, IV–VII. In Halliwell (ed. 1865) are further illustrations provided by Frederick W. Fairholt from French sources. Hotson (1952, p. 5 n.) quotes contemporary references to the fool’s cap. Felver (1961, p. 60): The only time this old-fashioned article of Fool’s wear appears in Shakespeare. Hunter (ed. 1972): Have my fool’s cap (for your earnest, for you show yourself apt to act as a fool if you bind yourself to one who’s out of favour). Dent (1981, C492.1): Proverbial: To wear a Cock’s-comb.

626 How now]
See n. 361.

626 prety]
Here the word has perhaps a range of meanings: clever, fine, and attractive (OED, a. 2, 3, 4). Cf. 705, 909.

626 knaue]
See n. 573. Lloyd (in Singer, ed. 1856, 9:527): The fool is a boy, a pretty knave, young that is, and of pleasant aspect, and boundaries of his intelligence lie somewhere between innocence and acuteness. White (ed. 1862): The poor fellow had plainly had many years’ sad experience of the world.
