Idem (1880, p. 120): He has wisdom enough to stock a college of philosophers,—wisdom which has come from long experience of the world without responsible relations to it. For plainly he and Lear have grown old together. The king is much the older; but the Fool has the marks of time upon…his mind. They have been companions since he was a boy; and Lear still calls him boy and lad. Clarke (1873, pp. 397–8): Lear’s fool is a youth, not a grown man; a petted lad.…This tenderness with which the lad is treated [by Lear and Kent] partly arises from his delicacy of frame, which is indicated by…his pining away on his young mistress’s departure [603],…his sensitiveness to churlish weather [1665–6, 1858–9],…[and] his withdrawal from the play.…The fragile lad…never recovered from the rigours and terrors of that tempestuous night. Furness (ed. 1880): Not a boy, but a man—one of the shrewdest, tenderest of men, whom long life had made shrewd, and whom afflictions had made tender; his wisdom is too deep for any boy, and could be found only in a man, removed by not more than a score of years from the king’s own age; he had been Lear’s companion from the days of Lear’s early manhood. Rolfe (ed. 1880), agreeing with Furness: Lear’s addressing him as boy and pretty knave…may be explained, partly by the force of habit…and partly from his slight and frail physique. Craig (ed. 1901): Lear several times addresses the fool as my boy; see [636, 662], and as lad [669]. Bradley (1904, p. 313): This is not decisive; but Lear’s first words to him…are difficult to reconcile with the idea of his being a man.…But even if…the Fool were imagined as a grown man, we may still insist that he must be imagined as a timid, delicate and frail being, who on that account and from the expression of his face has a boyish look. Stroup (1961, p. 128): His pining away may suggest the smallness of the person who will appear in the role and double as Cordelia (see n. 3277 and ). Brown (1963, p. 164): No adult actor can do justice to the part’s little-boy language and qualities of mind. In support McEwan (1976) cites Lear’s epithet pretty (626), similarities with the precocious Lylan page, the proverb children and fools speak the truth (Tilley C328), and emblems associating rulers and old men with a child-fool. Elton (1966, p. 320), relating the Fool to the puer senex (wise youth) tradition: In contrast to Lear’s imprudence, the boyish Fool is full of practical worldly wisdom…apt perceptions, sage counsel, and prudent forebodings.…The Fool sums up Lear’s immature old age.
Hotson (1952, pp. 96–101): This is not the artificial court jester but a natural or born fool, urging sharp truths in a vain effort to make his beloved master see better. Masked as bitter jests, their gnomic wisdom is like that of a Greek chorus.…God’s fools stand under a special protection, and are at times granted an insight denied to the merely sane. Hence the King’s treatment of the Fool shows his fundamental charity. Later, when Lear’s sufferings bring him to the brink of madness, the Fool’s presence is a continual reminder of God’s mercy to him in the past, and a spectacle of humility. Farnham (1936, p. 437): The fool is like another self of the protagonist, listened to perforce even as another self would be listened to. He searches as by inalienable right the holes in Lear’s fabric of mortal pride. The grossness of the fool is strangely touched with that unreasoning perception of truth which folk-belief credits to the insane man and the idiot. Stauffer (1949, pp. 202–3): The Fool is Lear’s conscience.…Again and again the Fool calls Lear back to an acknowledgment of his pride, his hasty temper, his mistaken judgments, his humiliation, his shadowy nothingness, his ignorance, his folly, his nakedness, and his own responsibility for his unnatural position under the power of his ungrateful daughters. Harbage (1963, p. 408): He has been, and to an extent remains, the professional irresponsible, with quick, clever, perversely irreverent mind, but he has ceased to be typical. He has become an earnest fool, a moral fool.…He nags compulsively.…This Fool is at once a wag, a fury, and a pitiful defective. For other criticisms, see . Rosenberg (1972, p. 105): Some conventions deepened [this] Fool’s stage role, conventions so immediately accepted over the centuries that they seem archetypal: the wise fool, the wise child, the wise madman,; the mascot; the scapegoat; the Vice, or Folly; the mad clairvoyant; the voice of a possessing spirit; the amusing lunatic; the compulsion of a fool…to speak uncomfortable truth; the magic and mystery of the unnatural; permitted vituperation as an amulet against bad luck; the instruction of the lofty king by his lowly jester; the voice of the king’s unconscious; the mock king; the interchangeability of king and jester…; the choric voice.…[Lear’s] Fool represents the kind of visionary folly Erasmus celebrated, that in its non-reason sees beyond itself to deeper realities. There is a touch of the magical—and the demonic—in his charm-like rhymes, his ritual, didactic utterances. He seems to command mysteries: as simple as his riddles and jokes,…or as subtle as his semi-oracular pronouncements. These conventions are discussed by Welsford (1935, passim) and applied to Lear’s Fool (pp. 253–70). Rosenberg reviews actors’ and critics’ various conceptions of the fool as childlike, unsophisticated, uninhibited,…a very symbol of sexuality,…bitter and sweet,…naive and world-weary, practical and idealistic, sensible and foolish, mad and sane, conformist and rebel, dependent and independent, privileged and underprivileged, jesting and melancholy, hurtful and loving. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 55): As Stephen Booth has noted, the Fool breaks out of every category in which he might be fixed (Booth, 39).…Most representations of the Fool tend to emphasize his strangeness, his difference from others, and give most weight to his close relationship with Lear. Brown (ed. 1976): The fool may seek to wound Lear, or to protect him by making him see himself more truly, or to help him laugh off his worries. Colie (1974, p. 132): One text for the Fool’s insistent harping on Lear’s folly is Proverbs 26:5: Answere a foole according to his foolishnes, least he be wise in his owne conceite. The more irrationally the king behaves, the more realistic seems the Fool’s treatment of him. Hammond (1991, p. 107): The Fool’s part is made up largely from quotations, near-quotations and pseudo-quotations. He repeatedly quotes the dramatic action which we have already observed on stage, miniaturising it and turning it into epitomes of proverbial or quasi-proverbial lore.…His own direct exchanges with Lear are themselves cast most frequently in the form of riddles, but the kind of answer which the riddles have is subtly different each time. Murphy (1984, p. 174) finds a source for the Fool in King Lear. Will Sommers, Henry VIII’s court fool and the best known fool in Tudor England, appears [twice] in Harsnett’s Declaration (1603, pp. 61, 138).

626 how do’st thou]
Verity (ed. 1897): The question is prompted by what the Knight has said of the Fool [603]. Only Gardner (ed. 1969): What are you driving at?

627 Sirra]
See n. 411. Spoken to Kent, not Lear, whose question is ignored; the Fool does not directly address Lear until 634. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Here used in jocose familiarity, comparing 645. Skillan (ed. 1967): He assumes a mock superiority as he does with Lear; cf. n. 631. Black (1984, p. 94), thinking Lear is addressed: The Fool here apprentices Lear and subsequently trains him in the fool’s profession, until certifying him at 911. Calvo (1992, p. 50): The Fool hardly ever addresses Lear with you.

627 you were best]
Abbott (§230): The old (to) me (it) were better, being misunderstood, was sometimes replaced by I were better.…When the old idiom is retained, it is generally in instances like [the present]…where you may represent either nominative or dative, but was almost certainly used by Shakespeare as nominative. Cf. Franz §293, and 1881. Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 179): The figure syllogismus, or abridged syllogism, presents a single vivid suggestion, from which the mind leaps to the desired inference.…You are a fool. A fool wears a coxcomb. Therefore you should wear a coxcomb. Vickers (1968, p. 360): If weak on logic and repartee, the Fool’s main weapon is the riddle,…not a device that we associate with the witty Fools [in Sh.], perhaps because its essentially static, prepared nature is not as brilliant a display of improvized wit as equivocation, repartee, comic logic, or the rhetorically structured set-piece. But in fact this limitation is here an advantage, for the riddle is unmistakably the solo utterance of the Fool and one which can therefore be seen as his own invention, and express his own attitudes.

628 Kent]
Since the Fool addresses Kent in 627 and again in 630, Q naturally gives this intervening response to Kent; F gives it to Lear. At 658 and 3285 F replaces Q’s easily likely Lear. with Kent., suggesting perhaps that the prefixes could be misread one for another, as they might if in the MS they were sometimes abbreviated to Ke., Le., or Ki. Alternatively White (ed. 1862): The mistake seems to be due to the fact that both Lear and Kent reply interrogatively [Why] to the Fool’s remark about his coxcomb. So Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 171): The F compositor’s eye has caught line [636] instead of line [628]. Only a few committed supporters of F adopt its attribution of this line to Lear. Knight (ed. 1840): The poet…would not permit Kent, in his character of serving-man, so soon to begin bandying questions with Lear’s favourite. But Kent is only replying to a remark addressed to him, as the word Sirra shows it is. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): His master was the proper person to question him step by step.…It was equally the rôle of the bystander to comment [as at F 658, Q 669+8] on the point when it came, whereupon the master felt pride or disappointment in the ability to jest thus shown off in his allowed fool. Kirschbaum (1945, p. 22): The wily fool…recognizes only Kent, and says to Kent what he wants the King to hear.…Part of the game is for Kent to remain silent. Taylor (1983, p. 119): F makes good dramatic sense, being part of the shifting of interlocutor or audience which characterizes the Fool’s comic technique. Kerrigan (1983, p. 219), convinced that F is an authorial revision: F is Q’s superior because it decisively marks the Fool’s first appearance in the play by establishing a King-jester duologue which runs unbroken for 32 lines. The evidence is however against an unbroken duologue; the Fool pointedly ignores Lear for Kent during his first 10 lines in both Q and F. This, taken with his pining for Cordelia (603) and his sharp criticisms of Lear’s folly in exiling her, suggests strongly and dramatically that the Fool feels aggrieved if not resentful, and so speaks with some acerbity throughout the scene.

628 Foole]
Jennens (ed. 1770), Dyce (ed. 1857), Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 171), Wilson (ed. 1960), and others explain F1 my Boy as the compositor’s erroneously taking line 636 for this. Jennens explains why: F1’s appellation is what Lear gives the fool, and not so natural in the mouth of Kent. White (ed. 1862): The King never calls him Fool. In speaking of him he gives him his official title; but in speaking to him he always uses some term of familiar and pitiful endearment,—generally my boy. See n. 626. Calvo (1992, p. 51): Kent, instead, consistently uses the vocative foole to address the jester. To Knight (ed. 1840) and later defenders of F, F’s word justifies its assigning the line to Lear.

629–31 Why…shortly]
Foakes (ed. 1997): If you cannot please those in power, you’ll soon suffer for it. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) compare Leir’s similar advice to Kent’s counterpart Perillus in Leir 872–5 (see ).

629 taking…fauour]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Evidently the Fool has witnessed Kent’s…tripping up Oswald’s heels. Colman (ed. 1982): I.e. siding with Lear, who is out of favour with Gonerill; but the Fool may also be seeing through Kent’s disguise and referring to his defence of Cordelia. There is no evidence in the play that the Fool ever thinks he is addressing Kent in disguise.

629 on’s]
Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 533): Since Shakespeare evidently often spelled one as on, Q1’s on’s probably means one’s (as in Q2 and F) rather than on his (which seems less idiomatic). Though one’s is never spelled on’s in F, it is in Q1 Tro. 5.2.89 (3077). OED (Take, v. 20) records the expression take one’s part, meaning to side or ally oneself with, as early as 1530; no comparable meaning of take on is attested, and such senses as assume or undertake (OED, 84b, 84d) seem to be chiefly modern idioms. Stone (1980, p. 132), uniquely: For on’s = of his see [632]; but there on is a separate preposition, not part of the verb.

630 nay]
Schmidt (1875): Used, not simply to deny or refuse, but to reprove, to correct, or to amplify that which has been said before (OED, adv. 5). Cf. 871, 1808, 3204.

630 smile…sits]
Hudson (ed. 1871): To fall in with and humour the disposition of those in power, or…who have rewards to bestow. Deighton (ed. 1891): Accommodate yourself to changes. Tilley S25 detects the proverb To set up his Sail (To sail with) every wind, comparing W439, To turn with the Wind (tide). Cf. 1151–2.

630 sits]
Schmidt (1875): Of the wind, = to have a direction, citing many Shn. exx. (OED, v. 13d). Falconer (1965, p. 75): To blow from, or be in, a particular quarter.

630–1 catch cold]
Farmer (in Reed, ed. 1785): Be turned out of doors, and be exposed to the inclemency of the weather. Muir (ed. 1952): Or, perhaps, it merely means it will be the worse for you. Seymour (1805, 2:95): A cant phrase for meeting with disaster. Wilson (ed. 1960): Become cold (not the mod. catch cold, see O.E.D. catch [42]). Skillan (ed. 1967): Be cold-shouldered. Sh. uses the phrase in several literal senses: to become cold, catch a chill (Err. 3.1.37 [660]); to become seriously ill after becoming cold (Cym. 1.4.180 [481]); to catch a head cold or cough (Ado 3.4.66 [1562–3], 2H4 3.2.181 [1715]), the usual modern meaning, and the proverbial one (Dent, 1984, C508.11). Any will do here, literally or as the basis for metaphor. Although Deighton (ed. 1891) thinks Farmer’s interpretation perhaps too literal, Traversi (1952, p. 53) finds the Fool’s speech prophetic of Kent’s later exposure to the elements, and Wilson of 1723–4. Hunter (ed. 1972): (1) the wind of power will make you suffer; (2) you’ll be turned out of doors.

631 fellow]
See n. 16. Skillan (ed. 1967): Again, we see his use of privilege; cf. n. 627. Gardner (ed. 1969): The professional familiarity of a fool to a king is useful to Shakespeare in proposing their present equality.

632 hath…done]
In Q both verbs are perfect; in F, for no clear reason, the second is simple past. F’s ha’s and did are both shorter forms, perhaps made so to fit into the full line, though its spacing might have allowed the longer forms. Franz (§174) derives ha’s from the short form ha’.

632 banisht]
Capell (1783, 1.2:149): Lost them as daughters, lost their love and obedience, and by an act of his own. Eccles (ed. 1792): Only spoken in the wanton levity of the [Fool’s] character, as being the contrary of those favours [Lear] had conferred. Traversi (1952, p. 53): The Fool’s speech implies, in its very form of expression, a reversal of reason, of logic, which at once reflects the state into which Lear’s initial action has plunged that part of the universe which depends upon him for its ordered functioning. Skillan (ed. 1967): He had actually alienated himself from gon. and reg. instead of ingratiating himself with them. Schell (1983, p. 160): Sent them into the alien place that England now is. Foakes (ed. 1997): Echoes 195.

632 on’s]
Abbott (§182): On…was frequently used even for the possessive of, particularly in rapid speech before a contracted pronoun.…When o’ [colloquial contraction of of] came before a vowel,…[it] was forced to assume a euphonic n. OED (On, prep. 27): In senses now expressed by Of.…In early times generally an actual difference of idiom, but from the end of the 16th c. due to confusion of of and on, esp. owing to the reduction of both of these to o’. Cf. Franz §500; n. 331, on’t; and 894, 1885, 1894.

633 blessing]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Made Cordelia queen of France by cursing her. Page (ed. 1889): In providing her with a good and noble husband, like the King of France, instead of a selfish bargainer, like the Duke of Burgundy. Perhaps so, though the Fool apparently did not witness that bargaining. Bevington (ed. 1992): Saving her from the curse of insolent prosperity.

633 against his will]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Unintentionally (OED, Will sb.1 14, quoting this l.).

634 needs]
OED (adv. c): Of necessity. Cf. 1517, 1591, 2400. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Emphatic: None but a fool would be Lear’s follower now.

634 how now]
See n. 361. Wilson (ed. 1960): He has so far impudently ignored Lear. Calvo (1992, p. 52): The Fool’s greeting to Lear.…Greetings always occur at the beginning of conversations.

634 nuncle]
Nares (1822): A familiar contraction of mine uncle [OED, Nuncle, citing Lr. 670; N 3b].…It seems that the customary appellation of the licensed fool to his superiors was uncle, or nuncle, citing only Fletcher’s The Pilgrim (1621–2), 4.1.57 as evidence for this custom. Cf. 647, 661, 670, 685, 692, 699, 726, 835, 913, 1398, 1665–6, 1820, 1891, 2007. Foakes (ed. 1997): Perhaps…not uncle, unsupported by OED.

635 two coxcombes]
Johnson (ed. 1765): To mark double folly in the man that gives all to his daughters. Delius (ed. 1854): He played the fool doubly, to each of his two daughters (Ger.). The logic of the joke is somewhat obscure. Apparently, having given his one cockscomb to Kent in 631, the Fool wishes for another to offer to Lear; this suggests to him that he (or anyone) ought to possess two coxcombs anyway, if he were so doubly foolish as to give all his living to his two daughters, as Lear has done. Since he has not been so foolish, but Lear has, the Fool retrieves his cockscomb from Kent, offering it to Lear as the first of his two.

637–8 If…selfe]
Brown (ed. 1976): I.e., as tokens of my folly. Tilley A187 detects the proverb He that gives All before he dies provides to suffer (is a fool); this line would be its first recorded instance. Elton (1966, p. 79 n.) adduces two similar proverbs, D570, G308.

637 any]
Weis (ed. 1993): Even the slightest. As at 770, F substitutes the more probable my, here adding all as well. Of the errors in both places Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 372) says, If the m had one stroke too many in the copy for Q it might be taken by the compositor for an [and so my for any].…[Here] it is possible that in the copy for Q all was missing (or the compositor may have carelessly omitted it).

637 liuing]
Malone (ed. 1790): Property (OED, vbl. sb. 4). Brown (ed. 1976): Means of livelihood.

638 ther’s mine]
Apparently Kent declined it at 631.

638 beg]
Capell (1783, 1.2:150): Having nothing to buy it with.

638 of]
From. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 512): Off, so emending. But the English and Shn. idiom is always to beg something of or from a person (OED, Beg v. 1b, 2a, 2c); to beg something off a person, possibly modern slang, is unattested in OED and appears nowhere else in Sh.

638 thy]
Verity (ed. 1897): It is a sign of his familiarity that he addresses his master almost always by thou.

640 whip]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): The punishment given to fools who exceed their privilege of uttering unwelcome truths in the form of jests, comparing AYL 1.2.84–5 (249). Verity (ed. 1897), Harrison (ed. 1937, rev. 1949), and Foakes (ed. 1997) provide evidence. Wells (ed. 2000): Lear may carry a whip (presumably from the hunt), and may threaten the Fool with it.

641 Truth…kenell]
F’s contraction Truth’s and omission of that are somewhat more colloquial. See nn. 589, 1667. Eccles (ed. 1792): An oblique allusion to the effects of Cordelia’s sincerity, thus explaining Lear’s reply in 644. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): The fool compares himself to the honest male dog whipped out. Lothian (1949, p. 8): The Fool was a constant reminder to all, especially to kings, of their subjection to Truth. Foakes (ed. 1997): May suggest Cordelia, Kent or the Fool. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Compare Launce’s pathetic soliloquy, TGV 4.4.21–8 (1841–8). Brown (ed. 1976): The fool probably slinks away from his master, imitating a dog.

641 must to]
On the omission of the verb of motion see n. 312.

642 Ladie oth’e brach]
Sisson (1956, 2:231): The Folio reading [theLady Brach]…is far more effective and relevant…with its plain hint at Goneril or Regan, braches of noble rank, and sycophantic. Wilson (ed. 1960): The F variant is seen to be an ordinary misprint of the omitted letter [’s] type. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 533): Q seems an error…but could have been corrected [as by Malone and Steevens; see textual n.] simply by striking out o. F looks instead like deliberate revision, perhaps prompted by Q’s error: instead of a bitch named Lady (Q, as emended), it offers a lady named Bitch. Given the ambiguous meaning of brach (see next n.) both Q and F may make a kind of sense, though each seems strained and odd. Though it is remotely possible that brach is plural and the Q phrase means chief female [OED, Lady sb. 2b] of the hounds or bitches, no such use of the singular form for the plural has been attested. To read the phrase as meaning consort, mate [OED, 7] of the hound seems without point. To make brach synonymous with the dog that must to kennel—i.e. truth in the person of the Fool— and to identify the Lady therefore specifically with his hostess-mistress Goneril, who stinks as she stands by the fire, would be, for the Fool, to risk certain whipping. That same objection applies almost equally to the F reading, though there the identification with Goneril is more oblique, less absolute; to try to avoid it altogether seems to result in redundancy—the female bitch or Madam Bitch (Ribner, ed. 1967)—though Rann (ed. 1794) takes the phrase, without capitals, to mean simply a favourite lap-dog, and Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 373) avoids tautology differently: Truth is a dog of low social status—the Lady Brach is pictured as of high social status. Edwards (ed. 1975): That refined bitch, untruth. Craig (ed. 1901) cites Samuel Rowlands’s Martin Mark-all (1610, p. 9), in which a grand jury includes Friskin Fitz-Fizler, my Lady Brache[’s] Gent. Vsher of Feuersham. In all probability Q is in error, but F is by no means clearly preferable; as Duthie (op. cit., p. 372) notes, F’s theLady could easily be an accidental inversion by the compositor of the Q reading without its possibly erroneous o. About half the eds. follow Malone in striking out Q’s o, taking Lady as a dog’s proper name, as it is in Q1 1H4 3.1.236 (1780), heare lady my brache (F, less probably, heare (Lady) my Brach). Steevens (ed. 1773): Still a common name for a hound. Horsman (ed. 1973): This reading weakens the contrast between outcast and aristocrat, with its glance at Cordelia expelled and disinherited for telling truth while her sisters were welcomed in. Possibly (Blayney, apud Halio, ed. 1994) Q’s o is a misreading of terminal e on Ladye, though Sh. elsewhere uses that sp. only in the pl. Several proposed emendations convert Ladie to some variant of lie in order to make an antithesis with Truth: see . Walker (1953, p. 66) refines on this idea, perhaps too ingeniously, in The lie o’th’ brach, detecting a double reference to lie (untruth) and lye (the detergent made from urine) and the latter word makes it clear why the stink was mentioned. Duthie (op. cit., p. 642) suspects that an aural error of Lye a for Liar in a reported text was misinterpreted by the Q compositor as a contraction of Ladie and an o. Similarly Stone (1980, p. 187) supposes Ly of Lye (mistaken for an abbreviation of Lady) and a detached e resembling, because linked to the succeeding word, an o. Muir (ed. 1952): Perhaps the anthithesis is not between Truth and Falsehood, but between Truth and Flattery. Shakespeare often associates dogs with flatterers. There may even be a suggestion that Cordelia is truth, and Goneril and Regan flattering bitches. So Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956): Fawning flattery like that of a petted bitch. Though many eds. suspect a glance at Goneril, Spilsbury & Marshall (ed. 1905), on a hint from Moberly (ed. 1876; see n. 644), suggest Oswald, as does Wilson (op. cit.), who adopts Letherland’s (apud Steevens, ed. 1773) emendation [the] lady’s brach, i.e. favoured animal: The effeminate puppy Oswald who, the Fool implies, had thrust him from his accustomed place by the fire. The abusive brach…forms a fitting climax to the epithets mongrel, whoreson dog, cur that the angry Lear had just been heaping upon the Steward. Moreover, by Truth’s a dog the Fool clearly means himself,…who had been whipped for speaking true [696]. His antithesis should therefore be another person, a member of Gon.’s household, and one that Lear w[oul]d know as a liar. Horsman (op. cit.): This is much less apposite—if indeed brach can be used abusively of a male at this date—for Oswald has just been driven out by Kent. And Lear has no reason to think Oswald a liar. Davidson (1998, p. 317): Stenographic spelling of Lady Oath, the Brach; but Goneril is never associated with swearing oaths.

642 brach]
Though Sh. uses the word at least four and possibly six times, it is not found in any contemporary English dictionary, though Florio’s Italian dictionary, World of Words (1611), defines Bràcca A brache, or a bitch, a beagle, and Cotgrave’s French Dictionarie (1611) defines Brachet as A kind of little hound and Braque as A kind of short-tayled setting dog. Barrett’s polyglot Alvearie (1580) defines Brache as Biche. Canicula…Petite chienne, Hound as Canis odorus. Canis odorisequus.…Braque, and Dog as Bitch, canis…chien, ou une chienne. Madden (1907, p. 51 n.): The word appears to have been originally synonymous with rache, meaning a hound hunting by scent (see the notes on Rache and Brach in the Appendix to The Master of Game [ed. W. & F. Baillie-Grohman, 1904; N. Y., 1909, pp. 246–7]). The meaning seems to have been in transition. Craig (ed. 1901): A species of small hound which hunted by scent. See [Tro. 2.1.114 (967; brooch in Q, F); Lr. 2026]; but it was generally in Shakespeare’s day used (to quote the Gentleman’s Recreation [by Nicholas Cox; 1674, p. 28]) as a mannerly name for all hound bitches. That this meaning for it was creeping in as early as Henry the Eighth’s reign appears from a passage in Sir Thomas More’s [d. 1535] Dialogue of Comfort against Tribulation, p. 199, ed. [1553]: I am so connyng <i.e. unskilful (ironical)>, that I cannot tell whither among them <i.e., in the phrase of hunting men> a bych be a bych or no. But as I remember she is no bych, but a brache [ed. 1976, 12:295]. OED does not clearly support Craig’s claim that the latter meaning was general in Sh.’s day, and Sh. seems to use both senses. As the modern term of abuse for a female the word appears in Jonson’s Alchemist 1.1.111 but not in Sh.

644 A…mee]
Moberly (ed. 1876) takes the line as referring to Oswald (see n. 642), an interpretation accepted by Furness (ed. 1880), Wilson (ed. 1960), and others. Craig (ed. 1901): Lear may be referring to himself: Are the words another expression of the bubbling-up sorrow for his conduct towards his younger daughter, as if he would say a plague take me for my folly? Most eds. follow Rolfe (ed. 1880): Why may it not refer to the Fool, who has just nettled his master into a hint of the whip? Cf. A bitter fool [666]. Page (ed. 1889): How bitterly the fool’s words come home to me! Though Deighton (ed. 1891) thinks Lear hit hard in the remembrance of the way in which he had allowed flatterers to deceive him, the Fool has not mentioned flatterers, and Lear may simply be making a real or mock complaint at receiving impertinence when he expected amusement. Verity (ed. 1897): Said, I think, half lightly but with a touch of displeasure. Brooke (ed. 1947): The Fool’s talk rubs me shrewdly where I am sore. Lear, however, whose conscience has begun to hurt him, is not ungrateful for this counter-irritant and encourages it for the distraction it affords; so Harrison (ed. 1948). Foakes (ed. 1997): Referring to the Fool, Cordelia, or both? Hunter (ed. 1972): The remark refers generally to memory of Gonerill’s household—How intolerably bitter is the situation I’m in! Weis (ed. 1993): Perhaps referring…to the Fool’s image of the stinking brach. Brown (ed. 1976): Possibly directed to his attendants, laughing at the fool.

644 pestilent]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Plaguy (OED, a. 4, citing Rom. 4.5.144 [2719] as its first ex.). In Marston’s Malcontent (1604, 3.1.131) Passarello is called A pestilent Fool.

644 gull]
F’s gall is universally preferred. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 373): Doubtless a misreading of a as u. Only Stone (1980, p. 224) defends Q as meaning deception or simpleton. Taylor (1983, p. 453): But this disregards to me. Kittredge (ed. 1940): An irritation; an irritating creature. To gall is, literally, to rub the skin off, so as to make a sore spot (OED, sb.2 2, 3; v.1 1). Muir (ed. 1952): But the word also means the secretion of the liver, bile, something intensely bitter (OED, sb.1 1).

645 Sirra]
See nn. 411, 627. Wilson (ed. 1960): As usual the Fool inverts, applying to his master the term his master has just applied to him [640]. More probably (and properly) addressed to the servant Kent; see textual n. and nn. 646, 647.

646 Doe]
Lear’s speech does not imply that the Fool has just spoken to him. Having heard some unwelcome sharp remarks heretofore, Lear encourages what promises to be a conventional fool’s routine, as the Fool resumes the instruction of Kent begun in 627. Capell (1783, 1.2:150): Kent is to be taught by [648–57], and…replies to’t when over, Lear is only call’d on to mark it. But Capell’s reassignment of this speech, as being so expressive…of Kent’s character, is unnecessary.

647 vncle]
The same as F’s Nuncle; see n. 634. Addressed to Lear, in answer to 646, but also to suggest that, though the Fool is speaking to Kent, every line of his speech reflects on Lear’s behavior.

648–57 haue…score]
Muir (ed. 1952): Florio, Second Fruites [1591], pp. 101–5, has some similar rhymed proverbs: The bottome of your purse or heart, | To anie man doe not empart. | Doe not giue your selfe to plaie, | Vnles you purpose to decaie [p. 101]; Shun wine, dice, and letchery, | Else will you come to beggery [p. 105]. Tilley A202 compares the proverb Speak not All you know, do not all you can, believe not all you hear. Blayney (1984, privately) points out that on the same p. of John Willis’s The Art of Stenographie (1602, fol. D4) with Merlin’s Prophecie (see n. 1735) are the verses Yf thou loose much, and gaine nought, | Yf thou spendest much, and mindest nought, | Yf thou borrow much, and pay nought, | And lookest in thy pursse, and findest nought, | Thou mayst be sory in thine hart, but say nought. Danby (1945, p. 19): The Fool’s model of cautionary excellence is the canny capitalist and self-denying puritan combined. Traversi (1952, pp. 52–3): The speech is simply a compendium of the moral principles followed by the new rich of the time in their progress to power; thrift, temperance, and a distrust of the more generous human impulses are the supreme virtues, and the successful practice of usury is their reward. The only factor that distinguishes the Fool’s expression of these contemporary commonplaces is the curiously wry, acid concentration with which they are uttered, and the use of deliberately monotonous rhyme, to deprive them of all moral attractiveness.…The observation of facts, and a keen sense of coming developments, prevent him from identifying himself with the opinions he has himself uttered. Wilson (ed. 1960): The speech bids Lear be everything a Fool is not: canny, close-fisted, unsociable, strait-laced, in short a miser or usurer whose sole aim in life is to make money breed. McCann (ed. 1964): A string of wise sayings not particularly relevant to Lear, except that they stress the importance of common sense. Hunter (1972, p. 338): Probably not sung; incantation through words alone, making music superfluous. For a modern musical setting, see Gooch & Thatcher (1991, 1:635). Brown (ed. 1976): The two rhymes of the set-piece are persistent, and its advocacy of prudence can be made funny in performance by a similarly persistent seriousness of delivery, or by an opposite and tantalizing flippancy. Taylor (1985, pp. 200–5) finds throughout the speech ambiguities designed not to enlightern but to bewilder…reason, ours and Lear’s,…thereby advanc[ing] the revolution of perspective, from Lear as malefactor to Lear as sufferer. Leinwand (1987, p. 230): A program for Stuart absolutism. Rather than drain the exchequer and challenge Parliament, a seventeenth-century king must go to school with the new men. Halio (ed. 1992): Set in sing-song rhyme to emphasise its conventional wisdom. Perhaps the very point is that in his actions Lear continually ignores common wisdom; see the following nn.

648 haue…shewest]
Craig (ed. 1901): Do not parade thy wealth. Wilson (ed. 1960): Hoard your goods. Perhaps more may include other things than wealth, such as power or authority. In any case, Lear has little left to show, as the Fool knows.

648 shewest]
Herford (ed. 1899): Seemest to have (OED, Show v. 30d?). Cf. n. 753. More probably, display (OED, 2).

649 speake…knowest]
Craig (ed. 1901): Be not a babbler. Kittredge (ed. 1940), more probably: Don’t tell everything you know. So the proverb; see n. 648–57. Lear has spoken more than he knows about the disloyalty of Kent and the ingratitude of Cordelia. Rosenberg (1972, p. 113), noting the tensions…between what [the Fool] says and what he is: He himself speaks less than he knows.

650 lend…owest]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Don’t lend your last penny. Lear has given away almost everything.

650 owest]
See n. 221.

651 ride…goest]
Crook (ed. 1907), following Craig (ed. 1901): Take things as easy as possible, ride rather than walk. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Cf. Roxburghe Ballads, ed. Chappell, I, 59: He is a foole will go a-foot and let his horse stand still. The aim is of course to husband one’s energy, not to save shoe leather (Wilson, ed. 1960; Skillan, ed. 1967). Though Lear calls to horse at 1600 he is afoot for the rest of the play except when driven to Dover (2050).

651 goest]
OED (v. 1): To walk, quoting this l.

652 learne…trowest]
Mrs. Griffith (1775, p. 357): Not to embrace all opinions. So Tovey (ed. 1896), proverbially: Don’t believe all you hear (cf. n. 648–57). Alternatively, following Capell (1783, 1.2:50) and Furness (ed. 1880): Learn more than you already know. Eds. are divided between these two readings; each applies to Lear, who has already leaped to conclusions and will long resist learning the truth. Tovey’s third alternative, Ascertain much, and don’t indulge in guesses, has been accepted by only Henley (ed. 1903).

652 trowest]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Believe (OED, v. 3, quoting this l.). Capell (1783, 1.2:150): Knowest, citing the know/trow variant at 726. Though OED does not attest the latter meaning exactly, think (v. 4) and the rare to verify; to ascertain (v. 7) are close, and Schmidt (1875) gives a few Shn. exx. in which Trow you? means Do you know? Caldecott (MS notes, 1813–33): First thinkest of.

653 set…throwest]
Griffith (1775, p. 357): Never set equal to the stake you throw for. Schmidt (ed. 1879): If [less] is an adjective, then the meaning is: Set a less sum than thou hast won by thy last throw; if an adverb: Keep on throwing, but set nothing (Ger.). Most eds. incline to some refinement of Mrs. Griffith’s reading. Deighton (ed. 1891): Stake a smaller sum than that which you hope to win…i.e., do not risk your money unless you can get odds given you. Tovey (ed. 1896): Let your stakes be always low.…It is a warning against high play. Lee (ed. 1908): A confused way of saying Keep something in reserve when you stake a throw of the dice. Harrison (ed. 1937): Don’t bet a larger stake than you can afford to lose. Craig (ed. 1931): Don’t bet all you can. Muir (ed. 1952): Don’t stake all your winnings at a single throw. Wilson (ed. 1960) compares 1H4 4.1.46–7 (2270–1), To set…Al at one cast, but the parallel may not be exact. All eds. assume that the line refers to play at dice except Chambers; see next n. The line’s general meaning—Play prudently—is clear enough; Lear’s actions have been rash.

653 set]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Stake (OED, v. 14, quoting this l.). Chambers (ed. 1906) alone: Call (at cards).

653 throwest]
OED (v.1 10): To play at dice. Rolfe (ed. 1880): Seems to be = throwest for. Neilson & Thorndike (ed. 1909): Seems equivalent to win.

654–5 leaue…doore]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Give up drinking and licentiousness and remain quietly at home instead of gadding about. Brooke (ed. 1947), more generally: Stay at home and tend to your business. Wilson (ed. 1960) compares MV 2.5.53–5 (890–2), emphasizing thrift. The lines refer more obviously to Gloucester’s past conduct than to Lear’s, though both, as the audience can by now recognize, are in the process of breaking up their families for different reasons.

655 in a doore]
OED (Door, sb. 5): In at door, -s, = indoors; (A-doors): A phonetic reduction apparently of both of doors, o’ doors,…and at doors…in the phrases forth a doors, out a doors, in a doors, for which also the full forms occur. Cf. Franz §239, and 1666, 2170. Brown (ed. 1976): At home.

656–7 more…score]
Griffith (1775, p. 357): Improving one’s capital. Eccles (ed. 1792): For the score which thou now possessest, thou shalt have more than two tens. Muir (ed. 1952): Meaning, I suppose, that for each pound one would have more than twenty shillings. Wilson (ed. 1960): You’ll make a score (of money) grow to more than two tens (through usury). See [660–1]. Brown (ed. 1976): You will gain in every transaction, with a pun on score = reckoning. The general idea is that such behavior is profitable in some way: Your savings will increase (Kittredge, ed. 1940), you will do better than break even (Harbage, ed. 1958), You will have more than maximum felicity (Brooke, ed. 1947).

658 Lear.]
Knight (ed. 1840): The folio with great propriety assigns [the speech] to Kent, in reply to the fool’s address to him [645]. Hudson (ed. 1856): As the Fool’s speech was addressed to Lear [see 647], there can be little doubt that the quartos are right. The Fool is probably speaking to both of them: see n. 647. The fact that the Fool addresses Lear in answer to this speech, at least by 660, may argue that Lear is its speaker. White (ed. 1862) thinks the vocative foole more likely to be Kent’s, since Lear characteristically addresses the Fool by familiar terms of endearment such as boy; but Lear’s last two speeches may not have been friendly either. On the possible confusion of the prefixes see n. 628. Taylor (1983, p. 108): Without [this speech] Kent, in F, would have nothing at all to say after the Fool’s entrance. Kerrigan (1983, p. 219) continues to prefer F (see n. 628): Kent’s interjection here ensur[es] that the exchange does not become monotonous. One four-word speech in 77 lines does not break the monotony of F very much; possibly Sh. intended to keep Kent in the background during this long exchange, and his single interruption in F is anomalous and unmotivated.

658 nothing]
OED (sb. 3): A thing…not worth reckoning, considering, or mentioning; cf. (6b): A trivial or trifling remark. Goggin (ed. 1910): Nonsense, citing MV 1.1.114 (123). Halio (ed. 1992): No big news, i.e. conventional wisdom.

659–60 Then…for’t]
Though the lawyer Furness (ed. 1880) quotes at length Campbell’s (1859, pp. 97–9) defense of the bar against the Fool’s sarcasm, the point of the quip is proverbial. Tilley L125: A Lawyer will not plead but for money (a fee). Hunter (ed. 1972), simply: No fee, no breath, nothing. Elton (1966, p. 325 n.) cites another instance from Francis Lenton, The Innes of Court Anagrammatist (1634, sig. C). Crook (ed. 1907), following Deighton (ed. 1891): The idea is that advice which is worth having is worth paying for. Skillan (ed. 1967) finds an additional meaning: It meant nothing to kent because he did not require the information.…kent was not the reason for the moral in the lines. The Sokols (2000, p. 198): Shakespeare’s references to attorneys-at-law…imply mockery or even reproach.

659–60 like]
F’s added ’tis must be understood to make sense of Q; it was probably omitted by accident.

659–60 breath]
Hudson (ed. 1871): Words. Harbage (ed. 1958): Voice, counsel.

659–60 vnfeed]
OED (ppl. a.): Not rewarded with, or engaged by, a fee; unpaid, quoting this l. as its earliest ex.

660 you…nothing]
Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): A fool’s reward for a clever jest or rhyme was a small coin from the bystander—e.g., Feste’s gratillity (TN 2.3.26 [726]). Muir’s (ed. 1952) parallel from Leir 654—He lou’d me not, and therfore gaue me nothing (see )—is remote.

660 you…you]
Johnson (1975, pp. 151–6): Here is the only time when the Fool addresses Lear with the properly respectful pronoun; his use otherwise of thou is a sign that fool and king become co-equals in foolishness, misery, and humanity. The point is unprovable, since we do not hear how the Fool addresses Lear before his abdication; his intimacy may be habitual, and no reason is given for the exception here.

660–1 can…nothing]
Spilsbury & Marshall (ed. 1905): A subtle hint that there is more in what he has said than Lear seems to think. Wilson (ed. 1960): You is emphatic. At least the question is clearly a lead into his next quip. Joseph (ed. 1966): (i) Get no interest out of nothing (use has the sense usury); (ii) employ nothing to any purpose.

660 vse]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Interest (cf. n. 656–7). But as the Fool’s next speech makes clear, he is thinking of rent (OED, Use sb. 4), not usury (OED, 5b). Fischer (1985): Benefit, profit.

661 vncle]
See n. 634.

663 nothing…nothing]
For the proverb, see n. 96. Verity (ed. 1897): So he had told Cordelia, and he does not yet see the applicability of the maxim to his own case; but the Fool points it out. Hunter (ed. 1972) unnecessarily limits the meaning to the arithmetical point that nothing cannot be multiplied into something.

664–5 so…to]
Wilson (ed. 1960): I.e. he must expect nothing now, having given the land away. Foakes (ed. 1997): Possibly a pun on rent = torn, alluding to the division of the kingdom.

664 Prethee]
A 17th-c. sp. of prithee, Archaic colloquialism for (I) pray thee (OED, Prithee int. phr. arch.). In Q1 of this play this form (3 occurrences) alternates with prethe (5 occurrences), prithe (3 occurrences), prithee (1 occurrence) and prithy (1 occurrence). Cf. 692, 885, 1080, 1512, 1804, 1891, 2007, 2047, 2228, 2755, 3231, 3285. (I) pray you occurs 10 times. Prethe and prithe are set by both Q compositors and may reflect MS spellings; all the rest are set by Q Compositor B.

666 bitter]
OED (a. 7): Of words (or the person who utters them): Stinging, cutting, harsh, keenly or cruelly reproachful, quoting this l. Craig (ed. 1901): Cruelly sarcastic, citing AYL 3.5.69 (1842). In Marston’s Malcontent (1604, 3.1.147) Passarello is called A bitter fool.

667–9 Doo’st…mee]
In Q the Fool’s question and Lear’s reply introduce another of the Fool’s satiric routines, about the sweet and bitter fool; in F the routine has been omitted, yet the introduction to it remains. The result is a striking non-sequitur as the Fool offers and the King encourages a line of thought that is straightway abandoned as the Fool begins a quite unrelated routine about the crowns of an egg. To most eds. the disjunction has seemed the result of incomplete and clumsy theatrical or censorial cutting—a bleeding cut—in F. Doran (1931, p. 76): The cut was carelessly made, because this question is left without a reply. Stone (1980, p. 234): The cut should have begun at line [667].…[F] Compositor E…miscalculat[ed] the length of the marginal line marking the deletion in his copy, which reproduced a deletion marked by the bookkeeper in a playhouse MS. Halio (ed. 1992, p. 79): Possibly the [deletion] marks did not extend fully enough or clearly enough from the beginning of the passage. Early eds., from F1 through Rowe (1714; see textual nn.), unaware of the Q version, let the discontinuity stand; since Theobald, eds. have removed the difficulty by restoring the Q lines; Halio instead removes lines 667–9. Taylor (1983, pp. 102–10), believing that Sh. made or approved of all the major changes in F, defends the result of the F omission: Shakespeare intended the passage to stand just as it does in the Folio.…In fact, the difficulty here is entirely of a piece with the difficulty of the Fool’s speech elsewhere: the promise of meaning followed by deliberate obfuscation, sudden changes of direction, reliance upon and frustration of the expectations and suspicions of his audience. Do’st…sweet one [667–8, F] can easily be no more than a rhetorical question; Lear answers it like a literal one…; the Fool pauses and then says something which appears completely out of the way. But is it? With the Fool we (like Lear) never know. The Fool’s remarks are generally clearly pertinent, however oblique; he is not given to non-sequiturs.
Baldwin (1944, 1:739): Indebted to Erasmus’s Quid inter fatuum & sapientem? (Colloquies, in Opera, 1703, 1:742).

667 Doo’st]
On Q2’s and F’s added thou see n. 562.

667 my boy]
Wilson (ed. 1960): As usual the Fool inverts, applying to his master the term his master has just applied to him. Wiles (1987, p. 191), fancifully: Addressed to his marotte or fool’s head on a stick,…not found in sixteenth-century English fooling, and…therefore a sign of antiquity. Not explicitly found in this play either; cf. n. 923–4. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 51), also assuming an old-fashioned bauble or marotte: To avoid suggesting any direct connection between the character in the play and Archie Armstrong, a favourite of James I, who came with him to London in 1603 as his official court jester.

668, 669+3 bitter]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Unlike 666, Pitiable, grievously afflicted (OED, a. 3).

668 foole.]
F’s substitution of one. is seemingly cosmetic, designed to avoid a fourth repetition in four lines.

669+1–+11 That…snatching]
Thirlby (MS notes, 1725–33): Not left out by Shakespear. Johnson (ed. 1765): This dialogue was…omitted in the folio, perhaps for political reasons, as it seemed to censure the monopolies. Many eds. have found censorship an adequate explanation for the omission. Collier (ed. 1842): The point and truth of the satire were likely to render it obnoxious to those against whom it was levelled. See n. 669+10. But Smith (ed. 1902), anticipated by Delius (1876, p. 141): This objection does not apply to the fool’s verses [669+1–+4], which Theobald restored, noting that the Retrenchment of them by the Players was very injudicious. For, without them, how very absurdly does Lear reply, Do’st…boy? Granville-Barker (1927, p. 225): Apart from politics, The whole cut is a useful tightening of the dialogue, though seeming at a first glance a little clumsy. Similarly Chambers (1930, 1:467): Though censorship is possible, we probably have to do with ordinary theatrical cutting. Doran (1931, p. 76): Perhaps the censor, Sir George Buc, objected to the slur cast by the Fool on Lords and great men, as in 1611 he changed a reference to great men fearing death to some men, in Second Maiden’s Tragedy 3.161 (ed. Lancashire, 1978; but see p. 277: Perhaps…an allusion to James’s pathological fear of death). Hart (1942, p. 147): A reviser cut these lines of crude clowning. Greg (1955, pp. 375, 387): The play was doubtless cut for representation; in this passage censorship is possible but uncertain. Taylor (1983, pp. 102–110): The cut represents both censorship and Sh.’s intent. Finding satirical allusions not only to monopolies but to a king’s excessive hunting, a surfeit of knights, courtly gluttony and promiscuity, bad advisers, and regal folly (see the following notes), the Master of the Revels, sensitive to a rash of recent dramatic satire, could not have allowed the passage. Indeed, its inclusion in Q is evidence that Q was not based upon a report or memory of the play as performed. Still, by a happy serendipity, the censor’s cut suited Sh.; indeed, he may have welcomed the deletion. Besides removing two troublesome references (see nn. 669+1, 669+8), the omission serves the laudable dramatic function of abbreviating the fairly repetitive exchanges between Lear and his Fool here,…hardly the Fool’s most brilliant.…Shakespeare’s own impulse to comment upon contemporary abuses may have led him to write at greater length than the play required. The censor, by curbing that impulse, may actually…have done the timeless work of art a service, one which Sh. acceded to, Taylor believes, rather than substitute a politically less offensive passage. Whether the cut was made by the company, a reviser, a censor, or Sh. is open to informed conjecture; but Sh.’s response to it, if he did not make it—resignation, welcoming approval, indifference—is a matter of pure imagination. The clumsy failure to cut 667–9 may suggest a lack of close authorial attention, and for that reason Stone (1980, p. 234), like many others, assigns the ensuing cut to the book-keeper in the theatre. Howard-Hill (1985, p. 168) is skeptical that the same man (Buc) who found the passage offensive in 1605–6 did not react to it in 1608 when he licensed the quarto for publication.…The notion that it was deleted in the prompt-book is a figment of the imagination. Richman (1986, p. 381): In performance, one of the Fool’s most successful sequences.…Every night the spectators laughed and gasped, fully understanding the comedy and growing pain of Lear’s situation. Calvo (1992, pp. 52–3): The only thing the Folio achieves by suppressing these lines is to deprive the audience of a punch-line…leaving the joke unfinished. Weis (ed. 1993, p. 17): Sh. would not have cut so many lines if only the two lines referring to monopolies were offensive, and he would not have made so bad a patch at 669–70: Perhaps the general disrespect shown by the Fool to purely symbolic royalty (and approved by Kent’s This…lord) may have been thought too subversive. Cf. Clare (1990, p. 134) in n. 473+1–+6, and .

669+1–+4 That…there]
Possibly sung. See n. 684. Thirlby (MS notes, 1725–33): Shakespear did not cast this out in revising, tis almost incredible that he shd. Wiles (1987, p. 669) imagines byplay with a fool’s bauble, a marotte who can swivel his gaze from the sweet fool in Motley (Armin) to the bitter fool (Lear). Neither Armin nor any contemporary English actor is known to have used such a prop, though Wiles identifies it with Armin’s cudgel Sir Timothy Truncheon; see nn. 667, 923–4.

669+1 Lord…land]
Page (ed. 1889): I.e. thyself. Tovey (ed. 1896): A figment of the fool’s, to point the sarcasm. There was no such lord; the notion was entirely Lear’s own. So Kittredge (ed. 1940), Harbage (ed. 1958), Wilson (ed. 1960). Brooke (ed. 1947): A masterpiece of indirect arraignment. The king can do no wrong, but the king can stand for the hypothetical lord who counselled the king to the king’s own folly. Bradley (1904, p. 447), without evidence: Gloucester may have given such advice. Craig (ed. 1901) and others: A survival from the source-play: Skalliger, a lord in the old play [Leir 32 ff.], who gives certain advice to Leir about the division of the kingdom, may have been in Shakespeare’s mind here; see . Taylor (1983, p. 108) approves of F’s eliminating this presumed hangover from the Leir version: F more clearly makes Lear himself singly responsible for the decision to abdicate. Lear otherwise seems to make his own decisions, sometimes against the court’s expectations (see 4–10); and the Lord is completely imaginary in 669+2 and is otherwise unidentified.

669+2–+4 Come…there]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): The Fool places himself opposite to Lear and at some little distance. He accompanies the recitation with gestures.

669+2 doe…stand]
For attempts to regularize the meter, see textual nn. and . Kittredge (ed. 1940): Thou and him are emphasized.

669+2 for him stand]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Stand where you are and impersonate that lord. Harbage (ed. 1958): The Fool thus identifying Lear as his own foolish counsellor. Skillan (ed. 1967): He goes and stands beside Lear.…[At there] he lightly points across himself to lear. But the meaning is anything but clear (see next n.). The Fool may simply be directing Lear to stand out there, in the same space just occupied by the Lord, who now stands next to the Fool, heere by mee.

669+3 sweet…foole]
Though Tovey (ed. 1896) identifies the sweet fool as Lear, and Verity (ed. 1897) the bitter fool as the Lord, Lear must be the bitter (see n. 668, 669+3) fool out there, and the Lord probably the sweet one, standing next to the Fool, who is acting as judge between them. Harbage (ed. 1958), less probably: Lear is the born fool as distinct from himself, the fool in motley, professionally satirical. Eccles (ed. 1792): The epithet sweet refers to the Lord’s effecting his purpose by flattery, and soothing language; more probably, Upon a comparison, himself should be considered as the sweet fool, the consequences of the other’s advice having been found so bitter. Skillan (ed. 1967): The one fool is sweet with sense, the other bitter (poor) without it.

669+3 presently]
See n. 431.

669+4 motley]
Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): The parti-coloured dress of the domestic jester, a modern misconception corrected by Hotson (1952, pp. 14–15, 43, 69–70, 100): Not the gaudy parti-color of the medieval fool, but the idiot’s long coat made of a coarse material of mixed color, probably green— an undemonstrative vesture of humility. The Lord is of course not wearing motley, but has given foolish, irresponsible advice that may allow him to be taken for a jester. The King, on the other hand, is fool in being a man who acts in folly. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 52): The long coat was derived from the coats children wore, as appropriate to the natural with impaired intellect who remained immature, and whose wisdom was instinctive; Shakespeare may have had this image of a natural fool in mind in making Lear address him as boy so frequently, and the Fool call Lear nuncle, as if he were an elderly relative. See n. 626.

669+4 found out]
Probably found means here is to be found, but Harbage (ed. 1958) and Brown (ed. 1976) take found out to mean revealed.

669+4 there]
Delius (ed. 1854): Pointing to the king. Halio (ed. 1973) compares the proverb He who takes counsel of himself has a fool for his client (Tilley F490; neither Tilley nor Dent, 1981, cites this l.). Taylor (1983, p. 105): In early 1606, it would have been hard not to see the Fool’s jibe at Lear as a reflection of King James’s own royal fool [Archie Armstrong] commenting on the folly of James himself in his managing of political affairs. Taylor concedes, however (p. 118 n.) that Anthony Weldon’s description of James as the wisest foole in Christendom cannot be dated before 1623. Shickman (1991, p. 80): The Fool hands a looking glass to Lear. Foakes (ed. 1997): Or his bauble? There is no textual evidence, however, for either property.

669+6–+7 All…with]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Thus he calls Lear a born fool—an idiot. Hunter (ed. 1972): Rather to make the point that we are all born with folly as a characteristic. Edwards (ed. 1975): Contradicting Lear’s view that he could keep his titles when he gave away his power ([144]). Taylor (1983, pp. 117–18, n. 54): James created sixty peers; he cites satiric references to the practice in several plays from 1603–7. Clare (1990, p. 133): A reference to the giving away of titles readily evokes the image of King James, as does the Fool’s dismissal of Lear as a fool: James was known as the wisest fool in Christendom. Though she concedes (p. 149 n.) that If the term originated with [Anthony] Weldon, it post-dates an early performance of King Lear, she nonetheless presumes, without evidence, that it reflects a common perception of the King, and argues that a censor therefore cut these lines from the F text. Taylor, op. cit., p. 188, n. 65): Weldon’s Court and Character of King James (1650) was written after 1618. Calvo (1992, p. 53): The Folio suppresses two crucial lines.…It is precisely in these two lines…that the Fool finally makes his point that Lear has been a fool for giving away his kingdom. Weis (ed. 1993, p. 17): The remark points to an Erasmian understanding of folly.…Lear, the Fool tells him, was born innocent of the wicked ways of the world.

669+8 altogether foole]
Furness (ed. 1880): The concrete for the abstract, evidently taking This to refer to the Fool’s remarks. Others think it refers to the Fool himself, who to judge from the pertinence of his speech, Kent humorously observes, is not altogether a fool—a phrase spoken of the Fool in Tim. 2.2.115 (782). Page (ed. 1889): The Fool wilfully mistakes the sense of…altogether. Kittredge (ed. 1940): And plays with it as if it meant one who has all the folly that there is—is altogether the fool, the sole fool. The missing article makes the wordplay possible. Dent (1981, A231.1): Possibly proverbial: Not Altogether (a) fool (ass).

669+9 faith]
Deighton (ed. 1891): ’Faith, i.e. in faith; to tell you the truth (OED, sb. 12b). Cf. 2347+26, 2393, 2828.

669+9 Lords…men]
Verity (in Irving & Marshall, ed. 1889): To not a few, [this] would have suggested [in 1623; but the lines were in Q (1608), not F]…Sir Giles Mompesson [see next n.],…the prototype of Massinger’s Sir Giles Overreach in A New Way to Pay Old Debts.…This famous monopolist long continued to be regarded as the type of evil and avarice in high places, citing Massinger’s The Bondman 2.3.[69–70] and Thomas Randolph’s Aristippus and Hey for Honesty [Works, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1875, pp. 16, 456].

669+9 let me]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Leave me alone…in sole possession of folly. Black (1984, p. 94): Professional fools guarded their places very jealously.

669+10 monopolie]
Jennens (ed. 1770): A patent out of court for being sole fool. Warburton (ed. 1747): A satire on the gross abuses of monopolies at that time; and the corruption and avarice of the courtiers who commonly went shares with the patentee. Steevens (ed. 1778): Monopolies were in Shakespeare’s time the common objects of satire, citing Dekker’s Match Me in London (ca. 1611–13, 1.4.140), Lording Barry’s Ram Alley (1607–8; ed. 1611, fol. F3v), and Birth of Merlin (?1608; ed. Brooke, Apocrypha, 1908, 5.2.58). Knight (ed. 1840): In the reign of Elizabeth almost every article of necessity—iron, skins, leather, wool, yarn, coal, beer, glass, paper, saltpetre, potash—was consigned by the prerogative of the crown to the monopoly of some patentee. Staunton (ed. 1859): These Monopolies had been carried to an outrageous extent in the reigns of Henry VII., Henry VIII., and Queen Elizabeth; and the evil was not much abated at the period when this tragedy was written; nor was it effectually remedied until the passing of the statute of the twenty-first of James, 1623. Verity (in Irving & Marshall, ed. 1889) quotes Henry Feilden’s Short Constitutional History ([1882], pp. 186–7): The system was much abused under Elizabeth, who granted her favourites monopolies.…In 1571 a question was asked in Parliament about the abuse, but the proposer was summoned before the council, and the subject dropped until 1597, when an address on the subject was presented to the Queen, who promised to recall the illegal monopolies. The abuse, however, continued, and in 1601, a bill against them was introduced by Lawrence Hyde, and so strongly supported that the queen had to yield. Monopolies, however, continued, and were freely sold by James I. Tovey (ed. 1896): The last address of Queen Elizabeth to the Commons of England was a concession abolishing certain monopolies; and thus for some years it became at once possible and popular to speak against them. Craig (ed. 1901): In spite of the Declaratory Act against monopolies, passed at the end of Elizabeth’s reign, James I. constantly granted them to his needy courtiers, and there was a great popular outcry in consequence. Patterson (1989, p. 109): When James succeeded,…many patents were still extant, and others were distributed in the first rush of liberality (what James called his Christmas) to his Scottish followers. Like Warburton, Kittredge (ed. 1940) thinks the satire is against not only the fact but also the means of gaining a monopoly: The courtiers who had helped…to secure the monopoly would insist on having their share—and so would the court ladies. Monopolies, and the bribery or corrupt influence by means of which they were often obtained, were constant subjects of satire in Shakespeare’s time. Cf. Rom. 1.4.77–8 [528–30].
Some eds. have speculated that the special sensitivity of the topic just before the publication of the Folio led to the excision of this presumed satire at that time. Knight (ed. 1840): By the 21st of James the First this most injurious prerogative of the crown was got rid of, and all commissions and letters patent for the sole buying, selling, making, or using anything are declared contrary to the laws of the realm. Patents for new inventions to be granted for a limited time were excepted by this statute. It is curious that this passage of the text is not found in the folio edition of 1623, at which time the struggle for the abolition of monopolies, and the resistance on the part of the monopolists, were no doubt carried to extremes that would have rendered such a direct allusion offensive to the court, which had an interest in supporting the corruption. Staunton (ed. 1859): In 1621, Sir Giles Mompesson was impeached for abusing his monopoly.…In 1624, monopolies were abolished by Parliament [Feilden, loc. cit.]. Note that the first folio appeared in what must have been the most critical year in the long struggle, viz. 1623. Taylor (1983, p. 102), who believes that this passage was censored before the play was ever staged in 1605–6: The King’s granting of monopolies was debated in Parliament in 1604 and 1606 (as well as in 1610, 1614, and 1621). Foakes (ed. 1997): It was only late in [James’s] reign that the number of awards grew so large as to lead to a parliamentary campaign against them in 1620–1 [citing Roger Lockyer, The Early Stuarts, 1989, pp. 190–6]. This is when censorship, or self-censorship [by the company, not Sh., of course], might have led to the cutting of these lines.

669+10 out]
Jennens (ed. 1770): Out of court. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Extant,…given out for my benefit. Smith (ed. 1902): Taken out, granted to me.

669+10 an’t]
Most eds. accept Q2’s on’t. Several Q words spelt with a are given an o in later texts: cf. 577–8, 655, 676, 700, 704, 1105, 1132, 1400, 1478, 1613, 1666, 1860, 2014+28, 2399, 2794. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 374) thinks these Q spellings are errors of transmission, due either to colloquial or dialectal pronunciation or to misreading of a as o such as Q’s uncorr. lodes in this very line. But an’t may very well be Shn.; OED attests that it is a frequent 16th-c. variant of on’t, citing LLL 5.2.460 (2399) ant (Q1598; on’t F), where it means of it as it does here (cf. 1478, and see n. 331). In Ham. 5.1.23 (3212) Q2’s an’t becomes F’s on’t, both meaning of it.

669+10 lodes]
Only a few eds. (see textual n.) have adopted Q’s uncorr. reading, taking it to mean a large part (Collier, ed. 1843). Having in an earlier ed. accepted Collier’s explanation, Dyce (ed. 1865) rejected it: Mark the ridiculous inconsistency of expression in the passage, if the Fool be speaking of lords only,—they would have part on’t—and loads too—they’ll be snatching. Most eds. adopt Q’s corr. Ladies. Greg (1940, pp. 152–3): To explain the original error we may suppose the spelling ladis in the copy. Heilman (1948, p. 326): The sexual innuendo…anticipates [923–4]. Hotson (1954, p. 169): A complacent boast of his physical irresistibility to the other sex. Hunter (ed. 1972): Presumably…illustrated by some indecency with the Fool’s bauble, of phallic shape (Kermode, in Evans, ed. 1974).

669+11 all the foole]
Clearly, says Taylor (1983, p. 103), there is a pun here in the sense all the custard (OED sb1 [earliest ex. dated 1598]). Such a pun, undetected for four centuries, would seem to have no relevance to the context, though Weis (ed. 1993) supplies one: To suggest that there is a greed for folly among the great. The presumed pun is Taylor’s entire evidence for a censorable reference here to the quite incredible competitive gluttony which had already become a notorious feature of banquets at the court of King James. The pun would also explain, Taylor suggests (p. 107), the request in the next line for an egg, out of which custards are made.

669+11 snatching]
Avaricious catching at a share in the monopoly, even a monopoly on folly. Joseph (ed. 1966): I.e., (i) ladies are also foolish; (ii) ladies are always grabbing at me, trying to take hold of parts of me. Apseloff (1980–1, p. 102): Also a bawdy reference to fast copulation. So also Taylor (1983, pp. 102–3, 117 n. 52), taking it as evidence of a censorable allusion to court promiscuity. Taylor’s authority, Colman (1974, p. 214), does not find the double entendre here, perhaps because the Fool is talking of folly, not vice; but Idem (ed. 1982): Fornicating. Bevington (ed. 1988): Snatching at the Fool’s phallic bauble or perhaps crotch (ed. 1992). Wells (ed. 2000) cites Williams (1994, p. 523): The natural fool was thought to be generously endowed genitally. Brown (ed. 1976): Quibbling; see OED (Snatch, sb. 9: A quibble; a captious argument, citing MM 4.2.6 [1861]).

670 Nuncle]
See n. 634.

671 crownes]
Taylor (1983, p. 107): A pun on crowns = coins; the Fool’s offer to pay Lear two crowns—ten shillings—for a single egg makes him seem momentarily, deceptively, an innocent half-wit, easily cheated of his money. Such a pun would be irrelevant to the train of ideas, and the Fool has already established his ability to be unexpectedly cogent.

672 What two crownes]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): The answer to the Fool’s conundrum is obvious, since crowns was a common term for the two parts of the eggshell [unattested in OED; not elsewhere in Sh.]; but Lear wishes to let him make his joke. Conundrums are not meant to be guessed.

674 eate…meate]
Eccles (ed. 1792): A rebuke to Lear, who had not acted so wisely.

674 two…egge]
The eggshell was proverbial for worthlessness. See Tilley E95, Not worth an Eggshell (egg); cf. Ham. 4.4.53 (2743+45). Dent (1981), not Tilley, cites this l. Hulme (1962, pp. 168–9): His egg-shell image is part of grammar school language, citing Withals’s Dictionarie (1553; 1616, p. 233): A peece of an Egge is better then all the shell. The Fool’s point is that any crown that the former King might wear is a mere mockery now that he has given away his real crown and the power it stands for, the empty eggshell being an image suggestive of his impotence. Deeper meanings have been found. Gorfain (1977, p. 250): The Fool’s natural analogy emphasizes the unnatural act Lear has committed. The wholeness of the egg and its simplicity underscore the basic relationship Lear has mistakenly sundered.…[Lear fails] to identify and discriminate bald and golden crowns, to know he is both king and a man. The quintessential image of oneness and life, the egg, cannot be eaten except by dividing its shell…[a] destructive/creative act. So Lear learns that his title alone yields him only his bald crown. The Fool does not, of course, make explicit any analogy between the eggshells and Lear’s bald and golden crowns.

675 clouest]
Not to be taken literally. See n. 147. Foakes (ed. 1997): Divided the kingdom.

675 crowne]
F’s Crownes is clearly an error. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 171): The F compositor may have repeated the plural from the previous line. Compositor E frequently adds a superfluous final -s.

676 borest…backe]
The allusion is to the fable of the old man (and his son) who, foolishly trying to please passers-by, carried their ass rather than riding it. In first identifying the allusion Fairholt (in Halliwell, ed. 1865), followed by countless eds., wrongly attributes the fable to Aesop; it originated in Poggio Bracciolini’s Facetiae (1471, no. c), and was later included in some expanded Latin Aesops, including Camerarius’s eds. of 1542 and 1571. Baldwin (1944, 1:636–7) reports that it was first Englished by William Bullokar in 1585, though Foakes (ed. 1997) finds it in Tales and quicke answeres (1532 [sigs. F3v–4]), adding, The moral is that in trying to please all he pleases no one. The fable also…provides another image of the inversion of order. Craig (ed. 1901): It appears in one of Sh.’s possible sources for this play, Warner’s Albion’s England (1586, p. 71). Montaigne (tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 3:13) describes AEsopes Asse: who…layde his two fore-feete very jocondly upon his masters shoulders; Rowse (ed. 1978) reproduces a mid-16th c. woodcut illustrating this act. There may be an additional allusion. In the 1570 ed. of Barclay’s tr. of Ship of Fooles the ch. Of fooles oppressed with their owne foly is illustrated (fol. 150v) with a woodcut, derived from Sebastian Brant’s Narrenschiff (1494), of an ass rearing its front feet over the back of a man. Among the men who of the slowe Asse shalbe troad downe to hell are they which will not apply their minde To wise mens counsell and aduisement, others who furious of intent, By wrath are driuen to diuers great offence, and suche fooles as suffer paciently, For lacke of beating their children folowe vice. Fraser (1962, Pl. XLIX) reproduces a woodcut from a French tr. of Brant (1497), showing the fool bearing the whole ass and his burden.

676 at’h]
For on th’. OED (A prep.1): A worn-down proclitic form of OE. preposition an, on. Q2 and F read on thy. See n. 700; cf. 1400. The Q1 form and meaning may be Shn., being found in good quartos; elsewhere in F the a is retained in Ham. 5.2.261 (3718) and Tro. 4.5.45 (2598), and changed to o in Tro. 2.1.19 (878) and 5.4.9 (3340). There is no need to think Q2 influenced F here, since as the natural thing to say, [on th’] was likely to be substituted by both printers (Doran, 1931, p. 114). Cf. n. 1955.

676–7 asse…durt]
Partridge (1947, p. 67) detects a scatologic pun, Rubinstein (1984, p. 17), impossibly, one on bared his arse.

677 wit]
OED (sb. 2): Mental capacity, understanding, intellect, reason; (6): Wisdom, good judgment, discretion, prudence. Cf. 680, 682, 700, 885, 1318, 1722, 1729.

677 bald crowne]
The Fool puns on another sense of crown: Schmidt (1874): The head (OED, sb. 17b). Lear’s head is not wholly bald (hairless) since he is repeatedly called white-haired; cf. 1622+1, 1661, 1678–9, 2781. The word bald could mean merely having no hair upon some part of the head (OED, a. 2), e.g. tonsured; Hulme (1962, p. 169) compares Withals’s Dictionarie (1553; 1616, p. 252): Euery one that hath a balde crowne is not called a Priest. An alternative meaning, piebald, white or streaked with white (OED, 5), seems to have been used only of animals, not men. Since Lear has given up his royal crown and appears hatless throughout the play (cf. 1622+7, 2131, 2783+4), bald may mean here nothing more than uncovered, bare-headed (OED, 4d, citing Cor. 4.5.194 [2854]). Wiles (1987, p. 190): Fools often had their heads shaved to prevent lice.…The fool contrasts his own literal baldness with the metaphorical baldness of Lear.…He proves that he speaks like himself…by removing his cockscomb to reveal his baldness. There is of course no evidence that the actor playing the Fool was required to shave his head, and the Fool is referring to Lear’s bald crown, not his own.

678 if…selfe]
Furness (ed. 1880): I.e. like a fool, foolishly. Cf. Tilley F459, A Fool cannot speak unlike himself; neither Tilley nor Dent (1981) cites this l. Lee (ed. 1908): The fool means that he is in earnest, anticipating Kelcy (1932, p. 362): Like a fool—fooling. Kittredge (ed. 1940): If I am a fool to be so outspoken. Foakes (ed. 1997): If I speak (truth) like a fool.

679 let…so]
Cf. n. 640. Why anyone should be whipped for finding a fool’s remarks foolish, and who that person might be, has been much discussed. Eccles (ed. 1792): Possibly…he will deserve to be whipped who does not, or cannot discover that in this instance, at least, he speaks good sense. Perhaps…better…thus—The Fool was accustomed to speak bitter and unpalatable truths, and had sometimes been chastised for so doing.…Let not me be whipped, but him who first finds it to be as I have said i.e. the king himself, who was likely to be soonest sensible of the truth and justness of the sarcasm, and who, he insinuates, deserved whipping for the silly part he had acted. Craig (ed. 1901): If my words are folly, yet it being your interest to believe them good sense, let the finder out of them for folly be whipped, for he can be no friend of yours. Goggin (ed. 1910): Any one who thinks [these words] folly deserves himself to be whipped as a fool. Fools were whipped for impudence, not folly, but perhaps the meaning is simply that if he speaks like a fool he must expect whipping, as a fool must. Kelcy (1932, p. 362): Let not me be whipped for saying it—for words spoken in jest cannot constitute an insult—but him who first finds it to be as I have said—for he will insult the king. However, like myself may mean just the opposite: not in my capacity of jester, but…according to my real opinion.…Let him be whipped who first finds that I am doing so. For by claiming that I really mean it he will insult the king and merit a whipping. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Let him he whipped who first discovers that I have told you the truth. So is emphatic. The implication is that Lear has already made this discovery and that he, if anybody, should be whipped for folly. Wilson (ed. 1960): Sc. as a lying fool, comparing 694, a line the audience has not yet heard. Horsman (ed. 1973): Let the man who will first find it is true <Lear> have the whipping which truth is due to get.

680–3 Fooles…apish]
It is not clear that the Fool sings these lines, and no music for them survives. For conjectural settings see , and for modern musical settings see Gooch & Thatcher (1991, 1:635).

680 Fooles…yeare]
Although most eds. accept F’s alteration of wit to grace, the Q line may have been familiar as a proverb (Tilley F535). Capell (1783, 3.2) discovered in Lyly’s Mother Bombie [1594 (ca. 1589), 2.3.76–7] Gentlemen had neuer lesse wit in a yeere; see n. 677. No instance of a proverb before Lyly and Lr. has been found; cf. Dent (1981, F535). Wilson (ed. 1960): Lyly was prob. parodying a proverb familiar to the audience.…Sh.’s Fool is clearly himself parodying either Lyly or the original proverb. Seng (1967, p. 201): Or echoing some popular song or rhyme of the day. Van Dam (1935, p. 70): Why was it stated that fools were out of grace? In the context it does not seem to be apropos; moreover, it clashes with the high favour Lear’s fool enjoyed.…If Shakespeare had written grace, the flavour of the travesty [of Lyly’s phrase] had vanished. We think the Q is right. Taylor (1983, p. 373): Lyly’s line is spoken by a foole [a shee foole, the simple maid Silena; not a court fool] (2.3.75), an idiot of the newest cut (2.3.47), to a scholler (2.3.51), who begins by complaining of a father who seekes to place affection by appointment, & to force loue by compulsion (2.3.2). The line in Lear is also spoken by a fool, criticizing a father guilty of a similar fault; and his rhyme proceeds to link its initial generalization to a statement about scholars (wise men) and intellectual fashions.…Q is (again) closer to [Sh.’s] sources than F. The parallels are not remarkably close. Q makes the harder reading (see n. 681); F’s grace—favour (Johnson, ed. 1765; see n. 251), opportunity of showing their folly (Meiklejohn, ed. 1879; cf. OED, sb. 10: Fortune), demand (Brooke, ed. 1947)—simplifies it. Doran (1931, pp. 55–6): Perhaps Sh. meant to write grace but mistakenly wrote wit (the word that stuck in his memory, presumably from the proverb or Lyly’s phrase), later correcting it. Seng (1967, p. 200): It was possibly the Q1 compositor’s error. His eye may have caught the word from the lines just preceding the song, Thou…away [676–7] or from the third line of the song itself. He suggests for grace favour or its manifestation…good-will (OED sb. 6).

680 in a yeare]
Clarkes (ed. 1868) alone: Idiom of indefinite time…used to imply now-a-days, at present; unattested in OED. More likely, within a year, as at 1327, Sh.’s only other use of the phrase; or within this year. Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): In any year, i.e. ever. The underlying logic seems to be that since a fool shows a certain lack of wit on any day, within a year’s time the cumulative, plentiful lack of wit is even greater.

681 For…foppish]
Foppish means resembling…a fop or fool (OED, a. 1, quoting this l., Sh.’s only use of the word, as its first ex.); cf. foppery, 447. Harder to explain is For. In Q the logic might be that since fools have less wit than wise men, now that wise men are foolish the fools have had either to reduce their wit accordingly, acknowledging superior competition, or to struggle to compete. So Van Dam (1935, p. 71): It is the people’s increasing foolishness which incites the (professional) fools to more foolery than ever. Alternatively, fools never had less wit (intelligence, good sense) than they show this year, in attempting to thrive by foolery against so much competition from formerly wise men. Or possibly had nere lesse wit means were never less appreciated for their witty folly, having been supplanted by wise men who are even more foolish—essentially what F states more simply. So Johnson (ed. 1765): They were never so little wanted, for wise men now supply their place.

681 wise men]
Schmidt (ed. 1879), on F’s wisemen: Generally written as one word in old edd. (Ger.). In F it occurs (sing. and pl.) 11 times as one word, 10 times as two. Cf. 1668.

681–3 foppish…apish]
Ellis (1871, 3:953) lists this as one of ten Shn. rhymes of short a with short o, including those at 923–4, 1271–2, and 2014+20–+21. Tovey (ed. 1896) notes the alternative spellings chaps and chops. Kökeritz (1953, p. 225): Perhaps its very inexactness is its sole raison d’être in the song. Cf. Cercignani (1981, p. 114).

682 They…doe weare]
In Q the referent for they and their, and They in the next line, is in all probability wise men; F’s alteration of doe to to introduces an ambiguity, allowing it to refer to Fooles. Stone (1980, p. 215), defending Q: Weare = diminish, fade [OED, v.1 13]: F, not very clearly intelligible, misses, in any case, the point—which is not simply that wise men have grown foppish, but that they are unaware of having done so. Foakes (ed. 1997): Presumably wear out or deteriorate. Wells (ed. 2000): Become threadbare. In F, wise men know not how to appear provided with brains (Clarkes, ed. 1868) or to display their wisdom (Brooke, ed. 1947); cf. OED (7): To exhibit or present, first ex. from WT 1.2.344 (445). Brooke adds, Behind this nonsense verse, and in other parts of the play, one detects a scornful protest against the new foppery and social extravagance that James I’s accession brought in.
