But McCann (ed. 1964) finds a different meaning in F: Fools do not [now] know how to behave; cf. OED (2b): To use, employ, handle, last ex. dated 1440, or perhaps (8) figuratively To carry about with one…. To possess and enjoy as one’s own. Seng (1967, p. 201): Ambiguous: Either…wise men in imitating fools are at a loss to manage the wit they should be using, or…fools are getting so much competition from wise men that fools do not know what face to put on their own natural wittiness. So Hunter (ed. 1972), F: The wise men, slavishly imitative of the manners of the time, don’t know how to show their wisdom; in attempting to follow fashion they become fools, and Edwards (ed. 1975): Fools don’t know how to show their talents.

682 wits]
OED (Wit sb. 3c): Pl. Mental faculties, intellectual powers.…Often practically equivalent to the sing. in sense 2 [intellect, reason]. Cf. 1722, 1941, 1950, 2001, 2046, 2789. Possibly (6): Wisdom, good judgment, in reference to a number of persons (2b). See n. 677 for both senses.

683 apish]
Most eds. agree with the Clarkes (ed. 1868): Fantastic (OED, a. 2: Fantastically foolish, affected, silly). But Harrison (ed. 1937): Like; Idem (ed. 1948): Like apes, who always imitate (OED, 3: Unreasoningly imitative). So McCann (ed. 1964): The wise men have so closely imitated them. Brown (ed. 1976): By following fashion, wise men…become fools. Sh. elsewhere uses the word in both senses.

684 full of songs]
This seems to imply previous singing in the scene; since 647–57 are a speech (645), the sung lines would most likely be 669+1–+4. Seng (1967, p. 201): But [Lear’s] use of the term may be merely generic. Reynolds (in Malone ed. 1790): Shakspeare’s fools are certainly copied from the life. The originals whom he copied were no doubt men of quick parts; lively and sarcastick. Though they were licensed to say any thing, it was still necessary to prevent giving offense, that every thing they said should have a playful air: we may suppose therefore that they had a custom of taking off the edge of too sharp a speech by covering it hastily with the end of an old song, or any glib nonsense that came into mind (cf. n. 728–9). Malone (op. cit., 10:680) quotes from Wager’s The Longer Thou Livest (1569, sig. A3): Entreth Moros…synging the foote of many songs, as fooles were wont. Busby (1923, pp. 66–8): Other fools who break into scraps of songs are Simplicity in Three Lords and Three Ladies of London (1588), Barnabe Bunch in The Weakest Goeth to the Wall (1600), and Much in The Downfall of Robert, Earl of Huntingdon (1598). Moreover (p. 76), Fragments of verse are scattered promiscuously throughout the clowns’ parts, giving exx. from several plays. Foakes (ed. 1997), however, of Lear’s question: Implying that the Fool did not usually sing? He may have spoken most of the rhyming passages, though (p. 51) [Armin’s] skills would have included singing.…Little early music survives that can be linked with him. See .

684 sirra]
See n. 411.

685 vs’d it]
Schmidt (1875), Use vb. 1b: To make a practice of, giving Shn. exx. of us(d) it in which it’s antecedent is, as here, somewhat indefinite. Cf. OED (Use v. 1, 4, 19).

685 nuncle]
See n. 634.

685 euer]
Since the passage is prose, F’s contraction ere is not metrical; possibly it is due to F’s full line, though there is probably room for the longer word.

685–6 mad’st…mother]
Malone (ed. 1790): When you invested them with the authority of a mother. Deighton (ed. 1891): I.e. by giving them the power of punishment. Wilson (ed. 1960): Perh. the Fool recalls Lear’s hope to find with Cord. a kind nursery [132]. But the Fool cannot recall what he was not evidently present to hear. F’s plural Mothers, which is unnecessary and may seem illogical in giving Lear two mothers, is adopted by most eds. and defended by Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 135): He has turned things topsy-turvy, and has made two daughters…into—as it were—two mothers. Colie (1974, p. 122) finds the doctrine of generations in Ecclus. 33:18–22 particularly relevant.

686–7 gauest…breeches]
Proverbial: Tilley R153, He has made a Rod (staff) for his own tail (head). Elton (1966, p. 313 n.) compares Nashe, To the Gentlemen Students (1589), the world turned vpside downe, since the child beateth his father (Works, ed. McKerrow, 3:315, who [4:448] traces the idea to Aristophanes, Nubes 1321 and 1408, a scene referred to in Wilson’s Rule of Reason, 1551, sig. X1).

687–91 then…among]
As prose in both Q1 and Q2; F sets as verse except for erroneously leaving the first one or more probably two words in prose. The error does not necessarily show F’s derivation from a quarto; the lining may have been wrong or unclear in a previous MS.
Danby (1945, pp. 17–18) finds the song typical of the Fool’s manner of comment: It can state with an appropriate sense of anxiety and bafflement, distress and bitterness—all shrugged off in a hideous flippancy—the crisis of the dichotomies.…The Fool’s trick is to keep a see-saw of ambivalencies constantly in motion.…There is no fixed centre, only a to-and-fro between extremes.…The paradoxes proliferate.… That the daughters have stolen the Fool’s tears and he their song throws a general doubt on human identity, and on the possibility of making clear distinctions.…The King is a fool playing bo-peep, the old man is a little boy, the daughters are his mothers, the wielder of the rod is the recipient of punishment.

687–9 they…sung]
As Rollins (MLR, 1920, pp. 87 ff.) has shown, the lines parody the broadside ballad of the Protestant martyr John Careless, published in 1586, 1624, and 1635. Its first lines, as quoted by Coverdale at the end of Careless’s letters in Certain most godly, fruitful, and comfortable letters (1564, p. 634), are Some men for sodayne ioye do wepe, And some in sorow sing. Rollins finds another version in the British Library’s MS Sloane 1896, fols. 11–12v, and Halliwell-Phillipps (1880, p. 53) reprints another from MS. Lansd. 98. As Rollins (op. cit.) notes, Nashe twice refers to the ballad, once quoting some men for sorrow singe (ed. McKerrow, 3:104, 5:196; cf. 5:suppl. 50); Steevens (ed. 1778) first notes a quotation from it in Heywood’s play Rape of Lucrece (1606–8; 1608, sig. C1v), and Seng (1958, p. 584) finds its opening lines incorporated in a prefatory sonnet in H[enry] L[ok’s] Ecclesiastes (1597, sig. N3). Rollins observes, Likely enough, as a broadside ballad sung through the streets of London John Careless came to the attention of Heywood and Shakespeare; he prints the whole in his Old English Ballads 1553–1625 (1920, pp. 47–53). Seng (loc. cit.): Its popularity is clear from the fact that it gave its name to the tune, citing Rollins, Ballads (1920, p. 55) and Chappell, ed., Roxburghe Ballads (1879, 3:168). For possible musical settings see . Crook (ed. 1907): The Fool means that both the daughters and himself hide their real feelings by pretending the opposite. Danby (1949, p. 104): The daughters have stolen the Fool’s tears; he is left to sing their song. It might be profound hypocrisy on the daughters’ part. Seng (1967, p. 205): Where the earlier song [680–3] had included the king in the roster of fools by implication—he is a man, and all men are fools from birth—this song, more audaciously, calls Lear by a title that he has earned for himself. Long (1971, p. 167): Sh. parodied a popular, catchy phrase in order to make the point that the Fool for sorrow sings when he beholds the foolishness of King Lear.

690 bo-peepe]
Opies (1951): Whether the game was once a form of hide-and-seek, or never more than a baby amusement of covering the head and peeping out…is uncertain. Johnson ([Dictionary,] 1755) defined bo-peep as The act of looking out and then drawing back as if frightened, or with the purpose to fright some other.…The earliest reference to the game appears to be in 1364 when Alice Canston had to play bo-pepe thorowe a pillory for giving a short measure of ale. OED’s exx. commence from 1524. Douce (1807, 2:146) quotes Robert Sherwood’s Dictionary (1672): Jeu d’enfant…se cachans le visage, & puis se monstrant. Craig (ed. 1901) quotes from Cotgrave’s French Dictionarie (1611), Faire les doux yeux. To play at boe-peepe; or to winke, and from Sir John Barnavelt 3.1, this blinded State, that plaies at boa-peep wth vs (Old Plays, ed. Bullen, 2:348). Kittredge (ed. 1940) cites from Dekker’s Satiromastix a passage that suggests hide-and-seek: our vnhandsome-fac’d Poet does play at bo-peepes with your Grace, and cryes all-hidde as boyes doe (5.2.153–4). Wilson (ed. 1960), citing Tilley B540, To play Bopeep, and quoting one of Tilley’s exx.: App. a game usual with fools as well as children. Cf. Skelton Image [of] Hypocrisy (Wks. [ed. Dyce, 1843,] II, 420), Thus you make vs sottes, And play with vs boopepe. But there sottes means dupes, victims of bo-peep and like gambaldes, deceptive tricks. Dent (1981), not Tilley, cites this l. Sh. does not elsewhere use the term. The metaphor as applied to Lear has been variously understood. Eccles (ed. 1792) and many others: Acting in a childish, silly manner. Kittredge (op. cit.): Be so childish as to hide himself—i.e., renounce his royalty. Brooke (ed. 1947): Erratically display and conceal his royal countenance. Muir (ed. 1952): Harsnett [1603, p. 61] uses the phrase.…The implication is that Lear has blinded himself, hidden himself (i.e. abdicated), or played silly pranks. Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956): Hide his royalty in behaving like a fool. Joseph (ed. 1966): Plunge [him]self into obscurity. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Hiding his own eyes and refusing to see the true state of affairs.

691 fooles]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 172): The sense shows that Q is right. The F reading [Foole] may be due to a slip by the compositor. Or a scribe. Compositor E frequently omits a final -s. Most eds. accept Q. Seng (1967, p. 203), however, defends F: NED gives an elliptical sense of the word among. Used adverbially it can mean During this period, at the same time…betweenwhiles, yielding and between whiles go about as a fool.

691 among]
Abbott (§203): Prepositions are often placed after their objects. Cf. Franz §544. Cf. prev. n.

692 prethe]
See n. 664.

692 Nunckle]
See n. 634.

693 I…lye]
Eccles (ed. 1792): He had sometimes been punished for telling truth. Wells (ed. 2000): Because the truth is so painful.

694 And]
See n. 630.

696–8 they’l…peace]
Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 202): The crocodile’s argument is one that harms the opponent either way, citing these ll. Weis (ed. 1993), fancifully: Pun on…piece, i.e. codpiece, a pun not found in Sh. (Wells, ed. 2000). Foakes (ed. 1997): Does the Fool draw attention to his conspicuous codpiece…to point up a quibble?

699–700 thou…middle]
Eccles (ed. 1792): He parted and gave away his wit, when he gave away his crown. Halio (ed. 1992): I.e. if a fool is only a half-wit, Lear is less. Murphy (1984, p. 175) suspects that the image was suggested by the same passage in Harsnett (1603, p. 61) that suggested bo-peepe (see n. 690), though there the phrase is pare away the deuil.

699 thee]
Abbott (§213): Thee for thou is…found after the verb to be.…In these cases thee represents a person not regarded as acting, but about whom something is predicated. Cf. Franz §283. OED (pers. pron. 3): Often so used dialectically.

699 Nuncle]
See n. 634.

700 wit]
See n. 677.

700 a]
This and F’s o’ may mean either on or of. See nn. 669+10, 676, 1105. Cf. 1400, 1613, 1860, 2399, 2794.

701 one…parings]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Goneril, he argues, must have half of the King’s wits. McCann (ed. 1964): The Fool suggests that Goneril and Regan are as worthless as peelings. The point is obscure; perhaps the Fool means that Lear’s dividing up his possessions was tantamount to losing his wit (since the act was foolish) and his self (since now he has no function); his two offspring, each being of his flesh and blood and having half his former possessions and duties over them, are what remain of the old Lear.

703–4 How…frowne]
Collier (ed. 1843): The folio prints [these lines] as prose, and makes them so by omitting Methinks. There being no apparent reason for either change, they may be inadvertent.

703 How now]
See n. 361.

703 makes]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Make for do is common in our old writers, citing Ham. 1.2.164 (352).

703 Frontlet]
Malone (ed. 1790): A forehead-cloth, used formerly by ladies at night to render that part smooth (OED, 1a). Though OED quotes this l. as its earliest ex. of a figurative use of the term, Steevens (ed. 1778) quotes from a sonnet (Canzon. 27) in Zepheria (1594): And vayle thy face with frownes as with a frontlet. Rann (ed. 1794): Goneril’s brow appeared to Lear as completely covered with frowns, as it would be by a frontlet. Deighton (ed. 1891): What business have you to approach me with a frown on your brow? Verity (ed. 1897): Probably Goneril has just seen Oswald and heard his report. Perrett (1904, p. 224), citing OED 1f, Coronet, perhaps a nonce-word: Probably Goneril appears…in a frontlet betokening higher rank than the coronet of a duchess. Joseph (ed. 1966): The torture, the frontlet, consisted of a cord tightened round the forehead, making the eyes start out. It is possible that Lear is referring sarcastically to Goneril’s eyes, protuberant in rage. Not attested in OED. Halio (ed. 1992): Possibly Goneril is wearing a bandage containing some medicament (OED, 1c) to support her fiction (cf. 515) that she is sick: Lear quibbles on the two senses, literal and figurative (= frown).

704 alate]
OED: Of late, lately. For a as a worn-down of, see OED (A prep.2 1), Franz §239. F’s of late is more formal, its prose less so; the change is insignificant.

704 frowne]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Habit of frowning (OED, sb. 1, quoting this l. as its first ex.; but see Tit. 1.1.458 [502] etc.). In 706 F gives the fuller frowning.

705 prettie]
Fine. See n. 626.

705 fellow]
See n. 16.

706 O]
OED (sb. 1): The Arabic zero or cipher O; hence, a cipher, a mere nothing, quoting this l. as its first ex. Adams (in Irving & Marshall, ed. 1889): Shakespeare uses the O either for zero or for anything round, citing LLL 5.2.45 (1933) (smallpox marks), MND 3.2.188 (1215) (stars), H5 1.pr. 13 (14) (the Globe or another Th.), and Ant. 5.2.81 (3297) (the Earth). The present is the only reference to its arithmetical use.

706–7 O…figure]
Malone (1783, p. 48): A mere cypher; which has no arithmetical value, unless preceded or followed by some figure. Idem (ed. 1790): The same idea is in WT 1.2.6–9 (55–7). Frost (ed. 1909): Possibly some antithesis between pretty fellow and without a figure (or face). Proverbial: Tilley C391, He is a Cypher among numbers. Baldwin (1943, pp. 166–7) cites schoolbook explanations of the idea, and Muir (ed. 1952) finds it in Florio’s Second Frutes (1591, p. 149). Elton (1966, p. 308 n.) cites several analogies between fool and cipher, including AYL 3.2.290 (1482). Edwards (ed. 1975): If the number 10 loses just a part of itself, the figure 1, it becomes nothing: so Lear has destroyed himself by losing a part of himself. Adelman (1992, p. 298): Signifying castration.

707–8 I…nothing]
Dent (1981, S623): Proverbial: Somewhat (Something) is better than nothing.

708–9 yes…nothing]
Generally understood as addressed to the frowning Goneril (see textual n.); Rosenberg (1972, p. 116) thinks it addressed to Lear.

710 Mum, mum]
OED (Mum int.): A command to be silent, quoting this l. Munro (ed. 1957) cites several proverbial uses: Tilley M1310, N279, W767. Duthie (ed. 1949): F [erroneously] agrees with Q in setting this as part of the verse.

710–11 he…some]
No source for these verses has been found. Though occasionally set to music, no contemporary setting is known. Hunter (ed. 1972, p. 339): The tone is more that of a proverb than a song.

710 neither…nor]
F’s nor…nor is perhaps a metrical change; correlative nor for neither is common (OED Nor conj.1. 2b).

710 crum]
OED (Crumb, crum sb. 3): The inner part of a loaf, not hardened in baking, and capable of being easily crumbled; the soft part of bread. Opposed to crust, quoting this l.

711 Wearie…some]
Delius (ed. 1854): Weary of all things when he has all in superfluity, he will be happy with some later (Ger.). Brooke (ed. 1947): The story of Lear in a nutshell. Wilson (ed. 1960): Tired of life…[shall] have neither, but adding, shall want some is inconsequent after weary of all. Wearie of all must modify the first verb: The man who keeps nothing at all for himself, [because] having become tired of everything, will find himself in want (Lott, ed. 1974, like Delius). See also .

711 want]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Feel the want of.

711 That’s…pescod]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 374): Set [erroneously] in both Q and F as if part of the verse.

711 sheald pescod]
OED (Sheel v.): To shell; to take off the husk, nowhere else in Sh.; (Peasecod, peascod): Pea-pod. Warburton (ed. 1747): Which is his condition, having parted with his power. Johnson (ed. 1765): A mere husk, which contains nothing. The outside of a king remains, but all the intrinsic parts of royalty are gone. Tollet (in Steevens, ed. 1773, 10:2N 4v–5), followed by many eds., finds the same symbolism for lost sovereignty in the effigy of Richard II in Westminster Abbey; in Steevens (ed. 1778) he cites as his authority Camden’s Remaines [1605; 1629, p. 181]. But according to Wright (ed. 1875), both Camden and Tollet are wrong: those pods are of the broom plant, the badge of the Plantagenets. Moreover, although the pods are open the seeds are indicated. Muir (ed. 1952, p. xxxv): This would be the only evidence that Sh. had read Camden. Alter (1989, p. 232): Perhaps there is an associative trigger here in the contiguity of the larder items, crust and crumb.…The new image, however, rather explicity suggests impotence, not only in the physical shape to which it refers but in its sound, for peascod…sounds very much like a spoonerism for codpiece, which, if empty, would be a striking emblem of the king unmanned. Adelman (1992, p. 298): Signifying castration. Hunter (ed. 1972): Since a peascod is the shell, one that is shelled is nothing. This is overnice; probably sheald means which has been subject to the action of shelling, of removing its contents, as Johnson understood. Dent (1981): Possibly proverbial: Not give two Peascods (P138.1), Not worth a Cod (seed pod) (C501.1).

712–25 Not…proceedings]
Verity (ed. 1897): Goneril always goes straight to the point, wasting no time in preliminaries and sparing no one’s feelings. Note how skilfully her complaint is introduced, viz. in immediate connection with the witticism of the Fool. Harbage (1963, p. 408): The writing is implacable. Much of what Goneril says is true, but it is terrible that she should say it. Vickers (1968, pp. 351–2): The fact that Goneril enters on to a prose scene…and addresses Lear and the Fool in verse shows the sharpness of her isolation from them—Lear of course then ascends to the anger and intensity of verse too. Hunter (ed. 1972): The rhetoric of Gonerill’s [whole] speech seems designed to convey an impression of cold venom. Notice the length of sentence,…the elaboration of the subordinate clauses, the lack of concrete imagery, the sharpness of the alliteration…, the balance of abstractions, the deviousness of the rhythm. Brown (ed. 1976): Goneril’s speech has careful, short parentheses, qualifying clauses, and a firm, sustained return to meter.…It is a show of force and independence, cloaked in political urbanity. Reibetanz (1977, p. 63): Goneril’s intricate opening speech betrays much preparation.…Only two sentences thread their labored way through these fourteen lines. The first sentence makes us wait until the third line for its cargo of verbs, and the awkwardness of not-to-be-endured riots exposes its lack of spontaneity. The labyrinthine syntax of the second sentence (including three bys, two ands, one but, one nor, three thats, and three whiches) unfolds in highly wrought periodicity, with a series of abstractions that artfully gloss over the ugly threats within. Smidt (1990, p. 136): Q’s prose, from here to the end of the scene, in place of F’s verse, may be symptomatic of the worked-over state of Shakespeare’s foul papers, first hinted by Doran (1931, pp. 126, 128). Patterson (1984, p. 72), topically: Goneril’s language of parliamentary reformism—redresses, wholesome weal, discreet proceedings—shows that Sh. did not support without question the parliamentary opposition against the king.

712 all-licenc’d foole]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Fool to whom all license is permitted. On all = altogether see n. 107, 110+1. Verity (ed. 1897): Understand some words like annoys us, is troublesome, since the verbs in [714] are hardly appropriate to him. But see n. 714.

713 other]
Abbott (§12): Originally both sing. and pl. (OED, absol., pron. 5b, 6b). Cf. Franz §357, and 2077.

713 retinue]
Kemshead (ed. 1875): Accent on second syllable; so pronounced by Milton, and Dryden as well. OED (sb.): The usual stressing in the 16–18th centuries.

714 carpe]
Schmidt (1874): Find fault (OED, v.1 5). Verity (ed. 1897): With the household arrangements. Craig (ed. 1901), anticipated by Todd (1810, p. 326): But it may also mean to prate, to talk noisily (OED, 4, latest ex. 1557), comparing 1H4 3.2.63 (1882), carping (Q2, F; capring Q1). Wells (ed. 2000): Could mean contend, fight (OED v.1 8). In Sh.’s three earlier uses of carping and one later of carp’d the reference is always to censure, not prattle or fighting.

715 ranke]
Schmidt (1875) and most eds.: Disgusting, gross. Tovey (ed. 1896) and a few others.: Excessive. Properly used of weeds overgrown, as in Ham. 1.2.136 (320), where, as here, both meanings may apply.

715 (not…riots,)]
Q2 repeats Q1’s puzzling parentheses; F1 half-corrects by moving the second parenthesis back a word; for perfect sense, the same should have been done to the first. Simpson (1911, pp. 93–4) cites several examples of compound nouns or adjectives…enclosed within brackets where we should employ the hyphen.

715 riots]
Schmidt (1875): Tumultuous disturbance[s] of the peace (OED, sb. 4b). Joseph (ed. 1966): Arising from debauchery (OED, 2). A few eds. follow Verity (1897) in taking Goneril’s charge as true: Her complaint…very likely has some justice, on the principle…of like master, like man. Moreover, Lear not only sets them the example of fault-finding [513–14] and treating her servants ill [507], but seems [719–20] to Goneril to encourage them. But we have only Goneril’s word, who has the ability to avail herself of every opportunity of criticism, and to turn every fault, however small, into an excuse for her conduct (Smith, ed. 1902). As Kittredge (ed. 1940) points out, there is not the slightest objective evidence in the play of the knights’ misbehavior: see n. 586–872. Brown (ed. 1996), though agreeing: However, Lear’s peremptory orders can be echoed by his knights and lead to enough rowdy behavior to justify any strictures; some directors take this hint and in rehearsals work up brawls and rank behavior which looks dangerous and even criminal. Taylor (1985, p. 210): By shifting her main attack from Lear to his train Shakespeare severely weakens Goneril’s credibility, for…we have no a priori reason to think ill of them.…Goneril thus appears to malign the knights only as a means of getting at Lear, as Lear himself deduces.

715 Sir]
This word is hypermetrical in F’s verse, as it would be if it began the next line, where perhaps it belongs. It may have been intended to introduce the main body of Goneril’s attack. See n. 60.

716–17 I had…to haue]
Both pairs of words are naturally elided in speaking F’s verse. There is no need to assume, as Halio (ed. 1992) does, that in correcting Q’s prose, the F editor or reviser failed to make all the necessary adjustments to verse.

717 safe]
Schmidt (1875): Affording security and safety (OED, a. 7). Since safety may not be Goneril’s concern, Wright (ed. 1875) proposes Sure, certain (OED, 9: Guaranteed against failure).

718 what…done]
Verity (ed. 1897): Referring to Lear’s treatment of her gentleman [507] and perhaps of Oswald [614]. They may be the same person; see n. 507.

718 too late]
Page (ed. 1889): Also lately (OED, Late adv. 4), referring too to your selfe. Most eds. refer it to late. Muir (ed. 1952): Lear has been tardy in reproving; but Bhattacharya (1980–1, p. 99): There is no indication that Lear has ever rebuked his retinue. Wilson (ed. 1960) and most others who comment: Only too recently; see prev. n. Cf. 1192, 1948, 2109, 2112, 2411.

719 put on]
Stone (1980, p. 203): A careless error for F’s put it on. Warburton (ed. 1747): Promote (OED, Put v.1 46h, To urge onward, to encourage; to incite, quoting this l. as its second ex., after Ham. 5.2.397 [3897]). See 1038. Tovey (ed. 1896): In [519], put on means assume. Not here.

720 allowance]
Malone (1783, p. 48): Approbation (OED, sb. 2). Cf. 1181.

720–5 which…proceedings]
Moberly (ed. 1876): The rest of the sentence labours under a plethora of relatives. The meaning, however, is simple: If you instigate your men to riot I will check it, even though it offends you; as that offence which would otherwise be a shame, would be proved by the necessity to be a discreet proceeding. Verity (ed. 1897): She is threatening Lear, for the first time in her life, and designedly wraps up her menace in rather vague language. Smith (ed. 1902): The somewhat embarrassed syntax and the indirect expressions betoken Goneril’s hesitation. Her statements have been direct enough while she merely objected to Lear’s conduct. Now for the first time she threatens him to his face. Gardner (ed. 1969): With taut, involved formality. Lott (ed. 1974): In the obscurity of so complex a sentence…she avoids a direct confrontation with her father.…Whenever possible she uses impersonal forms: the fault, the redresses. So Foakes (ed. 1997): Veiling her threat in abstractions and obscure syntax in an attempt to be easy on Lear. Her threats, of course, are not easy on him.

721 would]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Ought, citing Ham. 3.3.75 (2352). For most eds., a simple future conditional.

721 scape]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Not ’scape, as usually printed. OED (v.1): Aphetic var. of Escape.

721 censure]
Goggin (ed. 1910): Here blame [OED, sb. 4]; but the usual meaning in Shakespeare is judgment, opinion [OED, 3], comparing 1972, 2942.

721 redresse]
F’s redresses seems required by their in 723. Possibly the Q compositor repeated the singular from 717, or misread final s as Q’s illogical comma. Wells (ed. 2000): The plural ending was often omitted after s, citing Abbott §471.

721 sleepe]
Page (ed. 1889): Be unused.…A mixture of simple and metaphorical language (OED, v. 4).

722 which]
Craig (ed. 1901): I.e. which remedial proceeding.

722 tender]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Regard and concern (OED, sb.3 3, quoting this l. and 1H4 5.4.49 (3010) as its only exx.).

722 wholsome weale]
Valpy (ed. 1833) and many eds.: Well-governed state. Verity (ed. 1897): A proper state of things. Some interpret weal = commonwealth,…but she is thinking rather of her own household. Wright (ed. 1875), wholesome: Sound…healthy (OED, a. 3). Hudson (ed. 1879): Here used proleptically (OED, 2).

723 working]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Execution.

724 that else]
Perhaps F’s Which else was substituted to avoid three thats within seven words. The meaning is the same. See n. 235. Doran (1931, p. 45): When that is applied to the antecedent, the form of the relative preferred by Shakespeare is which, citing Abbott §§258–73.

724 shame]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Shameful. Wilson (ed. 1960): I.e.…in us.

724 necessitie]
Goggin (ed. 1910): The obvious necessity for it. No one seems to read necessitie as personification.

725 must call]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Will make men call. F’s Will call is equally elliptical and less emphatic.

725 proceedings]
F’s proceeding seems intended to parallel the singular offence or shame; Q’s plural, rejected by all eds., makes a more logical parallel of two nouns for plural action—proceedings, and the plural redresses referred to by their.

726–9, 735–7 For…darkling, May…thee]
Presumably the Fool interposes these two speeches while Lear stares in disbelief at Goneril, as his succeeding questions indicate. So Rosenberg (1972, p. 117): Lear is speechless. Kent, uncharacteristically, does not speak at all here. Fool twists the knife.

726 trow]
Means the same as F’s know. See n. 652.

726 nuncle]
See n. 634.

726–8 the…young]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 375): F follows Q in printing verse as prose. Or follows the lineation in the playbook derived from the same MS as Q; or had no room for verse at the end of this crowded column. Hunter (ed. 1972, p. 339): More a proverb than a song. Though no source in proverb or song has been found for this jingle, it is based on traditional bird-lore going back to Pliny’s Nat. Hist. 10.11, as Baldwin (1935, pp. 157–63; 1944, 1:633–4) has shown. The idea appears also in 1H4 5.1.59–64 (2696–2701), on which the Clarkes (ed. 1868) comment: The cuckoo frequently lays its eggs in the sparrow’s nest; which, when the young cuckoo grows big, is oppressed by its presence. Hudson (ed. 1871): They get so big and so voracious as to scare away or kill their feeder. In Pliny the victim is the wood pigeon; that the English victim is the hedge sparrow, or haysugge, Wilson (ed. 1960) documents from Chaucer, Parl. of Foules 612–13; Massinger, The Picture 2.2.114–15; and Bullokar, Engl. Expositor (1616, s.v. Heisugge). OED (Cuckoo, sb. 1) lists other victims, found in many allusions. Moberly (ed. 1876) makes the Fool’s speech not so much a judgment on Goneril’s cruel rebuke as an explication of its logic: So the young cuckoo, wanting the nest to itself, was under the regrettable necessity of biting off the head of its foster-mother the sparrow; which, under the circumstances, was not a shame, but an act of discretion. Heilman (1948, p. 93): This begins a pattern of animal imagery applied to Goneril and Regan to emphasize the ferocity and bestiality into which human beings can fall. Adelman (1992, p. 298): Signifying castration. Rather, killing. Foakes (ed. 1997): Implying a kind of cannibalism. Halio (ed. 1992): The Fool alludes figuratively to Gonerill’s illegitimacy (compare [764]) or usurpation and certainly to her ingratitude. Williams (1994), hedge-sparrow: Cuckold fathering his wife’s bastard.

727 it had]
Q’s simple past is consistent with the other verbs, and better for a traditional jingle (Wilson, ed. 1960). Most eds. (see textual n.) agree with White (ed. 1862) that F’s it’s had is a misprint rather than an abbreviation of it has had. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 533): Possibly another example of Compositor E’s weakness for terminal s. Only Foakes (ed. 1997): F, perhaps anxious about the repeated it, changes…to it’s.

727 it]
To a number of modern eds. this archaic form of the possessive its (OED, It pron. 10) sounds, as it did to Tiessen (1877, p. 160), like baby talk, such as it may be in Jn. 2.1.160–1 (461–2) (though there that effect may be due to the use of it for he rather than of the possessive form it). It is not baby talk at 2303+1; see n. Brook (1976, pp. 78, 118): Used with reference to children or when a child is addressed. Juliet’s Nurse may be using it colloquially in Rom. 1.3.52 (399), but it is used formally and seriously in Ham. 1.2.216 (409), Cym. 3.4.157 (1847), WT 3.2.100 (1279), and in the seven occurrences of it own—H5 5.2.40 (3027), Ham. 5.1.221 (3410), Tim. 5.1.148 (2384), Ant. 2.7.44, 47 (1382, 1386), WT 2.3.178 (1110), and Tmp. 2.1.164 (841). Bronisch (1878) finds possessive it only once in the Bible (A.V.; also G.), in Lev. 25:5 (it owne accord). Thirlby (MS notes, 1733–47) cites Andrew Willet, An Harmonie upon the First Booke of Samuel (1607, p. 57): it owne nature. Sh. uses its, usually spelled it’s, only a dozen times; Jonson uses both forms several times. Until the end of the 16th c., the usual possessive for it was his or her; see Abbott §228 and Franz §320, and cf. 1173, 1428, 2529, and perhaps 130, 899, 904–5. Goggin (ed. 1910): Its does not occur in Spenser…and is found only three times in Milton. The five occurrences of it’s in WT, the two in Tmp., and the single its in MM may be due to the scribe Ralph Crane. In view of the novelty of the possessive pronouns it and its, and of their rarity and unsettled usage in Sh.’s texts, perhaps the Fool’s use of it here may not safely be interpreted as jocular or otherwise significant.

727 beit]
F corrects to by it. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 375): Probably a misreading (e/y), comparing 177. Stone (1980, p. 193): A phonetic error: By was pronounced [bəi] (see [Dobson, 1957, 2:451]). A compositor might have made either kind of error, the second by carrying the words in memory.

728–9 so…darkling]
Though Steevens (ed. 1793) suspected that this was based on an old song, and Knight (ed. 1840) and Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) on a proverb, no sure sources have been found. Knight, however, notes a similar image in Spenser’s account of the Lear story: But true it is that when the oyle is spent, | The light goes out, and weeke is throwne away; | So when he had resignd his regiment, | His daughter gan despise his drouping day; see . Reynolds (in Malone, ed. 1790) remarks on the incoherent words with which Shakespeare often finishes this fool’s speeches (see n. 684), but many eds. rebut him in this case. Halio (ed. 1992): Possibly a nonsense tag to take off the edge of the Fool’s bitter couplet, but even so it conveys a sense of disaster. Eccles (ed. 1792): These words glance probably…at the forlorn condition to which the king is likely to be reduced. Knight (op. cit.): May have been proverbial to signify the desertion of a man by his mercenary friends, when he is become a sheal’d peascod. Moberly (ed. 1876) refers the words to the preceding two lines: And so it happened that we were all snuffed out in a moment. Verity (ed. 1897): Meaning perhaps that Lear’s days of power are all over, or that Goneril’s speech has, as it were, snuffed him out. Porter & Clarke (op. cit.): Proverbial phrase for a man left in the lurch by improvidence, as the foolish virgins in the parable [Matt. 25:1–13] were for lack of oil. Goggin (ed. 1910): May mean that Lear is like a burnt-out candle. His power (the oil) is gone and he himself is like the wick, only fit to be thrown aside. Houghton (ed. 1957): The words may suggest the moral chaos of daughters teaching fathers. Hunter (ed. 1972): Lear is presumably the candle of the state, whose extinction plunges the people into darkness. Dent (1981): Possibly proverbial: A Candle (torch) lights others and consumes itself (C39). Dent also cites Shn. and other instances of the Candle of life image (CC1). Foakes (ed. 1997): Does the Fool here perceptively anticipate the afflictions soon to come…or does he provoke them?

728–9 darkling]
Hudson (ed. 1856): In the dark (OED, a. 1). On the old adverbial suffix -ling see Franz §243. Clarkes (ed. 1868): The expression probably included a figurative meaning of baffled, deserted, bereft of light and help. Harbage (ed. 1958): Like the dead hedge-sparrow and the threatened Lear. Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960, p. xxx): Lear’s folly has produced a figurative darkness in the kingdom. Sh. uses the word in MND 2.2.86 (740) and Ant. 4.15.10 (3011).

730 Are…daughter]
Verity (ed. 1897): There is (I think) no touch of irony or anger; merely a dazed bewilderment, which has held him silent for a moment. The sudden revelation of what his daughter is stuns the king; only with self-recovery comes passion. Weidhorn (1969, p. 307): He would rather think that [Goneril] was someone else than that a daughter of his could speak so, comparing 287–8, we…daughter. Edwards (ed. 1975): There is deep irony in his comic turn, for to rediscover who he is and his children are becomes his most serious need.

730 our]
The royal plural.

731 Come sir]
By F’s omission, as Knight (ed. 1840) remarked, the line is rendered strictly metrical. But like several other vocatives beginning speeches in this play, it may be equivalent to a separate introductory line, or in this case as a kind of completion of the previous short line, which may be read with three or four heavy stresses. See n. 60, and cf. 746. In either case, regular meter would result in this line. Doran (1931, p. 128): Possibly Sh. removed the phrase here and in 746 and 833 to get rid of its repetition in Goneril’s part.

731 that]
Jennens (ed. 1770) prefers Q’s reading to F’s your: If we read your, we make the next clause of the sentence, whereof…fraught, unnecessary.

732 whereof]
Franz (§347): Of which (OED, adv. 4: Wherewith).

732 fraught]
Schmidt (1874): Filled (OED, ppl. a. 2b, quoting this l.); Idem (ed. 1879): Equivalent to freighted; usually followed by with; only in this passage by of (Ger.).

733 dispositions]
See n. 329.

733 that]
On F’s which see n. 235.

733 transforme]
Schmidt (ed. 1879) defends F’s transport by citing similar uses of the word at Cor. 1.1.75 (76) and WT 3.2.158 (1343); but the same kind of example supports Q’s transform—e.g., Ado 2.3.24 (855), JC 1.3.24 (456). Kirschbaum (1945, p. 23): Q’s term is hackneyed, F’s includes covert insult. But transform is Sh.’s more usual word for a man’s alteration to something lower—a dog, a beast, an oyster, an ape, etc.—and Goneril speaks with insulting sarcasm in both texts. Duthie (1949, p. 42): A likely synonym-substitution. Foakes (ed. 1997), transport: Carry you away emotionally.

735 an Asse]
Eccles (ed. 1792): I [the fool]. Foakes (ed. 1997): Even a fool.

735–6 cart…horse]
Proverbial: Tilley C103, To set the Cart before the horse. Eccles (ed. 1792), literally: The preposterous enormity of such base and unnatural behavior. Brooke (ed. 1947): When the relation of father and child is unnaturally inverted. Muir (ed. 1952): When a daughter gives instructions to her royal father. Elton (1966, pp. 312–13) places this and similar statements by the fool in the medieval and Renaissance tradition of the world-upside-down topos; cf. 676, 685–6, 744+4.

737 whoop…thee]
Steevens (ed. 1773): From the burthen of an old song. Though Malone (1780, 1:259) compares the song burden in WT 4.4.198–200 (2023–4), Whoop, do me no harm, good man, and the Clarkes (ed. 1868) cite a line, Whoop, Jinny, come down to me, from a related song in Chappell’s Popular Music (1859, p. 774), no song bearing the Fool’s line has been found. Some eds. follow Reynolds (see n. 684) in supposing the line intentional nonsense to cloak his plain speaking (Herford, ed. 1899); others think that the words have a point, possibly conveyed by an accompanying grimace and a caper (Kittredge, ed. 1940). Hunter (ed. 1869) evidently thinks it addressed to Lear: Pull away! jog on! Armour (ed. ca. 1930): Probably addressed to the horse, which he calls Jug. So Lott (ed. 1974), adding, It plainly refers to putting the cart before the horse. Others imagine it is a response to placate an angry Goneril. Moberly (ed. 1876): As things have got the wrong way forward, I know what fair lady I must pay my court to now. Tovey (ed. 1896): Perhaps with a start of pretended terror at the angry face of Goneril. Hunter (ed. 1972): It repudiates the involvement with others which appears in the preceding line. Others find a sarcasm. Rolfe (ed. 1880): Perhaps to express ironically the Fool’s estimation of Goneril. Brooke (ed. 1947): With sardonic reference to Goneril. Wilson (ed. 1960): An ironical cry of admiration for Gon., here called a whore (see following notes). Rosenberg (1972, p. 118): Pretending mock love to her. Halio (ed. 1992): Gonerill makes a threatening gesture that elicits this mock protestation of love. Weis (ed. 1993): Ironic admiration for Goneril’s shameless boldness.

737 whoop]
The exclamation served many purposes, expressing excitement, surprise, derision, exultation, incitement, etc. (OED, int., quoting this l.).

737 Iug]
First explained as a nickname for Joan in Boswell (ed. 1821, 21:391 n.). OED (sb.1 1): Applied as a common noun to a homely woman, maid-servant, sweet-heart, or mistress; or as a term of disparagement. Verity (in Irving & Marshall, ed. 1889) provides exx. of both affectionate and disparaging usage, commenting: It signifies a mistress; and sometimes, less offensively, a friend. Wilson (ed. 1960): Jug = contemptuous for Joan, and Joan often = whore, citing Cambyses 251–2. So Williams (1994). Edwards (ed. 1975): Or the bottle.

738–829 Doth…thee]
For the remainder of the scene Lear apparently speaks verse, all of it incorrectly set as prose in Q. See .

738–40 Doth…doth]
F’s change to Do’s…Do’s seems insignificant, and may be scribal or compositorial. Blake (2002, p. 66): Any anyone, anybody usually takes a singular verb.

738–9 Doth…Lear]
Roderick (in Edwards, 1758, pp. 218–20): Lear’s question and answer are an ironical response to Goneril’s claim that he is transported beyond his former self. Heath (1765, p. 325): Lear is too astonished and excited to be ironical. Page (ed. 1889): Lear expresses his astonishment by professing to doubt his own identity. Goggin (ed. 1910): Lear’s bewilderment and astonishment at Goneril’s attack are so great that at first he cannot believe he is really himself. Hence he does not at once break out into the outburst of passion which would be natural to his character. Goneril, of course, recognizes the irony behind both of Lear’s questions (730, 738) when she disdains his performance as a pose of admiration, a pranke. Jorgensen (1967, pp. 74–5): There is something like an ancient clown in [Lear’s] behavior.…Never having learned to think,…he can only ludicrously dramatize his sense of outrage and self-pity. Harbage (1963, p. 408): His attempts to answer with irony are lamely ineffectual—in this kind of warfare he is completely outgunned. Mahood (1992, p. 161): His Knights are one set of coordinates, his children being the other, which plot his very identity, and any threat of withdrawal leaves him disoriented. Foakes (ed. 1997): Lear’s dawning recognition of a gap between his role (as king) and his identity (as human being) begins here.

738 any]
I.e., any one. Cf. Franz §352.

740 walke thus]
Lear may be staggering. Rosinger (1983) suggests walk in one’s sleep, citing OED (v.1 10): To act in sleep (J[ohnson, 1755]);…as a somnambulist, quoting Mac. 5.1.3 (2096) as its first ex.

741–2 either…so]
Since 740 and 743 are regular iambic lines, eds. attempt to tailor these intervening lines as verse also, usually as F does, by dividing after discernings and omitting sleeping. But possibly Q’s prose reflects a verse line intentionally full, to be divided after lethargie; such a line may be read as rough pentameter with elisions to either’s and or’s.

741 notion, weaknes]
Compositorial misreading or transposition of letters in Q, for which F’s Notion weakens, accepted by all eds., is the obvious correction. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 375): The [Q] punctuation suggests that weaknes was definitely intended. On the intransitive use of the verb, see n. 485. Heath (1765, p. 325), notion: Apprehension (OED, sb. 5a: Understanding, mind, intellect, quoting this l. as its first ex., before Mac. 3.1.82 [1078], a Notion craz’d). Verity (ed. 1897): The first hint from Lear’s own lips of what becomes so tremendous a feature of the play, viz. his insanity. His words are truer than he suspects.

741 or]
Q’s word is useful if discernings means other than notion (see next n.); F’s omission may be intended to smooth the meter, but it also creates a puzzling ellipsis. Thus Lott (ed. 1974): Ha!…breaks off the sentence before he ever reaches the or that one would expect to follow Either. Halio (ed. 1992), defending F: Moved almost to incoherence, Lear does not complete the either/or construction.

741 his discernings]
The second his in the line is usually taken in parallel with the first as referring to Lear; but Page (ed. 1889): Perhaps his here signifies its [see n. 727], and refers to the mind. Sh. does not elsewhere use discernings. Most eds. understand it as Heath (1765, p. 325): His faculty of discernment, whereby he is enabled to distinguish persons and things, and know one thing from another (OED: Distinction, discrimination; intellectual perception, discernment)—i.e., a particular faculty of mind. But Hudson (ed. 1879): Notion and discernings are evidently meant here as equivalent terms…for mind, judgment, or understanding. Just as probably, the word refers to the sense of sight, and repeats the doubt expressed in where…eyes; OED (Discern, v. 5): To distinguish (an object) with the eyes.

742 are lethergie]
F’s Lethargied has been universally preferred, because it makes good sense— Dulled as with a lethargy (Wright, ed. 1875)—and because confusions of terminal e and d are common (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 375). Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 512): Possibly a misreading of lethergic. Still, it is just possible that lethargie is right, but that the Q compositor who botched weaknes in the previous line tried to make lethargie a parallel noun by supplying are. Stone (1980, p. 225): Perhaps his discernings are <mere [ = nothing but, no more than]> lethargy. F’s participle Lethargied requires a transitive verb to lethargy; OED quotes this l. as the only evidence for such a verb before 1769, and Sh. uses it or its participle nowhere else. If he were coining a nonce-word, he could as easily have intended the verb to be intransitive, parallel to weakens. In any case the idea of a lethargy leads to Lr.’s next idea: are his mind weak and his perceptions dull because he is asleep?

742 sleeping…ha!]
In Q Lear either wonders whether he is asleep or awake, or (less probably) says that his mind is dull whether he is asleep or awake. There is a clear sequence of ideas; see prev. n. F’s Ha! Waking? simply expresses astonishment that he is awake, without the transitional doubt whether he is asleep. Kirschbaum (1945, p. 24), however: Q’s use of the conventional pair of terms is vulgar and debilitating, F’s substitution is dramatically abrupt.

742 ha!]
The exclamation occasionally expresses indignation in Sh. (Schmidt, 1874), though more usually wonder, surprise, or impatience. Presumably here it is in reaction to some bit of stage business, such as the pin prick he gives himself at 2807–8, or pinching himself (Harbage, ed. 1958) or shak[ing] himself (Halio, ed. 1973), to decide whether he is sleeping, or wakeing. Possibly, however, it is a scornful rejection of the possibilities he has been enumerating. See n. 592.

742 tis not so]
Generally taken to refer to wakeing; but the following question allows the possibility that it refers to 739—’tis not so that I am Lear—or, perhaps most probably, that it answers the implied question whether he fails to recognize himself because his perception is dulled by weakness or sleep. Rejecting this possibility (tis not so) and assured that he is fully awake and sentient, he returns (with heavy irony) to the first explanation—that he must indeed not be Lear. Foakes (ed. 1997): In Q Lear denies with these words that his discernings are dulled, sleeping or waking. But why would Lear first announce the obvious—that his discernings were dulled while sleeping—and then deny it? More probably Q and F mean the same thing: Lear determines he is awake, and so rejects sleep as the cause of his confusion.

743 who is…am]
Weidhorn (1969, p. 308) finds this a more despairing question than the former (738): It implies not only I don’t know but also Is there anyone at all who does know? But if Lear is being ironic, the question is rhetorical, a challenge. Foakes (ed. 1997, pp. 18–19): It highlights at once a rift in Lear himself that will lead to madness, and his failure to perceive the nature of what he has done, viz., divide[d] not only his lands but himself. He cannot stop being King, yet gives his power away. The context makes clear, however, that Lear is not thinking only of the office of kingship, but of his identity as a man and especially a father: Are you our daughter? The lines cut from Q (744+1–+4) reinforce this idea.

743 who I am?]
Walker (1953, pp. 64–6): This query may make a pentameter line with 744+1 I would…markes, if Lears shadow is considered a prose interjection and not part of the verse line. Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960, p. 138): This can be scanned, in more than one way. But…in no way that seems to me convincingly Shakespearian.

744 Lears shadow?]
Shadow means unreal or unsubstantial image (OED, sb. 6). Brown (ed. 1976): Also departed spirit (OED, 7). Q lines as prose continually with I…that (744+1), with which it may make a pentameter line, of five stresses but lacking unstressed syllables between the first two and last two words. F, cutting the following four lines, assigns 744 to the Fool. There are two reasons, neither conclusive, to think that in the MS behind Q the words were spoken by Lear. Verity (ed. 1897): In the old play [Leir 1110–11]…the king says, Cease, good Perillus, for to call me Lord, And think me but the shaddow of my selfe; see . Righter (1962, p. 133): In 1H6 5.4.133 (2775) Alençon, a king whose authority has been given up,…is now as shadow of himself. Rosenberg (1972, p. 107): A mirror in Fool’s hand would multiply ironies. He is Lear’s looking-glass. Does Lear himself carry a mirror? Shickman (1991, pp. 77 ff.), finding several illustrations of a fool holding a mirror, argues that Lear’s Fool has one, and holds it up for Lear to look into; he provides no evidence from contemporary stage practice, however. Kerrigan (1983, p. 219): A misattribution in Q would presuppose not one but two omitted prefixes. He suggests that giving this speech to the Fool in F makes up for cutting his speech at 744+4, but he does not say why the replacement is necessary—Q is excellent in itself; and his appreciation of Lear’s growing understanding of himself in Q as he concedes that he has become his own shadow is dubious, since Lear’s question is more likely an ironic challenge than a concession. In F Kerrigan finds virtue in the non-sequitur between 744 and 745: The Fool’s words resonate, and…the King takes a silent step towards self-discovery. Stone (1980, p. 229): In a speech largely consisting of rhetorical questions there is nothing untoward in Lear’s answering his own question. Richman (1986, p. 378): Lear’s answering his own question with another question and then switching to sarcasm is a wild see-sawing of moods taxing to the actor and too close to madness this early in the play. Foakes (ed. 1997): Q is simpler.…F is more complex: does the Fool mean both that he is Lear’s shadow (or the mirror-image in which Lear may see himself as a fool), and that Lear has become a shadow of his former self? But perhaps the Fool answers only Lear’s immediate question (who I am), not both it and the previous one (who is it) with one and the same answer having quite different meanings for the two questions. (Ibid., p. 19 n.): Lear continues to act as if he retains royal authority until well into Act 2, and the change in F makes the action more consistent. Such is Goneril’s self-serving (and therefore doubtful) claim in 522+1–+2; but it may as easily be claimed that after his abdication Lear never asserts royal authority, but simply insists upon the treatment that was a pre-condition for his daughter’s receiving his land (see nn. 143–4, 144) and that is consistent with normal decency and his dignity as former monarch and father.
Although the attribution in F to the Fool suits his character and previous comments, it may possibly be an error. If 744+1–+3 were cut as redundant (see next note), 744+4 would also have been cut to avoid a non-sequitur. If the speech prefix for the Fool still stood legibly in the margin after 744+4 had been marked for deletion, a Folio scribe or compositor might have assigned it to the last remaining line before 745, thinking some remark by another character was intended to stand between the end of Lear’s concluding speech and the beginning of a new speech also bearing Lear’s speech prefix. Knight (ed. 1840) puts dashes at the end of this line and the previous one, indicating that Lear ignores the Fool’s interruption and goes on to his next speech. Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 375–6): The question mark in Q…may be intended for an exclamation mark.

744+1–+4 I…father]
By introducing the subject of daughters the Q lines serve as a transition from Lear’s play-acting and rhetorical questions to a direct confrontation of Goneril. Without them, in F, Lear goes abruptly from asking who he is to asking who Goneril is—an apparent non-sequitur. Lettsom (in Walker, 1860, 1:5 n.): The quartos give an unsophisticated text, though one disfigured by some palpable blunders, while in the folio we have a text derived from a good original, but sophisticated in a blundering way for the sake of the metre. Delius (1876, p. 141): An un-authorial cut: Consequently there is no motive for Lear’s [preceding] passionate question. Schmidt (ed. 1879): Perhaps there is here a real gap in the Ff, but the lines which the Qq offer in its place are too questionable to be adopted in the text (Ger.). Chambers (1930, 1:467) and Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 376) also find a lacuna. Possibly the cut was made intentionally because Lear had already once questioned whether Goneril were his daughter (730) and whether he had his true knowledge and reason. Doran (1931, pp. 69–70), however, suspects accidental omission: In F the phrase Lears shadow is rightly assigned to the Fool. It is a gratuitous remark which Shakespeare may have inserted in the quarto manuscript after he had written the passage. Perhaps he omitted the speech heading. In any case, the printer of Q1 thought it was to be inserted in the middle of Lear’s speech. What is lacking from the folio appears to be necessary to the sequence of Lear’s thought.…The Fool’s two comments are of the nature of asides. If Lear hears them, he pays no attention. Therefore the passage does not appear to be a deliberate omission from the folio. Perhaps the transcriber [preparing playhouse copy], in copying the quarto manuscript, had sufficient acumen to perceive that Lears shadow was meant for the Fool, but misunderstood its purpose, thought it was intended to be the answer to Lear’s question and to supplant Lear’s own answer. Kirschbaum (1945, p. 25): Of course, it is possible that the F compositor unconsciously selected the wrong Lear speech to follow the Fool’s speech, but I do not think [so]. Duthie (op. cit.), on the other hand, suspects such a compositor’s error: first the F scribe assigned 744 to the Fool; then the F compositor, having set up this short speech of the Fool, may have accidentally let his eye return to the copy after the Fool’s next speech. Horsman (ed. 1973): An obvious gap is left unless the actor could, by emphasizing Your name…, imply the connection: If I am not Lear who are you?. Capell (1783, 1.2:151–2) defends the cut as one of Shakespeare’s own mending: Q is in many parts nonsense, verse rarely, whereas F has simplicity, clearness, and the beauty of making Lear’s last question answer’d to by the Fool. Kerrigan (1983, p. 220) admits the lacuna but finds it a virtue: F surpasses Q. It opens a gap between Lears shadow and Your name… which is both painful and unignorable. The poetic space can scarcely be played across. Within it, the Fool’s words resonate, and…the King takes a silent step towards self-discovery.

744+1–+3 I…daughters]
Brooke (ed. 1947): Lear’s speech…, badly preserved in the Quarto, which alone contains it, was evidently in verse. Only the last line of it now scans. Wilson (ed. 1960): The scansion seems convincingly verse; the succession of strong accents underlining Lear’s agonized insistence. Wells (ed. 2000): He may mean either I wish I knew who I am (I can’t be Lear), or I should like to be persuaded I am merely Lear’s shadow, not Lear himself.

744+1 that]
This may refer to who I am, since Lear’s identity has been the burden of his last remarks; but it may refer to the proximate idea, that I am Lear’s shadow, since as Verity (ed. 1897) says, It would be a relief to him to find that he is only a shadow, i.e. that he has no daughters, and that the supposed existence of a monster like Goneril is only a nightmare. Knight (ed. 1840; see n. 744) punctuates so as to make the remoter reference possible, and his interpretation has been accepted by the Clarkes (ed. 1868), Deighton (ed. 1891), Tovey (ed. 1896), Lee (ed. 1908), Kittredge (ed. 1940), Muir (ed. 1952), Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960), and others. Hammond (1988, p. 101): Neither Q nor F suggests that Lear’s I would learne that is a reply to a remark by the Fool, as in the conventionally conflated text.

744+1–+3 for…daughters]
Rann (ed. 1794): Were I to judge my own identity and sanity by certain qualities which I once possessed, I might thence also erroneously conclude that I had daughters; whereas the contrary is clear from the treatment which I now experience. The present Lear, without daughters, is not the true Lear, or is dreaming.

744+1–+3 by…reason]
Most eds. take three nouns in parallel, following Tyrwhitt (1766, pp. 52–3): Marks of sovereignty, of knowledge, and of reason. The Clarkes (ed. 1868) understand a double parallelism: By the tokens of sovereignty that I still retain, by the knowledge and reason that are still mine; this makes superior sense, avoiding the obscure meaning of marks of knowledge and reason. Hudson (ed. 1879) and Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) make the last two nouns appositives to the first; the former interprets knowledge and reason, which are our supreme guides or attributes (see next note), and the latter The marks of sovereignty are knowledge of things and reason upon them—a doubtful proposition. Staunton’s (ed. 1859) attempt to elide three nouns into two terms by removing a comma—sovereignty knowledge and reason, i.e. of supreme or sovereign knowledge—involves unnecessary forcing of language.

744+1 markes of soueraintie]
Roderick (in Edwards, 1758, p. 219; 1765, p. 268), questionably: I.e. the distinction and respect due to; so Wilson (ed. 1960): Implies not self-recognition but a realization that he should command obedience and respect. More probably, Johnson (in Steevens, ed. 1773) and most eds.: Tokens [OED, sb.1 10] arising from sovereignty—presumably the name and all the additions to a king (Malone, ed. 1790), his dress, and his entourage of knights, Kent, and the Fool. Foakes (ed. 1997): Perhaps Lear displays some insignia; but Lear says the, not these. Mason (1785, p. 343), improbably: Those tokens of royalty which his daughters then enjoyed, as derived from him. Hudson (ed. 1879): Sovereign marks (see prev. n.); likewise Page (ed. 1889) and Lee (ed. 1908): Sovereign powers. Joseph (ed. 1966): Signs of Man’s pre-eminence on earth. So Stone (1980, p. 234): Sovereignty over the animals.

744+2 false perswaded]
Craig (ed. 1901): Falsely. Perhaps we should hyphen. So OED (False, adv. 2b, quoting this l.). Muir (ed. 1952) cites such compounds with false at 2H4 4.1.188 (2056) and Ant. 4.14.19 (2846), neither hyphened originally.

744+2–+3 I had daughters]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): That I am King Lear—and he, I know, had daughters.

744+4 Which]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Referred [to]…I [744+3], and is used [for]…whom. Abbott (§265): Which…is used interchangeably with Who; cf. Franz §335. OED (Which pron. 9): Used of persons…the ordinary word being who (objective whom). So most eds. Cf. 761, 1176, 1633, 2232. Knight (ed. 1840) and several followers who treat this line as an interrupted continuation of 744 (see textual n.): Refers to shadow. Wright (ed. 1875) and Tovey (ed. 1896), finding shadow too remote an antecedent, refer the pronoun to daughters, the former explaining, It is rather like an instance of which with the redundant personal pronoun for who, and the latter, Much as Chaucer uses that he for who, comparing LLL 4.2.29 (1180) Which we = we who. Stone (1980, p. 234), uniquely: Both sense and metre require the addition…of thee: Which < = as to which, see Abbott §272> they will make <thee> an obedient father.

746 Come sir]
F omits, substituting Sir in midline. See n. 731.

746 admiration]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Assumed wonder, pretended amazement. Hunter (ed. 1972): Perhaps astonishing behaviour. Walker (1854, p. 230): Five syllables. But the F line allows only four.

746 sauour]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Taste, character. OED (sb. 3b): Fig.…Character, style, sort, quoting this l. as its first ex. of two.

747 other your]
Craig (ed. 1901): Other of your. An old genitive construction; see Franz §329 on the word order, which Halio (ed. 1992) calls anastrophe. Rolfe (ed. 1880) compares 2H4 4.4.53 (2429), other his…followers. See Abbott §12 on the use of other as either adjective or pronoun.

747–8 you vnderstand]
F adds To to begin the second line, probably to regularize meter in 748 (though not 747). But you may have been intended to begin 748, thus making both lines regular. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 512): Shakespeare uses line-divided feet often in this period.

749 reuerend]
Schmidt (1875): Entitled to high respect, venerable.…Nearly equivalent to old (OED, a. 1; = Reverent a. 1). Cf. 1204. On the scansion see n. 154.

749 should]
Q2’s added you is unnecessary and lames the metre (Furness, ed. 1880). Hunter (ed. 1869) unnecessarily transposes a parenthesis and converts adjectives to nouns: Old and reverend, as you are, should be wise. Clarkes (ed. 1868): The word you…is elliptically understood as repeated before should…for the sake of metrical euphony.

749 wise]
Dent (1981, O37): Proverbial: Older and wiser. Carter (1905, p. 435) cites Job 32:7.

750 Knights and Squires]
In 141, knights only. There may be no serious inconsistency, since a squire, attendant on a knight and next in rank under him, was a kind of apprentice knight. Lott (ed. 1974): They were originally shield-bearers. Goneril, who may not know the rank of each of Lear’s men, is using a common verbal formula to describe his whole retinue. Muir (ed. 1952, pp. xxxiv): In Higgins’s Mirour [1574] Leire is granted threscore knightes & squires (see ). The squires are not mentioned in Holinshed, Spenser, or Leir; Perrett (1904, pp. 186–90), showing that they were first added in the account of Wace and had last appeared in Caxton (1502) and Higgins (1574; not 1587), concludes that Sh. probably knew one of the two latter versions of the Lear story. In Wace and many subsequent early accounts, to the number of knights is added an additional number of their squires; in Caxton and Higgins the their disappears and the more ambiguous enumeration of 40 (or 60) knights & squires is given, as here.

751 men…bold]
Sprague (1944, p. 284): From Ferrer’s promptbook we learn that in Kean’s performance…Knts turn slowly & look at each other in intense surprise. Cf. n. 586–872. Pearson (1949, p. 140) sees an allusion to James’s court during the visit of the Danish king in the summer of 1606.

751 disordred]
OED (ppl. a. 2): Morally…corrupt; disorderly, unruly, quoting this l.

751 deboyst]
This and debosh’d (F’s constant sp. of the word) are variants of debauched, meaning both debased (Schmidt, 1874) and led away from proper service and allegiance (Bevington, ed. 1992). OED treats Deboist (var. deboisht etc.) as a separate 17th-c. by-form.

752 our]
Goggin (ed. 1910) and McLeod (1983, p. 176) suspect a royal we here; but since Goneril refers to herself by singular pronouns throughout the rest of the speech and scene, it is more likely a simple collective, as in our liues in 848.

752 infected]
OED (ppl. a. 2): Contaminated in respect of moral character, opinions, etc. Cf. 1449.

752 manners]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Conduct and character (OED, sb.1 4).

753 showes…lust]
The line scans adequately if epicurisme is stressed only on the third syllable; Bailey, Dictionary (1730) stresses the second.

753 showes]
Wright (ed. 1875): Appears (OED, v. 30). Cf. n. 485, and 780.

753–4 epicurisme…lust…tauerne…brothell]
Furness (ed. 1880): An instance of what [Hiram] Corson calls a respective construction. The first word refers to the third and the second to the fourth.

753 epicurisme]
OED (2): Practical conformity to the (supposed) principles of Epicurus;…sensuality, quoting this l, the word’s only occurrence in Sh. Gardner (ed. 1969): The true epicurean philosophy, which advocated temperate pleasure and the virtue of tranquillity, was always misrepresented in this way. But Goneril is probably thinking of a more specialized meaning. Craig (ed. 1901): Gluttony (OED, 2b).

753 lust]
Not elsewhere one of Goneril’s moral concerns. Heilman (1948, p. 101): The first in a pattern of references to sex as a symbol of evil and corruption of creative energies. Main (ed. 1962): Later, in her lust for Edmund, she will try [to make her house] a brothel.

754 make]
F’s Makes it supplies the necessary complement, probably overlooked in Q. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 512) prefer a more convoluted construction…appropriate to Goneril, an understood which after Inne in the previous l.; but in that case the sentence says that an inn is being made like a tavern, which is neither very good sense nor Goneril’s point that the court is being degraded. Abbott (§336): Inflection in s [frequently occurs] with two singular nouns as subject. Cf. Franz §673, and 1055, 1256, 1536, 1923, 1931; cf. n. 1055.

754 or]
F’s or a regularizes meter. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 512): Though Q could easily have omitted an a, the line is metrically acceptable if a caesura is understood after tauerne.

755 great]
The likeness of orthography and sound to F’s grac’d suggests error in one of the texts, though Stone (1980, p. 215) holds for conscious revision: The contrast…which concludes the sentence reqires no more meaning or weight…than is given by great pallace: the added emphasis of grac’d is superfluous, and its meaning (if any) irrelevant. Grac’d was possibly suggested to the reviser by an untidily written greate [cf. Stone p. 100: grate?] in the manuscript he consulted; it may, on the other hand, represent compositor B’s misreading of manuscript copy. But misreading of grac’d by the Q compositor is also possible. Q is simple and clear, F’s grac’d less so. Schmidt (1874): Full of graces, dignified, honorable (OED, quoting this l.)—but the source of the honor is disputed. Warburton (ed. 1747): Graced with the presence of its sovereign—i.e., by his grace, the King (Hunter, ed. 1972). Frost (ed. 1909): Graced by such as Goneril. Muir (ed. 1952): The abode of stately decorum; so Skillan (ed. 1967): With good taste, morals and manners. Thomas (1995, p. 579): F’s grac’d is obviously right, a necessary antithesis to the squalid, ungraced Taverne or a Brothell. Elton (1966, p. 119 n.) cites Tilley W328, Whoredom and grace can never bide in one place, a rare proverb; neither Tilley nor Dent (1981) cites this l.

755 speake]
Schmidt (1875): Call (OED, v. 10b: Ask for, quoting this l.).

756 thou]
Both Q’s reading and F’s then make good sense, but Q’s thou may be suspect because Goneril addresses Lear by the more formal you throughout the rest of the speech, scene, and play. Wilson (1923, p. 119) notes other instances in Shn. texts where these two words have been mistaken for each other. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 376): Probably a misreading—o/e, u/n.

756 desired]
Muir (ed. 1952): Requested (OED, Desire v. 6).

757 that…begs]
Smith (ed. 1902): Goneril admits her own masterfulness. Her threats are no longer hesitating or cloaked in obscure phraseology.

758 a little]
See n. 810.

758 disquantitie]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:20): Lessen (OED, v. 1, quoting this, the only occurrence in Sh., as its first ex.). Abbott (§439): Dis- was sometimes used in the sense of un-. Cf. Franz §84, and 797. Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 133): Shakespeare is especially fond of negative terms, which are the contradictories of the corresponding positive terms. By them he achieves vigor and freshness. Blake (2002, p. 214): Shakespeare does not use a verb quantity.

759–60 remainder…to bee]
Abbott (§354): Noun and infinitive [are] used as subject or object. Cf. Franz §§656, 658.

759 remainder]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 136): F’s remainders, meaning those who remain, is found in Cymbeline [1.1.129 (154)].

759 still depend]
See n. 143. Wright (ed. 1875): Remain dependants (OED, Depend v.1 3). Cf. Tro. 3.1.4–6 (1482–4).

760 besort]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:6): To sort or suit with (OED, v., quoting only this l.). Abbott (§438): The prefix be is used…to convert…nouns into verbs. Cf. Franz §76, and 1638+8, 2311+2. Skillan (ed. 1967): I.e., elderly.

761 that]
This and F’s which mean who. See n. 744+4, Abbott §§258–9, and OED (rel. pron. 3b, quoting this l.).

761 know…you]
Wilson (ed. 1960): I.e. know how to behave and recognize that you are an old man whose foibles should not be encouraged. Note the ironical echo of [318–19]—and of the proverb (Tilley K175).

762 Darkenes, and Deuils]
Frost (ed. 1909): These words have no particular meaning; they suit his angry state of mind, and being full of dentals and sibilants, would come from clenched teeth with hissing sounds. They are different from the oaths to pagan gods in the first scene, and anticipate later references to madness as demonic possession. Elton (1966, p. 176 n.): Lear’s curse…leads eventually into the obscurity of the villains, threading…night ([1062]), and into the lust-ridden Edgar’s demonic underworld.

763 saddle…together]
Halio (ed. 1992): Lear’s servants seem frozen here; thus, he must order them again at [785]…and [803]. Nevertheless, Oxford [ed. 1986] adds sd Exit one or more. See n. 785. In Leir 852 (see ) the suggestion to seeke some other place comes from Gonorill, not Leir.

764 degenerate]
Joseph (ed. 1966): Devoid of ancestral virtues,…without family qualities (OED, a. 1).

764 bastard]
Traversi (1952, p. 55): An anticipation of the fateful curse shortly to come [789 ff.]. McCann (ed. 1964): Goneril has not only become base, but cannot be his lawful daughter. Cf. 1409–10. Foakes (ed. 1997): Equating her with Edmund. But Lear has no reason yet to think Edmund morally degenerate; see 2560–1. In his anger he is speaking in hyperbole; he does not, of course, believe that Goneril is actually illegitimate, and calls her daughter to the end of the play (1435, 1512, etc.). (Ibid., p. 97): Cf. Leir 312 ().

765 yet…daughter]
So Perillus to the king in Leir 909: You haue two daughters left; see . Wells (ed. 2000): Possibly a = one, implying that he disowns both Cordelia and Gonoril.

766 You]
Hodge & Kress (1982, p. 145): Goneril’s non-reciprocal pronoun following Lear’s intimate thee indicates [her] power. Or a certain coolness at being called degenerate bastard.

768 Duke.]
So Q here and in following SPs; F specifies Albany and Alb. Bullough (1973, p. 290): In both plays [Leir and Lr.] Goneril’s husband is amiable and mild. In Leir [966] (where he is Cornwall) he listens to his wife’s tirade until he can bear it no longer and goes out; see .

769 We…repent’s]
Although most eds. prefer F’s Woe…repents, Q makes sense as a sentence broken off at Albany’s entrance: We…repent us, a reading reflected in Q2’s repent’s vs. Wells (ed. 2000) replaces Q1’s comma with a dash to mark an aposiopesis, and glosses We—royal plural—who repent etc. Capell (1783, 1.2:14) interprets F’s Woe as either the subject of an interrupted sentence or as an ellipsis of Woe to him; no one suggests the equally likely Woe to us. Joseph (ed. 1966): The sorrow that repents too late. Stone (1980, p. 215): The ellipsis in F…for which no precedent has been found, is doubtfully idiomatic. Franz §542, however, lists analogous omissions of prepositions. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 376): The [Q] compositor probably misread woe as wee.…[repent’s] looks as if it were consequent on the error. But the reverse could be equally true of the F compositor. Whatever version is preferred, the sudden introduction of the notion of repentance is puzzling. Stone (op. cit., p. 231) suspects it begins a hypocritical sentiment at the end of Goneril’s speech, interrupted by her husband’s entrance. Malone (ed. 1790) compares a speech of Cordila in Higgins’s Mirour: Then he to late his rigour did repente | Gainst me; see . Muir (ed. 1952): It may originate in the proverb in Florio’s Second frvtes (1591), Yet, but too late repents the ratt, | If once her taile be caught by the cat (quoted by Tilley R32, Too late does the Rat repent in the cat’s paws, without citing this passage). Tilley M875, It is never too late to Mend (repent), cites this l.; Dent (1981) prefers A211, When All is consumed repentance comes too late and R80, Repentance never comes too late. Cf. n. 1523. Edwards (ed. 1975): Superficially…addressed to Goneril. You had better repent.…Lear, however, must also be thinking of himself, determined to repent in time of his indulgence to Goneril, conscious that he repented too late of his harshness to Cordelia.

769 O…come?]
F omits, perhaps accidentally (Doran, 1931, p. 69), leaving a metrically incomplete line. Kirschbaum (1945, p. 26): Q’s phrase makes Lear out as petulant.…In F he suddenly throws his question at Albany without any kind of preparatory greeting. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 172): The F arrangement is effective, Lear in his passion shouting…with no preliminary greeting. But I think that Q sounds better, and it is very possible that the F compositor accidentally omitted half a line. Or a scribe did. Weis (ed. 1993): Q has Lear acknowledge Albany’s presence and offers a complete line. Stone (1980, p. 231): In Q, 770–1, O…horses, should surely be given to one of Lear’s gentlemen.…The revision in F…is entirely unconvincing.

770 is…will]
In Q, Lear’s question to Albany makes no sense, since neither he nor Goneril has suggested that Lear should prepare to depart. Most probably the compositor read my (F’s reading) as any. That small (probable) error corrected, the Q line makes perfect sense: like the F line, it requires a midline pause while a dumfounded Albany fails to respond, whereupon the enraged Lear abruptly shouts to whichever of his retainers are within earshot, Prepare my horses. Some eds. punctuate a midline break: see textual n. F marks the pause more emphatically by adding speake Sir, dropping that wee to preserve meter. A few defend Q. Van Dam (1935, p. 98): The F line is illogical: Albany cannot know what will is meant, and after speake Sir one cannot expect Lear going on with Prepare my Horses. Weis (ed. 1993), retaining any: Q’s version is dramatically stronger in conveying Lear’s distraught state of mind, which in his encounters with Goneril (1.4) and Regan (2.4) repeatedly causes his sentences to be choked off in mid-flow from the sheer pressure of violent emotion. Lott (ed. 1974): As they are in Albany’s palace, he is properly their host, and should be able to overrule his wife. His entry gives Lear some faint hope of this.

771 marble harted]
Taylor (1925, p. 30) thinks Sh. derived this exceeding rare phrase from Florio’s tr. of Montaigne [ed. 1910, 1:21], but the metaphor, used in 3H6 3.1.38 (1436), was proverbial: see Tilley H311. Craig (ed. 1901) compares marble-breasted in TN 5.1.124 (2280) and Heywood’s Dialogues (Works, ed. Pearson, 6:300).

772 thee]
For thyself (Abbott §223). Cf. Franz §307.

773 Sea-monster]
Abend (1949, pp. 535–6) notes thirteen Shn. associations of ingratitude with monstrosity; cf. 912. Though Sh. does not here specify a particular kind of monster, commentators have. Upton (1748, p. 203): the Hippopotamus; the hieroglyphical symbol of impiety and ingratitude, citing Sandys, Relation (ed. 1637, p. 105): The River-horse [signified] Murder, impudence, violence, and injustice; for they say that he killeth his Sire, and ravisheth his owne dam. Wright (ed. 1875): His account is evidently taken from Plutarch’s Isis and Osiris, and Shakespeare may have read it in Holland’s translation. Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): But that animal is a river monster. A. (1909, p. 424) quotes OED citations from Bossewell, Armorie (1572, 2:65b) and Daniel, Philotas (1605, p. 274) placing it in the sea; but the first citation is illustrated by a sea-horse, not a hippopotamus, and the second animal only thrusts into the maine, which may mean seacoast estuaries, where it may in fact be found. Malone (Notebook, BL Add. 30,943, fol. 45v): Perhaps some particular sea-monster which had been exhibited in England, citing Wither, Britain’s Remembrancer (1628, canto 4): as rare a sight As…some great Monster spewd out of the Marine. Wright (loc. cit.): More likely…he meant the whale, in support of which Boodle (1884, p. 216) cites 2303+17 and Per. 2.1.30–4 (582–4). Hudson (ed. 1879): Probably…the dreadful beast that made such havoc with the virgin daughters of old Troy. Alluded to again in [MV 3.2.57 (1400)] as the Sea-monster. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): As told in Ovid, [Meta. 11].…Daughters were cast anciently to the sea-monster by unkind fathers; here the child casts away the father. Craig (ed. 1901): I think it is not likely Shakespeare had here any special kind of monster in his thoughts, but was thinking of those monsters of classical mythology slain by Hercules [saving Hesione] and by Perseus [saving Andromeda] in defence of beauty—these stories were then very popular. Bang (1903, p. 211) compares Jonson, Cynthia’s Revels 4.1.65, a sea-monster, that were to rauish Andromeda, citing Ovid, Meta. 4.670 ff. as the source. White (ed. 1866, 1:ccx f.): What is the sea monster? Yet how much more of horror is suggested by that definite indefinity than if the comparison had been in terms of a crocodile or a kraken. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The is manifestly the generic article. Gardner (ed. 1969): The context suggests a creature of human resemblance. The Nereids, or the Mermaids, were called sea-monsters: their body is rough and scaled all over, even in those parts wherein they resemble a woman (Pliny’s Natural History, tr. Philemon Holland, 1601 [p. 236]). They were, of course, treacherous. Hunter (ed. 1972): If any specific sea-monster is meant, that which destroyed Hippolytus…as described in the 1581 translation of Seneca’s Phaedra.…It is sent as a punishment for filial ingratitude. Bate (1989; 1993, p. 194): The image conflates two of the monsters slain by Perseus: marble-hearted and hideous come from the grotesque Gorgon’s head which turns to stone, and the sea-monster itself is that from which Perseus saves Andromeda. Weis (ed. 1993): The archetype of sea-monsters in the Judaeo-Christian tradition, however, is Leviathan from Job 41. Foakes (ed. 1997): Or Psa. 74:13–14. Dent (1981) detects two proverbs, Ingratitude comprehends (is the worst of) all faults (vices) (I66) and Ingratitude is monstrous (a monster) (I66.1).

774 Alb.…patient]
Adee (ed. 1890, p. xix): One of those purposed touches to make the future king, Albany, a favorite with the audience. Cunnington (1910, p. 447): Added in F to give emphasis to Lear’s rash temper.…[It] could be omitted without showing a gap. Doran (1931, p. 68): It is better than having Albany stand silent, as he does in Q1, despite Lear’s appeal to him, until Lear finishes his tirade of fifteen lines. Foakes (ed. 1997): Strengthening Albany’s role, and the play’s first call for patience, God’s medicine to heal grief and sorrow…[and] cure intemperate passion, comparing 1571, 1689. Honigmann (1965, p. 122): F’s addition interrupts Q’s pentameter line. Similarly Stone (1980, pp. 240–1): The speech is more likely an addition to F by a reviser than an omission from Q, since 773 and 775 make a pentameter if uninterrupted (he would line as 774–5; cf. textual n.).
