Moreover, It justifies, qua interruption, an apparently pointless discontinuity in Lear’s train of thought, an idea repeated by Urkowitz (1980, p. 44).

774 patient]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Calm. In this play the words patient and patience always have the root meaning of suffering or being able to endure trouble with composure (OED, a. 1), occasionally in the special senses of being forbearing with others (1b) or of waiting calmly (1c). Cf. 1416, 1524, 1571, 1689, 2016, 2347+16, 2475, 2525, 2620, 2998. Hoeniger (1992, p. 325): Patience [is] the virtue that alone can offer effective medicine to cure intemperate passion; cf. n. 1571. In Leir 755 the king is called the myrrour of mild patience; see .

775 detested]
See n. 284, cf. 1510.

775 kite]
Harrison (ed. 1948): The lowest of the birds of prey, an eater of offal. OED (sb. 2): Fig. A person who preys upon others, a rapacious person, quoting this l. Craig (ed. 1901): A term of strong opprobrium, when by Shakespeare applied to women, citing H5 2.1.76 (576), Ant. 3.13.89 (2261), where it means whore. Armstrong (1946, p. 12): Throughout Sh., a despicable creature symbolic of cowardice, meanness, cruelty and death. Foakes (ed. 1997): Listed in Leviticus, 11.14, as an abomination. Dent (1981) compares the proverb As kind as a Kite (K113).

775 list]
Collier (ed. 1843): May be right, taking to list in the sense of to limit or bound (OED, v.3 2b), presumably in the form list’st. This is possible if and is epexigetical, the equivalent of who are. Q2 guesses lessen for list, making traine, and men objects of this verb. All others follow F’s lyest, assuming that the Q compositor misread ly’st or li’st. Doran (1931, p. 23): List is misleading only because of its spelling and because it is not followed by a full stop. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 512): The manuscript probably contained no punctuation after list.

776 and]
See prev. n. Possibly a misreading of are (F).

776 choise and rarest]
Abbott (§398), followed by many eds.: The est of the second adjective modifies the first. Cf. 1220+3.

776 parts]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Qualities (OED, sb. 12). Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Accomplishments (OED, 11?).

778 exact regard]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Scrupulous observance. Craig (ed. 1901): Minute details. Fraser (ed. 1963), combining: Strict attention to detail.

778 support]
OED (v. 10a): Preserve, quoting this l.

779 worships]
Hudson (ed. 1871): Misprint of the plural for the singular. But OED (sb. 3b): With a and pl.: A distinction or dignity; a position of honour or high place, quoting this l. Tovey (ed. 1896): Plural…because there are many knights, each of whom maintains the honour of the knightly name. See n. 9, and Franz §680.

779 fault]
Lott (ed. 1974): Lack of gratitude. But since Lear has just cursed vehemently against ingratitude (771–3), and will again (802–3, 912, 1444–5, 1663–4, 1794–6), perhaps he means only Cordelia’s stubborn refusal to speak, which he misjudged (cf. 784–5). So Edwards (ed. 1975), who finds her failure to respond a small fault in comparison with Goneril’s callous ingratitude;…also small in comparison with its large effect in deranging Lear.

780 shewe]
See n. 753. Gardner (ed. 1969): The fault seemed the worse against the great virtue of Cordelia.

781 that]
On F’s Which see n. 235.

781 engine]
Many eds. follow Edwards (1750, p. 223) in identifying the engine of torture known as the rack (so OED, sb. 5b, quoting this l.). But the point of the sentence is not that Lear was tortured, but rather that a small fault exerted a great dislocation, as Delius (ed. 1854) notes. Beginning with Warburton (ed. 1747), who sees an allusion to the boast of Archimedes to move the world, others have identified the engine as a little lever which can dislodge a fixed mass (Harrison, ed. 1937). Wright (ed. 1875): In [Tmp. 2.1.162 (839)]…a warlike machine. Moberly (ed. 1876): Some windlass of terrible power. Kittredge (ed. 1940): A machine of any kind. Joseph (ed. 1966): Wedge.

781 frame of nature]
Deighton (ed. 1891): My natural disposition. Tovey (ed. 1896): The Natural affections of Lear. Salingar (1983, p. 139): His personality as a coherent whole. See nn. 185, 441. Maxwell (apud Muir, ed. 1952): Lear’s frame being prised apart. Gardner (ed. 1969): Frame…here seems to mean temperate control, the restraint of reason…which controlled his baser nature, comparing deere iudgement in 785. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The figure is that of a building that is thrown off its foundation. Mack (1965, p. 32): Or even a rupture in the cosmic frame itself. Hoeniger (1992, p. 319): The traditional conception of the human body as a building produced by nature.…By casting out of Cordelia in his bitterness of spirit, Lear has done violence to his own nature.

782 fixt place]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Proper station. Tovey (ed. 1896): Set or appointed by nature. Traversi (1952, p. 55): The natural order in which paternal love is met by filial devotion. Wilson (ed. 1960): Foundation or centre (i.e. Cord.). Horsman (ed. 1973): Center, fixed like that of the earth in the (Ptolemaic) universe. Joseph (ed. 1966): The position in which his nature was fixed. As a result it is changeable again. He is disconcerted by the rush of hatred for Goneril and remembers the same thing happening with Cordelia. Gardner (ed. 1969): Describing a stability that was. Hunter (ed. 1972): (1) the foundations of the frame of nature; (2) the natural affection which supports human existence. Lott (ed. 1974): The properly constituted body as part of the general order of the universe.

782–3 drew…gall]
Tovey (ed. 1896): The more love was taken from his heart, the more choler was added to his gall (OED, sb.1 2: gall-bladder), which is the seat of the dry choler and of bitterness,…rancour (OED, 3). More simply, as the heart, seat of the emotions (see n. 1029), is emptied of love it is filled with rancor; cf. 2H6 3.2.199 (1903), rancorous heart.

783 O…Lear!]
F’s third Lear completes the verse line.

784 gate]
Presumably his skull (see textual n.). But Joseph (ed. 1966): Nevertheless, Lear has just spoken of the love in his heart, and he consistently explains his misfortunes as the results of too great a love for his children. There are grounds, therefore, for interpreting gate as a reference to his heart, at which he beats. Hunter (ed. 1972): The ears, the eyes, or the mouth,…[or] his head as the general area of judgment.

785 deere]
Furness (ed. 1880): This word, which here means choice, precious…imports in general the excess, the utmost, the superlative of that, whatever it may be, to which it is applied. Cf. 1628, 2347+45. Deighton (ed. 1891): Which you should have valued highly. Verity (ed. 1897): That might have proved so valuable.

785 goe…people]
This seems to be one of three or four consecutive orders to prepare to leave (see 763 and n. 770), and it is repeated verbatim at 803. If the latter repetition is not an error, the sequence of commands may imply disbelief, astonishment, or misunderstanding in those spoken to that postpones their enacting the orders; or it may suggest that different people respond to each command. Smidt (1990, p. 137) finds them evidence of imperfect revision in Q. Who is being spoken to is unclear: the Fool would not carry such an important order; Kent would, but since his last speech in the scene is 669+8 (Q; 658 in F) it is uncertain how long he remains on stage. Possibly a few of Lear’s retainers who entered with him at 538 have remained in the background, though dramatic economy and the intimacy of Lear’s discussions with Kent and the Fool and with Goneril and Albany would suggest otherwise. See n. 624 and textual nn. 785, 829.

785 my people]
Naturally understood as a vocative, but Verity (ed. 1897) takes it as an ellipsis: Summon my train.

787 Of…you]
F’s added part-line both completes and clarifies Albany’s remark in 786 and makes a full line of verse with 788. Delius (1876, p. 135): Without it, Albany speaks most naïvely of his ignorance in general. It may represent either an accidental omission from Q (Delius) or an improvement in F. Halio (ed. 1992): Probably omitted accidentally by the Q compositor, who printed almost the entire scene as prose and omitted the third Lear in [783] as well. Van Dam (1935, p. 95): A needless interpolation in F.

789–803 harke…child]
For accounts of the delivery of this famous speech by the great actors, and of accompanying stage business, see Furness (ed. 1880), Sprague (1944, pp. 286–7: Until quite recent years, it was spoken kneeling), Rosenberg (1972, pp. 126–33), Brown (ed. 1976), and Bratton (ed. 1987, pp. 21–4); for its relocation by Tate and his followers, see , . Hazlitt (1820, p. 687): It should not be scolded, but recited as a Hymn to the Penates! White (1880, p. 117): Usually called [Lear’s] curse. But it is not a curse; it is a prayer,—a passionate plea to the powers of nature that they will inflict upon her the extremest agony of soul that can be felt by woman.…The prayer would shock and revolt the whole world, were it not that it closes with those lines that cause sympathy to flash like a flame from the hearts of all born of woman. Verity (ed. 1897): The speech…demands the measured enunciation of prayer. Delivered slowly, each word drives the terrible imprecation home. Neilson & Thorndike (ed. 1909): This speech, usually known as Lear’s curse, shows both the extravagance of his passion and the concentrated energy of his intellect. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 169): The actor who will rail and rant this famous passage may know his own barnstorming business, but he is no interpreter of Shakespeare. The merely superficial effect of its deadlier quiet, lodged between two whirlwinds of Lear’s fury, should be obvious. But its dramatic purpose far outpasses that.…With this deliberate invocation of ill we pass into spiritual darkness. Harbage (1963, p. 408): Lear’s wrath is understandable, but it takes a terrible form. His curse of sterility has the frightening beauty of volcanic flame. Goldman (1981, p. 34) remarks the thick play of clashing consonants. Against Knowlton’s (1936, p. 737) and Danby’s (1949, pp. 20–31) assertion that Lear conceives of Nature as a kindly, orderly, just system that takes for granted that parents are to be honoured and human decencies observed, Rosenberg (op. cit., 1972, pp. 125–6) opposes this evil, ugly, vicious, antinatural wish that his daughter be made sterile or that his grandchild be a monster—i.e., that nature act unnaturally. Hunter (ed. 1972) compares Deut. 28:15, 18: If thou wilt not hearken unto the voice of the Lord thy God…cursed shall be the fruit of thy body [AV]. Taylor (1985, p. 224): Lear’s curse…is an act of desperation…[which] is the measure of our sympathy. Hodges (1985, p. 82): Lear’s tongue-lashing in the language of dismemberment anticipates his later wishes that Regan be flayed (827) and anatomized (2033). Berry (1993, pp. 80–1): Lear’s curse on Goneril’s fertility…foreshadows the state of all three daughters.

789 harke…heare…heare]
There is a slight difference between Q’s beginning, which first invokes Nature and then begs her to listen, and F’s, which insistently repeats the imprecation Heare three times, the third to complete the meter. Van Dam (1935, p. 95): F’s Heare [for harke] may be a tautological misprint. Or the repetition may be for rhetorical emphasis. Wright (1999, p. 266): When characters are greatly excited, they may omit an expected unstressed syllable anywhere in the line and more than once, quoting this l.

789 Nature]
See n. 232. Harrison (ed. 1937; rev. 1948?): Lear also [cf. 335] calls on Nature, but as the goddess of natural affection. Empson (1951, p. 130): Lear, unlike Edmund, assumes that Nature is good and will punish wickedness, so that there are two views of Nature in the play; but one might also accuse Lear of believing that Nature is an amoral magical force which will obey his royal caprices. Elton (1966, p. 189): Lear continues to invoke this [fructifying] goddess for his curses; nature betrayed requires Nature to wreak vengeance. Edwards (ed. 1975): Not Edmund’s deification of natural impulse, but great creating Nature [WT 4.4.88 (1898)], the earth-mother. Foakes (ed. 1997): His horrible curse would make nature unnatural…and almost aligns him with Edmund.

789 heare deere]
Abbott (§480) and a few followers: Both dissyllables. Dear, as an address to a deity, usually means esteemed, beloved (OED, a.1 2b), but might mean glorious (OED, 1). Halio (ed. 1992): Precious (OED, 4); cf. n. 1628.

792 sterility]
Not used elsewhere by Sh. Taylor (1925, p. 65) suggests derivation from Florio’s tr. of Montaigne, but the word was common, and Sh. uses sterile repeatedly.

793 increase]
OED (sb. 2b): Procreation, quoting this l.

794 derogate]
OED (ppl. a.): Deteriorated; debased, quoting this l. Glosses tend to emphasize either moral debasement—unnatural (Warburton, ed. 1747), degenerate (Edwards, 1758, p. 194), dishonored (Delius, ed. 1854), depraved, corrupt (Schmidt, 1874)—or physical deterioration—damaged (Johnson, 1755), degraded, blasted (Johnson, ed. 1765), shrunk, wasted (Malone, ed. 1790), blighted (by barrenness) (Kittredge, ed. 1940). Clarkes (ed. 1868): The word thus comprises the effect of debased from her nature as his daughter…and damaged physically by the fearful malediction he here invokes. Sh.’s first use of the word; in later plays it appears as a verb. Taylor (1925, p. 60) suggests it derives from Florio’s tr. of Montaigne [as verb], though it appears as an adjective in a few other writers (OED).

794 spring]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Optative subjunctive.

795 teeme]
Schmidt (1874): Bear…children (OED, v.1 2). Callaghan (1989, p. 146): Empty, discharge, specifically excretion,…waste matter: a monstrous birth. OED (v.2) does not suggest or support such meanings, and in any case Lear’s is a different, intransitive verb (v.1)

796 spleene]
Rann (ed. 1794): Malice and disobedience. OED (sb. 6): Violent ill-nature. Evans (ed. 1898): The spleen was supposed to be the seat of anger and malice.

797 thourt]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 377): Misreading of thuart, a sp. variant, not attested after the 15th c. (OED, adj.), of F’s thwart. Athwart, however, was spelled athourt. Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): Perverse (OED, 2a). Schmidt (ed. 1879): As an adj. nowhere else in Sh.

797 disuetur’d]
The conjecture disfeatur’d (see textual nn.) is not graphically very similar, unlike F’s disnatur’d. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 377): N misread as u, and a misread as e, giving other exx. Becket (1815, 1:138) explains the former as ill-featured, Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:20) and most eds. the latter as Flown from Bias of Nature, without natural Affection. Neither is used elsewhere in Sh.; OED and Craig (ed. 1901) find disnaturing in Florio’s tr. of Montaigne [ed. 1910, 3:108]. Knowlton (1936, p. 737): She has acted unnaturally, contrary to Nature, and therefore she deserves to be punished by Nature.…An appropriate punishment, one in kind, would deprive her of offspring, or else afford her such as would treat her unnaturally.

799 accent]
Q does not make very good sense as a truncation of either accented or accenting, nor as a supposed participle of accend, to set on fire (OED, v.) whether spelt as intended or as an erroneous setting of accenst (Stone, 1980, p. 203). Schröer (1935, p. 390): Sharp, bitter, by analogy with a figurative use of the noun (OED, sb. 8: sharpness, intensity) not recorded before 1647 and without adjectival counterpart. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 512): Blayney provides an earlier English example of the Scots word eident (or ident) at John of Bordeaux 1026 (MSR); however, this word seems unlikely to have been spelled with an initial a here (as Blayney conjectures)—an unattested spelling which would make it indistinguishable from the incongruous aydant [2368].…Ardent, still widespread in the literal sense fiery, burning, would seem a more plausible emendation…; but we cannot claim that it is more likely than F’s cadent to have stood behind Q’s accent (though it does suppose only two misread letters, rather than three). In any case Q seems to represent a misreading of a difficult MS. F’s cadent, falling (Steevens, ed. 1773), makes adequate sense, though to Stone (1980, p. 203) it savours of elegant euphemism—most implausibly in the context of a passionate speech. Although not used elsewhere in Sh. nor recorded before Sh. in this sense (OED, a. 1), it had been previously used in the astrological sense of declination (OED, 2). Besides its rarity its chief difficulty is the uncertainty how it could be misread as accent. Though Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 377) rightly says that confusion between a and c is possible, he is less convincing that cce is a likely misreading of ade. It is possible that a badly written word in the MS was misread as both accent and cadent. A possibility is current, a word that Sh. twice uses to describe flowing tears (Luc. 284, brinish current; R3 2.2.68 [1342], All Springs reduce their currents to mine eyes; cf. Tro. 5.3.55 [3260], recourse of teares). It is consistent with Sh.’s frequent descriptions of tears as seas, floods, tides, and streams, and makes better sense with channels than do accenst or ardent. Graphically it is similar to both Q and F readings: initial cu is easily misread as a (with its usual initial or final flourish) or as ca, and rr is virtually indistinguishable from cc, while in Hand D of Thomas Moore the same is true of several exx. of medial r and d.

799 fret]
OED (v.1 5): To form…by wearing away, quoting this l. Falconer (1965): By the sea. The word is used with tears in R2 3.3.167 (1755); cf. Luc. 1712–13, The face…caru’d…with tears.

800 her…benefits]
Roderick (in Edwards, 1758, pp. 230–2) understands her as repeated before benefits and referring to the supposed Child as a Daughter, not a son. Heath (1765, pp. 328–9) and all others disagree: May it (that is, the child)…turn all the pains that she [the mother] felt, and all the benefits she conferred on it, as a mother, to laughter and contempt. Hunter (ed. 1972), benefits: Joys in motherhood, and Foakes (ed. 1997): Pleasures or advantages gained from having a child. Horsman (ed. 1973, pains: Anxieties, exertions…; birth-pangs.

801 laughter and contempt]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Hendiadys…for contemptuous ridicule.

801 that she may feele]
Adee (ed. 1890, pp. xxxvii f.): The repetition is clearly a printers’ blunder. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 512): This repetition could be mere compositorial dittography, but iterative incoherence is characteristic of Lear. Wells (ed. 2000): Indicat[ing] difficulty in finding the right words. Here probably erroneous, since it breaks meter.

802 serpents tooth]
Malone (in Boswell, ed. 1821) finds the image used in Psa. 140:3 to describe evil and violent men. Though the text does not support his statement, The viper was the emblem of ingratitude, several exx. cited in Tilley V68, To nourish a Viper (snake) in one’s bosom, a proverb elsewhere alluded to by Sh., do make that identification. Cf. 1443, 3029. Perrett (1904, p. 107): In Mirour (1587, fol. 35r; not in 1574) the daughters are compared to vipers vile, as also in Leir 811, 1653, 2345, 2558, 2584 (see , , , , ).

803 thanklesse child]
Harrison (ed. 1937): According to the accepted notion of the duties of children and parents, the child owed life (and therefore everything) to the parent. Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 256): Upbraiding another for ingratitude or impiety constitutes onedismus.

803 goe, goe, my people?]
To Jennens (ed. 1770) and most eds. F’s Away, away seems preferable to Q’s repetition of 785, which Greg (1933, pp. 253–4) attributes to an actor. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 169 n.) suspects that Q’s repetition as if his first order had not been obeyed might be mere muddlement of text, whereas F’s substitution is spoken to Albany, and has no reference to the servants, who have already been sent off, nor to Lear’s own departure.…The Folio’s change of phrase might cover a change of meaning too. Granville-Barker would not go to the stake for my reading, since it is hardly clear that all the servants have left the stage or that Lear is addressing these words to Albany. Doran (1931, p. 128): Possibly Sh. made the alteration to get rid of the repetition. Bransom (1934, p. 44 n.): Kent and attendants should leave the stage [at 770].…Away, away…must be addressed to the fool, who does not obey until 841. Van Dam (1935, p. 96): Q is genuine; F has an elucidatory synonymous change of which the plainness was considered to be more suitable to Lear’s exit, and more intelligible to the audience. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 512): Q’s repetition…might well suggest resumption of the exit earlier interrupted by 786–7. See n. 785.

803 Exit]
The singular form is often used for the departure of more than one person, esp. when a main speaker leaves accompanied by attendants. Though a few eds. have followed Q in having Lear remain on stage, most follow F’s exit here and reentrance at 809, to provide Lear the opportunity to learn offstage of the dismissal of fifty of his followers. Though his parting words in both Q and F seem to be an order to attendants, most eds. have marked a solo exit and reentrance. The Oxford eds. (1986, 2000) of Q and F, however, mark a group exit here in each text, differing only in keeping the Fool on stage in F. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 512): Blayney follows Duthie in calling for the rest of Lear’s train to exit at [785], but a straggle of exits seems unlikely, and the departure Lear calls for there might well be interrupted by Albany’s following speech. The exit here, by contrast, clearly takes place. (Ibid., p. 533): Since F calls for Lear’s re-entrance alone, the Fool presumably remains on stage while the others leave (as he does again below [829]). Editors retain F, and so must interpret Away, away either as an address to Fool (who must then deliberately ignore it), or as an exclamation directed at Lear himself, alone (a usage for which there are no parallels in Shakespeare). The Fool may of course exit and reenter with Lear in both texts; his remaining on stage at 829 is not a parallel with the situation here, since there Lear does not order attendants to accompany his exit.

804 Gods…adore]
Empson (1951, p. 130) imagines an emphasis on we: Perhaps implying that Nature was not one of the regular gods and should not be prayed to. More likely Albany is using a conventional formula. Wilson (ed. 1960): An oath, not vocative.

806 afflict…know]
Foakes (ed. 1997): Try to find out what will pain you.

806 the cause]
This phrase seems to answer Albany’s whereof more directly than F’s vaguer more of it, which finds a rare defender in Kirschbaum (1945, p. 27): In F, Goneril implies that Albany has already seen and heard enough to convince him of her rightness.…In Q, Albany is asked not to look behind Lear’s explosion to find the sufficient reason for it. In F, in short, Goneril takes her husband more for granted (in that she assumes he will be her ally). But both versions of her answer are impatiently curt and dismissive, hardly suggesting alliance. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 533): Few editors before Schmidt (who obsessively favoured F) accepted F’s reading, which is metrically awkward; but no emendation, or explanation of the suspected error, suggests itself.

807 disposition]
See n. 329.

808 that]
F’s substitution of as is unnecessary but idiomatic; see nn. 104, 588.

809 Enter]
Jennens (ed. 1770) explains the rapidity of Lear’s return: He flings out in a rage; but returns presently to vent more reproaches and curses, which his rage suggested. More probably, Steevens (in Johnson, ed. 1765, 8:2K4v–5r): He returns in a still greater passion, having been informed (as it should seem) of the express number without. Leech (1950, pp. 78–9): The exit is achieved with authority, but Shakespeare will not let him keep the dignity of his vituperation: almost at once he returns, unpacking his heart with words.…The authority is gone now.…There is a dreadful poignancy but an absurdity too. Jones (1971, p. 167): The sudden exit and re-entry are visible signs of lack of self-control.

810 What]
OED (int. 2): An exclamation of surprise or astonishment (sometimes mixed with indignation): usually followed by a question. Cf. 1030, 1158, 1533, 1551, 1844, 2588, 2594, 2633.

810 fiftie]
At 758 Pope (ed. 1725) changed a little to Of fifty in order to explain Lear’s knowledge of the exact number here, which…is no where specify’d by Gonerill. Koppel (1899, p. 37) speculates that after 758 a line was lost [from both Q and F] specifying the number, and Bradley (1904, p. 446) that the number was dropped when an earlier speech was shortened. Furness (ed. 1880): Surely, a simple oversight on Shakespeare’s part, or a trick his memory played him. In the old play of King Leir [807; see ], Gonorill says she has restrayned halfe his portion; cf. Leir 763, . In Higgins’s Mirour halfe his garde she and her husband refte; see . Perrett (1904, p. 190): The reduction by half begins with Geoffrey (see ) and continues through Higgins, though the actual number varies; cf. 1441, 1497. Most eds. accept Steevens’s explanation (see prev. n.), who adds that Goneril with great art avoids to mention the limited number, and leaves him to be informed of it by accident, which she knew would be the case as soon as he left her presence. Capell (1783, 1.2:152): During Lear’s execrations someone on the scene may be suppos’d to gather the lady’s will from herself, and to tell it their master, as he is about to go out, or does actually so. Smith (ed. 1902): Before the threat was uttered, it had been carried out. Perrett (op. cit., p. 191): Gon. does not dare tell her father what she has done. Noyes (1930, pp. 299–300): Goneril’s request in 758 is a brutal, hypocritical allusion…to the operation which she has just performed, and deliberately designed to make the blow of his discovery of that operation more stunning in its effect upon Lear. Cf. n. 538. But it is clear from 843, 845, and 854 that Goneril still imagines Lear’s retinue to be intact, and from 1525 that Lear still expects to be attended by all hundred knights several scenes later. Goneril had stipulated their dismissal as a condition for Lear’s staying with her, but had not herself actually dismissed them. Lott (ed. 1974): We must assume that at this point Lear has been told off-stage to get rid of fifty knights within the next fortnight.

810 at a clap]
OED (Clap, sb.1 7): At one stroke, at once, quoting this l. Used nowhere else by Sh., but not rare; see Franz §270 for analogues. Craig (ed. 1901) finds it often in North’s Plutarch and Harsnett’s Declaration (1603, pp. 51–2, 54, 164), and Taylor (1925, p. 59) in Florio’s tr. of Montaigne’s Of Moderation (Everyman ed., 1910, 1:215: they sacrificed fiftie men at one clap), all sources for Sh.

811–14 within…asham’d]
Though F properly lines to indicate two regular pentameters, Flatter (1948, pp. 78–81) absurdly redivides as shorter lines to be filled by actors’ pauses; he treats Albany’s speech as an extrametrical irrelevance.

811 within a fortnight]
Eccles (ed. 1792, p. 82) weighs whether this interval is the past time in which Lear has been resident with Albany and Goneril, as the Clarkes (ed. 1868), Wright (ed. 1875), and others (see n. 505) believe, or is the future time allowed Lear to dismiss his knights (see prev. n.). Eccles favors the former, to allow time for Cordelia to hear of her father’s mistreatment and invade England with a large army. As Daniel (1877–9, p. 217) points out, if a fortnight has already passed, we are now compelled to believe that Edgar has been hiding in the same house with his father the whole of that time; see n. 333. Daniel is willing to think so, since time is needed for rumors to develop of war between Cornwall and Albany and for Cordelia to land at Dover. If Lear had only recently arrived at Goneril’s, her proposed dismissal of his knights a fortnight hence, halfway through his scheduled visit, might at least partly satisfy her wish to punish (check) him and be rid of them. For the problematic time scheme, see Knowles (1999, pp. 36 ff.) and n. 926.

813 Ile tell thee]
Most eds. mark a change of address from Albany to Goneril after these words. Flatter (1948, pp. 78–81) alone thinks that only Goneril is addressed.

815 thus]
Harrison (ed. 1937): I.e. with sobs, presumably causing Lear to break off speaking after 813.

816 teares that]
On F’s which see nn. 235, 2911, and Franz §339. Doran (1931, p. 46): Probably both the awkward and inharmonious repetition of that and the fact that the relative introduces an accidental circumstance and not an essential characteristic account for the variation. Skottowe (1824, p. 108): So in Leir 865 Leir weeps after the vituperations of Gonorill, comparing Leir 1135; see , .

817 the worst]
Stone (1980, p. 216) prefers Q to F’s thee worth them.: Q’s phrase should be followed by a dash to indicate that Lear interrupts himself to break into impotent cursing.…F (as often) completes a sentence deliberately left unfinished. Halio (ed. 1994) puts a dash before Q’s phrase to indicate a similar interruption. All other eds. but Oxford (1986, 2000) think F makes better meter and sense—Give you the importance of being their cause (Edwards, ed. 1975)—by correcting an apparent misreading. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 377): The compositor may have been able to make out only the beginning of worth: taking the preceding word [thee, spelt the] as the article he may have guessed the worst and simply ignored the them. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 512), rejecting Stone’s reading as clumsy as well as unmetrical, Duthie’s explanation as unlikely—worst for worth is not an intrinsically easy error, especially when compounded by apparent omission of them—and Blayney’s conjectural emendation the worse: as paleographically easy…[but] strain[ing] both sense and metre, defend their own emendation the, worst (appearing in 1986 Q and Wells, ed. 2000, as thee—worst): Lear breaks off before finishing his sentence, thee distracting his attention from his own tears back to Goneril, whom he then curses. So emended, in Q Lear presumably intends to say that his tears should make Goneril repentant, or ashamed; precisely because they do not, he curses her. In F, Lear not only, more self-controlled, finishes his sentence; he makes the very different statement that his tears shame him by assigning to Goneril a value she does not deserve. He then curses her because she has made him weep shamefully, rather than (as [in Q]) because she does not weep herself. The graphical similarity of Q and F suggests misreading in one of the texts; rather than accept that likelihood, the Oxford eds. emend to confirm the differences between them, including an And presumably added for meter. It is hard to know how to take Lear’s supposed curse in Q. To gloss it as (the) worst winds and mists upon thee! seems bathetically meteorological, while the superlative in the alternative gloss, worst blights and pestilential airs, seems oddly forced, all blastments being dreadful. Neither reading quite makes a natural, spontaneous curse.

818 blasts and fogs]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Fog and mist were thought to contain the seeds of pestilence; blasts, Blighting strokes of pestilence (OED, sb. 6). Wilson (ed. 1960), blasts: Any blasting or withering influence, citing Tmp. 1.2.321–4 (459–61). Cf. 1451, 1840. Less probably, Schmidt (1874), blast: A cold and violent gust of wind (OED, 1).

818 the]
F’s thee: | Th’ satisfactorily corrects an evident mistake. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 378): If the copy read vpon the the vntented, the [Q] compositor may have thought the two thes an error.

819 vntender]
Though Q(u) may make a kind of sense—pitiless (Seymour, 1803, p. 48)—virtually all eds. adopt Q(c)’s and F’s vntented. Greg (1940, p. 153): The [Q] compositor was apparently guessing at the words in a difficult and obscure passage. Idem (1933, p. 252): The press-corrector, however, consulted copy: Guessing would have been impossible, since (1940, p. 135) the passage remained unintelligible. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 512): Stone [1980, p. 216] defends Qa, suggesting that the press-corrector may have been unfamiliar with vntender, and noting that the word’s first recorded occurrence is in Lear. But since that is at [113], both the compositor and the proof-corrector would already have encountered it; moreover, since untenderly dates from the 15th c., the negative adjective could hardly have caused much confusion in 1607. Stone objects that a wound may be untented…but it is hardly possible to speak of an untented wounding…; but OED notes two earlier examples of wounding (vbl. sb. 2) as a mere synonym of wound. Unappeased; not put into a way of cure, as a wound is when a surgeon has put a tent into it (Nares, 1822), Undressed (Valpy, ed. 1833), Unprobed, unsurgeoned (White, ed. 1883), and Uncleansed, and so festering (Dent, ed. 1927) are all fairly literal glosses of untented. OED (ppl. a.1): Unprobed, undressed, quoting this l. as its first ex.; (Tent, v.4): To probe.…To treat by means of a tent; (Tent, sb.3 1): A probe, (2): A roll…usually of soft absorbent material, often medicated,…formerly much used to search and cleanse a wound, or to keep open or distend a wound. Craig (ed. 1901) cites several references to the practice; Hoeniger (1992, p. 256) traces its history. Following Theobald (1726, p. 141)—A Wounding of such a sharp, inveterate Nature, that Nothing shall be able to tent it, i.e. to search the Bottom, or assist in the cure of it— some eds. interpret the participial ending -ed as equivalent to -able; see n. 284. Thus Too deep to be probed (Staunton, ed. 1859), Rankling or never-healing (Verplanck, ed. 1847), Incurable (Clarkes, ed. 1868), Undrainable (Tannenbaum, 1916, p. 63).

820 peruse]
Q1(c) and F correct to pierce. Greg (1940, p. 153): The copy may have had the common spelling perse or even perrse. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 512): Shn. pearse. The press-corrector very likely consulted copy, as in the previous line.

820 about]
Schmidt (1874): Carried by, or appendant to, a person. OED (prep. 5): Appertaining to. Blake (2002, p. 180): Belonging to.

820 the]
F prints thee. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 378): The copy may have had the for thee.

820 fond]
See n. 384–5. Heilman (1948, p. 322): Because by weeping they tell Goneril that she has power…thus.

820–1 eyes…out]
Milward (1987, p. 168) compares Matt. 18:9, Shaheen (1987, pp. 148–9) compares Matt. 5:29 and Leir 1906 (see ).

821 beweepe]
Rann (ed. 1794): Should you [beweep]. Abbott (§438): The prefix be is used…seemingly to give a transitive signification to verbs that, without this prefix, mostly require prepositions. Cf. Franz §76.

821 this cause]
Moberly (ed. 1876): For such a reason.

821 you]
On F’s ye see n. 490.

822 you cast]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 378): Probably the Q inversion…is an error of the compositor.

822 make]
Q’s waters commonly meant tears (OED, Water sb. 17d; cf. Ant. 1.2.148 [247] etc.), and make in Q has its common meaning of produce. F’s loose may have been substituted to avoid an unintended ribaldry; cf. OED (Water, sb. 18), TGV 4.4.38 (1856), TN 1.3.130 (238). Though most eds. adopt the unauthoritative F3 spelling lose, glossing it waste (Deighton, ed. 1891; Kittredge, ed. 1940; etc.), loose makes excellent sense as discharge [as an arrow] (Staunton, ed. 1859; OED, v. 4; cf. H5 1.2.207 [354]), release (OED, 1; cf. Ham. 2.2.162 [1196]), or give vent to, emit (Muir, ed. 1952; OED, 4c; cf. AYL 3.5.103 [1877]). Muir: There is no good reason for altering the F reading; for though loose is a frequent spelling of lose, the word does not certainly mean that here.…There may, however, be a quibble on loose and lose. Hunter (ed. 1972): Probably Sh., given the overlap of spelling, did not distinguish clearly between the two words.

823 temper]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): To work together to a proper consistence (OED, v. 10, used of clay or mortar). Deighton (ed. 1891): Moisten (OED, 11), and so Soften (Bald, ed. 1949); OED, 13). Lear may be saying simply that he will cast his eyes and their tears to earth, possibly as a sign of contempt for his own emotion (Wells, ed. 2000), but other figurative meanings have been found. Rook (in Wolfit, ed. 1956): Soften humanity. Wilson (ed. 1960): Since…tears cannot temper her hard heart. Taylor (1991, p. 494): An ironic reminiscence of the wise Prometheus, tempring earth with water, in Epistle 451 to Arthur Golding’s tr. of Ovid (1567, p. 10).

823 yea…so]
The original Q text made a pentameter line (though erroneously set as prose); the F substitution makes a pentameter with the next line; and both the omitted and added text, taken together as they have been in most modern eds., form a continuous train of thought, Lear asking a rhetorical question and then accepting its implications. The F version, on the other hand, leaves 823–4 with meter unimproved and a conspicuous gap between Lear’s threat to cast his eyes to earth and what follows: the Ha?, which might be a follow-up question, challenging an answer, has no question to follow and so must be treated as an abrupt exclamation, while Let it be so seems to assent (nonsensically) to Lear’s plucking out his own eyes, rather than (as in modern eds.) to the fact that the situation has come to this, i.e. humiliation by a daughter. Q and F, each imperfect, are perfected and complemented in sense and meter by conflation. So Foakes (ed. 1997): The phrase in F is a natural sequel to that in Q, and completes the blank verse lines. Doran (1931, p. 64): Each text has something which supplements the other.…Possibly the half-line Let it be so was added by Shakespeare in the transcript [for playhouse copy] to fill out a defective line ([824]), but was written in such a way that the folio printer [or a scribe preparing F copy?] interpreted it as replacing the question i’st come to this? rather than as being supplementary to it. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 172): Ha?…so may easily have been accidentally omitted from Q…; and [a scribe] may have written it into [the copy for F] in such a way that the F compositor thought it was to replace instead of supplement Q’s yea…this?. A few eds. question conflation, however. Van Dam (1935, p. 98): F replaces Q’s obvious interpolation; but Q’s phrase was probably part of Sh.’s original rough draft (see ). Halio (ed. 1992): Short lines are not uncommon in F.…Conflation…is unwarranted. Weis (ed. 1993): Q [is] dramatically more charged.

823 yea]
OED (adv. 4): Introducing a question or remark…expressing either vague assent or (more commonly) opposition or objection: = Indeed?; Well, Well then, quoting this l. and MND 3.2.411 (1455), Yea, art thou there? The usage seems to have been obsolescent; in R3 1.4.88 (927) Yea (Q1) is replaced by What (F1), and in Lr. 1410 by O. Possibly F’s Ha? here is a similar modernization. Hunter (ed. 1972): F has, throughout its length, a remarkable prejudice [against yea]. If so, then Ha should probably be regarded as a substitute rather than an addition.

824 yet…daughter]
F’s I haue another daughter avoids Q’s repetition of 765, and so is approved by Dyce (ed. 1865). Greg (1933, p. 254) scorns Q’s repetition as an actor’s redundancy. Van Dam (1935, pp. 98–9): Q’s more telling phrase has degenerated into [F’s] flatter [one]. Weis (ed. 1993): F’s effect is blander than the resonance of Q, which indicates Lear’s power of feeling. Greg (1940, p. 392) compares Leir 909, You haue two daughters left; see .

824 yet]
Walker (1860, 2:284): Means as yet. More probably, Kittredge (ed. 1940): Emphatic; see n. 245.

825 whom]
F corrects to who; Franz §334 gives other exx. of the error.

825 kind]
See n. 132.

825 comfortable]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): Ready to give comfort, comforting (OED, a. 6). See n. 367, cf. 1241.

826 shall]
Brook (1976, p. 114): Used in temporal and conditional clauses where today we use the present tense, citing Franz §610.

826 nailes]
Perrett (1904, p. 227) compares Leir 1906: And with these nayles scratch out her hatefull eyes; see . Cf. 2128–9.

827 flea]
Joseph (ed. 1966): An apt word to use of wolvish visage. A dead wolf had to be flayed if a reward was to be claimed for its skin. Possibly an authorial spelling, though its recurrences in Cor. 1.6.22 (629) and 3.3.89 (2373) may be scribal; flay appears only in WT, where it may reflect the preferred spelling of the scribe, Ralph Crane.

828 resume]
OED (v. 1c): To assume…anew, quoting this l. as its first ex.

828 shape]
Deighton (ed. 1891): I.e. of king. Joseph (ed. 1966): Clothes, robes; (figuratively), customary way of life. Brown (ed. 1976): Role (OED, sb. 8: both part and stage dress). Mahood (1957, p. 55): Also Essential form…his dignity as a human being. Skillan (ed. 1967): Full kingly state and authority. Edwards (ed. 1975): Lear sees kingship as something you can take off and put on again. The threat confirms the fear that Goneril intimates in 328–30 and makes explicit in 847–8.

829 thou…thee]
F omits these words. Capell (1783, 1.2:153): The period can ill spare them, ending lamely at ever. F’s omission here and of my Lord in the next line reduces one and a half verse lines to one; Greg (1933, p. 253; 1942, p. 90) prefers the regular F line 829–30, and supposes that Q’s additional words are an actor’s redundant insertions.

829 warrant]
Walker (1854, p. 65): Usually a monosyllable. Abbott (§463): R frequently softens or destroys a following vowel.

829 Exit]
Introduced without authority in Q2, repeated in F. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 533): Naturally some suspicion attaches to [F’s Exit], which may suffer from Q2’s influence; most editors since Rowe get the train off at this point. But Lear last addresses his train at [785]…, no one refers to them after that line, and it would seem most natural for them to leave then. There is no need to assume Q2 influence on F here; elsewhere (e.g., 1733, 2081) the singular Exit includes more than the departing speaker. Lear addresses someone at 785, but perhaps only Kent and the Fool. See n. 785.

830–3 Doe…more]
Coleridge (MS notes, 1818–19, ed. Foakes, p. 100): The baffled endeavour of Goneril to act on the fears of Albany—and yet his passiveness, inertia—not convinced, yet afraid of looking into the thing.…The influence of a princess whose choice of him had so royalized his state, some little excuse for Albany. Verity (ed. 1897): When he begins, rather timidly, to hint disapproval of her conduct she cuts him short. Their difference of opinion in this Scene is useful in foreshadowing their ultimate relations. Albany, well-intentioned but rather weak, is designed as a contrast to his wife and Edmund. Smith (ed. 1902): But events show that he is not wanting in moral force. Because these lines follow easily from 808, Smidt (1990, p. 137) suspects that the intervening lines, including Lear’s re-entry, are an interpolation added in a clearly imperfect revision of Q.

830 that]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Treason implied in Lear’s statement—as if he had said I shall take steps to recover the throne and so depose you.

830 my Lord]
See n. 829.

831 partiall]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Biased because of. At this point in Leir (841) Gonorill’s husband urges her to be not angry in a partiall cause; see .

832 you,]
F’s period is misleading. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 378): It is clear that Goneril interrupts him in his reproach.

833 Come…more]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 35), arguing that Her attitude to Albany at this stage of the play is certainly not such as to warrant her being so rude, prefers F’s Pray you content, spoken, I imagine, soothingly and in a conciliatory manner. Cf. 1438. One may as easily imagine the reverse. Each version is curt and elliptical, each interrupts Albany so as to shut him up. Deighton (ed. 1891), content: Be content, satisfied; do not trouble yourself about these matters (that do not concern you). Doran (1931, p. 66): F is not a printer’s variant of Q; see also n. 731.
F’s following words What…hoa (see textual n.) are more likely to be an F addition or transposition than an omission from Q, since in Q 832–3 form a verse line (though printed as prose), whereas the words unique to F (as perhaps at 857; see n. 857–9) destroy the regularity of both lines. Doran (1931, pp. 65–6): The phrase introduces metrical irregularity and looks like a transposition of the speech from its original place [–833, after 841]. The line [F 833] has only four feet, and the line preceding, which should rightly be combined with Pray you content, is left as a half-line.…[In Q] there is likewise no complete five-foot line, but Shakespeare frequently introduces single lines with two or three accents; Oswald’s reply, Here Madam, combines with [–833] to make a three-foot line. But Q’s text may be read as two regular pentameters: see n. 857–9. OED (What int. 3): Used to hail, summon…. a. in phr. what ho!…b. simply. Why Oswald needs in F to be called here so far in advance of his entrance at 856, and called again at 848, is unclear, since the superserviceable Oswald is nothing if not attentive; in F his appearance seems uncharacteristically tardy. The pattern in Q, where he is called once and appears promptly, is what we should expect. Honigmann (1965, p. 122): Shakespeare could have expanded the incident, to underline Goneril’s impatience. McLeod (1983, p. 176): The stage business in F is more complex and Goneril is more agitated because she addresses three people in succession rather than Q’s two. For other views see n. 842–55.

833 Oswald]
Wilson (ed. 1960): First mention of the name in the text. See 506, 575.

834 you]
F’s You Sir seems to be metrical polishing; sirrah would have been more conventional, but unmetrical. Honigmann (1965, p. 122 n.): The sir in Q [833] should stand [here], where Q omits it.

834 more…foole]
A common phrase: see Tilley K129 and n. 573.

834 knaue]
See n. 451.

835 Nunckle]
See n. 634.

836 and]
F omits perhaps to make regular meter.

836 take…with]
F adds thee; perhaps the Q compositor saw the a and took the as a redundant article. See n. 820. Kittredge (ed. 1940): An absolutely perfect pun. The literal sense is obvious; but the phrase was a regular farewell gibe: Take the epithet fool with you as you go! Good-bye, fool as you are!, comparing 1H4 5.3.22 (2914). Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Take me and your folly. Dent (1981, K137.1): Proverbial.

837–41 caught her…after]
The five near-rhymes were probably intended as comic, but how they were pronounced is unclear. Capell (1783, 1.2:153) would pronounce after ahter and halter hauter, as would Ellis (1869–89; 1871, p. 963), who notes the rhyming of daughter and after in Shr. 1.1.239–40 (547–8) and WT 4.1.27–8 (1606–7) and says (1869, pp. 193, 231) that the vocalization of l was established shortly after 1600. Tovey (ed. 1896) would pronounce an f in all five words, halter reflecting Anglo-Saxon healfter. Strachan (1927, p. 424), Jenner (1927, p. 408), Whitby (1927, p. 440), and Gill (1939, p. 15) provide evidence of the f sound in dialectal pronunciation of daughter and slaughter. Like Ellis, Kökeritz (1953, pp. 39, 183, 310) favors near-rhymes without l or f: The…rhyme is clearly a patchwork of colloquial pronunciations current in regional or class dialects within the London area or in its immediate vicinity. It is hard to believe, however, that the Elizabethan audience regarded such forms as vulgar or rustic.…The clever rhyming itself was undoubtedly a source of amusement and appreciative comment. With a good deal of cautious qualification of particulars Cercignani (1981, pp. 94, 211, 216, 325, 342, 353) seems inclined to agree. Dobson (1957, §423): Shakespeare’s rhyme…depend[s] on the reflex of ME au (with loss of <χ> in daughter, &c., and of <l> in halter. Wilson (ed. 1960): Now they are leaving Gon.’s house he can speak out. But Lear has not caught her.

837 fox]
Skillan (ed. 1967): Because she is cunning.

839 should sure to]
On the omission of a verb of motion see n. 312. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Should certainly be sent to. Joseph (ed. 1966), improbably: Would certainly want to go. Skillan (ed. 1967): She has preyed on her father and deserves to be hanged.

840 cap…buy]
Wilson (ed. 1960) compares 625, where he also treats his cap as current coin. Skillan (ed. 1967): I.e., if his fool’s wit should find a way. Lott (ed. 1974): The mark of his trade, but he would give up even this.

840 halter]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): A hangman’s rope (OED, sb.1 2). Foakes (ed. 1997): Also a rope to lead her like a beast (OED 1).

841 so]
McCann (ed. 1964): = therefore: The Fool follows the old man and does not remain where such [savage] creatures are. It may mean only thus, as you see.

842–55 Gon.…th’vnfitnesse]
Following Fleay (1879, p. 119), Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxx) imagines that the absence of these lines from Q represents censorship, since James’s wholesale knighting, in 1603–4, of several hundred of his needy Scotch followers still rankled in the popular mind. The idea is very doubtful: Goneril fears Lear’s knights as a source of military opposition, and that was not the complaint against James’s knights. More likely the passage is an addition in F to clarify motive. Cunnington (1910, pp. 448–9): The folio lines here show several indications of insertion, while there is no gap if they are omitted.…They greatly extend the time after Oswald’s first calling [Q 841, F 833] until his appearance [Q 857+1, F 856].…Thus [in F] Goneril is already waiting for Oswald…[and impatiently] she spends an idle moment with [Albany].…If the quarto had merely dropped the Goneril-Albany discussion there would be no reason to find Oswald’s first call displaced.…[It] seems purposely to have been put back in the folio…[so] that Goneril’s explanation should be in character and perfunctory.…[In 1.3, 522+1–+4] is omitted in the folio, and…possibly [842–55 here] takes its place.…It is better that Goneril should explain herself to her husband than to herself or to Oswald.…The passage moreover contains some slight inconsistencies which suggest a rather careless insertion; see n. 853. Moriarty (1913, p. 462) thinks that these lines replace others cut from Q (see n. 439–44); he does not explain why they are expanded so much here. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 225): The Folio gives us…a passage in which Goneril justifies herself to Albany; undoubtedly useful. Muir (1983, p. 107): Therefore A valuable addition,…a useful preparation for her later conduct, and goes some way to excuse Albany’s tame acquiescence. Doran (1931, p. 66): If [the passage] had been considered especially displeasing to James and had possibly been marked out by the censor, the actors would scarcely have been bold enough to restore it to the version of the play performed before the public. It seems to indicate better stage management in making the entrance of Oswald less abrupt, and it is a considerable addition to Goneril’s part—she finds an excuse to justify her ill-treatment of her father, and immediately accepts the excuse as though it were true. Greg (1946, p. 232): Telescoping, due to faulty memorial reconstruction in Q. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 378): This omission from Q may be due to abridgement, the lines presumably being later restored in F. Stone (1980, p. 79): The Q compositor must have omitted them by accident. McLeod (1983, p. 178): In F’s lines is a different characterization of Goneril than in Q: in F she is wrought in the extreme, but trenchant in irony and rational in argumentation, coming to the boil slowly. Foakes (1993, p. 187): The changes in F make Goneril’s behaviour here more reasonable and less disdainful.…If she seems hard, she is reflecting [Lear’s] hardness. Goneril’s reasonableness is of course entirely self-serving, and Lear offered no hardness or threat to her until provoked by her disdain and her attempt to strip him of his knights, whose maintenance was the condition of her inheritance of half a kingdom. So Watson (1960, p. 189): But this is a topsy-turvy view of the play. Not only do the daughters provoke Lear’s righteous indignation, but also, according to the Jacobean social code, they would be expected to suffer pacientlie, and indure willinglie their <father’s> imperfection, choller, or frowardnes [James Cleland, The Institution of a Nobleman, 1607, p. 128]. In this case, the prerogative of age is equally involved. Hence, the Renaissance audience would not have shown the least sympathy for the two daughters at any time after they had revealed their true intentions at the end of the first scene. So Mack (1965, pp. 31–2): To justify Goneril is to obscure from the audience the relentless movement by which the man who is cynically humored so long as…he bears bags is maneuvered into surrender by two daughters whom Kent calls dog-hearted, Albany calls Tigers, not daughters, and the gentlest voice in the play calls Shame of ladies.…The motivation of the sisters lies not in what Lear has done to them, but in what they are…paradigms of evil. Similarly Taylor (1985, p. 175): Such defenses of Goneril would be plausible only if scene iii did not exist. Weis (ed. 1993): Q’s brusque version of the conversation is more effective than F’s elaborate one: In Q Goneril single-mindedly attends to the business at hand—the conspiracy against Lear—and only then briefs Albany on her plans, thereby indicating that she thinks he is an ineffectual fool not worth consulting. Taylor (1983, pp. 380–1) argues for a source in the Life of Marius from North’s Plutarch. Sh., of course, knew many other precedents for sharking up a list of lawless resolutes.

842 This…Counsell]
Deighton (ed. 1891), followed by Crook (ed. 1907), takes the speech literally: I have given this father of mine good advice. But it may begin the sarcastic tone continued in the next lines: Who ever counseled this man to keep a hundred knights! Thus Wilson (ed. 1960): He would not insult me thus had he not been encouraged. Horsman (ed. 1973): Ironic = has been incited to insolence. Foakes (ed. 1997): Putting Lear in his place as a mere man…and pouring scorn on his good (ironically = bad) judgement), citing Job 12:13 (Geneva) for counsel = judgment (OED, sb. 3: judgement; prudence; sagacity). Goneril, however, uses the past tense, implying that Lear has had bad counsel, meaning probably bad advice; if she meant to disparage his present bad judgment in keeping a hundred knights, she would more naturally speak in the present tense.

843 hundred]
Noyes (1930, p. 301), believing that Goneril has already dismissed fifty knights, interprets her insistence on the original number here as part of her deliberate plan to keep Albany in the dark as to any real cause for Lear’s wrath. But it is hardly certain that she has dismissed any knights (see n. 810), much less that Shakespeare seems to have changed his conception of Goneril (Foakes, ed. 1997). No discrepancy is necessary: she could refer to the hundred knights that Lear still wants to keep, even though she had given orders that half of them be dismissed in the coming fortnight. See n. 811.

844 politike]
Schmidt (1875): Prudent (OED, a. 2).

845 At…dreame]
An alexandrine, though Elze (1886, p. 38) attempts to read -dred…that as one foot.

845 At point]
Florio (1611, s.v. Púnto): Essere in púnto, to be in a readinesse, to be at a point (OED, Point sb. D.1, quoting this l. of Lr. as its first ex.; cf. Mac. 4.3.135 [1963]). Steevens (ed. 1773) and many eds.: Completely armed, the implied, not the literal, meaning. Cf. 1638+3.

846 buz]
Schmidt (1874): Whisper. Kemshead (ed. 1875): Idle rumour (OED, Buzz sb.1 3b). Or possibly A groundless fancy, whim (OED, 3a, quoting this l. as its first ex. for either meaning).

847 enguard]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:22): Ensure with Guard. Abbott (§440): En- was…used, sometimes in its proper sense of enclosing. Schmidt (1874): To surround as with a guard. OED (En-, prefix1 3): With additional sense of in, or simply intensive (in poetry often merely to give an additional syllable, quoting this l. as its first ex. of enguard. No other contemporary use has been found. Muir (ed. 1952) cites several such compounds in Sh.

848 in mercy]
Wright (ed. 1875): At his mercy (OED Mercy sb. 5b, quoting this l. as its first ex. of the phrase). Horsman (ed. 1973): At discretion, in his power.

849 feare too farre]
Verity (ed. 1897): Let your fears carry you too far, i.e. in her treatment of Lear. More probably, Crook (ed. 1907): Fear beyond reason.

850 Safer…farre]
Proverbial. Tilley F135, Fear (Suspicion) is one part of prudence. Dent (1981) adds In Trust is treason (T549). Jones (1977, p. 270): Echoes Seneca’s exchange with Nero in Octavia [440–532].

851–2 Let…taken]
Tovey (ed. 1896): My rule is always to remove dangers, instead of always dreading them. Halio (ed. 1992): Antimetabole.

851, 852 still]
See n. 253.

852 taken]
Capell (1783, 1.2:153): Taken with harm, i.e. o’er-taken. Rann (ed. 1794): Surprised. Moberly (ed. 1876): Overthrown. Deighton (ed. 1891): Sc. as in a snare. Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Taken prisoner. Horsman (ed. 1973): Stricken, attacked. Foakes (ed. 1997): Seized or afflicted.

852 I…heart]
Verity (ed. 1897): I.e. that Lear is capable of trying to resume his shape. OED (Heart sb. 7): Intent, will, purpose, inclination, desire; (8): Disposition, temperament, character. See also n. 75, cf. 402, 852.

853 What…writ]
At 527 Goneril announced plans for a letter to Regan, and from 858 it is apparent that she has had Oswald either write it from dictation or fair-copy it. There need be no inconsistency (Cunnington, 1910, p. 449; Smidt, 1990, p. 137) of 853 with 858, though there may be another one, since as far as we know…Lear’s only utterances on the subject are during this scene. Greg (1940, p. 433): The letter has been rather mysteriously brought up to date and includes…What he hath uttered…[and] her intention to visit her sister; see n. 1470. Tamblyn (1922, p. 359): What…vtter’d refers to 828–9, and during the ensuing moments she has been writing an addendum to this letter, describing Lear’s parting threat. But this explanation makes nonsense of her question at 858 whether the letter, as yet unseen, is done. Possibly she means that she has already written (or dictated) her fears that Lear would attempt to manage those authorities that hee hath giuen away (522+1–+2), and that what he has just uttered simply confirms her written fears. Or possibly the F reviser has been inattentive. Foakes (ed. 1997): Foreshortening the action.…The effect is to hint that Goneril has planned more in advance than the scene shows. Oswald is her steward, controller of the household, and it would be appropriate for him to transact business on her behalf, as her confidential agent. Perrett (1904, pp. 207–8) compares Gonorill’s letter of slander, scandall, and invented tales in Leir 984 ff.; see .

853 writ]
On the curtailed form see nn. 103, 420. Sh. prefers participial writ to written by about 3:1.

854–5 If…vnfitnesse]
Rosenberg (1972, p. 135) thinks the implied conclusion is she’ll be sorry. But it might be I’ll be surprised. Urkowitz (1980, p. 46): By interrupting her sentence upon Oswald’s entrance, Goneril dismisses her husband.

854 sustaine]
See n. 142.

857–9 What…Madam]
Honigmann (1965, p. 123): In Q [where –833 is followed by 857+1 and 858], there are two verse lines ending writ…Madam.: F’s I Madam hangs loose from the metrical pattern, Q’s Yes Madam is part of it.

857 How…Oswald]
In Q the speech introducing Oswald’s entrance and Goneril’s colloquy with him (858 ff.) is What Oswald, ho. Since in F that summons appears earlier at 833 and another is added in 848, Q’s original line is here replaced by the direct address How now Oswald? when he appears, and his announcement in Q—Here Madam—is omitted as being redundant, Goneril having already noticed him. See nn. 361, 833.

858 What]
OED (adv. 21): As mere sign of interrogation, introducing a question. Cf. 1533, 1920, 2594, 2641, 2707, 2932.

858 letter]
See n. 853.

860 company]
Wright (ed. 1875): Companions. Harbage (ed. 1958): An escort.

860 away]
So in Leir 989–90 Gonorill’s Messenger carries a letter to Ragan; see .

861 full]
Wright (ed. 1875): Fully (OED, adv. 4).

861 my particular]
Schmidt (1875): My personal, individual, private (OED, a. 3, quoting 2871), as distinct from your owne (862). Page (ed. 1889): Special, that relating to this particular business (OED, 2). Verity (ed. 1897): Special, chief (OED, 7). In any case the reference is to the business threaten’d by Lear (Capell, 1783, 1.2:153) in 828–9. See nn. 1592, 2871.

861 feares]
F has feare; terminal -e and -es are easily confused in MS. Either word will do; Goneril has one main fear, Lear’s threat, but also is concerned about riot, insubordination, and expense.

862 reasons]
In Leir Gonorill sends a letter filled with thunderclaps Of slaunder, scandall, and invented tales (983–4), including the charges that Leir has slandered and maligned Ragan (1036), abused Gonorill (1037), caused divisions between Gonorill and her husband (1037) and intends the like between Ragan and hers, and made mutinyes amongst the commons (1038), Then stirring up the Commons ’gainst the King [i.e., of Cornwall—Gon.’s husband] (1191); see .

863 compact]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Confirm (OED, v.1 3, quoting only this l.). Johnson (ed. 1765): Unite one circumstance with another [OED, 1] so as to make a consistent account. Eccles (ed. 1792): And give it farther plausibility. Wright (ed. 1875): Elsewhere used by Shakespeare only as a substantive or participle. See n. 341. In Leir 1039–41 Gonorill instructs the Messenger to affirm her slanders With othes and protestations; see .

863 it]
Delius (ed. 1854): Has no antecedent, but goes with the whole sentence (or idea) (Ger.)—i.e., it refers to some understood word such as account, relation.

863 more]
Malone (ed. 1790): A dissyllable. See n. 789. Dyce (ed. 1865) suspects that a word has dropped out.

864 after your returne]
To make sense, the Q1 press-corrector altered after to hasten in the corrected forme, reducing and to & to make room; F follows either corrected Q1 or a MS word read as hasten. Greg (1940, p. 153): The h must have been obscured in the copy. Stone (1980, p. 201), less probably: Prompted by a phonetic mis-spelling asten. Taylor (1982, p. 123): OED gives no example of haste or hasten spelled without the initial aspirate; moreover, the line as emended remains unmetrical, an unaccented syllable being required between returne and now. He therefore alters returne to retinue, interpreting the line to mean Go and get your retinue or Go, and have your retinue follow. The sense is not especially good, since Goneril has already ordered Oswald in 860 to take some company, and company does not follow behind. Williams (1983, pp. 192–3): Goneril’s retinue (713) names the king’s attendants; it is unlikely that she would use the same word to describe Oswald’s, the traveling companions of a steward, a mere gentleman servant. Furthermore, after your retinue…must mean follow your retinue. (But surely retinue are followers themselves.) Therefore after your retinue would seem to mean follow your followers. Howard-Hill (1985, p. 171): The line in F is not unmetrical and makes good sense.…The reading after is plausible for hasten…perhaps with a blotted h. Idem (1986, p. 434 n.): Taylor’s construction requires the F collator [or editor, or scribe] to have overlooked two promptbook variants in the place where he made a correction that was not obvious. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 513): Alternatively, get you gon means leave my presence and after your retinue means look for the retinue to attend you. But in context get you gon almost certainly means the same as away to horse, to Regan’s, the counterpart of returne, the word agreed upon by both states of the Quarto and the Folio. A missing unaccented syllable is a minor irregularity, and may be otherwise explained (see next note), and an illegible h, perhaps mistaken for a blotted or deleted letter, provides a simple explanation and requires a minimum of correction to make good sense. So it seemed to the press-corrector, who, if he had consulted copy to make the correction, would have remedied a misreading of retinue before supplying a letter to change another word in the text. F follows a reading not in Q2, which Taylor supposes (1983, p. 359) was the F compositor’s copy; he must therefore further posit contamination of the F copy (Q2) from another source by yet another person to whom the Q1 correction made good sense—as it has to all other eds. Wells & Taylor (loc. cit.): Goneril follows Oswald (Sc. 7 [i.e., 2.2]), and so contradicts herself if she here calls for his quick return (though the inconsistency could result from Shakespeare’s own change of plan). Or Goneril’s; or Oswald did not return quickly enough. Bradley (1904, pp. 257–8): Lear and Goneril, intending to hurry to Regan, both send off messengers to her, and both tell the messengers to bring back an answer [actually Kent is directed by Regan, not Lear, to attend an answer]. But it does not appear either how the messengers could return or what answer could be required, as their superiors are following them with the greatest speed. (Ibid., p. 449): It may be said that they expected to meet them coming back, but there is no indication of this in the text. Muir (ed. 1952): Presumably both Lear and Goneril expected to meet their returning messengers on the road. Kent and Oswald, however, are both commanded by Regan to follow her to Gloucester’s house [1066–8, 1312–13].

864 now]
F’s no, no supplies an unaccented syllable to make regular meter. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 328): The copy for Q may have had no no and the second no may have looked like a w. Or the interval of a syllable may have been filled by Goneril’s turning from Oswald to Albany. To explain F’s double negative, McCann (ed. 1964) imagines stage business for which there is no textual evidence: Goneril stops Albany from making an attempt to speak to Oswald with the intention of tempering his message. More likely the words are a transition from her positive charge to Oswald back to her negative reproofs to her husband, and the repetition is simply emphatic.

865 mildie]
OED (Mildy) finds only one ex. of this variant of mild. F1 and all other eds. adopt the Q1 press-correction milkie, OED (a. 4): timorous, effeminate, or tender-hearted (Wells, ed. 2000), a word used elsewhere by Sh. At 2304 Goneril calls Albany Milke liuerd. Greg (1940, p. 153): The compositor was…guessing [at illegible copy], for there could be no real likeness between k and d. Stone (1980, p. 216): But mildie is the rarer, hence may not have been recognised by the corrector, who may simply then have substituted what he expected to see. It is doubtful…that a compositor would read k as d in a fairly common word; and not a priori likely that foul case would produce such an error. Tovey (ed. 1896): On Goneril’s lips the epithet milky has a tinge of contempt, implying faintheartedness and weakness [OED, a. 4], comparing Tim. 3.1.54 (970), faint and milkie heart. Wilson (ed. 1960): A mother’s milk is a symbol of the benign Nature which Gon. rejects, comparing Mac. 1.5.17, 48 (363, 399), etc.

865 gentlenes and course]
Interpreted variously as a hendiadys: gentleness of your course (Schmidt, ed. 1879), and gentle course (Hudson, ed. 1879), course of gentleness (Page, ed. 1889). Wright (1981, p. 173): The high style…expresses her distant contempt for him. It need not be a hendiadys, however, but merely refer to his gentle character and (cautious) course of action.

866 though…pardon]
The meter is sometimes regularized by adding an it before not. Abbott (§483): A conjunction like yet or but, implying hesitation, may naturally require a pause immediately after it; and this pause may excuse the absence of an unaccented syllable, additional stress being laid on the monosyllable.

866 dislike]
Eds. prefer F’s stronger condemne. Either word will do. Greg (1942, p. 93): She makes a concession to decency in saying that she does not condemn the gentlemanly behaviour of her husband—it would never occur to her to pretend to like it.

866 vnder pardon]
Deighton (ed. 1891): If you will excuse my saying so. OED (Under prep. 18): With words denoting protection, care, or benevolent interest. See n. 1181.

867 y’are]
F erroneously prints Your are. The same kind of error occurs at 929, 1407, 3217, and 3256; all five instances were set by F Compositor E. Doran (1931, p. 99) suspects a habitual mistake on the part of the printer; but conceivably it was a scribe’s mistake, or the result of an obscurity in his script. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 379) suggests possible misreading of MS you as yor. Y’are is also (elsewhere) an abbreviation of ye are: see Franz §288 Anm., and cf. 2442, 2444.

867 alapt]
Perhaps the Q compositor thought he saw in his MS a variant of alapat (OED v.: To slap or strike, quoting only one ex.), as Caldecott (MS notes, 1813–33) and Halliwell (ed. 1865) suggested; the Q2 compositor may have reproduced Q1(u) unthinkingly. An adjectival form, if one existed, of the only other word at all graphically close, alate (see n. 704), would not make good sense. Alapt made no sense to the Q1 press-corrector, who substituted attaskt, which in F somehow became at task. Mason (1785, p. 344) glosses F’s reading as taxed. The Clarkes (ed. 1868): Task and tax were sometimes interchangeable spellings, citing 1H4 4.3.92 (2562), taskt the whole state. OED records both task (v. 5) and tax (v. 6) in the sense to censure, reprove that both the Q (corrected) and F readings suggest; cf. 1671, taske (Q1), taxe (F). The past participle in this sense appears in AWW 5.3.206 (2932) in the form taxt. Greg (1933, p. 771): Possibly Q’s MS copy read ataxt (very likely a Shn. coinage), which the Q compositor misread as alapt, l and t being frequently confused in Q1 Lr., and x and p being all but indistinguishable in some hands. The Q corrector must have read the copy correctly, but instead of being content to reproduce it, he thought it necessary to emend…[and] substituted attaskt, doubling the t by analogy with words like attain.…Neither word is otherwise recorded.…The folio’s at task…is clearly wrong. The parallelism with prais’d shows that a participle is needed. The folio compositor or editor [or scribe] must have had before him the corrected reading [attaskt] of the quarto, and when he further emended it to at task he added yet another unknown locution to the English language. So also Greg (1933, p. 258; 1940, pp. 142, 154; 1942, pp. 98–9). Walton (1971, p. 282 n.): The argument that the F at task represents a further conjectural emendation of a conjectural emendation [attaskt] by the Q1 press-reader involves the assumption—see [Greg’s] Variants, p. 154—that the [theatrical] manuscript used by the F collator [in preparing F copy from Q1] was defective or at least illegible. But if the manuscript was illegible, then it would be at least as easy to suppose that the F collator unsuccessfully tried to correct alapt with reference to it [rather than to Q(c)]. Doran (1941, p. 472): The choice of readings is important [to Greg’s theory of F’s text], since on it hinges the determination of whether or not F was here printed from a corrected forme [of Q1], and hence the determination of several other readings [1063 prize, 1066 best]. That Q1 was F’s copy at all is questionable; see . To account for the Q correction Kellner (1925, p. 73) proposes that the Q MS read attaxt, but this is a word not so likely to have been misread alapt in Q. Q’s attaskt has been glossed as call’d to task (Jennens, ed. 1770) and take[n] to task,…blame[d] (OED, Attask v., quoting only this l.). Johnson (ed. 1765) finds the same meanings for F’s at task, but OED (Task sb. 4a) does not record another ex. and finds the sense blamed doubtful. Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 12–13): Miss Doran [1931] maintains…that Q was printed from a Shakespearian autograph manuscript and F from a transcript of the same manuscript in a later state. But the variant [here] cannot be explained on this hypothesis. The copy for Q read ataxt: F’s at task cannot be derived from this, but must be derived from the attaskt of Q corr.—a reading which owes its existence solely to the press reader. But the F reading could have appeared as a result of the F scribe’s or compositor’s consulting Q1 (see ), or even without such consultation: if the Q press-corrector, finding ataxt in his MS, could spell it attaskt, the scribe preparing the playbook behind F from that same copy could have made the word out to be at tax (spelled at task). Howard-Hill (1982, pp. 21–2): F may derive from ataxt through an intermediate MS in which the spelling may have already been varied. A fresh transcript made from the playhouse book for Jaggard’s printers is one such possible intermediate MS. It is even remotely possible that ataxt, correctly so transcribed from Sh.’s rough draft into the playbook, was there altered to at task for ease of pronunciation. And pace Duthie, it would have been as easy for F1’s scribe or compositor to change the word to F’s at task as for the Q corrector to change it to attaskt, since the interchangeable tax and task are simply instances of a common kind of metathesis, found contemporaneously also in the interchangeable ask and ax. Taylor (1983, p. 358): F’s reading may be an authorial revision. Davidson (1998, p. 318), by analogy with vent/vext (2352), suggests misreading of attaint as ataxt. For conjectural emendations, see .

867 want]
F supplies a for which must have been an accidental omission of either the copy or the compositor (Greg, 1940, p. 155).

868 praise]
Probably a common e/d misreading of praisd; F imperfectly corrects to prai’sd. Wilson (ed. 1960): Worthy to be praised.

868 harmfull]
Hudson (ed. 1881): In its effects.

869 pearce]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Into hidden events, but suggesting also 1456, her eies are fierce.

869–70 tell…well]
Crook (ed. 1907): Two rimed lines at the end of a scene. Traversi (1952, p. 57): The use of rhyme to underline certain moral sentences, generally of common acceptance, has characterized King Lear since the opening scene. Brown (ed. 1976): He probably intends to leave. But after the couplet, conventional for a scene ending, two more very short speeches show in a more realistic manner a husband and wife at odds.

870 striuing…well]
Malone (1783, p. 49): The same proverbial idea occurs in Son. 103.9–10: striuing to mend, To marre the subiect that before was well. Tilley W260: Let Well alone. Dent (1981) adds from Bodenham’s Bel-vedere (1600), oft they marre the worke before was well.

870 ought]
The word cannot mean aught—Albany is not so pessimistic—but is a spelling reflecting the frequent Elizabethan pronunciation of gh as f: see n. 837–41. Dobson (1957, §34): Hodges [Plain Directions, 1649] pairs ought with oft in his near alike list. OED records the 17th-c. spelling of loft as laught; in Gammer Gurton’s Needle (1553?; ed. 1575, sig. C3r) ought is spelled oft; and in PP 18.41–2 oft rhymes with nought. Oft is also spelled ought in a MS copy of the elegy On Mr. Richard Burbidg (ca. 1619) reprinted in Halliwell-Phillipps (1889, 2:88). The rhyme of oft : naught in PP 18.41–2, pointed out by Greg (1942, p. 94), may not be Shn.; see Cercignani (1981, pp. 211, 342). Since the spelling ought for oft does not occur elsewhere in F or the good quartos, it may not be Shn. here, but a compositorial anomaly or error. Doran (1931, pp. 124): An undoubted error of mishearing. The compositor, seeing oft in his copy, may have carried the word aurally in his memory and thus set it as ought. Ingham (1967, p. 83): If so, he himself pronounced the latter word with the vulgar [f] instead of the standard [χ]. Like Greg (loc. cit.), Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 79): The Q line in punctuated to accord with the…erroneous reading.

871 Nay]
See n. 630. Goneril cannot accept even Albany’s mild and conventional demurral, and is prepared to continue browbeating him in order to have the last word.

872 euent]
OED (sb. 3): Outcome. Page (ed. 1889): Let us await the event; or, the event will show (which is right). Proverbial: Tilley T338, Time tries the truth; E116, The End crowns (tries) all; neither Tilley nor Dent (1981), however, cites this l. Hudson (ed. 1871): Albany shrinks from a word-storm with his helpmate.…In their marriage, Goneril had somewhat the advantage of her husband; because…she was a king’s daughter, and he was not. Macaulay (1907, p. 28): Albany is amiable, and not deficient in spirit, but borne down by the violent temper of a wife who has brought him an immense dowry. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Albany is a feeble character—no match for Goneril. She despises her mild husband and has the last word in the quarrel in iv, 2. Charitable critics have tried to rehabilitate him.…[If he is] not wanting in moral force [see n. 830–3]…he is very tardy in its manifestation.

873 <Scena Quinta>]
Harbage (1963, p. 409): In wonderful fashion, the playwright lets us see inside [Lear’s] mind by words which escape his lips with an irrelevant relevance that stuns…. This slight scene is one of the greatest in dramatic literature. Bratton (ed. 1987): Omitted by eighteenth- and nineteenth-century actor-editors, except for Samuel Phelps, who was praised for restoring it.…[Irving and others transposed it] to Lear’s next entrance, II.4,…avoiding shifts of scene. Foakes (1993, p. 187): The scene does not advance the action…but in certain respects it is a turning point. In it Lear for the first time recalls Cordelia in recognizing that he did her wrong, and his final cry, O…not be mad, marks his (and the audience’s) recognition that madness indeed lies ahead. Kittredge (ed. 1940): This scene occurs on the same day as Scenes iii and iv. Wells (ed. 2000): The scene follows rapidly on the previous one—Lear still awaits his horses. Adams (1948, p. 318): It is near Albany’s Castle and…out of doors.

874 Enter Lear]
See n. 538.

874 Gentleman]
Brooke (ed. 1947): The Folio marks the Gentleman’s entrance (erroneously) with the rest at the opening of the scene. This is the textual convention known as massed entrances. Since massed entrances are infrequent in Shn. texts, here it may represent an editor’s or scribe’s attempt to supply detail for future readers of F. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 874): He is not required until line [919], where it seems clear from the dialogue that he has just entered. Following Jennens (ed. 1770), Verity (ed. 1897), and others in ignoring this possibility, Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) follow them in imagining an improbability: Shakespeare seems to indicate that letters had been sent by this nameless messenger to Gloucester at the same time that Kent was sent with one letter to Regan. This is confirmed by Lear’s learning from this Gentleman, who had been before Curan in visit there (see [1274–8]), that Regan had not been expected the night before ([928–43]). The same Gentleman apparently meets Kent confidentially, who says he knows him ([1616–53]). The information that the Gentleman relays to Lear at 1274 does not show that he had been to Gloucester’s house; he could have gleaned it from servants remaining at Regan and Cornwall’s house when he arrived there with Lear. The Oxford eds. (1986) adopt this idea of two sets of messages, but never give any reason why Lear should be writing to the Earl of Gloucester at this time. There is no hint of a reason in the text, here or elsewhere; and Lear’s obvious and immediate need is to forewarn Regan of his intention to visit her.
