So Halio (ed. 1992): Gloucester in the next scene gives no indication of receiving word from Lear, as Regan does. See the next n.
Perrett (1904, pp. 198–9): Nowhere in the play has more than one representative of the train a speaking part.…The text does not oblige us to consider the Knight or Gentleman of I, iv and v, and II, iv the same, but it is natural to do so; there is nothing against it; and…the audience would probably recognise him as the same Gentleman or Knight. It is natural too that the Gentleman whom Kent has noted ([1626–7, 1638+11]) should be he who in earlier scenes was prominent in zealous attachment to his master. And the Gentlemen of III, i; IV, iv, vi, and vii in F1 are identical. So that as far as F1 is concerned, the Knight or Gentleman, the representative of the train, is one and the same throughout the play. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 533): So interpreted, the Gentleman becomes an important minor role, linking the two halves of the play, Lear and Kent and Cordelia. Cf. n. 1615.

875 you]
Warren (1983, p. 72): To [2014+18] in Q Lear has used thou consistently to Kent-as-Caius except in [875–9].

875 Gloster]
Since there is no hint why Lear should be writing to the Earl of Gloucester (nor that the earl received a letter), and obvious reason why Lear should be writing to Regan and Cornwall, this name has proved confusing (see prev. n.). Anticipated by Thirlby (MS notes, 1725–33)—Gloster might be her dwelling place—Capell’s (1783, 1.2:153–4) explanation has satisfied most eds.: Glocester…is to be understood of the town of that name, as is evident from the there of l. [878]: it is made the residence of Regan and Cornwall, to give likelihood to an ensuing scene’s action,—their late quitting it, and evening visit to Gloster in a castle of his residence, which we may suppose in it’s neighbourhood; earls, in old time, had some dominion in the counties that gave them their titles, and resided there usually. Perrett (1904, p. 268): The old nobleman…has been named only once as yet, and that once four scenes back [39].…Lear’s…word there [878], would infallibly suggest the town of Gloucester. Brooke (ed. 1947): The residence of Regan and Cornwall, and the capital of the southwestern section of Lear’s kingdom[,]…about seventy-five miles southwest of Leicester, where Brooke locates Lear’s castle (see nn. 1, 505). Horsman (ed. 1973): Apparently the central place where it is usual to break a journey from Albany to Cornwall. Cornwall’s house may be in the town and Gloucester’s in the countryside, a night’s ride away. Since a good day’s ride in Sh.’s time was twenty miles (MV 3.4.84 [1812], Cym. 3.2.68–9 [1535–7]), and travel at night would be slower, Cornwall’s and Gloucester’s houses need not have been many miles apart, and could both have been within modern Gloucestershire. Cornwall and Regan cover the distance between the present euening (1040) when they receive warning of Lear’s imminent arrival and their descent upon Gloucester now, later that same night; see n. 1040. There is no doubt that Cornwall has jurisdiction over Gloucestershire: Gloucester calls him my maister, my worthy Arch and Patron (995–6), and Cornwall bestows the title Earl of Gloucester upon Edmund (1987–8). Perrett (op. cit., pp. 270–1) imagines that Gloucester’s house is between Albany’s house and Cornwall’s, that Lear naturally would stop there to break his journey to Regan, as Goneril soon does too, and that Lear naturally expresses surprise at not having met Kent returning from Regan’s home. The theory multiplies improbabilities: Cornwall and Regan, trying to avoid Lear, would be unlikely to head in his direction and stop where he was likely to stop; and clearly at 1274 Lear already knows that they have left home, as he could do only if he had been there before coming to Gloucester’s house.
A few continue to worry the point, suspecting carelessness or error. Bradley (1904, p. 259): The Duke of Cornwall, we presume in the absence of information, is likely to live in Cornwall; but we suddenly find…that he lives at Gloster. This seems likely to be also the home of the Earl of Gloster, to whom Cornwall is patron [996]. But no: it is a night’s journey from Cornwall’s house to Gloster’s. (Ibid., p. 450): As Koppel [1899, pp. 40–51] points out, Gloster is nowhere else used in the play for the place.…It would unquestionably be taken by the audience to stand in this passage for the Earl, especially as there has been no previous indication that Cornwall lived at Gloster. One can only suppose that Shakespeare forgot that he had given no such indication—unless we suppose that Gloster is a mere slip of the pen, or even a misprint, for Regan. But…Lear would hardly have spoken to a servant of Regan, and, if he had, the next words would have run Acquaint her, not Acquaint my daughter. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 229): I give a guess that Gloucester in this line is a slip for Cornwall, a conjecture accepted by Wilson (ed. 1960) and Greg (1940, p. 434), who adds (p. 431 and n.) that though there is no confirmation in the play, It is natural to suppose that Gloucester’s castle is near Gloucester, but not in the town, or even very near it, since for many miles about There’s scarce a bush [1604–5]. Foakes (ed. 1997): Shakespeare anticipated here the arrival of Cornwall and Regan at Gloucester’s house…as if Lear could already know they would be there. But why would Sh. suggest to an audience that Lear could know what he could not and did not? Wells (ed. 2000): Some Stratford productions (like the Elliott-Olivier film) have followed Duthie and Wilson [ed. 1960], others (including Gielgud in 1950) have altered to Regan, and one (Glen Byam Shaw, in 1959) even to Gloucestershire. Evans (ed. 1898): The matter is of no dramatic importance, and it is unlikely that Shakespeare ever troubled his head about it.

875 letters]
Craig (ed. 1901): This letter, comparing 877. Hoeniger (ed. 1968), questionably: Pages of a letter. OED (Letter sb. 4b): Pl. with sing. meaning, after L. litteræ. Schmidt (1874) gives many Shn. exx. of this usage; in Lr. it is apparent at 1108, 1304, 1309, 1470, 2391, 2400, 2701, and 2709, and possibly at 2109 and 2347+10; F changes to the singular at 1470, 2391, and 2400. On such grounds and others Perrett (1904, pp. 264–7) scouts Koppel’s (1899, pp. 40–51) elaborate theory that Lear gives Kent two letters, for Gloucester and Regan respectively: Kent’s diligence…must be speedy. But Koppel would have us believe that Kent goes first to the earl of Gloucester (p. 41) whose house is not on the way (p. 46, note 1 [but see prev. n.]) from Gon.’s palace to Reg.’s home: and further that Gon. knowing Lear’s purpose to go to Gloucester’s house, mentions this in her letter to Reg. advising her to leave home and go to the same place, Gloucester’s house, where she too will go, in order that they may confront their father together. All this latter assumption is to explain Reg.’s remark on Gon.’s arrival [1470–1], viz. that it was expected. On Lear’s purposed destination see the prev. n.; on Goneril’s motives for going to Gloucester’s house see n. 1470. Horsman (ed. 1973): The letters are for Regan and perhaps Cornwall, and are delivered to them at their home ([1303–4]). Weis (ed. 1993): The letter…Lear seems to have written straight after leaving Goneril and Albany.

876–7 acquaint…letter]
Hudson (ed. 1871): The old King feels mortified at what has happened, and does not want Kent to volunteer any information about it to his other daughter. Armour (ed. 1930): The helplessness of Lear is emphasized by the futility of his careful instructions.…She [Regan] knows everything already, having been posted up by Goneril. Hunter (ed. 1972): Lear already distrusts Regan, and wishes not to give her any ammunition for an attack on his interpretation of the recent past. Halio (ed. 1992) rejects Hunter’s inference as implausible, adding, Lear does not distrust Kent; unlike Gonerill, he is trying to keep a lid on the situation.

877 demand out of]
Verity (ed. 1897): Question arising out of.

878 diligence]
Joseph (ed. 1966): (i) Conscientiousness; (ii) speed. [Lear] remembers [566] (OED, sb. 3, 2).

879 before]
F’s afore is now dialectal (Brook, 1976, p. 93; OED, adv. 1).

880 I…sleepe]
Greg (1940, p. 433): Implying that the journey will…take him well into the night.

882 braines…heeles]
Moberly (ed. 1876) traces the idea to [pseudo-] Demosthenes’ On Halonnesus 45: If you carry your brains in your heads and not trodden down in your heels (Loeb ed., tr. J. H. Vince, 1930, 1:173). Longinus, On the Sublime 38.1 (Loeb ed., tr. W. Hamilton Fyfe, 1927, p. 229) calls this passage laughable. Kittredge (ed. 1940) finds it in Hoccleve, Male Regle (ed. Furnivall, 1892, p. 32, l. 232: No more than [if] hir wit were in hire heele), and Muir (ed. 1952) in Robert Armin, Nest of Ninnies (1608, sig. E4v): The braine is now lodged in the foote, and therevpon comes it that many make their head their foote, comparing 1684–5. Armin probably played Lear’s Fool; see . Dent (1981, H386.1): Proverbial. Halio (ed. 1973): The Foole first refers to Kent’s promise of speedy service, then to Lear’s foolish journey. Brown (ed. 1996): The fool may start by standing on his head.

882 braines]
OED (Brain sb. 1): In 16th c. it became usual to employ the pl. instead of the sing. when mere cerebral substance, and not a definite organic structure, was meant; this usage still continues.

882 where]
Compositor’s error; the obvious correction to were may have been made independently in Q2 and F1. Ingham (1967, p. 83): Q’s spelling reflects a vulgar pronunciation until the 18th c.

882 wert]
Tovey (ed. 1896): I.e., were it, the brains, used here as a singular.

883 kibes]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): A chap in the heel, an ulcerated chilblain (OED, Kibe sb. 1).

885 prethe]
See n. 664.

885–6 thy wit…slipshod]
See n. 677. Slipshod means wearing slippers (OED, a. 1), the customary resource of those who are afflicted with kibes (Eccles, ed. 1792). The implication, your wit will lack kibes, is an apparent sally whose point has been much debated. Although the remark seems to be an answer to Lear, who has just spoken (884), the reference to kibes makes it seem equally pertinent to Kent, who promises to make a rapid journey. Eccles (ed. 1792): An insinuation of the Fool’s that Lear wanted brains, or wit. If he has them not, they cannot be in his heels, and, consequently, are not in danger of kibes. Singer (ed. 1856): For you show you have no wit in undertaking your present journey. Evans (ed. 1898): Either in your heels or your head. Moberly (ed. 1876) sees a double application: The fool laughs at Kent’s promise of rapidity, and says, first, that when men’s brains are in their heels (that is, when they have no more wit than is needed to go fast) they may get brain-chilblains; and secondly, that as Lear has no brains, he is in no such danger. Hudson (ed. 1879): Thy wit is not in thy heels, and therefore will have no need of slippers; referring to what the King has just said,—I…you [878–9]. Page (ed. 1889): Thy heels (= feet) are not, in the journey you are setting out on, guided by understanding; thy heels have no brains in them. Tovey (ed. 1896): Lear’s wit is in his heels, for his only notion is to run from one daughter to another, and the fool congratulates him on having good boots on. Neilson & Thorndike (ed. 1909): Your brains aren’t in your heels…: i.e. there is no sense in your journey. Goggin (ed. 1910): The object is to point out to Lear the folly of expecting anything from his other daughter. Kelcy (1932, p. 364), emphasizing thy and slipshod: You will never expose your wit to the cold by wearing shoes out at the heel. Thus under cover of telling Lear that he does not have to fear…the Fool tells him that his wit is in his heels. That is,…not in the right place,…unsettled. Colman (ed. 1982): In expecting a welcome from Regan, you are not using your brain, so you won’t blister it with over-use.

887 Ha ha ha]
Skillan (ed. 1967): Lear does not see the point of the jest but only the comical figure; his laugh is hysterical. Or absent-minded; he sees that the Fool expects a laugh, and complies even though he has been too upset to attend to the joke.

888 Shalt]
On the omission of the nominative see n. 230.

888–9 kindly]
Following Mason (1785, p. 344), the Clarkes (ed. 1868): Here used with punning significance; ostensibly, in the sense of affectionately, and really in the double sense of according to her nature or kind, and with kindred cruelty to that of her sister. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): I.e. unkindly. Colman (ed. 1982): In the same kind as Gonerill. Steiner (1967, pp. 234–5): The word implies the entirety of King Lear, with its realization of a world in primal chaos.…In that small word, terrible queries and subversions lurk. Is there kindness in our human kind; if each man deal after his kind, what then? Did Shakespeare…implicate the common root which makes of kind the German word for child?

889 shees…this]
A. (1909, p. 424) mistakenly refers these pronouns to Goneril and Regan; but this, the nearer daughter, is Goneril, shee is Regan, consistently with 892. So Horsman (ed. 1973), Wells (ed. 2000).

889–90 as like…apple]
Page (ed. 1889): I.e. in appearance only. Wright (ed. 1875) compares Lyly, Euphues (ed. Bond, 1:258): The sower crab hath the shewe of an apple as well as the sweet pyppin. Joseph (ed. 1966): She is as sour as Goneril. The comparison may suggest Regan’s smaller stature. Craig (ed. 1901), citing TN 5.1.223–4 (2388–9), suspects that the comparison is based on a proverb. Tilley suggests As like as an Apple is to an oyster (nut) (A291), Dent (1981, A290.1) tentatively: As like as an Apple to an apple (crab).

889 crab]
Delius (ed. 1854): Refers to the sour taste of a crabapple (Ger.). Craig (ed. 1901): Possibly…the fruit of the wild apple, Pyrus malus, not that of the common crab. OED (sb.2 1): The wild apple, especially connoting its sour, harsh, tart, astringent quality; applied also to cultivated varieties having similar qualities, quoting this l. and citing Shr. 2.1.229–30 (1107–9) for a related meaning.

890 I con…tel]
Proverbial: Tilley K173, I Know (wot) what I know (wot). Wells (ed. 2000): I am in on a secret.

890 con]
F’s can tell is more symmetrical, though con = know (OED, v.1 1) makes perfect sense, as Collier (ed. 1843) and Stone (1980, p. 216) note.

891 thou]
On F’s omission see n. 562.

893–909 thou…reason]
Harrison (ed. 1937): This well meaning but perpetual fretting of the fool is partly a cause of Lear’s madness. Gordon (1944, pp. 126–7): Why these questions?…We are here in that wisdom of nature of which Gloucester spoke.…Shakespeare had been looking into it…in order to see what the old world of Nature was.…All kings formerly kept…a philosopher.…In the Middle Ages one of the most popular forms of instructive reading was the dialogue or catechism, in which one of these celebrated philosophers instructed his royal pupil.…Perhaps the most popular of these dialogues was the so-called Book of Sidrach, philosopher to King Boctris of Armenia.…It was translated into English, and four versions of it, one complete, were published in London in the sixteenth century [STC 3186–8a] including the questions What is the cause of eclipses?…Why are the planets seven?—Why has the snail a house? Unfortunately, these questions are not found in any of the four versions, though eclipses, the seven planets, and snails are discussed. Muir (ed. 1952): The Fool, reversing the usual procedure, puts the reasons of nature to his master. Wilson (ed. 1960): The Fool now tries to stop Lear brooding by asking some stock philosophical questions, but gives the answers a turn apt to his plight, comparing 1932–3. Skillan (ed. 1967): The Fool implies that lear makes no use of his faculties. Gorfain (1977, p. 251): The questions are mock riddles, implying a denial of justice and order.

893 not]
Used idiomatically in questions to imply a positive answer. F’s omission results in a simple question.

893 stande]
Probably a compositor’s misreading. The abbreviation for -es resembled an -e. Q2 and F1 may have supplied the obvious correction independently.

894 of his]
For F’s on’s see n. 632.

896 on]
For F’s of see Abbott (§175): Used locally in the sense of on. Cf. Franz §486 Anm. 2, and 2992.

896 side’s]
Page (ed. 1889): Side his, with of understood.

897 smell out]
Proverbial: Tilley S558, I Smell him out. Thompson (1965) compares 1341–2 and 2170–1. Cf. also 2549.

898–919 I…mad]
Herford (ed. 1899): Lear’s subsequent ejaculations to himself are in verse; his distracted replies to the Fool in prose.

898 I…wrong]
Virtually all eds. think that Lear is remorsefully admitting a wrong done to Cordelia. James (1951, p. 95), however: He is referring to Goneril on whom he had a little earlier called down a dreadful curse. Joseph (ed. 1966): Probably an indignant outburst against Goneril, signifying, She has the impertinence to claim that I did her wrong!

899 Canst]
See n. 891. Crook (ed. 1907): The omission of the pronoun is to give a more familiar tone to the conversation.

899, 904–5 his]
On the gender of the pronoun see n. 727.

901–4 why…in]
See n. 893–909. Proverbial for a stay-at-home: Tilley S580, Like a Snail, he keeps his house on his back (head). Cf. AYL 4.1.54–5 (1968–9).

905 daughter]
F’s daughters corrects a common Q1 error, omitted final -s.

905 hornes]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Shakespeare’s audience were at liberty to recognize the everlasting horns joke, for which they were on the alert. The Fool does not mean to call Lear a cuckold: he simply accepts horns as the inevitable adornment of married men. But Harbage (ed. 1958): The legitimacy of Goneril and Regan being, figuratively, suspect throughout. Skillan (ed. 1967): Refers to Lear’s powers of perception…, the horns being his sensitive feelers.

905 case]
Schmidt (1874): Sheath, cover (OED, sb.2 1, 2). Only Brown (ed. 1976): Also legal rights (OED, sb.1 7d); cf. 1740.

906 forget my nature]
Hudson (ed. 1881): He will renounce the kindness which is naturally his. Deighton (ed. 1891): Banish all thoughts of fatherly love. Edwards (ed. 1975): Or lose my identity. See nn. 185, 441.

906 so…father]
Deighton (ed. 1891): To think that so loving a father as I have been should receive such treatment at their hands!

906 be]
Abbott (§299): Be is used with some notion of doubt…; for instance,…in questions. Cf. Franz §171. Kittredge (ed. 1940): A common old form of the plural. OED (v.): Early in 16th c. are made its appearance in standard Eng.…Be continued in concurrent use till the end of the century (see Shakspere, and Bible of 1611).

908 Asses]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Stupid servants. Elton (1966, p. 313 n.): From horses to asses…is a Renaissance proverb, citing Tilley H713. Skillan (ed. 1967): The servants are asses because they are hard driven and patient. Or because they are so foolish as still to obey Lear; cf. 627–9.

908 them]
F substitutes the colloquial ’em for them here and at 1845, 2014, 2549 (twice), and for vm at 1399 (twice) and 2968 (e’m); at 2966 it substitutes them for em.

908–9 reason…reason]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): The Fool has intentionally prepared a conundrum so obvious that the answer is inevitable. Then he can make the point that he wishes. Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 198): The fallacy of begging the question…when the conclusion…stands as one of the premises. Elton (1966, p. 163): Possibly…pointing to…the Globe heavens [stage roof], perhaps painted with stars.

909 seuen starres]
Delius (ed. 1854): The Pleiades. Furness (ed. 1880): The Great Bear, whose seven stars are the most conspicuous group…in the Northern Hemisphere. Edmund names it at 458. Rolfe (ed. 1880): But that group was commonly known as Charles’ Wain, citing 1H4 2.1.2 (636). Tovey (ed. 1896) quotes Cotgrave (1611), Pleïade: f. One of the seuen starres, and a marginal gloss opposite Pleiades in Job 38:31 (A.V., 1611), Cimah or the seven stars. OED: a. The Pleiades. b. ?The Planets. c. The Great Bear. Brown (ed. 1976): Because of their grief for their father’s suffering, the seven daughters of Atlas were turned into stars, the Pleiades. So Weis (ed. 1993): The youngest daughter of Atlas and Pleion, the lost Pleiad, by analogy with Cordelia inspired the Fool’s stellar reference here. Sh. never uses the name Pleiades for the constellation nor refers to the myth. See n. 893–909.

909 more]
On F’s mo, Kittredge (ed. 1940): Not a contraction of more but an independent formation from the same root. OED (Mo a. 2): More in number (as distinguished from more, greater in amount or quantity). Hogan (1962, p. 79): F…could fit mo but not more.

909 prettie]
Craig (ed. 1901): Apt. Or clever; see n. 626.

912 tak’t againe]
Johnson (ed. 1765): He is meditating on the resumption of his royalty. Steevens (ed. 1773): Rather…on his daughter’s having in so violent a manner deprived him of…privileges. Lott (ed. 1974), specifically: The right…to have a hundred knights and squires. The it could mean the kingdom (Foakes, ed. 1997). Wells (ed. 2000): (For them) to take it (kingdom, power, or crown) back by force. The daughters make no such attempt, having no need. Crook (ed. 1907): Some see in it a reference to his conduct towards Cordelia, from whom, owing to her monster ingratitude, he has been compelled to take away the third which was her due (but againe makes nonsense of this interpretation). Most eds. think Johnson’s interpretation most consistent with Lear’s threats in 827–9 (Clarkes, ed. 1868) and 906 (Wright, ed. 1875). Verity (ed. 1897): The bitter words of the fool are designed to urge Lear to this course; else they would be mere witlessness or cruelty.

912 perforce]
OED (adv. 1): Forcibly.

912 Monster, ingratitude]
See nn. 238, 773. Since the subject of conversation has been both daughters, Lear’s singular Monster probably does not refer to either; apparently the phrase is elliptical for What a monster is ingratitude! Conceivably the omission of the comma from F’s MonsterIngratitude may be due to crowding in a full line. Eds. are curiously silent about their general preference for F (see textual nn.). If Ingratitude is capitalized as a personification, F’s phrase apparently means monster that is Ingratitude, a good sense; most eds., however, do not capitalize, thus making Monster adjectival, a usage not recorded by OED in any sense before the 19th c., and never in the sense unnatural, wicked. Watson (1960, pp. 358–9): Antonio de Guevara, echoing both the classical moralists [e.g., Cicero and Seneca] and common Renaissance opinion, had said that although a man might forgive all other injuries, ingratitude could never be forgiven.

913 Nunckle]
See n. 634.

914 beate]
See nn. 103, 853.

915 Hows that]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Wherefore?

916–17 old…wise]
See n. 749.

918 O…mad,]
Verity (ed. 1897), comparing 1512: One of the most terrible things…is the king’s consciousness…that it lies more with his daughters than himself to determine whether or no he shall be mad. Muir (ed. 1952): The first premonition. Wilson (ed. 1960): This sudden fear is occasioned by the Fool’s last remark; since wise often = in one’s right mind, citing Oth. 4.1.234 (2624) and OED (a. 4). Welsford (1935, p. 262): Sweet heaven rejects his prayer. Rosenberg (1972, p. 140): Lear’s first appeal to heaven…in which the note of humility enters; like all the other appeals—prayers, orders, demands—it will be denied. Brown (ed. 1976): Lear can be terrified or despairing, willful, determined, still able to control, or already mad. Foakes (ed. 1997), citing Rosenberg: In performance the line can be an ironic moment of lucidity for a Lear already mad, or, as often staged, a terrible premonition for a still sane Lear of what is shortly to come.

918 mad⁁]
Of F’s mad, not mad Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 85): Ploce, iteration of a word, is employed with admirable effect…to express intense feeling.

918 sweet]
Schmidt (1875): A general word of endearment. OED (a. 8b): In forms of address, freq. affectionate, but formerly also…respectful or complimentary. Both quote this l. Cf. 1862.

918 heauen]
Brown (ed. 1996): He…prays to sweet heaven and not to Apollo, Jupiter, or remorseless powers.

918–19 O…mad]
The duplication of I would not be mad makes Q’s 918 hypermetrical; F’s reduction of the first instance to not mad (in transposed position) makes a pentameter, and Blayney’s suggestion (apud Wells & Taylor, 1987, p. 513) that the Q MS read not be mad sweet heauen! not mad both supports F’s wording (though transposed) and offers an explanation for the compositor’s misreading, viz. eyeskip between two consecutive lines ending with mad. Wells & Taylor defend Q because Lear speaks rhythmical prose or broken verse elsewhere in this scene, though not another heptameter. Weis (ed. 1993): Q and F differ in their arrangement of emphases here, but not substantially in content.

919–20 keepe…readie]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 380): F follows Q in printing a verse speech as prose. But Doran (1931, p. 106): Apparent revision on the transcript [which became the playbook]…may account for the failure of the printer of the folio to set…verse. That is, the lineation in Sh.’s rough draft was, because of revisions, unclear both to Q’s compositor (who used it for copy) and to the scribe who prepared from the same draft the playbook underlying F.

919 in temper]
In the abstract the phrase means in…proper condition (OED, sb. 1); in contrast to madness it may mean in a moderate, calm, sane state of mind (Page, ed. 1889; OED, 3) or in one’s wonted disposition (Deighton, ed. 1891; OED, 9, = Temperament). Cf. 2775, temperance.

919 How now]
See n. 361.

921 Seruant]
Presumably one of Lear’s knights, as F’s Gent. may suggest. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 83): Just different appellations for the same small-part character. See n. 874. On the missing entrance see n. 538.

922 Exit.]
Greg (1940, p. 434 n.) believes that his knights do not accompany him, but pursue and catch up with him by 2075–6. In the interim, however, there are references to a traine (1336; F: number), my hundred Knights (1525), and a desperate traine (1609) that seem to refer to followers at hand. See n. 1336.

923–4 Shee…shorter]
Capell (1783, 1.2:154): The Fool’s addressing an audience is extravagant certainly,…but his rimes admit of no other colour. Eccles (ed. 1792): This concluding rhyme of the Fool seems to convey a hint of his expecting soon to return in consequence of the ill treatment there was a probability of their receiving at the place to which they were going. Steevens (ed. 1793): This idle couplet is apparently addressed to the females present at the performance of the play; and, not improbably, crept into the playhouse copy from the mouth of some buffoon actor, who spoke more than was set down for him.…Can such another offensive and extraneous address to the audience be pointed out among all the dramas of Shakspeare? Coleridge (apud Henry Nelson Coleridge, Literary Remains, 1836–9): The Fool’s conclusion of this act by a grotesque prattling seems to indicate the dislocation of feeling that has begun and is to be continued. Brown (1838, p. 292): These lines ought to be for ever expunged from the text.…[They are] not Shakespeare’s. They are omitted by Budd (ed. 1935). Petz (ed. 1839) suspects that something about the Fool’s dress is suggestive of obscenity and hence the occasion for laughter here; cf. 1692–3. Singer (ed. 1856): She who thinks that the journey we are now starting on will better us and bring us mirth, is such a simpleton, that if she is a maid now, she will be cheated before long of her claim to the title. White (ed. 1862): The indecency is entirely gratuitous.…The jest…is of the most miserable sort, and one which Shakespeare would hardly suffer in the mouth of this, the most thoughtful and subtly whimsical of all his thoughtful and subtle Fools. Moberly (ed. 1876): A vague threat of vengeance on some indefinite female. White (ed. 1883): Probably a tag, written by or for the actor of the Fool. Hudson (ed. 1881): To tickle the pruriency of the groundlings. It is so utterly irrelevant, withal so out of character, and so grossly petulant, that I can hardly bear to let it stand in the text. Bradley (1904, p. 452) finds the lines spurious because they are violently incongruous with 918–19, not only grossly indecent but irrelevantly indecent and evidently addressed to the audience, two faults which are not in Shakespeare’s way, and doggerel such as is not found in the plays after AYL. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 229): Shakespeare could write bawdry, and sometimes at what seem to us the unlikeliest moments. This does not smack of the Fool, though, or of what Shakespeare wants of him. Brooke (ed. 1947): The Fool, it should be remembered, is an adolescent boy (but see n. 626). Houghton (ed. 1957): The mental vigour and fertility of Shakespeare often expressed itself in puns and innuendo involving sex. The fool may also be anticipating his own speedy return from the fruitless mission. Harbage (ed. 1958): An indecent gag addressed to the audience, calculated to embarrass the maids who joined in the laughter, who merely find him amusing, unaware of Lear’s tragic situation and the Fool’s sympathy for him (Hoeniger, ed. 1968). Felver (1961, p. 61): This and Merlin’s prophecy (1735–49, F) are irrelevant sops to a conservative 17th century audience, lest Armin’s Fool be too different from his predecessors. Joseph (ed. 1966): Things has the normal sense of events…[and] the bawdy sense of male sexual organs.…The Fool’s point is that the girl who is stupid enough to find what he is doing funny has not the wit to preserve her virginity. Craig & Bevington (ed. 1973): A bawdy joke…implying universal carnality. Brown (ed. 1976): It half-masks his terror of what the future holds. Booth (1978, p. 105): Its substance participates in the thematic undercurrent of sexual wantonness in the play, but it is addressed to and concerns only the playhouse audience.…The humble seer turns momentarily and unexpectedly into an irresponsible, frivolous clown. Golding (1979, p. 128) finds some unlikely puns: The Quarto reading directs attention to both [sex and ambition].…Goneril may think she is made by sending the old man packing, but the Fool knows better.…Things (the pricks of circumstance) will eventually rise to undo her status as a false maid/made woman. Bratton (ed. 1987): An example of Shakespeare’s use of Robert Armin’s special, comic’s, relationship with the audience. He makes a joke combining a bawdy reference to himself out of the role (having the traditional lechery of the clown), with something that is part of the play: a foreboding about what is to come. Foakes (1993, p. 183): These lines can be explained literally in terms of laughter turning to dismay, but a reminder that the play is tragic is hardly necessary here.…The couplet marks the end of a stage in the action, momentarily interrupting it, to switch attention away from Lear, who is offstage for the next three scenes (320 lines). Idem (ed. 1997): Laughter was proverbially associated with sexual surrender, as in the phrase Laugh and lie down (Dent, L[92]). But the proverb refers to idle jesting, and neither Tilley nor Dent cites this l. as an instance of it.

923–4 departure…shorter]
Ellis (1869–89, p. 200) shows the pronunciation of -ture as -ter in Sh.’s day. Kökeritz (1953, p. 226) suspects the influence of Warwickshire dialect. Horsman (ed. 1973): The rhyme would be on the a vowel, citing J. C. Wyld, Colloquial English (1936, p. 240) and Dobson (1957, §87), neither of whom documents this vulgar pronunciation for shorter. Cercignani (1981, pp. 114, 263), however: Possibly an exact rhyme. Muir (ed. 1952): The word departure is a homonymic pun; OED (Depart v. 3): Separate. But the pun is doubtful, since departer in anything like this sense is not attested after 1400. Hotson (1954, p. 169) suspects a pun on deporter, which Cotgrave [1611] gives as the French for a sporting bauble. What roused the wanton wench to hilarity was not the Fool’s vanishing but the sight of his immoderate bauble. In fact Cotgrave’s word is deportet, defined as A sporting bable; a wenches &c. The pun, if any, would have been very obscure: deportet does not sound like departer, and OED gives no evidence that the Fr. word was adopted or had cognates in English. Nonetheless Wiles (1987, pp. 190–1) asserts that the fool puts his bauble between his legs…for phallic mime here and at 1682–5. The pun [discerned by Hotson] confirms that the regular French type of bauble, the marotte or fool’s head on a stick, was used in Lear, though unknown elsewhere in 16th-c. English fooling. Lott (ed. 1974) suspects a different pun on departure, verbal manipulations of the maids.

924 things]
Partridge (1947, p. 203): Penis (OED, sb. 11c). Colman (1974, p. 218) and Williams (1994) give other exx. Wiles (1987, pp. 190–1): The fool puts his bauble between his legs. There is no evidence for a bauble in the play. Foakes (ed. 1997), nonetheless: Wiles also notes that the bauble was no longer used in late-sixteenth-century fooling, and claims that Lear’s fool belongs to a vanished world, not to the social reality of 1605; if so, Shakespeare may have been anxious to avoid comparison with Archie Armstrong, King James’s fool. But in 1606 the rough horseplay and impudence of James’s young jester (d. 1672) was not likely to be confused with the wit of Lear’s Fool.

925 Exit]
Leech (1957, p. 260): An excellent place for an Act-end,…the end of the first phase in his way of humiliation.

926 <Actus Secundus>]
Verity (ed. 1897): Observe how much of the earlier, wilder action of the tragedy is associated with night: surely, for symbolical effect. Traversi (1952, pp. 57–8): The Second Act of King Lear is concerned, in the main, to develop further the situations already defined. It opens (II, i) with a noticeable deepening in the atmosphere of obscure foreboding which already begins to surround the main action. We hear at the outset of likely wars between Cornwall and Albany.…The very secrecy which enshrouds them is ominous, as is the insistence upon darkness as a cloak covering Cornwall’s movements which are thought to be connected with them; he is coming this night, now, i’ the night, i’ the haste, and, as we learn from Regan herself before the end of the scene, threading dark-eyed night. Once more these scattered and seemingly accidental repetitions have their part to play in the developing pattern; they link up with the disastrous revelation already made of Lear’s darker purposes and with his repeated invocations of obscure natural forces, and, together with these, look forward to the end of the act when, in Gloucester’s words, night comes on.…This and the following scenes (II, ii, iii)…are preludes to the next stage in Lear’s downward process—his meeting with Regan. Holloway (1961, pp. 82–3): The settled society of men, with their fixed abodes, [is progressively transformed] into a confusion of people constantly leaving their homes, constantly on horseback.…The society of men is becoming the chaotic world of the outlaw. Edwards (ed. 1975): The main-plot and the sub-plot are linked, and the lines between the opposing parties in the play are drawn more clearly when Cornwall and Regan adopt Edmund and identify Edgar as one of Lear’s followers.

926 <Scena Prima>]
Goggin (ed. 1910): As over a fortnight has elapsed since I. ii it is difficult to understand what has happened to the Gloucester family in the meantime. There is no indication that Edmund has kept the promise made to Gloucester in I. iii to enable the latter to hear his conversation with Edgar, and yet this Scene would appear to be in some way intended for its fulfilment, as Gloucester has set guard to catch Edgar (line [945]) and the latter is evidently hiding. It is difficult to think that Shakespeare would have made such a large demand of his audience as to leave him hidden in the castle for a fortnight, and that in the meantime Edmund has kept on poisoning Gloucester’s mind. It is a further sign of hasty composition that, though only a fortnight or so has elapsed since the division, we hear that a war is impending between Cornwall and Albany. But it is hardly certain that a fortnight has elapsed (see nn. 333, 811), and there is no evidence of impending war, only of rumors of war. Bransom (1934, pp. 54–6), having worked out a timetable of events from 1.2 through 2.4 : All these movements, with the possible exception of Goneril’s journey to Regan’s palace, can be made out with certainty from the text.…But in his elaboration of these [Sh.] did not make the course of events very clear.…The play is not really loosely constructed, but is apt to have that appearance. Kittredge (ed. 1940): This scene opens in the night that follows Lear’s departure for the Duke of Cornwall’s castle at the end of i, 5, and closes just before dawn on the next day. Daniel (1877–9, p. 217) thinks an additional day has passed: the action which ceased a little after noon…recommences here towards night of the following day. Perhaps Daniel, taking two dayes (1102) literally, allows Lear more time to arrive in Gloucestershire, but such a timetable would require an eighty-year-old man, after a morning of hunting, to ride without apparent rest for two days and nights before arriving at Gloucester’s house in 2.4. Leaving at noon, Kent expects to make the same journey before he sleeps; see 880 and n. Adams (1948, p. 319): In the Globe, the illusion of night was created by lighted candles, links, or torches. Hudson & Black (ed. 1911, p. liv): The chief link between the Lear plot and the Gloucester plot is Edmund’s association with Regan and Goneril, which begins in this scene. Dent (ed. 1927): It is in this scene that the two plots really begin to combine.…Gloucester’s cry, My old heart is crack’d, is an echo of Lear’s earlier cries, and points emphatically to the similarity between the two plots.
Though most eds. place the scene at Gloucester’s house (see textual n.), where Edgar has been hiding in Edmund’s lodging [489] (Foakes, ed. 1997), or just outside (Greg, 1940, p. 434; cf. n. 489), Brooke (ed. 1947) disagrees: This is on a treeless and uncultivated heath, a day’s ride from the city of Gloucester. Shakespeare was doubtless thinking of one of the British Camps, the remains of which are conspicuous on the crests of hills (e.g., the one near Dorchester on the Thames which he would have passed in going from Stratford to London). Gloucester’s castle may appropriately be located in the Vale of the White Horse or Salisbury Plain or, perhaps more plausibly, in one of the bleaker parts of the Cotswolds, e.g., near Chipping Norton. There is no clear evidence of locale; see n. 875. On the words castle and heath see nn. 333, 1614.

927 Curan]
See DP n. 11.

928 Saue]
Delius (ed. 1854): God save (OED, v. 3). Cf. n. 1234. Wright (ed. 1875): A common form of salutation. Kittredge (ed. 1940): To which Curan makes the conventional answer.

929–32 And…night]
Erroneously printed as verse in F, indicating that either the transcriber or the printer understood them to be such, and hence the F printer was probably not using Q for copy (Doran, 1931, p. 108). Alternatively, the compositor was stretching his prose copy, setting it in shorter lines of apparent verse in order to fill the column; see nn. 938–42, 961–2.

929 you]
On F’s erroneous your see n. 867.

932 to night]
F’s this night gives Q’s obvious meaning, as at 312, not the possibly ambiguous one at 359.

934–41 you…sir]
Gardner (ed. 1969): Curan, the informer, drops hints and fishes for information. The evasive half answers and the veiled questions establish the atmosphere of intrigue in this brief appearance. The dialogue is Shakespeare at his best.

934–5 abroad]
Delius (ed. 1854): Going around (OED, adv. 2); not in…foreign lands (OED, 4).

935 whisperd]
OED (ppl. a. 2): Reported quietly or secretly, quoting this l. as its first ex.

935 ones]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): News was originally a plural—new things. On the substantive use of the adjective see Franz §364, and cf. 1346.

935 there]
There is no reason to prefer F’s they.

936 eare-bussing]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Only whisper’d ones. Hudson (ed. 1856): Spoken with the speaker’s lips close to the hearer’s ear, as if kissing him. OED (sb.1 15b) quotes this l. as its only ex. of this and of F’s ear-kissing. Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 17, 192): Sometimes F substituted more familiar words for less familiar ones in Q which we must believe to be genuine.…It is possible that bussing is a misreading of kissing.…On the other hand bussing is a very pleasant reading, and…the F reading may be a sophistication. Sh. uses forms of kiss more than 300 times, of buss only 4 other times. Collier (ed. 1843): A play, probably, on bussing and buzzing, which here would have been hard to resist (Foakes, ed. 1997). Eds. often prefer Q because F eliminates such a quibble. Weis (ed. 1993): Q’s reading is more colloquial than F and better conveys the nuance of surreptitious topics of conversation,…i.e. rumours which are buzzed (told in a low murmur) at large. See n. 846.

936 arguments]
See n. 236.

937 Not, I]
Though all eds. adopts F’s Not I:, Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 513) give several contemporary exx. of the Not, I… phrase; thus Q’s reading is possible, though the idiom does not appear elsewhere in Sh.

938–42 Haue…Sir]
F erroneously prints as verse, not following Q1. See nn. 929–32, 961–2.

938 warres]
Petz (ed. 1839): Apparently over the equalizations of the part of the kingdom designated for Cordelia. Perrett (1904, p. 247): An anticipation of the civil war [in Mirour] that ensues when, after Cordeilla’s death, the two nephews, like the two dukes, hold each a half of Britain. Buck (ed. 1907): This rumor of civil war is here inserted to prepare us for the questions which Edmund asks Edgar with the object of confusing him ([953, 955]). Granville-Barker (1927, p. 148): But the wars themselves come to nothing. For his suspicion that this detail is therefore a loose end in the plot, see n. 1638+1. See also 1759–60. Halio (ed. 1973): A leitmotif…confuting one of Lear’s stated reasons for retiring, citing 49–50. Edwards (ed. 1975): It was accepted in Elizabethan political thought that a division of rule…would inevitably lead to civil war. Levin (1959, pp. 95–6): Gorboduc…foreshadowed King Lear in introducing a dissension between rival Dukes of Cornwall and Albany. Greg (1940, p. 442 n.): The rivalry was between the dukes, not, as Bradley has it ([1904], p. 250, n. 3), between Goneril and Regan: there is no hint of any quarrel between the sisters till Edmund comes to the fore. Reibetanz (1977, p. 39): Curan’s rumour colours the atmosphere of the tumultuous family division…by raising the even more fearful spectre of political chaos. But once the reference has served its purpose, it disappears. Smidt (1990, p. 131): Nothing comes of this strife, and just before he is killed, at [2060–71], Cornwall speaks as if he is oblivious of any conflict between himself and Albany. Foakes (ed. 1997): The first hint, following on Albany’s distress at seeing Goneril and Lear quarrel in 1.4, of…a rift between [Lear’s] sons-in-law. Indeed that distress might be the immediate cause of the rift. By the end of 1.4 Albany knows that Goneril and Regan (and conceivably Cornwall) are in collusion against Lear. As late as 4.2 (2270–86, 2304–2307+6) he remains reluctant to join his forces with Regan’s and Cornwall’s against Lear’s supporters, and he is still debating the question in 5.1 (2847–50, 2865–74). Oswald might have reported to Regan Albany’s initial reactions in 1.4 against Goneril’s course, and Cornwall might have smelled future opposition from Albany. The messenger who gave Curan advance notice of Cornwall’s and Regan’s approach might also have whisperd eare-bussing arguments about Cornwall’s new suspicions of an uncooperative or hostile Albany; Curan may now promote this gossip to rumor, perhaps improving it (in consideration of Cornwall’s sudden mysterious journey at night) to include likely warres. But no such reasons for the sudden rumors of division are ever clearly provided, and civil war never seems imminent.

938 towards]
All eds. adopt F’s toward, but Q is equally correct. Each means at hand (Dyce, ed. 1867, Gloss.): see OED (Toward adv. 2b; Towards adv. 1). Towards is usually a preposition in Sh., but is an adverb in Rom. 1.5.122 (704). Cf. 1770, 2652.

941 may]
F’s added do means hear (Tovey, ed. 1896).

941 Exit]
On Q’s omission see n. 538.

942 be]
Page (ed. 1889): To be; infinitive used absolutely. Or elliptical for is to be or will be. Lott (ed. 1974): The form of the verb shows that Edmund is reporting what he has heard.

943 better best,]
All Qq and Ff agree with Q1’s punctuation, which makes sense. Seymour (1805, 2:101): What was better is now best; what had thriven and improved, seems now to be perfect. Harbage (ed. 1958): Hyperbole. But most eds. mark a pause between the words to indicate two consecutive ideas. Deighton (ed. 1891): So much the better for my purposes, in fact the best thing that could possibly happen.

944 perforce]
Necessarily. Tovey (ed. 1896): This cannot but work in with my plans.

944 my busines]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Edmund sees the opportunity of winning over the duke, through Regan, to support him in his project of getting Edgar disinherited.

946 thing]
I.e., to persuade Edgar to flee, and perhaps in the process to give Gloucester something like the aurigular assurance promised him in 424–5. Gloucester, in the upshot, hears only the sounds of struggle and Edmund’s ensuing account of the conference. Lott (ed. 1974): Shakespeare thought of the events in this scene as following immediately on those in i.ii [comparing 425–6]. In any case there was a stage tradition that the working out of an evil scheme or plot takes place as soon as possible after that scheme is hatched. Cf. n. 952. The chronology is vague and obscure; see n. 333.

946 quesie question]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Of a suspicious, questionable and uncertain nature. Steevens (ed. 1773): Delicate, what requires to be handled nicely. Rann (ed. 1794): Of a ticklish nature. OED (a. 1b): Uncertain, hazardous, quoting only one other ex. Skillan (ed. 1967): edm. has to get his brother out of the way in order to be able to accuse him to his father without his being able to defend himself, and to do it in a way that will incriminate edg. A few eds. would add the sense of suffering or producing qualms. Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:54): Squeamish. Delius (ed. 1854): Nauseous (OED, a. 5). Bevington (ed. 1992): Matter not for queasy stomachs. Tovey (ed. 1896): At which a fastidious conscience might scruple (OED, 3c). Edmund must be talking generally; he himself does not have a fastidious conscience, nor does he seem squeamish. Few eds. comment on question, apparently taking it to mean nature, quality, a sense unattested in OED, or possibly a problem;…a subject involving…difficulty or uncertainty (OED 3; cf. 2997+4), an awkward and somewhat redundant sense. Herford’s (ed. 1899) Discussion (OED, Question sb. 1) fits the context, meaning either that persuading Edgar to flee will require some tricky argument (which follows), or that some actions will not bear much tender-minded discussion (Edmund’s own argument in 2975–6).

947 which]
Refers to thing.

947 must aske…helpe]
Q makes good sense, read as an ellipsis: this uncertain thing requires the help of speed and luck; it is of no importance whether the omitted and understood word is a that or an of after aske or a to or for before helpe. Duthie (1949, p. 43) compares Shr. 2.1.114 (979), my businesse asketh haste. Stone (1980, p. 216): There is no fault in Q’s syntax. We may even now say: I asked him a favour. Elizabethan English permitted, more than does our own, the dropping of prepositions before the indirect objects of certain verbs (see Abbott §201). Q’s line…is, of course, a foot short: no doubt the chief reason for F’s correction. It is possible that I has been omitted from Q before must aske: in that event, which = as to which (see Abbott §272 for this usage). The elliptical utterance and rough meter (which lacks only one or two unaccented syllables) suit Edmund’s urgency. F’s I must act,…worke, on the other hand, may be a sophistication. Doran (1931, p. 125): Though all editors adopt the folio reading, it is not necessarily better. Horsman (ed. 1973): In Q, The verb [is] influenced by question and the rest altered to fit it. Weis (ed. 1993): By splitting the clause into two, and by printing ask for act, F loses the urgency and syntactic tautness of Q. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 513): It seems unlikely that F…restores the reading of Q’s copy; resort to F here assumes that acte was (implausibly) misread as aske, and I independently omitted. The Oxford eds. (1986 Q; Wells, 2000) add (from 503) a monosyllabic noun Wit to the Q line in an attempt to improve meter and sense; see textual n. Skillan (ed. 1967), act: Put into operation and (possibly)…[use] the actor’s resource and skill.

947 breefnes]
Delius (ed. 1854): Speed of execution. Halio (ed. 1992): Edmond here personifies. Possibly in F (Briefenesse); but the F compositors capitalized hundreds of unpersonified Q nouns.

947 fortune]
Brooke (ed. 1947): Luck. Wilson (ed. 1960): May I be lucky enough to bring it off quickly! Elton (1966, p. 134), comparing 2973–4, 3124–5: Edmund wagers on the quick grab.…To the very end…he is inspired by the pragmatic test of fortunate or unfortunate outcome. Opportunism is all. F’s capitalization (cf. the prev. n.) leads Fraser (1962, pp. 47 ff.) to think this the first of many allusions to the superhuman influence of the goddess Fortune; cf. 1249, 1325, 2181, 2634, 2890, 2984, 3136, 3245.

948 Enter Edgar]
In Q this entrance is marked in the margin opposite 944, perhaps roughly where it appeared in the MS. McKenzie (1973, p. 128): A marginal note proper, comparing 462 and 1595. The Q compositor had placed all previous entrances in the center of the page, between speeches, before a speech either spoken by the entering character or (at 702 and 769) addressed to him. Only here and at 462, where Edgar appears in the midst of his brother’s soliloquies, does the Q compositor place the entrance in the margin rather than interrupt the speech. Possibly the Q compositor overlooked the direction, and then found that, in the midst of several very dense pages (containing many doubled speeches), he had no room for inserting the SD except in the margin. F centers the entrance direction in 948, just before Edgar is hailed by Edmund. Werstine (privately): If the SD appears in Q approximately where it appeared in the MS (left margin), then the MS is likely to have been a playhouse one, for by a convention already in place in the MS John a Kent, which is, after I. A. Shapiro, thought to date from the ’80s, the scribe or author puts SDs in the right margin, leaving the left clear for SPs and for the stage-reviser/book-keeper/playhouse annotator to use. This convention is in force with rare exceptions in four other playbooks from Sh.’s own time: More, Ironside, Charlemagne, John of Bordeaux, but not Second Maiden’s Tragedy, and Woodstock. Likely is not necessarily, of course; see Long (1999, p. 422). Sh. may have added the entrance as an afterthought in his rough draft, having finished writing Edmund’s long speech; he may not have thought it necessary to observe playhouse conventions in rough working papers; and none of the named plays belonged to Sh.’s company except Second Maiden’s Tragedy, which does not follow this convention.
At what point Edgar becomes visible to the audience, and whether he becomes visible to Edmund at the same time, has been a matter for conjecture. Granville-Barker (1927, pp. 229–30): Even the Folio…shows that he enters on the upper stage and is visible to the audience before Edmund sees him. It may be a small matter, but the difference between an independent entrance and being called on like a dog is appreciable, and can affect a character’s importance. Edgar does descend, of course. Greg (1940, p. 300): But there is no indication that Edgar is visible to the audience till he enters below; the balcony would not necessarily be required. Adams (1948, p. 319), questionably, would set this scene on the upper stage (see n. 333) and would have Edmund summon Edgar from an imaginary third level above. Joseph (ed. 1966): He can enter as if he had come down off-stage. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 513): In Q Edgar appears to the audience after 944 at a window above: Edmund’s first subsequent line (my…brother) explains to an audience why Edgar is peering nervously from an upstairs window.…That Edgar is above seems evident from Edmund’s call to him to discend; but no time is allotted (as usually happens) for Edgar to descend by the tiring-house steps. If Shakespeare had wanted the usual staging, he could easily have provided it by having Edmund call Edgar (brother…say) before addressing the audience for three lines.…It would be natural—and dramatically effective—for Edgar in these circumstances simply to climb over the upper stage railing and jump or climb down to the main stage. Since a jump from eight or ten feet above the stage would be hazardous, esp. while wearing a sword (see 491, 961), Edgar might instead appear above, see his brother below, and start down backstage stairs on his own before Edmund begins to call him, appearing on the main stage during or just after 949. Thus Horsman (ed. 1973): He has apparently been hiding from the guard and would first show himself rather gingerly. Edmund has been soliloquizing downstage; while Edgar is descending the stairs backstage, Edmund goes to one of the tiring-house doors and they converse beside it. Thomson (1988, p. 183): Edgar need not be seen above at all since he does not speak until he joins Edmund on the main stage. Surely there are enough staging problems without creating new ones. Halio (ed. 1992): The only occasion in the play where some kind of above seems to be used, contradicting Adams (op. cit., p. 316), who alone thinks (questionably) that five scenes (1.2, 2.1, 3.3, 3.5, 3.7) are played on the upper stage, representing an upstairs room in Gloucester’s house; see n. 333.

949 discend]
See prev. n. Eccles (ed. 1792): I.e. from the place in which he lay concealed. Kittredge (ed. 1940): In Edmund’s chamber. See [489].

950 watches]
Schmidt (1875): Is on the look-out (OED, v. 4).

950 O]
F’s Sir may have been added to smoothe out another of Q’s metrically rough lines (cf. 947). Wilson (ed. 1960), on the added word: Note the deference.

951 intelligence]
Schmidt (1874): Information (OED, sb. 7).

952 you…night]
Crook (ed. 1907): The darkness of the night will favour your escape. Goggin (ed. 1910): This suggests that Shakespeare did in some way conceive the events of this Scene as following immediately on those of I. ii. See [425–6]. Goggin accordingly makes now emphatic: At last, for the first time (today) since you were warned by me. But the time scheme is too vague for certainty (see n. 333), and now may mean simply at this hour.

953 haue…ought]
The absence of ought results in a line smoother in F than in Q.

954 hee’s…hast]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Edmund seems to grasp at every motive, however trivial or insignificant, that may appear to enforce…Edgar’s departure. Rosenberg (1972, p. 142): Edgar is hustled by Edmund’s pace. Exclamations, questions, the racing tempo involv[e] new dangers Edgar has never thought of.

954 it’h hast]
Abbott (§91): The was inserted in a few phrases which had not, though they now have, become adverbial; cf. Franz §268. Wright (ed. 1875) cites Ant. 5.2.196 (3432), put it to the haste. Page (ed. 1889): The is redundant, attracted (in the hurry of excited speech) from the preceding phrase. Deighton (ed. 1891): With great haste; the, emphatic. But the elision must prevent emphasis. Houghton (ed. 1957): The trisyllabic feet give the idea of urgency.

956 vpon his partie]
This apparently simple phrase has been given exactly opposite meanings and some highly ingenious interpretations. Many follow Hanmer (ed. 1743) in taking upon in its common Shn. sense of concerning, reflecting on, on the subject of (OED, prep. 22) and party in the sense either of a side in a contest (OED, sb. 5) or a faction of people on one side in a contest (OED, 6). So understood, Edmund’s question is merely a repetition of the one he has already asked in 953. Goggin (ed. 1910): It is…natural to think that Edmund merely repeats the question urgently. However, since on his party can and in Sh. sometimes does mean in his support, on his behalf (OED, Upon 4b; Party 5b; see, e.g., Jn. 1.1.34 [40], R2 3.2.203 [1562], Cor. 1.1.234 [255]), other eds. have followed Henley (apud Eccles, ed. 1792) in this reading, thus seeing the second question as different from the first. Eccles objects: His having spoken on behalf of the duke of Cornwall could be no reason for intimidation on account of his coming to his father’s habitation. Delius (ed. 1854), however, and many supporters: Edmund is trying to rattle Edgar by suggesting he is suspected of giving offense to the factions of both Cornwall and Albany. So Wright (ed. 1875): Edmund is endeavouring to alarm his brother to the utmost by suggesting every possible motive for flight. Evans (ed. 1898): He would thus suggest the idea that Edgar would find refuge with neither party. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): He was seeking material through which to fasten suspicion upon him, and if one question surprised no emotion or sensitiveness, he must try another in case of any chance to make capital against him. To the objection that Edgar would have nothing to fear from the approaching Cornwall for speaking against his enemy, Moberly (ed. 1876) opposes further ingenuity: War having not yet broken out, Albany would be in a position to demand the punishment of any one who spoke against him, and Cornwall not unlikely to concede it, as Elizabeth might have done, if his warlike preparations were not sufficiently advanced to make it safe to throw down the gauntlet. Many have doubted a theory which rests on so many suppositions; the immediate occasion is the arrival of Cornwall, and fear of his wrath alone should be quite enough to alarm Edgar. Tovey (ed. 1896): Edmund cunningly suggests to Edgar that he is accused of something like treason, and that the coming of Cornwall is upon his account. This, added to the fear of Gloucester already implanted (I. ii.) and Edmund’s volubility, completely confuses him. Hence he does not attempt to oppose Edmund, loses his head, and flees.…It could not be a motive for Edgar’s flight, that he had spoken in favour of the Duke of Cornwall. We have to suppose that Edmund’s intention is simply to bewilder; but there is not much cunning in it. More firmly Craig (ed. 1901), who takes upon in the sense of opposed to (OED, 21): Against, or to the detriment of, his (Cornwall’s) party, which is soon to be opposed to that of Albany, comparing Mac. 4.3.131–2 (1958–9), My first false speaking was this vpon my selfe. So also Bald (ed. 1949); and Chambers (ed. 1906) interprets party against to mean dispute.

956 Albany]
On the scansion see n. 47.

957 aduise]
Steevens (ed. 1793): Consider, recollect yourself (OED, v. 5). Craig (ed. 1901): Or perhaps a caution, be wary, citing H5 3.6.159 (1609).

957 your]
F adds selfe, making specific the reflexive meaning; but it is not likely that the Q compositor overlooked this word in his MS. The Oxford eds. (1986 Q; Wells, 2000) adopt the simpler correction of Q proposed by Blayney (apud Wells & Taylor, 1987, p. 513): Aduise you, which makes good sense and meter. Cf. TN 4.2.94 (2079), Aduise you what you say. The Q compositor might easily have mistaken a terminal mark of punctuation for an r.

958 on’t]
See n. 331.

960 crauing]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 381): Probably misreading—r/u, a/n, u/n. Most eds. adopt F’s cunning, which makes good sense. Kittredge (ed. 1940): As a trick—in order that I may not seem to be in collusion with you. No one suggests cravening; OED cites Cym. 3.4.78 (1752) as the first use of craven as a verb. Weis (ed. 1993) overingeniously defends crauing: Although OED restricts craving (meaning accusation) to Middle English,…Edmund may pointedly use it here, thinking his brother and father live in a medieval Morality play world. Miola (1994. p. 189) detects an analogue of Edmund’s deception in Terence’s Andria; see .

960 vpon]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Against (OED, prep. 21). Cf. 2048, 3213.

961–2 seeme…well]
Though set as prose in Q, these two lines, like those surrounding them, make one regular line of verse. F’s added Draw, without which the action is perfectly clear, produces a hypermetrical line which F sets as two incomplete ones. Abbott (§512) would make Draw an interjection on a separate line. Apparent sophistication. Werstine (privately): Folio Compositor E is spreading his copy…, setting Curan’s first (prose) speech as verse, splitting this line needlessly, and then wasting a whole typographical line on Edgar’s exit. Cf. nn. 929–32, 938–42.

961 seeme]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Not pretend, rather show yourself [OED, v.2 6].…The defence is to be lifelike.

962 quit]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Acquit, i.e. in swordfighting. Harrison (ed. 1948): Here they clash their swords together. Hunter (ed. 1972): Also, perhaps…depart. Weis (ed. 1993), less probably: Also, good luck with clearing your name; Edgar’s escape is at issue, not his good name. Lott (ed. 1974): Most probably he wants Edgar to react without thinking at all. Edgar’s natural response is to defend himself from attack. Rosenberg (1972, pp. 142–3) even wonders if Edmund means now to kill Edgar, who proves the better sworder here as in 5.3: Edmund would be much safer with Edgar dead. But since Edgar has not yet been proclaimed traitor, fratricide would be hard to justify. Halio (ed. 1992): [Lines 966–8] suggest…that the duel is a sham from first to last.

963–4 yeeld…here, torches, torches]
Delius (ed. 1854): Edmund speaks [yeeld…here, torches, torches] loud so as to be heard outside.

963 here, here]
F’s hoa, here has seemed more idiomatic to most eds. OED (Ho int. 2): An exclamation to attract attention. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 381): The Q word is probably a misreading—e/o…r/a. The Q compositor may have read hoa as her and set up here.

964 brother flie]
F omits flie, making smoother meter. Eccles (ed. 1792): As there does not any reason appear to have been intimated to Edgar by his brother for his father’s so violent resentment against him, there is something strangely unnatural in his being so easily made the dupe of Edmund’s cunning and treachery: Indeed the whole of this accusation and its consequences…is conducted in a manner highly artificial and improbable. Verity (ed. 1897): Some critics have considered it rather improbable that Edgar should fly instead of staying to clear himself of suspicion and at least have some explanation with Gloucester. But sudden confusion does make even sensible men lose their heads and act very unwisely.

964 torches]
Delius (ed. 1854): The pretended fight takes place in the dark. See 952, 954.

965 Exit Edgar]
On Q’s omission see n. 538.

966 beget opinion]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Induce a belief.

967 more]
Craig (ed. 1901): Particularly. Rather, more than would appear without such evidence; the phrase means of fiercer fighting on my part, that I have fought even more fiercely <than I seem to have> (Horsman, ed. 1973).

967–8 drunckards…sport]
Collier (ed. 1843): Many passages might be produced…to show, that young men out of gallantry sometimes stabbed their arms, in order to be able to drink the healths of their mistresses in blood. Steevens (ed. 1793) cites Marston, Dutch Courtezan, 4.1.[61] (ed. Halliwell, 1856, 2:299), Cooke’s Greene’s Tu Quoque (ed. Berman, 1984, ll. 1877–80), Dekker’s Honest Whore, Part I [2.1.435–6] (ed. Bowers, 1955), Jonson’s Cynthia’s Revels 4.1.208 (ed. Herford and the Simpsons, 1932), Middleton’s A Trick to Catch the Old One 5.2.195 (ed. Wayne, 2007), and The Man in the Moone (1609, sig. F4; ed. Halliwell, 1849, p. 43). Edmund, however, may be referring to an act of reckless bravado, not of gallantry.

969 no, helpe?]
All eds. before the Oxford (1986) follow Q2 in eliminating the comma to form a question meaning Is no one coming to help me? (Wilson, ed. 1960, comparing 2633, No rescue?). The Oxford eds. (1986; Wells, 2000) follow Stone (1980, p. 204): Emend: Ho! Help! The note of surprise, or desperation, in no helpe? might be attributed to Edmund’s clever play-acting, but I should be sceptical of any such interpretation. One expects cries of Ho! in situations of this kind…, and the comma after no in Q1 confirms, I think, a misprint. Foul case might well result in the mis-setting of n for h.…Whether the reading in F was inherited from Q2…or whether the F reviser and Q2 editor were tempted coincidentally to the same sophistication, it would be difficult to decide. The question-mark was commonly used to indicate exclamations. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 513): Stone’s conjecture is supported by the fact that n and h are adjacent in the type case, and by the absence of parallels for no helpe?…Ho is juxtaposed with help 13 times elsewhere in the canon.…The agreement of Q2 and F is meaningless, given Q2’s demonstrable influence on F. There need be no influence here, the correction being an apparently obvious one.

970 Enter…]
F adds the missing attendants; see n. 538. Urkowitz (1980, p. 27), however, argues that they do not appear on stage in Q; rather, Gloucester’s instructions at 979, interrupting Edmund’s speech in both F and Q, is in Q only directed to offstage pursuers, whereas in F their onstage presence makes the threat of pursuit…more real. Taylor (1983, p. 404) disagrees: The variants…probably reflect a difference in the provenance of the two manuscripts rather than a change of authorial intention, and editors or interpreters of Q Lear would be justified in supplying the attendants from F.

972–9 Here…after]
McKeithan (1934, pp. 46–7) finds a parallel with Edmund’s deception of Gloucester in a ch. of Sidney’s Arcadia 2.15.11–12 (see ), in which the frightened King of Iberia calls his guard, who find his son Plangus in the dark with his sword in hand.

973 warbling]
Perhaps because Q’s word seems mildly comical, implying birdlike trills and quavers (OED), most eds. have adopted F’s Mumbling, suggesting he was being quietly cautious (Foakes, ed. 1997). Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 381): Q may be a misreading of mumbling: w/m, a/u, r/m, are all possible graphic errors. Doran (1931, p. 132) compares the u/a misreading at 960. Weis (ed. 1993) prefers warbling, for its alliteration with wicked and its idea of Edgar’s wooing the moon; but wicked charms are not serenades. Similarly Wells (ed. 2000): Singing, chanting. Wright (ed. 1875) considers mumbling to be a verbal noun without a prepositional prefix a-, citing Abbott (§178), who, however, would consider it a participle. Rolfe (ed. 1880): The participle with of [needlessly] added. Verity (ed. 1897) finds the idiom in JC 5.3.38 (2519), and Smith (ed. 1902) finds the reverse, the omission of the posterior preposition, in 3238, a hanging thee. Franz (§669): Here the old and new constructions (with and without of) stand right next to each other. Cf. 2359.

973 charms]
Warburton (ed. 1747): This was a proper circumstance to urge to Glo’ster; who appears by [433 ff.] to be very superstitious. Hudson (ed. 1856): Edmund here takes hold of him by just the right handle. Hunter (ed. 1972): Gloucester’s reply is, however, severely practical.

973 coniuring]
Wright (ed. 1875): Binding by incantations.…In Shakespeare the accent is most commonly on the first syllable, though there are other instances of the other accentuation—as here, he seems to think (questionably).

973 Moone]
Perhaps following Root (1903, p. 54), Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): The moon-goddess Hecate, mistress of sorceries.…This…accords with Lear’s appeal [117]…, as well as with the astrological passages in scene ii.

974 stand’s]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 137): Equivalent to stand his. But it is quite possible that F [stand] is right and that to him is understood. OED (Stand, v. 15c): To act the part of, quoting this l. and other exx. in which a possessive pronoun is usual. Taylor (1985, p. 27): F could easily result from an incomplete or bungled attempt to correct Q2 [stand his]: his was crossed out, but either the annotator forgot to request or the compositor failed to supply the corresponding s at the end of Q2’s word. Or a scribe working from Sh.’s MS or the playbook could have overlooked or dropped the single letter s, without Q2’s being involved at all.

974 auspicious Mistris]
Malone (ed. 1790) finds the same phrase in AWW 3.3.8 (1550). OED (Mistress sb. 6): A woman, a goddess…regarded as a protecting or guiding influence, quoting this l. Verity (ed. 1897): Cf. [Leir 348–50; see ]…, If…Venus stand auspicious to my vowes.

976 Looke…bleed]
Muir (ed. 1952): Edmund must gain time to allow Edgar to escape; he does not wish to be confronted with him until Gloucester is convinced of his guilt. Quinn (ed. 1970): Interpreted by some critics as an indication of Edmund’s appeal for attention to a father who even now is more interested in Edgar. Hunter (ed. 1972): There is some comedy in the cross-purposes of Edmund trying to get Edgar out of the way…and Gloucester bent on [his] capture.

978–92 Fled…fled]
Clarkes (1879, p. 515): The ill-following sentences here serve to represent Edmund’s hurriedly concocted narration. Dry (1973, p. 15): In his moments of pure deception [Edmund’s] diction becomes hedged with double meanings…and his sentence structure becomes remarkably complex. Lott (ed. 1974): The clauses of Edmund’s speech are linked together loosely and without clear grammatical conjunction. He is deliberately speaking in starts to give the impression of confusion. Brown (ed. 1976): He is also preventing, by his talk, the pursuit of Edgar.

978 this way]
Capell (1783, 1.2:154): A wrong way should be pointed to. Wells (ed. 2000): But this would be difficult if there were only two stage doors as Gloucester must have entered by a different one from that by which Edgar departed.

978 could—]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 381): Q is right in indicating that the speaker is interrupted. Hogan (1962, p. 73): F, having no room for the dash, cut the punctuation.

979 him]
F’s added ho may be intended to regularize the meter, giving an unambiguous fifth stressed syllable to the line.

979 after]
On the absence of an exit see nn. 538, 970.

981 that]
Abbott (§285): The purely conjunctional use of that is illustrated by the Elizabethan habit of omitting it at the beginning of a sentence, where the construction is obvious, and then inserting it to connect a more distant clause with the conjunction on which the clause depends. Ibid., (§287): In order to give a relative meaning to words [such as when] that were originally interrogative,…that was frequently affixed.…This, with the above, explains [Lr. 977–81:] When by…But [when] that; see n. 273. Clark & Wright (ed. Ham., 1872, 4.7.157–9 [3148–50]): That follows when, after a parenthesis or other intervening words (compare [Lr. 977–81]), completing the conjunction When that. Cf. 2303+15, If that, 3098–9, since…that, cited by Franz §548, and n. 182. Brooke (ed. 1947) interprets but that quite differently as in spite of what he said. So does Joseph (ed. 1966): But instead.

981–2 reuengiue…thunders]
Elton (1966, pp. 200–12) treats at length of occurrences in classical, Christian, and contemporary skeptical texts and in Sh. of the question whether thunder is the clear instrument of the gods’ vengeance, and the gods are the clear agents of justice (p. 202). Cf. 1521, 1661–4, 1702–12, 1933.

981 reuengiue]
Wright (ed. 1875): Compare responsive = corresponding, in Ham. [5.2.151 (3620)]. OED (a.): Revenging, vindictive, quoting only this l. Most eds. follow F’s reuenging. Stone (1980, p. 225): Arguably, a form approximating to revengeful would be preferable to revenging in the context.

982 gainst Paracides]
Main (ed. 1962): Edmund ironically makes a self-fulfilling prophecy, comparing 3131–2.

982 all]
The point seems to be not that all the gods hurl thunder, or that all thunder is hurled only at parricides, both of which cannot be true statements, but that when a sinner so heinous as a parricide is to be punished, the maximum amount of thunder is hurled at him. See the next n.

982 their thunders]
Dyce (ed. 1865): F’s the thunder is a vile reading. White (1854, p. 424), however: There is a grandeur in the thought of the gods bending all the thunder against parricides, which dwindles away in the particularity of their thunders. Similarly Furness (ed. 1880) and Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 137) find the F text a stronger and more comprehensive expression. F’s reading may seem to imply what cannot be true—see the prev. n.—and most eds. have preferred Q. Foakes (ed. 1997): F’s reading is more vague and may be due to careless transcription.

982 bend]
OED (v. 17c): To direct…against, quoting this l. See n. 2318. Hunter (ed. 1972): Like a bow; but cf. Jn. 2.1.37 (330), our Cannon shall be bent.

983 many fould]
Joseph (ed. 1966): With many strands.

983 bond]
See n. 99.

984 in a fine]
The usual idiom is F’s in fine, meaning (1) to conclude, or (2) at last (Tovey, ed. 1896). OED (Fine sb.1 1b): Also, in short. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 381): The Q compositor may have repeated a from the latter part of the previous line.

985 loathly]
Wright (ed. 1875): With loathing or abhorrence (OED, adv. 1b, quoting this l.). Rolfe (ed. 1880): Loathingly; the only instance of the adverb in S., though the adjective appears twice.

986 with]
All eds. adopt F’s in, which avoids repetition of the same preposition in two consecutive phrases. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 381) on Q: Perhaps an anticipation of With at the beginning of the next line. Possibly the repetition is intentional, to make two parallel phrases.

986 fell]
Wright (ed. 1875): Fierce (OED, a. 1).

986 motion]
Schmidt (1875): An attack in fencing (OED, sb. 3c).

987 prepared]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Ready drawn. Cf. 972.

987 charges]
OED (v. 22): Attack or assail with impetuosity, quoting this l. Lott (ed. 1974): He cunningly slips into the present tense…to give immediacy to his fabricated report.

987 home]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): To the utmost. OED (adv. 3): To the point or mark aimed at;…so as to…penetrate effectually. Cf. 1763, 1796.

988 vnprouided]
Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Unguarded, unprepared. Page (ed. 1889): Not provided with defense.

988 lancht]
This and Q2’s launcht are variant spellings of launched, a cognate of lanced. OED (Lance v. 6): To pierce with, or as with, a lance or a lancet; to cut, gash, slit; (Launch v. 1a): Wound; cut, slit. Until recently even such Folio loyalists as Knight (ed. 1840) and Schmidt (ed. 1879) considered F’s latch’d a misprint. Greg (1933, p. 261), however: I believe that latch’d…is correct; if not, it is a literal error, not a misreading. Doran (1931, p. 91): A certain number of errors in F could have been caused, like many in Q1, only by the misreading of manuscript, comparing 1013, 1026, 1148, 1150, 1151, 1152, 1153, 1307, 1834, 2353, 2530, 2898. A few recent eds., however, despite the excellent sense of Q, defend and adopt the F reading. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905), latch: To drip, not to…catch, a use retained in the provincial latch-pan for dripping-pan. Here…denoting such a light lancing of the arm as would cause…a dribble of blood. But to catch or receive in (a receptacle) (OED, Latch v.1 3) means nothing like to cause blood to flow. Onions (1911), latch: Catch. Horsman (ed. 1973): This sense gives a more plausible tale than Q lancht, pierced. But the precise meaning given by OED (1), To take hold of, grasp, seize (esp. with the hand or claws) has little to do with thrusting a sword. Hunter (ed. 1972), followed by Colman (ed. 1982): Nick; unattested in OED. Apparently the edge of the sword is imagined as catching onto the flesh sufficiently to wound it. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 138) cites a third meaning (OED, 1c), To pull or strike swiftly off, but this is a Scots word last recorded in Stewart’s Chronicles in 1535, and Edmund has not had his arm struck off. Muir (ed. 1952): There is no evidence that [Sh.] had read [Stewart] before he wrote King Lear. Halio (ed. 1992) cites OED (4), to receive…a blow, but that is the opposite of giving a wound, the meaning required here. Stone (1980, p. 217): F’s reading cannot have derived from Q2…: it suggests nothing so much as a misreading of lãch’d [or lācht] in manuscript. Taylor (1985, p. 20): Possible foul-case error, since n lies immediately above t in the type-case.

989 but]
A handful of eds. have followed F’s And. Schmidt (ed. 1879): But…would indicate that the result of the scene was something unexpected (Ger.). Muir (ed. 1952): The Q reading But is more logical, perhaps; but Edmund is feigning agitation.

989 when]
Qq and Ff agree in this reading. Wright (ed. 1875): Either the construction is irregular [and to be explained only on the ground of Edmund’s perturbation (Furness, ed. 1880)] or the reading was most probably whe’r for whether, as Staunton conjectured [see textual n.]. Rolfe (ed. 1880): There may be a change of construction (cf. [Abbott (§415): Construction changed by change of thought]) in Or whether [991], or an ellipsis: Or whether (it was that he was) gasted, etc. Verity (ed. 1897): Greater symmetry (whether…or whether),…surely, is a quality that we do not want here, the broken, disjointed style of the whole speech being intended to indicate Edmund’s feigned agitation. Neilson & Thorndike (ed. 1909): Shakespeare mixes constructions here: And when he saw…or whether gasted. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 381): Q may have a misreading of r as n; but he prefers when, citing Verity.

989 best]
Eds. are divided on whether this is an adjective modifying spirits (Delius, ed. 1854) and so implying stoutest courage (Tovey, ed. 1896) or best powers (energies) (Kittredge, ed. 1940), or is an adverb modifying alarumd (Schmidt, ed. 1879) and so implying thoroughly awakened (Rolfe, ed. 1880) or roused…to do their best (Meiklejohn, ed. 1879).

989 alarumd]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Roused…as by an alarum (OED, Alarmed ppl. a. 1, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Cf. n. 2918, 2926.

989 spirits]
OED (sb. 16): One or other of certain subtle highly-refined substances or fluids (distinguished as natural, animal, and vital) formerly supposed to permeate the blood and chief organs of the body; (16b): Pl. Vital power or energy; (13): Mettle; vigour of mind; ardour; courage—attested only in the sing. Cf. 2291, 3094. Joseph (ed. 1966): Edgar is spoken of as seeing Edmund’s spirits as they issue from the wound with the blood, and (figuratively) in the energy of his response to the attack. But since spirits were invisible, only the figurative meaning applies.

990 bould]
Dent (1981, I82) detects the proverb Innocence is bold.

990 quarrels, rights]
Q2’s quarrels right has been all but universally followed. Deighton (ed. 1891): The justice of my cause. Stone (1980, p. 217) defends the minority view: The comma in Q1 is manifestly wrong, but there is no other reason for the alteration in Q2.

991 or whether]
Instead of being balanced against another whether, this phrase is apparently intended to parallel the when beginning the previous clause, suggesting two possible reasons for Edgar’s flight—Edmund’s boldness or his noise—without affirming either.
