Some eds. improve the parallelism by emending when to some form of whether: see textual n.

991 gasted]
Hanmer (ed. 1743–4, 6:Gloss.): Aghasted, frightened, dismayed (OED, Gast v.1, quoting this l.). Hunter (ed. 1869): Scared as if he expected a ghost. Wright (ed. 1875): For this derivation there is no foundation. Muir (ed. 1952): Elizabethans erroneously supposed that gastfull was etymologically connected with ghost.…Shakespeare may have intended a quibble.…Edgar, frightened, vanished like a ghost at cock-crow. Wright, Rolfe (ed. 1880), Craig (ed. 1901), and Muir (1952, p. 555) have pointed out the use of the words gastring, gaster, gastred, and gastful in Sh.’s source Harsnett (1603, pp. 73, 135, 137, 142; see , , ), and Craig suggests that gaster, a much more frequently-occurring form [than gast]…may well have been Shakespeare’s word. Sh. had already used gastnesse = ghastliness in F Oth. 5.1.106 (3211; ieastures in Q1).

991 made]
Capell (1783, 1.2:154) defends his punctuation made—: This, or words of this kind, is imply’d after made—Or how else it was, I know not, But suddenly he fled. Abruptions, and slips in construction, are the proper language of falsehood at first setting out. Likewise the Oxford eds. (1986 Q; Wells, 2000) supply I know not. This clarifies the sense, but interrupts the verse pattern, making 993 a part-line instead of the complement of 992. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 514): It seems likely that Q has accidentally omitted a verse line.…For the common idiom I know not, but see [586–7, 1581]. Stone (1980, p. 217), like Capell: I cannot tell is clearly understood without emendation.

992 but]
Stone (1980, p. 217): Q’s but appears clumsily to repeat the but three lines further up.…It serves a different function, in fact: that of introducing a certainty to set against the uncertainty implied in the previous clause.…Both buts are removed in F, which here prints Full. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 514): It is…difficult to believe that Q’s but…could be an error for F’s Full (or ful); but, if correct, must be contradicting a previous statement, but no such statement is available, a lacuna that the Oxford eds. partly supply: see the prev. n. According to Stone, the but contradicts not a previous statement but a previous lack of statement, and is the equivalent in meaning to but in any event.

993 Let…farre]
Muir (ed. 1952): However far he flies. Wilson, ed. 1960: Even if he flies far.…The construction is paratactic (J. C. M[axwell]). Joseph (ed. 1966), alternatively: He’ll have to fly a long way to evade me.

994 not…vncaught]
Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 135): Litotes…to veil a threat.

994–5 vncaught and found,]
Q2’s and F’s strengthening the comma to a semicolon, and the absence of punctuation after vncaught in all texts, have enabled some eds. to read these words as a single connected phrase meaning uncaught and (un)found, or similarly to emend it to uncaught, Unfound (Singer, 1852, p. 6; withdrawn, 1853, pp. 270–1) or uncaught And sound (Stone, 1980, p. 178). Others, such as Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 382), find F to be merely repeating and worsening an error in Q, and so alter the punctuation. All eds. since Hanmer have marked a medium pause after vncaught, and many have marked a heavy pause or break after found. Johnson (ed. 1765): The sense is interrupted. He shall be caught—and found he shall be punished. Despatch. Brae (1852, p. 82): There is an expressive pause after found, as though the punishment consequent upon Edgar’s capture were too terrible and indeterminate for immediate utterance. Deighton (ed. 1891): The pause after found gives expressiveness to the denunciatory despatch. Lee (ed. 1908): There is a similar elliptical construction at 1000. Hunter (ed. 1972): The pause is filled in by some gesture, such as drawing his hand across his throat. The meaning of the pause depends on the meaning of the word following it; see the next n.

995 dispatch,]
The Q1 punctuation allows this word to complete the previous line of thought or, as in Q2 and F, to commence another. In the first case dispatch may mean punished by exile (Davenport, 1953, p. 20), but most eds. cite 999 to interpret it as a common euphemism for kill (Delius, ed. 1854; OED, v. 4, quoting 2397). They differ whether the word is a noun—despatch is the word (Hudson, ed. 1856), death (shall be his lot) (Wilson, ed. 1960)—or an imperative, despatch him instantly (Hunter, ed. 1869); not by killing him on the spot, apparently, since to the stake seems to imply public execution)—or an ellipsis: (I will) dispatch him (Craig, ed. 1901). Horsman (ed. 1973) compares the ellipsis at 1000. A few eds. follow Warburton in emending to dispatch’d in order to form parallel participles: when he is found, he will be dispatched. If the word begins a new line of thought, it must mean make haste. Brae (1852, p. 82): Addressed to Edmund, and simply means, Get on with your story, which in fact he does. Dyce (ed. 1857): That here dispatch cannot be understood as make haste, is plain from the context (and Gloster has already sent attendants in pursuit of Edgar). Yet Stone (1980, p. 178): Addressed to the attendants who have earlier been ordered to pursue Edgar. Most eds. agree with Hudson or Hunter.

996 worthy]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Honourable.

996 Arch]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Chief (OED, absol. quasi-sb., quoting this l. and one other ex.). Heron (1785, pp. 305–6): A Latinism…for my worthy and arch-patron [so Kittredge, ed. 1940: Chief patron. Hendiadys]…Or arch may here mean support [so Caldecott, MS notes, 1813–33, as an arch is the strongest form of building, and Deighton, ed. 1891: An arch of a building, that which gives it its main support]. Gloucester’s earldom is evidently within Cornwall’s duchy; in any case a duke is superior in status to an earl.

997 proclaime]
Schmidt (1875): Make known to the public by criers (OED, v. 1). Cf. 1252. Following McKeithan (1934, p. 47), Bullough (1973, pp. 410–11 nn.) contrasts Sidney’s Arcadia 2.15.13 (see ), where Plangus, instead of opposing his duped father, choose[s] a voluntarie exile.

999 bringing]
Crook, (ed. 1907): For bringing.

999 caytife]
The Q reading makes doubly good sense, meaning both captive and base wretch (Wright, ed. 1875; OED, Caitiff sb. 1, 3). Brooke (ed. 1947): More expressive than F’s Coward. The Sokols (2000, p. 235): In Sh., suggesting either pity or contempt. Cf. 1708.

999 stake]
Deighton (ed. 1891): To be burnt alive. Craig (ed. 1901): I suppose bringing in, taking prisoner. I think it was customary to chain captives to a stake. Kittredge (ed. 1940): To the place of execution; to his death. A figure derived from the stake to which one was fastened for execution by fire. Not to be taken literally. So Bevington (ed. 1988): To reckoning. Wilson (ed. 1960): But perh. Glo. wishes him to be burnt for witchcraft; cf. [973–4].

1000 death]
Delius (ed. 1854): Elliptical; something like shall deserve death is to be understood. Crook (ed. 1907): Like dispatch in [995].

1001 disswaded]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Attempted to divert (OED, v. 2).

1002 pight]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Pitched, fixed, settled. Collier (ed. 1842): Determined (OED, Pitched, pight ppl. a.1 4, quoting this l. as its first ex.).

1002 curst]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Severe, harsh, vehemently angry (OED, Cursed, curst ppl. a. 4).

1003 discouer]
Wright (ed. 1875): Expose (OED, v. 3, 6).

1004 vnpossessing]
OED (ppl. a.) quotes this l. as its first ex. Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): Having no possessions, incapable of possessing or inheriting. Moberly (ed. 1876): For, says Blackstone, he [a bastard] is looked upon as nullius filius, and is therefore of kin to nobody, and he has no ancestor from whom any inheritable blood can be derived. Coleridge (MS notes, 1818–19, ed. Foakes, 1989, p. 100): = the secret poison in Edmund’s heart—and then poor Gloucester’s Loyal and natural boy, as if praising the crime of his birth? Harbage (1963, p. 410): Edmund is cleverly hinting a remedy: see 1022–3.

1005 would]
Abbott (§331): Not future conditional = should, but volitional: If I were willing.

1005 could…reposure]
F’s would is if anything weaker, and its reposall is synonymous. OED (Reposure) quotes one ex. (1602) earlier than Q1 and one later (1614); for Reposall it quotes this and one ex. (1614) earlier than the printing of F1. Presumably F substitutes a word about equally new and rare for one that seemed (to someone) less familiar. Sh. never used either again.

1006 trust]
Warburton (ed. 1747): That men have reposed. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Our father’s.

1006 vertue…worth]
Not objects of of, but coordinate with reposall (Delius, ed. 1854). Wright (ed. 1875): (Or the belief in any) virtue or worth, in thee. Hunter (ed. 1972): Or any virtue or worth that you possess.

1007 fayth’d]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:24): Credited (OED, Faith v., quoting this l. as its last ex.). See n. 223.

1007 what]
Wright (ed. 1875): As to what I should deny; the suspended object of the following sentence. Crook (ed. 1907): The object of turn [1009], in apposition with it. Schmidt (ed. 1879): Interjection; see next n.

1007 I should]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 173): The sense is in favour of Q, and so I suppose that the F compositor has accidentally inverted. Or a scribe. Schmidt (ed. 1879) prefers F as introducing an incomplete sentence—What, if I denied [what you say]—with the implied conclusion no one would believe you. Koppel (1899, p. 54) thinks the clause is complete: What, should I deny?

1008 this]
This intent (1001).

1008 I]
Ay. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 173): The line sounds very much better in Q. The F compositor may well have overlooked the I, having just set up I would. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 533): It might be an incomplete correction, I being struck out for replacement by yea.…Here I (ay) is potentially confusing.

1009 character]
See n. 397. Harbage (ed. 1958): Written testimony. Edmund may mean this generally, but Gloucester seems to take it as specifically referring to the fabricated letter of 382–9: see 1016, his letter. Weis (ed. 1993) detects also the modern sense true ethical nature, but Edgar’s true nature could not be blamed on Edmund’s suggestion.

1009–10 turne…to]
Harrison (ed. 1948): Make it appear to be.

1010 suggestion]
Warner (1768, p. 51): Pernicious counsel or advice (OED, sb. 2). Nares (1822): Temptation (OED, 1). Hunter (1845, 2:170): A theological word, one of three procurators or tempters of Sin, Delight and Consent being the others. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Instigation, incitement (OED, 1). Horsman (ed. 1973): False charge (OED, 3).

1010 pretence]
F prints practise. Q’s word could mean claim [to possess Gloucester’s wealth] (OED, sb. 1), expressed aim, intent, purpose, or design (OED, 3), or the assertion or alleging of a ground, cause, or reason for any action (OED, 6), all of which make excellent sense. Edmund uses both words elsewhere: see 421, 502. Most eds. prefer the more familiar Shn. word in F; see n. 502. Wright (ed. 1875): Practice is more in keeping with plot and suggestion. It is also redundant: see OED (Plot sb. 5, 7): Device, design, scheme, A plan…secretly contrived…to accomplish some wicked, criminal, or illegal purpose, and (Practice sb. 6a, 6c): Scheming or planning, esp.…in an underhand way, and for an evil purpose, A scheme, plot, intrigue, conspiracy, stratagem, manoevre, artifice, trick.

1011 make…world]
Rann (ed. 1794): Suppose all mankind superlatively stupid. Goggin (ed. 1910), less probably: Hoodwink men.

1011 dullard]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): S. uses the word only twice.

1012 they]
Tovey (ed. 1896): The world, taken as a plural.

1012 not thought]
Abbott (§305): Do [is sometimes] omitted before Not…[when] not precedes the verb.…Less commonly in a subordinate sentence. In effect, the negative and verb are transposed. Cf. Franz §405, and 2269, 2307+1.

1012 my death]
Moberly (ed. 1876): This skilful suggestion, that Edmund should be put into Edgar’s place, is acted upon at once by Gloucester; yet it is so indirect that Gloucester imagines the thought to have come from himself. Cf. n. 1004.

1013 pregnant]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Ready (OED, a.2 3d). Nares (1822): Full, or productive of something (OED, a.2 5). Wright (ed. 1875): Obvious. Each of these meanings has its adherents, but probably the last two, which have a different etymology, make best sense. OED (a.1): Of an argument, proof, evidence, reason, etc.: Pressing, urgent, weighty; compelling, cogent, forcible, convincing; hence, clear, obvious. Thus Verity (ed. 1897): Full of force, weight. Joseph (ed. 1966): Fruitful (astir with life) and powerful incitements. Craig & Bevington (ed. 1973): Teeming (with urgings). Horsman (ed. 1973): (a) pressing…, cogent, obvious…perhaps fits the Q reading spurres; (b) resourceful, inventive…goes rather with F spirits; (c) full of meaning, suggestive…would fit either. The word has still another meaning at 2670.

1013 potentiall]
Wright (ed. 1875): Powerful, potent (OED, a. 1). Horsman (ed. 1973), alternatively: Possible, as opposed to actual, latent.

1013 spurres]
Dyce (ed. 1865): Incitements (OED, Spur sb. 4, quoting WT 4.2.9 [1622]). Even Furness (ed. 1880), usually loyal to F, holds the majority view that its spirits is a misprint; cf. n. 988. Greg (1933, p. 261) is doubtful: Not an easy graphic error. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 173): Either simple misreading or confusion with profits in the preceding line. Delius (ed. 1854), spirits: Evil spirits. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Suggesting damned practise [but see n. 1010]…appeal[ing] to Gloucester’s superstition, an argument repeated by Sisson (1956, 2:232). Harbage (ed. 1958): The devils which possess him; but Edgar’s demons are not mentioned until Act 3. Muir (ed. 1952): It might mean incitements [unattested in OED].…In other plays Shakespeare juxtaposes potent and spirits; cf. Idem (1950, pp. 513–14). Halio (ed. 1992): Q gives a possibly mixed metaphor (pregnant spurs). But pregnant may simply mean potent; see prev. n. The F reading makes strained sense at best. Schmidt (ed. 1879) concedes that it forms a poor predicate to profits. Munro (ed. 1957): One could hardly describe the profits of my death as potential spirits. Wilson (ed. 1960): It is odd to call profits spirits, even evil spirits. Foakes (ed. 1997): F’s reading is a corruption, perhaps by attraction from spirit, [989], and profits, [1012].

1014 Tucket]
Nares (1822): A particular set of notes on the trumpet, used as a signal for a march.…From toccata (OED Tucket1). Manifold (1956, pp. 27–8): Tuckets announce arrival, not departure…[and] are played on a single trumpet.…Persons of importance had their own Tuckets, by which they could be recognized at a distance.…A fairly lengthy call—longer at least than the average Flourish. The term appears several times in F texts, not in the quartos. Of F’s addition here, Doran (1931, p. 84): Things for which the prompter must be responsible are provided for in the directions of the folio; cf. 1217, 1466, 1584, 1655, 1780, 1880. Halio (ed. 1992): And Gloucester’s preoccupation with Edmond’s news naturally suggests a delayed response.

1014 within]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Behind the scenes, offstage.

1015 Strong]
Both Q’s reading and F’s strange are possible; one is probably a misreading for the other (strange/stronge); somewhat more eds. favor Q. Steevens (in Reed, ed. 1803), strong: Determined [OED, a. 3]…term of obloquy [unattested in this sense]. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Steadfast in guilt. Idem (1879, p. 595): Confirmed. Schmidt (1875), Tovey (ed. 1896), and Craig (ed. 1901): Reckless; unattested in OED. OED (a. 11e): Of a malefactor: Flagrantly guilty, citing 2H6 4.1.108 (2276), Bargulus the strong Illyrian Pyrate, and R2 5.3.59 (2558), O heynous, strong, and bould conspiracy; cf. Tim. 4.3.46 (1649), strong Theefe. Formidable (OED, 7) may be remotely possible. Beginning with Delius (ed. 1854), supporters of F’s strange = abnormal (OED, a. 10) argue that Strong and fastned is almost a redundancy—but that is not so if strong means flagrantly guilty. Schmidt (ed. 1879): Unheard of, enormous, citing Ham. 1.5.27–8 (712–13), Murther…most foule, strange, and vnnaturall (F; beastly in Q2) and Ant. 4.15.3 (3001), All strange and terrible euents. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 139), followed by Sisson (1956, 2:232–3) and Wilson (ed. 1960): Not of one’s own kin or family [OED, 3]…along with…out of the ordinary: cf. I neuer got him [Q] in the next line. Sisson adds, Strange…is highly relevant here, when Edmund has been insisting on Edgar’s unnatural purpose ([986]), and Gloucester now contrasts Edgar with the natural boy Edmund ([1022]). Muir (ed. 1952): Unnaturalness. Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956): In planning the murder of his own father. Gardner (ed. 1969): Rare. Stone (1980, p. 217): Though strange is just possible (in the sense surprising, unaccountable, if hardly in the sense unfriendly), it gives, one might consider inappropriately, a colouring of wonder or puzzlement to Gloucester’s indignation.

1015 fastned]
Rann (ed. 1794): Obdurate (OED, ppl. a. 2: Rendered firm in consistency). So Craig (ed. 1901): Inveterate, hardened; perhaps a metaphor from the language of masonry. Wright (ed. 1875): Confirmed, determined (OED, 1, quoting this l. and one other ex.).

1016 his letter]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): See [382 ff.]; and n. 1009.

1016 said he]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 173): I should not like to sacrifice F’s said he?: it comes in very naturally, taking our minds back to the actual words imputed by Edmund to Edgar ([1007–10]). But Q’s I…him is very effective. It is possible that [a scribe preparing F copy] wrote in said he? in such a way that the F compositor wrongly thought it was to replace I…him. Honigmann (1965, p. 124): If so, F gives two consecutive long lines; if not, F has a long and then a short line. On the other hand, Q [1114–15] is perfectly regular (taking neuer as a monosyllable). Perhaps said he so? was intended in F; the added syllable would make a full line. Alternatively, F’s 1016–17 make two good pentameters if divided after Harke. The conflated line of most eds. can be read as a rough pentameter if the first three syllables are read rapidly and without accent. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 533), contra Duthie: The result [of conflation] is an irregular fourteen-syllable line, and F can be interpreted as a genuine question…which shows Gloucester on the brink of a thought which would destroy Edmund. But surely Gloucester is not seriously questioning Edmund’s guilt at this point. Halio (ed. 1992): Gloucester’s agitation lends itself to hypermetrical speech. Foakes (ed. 1997): F’s short line possibly mark[s] a pause as Gloucester notices the trumpet sound. It is by no means clear why F’s substitution, which merely repeats the previous phrase, should have seemed preferable to Q’s I neuer got him. The latter may have seemed somewhat a non sequitur after would he denie his letter, but it serves as a useful transition in the speech and the scene: it follows directly from Edgar’s supposed denial that he was bound to the father (984), and anticipates and explains Gloucester’s sudden choice of Edmund as his heir in 1021–3.

1016 I…him]
Furness (ed. 1880): I have followed the majority of editors in adopting a sentence from the Qq which seems in keeping with Gloucester’s agitation. Deighton (ed. 1891): He is no son of mine. See n. 349. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 206 n.): A stroke of irony—only to be fully appreciated perhaps by the shade of Lady Gloucester.…And this to Edmund his bastard!

1017 Dukes]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Gloucester recognizes this particular tucket [1014] as the Duke’s special signal.

1017 why]
Q is obviously right: Gloucester wonders momentarily at the duke’s unexpected arrival, then returns to a more pressing problem, his murderous son. Only a few defend F’s wher. Knight (ed. 1840) prints wher’ and glosses wherefore—the Q meaning. OED gives one ex. of this abbreviation of whether. Kirschbaum (1945, p. 35): It is the door by which the Duke will enter that concerns Gloucester…—Edgar may escape by it; hence the next line. Muir (ed. 1952): But there is no reason to think that Edgar is still in the castle precincts. Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 173–4): Misreading of y as e is sometimes found.…And it is possible that y might sometimes be misread as er.…[A scribe preparing F copy] may have misread the playhouse manuscript, taking why as wher. Stone (1980, p. 101): Superscript y read as r. Horsman (ed. 1973): Whichever gate (port) he [Cornwall] will need, I must bar them all;…my guest must concede that to me as a favor. But if the meaning is that the duke, as lord of this part of England, must concede that closing of all sea-ports…, then F wher is less apposite.

1018 Ports]
Delius (ed. 1854): Both gates [OED, Port sb.3 1] and harbors [sb.1 1, 2]. Most eds. have preferred one or the other; Craig (ed. 1901) attempts to generalize—means of exit—but that sense is unattested in OED. Since Edmund is now without the gates of Gloucester’s house, which is not within city gates but in the country, probably harbors, the way to flee the country, are meant. Cf. 1254, 1638+3. Colman (ed. 1982): Probably places of refuge [OED, sb.1 1b, fig.] rather than either gates or sea ports.

1019 picture]
Furness (ed. 1880): A printed portrait, citing Nobody and Somebody (1606, sig. D4): Let him be straight imprinted to the life: | His picture shall be set on euery stall, | And proclamation made, that he that takes him, | Shall haue a hundred pounds of Somebody. Halliwell-Phillipps (1880, p. 92): A written description? Harrison (ed. 1937; rev. 1949): During the plots of 1603 and 1605 descriptions of the wanted men were broadcast by proclamation. McCann (ed. 1964): Drawing, with a description.

1021 note]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Such information as will enable them to recognize him. More simply, suitable notice. F’s due note regularizes meter. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 514): Q’s metre is acceptable if kingdome | May is understood as a line-divided foot.

1022 loyall]
OED (a. 4): = legal in certain senses. a. Of a child: Legitimate, quoting this l. as its first ex. But this sense may only be an unconscious quibble on the usual meaning. Joseph (ed. 1966): As a bastard, Edmund is a natural son. But he is also natural in his filial behaviour; and loyal has the sense legal as well as faithful. Muir (ed. 1952) compares 1972–3.

1022 naturall]
Hudson (ed. 1856): The word…is here used with exquisite art in the double sense of illegitimate [OED, a. 13c] and as opposed to unnatural. OED (16): Feeling or exhibiting natural kindliness, affection, or gratitude, quoting this l. Muir (ed. 1952): Since natural could mean legitimate [OED, 13a] as well as illegitimate, he may also imply that Edmund is now his rightful heir.

1023 capable]
Steevens (ed. 1778): Capable of succeeding to my land, notwithstanding the legal bar of thy illegitimacy (OED, a. 7, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Moberly (ed. 1876): Which is, says Blackstone [Commentaries, 1765, 1:447], by the transcendent power of Parliament, and not otherwise. Keeton (1967, p. 33): A technical term of law. Verity (ed. 1897): Gloucester has in mind Edgar’s supposed taunt in [1004]. The Sokols (2000, pp. 29, 78): The anachronism in a play set in ancient Britain of indicating a legal means to disinherit the legitimate heir of lands (a means not available before the Statute of Wills 1540…) is consistent with reflections in the play of up-to-date social attitudes of Shakespeare’s time condemning bastardy.…In England before the 1540 statute…disinheritance of a male heir was not easily achieved.

1024 Enter…Cornwall]
On Q’s incomplete SD see n. 538.

1025 How now]
See n. 361.

1026 call]
Harbage (ed. 1958): Say was.

1026 but]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Only just.

1026 strange newes]
F’s strangenesse is clearly an error, whether a misreading of manuscript (see n. 988; Wilson, ed. 1960), compositor’s blunder of the memorial type (Greg, 1933, p. 261; Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 173), or other.

1027 if…vengeance]
Muir (ed. 1952) finds a weak parallel in Leir 1582: If it be so, that shee doth seeke reuenge; see .

1027 comes too short]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Is inadequate. Regan uses the phrase in 77.

1028 dost]
On omission of the pronoun see n. 562. Furness (ed. 1880): The fact that Regan at no other time addresses Gloucester in the second person makes me think that we should read…does. Kittredge (ed. 1940) compares 1723.

1029 heart]
OED (sb. 9): The seat of the emotions generally. Cf. 782, 1443, 1574, 1625, 1727, 1867, 1893, 2034–5, and 2396; and see next n.

1029 crackt]
Schmidt (1875): To break (OED, Heart-broken a.: Overwhelmed with anguish, despair, or crushing grief). Heilman (1948, p. 318): An unusual number of passages refer to the breaking of hearts, citing 1585, 3139, 3145, 3159–62, 3168+12–+13, and 3285, missing 1783 and 2586. Hunter (ed. 1972): The repetition suggests…sentimental self-pity, comparing 1032, 1035. On the physiology see n. 3168+12.

1030 What…life?]
Coleridge (MS notes, 1818–19, ed. Foakes, 1989, p. 100): Incomparable!…—compared with the unfeminine violence of [1027]—and yet no reference to the guilt, but to the accident. Goggin (ed. 1910): There is a hidden sneer in Regan’s words and in her mock surprise: it is quite natural, she suggests, that Edgar should turn out badly; look at his godfather! Kittredge (ed. 1940): Thus Regan venomously suggests a subtle association between her father’s character and Edgar’s plot of parricide. She is more outspoken in [1033–4].

1030 What]
See n. 810.

1031 he…Edgar]
For emendations to regularize the meter, see textual n. and . Abbott (§478) improbably suggests making the final syllable into two by prolonging the r, and more possibly by making your a dissyllable. But the line scans most naturally if the first two words are stressed.

1031 named]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Not…Christian sponsorship, but something corresponding to it in paganism—unspecified. Kemshead (ed. 1875): An allusion to Christian baptism and sponsorship. Brooke (ed. 1947): This tells us by Elizabethan convention that Lear’s name was also Edgar; but the reference to godson and the Anglo-Saxon name are both anachronisms. Foakes (ed. 1997): It hints that Edgar is the son Lear might have wished for. Lear never hints at such a wish.

1032 I]
Ay, in apparent response to Regan’s question. F substitutes the exclamation O. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 383): It might be suggested that F’s O is an erroneous repetition from the beginning of line [1029].…But it is much more effective, considering Gloucester’s mood here, that he should imply, but not directly give, an affirmative answer. Small i and o are easily confused in some 16th-c. hands.

1032 shame]
At the fact of attempted parricide, not at the disgrace to the King’s name. Gloucester’s woes are personal.

1033–43 Was…there]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): It is just one of Shakespeare’s subtleties in knowledge of human nature, making Regan seek to associate the accused man, Edgar, with the knights who belong to her father’s train, and whom she is determined to fasten blame upon, as an excuse for her refusal to receive and entertain them—as Goneril has encouraged her to do (see 527–8, 854–5). Hunter (ed. 1972): Gloucester’s response…is not very satisfactory; he is too sunk in self-pity to catch her drift. It is Edmund…who gives her the reply she wants, thus establishing at first sight the natural rapport between them. McLeod (1983, p. 179): Regan has received her sister’s letter informing her…of the ryotous knights.…She has also read Lear’s letter. As we have read neither, we have no reason to account Regan’s behaviour sinister per se. Unless sinister has here some special sense, this is a whitewash. Refusing to receive her unhoused father is hardly kind behavior, as even the Fool has foreseen (in 888). Skillan (ed. 1967): If edg. found his friends among the knights, they could not have been as bad as they are painted. The play nevers shows Edgar with the knights.

1034 tends]
Wright (ed. 1875): Attend. Cf. 1562, and see n. 1378. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 383): The terminal s is extremely common for a plural present-indicative verb. See n. 1697. F’s change to past tended is both unnecessary and problematic, since some or all of Lear’s knights still attend him, and Regan has no reason to think otherwise, indeed anticipates their arrival with Lear (see 1042). Likewise the common emendation tend is an unnecessary correction of tends, and as a truncated form of F’s tended, as Abbott (§472) thinks, it can only be defended by such doubtful logic as Duthie’s: The idea is that the Knights were attendant on Lear when, in the past, Edgar was a companion of theirs. But Regan is talking of the attendance of the knights, not of Edgar; he may have fled, but she still thinks that they accompany the king, and so she naturally speaks in the present tense. Foakes (ed. 1997), however: Regan uses the past tense, as if to distance herself from her father and his train. She has already distanced herself physically.

1034 too…bad]
Crook (ed. 1907): Gloucester, in his excitement, repeats his phrases, comparing 1029, 1032.

1036 Yes]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Prolonged and dissyllabic. Muir (ed. 1952): Presumably to fill out the metre and to suggest Edmund’s feigned hesitation in speaking of Edgar’s guilt.

1036 Madam]
Walker (1854, p. 173): Usually a monosyllable. But it seems dissyllabic in 1029, 1035, and may be here.

1036 of…consort]
F’s added phrase, which makes up a full verse, may have been overlooked by the Q compositor, though there is no apparent reason for such an oversight, and the sense is clear without the phrase. Possibly Q’s short line was intended: Edmund’s laconic, matter-of-fact reply effectively contrasts with his father’s voluble expressions of distress. Honigmann (1965, p. 127), however, rightly notes that in Q the verse is regular if 1035 is divided after Madam, and adds, F’s two irregular lines [1034, 1036] are less easy to explain. Foakes (ed. 1997): Edmund seizes another opportunity, stressed in F, to blacken Edgar’s name.

1036 consort]
Collier (ed. 1843): Company (OED, sb.2 1). Furness (ed. 1880): Probably here used as a strongly contemptuous term. It is not inherently such, as the exx. in OED attest. Abbott (§490): The accent falls on the second syllable, as it does in the verb. The evidence is ambiguous: the accent falls so in TGV 4.1.62 (1610), but the reverse is true in TGV 3.2.83 (1530) and 2H6 3.2.327 (2042), and according to OED the modern pronunciation begins appearing in the early 17th c. See also Kökeritz (1953, p. 336), Cercignani (1981, p. 38).

1037 though]
That (Crook, ed. 1907) or if (Kittredge, ed. 1940); OED (conj. 4a): After negative…phrases with…marvel. Franz §576 gives other exx.

1037 were]
Abbott (§301): Was.…No doubt or future meaning is implied. Brook (1976, p. 108): Were as a subjunctive…is used after if and though in dependent sentences. See Franz §645.

1037 ill affected]
OED (Affected ppl. a. II.1): Disposed, inclined.…b. Usually with the direction of the…disposition indicated by well, ill, etc. Here, in effect, a traitor (Abbott §301), disloyal…towards you (Kittredge, ed. 1940). Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956), less probably: Disaffected (toward his father). Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Badly influenced.

1038 put…on]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Incited him to (OED, Put v.1 27b, quoting this l. as its first ex.). See n. 719.

1039 these—and wast]
Furness (ed. 1880): Perhaps the [Q] compositor was baffled by the text of his copy, and left a dash to be filled up by the proof-reader, which was not done. Instead the Q press-corrector substituted the quite dissimilar the wast and spoyle, and F prints the still different th’expence and wast. Few eds. have followed the substitution of Q(c), which seems to have been made without reference to the MS. or consideration of…the ductus literarum (Ridley, ed. 1935). Muir (ed. 1952): The uncorrected [Q] version looks like a genuine attempt to decipher the copy, the corrected version being an emendation. Greg (1940, pp. 155–6): The intended reading was possibly The spoyle and wast or The spence and wast: The folio proves the [Q press-] corrector’s order to be wrong, and the object of the inversion is quite obscure. It may be accidental.…On the evidence we are bound to assume that the [proof-] reader correctly deciphered the word in the copy…and gave a rather tautologous reading. The compositor’s these— stands, then, for the spoyle. Of course, he cannot really have misread p as e: probably thes was all he could decipher, and he interpreted it as these. At the same time the corrector’s inversion and the comparative weakness of his reading…make me wonder whether the copy may not have had a reading rather closer to F.…There actually is a remote possibility that in this passage Shakespeare did write the spence and that the folio reading th’expence is a sophistication. Stone (1980, p. 208): Abbott [§338] says…that the Folio occasionally prints a dash or hyphen in place of final s…[because] that final s was indicated by a mere line at the end of a word in MS. If the dash here means final s, the correct reading might be the seise (…possession of). Howard-Hill (1986, p. 424): The F variant clearly reflects a fresh reading drawn from the promptbook, rather than the adoption of an existing variant from a quarto. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 514): The conjectures of Malone and Maxwell (see ) fail to explain Q[u]’s dash…; Greg’s…introduces a word [spence] for which there are no Shakespearean parallels.…Stone’s…provides a weaker meaning through the agency of a form only recorded once elsewhere (OED). It seems best to assume that the press-corrector properly deciphered Shakespeare’s manuscript, and that F represents a deliberate rewriting. The Oxford eds. (1986) accordingly alter F to th’expense and spoil, thereby changing the one reading (wast) on which Q1 (u, c), Q2, and the Folio agree, arguing further that (ibid., p. 533) Q[c]’s and Q2’s spoyle alliterates and contrasts better with F’s expence. More probably, the same difficult MS lies behind both Q and the playbook that ultimately supplied the text of F, and either the partly illegible th’expence or the spence was misread in that MS by the Q1 proofreader as the spoyle (and was transposed with wast to put the stronger of these two words second, in order of climax), while being more correctly read by the playhouse scribe, or else the spoyle was misread in that MS by the playhouse scribe as The spence or th’expence and his error survived in the playbook. Sh. never uses the rare expoyl (exspoil), and OED does not record the forms espoil or espence. As Greg says, wast and spoyle are somewhat redundant, and th’expense would have been the more likely to survive in the acting text if it is more or less what Sh. originally intended. F’s reading seems more probable on several counts than Q(c)’s. Knight (ed. 1840): Expense is expenditure, a step before waste. OED (Waste sb. 8): The consumption or using up of…resources [quoting this l. as its last ex.],…as distinct from [def.] 5 [= Useless expenditure or consumption, squandering]. Brooke (ed. 1947): Hendiadys: Wasteful spending. Hendiadys is unnecessary, however, and may be too often identified; see Wright (1981).

1039 this]
Greg (1940, p. 156): The omission of this [in Q(c) and F] is certainly correct. The compositor’s error was really one of duplication.

1039 reuenues]
Accent on the second syllable. See n. 145.

1040 present euening]
Tovey (ed. 1896): It is clear from this that Shakespeare places the seat of the Duke of Cornwall close to Gloucester’s castle. Goggin (ed. 1910): Cf. 1124, 1303–9.

1041 cautions]
Crook (ed. 1907): Warnings.

1042 my]
Foakes (ed. 1997): Regan asserts her personal authority, comparing 1062 ff.

1043 ile…there]
Bullough (1973, p. 291): In Leir the Messenger reaches Ragan [1161] after she has (however insincerely) welcomed her father [1126–40]; see .

1044 assure]
Page (ed. 1889): The imperative mood: assure thyself; be assured.

1045 heard]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 383): Perhaps a misreading of e as d. F: heare. A similar misreading is possible at 1252.

1046 child-like]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Twice only in Shakespeare.…Filial.

1046 office]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Dutiful service [OED, sb. 2], comparing 1382, 1462, 1638+12. Cf. 3206.

1048 betray]
Eds. generally prefer F’s bewray. Wright (ed. 1875): Bewray and betray are used almost interchangeably, but in the former there is no notion of treachery inherent. Weis (ed. 1993): Q’s betray conveys an ironic nuance (as Edmund is indeed a traitor to both his brother and his father). OED (Bewray v. 2b): To expose (a deception); (3): Reveal (secrets) prejudicially. The meaning is somewhat different at 2056+14. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) find bewraying his practise in Sidney’s Arcadia 2.29.6 (ed. Feuillerat, 1:334).

1048 practise]
See nn. 502, 1010.

1051 I my]
Abbott (§482): Both stressed.

1053 feard of]
Most eds. follow Abbott (§174): Of passes easily from meaning as regards to concerning, about; cf. Franz §517, and 2889. Tovey (ed. 1896): Dreaded lest he should do harm. Crook (ed. 1907): Feared as capable of.

1053 make…purpose]
Rann (ed. 1794): Take…steps, i.e. against Edgar.

1054 how]
I.e., however, as (OED, adv. 13, Franz §583 Anm. 2).

1054 in my strength]
Hunter (ed. 1869): With my authority. Foakes (ed. 1997): And resources.

1054 for]
Abbott (§149): As regards. Cf. Franz §483, and 2915.

1055 vertue…doth]
Capell (1783, 1.2:155): Figuratively for—virtuous obedience; and hence it is that itself [1056] is predicated of it, and doth follows it. Wright (ed. 1875): Two substantives closely connected and considered as expressing one idea are frequently followed by a verb in the singular, citing Abbott §336; see n. 754. Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): The virtue of obedience.

1056 ours]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): The royal we. But since Cornwall uses the singular my two lines earlier in the speech, he may simply mean here mine and Regan’s. Wilson (ed. 1960): I.e. one of our retinue.

1057 natures]
OED (sb. 3): An individual character, disposition, etc., considered as a kind of entity in itself; hence, a thing or person of a particular quality or character. Cf. 2303+1 and n. 185. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 192) explains F’s erroneous Nature’s: The F compositor has probably blundered while carrying the word in his head.

1057 trust]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Trustworthiness (OED, sb. 4). Foakes (ed. 1997): Full of irony, comparing 277, 1006, 2412.

1057 need]
Greg (1940, pp. 441–2 n.): He has the likely wars with Albany in mind, for as yet he knows nothing of the designs of France. Hunter (ed. 1972): Need in wars with Lear or wars with Albany. But a leader always needs loyal followers; Cornwall may have no more particular need in mind.

1058 first]
I.e., before anyone else does. Edmund is a free agent, as yet allied to no nobleman.

1058 seaze on]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Take into our service. Deighton (ed. 1891): Appropriate as an ally. See n. 277. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 122): No doubt an authorial spelling. Perhaps, but many other 16th- and 17th-c. writers use it (OED). In F1 it appears in TGV 5.4.33 (2152), Tit. 1.1.281 (313) and 4.2.96 (1779), and Oth. 4.2.37 (2729), as opposed to 36 instances of seiz-, two of them in Lr., here and at 277.

1059 you]
F’s added Sir is deferential but apparently extra-metrical; see textual n. for verse arrangements.

1059 how euer else]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Whatever else my shortcomings (OED, adv. 1b: To whatever extent, quoting this l.). Crook (ed. 1907): Whether successfully or not.

1060 your grace]
See n. 218.

1062 Reg.]
Jennens (ed. 1770): Regan may be here supposed officiously to complete Cornwall’s sentence. Capell (1783, 1.2:155): Regan’s breaking-in upon her husband, and finishing his speech for him, is highly in character. Smith (ed. 1902): It is not necessary to hold that Regan interrupts Cornwall, much less that the interruption is characteristic. She could not behave to Cornwall in the overbearing manner that Goneril does to Albany. Cornwall’s remark is complete in itself, and Regan merely takes it up and adds to it, as she is the person mainly concerned in their visit. It was to her that both her father and sister had written. Moreover, we are distinctly told in the following scene that it is the Duke’s disposition not to be rubb’d nor stopp’d. Cf. [1367–9]. Wilson (ed. 1960): Adding her elaborate rhetoric to Corn.’s simple query, Reg. indicates that he is second fiddle; but we need not suppose that she interrupts him.

1062 Thus…season]
OED (Season sb. 14): The right, proper, due or appointed time; a fit or favourable occasion. The conventional phrase out of season, meaning inopportune(ly) (OED, 16), occurs in Err. 1.2.68, 2.2.47 (233, 442–3). Most eds. take the phrase as an adverb modifying came to visit (1061). Regan acknowledges that a hasty arrival at night is improper. Hunter (ed. 1972): Or it may imply that it is winter, a bad time for travelling. Stone (1980, pp. 193–4), attempting to make sense of the Q line, would change Thus to This and take out of season as adjectival, modifying night: Regan’s description of night is, I believe, intended as a portent of the coming storm: [though] the storm does not break…until the following night.…The time of year, at least, causes no perplexity. Though the night of the storm is cold ([1863], the season is summer (cf.…[2357]), hence the epithet out-of-season. There is of course no mention in the line of a storm, summer storms are not unseasonable, and a naked beggar pelted by night rain would naturally be cold even in summer. Nonetheless the Oxford eds. (ed. 1986 Q; Wells, 2000), receptive to supposed differences between Q and F, adopt Stone’s conjecture. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 514): Although Regan has no reason to claim that she was threatning the night [as in unaltered Q], it does suit her purposes to claim that she has sought out Gloucester despite the unseasonable threatening weather. But she does not make that claim.

1062 threatning…night]
Most eds. take Q to be a misreading and accept F’s thredding. Though Stone and the Oxford eds. (see prev. n.) find such a misreading unlikely, Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 383–4), guessing that Q’s copy might have read threadding or thredding, provides examples from quarto texts of d/t and d/n confusions, including, from Lr., vntender/vntented (819), bloud in/bloodied (1505), deed/need (1564), countenadce/countenance (2910). Possibly only a single letter was misread, if the compositor read threading as threating and expanded it to threatning; or, as Duthie suggests, thredding was misread as thretning. No good sense can be made of Q; Rann’s (ed. 1794) attempt—threat’ning…braving all the perils of is unsupported by OED. Theobald (ed. 1733) proposes treading, finding too obscure and mean the allusions to the Cant-phrase of threading of Alleys, i.e. going thro bye-passages…or to threading a needle in the dark. Heath (1765, p. 330) rejects the emendation—For who can represent to his imagination, treading the night?—and refines on Theobald’s first interpretation: That is, slipping through it [night], as if afraid of being discovered. More probably, most eds. elaborate on Theobald’s second sense. Capell (1783, 1.2:1): Doing a work of day in the night, comparing the metaphor in Jn. 5.4.11 (2472), Vnthred the rude eye of Rebellion. Davies (1783, 2:283) understands the metaphor to imply that the night travel was as difficult as threading a needle. OED (Thread v. 4): To make one’s way through (…a passage presenting difficulties or obstacles), citing R2 5.5.17 (2682–3), It is as hard to come, as for a Cammell | To thred the posterne of a small needles eie, and Cor. 3.1.124 (1821), They would not thred the Gates. Hudson (ed. 1879): Threading is passing through. The word dark-eyed shows that an allusion to the threading of a needle was intended. Horsman (ed. 1973): The expression is so common in the seventeenth century that the quibble…seems unlikely. See the next n.

1062 darke ey’d]
Kittredge (ed. 1940) finds a similar epithet in Heywood, Love’s Mistress (1634) 3.1.4: Thou smooth-cheek’t negro night, the black-eyed Queene. Muir (ed. 1952): A quibble on the eye of a needle, and the dark eyes of Night—a pun that Wilson (ed. 1960) approves and Stone (1980, p. 194) finds incredible.

1063 Ocasions]
Schmidt (1875): Cause, motive (OED, sb.1 3; cf. 5: Circumstances…requiring action). Verity (ed. 1897): Understand some words like are the cause, i.e. of the visiting [1061].

1063 prise]
The Q1 proof-reader changed this reading to poyse; Q2, printed from a copy of Q1 having this sheet uncorrected, reproduces Q1(u) as prize. F repeats the latter reading, but whether it is derived from the playhouse MS, as Greg (1940, pp. 156–7), Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 139–40), Muir (ed. 1952), and others hold, or from Q2, as Stone (1980, p. 178) and Taylor (1983, pp. 362–3) suggest, remains uncertain. Greg, thinking that Q(c) sheet D was copy for F1, nonetheless rejects two of its press-corrections, poyse and lest (1066), hypothesizing that they were changed in the Q1 copy in accordance with the promptbook; Taylor, believing Q2 was the copy for F here, thinks that the F readings derive from it. Equally well, the F copy may have been a transcript, reproducing from the playbook the readings also found in Q(u) and Q2; see . Poyse, in the figurative sense of importance, was long preferred on several grounds. Warburton (ed. 1747): I.e. weight; Malone (ed. 1790): Or moment; OED (sb. 1). Hunter (ed. 1869): Requiring to be well weighed. Henley’s (apud Eccles, ed. 1792) conjecture peize means, he thinks, the same as poyse, balance or weight, and figuratively deliberation. Furness (ed. 1880): Sh. elsewhere use[s] poise in phrases similar to the present [e.g., Rom. 1.2.95 (344), Her selfe poysd with her selfe; Oth. 1.3.327, 3.3.82 (680–1, 1682), one scale of reason, to poise another of sensuality; full of poise].…It is a less likely word to occur to an actor [i.e., an unauthoritative intervenor in the text] than prize. Greg (1940, p. 157): Modern taste is offended by the rime or jingle [with prize] produced by aduise, and so prefers poyse. Taylor (op. cit.) thinks that F merely reproduces the unauthoritative reading from Q2, which he supposes was used as printer’s copy for F (see ). On the other hand, F’s prize has often been preferred. Johnson (ed. 1765): Why not prize or price for value? The meaning is unattested in OED, though the sense thing of value (Prize sb.1 3) is related. Heath (1765, p. 330): Of some consideration and importance in our esteem, unattested. Schmidt (ed. 1879): Prize seems to shade into the meaning worth in Ant. 5.2.183 (3415; make prize = make price?); the F reading thus means some account, unattested in OED. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): It is the matter of prudence in not permitting Lear and his riotous Knights to waste her Revenues…—in a word, the value at stake,—that is occupying Regan’s niggardly mind. The Qq and F generally maintain the distinct modern spellings of price and prize, though they are reversed in Tro. 1.2.289 (447; price Q, prize F). Prise is several times used for prize, in Ado 4.1.218 (1180; prisde Q, F), 2H4 3.2.101 (1521; Prize F), and AYL 2.3.8 (711; priser) and 3.2.152 (1350; pris’d). Greg (op. cit.), followed by Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 140), Bald (ed. 1949), Muir (ed. 1952), and others, takes Q1(u)’s prise as a variant spelling of the authoritative prize = importance, but the sense is unusual (Greg) and unattested in OED. Greg’s argument that the resulting rhyme adds a touch of stiff formality to the opening of Regan’s speech has been repeated by Munro (ed. 1957). Some senses of price—worth (OED, sb. 6), estimation (8), pre-eminence (11)—fit adequately though not exactly. Sh. uses the spelling prise for price only once elsewhere, in LLL 5.2.224 (2127; Q, F), but the variant is common, and may have been Q’s word here. Still, as Stone (1980, p. 178) argues, both price and prize seem unidiomatic if not forced, and since the o/r misreading is common, poise or poyse may be the true reading, misread by both the Q compositor and the scribe preparing the playbook that may lie ultimately behind F, but correctly deciphered by the Q proof corrector. Thus a false reading would have survived in the playbook behind F. Perhaps even more probably, the F1 scribe and Q1 compositor read the word (if not the spelling) alike and correctly, and the Q1 corrector introduced an unnecessary change because he was unfamiliar with the spelling prise. The phrase of some price does not appear elsewhere in Sh., however.

1065 he]
Franz §299 gives other exx. of the redundant pronoun. Here it is added for metrical purposes.

1065 writ]
Foakes (ed. 1997): Regan knows Kent has arrived, but it seems Gloucester, to whom Lear’s letter was addressed, does not know. But it is unlikely that Lear wrote to Gloucester; see n. 875.

1066 defences]
Q(c)’s diferences, disagreements, is certainly correct (Greg, 1940, p. 157). Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 514): The uncorrected reading suggests that the manuscript used the de spelling (see OED); the modern word deference is first recorded in 1647, so no ambiguity would have arisen. Deighton (ed. 1891): Disputes. Cf. 1125.

1066 which]
Delius (ed. 1854): This does not refer to differences, but to writ. Smith (ed. 1902): The antecedent is some such words as letters understood. Harbage (ed. 1958): Refers, indefinitely, to the whole situation.

1066 best]
Some eds. have accepted Q(c)’s lest (= least), understanding, as the Q proof-reader did, the following from our home to mean while at home (see n. 1067); so Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905), Kellner (1925, §60). Stone (1980, p. 212), following Greg (1940, p. 157) and Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 140): The corrector must have [erroneously] taken the phrase in its most obvious sense and altered the apparently contradictory best accordingly.

1066 thought it fit]
Furness (ed. 1880): Schmidt [ed. 1879] thinks that the misprint of the Folio [though it fit] is more likely to stand for thought fit than for thought it fit. The space is suspiciously large between though and it, and looks to me as though a letter had dropped out. The presence or absence of it need not affect the scansion. On the redundant object it after verbs of cognition see n. 294.

1067 from]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Not at home, but at some other place. Abbott (§158): From is frequently used in the sense of apart from, away from (OED, prep. 5b). Cf. 1498, n. 1246. Muir (ed. 1952): She wishes to answer the letters away from home, so that the King cannot quarter himself there before she has consulted with Goneril; who, we learn, is also coming to Gloucester’s castle (cf. [1476]). Edwards (ed. 1975): Regan has been appealed to by both sides in the dispute. She has already made up her mind what her answer is, and she prefers to give it on neutral ground, where the claim on her hospitality is less. Cf. n. 1470.

1067 hand]
Greg (ed. 1940, p. 158): Q(c)’s home is a certainly correct emendation of a three-fold graphic error. Weis (ed. 1993): Perhaps hand = letters written in Regan’s hand.

1067 seuerall]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Respective (OED, a. 8).

1067 messengers]
Walker (1854, p. 200): Frequently a quasi-dissyllable, citing 1124, 1222, 1275; cf. Abbott §468. Goggin (ed. 1910): I.e. Kent and Oswald.

1068 From…dispatch]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Await to be despatched from this place. OED (Dispatch sb. 2): Official dismissal…given to an ambassador after completion of his errand, quoting this l.

1069–70 Lay…busines]
Verity (ed. 1897): A polite way of telling Gloucester not to trouble about his own misfortune any more but to devote his attention to their business. Quinn (ed. 1970): Which requires immediate attention.

1069 Lay…bosom]
See n. 125. Deighton (ed. 1891): Do not allow yourself to sorrow at Edgar’s treachery. Harbage (ed. 1958): Be consoled.

1069–70 bestow…To]
OED (Bestow v. 6c): To confer as a gift, present, give.…(rarely) [with] to, quoting only this l. and Tit. 4.2.163 (1847), which lacks to.

1070 needfull]
Harbage (ed. 1958): Needed (OED, a. 3).

1070 busines]
Walker (1854, pp. 171–2): Very often…a trisyllable. Abbott §479 gives other Shn. exx. Cf. 3293. Defending F’s businesses, Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 140): The plural is found elsewhere in Shakespeare—see [AWW 1.1.206, 3.7.5, 4.3.85 (213, 1860, 2193), Jn. 4.3.158 (2163)]. And the verb craues in the next line does not necessarily support busines, citing Abbott §333 (see n. 1697; also n. 207).

1071 which]
Collier (ed. 1843) refers this to the previous word, but it may refer to Gloucester’s councell; see the next n.

1071 vse]
If the subject is business(es), this word must mean something like settlement (Moberly, ed. 1876), action (Harrison, ed. 1948), or attention (Bald, ed. 1949), senses unattested in OED. If the subject is councell, the meaning is the ordinary one, utilization or employment (OED, sb. 1).

1073 Exeunt]
For Q1’s misplacement of this direction after 1071, and Q2’s further error of omitting the turnover bracket and changing the word to Exit, see , and Blayney (1982, pp. 104–5, 179, 208). For F’s added Flourish see n. 202.

1074 <Scena Secunda>]
Goggin (ed. 1910): The events of this Scene take place early in the morning…of the same night as those of Scene I. Kent and Oswald, as directed by Regan and Cornwall, have followed them to Gloucester’s castle, and having travelled separately meet outside the castle. The length of the Scene is out of all proportion to its importance in the development of the plot. Its main purpose seems to be to prepare the way for the incidents of Scene IV. by the quarrel and the insult to Lear in the person of his messenger Kent, and by showing incidentally the attitude of Regan and Cornwall to the old King. Further it shows that the dramatist intends the characters of Kent and Oswald to be contrasted. Kittredge (ed. 1940): This scene begins and closes about sunrise on the same day on which Scene i ends, citing 1076, 1240. Daniel (1877–9, p. 218), less probably: 1 or 2 a.m. Adams (1948, p. 320) imagines, without textual evidence, use of a standard Globe setting, traverses…painted in imitation of castle walls…suspended at the rear of the inner stage. Houghton (ed. 1957): The quarrel between Kent and Oswald reflects that of their masters. In Leir 1920–70 the Gallian Ambassador follows Leir to Ragan’s court, engages in altercation with Ragan, and is struck by her ’gainst law of Armes; see .

1075 Kent, and Steward]
Verity (ed. 1897): The several messengers, 1067. Crook (ed. 1907), F’s seuerally: Separately. Although Oswald was ordered by Goneril to hasten his return (see n. 864), he follows Regan and Cornwall to Gloucester’s house because he has not yet received answer and formal dismissal from them; see n. 1068. Horsman (ed. 1973): Both speakers are messengers sent to Cornwall and Regan, and brought with them to Gloucester’s castle; but Oswald apparently arrives after the main party. Greg (1940, p. 435): It would be tempting to suppose that he had been sent back from Cornwall’s to report to Goneril…, and that he now arrives [back from Goneril] to announce that she too is on her way [to Gloucester’s]. However, he delivers no message (and at [1470] Regan expects her sister on the ground of her letter not of a message) and the time is probably too short to allow of a double journey. Moreover, Regan has just informed us that the seueral…dispatch ([1067]). There can be no question of a day intervening between ii, i and ii, for Kent has only recently arrived: I haue…hard ([1231]).

1076 deuen]
Q2 repeats Q(c)’s euen, F prints dawning. Greg (1940, p. 158): euen is An apparently obvious and yet certainly erroneous emendation. It is in fact not evening but early morning before sunrise. The folio presumably gives the correct reading, but [Q(u)] points to the copy having dauen. Dauing and dawin are seventeenth and eighteenth century spellings of dawn, while dawn itself is only a variant of dawing or dawning, and is not cited in OED before F1. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 384): Dawn cannot have been a very common word in 1608.…It may be suggested that F’s dawning is a substitution…of a more common form.…Dauen…may be Shakespeare’s word. The spellings dauen, dawen, and deuen do not occur elsewhere in Sh. Wilson (ed. 1960): But J. C. M[axwell] has pointed out that Good deuen is a coll[oquial] form of Good even. Cf. godden and god deuen (Gammer Gurton’s Needle, 4.3.5) cited O.E.D. under Good even. Stone (1980, p. 194), also defending Q1(c): F’s Good dawning was possibly invented (it is not an expression known to OED) to suit Oswald’s euphuistic style. So Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): The flunkeyism of Oswald shews itself in this affected phrase. Eds. have chosen between euen and dawning according to their understanding of the time of the scene. Johnson (ed. 1765): It is plainly past evening [OED, Even sb. 1: Close of the day; evening], and may…be supposed to be dawning. Capell (1783, 1.2:155): From 1104 we see…that ’tis night; but late in it, and drawing towards the morning. Mason (1785, p. 344): Very early in the morning, citing 1062, 1213–14. Malone (ed. 1790): The morning is just beginning to dawn, though the moon is still up, and though Kent early in the scene [1104] calls it still night. Towards the close of it, he wishes Gloster good morrow [1234]…and immediately after calls on the sun to shine, that he may read a letter. Delius (ed. 1854): As always in Sh., that time of day which is approaching is given by way of greeting, and not that which is then present; Oswald wishes Kent, whom he does not recognize in the dark, a good dawning (Ger.). Clarkes (ed. 1868): Sh. has marked the time throughout this scene with especial care; opening it with the hours before the breaking of the morning, when it is still night, yet the moon shines, and allows sufficient light to permit Kent to draw and attack Oswald; for the re-appearance of Regan and her husband, who have ridden through the night; and yet not sufficient light to permit Kent to read the letter he has received from Cordelia. Hudson (ed. 1879): It is still so dark, however, that Oswald does not recognize Kent. Kent probably knows him by the voice. Harbage (ed. 1958): Perhaps…it is too early for good morning. Taylor (1983, p. 454): Given the flexibility of dramatic time either Q or F is acceptable. Most eds. seem to agree with Johnson that the time is too late for the word even in its usual sense. Wells (ed. 2000), however: Good even might not seem inappropriate in darkness. Either word represents verbal scene-painting, since the Globe stage was fully lighted.

1076 art]
On the omission of the pronoun see n. 562.

1076 of the house]
F has this instead of the. Craig (ed. 1901): A servant, a dependant here—i.e., of the household; cf. 1718. But since Kent answers aye though he is not a servant of Gloucester, probably he interprets the phrase to mean inhabitant of the house. Cf. Mac. 2.3.83 (839), sleepers of the House. On the possibility that Gloucester might have retained possession or charge of the royal palace, Greg (1940, p. 431 n.): Being in Lear’s service, [Kent] might quite properly regard himself as of the household in any formerly royal residence at which the king was about to arrive. Kent thinks the king is going to Cornwall’s house, however, not about to arrive at Gloucester’s. Possibly Kent assumes that Cornwall, in whose company he has arrived, is by virtue of sovereignty temporarily the master of Gloucester’s house. Hunter (ed. 1972): Perhaps Kent says he is of Gloucester’s household…to give occasion for further attacks on Oswald, thus lying…as a way of picking a fight (Orgel, ed. 1999). Wells (ed. 2000): Kent is in disguise.

1077 I]
Foakes (ed. 1997): A surly refusal to talk?

1078 we]
Hunter (ed. 1972): The plural refers to [his] attendants. Cf. 860.

1078 set]
Schmidt (1875): To make to sit or stand (not lie) (OED, v. 17)—i.e., either tie up (Crook, ed. 1907) or stable (McCann, ed. 1964). Kent wilfully misunderstands: OED (104): To allow to get stuck, citing this l. Vickers (1968, p. 359): In this encounter Kent, like some of Sh.’s clowns, plays the obstructing equivocator.

1079 It’h mire]
Tilley D643 detects the proverb Dun <a horse> is in the mire (cf. Rom. 1.4.41 [494]), though its meaning—things are at a standstill—does not seem to apply. Dent (1981, M989) suggests another: To leave (lie) in the Mire. Colman (ed. 1982), mire: Mud, horse-droppings. OED attests to the first meaning (sb.1 2), not the second.

1080 Prethee]
See n. 664.

1080 if…me]
Delius (ed. 1854): A conventional phrase before a question or request, but which Kent takes literally. Cf. Shr. 4.3.50 (2032), JC 5.3.14 (2494). Foakes (ed. 1997): Be so kind as to.

1081 I…not]
Brooke (ed. 1947): The particular reason for Kent’s rage against Oswald appears in [1306 ff.]. Bransom (1934, p. 58): He was not a young man; he had had two tiring journeys, and the second one, from Regan’s palace to Gloster’s castle, must have been particularly annoying as well as wearisome. Goneril had outmanœuvred the king. This second journey was evidence of it. Oswald had been her instrument in doing it, and here the fellow was treating Kent as if he were a groom. This exasperation of Kent is a fine touch of Shakespeare. Like the king he did not find it easy to play his new part. The great nobleman will peep out in unguarded moments. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 67): His fierce verbal and physical onslaught…may satisfy the audience’s gut feeling that Oswald and Goneril deserve to be castigated, but his violence arguably does his master a disservice, confirms the riotous behavior of his followers, and exacerbates the conflict between Lear and his daughters. No other follower shows riotous behavior, however; see n. 586–872

1082 care…for]
Wilson (ed. 1960): A quibble—(a) like, (b) heed.

1083 Lipsburie pinfold]
Since no place called Lipsbury is known, a few commentators have conjectured that the name is a corruption, suggesting Ledbury (Rann, ed. 1794), Finsbury (Collier, ed. 1853), Lydbury (Halliwell-Phillipps, 1880, p. 92), Westbury Pen Hole (Sugden, 1925, p. 310), and Avesbury or some other Arthurian…Wiltshire-bury or even Salisbury (Sa)li[p?]sbury) (Smith, 1946, p. 154). Farmer (in Steevens, ed. 1773, 10:2Q3v): It may be a cant phrase, with some corruption, taken from a place where the Fines were arbitrary. Collier (ed. 1877): Every auditor knew Finsbury pinfold, an old jail there so-called, citing no evidence. Pinfold means a pound (OED, sb. 1), but since Kent’s intentions are obviously hostile, many suggest that here it means an arena. Capell (1783, 1.2:155–6): It was some village or other, fam’d for boxing;…the boxers fought in a ring or enclos’d circle, and…this ring was call’d—Lipsbury pinfold. Tovey (ed. 1896): A pound…would be an excellent place for a fair stand-up fight,…though where Lipsbury pinfold is no one can tell us. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Some wrestler’s ring…locally as familiar to Globe audiences as Yaughan’s alehouse in [Ham. 5.1.60 (3249), F only], and as utterly unknown now. Most, however, assume that it is a made-up name, possibly of Sh.’s coinage. Steevens (ed. 1778) suggests an analogy with Lob’s Pound, where pound may mean figuratively a place of confinement (Furness, ed. 1880; OED 2). Tilley L403 explains the proverb He is in Lob’s pound as meaning He is in difficulty but cites no Shn. references to it. Edwards (ed. 1975): There is no such place…; Kent makes it up, still pretending to be a humble and surly local. Most eds. follow the suggestion of Nares (1822) that the term here is a punning name, meaning the teeth, as being the pinfold within the lips. The phase would then mean, If I had you in my teeth. By analogy Wright (ed. 1875) provides the proverbial exx. of Needham’s Shore and Weeping Cross; Craig (ed. 1901) adds that In Beaumont and Fletcher, Wit at Several Weapons, I. i. [177]: Lipland means the lips and kissing. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Lipsbury means Lipsburgh, Liptown. In the Liptown pen, then, is in the enclosure adjacent to the lips, i.e., between my teeth, in my jaws,—and so in my clutches.…On such punning names see Jespersen, Nordisk Tidsskrift, 3d series, IX, 65–72. Examples are: Needham (for poverty), Cuckoldshire, Hempen Lane (the road to the gallows). Lott (ed. 1974) adds Bedfordshire for bed. Kittredge further provides examples of the teeth and lips as fence or jail for the tongue, from Homer [Od. 10.328, Il. 9.409], Plutarch (De garrulitate, cap. 3), Lyly’s Euphues (ed. Bond, 1:279), Marlowe’s 2 Tamburlaine 4.3.43–7, R2 1.3.166–7 (459–60), and Luc. 679, her lips sweet fold. Eds. have applied Nares’s idea in different ways. Verity (ed. 1897), over-literally: One can scarcely suppose that Kent would want to bite Oswald. MacCracken (ed. 1914): If I had thee in some place where lips are sealed and arms at liberty; cf. Jackson (1819, p. 321): Where the movement of thy lips should be of no avail. Hudson (ed. 1879): So…a place where neither Oswald’s legs nor his lips could help him,—where he could not run away, nor could his whining nor his yelling for help do him any good. But all this seems to me forced and far-fetched. Surely no theatrical audience would have understood the phrase. Brooke (ed. 1947): Lip-Town…where one may expect lippy creatures like Oswald, with vagrant tongues and habits, to wind up. Houghton (ed. 1957): To suggest…that Oswald used his lips too loosely. Hulme (1962, p. 61): Shakespeare is using…an existing joke on two senses of lip—to kiss and to shear (a sheep). Horsman (ed. 1973), finding in OED that bury could mean a court, or a manor-house: The whole may be…interpreted as the prison or trap belonging to the court of my lips or teeth. Brown (ed. 1976): To judge by your talk. Most eds. follow Nares’s own interpretation, in my teeth. Deighton (ed. 1891), unconvinced: Kent could hardly expect such a jest to be intelligible to Oswald. Musgrove (1981, p. 11) suspects thieves’ cant: It may be connected with Knapsbery, a thieves’ rendezvous (Harman, p. 109), or perhaps with Lypken, cant for a house to lye in. He does not explain why Kent should speak as if he were a thief.

1085 I…not]
Verity (ed. 1897): Because it is not yet light. Or may be that Oswald feigns ignorance, not wanting a second…encounter with Kent.

1086 I know thee]
Hunter (ed. 1972): I can see through you. Notice the pejorative second-person singular throughout this dialogue.

1087 for]
Deighton (ed. 1891): To be (OED, Know v. 11c).

1088–97 A…addition]
Henley (apud Eccles, ed. 1792): Kent is not only boisterous in his manners, but abusive in his language. His excessive ribaldry proceeds from an over solicitude to prevent being discovered, adding (in Steevens, ed. 1793), like St. Peter’s swearing from a similar motive. Knight (ed. 1840): Slang. It must be recollected that Kent has assumed the character of a serving man. White (ed. 1883): Kent’s store of billingsgate is rich and varied. He rails us into something like sympathy with Oswald. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Kent upbraids Oswald as a cowardly menial who parades as a gentleman. Wilson (ed. 1960): An outline of Osw.’s career from a menial in the kitchen to Gon.’s intimate.

1088 eater…meates]
OED (Broken ppl. a. 1b): Broken…meat: fragments of food left after a meal. Craig (ed. 1901): A common gird against serving-men, citing Cor. 4.5.32 (2686–7), Cym. 2.3.114–15 (1090–1). Gardner (ed. 1969): Menial servants were entitled to the leavings from table, as part of their payment, quoting from Middle Temple records.

1089–90 base…knaue]
Seymour (1803, p. 48): I.e. a fellow made up of inconsistencies, as well in his exterior habiliments, as in the composition of his mind. He is at once proud and beggarly,…insolent and mean. Verity (ed. 1897): All terms of contempt specially applicable to anyone who claimed the rank of gentleman with doubtful right to it; exactly expressive therefore of the disdain which, on social as well as personal grounds, Kent, the Earl, would feel for a pretentious, self-satisfied person like the steward. Foakes (ed. 1997): But Kent is himself disguised as a servant, and appears at best the equal of Oswald, probably his inferior, for Oswald calls him a ruffian [1135].

1089 three snyted]
The corrections of Q1(c) (shewted) and F (suited) apparently mean the same. Steevens (ed. 1778, 2:431) supports the pronunciation of suitor as shooter by citing a pun on those words in LLL 4.1.114 (1100) and the confusion of suter and shooter in The Puritan (1607) 2.1.95, 97 (ed. Brooke, 1908). To these Ellis (1869–89; 1869, pp. 215–17) adds another play on suiter and shoot from Rowley, Match in the Dark (1633) 2.1, and says of the present passage, three snyted [is] an evident misprint for three suyted. Now shewted…may indicate…transitional pronunciation [or]…it may be…a mere misprint for sewted, which would be a legitimate orthography for suited (so OED, Suit sb.). He quotes Wright’s (privately conveyed) demur: I suppose…the correction communicated verbally to the compositor, who inserted it according to his own notions of spelling. Greg (1940, p. 158): Clearly the [Q] copy had suyted and thus agreed practically with F. The corrector presumably intended the same word, but his spelling is peculiar and misleading (shute is elsewhere found as a var. of suit [so OED], but shewt does not appear to be recorded). Cercignani (1981, p. 347) gives other Shn. instances of s pronounced as sh. That the Q compositor intended to set suyted seems probable, but the spelling may not have been in his copy, since it never appears in any Folio or good Quarto text of Sh. Except for Tro. 1.1.97 (131) suite, suit and its derivatives (suits, suited, etc.) are always spelled sute in the Quartos and are divided between sute and suit(e) in the Folio. Neither does shewt appear in Quartos or Folio. OED (Suitor sb.) records the 16th c. variant shewter. Possibly Sh.’s spelling was sute, and suyt and shewt may represent the preferred spellings of Q compositor and corrector respectively. Werstine (privately) cautions, however, that spelling in manuscript is much more various than in print.
Farmer (in Steevens, ed. 1773, 10:2Q3v) and a number of later eds. suppose the epithet to mean luxurious dress, since Edgar [rather, Poor Tom], in his pride, had three suits, only (see 1914–15 and ). So Delius (ed. 1854): This signifies foppishness, changing his suits that many times, or else wearing them all at the same time. Hudson (ed. 1879): One who spends all he has…in dress, comparing 1128–9, a Tayler made thee. Phelps (ed. 1917): At the extortionate price of Elizabethan clothes the possession of three suits was quite beyond the ordinary man.…Kent is contrasting the pampered lackey’s outward exquisiteness with his mental and moral poverty. Most eds. follow Steevens (ed. 1773) in seeing three suits as the mark of servility: One who had no greater change of cloaths than three suits, citing Jonson, Epicoene 4.5.10–11, a pitifull poore fellow…and had’st nothing but three sutes of apparell. Hunter (ed. 1869): Hired for three suits of clothes and a hundred pounds. Wright (ed. 1875): It is probable that three suits of clothes a year were part of a servant’s allowance, citing Epicoene 3.1.39–41, who allowes you…your three sutes of apparell a yeere? Deighton (ed. 1891): What to [Edgar in 1914–15] in his then state would be comparative wealth, might be spoken of as poverty in the case of a steward; and the epithets beggarly, hundred-pound, worsted-stocking, are all in keeping with such a meaning. Verity (ed. 1897): Probably the yearly allowance of clothes to a servant…[and] a meagre wardrobe for a gentleman. Either way…a contemptuous estimate.

1089–90 hundred pound]
Steevens (ed. 1773): A term of reproach, citing Middleton’s Phoenix (1607) 4.3.56–7, How’s this? am I used like a hundred-pound gentleman? Staunton (ed. 1859) cites Oldys’s Life of Raleigh (Raleigh’s Works, 1829, 1:163): Nay at Milan, where there are three hundred pound Englishmen, they cannot so much as have a barber among them. Clarkes (ed. 1868): An expression formerly used to designate a pretender to gentry. Moberly (ed. 1876): Worth £100 and no more; that is, just up to being a juryman. So Verity (ed. 1897), adding, It does not mean having a yearly income of £100. Herford (ed. 1899): Implying pretentious poverty. Craig (ed. 1901): A hit at James the First’s profuse creation of knights, citing from the mock dedication to Middleton’s Father Hubburd’s Tales (1604) the phrase hundred-pound feat of arms. Neilson & Thorndike (ed. 1909): James I conferred knighthood freely, and the poverty of some of the recipients was a current joke. Onions (1911): App. contemptuous epithet for a pretender to the title of gentleman (perhaps referring to a minimum of property-qualification). Wilson (ed. 1960): Osw. is nothing more than a menial, though he aspires to be a gentleman.…A rich, if somewhat frayed, doublet-and-hose w[oul]d lend point to these references. Gardner (ed. 1969): A reference to some property qualification for a gentleman…seems too flattering. I take it to be the total weight of property belonging to the one trunk inheriting slave. Brown (ed. 1976): Sarcasm (a hundred pounds a year was a huge salary for a menial). But it is not clear that the hundred pounds is an annual salary, and Oswald may be a gentleman, not a mere menial; see n. 506. Wells (ed. 2000): Kent seems to veer between accusing Oswald of behaving like a despised menial and…a pampered favourite.

1090 wosted stocken]
Q(c) and Q2 print worsted-stocken, F woosted-stocking. Greg (1940, p. 158): The spelling worsted is no doubt more correct as representing an original worthstede, but the emendation was quite unnecessary, seeing that the r was no more pronounced then than now: wusted, wosted, and woosted are common spellings from the fifteenth century to the eighteenth. It is unlikely that F accidentally followed the spelling of [Q(u)]. The introduction of the hyphen is reasonable, but the passage calls quite as loudly for others, which were (all too freely) supplied in F. Q and F may both lack an r in the first word because they derive ultimately from the same authorial MS; Sh., however, does not elsewhere use the word. Stocken is a common 17th-c. spelling, and stockin is common 16th-18th c., though elsewhere in the Folio and Quartos the word is always spelled stocking. Wright (ed. 1875): At a time when everyone who could afford it wore silk stockings, worsted or woollen stockings were the badge of servants, or of those who from necessity or otherwise lived meanly. Steevens (ed. 1773) finds this opinion in Stubbes, Anatomie of Abuses (1583, sig. E3v), Tailor’s The Hog hath Lost his Pearl (1614, sig. B2) 1.1.92–4, and Beaumont & Fletcher, The Captain 3.3.154–5; Malone (ed. 1790), in Middleton’s Phoenix 4.2.54–7; and Craig (ed. 1901), in Jonson, Epicoene 3.1.41–2. See also Every Man in his Humour (F) 1.3.41–7.

1090 knaue]
See n. 610. Hulme (1962, p. 328) improbably finds a pun on the rare sense contrivance in which spool or spindle revolves (OED, sb. 5), in conjunction with the previous word.

1090 lilly lyuer’d]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Cowardly (OED, Lily adj. b). Wright (ed. 1875): The liver was regarded by the old anatomists as the seat of courage: hence a white and bloodless liver was the sign of cowardice, citing Mac. 5.3.15 (2232), 2H4 4.3.104 (2339–40), R3 4.4.464 (3262), and 2304. Deighton (ed. 1891) adds TN 3.2.61 (1441), and Tovey (ed. 1896), MV 3.2.86 (1432). Tilley F180, A white-livered Fellow, cites this l.; Dent (1981) adds As white as a lily (L296). Hoeniger (1992, p. 175): When the liver did not transform the chyle into blood, it became white from an abundance of phlegm.

1091 action taking]
Mason (1785, p. 344): A fellow who, if you beat him, would bring an action for the assault, instead of resenting it like a man of courage. OED (Action sb. 16): Litigious, quoting only this l. Verity (ed. 1897): So the coward Sir Andrew in [TN 4.1.34 (1950)], when beaten by Sebastian, says I’ll have an action of battery against him. Less probably Crook (ed. 1907): Not resenting any action done against him.

1091 knaue, a]
Since the epithet provides a welcome breathing space, its omission in F may be accidental.

1091 whorson]
Not necessarily bastard (cf. 26). Schmidt (1875): A term of reproach or ludicrous dislike (OED, attrib.). Cf. 1105, 1137.

1091 glassegazing]
Malone (ed. 1790, 10:680): One enamoured of himself; who gazes often at his own person in a glass (OED, Glass sb.1 16, quoting only this l.). Craig (ed. 1901): Vain, foppish, citing R3 1.1.15 (17).

1091–2 super-finicall]
The word does not occur in the OED. Eds. have universally preferred F’s super-seruiceable finicall, the second of the hyphenated words in Q and F being graphically enough alike that the Q compositor may have overlooked one of them through eyeskip. Johnson (1755): Over-officious (OED, a.: More serviceable than is required or fitting; doing or offering service beyond what is desired, quoting this l. as its first ex.). More exactly here, Joseph (ed. 1966): Always at one’s master’s disposal no matter what the service to be performed. Cf. other descriptions of Oswald’s character at 1095, 1146–53, 2704–6. Less probably, Wright (ed. 1875) and a few followers: One who was above his work. Deighton (ed. 1891), finicall: Foppish, over-fine. On F’s second word, Kittredge (ed. 1940): Fussy about trifles. Muir (ed. 1952): Affectedly fastidious (OED). The word is not used elsewhere by Sh., and Tobin (1983, p. 118) believes that he got it from Nashe, who may have coined it and used it repeatedly, though others also used the word; see Schäfer (1980. p. 147).

1092 one truncke inheriting]
Hanmer (ed. 1743–4, 6:Gloss.), inherit: To possess; all senses in OED retain the connotation of possession as heir, but Schmidt (1874) finds an absolute sense at 2568. Most eds. follow Steevens (ed. 1773): A fellow, the whole of whose possessions are confined to one coffer, and that too inherited. Johnson (ed. 1765), apparently supposing that truncke means trunk-hose: A wearer of old cast-off cloaths, an inheritor of torn breeches. Rann (ed. 1794): Possessing only a single pair of trunk-hose. Verity (ed. 1897): One trunkhose is not consistent with three-suited. Wells (ed. 2000): OED records this meaning of trunk only in the plural. Foakes (ed. 1997) alone: One is often hyphenated to trunk but not so in Q or F, and I take one to mark a shift from a, comparing one that (1092) and one whom (F only), where one is a pronoun, not, as here, adjectival. Strier (1988, p. 130): Many of Kent’s insults make no sense unless Oswald is finely, even ostentatiously dressed—not obviously implied by beggarly and wosted stocken.

1093 would’st…seruice]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Ready to act pandar to master or mistress. Kittredge (ed. 1940): If it comes in your day’s work. Hoeniger (ed. 1968), bawd: Used for both sexes (OED, sb.1). Foakes (ed. 1997): Oswald later carries letters from Goneril to Edmund; see 2716 ff.

1094 composition]
Schmidt (1874): Compound (OED, 19).

1095 sonne…bitch]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): A fine touch!—not merely the son, but the heir, inheriting all the mongrel’s qualities. Partridge (1947, p. 75), bitch: Connotes wantonness.

1096 clamarous]
Greg (1940, p. 140): Q1(c)’s clamorous is a slight but obvious correction; F1’s clamours is a misprint or an anomalous form (on the analogy of wonders for wondrous). Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 385): It is perhaps safer to regard it as a misprint.

1097 addition]
Title(s). See n. 144. Weis (ed. 1993): Sarcastically.

1098 monstrous]
See n. 238.

1098 fellow]
See nn. 16, 577.

1099 of thee]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): By thee.

1099–1100 nor knows thee]
