Goggin (ed. 1910): It is singular that Oswald, who had seen Kent only a few hours before, and who had good reason to remember Kent’s treatment of him at Goneril’s palace less than two days before, should now profess ignorance of him. It cannot be on account of the bad light, for Kent is able to recognize him. Cf. Hudson in n. 1076.

1101 brazen fac’t]
OED (a.): Impudent, quoting this l. The metaphor is proverbial: see Tilley F8, citing this l. Cf. 14.

1101 varlet]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Rascal;…diminutive of vassal (OED, 2). Cf. 1474.

1102 two dayes]
Verity (ed. 1897): Kent must have taken something over a day in the journey on which we saw him set out ([875–9]). Daniel (1877–9, p. 218) takes two dayes literally; see n. 926. Greg (1940, p. 435), however, Presumably two days since may by a stretch mean yesterday. Maxwell (ed. of Greg, 1966, p. 327 n.): Greg seems confused here. Is…since is presumably a question expecting the answer No; so that it is not by a stretch, but by the most natural interpretation, that the incident belongs to the previous day. Kent began his journey (1.5) near noon (cf. n. 539) of Lear’s day of hunting (1.4), and expected not to sleep before completing it (880); he arrived at Regan’s house late that night, and followed Regan and Cornwall throughout that same night to Gloucester’s house; having watcht and trauaild hard, he is now ready for sleep (1231–2; cf. n. 1075). In all probability the time is now still that night, before the dawning of a new day. To believe that another whole day intervenes would require Lear, who will not arrive until late this afternoon, to spend a morning hunting and then two more days riding without shelter and possibly sleep, before setting out at the end of 2.4 for yet another night of wandering on foot. Kent might survive that, but not an eighty-year-old man.

1103, 1106 draw]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Draw your sword. Wells (ed. 2000): Implying that Kent does so.

1105 sop…moone-shine]
OED (Sop sb.1 1): A piece of bread or the like dipped or steeped in water, wine, etc.; (2b) Used of persons in respect of some pervading quality, quoting this l. as its last ex. Warburton (ed. 1747): He would make a sop of his antagonist, which should absorb the…moon’s rays by letting them into his guts. Capell (1783, 1.2:155): He would lay [Oswald]…upon his back on the earth, like a sop in a dripping-pan, for the moonbeams to baste him. Malone (ed. 1790): After having beaten the Steward sufficiently, and made his flesh as soft as moistened bread, he will lay him flat on the ground, like a sop in a pan, or tankard. Caldecott (MS notes, 1813–33): By the light of the Moon…I’le make you float lifeless, like a toast in a tankard. Entwisle (1873, p. 84): In the sense of steeping him in his own blood, by the consenting light of the moon. Craig (ed. 1901): He would knock Oswald into a puddle, or pond, where he might look up at the moon. Gardner (ed. 1969): Toss him into moonshine reflected in water. Crook (ed. 1907): Leave him lying bathed in the light of the moon. Rea (1920): Figuratively, I’ll sop up the moonlight with you. MacCracken (ed. 1914): As we say, wipe up the floor with you. Most agree with Warburton; Kittredge (ed. 1940): I’ll drill you full of holes, so that the moonlight can soak into you until you are a mere sop—steeped in moonshine. So Quinn (ed. 1970): You can be used, spongelike, to sop up the moonshine, comparing Tate’s King Lear (1681, p. 14): I’ll make the moon shine through thee. Munro (ed. 1957): Cf. the phrase to let daylight into. Hunter (ed. 1972): Or while you talk moonshine—nonsense (OED, 2). Davies (1783, 2:284): Kent means, that, by the help of the moon, he will dispatch him as quickly as he would eat a morsel of bread. Only a few eds. follow Nares (1822), who detects a reference to a dish of fried eggs called eggs in moonshine (OED, Moonshine 3, quoting this l.). So Neilson & Thorndike (ed. 1909): Equivalent to—I’ll make an omelet of you; Wilson (ed. 1960): = make mincemeat of. Lit. = make into a dish of poached eggs; Joseph (ed. 1966): Eat you; and Wells (ed. 2000): Turn you into moonshine, a dish of eggs or custard.

1105 a’you]
F reads of you. Q1’s a’ is a worn-down of (OED, A prep.2 1). Cf. 1613, 1860, 2399, 2794, and n. 704.

1105 whorson]
See n. 1091.

1105 cullyonly]
Rann (ed. 1794): Scurvy. OED (a.): Rascally, base, despicable, quoting this l. as its first ex. The sense of foolish, doltish from the Ital. coglione, proposed by Hanmer (ed. 1743–4, 6:Gloss.), Nares (1822), and Wright (ed. 1875), is unattested by OED. Williams (1994), Cullion: Testicle, quoting this l. Orgel (ed. 1999): The insult is analogous to calling someone a prick.

1106 barber-munger]
Mason (1785, p. 344): A fop, who deals much with barbers to adjust his hair and beard (OED, Barber sb. 2, quoting this l.). Fraser (ed. 1963): Hence effeminate man. Farmer (in Steevens, ed. 1773) understands munger to imply taking fees [from barbers] for a recommendation to the business; but White (ed. 1883): Consorts with…as in whoremonger. Williams (1997, p. 330): May imply a pox condition, requiring a barber-surgeon’s services.

1107 haue…with]
OED (Do v. 33d): To have dealings or business with, quoting this l. as its first ex.

1108 letters]
Evidently one letter. See 527, 858, 1309, 1470, and n. 875.

1109 Vanitie]
All eds. take this as an epithet for Goneril except Spilsbury & Marshall (ed. 1905): Kent represents Oswald as suited to play Vanity, but only as a mere puppet. Johnson (ed. 1765): Alluding to the mysteries or allegorical shews, in which Vanity, Iniquity, and other vices, were personified. Ritson (1783, p. 168): Rather, the old Moralities. Dyce (1844, p. 224; ed. 1867), Halliwell (ed. 1865), and others doubt an allusion to the morality play. Meagher (1971, p. 246): Lady Vanity does not appear in the extant old moralities at all. The term Lady Vanity is common if not proverbial: Reed (ed. 1785) finds it in Jonson’s Volpone 2.5.21, Wright (ed. 1875) in Jonson’s The Devil Is an Asse 1.1.42, Verity (ed. 1897) in Marlowe’s Jew of Malta 2.3.116, Kittredge (ed. 1940) in Nashe’s Pierce Penilesse and Have with You to Saffron-Walden (ed. McKerrow, 1:241, 3:11), in Sir Thomas Moore 4.1.147 (ed. Brooke), and in Anthony Munday’s Death of Robert Earl of Huntington (1601, sig. E1v, as dame vanitie). Though Kittredge also cites Vanity in The Contention betweene Liberalitie and Prodigalitie (1602), that character is male. Hudson (ed. 1856): Vanity by way of antithesis to royalty; opposed to abstract in Kent’s figure (Kermode, in Evans, ed. 1974). Hunter (ed. 1869): The vanity that mimics greatness. Deighton (ed. 1891): Frivolous piece of worthlessness. Meagher (op. cit., p. 251): The epitome of the vain woman, perhaps provided with gorgeous dress and a hand mirror, as in emblematic depictions of Vanity. Edwards (ed. 1975): The personification of worldly self-interest. Bullough (1973, p. 339 n.) derives the term from Gonorill’s pride in new made fashion (Leir 102; see ); cf. 1569. Halio (ed. 1992) connect[s] Gonorill’s vanity with her servant Oswald’s, which Kent detests.

1109 puppets]
Collier (ed. 1843): She [Vanity] had also probably been represented in a puppet show. Munro (ed. 1957) cites Chambers (1903, 2:158–9): Representations [motions] of miracle-plays [and moralities] by means of moving puppets or marionettes make their appearance in all parts of Europe at a period when the regular dramatic peformances of similar subjects were already becoming antiquated, quoting WT 4.3.96–7 (1764–5), a Motion of the Prodigall sonne, Jonson’s Bartholomew Fair, etc. Meagher (1971, p. 258 n. 3): A list of known early puppet plays can be found in George Speaight, The History of the English Puppet Theatre (London 1955): neither there nor elsewhere have I found any evidence of a puppet Vanity. Dyce (1844, p. 224): Here…puppet is nothing more than a term of contempt for a female (OED, sb. 1). Wilson (ed. 1960): It can also = poppet or darling (unattested; cf. OED, 2: a child’s doll; 2b: an idol); see . Meagher (op. cit., p. 250): A vain and dolled-up woman (OED, 1: A dressed up mere doll or figure of a woman). OED (3c): A living personator in dramatic action; an actor in a pantomime, quoting this l. Hunter (ed. 1972): There is also…the sense of the unnatural revolt of the puppet against the puppeteer Lear.

1111 so]
McCann (ed. 1964): Merely emphatic. But possibly = thus: Kent may be striking Oswald’s shanks or hindquarters with the flat of his sword to provoke a fight, as Skillan (ed. 1967) suggests. So Brown (ed. 1976), adding, Some restraint does seem necessary to prevent Oswald running off.

1111 carbonado]
Edwards (1748, p. 30): Slash, scotch; Idem (1750, p. 147): Or cut as they do steaks before they make carbonadoes of them. To carbonado was to broil on coals (L. carbo); before cooking, the meat was slashed crosswise to allow heat to penetrate faster, juices to flow, and crust to form. The metaphorical sense, To cut, slash, hack (OED, v. 2, quoting this l.), appears elsewhere in Sh. (e.g., Cor. 4.5.187 [2845–6]); Kittredge (ed. 1940) and Muir (ed. 1952) give non-Shn. exx. The Sokols (2000, p. 234): Under the 1604 statute of stabbing Kent would have been guilty of murder if he killed Oswald, since Oswald refuses to draw a weapon. But Kent shows no such intent; he is trying to get Oswald to draw.

1111–12 come your wayes]
Schmidt (1875, Way): Come [on] (OED, Way sb.1 7b, 23b). Deighton (ed. 1891): The old genitive used adverbially, citing Abbott §25; cf. Franz §237.

1114 stand]
Not stand still, but stand at defence (OED, v. 10).

1114 neate]
Much debated. Since in reference to persons or their dress Sh. elsewhere uses neat in the sense of elegant, trim (OED, 5) or (less often) cleanly, tidy (OED, 9), most eds. understand some such sense as finical (Steevens, ed. 1773), dressed-up (Tieck, ed. 1833, 9:366), trim, spruce (Wright, op. cit.), dandified (Goggin, ed. 1910), or foppish (Kittredge, ed. 1940). Though OED records no negative sense, Kent intends a sarcasm. Joseph (ed. 1966): Kent refers to Oswald’s superficial elegance trying to hide a worthless nature. The senses mere…very (Johnson, ed. 1765), sheer (Chambers, ed. 1906) are unattested in OED. The sense pure, unmixed (Caldecott, MS notes, 1813–33; Walker, 1860, 2:352) and by extension unmitigated (Porter & Clarke, ed. 1905) does not appear elsewhere in Sh. (Rolfe, ed. 1880) and in Sh.’s time was used only in reference to the dilution of liquor with water (OED, a. 3). Capell’s (1783 [1774], 1.1:44) calvish has reappeared as cowherd (White, 1787, p. 479), base, dirty fellow (Rushton, 1867, p. 178), cattle-tending (White, ed. 1883); OED records no adjectival use of the noun neat = cattle, and though Staunton (ed. 1859) cites a pun on the senses cleanly and calf-like in WT 1.2.123 (198) and a similar one in John Taylor’s Epigram 23, On the husband of Mrs Parnell (Works, 1630, sig. 3D2v), both refer specifically to cuckoldry and in any case would have no especial point as addressed to Oswald (Wright, ed. 1875). Similarly Kelcy’s (1932, p. 365) accomplished in baseness is unattested in OED.

1115 strike.]
Explaining Q1(c)’s correction to strike?, Greg (1940, pp. 158–9): The question mark [is] used, as often, in the place of a mark of exclamation.

1117 Gloster…Dutchesse]
Wilson (ed. 1960) justifies a later entrance of the nobles (see textual n.): Edm. w[oul]d not take it upon himself to speak peremptorily to the brawlers if his seniors were present. On the unnamed attendants, supplied in F, see n. 538. Dessen (1978, pp. 62–3): To the modern editor or director, then, the scene makes far more literal and theatrical sense if the entrance of the larger group is delayed.…If we accept the original stage directons, Kent’s failure…is acted out in front of the figures who represent the new regime, emphasizing his helplessness and vulnerability…in the present world of the play. Foakes (ed. 1997): Edmund, hearing a disturbance, rushes in ahead of others who outrank him,…taking the opportunity to show how well he serves Cornwall.

1117 rapier]
Dessen & Thomson (1999): A slender two-edged sword.…Most common entrances are with a rapier drawn.

1118 How now]
See n. 361.

1118 matter]
Bevington (ed. 1980): Trouble. (But Kent takes the meaning cause for quarrel). See next n.

1118 Part]
Dyce (1844, p. 225): Undoubtedly a stage-direction, quoting Look about You (1600, sig. I3). Schmidt (ed. 1879): Not only to separate, but also to go away, to depart. Edmund means it in the former sense, and Kent understands it in the latter (Ger.). Most eds. keep the word in the text and understand the first sense only; see the next note.

1119 With you]
Rann (ed. 1794): I’ll exchange a thrust with you. Gardner (ed. 1969): Have at you. Dyce (1844, p. 225): The matter is with you, I will deal with you. Wright (ed. 1875): Kent intentionally misunderstands Edmund, and takes matter to mean cause of quarrel, comparing Ham. 2.2.193–5 (1231–3). Deighton (ed. 1891): Kent may mean only as you will not allow me to fight with him, I am ready to fight with you. Tovey (ed. 1896): For I’ll be with you used as a menace, cf. [Shr. 4.1.167 (1799)]; Munro (ed. 1957) adds MND 3.2.403 (1444), TN 3.4.320 (1838). Onions (1911, With 5): Used threateningly, almost = I’ll trounce you, I’ll give you what for. Skillan (ed. 1967): He will take on anyone who attempts to frustrate his practical judgment of osw. Brown (ed. 1976): Kent turns unthinkingly to engage with Edmund,…carried away by his own aggressive zeal. Idem (ed. 1996): Outstripping what would be appropriate to any disguise as a mere servant. Only Schmidt (ed. 1879) understands depart with you (see prev. n.), and only Brooke (ed. 1947) does not take you to mean Edmund: Kent continues to address Oswald, refusing to be diverted by Edmund.

1119 goodman]
Though the epithet is clearly derisive, eds. differ why it is so. Wright (ed. 1875): Contemptuously familiar, comparing Rom. 1.5.77 (653). Hudson (ed. 1881): About the same as master or mister [OED, 2]. With boy, it is contemptuous. Cf. yong maister in 1120. Deighton (ed. 1891): Usually employed towards old men. Craig (ed. 1901): A title of mock respect. Kittredge (ed. 1940): A form of address to a presumptuous youngster.…Goodman was the title regularly accorded to a farmer or other respectable person below the rank of gentleman (OED, 3b). Brooke (ed. 1947): A plebeian form of address. Joseph (ed. 1966): Prefixed to the names of those under the rank of gentleman, and could therefore be used ironically. Kent knows that Edmund is illegitimate. Weis (ed. 1993): And [of] junior status to Edgar. Perhaps further mockery lies in another sense: Prefixed to designations of occupation (OED, 3b, quoting Ham. 5.1.14 [3203]). Foakes (ed. 1997): Whipper-snapper; goodman is mildly insulting, as a term for a yeoman or an innkeeper.

1119 and]
See n. 630.

1120 fleash]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Initiate…in fighting (OED, v. 2a, transf. and fig.). Crook (ed. 1907): Contemptuously assuming that he has never fought before. Wright (ed. 1875) explains the literal origin: A hunting term, signifying to give a dog his first taste of flesh (OED, 1). Joseph (ed. 1966): The joke here lies in the fact that Kent is offering to initiate him by making him bleed. A few eds. follow Hunter (ed. 1869): Stir your valour (OED, 2c). Cf. 1199 fleshment.

1120 ye]
On the objective form see n. 490.

1122 Keepe peace]
Cornwall, having superior rank, assumes control though he is a guest in Gloucester’s house. See 1755 and n. 539–40.

1122 vpon your liues]
Deighton (ed. 1891): On peril of losing your lives (OED, Life sb. 3c).

1124 messengers]
On the scansion see n. 1067.

1124 King.]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 385), on F’s King?: The F compositor may have anticipated the punctuation mark at the end of the next line.

1125 difference]
See n. 1066.

1127 bestir’d your valour]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Shown such activity in fighting. Craig (ed. 1901): So over-exerted your valourous self; your valour may be a mock title, comparing Sir valour, Tro. 1.3.176 (636). Crook (ed. 1907): Kent implies that Oswald is out of breath through trying to screw his courage to the sticking point.

1128 nature]
See n. 232.

1128 disclaimes in]
Schmidt (ed. 1879): The only instance in Sh. of disclaim in. The idiom is common. OED (v. 2a): To renounce or disavow all part in, quoting this l. Deighton (ed. 1891): Disclaims all share in making you.

1128 Tayler]
Proverbial: Tilley T17, The Tailor makes the man, quoting this l. Addis (1873, p. 446) supplies many contemporary statements of the idea. Dent (1981) suggests another proverb, Apparel makes (Clothes make) the man (A283). Schmidt (ed. 1879): Because the best of you is your clothes (Ger.). Hudson (ed. 1881): Oswald is one whose soul is in his clothes, i.e. foppish. Harrison (ed. 1937): No natural man, but only fine clothes. Traversi (1952, p. 58) compares the difference between the essential man and the clothed creation of fashion in 1881–9. Colie (1974, p. 188): Kent records his anger at the upstarts who imitated their social betters. Hunter (ed. 1869) cites a different proverb, Nine (Three) Tailors make a man (Tilley T23), in which Tailors originally meant tellers, strokes on the death bell. Turner (ed. King and No King, 1963, p. 90 n.): Early on it was misunderstood to refer to fashioners of clothes, and a tailor became proverbial for weak or inadequate man (OED, sb. 1b, In proverbial and allusive phrases; often implying disparagement and ridicule, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Following Hulme (1962, p. 101), Brook (1976, p. 57): A possible obscene meaning [organ of generation, comparing Tmp. 2.2.53 (1092) and 2H4 3.2.152 (1688)]…makes the taunt more offensive, though it is not required. Weis (ed. 1993), without support: Tailors suggested sexually devious substance, sexual corruption.

1130 fellow]
See n. 16.

1131 I, a…sir;]
Collier (ed. 1843): The folio, by omitting Ay [i.e., I],…and by faulty punctuation, makes the passage read, as if Kent had contradicted himself. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 141): F is satisfactory as it stands, the comma being equivalent to a semicolon.

1131 Stone-cutter]
Hudson (ed. 1881): Sculptor (OED 1, citing this l.). Tovey (1896): Like the Painter, but unlike a tailor, taught to make some likeness of a man.

1132 hee]
F’s they is a grammatical slip (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 141).

1133 houres]
F’s yeares is an easy misreading of houres, and vice versa; in secretary hand both h and y go below the line. Defenders of F have found Q’s two houres an exaggeration of wit (Schmidt, ed. 1879), a vulgarization and absurd (Greg, 1942, p. 91), and ludicrous.…After two years one would still be a botcher (Sisson, 1956, 2:233), but most eds. have found Q’s sense superior. Thirlby (MS notes, 1725–33): Hours is the more like to be genuine for its superlative extravagance. Maguire (1996, p. 50): Given that a craftsman’s apprenticeship lasted seven years, Q’s reading is the greater insult.

1133 at the]
I.e., practicing the. Though possibly F’s o’the is an error for ath’, Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 141) defends it by comparing MM 2.1.197 (645), what trade are you of, where of has the slightly different meaning of belonging to not so apposite here.

1134 Glost.]
All eds. accept F’s change to Cor., presumably since Cornwall questions Kent in the previous and following speeches; but Gloucester may well be returning to his unanswered question in 1121: see n. 1119 on matter, and the next n. Stone (1980, p. 229), supporting Q: It is Gloucester (in both Q and F) who asks the same question several lines later [1159].

1134 yet]
Tovey (ed. 1896): At any rate,…at least. Brooke (ed. 1947): However. If the speaker is Gloucester, the word may signal his wish to return from Cornwall’s diversion to the main issue; he repeats the same question yet again at 1159. The disturbance has occurred in his house; he wants to know why.

1135 ancient]
Cf. 1204. Rolfe (ed. 1880): Aged, old (OED, adj. 6). Halliwell (ed. 1865): Although Kent was but forty-eight [570], that was considered a great age in former days. Since Kent is grizzled, and the term is clearly intended as an insult, there is no need to assume with McCann (ed. 1964) that he is disguised as an older man.

1135 ruffen]
A common spelling variant (OED, Ruffian).

1136 at sute of]
Harbage (ed. 1958): On the plea of, moved to mercy by. Oswald speaks figuratively: His age begged for mercy. Lott (ed. 1974) suspects a dramatic joke on suit and tailor in the previous lines.

1136 gray-beard]
Q lacks the unnecessary hyphen at 1140; F prints it in both places. Doran (1931, p. 110): Here it must have been in the manuscript, since it is in both Q1 and F; perhaps the hyphen in Q2 and F…[in 1140] may be a coincidence, both printers having been influenced by the previous occurrence. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 385): Kent interrupts Oswald.

1137 whorson]
See n. 1091.

1137 Zedd]
The name of the letter Z, here applied contemptuously (OED, 1). Johnson (ed. 1765) fancifully: An allusion to his bending or cringing posture.

1137 vnnecessarie]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Its place may be supplied by S, and the Roman alphabet has it not.

1138–9 tread…into morter]
Steevens (ed. 1773) finds the expression in Massinger, A New Way (ca. 1625) 1.1.87–8, and Dent (1981, M1182.1) thinks it is proverbial. Elton (1966, p. 289 n.) and Dent cite Tilley F447, Bray a Fool in a mortar, you cannot make him leave his folly (Biblical). See OED (Bray, v.2 1): Crush to powder; usually in a mortar, quoting Jonson, Alchemist 2.3.178.

1138–9 vnboulted]
OED (ppl. a.2): Unsifted, quoting this l. as a figurative use. Warburton (ed. 1747) takes the fig. sense as unrefined by education and Tollet (in Steevens, ed. 1778) as coarse, explaining to break the lumps [of lime in mortar] it is necessary to tread it; Moberly (ed. 1876), as unmitigated, which to Verity (ed. 1897) seems more appropriate here than coarse, since previously Kent charged Oswald with an affectation of refinement, citing 1092, 1114. Tovey (ed. 1896): The expression…applies to Oswald’s character, not to his language.…[He has] none of his vices stamped out of him. Lott (ed. 1974): Perhaps simply natural, since lime and sand in their natural state had to be trodden with water to make mortar. Muir (ed. 1952): Perhaps a quibble…: released or unrestrained; or, since unbolt is used [figuratively] in the sense of reveal (Tim. I. i. 51 [68; the literal sense is unlock]), unbolted might mean apparent. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Perhaps suggesting that he should be kept behind a bolt. Muir, alternatively: Since Boult (in Pericles) has a name suitable to his trade [i.e., he controls the bolt to the door of a brothel; see Hulme (1962, p. 54)], unbolted might…mean effeminate or impotent. Halio (ed. 1992): I.e. lacking a bolt. So Williams (1997, p. 48): Penis. Wells (ed. 2000): A eunuch.

1139 daube]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Plaster OED (v. 1, quoting this l.).

1140 iaques]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): A privy (OED, Jakes 1). Fripp (1938, p. 665 n.): Kent request[s] that he may treat him as Jehu dealt with the house of Baal, citing 2 Kings 10:27.

1140 wagtayle]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): A comically uneasy bird, so called from the spasmodic up-and-down jerking of its tail (OED, sb. 1, 2). The metaphorical application is less certain. Davies’s (1783, 2:285–6) a cant term for an eunuch or any impotent person and Rann’s (ed. 1794) effeminate are unattested, though reference to a mincing walk seems a possibility. Dyer (1884, p. 159): An officious person. Deighton (ed. 1891): Insignificant, contemptible creature. Craig (ed. 1901): A term of opprobrium for bustling or ducking pages and waiting men. Compare silly-ducking [1178]. It is sometimes to be met with in the sense of pert boy or child (OED, 3a, quoting this l.). Lott (ed. 1974): This bird struts about on well-kept lawns, and because of the quick movements of its head and tail looks very pleased with itself. Onions (1911), emphasizing the ducking motion: Obsequious person. Harrison (ed. 1937), emphasizing the bustling: A busy court knave. Kittredge (op. cit.): Oswald is too scared to stand still. Halio (ed. 1992): Kent may also strike out against him again. Rosenberg (1972, p. 148): Other implications are the servile spaniel and the whore. Dent (1981, D519) cites the proverb The worst Dog that is wags his tail. Wagging the tail may refer to sexual activity (as in Marston, The Fawn 4.1.268–73, The Dutch Courtesan 4.3.7) and wagtail may mean a prostitute (OED, 3b); Partridge (1947, p. 217) glosses a dissolute man (who wags his tail = penis) and Edwards (ed. 1975), Effeminacy. Williams (1994): One of the most frequently used terms for whore; but he quotes this line under the meaning womanizer.

1141 sir]
To most eds. F’s sirrah has seemed more consonant with beastly Knaue; see n. 411. But Cornwall may be addressing Oswald, forestalling his reply to the end of Kent’s speech.

1142 beastly]
Deighton (ed. 1891): More like a brute beast than a man. Craig (ed. 1901): In the sense of irrational or thoughtless. Muir (ed. 1952): And perhaps disgusting. Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): Because he shows no proper respect for rank.

1142 Knaue]
See n. 451.

1142 you haue]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 385) finds F’s know you less commonplace, and most eds. apparently think that Kent’s reply implies F’s query. Wells (ed. 2000): Accidental inversion [in Q] seems likely. But Q could equally be right.

1142 reuerence]
Schmidt (1875): Respect (OED, sb. 1). Harrison (ed. 1948): To raise your voice in the presence of your betters. Or to fight.

1143 anger…priuiledge]
Apparently proverbial. Tilley L458 detects here and in Jn. 4.3.32 (2031: impatience hath his priuiledge) a form of the proverb Give losers leave to speak; Dent (1981, P595.1) suspects a separate saying, Anger (impatience) has its Privilege, and Elton (1966, p. 289) suggests He that cannot be angry is no Man (Tilley M172).

1145–1216 That…so]
Like Crane (1952, pp. 162–3), Vickers (1968, p. 360): As Kent returns to his old self he returns to verse for more dignified anger, only dropping back to prose briefly after his inflated poetry mocking a courtier’s respect for Cornwall. Cf. n. 1185–9.

1145 sword]
McCann (ed. 1964): The mark of a man; yet, Oswald is not a man according to Kent—i.e., he is a coward. Edwards (ed. 1975): The wearing of a sword in civil life was a social privilege: it is Kent’s contention throughout that Oswald is a social pretender. Honesty in the next clause suggests another meaning, since oaths were sworn on a sword: see H5 2.1.99–101 (599–601), Ham. 1.5.147–61 (842–58), etc.

1146–7 That…twaine]
The Q lines scan regularly if divided after roges, as in Pope’s ed. (see textual n.). F’s addition of holly makes 1147 regular but leaves 1146 apparently hypermetrical as Q does.

1146–53 such…following]
Muir (ed. 1952; rev. 1957, p. 257) accepts Kirschbaum’s private suggestion that this description of sycophancy is derived from Jonson’s Sejanus 1.1.23–38, Sh. having recently acted in that play. Possibly; but the satire is conventional, and Jonson attributed it to Juvenal’s Sat. 3.100 ff. and other classical sources (Herford & Simpson, eds., 4:473).

1146 That]
On F’s Who see n. 235.

1146 honesty]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Honourable character. Lott (ed. 1974): The unwritten code of chivalry implied that men who bore arms carried them for honest ends.

1146 smiling]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Often associated with villainy in Sh., citing MV 1.3.100 (428), Ham. 1.5.108–9 (793).

1147 Rats]
Tilley M1235 cites the proverb A Mouse in time may bite in two a cable. Dent (1981) disagrees, finding it dissimilar and irrelevant. Stone (1980, pp. 52–3): A loose reference to Aesop’s fable of the lion released from a net by a mouse, comparing Leir 642–3; but such an allusion would hardly serve Kent’s invective.

1147 those cordes]
F’s the holly (corr. holy) cords may be a needless metrical improvement (see n. 1146–7) and is regarded with suspicion by Warburton (MS notes, 1747–79) and Malone (ed. 1790); it does complete a regular line. Without the addition of holy Kent’s speech may refer generally to all ties or restraints of honor that would guide an honest servant (such as himself) but that are lacking in a compliant slaue such as Oswald. Kermode (1994, p. 100) thinks that Q’s omission is accidental: Without holy the simile loses what must have been its original force; rats like Oswald are not the enemies of any old cords, but of those that bind friends, families, societies in sacred obligation. F’s added holy has invited greater specificity and much disagreement. Warburton (apud Theobald, ed. 1733): Union between Parents and Children. Theobald adds, Kent…supposes very justly, that [Oswald] has fomented the Quarrel betwixt that Princess [Goneril] and her Father. Warburton (ed. 1747; withdrawn, MS notes, 1747–): The cords of the sanctuary, explained by Crook (ed. 1907): The Sanctuary where the victims for sacrifice were bound to the altar by cords…[representing] virtues which bind men to each other. Frost (ed. 1909): Bonds between husband and wife, an interpretation seconded by several eds. incl. Wilson (ed. 1960): Kent hints that Osw. is duteous to the vices of his mistress ([2705]), comparing 3H6 3.3.243 (1991), holy Wedlocke bands. Though Kent has voiced a similar suspicion in 1093–5, and Oswald later does act as go-between for Goneril and Edmund, Kent has no actual grounds for such an accusation at this point. Harbage (ed. 1958) adds sacred bonds (between…man and God). Gardner (ed. 1969): Cord meant nerve, as well as sinew or tendon.…Flatterers destroy the God-given nerves that hold life together. Hunter (ed. 1972): Bonds of natural affection that bind the individual to society, specifying matrimony, filial obedience, royal duty. Barnes (1984, pp. 20–22), citing the Geneva Bible gloss on Eccles. 4:9–12: Unity of commonwealth.

1147 in twaine]
F’s a twaine means the same. Abbott (§24): In these adverbs the a- represents some preposition, as in, on, of, &c. contracted by rapidity of pronunciation, quoting this l., 1839, 1977, 2500, and 3238. Cf. Franz §§238, 240. OED (A prep.1 6): Partition: in, into. Wright (ed. 1875) notes the reverse variation between Q and F Oth. 5.2.206 (3495).

1148 to…to]
Greg (1928, p. 39): Evidently with an idea of mending the metre, [F] reduces to in both cases to t’, oblivious of the fact that in the first it stands for too. Doran (1931, p. 93): Too may have been written to in the manuscript; the two forms are frequently interchanged in both quarto and folio of King Lear. Even if too stood in the manuscript, it is not certain, in view of the habit of contraction in the folio for the sake of the meter, that the corrector or printer would have respected it any more than to. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 534): The first elision, made in anticipation of the second, would here make the nonce word intrince unintelligible. If the compositor did not know intrince, he may have misunderstood it as the first of two infinitives.

1148 intrench]
F prints intrince, of which Q’s word is a possible misreading (cf. n. 988), substituting consciously or not a familiar form for a newly minted one unknown outside this passage. White (1880, p. 828): Intrench…is merely a phonetic spelling of intrinse. Cf. shewted/suited at 1089. Stone (1980, p. 53) and Wells (ed. 2000) take the Q reading to mean entrench’d, embedded, and Weis (ed. 1993), who adopts it, to mean deeply engrained; these senses do not agree well with bite and cordes, though Weis argues, Rats can gnaw away under the surface. See textual n. Upton (1746, p. 327) thinks F’s intrince is a shortened form of intrinsicate, a word current for a half-century in the sense intricate, involved, entangled (OED, a.) before Sh. used it in knot intrinsicate in Ant. 5.2.304 (3556). He cites the similar abbreviation reverbs (164), and Malone (1783, p. 49), attent in Ham. 1.2.193 (383). OED (Intrince a.) endorses this possibility, noting also O.F. intrincé, var. f. intrinqué, intriqué intricate. Wright (ed. 1875) extends the meaning to tightly drawn, Deighton (ed. 1891) to closely interwoven, and Hunter (ed. 1972) to too inward, secret, hidden [OED, Intrinsic a. 2] (in their mode of tying) to be untied. Hanmer (see textual n.) emends to intrinsick, but no one has suggested the possible meaning for intrince of inherent, essential, proper (OED, Intrinsic a. 3; Intrinsical 3, var. sp. intryncicall in the 16th c.)—i.e., an essential part of their human nature or their marriage relationship. Kermode (1994, p. 101): Intrince lies behind both Q, which misunderstood it, and F, which didn’t.…The F version cannot derive from the Quarto tradition…[but] had survived in a manuscript tradition.

1148 inloose]
Probably a misreading for F’s vnloose, a word used several times by Sh.; inloose appears nowhere else in Sh. and is unrecorded by OED. A nonce-word enloose by analogy with enlarge (sometimes spelt inlarge in F) may also be a possibility.

1148 smooth]
OED (v. 6a): To allay, assuage, mitigate the force of (passion, trouble, etc.), quoting this l. Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.), followed by many eds.: To flatter; but though intransitively the verb may mean use flattering language (OED, 5), no transitive use (such as here) is attested in that sense; nor are others such as to stroke, to caress, to fondle (Steevens, apud Dyce), encourage (Hunter, ed. 1869), humour, extenuate (Wright, ed. 1875), aid and abet (Kittredge, ed. 1940), help to gratify (Harrison, ed. 1948), indulge (Foakes, ed. 1997). Brooke’s (ed. 1947) Make the way easy for may be possible (OED, 2), though it is the passions, not the way to them, that Oswald is said to smooth.

1149 natures]
See n. 185.

1149 rebell]
Jennens (ed. 1770): Perhaps ev’ry passion (i.e. all the passions) will admit of a plural verb; so Abbott §12. Alternatively Wright (ed. 1875): Attracted into the plural by the word lords. Wilson (ed. 1960): Sc. against Reason, which sh[oul]d rule the passions. [Rebel] often refers to lust, citing Shn. exx. Gardner (ed. 1969), quoting Burton, Anatomy of Melancholy [1.2.3.1]: Passions and perturbations were held to subvert the good estate of man.…They were compared to insurrections, rebellious inclinations, in man’s nature. Edwards (ed. 1975): Rebel against proper self-control.

1150 Bring]
F’s Being has mainly appealed to a few eds. having a general predilection for F1. But all parallel verbs in the passage are active and even transitive, as are the verbs in the proverb To add Oil to (pour oil on) the fire (Tilley O30; cf. O32), and most eds. favor Q. Doran (1931, p. 92): Probably due to misreading, comparing Q’s supposed r/e misreading in 347. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 387) infers Q to be an r/e misreading, but later (in Wilson, ed. 1960) concludes that F is an instance of the reverse.

1150 stir]
An obvious misreading (cf. n. 988) for F’s fire; perhaps the MS had the graphically closer fier. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 142) takes fire to mean wrath, as in 2H6 5.2.55 (3277), but in uses of the proverb (see prev. n.), as in AWW 5.3.6–8 (2703–5), it may mean other blazing passions. Harbage (ed. 1958): Intemperance.

1150 their colder-moods]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 142): F’s the, referring to a certain definite class of moods, is satisfactory as the specific reference to the Lords in Q, followed by most eds. Those moods are brought on by an excess in the body of either of the cold humours, melancholy and phlegm.

1151 Reneag, affirme]
F’s Reuenge is clearly a copyist’s or compositor’s misreading. Doran (1931, p. 92) compares a supposed n/a confusion at 1627. Greg (1933, p. 260): Possibly the foul-case substitution of u for n produced Reueag, corrected to Reuenge. Stone (1980, p. 101 n.): Possibly the misreading of a spelling correction, viz. Renegue. There are other known press-corrections on this F page, but not this one. Rann (ed. 1794): Deny (OED, Renegue 2a, quoting this l.). Harrison (ed. 1948): Oswald is a perfect yes man. Kittredge (ed. 1940) compares 2545–6.

1151 halcion]
Peck (1740, p. 251): Halcyon or kings-fisher [OED, Halcion a. 1, quoting this l.; Kingfisher 1], which bird (as the common people imagine) if [a dried specimen is] hanged up with a string…will, by its turning and varying with every gale, always shew what quarter the wind is in, citing also Sir Thomas Browne’s scientific disproof of the idea in Pseudodoxia Epidemica 3.10 (ed. Keynes, 2:187). Steevens (ed. 1778) quotes contemporary references to the idea. Dent (1981) cites the proverb To turn with (as) the Wind (W439).

1152 gale and varie]
Delius (ed. 1854): Equivalent to varying gale. Deighton (ed. 1891) and many other eds.: A hendiadys. Not necessarily: it may mean each gust and each shift of wind.

1152 gale]
Johnson (1755): A wind not tempestuous, but stronger than a breeze (OED, 1a). See prev. n. Since OED (sb.3) does not record it as a known variant, F’s gall probably represents a misreading of e as l; Doran (1931, p. 92) cites other Shn. exx. in Kellner (1925, p. 71). Colman (ed. 1982), however, accepts it: Varying resentment of insult or injury. Similarly Halio (ed. 1992): Varying irritation. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 534): [It] might mean a state of mental soreness or irritation ([OED,] sb.2 2; 1591+). However, F2’s independent emendation [gale] does support Q.

1152 varie]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): Variation (OED, Vary sb., quoting this l.). F’s sp. varry occurs also in F LLL 1.1.295 (290; varried) and 4.3.98 (1436; varrie), Ant. 1.4.46 (480) and 4.15.11 (3013), in passages set by three different compositors; F LLL reprints Q1’s spellings, apparently deriving from Sh.’s MS. Schmidt (ed. 1879): As a noun only here in Sh.

1153–5 Knowing…foole]
Hubler (1935, p. 436): Here and in similar cases the Q1 compositor compressed three lines into two to save the space of a line. But since Q1 was set seriatim, there was no need for such compression; the compositor need only have ended the page one line sooner to allow for all three lines. More probably the MS confused the compositor. Werstine (privately): Inexplicable mislineation such as is not found in Hand-D [Sir Thomas] More but is found in scribal MSS like [Middleton’s] The Witch.

1153 dayes]
Misreading of manuscript; cf. n. 988. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 387): Misreading—a/o [F dogges]. For the confusion of y and g cf. [Tro.], in which Q1 has at [5.1.61 (2927)] day for dog and at [3.2.160 (1792)] age for aye.

1153 following]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Their master,…whether he is right or wrong.

1154 epeliptick]
OED (Epileptic) quotes this l. as its first ex. Johnson (ed. 1765): The frighted countenance of a man ready to fall in a fit. Capell (1783, 1.2:157): Distorted…as such a fit would have done. Dyce (1844, p. 226): Distorted by grinning. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Grinning with suppressed rage, while striving to pass it off as a smile of contemptuous superiority. Bucknill (1860, p. 266) and Hunter (ed. 1869): Idiotic. Wright (ed. 1875) and other eds.: Distorted and pale. Hunter (ed. 1972): Twitching with terror. Betts (1998, p. 408): Pock-marked by syphilis. Wells (ed. 2000): Smiling twitchily. Foakes (ed. 1997): Another of Kent’s exaggerated insults?

1155 smoyle]
OED records both this and F’s Smoile as 17th-c. spellings of smile. Capell (1783, 1.2:157): Receive…with smiles, unattested. Deighton (ed. 1891): Ridicule…by your grins (OED, v. 7, quoting only this l.). On the omission of the preposition see n. 174. Brook (1976, p. 105): Cf. MnE deride. Wright (ed. 1875): Shakespeare uses smile more than once with a direct object, but never in this sense. This fact and the spellings not found elsewhere in Sh.’s Qq or F1 have raised suspicions of some corruption here (Furness, ed. 1880) and several defenses against them. Ridley (ed. 1935): A dialect form…not inappropriate to Kent when he remembers to borrow other accents. Brooke (ed. 1947): It looks as if Oswald was represented on the stage as a somewhat farcical Yorkshireman (cf. [615–16]), and Kent seems to parodying his accent. Munro (ed. 1957): The vocabulary of his present speech…is far removed from dialect. Wilson (ed. 1960): Why, in this scene, sh[oul]d dialect pronunciations be indicated in this word only? Moreover, the two words were prob. normally pronounced alike; cf. boil at [1517]. Kökeritz (1953, p. 217) compares arint (1903) and other analogues. Dobson (1957, §259) records ambiguous pronunciations of -ile/-oil words, though not of smile. Cercignani (1981, pp. 246–7) explains the Q and F forms here as inverted spellings on the analogy of words like employ and voyage.

1155 as]
Abbott (§107): If is implied in the subjunctive. Cf. Franz §582, and 1795, 3165, 3168+9.

1155 foole]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): A jester trying to make you laugh. Muir (ed. 1952): Or, less likely, as if I were foolish, and your butt.

1156 Goose]
OED (sb. 1f): A foolish person, a simpleton. Furness (ed. 1880): Oswald’s forced laughter suggests to Kent the cackling [1157] of a goose. Warburton (MS notes, 1747–79): Alludes to a Winchester Goose, one debauched in the Stews, which were the property and under the government of the Bishop of Winchester. Capell (1783, 1.2:27, 156) detects the same allusion, referring it to a venereal sore or tumor contracted in the stews, so call’d, from the resemblance it has to that fowl’s egg (OED, 3), also alluded to in 1H6 1.3.53 (421) and Tro. 5.10.55 (3590). A few eds. agree, and Jones (1950, p. 295) relates the allusion to the theme of immoral sexual relations in the play. But since Winchester is not named, such an allusion seems a little far-fetched (Craig, ed. 1901) if not pointless (Wilson, ed. 1960) and is not likely to have been noticed by an audience (Muir, ed. 1952). Williams (1994, 1997), s. v. Winchester, does not cite this l., though glossing goose as whore or a whore’s client. Muir adds, E. A. Armstrong, Shakespeare’s Imagination, [1946,] pp. 57–65, shows that the goose often appears as part of a chain of ideas, including disease, bitterness, seasoning, and restraint, as here (1154, 1090, 1172, 1147) and at 1322–38. For doubts about this chain or cluster see n. 1322–7. Joseph (ed. 1966): A goose is proverbially fierce in show, but really stupid and cowardly. Musgrove (1981, p. 11): Wild geese could mean the wild rogues associated with Poor Tom—whom Kent cannot be thinking of before meeting him in 3.4. See also n. 1157.

1156 and]
See n. 630.

1156 Sarum plaine]
Salisbury Plain. Capell (1783, 1.2:156): Some open country is wish’d for, that he might have no place to skulk in; and that of Sarum is named, as being widest and nearest. Clarkes (ed. 1868): If he had him in the broad open space of Wiltshire, he would drive him into the adjoining county of Somerset. Hudson (ed. 1871): Salisbury plain is the largest piece of flat surface in England, and used to be much noted as a lonely and desolate region. Since Merlin had literary connections with Salisbury, Smith (1946, p. 154) suspects some obscure allusion to Arthurian legend; see the next n. Similarly Guilfoyle (1987; 1990, p. 100): After landing at Dover, Arthur pursued Mordred to Salisbury, where both died. Elton (1966, p. 289 n.): Salisbury Plain, noted for its pagan relic, Stonehenge, lies between Kent and Cornwall. Hulme (1962, p. 65) thinks Kent may refer to his own bluntness, citing from Udall’s tr. of Erasmus’s Apophthegmes (1542) a malaparte speaker called Thom trouthe, or plain Sarisburie. Musgrove (1981, p. 11): Salisbury Plain was notorious as a dangerous haunt of vagabonds—an epithet applying to neither Kent nor Oswald. Sh. does not elsewhere use the word Sarum, and Tobin (1983, p. 119) thinks it echoes Nashe’s my old Sarum plaine song from Lenten Stuff (1599, ed. McKerrow, 3:184), which refers not to a place but to the well known Salisbury Psalter.

1157 send you]
F’s driue ye is clearly an intentional change, though not necessarily an improvement. Kent may not intend to be a drover, but merely to terrify Oswald into flight. Hunter (ed. 1972): I would make you add flight to your cackling laughter, like a goose being driven. On the objective ye see n. 490.

1157 Camulet]
Whether there is an allusion here to King Arthur’s court at Camelot, and why Kent would threaten to send Oswald in that direction, are questions that have much occupied commentators. Theobald (ed. 1733) identifies the Camelot in Somersetshire mentioned by Holinshed but is unsure whether Arthur kept his court there, or in Wales, or in Stirling County, Scotland. Steevens (ed. 1778) quotes from Drayton’s Polyolbion (1612), Third Song 397–8: Like Camelot, what place, was ever yet renownd? | Where, as at Carlion, oft, hee kept the Table-round (ed. Hebel, 4:48). Since Arthur’s table and sometimes Camelot were also frequently located in Winchester—in Malory’s Morte Darthur 2.19, 12.10 (Craig, ed. 1901), Jonson et al.’s Eastward Ho 5.1.44–5 (Brooke, ed. 1947), Selden’s Illustrations to Drayton’s Fourth Song [Hebel ed., 4:89] (Furness, ed. 1880), The Birth of Merlin 3.6.134–5 [ed. Brooke, 1908] (Verity, ed. 1897), etc.—Capell (1783, 1.2:156) finds reinforcement of an allusion to Winchester in the prev. l. (see n.), and Phelps (ed. 1917) remarks that Winchester is about a day’s journey by foot from Sarum. Furness (ibid.) notes that Selden (op. cit.; Hebel ed., 4:68) also locates Camelot and the round table by Cadbury in Somerset, and Tovey (ed. 1896) notes that Sarum Plain was once reckoned to extend over the borders of Somersetshire. Camelot is also located in Wales, as in Caxton’s Preface to Malory’s Morte d’Arthur [Works, ed. Vinaver, 1:cxiii] (Staunton, ed. 1859) and Drayton’s Heroical Epistles (Q. Catherine) [Hebel ed., 3:203] (Hunter, ed. 1869). Page (ed. 1889) denies any Arthurian allusion: A town in Cornwall, now Tintagel or Camelford, the residence of the Duke of Cornwall. Not to be confounded with the Camelot of Arthurian legends…in Winchester. Wilson (ed. 1960): Kent threatens to chase Oswald from Salisbury plain…to Reg.’s castle; a long drive. Bevington (ed. 1980): Cadbury and Winchester are in the general vicinity of Salisbury and Gloucester.
The point of the name here is also obscure. Hanmer (ed. 1743) sees Camelot as the natural home for a goose like Oswald: In the parts of Somersetshire near Camelot there are many large Moors upon which great numbers of Geese are bred. Warburton (ed. 1747): This alludes to some proverbial speech [unidentified] in those [Arthurian] romances. Staunton (op. cit.) and Smith (ed. 1926) point to the repeated pattern in Malory of sending defeated enemies to do homage to the king, and suggest that Kent intends a similar journey for Oswald. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) agree; or, As the geese-keepers drove their geese, also, from the moors to town, he could drive him, cackling, to slaughter. Neilson & Thorndike (ed. 1909): Kent seems to combine two images, one of the flocks of geese on Sarum Plain, the other of the defeated knights who were compelled to report to Arthur at Camelot. Goggin (ed. 1910): Camelot, the legendary capital of King Arthur, is probably here conceived by Shakespeare as Lear’s capital also. Kent’s point may simply be that Oswald, terrified, would flee a great distance; or, if he intends an allusion to Arthur’s Camelot, it may be a simple sarcasm, since Oswald is no knight and would have no business there. Joseph (ed. 1966): The word had the Elizabethan sense of shoddy. Rather, camlet referred to various high-quality fabrics (OED) and was almost always spelt chamblet, as in H8 5.3.89 (3351). Thus Weis (ed. 1993): Home to Camelot could be rendered as back to your costly tailors, an interpretation he concedes is far-fetched. Lott (ed. 1974): No particular significance seems to be attached to these place-names. They are ancient, and would be associated by the audience with the legendary history of Britain, and therefore with King Lear. Camelot may have been suggested because of its assonance and alliteration with cackling. Foakes (ed. 1997): Camelot is linked with Winchester…and Winchester goose was a name for venereal disease and for a prostitute…, so some hidden chain of association may have been at work here.

1158–89 What…too’t]
Brown (ed. 1996): Though this encounter is often much cut in performance [see ]…[it] establish[es] the social and political context for the main action, showing the danger of face values and the perversions which follow the exercise of unrestricted power.

1158 old]
See n. 570.

1158 fellow]
See n. 16.

1160 contraries]
Craig (ed. 1901): Coleridge’s contrast of Oswald and Kent (see ) may give us the key to the violent bearing of Kent in this scene and the unbridled and coarse language he uses. This is generally considered a blemish in the play; but we must, I think, try to look at Kent, the brave, the noble, the generous, the true, suddenly confronted and opposed in the execution of his duty, at the end of a long and wearisome journey, by Oswald, the basest of the base, who, without one spark of merit,…was yet putting on an air of provoking self-sufficiency, and who, unconscious that he is in the presence of a great nobleman, and, thinking he had only a common serving-man to deal with, was making an effort to cloak his real base motives of action; and is it strange that the meeting of two such men should be most stormy and that it should bring out all that was violent in Kent’s nature? Cf. n. 1081.

1160 hold]
Schmidt (1874): Have (OED, v. 6b).

1160 antipathy]
OED (sb. 1): Natural contrariety or incompatibility, quoting this l.

1163 offence]
F’s fault may be intended to avoid repetition in 1190. Doran (1931, p. 47): The substitution of a synonym has been accompanied by the expansion of a contracted form [what’s/What is], evidently with the purpose of preserving the meter.

1164 likes]
See n. 218.

1165 his…hers]
Petz (ed. 1839): Gloster’s and Regan’s.

1166 occupation]
Schmidt (1875): Trade, profession (OED, 4a). Tovey (ed. 1896): Custom, or wont; cf. OED (sb. 4b): Course of action in which one is engaged, esp. habitually.

1166 plaine]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Plain-spoken (OED, 11: Candid, frank). Cf. 1174, 1175.

1168 That]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 387): Perhaps…influenced by that later in the same line. Q2’s correction Than is so obvious and necessary that F’s agreement is insignificant.

1168 stands]
A subject, that which, must be understood.

1168 shoulder]
Craig (ed. 1901): The part [of the back or trunk] between the shoulders (OED, sb. 1).

1170 fellow]
See n. 577.

1171 praysd For bluntnes]
Muir & Danby (1950, p. 51) compare Sidney’s Arcadia 1.4.2, 5; see n. 137. OED (Bluntness sb. 3): Rudeness,…abruptness of manner or address, curtness, quoting this l. as its first ex.

1172 sawcy]
OED (Saucy a.1 2): Insolent towards superiors. Cf. n. 26.

1172 ruffines]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 387): Doubtless spelt as the…compositor pronounced it. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 514): The use of an ﬁ ligature implies that the compositor deliberately set ruffines, but he nevertheless probably misread the manuscript. Ruffines is not recorded elsewhere, and though it could be a neologism based on ruffy (= a devil or fiend…), Shakespeare never uses the root word, devilishness seems less appropriate than roughness, and ruffines is metrically anomalous. OED (Roughness sb. 5): Rudeness…of character or manners, quoting this l. as its first ex. and recording the sp. ruffenesse. Cf. 1779, ruffe. Macaulay (1907, p. 28): It is rather a fault…that Kent should behave so very insolently in this scene. A man of his rank and sense should have had more self-command and dignity even in his anger. One can hardly blame Cornwall for putting him in the stocks.

1172 constraines]
OED (Constrain v. 3b): To force…any behaviour, quoting this l.

1172–3 garb…nature]
Kittredge (ed. 1940), from: The emphatic from, which means literally away from, and so, contrary to, quite out of accord with (OED, prep. 8b). The main interpretive crux in this phrase is his, which may refer to Kent or, as Staunton (ed. 1859) first proposed, to garb as the standard possessive pronoun for it (see n. 727). Johnson (ed. 1765) assumes Kent: Forces his outside or his appearance to something totally different from his natural disposition. See n. 185. Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): Hypocritically. This interpretation suits well Cornwall’s own statement in 1176–7 that affected candor such as Kent’s may hide innate craft and corruption. Anon. (apud Craig, ed. 1901): Strips off the dress (so as to be) quite away from the natural man, goes naked, in his absence of manners and in the indecent plainness of his speech. The other line of interpretation begins with Caldecott (MS notes, 1813–33): Stretches the dress and habit, he wears, beyond its proper measure & compass. The Clarkes (ed. 1868): His here is used for its. Cornwall implies…that [Kent] distorts the style of straightforward speaking quite from its nature, which is sincerity; whereas he makes it a cloak for craft. OED (Nature sb. 1): The essential qualities or properties of a thing. Hunter (ed. 1869): Strains the manner beyond its proper character. Tovey (ed. 1896): Those who affect this manner distort it, and it looks, as it is, unnatural. Smith (ed. 1917): Carries the assumed manner to a wholly unnatural extent. Harbage (ed. 1958): Caricatures it. Though Johnson’s reading makes simple good sense, and the alternate line of interpretation is in some instances rather forced, commentators divide about equally.

1172 garb]
Wright (ed. 1875): Outward address and manner (OED, sb.2 2, not supporting Wright’s especially of speech). Hudson (ed. 1879): Style or manner (OED, 3a: of behaviour). Muir (ed. 1952): Not…fashion of dress (OED, 4).

1173 his]
I.e., its; see n. 727.

1173 he]
On the emphatic repetition of the pronoun see Schmidt (ed. 1879), Franz §298.

1174–9 He…nisely]
Coleridge (MS notes, 1818–19, ed. Foakes, 1989, p. 101): In thus placing these profound general truths in such mouths as Cornwall’s, Edmund’s, Iago’s, etc., Shakespeare at once gives them, and yet shows how indefinite their application. Hudson (ed. 1871): An inferior dramatist…would probably fill their mouths with something either shocking or absurd; which is just what real villains, if they have any wit, never do.

1174 he…truth]
The Q version of the line scans well enough if the first two words are emphasized, with the heavy irony that Cornwall clearly intends. F’s An honest mind and plaine smooths the meter but muddies the sentence, interrupting three parallel clauses with a more literary if uneasy appositive of mind with he. On F’s placement of the noun between two adjectives see Franz §686. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 514): It seems implausible to suppose that [in Q] an and mind have been omitted, honest misread he must, and be substituted for and. See .

1175 and…so]
Most eds. accept the emendations of Rowe and Pope (see textual n.), interpreting and as if (see n. 630) and so as so be it (Wright, ed. 1875) or well and good (Deighton, ed. 1891). But Q and F make perfect sense without any emendation: and they must accept it as the truth.

1175 If…plaine]
Deighton (ed. 1891): If not, the only excuse he troubles himself to make is that he is a plain-spoken man. Crook (ed. 1907): If not, at least he knows he has been outspoken. Brooke (ed. 1947): He forces it on them anyway. Edwards (ed. 1975): He is not the one who is distorting things.

1176 these kind]
Abbott (§412): Two nouns together connected by of seem regarded as a compound noun with plural termination. Cf. Franz §316, and 2001. OED (Kind sb. 14b): The feeling that kind of was equivalent to an adj. qualifying the following sb., led to the use of…these, those…when the sb. was plural, as in these kind of men.

1176 knaues]
See n. 451.

1176 Which]
See n. 744+4. Abbott (§266): Who indicates an individual, which a kind of person. Cf. 1633.

1176 plainnes]
See n. 137.

1177 harbour]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Give cover to; used in a bad sense (OED, v. 3). OED (4. fig.): To cherish privately.…Now usually in reference to evil thoughts or designs.

1177 more corrupter]
On the double comparative see n. 84.

1177 ends]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Purposes (OED, sb. 14).

1178 silly ducking]
F’s hyphen results in an awkward compound, often emended, without counterpart in Sh., and quite possibly inauthentic. Silly is usually an adjective in Sh., with the possible exception of Ven. 1151, sillie milde; sillily, TNK 4.1.40 (2198), occurs in Fletcher’s portion; silly is hyphened nowhere else in the Quartos or Folio. Schmidt (1874), Duck: To bow, citing also R3 1.3.49 (515) and Tim. 4.3.18 (1620). Joseph (ed. 1966): Cringing. Horsman (ed. 1973), reading (erroneously?) silly-duckling: Over-attentive. In F’s compound silly is taken by some to mean ludicrously (Craig, ed. 1901) or stupidly (Lee, ed. 1908); OED (Silly, a. 5b). Q’s adjective is interpreted variously. Steevens (ed. 1778): Simple, or rustic (OED, 3). Schmidt (1875), followed by Onions (1911): Poor;…as a term of pity (OED, 1). Tovey (ed. 1896): Here used contemptuously, but still with a notion of simplicity. They are innocents [unattested, but cf. OED, Seely 5] compared with the knave who affects a rougher manner. It could also mean, as in F, foolish; or simply lowly (OED, 3b, quoting Holinshed, sillie footman).

1178 Obseruants]
Nares (1822): Obsequious attendant[s] (OED, sb. 3, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Wright (ed. 1875): Who watch their lord with slavish attention. Muir (ed. 1952, rev. 1957, p. 257) compares Jonson’s Sejanus 1.1.36–8; see n. 1146–53. Abbott (§492): First syllable accented.

1179 that]
See n. 235.

1179 stretch…nisely]
I.e., in contrast to Kent’s bluntness. Stretch may mean simply tender (Eccles, ed. 1792; OED, v. 5), but in Sh. the word generally implies strain. Thus Schmidt (1875): To strain, to put to the utmost strength or effort (OED, 20), followed by most eds. Steevens (ed. 1778), nisely: Foolishly (OED, adv. 1). Malone (ed. 1790): With the utmost exactness, with an attention to the most minute trifle (OED, 5). Wright (ed. 1875): Hence, fancifully. Clarkes (ed. 1868) and most eds.: Punctiliously, precisely (OED, 4c, quoting 3100 as its first ex.), the meaning in 3100. Also possible is OED (3): Finely, elegantly, refinedly, daintily, citing TN 3.1.14 (1228). Edwards (ed. 1975): The image here is of fawning servants stretchng themselves into ridiculous postures as they make their elaborate bows.

1180–3 Sir…front]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Kent parodies the style and manner of a silly-ducking observant. Wilson (ed. 1960): Parodies the deferential language Corn. expects.

1180 Sir]
See n. 60.

1180 in good sooth]
Tovey (ed. 1896): The oath is an affectation of the city; he cites 1H4 3.1.248 (1795), 2H4 1.2.36 (309). F’s substitution of faith for sooth produces an even more common oath. The graphic similarity of the two words suggests misreading of one of them.

1180 in…veritie]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): An affected synonym for in good faith. Halio (ed. 1992): A deliberate redundancy. Wells (ed. 2000): A latinate word, grander than the Anglo-Sxon sooth.

1181 Vnder]
See n. 866.

1181 Allowance]
See n. 720.

1181 graund]
Knight (ed. 1840), on F’s great: The change was not made without reason. Although Kent meant to go out of his dialect, the word grand sounded ironically, and was calculated to offend more than was needful. Stone (1980, p. 218): The reading in Q is consistent with the stilted phraseology Kent affects in this speech, hence the correction in F is unusually obtuse.

1181–2 aspect…influence…Phœbus]
Muir (ed. 1952) finds the same language in Florio’s Epistle Dedicatorie, A Worlde of Wordes (1598, sig. a3v). Zitner (1974, p. 9): This unflattering allusion may be Sh.’s comment on fashionable Italianate verbal artifice.

1181 aspect]
Nares (1822): Almost always accented on the last syllable in the time of Shakespeare; OED (sb.) records the mod. pron. as early as 1609. All eds. agree with Delius (ed. 1854): Here used in a secondary astrological sense, like influence in the following line. That sense is explained as a planet’s position at a particular time, and its [resulting] influence…on mortals (Tovey, ed. 1896), or as the way in which a planet looks upon a man, i.e., with good or bad effect (Kittredge, ed. 1940); OED (4) supports both etymologies. The primary meaning is not entirely clear. Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Presence (perhaps OED 13: A thing seen, a sight; an appearance). Muir (ed. 1952): Appearance; cf. Schmidt (1874): Look, air, countenance (OED, 10, 11).

1182 Whose]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): The antecedent…is your (i.e., of you).

1182 influence]
See n. 454. Muir (ed. 1952): Kent implies ironically that Cornwall is a heavenly body. Foakes (ed. 1997): Cornwall’s countenance becomes a star affecting human destiny.

1182–3 wreath…front]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Probably an allusion to the wreath of curls round the head of the Sun-God [Phoebus Apollo] in old coins, representing the lambent rays on the circumference of the sun’s disc. Schmidt (1874), Front: Forehead (OED, sb. 1).

1183 In]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 387): Perhaps the Q compositor substituted In for [F’s] On owing to association with influence [1182]. But the Q reading may be right; one may as easily speak of fire in the sun’s face as on it; probably the phrase does not refer to wreath, which would be around rather than either in or on the sun’s face.

1183 flitkering]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 388): C misread as t, the reverse cause of the Q curre/terrer variant in 2280; (ibid., p. 15): The word required is flickering, or rather, for metrical reasons, flickring. OED (Flickering ppl. a. 5): That shines with, or is illuminated by, an unsteady or wavering light, quoting this l. as its first ex. Wilson (ed. 1960): Alludes to the uncertainty of royal favor. Possibly F’s flicking is a compositor’s error for flickring, though Duthie proposes a bungled MS correction in a copy of Q1 [or Q2, which is identical here] used for F printer’s copy. Doran (1931, p. 99): F has the appearance rather of an independent error made by the printer of the folio than of a blundered correction of flitkering. Sh. does not use either word again. Except for Rowe (see textual n.), only Colman (ed. 1982) accepts F’s flicking, glossing it flickering, though OED attests to neither form nor meaning.

1183 front]
Muir (ed. 1952): Forehead (OED, sb. 1). Harbage (ed. 1958): I.e. face (OED, 2).

1184 mean’st thou]
On F’s omission of the pronoun—an unnecessary improvement of meter—see n. 562.

1185–9 To…too’t]
Lott (ed. 1974): In addition to changing his tone by reverting to his frank manner, he now talks in prose.

1185 dialogue]
F’s dialect is an obvious and necessary correction. Wilson (ed. 1960): Manner of speech peculiar to a person or theme [OED, Dialect 1]; not necessarily local [OED, 2]—here Kent’s plainness. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 388): Perhaps the Q compositor could only make out the first four letters, thereafter misreading e as o, and t as e as in noystles for noyseles at 2307+3. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 514) imagine a possible MS sp. dialegte nowhere else recorded.

1185–6 discommend]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Disapprove; used by S. nowhere else (OED, v. 1). He could have found it in Harsnett’s Declaration, 1603, p. 38 (Salingar, 1983, p. 163), or discommendable in Florio’s tr. of Montaigne (Taylor, 1925, p. 60).

1186 no flatterer]
The implied sequel is but neither am I a knave, stated explicitly in 1188.

1186 he]
Page (ed. 1889): A person of the kind you speak of. Eccles (ed. 1792): Oswald. Moberly (ed. 1876): Kent himself, confessing to excessive plainness to Cornwall.

1186–7 beguild]
Schmidt (1874), beguile: To deceive, to cheat (OED, v. 1). Cf. 2505, 3111. Kent refers to the craft and corrupter ends mentioned by Cornwall in 1177. Capell (1783, 1.2:157) mistakenly imagines someone who cheated you by his flatteries into a good opinion of yourself.

1187 in…accent]
Capell (1783, 1.2:157) refers this to Kent’s immediate manner of speech: to speak plainly. But all other eds. think it describes the knave’s plainness described by Cornwall in 1171–6.

1187 accent]
Schmidt (ed. 1879): Not seldom, as here, equivalent to speech, language (Ger.). OED (sb. 4): The way in which anything is said;…utterance.

1187 plaine]
A pun on plain-spoken and evident (Page, ed. 1889; OED, a. 4) or out-and-out (Kittredge, ed. 1940; OED, 5).

1187 knaue]
See n. 451.

1189–90 though…too’t]
The sense is obscure, and depends in part on whether your displeasure refers literally to a state of mind in Cornwall or metonymically to Cornwall in such a state of mind. Johnson (ed. 1765) understands the second—You, displeased as you now are—as does Wright (ed. 1875), who compares some discretion (1429). Anon. (1786, p. 166), followed by Rann (ed. 1794) and many others, even takes the phrase as a mock-title, given to the angry Cornwall, in the same manner as we now say, your highness; your excellence; your grace, &c. If displeasure is taken literally, win your displeasure means incur your displeasure (Becket, 1815, 1:143). From that premise, eds. still differ on the meaning of the whole clause. Moberly (ed. 1876): Even if you should be so displeased at my new-fangled language as to entreat me to return to the old; but since Kent’s old language was not knavish, simply plain, it is not clear why he should need to be entreated to return to it from his new affected style. Verity (ed. 1897): Even though I should so displease you by my bluntness as to entreat me to be a knave (i.e. a flatterer); but a knave speaking in a plain accent can hardly be a flatterer. Similarly Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956), taking ’t as a reference to knavish flattery: Though your displeasure at my plain speech should be an inducement to offer flattery instead. Edwards (ed. 1975): Even though you hated me enough to beg me to become one (?). Craig (ed. 1901), followed by Munro (ed. 1957) and others, finds exactly the reverse meaning: Though as a great inducement to be [a plain knave]…I should win your displeasure, a thing far more desirable in my eyes than your favour, the favour of such a man as Cornwall. Horsman (ed. 1973): Even though I should evoke your anger so much that it would beg me to be one [an out-and-out rascal]. Brown (ed. 1976), more simply yet: Although your anger at my behavior should encourage me to be a knave. Bevington (ed. 1980): I will no longer use plain speech, despite the incentive of incurring your displeasure by doing so. (Kent prefers to displease Cornwall, since Cornwall is pleased only by flatterers, and Kent has assumed until now that plain speech was the best way to offend; but now he argues mockingly that he can no longer speak plainly since his honest utterance will be interpreted as duplicity).
On the other hand, if your displeasure is taken to refer figuratively to Cornwall himself, then win your displeasure may mean win over or overcome (Bald, ed. 1949; OED, v.1 2) your dislike. Thus Johnson (op. cit.): Though I should win you…to like me so well as to intreat me to be a knave. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Though I should win you from your displeasure sufficiently to make you entreat me to be a knave. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Even if I could induce you to lay aside your displeasure so far as to beg me to be [a knave]. Muir (ed. 1952): Though I should convert your grace, who are not gracious to me, to a more amiable frame of mind, so that instead of being annoyed with me you actually entreat me to be a plain knave, i.e. a flatterer. The weakness of this line of interpretation is that it demands a great deal from an audience: not only to take your displeasure figuratively but also, contrary to the familiar idiom win his (dis)pleasure, (dis)trust, etc., to understand win as effectively meaning its opposite: lose, escape from, your dislike.
The ultimate problem in the sentence is the syntactical connection of the infinitive to intreat. It seems at first adverbial, modifying win— win you to entreat me; but it may be adjectival, modifying either the you in your or the noun displeasure. The latter was suggested by Boodle (1884, pp. 216–17: I believe we have here one of those terse uses of to with the infinitive so common in Shakespeare, though I should win your displeasure by your entreating me to it (and by my not acceding), citing Abbott §357, indefinite use of the infinitive in a gerundive sense; see n. 1926–7. Of all interpretations this may be the simplest and most consistent with Kent’s overall meaning. The loose syntax reflects his impatience. Thus Harrison (ed. 1948): Even if you ask me and are angry because I refuse, and Sisson (1956, 2:233): Even though I should win your displeasure if you entreated me to it…(for I wouldn’t do it). This last line of interpretation seems to make the most consecutive sense with the previous speeches. Kent has called Oswald a knave (1161); Cornwall has responded with a tu quoque, calling Kent (rather than Oswald) the plain knave (1175–6); Kent speaks fancily to refute the first half of the charge, showing at least that he’s not necessarily plain-spoken (as he says, 1185–6); then, perhaps pointing to Oswald (as Eccles thought: see n. 1186), he goes on to refute the second half. It is Oswald, he says, who is the true knave present, having just beguiled Cornwall with a plain but false report of his clash with Kent; unlike Oswald, Kent will never be a knave, even though he were entreated to be so by the great duke Cornwall and would win Cornwall’s displeasure by his refusal.

1189–90 too’t]
I.e., to it. Franz (§656, Anm.): Now we would expect an infinitive: To’t = to be so.

1192 late]
See n. 718.

1193 strike at]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Aim a blow at. Cf. 615. OED (Strike v. 32b): Fig.…To aim at the overthrow, destruction, or defeat of, quoting this l.

1193 vpon his misconstruction]
Wright (ed. 1875): In consequence of his misunderstanding me (OED, Upon prep. 11c; Misconstruction 1: misconstruing…words or actions, citing this l.). Accordingly, his means the King’s (Thirlby, MS notes, 1725–33).

1194 coniunct]
MS conjunct might have been misread as F compact; or vice versa (Sisson, 1956, 2:233). Collier (ed. 1843): Either reading means in concert with, having entered into a compact (OED, Conjunct adj. 1: Conjoined; Compact ppl. a.2: Joined in compact). Both words in this sense occur elsewhere in Sh. (e.g., Oth. 1.3.367 (718), coniunctive; MM 5.1.242 [2619]), and coniunct appears again in 2859+2. Doran (1931, p. 47) would hesitate to attribute to a printer the striking F variant. It could be scribal.

1194 flattering]
Armour (ed. 1930): Probably referring ironically to [1186]. The word here apparently means something like approving (encouraging?) by agreeing with; its use here is glossed by neither Schmidt (1874) nor Onions (1911) and finds no exact support in OED. Bevington (ed. 1988): Gratifying.

1195 being…insulted]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): I is understood before being, and he before insulted. Abbott (§378): Participle without Noun.…The context often suggests a noun or pronoun. Cf. Franz §§306 and 663, and 1217, 1302, 1318, 1610, 1719, 2314, 2331. On a verb without a nominative see n. 230. Furness (ed. 1880): We might perhaps explain the absence of the nominative he by its absorption in the first syllable of insulted. Craig (ed. 1901), insulted: Triumphed, crowed, exulted (OED, v. 1).

1196 put vpon]
See n. 519.

1196–7 such…That]
See n. 240–1.

1196 man]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Manhood, courage (OED, sb.1 5c). Cf. 1318.

1196–7 that, That]
Malone (1783, p. 49): The meter…shews, that the concluding word of the first of these lines was inadvertently inserted by the compositor. F omits it. Possibly Okes’s compositor, who was inexperienced at setting dramatic verse (see ), saw belatedly that That belonged in the second line but then neglected to remove it from the previous one. Furness’s (ed. 1880) conjecture of the absorption of it in the final t of That is unnecessary; see prev. n.. See also .

1197 worthied]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): Rendered him worthy (OED, v. 1, quoting this l). Craig (ed. 1901): Gave him the appearance of worth. Abbott (§290): Any noun or adjective could be converted into a verb, quoting this l. Cf. 1211, 1764, 1900, 2014+18, 2056+2, 2112, 2868+3, 3222. Some eds. derive from the noun. Rann (ed. 1794): Made a hero of him. Wright (ed. 1875): Like one of the old [i.e., Nine] worthies. But the verb may derive from the adjective (OED, v., quoting this l.), or possibly from the ME verb wurthien (Perrett, 1904, p. 295).

1198 him attempting]
Delius (ed. 1854): Attempting him. Hudson (ed. 1856): The Steward means himself. Meiklejohn (ed. 1879), attempting: Attacking (OED, v. 9).

1198 selfe subdued]
Hudson (ed. 1871): Pretending that the poor figure he made was the result of virtuous self-control, and not of imbecility or fear. Neilson & Thorndike (ed. 1909), less probably: Who was already down, subdued by his own fall. OED (Self- 2a): The subject and object of the action, quoting this l.

1199 flechuent]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 388): Doubtless a u/m graphic error, a minim misreading. Or conceivably a compositor’s misreading of a nonce-word he had never seen, F’s fleshment. Cf. 3075 fleach. Henley (apud Eccles, ed. 1792): A young soldier is said to flesh his sword, the first time he draws blood with it; fleshment, therefore, is here metaphorically applied to [Kent’s] first act of service…in a sarcastic sense. Though Oswald cannot know that his tripping-up was Kent’s first act of service, his insults towards Kent are in general not notably careful of the truth. Closer glosses are ardor (Rann, ed. 1794), pride, encouraged by a successful attempt (Nares, 1822), elation (Hunter, ed. 1869), and ferocious mood (Kittredge, ed. 1940). OED (Fleshment): The action of fleshing [vbl. sb.: inciting (hounds) to the chase by giving them a taste of flesh]; hence, the excitement resulting from a first success, quoting only this l. Cf. n. 1120. Stone (1980, p. 179): An affected coinage…is appropriate in the mouth of Oswald, glossing it as receiving a reward. Rowse (ed. 1978), oddly: Embodiment.

1199 dread]
F’s dead accidentally omits a letter.

1200 againe]
Steevens (ed. 1793): Kent had not drawn on him before, and…again corrupts the metre. See textual n.

1201–2 None…foole]
Tovey (ed. 1896) suspects the speech to be a Shn. afterthought, since 1200 and 1203 make a verse line.

1202 A’Iax…foole]
Eds. cannot agree whether the allusion to Ajax refers to Kent, Cornwall, or Oswald, or why Cornwall seems to find it so offensive that he instantly calls for the stocks. The basic point of difference is whether Ajax is a hero who is unjustly ridiculed or is a man inherently foolish. Heath (1765, p. 331) proposes the former reading: Such a plain blunt brave fellow as Ajax was, is the person these rascals always chuse to make their butt, and put their tricks upon—as presumably Oswald is now doing in deceiving Cornwall with an invented story. Thus apparently Seymour (1805, 2:105): Any rogue or coward…can, by falsehood and cunning, overreach plain honesty, and outwit Ajax, and Verity (ed. 1897): He [Cornwall] thought that Kent had ridiculed him for being duped by Oswald. Steevens (ed. 1773), however, seems to suggest that Ajax represents Kent, not Cornwall: These rogues and cowards…have the subtlety to bring a man, as much above their match as Ajax, into disgrace. Or perhaps, these rogues and cowards speak of themselves as if Ajax was a fool to them, explaining foole in (ed. 1778) as their butt, their laughing-stock.…[They] never meet with a man superior to themselves, but they make him their jest, like Ajax with Thersites in Tro. Clarkes (1879, p. 360): A fool in comparison with them for courage. Tovey (ed. 1896), followed by Perrett (1904, p. 295) and Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905), makes the references explicit: Having recently written Tro., Sh. would have noted the resemblance between the character of Kent…stolid, brave, impetuous; and the character of the valiant Ajax, at whom the foul-mouthed Thersites gibes. Oswald is not foul-mouthed. Spilsbury & Marshall (ed. 1905): Oswald and the servants who are unable to meet Kent (Ajax) in fair fight…can misrepresent him to Cornwall, and so make a fool of him. Quinn (ed. 1970): Cowards like Oswald invariably picture anyone who is not a coward as a blustering oaf such as Ajax was reputed to be. Root (1902, pp. 452–3; 1903, p. 35): Sh. derives from Ovid, Meta. 13[.128 f.], his characterization of Ajax as a plain blunt fellow easily imposed on by smooth talkers (like Ulysses); here Kent sees himself as an Ajax figure, Oswald as a Ulysses. (The latter comparison is inherently unlikely.) Budd (ed. 1935): Kent, having recovered his sense of humour after his anger, is likening himself to Ajax, who during the Renaissance was often taken as a type of foolish anger, citing Campbell (1930, p. 197). Brooke (ed. 1947): In [LLL 5.2.578 (2531)], Ajax is runner-up for a place among the Nine Worthies. Malone (1783, p. 49) takes to as short for in comparison to: These rogues and cowards talk in such a boasting strain, as if the valiant Ajax were a person of no prowess compared to them, to which Mason (1785, p. 345) adds, alluding to the Steward’s account of their quarrel; Steevens (ed. 1793) came to prefer this interpretation to his earlier one. If Kent compares himself to Ajax, Cornwall’s anger may be directed at the perceived self-congratulation of a bragart (1204). There is no such clear motive for his sudden anger with Kent if the phrase means simply that Oswald and his ilk are overweening—e.g., that Ajax is a fool compared to them, according to their account of themselves (Kelcy, 1932, p. 365) or in their own opinion (Ridley, ed. 1935).
On the other hand, eds. think that Cornwall is offended at being himself compared to such a dolt as Ajax. This seems to be Capell’s (1783, 1.2:157) interpretation: Ajax is a fool to them, videlicet in bragging, as he is portrayed in Tro. This interpretation, approved by Furness (ed. 1880), has also been made to reflect on Oswald, not Cornwall: so Deighton (ed. 1891): There is not one of these rogues and cowards to whom in the matter of boasting Ajax is not a mere tiro. An allusion to the proud boasts of Ajax after his slaughter of the Grecian flocks and herds which in his madness he mistook for his enemies, the chieftains of the army. But, asks Phelps (ed. 1917), has Oswald bragged? (Or has Cornwall?) Perhaps Deighton has in mind 1135–6. Brown (ed. 1976): Men like Oswald learn wisdom (folly) from the Greek hero (braggart). Jespersen (1929, pp. 424–5) adds a refinement: If Kent, in applying the name of Ajax to Cornwall, alludes to a jakes [cf. 1139–40], we can easily understand Cornwall’s rage. This explanation is supported by the spelling of the quartos A’Iax. He cites Cotgrave (1611), Retraict : An Aiax, Priuie, OED (Ajax), LLL 5.2.578 (2531), AYL 3.3.73 (1681), &c. So Harrison (ed. 1937): A very evil-smelling apartment; Idem (ed. 1948): Kent thus implies All these knaves and cowards are fooling this stinking braggart. Many eds. think the point is merely that Ajax is a simpleton, a warrior but of slow perception (Houghton, ed. 1907), a brave but dull-witted hero, and…easily fooled (Goggin, ed. 1910), stupidly belligerent (Harbage, ed. 1958). Foakes (ed. 1997): Thus, a compound insult (stupid, privy). Petz (ed. 1839) alone infers an allusion to the strife of Ajax and Odysseus over Achilles’ shield, and Ajax’s resultant madness at being thought less deserving of it than others.
Furness (ed. 1880): The a in Ajax was pronounced long. Sir John Harington in the Prologue to his Metamorphosis of Ajax [ed. Donno, p. 78] says, that [it] agrees fully in pronunciation with age akes—i.e. aches, and Ben Jonson [Ep. 133.195–6]…makes it rhyme with sakes.
