The sound was not the modern long a [e] but, according to Cercignani (1981, p. 103), the Late Middle English a [ā].

1203 Bring]
F’s Fetch is consistent with 1212 but not therefore more authoritative. Q avoids alliteration with foole (1202).

1203 ho]
F omits, to smoothe the meter. In Q the speech is unambiguously a call directed offstage, where the stocks are, not an order to an onstage attendant. Cf. n. 1217. Wells & Taylor (ed. 1986) remove ambiguity in their F text by having onstage servants respond (see textual n.). Thomson (1988, p. 184): At 1212, [calling] is added, suggesting that Cornwall’s impatience to punish Kent is what causes him to repeat the command [Bring/Fetch…stockes, 1203, 1212].…The absence of information in other editions prompts the inference that Cornwall calls off stage both times.…The question is whether they [the F servants] obey him the first time he speaks or are hesitant and must be commanded again.…All three versions of the staging seem equally possible.

1204 stubburne]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Fierce (OED, Stubborn a. 1). But perhaps only Pertinacious…in refusing obedience or compliance;…unreasonably obstinate (ibid.).

1204 ausrent]
Q1(c)’s miscreant is a palpable case of ingenious failure of conjectural emendment (Adee, ed. 1890, p. xiii), a good example of conjecture by the Q press-reader (Wilson, ed. 1960). Greg (1940, p. 159): F’s antient proves that [Q(c)] is a mere graphic error, a misreading no doubt of ansient. See n. 1135.

1204 knaue]
See n. 451.

1204 reuerent]
See n. 749. Brooke (ed. 1947): Old enough to know better. Wilson (ed. 1960): Sarcastic. Sh. uses the two forms [reverend, reverent] indiscriminately.

1206 I]
F’s added Sir, is an apparent metrical improvement, unnecessary if 1205 is spoken naturally with two stresses.

1206 too old]
Dent (1981) detects an echo of the proverb Never too old (late) to learn (L153).

1207–11 I…messenger]
Bullough (1973, p. 291): Parallel to Ragan’s striking the ambassador in Leir [1966–7]; see . Foakes (ed. 1997): The title of King is merely ceremonial now, and Kent’s appeal means little.

1209 should]
F’s shall is an apparent sophistication. Furness (ed. 1880) cites Abbott (§315)—Shall for will,…are sure to—who does not cite this l. OED (Shall v. 8g): In statements of a result to be expected from some action or occurrence, quoting this l. Cf. 1216.

1209 respect]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Do homage, do reverence. Brooke (ed. 1947): In the way of compliment (ironic). F’s respects is inferior and probably erroneous, for the Q line is quite full of s sounds already (Furness, ed. 1880), and the Q singular admirably balances the singular malice at the end of the line. Indeed it is hard to see how the plural would make sense (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 174).

1209 malice]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Ill will [OED, sb. 4]. Not here used in the limited modern sense.

1210 Grace and person]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Not only an outrage on the King’s grace (i.e., his royal honour) but a personal insult to him, comparing 1221–3. Hunter (ed. 1972): Both his mystical body as King and his person as man. Brooke (ed. 1947): As a royal messenger, Kent had the immunity of heralds.

1211 Stobing]
Greg (1940, p. 159): Q1(c)’s Stopping is a false emendation. F [Stocking]…convicts Q1(u) of a graphic error, evidently for Stoking. The confusion of b and k occurs elsewhere in the quarto (e.g. bitt for kill at [2222]), which again refuses to recognize the verb stock at [1477, 1914]. On the formation of transitive verbs from nouns, see n. 1197. The punishment was customary for low miscreants; cf. n. 1220+3–+4. Farmer (in Steevens, ed. 1773, 10:2Q4r): Formerly in great houses, as still in some colleges, there were moveable stocks for the correction of the servants. Young (1949, p. 633) quotes from the household rules of the fifth earl of Huntingdon (1604–): If any doe unseamly behave themselves towards there betters, the offence to be punnyshed first by the stockes. Mack (1965, pp. 56–7) takes the scene to be emblematic, comparing the stocking of Pity and Charity in medieval moralities probably unknown to Sh. Craik (1958, pp. 93–6; 1966, pp. 52–3) shows in several moral interludes such as Hickscorner, Youth, and the Satire of the Three Estates the tradition of the vices putting the sage virtues in the stocks. Salingar (1986, p. 99): The Morality-play icon of virtue martyred in the stocks becomes an icon of social transposition, of the confusion of moral values.

1212–13 Fetch…noone]
Hogan (1962, p. 74): Q’s lineation (see textual n.) is surely right…. F, seeing little chance of getting as…Honour into a line shortened by a speech-heading…rearranged so as to produce the needless alexandrine which some editors have accepted.

1213 set]
Q1(c)’s sit is certainly correct (Greg, 1940, p. 159).

1214 Till…too]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Very artfully is this speech thrown in. Not only does it serve to paint the vindictive disposition of Regan; it also serves to regulate dramatic time, by making the subsequent scene, where Lear arrives before Gloster’s castle and finds his faithful messenger in the stocks, appear sufficiently advanced in the morning to allow of that same scene closing with the actual approach of night without disturbing the sense of probability.…[Sh.] makes a whole day pass before our eyes during a single scene and dialogue, yet all seems consistent and natural in the course of progression. Verity (ed. 1897): Whenever anyone suggests something evil, especially something cruel, she quickly suggests something worse, more cruel. She delights in causing and seeing purposeless suffering…whereas Goneril is composed and thoroughly business-like in her malevolence, ready to stab anyone to the heart if her schemes require it, but self-restrained and not so wanton in causing pain.…To my mind Regan is more odious, though less formidable, than Goneril. Miriam Joseph (1947, pp. 82–3): By anadiplosis,…the repetition of the last word of one clause or sentence at the beginning of the next,…Cornwall…is echoed and outdone by the more cruel Regan.

1215 dogge]
Dent (1981) cites the proverb To use one like a dog (D514).

1216 could]
Since F’s should is weaker if it means ought (Crook, ed. 1907; OED, Shall v. 2, 18), it is often glossed would certainly (Kittredge, ed. 1940). Cf. n. 1209.

1216–17 you…will]
A pentameter if me so and being his are elided without accent.

1217 Sir]
See n. 60.

1217 being]
On the omitted you see n. 1195.

1217 knaue]
Rann (ed. 1794): Servant. But Regan implies someone worse than a dog; see n. 610.

1217 I will]
Brown (ed. 1976): Some Regans…kick Kent like a dog.

1217 Stocks…out.]
On F’s added stage direction see n. 1014. Dyce (ed. 1857): In the folio [this] stage-direction…is placed two lines earlier [than 1219] (as it no doubt stood so in the prompter’s book, that the stocks might be in readiness). See . Werstine (privately): Dyce’s suggestion is absurd—two lines’ advance notice is about as good as none at all. Prompters’ warning directions for the provision of properties appear dozens of lines prior to their actual use, as the first quarto of TNK indicates. Sisson (1956, 2:232–3): I suggest that the conduct of this scene, as of Sc. 3 and 4 following, is best met if the stocks are not brought on and off, which offers difficulties, but if the stocks are set in the inner stage, to be discovered [i.e., by opening curtains], closed off, discovered again, and finally closed off, as required in this and the following scenes. This is not incompatible with the indications in the dialogue, the stocks being fetched forth ([1203, 1212]) into the curtained inner stage. The Quarto text [1203] shows more clearly that Cornwall is shouting (to servants within). Horsman (ed. 1973): The stocks would be brought downstage and well to one side to allow for the playing of the next two scenes. Soellner (1984, p. 278): Kent was placed prominently on the forestage; perhaps he was put against one of the two pillars to make Edgar’s [and Lear’s] failure to see him more plausible. See n. 1251. Dessen & Thomson (1999, out, stocks) cite many SDs for moving large objects onto the stage; this is the only one for stocks, though stocks appear (somehow) on stage in other plays.

1218 fellow]
See n. 577.

1218 nature]
F’s colour means the same: Clarkes (ed. 1868): Character,…kind (OED, Colour sb. 16, quoting this l.). See n. 185.

1219 Our sister]
Tovey (ed. 1896): In the letter actually written by Oswald, but inspired by Goneril. Cf. 858. Schmidt (1875): Sister-in-law (OED, sb. 1a). Cf. 2066, 2070, 2865, 3029.

1219 speake]
Q2 corrects to speakes, but Stone (1980, p. 54) prefers spake, its homonym—a slight exaggeration, since the two words, though sounding similar, were distinguishable: see Cercignani (1981, pp. 158–62, 167–8, 171–3).

1219 away]
Schmidt (ed. 1879): Here. Tovey (ed. 1896): Properly on the way (a- meaning on), hence this way or hither (OED, adv. 1). So Harbage (ed. 1958): Along.

1220 your Grace]
See n. 218.

1220+1–+4 His…with]
Delius (1876, p. 142): In these lines Gloster admits the guilt of Kent…and gives assurance that Lear himself will punish his follower, although not in such a degrading manner.…This, at once, justifies and anticipates Lear’s wrath at the sight of his servant sitting in the stocks. It is hardly to be believed that the poet would himself have omitted this delicate and well-considered stroke of art. Fleay (1879, p. 119): Clearly a purposed [though non-Shn.] omission, not accidental, the meter being set right by inserting, need. So Doran (1931, p. 127): Since 1221–4 in F are as metrically regular as in Q, F’s changes are deliberate revision, a case of omission with patching required (Idem, 1935, p. 141). Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 174–5): The F omission would seem to be a deliberate cut: and the abridger left himself with an incomplete line. Q lines [1220+2–1221] are incorrectly divided: with corrected lineation line [1221] runs thus in Q—are punisht with, The King must take it ill,. The first three words conclude the F cut. The abridger has presumably filled out The King must take it ill to The King his Master, needs must take it ill, thus achieving regular metre despite the 4½ line excision. In patching line [1221] he took his Master from line [1220+1], the first of the excised lines. The expansion of 1221 to a pentameter was earlier pointed out by Knight (ed. 1840), Collier (ed. 1843), Dyce (ed. 1865), and others. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): The F cut is a decided improvement upon the wordy Q, yet the missing Q lines sound Shakespearian. Only if we were sure that Shakespeare made the change would we be entitled to adopt the briefer F version. Stone (1980, p. 235): F’s cut is probably theatrical rather than editorial…, since the lines raise no serious textual or contextual difficulties. It seems to have been found desirable to shorten the episode of Kent’s stocking. Halio (ed. 1992, p. 267): The lines are not essential to the action, although they spell out the situation in fuller detail and show Gloucester pleading more earnestly. Weis (ed. 1993): They expand the train of thought rather than to alter or radically redirect it. Foakes (1993, p. 190): By omitting this passage, F allows us to think that Kent’s punishment is not inappropriate for his offense (see n. 1211). But in Q and F 1207–11 Kent has rightly asserted his immunity from such punishment; see n. 1210. Idem (ed. 1997): Perhaps omitted as mere elaboration.

1220+1 much]
Abbott (§51): Frequently used as an ordinary adjective (OED, adj. 1: Great).

1220+2 check]
Wright (ed. 1875): Rebuke (OED, v.1 11).

1220+2 purpost low correction]
Deighton (ed. 1891): The indignity with which you propose to punish him. Greg (1940, p. 159): [Q1(c)’s] removal of the comma after correction is no doubt in accordance with grammar, and so may be allowed as correct: at the same time the comma does mark a pause, and there is even less excuse for the one which the corrector left standing in the next line.

1220+3–+4 such…with]
Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) instance the ignominy of the stocks from Randle Holmes’s Academy of Armory (1688, 3:312): The stocks keep safe…Night Walkers, common Drunkards and Swearers, that have no Money,…Strippers of Hedges, Robbers of Hen-roosts…Wandring Rogues, Gipsies, and such as love Begging better than Labour. Statutes under Henry VII, Henry VIII, Edward VI, and Elizabeth put vagabonds in the stocks. Cf. nn. 1211, 1285. For citations of these statutes, and texts of some of them, see Chambers (1923, 4:260–1, 269–71, 324–5, 336–7).

1220+3 belest]
Duthie (1949, pp. 50–1): Q1(u)’s reading results from graphic confusion of a/e and l/s. Q1(c)’s basest is certainly correct (Greg, 1940, p. 159), as most eds. agree. See textual n. and .

1220+3 contaned]
Q1(u) probably results from a/e misreading (Duthie, 1949, p. 50) and perhaps m/n misreading. Greg (1940, p. 159) explains Q1(c)’s temnest: The proofreader must have crossed out or underlined taned and written temnest in the margin, meaning the compositor to alter the word to contemnest (for either contemnedst or contemndest); whereupon the latter, misunderstanding his directions, substituted the marginal correction for the whole word in the text, thereby making nonsense. Most eds. print contemned’st. Foakes (ed. 1997): The rarer superlative probably led to the confusion in Q. Stone (1980, p. 201): The copy must have read conte[m]ned: the compositor could hardly have overlooked a final -st in the first instance. Contemned requires no alteration: Elizabethan English, possibly for reasons of euphony, permitted the omission of -[e]st in either of a pair of superlatives, citing Abbott §398. See n. 776. Blayney (1982, 1:248) agrees mostly with Greg but not that the reader’s intention was correct: When he altered belest at E2v20, the proof-reader wrote as in the [right-hand, gutter] margin.…He would then have crossed out taned and have started to write temn… after the first marginal annotation. Each letter he wrote would have brought his pen, and consequently his eye, closer to [a line on the facing page of the proof-sheet].…Coincidentally, E3r20 reads: To take the basest and most poorest shape, [1258]. That line, I believe, is probably where the idea of changing contemned to contemnest originated. Tovey (ed. 1896): Most despised. Harbage (ed. 1958), less probably: Most harshly sentenced; stocking is hardly the harshest sentence.

1220+4 trespasses]
The Sokols (2000, pp. 380–1): Here and in 1320 the term seems to refer to an offence particularly distinguished by its lesser importance, and meriting a punishment which is shaming and unpleasant rather than capital.

1221–3 The…restrained]
Doran (1931, p. 128) suspects that Q’s momentary misalignment of verse here occurred because the lines were additional or revisional matter written in the margin without clear line-divisions.

1222–3 hee’s…should]
F’s he makes the King the subject of should; Q implies an ellipsis of the nominative; see n. 230. Thus Abbott (§399): (That he or ? you) Should. Cf. n. 1223. Neither reading requires one to suspect a line dropped out after [1222] (Brooke, ed. 1947). Possibly a phonetic error: the F compositor, carrying hee’s so in his memory, elided the s’s and dropped the first. Compositor E often omitted terminal s.

1222 In]
Harbage (ed. 1958): In the person of.

1222 messenger]
On scansion see n. 1067.

1223 haue]
See n. 1222–3. If the King is the subject, have must mean something like endure to have; OED (v. 18): To have something done to one;…to receive, experience, or suffer it as the action of others. Cf. 1226. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Find. If Cornwall is the subject, have means cause to be; OED (17b): To cause…something to be done, or a person to do something.

1224 answer]
See n. 517.

1225 more worse]
On the double comparative see n. 84.

1226 Gentlemen]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 389): Q may have an a/e misreading: F [Gentleman; also Q2] is right, of course—the reference is to Oswald.

1226 abus’d]
Wright (ed. 1875): Misused, ill-treated (OED, ppl. a. 2, adding Wronged, done violence to, quoting 2764). Cf. 2168, 2764.

1226+1 For…legges]
Doran (1931, p. 69): F’s omission may have been accidental. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 175): There can, I think, be no doubt about the authenticity of the line. In its first half it refers to a very important element in Kent’s offense. The F compositor would seem to have been guilty of a careless omission. Seymour (1805, 2:105) suspects that put in his legges is a stage direction: It was useless to the servants, (who could not be ignorant how they were to use the stocks,) and is an awkward encumbrance to the verse [if 1227 completes a verse line]. But of course the line is an order, not an instruction. Gloucester’s servants have hesitated to stock Kent during their master’s objections to that act; now Regan insists they do so. And 1227 is a part-line in F as well as in Q. Mahood (1992, p. 170): It makes sense for Gloucester’s servants to obey Cornwall’s orders to bring the stocks (they know where they are kept) and for Cornwall’s to thrust Kent into them with a brutality which presages their behaviour in the blinding scene. Foakes (ed. 1997): The line is omitted possibly because Kent was already thus restrained [1223]; but that reason would apply to only the last four words of the line.

1226+1 following]
Schmidt (1874): To pursue, to apply one’s self to (OED, v. 9).

1227 Come…away]
F assigns the line to Corn. and like Q2 omits good. Doran (1931, p. 81): Cornwall’s part has twice been enhanced at the expense of Regan’s, in places where short speeches could be indifferently assigned, i.e. [here and 1597, 1601]. The shifts were probably made for some practical reason concerned with stage management, such as keeping rapid dialogue moving among more characters. Urkowitz (1980, p. 38): Either version is Shakespearean, purposeful, and theatrically intelligible. Only a few ardent Foliolaters prefer the reassignment. Kirschbaum (1945, p. 38): Q not only gives the line to Regan, but it also apparently does not know to whom the line is spoken, Gloucester or her husband. In F we know that [1227] is spoken by Cornwall to Gloucester as the former leaves the stage with Regan. In Q the point which F makes is lost: Cornwall’s adjuration to the delaying Gloucester is the first indication of the rift that is to come. Kirschbaum (apud Muir, ed. 1952): Nevertheless, Gloucester remains, though obviously nervous. It is doubtful that Regan would urge Gloucester rather than Cornwall to exit with her, and even more improbable that Gloucester would risk Cornwall’s displeasure by refusing to accompany him in order to remain and talk with a knave whose insolence has put the Duke in a rage. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 175): F omits one line…and misassigns the next one. I am at a loss to account for this patch of corruption unless by supposing a moment of quite unusual absent-mindedness in the compositor. Wilson (ed. 1960): Poss. the copy for F had to Corn. as a S.D. Werstine (privately): The formula to so-and-so occurs only in entrance directions to indicate whom newly entering characters approach or join, citing Dessen & Thomson (1999, pp. 231–2). The omission of good from F might be an intentional or unconscious consequence of Cornwall’s being misassigned the line, since a note of compliment would not suit his present mood; but that is not the reason for its absence also from Q2, which might have influenced Compositor E or a scribe here. Evans (1961, p. 325): Q2, here printed from a corrected state of Q1, also omits good and seems at this point to have served as copy-text [i.e., printer’s copy] for F1. It is, therefore, likely that the F1 omission is without authority. That Q2 was F’s copy is questionable, and the changes might be scribal error or interference; see . Sprague (1944, p. 288): Traditionally Oswald sometimes remains to offer various pantomimed threats and indignities to the stocked Kent; so Rosenberg (1972, p. 149), Bratton (ed. 1987).

1228 Dukes]
F Duke. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 175): The F compositor has presumably carelessly omitted a letter. Compositor E often omits terminal -s.

1229 disposition]
See n. 329.

1230 VVill not be]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Will not allow itself to be.

1230 rubd]
Rann (ed. 1794): Impeded (OED, Rub v.1 3b, quoting only this l.). Warburton (ed. 1747): Metaphor from bowling—as often in Sh. Craig (ed. 1901): When a bowl thrusts another from the neighborhood of the small bowl which all aim at, called the mistress, the jack, and more rarely the block. Kittredge (ed. 1940): A rub is anything that hinders or deflects the course of the bowl (OED, sb.1 2; figuratively, 3).

1231 you]
F omits, either to make more regular meter or to avoid a turned line.

1231 watcht]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Been without sleep (OED, Watch v. 1).

1232 ont]
Q2 corrects to out. Doran (1931, p. 21): The n does not appear to be a reversed u. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 389): Doubtless an n/u misreading. OED (Sleep v. 10): With out or away: To pass or spend (a certain time) in sleep.

1233 A]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Even a.

1233 out at heeles]
OED (Heel sb.1 12): With stockings or shoes worn through at the heel;…fig. in unfortunate or decayed circumstances; for at see n. 1285. Proverbial: see Tilley H389. Eccles (ed. 1792), misinterpreting grow out as a verb phrase: To a good man may arise prosperity and advantage from circumstances seemingly…ignominious. Delius (ed. 1854): With a pun on Kent’s heels’ protruding from the stocks. Hudson (ed. 1871): A man set in the stocks was said to be punished by the heels [cf. 2H4 1.2.123 (392)]. Furness (ed. 1880): Is it not likely that Kent jocosely means that what is usually but a metaphor is with him a reality? Verity (ed. 1897): Kent is philosophical…and says a good man must expect reverse of fortune like his neighbours. Harbage (ed. 1958): I.e. it is no disgrace to decline in fortune. Quinn (ed. 1970): Bad luck can happen to anyone. Colie (1974, p. 128): The feet-heels-stocks cluster of images suggests a possible echo of Job 13:27.

1234 Giue you]
Craig (ed. 1901): Ellipsis, God give you (OED, Give v. 17). Cf. n. 928.

1234 good morrow]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Considered proper only before noon, citing Rom. 2.4.109–13 (1209–13). Rosenberg (1972, p. 149), without textual support: Kent may slip to Gloster…the message, betrayed by Edmund, that will cost Gloster his eyes.

1235 to]
For the too of Q2 and F, see n. 378. Horsman (ed. 1973), however: The sense is not that it is the duke’s fault, but that he has gone too far.

1236 tooke]
A Shn. form; F’s change to taken is unnecessary. On curtailed forms of past participles see n. 103. Abbott (§343): Where…the form thus curtailed was in danger of being confused with the infinitive, as in taken, [Elizabethan authors] used the past tense for the participle. Muir (ed. 1952): Received (OED, Take v. 42).

1237 must]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Art fated. Wilson (ed. 1960): Reg.’s attitude has shown Kent what treatment his master will receive at her hands.

1237 approue]
See n. 198.

1237 say]
All eds. but Oxford (1986; Wells, 2000) and Weis (ed. 1993) follow Q1(c)’s saw. Greg (1940, pp. 159–60): The word say, with the same sense as saw (i.e. saying), had a restricted currency in the first half of the seventeenth century: Marston has Tis an old say [1 Antonio and Mellida 3.2.170, quoted by OED, sb.4 2]. It is therefore possible that [Q1(u)] may preserve Shakespeare’s own reading which was independently normalized by the corrector and by the prompter or folio editor. One does not quite see why the compositor should have printed a y for a w.…Still say may be no more than a literal error, and the agreement of [Q1(c)] and F must be allowed due weight. Sh. often uses saw and saying to refer to a proverb, but the rare say nowhere else. On y/w variants see n. 2710.

1238–9 Thou…Sunne]
Proverbial: Tilley G272, Out of God’s blessing into the warm sun. Tilley’s many examples, and those provided by other commentators, show that the proverb was indeed common, both widespread and enduring. The parallel proverb, Tilley H56 Out of the hall into the [hot] kitchen, implies the same movement from relative comfort to discomfort, from better (or merely bad) to worse. Most eds. accept Capell’s (1783, 1.2:157) application: Lear…[erroneously] thinks to mend his condition by leaving his eldest daughter and coming to Regan,…such opinion had [Kent] now entertain’d of Regan’s superiority in badness. Proposing alternative applications to Lear’s more general sitution are Nicholson (1867, p. 413)—Having had God’s blessing and annointing as a crowned king, thou hast voluntarily given away thy right—and Carver (1930, p. 480)—Exchanging power and dignity for impotence and humiliation. The exact metaphor underlying the proverb has been much debated: the lost blessing has been specified as house and home,…all the comforts of life (Hanmer, ed. 1743; Furnivall, 1875, p. 223; Hudson, ed. 1879); the shelter of an hospital, or house of charity…for travellers (Johnson, ed. 1765); family connections (Hunter, ed. 1869); the cool and tranquility of church after receiving the priest’s blessing (Skeat, in Wright Shakespeariana, 21 Sept. 1880; followed by Gollancz, ed. 1895 and others); sanctuary in churches (Lee, ed. 1908); religion as opposed to worldliness (Bond, 1903, pp. 220–1); divine blessings as opposed to the ordinary chances of mortal life (Sisson, 1956, 2:234); shade as of a spreading tree (Craig, ed. 1901); the benefits (including shade) of clouds and the fruitful rain (Nicholson, op. cit.; Brooke, ed. 1947; Stewart, 1948, pp. 188–90). Biblical passages comparing God’s protection to shade from the hot sun are Psa. 121:5–6 (Tovey, ed. 1896); Isa. 25:4 and 35:2 (Bond, 1902, 1:374). LeComte (1975, pp. 3–9) records forty-four applications of the same proverb in Ham. 1.2.67 (247), most of them not relevant here. Muir (ed. 1952) compares Leir 1154 (see ): He came from bad to worse. Hunter (ed. 1972): This particular saw is no doubt suggested by the rising of the sun.

1240 beacon]
See textual n. Malone (ed. 1790): Kent is surely here addressing, not the moon, but the sun, which he has mentioned in the previous line, and for whose rising he is impatient, that he may read Cordelia’s letter. He has just before said to Gloster, Give you good morrow! The comfortable beams of the moon no poet, I believe, has mentioned. Those of the sun are again mentioned by Shakespeare in Timon of Athens [5.1.131 (2361): Thou Sunne that comforts burne]. Cf. Ven. 799: Loue comforteth like sun-shine, and 529: Looke the worlds comforter…His dayes hot taske hath ended in the west; and cf. Tit. 2.2.10 (710). Steevens (ed. 1793): The term, beacon, was more applicable to the moon, being, like that planet, only designed for night-service.…The mention of the sun in the preceding proverbial sentence is quite accidental. Tieck (ed. 1833, 9:367): Moonlight seldom shines bright enough to read letters by. Daniel (1877–9, p. 218): Address [to the moon] was unnecessary, as the moon was already shining. Though a beacon could be a post or tower, it usually involved a fire (OED, sb. 2–4, 6; Falconer, 1965), which suggests the sun rather than the moon; cf. 1H6 3.1.29–30 (1456–7), Per. 1.4.87 (478). Tovey (ed. 1896) is mistaken to say The sun has just risen: see goodnight in 1249. Perrett (1904, p. 254): Kent could not suggest the sun [1239], and proceed to address the moon.…Further the epithet comfortable is better suited to sun-beams than to moon-beams. Cf. Timon, V, i, [131], Thou sun that comfort’st.…The rising hope with the letter is made to synchronise with the rising of the sun. Edwards (ed. 1975): Kent reflects that in spite of the proverb, you cannot do without the sun.

1240 vnder gloabe]
Rolfe (ed. 1880) compares Tim. 1.1.44 (60), this beneath world, and Craig (ed. 1901), R2 3.2.38 (1394), the globe that lights the lower world. Foakes (ed. 1997): Perhaps another sardonic joke for Kent, if he pointed to the structure of the Globe theatre above him.

1241 comfortable]
See n. 825. But Craig (ed. 1901): Helpful (OED, a. 2); and possibly encouraging,…cheering (OED, 1). The word may be proleptic: though the warme Sunne sometimes brings discomfort, tomorrow’s sun, by enabling Kent to read Cordelia’s letter, will bring comfort.

1242 this letter]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Possibly being supposed to draw it forth and look at it by the still imperfect light of coming dawn. Eccles (ed. 1792): This letter, which he appears to have very lately received, may be supposed to have been directed to him under a fictitious name [Caius?], by his own desire, at the castle of Gloster. Bradley (1904, p. 459): We may suppose that this intelligence came from one of Albany’s or Cornwall’s servants, some of whom are, he says ([1633–4, F only]),…spies. Goggin (ed. 1910): When did Kent receive this letter from Cordelia? This is one of the insoluble difficulties of the play. Apparently it is from the letter that Kent derives the information he communicates to the Gentleman in [1638+1–+4]. But if that be so, apparently Cordelia hears of her father’s misfortunes before they take place. Greg (1940, pp. 442–3 n.): It is clearly on the strength of [this] letter that Kent informed the Gentleman that the French have…banner [1638+3–+4], and that Cordelia is at Dover.…[Kent] has only just arrived at Gloucester’s after posting hard all night, and it is difficult to understand how he can have received it at any time after he left Albany’s, which was immediately upon Lear’s quarrel with Goneril. Moreover, Cordelia, informed of his obscurèd course, would of course have sent the letter to Albany’s, where Lear was resident, no doubt through one of the spies that she had planted in his house ([1633]). There can be no doubt, therefore, that the French army had actually landed before Lear had any quarrel with his daughters.
None of these theories of the letter’s contents or provenance or implications for the plot is necessarily true. Kent says only that Cordelia has written to him, not that she has any knowledge of his and Lear’s misfortunes (see n. 1636). His remark I know tis from Cordelia seems to indicate the extent of his knowledge of the letter; the remark would be pointless had he already read the letter and seen its signature. The play provides no evidence as to when Kent might have informed her about his obscured course. Although as early as the night of Cordelia’s departure with France Kent could have confided plans to remain in Britain in disguise, could have arranged to exchange messages with her, and accordingly could now be sure that this (yet unread) letter is from Cordelia, in fact the play tells nothing at all about any such arrangements, or why Kent is sure the letter is hers. How it reached him is also unclear; conceivably it might have been conveyed through a prearranged network of household servants friendly to Cordelia, France, or Lear—the spies alluded to in 1632–3 (F only). Conceivably it was delivered first to a servant in Goneril’s house, where Cordelia expected Lear and Kent to be, and subsequently it (or a duplicate) followed him to Regan’s or Gloucester’s house and was transmitted by a servant in Gloucester’s house who was acting as intelligencer for Cordelia and France. Gloucester, it may be recalled, also somehow receives the next night a dangerous letter (cf. 1761) about a power already landed. But the play is silent about how Kent receives the letter. Nor are his and Cordelia’s intentions any clearer. Having now heard from her, Kent can soon inform her (and he does: see 1626–1638+12 and nn.) of the enormious state of affairs in England. It is not clear what losses Kent has in mind—Lear’s, Cordelia’s, his own, or the country’s (see n. 1247)—and his anticipation of future remedies for them may be mere prediction, hope, or resolve, not the result of anything specific that Cordelia says in the letter. There is no basis at all for Ioppolo’s (1991, p. 172) claims that Kent had already appealed to Cordelia for aid, nor could Cordelia have responded to such an appeal, made only half a day earlier after Lear’s break with Goneril. Cf. nn. 1638+1, 2347+2–+7. Bullough (1973, p. 368) compares the Gallian King’s embassage to Leir at Cornwall’s court, but the parallel is remote at best.

1242–3 nothing…miserie]
Granville-Barker (1927, p. 230): Cut this much, and an actor can make sense of a passage otherwise as obscure as it is evidently corrupt. Only Stone (1980, p. 188) agrees, interpreting these words as a line from Cordelia’s letter which interrupts the pentameter line Peruse…Cordelia. All others understand it as Kent’s own generalization. It sounds proverbial, but no exact analogue has been found. Neither has agreement on its meaning. Much depends on whether sees is interpreted as discovers, attends to (i.e., notices) (Davies, 1783, 2:287), experiences (Hudson, ed. 1871), expects (i.e., foresees; Brae, 1879, p. 366), perceives (Verity, ed. 1897), or appreciates (Harrison, ed. 1948). Capell (1783, 1.2:158): Only people born to ill-fortune…and living under her frown…can be said to see miracles; so wonderful are the situations…which she is pleas’d to reduce them to. Rann (ed. 1794): The wretched are almost the only persons that attend duly to the wonderful dispensations of providence; thus Verity (op. cit.): The prosperous are blind to all the miracles of man’s existence. Moberly (ed. 1876) finds a version of the proverb Darkest before the dawn: It is only when things are at the worst that Providence interposes with a miracle; similarly Houghton (ed. 1957) supplies from the old ballad of Sir Aldingar the line When bale is att hyest, boot is at next. Hudson (ed. 1871): Miracles are hardly ever wrought but in behalf of the wretched; Idem (ed. 1879): In the Gospels. Milward (1987, p. 170) cites Isa. 61:1, Matt. 5:3 and 9:5. Theobald (1888, pp. 411–12) compares Bacon’s Of Adversitie (1625; ed. Kiernan, 1985, p. 18): It was a high speech of Seneca [Epist. 66.29, illa bona optabilia haec mirabilia sunt]…That the good things, which belong to Prosperity, are to be wished; but the good things, that belong to Adversity, are to be admired.…Certainly if Miracles, be the Command over Nature, they appeare most in Adversity. Armour (ed. ca. 1930): Help coming when we are in the depths of misery is the most truly a miracle. Kelcy (1932, p. 366): Hardly any but those who are in distress can get the sensation of a miracle out of a stroke of good fortune. Kittredge (ed. 1940): When we are in despair, any relief seems miraculous. Muir (ed. 1952) compares 2180–4. Mack (1965, p. 56): Perhaps a reminiscence of the story [Acts 16:22–6] of Paul and Silas, when by the magistrates of Philippi they were thrown into prison and the stocks, only to be miraculously released at midnight by an earthquake as they sat singing psalms. Skillan (ed. 1967): Miracles are almost only known to misery, as they relieve where relief seems impossible. Quinn (ed. 1970): Natural phenomena (such as the sun rising) are really appreciated only when one is miserable. Verity (op. cit.), followed by Brooke (ed. 1947): Possibly…not so much a reflection on the part of Kent as the dramatist’s own way of preparing the audience for something rather improbable. See next n.

1242–3 my rackles]
Greg (1940, p. 160): Q1(u)’s reading may be nothing but a mis-division of an unusual spelling, and Q1(c)’s my wracke can be nothing but a rather desperate guess on the part of the corrector. Ridley (ed. 1935): One would feel happier about the F reading [miracles] were it not that the Q compositor had no difficulty with miracle, either in [243] or [2497]. Myracle appears in F 1H6 5.3.54 (2491) and 5.4.66 (2681), Cym. 4.2.29 (2279), Lr. 2497, and Q1 1H4, and myraculous in F Ham. 2.2.594 (1634) and Mac. 4.3.147 (1979). Myrackle, one of several 16th-c. variants with k or ck recorded in OED, does not appear elsewhere in Sh.’s texts; it may have been a spelling of the Q1 compositor, who added a k to a common Shn. spelling. Werstine (privately) cautions, however, that spelling in manuscript is much more various than in print. Only Seymour (1803, p. 48) and Jackson (1819, p. 327) defend my wrack (= wreck), Jackson comparing Sidney’s Arcadia 2.10.1 (see ), where the blind king says, nothing doth become me but miserie. All others prefer miracles but interpret it variously; cf. n. 243. To Capell (see prev. n.) it means Kent’s wonderful misfortune. Delius (ed. 1854): That Cordelia should have thought of him, or that her letter should have reached him. Knowles (1999, p. 35): She must have had available to her some unmiraculous means of communicating from France to her friends in England. White (ed. 1862): And her knowledge of his sad fortunes; or of his obscured course (Hunter, ed. 1869). Clarkes (ed. 1868): The coming miracle of redress; so Joseph (ed. 1966): The fact that Cordelia…has set about changing the situation in Britain which seems so hopeless for Lear. Hudson (ed. 1871) and others: A hoped-for miraculous providence…able to turn their course of misfortune. Brae (1879, p. 366), improbably: Sunrise before its time. Perrett (1904, p. 254): The beautiful phenomenon of sunrise. Theobald (1888, p. 411): The miracle is in his own mind—he has conquered circumstances, and remains calm and cheerful amidst the greatest reversals of fortune. Deighton (ed. 1891): Such miraculous comfort as this letter brings me. Mosley (1911, p. 304): By some miracle I know ’tis from Cordelia though I am unable to read it yet. On the scansion see n. 154.

1243 miserie]
Following Capell (1783, 1.2:158), most eds. think that Kent refers to his own condition. Verity (ed. 1897): Miserable people; abstract for concrete. Bradley (1904, p. 458): Surely not that of Kent but that of Lear.

1243 Cordelia]
Tieck (ed. 1833): Sh. wishes to call Cordelia to mind and to give us a hint that wholly new events are about to happen. McNeir (1969, 175): The convergence of the action on Dover in the last two acts is repeatedly anticipated by references to Cordelia’s return and the French invasion in Acts II and III.…There are six distinct references to this theme between II.ii and III.vii [1638+1–+9, 1760–4, 2049–51, 2060–1, 2074–9, 2120–30]. Their effect is to counteract, in a muted manner, the signals of a society becoming increasingly chaotic…by suggesting stability, repose and relief from torment if the protagonists of the two plots can reach the sanctuary offered by Cordelia.

1244–7 VVho…remedies]
The obscurity that editors have found in this speech has been attributed to Kent’s reading aloud fragments of Cordelia’s letter (Jennens, ed. 1770; Kittredge, ed. 1940; see textual n.) by moonlight (Steevens, ed. 1773; Collier, ed. 1843), to his ruminating elliptically to himself (Capell, 1783, 1.2:158), to the accidental loss of a line or parts of lines (Malone, ed. 1790; Collier, ed. 1877; Bradley, 1904, p. 459; Hoeniger, ed. 1968), to Kent’s inability to follow his train of thought for weariness (Singer, ed. 1856; Verity, ed. 1897), and to the author’s making the speech purposely confused in phraseology to indicate the situation of Kent (Clarkes, ed. 1868), or to tantalize the audience and make it jump to conclusions (Pechter, 1978, p. 190). In neither Q nor F is there italicized text or a stage direction to indicate reading, as is usual in F: cf. 382–9, 2715–23, 3059–63. Knowles (1999, p. 36): He has just said that he needs sunlight…to read by; that sunlight cannot have arrived three lines later. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 515): Such naturalistic explanations…only indicate the state of desperation to which critics have been driven.

1244 not]
Greg (1940, p. 160) and virtually all eds. approve of Q1(c)’s most as certainly correct. Taylor (1982, pp. 122–3), however, proposes now on the grounds that it would have been difficult for the original compositor to overlook the medial long s, and citing the substitution of not for now in Q1 R3 1.3.340 (818) and 5.3.180 (3642). See textual n. It is however possible that the Q compositor misread the long s as t, nott being a 16th-c. sp. of not (OED).

1244 fortunately]
Since only Kent could have informed Cordelia of his obscured course, by intent, fortunately must mean not accidentally but happily.

1245 obscured course]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Disguise. Harrison (ed. 1948): Actions in disguise. See n. 201.

1245 shall]
Mason (1785, p. 346) and Hudson (ed. 1879) think that the implied subject is I (1243). Knowles (1999, p. 36): In the Folio a period marks a sentence break between course and And in line [1245], but in the Quarto there is only a comma, which makes a mere parenthesis of Who hath…course and allows the sentence to continue after it. In the Quarto, then, the understood subject of shall is not Cordelia but Kent: I [Kent] know ’tis from Cordelia (Who…course) and [I, Kent] shall find time to remedy losses.…Having now heard from Cordelia, Kent says that he may soon send news to her (as he does in 3.1) of the enormous State of affairs in England. Or…I shall seek out remedies, with the help of Cordelia, for present losses. Most eds., however, follow Capell (1783, 1.2:158) in thinking the subject to be the nearer antecedent VVho (1243). Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 515): In the circumstances we expect news of Cordelia.…We expect Cordelia to find time for something, or to do something. Logic may favor this second reading, since Kent seems to find hope in Cordelia’s words. Still, that hope may come simply from her presence in England with her army, which may inspire him to imagine other remedies of his own. At best the audience gets a vague assurance that someone or other plans to do something to improve matters.

1245 find time]
To raise us (Capell, 1783, 1.2:158) or to deliver us (Delius, ed. 1854). But there may be no ellipsis, or a different one: find time, (for or in the endeavor of) seeking; Perring (1885, pp. 325–6) proposes the comma after time. Similarly Sullivan (1923, p. 896): Find time when seeking. Hunter (ed. 1869), followed by Walker (1953, pp. 158–9), reads find Time itself…seeking.

1246 From]
If the phrase refers to Cordelia, this word may mean while away from, as Sullivan (1923, p. 896) suggests: Removed as she is from the lawless state of things prevailing here; see n. 1067. It may however mean out of or on account of, either of which makes easy and excellent sense. OED (7): Indicating a state, condition, etc. which is abandoned or which is changed for another, quoting Jn. 5.4.25 (2486); (14): Denoting ground, reason, cause, or motive: Because of, on account of, owing to, as a result of, through, quoting Cym. 1.5.24 (516) as its first ex. Bevington (ed. 1980): To provide relief from (?). Rowe’s emendation For has recently been defended by Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 515) and adopted by them (eds. 1986, 2000) and Halio (ed. 1992): For…leaves Cordelia at the centre of attention, produces an intelligent idiom, and presupposes an easy error. Foakes (ed. 1997): It would then be possible to anticipate the letter as anticipating 3.1 (Q) in hinting to Kent that France is planning an invasion; but there is no reference to a French invading force in 3.1 in F. It may not be necessary to presuppose any error, difficult though the passage seems to be.

1246 enormious state]
Johnson (ed. 1765), enormous: Out of the ordinary; so the Clarkes (ed. 1868): Abnormal, and more emphatically Craig (ed. 1901): Monstrous (all OED, Enormous a. 1). OED (Enormious a. 2): Extraordinarily wicked, outrageous,…; = Enormous 2, which latter quotes TNK 5.1.62, enormous times, the only other occurrence in Sh. Kent may be speaking only generally—the present monstrous state of things in this country—but eds. have specified the enormous misrule of Regan (Steevens, ed. 1773), Kent’s strange disguise and situation (Mason, 1785, p. 346), the confusion subsisting in the state, in consequence of the discord which had arisen between the Dukes of Albany and Cornwall (Malone, ed. 1790), and the wickedness of Goneril, the unhappy condition of the king, [and the fact that] he himself, a nobleman, has been stocked like a low, common rogue (Tieck, ed. 1833, 9:366). Tovey (ed. 1896), followed by Brooke (ed. 1947), refers the phrase to Cordelia: The cares which the disorder of public affairs puts upon her. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 515): Blayney alters this to hir; the conjecture is paleographically plausible, but we have no reason to believe that Cordelia’s state (i.e. France) is an enormity. We do not hear that France may be preparing for war until 3.1, and we do know of enormities in Britain now.

1247 Losses]
Henley (apud Eccles, ed. 1792) specifies Kent’s loss of Lear’s favor and Lear’s loss of his kingdom; presumably Kent might also regain his rights and titles (Hudson, ed. 1879) and Cordelia might regain Lear’s favor but not, as queen of a rival country, her patrimony. Knowles (1999, p. 36): By that word, if it were in her letter, Cordelia could not possibly refer to Lear’s loss of status in Goneril’s household, or Goneril’s threat to diminish his train, or Lear’s being goaded to reject her straitened hospitality, or Regan’s flight from offering hers. Cordelia can know nothing of these events, since they happened only a half day ago, on the previous afternoon and night; and Lear’s being locked out in the storm will not happen for some hours yet.…It is not Cordelia who knows of Lear’s recent losses but Kent, who in 3.1 would naturally want the Gentleman-messenger to inform Cordelia of them instantly. Indeed, in 4.3…it is evident from his description of her reaction that the information is new and shocking to her. Nagarajan (2002–3, pp. 132–3) believes that Cordelia could have written the letter before embarking for France, anticipating losses of the State, specifically political chaos, civil war and internecine conflict; but she saw nothing in the opening scene to arouse such fears, and her expressed worries (296–9) are only about her father’s future care.

1247 and]
Q1(c)’s their is Certainly correct. To account for the compositor’s error we might suppose that his copy had the contraction yr, and that he mistook this for an ampersand, which in some hands would be by no means impossible (Greg, 1940, p. 160).

1247 all]
Crook (ed. 1907): Quite.

1247 ouerwatch]
Q2’s ouer-watcht supplies the omitted participial ending, and F’s o’re-watch’d smoothes the meter. Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): Worn out with watching. The word is so used in JC 4.3.241 (2249), and Craig (ed. 1901) compares Sidney’s Arcadia 2.11.[8] (ed. Feuillerat, 1:225), to pacifie with sleepe his ouer-watched eyes. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Kent is dead tired for want of sleep, having been traveling since he left Lear.

1248 Late]
Greg (1940, p. 160): Q1(c)’s Take is certainly correct. In the copy the initial t would be a minuscule…while k…was apt to be misread.

1248 vantage]
Schmidt (1875): Good opportunity (OED, sb. 4b, 5b). Deighton (ed. 1891): Advantage of your weariness.

1249 This…goodnight]
One line in both Q and F, and acceptable pentameter if the first two words are stressed. Foakes (ed. 1997) justifies the usual editorial division after lodging and the resultant short line: Kent makes himself comfortable in order to sleep and then makes his appeal to Fortune.

1249 lodging]
OED (vbl. sb. 4, trans. & fig., quoting this l.): Sc. the stocks. Not Gloucester’s house.

1249 goodnight]
Perrett (1904, p. 254): Though sunrise approaches, the remark is quite natural, since he is now going to sleep. Cf. n. 1240.

1250 Smile…more]
Though most eds. follow the F punctuation (see textual n.), Collier (ed. 1858) defends Q: Kent does not mean to ask Fortune to smile once more; but to smile, and when smiling, to turn her wheel once more. Deighton (ed. 1891), however: Though frowning upon me now, once again look upon me with favour. The sense is good either way. Dent (1981, F598.1) detects a proverb, Fortune can both smile and frown. Bevington (ed. 1980): Since Kent is at the bottom of Fortune’s wheel, any turning will improve his situation. Cf. 2181–4 for this idea, and the proverb Fortune’s wheel is ever turning (Dent, F617).

1250 wheele]
Page (ed. 1889), Fortune: Represented, allegorically, as a goddess with a wheel, the turns of which denote the vicissitudes of fortune. Verity (ed. 1897) cites Fluellen’s description of Fortune in H5 3.6.32–5 (1481–4). See H. R. Patch, The Goddess Fortuna in Medieval Literature (1927); Fraser (1962, pp. 46–60 and Pl. XVII, XX, XXII); Frederick Kiefer, Fortune and Elizabethan Tragedy (1982); and other studies cited by Soellner (1984, p. 275 n.), who finds allusions to Fortune’s wheel at 3136 and, more dubiously, at 1344 and 2796.

1250 sleepes.]
F’s omission of the stage-direction may be due to oversight, or perhaps the direction was thought unnecessary.

1251–72 Enter…Exit]
MacCracken (ed. 1914): Edgar’s entrance during Kent’s sleep, like the modern lowering and raising of a curtain, serves to convey the impression of lapse of time…between Scenes ii and iv. Dent (ed. 1927): We have got to learn in some way or other of Edgar’s intention to play the part of poor Tom o’ Bedlam, so that when we hear his name ([1819, 1824]) and see him ([1818]) we know with whom we are dealing (Hunter (ed. 1972).
Daniel (1877–9, p. 218): The time of this scene may be supposed the morning following his flight. No scene division is marked in Q or F. Bradley (1904, p. 260 n.): What modern editors call Scenes ii., iii., iv. of Act ii. are really one scene, for Kent is on stage through them all. Greg (1940, p. 435): To this conflation [which he calls irrational] there are two objections.…One is the improbability of the fugitive Edgar returning to the castle, even at daybreak, until he has assumed a disguise: the other is that it makes one continuous scene run from early dawn to nightfall. Koppel (1874, pp. 273–4; 1899, pp. 145–7) and Schmidt (ed. 1879), who first protested the conventional division on the grounds that the stage was not cleared, contend as well that the locale does not change to a wood or part of a heath (see textual n.) but remains before Gloucester’s house. So Goggin (ed. 1910): Most editors, following Pope, give the stage direction A wood, but the appearance of a wood close to Gloucester’s castle is rather in contradiction of [1604–5].…It seems best to imagine Edgar as coming away from the castle, whence he has just escaped; in the darkness and in his agitation he fails to observe Kent. Other eds. mark a change of scene precisely because they think the locale changes. Eccles (ed. 1792): Edgar would have stood the hazard of being taken by remaining so near the scene of danger. Muir (ed. 1952): Presumably Kent remained on the stage during Edgar’s speech, though he must not be supposed to be in the immediate neighborhood of the castle. Edgar’s hollow of a tree (1253) is in conflict with 1604–5 and so may imply a locale away from Gloucester’s house. Rosenberg (1972, p. 151): He could be in another part of the castle grounds. His speech, however, suggests longer flight: he has learned that no port, no place, is safe for him. Ellis (1974, p. 142): Edgar…attempted not to outrun his pursuers but to elude them.…When the search dies down, he steals from his hiding place [in a tree] close to the castle, fails to notice the motionless, sleeping Kent, delivers his soliloquy, and escapes.…[Scarce a bush (1605)] refers not to the immediate locality but to the outlying district. Orgel (ed. 1999): Kent remains onstage…but he and Edgar are clearly not part of the same scene.
Whether the locale changes or not, the continuing presence of Kent onstage in the stocks during Edgar’s soliloquy has seemed to call for explanation, since it does not correspond with normal Elizabethan dramaturgy (Hunter, ed. 1972, p. 320). Bradley (op. cit., p. 451): Kent is on the lower stage the whole time, Edgar in the so-called scene iii being on the upper stage or balcony. Greg (1940, pp. 301–2): The natural thing would be to discover [the stocks] on the back stage, and have Kent put in them there. Then at the end of the scene the traverse could be closed, Edgar could speak his short soliloquy before it, and it could be withdrawn once more to disclose Kent still in the stocks in the scene that follows.…But it is not how the action is arranged in the Folio, and it is not how Shakespeare wrote it, since two speeches (1203, 1212) and a Folio stage-direction (1217) indicate that the stocks are carried onto the stage. Greg therefore imagines that the play was written, not with the ordinary theatre in view, but for a plain stage with no alcove and probably no balcony. He does not say what stage that was, but rules out the Great Hall at Whitehall, where the court saw Lr. performed on 26 Dec. 1606, since there ample resources must have been to hand. Idem (1955, p. 386): It is, however, rather unlikely that Edgar would return to Gloucester’s castle, and the staging assumed in F would therefore be unexpected on a stage duly provided with an alcove and traverse. Adams (1948, p. 321) prefers the stocks in the alcove: The stage curtains close…to mark the passage of time. When next they are opened, it will be supposed that Kent has sat in the stocks all day. Soellner (1984, p. 278), citing 1253: Edmund may have entered from the…discovery space,…and he would presumably have remained upstage; cf. n. 1250. Bratton (ed. 1987) records 19th-c. use of groove scenery to mask Kent during the scene. The fact that F does not seem [in the SD at 1217] to make natural (Greg) use of the Globe’s stage resources may reflect re-writing for a different venue or for touring; see .
The usual solution now is to deny any problem. Creizenach (1909; tr. 1916, p. 360): The Elizabethan public was obviously quite unconscious that the stage was here serving to represent two different places at once; or, at any rate, they were not in the least offended by it. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 230): On an unlocalised stage I doubt its puzzling even a modern audience. Harrison (ed. 1937): Kent in the stocks at the back of the stage would not be noticed by Edgar in his passage from door to door across the front of the stage. Reynolds (1962, p. 87): The open stage as only a stage was an accustomed feature, inherited from the fifteenth century and earlier. The convention to be illustrated is: nothing was dramatically on it unless it was made use of or alluded to as present. Kent, whose presence is not acknowledged by Edgar is, by this convention, dramatically considered, just not there. Fraser (1962, p. 14): Sh. puts this legacy…of the medieval drama to novel use: by presenting Kent and Edgar at once together and apart in unrealistic defiance of the possible, and thus bringing the two good men, unjustly made wretched, together, he voices an appeal to a higher reality, an unspoken comment close to the heart of the drama. Mooney (1985, p. 156): Each…depicts the disastrous consequences of loyal behaviour and filial faithfulness in Lear’s shaken kingdom. Horsman (ed. 1973): The stage is big enough for Kent to sleep on one side while Edgar, on the other, is assumed to be in another, unspecified place. Hunter (1976, p. 28): That a character asleep and not seen by others counts as absent…is an eminently practical assumption. Dessen (1984, pp. 103–4): Directors usually use their lighting to black out Kent and highlight Edgar during his speech, thus preventing the audience from seeing them on stage simultaneously and thereby from recognizing the parallels between them, viz. that each has lost his identity and been subjected to injustice.…The stocks would then signal not a courtyard or other specific public locale but rather a general sense of imprisonment or bondage…just as Edgar would be assumed to be in flight, anywhere. Moreover, Edgar’s stage behavior in itself could have been a major signal for stage night. Bevington (1984, p. 121): The juxtaposition is symbolic, not illusionistic. Thomson (1988, p. 184): Kent is on stage asleep in the stocks throughout Edgar’s self-pitying speech, providing a silent but eloquent commentary. Foakes (1993, p. 189): The two are thus visually linked in degradation and as outcasts, anticipating their association in Act iii with Lear. Idem (ed. 1997): A powerful visual emblem of the enormous state produced by Lear’s folly and Edmund’s machinations. No one attempts to deal with Greg’s second objection, that during the continuous scene 2.3–2.4, lasting fewer than 330 lines, a whole day passes, from before dawning (1076) to the coming of night (1603).

1252–72 I…am]
Muir (1997, p. 148): An extreme case, perhaps a unique case, of rich internal harmonies provided by internal rhyme, alliteration, and consonance. Edgar has been confined to prose…so it is important that his first verse shall be a step towards his rehabilitation.

1252 heare]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 389): Perhaps a misreading of d as e. F’s heard is consistent with escapt (1254). Cf. n. 1045.

1252 proclaim’d]
Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): As an outlaw (OED, v. 2b, quoting this l.); see also n. 997. Eccles (ed. 1792): By the authority of Cornwall after that he had entered the castle. The idea was Gloucester’s: cf. 997, 1019–21.

1253 happie]
Hudson (ed. 1879): Propitious, or lucky (OED, a. 3). Cf. 2676. Craig (ed. 1901): I.e. which luckily presented itself. Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 56): Transferred epithet, or hypallage; see n. 1319.

1253 hollow…tree]
In several Bedlamite songs from the 17th c. Poor Tom reports that In an oken Inne I pound [poun, pawn] my skin: see Graves (1927, p. 23), Wells (1961, p. 312).

1254 Port]
See n. 1018.

1254 free]
Schmidt (1874): Not obstructed (OED, a. 11)—by guards.

1255 That]
Wright (ed. 1875): Loosely used for Where, the preposition in being omitted (OED, relative pron. 8). Page (ed. 1889): No place (is free), so that (OED, conj. 4b). Schmidt (ed. 1879): That = but that or but (OED, conj. 5). Schmidt’s construction would make not (1256) redundant.

1255 vnusuall]
Doran (1931, p. 110): The misprint vnusall in F…appears…to have been copied from…Q2. It could not have been set by the same Jaggard compositor, since in F it was set by Compositor E, a novice in 1623. Walton (1971, p. 283) doubts Q2’s influence: A common type of error, haplography. Here the second u has been forgotten on account of the first, citing other coincidental agreements between F and a quarto. Van Dam (1935, p. 31) finds other instances of syncopic pronunciation of -ual as -al in Elizabethan texts, including vsalley in the Henslowe Papers (ed. Greg, p. 105). Usall is not attested by OED.

1256 attend]
OED (v. 13b): Look out for…a future…event.

1256 while]
F’s Whiles is the old adverbial genitive (Abbott §137). Either form may mean during the time that or until (OED, While conj. 1, 3; Whiles 4, 5).

1257 am bethought]
OED (Bethink v. 9): Propose to oneself, resolve; (v. 11): To be bethought: to bethink onself, quoting this l. as its first ex.

1258–67 To…rosemary]
Pyle (1948, p. 453): The idea of Edgar’s disguise as a beggar may have been prompted by the Paphlagonian king’s plight [in Sidney’s Arcadia 2.10.3; see ], with alms his onelie sustenaunce. Muir (1951, p. 13): Edgar uses several phrases which recall Harsnett.…Harsnett mentions penurie [1603, p. 24; see ].…He speaks of what wind or weather so euer [p. 52; cf. p. 61], and of thunder [pp. 24, 72, 108, 133, 136, 175; see , , ], lightning [pp. 24, 73, 107, 136, 175; see , , ], and hail [pp. 133, 136; see , ]; he uses the word Bedlam [p. 116; cf. bedlamit, p. 86];…he tells how there were two needles thrust into the leg of one of the girls [p. 42, 214–16; cf. p. 93] and quotes Friswood Williams’s complaint that a priest did thrust a pinne into her shoulder [p. 214]; he tells us of a demoniac who thought he was rent with a thousand nayles [p. 73; see ] and another who would winch, skip, and curuet, hauing so many fiery needles in his skin at once [p. 93]; and he uses the phrase mortified patience [p. 41]. Bullough (1973, p. 284): The king and his son in Sidney are both poorely arayed, extreamely weather-beaten (2.10.1; see ); but (pp. 299–300) Edgar’s original in Sidney did not assume madness. No doubt Shakespeare recalled Hamlet and the possessions in Harsnett, where Marwood, like Edgar, lay abroad in the fieldes and was scared with lightning and thunder, that happened in the night; see . Salingar (1983, p. 145), less probably, suspects a source in Montaigne’s essay Of the Caniballes, where full gorged Frenchmen are contrasted with hunger-starved beggars at their gates (tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 1:229). On the analogy with Kent, see n. 531–7.
Traversi (1952, p. 59): His explicit references to penury and nakedness, to lunacy and to the potential presence of the beast in man will all find their realization later in the play. Rosenberg (1972, p. 151): Edgar almost certainly repeats…Kent’s onstage change into final disguise, or his new identity, too, may bewilder audiences.…The process of stripping before the audience…will anticipate Lear’s action. Bratton (ed. 1987): Mad Tom has become progressively more naked in productions. Foakes (ed. 1997): However, Edgar speaks of what he will do, and his abrupt emergence as Poor Tom at [1818] might be more startling if he remains in costume as Edgar here.

1258 most poorest]
On the double superlative see n. 84.

1259 in contempt of]
Verity (ed. 1897): So as to bring contempt on, or debase. Kittredge (ed. 1940): As if to show how contemptible a creature a man may be. Hunter (ed. 1972): Despising the pretensions of humanity (to be superior to the beasts). OED (Contempt sb. 1): The action of…holding or treating as of little account, or as vile and worthless; the mental attitude in which a thing is so considered, quoting this l.

1260 grime]
Begrime, blacken (OED, v., quoting this l.).

1261 else]
F’s elfe repairs Q’s misreading of long s. The verb is apparently Sh.’s coinage (OED quotes this l. as its first ex.); elf-locks, referred to in Rom. 1.4.90 (538), were locks of tangled hair by Superstition suppos’d to have been twisted by Elves, or Fairies (Theobald, ed. 1733). Craig (ed. 1901) finds in Dekker’s English Villanies Discovered (1608; ed. E. D. Pendry, 1967, pp. 290–1) a description of the Ab’ram cove (i.e., Bedlam beggar) as a lusty strong rogue…his hair long and filthily knotted, for he keeps no barber.

1261 haire]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 143) prefers F’s haires as picturesque exaggeration, of elfing all the hairs of his head.

1261 with]
F has in. Jennens (ed. 1770) thinks that Q’s word derives accidentally from the previous line; but the parallel may be intentional.

1262 presented]
Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Which I offer or present to the winds (OED, ppl. a., quoting as its earliest ex. Ven. 405, Sh.’s only other adjectival use). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Meeting them boldly. Craig’s (ed. 1901) assumed is unattested, and Muir’s (ed. 1952) exposed to view, as on a stage (OED, Present v. 7b) does not seem to fit the context.

1262 nakednes]
For the half-naked state of Bedlam beggars see n. 1265. The meaning destitution; bareness, poverty (OED, 2) seems usually to have been applied to places or things, not persons. Lascelles (1973, p. 76): An allusion to the nakedness of sinners in Doomsday paintings in English churches, waking a deep and powerful fear in the audience. Reibetanz (1974, p. 43): Rather, Sh. follows the practice of Renaissance iconographers in depicting Truth without clothes. Since the sources do not mention this detail, Tobin (1978, p. 39) notes the striking parallel of a beggar with belly naked in Apuleius’s Golden Ass. But any beggar might show skin.

1262 outface]
Schmidt (1875): To brave (OED, v. 2: Defy, quoting this l.). Mack (1965, p. 88): The peculiar frequency of this kind of locution (out + verb) in Lr. instances a pattern of pugnacity which pervades this tragedy, comparing 1622+3, 1624, and 2946 but not 1871.

1263 wind]
Taylor (1983, p. 370): F’s Windes was set by Compositor E, who had a particular weakness for errors involving addition or omission of terminal s. The same change occurs in his stint at 1828, but not at 630, 1620, 1670, 1699, or 1730; Compositor B also makes this change at 1656. Sh. generally prefers the singular by about 3:1, and in Q of this play by 12:2.

1263 persecution]
On F’s plural see the prev. n. OED (1c): Persistent or continued injury or annoyance from any source, quoting this l.

1264 proofe]
Schmidt (1875): Knowledge gathered by experience (OED, sb. 5). Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Example.

1265 Bedlam beggers]
OED (Bedlam): ME Bedlem = Bethlem, Bethlehem; applied to the Hospital of St. Mary of Bethlehem, in London, founded as a priory in 1247.…In 1330 it is mentioned as an hospital, and in 1402 as a hospital for lunatics…; in 1346 it was received under the protection of the city of London, and on the Dissolution of the Monasteries, it was granted to the mayor and citizens, and in 1547 incorporated as a royal foundation for the reception of lunatics. (5): An inmate of Bethlehem Hospital…; spec. one of the discharged, but often only half-cured, patients…, who were licensed to beg, wearing as a badge a tin plate on their left hand or arm; called also bedlam-beggars. Cf. 465, 2176+5. Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): These were patients who were discharged…because the space in the hospital was very limited; and they were, as now, allowed to remain only one year. Staunton (ed. 1859): The sympathy excited by these unfortunates, occasioned many sturdy vagabonds to counterfeit and exaggerate their dress and peculiarities. Berlin (1968, p. 203): They were the most wretched members of the underworld. These beggars, both legitimate and rogue, were often called Abraham Men, after the leprous beggar Lazarus in Luke 16:20–22 who went to Abraham’s bosom (OED). Steevens (ed. 1778) quotes from a description of such beggars in Dekker’s Belman of London (1608, sig. D2) based partly on Harman’s Caueat for Commen Cvrsetors (2nd ed., 1567, sigs. D1v–2). This is Dekker: Of all the mad Rascalls…the Abraham-man is the most fantasticke: The fellow (quoth this old Lady of the Lake vnto me) that sat halfe naked (at table to day) from the girdle vpward, is the best Abraham-man that euer came to my house, and the notablest villaine: he sweares he hath beene in Bedlam, and will talke frantickly of purpose: you see pinnes stuck in sundrie places of his naked flesh, especially in his armes, which paine hee gladly puts himselfe to (being indeed no torment at all, his skin is either so dead with some fowle disease, or so hardened with weather, onely to make you beleeue he is out of his wits) he calls himselfe by the name of poore Tom, and comming neere any body, cries out, Poore Tom is a-cold. Of these Abraham-men, some be exceeding merry, and doe nothing but sing songs, fashioned out of their owne braines; some will dance, others will doe nothing but either laugh or weepe; others are dogged, and so sullen both in looke and speech, that spying but a small company in a house, they boldly and bluntly enter, compelling the seruants through feare to giue them what they demaund.…The Vpright-man and the Rogue are not terribler enemies to poultry ware, than poore Tom is: neither does any man shift cleane linnen oftner than hee does his wenches. Knight (ed. 1840) quotes from Harrison’s Description (in Holinshed, 1577, pt. 3, ch. 5, fols. 106v–7; 1587, pt. 2, ch. 10, pp. 183–4), who reports that in sixty years the trade has grown to 10,000 persons of both sexes who, among other practices, apply irritants to their skins to make sores; Knight also quotes from Aubrey’s MSS (Lansdowne 226): They wore about their necks a great horn of an ox in a string or bawdry, which, when they came to a house, they did wind, and they put the drink given them into this horn, whereto they put a stopple. Similar descriptions are found in Awdely’s Fraternity of Vacabondes (1565, sig. A2), Dekker’s O per se O (1612, sigs. M2–3), and Holme’s Academy of Armory (1688, 3.3, p. 161). See A. L. Beier, Masterless Men: The Vagrancy Problem in England 1560–1640 (1985). For arguments that Tom o’Bedlam was not a sympathetic figure but a repulsive, fearsome kind of con-man, and for a survey of literature about him, see Carroll (1987, pp. 431–4; 1996, pp. 190–4). Idem (1987, p. 441; 1996, p. 203): As Poor Tom, Edgar has performed the role of suffering and marginalization, but has also profoundly experienced it, just as the counterfeit madmen of the period may have feigned self-mutilations that were essentially indistinguishable from the real thing.
The Q1 title page advertises Edgar’s sullen and assumed humor of Tom of Bedlam as one of the play’s attractions. Dekker uses the word sullen to describe Bedlam beggars (see above), apparently meaning something like gloomy, ill-humored, or moody (OED, a. 1). Bratton (ed. 1987): Edgar’s assumed madness was seen by the eighteenth-century audience as chiefly comic, as it sometimes was in the 19th c.; In the twentieth century Tom has been taken much more seriously, as a parallel to Lear’s descent to a natural state. Leggatt (1996) discusses Jacobean treatment of madness, real and theatrical. (P. 137): Other plays of the period cope with the horror of madness by stylizing and distancing it; King Lear confronts it directly.

1265 roring voyces]
Muir (1957, p. 151): Harsnett (1603, pp. 38, 45, 72, 127) describes frequently the roaring of the devils possessing the demoniacs.

1266 Strike]
Dyce (ed. 1865): Strike into (OED, v. 36d, Thrust…into, quoting this l.).

1266 numb’d]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Because exposed to the cold. Greg (1940, p. 160): The insertion of and…after numb’d is an obvious necessity; see textual n.

1266 mortified]
Wright (ed. 1875): Deadened, insensible (OED, ppl. a. 3, quoting only this l. and JC 2.1.324 [968]); the word is also in Harsnett (1603, p. 41; see n. 1258–67). See the quotation from Dekker in n. 1265.

1266 bare]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 175): Bare adds an effective touch to the picture, and the F compositor may have omitted it accidentally. Halio (ed. 1992): But accenting -ed in mortified makes the metre regular.

1267 Pies]
Q1(c)’s Pins is certainly correct (Greg, 1940, p. 160).

1267 wodden]
A common spelling variant of wooden (OED), found also at 1285 (F) and in Tmp. 3.1.62 (1308). The usual sp. in Shn. texts is woodden.

1267 prickes]
Steevens (ed. 1778): Skewers (OED, sb. 14). See the quotation from Dekker in n. 1265. The details of needles and nails in the skin found by Muir (ed. 1952; 1957, p. 151; see n. 1258–67) in Harsnett (1603, pp. 42, 73, 93, 214–16) refer to the demoniacs, not to beggars.

1267 sprigs]
The word does not appear elsewhere in Sh.; Muir (ed. 1952) thinks it may derive from Florio.

1267 rosemary]
Weis (ed. 1993): Along with other ever-greens such as ivy and laurel, rosemary was a common emblem worn at funerals to denote the immortality of the soul, hence its association with dead bodies, comparing Rom. 4.4.79–80 (2659).

1268 obiect]
Delius (ed. 1854): Appearance. OED (sb. 3b): Something which on being seen excites a particular emotion…; a sight, spectacle, quoting 3194.

1268 frame]
Greg (1940, p. 160): Q1(c)’s from is certainly correct, and clearly derived from inspection of the copy, since it only becomes obvious when a further emendation is made as in F (Farmes for seruice).

1268 low]
Schmidt (1874): Humble, mean.

1268 seruice]
All eds. but Weis (ed. 1993) and Halio (ed. 1994) accept F’s Farmes. Doran (1935, p. 141 n.): Farmes perhaps thought to be saruis [spelled with long s] by the Q compositor. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 389), alternatively: The copy for Q may have had ferms, and the compositor may have taken it to be seruis. The spelling ferm(e) is not found in Shn. texts. Weis, explaining Q: Lowly, poor servants, perhaps tenant farmers.

1269 pelting]
Peck (1740, p. 242): Paltry (OED). The phrase pelting village is found repeatedly in North’s Plutarch (Hunter, ed. 1869; Craig, ed. 1901), in Taylor’s Workes 1.124 (Halliwell, ed. 1865), and elsewhere. Verity (ed. 1897): The point of the epithet and of low is that these Bedlamites sought out lowly habitations like sheepcotes where they could terrorise the few inmates.

1269 sheep-coates]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 175): F’s Sheeps-Coates is an obvious slip. Tovey (ed. 1896): Shepherd’s cottage. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Like milles, often distant from any village.

1270 Sometime]
F changes to Sometimes. Wright (ed. 1875): The two forms of the word are used indifferently. But Q is consistent: cf. 697, 1232, 2347+40. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 143): Q’s exact symmetry in this matter is not necessarily a guarantee of authenticity. Werstine (1983, p. 285): But asymmetry produced by the addition or deletion of final s in a line set by Compositor E almost guarantees that the Folio is here corrupt, since the addition or deletion of final s was habitual for the compositor.

1270 bans]
Schmidt (1874): Curse[s] (OED, Ban sb. 6, quoting this l.). MacCracken (ed. 1914): To terrify country people. Tovey (ed. 1896), less probably: Or an exorcism, to keep off evil from the house, as the opening lines of a Tom-a-Bedlam song [see n. 464–5] suggest: From the hog…defend ye.

1270 prayers]
Heilman (1948, p. 259): Edgar’s pretended madness takes, in large part, the form of religious mania, citing his repeated warnings of the foul fiend (1827, 1833, 1841, 1860, 1878, 1895, 1910, 2005, 2248), abridgement of the decalogue (1860–3), catalogues of sins (1865–78), and names of devils (1895, 1919–22, 2004, 2014+12, 2248+2–+4). Harsnett’s Declaration, their source, is of course a study in religous mania.

1271 charitie]
OED (sb. 4b): As manifested in action: spec. alms-giving, quoting 1841.

1271 poore…Tom]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Edgar practises the Bedlam beggar’s whine. Cf. [1832]. Harrison (ed. 1948): Edgar rehearses the names which a bedlam calls himself. See nn. 464–5, 1265. The name poore Tom appears again at 1819, 1832, 1841, 1908, 1925, 2014+11, 2032, 2209, 2241, 2247, 2248+1, and 2265.

1271 Tuelygod]
Since neither this name nor Q1(c)’s Turlygod is known elsewhere, thought has been free in finding substitutes. Hanmer (ed. 1743): Turlurú, a foole, a gull, a ninnie, a patch (Florio, 1611). Warburton (ed. 1747): Turlupin, one of a sect of 14th-c. heretics, a new species of gipsies,…a fraternity of naked beggars; they are said to have maintained that one ought not to be ashamed of anything that is natural (OED, 1, earliest citation 1639) and to have practiced nudity by way of returning to the condition of man in Paradise (Tovey, ed. 1896). Heath (1765, p. 331): This name of Turlupin was known only in France and Germany. Douce (1807, 2:148): Turlygood (unattested); Turlupino and Turluru are old Italian terms for a fool or madman; and the Flemings had a proverb, As unfortunate as Turlupin and his children. The Italian word and the proverb seem to derive from the farcical character Turlupin created in Paris by the famous Henri Legrand, probably after 1615; the character, a roguish valet, is in any case unlike a Bedlam beggar; cf. Cotgrave (1611): Turlupin: m. A grub, mushrome, start-up, new-nothing, man of no value—again, not a pertinent sense. Nares (1822): Sh.’s term is too remote in form from the other, to be a corruption from it. Collier (ed. 1843): Turlygood is perhaps a corruption of Thoroughlygood—but again the epithet seems without point. Foakes (ed. 1997), however: Truelygood…makes a kind of sense, though no explanation is necessary if he is putting on the cries of madness. Mackay (1887, p. 430), as usual, turns to Gaelic: Guid or guidh…signifies earnest entreaty.…Tuir means…to chant dolefully, and le, with; whence Tuir-le-guid, anglicized into Turlygood, is one who beseeches or importunes for alms, with a doleful pertinacity. Smith (1946, p. 168): Turlygod looks like a perfectly acceptable anglicized form of Ir. Toirdhealbhach god, of which the first element is the Irish proper name, often anglicized Turlough or Turley, and the second element the epithet god, which means stammering [n.: or dumb]…[and] may even have been confused by careless Elizabethans with the epithet gealt, geilt, madman. So Musgrove (1981, p. 11): Harman (p. 113) records that there is above an hundred of Irishmen and women that wander about to beg for their living who have come over within these two years.…If the name does mean dumb Turley he could alternatively be a dummerer (Harman, p. 91), a rogue who pretends to be dumb—which Edgar never does. Muir (ed. 1952): None of these senses is satisfactory. Brooke (ed. 1947): It may be a form of twirligig (whirligig). A word grinagod (also grinagog) means one who is always grinning, on the analogy of which turligod would come to be one always whirling or being whirled about, the sport of chance. Stone (1980, p. 195): Tirl(er)y-gaud, poor good-for-nothing: OED defines tirlery as: ?Whirling, flighty, trifling, trumpery. Wells & Taylor (1987, pp. 515–16): Q1(u)’s Tuelygod possibly means towelly-god, referring to the beggar’s loincloth, or sickly, weak god, from tewly; god has an obvious pertinence to the beggar’s cry, and suggests the numinous awe accorded to the naked, half-human outcast by most cultures. This awe is not evident in contemporary descriptions: see n. 1265. From other stems—tirlie (tirlery etc.), turl (tirl), trely, turely, tuery, truely, trull, trowel, troll, trolly(-lolly), gord, and grod—Wells & Taylor can find no probable explanation of Q1(c)s Turlygod, though Truelygod is conceivable and troll—which could mean to ramble,…, or to sing in the manner of a round or catch…—seems relevant. No one has suggested god to be an easy misreading of goe or gad, either word suggesting wandering; the latter verb, used in Rom. 4.2.16 (2441), is apparently derived from gadling, vagabond (OED, Gad v.2 1; Gadling sb.2 3). Davidson (1998, p. 314), improbably: Stenographic spelling, yielding Poor two-legged Poor Tom! Whether it is correct or not, Q1(c)’s change to Turlygod is clearly deliberate, and to Greg (1940, p. 160) seems guaranteed by F: moreover, the spelling of [Q1(u)] does not look natural. Either form may be a proper name or nickname now lost, with no more meaning than those of some of Harsnett’s and Edgar’s fiends; cf. 1919–22.

1271–2 Tom…am]
Walker (1860, 3:277): Rhyming couplet. So Ellis (1869–89; 1871, p. 953), Kökeritz (1953, p. 224: dialectal), and Cercignani (1981, p. 114). Halio (ed. 1992): Probably dialectal…; Edgar doubtless means to disguise his voice as well as his person.

1272 something]
Dent (1981, S623) cites the proverb Somewhat (Something) is better than nothing. Wells (ed. 2000): At least I shall have some identity.

1272 Edgar…am]
Johnson (ed. 1765): I am out-lawed, dead in law; I have no longer any political existence. Ritson (1783, p. 169), agreeing with Capell (1783, 1.2.158) and followed by most eds.: In assuming this character…I may preserve myself; as Edgar I am inevitably gone. Moberly (ed. 1876): As Edgar I am annihilated. Lee (ed. 1908): I have rid myself of his likeness. Brooke (ed. 1947): As Edgar I am nothing. Graves (1927, p. 16) proposes that here Edgar sings the 17th-c. Bedlamite song, From the Hagg & Hungry Goblin, which Graves thinks may be Shakespearean, to give scene-shifters time perhaps to ready Kent’s stocks for the next scene. Wells (1961, p. 312): The song is too long, is not known to be Sh.’s, and if performed would probably have appeared in one of the play’s texts.

1273–1613 Enter…Exeũt]
Houghton (ed. 1957): The first of those very great scenes that have made King Lear supreme even among Shakespeare’s tragedies for depth and width.…Lear’s final speech ([1564–86]) may be considered as dramatic poetry to achieve a height even beyond the soliloquies of Hamlet.
