David (1935, p. 44): Lear’s persistent questions flog the emotions ever to a greater agony of intensity. Harbage (1963, p. 414): In this scene the shape of the tragedy alters in our eyes; whereas previously we have been weighing circumstances and viewing Lear’s reverses at least partly in terms of their provocation, we now cease to do so. Our emotions instruct us that the disaster is not traceable to measurable faults, or misunderstandings, of unfortunate circumstances, but to immeasurable evil. Skillan (ed. 1967): For the actor, this is the most difficult scene in the play. Quinn (ed. 1970): With this scene the play moves inexorably into the tragic sphere, asking unanswerable questions about the nature of evil and of man. Hunter (ed. 1972): The climactic scene at the end of the protasis or exposition of the play. Beginning at the level of the affront to Kent, the tension mounts through Lear’s dispute with Regan and Cornwall—conducted via Gloucester and so avoiding full-scale confrontation—and reaches its first full climax when Gonerill arrives and we have the full orchestration of I.i repeated, answering the I give you of the opening with a conclusive We take. This dispute only dies into another kind of climax as Lear’s speeches expand to prophetic frenzy, as the storm thunders closer, and as Lear rushes to join the cosmic furies, and the wicked withdraw to safety. Bieman (1968) and Taylor (1985) comment progressively on the scene. Styan (1967, pp. 111–12, 184–6) discusses the scene’s crescendos of emotional pressure, and Howard (1984, pp. 123–4) its dialectic of a power struggle.

1273 Enter King]
See n. 538. Wilson (ed. 1960): Sh. does not tell us what has happened to the knights, but when Kent asks at l. [1336], the Fool hints that they have thought it better to leave the king. This is doubtful speculation: it is evident from 1524–5 that Lear expects to maintain all hundred knights (who should therefore be still in attendance) or, from 1557, as the best of a bad bargain, at least half of them; and cf. 1589, 1609, both of which indicate a sizable train. We might as easily imagine that they are waiting nearby, offstage, much as they were at the end of 1.5. Here no one questions their whereabouts for another 63 lines, and the play offers not the slightest indication of where they might in fact be. Only after both daughters refuse them entrance is Lear clearly separated from his knights, some of whom later search after him; cf. 2075–6. There is no reason to bring onstage here more than Q’s one Knight (F’s one Gentleman) to represent them, and even he is mute after 1334 though he may remain until Lear’s exit. See also n. 874. Greg (1940, p. 434 n.) proposes an alternative explanation that Lear’s knights are pursuing rather than accompanying him, and that references to their presence are anticipatory. Some of them are apparently pursuing him at 2075–6, but that is after Lear has become separated from all his followers (except the Fool) in the storm, between this scene and 3.2. At this point in 2.4 we would naturally expect (if we were led to think about it) that the knights were performing their main function of accompanying and protecting Lear on his journey from Regan’s house to Gloucester’s. Only the Fool’s later impromptu (and perhaps merely hypothetical) routine about how followers ought to abandon a weak patron may suggest otherwise. All other evidence (see above) indicates that Lear believes them still to be in attendance, and there is no indication or reason given in the play to support Greg’s conjecture that they have somehow become separated from him. Foakes (1993, p. 193): The absence of [knights] from ii.4…may be to reduce the impact of Regan’s anxiety about Lear’s riotous followers. The followers are never shown as riotous, however; see n. 586–872. Idem (ed. 1997): Visually it is as if his train has already been reduced.…At [2075] Lear has regained some thirty-five or thirty-six knights. Regained seems to imply that some were already lost at this point, a notion without evidence to support it; see nn. 1336, 1441.
On the location of the scene, see nn. 875, 1251. Kittredge (ed. 1940): This scene takes place on the day that was dawning at the end of Scene ii—on the same day, therefore, as Scene iii. Cf. n. 873. Buck (ed. 1907): The time is now late in the afternoon. During the interval Kent had been asleep in the stocks [and presumably Cornwall and Regan are sleeping late? Cf. 1062, 1363]. At the end of this scene [1603, 1612] we find that night has already set in.
Eds. have offered four explanations for Lear’s going to Gloucester’s house. (1) Johnson (ed. 1765): He seems to have gone [from Regan’s] to visit Glo’ster while Cornwall and Regan might [in the interim] prepare to entertain him. To this Eccles (ed. 1792) sensibly objects that Lear would have told them so, hence they would not have subsequently tried to avoid him by going to Gloucester’s. Eccles therefore concludes (2) that Lear had always intended to visit Gloucester, and had written him of his plans. But it is doubtful that Lear did so write: see n. 875. (3) Clarkes (ed. 1868): Lear has come to Gloster’s castle, instead of going to his daughter Regan’s residence, having heard from his attendant gentleman that the Duke and Duchess of Cornwall have left their home and repaired thither. The attendant gentleman is of course not Kent, who has been ordered to attend Regan and Cornwall rather than return to Lear, but the Knight who enters here with Lear. Horsman (ed. 1973): The Gentleman has gone on ahead after Kent; finding them away, he has returned to tell Lear, who has reached only the intermediate place where Gloucester lives. See [875]. (4): Tyrwhitt (in Steevens, ed. 1778): Lear comes to the earl of Glocester’s, in consequence of his having been at the duke of Cornwall’s, and having heard there, that his son and daughter were gone to the earl of Glocester’s.
Many eds. accept (4), though (3) is equally possible. Option (4) would require Lear to ride a double journey as long and almost as hard as Kent and Oswald (who was Stewd in his hast) from Albany’s to Cornwall’s house, and then as Cornwall and Regan from their house to Gloucester’s. Since the latter arrive in the night before dawn and Lear not until sometime the next day, he might have traveled the whole circuit, arriving well after them; or he may have traveled the shorter distance (3) slowly because of his age. Greg (1940, p. 435): The company has either journeyed comparatively slowly (in spite of [878–9]…) or perhaps baited (at Cornwall’s) on the way.

1274–5 Tis…messenger]
Greg (1940, p. 393) compares Leir 1355–6: I wonder that the Messenger doth stay, Whom we dispatcht for Cambria so long since; see . Cf. 2851.

1274 so]
Deighton (ed. 1891): In this sudden and mysterious manner.

1274 hence]
F corrects to home. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 390): Perhaps a misreading of home: (i) e for o, (ii) nc for m, the latter a minim misreading. Or possibly the Q MS read thence.

1275 messenger]
F’s Messengers is apparently erroneous. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 175): Lear had sent only one messenger—the disguised Kent. See 875; on scansion see n. 1067.

1276, 1333 Knight]
F’s Gent. and Gen. are doubtless just different appellations for the same small-part actor (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 83).

1276, 1333 I learn’d]
He must have learned this at Cornwall’s castle while attending (or preceding) Lear there. See n. 1273.

1277 night before]
I.e., the night just past. The Clarkes (ed. 1868) note how the phrase, making the events of the past three scenes seem already remote, prepares the audience to accept the rapid progress of dramatic time indicated by 1603 and 1612.

1277 purpose]
F’s added in them could have made an even more regular pentameter after was.

1278 his]
F’s this is consistent with them. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 390): The [Q] compositor may have failed to notice a t in the copy.

1278 remoue]
Schmidt (1875): Change of place (OED, sb. 5: esp. one’s place of residence).

1280 How]
See nn. 96, 100. F’s Ha means roughly the same, perhaps expressing surprise more than shocked incredulity; see n. 592.

1281 Kent.…Lord.]
It may be that the Q compositor overlooked this line, but Kent’s silence in Q is more eloquent than this feeble reply in F, which looks suspiciously like sophistication.

1282–5 Ha…neatherstockes]
Q’s false verse betrays the inexperience of the Q compositor in setting dramatic texts. See . Crane (1952, p. 163): In this scene and 3.2, only the Fool speaks prose, removing himself from direct participation in the events he witnesses. His comments retain their ironic appositeness, but they are uttered as by a creature apart, barely heard and not at all heeded.

1282 looke]
F’s omission is apparently accidental.

1282 crewell]
OED (Crewel sb. 3): A thin worsted yarn…used for tapestry and embroidery; also formerly for making fringes, laces, vestments, hosiery, etc. Wilson (ed. 1960): Worn by menials, comparing 1090. F’s Cruell was an alternate spelling in the 16th-18th c., but crewell ceased in the 15th c. to be a variant sp. of cruel. The pun is first pointed out by Steevens (in Johnson, ed. 1765, 8:2K5v), and many other contemporary examples of it are supplied in Steevens (eds. 1773, 1778), Halliwell (ed. 1865), Kemshead (ed. 1875), Verity (ed. 1897), and Craig (ed. 1901).

1282–5 Horses…neatherstockes]
Muir (1951, p. 14) compares Harsnett, as men leade Beares by the nose, or Iacke an Apes in a string (1603, p. 106 [107]; see ), and his word neather-stockes (pp. 100, 199), used elsewhere by Sh. only once.

1283 heeles]
All eds. follow F’s heads; though horses may be hobbled by the heels, they are tied by the head. Anticipated by Thirlby (MS notes, 1722–33), Jennens (ed. 1770): The fool makes a progression downwards, from the head…to the legs. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 390): The compositor may have misread the a as e and the d as l, citing several exx. of such errors.

1284 bit’h loynes]
I.e., around the waist. Though the loins were considered the seat of generative power and an erotic zone (Williams, 1994), the word does not refer to the genitals, as is sometimes supposed, but to the region of the body between the ribs and hips (OED, sb. 1a) that could be girdled (girded, girthed). Kittredge (ed. 1940) quotes Brome, The Damoiselle 2.1 (ed. Pearson, 1:396): tyed up by the Loines, like a Monkey to the Bed-post.

1284 mans]
F’s man is probably a simple error, though Hogan (1962, p. 73 n.) suggests that the omission of ’s may be due to a crowded line.

1285 lusty at legs]
OED (Lusty a. 5a): Vigorous. Steevens (ed. 1778) finds a doubtful pun: Lustiness anciently meant sauciness (OED, a. 6: Insolent). Becket (1815, 1:148) finds puns on corpulent (OED, 10, first recorded 1772) and sturdy, resolute, neither sense giving a reason for stocking. Caldecott (MS notes, 1813–33): Prances too high, carries hmself too haughtily. Thirlby (MS notes, 1733–47): Does this hint at Kent’s tripping up the Steward’s heels? So Deighton (ed. 1891): Too free in the use of…(sc. in kicking), and Budd (ed. 1935): In tripping and kicking Oswald. Most probably, Kittredge (ed. 1940), followed by several eds.: Too vigorous in using his legs; too much of a vagabond. See n. 1220+3–+4. So Gardner (ed. 1969): At running away; from service (Kermode, in Evans, ed. 1974). Skillan (ed. 1967): Over-strong because of his haste to deliver lear’s message to reg., adding, He laughs cynically to see what kent’s eagerness and swiftness to carry out lear’s orders has led him into. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Possible sexual innuendo of chasing after women; so McCall (1977, p. 127). Craig (ed. 1901) finds the phrase in several contemporary plays, and Dent (1981, L192.1) calls it proverbial.

1285 at]
OED (At prep. 9): Expressing the relation of an attribute to a particular place or part, quoting this l. Cf. 1233. Furness (ed. 1880) prints at’, unnecessarily assuming an absorption of the definite article. Abbott (§90): The is…omitted after prepositions in adverbial phrases. Cf. Franz §268, and 2076, 2170.

1285 neatherstockes]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Stockings (OED), as distinct from upper stockes or (ed. 1778) overstockes, names for breeches. Kittredge (ed. 1940) gives exx. of contemporary puns on stocks and stockings.

1286–7 Whats…mistooke]
F’s division of the verse line is not due to column width, and seems simple error.

1286 Whats]
See n. 540. Crook (ed. 1907): What kind of man can he be?

1287–8 so…to]
On the omission of as see n. 229–30.

1287 place]
Delius (ed. 1854) and several later eds. find a pun on the two senses of location (in the stocks) and position (as king’s messenger). Cf. 1221–3.

1287 mistooke]
On the curtailed form of the participle see n. 103. Sh. uses this form slightly more often than mistaken (15:11).

1290 sonne]
See n. 46–7.

1294+1–1296 No…I]
Much has been made of the small differences between Q and F. Steevens (ed. 1773, 1:E3) is reluctant to restore the pair of Q speeches in 1294+1, omitted from F: Would any new idea be gained? Idem (ed. 1793), having made the restoration: The combined lines, as they are collected from discordant copies,…were not all designed to be preserved, and therefore cannot…be arranged as verse. Accidental omission by scribe or compositor is possible, since the speech prefixes and initial words duplicate those of previous lines; or possibly the speeches were deleted from the playbook behind F as being merely repetitive, though 1291–6 are intentionally repetitive anyway in both Q and F, and little is gained by the deletion. Indeed Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 176), who ordinarily would suspect the two speeches to be actors’ expansions, is unable to do so here: Observe the climax effect: first a simple No—Yes ([1291–2]), then a longer statement and counter-statement, then a still longer one, and then oaths: it seems to me to bear the stamp of Shakespearian calculation. Halio (ed. 1992, p. 268): The accumulation is excessive: Evidently the cut was made to allow for the [F] addition.…Within the puerile, see-saw argument…effective for three interchanges in either Q or F, a fourth seems tedious and unnecessary. The addition of F’s 1296 may be suspected of being non-authorial playhouse intervention: unlike Q, it adds a jocular note to Lear’s dismay—Delius (ed. 1854): Kent humorously tops Lear’s oath (Ger.)—and disrupts the opening pentameter line of Lear’s speech. Still, sardonic humor is typical enough of Kent—this is a characteristic reply (Delius, 1876, p. 135); F’s 1296 adds yet another symmetrical exchange of speeches, and the result is a good, if different, pentameter line, so that 1296 may be authorial. Herford (ed. 1899): It is part of the original exchange of speeches, but accidentally omitted from Q: The compositor’s eye seems to have been misled by the similarity of Kent’s speech to Lear’s [1295]. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): 1296 is thematically relevant: These oaths are not merely in accord with [116–19, 172–3], and the pre-Christian atmosphere with which these Roman and Greek deities are meant to give the play, but amount here, also, to a jest upon the situation; for the king swears by the chief male god, Jupiter, and Kent contradicts with an oath by the equally supreme feminine power of Juno, capable through cunning of frustrating Jove, as Lear’s rule is frustrated by that of his daughters. Similarity between Lear’s daughters and Juno is far from obvious. Doran (1931, p. 53): It is improbable that each of the printers [of Q, F] would have omitted a different portion of the text. It is more likely that Shakespeare, possibly having By Juno suggested to him when he read By Jupiter, decided to put in Kent’s oath for the sake of the antithesis. Either he at the same time deleted two other speeches in order to preserve the regularity of the meter, or the printer of the folio mistook the new line ([1296]) as a substitution for lines [1294+1] instead of as an addition to be interposed between the two halves of Lear’s line [1295, 1297]. The reviser need not have been Sh., of course. Thus Van Dam (1935, pp. 67–8): The F addition…must be a theatrical interpolation, for it is clearly out of place, it makes a farce of an earnest dialogue, and is inserted for the amusement of the audience. It is such a kind of insertion as Hamlet warned against in Ham. 3.2.37–45 (1886–92). Elton (1966, p. 189) finds a possible religious significance: The traditional dissension of Jupiter and Juno…anticipates…the disintegration of Lear’s pagan pantheon;…the clash…may foreshadow some impediment in the workings of a helpful pagan providence. This interpretation loads a facetious retort with much serious meaning for an audience to apprehend. Brown (ed. 1976): The cross talk often has comic effect.…But Lear grows more emphatic, or more weightily in command. Similarly Foakes (ed. 1997): Kent’s swearing by Juno is a more powerful rejoinder. Warren (1978, p. 98), followed by Wells (1983, p. 15): F’s omission of 1294+1 is presumably for a purpose (unstated) and the addition of 1296 appears to make up for the omission, hence the conflation of F and Q has no authority. But the assumptions that the two changes were made simultaneously, one in relation to the other, and by Sh., are not necessarily true, let alone provable.

1297 durst]
See n. 398.

1298 would…could]
F’s inversion is anticlimactic.

1299 vpon respect]
Warburton (ed. 1747) and most eds.: Respect, for one in honourable employment, i.e. as the king’s messenger (Edwards, 1758, p. 206), and ultimately respect towards the king who is represented in his messenger (Heath, 1765, p. 332). Cf. 1209. Malone (ed. 1790, 10:681) generalizes the meaning, considering respect as personified. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Elliptical for that which should command respect. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Upon a respectable person (like a king’s messenger). Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974), alternatively: Against the whole principle of subordination. A few eds. follow Chedworth (1805, pp. 317–18): Deliberately, upon consideration, citing Jn. 4.2.214 (1939).

1300 Resolue me]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Inform me, satisfy my desire to know (OED, v. 11, 17b). Kemshead (ed. 1875): Explain to me (OED, 15c). Joseph (ed. 1966): Let me be certain. Cf. 430. The use of pronoun object with dependent clause is common for all senses.

1300 modest]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Reasonable. Wright (ed. 1875): Moderate, well-measured (OED, a. 4). Schmidt (1875): Neither going beyond nor falling short of what is required, corresponding, satisfactory, becoming; specifically of this line, as much haste as may consist with telling the full truth. Rolfe (ed. 1880): Cf. [2751], where modest is exactly explained by Nor…so, that is, not too much nor too little, but just the measure (Latin modus). OED (2): Unobtrusive, quoting this l. Muir (ed. 1952): Becoming, sober. Skillan (ed. 1967): Lear really means…in the shortest form.

1301 may’st]
Though there is no reason to doubt the Q reading, virtually all eds. adopt F’s subjunctive might’st.

1301 purpose]
Q makes excellent sense: resolve upon the performance of (OED, v. 3; Stone, 1980, p. 218), or possibly intend (OED 5, to mean (well or ill) to any one; 6, to design or intend for some purpose). F’s alteration to impose, followed by virtually all eds., may have been made for metrical reasons, as in part is the new Oxford eds.’ propose, a doublet of purpose (1986 Q; Wells, ed. 2000). Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 516): None of Shakespeare’s other 172 uses of purpose has the accentuation Q requires.…Propose…is [also] better sense (display, propose for acceptance). F’s impose also makes sense, but seems less likely to lie behind Q’s error. In fact Sh. uses purpose as a verb only 23 times, once with the accent apparently (or possibly) on the second syllable (1H6 3.1.7 [1211]). This accentuation was familiar in the rhyming proverb Man purposes, God disposes (OED, Purpose 5; Dispose v. 7), and was made easy by the contemporary [oz] pronunciation of the verb (see Dobson, 1957, pp. 848, 928).

1301 vsage]
Schmidt (1875): Treatment (OED, sb. 7b, quoting this l. as its first ex.).

1302 Coming]
I.e., thou coming; cf. n. 1195. Abbott (§377): I.e. since thou comest, explaining, The participle is sometimes so separated from the verb that it seems to be used absolutely.

1302 vs]
Harrison (ed. 1948), following Kittredge (ed. 1940): The royal we. Foakes (ed. 1997): For the last time; Cornwall and Regan have already taken over this speech habit of power.

1304 commend]
Schmidt (1874): To commit, to deliver (OED, v. 1).

1304 letters]
See n. 875.

1306 kneeling]
Tovey (ed. 1896): As I knelt. Kneeling might be a substantive, in opposition to duty, or a participle agreeing with duty or me (my = of me), but is best taken absolutely, comparing Tro. 1.2.286 (444).

1306 reeking]
Schmidt (1875): To emit vapor or steam (OED, ppl. a. 2d, quoting this l. as its first ex.).

1306 Post]
Strictly speaking, from the 16th c. onwards a royal messenger riding, in relay, horses stationed or appointed in places [posts] at suitable distances along the post-roads (OED, sb.2 1); but also applied to similar bearers of messages or letters in ancient times (OED, 2b). Cf. 2069, 2727.

1307 Stewd]
OED (Stew v.2 3a): Bathe in perspiration, quoting this l. as its first ex. Armstrong (1946, p. 100) finds a characteristic image cluster of associations with brothels and disease in this line and 1322–6, associations of no relevance to Kent’s description of an unnamed messenger’s haste. Both Weis (ed. 1993) and Foakes (ed. 1997), however, detect hints of sexual corruption echoing 1091–5.

1307 in his hast]
If this does not mean as a result of his haste, it may be understood, as by Wilson (ed. 1960), to be metonymy: Sc. in his sweat.

1307 panting]
OED (Pant v. 5a): To utter gaspingly, quoting this l. as its first ex. Doran (see n. 988) takes F’s painting to be a misreading of manuscript; Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 176), either a minim misreading or a compositor’s conversion while carrying the word in his head. All except the recent Oxford eds. (1986, F) agree that Q’s breathles, panting makes the better and more obvious sense. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 534) defend the more pertinently abusive painting, to depict or describe in words (OED, v.1 2b) either decoratively (3c) or speciously (6). Such actions are incongruous with breathless haste, and salutations are delivered, not depicted. Weis (ed. 1993) compares 2347+27 Pantingly forth.

1309 letters]
Though Eccles (ed. 1792) imagines two letters, one inviting her to an interview and the other exciting her to affront her father, there need be only one: cf. 527, 858, 1108, 1470, and n. 875.

1309 spite of intermission]
Cawdrey (1604), intermission: A pawsing or breaking off (OED, sb.1 1). Most eds. from Warburton (ed. 1747) onwards take the phrase to mean an interruption or delay in the delivery or reading of Kent’s message. Buck (ed. 1907): This shows Oswald’s officiousness, and furnishes the motive for Kent’s anger in Scene 2. A few understand without pause on Oswald’s part (Steevens, ed. 1778) either to take breath (Malone, ed. 1790) or for me to rise from my knee and receive my answer (Clarkes, ed. 1868). Hunter (ed. 1972) understands just the opposite: In spite of the gasps and pauses that his breathless condition required. Wright (ed. 1875): In spite of interruption…from Kent, who had the prior claim. White (ed. 1883): Intrusion; that is, notwithstanding he intruded his letter. The latter two senses of intervention or interposition (OED, Intermission sb.2 2; from Intermit v.2 = Intromit) are attested by only two examples, the earliest dated 1628. Tovey (ed. 1896), elaborately: Although my business should have delayed theirs, and although my business was thus delayed. Halio (ed. 1992): Cornwall and Regan not only permit the interruption, they extend it by reading the letters Oswald delivers.

1310 presently]
See n. 431.

1310 on]
Most simply, Smith (ed. 1902): In accordance with, on the ground of, comparing 2151. Hunter (ed. 1869): Moved by. Wright (ed. 1875): On reading. Crook (ed. 1907): On account of. Kittredge (ed. 1940): As the result of.

1310 whose]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 176): Much better sense than F, those. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 534): An easy substitution for Compositor E.

1311 men]
F’s meiney, a word used also in Cor. 3.1.66 (1756), seems necessary to correct irregular meter. The spelling meinie could easily have been misread as menne and regularized to men by the Q compositor, as Taylor (1983, p. 368) suggests. Stone (1980, p. 179): Spelt, perhaps, meyne. OED (Meinie 2): A body of retainers, attendants, dependents, or followers; a retinue, suite, train, quoting this l. Verity (ed. 1897) finds the word, spelt meany, used several times in Gesta Romanorum to describe Lear’s train (ed. Herrtage, 1879, pp. 50–1), and Muir (ed. 1952) finds the spelling many in Harsnett (1603, pp. 50, 52; see ).

1311 straight]
See n. 527.

1312–13 attend…of]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Wait until they were at leisure to give me.

1314 And]
An I must be understood. Deighton (ed. 1891) notes Sh.’s frequent omission of the nominative, though seldom where the context, as here, might make it doubtful. See n. 230.

1316 fellow]
See nn. 16, 577.

1316 that]
On F’s which see n. 235.

1317 Display’d so sawcily]
See nn. 26, 1172. Rolfe (ed. 1880): Made so impudent a display; the only instance of the intransitive verb in S. OED (Display v. 5b, quoting only this l.).

1318 Hauing]
On the omitted I see nn. 1195, 1314 and . Alternatively, Abbott (§379): Sometimes a pronoun on which a participle depends can be easily understood from a pronominal adjective, i.e. 1315 mine. Cf. n. 230.

1318 more…wit]
See n. 677. Verity (ed. 1897): Indeed, his conduct has been ill-advised from his master’s point of view. Through him, Regan and Cornwall are even less disposed than before to receive Lear kindly, while the punishment which his plain speech towards himself and his treatment of Oswald have led them to inflict is an insult to the king which cannot but lead to dissension.…Thus when they meet, all three are in an angry, offence-taking mood. Smith (ed. 1902): In a sense all Lear’s friends are his enemies, as they play into Goneril’s and Regan’s hands. Foakes (ed. 1997): He did more to deserve being put into the stocks than he admits.

1318 drew]
See nn. 230, 1314. Singer (ed. 1826): The personal pronoun…is found in the preceding line, i.e. 1315 I. Brooke (ed. 1947): Kent is too angry to be coherent.

1319 raised]
Schmidt (1875), raise: To rouse (OED, v.1 4a).

1319 coward]
On nouns used as adjectives see Franz §367. Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 560): Transferred epithet.…Hypallage of this kind confers vitality and compression.

1320 sonne]
See n. 46–7.

1320 trespas]
See n. 1220+4.

1320 worth]
Deserving; cf. 305. Clarkes (ed. 1868) detect a second, contemptuous meaning: found it worth while to put me to [this] shame.

1321 This]
F’s The avoids repetition of this from 1320; either reading makes sense.

1322–7 Foole.…yeare]
The merits of F’s addition have been debated. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxx): To the actor who plays Lear, and who is visibly incubating insanity just now, the Fool’s gibes are irrelevant because not involving acting-dialogue. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 225): The Folio gives the Fool a little piping song, while Lear still stands speechless, his agony upon him. The dramatic effect will be appreciably different. Doran (1931, p. 66): The lines might be lifted from the text without spoiling either sense or meter.…Lear’s exclamation immediately following…has no bearing on what the Fool has said.…The new lines in the folio appear to have been an afterthought given to the Fool to enhance his part. Hart (1942, p. 147): Crude clowning. Stone (1980, p. 241): These proverbial sallies (for the most part in doggerel) doubtless have their relevance to the dramatic situation, but have been very clumsily misplaced here between Kent’s account of his mistreatment by Regan and Cornwall and Lear’s vehement reaction to it.…An obvious interpolation, though not in the style of the [F] reviser. Its banality suggests theatrical origin, as does the fact that F prints the verse incorrectly, each pair of lines being strung out as one: if the passage appeared thus in the prompt-book copy, that was very probably because it had been added, written sideways, in the margin, i.e. as an afterthought. Kerrigan (1983, p. 220) ingeniously defends the lines because they seem distressingly irrelevant: they both interrupt Q’s extended duologue between Lear and Kent, preventing predictability, and, far from helping Lear see better, are disengaged from the King. The two characters no longer speak the same language, because Lear is losing touch with the way things are. Weis (ed. 1993): [The] lines moralize Lear’s predicament in general terms and thereby break the almost stychomythic tautness of the exchange between Lear and Kent. But the stichomythy has already been broken by Kent’s preceding nineteen-line speech. Taylor (1983, p. 396): The added lines are clearly Sh.’s because they contain two striking Shakespearian image clusters originally pointed out by Armstrong (1946, pp. 57–65), namely geese-stocks (or restraint) and geese-blind-dolors. Cf. n. 1156. The evidence is weak for both clusters. Armstrong’s evidence for the first is that Launce was stocked when Crab his dog killed geese (TGV 4.4.32 [1852]) and that two geese are stolen from a pen (Wiv. 3.4.40–1 [1608]); his other three examples are completely specious, since stockish (MV 5.1.81 [2494] ) means blockish, wooden, stocks in 1H4 2.4.130 (1079) means stockings, and penned (1H4 3.1.206 [1747]) means written with a pen, not pent up. Similarly geese and blindness are referred to in unrelated and widely separated speeches in TGV 4.4.4, 32 (1825, 1852: Crab was a blind puppy), LLL 1.1.75, 97 (81, 103: truth blinds; geese breed), Rom. 2.4.16, 71 (1120, 1174: Cupid is blind; wits run a goose-chase), and MV 5.1.105, 112 (2519, 2528: geese are unmusical; a blind man can recognize a cuckoo); but Armstrong gives no example of an association with dolors (or dollars), only with medical diseases. These few tenuous associations seem coincidental. Halio (ed. 1992, p. 280): If the reference to wild geese is an allusion to the Wildgoose family (see [n. 1322]), then the addition was probably early. The Folio lineation, obviously crowded, may result from faulty casting-off of copy for signature rr1r, set by Compositor E.…Possibly the verses were sung, but neither Q nor F indicates this, they do not sound like traditional ballad material (Hunter, [ed. 1972], p. 340), and actors often speak the lines, though in sing-song fashion. Except for its possible irrelevance, there is no reason, stylistic or otherwise, to think that the speech is or is not Sh.’s. No source has been found for the lines; for modern musical settings see Gooch & Thatcher (1991, 1:635). Duffin (2004, p. 140) suggests two contemporary tunes.

1322 Winters…way]
Kemshead (ed. 1875): I.e., If such be their conduct the King’s troubles are not yet over. Tovey (ed. 1896): His daughters shun Lear, as migratory birds a land where winter reigns. Cf. 1341. Verity (ed. 1897): No doubt a proverbial saying; and Harbage (ed. 1958): With Cornwall and Regan equated with wild geese, proverbially evasive, perhaps referring to To run the Wild-goose chase (Tilley W390); no other proverb has been found. Halio (ed. 1973): Proverbial for we’re in for more trouble (bad weather), to judge from these portents. There is no need to identify wild Geese with Gonorill and Regan. Foakes (ed. 1997) quotes from an Italian book on weather prognostication tr. by I. F. (STC 10642; 1598, sig. B4v): If Geese doe flye aloft crying and cackling, it is a token of foule weather to follow. The Fool seems to be speaking specifically of winter migration. Muir (ed. 1952, rev. 1957, p. 258) notes the coincidence that one of Brian Annesley’s daughters was called Lady Wildgoose, and Akrigg (1968, p. 258) suspects an intentional play on the Wildgoose name; see .

1322 wil’d]
Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 534): An apostrophe error characteristic of Compositor E, comparing 1612.

1323 blind]
Crook (ed. 1907): To their misfortunes. Brooke (ed. 1947): To filial duty. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): To their father’s needs.

1324 beare]
Muir (ed. 1952): Hang on to. More probably Have upon the body (OED, v.1 6b) as a purse, in parallel with 1323 weare; cf. AYL 2.7.159 (1138).

1324 bags]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Full money-bags.

1324 kind]
See n. 132.

1325 arrant]
Chambers (ed. 1906): Regular (OED, a. 4). Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956): Notorious (OED, 3). Probably some of the root meaning of errant, vagrant (OED, 1) survives.

1325 whore]
Proverbial comparison: Dent (1981, F603.1), Fortune is a strumpet (whore, huswife). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Fortune is often called a harlot because she shows favour to every man and is constant to none, comparing AYL 1.2.32 (200), Mac. 1.2.14–15 (33–4). But here, Her favours are available only to those who have money (Lott, ed. 1974).

1325 turns the key]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Opens the door. Cf. 2136. Rubinstein (1984, p. 141), characteristically: Fornicates with.

1326 Dolors for]
Most eds. since Hanmer (ed. 1743) point out the pun on dollars, the English word for an Austrian or Spanish coin (Bevington, ed. 1980; OED, 1 [=thaler], 2 [=peso]), and Steevens (ed. 1778) gives other Shn. exx. Orgel (ed. 1999): The international European currency. Tovey (ed. 1896) explains the pun: Sorrows on account of thy daughters,…money to give them. Malone (ed. 1790), for: On account of (OED, prep. 21a, quoting this l.). Bevington (ed. 1992): In exchange for. Moberly (ed. 1876) alone interprets as despite: Poor though you are. Wilson (ed. 1960), who would read from: The F scribe or compositor may well have caught up the for from earlier in the line.

1327 tell]
Wright (ed. 1875): Count, or recount; according to the sense in which dolours is understood.

1328 mother]
Percy (in Steevens, ed. 1778): Lear here affects to pass off the swelling of his heart ready to burst with grief and indignation, for the disease called the Mother, or Hysterica Passio.…It is at least very probable, that Shakspeare would not have thought of making Lear affect to have the Hysterick Passion, or Mother, if this passage in Harsnet’s pamphlet had not suggested it to him. Harsnett (1603, p. 25): Ma: Maynie had a spice of the Hysterica passio, as seems, from his youth, hee himselfe termes it the Moother; in his deposition (p. 263), which Sh. doubtless read, Mainy describes the disease called the Mother or Vertiginem capitis that sometimes afflicted him, Edmond Peckham, and (fatally) Mainy’s eldest brother Thomas: It riseth…of a wind in the bottome of the belly, and proceeding with a great swelling, causeth a very painfull collicke in the stomack, and an extraordinary giddines in the head; see . Murphy (1984, p. 207): Thomas Mainy had died of this affliction; a few weeks later, Mr. Edmund Peckham, who suffered from this disease, died at Denham.…Richard Mainy was convinced that he would die of this illness. Foakes (1993, p. 253): Stephen Greenblatt [1988, p. 107]…argue[s] that hysterica passio could be regarded as a sign of demonic possession, but Harsnett specifically refers to the mother as a disease [and rejects the idea of possession; see p. 25].…It suggests primarily the emergence in Lear of the woman, the word recalling the mother of his children…and also the dawning of womanish feelings and breaking down of his masculine hardness. Idem (ed. 1997): This is the only scene in which Lear mentions the mother of his children [1409],…so the word mother has resonances beyond the reference to a disease; (ibid., pp. 39–40): This disease [1516] is identified as the mother.…Here may be seen the…presence of the mother of Lear’s daughters as a terrifying femaleness within himself. He is quoting Adelman’s (1992, p. 104) psychoanalytic theory that here Lear (p.114) discovers his origin in the suffocating maternal womb.…It is now inside him. Lear is describing literally his present symptoms of acute physical distress, not (metaphorically) his origins or (metaphorically) the disease that is Goneril (which Adelman elsewhere identifies with gonorrhea, not suffocation; see n. 1516); and it is unclear how, for an audience, this speech resonates from another not to be heard yet for some hundred lines. Kahn (1986, p. 36): In exiling Cordelia Lear brings about the return, in the form of hysteria, of the feminine he sought to repress. But Goneril and Regan, not Cordelia, give him the attack of hysterica passio, which is hardly synonymous with femininity. Hysterica Passio, also called Hysteria (from the Gk. hystera, womb), Vertiginem Capitis, Suffocatio, Praefocatio, Strangulatio Uteri, and Globus Hystericus, affected both men and women, though women were thought much more susceptible, as the name suggests. It was believed to be a swelling upwards or rising of the womb or abdomen towards the heart, caused by vapors; Horsman (ed. 1973), Hysterica passio: The old name (= suffering belonging to the womb) for hysteria. Not until later in the 17th c. was its cause sought in the brain rather than in the uterus. Considered strictly, the Mother was a different disease; its symptoms, including a sense of suffocation (OED, Mother sb.1 11b, 12, quoting this l.), could be experienced by men having an attack of hysteria. Since Sh. here derived this term from Harsnett, never using it elsewhere, and since in Harsnett it is a disease experienced by Maynie and his brother, there is no need to think that it signified to Sh. an internal femaleness, in Lear or in the Maynies. Bucknill (1860, p. 267) quotes from Marchamont Nedham’s discussion (Medela Medicinae, 1665, p. 48) of the disease, which he also calls Rising of the Lights: Men too sometimes have something like it. Adelman (1992, p. 300) asserts that Lear associates it unmistakably with the rising womb itself, but in fact in his only two references to its symptoms Lear specifies his heart (1397; F, rising heart), making no mention of a woman’s womb. The disease is described in Drayton’s Poly-Olbion 7.19–28 (ed. Hebel, 4:128), Edward Jorden’s A Briefe Discourse of a Disease Called the Suffocation of the Mother (1603, sigs. C1r–2r), denying demonic possession as a cause, and John Sadler’s The Sick Woman’s priuate Looking-glasse (1636, p. 61), and recipes to cure it are offered in John Partridge, The Treasurie of hidden Secrets (1600, sig, E3). See also Adams (1903, pp. 323–4), C. C. B. (1903, p. 324), Camden (1948, pp. 390–3), and Elton (1966, p. 91 n.). Craig (ed. 1931): Lear mistakes the epigastric discomfort of extreme grief for the disease. Gardner (ed. 1969): The symptoms of sorrow as described by Burton, Anatomy of Melancholy [1.2.3.5, quoting Melancthon] resemble Lear’s: The black blood drawn from the spleen and diffused under the ribs on the left side makes…perilous hypochondriacal convulsions. Hoeniger (1992, pp. 321–3), insisting that the mother affected only women, and that Harsnett and Sh. were mistaken to use the term for Lear’s discomfort: Galen…saw the cause of the illness as poisoned blood in the uterus, produced by excess black bile.…The swelling of the organs impedes breathing, and in acute cases the [melancholic] vapors rise to the head, causing dizziness and disturbing the brain.…We gather that Mainy and perhaps other simple folk were accustomed to speak of their illnesses with its suffocating fits as like the mother, though doctors diagnosed it in male patients by a different name—for instance, catalepsy, epilepsia passio, or, as in this case, vertigo of the head. Brown (ed. 1976): At last Lear speaks, fighting for breath and for control of his body, now violently shaking. Hotine (1981, pp. 138–9), without explanation: Lear’s symptoms are modelled on those suffered by King James himself. Rowse (ed. 1978), oddly, finds a quibble on a scummy contamination occurring in the fermentation of vinegar (OED, sb.2 2).

1329 Historica]
See prev. n. Doran (1931, pp. 96–7): Hysterica must have been spelled histerica, and the e must have been written in such a way that both the printer of Q1 and the transcriber [preparing the playbook] took it for an o. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 391): F Preserves an error from Q, which has a misreading of e as o. Wells (ed. 2000): OED’s first instance of hysterica [sic] passio…is from Harsnet, where Shakespeare may have picked it up.

1329 climing]
Wilson (ed. 1960): In [1328] the pain is climbing from below towards the heart; in [1397] it is rising from the heart upward. Or rather, constriction seems to be pushing his heart upward. Hoeniger (1992, p. 323) suggests that Lear’s heart may be simply swelling with wrath, but the terms swels vp (1328), climing (1329), and rising heart (1397) all suggest a different sensation.

1330 element’s]
Schmidt (1874), element: Proper and natural habitation (OED, sb. 12: That one of the four elements <earth, water, air, fire> which is the natural abode of any particular class of being). Dent (1981, E107) cites the proverb He is (To be) out of his Element.

1330 below]
Hunter (ed. 1869): In the region of the womb. Moberly (ed. 1876) quotes Harsnett: It riseth…of a wind in the bottome of the belly; see n. 1328. But if Thy refers to sorrow in general, possibly Skillan (ed. 1967) is right: It belongs to the spleen which was popularly believed to be the seat of the passions (OED, sb. 1b), specifically of the humour melancholy (Gardner, ed. 1969). Hunter (ed. 1972): The mother is a visceral symbol of the breakdown in hierarchy, when the lower elements climb up to threaten or destroy the superior ones.

1330 daughter]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Contemptuously. Verity (ed. 1897), agreeing, compares 2947.

1331 within]
F’s added here seems designed to make a rough pentameter of the line, but the result is disrupted meter in several successive lines which are regular enough in Q.

1332 there]
F here; either is acceptable. Brown (ed. 1976): The gentleman, about to follow Lear, stops in his tracks.

1332 Exit.]
On Q’s omission see n. 538.

1333–4 Made…of?]
One apparent verse line is set as two. The compositor may be stretching his copy to fill the column, having compressed it a few lines earlier. Cf. n. 1322–7.

1333 more]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Greater (OED, a. 1), which suits Q’s than; F’s But requires the meaning other, additional (OED, 4).

1335 No]
Meter demands that this be a separate line, as is F’s None, a response which is both more emphatic and avoids repetition of 1333 no. Hogan (1962, p. 76): F’s None and number [1336] gain some confirmation from the fact that Q could not have fitted these words into its single line of type.

1336 how chance]
Delius (ed. 1854): Elliptical: How does it chance (OED, v. 1). Abbott (§37): Chance appears to be used as an adverb.…But the order of words…indicates that Shakespeare treated chance as a verb. Cf. Franz §627.

1336 the]
Foakes (ed. 1997): F’s the the may have resulted from a misreading of scribal abbreviations, yt ye = that the.

1336 traine]
The word at 763, 776. F’s number makes no practical difference, and may be a memorial corruption (Duthie, 1949, p. 45) by scribe or compositor carrying Q’s word in his head. As far as either Q or F indicates, the train that Kent can see is only the one Knight/Gentleman and the Fool; how much of the rest of Lear’s train still accompanies him is indeterminate. Bradley (1904): The Fool…intimates that the rest have deserted him ([1341–5]). He and his daughters, however, seem unaware of any diminution; and…the doors are shut against him partly on the excuse that he is attended…train ([1609]). Nevertheless in the storm he has no knights with him…as though…he had hurried away so quickly that many of his knights were unaware of his departure. Bradley finds these obscurities mere carelessness as to matters which would escape attention in the theatre. Greg (1940, p. 434 n.): The Fool affects to see in [Kent’s question] an allusion to the dismissal of fifty of the knights; but it may equally well refer to the absence of the rest. Regan’s statement at the end of this scene that He is attended with a desperate traine (1609) may refer to their expected arrival quite as well as to their presence—but this argument is improbable, since at that point Regan had already used them as a reason for excluding Lear, and without their presence she would have had no reasoned justification for not admitting him alone. Greg continues, From [2075–6] it is clear that the knights have been pursuing the king all the way from Albany’s (via Cornwall’s, of course) and have at last more opportunely caught up with him as he is leaving Gloucester’s. But it is more likely that they became separated from Lear when he rushed out into the storm at the end of this scene than that he had traveled all night without them when they were ready (see 920–1) to accompany him. Muir (ed. 1952) half agrees with Greg: Shakespeare wished to give the impression in II.iv that Lear was deserted by his followers. The thirty-six hot questrists [at 2075–6] seem to have just arrived at Gloucester’s house in III.vii, following Lear from Goneril’s; but even if they had arrived earlier, and they are the desperate train mentioned by Regan, who is hardly a reliable witness, they might be regarded by Kent as a small train. Mahood (1992, p. 163): As the audience is swept along in this most headlong of Shakespeare’s plays, it does not occur to them to ask why an old man attended by a Fool and one other is able to outride the Knights…or [lose] fifteen of their number en route. Apart from Kent’s vague remark and the Fool’s descant on it, there is in fact no clear suggestion at this point that the majority of knights have abandoned Lear, nor any hint at 2075–6 whether the thirty-six knights are arriving from Goneril’s or Regan’s house. Cf. nn. 810, 1273.

1337 And]
See n. 630.

1338 thou ha’dst]
There is no metrical reason for F’s thoud’st, and little difference in pronunciation.

1338 deserued]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Because it’s a foolish question, since the answer is so obvious. But since folly is not normally punished by stocking, perhaps the further implication is that only a knave could be so foolish (cf. 1348–9), or that such folly will surely result in vagabondage or other knavery, hence that Kent as good as deserves punishment now. Hunter (ed. 1972): The question is subversive, for the answer must be that kings who lose their power also lose their followers.

1340–6 Weele…after]
Verity (ed. 1897): Why trouble about one who has fallen on wintry days? Kittredge (ed. 1940): In a series of brief parables the Fool explains that Lear’s fortunes are in a bad way. Harrison (ed. 1948): The fool is so much amused at Kent’s discomfiture that he strings off a series of wise sayings to show his own clearer understanding of Lear’s state. Butler (1992, pp. 3–5), who attempts to blacken Lear’s knights by associating them with Jacobean retainers who were indistinguishable from hired bullies, takes as clinching evidence this speech, the Fool’s indictment of them as timeservers and deserters. It is not clear what desertion if any has taken place (see n. 1336), and there is no evidence whatever that Lear’s knights are not enfeoffed men…owing sacred allegiance to their king but mere hirelings or mercenaries. Lear has retained them (see with reseruation, 133) from previous service, and praises the dutie with which they support the worships of their name, i.e. the name of knight. Since they are pre-Christian, Jacobean analogies may be tenuous.

1340 schoole]
OED (sb.1 1c): Set to school: to subject to teaching;…to correct, quoting this l.

1340 Ant]
Grey (1754, 2:108–10) cites many proverbs on ants laboring to prepare for winter, including Prov. 6:6–8, to which Eaton (1858, p. 137), Wordsworth (1864, p. 332), and Carter (1905, p. 435) add Prov. 30:25, and Green (1870, pp. 148–9) adds Prov. 20:4, citing emblems on the theme. Thaler (1955, p. 38): The language and imagery of the play are anything but consistently heathen. No popular contemporary proverb is cited by Tilley, but Aesop’s fable of the fly (or cicada, or grasshopper) and ant was well known: see Baldwin (1944, 1:610, 620–1) and, for a woodcut, Fraser (1962, Pl. XLIII). Dent (1981, W510) cites the more general proverb Winter eats that summer gets. Muir (ed. 1952, p. 252): Montaigne notes how ants provide for winter; see . Noble (1935, p. 230) notes that the biblical translations before the Authorised version of 1611 use the words pismire or emmet, not ant; Shaheen (1987, p. 149), however, finds antes in the related Scripture of Douay Prov. 30:25. Malone (ed. 1790): The king’s train, like that sagacious animal, prefer the summer of prosperity to the colder season of adversity. Wright (ed. 1875): The Fool preaches the faithlessness of summer friends in the winter of adversity, and the keenness with which men seek and follow their self-interest, and desert one whose fortunes are falling, comparing Tim. 3.6.29–32 (1412–15). Houghton (ed. 1907): An ant was a specimen of a busy intellect. Muir (ed. 1952): He may be telling Kent that he is foolish to remain with the King. Harbage (ed. 1958): Lear…is equated with winter bereft of workers. Wilson (ed. 1960): The knights…reappear at [2075]…, so the Fool may be mistaken. Or commentators may be mistaken to apply the Fool’s general remarks to Lear’s train. Fraser (ed. 1963): Lear, trusting foolishly to summer days, finds himself unprovided for, and unable to provide, now that winter has come.

1341 winter]
Craig (ed. 1901): For winter in the sense of adversity, compare [Cym. 2.4.5 (1149), 2H4 4.4.92 (2471)] and 1322.

1341–4 all…stincking]
Though Johnson (ed. 1765) found here no clear series of thought and proposed to emend (see ), he interpreted the original well enough: Men who are led by their eyes see that he is ruined, and if there were any blind among them [i.e., his train], who, for want of eyes, followed their noses, they might by their noses discover that it was no longer fit to follow the King. Malone (ed. 1790) compares AWW 5.2.3–5 (2643–5), I…smell somewhat strong of her [i.e., Fortune’s] strong displeasure. Whatever obscurity exists here is caused by a change of meaning of the phrase follow their noses. Kittredge (ed. 1940): To follow one’s nose is an old jocose idiom…for to go straight ahead in the direction in which one’s nose points (OED, Nose sb. 8a, Tilley N230, both quoting this l.); and as Tovey (ed. 1896) explains, in this sense…we are led by our eyes. The fool means that…Lear’s followers have seen how things are faring with him; but in the latter part of the sentence the quick-witted fellow plays on a second meaning, to be guided by the smell. Halliwell (ed. 1865): Kent has neither used his eyes to see, nor his nose to smell; in short, had not made use of his senses. Verity (ed. 1897): A hint to Kent. Hulme (1970, p. 530): Those of the audience accustomed to the notion that simply to follow one’s nose…must be the right way forward, are jarred into uncertainty: the words led by in a nose context carry a contrary implication. To be led by the nose is to be made a fool of (Tilley: N233, from 1598).…[Moreover,] certain things may be as plain as the nose on your face (Tilley: N215, from 1581), yet many a man cannot see further than the end of his nose (Tilley: N220, from c.1594).

1343 a 100.]
This is the number in Lear’s train; no good reason has been given for F’s change to twenty. Just possibly a manuscript i.C, a usual abbreviation for centum, a hundred (OED, C III.1), was misread by a scribe or compositor for 20. On Sh.’s possible use of Roman numerals, see n. 187–9. Wilson’s (ed. 1960) explanation for F’s word—indefinite for any large number, comparing 1178—applies equally to Q’s hundred, as often in Sh. Steevens (ed. 1778): Twenty refers to the noses of the blind men, and not to the men in general. This interpretation is impossible for Q and not certain for F; see Halliwell in the prev. n. Honigmann (1965, p. 141 n.): Q’s hundred may be contaminated by the hundred knights, yet a sly reference to the disappearance of the knights would be very much in character. Weis (ed. 1993): F indicates the ever-dwindling numbers of Lear’s retainers. But the Fool may be referring to men in general, not the knights, and there is no clear evidence of their dwindling: see n. 1273.

1343–4 stincking]
In bad odor with Fortune; see n. 1341–4. Foakes (ed. 1997, however: Stinking of downfall and loss. Wells (ed. 2000): Like a corpse. See .

1344–6 let…after]
The King gives similar advice to Perillus in Leir 872–5; see .

1344 wheele]
Deighton (ed. 1891) compares the wheel of majesty in Ham. 3.3.17–22 (2290–5). Danby (1945, p. 19): The wheel of Fortune, or alternatively a piece of the new haulage machinery. Elton (1966, pp. 135–6): The wheels in Lear include the Mirror-for-Magistrate-like ones on which the wicked characters have ridden, of these only Edmund recognizing the futility of the ride as he drops off [3136]; the practical wheel which the prudent man will either dismount as it heads into peril or mount as it ascends…; the wheel of fire…upon which Lear himself is bound [2795–6]; and, finally, the larger wheel, the unmentioned mysterious wheel of the universe and the mysteries of things, which the Divine Power turns.…Whatever meaning King Lear has perhaps lies in the celebration of the mystery of that ultimate wheel. Skillan (ed. 1967): The figure epitomizes lear: a large object whose very nature and construction makes its progress…swift and incapable of halting itself or being halted. Bate (1989; 1993, p. 195) suggests Sisyphus.

1345 it]
F’s omission is unnecessary and makes little difference.

1346 vp the hill]
F’s vpward means the same, though perhaps to the injury of the antithesis (Collier, ed. 1843).

1346 one]
On the adjective as substantive see n. 935.

1347 wise man]
F’s wiseman is a common variant. Both forms appear in about equal numbers in Sh.’s F and good quartos. Cf. 1355, 1693. Tovey (ed. 1896): Perhaps ironically (as in the doggerel that follows) for a would-be wise man, a shrewd fellow, keenly alive to his own interests. But he may mean, when a really good and wise man advises you better, reject my worldly advice. Hulme (1970, pp. 531–2): I.e., this will never happen, comparing Tilley F469: A Fool may sometimes give a wise man counsel.

1347 giue mee mine]
Hulme (1970, p. 531) detects three proverbs: Throw no gift again at the giver’s head (Tilley G101), Giff Gaff [Give gave] was a good fellow (G94), and Own is own (O100, O101).

1348 haue]
Sledd (1940, p. 595) suggests that F’s hause may be variant of halse = beseech, abjure (OED, v.1 2, not recording hause as a variant). Most eds. agree with Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 176): An obvious error in F. Wilson (ed. 1960): J. C. M[axwell]…conj. that the F collator [preparing copy for F], wishing to alter Q’s haue to ha’ and follow to use, stroked out haue and, writing ha’ and use close together in the margin, forgot to delete follow. Thus the F compositor set up follow and thought that hause was to be substitutes for haue. The explanation depends on a doubtful theory of copy (see ) and on the coincidence of error and carelessness in making an unnecessary change, and few eds. have followed it (see textual n.). Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 534): It leaves unexplained F’s use of terminal s for medial [long-s]. It seems more likely that the intrusive s has slipped from the end of F’s giues in the line above—which in F’s uncorrected state is giue.

1348 knaues]
See n. 451.

note.p: foole] Welsford (1935, pp. 255–6): The Fool is being as subtle, ambiguous, and volatile as Erasmus himself in his play upon the various meanings and relations of the words fool and knave.…The Fool suggests that there is ambiguity in the words wisdom and folly, but that…[he is] devoid of worldly wisdom. Wilson (ed. 1960), fool: Alternately in the pejorative sense ([1349, 1356]) and in the sense of the wise and loyal Fool (1354, 1357]). The two senses seem to be fused in [1360]. Elton (1966, p. 306 n.) gives literary exx. of the impractically loyal fool. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Faithlessness is true folly. Hulme (1970, p. 533) finds several proverbs pertinent: He is not the Fool that the fool is but the fool that with the fool deals (Tilley F486), A Crafty knave needs no broker (ODEP, s.v. Crafty), and Better be a Fool than a knave (Tilley F446, from 1640).

div.note:
1350–7 That…perdy]
Carter (1905, p. 436) compares John 10:13 and Prov. 19:4–6. Kittredge (ed. 1940) finds a parallel in Ovid, Tristria 1.9.5–6. Hunter (ed. 1972, p. 340): There is no reason why this should not be a ballad; but there is no evidence to connect it with one. Duffin (2004, 383) suggests the tune of Peg a Ramsey. For modern musical settings see Gooch & Thatcher (1991, 1:637). Wittreich (1984, p. 71): The Fool’s first prophecy, of imminent events, balancing that at 1736 ff.

1350 Sir]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Used substantively (OED, sb. 10: A gentleman). Page (ed. 1889): With a touch of irony. Foakes (ed. 1997): Referring to Lear’s knights. There is no need to think so (see n. 1273), and the Fool is giving councell about blind men and the wise man generally.

1350 that]
On F’s which see n. 235.

1350 and seekes]
Most eds. accept F’s addition because it makes 1350 fit the metric pattern of its rhyming line 1352 and counterpart lines 1354 and 1356. The Q compositor may have overlooked a second word beginning with se.

1351 forme]
Schmidt (1874): External appearance, empty show (OED, sb. 15: Mere outward ceremony or formality).

1352 packe]
Schmidt (1875): Go off in a hurry (OED, v.1 10).

1352 begin]
Though Sh. occasionally uses the subjunctive after when (Franz §643), all eds. adopt Q2’s begins.

1354–5 But…flie]
Goldsmith (1955, p. 21), Elton (1966, pp. 310–11 n.) and Carpenter (1979, pp. 128–9) suspect an allusion to a lost proverb, citing Godly Queene Hester (?1525–9), line 673 (ed. Greg. 1904), And fooles be fayne to fyght when wise men runne away.

1355 wise man]
See n. 1347.

1356–7 The…perdy]
On the fool-knave pairing see n. 573. The fool’s apparent contradiction of his own advice has puzzled commentators and resulted in various transpositions of the words knaue and foole: see textual nn. and . But the received text can be explained. Delius (ed. 1854): The knave, by following a fool’s advice [to desert the king], shows himself a fool; the Fool, by ignoring it, shows himself no knave to his master. If fool is first [1356] taken in its general sense, and then [1357] as the particular person of the speech,…emendation is superfluous (Ger.). White (ed. 1862): And if knave in [1356] is used in the sense of servant, in [1357] of rogue. Halliwell (ed. 1865): The knave…is really the fool who chooses not to act justly and uprightly.…the fool does not become a knave by remaining, although he might be thought a fool. Clarkes (ed. 1868), agreeing: The cunning rogue…shows himself…moral miscalculator as well as moral coward. Similarly Welsford (1935, p. 256): The knave who runs away, comes out into the open, and is at once seen as the abject contemptible ludicrous creature that he has always been. The fool is at least true to himself. Danby (1945, p. 18): Wiseman and Knave were kept opposed in the first part of the speech. Now they merge. Similarly, at the beginning Folly partnered with Knavery. Here the Fool contrasts them. Moberly (ed. 1876): The touching faith of the fool to his master is one of the most beautiful points of the play. The history of court-fools does not offer anything quite like it. It, however, took six strong men to drag away Patch, Cardinal Wolsey’s fool, from his disgraced master, who wished to send him as a propitiatory offering to Henry VIII. Bradley (1904, p. 460), interpreting as Delius because of what the Fool says in 1347–8, compares Tim 1.1.63–88 (81–110). Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): The quibbles turn on the double sense of knavery as good and bad, as sharpness and dishonesty, and of foolishness as good and bad, as stupidity and disinterestedness; also on himself as a professional fool, and on Kent as, in a sense, a professional knave or servant. Goggin (ed. 1910): The knave does what a fool would do. Kittredge (ed. 1940): That fellow that forsakes his master is (from the point of view of the higher wisdom) a fool, since true wisdom implies fidelity; and the fool who, like me, remains faithful is, at all events, no knave. Hunter (ed. 1972): A sudden switch from worldly wisdom to spiritual truth. Others disagree. Hunter (ed. 1869): The knave that runs away turns jester at misfortune. Danby (1949, p. 105): He really does believe that to follow Lear to disaster is foolishness. Absolute loyalty is irrational, and the Fool never suggests that there is a supernatural sanction for such irrationality. Folly is an alternative to knavery, certainly. But that does not make it a virtue. Elton (1966, p. 307): The Fool…preaches the new bourgeois ethic, [but] he lives the traditional one. Similarly Hulme (1970, pp. 535–6): Although the Fool’s actions accord with a higher wisdom, his words express the values of a society in which only the unsuccessful are contemptible and ludicrous. She adduces several proverbs—Fools have wit enough to come in out of the rain (Tilley F537), A Hood for this fool [to kepe him from the rayne] (H585), and He should be called a Fool to his face that being well does quit his place (F487)—and concludes, In this sense therefore…in deserting his master the disloyal servant takes on that quality of restlessness proverbially attributed to the fool. Dent (1984, F446) compares Better be a fool than a knave. Rosenberg (1972, p. 156): He gives shrewd advice, but let knaves follow it: he will not; he is a Fool.

1356–7 knaue…knaue]
For the quibble see n. 610 and prev. n.

1357 perdy]
Valpy (ed. 1833): A corruption of the French oath par Dieu (OED, Pardie).

1360 Not…stockes]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Had you been worldly wise instead of foolishly loyal you would not be where you are now. So Skillan (ed. 1967): Lightly tapping Kent with the bauble. F’s added Foole makes explicit the implied tu quoque, throwing Kent’s last word back at him. But Schmidt (ed. 1879): A title of respect, which Kent has earned by his fidelity. So Muir (ed. 1952): Kent, too, is a loyal fool, and not a politic knave. Hulme (1970, p. 535): The common proverb Who’s the fool now? (ODEP [1970, p. 886]: Fool, from 1588) underlines the triumph of [the Fool’s] last retort…: Kent’s particular in the stocks folly outdoes the general foolishness that runnes away.

1358 Enter…]
Doran (1931, p. 83): A number of entrances in F are moved up a few lines because the prompter desired to get the characters on the stage in time so that they would not miss their cues. Cf. 1468, 1890, 2039, 2072, 2088, 2188, 2267, 2526, 3182, 3264. Cf. 3184. Dessen (1995, pp. 74–5) senses some ironic counterpointing in the Folio placement which juxtaposes two fools who have yet to learn through suffering.

1361–2 Denie…weary]
F apparently breaks Q’s verse line into two short lines for reasons of space. The Q line is too long for the F margins, there is not enough room for a turnunder on the same line with 1363, and a turnover is never made at the beginning of a column.

1361 Denie]
Schmidt (1874): Refuse (OED, Deny v. 5).

1362–3 th’are…th’are…They]
F expands both elided pronouns to They. Rosenberg (1972, p. 157) imagines all three to be emphasized, sardonically,…for Lear himself travelled twice as far, wearily, unfed, sickening in mind and body. The emphasis is not possible in Q, nor in F if 1361–2 is to be read as the verse line that all editors agree it is. Q’s explicit elisions may have been caused by the compositor’s short measure that also caused wearie to be turned under.

1363 They]
F’s They haue makes a more regular line. Possibly Q’s extrametrical I at the beginning of 1364 should have ended this line (see textual n.), making F’s addition needless.

1363 hard to night]
Hard this past night. See n. 359. F’s all the night makes no practical difference.

1363 Iustice]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 391): A desperate guess by the compositor of an almost completely illegible word in the copy. Virtually all eds. accept F’s fetches. Though Stone (1980, p. 49) doubts that F’s word could be misread as Q’s, and Halio (ed. 1994, p. 132) that it originally stood in the MS, fetches is graphically fairly similar to Iustis. Schmidt (1874): A shift, a stratagem (OED, Fetch sb.1 2: Dodge,…trick). Davenport (1953, p. 21) thinks a nautical sense is also present, though there are no clear grounds for his equating tacking with evasive movements. The Oxford eds.’ (1986 Q; Wells, 2000) Insolence (written Insolēce), proposed by Blayney (see textual n.), could also have been misread Iustice, though Lear has yet no reason to suspect Regan of arrogant contempt, only of disobedient evasion. Weis (ed. 1993) attempts to explain Q: A sarcastic reference to the stocking of Kent. Similarly Orgel (ed. 2000): Presumably Cornwall’s explanation of that act. Cf. 1365. Davidson (1998, p. 317): Q represents an incorrect expansion of a stenograph for jests; but Lear suspects revolt, not a jest.

1364 Images]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Indications. Schmidt (1874): Appearance and semblance. Wright (ed. 1875): Signs. Moberly (ed. 1876): Visible tokens. Craig (ed. 1901): Or else types, embodiments (OED, sb. 4c: Typical example, quoting this l.). The sense exact likeness proposed by Harrison (ed. 1948), Kittredge (ed. 1940), and Wilson (ed. 1960) seems more appropriate in 2602, 3225.

1364 reuolt…off]
Wright (ed. 1875): Rebellion and desertion. Halio (ed. 1992): Serious disobedience, tantamount to…the breakdown of order. Foakes (ed. 1997): Lear still speaks as if he were in authority as King. But he may simply be protesting his daughter’s flight from filial office (1382, 1462) and the seruise (1378) due to him not only in curtesie and gratitude (1463) but as a condition of her inheriting half his kingdom (see 140–3). Though OED (Fly v.1 8d) does not record fly off = break away before Milton, Deighton (ed. 1891) compares Ant. 2.2.152 (855). Kittredge (ed. 1940) sees the two terms as close synonyms, a rhetorical device he also finds in 251, 381, 599, 776, 1264, 1266, 1549, 1633, 1657, 1812, 2248+4–+5, 2303+3, 2478, 2516, 3088, 3101, 3254, 3273.

1365 Fetch]
Verity (ed. 1897), followed by others: Said perhaps in grim reference to mere fetches [1363]—and perhaps thereby confirming the F reading.

1366–9 My…Course]
Moberly (ed. 1876): For a man so passionate as Lear to be asked to humour the vehement temper of one whom he considers his inferior, is the most stinging request that can possibly be made. Verity (ed. 1897): Gloucester’s description of Cornwall…becomes terribly significant in the light of his own sufferings at the duke’s hands.

1367 fierie]
Schmidt (1874): Irritable, passionate (OED, a. 5b). Perhaps choleric, governed by the fiery humor.

1367, 1371 qualitie]
Schmidt (1875): Nature, character (OED, sb. 1: Disposition). Cf. 1415.

1368 vnremoueable]
Wright (ed. 1875): Immoveable (OED, a. 1). Craig (ed. 1901): Stubbornly firm.

1369 Course]
See n. 201. Lott (ed. 1974), fancifully: With reference perhaps to stars in their courses (cf. fiery).

1370 confusion]
Schmidt (ed. 1879): Ruin, overthrow (OED, 1c, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Edwards (ed. 1975): The strongest in Lear’s crescendo of curses, consigning the objects of his wrath to perditon.

1371 what fierie]
Though F’s Fiery? What makes poor sense, Gloucester having just said what the quality is, meaning has been wrested from it. Page (ed. 1889): Why does he show off his nature to me? Tovey (ed. 1896): What character is this that should prevent my speaking to him and his wife? Kittredge (ed. 1940): What has his character to do with the matter? Hunter (ed. 1972): Lear is still in a world where individuality is far less important that status and relationship. When king and father command, character is no excuse.

1373–4 Glo.…man]
The two-line exchange supplied in F is seen by Adee (ed. 1890, pp. xxx f.) as delaying the business between Gloucester’s reference to the fiery quality of the Duke and Lear’s angry reply. It seems more likely to have been cut [from Q]…than to have been interpolated [in F] as a ripe afterthought. Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 37–8) agrees that a cut was made, but detrimentally—for line [1375] follows line [1374] much more naturally than it follows line [1372]—though the cut was made concurrently with that of the linked line 1379. Duthie’s logic, however, could as easily justify the concurrent addition of the two passages to F. Cunnington (1910, p. 449): Koppel [1877, p. 78] has already noticed that these passages are related together, the first leading up to and accounting for the second. It is most unlikely that accidental omission in the quarto should have affected both, and as intentional omissions to shorten they are not worth making.…There is no gap if they are omitted. Honigmann (1965, p. 127): The added lines [here and at 1379] give edge to the dialogue—and, if we are to regard them as deliberately cut in Q would save very little time. They cannot be accidental omissions in Q. Stone (1980, p. 241): In Q Gloucester replies…without making any move to comply—clearly because he is persuaded that the errand would be hopeless.…The [F] reviser must have thought this implausible or insufficiently clear and has Gloucester demurring explicitly.…That these lines did not belong in the original text is shown by their association with the next addition (see [1379]): to suppose that both passages were omitted from Q would be virtually to assume a method and purpose in the omissions. Honigmann (1982, p. 150): By adding [two passages], several lines apart, [the F reviser] shows Lear’s mind struggling with the enormity of the insult. Foakes (ed. 1997): These [F] lines take the heat off Gloucester by playing on the word inform; all Gloucester could do is convey a message, not give orders in the way Lear wants. Actually Lear demands only a better answere. He would expect Gloucester to urge one, not to demand one from a Duke or Duchess.

1375 I…Lord]
Flatter (1948, p. 58): Gloucester’s reply, an interjection only, should not stop the continuous flow of Lear’s speech.

1377 fate]
Greg (1940, p. 161): Q1(c)’s father is certainly correct. The copy may have had fatr.

1378 the]
Greg (1940, p. 161): Q1(c)’s his is certainly correct on the assumption that the folio was printed from an uncorrected sheet. But it was probably printed from a correct transcript: see .

1378 come and tends]
Q1(c)’s (and Q2’s) commands her looks like a mere guess, since her can hardly have been a misreading of tends. It has, however, been adopted by many editors and adapters since Tate (see textual n.), perhaps because it is simpler, more immediately comprehensible onstage (Bate & Massai, 1997, p. 147). F’s commands, tends, lends weight to the authenticity of tends, suggesting agreement between the word in Q’s copy and that in the playbook lying somewhere behind F (see ). Schmidt (ed. 1879), noting that Lear expects service from both Regan and Cornwall, suspects behind Q1(u) a possible copy reading of commands them but accepts F’s reading, emended to commands, ’tends (for attends = awaits: OED, Tend v.1 6; Attend v. 13b, 15). Conceivably tend could be an aphetic form of intend = purpose (OED, Tend v.1 7; Intend v. 18), here meaning intends to have or intends that you provide service; but the usage is apparently not elsewhere in Sh. Adee (ed. 1890, p. li): The true reading is, comes and tends service. Doran (1931, p. 100): If Q1(c)’s reading was the original, it is difficult to explain the absence of her from both Q1(u) and F; moreover, To account for the word tends in the folio by supposing that the printer got it from an imperfectly corrected reading in Q1 [presumed to be used for printer’s copy], in which the corrector [preparing F copy] had substituted commands for come and but had forgotten to cross out tends [=attends], is not a sufficient explanation. It does not account for the presence of tends in the quarto, which can be explained only by there having been a word like it in the manuscript. It is therefore just as probable that the reading of F is based directly on the manuscript as that it is derived from Q. Greg (1940, p. 161) accepts commands but considers tends an insoluble crux, since the phrase in F may be read either to mean commands and attends or, if punctuated commands—tends—, to mean commands her service—nay rather tenders [OED, Tend v.2 5] his own!, neither reading satisfactory to Greg. Sh. uses tend = await absolutely in Ham. 1.3.83 (548) and 4.3.45 (2706) though never transitively, and he does not elsewhere use tend = tender. Muir (ed. 1952): Lear’s tendering of his own service might be taken as a conciliatory afterthought, or [following Greg] as an ironical reinforcement of his words. Joseph (ed. 1966), alternatively: Lear sarcastically…offers his service. Nowottny (in Sisson, ed. 1954, pp. xxiii f.; cf. 1960, p. 55): As a king he commands Cornwall’s service, as a father he expects it of Regan as natural. Sisson (1956, 2:235), rejecting this idea: Lear commands her service, being her King and father, and tenders his own courtesy to a Duchess, King though he be.…Tend in the sense of attend, wait is weak and pleonastic after commands, and is unacceptable. So also Stone (1980, p. 86): Improbably clumsy as to rhythm and rhetorically extremely weak; tends seruise is in the wrong line: see . Honigmann (1982, p. 147): Stone’s emendation, introducing a short line, is clumsier. Foakes (ed. 1997): As Lear slips from King to father, so he slides from giving orders to tends = attends, or waits for. Bhattacharya (1980–1, pp. 101–2), however: The intent is emphatic and insistent: I am commanding, and I am waiting for my command to be obeyed. Hunter (ed. 1972): Tends is an easy misreading of true. Horsman (ed. 1973): Their could be misread as tends; but the mistake would have to be repeated by both the Q compositor and the scribe preparing the promptbook or transcript behind F.
No one has suggested another simple explanation for Q1(u): that it is correct except for an extraneous s on tends, added by the compositor by attraction from the first letter of the following word seruise, or except for an s missing from come. Either alternative would make the two verbs parallel, as they would more naturally occur in the speech. In the first case the line would read the deare father Would…speake, [would] come and tend seruise [i.e. expect dutiful treatment], thus continuing the subjunctive instead of suddenly shifting to a declaration of commands. In this form the line is still somewhat difficult, and a Folio scribe or compositor (in this case the novice Compositor E) puzzled by his manuscript’s come and tend might have consulted Q2 and adopted its apparently easier (though unauthoritative) commands. In the second case the line would read the deare father Would…speake, comes [i.e., has come, is here] and tends seruise; in this case the compositor might have unconsciously made comes singular following the singular speake, or simply have had difficulty reading the words comes and or (if badly spaced) comesand. In either case, if the playhouse scribe preparing fair copy for the playbook worked from the same MS that was later used as copy for Q1, his command may be no more than a different deciphering of a badly written pair of words, comeand or comesand.

1378 seruise]
If the word means attendance of servants on a master (OED, sb.1 6), Lear’s request seems to mark a sudden change from considerate moderation to peremptory haste (Greg, 1940, p. 161). So Hudson (ed. 1881): Lear is here asserting something of the regal authority which he has abdicated; and his meaning depends somewhat on an emphasizing of the words King, commands, and service. But service may as well mean dutiful respects (9), as Stone (1980, p. 188) suggests and as it does at 32, or else helpful, beneficial acts (19), or supply of one’s needs (23), or possibly even loving devotion (10)—all reasonable requests of a daughter and hostess.

1379 Are…blood]
The absence of this line from Q may be a result of obscurity in the MS which gave the compositor difficulty, resulting in six press corrections in five lines. It is hard to imagine that the press-corrector would have missed a whole line, but equally there seems no need for its addition to F except to remedy an apparent omission. Stone (1980, p. 241), however, sees the F line as a response to Gloucester’s embarrassed inaction (see n. 1373–4): Lear…repeats his wishes—not as fresh commands, but by way of reminder—and adds Are they inform’d of this?

1379 inform’d]
The repetition of the word from 1373–4 suggests wordplay—probably ironic emphasis.

1379 My…blood]
Schmidt (ed. 1879) cannot decide whether this is an oath—By my breath and blood—or a reference to Cornwall and Regan, whom he considers creatures of his breath and blood. Most eds. take it as an oath, though it does not appear elsewhere in Sh.; Schmidt finds the same words used together for the essence of life in Jn. 4.2.246 (1971), this Confine of blood, and breathe.

1380 The fierie]
Q1(c) changes to Fierie, of which Greg (1940, p. 162) says, The folio [Fiery? The fiery] suggests that here [in Q1] we have an emendation gone wrong. I conjecture that the quarto copy agreed substantially with F, and that the [Q1] compositor omitted the first word under the impression that it was an accidental duplication. It is, in fact, metrically redundant. Then the corrector wrote Fierie in the margin, intending it to be prefixed to the line as it stood, but the compositor, still convinced of the duplication, took it to be meant as a substitute for the first two words he had set up. The folio reading is certainly not derived from either state of the quarto, and it must therefore be supposed to represent that of the playhouse manuscript. Blayney (1982, pp. 245–6): F could…be a conflation of uncorrected Q and the corrected state as reprinted by Q2, but I suspect rather that there were two emendations that went wrong.…Both later versions begin with Fierie.…Had the compositor met the words fierie the duke, he might easily have transposed the first two words by design (…[or] simple error). The proof-reader could…have deleted The f, added a caret before Duke, and written the dele symbol, F, and the in the margin. I suspect that the compositor simply forgot to insert the after performing the first part of the correction. The Folio reading…looks very like the result of a different attempt to perform exactly the same correction. Fiery? was added before the uncorrected Q reading, but the second fierie was not deleted with sufficient clarity. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 534): One could as easily conjecture that [Q1(c)]’s Fierie was meant as an addition to, rather than a replacement for, [Q1(u)]’s The fierie. Foakes (ed. 1997): F simultaneously added one word and dropped another, Lear: The repetition of this word [Fiery] sharpens the dramatic effect of the line, by making Lear break off abruptly at that. It also disrupts the meter.

1380 hot]
Craig (ed. 1901): Passionate, hot-tempered (OED, a. 6b). Joseph (ed. 1966): A sarcastic reference.

1380 that Lear]
Blayney (1982, p. 245): What the Folio prints is, metrically, even worse than corrected Q [see prev. n], despite the substitution of a dash for Lear in order to reduce the number of syllables. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 534): There seems little reason to impugn F’s effective and metrical reading.
