The meter of Q’s lines 1376–81, with or without 1379, is regular; F’s lineation produces a short 1377 and a long or rough 1380.

1381–5 Mo…bodie]
Coleridge (MS notes, 1818–19, ed. Foakes, 1989, p. 101): The strong interest now felt by Lear to try to find excuses for his daughter—most pathetic. Smith (ed. 1902): Lear’s generous attempt to excuse Cornwall suggests that he is mellowing with his misfortunes,…[which] have so far dazed him that he almost seems to be learning self-control. Soellner (1968, p. 67): Here Sh. sides with Aristotle, not Plato and the Stoics, in recognizing the body’s influence on the mind. Salingar (1983, p. 138) finds the idea in Montaigne’s Sebond; see . Like Bucknill (1859, pp. 146–53), Hoeniger (1992, pp. 324–6) sees Lear’s flightiness of thought and emotional changeableness in such reversals as occur in 1375–1586 as signs of a growing mental illness which in Sh.’s time would have been understood as (p. 330) acute hypochondriac melancholy developing into mania.

1382 Infirmitie]
The condition of sickness. Gardner (ed. 1969): I.e., one who is ill.

1382 still]
See n. 253.

1382 neglect]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Omit, leave undone (OED, v. 3).

1382 office]
See n. 1046.

1383 where…boũd]
Crook (ed. 1907): Which, when in health, we are bound to perform.

1383 not our selues]
Proverbial phrase: Dent (1981, O64.1).

1384 nature]
Elton (1966, p. 189): Human nature,…natural condition, perhaps as a derivative of the all-embracing Nature; see n. 441, cf. n. 1427.

1384 oprest]
OED (ppl. a. 1): Weighed down physically or mentally; burdened, troubled, depressed, quoting 2945. Cf. 2056+1.

1385 suffer with]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Act in sympathy with. Or perhaps, be affected along with.

1386 fallen out with]
Most eds. agree with Deighton (ed. 1891): Angry with. Wells (ed. 2000): Repudiated. A few follow Craig (ed. 1901): Owing to my excessively impetuous nature, I have erred.

1386 more]
On the double comparative see n. 84.

1386 hedier will]
Delius (ed. 1854), heady: Impetuous, violent. Schmidt (ed. 1879): Not = headstrong, but headlong.…Will occurs frequently in Sh. as the blind impulse in opposition to wit (reason). Will is variously glossed as temper (Page, ed. 1889), impulse (Tovey, ed. 1896), mood (Crook, ed. 1907), disposition (Goggin, ed. 1910), inclination (Wilson, ed. 1960), etc. Smith (ed. 1902): The comparative has here merely an intensive force,…very heady, too heady.

1387 To take]
Moberly (ed. 1876): In mistaking. Hudson (ed. 1881): The infinitive…is here used gerundively…in taking. Deighton (ed. 1891): For taking: the indefinite infinitive. Cf. 376.

1387 indispos’d…fit]
Craig (ed. 1901): An attack of illness which indisposes [the] mind. Gardner (ed. 1969): A fit was an attack of lunacy, thought to show itself periodically (OED, sb. 3b). But it could mean any recurrent attack of illness (OED, 3a). Surely Lear is not attributing lunacy to both Regan and Cornwall.

1388 Death…state]
Deighton (ed. 1891): May I be accursed! an imprecation called forth by his eyes suddenly falling again upon Kent in the stocks. Crook (ed. 1907): An end to all my state. Delius (ed. 1854), state: Both station and dignity. Tovey (ed, 1896): All that makes up the life of man, comparing Mac. 1.3.140 (251). Kittredge (ed. 1940): My royal power. If the latter, Wilson (ed. 1960): Sh. irony. Lear’s kingly power is already dead. Foakes (ed. 1997): Condition as an old man.

1388 wherfore]
Walker (1854, p. 111) would accent the second syllable more strongly. Abbott (§490) prefers to retain the usual accent by making Death…state a separate line.

1389 he]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Emphatic.

1390 remotion]
OED (sb. 4): The action of removing or departing, quoting this l. as its first ex. Malone (ed. 1790): From their own house to that of the earl of Gloster. Cf. 1278 this remove. But many eds. follow Schmidt (ed. 1879): Keeping away, non-appearance (perhaps OED 1: Remoteness), referring to 1361–2. Kittredge (ed. 1940) compares Tate’s substitution in his King Lear (1681, p. 19): this Retiredness. Gardner (ed. 1969): Aloofness.

1391 practise]
See n. 502.

1391 giue…forth]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Release. Craig (ed. 1901): Out of the stocks. Though the idiom with this meaning is not recorded in OED, forth was formerly used in many idiomatic combinations with verbs (adv. 8), and there are many close analogues for give such as give out and give up.

1392 Tell]
F’s Goe tell is apparently metrical improvement.

1392 and’s]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): And his. Cf. 1588.

1392 Ile]
F’s Il’d is generally preferred, though Q is acceptable. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 392): This may be a misreading (e/d).

1393 presently]
See n. 431.

1394 beat the drum]
Since Lear’s knights seem not to include a drummer, presumably he is speaking metaphorically; but if so, it is an oddly fanciful expression for a man in a rage. Mason (1785, p. 347) finds this and the next line a mere nonsensical rhapsody, needing emendation; see . Perhaps Lear means that he will beat on their door as if it were a drum; but the preposition is at. The sound of military drums rouses sleepers in R2 1.3.134 (427) and Ant 4.9.29 (2732); no one has instanced the possibility of drums as a summons to execution. See next n.

1395 cry…death]
Eds. have taken to to mean until or unto. Assuming the former, Steevens (in Reed, ed. 1803): Till it cries out Let them awake no more; Let their present sleep be their last. Thus Moberly (ed. 1876): Till their pretended sleep becomes real death. Many eds. confirm this sense by putting the presumed cry in quotation marks; see textual n. Wright (ed. 1875): It is difficult to see how such an interpretation could be appropriate. Mason (1785, p. 347) initiates the alternative explanation, rewriting the line cry—death to sleep. So, without emendation, Tieck (apud Knight, ed. 1840, apparently translating from ed. 1832), and the majority of eds.: Till the noise of the drum has been the death of sleep—…has forced them to awaken. Harbage (ed. 1958): Pursue with noise (like a pack or cry of hounds).

1396 all well]
Muir (ed. 1952) compares Cornwall’s sympathetic remark in Leir 831, I feare that all things go not well; see .
F supplies the necessary Exit., missing from Q.

1397 O…downe]
Ridley (ed. 1935): The Quarto reads simply, and with vigorous brevity,…whereas the Folio makes a polished line of it. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 45): The Q version results in a total loss of the point of the following speech…with its downe, wantons, downe.…Q does not give us a Shakespearian first shot. Lear, of course, need not speak regular verse while suffocating, and downe might have been suggested to the reviser by 1400. F’s Oh me is a common Shn. interjection, but rising heart does not occur elsewhere in Sh.

1398–1402 Cry…hay]
Halliwell (ed. 1865): A reference to some absurd tale of a London cockney well known in Shakespeare’s time. Joseph (ed. 1966): Which has been lost. Macaulay (1907, p. 27): The Fool’s nonsense, coming in between the bursts of the King’s agony, heightens the effect beyond description. Some see in the nonsense a general moral lesson. Hunter, ed. 1869): The fool here intimates that absurd cruelty and absurd kindness have the same origin. Empson (1951, p. 133): The Fool satirizes Lear’s habit of giving orders. Wilson (ed. 1960): The point of the speech, the folly of Lear’s heart, has been missed. The cockney…and her brother are examples of a like foolish tender-heartedness; he goes so far as to butter his horse’s hay: she cannot bring herself to kill the eels before putting them into the pastry.…Lear’s heart has been as foolishly tender towards his daughters, but it is too late now to cry down to it and play the stern father. The mischief is done. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): The Fool echoes Lear’s cry [1395] and down [1397]. Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): The Fool implies that Lear’s cry to his heart will be just as effectual. Murphy (1984, p. 174) cites Harsnett’s (1603, p. 61) emblem of stupidity, them that drowned the Eele. Foakes (ed. 1997): The point…is that the cockney…acts too late…as Lear is doing.
Others find more specific meanings for the eel and buttered hay. Johnson (ed. 1765): Hinting that the Eel and Lear are in the same danger. Eccles (ed. 1792): The fool supposes Lear to stand in the place of the cockney, and his heart in that of the eels. Mason (1797, Addit. p. 59): For the fool does not mean to compare Lear himself to the eels, but his rising choler. Elton (1966, pp. 316–17): The eel, as in Rabelais and Pericles (IV.ii.[142–4 (1658–60)]), is…a generative symbol. The Fool, in effect, seems to imply that Lear could have avoided heartache, putting down both the hysterica passio…and the rising heart itself, had he also put down his wanton impulse to reproduction. Colman (1974, p. 192), followed by McCall (1977, p. 127): Likened to rising penises. Cf. n. 1400–1. Besides providing many exx., Williams (1994) adds, not quoting this l., Eel dishes are a favourite aphrodisiac.
Tovey (ed. 1896): The brother’s behavior is certainly the sort of silliness that country folk would attribute to the Londoner. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): As one city-bred in the country, who butters the hay…and who is as green as a rustic in the city, viz. his sister. Madden (1897; 1907, p. 298): The Fool notes a horse’s abhorrence of any greasy matter. Craig (ed. 1901): A stupid act, as the horse will not away with grease. A common trick of cheating ostlers formerly was to grease the hay, etc. of horses committed to their care, and so keep the horse from feeding, and then steal the provender—to which Muir (ed. 1952) adds: The cockney’s brother, however, did it in all innocence. Cf. Beaumont’s Knight of the Burning Pestle (1607), And never grease their teeth with candle-snuffe (2.364). Elton (op. cit., p. 317): Although in Robert Wilson’s The Three Ladies of London (ca. 1581) it is charged, Thou didst grease the horses’ teeth, that they should not eat hay, [ed. Hazlitt, 1874, 6:255]…the cockney’s foolish brother presumably acted merely out of the goodness of his heart. In an upside-down world, which binds generation to filial ingratitude [1794], pure kindness becomes perversity where thanklessness is the norm. Somerset (1982, p. 118): The passage [from Wilson’s play] suggests that the cockney’s brother…[was] planning to substitute better provender when the hay was refused; it was a simple-minded act because the horse naturally would prefer other provender over hay, buttered or not.

1398 Nunckle]
See n. 634.

1398 Coknay]
Q1(c)’s Cokney improves a common spelling (Greg, 1940, p. 162). OED (Cockney sb. 2d): A squeamish, over-nice, wanton, or affected woman, quoting this l. as its first of only two exx.; so glossed by Reed (ed. 1785). Verity (ed. 1897): The notion…is brought out…by the absurd words which the cockney uses to the eels. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Here it seems to denote a city woman, unfamiliar with such vulgar things as the making of eel pies. Commentators have traced the derivation of the term from the original coken-ey, cock’s egg (OED, 1) to a cockered child and hence to a squeamish or affected fellow or woman (OED, 2) to a townsman, considered more effeminate than a countryman (OED, 3) and on to the modern meaning, a Londoner born within the sound of Bow Bells (OED, 4; first ex. dated 1600). There seems to be no support for derivation from cock’s neigh (Minsheu, 1617), cook (Tyrwhitt, apud Steevens, ed. 1778), or Cockaigne (Douce, 1807, 2:151–6, and Albert Way, ed., Promptorium Parvulorum, 1843–65), or for the senses of simpleton (Rann, ed. 1794; Mackay, 1887, p. 88), a cooked dish (Whalley, in Reed, ed. 1785), a cook (Nares, 1822), one who is coaxed (Burgess, 1859), slut (Bulloch, 1878, p. 244; unsupported by Williams, 1994), or scoundrel (Crook, ed. 1907), though most of these ideas have been repeated by eds. Rushton (1871, pp. 74–5) was the first of many to cite its use in a passage in Lyly’s Euphues (ed. Bond, 1:244), where other terms in this passage—wanton, foole, and cockscomb—also appear. Munro (ed. 1957): The word was often accompanied by wanton, citing exx. from Tilley C501 and OED; the epithet probably meant spoiled, pampered.

1399 vm]
A common variant of F’s ’em; see n. 908. Daniel (facs. 1885, p. xiv): Q2’s vm vp might be an independent reading. Doran (1931, p. 32), however, finds it no different in nature from other unauthoritative additions in Q2.

1399 past]
OED (Paste sb.): Dough…as used in making pastry, quoting this l. Greg (1940, p. 162) thinks Q1(c)’s pâst a strange alteration…[probably] to indicate a long vowel without adding a final e in a crowded line. There is, of course, no authority for such use of the circumflex in English (except ô), but it may have been suggested by a contemporary convention in Latin. Blayney (1982, p. 112) suspects an incorrect replacement of a defective letter.

1399 rapt]
F’s knapt means the same: Knock, rap (OED, Knap v.1 1). Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 392) suspects that the Q compositor misread napt, but knap was echoic, and the word does not appear spelled nap until the 19th c.

1400 ath]
See n. 676.

1400 coxcombs]
Wright (ed. 1875): Used jocularly for heads (OED, 2).

1400–1 downe wantons downe]
OED (Wanton sb. 2b): A sportive or roguish animal, bird, etc., quoting this l. as its first ex. Muir (ed. 1952): Even without Robert Graves’ poem of this title one might suspect that the phrase was equivocal (OED, 3: A lascivious or lewd person). Orgel (ed. 1999): A quibble on lechers and on deflating erections.

1403 Enter…]
On Q’s incomplete entrance see n. 538. F’s addition of Gloster, who does not speak for almost 200 lines and has an entrance at 1596, is justified by 1597; his exit is specified in Q at 1586. Foakes (ed. 1997): Regan wears gorgeous clothes [1569].…If she and Cornwall are dressed for the day, their social excuse of being sick and weary is exposed as a fiction, citing Rosenberg (1972, pp. 161–2) for other dress.

1404 Good morrow]
Perrett (1904, p. 223): An ironical greeting, late in the day. See n. 1273.

1405 your Grace]
See n. 218.

1407–9 Regan…Regan]
Horsman (ed. 1973, p. 225): One can observe the change from the common you to the affectionate thou, and back again.…She replies, of course, with the respectful you. For the counterpart meeting of Leir and Ragan, see Leir 1118–56 (). Foakes (ed. 1997): If Lear’s anger melts away briefly his greeting of Regan can be very affecting, citing Bratton (ed. 1987, p. 123) and Rosenberg (1972, pp. 161–2).

1407 you]
On F’s erroneous your see n. 867.

1407 reason]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Sc. all his kindness to her.

1409–10 deuose me from]
Q1(c)’s diuorse is certainly correct (Greg, 1940, p. 163). The spelling deuorse, conjectured by Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 516), does not occur elsewhere in F1 or the good quartos; it might be compositorial. Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956): Refuse to be buried in.

1409 mothers]
Greg (1940, p. 392): Presumably the F compositor [setting Mother] carelessly omitted a final -s. Compositor E often does so. Craig (ed. 1901): The only place, I think, in this play where there is any allusion to the mother of Lear’s three daughters. In the old play she is mentioned at the opening [Leir 1–4; see ] as just being dead. Using the argument from absence, psychoanalytic critics find great significance in these facts: see n. 43–6.

1409 fruit,]
Greg (1940, p. 163) finds Q1(c)’s tombe certainly correct.…If an accidental stroke or smudge gave a tail to the t, the misreading would be a possible one. One would expect a comma: probably the printer left it out accidentally when inserting a slightly longer word. Doubting, as Stone (1980, p. 201) does (see ), such a misreading, Taylor (1982, p. 122) proposes that original scrine (for shrine; see textual n.) was misread fruit, which the puzzled Q1 corrector, seeing Sepulchring in the next line, replaced with the conjectural tombe. This misreading seems hardly easier than Greg’s, and the spelling in Sh.’s texts is always shrine. Joseph (ed. 1966): As the mother is dead he cannot divorce her. He therefore threatens to do the next best thing and disown her tomb, its contents and all that it represents of her on earth.

1410 Sepulchring]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): As being the tomb of (OED, v. 2, quoting this l. as its first ex.). The stress is on the second syllable (Abbott §490; OED).

1410 adultresse]
Foakes (ed. 1997), citing Adelman (1992, pp. 108–9): Lear invents a fantasy of illegitimacy, so linking his daughters (he called Goneril degenerate bastard at [764]) with Edmund’s bastardy, and siting the origin of viciousness in the female. But Lear is here rejecting the possibility his wife was an adultress, is yet unaware of any evil in Edmund (see 2560), continually reprehends both men and women for their evil, and explicitly says thou art my flesh, my bloud, my daughter (1515) and twas this [father’s] flesh Begot those Pelicane daughters (1855–6). Cf. n. 2567–71, however.

1410 yea]
On this word and F1’s O see n. 823.

1411 that]
A few eds. (see textual n.) have Kent exit here; though his exit at 1586 is clearly marked in Q, it is not explicit in F. He has no lines to indicate his presence after 1405. Ringler (1960, pp. 311–17) argues that the exit of Kent here would explain both his separation from Lear by line 1615, a few moments after Lear’s exit, and Kent’s uncharacteristic silence during Regan’s and Goneril’s insults to Lear in the rest of the scene. He interprets Q’s Kent at 1586 as a misinterpretation of K or Knt indicating the Knight who entered at 1273. Thus his emendation (to send Kent off here) would assume an Exit missing from both Q and F and a misreading of a later SD. But Kent’s silence may be otherwise explained—having disgraced his master by his outspokenness and being now dismissed to the background in 1411, he is hesitant to interpose himself again during the scene—and the king becomes separated from all his remaining knights, not just from Kent.

1411 Some…that]
Deighton (ed. 1891): I will come to that matter later on. Goggin (ed. 1910): In the thought of his greater grievance Lear puts aside for the moment the insult to his messenger. Petronella (1981, p. 9): The words point to the worsening plight of Lear.

1411–15 Beloued…Regan]
Q puts medial and terminal commas in each of these lines. Halio (ed. 1973): They are rhetorical: The Q punctuation (substantially also F’s) clearly indicates Lear’s over-wrought state and near incoherence.

1412 naught]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Worthless, good for nothing (OED, a. 1). Schmidt (1875): Naughty,…wicked (OED, 2).

1412–13 tyed…heare]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Alluding to the fable of Prometheus. Capell (1783, 1.2:159): But here it is the vulture that is tied, not its victim, and heare apparently refers to the heart, not the liver. Rolfe (ed. 1880) finds the same allusion in 2H4 5.3.139 (3164), 1H6 4.3.47–8 (2057–8), Tit. 5.2.31 (2317), etc., and Muir (1951, p. 15) cites Harsnett (1603, p. 73): Prometheus with his Vulture; see . The image was common: see Samuel Daniel, Delia 15, my Vultur-gnawne hart. For the frequency of the Prometheus allusion in the Renaissance see Elton (1966, p. 213 and n.). Fraser (1962, p. 79 and Pl. XXXI): In Alciati, Emblematum Libellus, an emblem of the self torment of a guilty conscience. Houghton (ed. 1957) compares 775. Like Thirlby (MS notes, 1725–33), Root (1903, p. 112) suggests, alternatively, the fate of Tityus as described in Æn. 6.595–600 and Met. 4.457. For conjectural emendations of tyed to tired (OED, Tire v.2 2: To tear flesh in feeding, as a hawk or other bird of prey) see .

1413 vnkindnes]
See n. 132.

1414 thout]
The same as F’s thou’lt, thou wilt; see Franz §176.

1415 Of…qualitie]
See n. 1367, 1371. F’s With…quality might refer to Goneril’s actions rather than her character (OED, Quality sb. 7b: Manner, style.…Obs. rare.). Thus Tovey (ed. 1896): Either, with what a depraved creature I have had to do, or, in what a base way she has treated me.

1415 deptoued]
Q1(c)’s depriued is obviously wrong as it stands. But the o in [Q1(u)] suggests that the copy had a rather than i, so that depriued may be a literal error due to the printer (Greg, 1940, p. 163). F’s deprau’d is usually accepted as correct. Stone (1980, p. 180): deplor’d is more likely to be what the Q compositor saw in his MS, since the mistaking of r for t, intrinsically unlikely, is unexampled elsewhere in the text. See textual n.

1416 pray]
F’s pray you makes regular meter; Q may have omitted the prounoun accidentally.

1416 take patience]
See n. 774. Rolfe (ed. 1880): The idiom occurs in WT 3.2.231 (1422), H8 5.1.105 (2901–2).

1417–18 You…dutie]
Beginning with Johnson (ed. 1765), many commentators have noted that these two lines seem to give a meaning directly contrary to the sense intended. Capell (1783, 1.2:160): Sh. should have written You more know how to lessen her desert. So Malone (1783, p. 49): The inaccuracy of the expression will clearly appear from inverting the sentence without changing a word: I have hope (says Regan) that she knows more (or better) how to scant her duty, than you know how to value her desert. Idem (ed. 1790): If [Sh.] had written I have hope that you rather know how to make her desert less than it is…than that she at all knows how to scant her duty, all would have been clear; but by placing less before know this meaning is destroyed. The intended meaning is clear enough, as Steevens (ed. 1778) asserts: You less know how to value her desert,…than she can be capable of being wanting in her duty. Even more simply, the Clarkes (ed. 1868): You are less capable of appreciating her merit than she is of failing in her duty. Schmidt (1875, p. 1420): An example of the double negative common in Sh. and his contemporaries. Wright (ed. 1875), agreeing: We should have expected some word the very opposite of scant. Viewed differently, the difficulty arises from a comparison that seems to make a positive (knowing how to value) somehow less in its performance than a negative (slacking or scanting). Thus Hudson (ed. 1879): The difficulty grows from putting a positive and a negative clause together in a comparison. Change the positive clause into a negative, and the sense comes right, thus: You know not how to value her desert, rather than she knows how to be wanting in her duty. Still better, perhaps, if we change the negative clause into a positive: You less know how to value her desert than she knows how to do her duty. Similarly Tovey (ed. 1896): The second member of the comparison is given, as if the first member had run, you more know how to under-value, i.e., You are more apt to underrate her merit than she to scant her duty. Sisson (1956, 2:236) simply understands a third negative: The construction is, You less know how to value her desert than she (little knows how) to scant her duty. Greg (1933, p. 771): The confusion is due to Shakespeare himself, who has mistaken his construction. The obscurity has its defenders. Furness (ed. 1880): Perhaps Regan’s speech puzzles poor old Lear himself, quite as much as his commentators, and he has to ask her to explain: Say, how is that? Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): An example of Regan’s hard glibness of tongue, just cleverly empty enough to bewilder Lear, but meaning nothing except that she sides with her sister. Muir (ed. 1952): Perhaps Shakespeare meant Regan to say the opposite of [what she means], and so tell the truth against her will.

1418 slacke]
OED (v. 1): To be slack or remiss in respect of (some business, duty, etc.), quoting the word’s reappearance in 1542; the adjective with the same meaning had appeared at 512. F substitutes scant, whose meaning is similar: see n. 304, and cf. 1459, 1721. Stone (1980, p. 218): Needlessly corrected in F. The double negative (see prev. n.) leads many eds. to expect a word with the opposite meaning such as do (Moberly, ed. 1876) or perform (Brooke, ed. 1947).

1419–24 Lear.…blame.]
These F lines seem more probably an addition to Q, continuing and expanding on Regan’s previous speech, than an accidental omission from Q, though Delius (1876, pp. 135–6) thinks only the latter can explain the absence of such valuable lines, Regan’s pretext for justifying still farther her sister’s conduct. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxi): The Lear-actor is in a hurry to get to the cursing, and Regan’s icy argument, although a fine closet touch, delays his outbreak. Cunnington (1910, p. 449): To make it clear that Regan knows the details of the quarrel between Lear and Goneril, Sh. inserted…two passages, the one where Goneril describes the contents of her letter [853–5] and this one. Moriarty (1913, p. 461): The added lines are intended as preparation for what follows and give a better sequence to the speeches between the king and Regan. Doran (1931, p. 60): Long for an accidental omission, but the pattern of the omitted lines, a short line by Lear and several lines by Regan, is the same as that of the two speeches by Lear and Regan immediately following. Having in his mind a visual impression of what came next in his copy, the printer might have picked up the second of Lear’s speeches instead of the first. Stone (1980, p. 242): Following Regan’s convoluted syntax, Lear’s request for clarification comes in with unintentionally comic effect, but it does enable the reviser to add a longer speech in which Regan makes her meaning perfectly plain. It is impossible to regard this clumsy procedure as original. The wonder is that the reviser did not simply substitute the new speech for Regan’s original one. Honigmann (1982, pp. 150–1): This is not Lear’s only request for clarification with comic potential…[but] a characteristic prank…that prepares for a characteristic kink in his madness [citing 1830]. Second, the F lines provide a bridge…[to] the sudden viciousness of O…old.…Third, F’s lines are connected with an earlier F insertion [842–55].…Someone…wished to make it clearer that the sisters saw the knights as a threat. Weis (ed. 1993): Lear’s reply (My…her) follows more naturally in Q than F where he might be expected to protest against her impudent riots…followers. McLeod (1983, p. 179), who sees no reason to account Regan’s behaviour as sinister per se since she frankly reveals in 1422 her grounds for siding with Goneril: Regan’s second F speech mitigates the bluntness of the first (her only one in Q), and so may render us less sympathetic to Lear’s repetition of his curse on Goneril, which it postpones. But of course Regan’s behavior must seem sinister because of her compact with Goneril in 310–322; her unhesitating acceptance of Goneril’s rationalizations, which the audience knows are exaggerated (see 853–5, 861–3) if not unfounded (see nn. 586–872, 715); and her prompt and heartless attempts to avoid seeing her father at all, either at her home (1041–3, 1067) or here at Gloucester’s (1361)—not to mention her contempt for Lear’s servant (1216, 1225–6). These added lines serve notice to Lear and the audience how firmly she has allied herself with Goneril and prepare for the ensuing events in the scene.

1419 Say]
OED (v.1 6c): In the imperative, introducing a direct question, quoting this l. Harbage (1963, p. 415): His ears refuse to take in Regan’s initial rebuke…and he treats her successive rebuffs as if they came from Goneril.

1421 faile]
OED (v. 10): Omit to perform.

1422 haue]
Abbott (§366): The subjunctive with have…is used where a past event is not indeed denied, but qualified conditionally, in an argumentative manner.…If it should be hereafter proved that she have, if so be that she have.

1422 Riots]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Regan and Goneril use the same vocabulary for the knights, comparing 513, 715, 753, 1033. Foakes (ed. 1997): Another reference [added in F] to the riotous behaviour of Lear’s train. Regan simply parrots Goneril’s claim, from her letter; there is no independent evidence of the Riots. See n. 586–872

1426–30 O…selfe]
Doran (1933, p. 57) suspects that the lines are owing to Montaigne; cf. n. 522+1–+4 and see .

1426 O…old]
Coleridge (MS notes, 1818–19, ed. Foakes, 1989, p. 101): Nothing so heart-cutting as a cold, unexpected defence etc. of a cruelty complained of passionately—or so expressive of hard-heartedness. And the horror of O…old; and then drawing from that universal object of reverence and indulgence the reason for Say…her [1432]. All Lear’s faults increase our pity—we refuse to know them otherwise than as means and aggravations of his sufferings and his daughters’ ingratitude.

1427 Nature]
Joseph (ed. 1966): Life, the natural forces which keep life going. OED (sb.): The vital or physical powers of man; (a person’s) physical strength or constitution. Cf. 1700, 1780, 2056+1, 2362.

1427 on you]
F corrects to in you. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 392): The compositor, carrying a group of words in his head, may have anticipated the on later in the line.

1427 verge]
Schmidt (1875): Brink, edge (OED, sb. 14). Falconer (1965, p. 91): Specifically of sea, cliff, or river (OED 15). Cf. 2462.

1427–8 standes…confine]
Wright (ed. 1875), confine: The accent is on the last syllable (OED, sb.2). Most eds. take the meaning of confine to be limit, boundary (OED, 1b), but that repeats the meaning of verge. Horsman (ed. 1973): Place of confinement (OED, 5). Possibly it means region, territory (OED, 2). Page (ed. 1889): Boundary (between sanity and madness). Tovey (ed. 1896): A euphemism for death. Brooke (ed. 1947): A very fine figure. Lear’s powers (like the owner of an estate) have travelled over all the territory that is theirs and now stand on the extreme edge, viewing that over which they have no control. Muir (ed. 1952): Regan may mean that Lear is imprisoned in the flesh and about to be released by death. Skillan (ed. 1967): At the extremest edge of her span with its consequent weakness.

1428 her]
Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 176–7): F’s his might be accepted as equivalent to its, were it not that Nature is being personified: and Nature is personified as a female in Shakespeare as to-day. His may be a careless substitution by the F compositor. See n. 727. Foakes (ed. 1997): F’s his makes a kind of sense as drawing the emphasis towards Lear. But in that case Goneril, who is addressing Lear, would have said your confine.

1429 some discretion]
Wright (ed. 1875): The discretion of some one; unless discretion is used for discreet person as speculation in [1633]. Furness (ed. 1880): The abstract for the concrete, comparing 1807 You houselesse pouertie.

1429 state]
See n. 44. The general meaning here of condition (OED, sb. 1) is further specified as weakness due to your age (Deighton, ed. 1891), condition of mind (Kittredge, ed. 1940), and dependent position (Muir, ed. 1952). Hoeniger (ed. 1968): And (possibly) kingdom. Hunter (ed. 1972): An ironic echo of state meaning power, royalty.

1431 make returne]
Return. Schmidt (1875) gives Shn. exx. of the idiom. Rolfe (ed. 1880): S. does not use the phrase in the modern sense (= make requital).

1432 Sir]
F’s omission does not improve the meter. Burton (1973, p. 114): Here and at 1485, 1511, and 1533 the verbless sentence and final position of sir are impolite. Since Regan is commanding rather than inquiring or exclaiming, Q’s question mark, omitted by all eds. except Halio (ed. 1973), is probably a printer’s error.

1434 you]
F’s you but is apparently metrical polishing.

1434 marke]
OED (Mark v. 16): Followed by indirect question: To ascertain by observation (what, whether, etc.).

1434 this]
Hunter (ed. 1869): The form of supplication Lear is about to utter.

1434 house]
The literal meaning is either household, family (OED, sb. 5), proposed by Delius (ed. 1854) and the Clarkes (ed. 1868), or (royal) family line (OED, 6), proposed by Staunton (ed. 1859), Perrett (1904, p. 250: the house of Brute), Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905: and the dignity befitting it) and many others. Most eds., however, interpret the word as a synecdoche, most commonly for family order and relationships (Warburton, ed. 1747; Hudson, ed. 1871; and others). Thus Kittredge (ed. 1940): Spoken with bitter irony: fathers would not kneel to the children in any normal family. Schmidt [ed. 1879] compares the horrified protest of Coriolanus [5.3.55–62 (3406–12)] when his mother kneels to him. The other figurative meaning is Lear himself, head of the household and royal family, and king, as is understood by Capell (1783, 1.2:160), Craig (ed. 1901), and others. Dent (1981, H782.1) suspects the phrase is proverbial.

1435–7 Deare…food]
Sprague (1944, p. 289): A serious petition when spoken by some 19th-c. actors, but spoken with a compound of real anger and affected levity by their 18th-c. predecessors.

1436 Age is vnnecessarie]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Old age has few wants (OED, Unnecessary a. 2, quoting only this l.). Steevens (ed. 1778): It seems unnecessary to children that the lives of their parents should be prolonged. [The phrase] may mean, old people are useless. Tyrwhitt (in Steevens, ed. 1778): Age is in want of necessaries, unable to procure them, unattested in OED. Heron (1785, p. 307): Age is now without respect, and without happiness…unnecessary evil! Halliwell (ed. 1865): An useless article, superfluous,…not wanted. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Living beyond a certain period is unneeded. Wright (ed. 1875): Lear is merely apologizing ironically for his useless existence. Most eds. agree with Steevens and Wright. Heilman (1948, p. 143): Lear’s ironic prayer is a ruthlessly logical display of the doctrine of the survival of the fittest.…Age is a crime in a world where the chief value is physical force. On the scansion see n. 154.

1436 on my knees]
Knight (ed. 1840) doubts the propriety of the usual stage direction here (see textual n.), on the grounds that Lear is not addressing these words to Regan; but later (ed. 1867), persuaded by Dyce, he restores it on the grounds that the action might be appropriate even if Lear were only rehearsing what he would say to Goneril. Dyce (1844, p. 227): Wishing to impress Regan with the full absurdity of his asking forgiveness of her sister, he drops upon his knees,—the immediately-following speech of Regan [is] decisive on the point; Good…tricks. Goggin (ed. 1910) compares 2812–14, where Lear kneels before another daughter and begs forgiveness for the folly of age. Actors almost always kneel, to different effects, as Rosenberg (1972, pp. 164–5) records, adding, This echo of his posture for the curse in I. iv is a reverse of the visual imagery in I, i, when his daughter may have, as usually in the theatre, knelt.…It is also a foreshadowing of another curse to come, and a reverse of his kneeling seriously to pray in III, iv, to beg forgiveness of Cordelia in IV, vii, to kneel by her corpse at the end. It is a focus of many thematic energies: the mighty king on his knees, the father become a child to the child, the old submissive to the young, the rich and powerful engulfed by the darkening shadow of poverty. Colie (1974, pp. 210–11): Here, bitter mockery: In England, a mark of respect paid parents by their children was kneeling for their blessing, comparing 2950–1. Leggatt (1992, p. 185): It was a daily custom…; even grown children performed this ritual on entering or leaving their parents’ houses. Halio (ed. 1992): Deliberate bathos. Lear is hurt and angry but still has enough wit left for sarcasm. Foakes (ed. 1997): A visual emblem of the inversion of order in the play, contrasting 2811 and citing Bevington (1984, pp. 169–71) on the erosion of proper custom in Lr.

1438 vnsightly]
Craig (ed. 1901): Unbecoming. OED (a. 1b): Unpleasing to the eye, quoting this l. as its first ex.

1438 tricks]
Craig (ed. 1901): Lear’s kneeling, and perhaps Shakespeare here girds at the kneeling Leir and Cordella, Leir 2298–2353; see . Halio (ed. 1992): Rhetorical devices.

1440 No]
F’s Neuer makes regular meter. Doran (1931, p. 126): Failure of a printer’s memory may account for Q’s word.

1441 abated me of]
OED (Abate v.1 7): To abate of;…to deprive of, curtail of, quoting this l. Rolfe (ed. 1880): Not found elsewhere in S. There is no reason to agree with Foakes (ed. 1997): Dramatically, an impression is conveyed that Lear’s train has already been slashed. Goneril’s abatement was conditional: Lear would have had to reduce his train, perhaps in the coming fortnight (see n. 811), if he were to stay with Goneril. He has rejected that option, and speaks of his hundred knights at the beginning of this scene as if they were still in attendance; see n. 1273. Goneril could decide how many knights she would support in her household, but not how many accompanied Lear to Regan’s. Ibid., abated: The word was used by Spenser, Faerie Queene, 2.10.30: see .

1441 halfe]
See n. 810.

1442 blacke]
Probably not clowdy or gloomy (OED, a. 10), as Johnson (ed. 1765) thought, but having dark or deadly purposes, malignant (OED, 9). OED (10b) does not record an ex. of Of the countenance:…clouded with anger, frowning; threatening, boding ill before 1709, or of the phrase To look black; to frown, to look angrily (10c) before 1814; but Sh. had previously referred to black-fac’d Clifford (R3 1.2.158 [349]), the black brow of night (Jn. 5.6.17 [2573]), etc. Warburton (ed. 1747): It alludes to a serpent’s turning black, when it swells with rage and venom, the very creature to which Lear here compares his daughter. He cites no source for this belief. Hicks (1995, p. 322) rejects Q2’s backe as an easy misprint and Theobald’s blank as unsuitable to the context.

1442 strooke]
OED (Strike, v. 37): To wound (a person) with…fangs. On the short participle see n. 615. Craig (ed. 1901): Perhaps an echo of the old play,…I will so toung-whip him [Leir 1048]; see . Baldwin (1944, p. 617): An allusion to Aesop’s fable of the country-man and the snake.

1443 Serpent-like]
OED (adv.): With serpentine motion,…disposition, quoting this l. as its first ex. Cf. n. 802. Foakes (ed. 1997): It was generally supposed that a serpent’s venom was in its tongue (OED, Tongue sb. 1[c]).

1443 heart]
See n. 1029.

1444 stor’d vengeances]
Deighton (ed. 1891) finds the idea in R3 1.3.216 (686) and Cor. 4.2.11 (2518), and Craig (ed. 1901) the very phrase in Beaumont & Fletcher’s The Coxcomb (ca. 1609) 1.1.22.

1444 fall]
Subjunctive used optatively or imperatively (Abbott §§364–5); cf. 161. Tovey (ed. 1896): Might be transitive,…but best taken as intransitive here. Cf. 1451.

1445 ingratful]
Abbott (§442): In- for un-. Rolfe (ed. 1880): S. uses ingrateful much oftener than ungrateful. Cf. 2090.

1445 top]
Schmidt (1875): Crown of the head, giving Shn. exx.

1445 yong bones]
Although there is no evidence in the play that Goneril has or is expecting children, a surprising number of eds. have followed the interpretation of Jourdain (1860–1, p. 141), that yong bones means infants just born, or yet unborn (Addis, 1867, pp. 251–2). To Bransom (1934, p. 45) the phrase is conclusive that Goneril was in the early stages of her first pregnancy. The phrase could have such meanings; Jourdain cites Leir 844 (see ), she breeds yong bones (OED, Bone sb. 2: The skeleton;…the bodily frame, body, person <with pathetically humorous force>, citing Leir), and other examples are supplied by him, Addis, Furness (ed. 1880), and Craig (ed. 1901). Verity (ed. 1897): His curse therefore keeps the same lines as before, viz. of imprecation upon Goneril’s unborn child [795–7]. Kellett (1923, p. 40), seconded by Muir (ed. 1952): The curse gains greatly in meaning if we assume that Shakspere’s Lear, like the old playwright’s Leir, knew or suspected that Goneril had already an unborn child. Lear hints no such suspicion, Leir did not curse an unborn child, and there is a vast difference between wishing that a child be so ill-natured as to torment the mother and wishing that it be born lame. Such a wish, monstrous in itself, would require Lear to change the focus of his curse from Goneril to her putative children back to Goneril. Perring (1885, pp. 326–7) offers a more consistent reading: King Lear, after denouncing Goneril in general terms, proceeds to frame against her a three-fold curse: her bones are young; lame them: her eyes are scornful; blind them: her beauty carries her away; blast it.…There is a special fitness in her father’s cursing her young bones, as she had taunted him with being old. Nor is it likely that the king, after he had petitioned the gods to carry into her womb sterility, would assume that there was an unborn infant to strike with lameness. Perrett (1904, pp. 275–6): What kind of disgusting Mumbo-Jumbo does it turn Lear into to believe that he vents his wrath in a horrible curse upon a babe unborn, the creature of proverbial innocence? What further sympathy could we have with such a foul-mouthed, inhuman savage?…The idea…is only saved from being revolting by being nonsense. How could the taking airs strike with lameness an unborn infant? Sh. and Lear knew too well as if they had read it in the words of a modern scientist that the human embryo is entirely withdrawn from the direct influence of the outer world…by enclosure in its protective membranes. He cites from Gascoigne’s Supposes (1566) 4.2.4 a remark addressed to a young man: A rope stretche your yong bones. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The context makes it certain that this applies to Goneril’s own youthful frame. To breed young bones is, to be sure, an old phrase for to be with child, but that does not justify the strange interpretation (Strike her unborn child) which has found favour with some critics. Lott (ed. 1974): Shakespeare may have recalled the phrase [from Leir] but given it a more literal meaning.

1446 taking]
Theobald (1726, p. 140): Blasting, bewitching, citing 1840–1, Ham. 1.1.163 (162), Wiv. 4.4.32 (2154). OED (ppl. a. 3): Seizing or affecting injuriously; blasting, pernicious…; infectious, catching, quoting this l. as its first ex. Cf. 1840–1. As Theobald’s gloss and examples suggest, taking could be effected by natural along with supernatural or magical agencies (OED, Take v. 7). Here it is apparently the natural agency of bad airs; for suggestions that ayrs be emended to fairies, see .

1448–51 You…pride]
Clemen (1961, pp. 242–3): Conventional prayer for annihilation, citing precedents in Seneca and in Elizabethan drama, including Gorboduc 3.1.25–6, 163–5. Elton (1966, p. 189): Here, as elsewhere, Lear is motivated by a polytheistic animism, in which all nature is alive and shares in the divine.

1448 You]
Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 392, 84): The Q omission of the speech-heading is doubtless accidental, since Q insets the line. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 516): As though it were the beginning of a speech. Perhaps the Q compositor’s use of a narrow measure on this page is at least partly responsible for the omission. Q2 supplies an obvious lack.

1449 infect]
Wright (ed. 1875): Taint, pollute (OED, v. 2: Spoil or corrupt). Cf. 752. Weis (ed. 1993), overspecifically: With swamp fever or malaria; cf. the next n.

1450 Fen…Sunne]
Craig (ed. 1901) compares Tmp. 2.2.1–2 (1040–1), All the infections that the Sunne suckes vp From Bogs, Fens, Flats, on Prosper fall, and MND 2.1.88–90. Kittredge (ed. 1940) compares 818 and 1 Tamburlaine 4.2.5–7, Make…every fixed starre To sucke up poison from the moorish Fens, And poure it in this glorious Tyrant’s throat.

1451 To fall]
The infinitive may be attached to either infect or drawne, the meaning in either case being in order to fall; Gardner (ed. 1969), followed by Lott (ed. 1974), attaches it to the more remote beautie: I.e., so that it (her beauty) falls away. Eds. are further divided whether fall is used transitively or intransitively. Malone (in Steevens, ed. 1778), reading transitively: To fall and blast, (i.e. humble and destroy) her pride. OED (v. 51): To bring or throw to the ground; to overthrow. lit. and fig., with exx. from ca. 1300 to 1625. Neither Abbott (§291), Schmidt (1874), nor Onions (1911) finds such a sense here or elsewhere in Sh. Stone (1980, p. 218), uniquely reads To-fall: To in Q is an intensive particle, and to-fall an imperative, citing several Shn. analogues. Mason (1785, p. 348), like Capell (1783, 1.2:160): Drawn up by the sun, in order to fall down again. Though either sense is possible, Wright (ed. 1875), like most modern eds., prefers the intransitive, as more in keeping with drawn which precedes and blast which follows. Cf. n. 1444. Kittredge (ed. 1940): To fall upon her. Only Lee (ed. 1908): Perhaps Fall to ruin.

1451 blast her pride]
Most eds. prefer Q; those who accept F’s blister usually emend it; see textual n. and . OED (Blast v. 7): Trans.…To wither, shrivel, or arrest vegetation; to blight. Said of a malignant wind; (v. 8): Trans. and fig. (Blasting withers up the brightness, freshness, beauty, vitality, and promise of living things.) Cf. 818, blasts and fogs vpon the, and 1840. Nichols (1862, p. 1): F’s blister refers to the inflammation and vesications of erysipelas (St. Anthony’s Fire) caused (he believes) by England’s foggy air. Schmidt (ed. 1879) finds such an idea in Tmp. 1.2.324 (461). OED does not attest to F’s blister as a verb used absolutely in the sense raise blisters (Foakes, ed. 1997), nor is it so used elsewhere in Sh. Sisson’s (1956, 2:236) grounds for preferring F—Sun-drawn fogs do not infect pride, but can…blister her skin—are not pertinent: Q says clearly that the fogs will infect her beauty, the obvious implication being that her pride will thus be withered. Q’s reading echoes Lear’s language in a counterpart curse at 818, makes perfect sense, and is grammatically and metrically superior to F, which is usually emended by the addition of an object (from Q) and an extra syllable; Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 144–5) would add two syllables, her pride, but elide the -er of blister. Kirschbaum (1951, p. 173) rejects Q’s pride as unauthorial: The alternatives are not blast and blister. They are blast her and blister. Muir (ed. 1952): Blast and blister were probably thought to have a common derivation [see OED (Blister sb.)], so that the substitution of one for the other would be simple enough.

1452 blest Gods]
Elton (1966, pp. 118–19): Like Goneril, Regan also spares mentioning the gods, except once, hypocritically, before Lear…—a silence which may be eloquent regarding her beliefs. She thus represents an antithesis to Gloucester’s concern regarding the heavenly forces.

1453 the rash]
See n. 321. Only Deighton (ed. 1891): The implies such a mood as being habitual to him.

1453 mood—]
Though most eds. accept F’s moode is on., there are demurs. Steevens (ed. 1773): Q may intentionally leave the sentence unfinished. Sisson (1956, 2:236): The Folio…seems weak as well as unmetrical, and Lear is plainly impetuous and breaks in upon Regan. Wilson (ed. 1960): Corruption induced by on me earlier in the line. Craig (ed. 1901), mood: Passion-fit, comparing TGV 4.1.49 (1597). OED (sb.1 2a): Anger. OED (On adv. 13b): In progress or course of action, quoting this l. as its first ex.

1455–6 The…harshnes]
Deighton (ed. 1891): It seems doubtful whether these words go with the line above or with those that follow, whether…harshness means…harshness as your sister has shown, or…to be cursed by me as I have cursed your sister.

1455 The]
An easy misreading; all eds. adopt F’s Thy. Conceivably Lear might be referring to The…nature different from the destructive nature of taking airs, lightnings, and fogs just invoked upon Goneril; but the subject of the rest of the speech is Regan’s nature.

1455 tẽder hested]
With few exceptions eds. consider Q a long-s/f misreading and accept F’s tender-hefted. Neither reading makes easy sense, but Q’s may be the more straightforward and simple.
Q: hested. Steevens (ed. 1773): Governed by gentle passions. Hest is an old word, signifying command (OED, sb. 1, v. 2). Seymour (1805, 2:111): Formed to gentleness by…the creator. Becket (1815, 1:154): Tenderly ordained. Verplanck (ed. 1844): Subject to tender laws, to the commands of natural kindness. White (1880, p. 829): Tenderly ruled, tenderly ordered. Lee (ed. 1908): Tender-vowed, plighted to gentleness (OED, Hest sb. 2, v. 1: Promise). Muir (ed. 1952), doubtfully: Commanded by a tenderness. Stone (ed. 1980): Hest (= will) [OED, sb. 3: Purpose; cf. v. 3]: the formation of quasi-participial adjectives from nouns is common in Sh., citing Abbott (§294), who does not list hested. Sh. never uses hest as a verb, and in its four appearances as noun it means behest, command.
F: hefted. (1) Theobald (ed. 1733), followed by several eds.: I.e. whose Bosom is heav’d with tender Passions, citing WT 2.1.45 (642) violent Hefts, Sh.’s only use of the word (as a noun) and OED’s only ex. for the meaning a heaving effort (sb. 4). Comparing the use of heave to mean sigh at 2347+26 and in Ham. 4.1.1 (2587), the Clarkes (ed. 1868) add that Sh. sometimes uses a passive participle instead of an active one and thus interpret tenderly-sighing nature or tenderly-breathing nature, as signifying tenderly-compassionate nature. Hunter (ed. 1869): Prone to the heavings of tenderness. Lee (ed. 1908): Heaving of the breast implies tender disposition. OED records neither the participle hefted nor the verb heft with such meanings. Harbage (ed. 1958): Swayed by tenderness, gently disposed—which seems a gloss on hested.
(2) The majority of eds. interpret the word as a variant of hafted (OED, Haft sb.1), a word found in Florio, meaning handled (Muir, ed. 1952), though Sh. never uses any form of the word haft. Davies (1783, 2:293–4): Smooth, or soft-handled,…for gentleness of disposition. Baynes (1869, p. 54): Heft, handle, that which holds or contains, and tender-hefted is simply delicately housed, daintily bodied, finely sheathed,…delicately-organised, or, more literally, fine-fleshed, comparing the phrase loose in the heft, signifying dissipated ways (OED, Haft sb.1 2a: Phr.…(fig.), unstable, unreliable). Schmidt (1874, Tender-hefted): But is haft or heft, i.e. handle, indeed that which holds or contains, or not rather that by which a thing is held?…Perhaps…tender-handled is = tender, gentle, to touch or to approach; of an easy and winning address, affable. Crook (ed. 1907): Handles things tenderly, i.e., is gentle and affable in demeanour. Wright (ed. 1875): Set in a tender handle or delicate bodily frame. Regan was less masculine than Goneril; so OED (Tender adv. C), quoting only this l. Kittredge (ed. 1940): This seems too grotesque to be probable; nor does it fit the context, for it is the tenderness of Regan’s nature, not of her bodily frame, that Lear has in mind. Verity (ed. 1897): Which must be handled with tender care. Brooke (ed. 1947): Responsive to the hilt, easily managed. A figure from a knife or other instrument in which the haft or handle easily accommodates itself to the master’s use, comparing Ham. 5.2.150–2 (3620–1). Wilson (ed. 1960): Complaisant; lit. easily handled (heft = haft). A Sh. coinage, because haft suggests knife, symbol of Reg.’s true nature. Joseph (ed. 1966): (Literally) has a pliable handle; (figuratively) does not cut so rigorously. Hulme (1962, pp. 75–7) strains to find additional senses, haft = to haggle and to accustom…to a pasturage (first dated 1725 in OED), and echoes of proverbs : Close companions are proverbially like heft and blade (1884),…to be loose in the haft is to be unreliable,…[and] the heft image may suggest the proverb question If the axe were gone, is this the remedy to hurle the helue after it? (1587).
(3) Knight (ed. 1840): Heft—haft—is that which is haved—held; and thus…thy nature which may be held by tenderness, or which has tenderness (Kemshead, ed. 1875). Similarly Moberly (ed. 1876): Tenderly-constituted nature; literally, tenderly held. The etymology is possible for haft (OED, sb.1), not for heft.
(4) Tovey (ed. 1896): Of slight weight [OED, Heft sb. 1], and therefore liable to give way under any heavy pressure. Craig (ed. 1901): Unlike dead-heft, a weight that cannot be lifted, tender-hefted might simply mean pliable, manageable. Lear might be thinking of the dogged, stern, unmoving nature of Goneril. This gloss is anticipated, without the etymology, by Eccles (ed. 1792): Tractable, compliant, easily manageable. Lee (ed. 1908): Weighted with tenderness.
(5) Hudson & Black (ed. 1911): That has established itself in tenderness. OED (Haft v.3) does not record this Scots and northern dialect usage before 1725.
(6) Muir (ed. 1952): Wright does not draw the conclusion [from Cotgrave, 1611, s.v. Emmanché Helved; set into a haft] that if lasche emmanché can mean faint-hearted, then tender-hefted may reasonably be taken to mean tender-hearted. But a French idiom does not imply analogous English idioms. The emendation by several eds. to tender-hearted is called specious by White (ed. 1862), and by Rolfe (ed. 1880) tolerable and not to be endured. S. could never have written tender-hearted nature (though he does refer several times to the tender hearts of persons).

1455 nature]
See n. 185.

1455–6 giue the or’e]
OED (Give v. 63d: Give over): To devote, resign, surrender, hand over: (a) with obj. a person, oneself (to a passion, form of behavior, condition, etc.).

1457 burne]
As the sun. Malone (ed. 1790) compares Tim. 5.1.131 (2361).

1457 in]
OED (prep. 25): Within the ability, capacity, thought, etc. of, quoting this l.

1459 bandy]
See n. 614.

1459 scant]
See n. 304.

1459 sizes]
Minsheu (1617), Size: A portion of bread or drinke, i[t] is a farthing, which Schollers in Cambridge haue at the butterie (OED, sb. 7, quoting Minsheu and this l.). Steevens (ed. 1773): A sizer is one of the lowest ranks of students at Cambridge, and lives on a stated allowance. Delius (ed. 1854): The same as exhibition [360]. Boas (1923, p. 48): To be scanted of sizes was a punishment for undergraduates, an indignity that might well stir Lear to a transport of rage. Muir (ed. 1952): In Leir, Perillus complains (763): His pension she hath halfe restrain’d from him. Skalliger urges Gonorill ([799–]801): The large allowance which he hath from you…Therefore abbridge it halfe; see .

1460 oppose the bolt]
Hunter (ed. 1972): The climax of these deprivations is, ironically enough, the one which Regan is shortly to put into practice. Halio (ed. 1992): Exaggerated: Gonerill did not lock Lear out.

1462–3 offices…gratitude]
Craig (ed. 1931): Lear enumerates what are ethically the pillars of society.

1462 offices of nature]
See nn. 441, 1046. Deighton (ed. 1891): Duties which natural affection bids you render. Danby (1949, p. 28) compares the Elizabethan view of benignant Nature in Hooker’s Ecclesiastical Polity 1.8.3–5: Lear’s theology of Nature here is neither pagan nor Ancient British.…[It assumes] that parents are to be honoured and human decencies observed. It assumes as the absolute shape for man an image of tenderness, comfort, generosity, charity, courtesy, gratitude.

1462 bond of child-hood]
OED (Childhood sb. 5): = Childship; filial relation, quoting this l. as its first ex. Smith (ed. 1902): Lear himself is now constrained to refer to the bond of childhood. Cf. Cordelia’s words, [99]—in which some hear biblical echoes: see n. 105.

1463 effects]
See n. 139. A few eds. read as in 199. Tovey (ed. 1896): Courteous attentions, as the results of a courteous disposition. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Actions. Joseph (ed. 1966): Lear is talking of the ways in which courtesy actually occurs. Lott (ed. 1974): Forms. Foakes (ed. 1997): Outward marks. Orgel (ed. 1999): Obligations.

1464 hast thou]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Transposed construction;…An emphasis is laid on thou.

1466 too’th purpose]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Come to the purpose, or point (Harbage, ed. 1958).

1466 Tucket within]
See n. 1014. Cowling (1913, p. 48) describes a tucket as a fanfare used to announce the arrival of heralds, messengers, and [lesser] courtly persons. Naylor (1896, p. 180; 1931, p. 174): Certainly in Shakespeare it seems to be used as a personal trumpet call. See n. 1470.

1469–71 What…here]
Verity (ed. 1897): This conversation between Regan and Cornwall is not heard by Lear; hence his astonishment at Goneril’s entrance. Apparently too he did not notice the trumpet-sound. His thoughts are occupied with the indignity to Kent. But Lear’s reaction may be dismay or outrage, not astonishment.

1468 Enter…]
On F’s earlier entrance see n. 1358. Greg (1940, p. 436): Presumably he has been sent out, or had gone out, to meet [Goneril]. But those who might have sent him have been asleep, and Oswald has no apparent reason to expect Goneril at Gloucester’s house. He could simply have met or been summoned to her upon her arrival.

1470 I know’t]
See n. 1466. Steevens (ed. 1793): Cornwall knows not the present sound; but to Regan, who has often heard her sister’s trumpet, the first flourish of it was as familiar as was that of the Moor to the ears of Iago, citing Oth. 2.1.177–8 (951–2). Delius (ed. 1854) disagrees, thinking that Regan already knows from the letter that Goneril approaches. Furness (ed. 1880): Delius evidently takes this as the object of approves.

1470 approues]
See n. 198.

1470 letters]
On F’s Letter see n. 875. Bradley (1904, p. 449): Goneril arrives at Gloster’s house, in accordance with an intimation which she had sent in her letter to Regan. [See n. 1309]…Thus all the principal persons except Cordelia and Albany are brought together; and the crises of the double action—the expulsion of Lear and the blinding and expulsion of Gloster—are reached in Act III. And this is what was required. But it needs the closest attention to follow these movements. In fact both Regan’s approues her Letter and here (1471) are surprising: there is no evidence that her letter expressed an intention to visit Regan (see n. 853) either at her own house (where Oswald was sent) or here at Gloucester’s (where Goneril could not have expected Regan to be). Goneril’s motive for going to Gloucester’s house is never made clear, nor why, if she warned Regan of that intent, she should appear there without such advance warning to Gloucester as Curan gives (929–32) of Regan’s approach. Presumably she expects to support Regan against Lear, and presumably Sh. wishes her arrival to surprise the audience as well as the king. So Bransom (1934, p. 39): The decision to go that night was taken suddenly, after Oswald’s dispatch, since 863–4 shows no intention of following him. Knowing of disputes between her husband and brother-in-law which might lead to war [see 938–9, 1635], she pursued Lear to prevent an alliance between her sister and father. More kindly, however (p. 75): I think Goneril had quite reckoned on the king’s coming back with her; to bring him back may have formed part of her purpose in following him. Houghton (ed. 1957): Her conduct may be dictated less by wanton cruelty than by her ambition to rule the country; and she succeeds in imposing her will on Regan. Goneril gives no hint of such a motive, and it does not explain her plan (in her letters) to arrive at Gloucester’s rather than at Regan’s; possibly, as Bransom suggests, she went to Regan’s first and thence onwards to Gloucester’s, as Lear may have already done (see n. 1273). Greg (1940, p. 436): She comes apparently straight from home, having no doubt had notice of her sister’s movements; but there is no evidence of such a notice, which presumably would have gone out from Regan’s house just the night before. Albany evidently does not accompany her (see 2268–75) and so remains guiltless of Lear’s expulsion; his absence may reflect his growing doubts about his wife’s purposes (cf. 869–72) or, as Bransom speculates (op. cit., p. 42), her increasingly poor opinion of her husband’s character and consequent decision not to discuss her fears or plans with him. Critics of course have the leisure to satisfy their natural desire to reconstruct and explain offstage actions, to infer motives and chronologies for them, to imagine the contents of letters, and the like, in order to see how coherent the action is or is not. Apparently Sh. does not expect his audience to do the same, since he is not at pains to provide the explicit evidence that would make it possible during the headlong rush of events.

1472 easie borrowed]
Most eds. hyphenate (see textual n.), perhaps unnecessarily, as Craig (ed. 1901) suspects: Easy may mean easy-going, coolly impudent. Similarly Horsman (ed. 1973): Easy, i.e. compliant, and Foakes (ed. 1997): Casual or effortless. Warburton (ed. 1747), of the compound form: Natural to him. Eccles (ed. 1792): Pride that requires no cause of importance to produce it; derived from an insignificant source…depends upon the uncertain favour. Moberly (ed. 1876): Borrowed without the trouble of doing anything to justify it. Deighton (ed. 1891): As a consequence of being employed by Goneril, but of which his dismissal…would as readily strip him. Budd (ed. 1935): From the example set by Goneril. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Easily borrowed because it does not take much to make him proud. Muir (ed. 1952): As one who borrows money without offering any security. Bevington (ed. 1980): I.e., Acquired with little effort at deserving and with weak commitment. Wilson (ed. 1960): Particularly a ref. to Osw.’s clothes, comparing 1089–90; cf. OED (sb.1 7): Ostentatious adornment. Lott (ed. 1974): Lear has found Goneril’s favour towards himself uncertain, and so, he suggests, will Oswald.

1473 Dwels in]
Rann (ed. 1794): Depends upon. Hudson (ed. 1871): Or comes and goes with the shifting favour of his mistress.

1473 fickle]
F’s fickly is evidently erroneous; Halio (ed. 1992) suspects that the [F] compositor got the wrong ligature, probably through foul-case error, but an e/y misreading is quite possible. Though Fickle seems to be required by the context (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 177), a few eds. adopt F3’s conjectural sickly. Wilson (ed. 1960): The context suggests, not that Osw. will one day find himself abandoned by Gon., but rather that her favour is a diseased, repulsive thing. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 534): Q’s fickle is a pertinent dig at Goneril’s inconstancy (and hence undercuts Oswald’s pride in her favour); but it might suggest or provoke some sympathy for Oswald’s predicament. Moreover, diseased grace is a possible oxymoron (he calls her a disease at [1516], for instance), and sickly could also mean Causing sickness or ill health [OED, a. 5: also producing discomfort or nausea] (usually of a climate), in a way which goes with Diuels in. This sense of sickly is attested once from a 1604 translation from Italian, not again until 1697, and always refers to qualities of the air. No then-current sense of sickly (weakened, unhealthy, etc.) makes an oxymoron so much as a strained epithet with grace, and there seems little danger of sympathy for Oswald at this point. Weis (ed. 1993): Fickle, for Oswald pliantly plays to every whim (gale and vary [1152]) of his betters.

1473 grace]
See n. 251.

1473 her, a]
Greg (1940, p. 163): The introduction of a comma [in Q1(c)] is quite uncalled for and is not supported by F. For a = he, see n. 585.

1474 Out]
Sprague (1944, p. 290): Some Lears have struck Oswald. See textual n.. Weis (ed. 1993) has Oswald exit here but be onstage at 1510. Wells (ed. 2000): Perhaps his mistress encounters him as he is about to leave.

1474 varlot]
Q1(c)’s varlet is No doubt a more correct spelling (Greg, 1940, p. 163); both are recorded. See n. 1101. Blayney (1982, pp. 116–17): The e replaces a defective zero.

1475 your Grace]
See n. 218.

1476 Enter…]
Q and F agree on Goneril’s entrance, but because in F she does not speak for several lines many eds. delay it (see textual n.). Halio (ed. 1992): But in the growing tumult, Lear may not at first see her. Adams (1948, p. 322): Goneril with Attendants? Bratton (ed. 1987): Often a magnificent entry: trumpets sounded, and Goneril’s train was numerous. Harbage (1963, p. 415): Goneril is unaccompanied by Albany, who is being saved by the playwright from contaminating participation in this episode.

1477 Gon.…struck]
F’s correction to Lear.…stockt has been almost universally adopted. Doran (1931, p. 80): The alterations [of speech prefixes] do not appear to have been accidental,…[being] accompanied by an appropriate change in the words.…In Act II, Scene ii, Kent has beaten Oswald, who, since he re-enters again in Scene iv just before Goneril does, must be understood to have gone off to meet her and to have told her what happened. In the folio, however, Lear, who has demanded several lines earlier how Kent comes to be in the stocks and has received no answer, makes an impatient reiteration. Urkowitz (1980, pp. 36–7) thinks the changes intentional, shifting audience attention from Goneril’s entrance—a vigorous piece of stagecraft—to Lear’s reaction to it. Since the two versions are of equal dramatic validity, it is unclear why such a change would be made. Edwards (1982, p. 696) rejects authorial change: In Q, Lear has to strike Oswald. Goneril must enter immediately and see Oswald on the ground or holding his jaw. She wants to know who struck him and hopes that Regan of all people was not a party to it. The incident does not make theatrical sense.…Q must be a mistaken attribution with an erroneous variant (struck for stockt). McLeod (1983, p. 181): Here in Q Goneril resumes harping on the same theme as in the third scene. But Q’s reading is implausible and probably erroneous: Goneril has won the argument in 1.4 and has no motive for resuming it now immediately on entrance after a long journey. She can hardly object to Regan’s merely speaking to Lear outside Gloucester’s house. Nor does the question itself make much sense: had Goneril instructed Oswald to report to Regan on his being struck, she could not hope that Regan knew nothing of the incident; had she not so instructed Oswald, she would have no reason to expect that Regan would know of it. From Goneril such a question seems both nonsensical and irrelevant to the occasion. Greg (1946, p. 232): Q always misunderstands the word stock [see 1211, 1914]; and struck seems the obvious substitute.…But if we read struck, the lines can only belong to Goneril, and the fact that she enters at this point makes their assignment to her all the easier. Foakes (ed. 1997): In Q Goneril seems already to be quarrelling with her sister, but Regan takes Goneril by the hand at 1484. Stone (1980, p. 219) and Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 516), like some directors, provide a motive for Q’s question by having Lear strike Oswald, upon no provocation whatsoever, at 1474; see n. The graphic resemblance of struck and stockt and the difficulty the Q compositor had with forms of stock at 1211 and 1914 make Q misreading and F restoration more likely here than substantive revision. Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 392–3) suspects that a badly written stockt in Q looked like struke; he gives many exx. of o/r, c/u, and e/t misreadings, and proposes that a scribe or editor of Q’s copy, having misread this word, changed the speech prefix accordingly. Since Lear insists to know who stocked Kent both before and after this speech (1467, 1490), there is likelihood that he does so here as well, before reacting to Goneril’s entrance. Van Dam (1935, p. 100): Gon. for Lear is a tautological misprint because in Q Enter Gon. precedes [this line]. Both entrance directions and speech prefixes were commonly marked in the same margins of MSS (see nn. 948, 1596), where they might compete with each other for space. The Q compositor may have thought the first line and a half, opposite Goneril’s entrance direction, were spoken by her as she entered, and that the succeeding half-line, more or less opposite Lear’s marginal speech prefix under the entrance, began Lear’s speech. Having made that misassignment, and remembering Goneril’s complaints in 1.3 and 1.4, or Oswald’s in 2.2, or Kent’s actions in 2.2, or his account of them at the beginning of this scene, the compositor may have been the more inclined to misread struck. Werstine (privately, as in n. 948) is inclined to think that an entrance in the left margin would be more characteristic of a theatrical than an authorial manuscript, citing line 2133 of Charlemagne (MSR), where a stage reviser or prompter has written in the left margin an entrance SD over the SP for the same character. Even if the case were exactly analogous with the one here, however, it would not establish that such a marginal addition could be made only by someone in the theater, and not by the author during composition. The question remains, however, why the verse line 1478–9 was divided into two part-lines in all three texts. Taylor (1985, p. 24) suspects that F replicates Q lineation. Conceivably that lineation originated with the Q1 compositor, trying to assign to Gon. and Lear. the parts that each actor might speak. If F derives from a transcript of the playbook, however, that lineation may ultimately derive from the original MS behind both playbook and Q1. If so, the line must have been (at least apparently) divided there, perhaps indicating the place where Lear turns from addressing Regan and Cornwall to addressing the entering Goneril.

1479–82 Who…part]
Lamb (1811; 1818, 2:25–6), arguing that the Lear of Shakspeare cannot be acted: What gesture shall we appropriate to this?

1479 O heauens]
Bradley (1904, p. 274): Lear’s first appeal to something beyond the earth…is immediately answered by the iron voices of his daughters.…His second appeal…[1572–3] is immediately [1584] answered from the heavens by the sound of the breaking storm. Empson (1951, pp. 134–5): This speech in fact touches off the storm.…Every time Lear prays to the gods, or anyone else prays on his behalf, there are bad effects immediately.…Thunder could be ironical even in the crude revenge plays; the revenger can take it as approving his plot though it really threatens him for his crimes; here, perhaps the heavens are supposed to resent what was said, as blasphemy.

1480–2 If…part]
Warburton (1739, p. 194): The exclamation, O…are old, may appear to the unlearned reader low and ridiculous. But we are to consider this Pagan King as here alluding to the antient Heathen Theology, which teaches that Cœlus or Ouranos was deposed by his son Saturn, who rebelled and rose up in arms against him. His case being the same with Lear’s makes this exclamation exceedingly pertinent and fine. Quoting Lamb (1811; 1818, 2:25), Hazlitt (1817, p. 176) speaks of Lear’s sublime identification of his age with that of the heavens. Carter (1905, p. 436) compares Psa. 71:9, 18, and Milward (1987, p. 172), Psa. 68:33 and Dan. 7:9, 13, 22. Kittredge (ed. 1940): So that you may well sympathize with old men in their troubles. Elton (1966, p. 246): As Lear’s O…are old…suggests the senectus mundi and decay-of-nature theme, it may further recall Renaissance disclosures that corruption afflicted not only the sublunar world but also the heavens themselves…[and] may anticipate his final hyperbolic onslaught ([3218–19]) upon their permanence.

1480 you]
F corrects to your. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 393): The compositor may have unconsciously repeated you from earlier in the line (in both cases it is preceded by if). Weis (ed. 1993), however: Q’s you produces a more complex reading…: if you grant (Allow) to humility gentle government. Wells (ed. 2000): A possible but tortured construction.

1480 sweet sway]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Mild government. McCann (ed. 1964): Loving authority.

1481 alow]
Q1(c)’s allow is another spelling correction (Greg (1940, p. 163). Upton (1748, p. ix): Approve (OED, v. 2). Cf. allowance, 720, 1181. Possibly (v. 8), Concede, permit (cf. 2176+7), or (v. 11): To give, or let anyone have,…as appropriate to his needs (see next n.).

1481 Obedience]
Presumably eds. understand by this the obedience of Lear’s daughters. But McCann (ed. 1964): Your obedience to my wish.

1482 make…cause]
Eds. disagree whether it is indefinite—Interest yourselves, make it your business to aid me (Craig, ed. 1901)—or has specific reference: My wrongs (Deighton, ed. 1891), Punishment of the fault (Crook, ed. 1907), My cause (Harbage, ed. 1958), or [Age’s] privileges (McCann, ed. 1964).

1482 Send downe]
Delius (ed. 1854): A token. Deighton (ed. 1891), more probably: Sc. your messengers, agents. McCann (ed. 1964), improbably: Someone (to explain why Kent was put into the stocks).

1483 Art…beard?]
Addressed to Goneril, not the heavens.

1483 Art]
On the omission of the pronoun see n. 562.

1483 beard]
Metonymy. Deighton (ed. 1891): Me so venerable. Hunter (ed. 1972): An emblem of age, and therefore of authority and deserving. Cf. 2594–5.

1484 O…hand]
Reibetanz (1977, p. 43): An unmistakable emblem of their affinity. Granville-Barker (1927, pp. 171–2): He is brought to a stand and to face the realities arrayed against him. The confronting must be made very plain to us [by the director]. On the one side stand Goneril and Regan and Cornwall in all authority. The perplexed Gloucester hovers a little apart. On the other side is Lear, the Fool at his feet, and his one servant, disarmed, free but a minute, behind him. Things are at their issue. Halio (ed. 1992): Alternative kinds of blocking are also possible.

1484 wilt thou]
The thou is consistent with Lear’s address in 1478; McLeod (1983, p. 181): F’s will you is a sign that Lear’s respect for Regan seems to continue. Foakes (ed. 1997): His shift from the intimate thou to the more distanced you signals his recognition of the realities. See nn. 1477 and 1432.

1486 finds]
Edwards (1748, p. 23): An allusion to a Jury’s verdict (OED, v. 17). Steevens (ed. 1773): To think; Idem (ed. 1778): We still say I find time tedious…without thinking on a jury (v. 6: Consider or regard as). Similarly Takes (so) (Craig, ed. 1901), Judges, esteems (Lee, ed. 1908), Deems (Muir, ed. 1952).

1487 dotage]
Goggin (ed. 1910): Cp. [847]. In the old play Goneril is described as calling her father foole and doterd to his face [Leir 758]; see . Heilman (1948): Dotage is Goneril’s favorite word for age: it is her way of denying that age has dignity or deserts, and that it has a place in Nature; she conceives of it only as a state which compels submission to her and her sister’s desires.

1487 so]
Dodd (1752, 2:121), followed by Delius (ed. 1854): Relates to [finds] as well as to terms (Ger.).

1488–9 O…hold?]
Craig (ed. 1931): This is not figurative but indicates belief in an actual swelling of the heart so that it might break through the sides. The idea occurs in Ant. 4.14.39–41 (2872–4), TN 2.4.93–4 (980–1). Schmidt (1874), Hold: To be firm, not to break (OED, v. 16).

1489–90 Will…stockes]
Werstine (1983, p. 293, n. 85): Compositor B…split a line of verse…to stretch his copy to fill the column, the next page having been already set.

1491 disorders]
Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Disorderly actions (OED, sb. 2b). Wilson (ed. 1960): This rubs in Gon.’s case ([750–5]) against Lear’s retainers.

1492 lesse aduancement]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Ironically used here for conspicuousness of punishment. Percy (in Steevens, ed. 1778): A still worse or more disgraceful situation; a situation not so reputable. Capell (1783, 1.2:160): He did not deserve so good a place as the stocks. Goggin (ed. 1910), aduancement: Promotion. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Honour.

1494 seeme so]
Rann (ed. 1794): Be content to think yourself so, and to be treated accordingly. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Speak and act like a feeble old man, and submit without protest to those who have you in charge. Collins (1903, p. 851) compares Euripides, Troades 729, And being weak, seem weak.

1496 will]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Are willing to (OED, v.1 6a, quoting this l.).

1498 from]
See n. 1067.

1498 prouision]
Schmidt (1875): Stores (OED, sb. 6). Cf. nn. 187, 2055.

1499 shall]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Will certainly.

1499 entertainment]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Proper maintenance; care and attention (OED, sb. 3).

1502–3 To…owle]
A few eds. prefer Theobald’s transposition of these two lines (see textual n.) in order to make Necessities sharpe pinch the object of wage (see following nn.). Jennens (ed. 1770): Necessity’s pinch is the cause or motive of waging war, not its object. Blayney (1982, 1:215), explaining an anomalous extra line on Q’s sig. F2r: Something is certainly wrong with the way in which the thought develops.…The transposed lines both begin with To, and it would have been extremely easy for the compositor to omit one of them by eyeskip. Line [1504] would therefore have been set as F1v38, and both pages would have contained 38 lines. If, during proofing, the omitted line had been noticed, one of the pages would have needed to be extended. To add a line to F1v would create an obvious discrepancy, with the catchword in F1v40 two lines lower than the left-hand margin of F2r38. Adding a line to F2r, however, would leave the F1v catchword on a level with F2r39.…Therefore, we can envisage line [1504] being taken over to become F2r1 while the original F1v39 (the direction line, consisting of quads and the old catchword) was removed. This left a gap of two lines at the bottom of F1v, and the compositor then set line [1503] and the new direction line. What he forgot was that line [1502] belonged between the two new lines that he transferred straight from his composing stick into that gap. This explanation of a supposed error in Q does not account for the repetition of the same text in F, derived ultimately from the playbook. Foakes (ed. 1997): Theobald’s transposition is unnecessary, and does not improve the sense.

1502 wage]
As early as Hanmer (ed. 1743–4, 6:Gloss.: To combat with,…to encounter) and Warburton (ed. 1747: Strive or fight) editors have taken this verb in an intransitive or absolute sense, as does OED (v. 10c): To struggle, contend against, quoting this l. and Per. 4.2.31 (1552) as its first exx. Cf. n. 485. Wells (ed. 2000), however: Wager.

1502 enmitie]
OED (sb. 3): Baneful influence, quoting this l. So Wilson (ed. 1960): Fresh air was considered unhealthy in Sh.’s day. But Lear hunts and rides in open air without hesitation. Halio (ed. 1992): Storms and in general the harsh condition of houseless poverty. Sh. elsewhere describes rough winds as opponents or combatants: cf. 1262–3, 2783, 3H6 2.5.6, etc.

1503 Comrade]
Hudson (ed. 1871): Not…that he would literally cohabit or herd with wolves, but merely that he would be like them, or in the same condition with them, in this respect. OED (sb.): An associate in…fortunes, quoting this l.

1503–4 owle…pinch]
See n. 1502–3. Warburton (ed. 1747) makes good sense simply by putting a semicolon after Ayre and a dash after pinch, commenting, The verb is is understood: i.e., To be…Owle, [Is or Which is] Necessities…pinch—. Similarly Jennens (ed. 1770): Necessities sharpe pinch is in apposition to To be…owle, and many eds. so treat it as a kind of parenthetical summary of the previous lines. So Hunter (ed. 1972): The phrase is governed by choose. The majority of editors (see textual n.) treat it instead as a sudden break in sentence structure, usually an exclamation: The reflection of Lear on the wretched sort of existence he had described in the preceding lines (Steevens, ed. 1778). Collier’s (ed. 1853) emendation of owle to howl makes Necessities…pinch the object of a verb and thus grammatically a part of the sentence. Furness (ed. 1880) vigorously defends this change: In the old reading, which renders Necessity’s sharp pinch parenthetical, there is a tameness out of place at the close of Lear’s wild outburst.…In the present text there is a climax, terrible in its wildness: roofs are to be abjured, storms braved, and famine howled forth among wolves. What companionship is there between wolves and owls, beyond the fact that they are both nocturnal?
