Yet what grates me in the old reading is…the un-Shakespearian feebleness of bringing in…an explanation of what it is to abjure roofs and to be comrade with wolves. As if Lear would stop to explain that people did not usually prefer such houseless poverty or such companionship, but that it was only the sharp pinch of necessity that drove them to it.…Theobald’s transposition of the lines, or any change that will avoid putting Necessity’s sharp pinch in apposition with the rest of the sentence, is better than the old text.…If it be objected that to howl a pinch is a violent metaphor, I reply that it is not more violent that to take up arms against a sea. Furness further adduces the frequent occurrence of silent h (including howlet for owlet in Mac 4.1.17 [1544]) to explain the confusion, and the slight corroboration of belly pinched Wolfe (1622+6) and Wolues…howl’d (2135, F). Rolfe (ed. 1880): But, as we take it, Necessity’s sharp pinch! is an exclamation that has no such connection with what precedes. It may mean, Is this the pinch to which Necessity brings me? Or is it barely possible that it is a sarcastic reference to the excuse which Regan has given for not receiving him.…The worst of these attempts to explain the old text is better than making him swear not only to be a comrade with the wolf, but to howl with the wolf! And to howl a pinch at that!…The poets often put [wolves and owls] together, as S. himself does in [Luc. 165]. White (1880, p. 829), rejecting Collier’s reading as insufferable, refers the word to Regan’s adjuration in 1494: That is, submit to the hard necessity of your condition. To this Lear…replies, <Shall I yield to> necessity’s sharp pinch <and> return with her! Verity (ed. 1897): Moreover, as the owl is traditionally a symbol of night…the mention of it indicates the time intended and thus adds something to the picture. Koppel (1899, p. 78): An interjected cry of inner pain. Hudson (ed. 1871) notes Job 30:29: I am brother to dragons, and a companion to owls (A.V.); the Geneva and Bishops’ Bibles read respectively ostriches and estriches. Williams (1951, p. 59): The wolf, symbol of greed, and the owl, of malevolence, are the evil companions the king expects to meet. Hunter (ed. 1972): Solitary and rapacious animals, hunting by night.

1504 Necessities]
Schmidt (1875): Extreme indigence, distress, want of what is needed (OED, Necessity sb. 10, quoting this l.). Cf. 1725. Hunter (ed. 1972): Both poverty and fate. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Anticipating the end of the scene. Lott (ed. 1974): The need to avoid at all costs a return to Goneril.

1504 pinch]
Hudson (ed. 1879): The pang [OED, sb. 3], of hunger, or of cold, or of both. Tovey (ed. 1896): Not merely pang, but pressure [OED, 2: Difficulty, hardship, quoting this l.].…Lear means, that painful pass to which men are driven by need. Taylor (1925, p. 11) compares Florio’s Montaigne (ed. 1910, 1:287): Necessitie must first pinch you by the throat, noting the occurrence of two words found here; Montaigne is discussing miserliness, however.

1505–8 Why…afoot]
Clarkes (1879, p. 515): The disturbed mode of construction in this speech consists perfectly with the agitation of the hapless old king’s mind.

1505 hot bloud in]
Most eds. prefer F1(u)’s hot-blooded, a few F1(c)’s hot-bloodied. Hinman (1963, 1:309–10): The last reading is quite unsatisfactory, to be accounted for only as a mistake on the part of the Folio [proof-]reader. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 534): But it is the form used in OED’s only early citation of the compound, Wiv. 5.5.2 (2483). Similar compounds always use the -ed spelling in Q and F texts: sober blouded/-blooded (2H4 4.3.87 [2323]), cold blooded (Jn. 3.1.123 [1049]), Halfe blouded/-blooded (Lr. 3025). Doran (1931, p. 99): F is closer than the quarto to what must have been the original word. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 383) includes Q’s bloud in among other misreadings of d as n, including deed in 1564 and countenadce in 2910. Stone (1980, p. 219) defends Q: Bloud = A hot spark, a man of fire (Johnson [1755; OED, Blood sb. 15]). The word is used in [Jn. 2.1.278 (585)]. Hot = ardent, passionate, eager. Foakes (ed. 1997) and Wells (ed. 2000) so interpret Q. Q does make sense, and Sh. had so used Hot-blouds in Ado 3.3.132 (1457); OED does not record the compound noun. The following comments apply to either Q or F. Wright (ed. 1875): For instances of nouns put prominently forward in a sentence to express the subject of the thought, without any grammatical connexion, see Abbott §417 [Nominative Absolute, quoting 2522–3]. Tovey (ed. 1896): A nominativus pendens. Craig (ed. 1901): France was before [358] said to have in choler parted. Crook (ed. 1907): Lear thinks [France] allowed the ardour of his love for Cordelia to overcome his wisdom. Hunter (ed. 1972): Passionate (supposed to be a French characteristic) and therefore likely to be violent. Edwards (ed. 1975): Amorous.

1507 knee]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:37): Bend the knee to (OED, v. 2, quoting this l.). Only Schmidt (ed. 1879): To travel thither on the knees, citing Cor. 5.1.5 (3156). Furness (ed. 1880): The passage in Cor. is not parallel. Craig (ed. 1901) compares Cordella’s speech in Leir 2294, Ide creep along, to meet him on my knee; see . Joseph (ed. 1966): There is an ironical flash of wit here. Lear says he would not go on his knees to France’s throne to keep dishonourable life on its feet (afoot).

1507 Squire-like]
Deighton (ed. 1891): As if I were a dependant; as the squire…was of the knight (OED, adv., quoting only this l.). Gardner (ed. 1969): The pension his allowance. Hunter (ed. 1972): Like a body-servant.

1507 bag]
Error for Q2’s and F’s beg. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 393): Doubtless an a/e misreading.

1508 base]
Johnson (ed. 1765): In a servile state.

1508 afoot]
Deighton (ed. 1891): On foot, going (OED, adv. 3). Only Brown (ed. 1976): Pun on knee.

1509 sumter]
Hanmer (ed. 1743–4, 6:Gloss.), sumpter: A beast which carries necessaries on a journey (OED, sb. 2: A pack or baggage-horse; a beast of burden, quoting only this l. as an ex. of figurative use). Wright (ed. 1875) compares R3 1.3.121 (590), I was a packe-horse in his great affaires, and cites Cotgrave (1611), Sommier: A Sumpter-horse; (and generally any toyling, and load-carrying, drudge, or groome). Skeat (1880, p. 343), followed by Craig (ed. 1901), prefers the original meaning of baggage-driver (OED, 1).

1510 detested]
See n. 284, cf. 775.

1510 groome]
Oswald. Foakes (ed. 1997): Servant (or stableman) (OED sb.1 3, 5).

1512 Now]
F’s omission is metrical polishing.

1512–23 I prithee…thy leasure]
Macaulay (1907, p. 27): This last struggle between rage and tenderness is, I think, unequalled in poetry. Johnson (1975, p. 154): He is so furious with Regan that he refuses from this point on to address her other than as you, but with Goneril he shifts back again to the intimate form of address, appealing to her daughterly feelings.

1512 prithee]
See n. 664.

1512 mad]
See n. 918, cf. 1586. Crook (ed. 1907): The indecision of Lear during the rest of this scene marks the first stage of his real madness.

1515 flesh, my bloud]
See n. 121. OED (Flesh, sb. 7): One’s near kindred or descendants.…Flesh and blood. Also OED (Blood, sb. 11b). Tilley F366 and Dent (1981): Proverbial. Cf. 1923. Milward (1987, p. 172): Biblical: see Gen. 37:27, Rom. 9:3, Gal. 1:16, Eph. 5:29.

1516 disease]
Muir (ed. 1952, rev. 1963, p. 258): Clifford Leech compares the following passage from Elyot’s The Gouernour, II.iv. [1531, sig. O5v]: for the bloode in our bodies beinge in youthe warme, pure, and lustie, it is the occasion of beautie…; but if in age it be putrified, it leseth his praise. And the goutes, carbuncles, kankers, lepries, and other lyke sores and sicknesses, whiche do procede of bloode corrupted, be to all men detestable. Leech suggests that Lear may be seeing Goneril…as a disease incident to his age. Adelman (1992, p. 109): He is intolerably implicated in [Goneril’s and Regan’s] femaleness.…He identifies her as the [sic] disease [venereal; see DP n. 15] in his own body.…His language figures his body as grotesquely female, pregnant with the disease that is his daughter. Lear of course says nothing here of femaleness, pregnancy, or veneral disease. He says, rather, that he is afflicted by his daughter as by a disease; cf. Claudius’s like the Hectique in my blood he rages (Ham. 4.3.66 [2731]). Foakes (1993, p. 192): Lear half-recognizes that the corruption of his daughters is also his own corruption, derived from him. But Goneril is the agent, not the recipient, of the (metaphorical) corruption of Lear’s blood; see n. 1519, and Idem (ed. 1997): Lear finds the source of his own corruption in that of his daughters.

1516 that lies within]
F’s that’s in makes regular meter. Doran (1931, pp. 126–7): Failure of a printer’s memory may account for Q’s phrasing. Greg (1933, p. 253): This flabby and vicious phrasing is an actor’s redundancy. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 516): Hexameters are common enough in Shakespeare, but the phrase which creates this one seems exceptionally feeble. Perhaps within was a currente calamo replacement for that lies. The Q line may be read as a pentameter if a is elided with the previous syllable. Van Dam (1935, p. 95): The F line is one of Heminge’s (or Condell’s) metrical corrections, a second remove from Shakespeare’s original line.

1517 needs]
See n. 634.

1517 bile]
Malone (1783, p. 50): The word boil, being pronounced as if written bile. OED (Boil sb.1) records the Q sp. from the 13th to 19th c., and F’s Byle from the 14th to the 17th c. Wilson (ed. 1960): Correct phonetic spelling of the period, comparing 1155 smoile. Muir (ed. 1952, p. lxi, n. 4) and Aberbach (1979, p. 131) find a parallel to Job’s boils (Job 2:7). Cf. nn. 1584, 1702–12.

1518 plague sore]
Verity (ed. 1918): Plague meant bubonic plague…of which there were bad outbreaks in London in 1582, 1606. Kaula (1975, p. 26) suggests that the term, not found elsewhere in Sh., derives from Christopher Bagshaw’s True Relation (1601, p. 65), but it was current elsewhere (OED), and Sh. uses both words often.

1518 an]
Wilson (ed. 1960), of F’s or: The words are graphically alike. And equally correct.

1518 imbossed]
Despite extensive and fanciful commentary, the meaning is clear. OED (Embossed ppl. a.1 4): Bulging, convex, swollen, tumid, quoting this l. Cf. AYL 2.7.67 (1041), imbossed sores, and headed euils. Craig (ed. 1901) cites Palsgrave (1530): Botche[,] a sore[;] bosse de pestilence.

1518 carbuncle]
OED (sb. 3): An inflammatory, circumscribed, malignant tumour.…It differs from a boil in having no central core; an anthrax, quoting this l.

1519 Corrupted bloud]
See n. 1516. Armour (ed. 1930): My blood which has become tainted in you. Foakes (ed. 1997), blood: lineage,…that part of the body parents and children share, comparing 1515 and citing OED, sb. 8. Wells (ed. 2000) invokes the legal concept of attainder, whereby blood inherited from a criminally corrupted person deprived his heirs of rank and title. Possibly, but Lear has begun by describing his own diseased flesh, not his lineage, and the other ills named—boil, plague sore—are fleshly, and may all be death tokens of the plague (Bucknill, 1860, p. 268; Hoeniger, 1992, p. 216). Perhaps bloud is simply metonymic for flesh-and-blood. A carbuncle is literally a small coal, and the name refers metaphorically to a feverish inflammation and swelling of the skin, easily imagined as originating in and erupting from corrupted blood within, as Old Hamlet’s tetter erupts from his poisoned blood.

1520 come]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Scil. upon thee.

1520 call]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Invoke.

1521 thunder bearer]
Hudson (ed. 1879): Jove the Thunderer (OED, quoting this l. as its first ex.), who shoots thunderbolts.

1522 Nor]
Nor do I.

1522 high Iudging]
Q is ambiguous: Jove the high, the supreme Judge (Craig, ed. 1901), or judging in heaven (Schmidt, 1874). F’s hyphen removes the ambiguity. On Shn. compounds with high, see OED (adj. 10, quoting this l.), and cf. 1678, 2357.

1523 Mend]
Improve yourself, be better (OED, v. 1c: Intr. for refl., quoting this l.). Dent (1981, M875) cites the proverb It is never too late to mend (repent); cf. n. 769.

1524 patient]
See n. 774. Bransom (1934, p. 68): The king does refrain from cursing,…because he is making a conscious effort to get this new thing, patience.

1526 not altogether]
Rosenberg (1972, p. 172): Now begins the reverse auction.

1527 sir,]
F’s omission makes a more regular line. See n. 60.

1527 looke]
F look’d. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 393): Perhaps a misreading of d as e. Wells (ed. 2000), adopting Q: Indicative simple present for complete present (Abbott §346). Deighton (ed. 1891): Expected.

1529 those]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Those who, like my sister.

1529 mingle…passion]
Rann (ed. 1794): Judge most candidly of your extravagant behaviour. Seymour (1803, p. 49): Correct the influence of those complaints with a due mixture of reason. Hunter (ed. 1869): Speak temperately to you when your language is intemperate. Reason is here moderation. Tovey (ed. 1896): Deal reasonably with the things that put you in a passion. Craig (ed. 1901): Examine your passionate utterances by the light of plain reason; or pour in some cold, calm reason to mitigate the stings of your hot, passionate utterances. Brooke (ed. 1947): Do not receive your wild words at face value, but discount them in the light of reason. The figure, however, is that of mixing a drink. Gardner (ed. 1969): Make some sense of your violent tirades.

1530 are]
F’s omission is metrical polishing.

1530 old]
Wilson (ed. 1960): I.e. senile.

1530 so,]
Capell (1783, 1.2:1) defends a break here: She could like to finish with—foolish; but is contented, we should…guess her meaning. Tovey(ed. 1896): So takes the place of further explanation: and treat you accordingly. Kittredge (ed. 1940): She breaks off abruptly, with a gesture: You are old—and no further explanation is necessary! Foakes (ed. 1997): As if she were about to repeat what she said at [1426–30]. Wells (ed. 2000): Or perhaps she holds back from saying what she really means.

1532 now]
F omits to make a pentameter.

1533 auouch]
Schmidt (1874): Assert, maintain (OED, v. 7). Cf. 2888.

1533 followers]
On the scansion see n. 154.

1534 of]
Wells (ed. 2000): Possibly have, comparing 3278.

1535 Yea]
OED (adv. 3): Used to introduce a statement, phrase, or word, stronger or more emphatic than that immediately preceding: = indeed; and more.

1535 sith]
See n. 194.

1535 that]
See n. 273.

1535 charge]
Schmidt, 1874): Expense, cost (OED, sb. 10).

1535 danger]
Delius (ed. 1854): Explained in the next sentence. But Regan and Goneril also have a somewhat different danger in mind: cf. 325–30, 521–522+2, 844–8, 853–5, 1040–3, 1609–11. Colie (1974, pp. 200, 201–2): Regan states the general argument against a mobile retinue in a speech far more neutral and sensible, in social terms, than it is usually considered.…Goneril and Regan were, of course, afraid of something other than mere inconvenience; they were afraid that their father, invested with his military power, might discover their aims and seek to stop them by turning that power against them. Cf. n. 141. Mahood (1992, p. 161): There is never any hint in Lear’s behaviour that he might, as Goneril says, enguard his dotage ([847]) with what her sister calls a desperate train ([1609]). What really rankles is the expense.

1536 Speakes]
F’s alteration to Speake is unnecessary: see n. 754.

1536–8 how…amytie]
Mahood (1992, p. 161): It is a good question.…Some Jacobean magnates tried to avoid confrontations between their own and the [visiting] royal household by building what were in effect twinned mansions, to accommodate James’s entourage side by side with their own. Others, less wealthy or less loyal, adopted the solution favoured by Cornwall and Regan [cf. 1042–3, 1498–9]. In 1608 the great ones of Nottinghamshire who found themselves in the path of the royal progress simply packed up and fled. Cf. n. 539–40. Foakes (ed. 1997) compares Cor. 3.1.108–12 (1802–6).

1536 a]
Q’s a means one; F’s one stresses the antithesis with two in the next line.

1537 commands]
OED (sb. 3c): With a and pl. Authority, quoting only this l. Elton (1966, p. 119 n.) compares Tilley M729, One Master in a house is enough; neither Tilley nor Dent (1981) cites this l.

1538 Hold]
Schmidt (1874): Keep,…maintain (OED, v. 7b).

1542 chanc’st]
On Q’s sp. of F’s chanc’d, see n. 217.

1542 slacke]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): To be remiss in, to neglect (OED, v. 1, adding in respect of some business, duty, etc. and quoting this l.). Cf. 516.

1542 you]
Ethical dative: towards you. On F’s ye see n. 490.

1546 giue…notice]
Rolfe (ed. 1880), notice: Attention, recognition (OED, sb. 5, quoting this l.). Deighton (ed. 1891): Admit into my castle or acknowledge as your attendants.

1547 I…all]
See n. 637–8. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xlvi) and Muir (ed. 1952) compare Leir 2144 (see ): Ah, cruell Ragan, did I giue thee all?

1548 And…it]
Hudson (ed. 1871): Observe what a compact wolfishness of heart is expressed in these few cold words! It is chiefly in this readiness of envenomed sarcasm that Regan is discriminated from Goneril; otherwise they seem almost too much like mere repetitions of each other to come fairly within the circle of Nature, who never repeats herself. Idem (ed. 1879): This spurt of malice…is the ne plus ultra of human fiendishness. Flatter (1948, pp. 81–2): The line is an aside. Munro (ed. 1957): This would lessen its dramatic value. It seems to be uttered amidst Lear’s continuous speech. Wright (1999, p. 272): The shared line was one device for intensifying the dramatic bond between…personages involved with each other on the stage, quoting this l.

1548 in good time]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Before it was too late; if you had retained it longer, you would have made a bad use of it. The implication of increasing senility is clear.

1549 guardians, my depositaries]
Since the second noun is unusual and Sh. uses it only here, Taylor (1925, p. 49) thinks the phrase echoes depositary and guardian from Florio’s recent tr. of Montaigne (ed. 1910, 3:208). Eds. generally agree with Moberly (ed. 1876) that Sh.’s first word means The guardians…of my realms, not of Lear’s person. Wilson (ed. 1960): An official title, now Warden, e.g. Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports, citing OED (Guardian sb. 3). Lear would of course not intend the more specific legal sense, custodian for one who is legally incapable (OED, 2). Deighton (ed. 1891), depositaries: Trustees of my power (OED, 1, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Here the terms are virtual synonyms.

1550 But]
Joseph (ed. 1966): Only. Cf. n. 1026.

1550 reseruation]
See n. 141.

1551 With]
By (Abbott §193; OED, With prep. 40). Cf. 1609 and 2H6 2.4.32 (1208).

1551 such]
Generally taken to mean the previously referred to (OED, dem. adj. 1a[c]), viz. one hundred. Delius (ed. 1854): Fifty. Idem (ed. 1872): Such and such a number (OED, 16b).

1551 what]
See n. 810.

1553 And]
Abbott (§97): And is frequently found in answers in the sense of you are right and or yes and.

1554–6 Those…prayse]
Most eds. follow the Q and F division, keeping not…prayse as an independent comment following on the preceding statement. Parallels to the thought of Those…wicked have been found in Cym. 5.5.215–17 (3497–9) (by Steevens, ed. 1778) and Cym. 3.4.48–9 (1719–20) (by Malone, ed. 1790, 10:681); Dent (1981, W914.1) compares the proverbial None of (Not) the Worst. A few (see textual n.) have been persuaded by Capell’s (1783, 1.2:161–2) argument for a full stop after fauor’d, changing 1554 from a generality to an expression of Lear’s astonishment that his daughters’ beauty has not been blasted as he had imprecated (cf. 818, 1449–51).

1554 seem]
F’s look means the same.

1554 wel fauor’d]
Schmidt (1875): Well-looking, handsome (OED).

1556 some ranke]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Not a high place, but better than none at all.

1556–8 Ile…loue]
Wells (ed. 2000): Lear still thinks that love can be quantified. Not all find this to be pathetic bargaining. Moberly (ed. 1876): Said in bitter irony to try what their real meaning is, and how far they intend to trample on him. In Mirour Leire returns to Albany’s house; see .

1557 doth]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Fifty is taken as a concrete whole.

1557 double]
OED (v. 1c): Amount to twice as much, quoting this l. as its first ex.

1558 art]
Clarkes (1879, p. 516): The word is better than [Pope’s] conventionally correct hast (see textual n.). It gives the characteristic touch of confused idea to Lear’s diction.…He embodies the love here; making it the representation of his daughters.

1558 her loue]
Harbage (ed. 1958): I.e. as loving as she.

1560–3 What…one]
Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): A splendid Sorites of selfishness. Perrett (1904, p. 190): The numbers 10, 5, 1 found without exception in the series [of Lear narratives] from Wace to [Higgins’s Mirour] (i.e. [the French and English Prose Bruts, Caxton’s Chronicle]) recur in Sh. Perrett quotes from Higgins the pertinent passages: But then they [Regan and Cornwall] tooke, all his retinue from him quite | Saue only ten,…Though in disdayne they laste alowde but fiue; subsequently Gonerell and Albany Bereaude him of his seruauntes all saue one, | Bad him content him self with that or none (see ). In Leir 807–8 (see ) Gonorill says much earlier in the action that, having restrayned halfe his portion, she will presently restrayne the other.

1560, 1563 What]
Abbott (§253): Used for for what, why (quid) (OED, What adv. 19; Need v.2 2b). Cf. Franz §342.

1561 follow]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Attend upon you (OED, v. 14).

1561 twise so many]
Colie (1974, pp. 200–1): I.e., at least fifty servants.…[These daughters] have their modern ways of conspicuous consumption no less grandiose than their father’s old-fashioned train—and far more centered on themselves, on their own comforts and the projected image of their own greatness.

1562 tend]
See n. 1034.

1563 one]
Verity (ed. 1897): Regan never fails to catch an ill suggestion and carry it a point farther.

1564–71 O…need]
Coleridge (MS notes, 1818–19, ed. Foakes, 1989, p. 101): The tranquillity from the first stun permit[s] Lear to REASON. Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Here Lear argues the whole question of humanity as against mere animalism. Lee (1909, p. xl), followed by Bullough (1973, p. 359): Sh. took the cue for this famous speech from Leir 896–905: Nay, if thou talke of reason, then be mute;…What reason moueth thee to sorrow for me; see . Jones (1971, p. 168) compares Constance’s speech on need in Jn. 3.1.211–16 (1142–7). Taylor (1925, p. 10) compares remarks by Montaigne (tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 3:260) concerning how little nature doth exactly and originally require at our handes, for the preservation of our being and how good cheape our life may be maintained. Craig (ed. 1931): Lear’s answer…is in some respects an expression of the underlying theme of the story: Why reason, i.e., discuss, the need, since it is not a question of need? It is a spiritual, not a temporal matter which is involved. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Lear distinguishes between absolute necessity (in which sense his daughters may have used the word need) and that which may be properly regarded as necessary for comfort and dignity. Heilman (1948, p. 169): Lear not only defines the effect upon humanity of the use of mere need as a measuring stick for perquisites, but he shrewdly demonstrates that his daughters do not themselves observe the canon of need; their values are wrong, and they themselves are dishonest in the bargain.…Need, cheap, beggars, superfluous connect his lines with other passages that approach values through economic terms; nature and beast’s introduce the nature and animal themes; gorgeous and wear’st, the clothes theme. Houghton (ed. 1957): Lear’s knights are to him…a mark of human dignity. Hulme (1962, p. 191): Udall [tr., Apophthegmes of Erasmus, 1542; 1564, p. 101] hopes that The frugalitee of Diogenes may shame our superfluitees and excesses. Harbage (1963, p. 415): This man needs what he is used to, needs what he expects.…He needs mercy and love. Elton (1966, p. 228) compares Guyon’s debate with Mammon in Spenser’s F.Q. 2.7.15 on the disparity beteeen Nature’s needs and superfluities. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Human nature…requires not merely satisfaction of its biological needs to maintain itself but also of certain other needs sanctioned and advocated by a civilized community—needs which are not the same for men of different social stations. This idea, frequently expressed in Renaissance writing, was derived from Seneca [Epist. 16] and Boethius [Cons. 2.5], comparing Jonson, Discoveries [1387–92]. Cf. n. 1569. Foakes (ed. 1997): Need cannot finally be calculated, any more than love. Granville-Barker (1927, pp. 160–1) remarks on the rhetorical reiteration in the passage. Jorgensen (1967, p. 76): It is not an impressively coherent argument.…[But] it reveals…the growing flexibility of Lear’s mind. His thought changes directions several times.

1564 O]
Fisher (1990, p. 88) sees in this single letter the moment of both anagnorisis and peripeteia in the tragedy: it signifies a groan, an exclamation of recognition, the abstract mathematical sense of…zero, and even (paradoxically) all—senses that would seem to require very different vocal inflections.

1564 reason]
Schmidt (1875): To argue, to debate (OED, v. 5). Cf. 2869.

1564 deed]
F’s need corrects an obvious error—possibly foul-case, since d and n were in adjacent boxes in the compositor’s case.

1565 in]
Brooke (ed. 1947): I.e., in possessing.

1565 superfluous]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Have in their deepest poverty some very poor thing which may be called superfluous. Craig (ed. 1901): Over and above what is necessary for bare existence; or superfluous may have the sense of generous, bountiful [unattested in OED]; and it may mean the very poorest are not stingy of their poor enjoyments, comparing 2252, where the word has the following meaning. OED (a. 4): Having, consuming, or expending more than enough; superabundantly supplied; extravagant in expenditure, quoting this l. So Hoeniger (ed. 1968), as alternative to the first meaning: Possess certain basic things in superfluity, e.g. air to breathe, water to drink. Cf. 1816 superflux.

1566 nature…nature]
Muir (ed. 1952; rev. 1957, p. 258): The first nature is human nature, the second animal nature (G. K. Hunter). See n. 441 and OED (sb. 10): The inherent power or force by which the physical and mental activities of man are sustained; (10b): The vital functions as requiring to be supported by nourishment. Cf. 1569, 2362, 2478.

1566 needes]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Emphatic: needs in the strict sense of the word. Hunter (ed. 1972) defends F’s and his own strong pause after the word (see textual n.): The usual [Q] punctuation…with the sense: If you do not allow…then man’s life…seems to me too rational…for Lear at this point. He is (I take it) angrily mimicking the computational arguments of his daughters: In your terms even the beggar’s rags are superfluous. Don’t bother to believe that human nature has needs greater than those of animal nature, for it is as easy (or cheap) to buy a human life as an animal life.

1567 Mans]
Hunter (ed. 1869): And then man’s.

1567 life as]
Though most eds. follow F’s life is, Q2’s life’s as is equally plausible. The Q compositor thought he saw as in his copy, and may have, and could easily have missed the final s on lifes, or read the -es abbreviation as e. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 516): No other examples of is/as error are found in Shakespeare.

1567 cheap]
Singer (ed. 1826): Little worth (OED, a. 5). Less probably Deighton (ed. 1891): In cost (OED, 1).

1568–70 If…warme]
Hudson (ed. 1871): You need clothing only for warmth; yet you pile up expense of dress for other ends, while your dress, after all, hardly meets that natural want. Kittredge (ed. 1940): If mere warmth were all the gorgeousness that a lady required of her apparel, then the gorgeousness of your attire would not be needed, for gorgeousness is certainly not—like warmth—a natural necessity. Danby (1949, p. 30) finds an intellectual pun: Gorgeous at first calls up the image of overdress. Then,…undress. The lewd daughters are perverting clothes from their proper use, mimicking the half-nakedness of the Beggarman. Muir (ed. 1952; rev. 1957, p. 258): Even the little clothing worn by a lady is superfluous to the needs of man the animal; but the needs of man the spiritual being—they are quite different (G. K. Hunter). Hunter (ed. 1972): Let us define the gorgeous in dress as able to keep you warm; yet nature does not even need that kind of gorgeousness in spite of the little warmth your gorgeous dresses do provide. Horsman (ed. 1973) supplies an ellipsis: If merely to be warm were to be sumptuously dressed [you would be poorly, because scantily, clothed]; your natural need is not for these sumptuous clothes, which hardly keep you warm at all. Perrett (1904, p. 223) compares Leir 782–5 (see ).

1568–70 beasts]
Elton (1966, p. 190): The human-beast equation, which is to be a major motif of the tragedy,…is fully explicit here.

1568 gorgeous]
Walker (1854, p. 178): Trisyllabic here, not in 1569. OED (a. 1): Splendid; showy, magnificent. Wells (ed. 2000): Colourfully. Foakes (ed. 1997): An unusual textual indication of costume.

1569 nature…wearest]
See n. 1566. Hankins (1953, p. 212) finds a parallel in Palingenius’s Zodiake (tr. Googe, 1576, p. 14). Elton (1966, pp. 125 n., 228 n.) relates the line to the commonplace natura paucis contenta, citing Tilley N45 (Nature is content with little) and classical and Renaissance texts, and to contemporary sumptuary legislation controlling excess in apparel. Dodd (1752, 2:122–3) earlier cites Lucretius, De Rerum Nat. 2.14–22, and Lucan, Phars. 4.373–8; cf. also Epicurus, Ep. ad Men. 130–1 and Sent. 3, 18, and Cicero, Fin. 1.11.38.

1570–1 but…need]
Mason (1785, p. 348): But to supply a real need. Heilman (1948, p. 169): Values entirely different from demonstrable material needs—higher needs (his own need, at the moment, is for symbols of respect and love). Moberly (ed. 1876): The poor king stops short in his definition; it is too plain that his true need is patience. Verity (ed. 1897): He suddenly passes into a direct statement. The change of construction indicates a sudden intense consciousness of what is his true need. Horsman (ed. 1973): Lear breaks off to pray for self-control or fortitude, his own true need. The break in sentence structure is marked by the apostrophe beginning 1571. Eccles (ed. 1792) would also make me emphatic.

1571–86 You…mad]
Smith (ed. 1902): The disjointed syntax, the short words, and their directness show Lear’s difficulty in expressing himself. In this awful picture of passion the very structure of the lines reflects the incoherence of Lear’s rage. He begins by asking Heaven for patience, but in the next breath asks to be touched with noble anger, and, struggling against his gentler impulses, defiantly threatens the terrors of the earth. Traver (1934, p. 181): Cf. Isa. 1:2. But Lear is not the Lord.

1571 that…need]
Capell (1783, 1.2;162): The repetition of patience is energetical, and that a word of great force; importing—that patience which is seen in you heavens,…that patience which none but you can bestow on one in my situation. Tovey (ed. 1896): Patience is repeated by Lear in his trouble. Perrett (1904, pp. 295–6) compares Macilente’s repetition of the word in Jonson’s Every Man Out 2.5.44. The metrically full line has aroused suspicion of compositorial error and has led to several attempts at emendation: see textual nn. and . Abbott (§476) would divide the line after heauens. It is remotely possible that the compositor misread yet as yt = that.

1571 patience]
See n. 774. Anderson (1927, p. 113): In psychological treatises, there is a repeated urging to patience as the only sure safeguard against the enemy within the heart, passion. Craig (ed. 1931): Patience seems to have been a term for the counterbalance which reason might set up against the passions. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Fortitude, which may keep him from the shame of tears. Danby (1949, p. 29): The prophylactic against the mortal sin of forsaking charity and falling into wrath. Fraser (1962, pp. 124–5) discusses the iconography of fortifying patience; cf. 774, 1416, 1524, 1689, 2016, 2475, 2525, 2620. The importance of the term and concept in Lr. is discussed by Welsford (1935, p. 266), Danby (1952, pp. 108–27), Mack (1965, pp. 111–14), Elton (1966, pp. 98, 104, 253–4), and many others. Foakes (ed. 1997) finds Christian overtones, citing Rom. 5:3–4. Milward (1987, pp. 172–3) cites also Heb. 10:36, James 5:11, and the example of Job.

1572–86 You…mad]
Verity (ed. 1897): The number of simple monosyllabic words is designed, I suppose, to create an effect of absolute simplicity, the simplicity of those moments in life when speech is almost impossible. Cf. n. 1570–1.

1572 you Gods]
See n. 1479.

1572 fellow]
Though the Fool calls Lear fellow at 631 and 705, Wilson (ed. 1960) finds the epithet unthinkable! here, and Richman (1986, p. 377) that it deflates, trivializes Lear. Most eds. adopt F’s man. Taylor (1983, p. 97): F offers a more dignified poore old man. The term fellow is familiar but need not be undignified: see n. 16, cf. Ham. 5.1.185 (3372), etc.

1573 both]
Hunter (ed. 1972): The first time that Lear deplores age.

1574 stirres]
On the singular verb see n. 207.

1574 hearts]
See n. 1029, and cf. OED (sb. 9b): The feeling or sentiment which one has in regard to a thing.

1575 foole]
Thirlby (MS notes, 1733–47) and Eccles (ed. 1792): Make…a fool (OED, v. 4: To make foolish, quoting this l. as its first ex. of two).

1575–6 to…To]
Q’s to is a possible misreading of F’s so, written with long s; cf. n. 3087. On the omission of as see n. 229–30.

1576 lamely]
Q is an easy l/t misreading. Doran (1931, p. 48): Lame and tame again appear as variants in [2668]. All eds. adopt F’s tamely.

1576 touch]
Craig (ed. 1901): Move, affect (OED, v. 24).

1576 noble anger]
Rann (ed. 1794): A just spirit of resentment. Craig (ed. 1931): One cannot understand either the character of Lear or the significance of his story without a sound conception of righteous indignation as a noble virtue; with it is connected the ethical propriety of revenge. So Watson (1960, p. 351), citing Aristotle’s definition [Rhet. 2.2] of anger as a longing for revenge for an undeserved slight: For the Renaissance aristocrat the meek acceptance of insult was a sign of great cowardice and weakness. Miola (1992, pp. 158–9) cites biblical, patristic, and humanist defenses of zealous anger. Hunter (ed. 1972): But here Lear’s alternative to weeping…[is] absurd boasting. Foakes (ed. 1997): Actors such as Garrick and Irving have wept or sobbed as they left the stage here, recalling [816].

1577 O]
Either this exclamation or F’s And may have resulted from the graphic similarity of O and ampersand.

1577 womens]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): That tears are womanish is an idea often repeated in Shakespeare, citing Mac. 4.2.29 (1744). Dent (1981, T82.2) suspects that Tears are women’s weapons is a proverb.

1578 Stayne]
Joseph (ed. 1966): (i) make marks on; (ii) dishonour.

1578–86 no…mad]
Anon. (1771, p. 218): The broken Sentences…require the utmost spirit, force, and violence, in order to fill the Idea of the Poet, and support the dignity of the Character, that he may be every inch a King. Knight (1930, p. 163): The lines are not far from the ridiculous. Brower (1971, p. 395): A Senecan-Marlovian parody of the hero’s vein. Barton (1971, p. 25): The breaks in his utterance here, the disjointed phrases, are not due entirely to climbing sorrow and the madness it portends. The fact is that the old king cannot find words adequate to his anger, cannot give his intentions a linguistic shape that is worthy of them. There is no vocabulary for what he feels. Braden (1985, p. 216): A new and frightening poignance.…He genuinely does not know what he is going to do. Cf. n. 1571–86.

1580 shall,]
Theobald (ed. 1733) identifies this fine abrupt Breaking off, and Suppression of Passion in its very height as aposiopesis, as does Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 245).

1580–2 I…earth]
Analogues for this train of thought have been found in Seneca’s Thyestes 270 and in Ovid’s Meta. 6.618–19 (by Theobald, ed. 1733), in Thyestes 192 (by Whalley, 1748, p. 58), and in Seneca’s Medea [423–4] (by Dodd, 1752, 2:123 and C., 1785, p. 430), and in the Senecan The Misfortunes of Arthur (1588; ed. Cunliffe, 1912, 1.2.43–5) (by Steevens, Bodley MS, 1793–1803).

1582 terrors…earth]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Things so terrible as to affright the earth.

1582–6 you…mad]
Harrison (ed. 1937): In great mental distress Nature gives a man four degrees of relief: words, tears, madness, death. In cursing Goneril, Lear has exhausted the relief of words; he will not weep; a little more, and his sanity must crack. Dunn (1952, pp. 329–30): The lines gather into one the various terms of the metaphor which is to envelop Act III: madness, heartbreak, a world cataclysm of cosmic proportions.

1583, 1585 No…flowes]
Against the agreement of Q and F most eds. reline the verse, leaving No…weepe as a short line. But Q and F make perfectly good meter if But this and in a (F into a) are elided.

1584 Storme and tempest]
Muir (ed. 1952): The Heavens answer. Foakes (ed. 1997): If so, against whom is the thunder directed? Wilson (ed. 1960): Storm in Sh. gen. means a violent wind attended with rain (Schmidt [1875]), and tempest a storm with thunder and lightning—as in JC 1.3 and Tmp. 1.1. Cf. O.E.D. tempest [sb. 1]. Delius (ed. 1854): The placing of the F SD is typical of the playbook in being several lines earlier than needed; cf. n. 1358. On F’s addition of the stage direction see n. 1014; cf. 1655, 1780, 1880. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 516): Q gives no directions at all for the storm, but some stage effect seems likely before Cornwall’s [line 1587], and this seems as good a place as any. Trewin (1978, p. 207): It is the fiercest known to the theatre.…After the first words, an actor will not attempt to match the cataracts and hurricanes. Halio (ed. 1992): At the Globe, thunder was created by rolling an iron ball, or cannon-ball (roul’d bullet), on a sheet of metal, or by drums beating, or by both; lightning was suggested by a squib, or firework set off, citing Gurr (1980, p. 170). Dessen & Thomson (1999, storm; cf. thunder and lightning) cite other plays in which storms are heard. Bratton (ed. 1987): The earliest ways of suggesting rain were simple—the creation of a pattering noise by dropping peas or some sort of hard grain onto a reverberating surface such as a drum.…Lightning was made for many years by blowing a pinch of highly inflammable powder, resin or some other substance, forcibly into a flame, either with ordinary household bellows or in a device called a flashbox. Foakes (ed. 1997): Increasingly naturalistic effects have been devised.…It has often proved more effective to symbolize the storm.…The actor playing Lear has to compete in voice with the noise.
Gollancz (ed. 1895): Possibly the first rumblings of the wild storm-scene of Lear may be heard in the mimic thunder which in Leir [1634, 1739; see , ] strikes terror in the heart of the assassin hired to murder the king and comrade. Following Adee (ed. 1890, p. xlvi), Brooke (ed. 1947): The storm…had no place in the Lear story before Shakespeare. He took it, along with the tale of Gloucester and his sons, from Sidney’s Arcadia [2.10.1; see ]. Muir (1951, p. 15): Harsnett [1603, pp. 52, 73, 108] mentions a shelter against what wind or weather so euer and lightning from heauen; he speaks of…thundring, clapping, and flashing out…hearing the huge thunder cracke of adiuration. Hamilton (1974, p. 178): A severe storm occurs at the outset of the material which [she believes] Shakespeare used in…Lodge’s Robert [Second Duke of Normandy, 1591]. Taylor (1982, p. 397) compares the storm described in 4.1 of Eastward Ho, the only storm in any of these potential sources which is described or dramatized at any length, or given any structural importance; but that tempest upon the Thames that deposits a boatload of drunkards at Cuckold’s Haven is quite unlike Lear’s storm. Cf. nn. 1604, 1702–12. For theories that the storm in Lr. is owing to the tempests of 29–30 March 1606 and the floods of the following June, see .
The central symbolic importance of the storm has long been appreciated. Smith (1739, p. 138): Shakespeare has with inimitable Art made use of a Storm in his Tragedy of King Lear, and continued it through seven Scenes.…The Anger, Fury and passionate Exclamations of Lear himself seem to rival the Storm, which is as outrageous in his Breast, inflamed and ulcerated by the Barbarities of his Daughters, as in the Elements themselves. Verity (ed. 1897): The storm is at once a fit setting for the action and a symbol of it. The convulsion in the physical world corresponds (1) with the convulsion in the moral world which has overthrown all the natural relations of family, and (2) with the tempest in Lear’s own heart (a thought specially indicated in [1622+3–+4]). Granville-Barker (1927, p. 142): The effect of the storm upon Lear is Shakespeare’s true objective. So he has to give it magnitude without detracting for one precious moment during the crisis from Lear’s own dramatic supremacy. And he solves his problem by making the actor impersonate Lear and the storm together, by identifying Lear’s passion with the storm’s. Gardner (1948, 1:175): The storm…may be considered as much a symbol of divine intervention and judgment as the rain, snow, thunder, lightning and whirlwind which precedes the Voice of God in Job (Chapters 36–7); cf. n. 1517. Heilman (1948, p. 26): It is obviously a symbol of subversion and perversion, of a turning upside down of the nature of things, of human unnaturalness. Danby (1949, pp. 180–5): The Thunder breaks in on his tirade. It may be in sympathy with Lear’s threats. It may be the ally of the pelican daughters, adding its own quota of cruelty to theirs. The Thunder brings a new nature on to the stage. With its appearance a fresh movement begins. It is Lear’s agent and master, his daughters’ servile minister, and the sign of some vague disturbance among the great gods.…It is the super-natural and the super-rational and the super-human. Holloway (1961, pp. 76–7), comparing Rev. 16:18: The storm on the heath recalls Armageddon.…For Shakespeare’s time collapse into universal chaos was…part of created Nature’s route to salvation.…Lear is in part a rehearsal of this terrible potentiality of Nature. Merchant (1964, p. 121): Lear’s personal reading of the storm is clear enough—it is a cosmic court of judgment, the thunder-claps are the dreadful summoners of the gods. In face of this dreadful pudder all wrongs shall be divulged,…indeed all pent-up guilts. In this respect the storm takes on the quality to which Lear invokes it, to become the image of that end, an eschatological pattern prefiguring the final judgment. Henry (1972, pp. 130–1): The storm is…the voice of the elements and supernatural powers—devised by Shakespeare as the executor of their sanction against Lear. Howard (1984, pp. 11–12): The sounds of the storm…, objectifying and magnifying the passionate storm of emotions within the old king, help to convey to the audience the enormity of his suffering. Colie (1974, p. 130) compares the great tempest of the Apocalypse (Rev. 6:15; cf. Luke 21:25–6). See further n. 1614 and . Williams (1952, p. 58): The Storm of the Third Act is prepared for with the greatest care…[by] several references to its approach: cf. 1587, 1603–4, 1612–13, 1616–1622+8, 1646.

1585 breake]
OED (Break v. 7c): To break the heart: to kill, crush, or overwhelm with sorrow. Cf. 1625, 1783, 2586, 3139, 3145, 3159.

1585 in]
F’s replacement of Q’s in by into, besides changing the meter (see n. 1583, 1585), makes quibbles on gusts of wind or passion less likely (see next n.). Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 516) note a similar Q/F variation in 2H4 1.2.50 (323).

1585 100.]
The compositor’s use on this page of an indented stick, making a shorter measure, explains the recourse to numerals.

1585 flowes]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 394): Doubtless an o/a misreading for F’s flawes. Bailey (1749): A fragment (OED, sb.1 2, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Goggin (ed. 1910): The ordinary meaning crack [OED, 4, first ex. 1626] will do as well. Cf. 3159. Muir (ed. 1952): Also gust of passion [OED, sb.2 2, citing Mac. 3.4.62 (1332)].…There may be a quibble on two or three of these meanings here. Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956): Also A squall of wind and rain [OED, sb.2 1], referring to the previous SD. See prev. n.

1586 Or ere]
Schmidt (1874) and Franz §558 cite many Shn. exx. of the idiom. Or = ere, before (OED, C. conj.) and ere = e’er, ever (OED, C. conj. 1d, quoting this l.). OED (Or C.1d, e): Ever [or ere] adds emphasis: or ever [or or ere] = before ever, before even, before…at all, or in any way, quoting this l.

1586 foole]
White (ed. 1883) alone: Not the coxcombed, but the crowned. More generally assumed to be addressed to the Fool, who has remained a silent supporter of Lear from [1403].

1586 Exeunt]
Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 193, 394): The F direction is inadequate.…Q’s Leister may be explained by supposing that the initial G of Gloster was illegible in the copy; there is an e/o misreading, and perhaps an extra stroke, interpreted by the compositor as an i, intervened between the o and the s. See n. 1. Q2 corrects to Glocester. On Kent, see n. 1411. Presumably the Gentleman exits here, as he entered, with the King. Rosenberg (1972, p. 181): Often, in the nineteenth century theatre, the scene—indeed the first act—ended here, to give Lear the grand curtain. But the remainder is indispensable.

1587–95 Let…Gloster]
If the Q and F lines make verse, it is very odd verse indeed; each text leaves four speakers, and F a fifth, with uncompleted lines. No attempt at relineation has seemed entirely satisfactory (see textual n.). Something like continuous pentameter may be achieved by dividing after little, bestowed, rest, particuler, and follower, though the result is rough, requiring several elisions: Let’s, th’old, and’s, and partic’ler. Possibly a brief prose interlude has been mislined as verse in both Q and F.

1587 Let…storme]
Abbott (§507) improbably considers this an instance of Lines with four accents where there is a change of thought, the cesura after withdraw serving as a fifth foot; see the prev. n. Wilson (ed. 1960): N.B. the complete indifference to what has just happened.

1588–90 This…rest]
Traversi (1952, p. 64): It is all impeccably logical, and…completely inhuman.

1588 and his]
On F’s an’ds see n. 1392.

1589 well]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Either (a) fittingly, comfortably (to them), or (b) easily, conveniently (to us).

1589 bestowed]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): To stow, to lodge (OED, v. 3). Cf. 2742.

1590 blame hath]
Some eds. follow Q and F literally, making the two words subject and verb. So Collier (ed. 1858): ’Tis his own fault or misconduct that hath put him out of rest. Schmidt (1874) gives doubtful exx. of blame = that which deserves disapprobation, crime, sin; the sense is unattested in OED, and Schmidt glosses this occurrence as fault (OED, sb. 3: Blameworthiness, culpability; fault). No one suggests the rare and doubtful sense Injury, hurt (OED, 5). Agreeing with Greg (1928, p. 40)—The construction was evidently misunderstood—the majority of eds. put a stop after blame, giving it the sense fault or responsibility, culpability (OED, 4), and assume that the pronoun he is implied, absorbed, or elided in hath. Malone (ed. 1790): He hath was formerly contracted…H’ath. On nominatives omitted with hath see n. 320. Tovey (ed. 1896): Sometimes a is used colloquially for he; sometimes even this is omitted. Verity (ed. 1897): He is readily supplied from his. All Qq and Ff lack a stop after blame, and it is unnecessary if the sentence is read as elliptical: ’Tis his own blame [that he] hath put etc.

1590 rest]
Muir (ed. 1952): Repose of mind. Harbage (ed. 1958): Or Place of residence. Hunter (ed. 1972): His bed.

1591 needs]
See n. 634.

1591 tast]
Schmidt (1875): Experience (OED, Taste v. 3). Cf. 3275.

1592 particuler]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Individual self. See n. 861.

1594, 1597, 1601 Duke., Reg., Re.]
Though all eds. follow the F reassignments Gon., Corn., and Corn. respectively, there is no reason to think them preferable to Q. Urkowitz (1980, p. 38): Either version is Shakespearean, purposeful, and theatrically intelligible. For a possible explanation see n. 1227. At 1594, reassigning the speech to Goneril merely repeats what the audience already well knows, whereas Q’s assignment to Cornwall lends new ducal authority to Regan’s evil, as at 1613, consolidating the opposition to Lear. Q’s assignment of 1597 to Regan seems plausible, both as an answer to her husband’s question and because it repeats her scornful old man epithet from 1588. From Regan, 1601 sounds like her typical rationalizing, something Cornwall is not much given to. Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 85–6), convinced a priori that Q’s assignments are wrong, imagines a scenario in which an original Q misassignment of 1594 to Regan, resulting in two consecutive speeches (1592, 1594) by Regan, led to a later erroneous transposition of the prefixes of 1594 and 1597 and was followed by a further accidental misassignment of 1601 to the Duke—in short, three or four imagined accidents in a row. It is easier to think that the addition of 1599–1600 in a MS behind F led to crowding and confusion of speech prefixes in the margin, or contributed to two cases of eyeskip, Gon. (1594) answering Reg. as at 1590, and Corn. (1601) answering Glo. as at 1599. No one seems to have argued either that the original Q assignments are demonstrably erroneous or that the F reassignments reflect changed authorial conceptions of the characters; see . Foakes (ed. 1997): F gives Cornwall and Goneril more prominence, at the expense of Regan, who has had the lion’s share of the dialogue with Lear.

1596 Enter Glo]
Q’s marginal entrance is far right of 1595. Cf. 462, 944 (n. 948). Here the text was set to a shorter measure, leaving no room for a SD, which was added after the text was transferred to the galley or when the page was made up.

1597 Followed]
On the omitted nominative see n. 230.

1598 rage]
OED (sb. 2): Violent anger, furious passion, usually as manifested in…words or action. Cf. 2370, 2505.

1599–1600 Corn.…Horse,]
Almost certainly a later interpolation rather than an accidental omission from Q. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxi): Without it giue him way may refer to Lear’s rage instead of (with this addition) to his riding off. Doran (1931, p. 60): A different conjunction [&/but]…may indicate revision in F instead of omission from Q. Stone (1980, p. 242): The [Q] line being hypermetrical, the [F] reviser has split it in two and, with interpolated matter, makes two good pentameters. Since the plot involves frequent journeys on horseback, he probably felt it safe to introduce the detail of Lear’s calling to horse.…[But] Lear departs on foot. See n. 1600. Halio (ed. 1992, p. 281): The hypermetrical line could have been the result of an accidental omission that F either recovers or substitutes for.

1599 Whether]
Common sp. variant of whither.

1600 cals to Horse]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Summons his attendants to mount and ride with him (OED, Call v. 4, Horse sb. 16). Thirlby (MS notes, 1725–33): Tho’ it does not appear yt he did take horse. Edwards (ed. 1975): Shakespeare seems to forget the horses. The detail was added to F, perhaps not by Shakespeare. It is inconsistent with both Q’s specific vnbonneted he runnes (1622+7), omitted from F, and the impression of the following lines in both Q and F that Lear’s attention is not on travel but on braving the storm and being distracted by the Fool—as we find is the case moments later in 3.2. No reason is suggested (or easily imagined) why Lear, having started out on horseback, should almost immediately have reverted to foot travel in the storm; had he been thrown from a horse with or without injury, one would expect some notice of that fact, and had he ridden off on horseback for any length of time he would not still be near Gloucester’s house in 3.2 (see 1717–21, 1928–31, and 2074–6). This added detail serves no useful purpose, unless to suggest how Kent (though not the Fool?) might have become separated from Lear, and its inconsistency with all the other known facts of Lear’s wanderings suggests that it was added by a reviser not overly familiar with the play. It has led to such lame excuses as Bransom’s (1934, p. 76): The king…does not seem to have waited for his horses. He probably wandered off on to the moor and, occupied with other thoughts, forgot them. Lear does call for horses at 763 and 906–7, for his journey to Regan’s house; here, however, he has no such destination: rather I abiure all roofes (1501). Foakes (ed. 1997): A king would be expected to travel by horseback or in a coach.…It would help to explain why Kent cannot easily find him. Of course, he would be hard to find in a storm at night; he obviously does not travel, for Kent finds him not far from where he started, and on foot.

1600 wil]
See n. 312.

1601 giue him way]
Either Do not interfere with his going (Craig, ed. 1901) or Let him have his own way (Crook, ed. 1907). See n. 1599–1600.

1601 leads himselfe]
Deighton (ed. 1891): He is not driven to act as he is doing. Kittredge (ed. 1940): He submits to no guidance.

1602 My Lord]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Addressed to Glo.

1603 bleak]
OED (a. 3): Cold, chilly; usually of wind or weather. Clarkes (ed. 1868): We think [bleak] is more probably the poet’s epithet [than F’s high], because it adds the effect of cold to a description where boisterous or high is sufficiently indicated by the expression ruffle. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 177): The F compositor has [probably] substituted high…owing to a recollection of high in [1598]. Sh. had used bleake windes in Jn. 5.7.40 (2648). Though high obviously means strong (OED, a. 10), Weis (ed. 1993) suggests advanced (OED, 11).

1604 sorely]
OED (adv. 4): To a great extent; in a high degree, quoting this l.

1604 russel]
Though rustle is possible, it fits poorly with sorely, and most eds. prefer F’s ruffle. Thirlby (MS notes, 1733–47): Russle seems too gentle. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 394): A double [long-]s/f misreading. Taylor (1983, p. 370): Typographically…ruffle would be an easy error for russle, since the ffl and ssl ligatures were adjacent in the typecase. Wells (ed. 2000) defends Q: To make a great noise (OED, v. 1a). Malone (1783, p. 50): A ruffler…was a noisy, boistrous, swaggerer. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Here it means roughly blow [OED, v.2 3]; in…[2107; see n.] it means roughly tear, rend. Joseph (ed. 1966): Bluster. Muir (1951, p. 15): In Harsnett (1603, p. 18; see ), a devil will ruffle, rage,…and blowe downe steeples. Cf. 1658, n. 2107.

1605 not a bush]
F’s scarce a bush is indifferent. Perrett (1904, p. 259): Gloucester’s emotion caused him to exaggerate, citing a tree (1253). See n. 1614. Hogan (1962, p. 76 n.): F is right; Q shortened scarce to not to make one rather than two lines.

1607–8 The…schoolemasters]
Traversi (1952. p. 64): Regan’s last comment…besides echoing the characteristically selfish moralizing of the speaker, contain[s] a truth the depth of which she is not herself aware,…[as] Lear’s own growth in self-knowledge, his development during the storm scenes will show. Milward (1987, p. 173) compares Psa. 119:67, 71. Watson (1960, p. 331): Regan is surely not speaking as a choral character. Thirlby (MS notes, 1725–33): Themselues is the object of procure.

1609 with]
See n. 1551.

1609 desperate]
Schmidt (1874): Reckless (OED, a. 4). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Regan, like Goneril, shamelessly misrepresents the character of Lear’s knights. Cf. 593.

1609 traine]
Craig (ed. 1901): It is not very clear where Lear’s knights are supposed to go, or if he brought them with him. See n. 1273. Speculations that Lear’s…attendant knights had not yet arrived (Eccles, ed. 1792) or have deserted him (Goggin, ed. 1910) or that Lear had apparently not brought his train with him (Houghton, ed. 1957), and that therefore Regan is making a barefaced pretence (Clarkes, ed. 1868) to make a fictitious excuse for her cruelty (Craig, op. cit.), are without clear textual support. Cf. n. 1336.

1610 incense]
Malone (ed. 1790): Instigate (OED, v.2 4).

1610 being]
I.e., he being. See n. 1195.

1610 apt]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Ready. Much more active in sense than in modern usage. Joseph (ed. 1966): Accustomed. OED (a. 4b): Customarily disposed, given, inclined, prone. Cf. 2311+4.

1611 abusd]
OED (ppl. a. 3): Imposed upon, deceived, mistaken, misguided. Craig & Bevington (ed. 1973): By wild counsel. Cf. 522+4, 2203, 2805, 2836, 2859+2. Buck (ed. 1907): Perhaps an unconscious reference to the time when their flattering speeches has so abused the king’s ear.

1611 wisedome]
Heilman (1948, p. 233): That is, looking out for oneself—a meaning wholly in harmony with all we have seen of the sisters who keep their minds strictly on business. Here a veritable exaggeration of cool sanity is transmuted into moral madness. Wilson (ed. 1960): Common prudence.

1612 Shut…doores]
Verity (ed. 1897) compares 1460. Muir (ed. 1952): Gloucester, in spite of his feelings (cf. [2135] ff.) obeys. Leech (1957, p. 260): A particularly effective Act-ending. Halio (ed. 1992): Cornwall’s repetition of Regan’s request, or command ([1608]), indicates Gloucester’s hesitation or reluctance to comply. Liebler (1995, p. 207): Goneril’s and Regan’s behavior is not only a filial fault; it is also illegal, according to Eizabethan Poor Relief legislation of 1598 and 1601. Wells (ed. 2000): The stocks would presumably have been removed.

1612 wild]
On F’s wil’d see n. 1322.

1613 at’h]
F oth’; both mean of the. See nn. 669+10, 704, 1105, and cf. 1860, 2399, 2794.

1614 <Actus Tertius>]
Dent (ed. 1927): Throughout this Act the alternating scenes of high and low tension…not only help the manipulation of the story, but they provide emotional relief for the audience. Traversi (1952–3, pp. 126–7): This Third Act of King Lear, which covers the storm and its counterpart in human behaviour, is the key-stone upon which the whole elaborate construction of the play rests. It is, above all, a marvellous example of poetic elaboration for dramatic purposes. At the centre of it, at once the main protagonist and symbol of the spiritual state of a humanity exposed to fundamental disorder, wrenched out of its fixed place in the frame of nature, stands the figure of the aged King. The intimate dove-tailing of personal conflict with external convulsions has often been noted, and is indeed an essential part of the conception. The storm which has broken out in Lear’s mind, the result of his treatment at the hands of his children, is admirably fused with the description of the warring elements, mainly entrusted to his lips; the external storm, whilst exercising upon his aged physique the intolerable strain under which it finally breaks, is itself a projection of his inner state, being fused with it in a single poetic reality. The opening dialogue between Kent and the Gentleman, as they meet on the wind-swept heath [1616–17], makes this perfectly clear…; from this moment the spiritual disorder and its external projection are related.…Lear…now clearly assumes a stature that is more than merely personal, becomes man, the microcosm of the universe, exposed to a suffering to which the frame of things itself contributes, but which finds its acutest symbol in the intimate disunion, which the earlier action of the play has introduced into the family bond. ¶ The whole Act is beautifully contrived around this central situation. If Lear has himself become unaccommodated man, it is clearly felt that he is unable to bear alone the whole weight of the situation for which the tragic conception has destined him.…The Fool, Kent, and Edgar each, from his own point of view, bear some fraction of Lear’s tragic burden, show an insight into some part of its significance; and before the Act ends, he is further joined by Gloucester, whose fortunes have been from the first evidently parallel to his own. The result is an intricate and progressive dovetailing of characters and situations which lead us, step by step, further and further into an understanding of the full depth and meaning of the universal tragedy which Lear’s outraged fatherhood and shattered royalty embody. Goldberg (1974, p. 115): The storm-scenes of Act III bring Lear and Edgar together for the first time. Each has been reduced to rock-bottom necessity; each, moreover, forms a kind of commentary on the other. Bullough (1973, p. 292): The hapless wandering of Lear and his Fool were suggested by Leir (Sc. 14 [1094–1117]), where the two old men are creeping towards Ragan’s home, and by their later extremity in France (Sc. 24 [2036–90]); see , .
Pye (1792, p. 133; rev. 1807, pp. x–xi): Events are made to take place in that time which could not possibly happen.…In the second Act [2.4], Lear comes in with his train to Regan.…From the circumstance of the storm continuing, it is obvious that the interval between the second and third Acts does not comprehend a period of time much exceeding that which really passes, and yet, in this time, we are told that there is a power already footed…; and Cornwall says, the French are now landed. The difficulty arises from the assumption that France’s invasion is occasioned by Lear’s mistreatment; see n. 1638+1. Hunter (1976, pp. 32–3) argues that the theatrical pacing of the play seems to cry out for a pause at this point, the nadir of Lear’s powerlessness, before we move forward into the storm, the heath, and the desolations of act III and discover there a world as new as the seacoast of Bohemia. Howard (1984, pp. 160–1): The scenes of Act 3 form an integral theatrical movement orchestrated climatically. The interrupting scenes within the castle, which form a dialectic with the scenes in the storm, do not dilute, but progressively heighten, the terror and pity with which we observe Lear.

1614 <Scena Prima>]
Verity (ed. 1897): This Scene lowers the pitch of the passion after the tension of the last Act, gives relief to the feelings, and prepares us for the wilder mood, verging more on madness, in which Lear is next brought before us. Also, it leads naturally to the arrangement (essential to the plot) by which Kent communicates with Cordelia. Budd (ed. 1935): The calm manner in which Kent mentions activities that hold out hope for Lear’s cause enables us to find momentary relief from the tension of the preceding scene. Kittredge (ed. 1940): This scene takes place on the same day as ii, 4, with which it is practically continuous. Gloucester follows Lear forth at [1586], returns ([1596]), and then goes out to rejoin Lear, pretending that he is ill and gone to bed ([1767–8]). Meanwhile Kent has been separated from Lear in the storm but means to search for him. He finds him at [1688]. Greg (1940, p. 436): Kent, who started with him, appears to have lost him again and returned to the castle demanding after him, where he has been refused entrance ([1720]). The Gentleman too has got separated from him, though he had evidently followed for a while ([1619–1622+8]). Kent and the Gentleman now meet accidentally, and the former, without revealing his identity, imparts the contents of Cordelia’s letter, namely that she is in Dover, and persuades his hearer to seek her out and inform her of what has happened. Their more pressing business, however, is to find the king. Houghton (ed. 1957): Hitherto everything has gone easily for the cruel sisters. Now we hear both of dissension between their husbands and of a move from Cordelia’s side. For this some lapse of time would naturally be supposed, but Shakespeare is deliberately vague, so that the picture of Lear driven straight out into the storm may not be impaired. In fact there is a double time scheme, though not so marked as in Othello. But see nn. 926, 1638+1 on the uncertain possibility of double time. Brown (ed. 1976): The exposition provides a breathing space for the actor of Lear (and an opportunity to change into storm-rent clothes).
The barrenness of the scene is indicated in 1605, but the term Heath, nowhere occurring in the text of the play, has been used to describe the locale by most eds. since Rowe, who probably took it from Tate’s History of King Lear (1681); see textual n., and Scouten (1983, pp. 46–7) and Ogden (1987, pp. 19–20; 1997, pp. 136–7). Joshi (1964, pp. 91, 93): Without any justification. It could be a plain, a champaign, or an open space.…The heath…meant for Shakespeare a waste-land utterly barren and blasted.…The theme demanded a different kind of landscape, unlike that of Macbeth, where the word occurs. Ogden, however, thinks Tate derived it from Davenant’s Macbeth (1671). Brown (ed. 1976): This scene is best played as if both characters enter to find shelter from the storm that rages offstage.

1615 Storme]
See n. 1584.

1615 still]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Perhaps as before (at [1584]), but more probably continuously. See n. 253. Leggatt (1992, p. 184): Evidently the sound effect, a beaten drum or rolled cannonball, was not just occasional punctuation (as in plays where thunder signals the entrance of a devil) but sustained over three out of four scenes—a daring, unusual and possibly exhausting effect. Wells (ed. 2000), however: Possibly the sound effects only punctuate the speeches, not overwhelm them.

1615 Kent]
Adams (1948, p. 323): The law of re-entry is observed.…To make [Kent’s] remove [some distance from Gloucester’s house] seem possible in a scheme of dramatic time, he was withdrawn ten or more lines…before the close of [2.4]. The law, formulated by Robert Prölss in 1905, is doubtful in Sh.

1615 a Gentleman]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Lear apparently has rushed hastily out of the castle unattended by any person but this gentleman and the fool.…It may naturally be supposed that this his attendant finding all his entreaties and persuasions ineffectual to prevail on the king to return, is now coming back to summon some others of his train to his assistance. How Lear…happened to be so poorly attended, it is not easy to determine, especially as Kent is seen to leave the stage with him at the conclusion of the preceding act. See nn. 1336, 1609. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905), improbably (see n. 874): This is the Gentleman sent to Gloucester when Kent was sent to Regan ([875]). He had turned back and joined the king on his approach ([1273]); and now, like Kent, he was ready to invite and welcome the succor of Cordelia. Houghton (ed. 1957): The Gentleman may be supposed to be one of Lear’s followers, now arrived, or someone Kent had known at court in old days. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 516): This gentleman reappears in 4.3…, 4.6…, and 4.7…, associated with Kent and Cordelia; he should be distinguished from the messenger figure (associated with Regan and Goneril) who appears in 4.2…and 5.3. The Oxford eds. (1986; Wells, 2000) accordingly call him First Gentleman. (Ibid., p. 534): In Q, no Gentleman has yet appeared: 1.5 calls for a servant and 2.[4] for a knight. So in Q the article makes sense; here in F, it seems to imply a new character. Elsewhere F calls for Gentleman only, reserving a Gentleman for the character, clearly different, who appears in 5.3.…F therefore probably retains the article here inadvertently. There is no need to differentiate between the Servant, Gentleman, and Knight, or to find disagreement about them between Q and F. Lear’s one hundred reserved servants were knights and therefore gentlemen. Perrett’s reasons for thinking that Q’s servant, knight, and gentleman are the same character played by the same actor (see nn. 580, 874) are reaffirmed by Halio (ed. 1992) and Foakes (ed. 1997). See also n. 1626. Mahood (1992, p. 165): Discreet and self-effacing in his attendance on the King [1276, 1335], the Gentleman talks freely with the disguised Kent, whom he appears instinctively to trust. His eloquence calls for a good voice, and it is tempting to speculate that the original actor of France took on this further role.

1615 at…doores]
Foakes (ed. 1997), on F’s seuerally: Separately, as at [927], or by different doors (as Q).

1616 Whats]
Q’s idiom is Shn.: see n. 540; the pronoun may refer to either a thing (like weather) or a person. F’s change to the more limiting Who’s is unnecessary. Baldini (1966, 1:170): F is banal, Q much more grandiose and mysterious.

1616 here beside]
F’s there besides is indifferent. See OED (Beside, Besides prep. 2, 3).

1617 minded]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): With his mind disposed. Hunter (ed. 1972): The play’s first equation between the inner world and the stormy weather.

1619 Contending]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Both (1) Physically struggling against and (2) competing in violence and anger. Edwards (ed. 1975): Only the latter meaning.

1619 fretfull]
Lott (ed. 1974): Would usually be applied to a person, ill-tempered, and may therefore extend here the train of thought in [1617], comparing impetuous (1622+1). OED (a. 3): Of water, agitated, of wind, gusty, first ex. 1613.

1619 element]
Nares (1822): The air, or visible compass of the heavens [OED, sb. 10: The sky; ?also, the atmosphere].…There was a notion, that all the elements were combined in the atmosphere, which therefore was the element of elements. He cites several Shn. exx., as does Schmidt (1874, quoting this l.). Many eds. follow Capell (1783, 1.2:163) in limiting the sense to one of the four elements, air, and since the air was not now the only element with which he had to contend, prefer F’s plural elements, comparing 1671; but there, three elements—air, water, and fire—are specifically named. Schmidt gives several Shn. exx. of the plural used of the air in commotion by tempests; cf. OED (11): Atmospheric agencies or powers, quoting 1671.

1620 Bids]
On the omitted nominative see n. 230.

1620–1 earth…maine]
Brower (1971, p. 395): The Gentleman pictures Lear as a Jove-Neptune. Shaheen (1987, p. 149) compares Psa. 46:2–3, at best an analogy rather than a reference.

1621 swell]
Schmidt (1875): Cause to rise (OED, v. 2b, quoting this l. as its first ex.).

1621 curled]
Rolfe (ed. 1880) finds the same metaphor in 2H4 3.1.23 (1443).

1621 maine]
Steevens (ed. 1778): Main land, the continent [OED, sb.1 4].…He wishes for the destruction of the world, either by the winds blowing the lands into the waters, or raising the waters so as to overwhelm the land. Malone (1780, 1:260) finds the latter idea in Tro. 1.3.111–13 (570–2). Hunter (ed. 1972): Lear commands the earth to return to the state before creation separated water and earth—in the Judaeo-Christian account, presumably; but Lear is pagan. Wells (ed. 2000) points to the confusion of the elements at Oth. 2.1.3–17 (757–68), WT 3.3.82–93 (1525–35), Tmp. 1.2.3–5 (84–6).

1622 things]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Everything in nature. Craig (ed. 1901): The order of the world, comparing 2956 and Mac. 3.2.16 (1170).

1622 change or cease]
Harbage (ed. 1958): Revert to chaos (?) or, improve (?). Edwards (ed. 1975): Be transformed, i.e. from their present state, or else come to an end. Foakes (ed. 1997): An image recalled at [3224).

1622–1622+8 teares…all]
Johnson (ed. 1765): The whole speech is forcible, but too long for the occasion, and properly retrenched. Wilson (ed. 1960): Few will now agree. Capell (1783, 1.2:162): The first folio omission, if not occasion’d by negligence, was occasion’d by ill judgment: for the omitted passage’s beauties are great; the description not full enough, and not striking without it. Delius (1876, p. 142): One of those explanatory passages which our poet loves to insert as a resting-place between two passionate scenes. The actors for this reason may have considered it superfluous.…[It is] a description of Lear’s mad defiance…in characters which are so essential to the delineation of the whole situation, that it is impossible that Shakspere should have omitted it. Moriarty (1913, p. 459): Its inclusion weakens the actual presentation of Lear in the storm in 3.2. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 225): An inefficient actor might have been the cause of this [cut]. Doran (1931, p. 76): [A] very fine passage.…The only excuse for its omission is that it is descriptive rather than dramatic and repeats what is elsewhere either acted by Lear or said about him, comparing 2783+1–+4. Hart (1942, p. 147): Omitted by an adapter, probably because Lear will be on the stage two or three minutes later. Urkowitz (1983, p. 32): Cut by a revising author. He gives no reason for thinking so; cf. n. 1631–1638+12. Halio (ed. 1992, p. 269): Theatrical abridgement, reducing the prominence Q gives the Gentleman. Mahood (1992, p. 165), contra Granville-Barker: If the player was less than fully competent, it is odd that the later version should make over to him almost the whole of the Doctor’s part [see nn. 2349, 2744].…[Rather,] once Burbage had brought 3.2 to life in rehearsal, Shakespeare realised Lear’s madness needed the minimum of preparation. Weis (ed. 1993): F reserve[s] the climax of the storm for 3.4. Foakes (ed. 1997): The lines are neatly excised…so as to maintain the metre.

1622+1–+2 Which…of]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Some player’s trash. Heath (1765, p. 325): On the contrary, they seem to me very much in Shakespear’s manner, and present us with a very picturesque image.

1622+1 eyles]
Heath (1765, p. 325): Undiscerning. Schmidt (1874): Blind. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Without discrimination or definite object. Muir (ed. 1952): Invisible, comparing Mac. 1.7.23 (497). Wilson (ed. 1960): Poss. implies they might spare Lear c[oul]d they see he is old. Williams (1951, p. 59): The anthropomorphic terms, eyeles rage, remind us of Lear’s rage and spiritual blindness and heighten the identification of Lear with the storm.

1622+1 rage]
OED (sb. 4): Violence, violent operation or action, fury (of things, e.g. wind…). Cf. 1656, 2134.

1622+2 make nothing of]
Heath (1765, p. 325): Scatter or disperse to nothing. Goggin (ed. 1910): Reduce to nothing. Delius (ed. 1854) and most eds.: Treat with irreverence (OED, v.1 21). Schmidt (ed. 1879): The opposite of make much of.

1622+3 little…man]
Hunter (ed. 1869): This alludes to the ancient notion of man being a microcosm, or little world, composed of elements corresponding to those of the external world. Foakes (ed. 1997): And so establishes the link between the storm in nature and the storm in Lear’s mind. OED (Little World) cites exx. from ca. 1200, including this line. In Cor. 2.1.63 Menenius calls himself a microcosm, and Craig (ed. 1901) finds the phrase little world of man in Jonson’s Hymenæi 125 and Tourneur’s The Atheist’s Tragedy (ed. Nicoll) 3.3.47. Horsman (ed. 1973) cites the heading of Raleigh’s History (1614) 1.2.5: That Man is (as it were) a little world. The comparison of man to a larger world is a medieval and Renaissance commonplace. Astrologers saw correspondences between man and the whole universe, and Furness (ed. 1880) provides citations for this idea; political thinkers drew analogies between man and the body politic. E. M. W. Tillyard, Elizabethan World Picture (1943, pp. 84–91), discusses both analogies; many other studies are cited in David G. Hale, The Body Politic (1971, pp. 12–14). Sh. compares the body to a kingdom in Jn. 4.2.246 (1970), 2H4 4.3.109 (2344–5), JC 2.1.67–8 (688–9), etc. Cf. LC 7, where a maid is Storming her world with sorrowes, wind and raine, and Sidney’s Arcadia 2.7.4 (ed. Feuillerat, 1:192), where the windes began…as in a tumultuous kingdome, to thinke themselues fittest instruments of commaundement.

1622+3 outscorne]
OED (Out- 18c: To overcome or defeat by the action) gives no other ex. of the word. Steevens (ed. 1793) proposes out-storm, citing LC 7 (see prev. n.), persuading Muir (ed. 1952): This line contains the same reference to the microcosm, and the Q compositor elsewhere confused c/t and m/n, citing 2280, 1067. Debate about changing scorn to storm occurs also in Tro. 1.1.37 (72) where, as here, most eds. resist emendation. Verplanck (ed. 1844): The original text…gives a good sense: Lear returns with scorn the scorn of the elements. Wright (ed. 1875): Lear’s speech in the next scene is true scorn and defiance.

1622+4 too…conflicting]
Craig (ed. 1901) compares conflicting Elements in Tim. 4.3.230 (1851), OED’s first ex. of the participle, and warring winds in 2783. Muir (ed. 1952): Swaying about in mad, angry conflict. Joseph (ed. 1966): Violent gusts of wind [blow] the rain hither and thither. Brook (1976, p. 137): Some compound words have more than two elements…not always linked by hyphens.

1622+5 cub-drawne]
Pope (ed. 1725): Drawn by nature to its young. Hanmer (ed. 1743; in ed. 1745, crediting Warburton): The she-bear drawn dry by the sucking of her cubs, and thence most ravenous and greedy of prey, and so most restless and furious (Upton, 1746, p. 311). Warburton (ed. 1747): Even hunger, and the support of its young, would not force the bear to leave her den in such a night. Milward (1987, p. 174): Robbed of its whelps. Most eds. agree with Warburton, Steevens (ed. 1778) citing as a parallel the suck’d and hungry Lyonnesse in AYL 4.3.126 (2278), and Kittredge (ed. 1940) as another Arden of Feversham 2.2.118–20 (ed. Brooke, p. 14).

1622+5 couch]
Schmidt (1874): To lie close and hidden (OED, v.1 16b). Craig (ed. 1901): I.e. through fright [OED, 17a]…not range abroad for prey. Colie (1974, p. 130): Just as, in Job’s storm, the beasts go into the denne, and remaine in their places (Job 37:8). Milward (1987, p. 174) notes couch in Job 39:2 (KJ), Psa. 104:22 (Geneva).

1622+6 belly pinched]
Pope (ed. 1725): Provok’d by hunger. OED (Pinch v. 6): Said of the painful action of…hunger; (Belly sb. 16b): Locative and adverbial, quoting this l. Brownlow (1993, p. 116): Cf. Harsnett (1603, p. 24), pinched with…hunger. Cf. 1H4 3.1.28, with…colic pinch’d.

1622+7 vnbonneted]
Craig (ed. 1901): Bonnet denoted the headdress of men as well as of women (OED, sb. 1a, 1d). Sisson (1956, 1:32): To go hatless out-of-doors would be almost indecent; cf. nn. 1714, 2625. Skillan (ed. 1967): The detail reveals lear’s distraction. Hunter (ed. 1972) He is totally abandoning self-respect as well as self-protection. Fischer (1985) suspects a possible pun on penniless, bonnet being perhaps a slang name for a coin. Foakes (ed. 1997): The image of Lear hatless and tearing his hair has been suggestive for actors.

1622+8 what will]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Anyone or anything that will. Schmidt (ed. 1879), less probably: wagers that which will win all, sets all against all. See next n.

1622+8 take all]
OED (Take v. 2d): In various games, as chess, cards, etc.: To capture, not recording this idiom. Verity (ed. 1897): Take-all is said to have been the name of a game at dice, citing Heywood’s Wise Woman of Hogsdon, where dice are repeatedly thrown at all (ed. Leonard, 1980, 1.1.73, 79, 88, 100, 105). Kittredge (ed. 1940), following Schmidt (ed. 1879): The cry of the gambler when he stakes, at a final cast of the dice, all the money that he has left. Hence it is used figuratively as a cry of despair or desperate defiance, citing The Weakest Goeth to the Wall 401, Daniel’s Civil War 7.20, and Ant. 4.2.8 (2420).
