Elton (1966, p. 307 n.): Recalling Lear’s I gave you all [1547]. Wilson (ed. 1960): But by all Lear means the whole world. Edwards (ed. 1975): He who has been so concerned about apportioning out his kingdom is now totally indifferent to who owns what. Dent (1981, A192.1) cites the proverbs He that wins shall take All (A192.1) and, more doubtfully, To make (let) All split (A205.1).

1624 out-iest]
Craig (ed. 1901): To drive out, exorcise by jesting [OED, Out- 16, quoting only this l.]; or perhaps, to outdo the greatness of his master’s wrongs by the wild extravagance of his jests. Kittredge (ed. 1940): To relieve by his jests. It is the Fool’s tragedy that his efforts to cheer up his master serve only to emphasize Lear’s folly and its dreadful results; for the Fool’s mind instinctively concentrates on that one idea and he calls Lear fool over and over again. Muir (ed. 1952, pp. lxiii f.): Nearly every one of his jests reminds Lear of the sorrow that is gnawing at his heart.…It might almost be said that these jests, coming on top of Lear’s afflictions and concerned as they are with the afflictions, help to drive him mad. He stands, perhaps, for worldly common sense [citing Orwell, 1947, p. 11]; he is not without malice [citing Empson, 1951, p. 133], and he can never forgive Lear’s treatment of Cordelia.…His dramatic function is of great importance. He provides not so much comic relief as a safety-valve for the emotions of the audience. Lear’s conduct is absurd, if judged critically; and the representation of madness is apt to arouse more laughter than sympathy. The Fool was therefore inserted to draw the laughs of the audience, and so preserve Lear’s sublimity, citing Hazlitt (1817, p. 158) and Keats’s marginalia in Hazlitt (Keats, Works, ed. Forman, 1938–9, 5:283).

1625 heart strooke]
OED (Heart-struck ppl. a.): Smitten with mental anguish or dismay, quoting this l. as its first ex.; see nn. 1029, 1585. For the participle see n. 615. Tovey (ed. 1896): Really an epithet of Lear. Goggin (ed. 1910): By hypallage transferred to the injuries. Hunter (ed. 1972): That are like blows on the heart.

1626–53 Sir…other]
Vickers (1968, p. 351): When [Kent] drops [his] role of the bluff serving man (he in fact plays the man he is) and looks after Lear with more protectiveness he returns to verse (III, i and after).

1626 doe know]
Know to be one of Lear’s loyal knights, apparently, since Kent entrusts to him both confidences and an errand on behalf of the king. See n. 1615. Horsman (ed. 1973): The emphatic do and the repetition of know you from [1618] perhaps indicate that they now meet at close quarters.

1627 warrant]
Schmidt (1875): Assurance (OED, sb.1 8). Craig (ed. 1901): Strength of.

1627 Arte]
F’s note is generally preferred. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 394): Probably a misreading—a for n, r for o. Steevens (ed. 1778), however, interprets Q’s word to mean skill in phisiognomy. Similarly Capell (1783, 1.2:163): Art of manners and face-judging, skill in knowledge of men. Malone (ed. 1790) compares Mac. 1.4.11–12, Art, To finde the Mindes construction in the Face. Hudson (ed. 1856): But it appears that Kent knows his man, and therefore has no occasion to use the art or skill in question. On such grounds most eds. follow Johnson (ed. 1765), note—My observation of your character—or Knight (ed. 1840)—knowledge. But the logic is questionable; Kent may know his man mainly from artful observation, not familiarity.

1628 Commend]
Hudson (ed. 1881): Commit. Deighton (ed. 1891): Entrust. Cf. 1304. In Q Kent commends to the Gentleman an errand to inform Cordelia of Lear’s distress; in F, which may be incomplete (see n. 1631–1638+12), no definite commendation is made.

1628 deare]
See n. 785. Craig (ed. 1901): Important, urgently pressing, of weight or moment (OED, a.1 4b, quoting this l.). Cf. 2347+52.

1628 thing]
Eds. generally assume that the thing being commended to the servant is Kent’s subsequent account of events in the kingdom: in Q, news of diuision and a power come from France, in F of French spies, snuffs and packings, a hard Reine against Lear, and perhaps something deeper. They further assume that Kent derives most of his news from Cordelia’s letter (at 1242). Thus Eccles (ed. 1792): The intelligence which Kent here communicates…may be imagined to have derived from the letter, which…he had so lately received from Cordelia. The contents of Cordelia’s letter, however, are a mystery, and insisting that that letter is the source of Kent’s news creates serious problems of chronology. So Gildersleeve (ed. 1912): Not much more than two weeks can have elapsed since Lear divided his kingdom and the disinherited Cordelia departed to France, and not more than two days since Goneril instructed her steward to begin to treat the king with discourtesy and neglect. Yet here Kent speaks as if months had passed,—time for France to send spies, to learn of divisions between Albany and Cornwall and of the unkind treatment accorded the king, and to send forces which have secretly landed in several ports. When hearing this play performed one does not note the inconsistency. At some points Shakespeare seeks, by the use of short time, rapidity of action; at others, by long time he lends plausibility; and he does not permit considerations of theoretical consistency to hinder dramatic effectiveness. On the uncertain theory of double time, see nn. 811, 926, 1638+1; and Kent may have learned his news from several sources, including servants of Cornwall and Gloucester and the man who delivered Cordelia’s letter; discord between the dukes was known at Gloucester’s house before 938.
Less problematically, the thing commended to the Gentleman is not the news, which are mere preamble (see Now to you, 1638+5), but the Gentleman’s very errand to Cordelia ([I] Offer this office to you), including the showing of a ring (1644) and contents of a purse (1643) which may hold one or more letters (see 2347+10–+11). The news in F 1633–7, instead of being things that Kent learned from Cordelia, are more probably things that Kent wants to inform Cordelia of; see n. 1634–8.

1628 diuision]
See n. 938.

1629 face]
Schmidt (1874): Appearance (OED, sb. 8).

1629 be]
Abbott (§361): The subjunctive is…found, more frequently than now, with if, though, &c.; cf. Franz §645. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 145) sees grammatical nicety in F’s indicative is, since there is no reference to futurity and since no element of doubt is involved; but it may merely represent casual if not unconscious substitution.

1629 couer’d]
Verity (ed. 1897): But it was known to the courtier Curan; cf. 938.

1631–1638+12 Who…you]
In the Q text (1638+1–+12) Kent conveys to the Gentleman the news of threatened civil strife, informs him that French forces have landed at Dover who will be sympathetic to Lear, exhorts him to carry news of the king’s plight to those forces, and gives him assurances of his [Kent’s] own credibility and authority in urging such a course. The train of thought is logical, consecutive, and complete, supplying all the information necessary to the understanding of what follows; and if lines 1638+2–+5 are properly relined (see textual n.) they and the rest of the passage make good verse. The F text (1631–8) retains only the news of domestic diuision, adds news of French spies in the dukes’ households, intimates that Albany has given Lear hard treatment (otherwise not indicated in the play), hints obscurely of something deeper (see n. 1637), and breaks off with an incomplete sentence. Capell (1783, 1.2:162–3) finds the information that is added (as ’twere in recompence) in the F-only passage to be necessary knowledge: From it we learn the motives of France’s invasion. (In fact we never learn the motives of France’s invasion.) But while adding details, the F text omits from Q details that seem essential. Delius (1876, p. 142: The omission of [1638+1–+12] renders that which follows incomprehensible. How could the nobleman find Cordelia, and deliver Kent’s message to her, if he did not know that she was with the French army at Dover? Naturally such a palpable error cannot have emanated from Shakspere, who better understood the plan of his drama. Doran (1931, p. 75): The lines are grammatically incomplete, and they do not contain Kent’s commission to the Gentleman; it is therefore impossible to understand what Kent means [in 1643–4 if…ring]. The dramatic reason for having the scene at all is gone. Although the F text does not provide the Gentleman with the facts, message, or motive that he needs to undertake a mission to Cordelia, yet he immediately sets out to find her anyway, apparently with no further end than to confirm Kent’s identity. Pope (ed. 1725): The Q lines seem necessary to the plot, as preparatory to the arrival of the French army with Cordelia in Act 4.…The [F] lines which have been put in their room are unintelligible, and to no purpose. Johnson (ed. 1765) believes that the Q and F texts are alternative versions, but instead of choosing only one he combines both, the F lines in italics and the Q lines in brackets: The speech is now tedious because it is formed of a coalition of both. The second edition [sc. F] is generally best, and was probably nearest to Shakespeare’s last copy, but in this passage the first [Q] is preferable; for in the folio, the messenger is sent, he knows not why, he knows not whither. Virtually all eds. since Theobald have included both Q-only and F-only lines; the result is a speech longer than any other in the play. Jones (1971, p. 185) finds the whole dialogue very clumsily inserted in the scene. Richman (1986, p. 380), describing his stage experience: combining Q and F creates an obscure passage that Shakespeare probably did not write. Q’s version is dramatically stronger than F’s. Heretofore, following Theobald, eds. have retained both passages as integral units, as in the present text; but Blayney (MS) proposes rather that 1634–8 are separate lines intended to go after plaine in 1638+9, where they would not be an incomplete sentence but either a series of appositives making up a full list of items that the Gentleman should report or, as Blayney believes, a concessive clause—Whatever else etc.—introducing Kent’s final sentence, I am a Gentleman…you. Knowles (1995, p. 44): Kent hardly needs to acknowledge that troubles are abroad in order to assert that he, despite his appearance, is a gentleman like his auditor and therefore to be trusted. See further n. 1634–8. Weis (ed. 1993, pp. 30–1, 165): Both Q and F at this juncture may be differently cut versions of an original composed of the two passages together.…The absence from Q of the spies and speculations certainly results in the sacrifice of a significant link between 3.1 and 3.3 when Gloucester, it turns out, is one such party.…[In 3.3] Gloucester clearly echoes the first part (F) of Kent’s speech to the Gentleman in 3.1…[and in] the F-followed-by-Q order of the conflationists’ 3.1; (p. 165): F’s text on its own begs questions of both rhythm and sense…[and] sounds a homiletic and equivocal note.…F restricts itself to a glancing allusion to a threat from France…in the hope perhaps that the reference to Cordelia would by itself render clear the geo-political movement of the play.…[Yet F] by referring to a possible something deeper as the reason for the French invasion, strips it of its crusading character, the restoration in England of true domestic and national harmony. In fact, furnishings would suggest that, if anything, France’s motives may be more sinister, perhaps using moral grievances as pretexts for territorial expansion.
The F cuts and additions have been variously explained. Capell (see above): F is an inferior substitution by the folio editors. Fleay (1879, p. 119): The Q lines are an innocuous substitution by Sh. for the lines in F, which would have been offensive to the court. See the next n. Koppel (1870, p. 88): Since in F Cordelia already knows of Lear’s suffering, sending the gentleman to her is pointless; instead, in F Sh. provides a cheering pause in the action, hinting at Lear’s future deliverance. Moriarty (1913, p. 468): The added F lines are an evident attempt to patch up a more plausible sequence between the abuse to which the king has been subjected and the prompt appearance of the armies of France within two weeks, though the patch with the original quarto lines, some of which are necessary, has [470] for some reason or other not been correctly made. Granville-Barker (1927, pp. 225–6): Folio and Quarto offer us alternative cuts [of a speech originally overlong]. That of the Folio is perhaps the clumsier of the two. It stresses the call for Cordelia’s help but barely hints at her army’s landing, which the Quarto emphasises.…The object of the cut in both cases—and possibly the cutting of the Gentleman’s speech [1622+1–+8] also—is evidently to shorten this prelude to Lear’s great entrance.…Shakespeare leaves us to the end a little unconvinced by the machinery of Cordelia’s return. There is no dramatic profit in the confusion. Neither text may be as Shakespeare left it. But in this instance I prefer the Quarto’s to an amalgam of the two. Walker (1953, p. 52): To omit eight lines of Kent’s speech in the first version [Q], restore them in the next [F] and omit the following dozen lines instead seems pointless and we should avoid postulating two acting versions with alternative cutting if we can. Greg (1942, p. 93): Cutting [for acting] seems to have overlapped, so that a portion of the text is irretrievably lost.
The incomplete instructions to the Gentleman and the break in the thought after 1638 both raise the suspicion that the F lines were intended to supplement the Q lines but, through scribal or compositorial error, supplanted them instead and thus damaged the sense of the whole passage. Cunnington (1910, p. 450): The folio text must have been printed from a corrected quarto and the addition (in the folio) taken by the printers as a substitute for the quarto text.…The two halves of the speech are of a totally different character, and the half which the folio omits is much the more important…[and] was not intended to be dropped. Following Chambers’s (1930, 1:467) suggestion of censorship (see n. 1631–8), Doran (op. cit., pp. 75–6) provides two possible scenarios: The Master of the Revels was on guard to catch any matter in plays which might be offensive to the court or to the foreign ambassadors.…On the transcript [copied from Q, to make the playbook] of this scene, which was just like the quarto, Shakespeare wrote an addition of nine lines and perhaps more that are now lost; the lines seem to be incomplete because there is no verb for the noun clause beginning…in [1634]. He intended the passage to be an insertion between [1630 and 1638+1]. When the transcript went to the Master of the Revels [George Buc, for license of public performance, or later approval of performance at court] he objected to the direct [Q] reference to France as an invading power and marked it out, but without making clear the exact limits of the omission. As a result the printer of the folio [using this same playbook MS as copy in 1623] set only an incomplete portion of the additional matter, and left out of the original what was necessary to the reader’s comprehension of the scene. One would expect the censor to have cut also the lines in the addition which refer to French spies in the households of the dukes; he may indeed have intended them to be cut, but not have marked them in a way that the printer understood. Another possibility is that the addition was not in the transcript when the censor had it, but that Shakespeare wrote in these lines and more to replace what the censor had deleted; the text was not clear to the printer, with the result that in the folio we have an incomplete patch. The idea of censorship is questionable: see . Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 394–5) similarly suspects that the F lines may have been a marginal addition to F’s copy that the compositor mistook as a replacement for the Q lines; this general idea is accepted as possible by Muir (ed. 1952; 1983, p. 108), Halio (ed. 1973), and others. The confusion might equally have been on the part of a scribe making a transcript from the playbook. Stone (1980, p. 119; cf. p. 235) explains the possible mechanics: It is quite likely that a slip containing the additional line was pasted by its lateral edge to the left margin of the manuscript and positioned immediately beneath line [1630] so that, when folded down, the flap obscured the rest of the speech. A prompt-book belonging to the King’s Company survives in which this method of interpolation has been employed (see Second Maiden’s Tragedy, ed. Sir W. W. Greg). The theory of mistaken replacement is indeed attractive: if the F-only lines were meant to be one or more expansions of the Q text rather than a discrete unit substituted for it, the obscurity and incoherence of the scene in F is easily accounted for.
Others assume that F as it stands is Sh.’s intentional revision of Q. Thus Urkowitz (1980, pp. 70–9): F, while lacking most of Q’s information, shows by the Gentleman’s forceful interruption of Kent’s speech (see n. 1639) more urgency and energetic action than exists in Q or a composite Q + F text. In F the French do not need the Gentleman’s message at all because the presence of French spies implies, Urkowitz thinks, that the French already know of the daughters’ mistreatment of Lear (though Goneril’s had occurred only the previous night, and Regan’s and Goneril’s in concert perhaps an hour or so before this scene; see n. 1614). Moreover, by postponing specific mention of a French invasion until 2061 in F (Urkowitz believes; but see n. 1764) Sh. adds a note of surprise for the audience. The Folio text represents a careful revision of the Quarto version, affecting the local dramatic action, the overall plot, the relationships between characters, and the meaning of the scene in the greater context of the play. So Taylor (1980, p. 32): Both texts offer coherent but incompatible alternatives, the Quarto beginning act iii with the imminence of a dubiously motivated French invasion, the Folio with the news that France knows what is happening, and that Cordelia—and Cordelia alone—is already on her way, somehow. I need hardly say that the Folio produces a more benevolent impression, one more clearly personified by Cordelia herself, as the sole representative of that apocalyptic counter-movement which culminates, disastrously, in v, ii. The notion that Cordelia alone is invading Britain is improbable; see n. 1631–8. Ioppolo (1991, pp. 173–4): The Quarto links [Cordelia] with the French army while the Folio does not. In the Quarto, she remains a character who has evidently been taking action.…In the Folio, she remains the more submissive character who is only incidentally involved in remedying her father’s situation. Ioppolo does not explain what Cordelia’s submissive presence is incidental to, and elsewhere in the play Cordelia is repeatedly linked to the French army in both Q and F. Halio (ed. 1992, p. 296 n.): If censorship was not an issue, then motivation on dramatic and/or thematic grounds must explain F’s alteration.…Shakespeare de-emphasises invasion by a foreign power [cf. nn. 2307+1–+6, 2347+1–+56] in favour of Lear’s rescue by his youngest daughter, Cordelia, whom he had rejected and cast out. Love, not politics, thus becomes central. These distinctions between Q and F rest on unproved assumptions—that 1631–8 were intended as a substitution for Q’s 1638+1–+12 (see above, and the notes below on each passage) rather than as additions, and that they were written by Sh.—as well as on questionable critical interpretations of several terms: see, e.g., nn. 1637, 1638+1, 1638+3, 1639–40, 1764, 2111–12. Halio (ed. 1992): In F, Kent does not send the Gentleman to Cordelia, but knowing her approach, he knows that Lear’s followers will meet her. Still, as Edwards (1982, p. 697) notes, he does give the Gentleman a ring; in Q this has a purpose—to confirm to both Gentleman and Cordelia the reliability of his messages to her—but in F it seems a pointless loose end, since in the absence of any messages there is no practical reason why Cordelia need reveal Kent’s identity to the Gentleman, or why Kent should wish her to do so. In Edwards’s view, Each text needs what the other can supply.

1631–8 Who…furnishings]
Fleay (1879, p. 119), believing Q to be an altered version played at court in 1606, concludes that these lines were censored for that performance and were stricken from Q, though they survived in F: they would in the winter of 1604–5, when the peace with Spain was not six months old—a peace procured by the [Spanish] bribery of Suffolk, Northampton, Pembroke, Southampton, Dirleton, &c., &c.,—be taken by the populace as a direct allusion to this scandalous corruption. But those lords (including Cecil) who received Spanish pensions to assure the peace were not secret spies for Spain. Chambers (1930, 1:467) also: The F lines were censored because of their political and social criticism. Q is more likely to be Sh.’s rough draft than an acting version, and of later date than 1604–5 (see , ); and there are reasons to think that the F lines may be a later addition intended to supplement rather than replace Q lines (see prev. n.).
Moreover, besides lacking the information necessary to send the Gentleman on his errand, as Johnson and Doran remark, the added F lines are stylistically troublesome, being convoluted with parentheses in a way uncharacteristic of Kent, and ending with an unfinished sentence (see n. 1634–8). Pope (ed. 1725) degrades them from the text to a footnote as excessively bad and seeming Interpolations…being so inserted that one can intirely omit them without any chasm, or deficience in the context (1:xxii; and see prev. n.). Theobald (ed. 1733), disagreeing: For my part, I see nothing in them but what is very easie to be understood; and the Lines seem absolutely necessary to clear up the Motives, upon which France prepar’d his Invasion: nor without them is the Sense of the Context compleat. Similarly Capell (1783, 1.2:163): The passage provides the motives of France’s invasion, a necessary knowledge; which should induce us to think these eight lines a part of the first plan, lost to us by the quarto’s compositor among other his negligences. The motives for France’s invasion, however, are never made clear: see n. 1638+1. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxi): The F lines are involved and tame, unlike the spirited twelve-line passage of the Quarto. Walker (1953, p. 51): They form a dramatically unnecessary and extraordinarily involved parenthesis. Zitner (1974, p. 7): Kent momentarily adopts a courtly style to undo the impression of his dress and situation. Pechter (1978, pp. 191–2), however: Astonishingly clumsy writing.…We hear a stutter of interrupting and qualifying relative clauses, culminating in an awkward redundancy [Speculations Intelligent]…a noun phrase (though for a moment we probably think we are hearing the beginning of a question), with an appositive range of three alternatives that is perplexing. Urkowitz (1980, pp. 75–6), as elsewhere, finds F’s inordinately complex speech an authorial improvement over Q: When…this gruff fellow suddenly begins speaking of state secrets in a rhetorical style alien to his habit, the Gentleman quite reasonably distrusts the medium even before he hears the full message. The Gentleman’s rejection of Kent must be based more on Kent’s mannered language than on any other factor, because he hears little of Kent’s matter. Kent’s next speech…suddenly drops from polysyllabic and complicated obscurity down to plain words in clear syntax. In contrast, both of Kent’s speeches are simple in the Quarto.…The Folio’s change in style adds another dimension to the dramatic exchange. The Folio consequently makes more believable the Gentleman’s shift from suspicious rejection…to friendly concern. Urkowitz does not explain why adding this dimension at the cost of making Kent’s instructions incomplete and obscure seems advisable; and for the Gentleman’s supposed rejection of Kent, see n. 1639–40. Similarly Taylor (1980, p. 32) denies any real incoherence or obscurity in F: Kent merely tells the Gentleman—and the audience—that he will see Cordelia, presumably soon, presumably nearby, presumably as she has made clear in her letter. There is no likelihood that Cordelia intimated such a plan in her letter, or could have carried it out. Knowles (1999, p. 277): No reason [is] given anywhere in the text to make an audience think, against all probability, that the Queen of France would have slipped into a hostile Goneril’s duchy alone, without an armed escort, as sole representative of th[e] apocalyptic counter-movement, that she would be traveling unguarded all the way across Britain to Gloucester’s house or nearby, that Kent would feel assured that the Gentleman would somehow see her soon by chance meeting, and that then without incident or notice to the audience she would return to Dover to meet Lear and fight the British forces.…Such a trip by Cordelia would cover almost four hundred miles and take several weeks, not the few days she has. Surely such an extended absence of the French queen from the French army at Dover would require notice and explanation within the play; there is none. Honigmann (1982, p. 153): F’s addition unfortunately contains no Shakespearian felicities of style. It seems to have been hurriedly thrown together, resulting in some obscurity, potentially confusing parentheses and changes of direction, and too much who-ing and which-ing.…Would an outsider, brought in to revise and tidy the text, be guilty of such messy writing? I am reminded of some of the tumbling (almost jumbling) sentences in Shakespeare, citing lines from Sir Thomas Moore and WT 1.2.308–14 (405–11). But Leontes’ frenzied ranting is a very different kind of speech, and Sh.’s part in Moore is dubious. Similarly Taylor (1983, pp. 393–5), arguing that F is a revision made in 1609, analyzes this passage as an impressionistic illustration that the F additions are markedly closer to the widely-recognized grammatical complexity of Shakespeare’s late style, concluding that here F’s incomplete second sentence, multiple qualifying clauses, lack of transitions, ambiguity and complexity of syntax, doublings, puns, and subterranean associations among images combine to give an impression of stylistic density which is entirely typical of the late plays—and markedly atypical of Kent.
An alternative explanation of the passage’s anomalous style, suggested (privately) by Blayney, is that the additions are not Sh.’s but someone’s else’s. Stone (1980, pp. 72–5) so argues: The additional [i.e., F’s] suggestions [about French motives for invasion] are wrong—one of them, at least, quite clearly so. The news of the King’s mistreatment cannot have reached France before the invasion [see n. 1638+1].…Not even the convention of double time will allow the French invasion to be prompted by news of the King’s misfortunes: the two sets of events are clearly contemporaneous.…[Moreover,] Kent is made to say that both the Dukes have borne a hard rein against the King. It is quite clear, however, that Albany has not done so.…[Furthermore,] Kent does not speak elsewhere in the high-falutin’ style here attributed to him…[and] so scornfully parodied by Kent himself [1180–3].…We may be surprised, too, that Kent of all personages in the play, should refer to Lear sentimentally as the old kind King.…Whoever wrote these lines was not as intimately familiar with the play as he ought to have been. The passage, therefore,…may be…emphatically categorised as spurious. Stone (p. 127) tentatively proposes Philip Massinger, who is known for his involuted syntax, his fondness especially for periodic sentences and for every kind of parenthetic construction, as the author of this and other F revisions. Knowles (1995, p. 45; cf. 1997, pp. 60–1): These eight lines contain several words or usages not found elsewhere in Sh.: Speculations = spies; snuffs = huffs, pl. and without in; furnishings; and packings = plottings (a usage that occurs once in [Shr.] in the singular), suggesting a writer with a different vocabulary. See .

1631–4 Who…State]
Knowles (1995, pp. 42–3): The first three-and-a-half lines of the F addition are clearly intended to follow Cornwall, as they do in F, and to complete the sentence that in Q was completed by But true it is.…Instead of supporting the surprising news of a French invasion with a mere affirmation—But true it is—the reviser may have wished to add circumstances to make it seem more plausible: the King of France may have previously prepared for invasion by establishing spies in the households of both dukes, and now he has in fact begun to invade.…The news that the French are in some English ports is a natural preparation for Kent’s instruction that the Gentleman should go to one of them, Dover, in expectation of finding Cordelia there. Knowles argues that the remaining lines of the F addition were intended to be inserted later in the scene—see n. 1634–8—and that the three-and-a-half F lines here were intended by the reviser to continue with the original Q passage, midway in 1638+1. There would probably have been some kind of metrical adjustment, since linking Intelligent of our State to From France there comes a power would make a hypermetrical line. Possibly some confusion about the markings to delete But true it is and perhaps (for the sake of meter) another word or two in the Q line (possibly there or even from France) was partly responsible for the accidental deletion of the rest of the Q speech from F. See nn. 1631–1638+12, 1638+1–+12.

1631 that]
Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Whom.

1631–2 as…high]
Rann (ed. 1794): As what potentates have not servants.

1631 Starres]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Here used for fortune, ruling fate or destiny. See n. 447–61.

1632 who…lesse]
Rann (ed. 1794): That seem to emulate their master’s greatness. Stone (1980, p. 75 n.) agrees. Delius (ed. 1854) and most eds.: Servants who seem to be no less, or no other, than what they are—namely, servants (Ger.). Page (ed. 1889): When in fact they are spies.

1633 Spies]
Taylor (1983, p. 378) suggests an origin in Holinshed or Plutarch for the notion of household spies. Sh. needed no literary source for the idea.

1633 Speculations]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Examiner, spy. Hudson (ed. 1856): Observer. OED (sb. 3b) gives both meanings, quoting only this l.; the word in this sense occurs nowhere else in Sh. Redundancy with Spies may not be complete: thus Hunter (ed. 1869), Means of observation, Chambers (ed. 1906), Intelligences, and Edwards (ed. 1975), Eyes. Wright (ed. 1875): Abstract for concrete, comparing 1429 discretion; Furness (ed. 1880) cites the many other exx. in Schmidt (1875, p. 1421). Skillan (ed. 1967): Duplication to effect emphasis.…The alliteration also assists. Wright (1981, p. 191): A hendiadys—spies and observations—for spies…giv[ing] information.

1634 Intelligent]
Johnson (1755): Giving information (OED, a. 4, quoting only this l., 1981, 2070, and WT 1.2.378 [484]). Clarkes (ed. 1868): As well as knowing, cognisant (OED, 3).

1634 State]
Delius (ed. 1854): Either situation or country.

1634–8 What…furnishings.]
This series of clauses is printed in F as a complete sentence, which it is not, though it begins with a sentence capital, following the sentence period after State. Most eds. since Rowe have marked it as broken off at 1638 (see textual n.). Capell (ed. 1768) and Jennens (ed. 1770) introduce the clauses with a colon after State, making them all appositives descriptive of the present state of England; other eds. seem to indicate the same relation by a semicolon, as Steevens (ed. 1778) clearly does: What follows, are the circumstances in the state of the kingdom, of which he supposes the spies gave France the intelligence. Others understand an ellipsis: Supply from intelligent (informing them) what, etc. (Tovey, ed. 1896): I.e. to note, and to report, what (Craig, ed. 1901); on such matters as what (Lott, ed. 1974). Perhaps a comma would do as well: Intelligent of our State, [of] what hath bin seene, etc. Moriarty (1913, p. 469) would supply a noun clause for the verb—What hath been hath been seen—assuming that such an extrametrical repetition of hath been might have been mistakenly struck out by F copy-reader or compositor. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 398), justifying his use of a dash after State: I…suppose that the punctuation is erratic, as so often in F, and that the full point after State is no more reliable than the semicolon after set high, and that both should be commas. But F’s punctuation throughout is much more reliable than Q’s, and its (midline) semicolon for a comma was quite usual: see Graham-White (1995, pp. 34, 72).
The syntax is in any case more or less awkward, and eds. excuse it variously. The Clarkes (ed. 1868): The irregularity of the diction…suit[s] with the wild circumstances of the scene, with the mysteriously hinted nature of the communication, and with the concealed rank of the speaker. Similarly Lott (op. cit.): Kent is disturbed…and rushes ahead with sentences which are not properly shaped. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 398): Kent’s message is meant to be mystifying, its hesitations and alternatives expressing his own uncertainties.…Kent changes the subject on the word furnishings to give directions to the Gentleman or Knight. Knowles (1999, p. 285): In fact the only uncertainty evident in the speech is whether (perchance) something deeper underlines the dukes’ recent hostilities to Lear and each other. On the whole Kent sounds, as usual, downright, confident, and authoritative: dare, warrant, But true it is (Q), my credit, will thanke, I am a Gentleman, From some knowledge and assurance (no uncertainty there!), and later confirmation, feare not but you shall, and Ile this way, you that. Muir (ed. 1952): Shakespeare may have intended him to break off in the middle of his explanation. Hunter (ed. 1972): The dash expresses a refusal by Kent to speculate further; he returns to what is known as a fact—the French invasion. Urkowitz (1980, p. 71): However, it should be noted that Shakespeare generally uses this rhetorical figure, aposiopesis,…only for occasions of emotional intensity, an argument he uses to oppose conflation of two texts that he believes are alternatives (see n. 1631–1638+12).
Many editors have suspected textual corruption. Schmidt (ed. 1879): Whether these incomplete sentences are due to the poet, or to the style in which the scene has been transmitted to us, cannot be decided;…it is easily conceivable that between [1638] and [1638+1] there were other lines which have been omitted in both texts (Ger.). So also Greg (1940, p. 436 n.): The transition…is harsh and obscure, and I have no doubt that at this point something was cut out of both texts and is consequently lost. Brooke (ed. 1947), Muir (ed. 1952), Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960), and others are inclined to agree. Knowles (1995, pp. 42–5), following a suggestion of Peter Blayney (see n. 1631–1638+12): Perhaps these lines were originally intended by an F reviser to follow plaine in 1638+9, where they would fit metrically, would avoid F’s awkward non-sequitur and sentence fragment, would instead make up a series of noun clauses parallel with how…plaine, and thus would give a complete list of things that the Gentleman should report to Cordelia. In this latter case, it would be clear that Cordelia had not reported in her letter to Kent (1242) the impossibility that she had already heard of Lear’s mistreatment; instead, that is one of things that Kent now wants reported to her, to inform her about conditions in Britain and to motivate her to do battle with her sisters’ forces. What hath bin seene by Kent, the Gentleman, and others is exactly the news that now needs to be relayed to Cordelia by the Gentleman (and which she later receives from him, as is reported in 4.3). Such a reading would avoid some of the difficulties that eds. have found with the time scheme of the play: see n. 1638+1. Following a hint from Stone (see n. 1631–1638+12), Knowles conjectures (p. 45) that these lines (1634–8) were by mistake printed continuously with the previous lines in F (1631–4) because both passages, though separate revisions, were written on the same slip of paper inserted into the playbook over the original page, an expedient that the bookkeeper of Sh.’s company also resorted to in 1611 in the playhouse manuscript of The Second Maiden’s Tragedy. A scribe making a transcript from the promptbook [of Lr.] to serve as printer’s copy for the F compositors…might have misinterpreted the marks for insertions and deletions in the original…text of the promptbook and have copied the eight lines from the slip as one consecutive passage, substituting them for the latter lines of Kent’s speech—instead of putting the second passage, lines 1634–8, after plaine in 1638+9 as the reviser intended. This explanation of how the F passage became so corrupt and problematic is dismissed as unnecessary by Foakes (ed. 1997, pp. 393 ff.) and defended by Knowles (1999, pp. 277–9). See .

1634 seene]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Sc. by all and sundry.

1635 snuffes]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): Angers, offence-takings. OED (sb.1 5): A fit of indignation; a huff, pet, rage, passion, quoting this l. The usage is unique in Sh.; he occasionally uses in snuff, referring to the proverb To take in Snuff (Tilley S598), but nowhere else uses the noun alone in the sense of anger, and never uses it in the plural. Greg (1940, pp. 441–2 n.): This antagonism is an undeveloped motive in the play, either because Shakespeare was content only to hint at it, or because he found he lacked room for elaboration.…There are…several clear statements on the subject [938–9, 1635, 1759–60, perhaps 955–6, 1057]…[Granville-Barker (see n. 1638+1)] puts the importance of the division too high; it may have been the occasion, hardly the cause, of France’s action.

1635 packings]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Underhand contrivances. OED (vbl. sb.2 a): Private or underhand arrangement; fraudulent dealing or contriving, plotting: see Pack v.2; (Pack v.2): Origin obscure.…The sense suggests some connexion with Pact…(also Compact…); the implication here being however always bad—as in the proverb There’s Falsehood in packing (Tilley F42). Craig (ed. 1901) compares Leir 1932, There is good packing twixt your king and you; see . Sh. uses the noun elsewhere only in Shr. 5.1.118 (2499), and there in the singular, though the verb several times. Cf. also 2958.

1636 hard Reine]
Most eds. agree with Spilsbury & Marshall (ed. 1905): As the rider holds in the horse with a tight rein. Horsman (ed. 1973): The way they have ridden, i.e. acted against, him. Craig (ed. 1901) finds the phrase hard of reine in North’s tr. of Plutarch’s Lives (Antonius; ed. 1612, p. 927), and compares Tro. 1.3.188–9 (648–9), beares his head In such a reyne; he alone, however, imagines the rein on the dukes rather than Lear, proposing the alternative reading how inflexibly firm, how stiff-necked they have been in their relations with the aged king. Hunter (ed. 1972): Pun on reign. As many commentators have noticed (see n. 1638+1), there can hardly have been time for Cordelia, in France, to have learned of Goneril’s mistreatment of Lear on the day before let alone of Regan’s mistreatment this very night; such hard rein could certainly not have been alluded to in the letter from her that Kent had received a day ago (see n. 1242). Kent’s reference here to the daughters’ treatment of Lear as a motive for Cordelia’s raising an army and invading England therefore makes no sense at all. If however, 1631–8 were intended to follow 1638+9, the daughters’ mistreatment of Lear would quite rightly be one item, if not the item, of recent news to be conveyed to Cordelia.

1636 both]
Crook (ed. 1907): This is hardly true of Albany. Though at 589–90 Albany is charged with an abatement of kindnesse (F), he soon thereafter protests I am as giltless as I am ignorant (786), and is notably absent from 2.4 when Goneril, Regan, and Cornwall drive Lear out into the storm. Skillan (ed. 1967): The concentrated nature of the speech may pass the men’s wives’ responsibilities on to themselves. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 399): Since [Albany] has done nothing to mitigate Goneril’s harshness to her father, as her husband he is a party to the way Lear has been treated. Kent may mean that Albany has acceded to his wife’s hard rein on Lear, but that is not what he says; his actual statement here in F so contradicts the evidence in the play as to raise doubt of its authenticity. See n. 1631–8. As for the other duke, Cunnington (1910, p. 450): It is quite impossible of course that France could then have heard anything of Cornwall and Regan’s action. Knowles (1999, p. 37): The mistreatment of Lear by both the dukes cannot have been the motive for Cordelia’s having landed in England, since Cornwall’s treatment is scarcely an hour old.

1636 hath]
Smith (1902, pp. 5, 12): F2 corrects F1’s popular and conversational concord to haue. Abbott §334 and Franz §156 give other exx. of third person plural in -th. Cf. 1918.

1637 something deeper]
Brown (ed. 1976): Something more secret/serious. If this phrase refers to domestic conditions, it must mean something more than the snuffs and packings of the dukes just mentioned, and so probably means outright rupture in civil war between them, or even an attempt by one of them to seize all the power that once belonged to Lear—indeed, the very things that Lear had hoped to avoid by his division of the kingdom. If the phrase refers to France’s and Cordelia’s motives for invasion, it could mean a number of things: foreign conquest of England, invasion to prevent civil war, or an attempt to recover Cordelia’s portion of the former kingdom. See n. 1638+1. Bransom (1934, p. 197), without evidence: Goneril’s ambition to possess the throne of Britain with Edmund as prince consort. Hunter (ed. 1972): It seems pointless to speculate on the nature of this something deeper; it is part of the deep shadow that belongs to the picture. Stone (1980, p. 74), who thinks the F-only lines here are spurious: Gloucester’s reference in 1759–60 to a worse matter than diuisiõ betwixt the Dukes was transferred to Kent by an F reviser not familiar enough with the exposition of the plot to notice that Gloucester’s mystery does not and cannot concern some further circumstance, hitherto unmentioned.

1638 furnishings]
The word appears nowhere else in Sh. A few eds. understand by it something furnished or provided, whether colours, external pretenses (Johnson, ed. 1765), sample[s] (Steevens, ed. 1778), a foretaste (Delius, ed. 1854), or means towards an end (Hunter, ed. 1869), but most agree with Eccles (ed. 1792), Trappings, the Clarkes (ed. 1868), External adjuncts, outward appendages (OED, vbl. sb. 3, quoting this l. as its first ex.), and Horsman (ed. 1973), Embellishments. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Pretexts that conceal the real purpose.…The French are invading Britain—whether because of what spies have informed them about the quarrels and plots of the dukes or about their harsh treatment of the King, or, perhaps, for some purpose that the invaders conceal, using these things as pretexts.

1638+1–+12 But…you]
For possible reasons for the absence of these Q lines from F, see n. 1631–1638+12. Johnson (ed. 1765), imagining Shn. revision: I suppose Shakespeare thought his plot opened rather too early, and made the alteration to veil the event [of invasion] from the audience; but trusting too much to himself, and full of a single purpose, he did not accommodate his new lines to the rest of the scene—i.e., did not prepare adequately for the Gentleman’s mission. Capell (1783, 1.2:163): That passage is preparatory to Cordelia’s appearance, and to other short notices of her army’s arrival that follow in this act. Theories that the lines were censored because of allusions to France as an invading power (Doran, 1931, pp. 74–6; see nn. 1631–1638+12, 2307+1–+6) or to neglect of port defences (Greg, 1955, p. 387) are rejected by Taylor (1983, pp. 80, 112–13): The old Leir play had been much more explicit in dramatizing the French invasion than Shakespeare was, even in the Quarto; Leir, moreover, dates from a period (c. 1590) when invasion of England by a continental power was a real and feared possibility. James I had little to worry about on that score: England had been officially and actually at peace since 1604.…Moreover, Jacobean censorship of references to foreign powers always involves negative portrayal of contemporary figures.…But in Lear the unnamed, pre-Christian French King…twice intervenes on the side of truth, justice, and an audience’s sympathies.…Greg presents no evidence that this [other] issue [of port defences] much exercised contemporary critics of the government…[and] such sensitivity could only account for the omission of two lines [1638+2–+3]. Taylor prefers to believe that references to France have been systematically eliminated from F on artistic and thematic grounds: see nn. 2307+1–+6, 2868–2868+4, and . Clare (1990, p. 136): The censor’s concern may have been generalised: The tradition of Franco-Scottish friendship and James’s policy of rapprochement would have made a reminder of past hostilities discordant and unwelcome.…Scenes depicting the successful invasion of Britain by a French army in a play which touched directly on matters of current political debate [i.e., the union of England and Scotland] would have been unwelcome to James. But of course the invading army is clearly French in both texts.

1638+1–+4 But…banner]
Moriarty (1913, p. 469): Mere smoothness could be…secured in combining these two passages by omitting only these lines; he offers no explanation why F excluded 1638+5–+12 as well. Nor does Foakes (ed. 1997), who in fact excludes these lines (but not the rest of the Q-only lines that follow), on no bibliographical grounds but simply because it seems premature for the French to have landed, hence probable that F1 meant to exclude the reference to France’s invasion here. See . Knowles (1999, p. 278): Foakes’s more consistent arrangement solves none of the stylistic problems that have troubled many editors and commentators. It still preserves a faulty (here called indirect) apposition (our state—what hath been seen), and requires the emendation of a terminal period and sentence capital (State. What) to create this apposition [see n. 1634–8]. It still includes a clotted string of parentheses and relative clauses, and then causes Kent to abandon his long sentence ten lines later without finishing it.…. [It also] creates a metrically short line—Now to you—where Q had metrical regularity. Most important, Quite possibly in this case the Arden edition supplants Shakespearean lines [Q] by non-Shakespearean ones [F; see n. 1631–8].

1638+1 But…is,]
This clause was cut when F substituted 1631–8 for twelve Q lines; when Theobald and modern eds. restored the Q lines while retaining F’s additions, the clause was naturally but perhaps mistakenly placed after the F-only lines, where it appears to be a transitional introduction to the restored Q lines that follow. It makes poor sense there: Hanmer changed the meaningless But to And (see textual n.), and Stone (1980, p. 70) even finds an awkward break both in sense and syntax that suggests the accidental omission of one or more [Q] lines. The clause makes excellent sense, however, in its original position directly after 1630, as an affirmation of the facts as yet…couer’d With mutual cunning reported in the preceding Q lines. So Delius (1876, p. 136): The clause refer[s] to what the [F] editor omitted; so Doran (1931, p. 74): The clause…is probably a confirmatory statement that there is division between the dukes, and would be so understood if it had a period following it instead of the comma used ordinarily in the first quarto for ending sentences within speeches. Weis (ed. 1993): I.e. it is indeed the case, although Albany and Cornwall are still trying to disguise it. Knowles (1995, pp. 38–9): There is a division, Kent reports, admittedly a hidden one, But true it is—a true division exists (or a division truly exists) even though hidden.…[The words] conclude the previous thought. In their location in modern texts, as an introduction to from France there comes a power, these four words make no sense, there being no reason for the But: no contrary opinion in the previous lines is being opposed, since France’s invasion has not yet even been mentioned. What has happened here…is that four words…intended to complete the sentence in Q were left out of F along with the rest of line [1638+1] and the succeeding twelve lines ([1638+2–+12]). When Theobald and other modern editors restored lines [1638+1–+12], they misinterpreted But true it is, reading the words as the beginning of the following sentence because Q’s But was capitalized (though with a verse capital, not a sentence capital) and the phrase was followed by a comma, not a period. Theobald was further misled by erroneous punctuation earlier in the passage. The text of Q that he owned and used for his edition was not Q1 but Pavier’s close imitation of it, Q2 (1619); and Pavier’s text mistakenly puts a period after Cornwall in line [1630], thus forcing Theobald’s misreading of the next line—But true it is—as the beginning of a new sentence. So it came about that four words which ended a sentence in Q1 were restored in modern editions as the beginning of a new sentence where they have no relevance.

1638+1 from France]
Thirlby (MS notes, 1733–47): How does it agree with Cordelia’s being landed with an army to right her father yt she shd not hear of his wrongs (nb. Gonerill’s first ill usage) till after her landing (see 2347+10, and cf. nn. 2347+37, 2376–81). Theobald and Capell (see n. 1631–8) find the motive for the invasion in the reports of diuision between the dukes. Greg (see n. 1635) minimizes this motive. Goggin (ed. 1910): We learn that a French force has actually been landed in the kingdom, and that Cordelia is at Dover. It is noteworthy that this expedition is stated [1635–7] to be the result either of the quarrels of the dukes or of their ill-treatment of the old king. Yet this ill-treatment of Lear could not possibly be known in France, for Regan and Cornwall had only just refused to receive him, and Goneril’s conduct was not yet two days old. The impression that France’s invasion is motivated by the dukes’ behavior, however, is entirely the result of Theobald’s particular, and dubious, way of reconstructing the text from Q and F lines; see nn. 1631–1638+12, 1634–8. Daniel (1877–9, pp. 219–20): Before any news at all of her aged father’s troubles can have reached her, Cordelia is already landed in England for his relief [citing 2379–80].…We must suppose then, that from the spies, darkly hinted at by Kent, she had gained sufficient knowledge of her sisters’ intentions to convince her that her return to England was urgently required. Knowles (1999, p. 37 n.): Neither sister evidences any actual intentions until Goneril confides hers to Oswald in 1.3, a few minutes before putting them into action in 1.4. Granville-Barker (1927, pp. 148–9): Kent, in an involved speech…(for him most uncharacteristically involved), suggests that it is the threat of [likely warres (938)] which is bringing the French army to England. But the vagueness is suspicious. It looks a little as if Shakespeare had thought of making the hypocrite inheritors of Cordelia’s portion fall out over it (an obvious nemesis) and had changed his mind.…The King of France comes armed with Cordelia to Lear’s rescue, as is natural. Then, by virtue of the clumsiest few lines in the play [2347+2–+7], he is sent back again. Did Shakespeare originally mean Cordelia to restore her father to his throne as in the old play; but would a French victory in England not have done? Doran (1931, p. 70): The connection between the invasion and the internal dissension of the dukes, which is several times rumored ([933–41, 1628–38, 1759 ff.]) but which is never brought to a head, is missed because of the omission of these lines; cf. n. 1631–1638+12. Idem (1933, p. 45): In Shakespeare’s sources for the Leir story, Cordelia did not come into Britain until after she had been reconciled with her father, who had gone to her in France.…If…Shakespeare intended her to be in Dover thus early in the play, it is readily apparent that he has given the invasion a dramatic importance which it did not have from the beginning. Primarily, it is made an effective tool in Edmund’s hands in accomplishing his father’s ruin.…[Secondly,] by bringing Edmund into frequent contact with Cornwall, Shakespeare has brought the minor plot into important relations with the principal story. In the third place, he has heightened suspense by the mysterious and ominous rumors, often repeated, of a foreign power afoot in the kingdom; he has increased anticipation of the speedy avenging of Lear’s sufferings. Finally, by suggesting that division between the dukes in Britain is the direct occasion for the coming of the French, he has increased the political significance of Lear’s abdication. Bransom (1934, p. 82): Kent was in possession of exactly the same information as Gloster learned on the same evening; see 1759 ff. Bransom sees a direct connection between the invasion and the rumored dissension: see n. 2376–81. Greg (1940, pp. 441–5): The author of the old play [Leir]…sought to lessen [the political difficulty] in two ways. In the first place, he made the husbands of the elder daughters independent sovereigns, the kings of Cornwall and Cambria (in this departing from Holinshed); so that…the battle was in fact fought between three foreign powers. In the second place, he made Leir appeal directly to Gallia for aid.…This Shakespeare’s Lear could never do.…We are not really concerned with the time allowed for the levying and transport of the army, whether it be a day or a fortnight.…There is…no difficulty about allowing what time we will for the preparation of the French invasion—provided always that the preparations began as soon as the king left the British court. ¶But this at once raises the question of France’s motive.…Lear’s quarrel with Goneril ends act i, that with Regan ends act ii; the landing of the French army is known certainly in iii, iii, on the night of the second quarrel, probably in ii, ii, before it took place.…Moreover, on the day of the second quarrel the letters reporting the invasion have already arrived: they must have taken at least as long to come from Dover as Kent, Lear, and Goneril took to come from Albany’s.…Now, when Kent reads the letter (in the stocks) he has only just arrived at Gloucester’s after posting hard all night, and it is difficult to understand how he can have received it at any time after he left Albany’s, which was immediately upon Lear’s quarrel with Goneril. Moreover, Cordelia, informed of his obscurèd course, would of course have sent the letter to Albany’s, where Lear was resident, no doubt through one of the spies she had planted in his house ([1633]). There can be no doubt, therefore, that the French army had actually landed before Lear had any quarrel with his daughters. The interview in 4.3 between Kent, now near Dover, and the Gentleman, who has delivered his message to Cordelia, confirms that this was, of course, the first report she had received of the final quarrel with Regan: and she had been already some time encamped at Dover. When therefore France and Cordelia planned their invasion they cannot possibly have known of Lear’s rejection by his elder daughters, for the simple reason that it had not yet happened. What then can be the justification of Cordelia’s boast, at [2379–80] that she pursues No blowne ambition but only her fathers right? On the basis of 358, France in choller parted, Greg imagines that France, incensed at some fresh insult to Cordelia, departed in a rage, determined to wrest by force her portion from the favoured son-in-laws, Albany and Cornwall.…But it is impossible to imagine the gentle Cordelia spurring on her husband to the recovery of her portion.…What Cordelia’s mourning and importuned tears [2378] brought about was not the original expedition, but a change in its purpose.…Cordelia succeeded in persuading her husband to abandon his purpose of wresting a portion of the kingdom for himself and retire to his own land, thus leaving her free to use his army in defence of her father, should the occasion arise.…Kent goes out of his way to ask whether the departure of the French king was due to the news that he had sent, and he is told [2347+37–+38] that it was not.…Shakespeare wanted to make it quite clear that France, yielding to Cordelia’s entreaty, had in fact already abandoned his own claim and its prosecution.…No doubt all this elaboration of motive proved too cumbersome of development at this point in the play’s action. The hints that survive are in a scene [4.3] that was in fact cut out of the Folio text. One may differ as to details: Cordelia could have sent letters for Kent to spies at both Albany’s and Cornwall’s to ensure his receiving one of them; France may have decided on invasion on Cordelia’s behalf, not simply his own. Muir (ed. 1952): This is to scrutinize the chronology of the play too curiously, for an invasion could not in any case be planned and executed in the two or three days that have elapsed since the first scene of the play. But the time may be longer; see nn. 505, 811. Horsman (ed. 1973): In the theater we are not troubled by the possibility that, because news of the invasion reaches Kent by II.ii, it must have been planned before Cordelia could have known anything of her father’s ill treatment. We are uncertain of the strict time taken even by the events on the stage and we readily accept the swifter movement of those which are related or implied rather than shown. The idea that Sh. simultaneously employed two time schemes, a rapid one (short time) for foreground events and a more leisurely one (long time) for background events, was first proposed for Mac. and Oth. by Christopher North (1849–50) and for MV by Halpin (1849) and is applied to Lr. by Greg (op. cit., pp. 439 ff.) and others. Stone (1980, p. 73) emphasizes dramatic rather than personal motive: The audience is intended at first to gain the impression…that the King of France is seizing an opportune moment to restore Cordelia to her rightful inheritance. Both Kent and Gloucester make the connection between the Dukes’ quarrels and the invasion.…Regan and Cornwall are convinced that Gloucester is an agent of the French.…[But in Act IV the audience finally discovers that] There is no plot; and there cannot possibly be one. The French King has returned home before Lear arrives at Dover; there is only Cordelia to meet him, and no suspicion can attach to her motives. Then (in [2376–80]) she reveals the full truth: her husband has merely yielded to her entreaties, and those have been prompted by love, not ambition. There can be but one implication: she has meant all along to rescue Lear from her sisters, whose true nature she had penetrated [cf. 306–7] though he had not; she has not needed to wait for evidence of their cruelties. It is of course possible that France began with a motive different from Cordelia’s. Knowles (1999, pp. 48–9): Sh.’s vagueness about chronology is intentional and artful. France’s early invasion is designed to move the play quickly towards a denouement and to avoid prolonging Lear’s madness. But since an early invasion, before knowledge of Lear’s mistreatment could have reached France, must have been for selfish motives on France or Cordelia’s part, Sh. leaves both motive and chronology vague. Cf. n. 926.

1638+2 scattered]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Divided, unsettled, disunited (OED, ppl. a. 1, quoting 3H6 2.6.93 [1378], scattred Foe). Hudson (ed. 1879): Or perhaps distracted by the feud between Albany and Cornwall (unattested in OED, 1b, before 1638). Caldecott (MS notes, 1813–33): Parcelled out; not compact or having its powers concentrated. Hunter (ed. 1972): Presumably refers to the dispersal of the royal power shown in [1.1].

1638+2 who]
Lott (ed. 1974): Refers to power.

1638+2 wise…negligẽce]
Wilson (ed. 1960), wise in: Taking advantage of. Or simply knowledgeable about, apprised of. Budd (ed. 1935): Knowing of our negligent watch on the coast. Joseph (ed. 1966): Either (i) wise in those respects in which we are negligent; or (ii) well informed of our negligence. Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): Profiting by. Ioppolo (1991, p. 172): The mislining…signals that wise…negligence was marginally added. But Q mislines hundreds of lines of verse quite regular in themselves, as these are (see textual n.); no disruptive marginal addition need be imagined, since there is no disruption in the meter. Ioppolo adds that negligẽce could represent the mistreatment of Lear…rather than the misgoverning of the kingdom. It probably means neither, but rather simple inattentiveness on the part of its leaders, or of the port authorities, as in the source. Bullough (1973, p. 281): In Leir, The invasion of Britain is made easy by the neglect of the beacon-watchers who…prefer the alehouse (sc. 27 [2434–63]); see .

1638+3 Haue]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): The word have here treats power [1638+1] as a noun of multitude.

1638+3 secret feet]
Though the general sense of concealed intruders is clear, the precise meaning is not, and the phrase has not been found in Sh. or elsewhere. Since F 1764 speaks of a Power already footed and both texts of tratours late footed (2112), and Lear imagines shoeing horses with felt (2626–7), here feet may be a synecdoche for men on foot, or possibly a term for foot-soldiers (OED, Foot sb. 4), though the term in that sense, which appears elsewhere in Sh., is attested only in the singular. The Clarkes (ed. 1868) and most eds. gloss as footing by extension from foothold (Muir, ed. 1952; OED, 23). Gardner (ed. 1969): Undercover agents; but they would not in time shew their open banner, as foot-soldiers would. Craig (ed. 1901): In [Leir 2434–94; see prev. n. and ] the French manage to effect a landing while the Captain of the watch and his brother-watchman are engaged in a drinking bout.…This was a subject which had to be treated with much caution before Elizabethan audiences. But it is not so treated in Leir, and cf. n. 1638+1–+12.

1638+3 Ports]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Probably harbours here, without the possible sense of gates in 1018.

1638+4 at point to]
Either in readiness to (Rann, ed. 1794; cf. n. 845) or just about to (Verity, ed. 1897; OED, Point sb.1 D.1c, quoting this l.).

1638+4 shew…banner]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Unfurl their banner in declaration of war.

1638+4 open]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Emphatic. Clarkes (1879, p. 316): Openly displayed, as well as unfurled.

1638+5 Now to you]
Tovey (ed. 1896): To address myself to you particularly; to show how this concerns you. Hunter (ed. 1972): To suggest what you can do.

1638+5 credit]
Page (ed. 1889): Believability (OED, sb. 2). Beyond that, commentators divide. Schmidt (1874): Good opinion entertained of a p. and influence derived from it. Verity (ed. 1897): The faith of what I say; not reputation, since Kent, being disguised, is unknown to the other.

1638+5 build]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Rely (OED, v. 6).

1638+6 Douer]
Perrett (1904, p. 258): Sh. in choosing Dover rather than any other of our best ports…follows [Leir]. But Dover is not mentioned in any source. In Leir (2392, 2431) the Gallian king lands by a port near a beacon, foure houres sayle from France; see , . Guilfoyle (1987; 1990, pp. 98–9): Possibly suggested by King Arthur’s landing at Dover to confront Mordred in Malory’s Morte Darthur (Caxton, 1485). Horsman (ed. 1973): Not a town but a coastal district where Gloucester may believe he can fall from a cliff and where Cordelia’s army from France may quickly encounter the British under Albany. Goldberg (1988, pp. 246–7): The word names a site of desire, the hope for recovery or…repose.…It is the place of illusion—the illusion of recovery and the illusion of respite and end. Turner (1988, p. 117): Symbolically, the very verge…of their confine, and there they [all his cast] meet with despair, madness, disillusion and death. Guilfoyle (1989; 1990, p. 119), a redemptionist: symbolically Jerusalem, a holy city and sanctuary for the faithful. Foakes (ed. 1997): The first hint that Lear is on his way there. But the line says only that Some will be there.

1638+7 Some]
Wright (ed. 1875): Not infrequently used as a singular [OED, indef. pron. 1], but it is not clear…whether Cordelia alone is intended.

1638+7 making]
Tovey (ed. 1896): When you make. See n. 1302.

1638+7 iust]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): True and accurate (OED, a. 6). Cf. 197.

1638+8 how]
Lott (ed. 1974): How much. But it could mean in what degree.

1638+8 vnnaturall]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Caused (unnaturally) by his own flesh and blood.

1638+8 bemadding]
See n. 760. OED (Bemad v.): To madden, quoting this l. as its first ex.

1638+9 plaine]
Like complain, the word may mean either lament (Tovey, ed. 1896; Harbage, ed. 1958; OED, v. 2) or utter feelings of ill-usage or injury (most eds.; OED, 4).

1638+10 blood]
Schmidt (1874): Noble birth. OED (sb. 12): Blood worth mention,…good parentage or stock; (12a): Gentle birth, good family. Cf. 3128.

1638+11 knowledge and assurance]
Rann (ed. 1794): Of you. Eds. often assume a hendiadys: Brooke (ed. 1947): Sure knowledge. Joseph (ed. 1966), assurance: Confidence, reliable information. Skillan (ed. 1967): Knowledge of facts and confidence that they are true.

1638+12 office]
See n. 1046. Muir (ed. 1952): I.e. the journey to Dover.

1639–40 I…not]
In either Q or F Lear’s knight might have good reasons to wish more conversation with Kent—to learn more of developments in England, to get further details of the errand given him in Q, to be assured that Kent speaks with authority; and in each text Kent, who is inquiring after the king at the beginning and end of the scene, clearly wishes both to resume his search and to send the Gentleman to Dover straightway, and so might wish not to prolong the conversation unduly. Thus Deighton (ed. 1891) on the knight’s reply: A courteous way of showing hesitation about undertaking the mission; and so others, explaining his motives: being ignorant who the disguised Kent is (Verity, ed. 1897), suspicious of the truth of what one who appears to be a mere servant has just told him (Evans, ed. 1898), wary of being trapped in treasonable plots by Regan’s tools (Porter & Clarke, ed. 1905). If these two speeches are taken literally, Kent seems eager to get into action and the Gentleman desirous to talke farther before he does so; the impression is reinforced in 1649 and 1652, when the Gentleman, by then at least persuaded of Kent’s bona fides, invites further talk and Kent insists that first they find the king. A number of commentators, however, interpret the speech as meaning the opposite of its literal meaning: to them, the Gentleman seems to wish not further audience with Kent but rather a breaking-off of the conversation and a refusal to accept any of Kent’s suggestions; in this reading, Kent’s No doe not refers not to talke farther but to the Gentleman’s assumed attempt to disengage himself and leave. Delius (ed. 1854): The Gentleman’s speech implies a courteous postponement or dismissal of a request; this explains Kent’s reply (Ger.). Moberly (ed. 1876): The gentleman intends to put off Kent’s request; but is persuaded by his tone of authority…and by the sight of the ring. Urkowitz (1980, pp. 68–70): To make sense out of Kent’s otherwise inexplicable objection, No, do not, it is necessary to recognize that the Gentleman’s line…is a conventional code for breaking off a conversation, not for continuing [comparing 331 and Mac. 1.5.71 (426)].…Kent prevents the [Gentleman’s] exit, however, with his urgent appeal. In the Folio text the Gentleman interrupts Kent’s speech abruptly at these are but furnishings, a sharp contrast to the complete hearing he gives…in the Quarto.…Because he forcefully interrupts Kent’s speech in the Folio, he means I will not listen to anything else you say, rather than I will not respond to your proposal, his meaning in the Quarto. In the Folio version of this speech, the Gentleman rejects Kent himself, not Kent’s proposal [which is never made].…Kent’s next speech, in which he prevents the Gentleman’s departure, is of necessity more forceful in the Folio than in its verbally identical Quarto counterpart since it must overcome a much stronger rejection. Taylor (1983, pp. 441–2): The Gentleman’s interruption is the result of the involuted style of Kent’s F lines, motivated by no more than a sense of urgency about finding the king: the product of impatience, not suspicion. He adduces in support of Urkowitz’s conventional code for breaking off conversation Ado 2.3.205–6 (1031), AWW 1.3.127 (448), H5 2.4.113 (1007), and Oth. 4.2.244 (2963). These arguments are questionable: except for Macbeth’s temporizing answer, the supposed parallels do not show a breaking-off of discussion according to a supposed formula, but rather the anticipation or appointment of a future interview; and in this scene the Gentleman, who seems willingly to have left Lear Contending with the fretfull element, shows no urgency to find him. Furthermore, Urkowitz’s impression of an abrupt interruption of Kent’s speech in F may be due to a faulty F text (see nn. 1631–8, 1634–8), and Kent’s reply is inexplicable only if we take the Gentleman’s reply in other than its literal sense. Kent apparently says doe not talke farther; had he been preventing the Gentleman’s exit, he would less misleadingly have said goe not or hear me now. Clearly in Q the Gentleman is hesitant and doubtful about undertaking his office, but instead of further colloquy Kent gives him a purse and a ring and promptly leaves to find the king. Deighton (op. cit.) thus interprets Kent’s reply: There is no necessity for any hesitation on the subject, for I will give you good proof that you may trust me. The Gentleman’s hesitation is clear, but that in Q he is breaking off a conversation or in F is forcefully rejecting Kent—an action of no apparent point in the scene—is hardly obvious.

1641 I]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 395): Q’s omission of am is doubtless a compositorial slip.

1641 more]
Pope (ed. 1725): I.e., I have some intrinsic worth.

1642 outwall]

1643 VVhat]

1643 shall]
Abbott (§348): Future for Subjunctive; cf. Franz §644 Anm. 1.

1643 Cordelia]
On the scansion see n. 47.

1644 As]
Abbott (§111): Used parenthetically…in a transitional manner for as regards which or for indeed, citing 1768. Deighton (ed. 1891): What Ingleby, Shakespeare, the Man and the Book [1877], Pt. i, p. 147, calls the conjunction of reminder, being employed…to introduce a subsidiary statement, qualifying, or even contradicting, what goes before, which the person addressed is required to take for granted. 1644 Ring]
Dundes (1976, p. 361): Kent’s use of a ring to summon Cordelia hints at incest. But Kent intends to introduce the Gentleman to Cordelia, not summon her to her father-lover (or anyone else).

1645 your fellow]
Rann (ed. 1794), fellow: Colleague; see n. 526. Schmidt (ed. 1879): Companion [OED, sb. 2].…As a general rule this word is found in this sense joined to a possessive pronoun, and therefore many editors prefer your fellow of the Qq. (Ger.). Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Also, as an equal [OED, 5a], both of them being gentlemen in the king’s service. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 145): Kent…cannot be using Fellow in a derogatory sense [here]. It must mean companion. Q’s your makes this clear: but it is quite possible that Shakespeare wrote [F’s that Fellow]—who that companion is that yet you do not know. Joseph (ed. 1966): The sense common person…seems to be involved. Wilson (ed. 1960): F’s that is obscure and harsh before That ([1646]) which [perhaps] the F comp.’s eye caught. Or possibly manuscript yr (for your) was misread as yt (for that), or vice versa. In fact Cordelia does not inform the Gentleman of Kent’s identity: see n. 2347+54.

1648 Giue…hand]
Wright (ed. 1875): The hesitation [in 1639]…is at an end. Tovey (ed. 1896): The gentleman consents.

1650 to effect]
Wright (ed. 1875): As to effect. Cf. Abbott §186; OED (To prep. 22). Hunter (ed. 1869): In their object or purpose. Deighton (ed. 1891): In their consequence. Skillan (ed. 1967): In substance. OED (Effect sb. 2): Purport;…essential significance.

1650 more…yet]
Hunter (ed. 1869): More important than all I have yet said. Verity (ed. 1897): More to the immediate purpose.

1651 That]
Anon. MS note (1608–23) in Q1, BL Copy 2: Sc. of yt—i.e., we’ll speak of that. Thirlby (MS notes, 1725–33), adding a comma: He will say wt he has to say more, when they have found the King. So Steevens (ed. 1773): That secret, however, you shall not hear till we have found the king. Most eds., however, take That to be a conjunction, giving the impression that lines 1651–3 are somehow an expansion or continuation of the sense of 1650; but the word has no real function in the clause that follows, and makes the next lines difficult to parse. Thus Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 516): Q can only be defended by interpreting Ile…you that as parenthetically (and unmetrically) interrupting Kent’s sentence; F [see next n.] suggests that Shakespeare would have found such an interpretation as impossibly strained as we do. The Oxford eds. accordingly emend Q (see textual n.) and propose a thorough relining of the verse which is not necessary: see next n. In fact the Q sense is clear if King is followed by a full stop, which Q usually punctuates in mid-speech by a comma, as it does here.

1651 in…pain]
F’s addition may have been made to fill out a verse line, but it is unnecessary to either meter or sense. Q’s lines 1651–3 make two passable pentameters if divided after you that, as would the F lines without the added phrase. Doran (1931, p. 127): Possibly added by actors. Eds. interpret the F phrase to mean either in which your pain (will) be (Hunter, ed. 1869) or in which I ask you to bestow your pains (Moberly, ed. 1876), the punctuation in the latter case presumably being omitted from F because of the full line. The F phrase is unnecessary to the sense because the Gentleman’s aid is already implied in when we haue found. Sh. seldom ends a scene with an incomplete line of verse, and in such cases it is usually some word or two of parting.

1651 which]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Which matter. Muir (ed. 1952): Which task.

1651 pain]
Schmidt (1875): Labour or trouble, giving Shn. usages in both sing. and pl.; cf. OED (sb.1 5, 6).

1652 Ile…that]
F’s reverse order seems without point; even if the added F phrase in 1651 is syntactically related (which it may not be: see prev. n.), F’s alteration could as well have read in which my pain This way, yours that.

1652 lights On]
Schmidt (1874), light: To meet, to find (OED, v.1 10d).

1652 On]
This should be the catchword on Q’s previous page, but Enter is. Apparently On…Exeunt. (1652–3) was originally the last line on F3v but at some time before final printing was moved to the top of the next page, very likely to make room on F3v for the addition of an overlooked line of text. The catchword was not accordingly changed. Such is Blayney’s theory as reported in Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 517).

1653 hollow]
F Holla. OED (Hollo v. 2b): To call after (in hunting); to call or shout to, quoting this l. as its first ex.; cf. n. 1857. Bradley (1904, pp. 445–6): But when Kent finds the King [at 1694] he does not halloo. Muir (ed. 1952, p. li n.): Either the actor could insert an halloo, or else the King’s plight made Kent forget the arrangement. The Gentleman apparently continues on to Dover and delivers a letter to Cordelia (see 2347+10); Kent, appalled at Lear’s condition, first seeks to bring him to shelter (1715), intending later to seek better care in Gloucester’s house (1717), but on hearing of a plot on Lear’s life (2048) helps drive him to Dover (2050). Circumstances force Kent to do first things first, and so deprive him of time and opportunity to pursue the Gentleman. Edwards (ed. 1975): Not clear in this scene is why the Gentleman, who gives no reason why he has left the King, should now be sent to search for him, as well as being sent off to Dover.

1653 Exeunt]
Horsman (ed. 1973): A brisk exit from opposite sides of the platform—for the King is to enter immediately through one of the doors at the back of the stage.

1654 <Scena Secunda>]
Daniel (ed. 1824): The scene…defies all powers of description. We can feel the force of the poet’s genius, even to agony: but we must inherit a portion of that genius, ere we can describe what we feel. Here are no supernatural agents called forth to deepen the horror of the scene—no furies weaving the web of fate.…But a dethroned monarch, an unhappy father, in the simple grandeur of unparalleled misery, invoking those servile ministers, the elements, to pour down their extremest vengeance upon his head.…Here we make a stand, and call upon the genius of every age and nation to produce a parallel to this scene. The most affecting image in all antiquity is Priam supplicating Achilles for the dead body of Hector. But Lear, wandering over the barren heath, amidst storm and tempest, with a broken heart, and a bewildered brain, is so transcendently sublime and awful, that antiquity must acknowledge the supremacy of Shakspeare, and bow to the immortal. Kittredge (ed. 1940): This scene takes place in the stormy night mentioned at the end of ii, 4. Kent, who has been seeking Lear ([1651–3]), finds him and conducts him toward a hovel that is hard by ([1715]). Vickers (1968, p. 352): Lear speaks in the most powerfully felt verse while the Fool continues in his comic prose—thus Lear’s rage is still more clearly defined.

1655 Storme]
See n. 1584.

1656–64 Blow…man]
Tillyard (1943, p. 59): Lear’s first words in the storm invoke explicitly all four elements in their uproars;…basic elemental conflict is as much a part of his thought as is the actual violence of the weather. Heninger (1956, p. 1): The riot of the four elements air (wind), water (caterickes, & Hircanios), fire (lightning), and earth (thunder-stones) shows imminent chaos. Fraser (1962, pp. 61–2): The last and most terrifying role played by the impious man is that of an anarch.…[Sh.] expresses in [such passages] his sense of the ultimate horror. Whenever he wishes to get at the nadir of human experience, he uses language of this kind, comparing 2H6 5.2.40–2 (3262–4), Tim. 4.1.15–21 (1518–24), WT 4.4.478–9 (2330–1), 2H4 1.1.153–4 (213–14), and Mac. 4.1.53–60 (1584–90), and citing Curry (1937, pp. 29–49). Rosenberg (1972, pp. 191–2), perhaps following Kanzer (1965, p. 5), detects a sexual undercurrent suggesting Nature’s orgasm; the analogy is forced. Foakes (ed. 1997): There is a bitter sexual undercurrent, feeding his misogyny, in Lear’s wish to destroy all the seeds that make man, citing Adelman (1992, pp. 110–12); but the seeds (Germains) are very likely male, not female (see n. 1663). Bain (1892, 2:105): Among the loftiest flights of Shakespeare’s sublimity, though some details are wanting in dignity, badly expressed, and extravagant.
