Saintsbury (1908, 2:44–5): More than Æschylean, admiring the monosyllabic feet in rage and blow, the trisyllabic (nearly if not quite tribrachs) at sul|phurous and, and vaunt cou|riers to and rotun|dity o’ | the world. Williams (1952, pp. 58 ff.) analyzes at length the poetic features and techniques of this speech, including its animal, anthropomorphic, and cosmic imagery; its rough onomatopoetic diction; its patterns of nasals, sibilants, and low vowels; its mixture of native or vernacular words with striking foreign importations, of monosyllables with polysyllables, etc. Houghton (ed. 1957): There is almost a new element of cosmic force in the verse here, partly produced by the predominance of spondees. Goldman (1981, p. 36): Each word threatens to stop the line dead.…The consonants clash, the vowels expand. Brandl (1922, p. 372) and Miola (1992, p. 160): Cf. Seneca, Hercules Furens 1202–5. So Bulman (1985, p. 156): Such mad rant links him to a long line of revengers who find their prototype in Hercules Furens. Hankins (1946, pp. 88–90; 1978, pp. 233–5) finds echoes of the invocation of heavenly lightning as deliverance from straunge chyldren in Psa. 144:4–8, 11. Tilley W446 detects the proverb Wind and weather, do your worst, though his first ex. is dated 1678; Dent (1981) doubts that the saying is proverbial or relevant. Velz (1989, p. 180): Sh. is evidently remembering Ovid’s [Meta. 1.254–9], the terrible storm Jupiter’s wrath evokes against Lycaon. Greg (1936, p. 179): Here the quarto compositor began by simply filling his (narrower) measure and in effect treating his copy as prose, though he [eventually] prefixed perfunctory capitals to the lines. He then decided for verse and cut up his copy into irregular lengths, though with no apparent regard for metre. The second speech is in fact prose, but having made up his mind for verse, the compositor proceeded to cut this also into lengths. For modern musical settings, see Gooch & Thatcher (1991, 1:634–5).

1656 Blow…blow]
Goldman (1985, pp. 82–3): Each word in the line threatens to stop the line dead.…It is hard to move from blow to winds and to get up further energy for crack your cheeks, citing the disparate consonants and the number of imperatives. Graham-White (1995, pp. 134–5): Neither text [Q, F] has a comma between Blow and windes. Without it, elision here is natural—and quite possible between & and crack if the d is not sounded. Far from each word threatening to stop the line dead, each can elide into the next.…Nor [in Q, F]…does the first line stop at an exclamation mark [see textual n.]; rather, it swings into the next. Williams (1949–50, pp. 177 ff.) defends Pope’s full stop after blow, adopted by almost all later editors; see nn. 1656, 1658.

1656 wind]
On F’s windes see n. 1263.

1656 cracke]
OED (v. 13b): Split asunder, quoting this l. as its first ex. Joseph (ed. 1966): Also make a roar, blast. Cf. 1663.

1656 cheekes]
Mason (1785, p. 2): The allusion…is to the manner in which the winds were represented in antient paintings, comparing Tro. 4.5.8–9 (2557–8). Williams (1951, p. 64 n.): Or the cartographer’s decoration of the little wind-god. Cf. Mikalachki (1998, p. 89). Cor. 5.3.151 (3508). Kittredge (ed. 1940): This and the next word are prolonged in utterance with a change in pitch and each counting for two syllables.

1656 rage]
OED (v. 4a): Transf. of things (e.g. wind, the sea, etc.): To be violent and boisterous.

1656 blow]
Most eds. adopt Pope’s punctuation (see textual n.), since blow makes apparently better sense if addressed to winds than to a downpour of water (cataracts). Williams (1949–50, pp. 178–82) also prefers the resultant epanalepsis (i.e., repetition of the same word at the beginning and end of a verse line), and explains Q’s omission of a terminal mark of punctuation (probably a comma) as possibly being due to the Q compositor’s use of a shorter measure, or printer’s stick, for setting verse, as distinct from the longer measure used to set prose the full width of the type-page. Lines 1656–8 in Q all end flush at the width of this shorter measure, and in 1656 the use of thin spaces between words and the lack of spaces after its two commas suggests that terminal punctuation was omittted for lack of room. The same lack of terminal punctuation in F seems more likely to be intentional on the part of scribe or compositor, since the semicolon after cheeks makes blow necessarily addressed to cataracts in the next line, resulting in apparently inferior sense. Unless F was influenced by the punctuation of Q, the absence of punctuation after blow in both Q and F may be due to indistinct or missing punctuation in a Shn. rough draft first transcribed to make the playbook and subsequently used as copy for Q; see . Graham-White (1995, p. 135): In Quarto and Folio the Cataracts blow and the Hyrricanos spout. But in most modern editions blow has been transferred to winds, even though it might seem stronger as an intensification of the opening command—Blow windes…blow / You Cataracts—than as a logically redundant repetition of that first command. Conceivably, since the rain and wind occur together, Lear bids them together to blow and spout, reversing the verb order to emphasize their inseparability, in a hypallage similar to With raynie Marching in the painefull field in H5 4.3.111 (2358).

1657 caterickes, & Hircanios]
OED records neither Q spelling. The first is probably a misreading of the 16th-c. spelling catarack (or some unrecorded variant of it). The second word may have been formed by metathesis from Hiricanos; cf. F’s Hyrricano’s. If the punctuation of 1656 by modern eds. is accepted (see prev. n.), both of these nouns are subjects of spout; otherwise the first is subject of rage, blow. Kittredge (ed. 1940) considers the two nouns synonymous, and OED (Cataract sb. 1b, not recording the Q sp.; Hurricano sb. 2) quotes this l. in giving both words the meaning waterspout. The gloss may be misleading to modern readers, since for Elizabethans a waterspout meant water falling as from a spout (see OED, sb. 2), rather than either a whirling column of water or a cloudburst (OED, sb. 3a, 3b), usages first attested in the 18th c. Cf. 1669, spout raine, and next n. OED’s first ex. for Cataract (1b), from Sh.’s source for the name Setebos, Eden’s Decades, the New World, or West India (ed. Arber, 1885, p. 386), associates spoutes faulynge owt of the ayer into the sea with the catractes of heaven…at Noes fludde. Williams (1949–50, p. 177): It would seem that Shakespeare in this passage had in mind the distinction from Genesis 7:11[–12] between the floodgates of heaven (or cataracts) [Vulgate: cataractae caeli] and the fountains of the deep (or hurricanoes) [fontes abyssi magnae], both of which were set in motion at the time of the Deluge. Idem (1951, p. 66): Cataractes are descending waters, of the heavens, and hurricanoes are rising waters, of the earth.…Lear orders a return of the Hebraic deluge. Such a distinction is doubtful here; Sh.’s only other hurricano is the dreadful spout…In his descent (Tro. 5.2.172–5 [3169–71]); cf. OED’s only non-Shn. ex. for Hurricano (2), from Drayton’s Moone-Calfe (1627; ed. Hebel, 3:183, ll. 667–8): And downe the shower impetuously doth fall, | Like that which men the Hurricano call. Though hurricanes involve heavy rains, all OED’s contemporary quotations emphasize only their violent winds; probably Lear is simply invoking both downpours and tempests.

1657 spout]
OED (v. 1): To discharge a liquid in a copious jet or stream, quoting this l. Cf. 1669.

1658 drencht,…drown’d]
Williams (1949–50, pp. 179–80): Possibly through a memorial or visual error the compositor misplaced the punctuation concluding one line by dropping it to the end of the line immediately below; or he made a faulty inversion of the comma that should have followed steeples in the next line. Drencht and drown’d are practically synonyms, each meaning submerged (OED, Drench v. 2; Drown v. 5). Q makes them parallel participles after the auxiliary haue; F’s drown could conceivably be an imperative like spout, as Foakes (ed. 1997) thinks, but the obviously parallel ideas of drenching steeples and drowning cocks seems naturally to demand Q’s parallel structure, and drownd is easily misread drowne (Doran, 1931, p. 94; Duthie, ed. 1949, pp. 177–8). Hogan (1962, p. 78): F, with his measure full, could not easily have made the correction himself.

1658 steeples]
Cf. n. 1604. Paul (1950, p. 252): In France and the low countries, steeples and churches were blown down in the tempests of 29–30 March 1606; cf. Mac. 4.1.52–60 (1582–90). Wells (ed. 2000): Like cockes, anachronistic.

1658 The]
F’s our, though generally preferred by eds., further reduces the parallelism with the cockes.

1658 cockes]
Schmidt (1874): Weathercock[s] (OED, sb.1 5, quoting this l. as its first ex. of two).

1659 sulpherous]
Elton (1966, p. 203) quotes Seneca, Quaestiones naturales [2.53.2; tr. Corcoran, 1971, 1:183]: Wherever lightning has struck there is sure to be an odour of sulphur. Cf. MM 2.2.115 (872), sulpherous bolt, Cym. 5.5.240 (3527), the Gods throw stones of sulpher, and Cor. 5.3.152 (3509), cha[r]ge thy Sulphure with a Boult. Gardner (ed. 1969) quotes William Fulke’s explanation, in A Goodly Gallery (1563, sigs. D3v–4), of how sulphur and thunderstones came to be in the clouds: In the exhalation which is gathered out of the earth, is much earthly matter…consisting of brimstone and other metallic substance…hardened as a brick is in the fire. Milward (1987, p. 175) is reminded of eschatological fire in 2 Pet. 3:12, Gen. 19.24, Rev. 18:20.

1659 Thought executing]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Doing execution with rapidity equal to thought. Absent any specific reference to speed, This idea seems rather to be involved in the compound than expressed by it (Moberly, ed. 1876). Though the proverb As swift as Thought is commonly alluded to in Sh., neither Tilley T240 nor Dent (1981) finds it here. Some eds. follow Baret (1928, pp. 316–17) in comparing Tmp. 1.2.201–3 (313–15), Lightning…momentarie And sight out-running, but there the idea of speed is explicit, as it is in R2 1.3.79 (376), swift like lightning in the execution. Kemshead (ed. 1875) and others, alternatively: Executing the thoughts of God. Harbage (ed. 1958), tentatively: Dazing, benumbing—i.e., putting an end to thought. Cf. R2 1.3.81 (378), amazing thunder, and JC 1.3.49–56 (487–94), the Thunder-stone: And…Lightning, dreadfull Heraulds, to astonish vs. Rosenberg (1972, p. 192): Mind destroying. Davis (1987, pp. 39–40), biographically: In writing Lear…Shakespeare simultaneously carried out his thoughts into words and felt his thoughts, and almost his mind itself, executed, destroyed in so doing. Weis (ed. 1993): Lear’s inner storm will indeed drive him mad. The verb execute did not mean destroy, but cf. OED (Execution 5): Destructive effect, infliction of damage, quoting Tit. 2.3.36 (771) and 4.2.84 (1767) and Mac. 1.2.18 (37) as its first exx.

1660 vaunt-currers]
Pope (ed. 1725): Fore-runners (OED, Vaunt-courier 2, quoting this l). Malone (ed. 1790) finds the same image in Tmp. 1.2.201 (313). Hunter (1845, 2:270) finds the term, not used elsewhere in Sh., in Harsnett’s Declaration (1603, p. 12), and Ashe (1950) in William Strachey’s sonnet prefixed to Jonson’s Sejanus (1605, sig. A3), a play in which Sh. acted.

1660 to]
F’s substituted of is the more usual preposition in OED’s exx. Walker (1953, p. 63) finds the change typical of F Compositor B’s customary negligence.

1660 Oke-cleauing]
Craig (ed. 1901): A very favourite image of Shakespeare’s, citing several exx.

1660 thunderboults]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Fiery bolts, or stone missiles, were supposed to be discharged from the clouds by the thunder (OED, Thunderbolt 1, 3, Thunder-stone 1). Cf. 2783+1 and n. 1659.

1661–4 thunder…man]
See nn. 981–2, 1702–12. Williams (1951, pp. 65–7), citing J. G. Frazer, The Golden Bough (New York, 1935, 2:181–3): Lear is acting in conformity and parallel with Roman and Celtic tradition. These mythologies both state the ancient position of the king as the creator of the weather, especially of the stormy weather.…This power of calling on the thunderbolt, which is granted to the king, exalts him to a position equal to that of Jupiter and identifies him with the Thunderer, the Rain-god, and the Hurler of the Lightnings.…The concluding images suggest the ruin of the Last Judgment. Cf. nn. 441–2, 3224–5.

1661 smite]
F’s Strike is indifferent, though Foakes (ed. 1997) finds it more euphonious. Weis (ed. 1993): Q’s…sounds a more biblical note. Wells (ed. 2000): As affliction by God (OED, v. 4).

1662–3 thicke Rotunditie…natures Mold]
Delius (ed. 1854): Not only the sphere of the globe, but the roundness of pregnancy (Ger.), comparing WT 4.4.478–9 (2330–1); see n. 1663. Baldwin (1952, p. 238): The thunder will cause miscarriage, not wholly flatten the globe. Houghton (ed. 1957): He uses language suggested by the sexual organs of men and women; for he wishes the human race to be abolished. Possibly there is a sequence of associated thoughts here: the roundness of the globe suggests the round womb; thus smiting flat the world, which presumes to raise her teeming and pregnant orb towards you (Moberly, ed. 1876), suggests destroying specifically the human matrix and all mankind. See next n.

1663 cracke]
Joseph (ed. 1966): Both split…[and] explode, as in [1656].

1663 Mold]
F’s moulds, preferred by most eds., may be erroneous: it can imply that Lear wishes reproduction of all forms of natural life to cease, but he specifies only one, Ingratefull man, as is consistent with Q’s singular Mold. Besides, to break the mold is a common formula for To render impossible the repetition of a certain type of creation (OED, Mould sb.3 2c, quoting this l.). The word means Matrix (OED, 2), in which nature shapes her products (Deighton, ed. 1891) or in which men are made (Harrison, ed. 1948). Wells (ed. 2000): Tantamount to womb. Williams (1951, pp. 67–8): The forms of Plato existent in the creator’s mind in accordance with which everything was made…[and] the womb. Baldwin (1952, p. 237): But elsewhere in Shakespeare these moulds are of the earth earthy, the shaping forces of great creating-Nature (Natura naturans) (WT 4.4.88 [1898]). Cf. next n.

1663 Germains]
Sh. seems to have invented the term, unattested before this line and Mac. 4.1.59 (1589) (OED, Germen), and its meaning is not entirely clear. Pope (ed. 1725) relates it to the L. germanus: All relations, or kindred elements that compose man. Instead it is derived from L. germen, meaning literally a sprout or bud and figuratively the germ or origin; the form may be influenced by common contemporary spellings of German and germane. Hanmer (ed. 1743–4, 6:Gloss. s.v. Germin) defines literally: The first sprouting of seed or of a branch. Confuting Pope, Theobald (1729; in Nichols, 1817, 2:217), followed by Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:28), Craig (ed. 1901), and others, extends the meaning to Seeds, by analogy with the parallel Seedes of Time (Mac. 1.3.58 [158]) and Let Nature crush the sides o’th earth together, | And marre the seeds within (WT 4.4.478–9 [2330–1]). Partridge (1947, p. 120): Semen of a man. Colman (1974): Spermatozoa. Theobald (ed. 1733) specifies: Seeds of Matter. Craig (ed. 1931, p. 921): Seeds or elements, from which nature operates. Curry (1937, pp. 31–42) understands an Augustinian and Renaissance neoplatonic sense: rationes seminales, the material essences which correspond to the exemplars in God’s mind. Danby (1949, pp. 21–3) paraphrases from Bacon, Advancement of Learning 2.13, the [Greek] theory of [the universe’s] origins in matter—either as a collection of potentially infinite seeds, or as a primordial substance capable of configuration through its union with form.…Lear’s germens are Bacon’s seeds, his moulds Bacon’s forms. Elton (1950, p. 196) cites Timothy Bright’s A Treatise of Melancholie (1586, p. 34): This earth [God] had endued with a fecunditie of infinite seeds of all things. Baldwin (1944, 2:657): Possibly directly echoing the generandum…semina rerum of Palingenius (Zodiacus Vitae, 1537, p. 80). Idem (1952, pp. 239–40): The semina rerum of Ovid (Meta. 1.6–9) and Lucretius though not, as Raphael Regius had glossed the term, the four elements. Paul (1950, pp. 253–4): The term appears in Mac. and Lr. because while the plays were being written [spring 1606] rivers were overflowing their bounds, causing disastrous upland floods which lodged and destroyed the corn. See .

1663 spill]
Steevens (ed. 1778): Destroy (OED, v. 1, Kill; 4a, 5c, Spoil). Tovey (ed. 1896) finds the added sense Shed, but this is said only of blood (OED, 9); possible however is OED (6): Waste by scattering. Williams (1951, p. 70): A hint of coitus interruptus. The Oxford ed.’s (1986) spoil excludes some of these senses.

1664 make]
For F’s singular makes see n. 207. Colman (ed. 1982): Prob.…the compositor’s eye was caught by -s of natures in the line above.

1664 Ingratefull]
Williams (1951, pp. 63 n., 70–1): Applies in three senses: 1) displeasing…, 2) harsh or unfriendly, and 3) not showing gratitude [OED, a. 1, 2, 3].…This is a destruction which like the Noachic Deluge and the Final Judgment is sent as a punishment for filial ingratitude…[and to prevent] another generation of ingrateful creatures.

1665, 1666 Nunckle]
See n. 634.

1665 Court holly water]
Holly is a 17th-c. sp.; Q1(c) corrects to holy. Steevens (ed. 1778): Proverbial…to mean fair words (OED, Flattery without performance or sincere intention, and Tilley, H532 both quoting this l.). Kinney (1980, p. 20): So used in Lipsius, Politickes (tr. W. Jones, 1594, sig. G2v). Hunter (ed. 1972): The flattery a man must sprinkle to belong to the court. Traversi (1952–3, p. 128): A deliberate reminder of the folly that has brought [Lear] to his present situation. McCann (ed. 1964): Flatter your daughters into giving you shelter for the night.

1665–6 drie…doore]
Elton (1966, pp. 308, 310) compares Tilley F537, Fools have wit enough to come in out of the rain, and the similar K10; Tilley does not cite this line, Dent (1981) does.

1666 out a doore]
See n. 655.

1667 and]
F omits. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 146): May well have been interpolated in Q in order to make the verse smoother.

1667 aske…blessing]
Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): I.e. submit to their authority (since the normal procedure would be for them to ask a blessing of him).

1667 daughters]
Delius (ed. 1854): Plural possessive, since both daughters are within Gloucester’s house. Kittredge (ed. 1940): No possessive: From your daughters. Ask (like cry in [1711]) takes two objects (the person and the thing), comparing 2950.

1667 pities]
Furness (ed. 1880): Although the omission of the relative is common enough (see [n. 589]), in dignified speech, yet here in the Fool’s speeches this and many other colloquialisms are to be expected. Smith (ed. 1902): But it is really a survival of the construction…in which one subject serves for two predicates, and from which the relative clause was developed, citing Kellner (1892 §§109–11). Cf. 588–9, 641, 1885–6, and Franz §348.

1668 wise man nor foole]
F’s Wisemen, nor Fooles is practically indifferent; see n. 681.

1669–79 Rumble…foule]
Williams (1951, p. 65): The second group of eleven lines is anti-climactic; the destruction does not occur. The tempest continues, however, to beat down on Lear’s unprotected head. Dunn (1952, p. 331) disagrees: It seems to be a conclusion of the first apostrophe, and both of them appear to be Lear’s curse upon himself. The curse is bitterly ironic, of course. Bradbrook (1978, p. 199) compares Job 38:34–5. Milward (1987, p. 173): Lear now appears as it were in the character of Job, disputing with God amid the whirlwind, quoting Job 36:10, 38:1, 8, 11.

1669 thy belly full]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Send forth all the wind in your belly. Muir (ed. 1952): The storm here, as in the opening lines of the scene, personified. Full is not an adv. modifying Rumble and meaning to the full, but an adj., later replaced by the suffix -ful, forming a compound with belly meaning A sufficiency (OED, 2). Dent (1984, B306) compares the proverbial To have a bellyful.

1670 Nor]
Schmidt (1875): Neither (OED, conj.1 5). Wright (ed. 1875): For neither.

1670 fire]
Delius (ed. 1854): Dissyllable.

1670 are my daughters]
Deighton (ed. 1891): And therefore I cannot complain of their treatment.

1671 taske]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Accuse, blame for. F’s taxe is a doublet of task; cf. 867, where attaskt was substituted for…copy ataxt (Wells & Taylor, 1987, p. 517).

1671 elements]
See n. 1619.

1671 vnkindnes]
See n. 132. OED (sb. 2): Ingratitude, quoting this l. as its last ex. Moberly (ed. 1876) compares the same association of storm with ingratitude in AYL 2.7.175–6 (1157).

1672 I…kingdome]
Skottowe (1824, pp. 111–12) compares Leir 888–9, 892–3, 898–905; see .

1672 children]
Deighton (ed. 1891): I.e. by the endearing name of children. But Lear’s point seems to be that the elements have no obligations to him, such as children would have.

1673–5 why…man]
Proudfoot (1992, p. xxviii) finds an echo in the anonymous (Heywood’s?) Tom a Lincoln (ca. 1611), 2661–70. Prester John defies the sacred powers to strike him with thunder and to destroy the globe.

1673 subscription]
Here used to mean that which is subscribed to (as if by signed agreement), and specified by eds. as obedience (Warburton, ed. 1747), allegiance, submission (Upton, 1746, p. 292; OED, 6b, quoting only this l.), service (Rann, ed. 1794), contribution (Caldecott, MS notes, 1813–33), the obligation towards Lear agreed to by his daughters (Ger.) (Delius, ed. 1854), kindness (Hudson, ed. 1879), etc. Cf. 359, 2137.

1673 why then]
F’s omission smoothes the meter.

1674 horrible plesure]
Crook (ed. 1907): The horrors it may please you to inflict.

1674 slaue]
Heath (1765, p. 338): Submitting to every indignity…[and] your power. Johnson (ed. 1765): By necessity and compulsion.

1675 infirme]
See n. 323. Harbage (1963, p. 417): Yet he seems more impressive than ever before. There is something in him uncrushed and uncrushable, and his magnificent addresses to the warring elements, the gods, and the sly sinners of the world lend him the stature of spokesman for erring, suffering, aspiring mankind.…He is both titan and old man in distress.

1676 yet…seruile]
OED (Servile adj. 3): Slavish, quoting this l. as its first ex. Heath (1765, p. 338): Notwithstanding this my submission…, I have a right to expostulate, and to call you servile. Deighton (ed. 1891) sees an opposition with 1671: Though I cannot charge you with ingratitude, I do accuse you of being mere slavish agents. Nearer and more probable is comparison between I and you: though I am your slave, yet you also are servile; so Edwards (ed. 1975). Skillan (ed. 1967): Co-operating with reg. and gon. with…abominable servility.

1676 Ministers]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Agents (OED, sb. 2). Or possibly servants, attendants (OED, 1). Elton (1966, p. 199): Intermediaries of the gods. Milward (1987, p. 175) compares Ps. 104:4: Which [i.e., God] maketh the spirits his messengers, & a flaming fyre his ministers (Geneva).

1677 haue…ioin’d]
F’s will…ioyne means are willing to join (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 146).

1678 high engẽdred battel]
F’s pl., Battailes, is unnecessary but is generally adopted. Rann (ed. 1794): Celestial forces. Rolfe (ed. 1880): High = in the heavens, comparing 1522. Craig (ed. 1901): Battalions nurtured high, in the heavens.…Battle has usually this sense (OED, sb. 8). Brooke (ed. 1947): Battalions of rain and wind, produced high in the air. Moberly’s (ed. 1876) battles begun high up in the air makes inferior sense, as does Joseph’s (ed. 1966) ethereal.

1678 head]
Though Lear clearly refers to his own white head, Brown (ed. 1976) finds puns on head = armed force/head of a family.

1679 foule]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Shameful (OED, adj. 13). Heron (1785, p. 30): Applies to the storm (OED, 15).

1680–7 Hee…glasse]
Wilson (ed. 1960): As usual the Fool comments upon Lear’s last words (a head, etc.). Your head, he says in effect, deserves to go houseless (unbonneted), since it was foolish to prefer Gon. and Reg. who despise you to Cord. who loves you. Dent (1981, H784.1) cites the proverb To have a (no) House to put (hide) one’s head in. Danby (1945, p. 22) This is the Fool’s counterpart to Lear’s prayer (1807–17), the negative to Lear’s positive.

1681 headpeece]
OED (Head-piece sb. 2): Any covering for the head, quoting this l. Delius (ed. 1854): Pun on helmet [OED, 1] and brain [OED, 4]; in opposition to codpiece, as something that ought by nature to take precedence (Ger.). Dent (1981, H282) detects the proverbial To have a good headpiece.

1682–5 the Codpeece…wake]
Eds. almost never follow Capell (see textual n.) in indicating song. Hunter (ed. 1972, p. 340): The compression and obliquity of language makes this unsuitable for music. Halio (ed. 1992): Both quatrains deal with foolish inversion of values.

1682 Codpeece]
Literally, a piece covering the cods; an anachronism. OED (sb.): A bagged appendage to the front of the close-fitting hose or breeches worn by men from the 15th to the 17th c.: often conspicuous and ornamented. Partridge (1947, p. 89): The penis (OED 1c; Williams, 1994). Hunter (ed. 1972): By metonymy. Douce (1807, 2:153–4): Shakspeare has with some humour applied [in 1692–3] the above name to the fool, who, for obvious reasons, was usually provided with this unseemly part of dress in a more remarkable manner than other persons. To this custom [Edmund] Gayton thus alludes, when speaking of the decline of the stage: No fooles with Harry codpieces appeare. Festivous [or Pleasant] notes upon Don Quixote, [1654], p. 270). The obvious reasons are the licentious behavior expected of the stage and court fool, also suggested by his bladder-and-stick or his emblem of office the bauble, whose carved form in some instances was obscene in the highest degree (ibid., 2:319); cf. Rom. 2.4.92–3 (1192–3), AWW 4.5.30–1 (2511–12). Wiles (1987, p. 190): There is no iconographic evidence to suggest that a fool’s costume ever incorporated a prominent codpiece. Rather, the fool puts his bauble between his legs in order to mime; but see nn. 669+1–+4, 923–4. Goldsmith (1955, p. 63): Has [Lear] not acted the part of a codpiece covering and protecting those baser parts—his lecherous and ungrateful daughters, Goneril and Regan? Gardner (ed. 1969): The Fool is glancing at Lear as the codpiece. Rather, he implies that Lear has been as foolishly improvident in his own way as the beggars have been in theirs, and consequently is as homeless.

1682 house…any]
Proverbial: Tilley H749, Before thou marry be sure of a House wherein to tarry. Horsman (ed. 1973): To copulate before taking a house (to give a home to the penis before the head).

1682–3 that…lowse]
Croft (1810, p. 19): A man who spends his all on his lusts, and after marries without a house to put his head in, shall become lousy like a beggar. Cf. the proverb in n. 1870–1. Similarly Kittredge (ed. 1940), reading The man who begets children, and Muir (ed. 1952), reading The man who satisfies his sexual appetites and will end up by sharing his wife’s lice. Danby (1949, p. 111) compares the Rake’s Progress from gallant to Abram Man described by Edgar in 1865–78. Craig (ed. 1901), apparently taking Codpeece to mean a fool: He that will house, provide for, a Goneril or a Regan, before taking proper measures for his own welfare, shall suffer much ignominy therefrom.

1682 house]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Equivocal, referring to shelter and sexual congress. Capell (1783, 1.2:164) conjectures that his hands have found a house in his cod-piece, into which he has stuff’d them to keep them warm.

1682 any]
Delius (ed. 1854): House is understood.

1683 head and hee]
Harbage (ed. 1958): [With] head-lice and body-lice.

1683 shall lowse]
Eds. understand will be lousy (OED, v. 2, quoting only this l.). Gardner (ed. 1969): A pun on…lose is also probable. Only Gilliland (1984) interprets Ought to de-louse [OED, 1], as a preparation to seeking sexual gratification, concluding implausibly, The Fool is urging that Lear present himself to his daughter in a pleasing manner to get shelter.

1683 so beggers]
Beggars’ lice were proverbial. See Tilley B230, B240, B249, L471, not citing this l.

1683 mary many]
Johnson (ed. 1765): A beggar marries a wife and lice. Mason (1785, p. 348): Rather, Many beggars marry. Hudson (ed. 1881) compares Wiv. 1.1.19–21 (21–2), Lowses…signifies Loue. Danby (1949, p. 111) understands the Beggarman and his long train of doxies.

1684 makes…make]
Proverbial. Wilson (ed. 1960) cites Tilley F562, Do not make the Foot the head. Tilley and Dent (1981) quote this l. instead under H317, I will not set at my Heart what I should set at my heel. Capell (1783, 1.2:164): Making that our last object which should be our first, implying Lear’s surrender of his power to women. Croft (1810, p. 19): Making his toe merry by dancing, instead of his heart, may bring corns. Moberly (ed. 1876): Exposes his nature where it is most sensitive. Hudson (ed. 1879): Who has set his children above himself. Furness (ed. 1880): Prefers or cherishes a mean member [Goneril and Regan] in place of a vital one [Cordelia]. Deighton (ed. 1891): Suffers his toe to become as callous as it would be well for him to make his heart. Danby (1949, pp. 111–12): Who makes his toe [= phallus] the centre of all his hopes, aspirations, and satisfactions. Harbage (ed. 1958): A parallel instance of misery deriving from reckless impulse: to transpose the tender and precious heart and the tough and base toe. Horsman (ed. 1973), questionably, though followed by Foakes (ed. 1997): To kick away Cordelia.

1684 toe]
Eccles (ed. 1792): An immodest and gross allusion. Page (ed. 1889) compares Cor. 1.1.155 (163), where one of the lowest, basest, poorest Romans is called the great Toe of this Assembly. Danby (1945, p. 23): Like the gallant’s codpiece, the courtier’s toe pinched in his shoe represents both sexuality and pride.

1684 heart]
OED (sb. 2): The centre of vital functions: the seat of life. Cf. n. 418. Harbage (ed. 1958): Also suggestng Cordelia (see DP n. 17). Halio (ed. 1992): The line…contrasts sexual promiscuity with love.

1685 haue]
Though most eds. accept F’s of, Q makes good sense. Stone (1980, p. 219): To have something happen to one is good English idiom. Or shall haue may mean acquire, if a comma is missing after corne. The logic of the metaphor is unclear in both Q and F. Why should cherishing a toe result in either a corn or the experience of pain, and from the very part he so foolishly cherishes (Craig, ed. 1901)? Or why should the toe, if exchanged with the heart, be more sensitive or subject to pain than the heart would have been, or yield enduring pain where others [who had not exchanged heart and toe] would suffer merely a twinge (Furness, ed. 1880)? Is it implied that physical pain is more noticeable than emotional pain, contrary to what Lear says elsewhere (1791–4)? Or is it that toes are likely to have corns that will give twinges of pain, whereas the heart in itself offers no cause of discomfort? Kittredge (ed. 1940): He will get a corn on his heart instead of his foot, and that will give him…heartache. Hunter (ed. 1972): If you valued your toe as highly as you should value your heart, its ailments would loom as large.

1685 cry woe]
Malone (ed. 1790): Be grieved, or pained. OED (Cry v. 4): The object may be a. a description or term for the utterance; b. the word or words uttered. The phrase occurs in R3 3.3.7 (1940), R2 3.2.102 (1460), etc.

1685 wake]
See n. 349.

1686–7 for…glasse]
Many eds. agree with Furness (ed. 1880) that the remark is inconsequential: This is the Fool’s way of diverting attention after he has said something a little too pointed; the idea of a very pretty woman making faces in a looking glass raises a smile. Kittredge (ed. 1940) compares 729, 737. Edwards (ed. 1975): Perhaps, finding himself growing sententious, he clowns this solemn saying with a wink at the women in the audience. Others see a glance at the self-absorption, vanity, hypocrisy, or contempt of Goneril and Regan which are causing Lear’s woe. OED (Mouth sb. 4b): To make a…mouth, or mouths: to express disapproval, derision, etc. by distorting or putting awry one’s mouth, to grimace. In Sh.’s other three uses of the phrase (MND 3.2.238 [1265], Ham. 2.2.364 [1410] (Q), 4.4.50 [2743+44]) it implies mockery, and has been so interpreted here. Eccles (ed. 1792): Descriptive of the treachery of a woman shewn, by her first addressing a man with kind speeches…and then turning suddenly round and making mouths at his figure represented in a looking-glass. Wilson (ed. 1960): And no marvel if Gon. and Reg. despise him, for all pretty women practice grimaces in their glass. He uses make mouths in both literal and fig. senses;…= make faces (at), treat with contempt. Hunter (ed. 1972): Women are by nature likely to despise what they see. Most eds., however, take the phrase as analogous to making practis’d Smiles | As in a Looking-Glasse (WT 1.2.116–17 [189–90]), sometimes as if it meant making gaping or wry mouths…when occupied with the duties of the toilet (Hunter, ed. 1869), but in any case implying a range of faults. Rann (ed. 1794): Was apt to consult her glass, to grow vain of her charms. Page (ed. 1889): Was a vain, giddy, thoughtless creature who practised looks and attitudes before her mirror. Muir (ed. 1952): Practising pretty faces…glancing obliquely at the vanity and hypocrisy of Goneril and Regan. Harbage (ed. 1958): Irrelevant, except as vanity is a form of folly, the Fool’s general theme. Elton (1966, p. 325, n. 82) details an extensive iconographical tradition in which a woman gazing into a mirror, sometimes observed by a fool, symbolizes pride, self-love, lechery, and avarice. Quinn (ed. 1970): The general sense…is that no one is exempt from human folly. Shickman (1991, p. 76) speculates that the Fool carries a mirror; see n. 744).

1687, 1689 glasse…patience]
Steevens (ed. 1773) compares Perillus’s description of the king in Leir 755 as the myrrour of mild patience; see . Greg (1940, p. 388): The only case of certain verbal dependence on Leir. But many verbal parallels have been suggested: see , , , .

1689 all]
Joseph (ed. 1966): Every sort of. Or complete.

1689 patience]
See n. 774. Tayler (1990, p. 28): Understood by the audience to allude to Job. Milward (1987) cites also Jas. 5:10–11, 1 Pet. 2:20–1.

1690 nothing]
Jennens (ed. 1770) defends his SD (see textual nn. and 1694): What can be more proper than Lear’s seating himself, after his last speech? Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 517): The reference to patience would be a natural cue for such action, citing TN 2.4.114 (975).

1692 Marry]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Originally an oath by the Virgin Mary, but used as a mere exclamation (OED, int.). Cf. 2311+7.

1692 Grace, & a codpis]
Hudson (ed. 1856): Meaning the king and himself. Wilson (ed. 1960): Then with a motion of the hand [he] reverses the roles by pointing to himself as the wise man and to Lear as the fool. See next n. Malone (ed. 1790), grace: In Shakspeare’s time the king’s grace was the usual expression [for address to a sovereign]. Kittredge (ed. 1940): An honourable person. For codpis, see n. 1682. Hunter (ed. 1972): The spiritual and the physical, the King (his grace) and the fool.…But Lear, like the cod-piece above…had children before he had wisdom.

1692–3 that’s…foole]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): He leaves it to Kent to decide which is which. Muir (ed. 1952): After the Fool’s allusion to the King as a codpiece in l. [1682], the audience, too, will share the ambiguity. Rosenberg (1972, p. 195): Fool may be describing…opposing pairs, among Kent, Lear, himself. Then the ambiguity spirals: which is lust, which love, which wisdom, which folly?

1693 wiseman]
See n. 1347.

1694 Alas]
See n. 1653.

1694 sit]
F’s are is ambiguous. Urkowitz (1983, p. 37): Lear might be sitting, even in the Folio;…[or] standing up to the elements. Cf. n. 1690. Weis (ed. 1993): Q’s implied SD is theatrically effective in conveying Lear’s exhaustion.

1694 Things]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Even those creatures.

1696 gallow]
Pope (ed. 1725): A West-country word, signifies to scare or frighten (OED, Gally v., quoting this l. as its first ex.). Delius (ed. 1854): Only instance of the verb in Sh.

1696 wanderer]
F’s wanderers agrees with them in 1697. Crook (ed. 1907): Fierce beasts which wander.

1697 makes]
On the common use of third-person plural in -s, see Abbott §333, Franz §155. Cf. 1034, 1070, 2608, 2658, 3019. Possibly the subject is the singular idea expressed in the previous clause: their terror (see Abbott §337).

1697 keepe]
OED (v. 33): Remain in. Cf. 1622+5, couch, and Luc. 1250, Caue-keeping.

1697 was man]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Arrived at manhood. OED (Man sb.1 1d): Assume[d] human nature, quoting this l.

1698 sheets]
OED (sb.1 7): A continuous extent…a. Of light, lightning.

1698 bursts]
Muir (ed. 1952): Peals (OED, sb. 3).

1699 grones]
OED (sb. 1b) quoting this l. as its first ex. of attribution to inanimate objects.

1700 nature]
See nn. 441, 1427.

1700 cary]
OED (Carry v. 39): Bear, endure, quoting this l. Bayfield (1920, p. 130): Completes an alexandrine.

1701 affliction…force]
Schmidt (1874), affliction: Any painful sensation (OED, sb. 2, 3). Though Weis (ed. 1993) explains Q’s force by metonymy—The awesome spectacle of the unleashed forces—, and Wells (ed. 2000) as meaning violence…of weather (OED sb.1 2d), the word makes a sense inferior to F’s generally accepted feare and may represent o/e, r/a, and c/r misreadings (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 395). Capell (1783, 1.2;163): The storm’s actual battery, and the terror inspir’d by it. Stone (1980, p. 225): On the other hand, perhaps a distinction is intended: psychological affliction, physical force. Foakes (ed. 1997) particularizes the feare: of the gods.

1702–12 Let…grace]
For thunderbolts as punishment of the guilty, see nn. 981–2, 1661–4. Craig (ed. 1931): Lear’s faith in the power of the gods…is the symbol of the retention of his sanity. When he loses his reason he loses also his faith in divinity. Edwards (ed. 1975): Having crie[d] out to the gale to obliterate a world which is unjust…in a moment of insight, he hears in the wind, rain, and thunder an apocalyptic voice challenging the values of the world…, unmasking the secret sinners. N. (1799, p. 790) cites as a parallel to this passage Lucretius, De rerum natura, 5.1217–25. C. (1855, p. 348), Collins (1904, p. 29), and Baldwin (1944, 2:532) compare Juvenal, Satire 13.192–5, 223–32. Hankins (1953, p. 88) finds a parallel in Palingenius’s Zodiake (tr. Googe, 1576, p. 3). Aberbach (1979, p. 132) cites Job 37:13; cf. nn. 1517, 1584. Following Armstrong (1949, p. 665), Bullough (1973, p. 412 n.) compares Sidney’s Arcadia 3.10.4 (ed. Feuillerat, 1:405), where Cecropia scoffs at the primitive attribution of thunder to some angrie body aboue, that spake so lowde.

1703 Powther]
Schmidt (1875): Turmoil. Kemshead (ed. 1875): Tumult, noise (OED, Pother sb. 2: Din). Q2’s Thundring is without authority, though striking (Doran, 1931, p. 33). F’s form pudder is rarer and dialectal (OED) and may not be Sh.’s, since in his only other use the word appears as poother (Cor. 2.1.218 [1137]). OED records one instance of pudder in 1609, Steevens (ed. 1778) finds it in Beaumont & Fletcher’s The Scornful Lady (1616) 2.2.92, and Tilley P619 records it in 1626; it seems somewhat more frequent in mid-century.

1704 find out]
OED (Find v. 20c): Discover the identity or true character of. Kittredge (ed. 1940): By the terror which such offenders must show [when they hear thunder]. Elton (1966, p. 205 n.) cites Tilley T118, When it thunders the Thief becomes honest, first recorded in 1640. Cf. Mac. 4.1.85–6 (1626–7).

1705, 1706 Vndivulged, vnwhipt]
OED quotes this l. as its first ex. of both words.

1706 of]
Abbott (§170): Placed before an agent (from whom the action is regarded as proceeding) where we use by. OED (prep. 15): Introducing the agent after a passive verb.…It is also occasional with ppl. adjs. in un-. Cf. Franz §519, and 1766, 3192.

1706 Iustice]
Lascelles (1973, p. 77): The first intimation of Lear’s preoccupation with Judgement and of the play’s several allusions to scenes from Doomsday, such as 2794–7, 3224–5.

1706–8 Hide…incestious]
Eds. obscure how many sinners Lear is addressing here. In the previous two lines he has addressed the wretch with undivulged and unpunished crimes, and he continues the theme of pent vp guilts to the end of the speech. It seems likely that 1706–10 specify particular kinds of undivulged crimes—bloody violence, perjury, incest, and secret murder. The agent committing the last and worst of these is told to shake; the previous three, each addressed in turn as thou in phrases ending with a comma, are told to Hide in terror. In Q the punctuation allows such a reading; in F the semicolon after hand, generally followed by modern editors, breaks the parallelism, leaves the ensuing line and a half without a verb, and gives the impression that the perjurer and the incestuous man may be the same person (though one sin hardly involves the other). Possibly Q’s meaning is thou bloody hand [that committed violence], thou perjured hand [that subscribed or gestured false witness], and thou man who has committed incest; the parallelism is imperfect but not lacking, since the bloody and perjured hands stand by metonymy for the first two sinful men. Alternatively, only bloudyhand may be a metonymy, possibly even a compound as the Q spacing suggests, and periur’d and simular are parallel adjectives: thou bloody-hand, thou perjured [man], and thou simular [i.e., dissembling] man. It is even possible that bloudyhand is a truncated participle, making three parallel adjectives qualifying man: thou bloudy-hand[ed], thou perjured, and thou simular man. Had F put a semicolon after Periur’d, its lines could have been read thou Bloudy hand; Thou Periur’d [one]; and thou [who art a] Simular of Vertue; the parallelism, though improved, would still have been inferior to Q’s.

1707 periur’d]
Craig (ed. 1901): Perjured one (OED, ppl. a. 1b: Absol. and quasi-sb., quoting this l. as its latest ex.). Furness (ed. 1880) rejects Theobald’s alteration (see textual nn.) to the noun Perjure (OED sb.1: Perjurer), found once elsewhere in Sh.: Where the QqFf all agree, and the sense is clear, change seems needless, although perjure with simular gives greater symmetry to the line.

1707 simular man]
F’s omission of man is possible because simular may be either noun or adjective (OED, One who…puts on a false appearance; Pretended, counterfeited); in Sh.’s only other use (Cym. 5.5.200 [3481]) it is an adjective, as in Q here. Abbott (§419a) thinks that here is a Transposition of adjectival phrase from the normal simular of virtue: The Elizabethans sometimes preferred to place the adjectival part…before, and the adverbial part after, the noun. Cf. 1981, 2181.

1708 incestious]
Deighton’s (ed. 1891) Unchaste is unsupported by OED, whose most extended meaning is adulterous (Incestuous a. 1b), first recorded in [1612]. Dundes (1976, p. 361) imagines that Lear refers to himself.

1708 Caytife]
See n. 999.

1708 in]
Cf. 418, shake in peeces. F’s indifferent variant to appears in AWW 4.3.169 (2274–5), shake them-|selues to peeces.

1709 couert…seeming]
Covert means literally hidden, but here means hiding (Joseph, ed. 1966). OED (a. 3a): Of persons:…sly, deceitful, quoting R3 3.5.33 (2119); (3b): Of words: Of hidden or obscure meaning. Seeming means Appearance (Schmidt, 1875; OED, vbl. sb. 1), as often in Sh. with a sense of speciousness or Hypocrisy (Lott, ed. 1974; OED, 3). Cf. n. 216.

1709 conuenient]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Suitable [OED a. 4]…such as may promote his purpose to destroy. Heath (1765, p. 339): Adapted to the views of the person who would seem to be what he was not. Hunter (ed. 1869): Seeming propriety (OED 5: Becoming; proper). Cf. 2418, 2877.

1710 hast]
Q’s verb is grammatically regular, F’s singular Ha’s may be defended: see n. 207. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 146): It may be a case of the northern s ending for the 2nd person singular. Presumably the change is scribal or compositorial.

1710 practised on]
Wright (ed. 1875): Plotted against. Cf. the noun in 502.

1710 Close]
Either an adjective, Hidden, secret (OED, adj. 4), or an adverb, Secretly (OED, adv. 2), Tightly (4); see also (C.Combinations.2): .…The adv. with participles, as…close-pent.

1710 guilts]
Schmidt (1874): Criminality (OED, sb. 5). Craig (ed. 1901): Guilty deeds (OED, 1). Cf. 1705, Vndivulged crimes.

1711 riue]
Page (ed. 1889): Rend, cleave (OED, v.1 1, 3, 4). In Q, possibly Pierce (3a, 3b) or To rend (the heart, soul, etc.) with painful thoughts or feelings (6).

1711 concealed centers]
F’s alliterative concealing Continents makes a regular line of verse and, despite a certain redundancy, better sense. Lear calls for stripping away the coverings that hide guilts, so that the guilts may be acknowledged and possibly forgiven. Johnson (ed. 1765), continent: That which contains or incloses (OED, sb. 1, quoting Ant. 4.14.40–1 [2873–4], Heart, once be stronger then thy Continent, | Cracke thy fraile Case). It is not so clear what could be meant in Q by splitting or piercing the hidden centers of guilt, unless centers means hearts (Becket, 1815, 1:157) or hidden cores (Weis, ed. 1993; Wells, ed. 2000). Van Dam (1935, p. 105): Obvious misprint in Q. Perhaps the Q compositor found a few letters illegible and guessed at a familiar word (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 396).

1711 cry]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Beg. OED (v. 1b): With the person addressed as indirect (dative) object, and the thing begged as direct object; esp. in to cry him mercy, and analogous phrases. Cf. 1952, 2014+26, 2950.

1712 summoners]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Officers that summon offenders before a proper tribunal (OED, sb. 2, quoting this l.). Hudson (ed. 1879): Lear is regarding the raging elements as the agents or representatives of the gods, calling criminals to judgment. Harrison (ed. 1937): The officers of the Ecclesiastical Court who summoned those guilty of immorality to appear. Muir (ed. 1952): Ministers of vengeance.

1712 grace]
Brooke (ed. 1947): Mercy (OED, sb. 15: Hence, pardon or forgiveness).

1712–13 I…sinning]
This sounds proverbial, but no proverb has been found. Tyrwhitt (in Steevens, ed. 1778) and C. (1855, p. 348) find a similar idea in Sophocles’ Oedipus at Colonus 266–7. Delius (ed. 1854): Lear places himself in direct contrast to the evildoers and sinners whom he has just spoken of (Ger.). Tovey (ed. 1896): The emphasis is on I. I am not the proper object of this vengeance of heaven. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Thus Lear points out his reason for not fearing the storm. Wilson (ed. 1960): Lear is not yet radically changed. Edwards (ed. 1975): One of the pinnacles of Lear’s vision.…He recognises his guilt, that he is a sinner; but he recognises also that he is not one of those criminals he has just talked of.…He neither excuses nor pities himself. Foakes (ed. 1997): If he is seen as still refusing to admit his own shortcomings, and failing to realize that the gods may be trying and punishing him as well as others, this remark will seem self-pitying.

1713 their]
F corrects this scribal or compositorial misreading to then. Duthie (1949, pp. 47, 57): Possibly then misread as ther.

1714 bare headed]
Foakes (ed. 1997): Kent’s concern here shows how unusual it would have been for a king to be out of doors with no hat, let alone in a storm. Cf. nn. 1622+7, 2625.

1715 gracious my Lord]
On the transposed adjective see n. 102.

1715 hard by]
Schmidt (1874): Close by (OED, adv.).

1715 houell]
Tovey (ed. 1896): An outhouse (OED, sb.1 1: An open shed…for cattle [etc.]); not necessarily A human habitation; a rude or miserable dwelling-place (2). Perrett (1904, p. 260): The hovel corresponds to that certain hollow rocke in the Arcadia [2.10.1; see ], which [hovel] Kent no doubt discovered while searching for the king. Bullough (1973, p. 330 n.) points to Cordila’s contrast of her former worldly pomp to her dungeon in Mirour (see ), esp. to From deinty beddes of downe, to be of strawe full fayne, comparing 1724; he concludes, This contrast may have led Shakespeare to invent the hovel and Lear’s realization of what poverty means.

1716 friendship]
OED (sb. 3): Friendly aid, quoting this l.

1716 lend]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Afford (OED, v.2 2).

1717 whilst]
The word, elsewhere spelled whil’st (2307+5, 3168+4), means the same as F’s while (1717).

1717 this]
Petz (ed. 1839): Gloster’s. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Used…to designate an object referred to, with an admixture of disdain and disgust; unattested in OED.

1717 hard]
Schmidt (1874): Unfeeling,…Cruel (OED, adj. 8, 12).

1717 house]
Harbage (ed. 1958): Household (both buildings and occupants). Cf. 1076.

1718 hard then is]
On F’s more harder than see n. 84.

1718 stone]
The comparison is proverbial: see Tilley S878.

1719 which]
Which household; see n. 1717.

1719 euen but now]
Abbott (§38): Both even now and but now can signify just at this moment, citing MV 3.2.169 (1516); cf. Franz §438. Verity (ed. 1897): After losing him, Kent had evidently gone back to see whether Lear had returned to Gloucester’s house.

1719 demaunding]
Valpy (ed. 1833): Inquiring. OED (Demand v. 8): Ask for or after, quoting this l. Deighton (ed. 1891): When I made inquiries. On the referent for the participle, see Abbott §378: The context often suggests a noun or pronoun—here I in 1717; cf. n. 1195.

1719 me]
F corrects to you. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 396): The compositor may have anticipated the me in the next line.

1720 denide]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Forbade (OED, Deny v. 9).

1720–1 force…curtesie]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Compel them to show that courtesy of which they are so niggard. Kent is unable to do this.

1721 scanted]
OED (ppl. a.): Stinted. Cf. n. 304.

1722–8 My…thee]
Bucknill (1867, p. 196): Shakespeare contemplated this exposure and physical suffering as the cause of the first crisis in the malady, Lear’s insanity. Granville-Barker (1927, pp. 174–5 n.): These lines show us some further battering at Lear’s sanity. Note in particular the ominously broken thoughts and sentences…and these, as ominously, are set between connected, reasoned passages. Hoeniger (1992, pp. 307 ff.) traces a gradual growth of insanity in Lear, beginning with his anger in 1.1 Bransom (1934, p. 91): Apparently for the first time since they entered the storm together, he notices his poor shivering fool. Lear’s infinite tenderness to his fool at this point is one of the sublimest and most touching things in the play. But it is something more. It is…Lear’s first act of disinterested kindness. Wilson (ed. 1960): From this point on he becomes aware of the sufferings of others.

1722 wit begins]
Though eds. all accept F’s wits begin, Q is perfectly correct, whether wit is understood as mind (OED, sb. 1), understanding, intellect, reason (2; see n. 677), or right mind,…sanity (4). Hoeniger (1992, p. 157): Reason or rather, one’s power of control over it. Cf. 2458, Least my braine turn. For F’s plural see n. 682.

1722 turne]
Schmidt (1875): Grow giddy (OED, v. 2b: To have a sensation as of whirling, quoting 2458). Cf. Shr. 5.2.20 (2558), TN 1.3.41 (157).

1723 dost]
For omission of the pronoun see n. 562.

1724 this straw]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Though no straw has been mentioned, it is implied by houell. Cf. n. 1715. Lott (ed. 1974), oddly: Thatched with straw, comparing 1825–6. But 2788 clearly refers to bedding, as here.

1724 fellow]
See n. 557.

1725–6 art…precious]
Hudson (ed. 1871): An allusion to alchemy, which was supposed to have the art of transmuting base metals into precious. Tovey (ed. 1896): But there is some notion also of experience, comparing 2669. Kittredge (ed. 1940) compares Marlowe, Dido, Queen of Carthage 1.1.169, See what strange arts necessitie findes out, and the proverb Necessity is the mother of invention (arts) (Tilley N61; cf. P527, Poverty is the mother of all arts). Foakes (ed. 1997) adduces Tilley V73, Make a Virtue of necessity. Neither Tilley nor Dent (1981) cites this l. to exemplify any of these proverbs. Kettle (1988; 1992, p. 24), in a Marxist reading: the context, when Lear is first beginning to feel his way towards a new freedom,…forbids any but a materialist significance.

1725 necessities]
See n. 1504.

1725 strange]
Page (ed. 1889): Rare, excellent (OED, a. 8, 9). But also (10): Unfamiliar, abnormal, or exceptional to a degree that excites wonder or astonishment; difficult to take in or account for; queer, surprising, unaccountable. So Brown (ed. 1976): Unheard of, odd.

1726 that]
F’s And weakens the logical connection between the two clauses. Possibly a misreading of yt as &.

1726 vild]
This variant of vile was extremely common from c 1580 to 1650 (OED). Cf. 1924, 2158, 2303+7, 2303+16, 2733. Page (ed. 1889): Cheap, worthless (OED, a. 5).

1726 you houell]
A vocative being unlikely, eds. accept F’s your.

1727 poore,]
Wilson (ed. 1960): An excellent example of Q’s defective comma punctuation.

1727 knaue]
See n. 573.

1727 part]
Hunter (ed. 1972): So as not to imply a radical limitation on Lear’s sympathy, perhaps we should read …sorry yet—for thee (I have a part of me still capable of feeling sorrow, and that part is concerned with you.)

1727 heart]
See n. 1029.

1727–8 of…That sorrowes]
F’s in…That’s sorry makes further unnecessary changes in this scene. Q gives a reading certainly not inferior (White, ed. 1862). On w/y variants see n. 2710.

1729–32 Hee…day]
Muir (ed. 1952): An adaptation of Feste’s song [TN 5.1.389–408]…and probably sung by the same actor [Robert Armin]. The Fool may be referring to Lear, or to himself. Bransom (1934, p. 91): Perhaps the song is to keep back the [Fool’s] tears. Noble (1923, pp. 85, 87, 149) supposes that the tune was newly popular, and later conjectures (see J. D. Wilson, ed. TN, 1930, pp. 92–101; Greg 1955, p. 297; Sternfeld, 1963, pp. 172–3 n.) that both Sh. and Armin may have provided words to it, first for Lr. and soon thereafter for a revival of a revised TN. Sternfeld notes that several phrases in the lyric reappear in Armin’s published works, though he is inclined to think Sh. the author of the song. So Seng (1967, p. 206): Sh. simply transplanted it [the song in Lr.] from the earlier play, changing the first and third lines, and a single word in the fourth, making it perfectly congruent with its surrounding text. The scene had opened with a paroxysm of rage; the serener pathos which closes the scene and Lear’s assent to the song’s moral prepares for his concern in 1809–17 about houselesse pouertie. For musical settings see and Gooch & Thatcher (1991, 1:636). Hunter (ed. 1972): Lear’s mention of his wits (line [1722]) reminds the Fool of the song, with its obviously appropriate refrain line, and he uses it to enshrine the lesson that our wits must be adapted to our fortunes. Dent (1981) doubtfully suggests the proverb Fools (Women) have wit enough to come in out of the rain (F537).

1729 a]
F’s and a also appears in the first line of Feste’s song (see prev. n.) and in Oth. 2.3.89 (1201; Q only). No satisfactory explanation of the and has been given. Dyce’s (ed. 1867, Gloss.) statement, Used redundantly, as it occasionally is in old ballads, is often repeated, but no such examples from ballads have been cited, and OED does not record such a use. Furness (ed. TN, 1901): A meaningless redundant expression, not uncommon in old ballads, where some syllables are needed to complete the measure; Idem (ed. Oth., 1886): It pieced out the line, giving a swing to the rhythm and a charm of homeliness to the verse which are to me as indescribable as they are indispensable; but the meter does not require it, and it does not appear in the Qq of Oth. or Lr. A sort of hum, a note in the music (Tovey, ed. 1896); It merely serves to carry a note in the tune (Kittredge, ed. 1940); but the earliest extant music, dating from 1772, has no note for such a syllable. J. Dover Wilson (ed. TN, 1930): Since it is not found in the Qq, It is possibly therefore an insertion of the playhouse musician entrusted with the arrangement of the songs. Abbott (§§95, 96) questionably assigns it the meaning and that too: I.e., a little and that a very little; cf. OED (And conj. 9). More possibly, he assigns it the meaning even; but OED (13) identifies such a quasi-adverbial use as a Latinism—perhaps unlikely in a ballad or fool’s song. Lott (ed. 1974): But, only, giving no support.

1729 little tine]
In its four occurrences in F tiny is spelled with terminal ne. OED (Tine adj.): App. always preceded by little. Skeat (1901, pp. 301): Originally a substantive, like bit.

1729 witte]
See n. 677.

1730 hey ho]
Though as used in the burden of songs this phrase derived from a nautical utterance marking heaving or hauling (OED, int., quoting this l.), it later blended with heigh-ho, F’s spelling here, indicating a sigh (OED, int. A).

1731 make…fit]
Most eds. follow Delius (ed. 1854), construing fit as a verb: Make contentment fit his fortunes (Ger.). The implication is that a tiny wit is unable to improve one’s fortunes. So Kittredge (ed. 1940): Must be contented and happy, even when his fortunes are bad. A few eds. seem to construe make content as be content, by analogy with such phrases as make mirth or make merry, though OED (Make v. 62, 69) does not list this phrase and Sh. does not use it elsewhere. Harrison (ed. 1948): Must be content with a fortune as slim as his wit, apparently taking fit as an adjective meaning appropriate (OED, a. 1, 2). The reading fortune’s fit is impossible, since fit meaning adjustment of dress (OED, sb.4 2) is a modernism. Milward (1987, p. 176), nonetheless: This is the lesson of I Tim. vi.6–8. Weis (ed. 1993) sees the remark as a warning to Lear, whose wit is turning.

1732 for]
In the song in TN (see n. 1729–32) the refrain begins For the rain throughout, and as here it means for bad fortunes are with us daily. F’s Though means even though his fortunes are all bad.

1733 True]
Kelcy (1932, p. 366): He may or may not mean that he has not much wit by giving his kingdom to Goneril and Regan, and now he will have to make content fit with the situation.

1733 come]
Addressed to Kent, as Capell (ed. 1768) first noted; cf. 1715–17.

1733 my good]
F’s omission destroys the pentameter, perhaps to fit the F column. Hogan (1962, p. 75): Its verse is neither a verse nor a partial verse, but a verse scotched at the head. F could have got in good, but not my good, even though the compositor began with the minimal speech-heading Le. The line is crowded by both a speech prefix and an Exit missing from Q.

1733 vs]
Wilson (ed. 1960): May include the Fool (cf. [1807]); but attractive to suppose it the royal plural, the sovereign formally commanding to be conducted to the straw-carpeted hut. In Q the Fool accompanies Lear; F’s added lines require his remaining behind.

1734–49 Foole.…time]
The Fool’s long solo address to the audience, consisting of an initial ribald joke followed by a comic mock-prophecy, because it interrupts both dramatic illusion and tragic mood for no obvious motive, has long been suspected to be un-Shn. Brown (1838, p. 292): The unfeeling players…have put into thy [i.e., the Fool’s] mouth words so foreign to thy nature, that they might, with as much propriety, be given to Cardinal Wolsey. White (ed. 1862): I believe [this is]…an interpolation. This loving, faithful creature would not let his old master go off half-crazed in that storm that he might stop and utter such pointless and uncalled-for imitation of Chaucer. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Clearly a scrap of ribaldry tacked on, by the actor who played the fool, to please the barren spectators…; just one of those instances of irrelevant and extemporaneous jesting to which Shakespeare himself, through his character of Hamlet, so strongly objects [Ham. 3.2.38–45 (1886–92)].…The fact of the Fool’s present speech occurring after Lear has left the stage, alone serves to condemn it as spurious. Cf. n. 923–4. Delius (1876, p. 136): It is [a] question whether Shakspere…took the trouble to introduce a stereotyped fool’s interlude merely meant to amuse the public, particularly as the drama rather required curtailing than amplifying? Hudson (ed. 1879): The whole passage, besides being a stark impertinence dramatically, is as unlike Shakespeare as it is unlike the Fool; unlike Shakespeare, I mean, in poetical texture and grain. Tovey (ed. 1896): We must keep it out of sight in forming our conception of the Fool. Bradley (1904, p. 452): Spurious. (1) The scene ends characteristically without the lines. (2) They are addressed [not in Shakespeare’s way] directly to the audience. (3) They destroy the pathetic and beautiful effect of the immediately preceding words of the Fool, and also of Lear’s solicitude for him. (4) They involve the absurdity that the shivering timid Fool would allow his master and protector, Lear and Kent, to go away into the storm and darkness, leaving him alone. (5) It is also somewhat against them that they do not appear in the Quartos. At the same time I do not think one would hesitate to accept them if they occurred at any natural place within the dialogue. Tolstoy (1906; 1937, 21:321): The fool…utters a prophecy quite unrelated to the situation. Goggin (ed. 1910): A tactless and senseless anti-climax. Warde (1913, p. 210): Though usually the first soliloquy [is] the keynote to the character, here the shrewd satire of the parabolical epigrams…would indicate a worldly wisdom and embittered sarcasm, rather than the loyalty and love which is his distinguishing characteristic. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 201): Certainly spurious. Its own incongruity can be left out of the question; its offense against the dramatic situation disallows it. The very heart of this is Lear’s new-found care for the shivering drenched creature at his side.…Shakespeare is incapable—so would any other dramatist in his senses be—of stultifying himself by despatching Lear from the scene immediately after, and letting him leave the Fool behind him. Chambers (1930, 1:466): Generally, and I think rightly, taken as an incongruous theatrical interpolation. Doran (1931, pp. 66–7): It is poor stuff to have been added by Shakespeare.…It is in a position where [an actor’s] interpolation might occur; it is spoken at the end of the scene, after Kent and Lear have left the stage. If the speech is an interpolation, it must have been written into the prompt-book. Budd (ed. 1935): A pointless mixture of statements of everyday happenings and of possibilities as remote as the destruction (confusion) of England itself. Hart (1942, p. 147): Crude clowning. Parrott (1949, p. 303): It is the Clown’s direct address to the audience and must have gotten into the text after Shakespeare severed his connection with the company and retired to Stratford. Lott (ed. 1974): Pointing out an anachronism and making a joke of it…sounds un-Shakespearian. Stone (1980, p. 242): The style, the irrelevant subject-matter, the clumsy rupture of dramatic illusion…; the printing of [1746] as one [line] and [its] apparent misplacement (suggesting a misreading of marginal addenda)—all indicate a theatrical interpolation for which the reviser cannot be held responsible. Richman (1986, p. 381): The lines stop the action. I do not think their presence compensates for the loss of the first-act sequence [669+1–+11].…Having newly taken pity on the drenched and shivering Fool, Lear would never leave him alone on stage to chatter about malt and tailors. Bratton (ed. 1987): Tate, and eighteenth- and nineteenth-century actor-editors…, simply cut this as an intrusive interpolation that detracted from the pathos of Lear’s exit.…It was commonly cut, for its obscurity and dramatic difficulty, up to 1970; but after that point the satirical Utopian vision it contains began to be recognised by socially and politically oriented interpreters of the play as of central significance.…Edward Bond pronounced that it was the most important speech in the play.
Partisans of the Folio and more recently those maintaining that F Lr. represents a Shn. revision also defend the speech, often making a virtue out of its egregiousness. Koppel (1877, p. 80) sees a later Shn. addition: The poet was generous to this, the most amiable of all his Fools, and even added somewhat to his part (Ger.). Weis (ed. 1993, p. 20): It is not impossible that a revising dramatist…realizing that Poor Tom would be usurping the Fool’s part as Lear’s confidant, decided to put the Fool at the centre of the action here…through a soliloquy. Fleay (1879, p. 119), fancifully: F preserves lines that a censor deleted from Q: James would not have tolerated even so distant a prospect of a time when the realm of Albion should come to great confusion, and any allusion to the cutpurse who came to the throng during his first progress is known to have been very obnoxious to him; see J. Nichols, Progresses…of King James I, 1828, 1:89. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxii): The censor condemned it as unmeet for the ears of the King’s Majesty. The mere allusion to the poore Knight in debt was enough. Fleay and Adee think Q is a theater version; but see . Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): The subtle double irony…and the hit at anachronisms such as are involved not only in the Merlin allusion but in quoting Chaucer, make just the sort of elaborate fooling more likely to be devised by an author for a fool’s mouth than by the fool himself impromptu in the course of acting. Why Shakespeare should not be the fittest and likeliest person so to adapt another great poet’s trifle in verse, suiting it to a trifling use of his own in the speech of the fool, who is one of his wisest, it is hard to see. Taylor (1983, p. 410) argues against unauthorized interpolation by the clown, since Armin left the company before Sh. did and no later clown had his reputation or power. Mackail (1930, p. 22): The verses…are stigmatized as an interpolation simply because they do not fit in to the artificial picture…[of the sympathetic, sentimentalized fool], or because they jar on the good taste of critics. Shakespeare is above the rules of good taste. Bethell (1944, pp. 85–6): The references to religion, to the disturbed social order…, to the distribution of wealth, and to sexual sin, are significant, since these very themes are of major importance in the play itself. Under a cloak of nonsense, the prophecy collects a number of the Lear themes in the form of a popular broadside, and with contemporary application.…Direct address to the audience shatters all possibility of dramatic illusion, in order to make clear the need for alert cross-reference between ancient and contemporary Britain.…The style is deliberately simplified and pedestrian…to parody the broadside manner; but the lines are not doggerel, and a suggestion of speech rhythm…indicates the work of an accomplished writer of verse. Brooke (ed. 1947): Comic relief, which at this point is badly needed. Empson (1951, p. 137): Mr. Bethell rightly pointed out that this joke makes the clown step out of the remote period as a contemporary, and that Edgar as Poor Tom is also a contemporary figure belonging to the Elizabethan unemployment problem. The shock of the thing depended on its realism. Munro (ed. 1957): The verse is typical of the Fool’s utterances; we should expect reference to Merlin who was much associated with early Britain; and the concluding lines fix the even earlier period of the action. Main (ed. 1962): A satiric parody of the new, purified heaven and earth that follows the apocalyptic dissolution.…The realm of England would be utterly destroyed by such perfection. Zitner (1967, pp. 79–80): The end of III.ii shows us Lear…being led to shelter at last. And the beginning of iii shows us Gloucester having second and better thoughts about his duty toward the King. Between these events we require the Fool’s [satiric, pessimistic] utterance lest we be misled by some slight hope that there is for Albion a possibility other than confusion. Vickers (1968, pp. 363–4): The effect of this speech [is] to detach him from his relationship to Lear and to restore his role as the Fool, a device analogous to that whereby Edgar is given verse soliloquies to remind us of his real part. Edgar’s real part is still within the world of the play, however; even in soliloquy he does not step out of it to address the audience. Hoeniger (1974, p. 91): His joke…amounts to Shakespeare winking at his audience: we all know by now, don’t we, that whatever this play is, it is not a chronicle history. Brown (ed. 1976): Sometimes used…as a Brechtian alienation device. The fool…mak[es] no attempt to sustain a dramatic illusion or to motivate the parting from Lear.…Other plays then current allowed fools such liberty; he gives no ex. Gorfain (1977, p. 253): As the Fool steps out of the frame of the Lear world to speak to us, he violates rules of order just as his prophecy does…, join[ing] now and then, life and art.…The Fool’s forecast enigmatically foretells the future by describing the present. His subject…is confusion. Moreover, its means are confusing. Weimann (1967; 1978, p. 43): The inverted form of the Fool’s prophecy should be accepted as it stands, and its obscurity viewed as a nonsensical and nonrepresentational heritage from the topsy-turvy patterns of the popular tradition of the folk-play. Booth (1978, p. 107): The prophecy duplicate[s] the general pattern of the play by failing to come to a conclusion when it signals one. Kerrigan (1983, pp. 221–6): The speech marks an important stage in the Fool’s extrication of himself from the action.…The speech dramatizes…the F Fool’s growing sense of his own irrelevance.…As he recites Merlin’s prophecy, the F Fool begins to leave Lear. Halio (ed. 1992, p. 282 n.): But this view is inconsistent with the Fool’s lines about the knave who runs away, [1354–7]. Foakes (1985, p. 39; 1993, p. 102) also denies to the Fool any sense of irrelevance or imminent departure: The effect in the Folio of foregrounding the Fool with a kind of epilogue or farewell speech…is to give him a greater prominence here than in the Quarto, and his prophecy symbolises the topsy-turvy, disordered world that Lear has brought about. Indeed (1993, p. 195; cf. 1985, p. 41), The speech has a generalizing force, like the songs in a Brecht play, stressing the larger impact of Lear’s division of the kingdom, and satirically linking disorder and corruption in the play with the corruptions the audience would be aware of in their own society. Possibly, but Lr. is anything but a Brechtian play; the larger impact of his division includes attempted regicide, patricide, fratricide, and adultery, civil unrest, foreign invasion, and war; and nothing in the Fool’s prophecy limits verbose sermons, watered beer, foppery, venereal infection, slander, petty theft, etc. to either Lear’s or the audience’s time, nor makes them the effect of Lear’s division; they are more general (and trivial) failings, and are satirized as such. They have nothing in particular to do with Lear’s deeds, and except for one or two passing references to foppish dress, legal corruption, usury, and venereal burning, none of them is a theme (Bethell) or any significant part of the play. Booth (1983, pp. 41–3): The confusions in this speech between fool and wise fool, present fact and prophetic future, and play and audience are typical of indefinition throughout the play. Wittreich (1984, pp. 47, 49): This utterance…is what the play itself is: a warning prophecy full of apocalyptic suggestion. The Fool’s prophecy thus imparts a political edge to King Lear.…Neither spurious nor irrelevant, the Fool’s prophecy is essential to King Lear—a quintessential manifestation of its cosmos. So read, the speech is essential to Wittreich’s apocalyptic reading of the play. He finds in it (p. 70) a possible reminiscence of Isaiah’s prophecy (Isa. 24) of God’s utter despoiling and dissolution of the earth, though the Fool hardly predicts that.
Dobin (1990, pp. 195–6, 235–6), less concerned with the prophecy’s authorship than its chronology: When Shakespeare wrote Lear,…Merlin’s prophecies were popularly…vindicated and glorified by the reunification of England and Scotland under James.…To mock Merlin’s predictions as nonsensical babble…could have had unpleasant repercussions for the playwright and the company. Probably the Fool’s prophecy was not performed in 1606 and did not appear in whatever text served as the source for the 1608 Quarto [but was added in a later revision].…As the Stuart regime wore on, Merlin and his prophecies were subjected to…more stinging parody in the public theater, such as in Rowley’s Birth of Merelin. It is unclear why Shakespeare would have added the prophecy later.

1734 braue]
Schmidt (1874): Fine (OED, adj. 3, quoting this l.).

1734 night]
Hunter (ed. 1972): A pun on knight would explain the sudden switch to medieval parody in the lines following.

1734 coole a Curtizan]
I.e., would cool even a hot whore. Partridge (1947, p. 93), cool: Cool the sexual heat. Bevington (ed. 1992): Put courtesans off from streetwalking (?). Skillan (ed. 1967), more fancifully: Turn a harlot to repentance. McCann (ed. 1964), questionably: Make use of a harlot. The Fool lewdly pretends that the group is entering a brothel.

1735 Prophesie]
The thirteen lines that follow imitate, somewhat, a six-line 14th- and 15th-c. jingle widely known in Sh.’s time as Chaucer’s prophecy. In one of the seventeen surviving MS versions (see R. H. Robbins & J. L. Cutter, Supplement to the Index of Middle English Verse, 1965, no. 3943) the (eight) verses are titled Prophecia merlini doctoris perfecti; these are printed by Walter W. Skeat in Chaucerian and Other Pieces (Oxford, 1897), pp. lxxxi f.; cf. p. [450]. The Welsh magician Merlin of Arthurian legend had prophesied British supremacy over the Saxons; this poem, predicting instead the downfall of England as the result of corruption, is an example of the indiscriminate assigning of Merlin’s name to political vaticinations. See n. 1749. Campbell (1914, p. 196): It was first printed by Caxton at the end of an edition containing Chaucer’s Anelida and Purse, from a ms. (Trin. Coll. Cam. ms, R 3 15) where it chanced to stand among a number of genuine Chaucerian poems. Thynne included it in his edition of Chaucer, 1532.…It was reprinted in the editions of 1542 and 1550, and in the editions of Stow and Speght [1561, 1598, 1602]; but in none of these editions was it definitely ascribed to Chaucer. In the first ed. (1532) it appears as follows: Whan faithe fayleth in preestes sawes | And lordes hestes are holden for lawes | And robbery is holden purchace | And lechery is holden solace | Than shal the londe of Albyon | Be brought to great confusyon. This jingle was frequently quoted from or alluded to in Sh.’s time, always as Chaucer’s prophecy, not Merlin’s. Blayney (privately) notes its appearance in John Willis, The Art of Stenographie (1602, sig. D4), on the same page with some rhyming proverbs about thrift similar to one or two lines of the Fool’s verses in 648–57. As Steevens (ed. 1773) points out, it appears also in Puttenham’s The Arte of English Poesie (1589, p. 232) as an example of merismus, or the distributor, a rhetorical figure of amplification. Because Puttenham’s quotation refers to the Realme rather than the londe of Albion, and Sh. appears in WT to have been familiar with Puttenham, Taylor (1983, pp. 382–5) argues that Sh. was the author of the F addition; but Puttenham, whose book was issued twice in 1589, was read by and influenced many writers (see G. D. Willcock & A. Walker, eds., 1936, pp. vii, xi f.), including Ben Jonson, who owned a copy. Taylor argues further that Puttenham influenced the theme of the Fool’s prophecy. In fact, except for one line (1746), the words priests and law, and the When…then form, there is little exact correspondence between Chaucer’s prophecy and the longer passage in Lr., though they share the general theme that injustice and corruption lead to a country’s downfall. Davidson (1992, p. 91): A stenographer could have left out the lines…since a version of them appeared in [Willis’s] Stenographie, and then could have neglected to replace the passage in the longhand manuscript he made from his notes. But Q1 Lr. is almost certainly not a stenographic text (see ), and the two versions of the prophecy are quite dissimilar. Cutts (1972, p. 263) discusses a mid-17th-c. eight-line version that closely follows some of the lines in Lr. in changed order. Busby (1923, pp. 69–70) compares similar fools’ prophecies, of Haphazard in Appius and Virginia (1575), beginning When gain is no grandsire, and of Frog in The Faire Maid of Bristowe (1605 [4?]), beginning When tinkers leave to drinke good ale. Leggatt (1992, p. 194): The anti-Catholic satire of [Dekker’s] The Whore of Babylon [1606–7] includes a mock-prophecy along similar lines. Serious prophecies in the when…then form are spoken by Oseas and Jonas in Greene & Lodge, Looking Glass for London 4.5.
Many see the passage as a satire of prophecy itself. Knight (ed. 1840): Nor was the introduction of such a mock prophecy mere idle buffoonery. There can be no question, from the statutes that were directed against these stimulants to popular credulity [e.g., Statute 5, Elizabeth c. XV], that they were considered of importance in Shakspere’s day. Bacon’s essay Of Prophecies shows that the philosopher gravely denounced what our poet pleasantly ridiculed. Taylor (1911, p. 129): Shakspere introduced…a parody on the paradoxical prophecy. and showed by the words he puts into the mouth of the speaker his contempt for the whole tradition from Merlin down. Hawkes (1960, pp. 331–2) likewise sees the speech as broadly satiric of the conventional form of the merlinesque prophecy. Hobday (1979, pp. 72–3): Shakespeare’s own attitude to prophecies was extremely sceptical. Those of Peter Pomfret, the spirit in 2 Henry VI and the witches in Macbeth are all fulfilled, but in a different sense from that understood by those who put their trust in them, and Buckingham in Henry VIII is ruined by his faith in prophecies. Shakespeare’s Hotspur dismisses the famous Mouldwarp prophecy…as skimble-skamble stuff (1 Henry IV III.i.148). The rude harsh-sounding rhymes of the popular prophecy are burlesqued in the fool’s prophecy…, which passes from satire to irony and in the final attribution to Merlin, whose supposed prophecies were used as political propaganda from the middle ages at least until the Restoration, becomes almost surrealist in its humour. Dent (1981, F526.1) doubtfully suggests a proverb, Fools and children prophesy. Kerrigan (1983, pp. 224–5): Lr. is preoccupied with prophecy, and the expectations (predictions) of characters and audience are frequently frustrated. What he tells us, the play confirms: that the only safe prediction is not. For the Fool’s prophecy is a studiously careful exercise in the avoidance of prophecy, citing 1749. Wittreich (1984, p. 47): The Fool’s prophecy imparts a parodic element that targets not prophecy in general but rather those [anti-Stuart] prophecies current in England which saw in the termination of Elizabeth’s reign the ruin of a nation.
