In its parody of this form of (often Merlinesque) prophecy, the Fool’s prophecy harbors a compliment in its criticism of a king who, even if sometimes foolish, is finally no fool. None of these commentators explains why Sh. or anyone else should have added such a satire at this point in the play. Carroll (1988, p. 243) notes wryly that defenders of Shakespearean revision in F do not object to this speech of the Fool on the grounds they use to justify cuts of several Q passages, even though his speech suffers all the same alleged liabilities as the mock-trial and Edgar’s speech in 3.6—that it is untheatrical, impedes the narrative momentum, is an eccentric digression likely to tire the audience, etc.: The Folio reviser can do no wrong.

1736–48 When…feet]
Warburton (1739, p. 198), noticing two contrary inferences (1746, 1747–8), argued that This is not one but two prophecies: 1. The first a satyrical description of the present manners as future [1736–9: i.e., Now]: 2. And the second a satyrical description of future manners, which the corruption of the present manners would prevent from ever happening [1740–5: i.e., Never]. He accordingly moved 1747–8 to follow 1739, thus ending each description with its proper deduction. Edwards (1748, p. 7): I shall not dispute…whether it is necessary to make the fool divide his discourse with the method and regularity of a sermon. Capell (1783, 1.2:165–6): Warburton’s transposition is destructive of humour, and of the speaker’s wild character which disclaims regularity. Malone (ed. 1790): It is as unnecessary as it is unwarranted. Capell imagines that the second part was intended as a substitute for the first but that, the latter remaining in the promptbook, both were printed by mistake. Brooke (ed. 1947): The first four lines describe conditions current in Shakespeare’s England; the next six describe absurdly utopian conditions; and the conclusion…is that when these things come together, the realm of Albion will be in great confusion. Wilson (ed. 1960) makes a bipartite division similar to Warburton’s but transposes the two conclusions. When things shall be as in fact they are, Britain will be in a state of ruin, as in fact she is; when things shall be as they should be, then walking will customarily be done with feet, i.e. the proper order will prevail, and men will walk uprightly—but no one will ever live to see this. Note that [1746 is] set as a single line in F, which suggests a marginal insertion misplaced. Stone (1980, p. 121 n.) agrees: The book-keeper, in writing out the interpolated speech (perhaps on a separate slip), must have accidentally omitted this couplet and inserted it later in the margin without showing its division into two lines. The compositor [or scribe] then committed a double error in setting the two lines as one and inserting them at the wrong point. Hawkes (1960, p. 332) objects to Wilson’s heavy-handed reordering as destroying the whole point of the speech: it is a parody of the conventional merlinesque political prophecy (see prev. n.) because of its delicate and delightful misplacing of the traditional prediction of Albion’s confusion, in such a way that the whole passage is rendered meaningless (or…foolish); the Fool should not be made to speak apparent good sense. Similarly Zitner (1967, p. 79): The waywardness of the law, the debts of knights and squires were proverbial, apparently irremediable.…And a Utopia with cutpurses, however forbearing, usurers, however secure, bawds and whores, however pious, is no Utopia at all. The speech, for all its apparent shift at [1740], is in tone satiric throughout, and in matter an expression of the incorrigibility of man.…No wonder, then, the burlesque aspect of the conclusion.…All prophecy is nonsense. Weimann (1967; 1978, p. 42): The prophecy provides both a vision of Utopia and an inversion of it. Weis (ed. 1993): The Fool is saying…that both the world as it is and the world as ideally it would be are equally confusing and meaningless.

1736 more…matter]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Better in talk than in substance; or better in preaching than in practice. See n. 398. Wilson (ed. 1960) compares Ham. 2.2.95 (1123). Harbage (ed. 1958), oddly: I.e. can outshine the gospel message (at present their ability to speak is quite unworthy of their theme). Creighton (1913, pp. 8, 75): The prophecy is a manifestation of England’s struggle to free itself from religious servitude and priestcraft.

1737 marre…water]
Spoil by dilution. Malt is roasted barley or other grain (OED, sb. 1, quoting this l.), which is brewed into beer by infusion, boiling, and fermenting. Diluting the wort excessively with water as an economy results in thin or small beer.

1738 Nobles]
Stone (1980, p. 121): Possibly an improper allusion…[to] the King himself, who affected to tutor his favourites— in 1607 or 1608 Robert Carr, and from 1614 onwards George Villiers.

1738 are…Tutors]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Invent fashions for them. Hunter (ed. 1869): Dictate fashions to them. Schmidt (ed. 1879): Better understand the handicraft. Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): Pay so much attention to clothes that they can instruct their tailors. Kittredge (ed. 1940) compares Petruchio’s captious treatment of the Tailor in Shr. 4.3.86 ff. (2071 ff.). Harbage (ed. 1958): Are no longer subservient to fashion. Wilson (ed. 1960): A glance at fantastic developments in male dress. Possibly the nobles will teach their tailors to make more fantastic clothing than they would ordinarily produce. Other readings are less probable. Delius (ed. 1854): Taking care of their tailors, and not ruining them by failing to pay their bills (Ger.). But that is not what tutor means. Moberly (ed. 1876), fancifully: Paying their bills by initiation into fashionable life instead of cash. Edwards (ed. 1975): When proud aristocrats are reduced to taking employment as tutors in the families of the working-men.

1739 Heretiques]
Stone (1980, p. 121): The last heretics to be burned in England [the Arminian Edward Wightman and Bartholomew Legate] went to the stake in 1612.…In 1618 the King reprieved a Portuguese ex-monk.…The observation…would make little sense before 1612, or for some time after, and…would not altogether pass for apt or accurate until the latter part of 1618. Kerrigan (1983, pp. 221–3): But the last burnings in Jacobean England were also the first.…James’s tolerant attitude towards Heresie was widely remarked. It was a matter…in some quarters of grave concern.…The couplet…could…have been written between about 1606 and 1611. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 131): Unlikely to have been written after 14 December 1611. In fact burning of heretics had been almost non-existent for a half-century. Mary, beginning in 1555, had burned some three hundred victims in three-and-a-half years. Foxe’s Book of Martyrs associated the practice with papism. The Act of Parliament authorizing it was repealed in 1559, and Elizabeth preferred to control heresy by fines, exile, or, when treasonous, by hanging and evisceration. Two burnings in 1575 and one in 1588 were rare exceptions. Romeo had referred to the burning of heretics (Rom. 1.2.91 [340]); neither his nor the Fool’s remark here need be a topical allusion; both refer to love-heresy. The Sokols (2000, p. 132): Here the senselessness of burning heretics is suggested.

1739 burn’d…Sutors]
The double meaning depends on two senses of wench: maid, and wanton woman (OED, sb. 1, 2). Heresy in the worship of love is an idea elsewhere referred to by Sh. (e.g., Rom. 1.2.91 [340], Ado 1.1.235 [227], TN 1.5.228 [520]). Hunter (ed. 1972): When love is more important than religion. Lott (ed. 1974): Only men who get girls into trouble [are made to suffer]; but such men are not necessarily Heretiques. Edwards (ed. 1975): Heretics…because they are faithless. So Bevington (ed. 1988): When heresy is a matter, not of religious faith, but of perjured lovers. Hoeniger (ed. 1968), suitors: I.e. libertines. Johnson (ed. 1765): The disease to which wenches suitors are particularly exposed was called…the brenning or burning (OED, vbl. sb. 4; Williams, 1994). Craig (ed. 1901) cites Err. 4.3.57 (1238–9), Tim. 4.3.142 (1756), Cor. 3.2.24 (2111). Brown (ed. 1976): Alternatively, the flames of love. Orgel (ed. 1999): Either the only people who burn are lovers (who burn with passion), or the only heretics who burn are faithless lovers (who burn with venereal disease).

1740 right]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Genuine or just.

1741 nor no]
On the double negative see n. 427+1.

1741 poore Knight]
Tovey (ed. 1896): The crown had exorbitant claims on tenures by knight-service. Moreover, under James I., many were knighted who had not wealth to keep up their dignity. See n. 1089–90.

1742 liue in Tongues]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Are actively circulated.

1743 Cut-purses]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Literally, thieves who slash purses (worn as a pouch at the girdle) and steal the contents; then, in general, pickpockets (OED). In Marlowe’s Massacre at Paris, sc. 14, the Cutpurse cuts off gold buttons.

1743 come…throngs]
Wilson (ed. 1960) compares WT 4.4.685–6 (2567–8), euery Shop, Church, Session, Hanging, yeelds a carefull man worke.

1744 Vsurers]
Hunter (ed. 1972): A part of city life, opposed to the traditional agricultural sources of wealth. Perhaps gold i’the field refers to grain, so that the phrase means when usurers turn farmers, or perhaps are willing to lend to farmers. See below.

1744 tell]
See n. 1327.

1744 i’th’Field]
Harbage (ed. 1958): Instead of in secret places. Lott (ed. 1974): In the open, not secretly for shame. Orgel (ed. 1999): Because they have nothing to hide. Halio (ed. 1992): Moneylenders [were] notorious for secrecy. Danby (1945, p. 20) finds in this line and the next an ambiguity of interlocking contraries: present corruption is mixed with Utopia; This is either complete conversion or utter brazenness: we can have it both ways.

1745 Churches build]
Muir (ed. 1952): As a sign of repentance. Edwards (ed. 1975): It was a common libel that women made fortunes out of vice, then turned pious and used the money for charitable ends.

1746 Albion]
See n. 5. William Harrison’s Description of England, in Holinshed’s Historie (1577, p. 5; 1587, 1:4) devotes a ch. to Albion, fourth son of Neptune, who was made by his father king of the Isle of Britayne and who changed its name to his. Spilsbury & Marshall (ed. 1905): The island of Great Britain, so named from its ancient inhabitants, the Albiones. Aristotle mentions the islands of Albion and Ierne [Hibernia] four hundred years before the invasion of Britain by Julius Caesar, so the common notion that the name was given by Caesar in allusion to the White Cliffs (Lat. Albus = white) has no foundation. The pseudo-Aristotelian references (De mundo 3; cf. Stobaeus, Ecl. Phys. 1.34.73) repeat the description of a Massilian captain c. 525 B.C. quoted by Avienus, Ora Maritima 5.108.

1746 Then…confusion]
Halio (ed. 1973): The fact that F prints two verses on the same line suggest[s] some confusion either by the collator [preparing F copy], the compositor, or both. Not necessarily. The fact that the F column is somewhat crowded, containing three turned-over lines and three stage-directions on the same lines as text, suggests that the F compositor may simply have been economical of space here by setting two short verses in one line. Hulme (1970, p. 533) finds a meaningful echo of line 1722, pointing to the source of Lear’s mental confusion: the when that for Lear (both as king and father) could never happen, has turned before his eyes into what others have foreseen. Edwards (ed. 1975): In so far as the prophecies are happening now, England…is already in confusion; in so far as they are unrealisable ideals, there would certainly be confusion of the present state if they were to come about. Wittreich (1984, p. 69), discussing the When…Then formula for prophecies, quotes from The Prophecie of Berlington lines which conclude, Then shal the Land of Albany, Be put to great Perplexity.

1746 confusion]
Harbage (ed. 1958): Ruin (ironic: an edifice of abuses is ruined by reform). Skillan (ed. 1967): Will find itself confounded…[to] realize that the above things are not but should be.

1747 who]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): If anybody.

1748 going]
Schmidt (1874): To walk (OED, vbl. sb. 1a, 1c).

1748 vs’d with feet]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): An intentionally absurd truism—such as fools frequently pronounced with a solemn air as a burlesque on the philosophers’ profound adages. The audience is at liberty to make it mean: The world shall once more be in a normal condition. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Men shall walk uprightly. Edwards (ed. 1975): These things are happening now—the bad things; when the good things happen, we shall actually be behaving in the proper manner.

1749 Merlin]
Upton (1748, p. xix): This Merlin is the prophet Dan Geoffrey Chaucer (see n. 1735). Moberly (ed. 1876): Perhaps by this name Shakspere may have meant his great forerunner [Chaucer],…quoting him as he does the dead shepherd Marlowe in AYL. In 1H4 3.1.148 (1680) Sh. refers to the dreamer Merlin and his prophecies, and would have known him as the type of seers and prophets (Verity, in Irving & Marshall, ed. 1889, quoting Greene’s Address to Perimedes the Blacke-Smith, 1588 [sig. A3]: propheticall spirits as bred of Merlins race). Merlin’s prophecies were translated into Latin by Geoffrey of Monmouth (who also wrote a life of Merlin) and appeared in a section of his Historia (ca. 1135) not many pages from the story of Leir. Though the prophecies were printed in English in 1499, 1510, 1529, and 1603, Shakespeare probably derived his knowledge of Merlin’s prophecies from Holinshed (Muir, ed. 1952). Spenser treats of some of Merlin’s marvels in F.Q. 3.2.18–21 and gives a prophecy of England’s future in 3.3.21–49; and an apocryphal Shn. play, The Birth of Merlin (1608?), includes earls of Cornwall and Gloucester and a courtier Oswald. Boswell (ed. 1821, 3:463) notes that Merlin’s name had long been invoked by political reformers (see Taylor, 1911, passim) and more recently by religious activists. Whalley (1748, p. 37): The Fool may hint at certain Forgeries of that kind which were newly coined by the Papists, citing Bp. Joseph Hall’s Virgidemiarum (1597–8) and James Maxwell’s Admirable and Notable Prophecies (1615). Harsnett alludes to neither Merlin nor prophecies. Wittreich (1984, p. 60): Subsequent to Geoffrey, Merlin’s prophecies invaded the chronicle histories not only to identify the tendencies that were laying Great Britain to waste but to set national history within the context of the Antichrist legend and the story of the Last Judgment.

1749 before his time]
See n. 39. Tovey (ed. 1896): The point of this sorry jest is that the place of Lear and his times, and therefore of the fool, is long prior, in the legends of Ancient Britain, to that of Arthur, to whose story Merlin, the famous prophet and magician, belongs. Phelps (ed. 1917): The Fool would have lived about 1300 years before Merlin. Hunter (ed. 1972), citing Geoffrey of Monmouth: Lear lived during the eighth century b.c., and Arthur during the sixth century a.d. Following Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) (see n. 1734–49), Creizenach (1916, p. 156): A hit at the pedants who charged [Sh.] with anachronisms. Harrison (ed. 1937): Mock pedantry from Shakespeare, who was not usually careful about his historical sequence. Kittredge (ed. 1940): This line makes the Fool a real prophet.

1751 <Scæna Tertia>]
Buck (ed. 1907): This scene brings the plot and the underplot together. From this time on their threads are tightly interwoven. Budd (ed. 1935): In their sordidness these scenes [3, 5] form a striking contrast to the surrounding magnificence of the storm scenes. Bransom (1934, p. 91): The time allows Lear to wander…[to] the hovel. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The same stormy night as in Scene ii. Gloucester means to find Lear and relieve him. He finds him in the next scene [1890].

1751 with lights]
Granville-Barker (1927, p. 230): The Q SD shows,…if nothing else does, the use of the inner stage for this scene. This is hardly necessary. The torches or candles may simply indicate the nighttime setting. Foakes (ed. 1997): The usual theatrical technique at the Globe, where plays were performed by daylight, for suggesting an interior night scene. Unlike Foakes, Wells (ed. 2000) infers a scene outside Gloucester’s dwelling. Either is possible. Adams (1948) questionably assumes use of the upper stage; see n. 333. Possibly the omission of the SD from F reflects performance on the Blackfriars’ indoor, candle-lit stage.

1753–70 Alacke…careful]
All eds. since F print these lines as prose, but the last speech in the scene is in verse, and these lines also make passable verse if 1753–64 are divided as in Q (with Go toe completing 1758), if We…King is left as a short line, and if the remaining lines are divided naturally where commas occur, after releeue him, Duke, Perceiued, bed, me, releeued, and careful. It is altogether possible that the Q compositor followed the verse division in the MS until being thrown off by a short line. Doran (1931, p. 108): The quarto prints correctly the first six lines as verse:…[they are] printed as prose in the folio, whose extrametrical substitution (see n. 1756) suggests a deliberate, even if slight, effort to turn the passage into prose. It does not seem likely that…the printer of the folio was using Q1 as copy.

1753 this,]
Another instance of Q’s mispunctuation; but it may suggest that the compositor perceived verse division in the MS: see prev. n.

1753–4 Vnnaturall dealing]
Muir & Danby (1950, p. 49): Sh. seems to have taken the the phrase from Sidney’s Arcadia 2.10.2 (see ). Hunter (ed. 1972), unnatural: Because it is their father that Gonerill and Regan have mistreated. See n. 473+1, cf. 1757.

1754 pitty]
Deighton (ed. 1891): By action, not by mere sympathy. Cf. Cor. 1.6.36 (647). Hunter (ed. 1972): Be merciful to (a use of the verb not elsewhere recorded, but cognate with have pity on in the same sense).

1755 tooke me]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 396): The compositor has anticipated the next word but one.

1755 vse…house]
Delius (ed. 1854): In that Lear’s daughters and their husbands forbade Gloster to give shelter to Lear (Ger.). Clarkes (ed. 1868): Or to give entrance to Kent: see 1717–20.

1756 their]
F’s stronger perpetuall leaves an ellipsis (to be entertained by them towards him [Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 147]) and is extrametrical if the line is verse (see n. 1753–70).

1757 nor…him]
Deighton (ed. 1891), sustain: See n. 142. Muir (ed. 1952): Care for, support (OED, v. 1). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Nor do anything whatever to relieve him, comparing 1943.

1757 nor]
Schmidt (ed. 1879) defends F’s or, finding neither…or in MM 4.2.104 (1969).

1759–70 Go…careful]
Of Q’s false verse, Doran (1931, p. 129): Some of the prose is rhythmic and it is possible to pick out several blank verse lines from the first part of it. The indications are that it was once entirely in verse, but that it has been partly rewritten in prose. But much of Sh.’s prose is rhythmic; these lines need not have been rewritten.

1759 Go…nothing]
For go toe, see n. 100. Tovey (ed. 1896): Here a mild word of warning. Explained by the next three words: Be more careful what you say, these are dangerous times. An alternative reading for say you nothing—that’s putting it lightly, that’s not the half of it—seems not to be a Shn. idiom.

1759 ther’s a]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 147) defends F’s indifferent There is, comparing 1628.

1759 diuisiõ]
See n. 938.

1759–60 betwixt]
On F’s betweene see n. 147.

1760 worse matter]
Craig (ed. 1901): I.e. a French army has landed. Hunter (ed. 1972): Cf. n. 1637.

1761 letter]
The sender is not identified. Pechter (1978, p. 194): Sometimes assumed…[to be] from Kent, though this is never verified. Ioppolo (1991, p. 175): In the Quarto text the audience could assume that the letter advising Gloucester to send Lear to Dover came from Cordelia. In the Folio…the author of the letter remains ambiguous. There is no evidence that the letter advises Gloucester to send Lear to Dover, and the idea does not occur to him until later when he hears of a plot on Lear’s life (2048). The sender and contents of the letter are equally obscure in Q and F. Halio (ed. 1992): Like Kent, Gloucester is in communication with Cordelia and the French forces. Or with British sympathizers; in 2109 Cornwall charges that the letter is from France, but Gloucester replies that it is from a neutrall.

1761 spoken]
Spoken of (OED, Speak v. 25). See n. 174.

1762 closet]
Either a private room (Deighton, ed. 1891; cf. n. 396) or a private cabinet for valuables (Schmidt, 1874; OED, sb. 3a, quoting this l.).

1763 home]
See n. 987.

1764 power]
See n. 1638+1.

1764 landed]
F reads footed. At 2061 in both texts the French army is landed; at 2112 in both texts English traitors, apparently those described in 2075–9, are footed (they would have marched, not landed). OED does not define footed, and the Clarkes (ed. 1868) and Schmidt (ed. 1879) think it may mean here either on foot or landed (got a foothold). Sh.’s only other use of the word, in H5 2.4.143 (1039), footed in this Land, may have the same ambiguity, as may also Haue secret feet (see n. 1638+3). Foakes (ed. 1997): F’s change to a more ambiguous term is deliberate, and made to remove explicit references to a French invasion before 3.7, adding (p. 400), here footed could refer to the forces of Albany or Cornwall. No previous editor has ever imagined such an unlikelihood. If the only previous explicit reference to a French invasion (1638+1) was only accidentally omitted, not deliberately excised, from F, as many eds. believe, this interpretation collapses; to assert and support it, Foakes removes that line and reference from his own text. But even without it, the audience has by now heard (in F) that Kent seems to anticipate help from the French queen Cordelia (1243 ff.), that France has spies in British ports (1633), and that Cordelia has returned to Britain (1643) (necessarily through one of those ports and almost certainly not alone), and soon Cornwall will learn of the aduantages of France (1981) upon Britain. Here in 3.3 Gloucester clearly implies that the Power is expected to revenge Lear’s injuries, and clearly neither Albany nor Cornwall is planning to do that. Since the only likely opposing force so far mentioned is a French one (neither Albany nor Cornwall has been reported yet to have raised any forces), who else would an audience here imagine was footed? Indeed footed may have been substituted for landed to suggest that armed conflict was even more, not less, imminent. Since Sh. refers several times to a power on foot (AYL 5.4.156 [2732], Cor. 4.5.119 [2777], etc.), perhaps footed means afoot, poised to march, at the ready (Brown, ed. 1976), or even On foot, on their March (Theobald, ed. 1733). So Rosenberg (1972, p. 199): On the move. See n. 1197.

1764 incline to the King]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Show ourselves on the king’s side. Craig (ed. 1901) compares WT 1.2.304 (400). OED (Incline v. 8): Take sides, or show practical sympathy.

1765 seeke]
Dyce (ed. 1865), though preferring seeke, says that F’s looke is equally good sense, and Schmidt (ed. 1879) finds look with a direct object in Wiv 4.2.81 (1971) and AYL 2.5.33 (920) (OED, Look v. 6d). See n. 174. Either word could have been misread for the other.

1765 Priuily]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Secretly.

1765 releeue him]
OED (v. 1): To raise (a person) out of some trouble, difficulty, or danger. Cf. 1926–31.

1766 Duke]
Cornwall.

1766 charity]
Verity (ed. 1897): Kindness (OED, sb. 4).

1766–7 of him]
See n. 1706.

1767 I am ill]
Verity (ed. 1897): I.e. say that I am—lest Gloucester’s absence from his house be noticed by Cornwall. Wilson (ed. 1960): Perh. ironical echo of [1362, 1382]—the same artifice used for benignant and malignant purposes.

1768 though]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 148): F’s if might be an erroneous repetition of If in the preceding line: but…it is quite satisfactory.

1768–9 King…releeued]
Muir (ed. 1952): Gloucester, who had earlier offered reasons of policy…now displays some moral stamina for the first time. Warren (1983, pp. 62–3) sees Gloucester’s initiative here as the beginning of the diminution of Kent’s part in the play’s action to a merely emblematic or choric function; but Gloucester’s help ends two scenes later, while Kent’s care continues to the end of the play.

1769 is Some…thing]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 148) defends F’s is…things, citing Abbott §335; see n. 204.

1770 toward]
See n. 938.

1771–5 This…fall]
Q mislines the verse despite the obvious concluding couplet.

1771 curtesie]
OED (sb. 6): Courteous act.

1771 forbid]
Schmidt (1874): Forbidden…prohibited. Rolfe (ed. 1880): The usual form of the participle in S. [by a ratio of 76:5]. See n. 103. For the prohibition, see 1601–12, 1753–7. Hudson (ed. 1871) misunderstands as a curse upon thee; see textual n.

1773 this…deseruing]
This, the subject of both seems and must draw, apparently refers to Edmund’s intended denunciation of his father; seems means has the appearance of (Delius, ed. 1854), or possibly promises to be; faire may mean either equitable or auspicious; and deseruing may mean desert in several senses: merit, that which is due a person, or that for which he may claim something (Schmidt, 1874): cf. Edmund’s use of the word in 34, and Albany’s in 3276. Most eds. think that Edmund refers to his own desert: the denunciation seems or promises to be a good opportunity of earning desert (Meiklejohn, ed. 1879), a good turn which should win the gratitude of Cornwall and Regan. Cf. Scene 5 of this Act (Verity, ed. 1897). Though such a reading is consistent with Edmund’s egoism and with the event, it may be somewhat forced, since deserving does not mean opportunity to win reward. Delius (op. cit.) apparently thinks the desert is Cornwall’s, whose servant Edmund now is: This denunciation has the appearance of a genuine service. No one suggests that the desert is Gloucester’s, who seems (to Edmund) fairly to deserve denunciation as a traitor to Cornwall.

1773 draw]
See n. 91.

1775 then…fall]
Proverbial: Tilley R136, The Rising of one man is the falling of another. Main (ed. 1962) sees an allusion to Fortune’s wheel, comparing 3136.

1775 then]
Though Q is possible, most eds. accept F’s The. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 396) suspects that the Q compositor was influenced by Then two words earlier or by when three words later.

1775 doe]
Though Q is possible, most eds. accept F’s doth, giving the line the symmetry of the proverb.

1776 <Scena Quarta>]
Coleridge (MS notes, 1818–19, ed. Foakes, 1989, p. 101): What a world’s convention of agonies—surely, never was such a scene conceived before or since. Take it but as a picture, for the eye only, it is more terrific than any a Michael Angelo inspired by a Dante could have conceived, and which none but a Michael Angelo could have executed. Or let it have been uttered to the blind, the howlings of convulsed nature would seem concerted in the voice of conscious humanity. (Ibid., pp. 101–2): This scene ends with the first symptoms of positive derangement; and the intervention of the fifth scene is particularly judicious,—the interruption allowing an interval for Lear to appear in full madness in the sixth scene. The additional phrases found in Furness (ed. 1880), including the often quoted the real madness of Lear, the feigned madness of Edgar, the babbling of the Fool, the desperate fidelity of Kent, were apparently added by Henry Nelson Coleridge in Literary Remains (1836–9, 2:201). Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): A play called Le Stravaganze d’Amore, by Cristoforo Castelletti (1585), also brings upon the scene in contrasting accord three similar types of madness: an old man, Metello, insane with grief for his children, as Lear is on account of the unkindness of his, Alessandro, an assumed madman, as Edgar is, and a professional fool. Bullough (1973, p. 416 n.) compares Harsnett (1603, p. 47), where the devil Hiaclito was of the new Court cut, affecting no other traine then two crasie fellowes, and an urchin butter-flie boy; see . Macaulay (1907, p. 26): Here begins the finest of all human performances. Hudson & Black (ed. 1911, p. lv), paraphrasing Moulton (1885, pp. 215–17): In the hovel scene the Lear plot and the Gloucester plot are interwoven as one.…Edgar is the victim of the Gloucester plot, and his disguise as a Bedlam beggar is the climax to the tragedy of his own sufferings; contact with the feigned madness of Edgar completes the overthrow of Lear’s mind, and, while the storm continues to rumble, the old king begins to tear off his clothes. Gloucester, seeking to save Lear, reaches the hovel, and in his words to Kent [1946–50], Edgar learns how his father has been deceived, and his anger against him is turned to pity. Dent (ed. 1927): We have reached the climax of the play. Lear’s mind totters on the verge of insanity. Two emotions strive for supremacy—rage and self-pity.…Had Lear been able to rest awhile in shelter he might have been restored. But…at the sight of [Edgar] something seems to snap inside Lear’s brain. See n. 1830–1. Hunter (ed. 1972): The appearance of naked Tom…releases Lear’s last hold on his own identity and submerges his sanity in his sense of all the oppressed and dispossessed of the world. Fool, King, and Bedlam begin to forge a new dialect, a rapt recitation of inner visions, compared to which the common-sense solicitudes of Kent and Gloucester seem external and superficial. Howard (1984, p. 25): The crack of thunder and the swirling voices of gibbering madman, frightened fool, and raging king create an overall impression of aural cacophony that is as important to the viewer’s understanding of what the scene means in psychological and social terms as is the exact language of any of the figures before us.
Kittredge (ed. 1940): The same stormy night as in Scene iii. Gloucester finds Lear ([1890]) and leads him to a farmhouse for shelter ([1930 ff.]). Cowling (1927, p. 176): The hovel was the stage middle door, behind an arras. Adams (1948, p. 324): The Fool enters [the hovel] by slipping through the edges of the rear-stage curtains. Reynolds (1962, pp. 89–91): Act III may be an extended illustration of the convention that exit and immediate re-entry directions mean a change of one location to an adjacent one or one almost adjacent.…Perhaps…Kent enters from the Left [at 1688] to persuade Lear to go to a hovel Kent has found…and they go back with him Left.…Kent, Lear, and the Fool, having crossed behind the tiring-house wall, now enter Right, cross the front stage to the Left door, which is now to be accepted as the entrance to the hovel.…The door convention does offer a consistent solution. An attempt to get a tumble-down shack into place for a scene outside it…would be absurd. Horsman (ed. 1973): They enter by one door; the other is taken to be that of the hovel. Halio (ed. 1992): [The] hovel is an imagined place, entered perhaps from a trap…or from behind curtains upstage center.

1778, 1782, 1785, 1803 good my Lord]
On the transposed adjective see n. 102.

1778–9 the the]
Q(c) corrects an obvious dittography.

1779 tyrannie]
Schmidt (1875): Cruelty, injurious violence (OED, sb. 4b). In Sidney’s Arcadia 2.7.4 (ed. Feuillerat, 1:193) Pyrocles and Musidorus endure the tyrannie of the winde. Cf. 1929.

1779 open nights]
Schmidt (1875): Not covered, not sheltered (OED, a. 5). Page (ed. 1889): A phrase similar to the open air (OED, Open air 1: Space…exposed to the weather). Skillan (ed. 1967): Night in the open.

1780 nature]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Human nature. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Man’s natural strength. See nn. 441, 1427.

1780 Storme still]
See n. 1584. Edwards (ed. 1975): This direction…indicates that the sound effects for the storm continue (intermittently) throughout the scene.

1782 enter]
F’s added heere is already implied by 1778, but may have been inserted to avoid verbatim repetition in 1778, 1782, and 1785. Halio (ed. 1994): F’s addition corrects the metre. Since just before and just afterwards…Kent says simply enter, the Q compositor may accidentally have omitted here. Wells (ed. 2000): A missing syllable at the caesura is acceptable.

1783 Wilt]
For omission of the pronoun see n. 562.

1783 breake my heart]
See n. 1585. Steevens (ed. 1793), believing that Lear does not address this question to Kent, but to his own bosom, would put a comma after breake; but as Pye (1807, p. 288) says, that sense and punctuation…is confuted by what Kent says [in 1784], who must know how Lear spoke it. Cf. 1805–6. In his next speech Lear explains why his heart will break. Edwards (ed. 1975) gives a different reason: It is Kent’s courtesy and concern for his comfort that Lear fears will make him break down. He has scores to settle in the storm—whatever they may be. He needs rest, but to relax from his scarcely defined purpose is to admit defeat.

1786–94 Thou…their]
Soellner (1968, p. 69): As Lear now for the second time [cf. n. 1381–5] touches on the question of the sympathy of body and mind, he gives the latter predominance. His is a Platonic emphasis of the same kind as that in a tract by Thomaso Buoni, Problemes of Beautie and all humane affections (translated 1606, p. 232).…Most apropos Lear, Buoni asked in Problem 103 [p. 232], Why are the griefes of the minde farre greater then those of the Body? What Buoni took for granted, Lear has to learn through suffering.

1786 think’st tis much]
Rolfe (ed. 1880) finds the expression in Tmp. 1.2.252 (377).

1786 crulentious]
F correctly reads contentious; Q1(c)’s press-correction tempestious could not have been made with reference to the MS or concern for ductus literarum (Ridley, ed. 1935, p. ix) and is evidently a mere guess: that the i was retained may be due to the printer (Greg, 1940, p. 164). Meyer (1994, pp. 132–3): A carelessly written o in secretary hand, open at the top, resumbles [sic] a u. And an Elizabethan secretary r, with its many different forms, is often confused with v or u and, therefore, with o. Conceivably, then, the manuscript o was misread as r. Similarly, both a secretary u and a secretary n appear as two minims and are frequently indistinguishable from one another. Further, the downstroke of a secretary l curves not from left to right, but from right to left, and is terminated by a small spur to the left across the middle of the upstroke. Since a secretary t also contains a cross bar and was generally looped, l and t were commonly confused with one another. Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960): Tempestious…involv[es] tautology (tempestious storme). OED (Contentious a. 1b): Prone to strife, quoting this l. as its first ex. So Lott (ed. 1974): In the war of human nature against the elements, comparing Inuades (1787). Blayney (1982, 1:249): Sometimes, I suspect, a group of marginal notes might not have been written until the proof-reader reached an obvious break in the copy.…If that happened while [this] speech…was being marked, the proof-reader would have made four marks in the text [1786, 1790, 1792, 1794] before adding the marginal notes. He would therefore have half-corrected the tempest to this tempest at line [1792] before he wrote the letters that changed this crulentious to this tempestious at line [1786]. I believe that here…we have what can be called a memorially contaminated proof-correction. But it is possible to imagine that the corrector, finding a nonsense word, simply skimmed a few lines ahead to find the clue in the context, and finding that the passage was based on a contrast of one tempest with another, guessed at this tempestious; see n. 1792. Foakes (ed. 1997) compares Oth. 2.1.92 (859).

1787 Inuades]
See n. 153.

1787 to the skin]
OED (Skin sb. 5e): Through all one’s garments; hence, thoroughly, completely, quoting this l.

1787 skin, so]
Doran (1931, p. 106): F’s erroneous skinso: reveals a misunderstanding of the sense on the part of the folio printer that could not have arisen if he had been printing from Q1. Hinman (1963, 1:310–11): Miscorrection.…The [proof]reader evidently meant a colon to be inserted after skin in place of the period.…[It] was inserted…in the wrong place.

1788–9 where…felt]
Proverbial: Tilley G446, The greater Grief (sorrow) drives out the less. Sayers (1793, pp. 68–9): It is an aphorism of Hippocrates [Aphor. 2:46; ed. Jones, 1931, 4:111]. Craig (ed. 1901): Lear may be supposed here, or after there [1794], to strike his breast. Shakespeare expressed nearly the same thought afterwards in [Cym. 4.2.243 (2557)].

1788 fixt]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Chronic, incurable (OED, ppl. a. 2: Securely established). Brown (ed. 1976): Irremovable.

1790 thy]
F’s they is doubtless a slip by the compositor (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 178).

1790 raging]
Q1(c)’s roring seems to Greg (1940, p. 164) Certainly correct, since it has the support of F [roaring]. The compositor must have accidentally substituted a more or less synonymous word: it is an error of the mind, not of the eye. Greg suggests (ibid., pp. 146–7) that in the copy of Q1 used (he believes) as printer’s copy for F, this sheet, G, was in its uncorrected state. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 148): If so, F’s roaring must have come from the playhouse manuscript. And the reading of Q corr. shows that the copy for Q had the same word. Stone (1980, p. 219): Except that (a) the compositor is most unlikely to have read an r as a g and (b) the raging sea was not yet a cliché, and is the more appropriate expression here, since the context requires an image representing mortal danger. In Sh. the sea often rages or roars or both (see Per. 3.3.10 [1323]), as does the storm in this play: cf. rage (1656), Roaring (1699). The corrector would have recently seen the first of these latter instances but not necessarily the second, since the outer forme of sheet F shows no sign of correction. Blayney (1982, p. 248): The [Q] copy must have been carefully checked [by the proof-corrector]. The uncorrected reading is so perfectly apt in context that nobody emending by guesswork would have had any reason for suspecting an error—and much the same is true of the correction of the to this two lines later. See n. 1792.

1791 meet]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Like Camillo in WT.

1791 it’h mouth]
OED (Mouth sb.): Face to face, quoting this l.

1791–4 whẽ…their]
Taylor (1925, p. 11) compares Montaigne: Our senses are not onely altered, but many times dulled, by the passions of the mind; see . Brownlee (1960, p. 276) compares Burton’s Anatomy of Melancholy 1.2.3.1: So we look upon a thing, and see it not; hear, and observe not; which otherwise would much affect us, had we been free [of passion]. At 2427–8 one sense is dulled by another.

1791 free]
Seymour (1805, 2:119): Free from inquietude (OED, a. 1b: Fig.…not in bondage). See prev. n., and cf. 2056+8, 2525.

1792 delicate]
Schmidt (1874): Tender (OED, a. 8).

1792 the]
The agreement of Q1(u) and F may suggest that they derive in common from Sh.’s MS, but there is no obvious reason why the Q proof-reader should have substituted Q1(c)’s this. Greg (1940, p. 164) suggests one possibility: It makes the fifth the in two and a half lines. Blayney (1982, p. 248), believing that Q copy was consulted by the proof-corrector at 1790, thinks that it probably was consulted here also; see also n. 1786. Alternatively, it is possible that the proof-corrector, having guessed at this tempestious at 1786 from the hint of the tempest in this line, then returned here to point up the contrast with this tempest. Greg infers that F’s reading derived from Q1(u), and Taylor (1983, p. 433, n. 33), that it came just as possibly from Q2; but their common assumption that F’s copy was a marked-up quarto is doubtful: see . It is perhaps also possible that the word was unclear in Sh.’s MS, that the scribe preparing the playbook and later the Q1 compositor both read the, but that the Q proof-corrector made out this.

1792 tempest…mind]
Muir & Danby (1950, p. 50): In Sidney’s Arcadia 2.12.[2] (see ) Basilius speaks of an inward tempest. Sh. had used the image previously in R3 1.3.44 (880), Ham. 3.2.6–7 (1854), etc.

1794 beares]
Q1(c)’s beates is certainly correct and evidently derived from the copy, since the reader cannot have understood the passage correctly (Greg, 1940, p. 164). Deighton (ed. 1891): Throbs. Craig (ed. 1901): A sort of quibble between beat, to be in a state of restless mental anxiety (see [Tmp. 1.2.176 (286)]) and beat as tempests do. Harrison (ed. 1937): The storm of passion within…is part mental, part physical, as the pulsations of his heart will not let him forget it. Lott (ed. 1974): (i) works laboriously, (ii) rages.

1794 their]
F’s there corrects an apparent compositor’s error. See n. 1788–9. Kittredge (ed. 1940): In my mind and heart. There is emphatic. Bratton (ed. 1987): Macready struck his forehead.

1794 filiall ingratitude]
The phrase has been punctuated as an appositive to what, as an apostrophe, and most probably as an expostulation; see textual n. Edwards (ed. 1975), filial: Belonging to a daughter or son (Schmidt, 1874; OED, a. 1).

1796 sure]
Though Q makes sense—most certainly (Weis, ed. 1993)—most eds. prefer F’s home, which has analogies in 1763 and elsewhere in Sh.; see Franz §381. In script the words are graphically enough alike for misreading. Pechter (1978, pp. 194–5) hears in F a secondary sense that points to the radical integrity of the family.

1798–9 To…this]
Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxiii): Omitted by the Quarto printer—a clear case of ductus literarum, for the next line repeats In such a night. Most eds. agree; Doran (1931, p. 59) adds, Evidence that something is wrong with the quarto text appears in a long line the meaning of which is not clear.…The folio gives what must be the original reading of the passage, inasmuch as it is metrically regular, and supplies what is missing in sense from Q1.…However, if the verse in the manuscript had been correctly divided, as in the folio, it would seem scarcely possible for [the Q printer] to have made such a mistake [as this eyeskip]. The improper alignment of the rest of the speech in Q1 may indicate that these few lines, from [1797] to [1802] and including those in the folio, were written in the margin of the manuscript as an addition. Stone (1980, p. 243) suggests that Q 1799–1801 should have been lined so as to end as this!…father…all,…shun that, and that F was revised to eliminate the part-line Whose…all and otherwise to smooth meter. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 517): The first in such a night occurs at the end of a verse line, the second at the beginning, which reduces (while not eliminating) the probability of eyeskip. Q of course makes sense as it stands.…The metrical irregularity might result from textual error; equally, though, it might have stimulated textual revision…[which] seems to us more likely…than the restoration of words originally included in Shakespeare’s foul papers. Q forms roughly regular verse if as this…Gonorill is read as one line. Clearly F is more effective, with its repeated expressions of amazement interrupted wildly by a cry of defiance. Foakes (ed. 1997): Its effect is to enhance the pathos of Lear’s situation.

1798 shut me out]
Edwards (ed. 1975): Self-pity blurs the truth that he left of his own free will. True enough; but Lear is right whether he knows it or not: cf. 1608–12, 1719–20, 1928, 2135–6. Stone (1980, p. 243) finds these words added to F suspicious, since Lear does not know that he has been shut out until 1928. Foakes (ed. 1997): Kent has made it obvious at [1719–20].

1798 Poure]
Elton (1966, p. 59): Anticipating Lear, Pyrocles in Sidney’s Arcadia 3.22.6 (ed. Feuillerat, 1:483) exclaims let it [i.e., blinde providence] poure out all his mischiefes vpon me.

1798 endure]
Dent (1981) compares the proverb He that Endures (suffers) is not overcome (E136).

1800 franke]
Schmidt (1874): Liberal, bountiful (OED, a.2 2). Halio (ed. 1992): Also open, without guile (OED, 3a).

1800 heart]
See n. 852.

1800 gaue you all]
F’s omission of you seems intended to improve meter, though Malone (ed. 1790) finds Q acceptable if father is read as a monosyllable. Brooke (ed. 1947): The Folio…gets the conventional count of syllables, but puts the accent on the wrong words. Stress fath’r, frank, and gave. See n. 1547. Milward (1987, p. 177): Lear seems to be identifying himself with the father of the prodigal in Luke xv.

1801 way]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Of thought (OED, sb.1 9b, quoting this l.). Tilley M866 compares Melancholy is the pathway to madness; Dent (1981) doubts it is a proverb. Lear may mean not melancholy but giving way to emotion, or dwelling on his own griefs (Foakes, ed. 1997).

1803 enter]
Cf. n. 1782. F’s added here completes a pentameter.

1804 Prethe]
See n. 664.

1804–8 goe…in]
Macaulay (1907, p. 29): The softening of Lear’s nature and manners, under the discipline of severe sorrow, is most happily marked in several places. Lott (ed. 1974): The Fool hesitates, not at first believing that the King wants him to go in first, against the accepted order of precedence. Wells (ed. 2000): Presumably addressed to Kent as he is the previous speaker.…[F’s] lines (perhaps accidentally dropped from Q) make sense of Lear’s I’ll go in as a deferred intention.…It seems desirable for Kent at least to stand unobtrusively aside…and for the Fool to enter.

1804 thy]
Eds. follow F’s thine, though thy own occurs elsewhere in Sh. and in this play at 1604 and 2604 (F).

1804 one]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 79): An aural error for a homophone own. OED (Own a.) records one as a sp. variant.

1805–6 This…more]
Edwards (ed. 1975): Lear has just said that he doesn’t notice the storm because of the distress in his mind; now he says exactly the opposite. Cf. n. 1786–94.

1805 ponder]
OED (v. 5): Reflect, quoting this l. as its first ex.

1806 would]
On the omission of the relative see n. 589.

1806 ile goe in]
Verity (ed. 1897): For the Fool’s sake. Stone (1980, pp. 231, 244): Possibly spoken by the Fool.

1807–8 In…sleepe]
Cunnington (1910, p. 451): These lines and the related 1819 are F additions, not Q’s accidental omissions. The effect of Edgar’s exclamation [1819] depends on our having seen the fool go in and having had our attention drawn to it. F’s In…first and Exit make explicit what is implicit in Q: that the Fool but not Kent (cf. 1818, 1822) enters the hovel. Terrified upon meeting the apparition of Edgar by himself alone, he rushes out again for protection and takes Kent’s hand. These two F lines also seem designed in part to express a motive for Lear’s (and his protector Kent’s) remaining behind: Ile pray. Some Lears kneel (Bratton, ed. 1987; cf. textual n.). Since in the following lines, original to Q, he does not pray, but rather reflects on suffering in his kingdom, one may doubt either that F’s lines were part of Sh.’s original intention or that he later added them. So thinks Stone (1980, p. 244), who also believes that Lear needs no more reason for remaining than he has already given Kent in 1804–6, even though a reviser thought so. Others suspect differently. Johnson (ed. 1765): These two lines were added in the author’s revision.…They are very judiciously intended to represent that humility, or tenderness, or neglect of forms, which affliction forces on the mind. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 226): The kindness to the half-drowned Fool is emphasised; and he is (I think) sent off the stage so that there may be no danger whatever…that some buffoon in the audience would vent an incongruous guffaw at the mere sight of him sitting there. But above all, by these two lines the meaning and intention of what is to come are emphasised.…This addition has to me all the air of being a second thought of Shakespeare’s own. Richman (1986, p. 378): Without the lines, the transition but ile goe in is too sudden and sweeping. Foakes (1993, p. 196): Lear’s sudden attention to the Fool in F leads him to think of other wretches; but see the next n.

1807 You…pouertie]
Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxiii): Of course the words…begin the apostrophe to the Poore naked wretches which follows, and Lear checks himself to repeat his command to the Fool. But…Doctor Johnson [thought (see prev. n.)] that Lear thus describes his jester. So Kittredge (ed. 1940): Synonymous with Poor naked wretches. Yet it is anything but clear why Sh. should have Lear begin his apostrophe before the Fool even begins to exit, only to interrupt it when he realizes the Fool is still there, and then start again; and though this phrase, by its abstractness, may be a bridge between the ideas of individual and general suffering, yet the singular pouertie seems to apply more easily and immediately to the single Fool than to unnumbered wretches. See next n.

1807 pouertie]
Schmidt (1875, p. 1422): Abstract for concrete, Poor people. Cf. n. 1633 on the plural speculations, which refers to several spies; but pouertie, being singular, may refer to only one case of impoverishment, not many poverties. Thus Craig (ed. 1901): Needy one, poor one. Verity (ed. 1897): The figure of speech is often intensive: e.g. to be poverty itself, personified, sounds worse than to be poor. Cf. pomp [1814].

1808 Nay]
See n. 630.

1808 pray]
See n. 1807–8. Since in the following speech there is no petition to God or man for favor or forgiveness, eds. have had to find special meanings to explain F’s word. Muir (ed. 1952): The prayer is not to the gods, but to the poor. Houghton (ed. 1957): Perhaps the prayer is no more to them than to himself. Wilson (ed. 1960): A prayer of repentance. Soellner (1968, pp. 69–70): This is not a prayer in the ordinary sense.…But…the warning to pomp has a touch of contemptus mundi rhetoric…and the last note, significantly, is a plea for divine order and justice.…Elizabethan moral literature accustomed Shakespeare’s contemporaries to associate house-garment metaphors with the body, the earthly house covering the soul, and with heaven, its ultimate house and garment, citing 2 Cor. 5:2–5 and Robert Cawdrey’s A treasurie or Store-house of Similes (1600). Hunter (ed. 1972): A highly unorthodox [prayer], not for his own safety during the night, but for that of wretches; and not to the gods, but to the objects of their power. Thomson (1988, p. 185): It is difficult to accept that the self-dramatizing Take physic, pomp would be spoken from a kneeling position—but perhaps Lear rises here.

1809–17 Poore…iust]
Bradley (1904, p. 287): This is one of those passages which make one worship Shakespeare. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 150): The supreme moment for Lear himself, the turning-point, therefore, of the play’s main theme. Bransom (1934, p. 97): There is the unexpressed admission of sin attaching to himself. Lear has never faced the facts of his life so honestly…; his moral sense has never been anything like so luminous. Danby (1949, pp. 185–6): The last and grandest act of his sanity, manifesting the traditional schema of spiritual regeneration, expressing the sentiment of Christian communism, charity, and a Christian levelling of society, and reflecting contemporary religious, social, and political concerns, particularly of the Anabaptists. Wilson (ed. 1960): We are pointed forward to ll. [1881] ff. Cf. Glo.’s words at [2449–55]. Both learn the same lesson from suffering. Harbage (1963, p. 418): The speech is alone sufficient to cancel any suggestion of nihilism in the tragedy; during the onslaught of viciousness, reserves of virtue are tapped. Mehl (1975, p. 156): The dramatic point of the two passages is not so much the proposing of a specific ethical or social concept, but a pointed illumination of the wretched state of the speakers themselves.…The basic identity of king and beggar, like Gloucester’s utopian longing for an even distribution of the world’s riches, are traditional homiletic and even pre-christian metaphors for the true state of man, but there is hardly anything in the play to suggest the idea that this should have practical political consequences.…The plight of the poor is not a major concern of the play, or only in so far as it affects the protagonists. Lear and Gloucester are not given any opportunity of proving that their attitude to the common people has really changed, nor is there any hint that Edgar will impose a new social order on the country he has taken over. Musgrove (1981, pp. 12–13): Sh. may have known the descriptions of miserable poor people in Robert Copland’s poem Highway to the Spital-House (ca. 1535). There are no verbal similarities, however. Answering Marxist critics who find in Lr. echoes of a contemporary assault on feudalism by enclosures, urbanization, etc., Liebler (1995, p. 208): Anglo-Saxon elegies such as The Wanderer, The Husband’s Message, The Wife’s Lament, and The Seafarer remind us that homelessness existed long before capitalism. Milward (1987, p. 177): Lear again assumes the figure of Job, citing Job 24:7–10, 29:12, 16. Foakes (ed. 1997): These lines exemplify Protestant teaching about the value of adversity, quoting from Otto Werdmuller, A Spiritual and most Precious Pearl, tr. Miles Coverdale (1593, pp. 151–2, 322). Liebler (op. cit., p. 206): Elizabeth’s Poor Relief Act of 1598 (reissued in 1601)…had made support of the poor a legal obligation of every parish. The Sokols (2000, pp. 265, 276): During the sixteenth century a transformation took place in the perception of poverty, and for the first time the English parliament began to legislate [in 1572, 1576, 1598] for universal secular provision for the relief of the deserving poor. The process culminated in the Elizabethan Poor Law of 1601.…[Lear’s] call for sympathy and greater sharing…was reflected…in society’s attempts through law at distributive justice. For modern musical settings see Gooch & Thatcher (1991, 1:636).

1810 bide]
Schmidt (1874): Abide,…to endure, to bear (OED, v. 9).

1810 pelting]
OED (vbl. sb.): Beating with missiles, quoting this l. as its first ex.

1810 night]
Q echoes 1667; F’s storme is more literal.

1811 sides]
Schmidt (1875): Considered as the part [of the body] principally fed by nourishment; unattested by OED.

1811–12 house-lesse…windowed]
James (1949, p. 147) sees a quibble on house (OED, sb.2: A covering of textile material) that fuses ideas of the body as the house of the soul and the house as protection for the body; but such a sense refers to a covering attached to a saddle, not to human clothing. Cf. n. 1808.

1812 loopt]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:39): Full of loop-holes (OED, Looped ppl. a.2, quoting only this l.). See n. 223. Malone (ed. 1790): Such as were made in ancient castles for firing ordnance or spying the enemy. Though Schmidt (ed. 1879) denies this sense in Sh., Rolfe (ed. 1880) cites 1H4 4.1.71, sight-holes euery loope.

1812 windowed]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:77): Full of Windows or Rents (OED, ppl. a. 3, quoting this l. as its first ex.). See n. 223. Craig (ed. 1901): The original meaning of window appears to have been wind-eye, i.e. eye, or hole, to admit the wind. Gardner (ed. 1969): An unglazed opening.

1813 seasons]
OED (sb. 11a): Transf.…A spell of…weather, quoting this l. as its first ex. of two.

1813 tane]
Common sp. of ta’en, elision of taken.

1814–16 take…them]
Jacox (1867, pp. 290–301) illustrates the topos from the Bible and modern French and English literature. Carter (1905, p. 437) compares Exod. 23:9, and Milward (1987, pp. 177–8), Luke 4:23, 1 Jn. 3:17. Henderson (1939, p. 219) finds a parallel in Lodovicus Vives’s letter to Leo X. Ransom (1947, p. 186): There is a slight flurry of latinity in the physic, pomp, expose,…superflux.

1814 physicke]
Schmidt (1875): A remedy for a disease (OED, sb. 4). Hunter (ed. 1972): To be (morally) healthy. Edwards (ed. 1975): To purge themselves of their pride. Empson (1951, p. 137): A pun: physical conditions, medicine.

1814 pompe]
Schmidt (1875): Magnificence. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Ye great and mighty ones of the earth. Wilson (ed. 1960): Including—especially—himself. Foakes (ed. 1997): Perhaps with special reference…to the regal costume stage tradition suggests he wore.

1816 shake]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Seems to convey the idea of the crumbs scattered from the rich man’s table. Ransom (1947, p. 187): I judge that we are all reminded more or less consciously of Lazarus. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Cast off…and bestow (OED, v. 15). Brooke (ed. 1947): The figure is from shaking the branches of an over-laden fruit tree (OED, 14).

1816 superflux]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): Superfluity (OED, sb. 1, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Verity (ed. 1897): Of your wealth and comfort. Bevington (ed. 1980): With suggestion of flux, bodily discharge, introduced by physic, purgative in l. [1814].

1817 shew…iust]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Make the differences of rank and fortune which heaven ordains appear less unjust. I.e., by lessening such differences. OED (Just adj. 2): Impartial…; rendering every one his due; equitable, quoting 3131. Empson (1951, p. 137): If the rich give their superflux.…This does not sound as if the gods are just of their own accord. Muir (ed. 1952) compares Leir 1909, The heauens are iust; see . Green (1870, pp. 488–90) cites an emblem, Providence making Rich and making Poor. Shuger (1996, p. 52): Not subversive heterodoxies…but the social teachings of the medieval church…[concerning] Christian caritas.

1818 Enter…Foole]
The F SD appears to be partly wrong: the Fool must be on stage by 1822, but Edgar is still off at 1826. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 535): He might reasonably appear at a window, or in a doorway, to speak his enigmatic entrance line, before disappearing back into the hovel. In Q, where he does not speak until 1827, there is no need even for that appearance.

1819 Edg.…Tom]
F provides a line that substantiates the Fool’s he sayes in 1823 and perhaps Kent’s dost grumble in 1825 (but see n.). Since it is not strictly necessary to the scene—Edgar could appear grumbling at 1825—and since there is no obvious reason why it should have been overlooked by the Q compositor, as Doran (1931, p. 60) suggests, it was very likely added later along with the SD above it; cf. n. 1807–8. Halio (ed. 1992, p. 283): Edgar’s interpolated scream dramatically motivates the Fool’s terrified re-entrance. It could be Shn., but the interjection Fathom, and halfe does not appear elsewhere in Sh., and Edgar’s succeeding lines are on the quite different subjects of possession and cold wind. Slater (1982, p. 160): The wholly debased Edgar appears at exactly the same moment to Lear and Gloucester. When each of them realises that…vilde things [may be] precious,…then Edgar, the basest of all creatures, appears, and becomes for one a moral, and for the other, an actual guide. Wells (ed. 2000): Edgar is often presented as virtually, sometimes (in modern performance) entirely naked, despite 1846.

1819 Fathom, and halfe]
Steevens (ed. 1778): Words used by those sounding the depth at sea. Capell (1783, 1.2:167): Allude to his being bury’d in straw. Hunter (ed. 1869): Refer to fields flooded with rain. Schmidt (ed. 1879): Is he not likely sounding the depths of Hell? (Ger.). Wilson (ed. 1960): Edg. pretends to be one of the fresh-water mariners or whip-jacks who run about the country with a counterfeit licence <from the Admiralty>, feigning either shipwreck or spoiled <sic> by pirates ([Harman], A Caveat [see n. 1265]). If so, it is a different pretense from Edgar’s usual role; see prev. n. Rosenberg (1972, p. 205): Reminder of the flood, of rainstorm, and even deeper, the mythic implication of depths from which water-creatures emerge. Foakes (ed. 1997): As if…measuring the depth of water in the hovel (the use of a trap-door would be appropriate).

1820, 1823 spirit]
OED (sb. 3): A supernatural…being—such as demons or angels. Cf. 2303+15, 2664.

1820 Nunckle]
See n. 634.

1823 a spirite]
F’s repetition is probably for emphasis rather than to make pentameter verse uncharacteristic of the Fool.

1825 What]
See n. 540. Elton (1966, pp. 84–7) finds this and the play’s many other questions about identity thematically significant.

1825 grumble]
OED (v. 1a): To utter dull, inarticulate sounds; to mutter, mumble, murmur; to growl faintly, quoting this l. second after Shr. 4.1.167 (1799). See n. 1819.

1827–1968 Away…man]
Theobald (ed. 1733): What Lear says, for the most part, springs either from the Source and Fountain of his Disorder; the Injuries done him by his Daughters; or his Desire of being reveng’d on them. What Edgar says, seems a fantastick Wildness, only extorted to disguise Sense, and to blunt the Suspicion of his Concealment. This makes it, that we are always most strongly affected with the King’s Madness, as we know it to be a real Distress. Coleridge (MS notes, 1818–19, ed. Foakes, 1989, p. 101): Edgar’s false madness taking off part of the shock from the true, as well as displaying the profound difference. Idem (in Raysor, ed. 1930, 1:58, from Literary Remains): In Edgar’s ravings Shakspeare all the while lets you see a fixed purpose, a practical end in view;—in Lear’s, there is only the brooding of the one anguish, an eddy without progression. Daniel (ed. 1824, p. 7): The ravings of assumed madness are rich in wildness of thought and luxuriance of fancy: the pathetic aberrations of a disordered mind, ever recurring to its own misery, are depicted with a truth that renders the contrast wonderfully impressive. Edgar wanders from subject to subject, from image to image; every object in the material and immaterial world—things most foul, strange, and unnatural are called forth with a facility that is any thing but akin to madness. Lear never for one moment wanders from his misfortunes.…Every exclamation bears some affinity to filial ingratitude. Moulton (1885, p. 218): In Lear we have the madness of passion, exaggeration of ordinary emotions; Edgar’s is the madness of idiocy, as idiocy was in early ages when the cruel neglect of society added physical hardship to mental affliction. In Edgar’s frenzy we trace rapid irrelevance with gleams of unexpected relevance,…a sense of ill-treatment and of being an outcast; remorse and thoughts as to close connection of sin and retribution; visions of fiends as in bodily presence; cold, hunger: these alternating with mere gibberish, and all perhaps within the compass of few lines. Crane (1952, pp. 163, 165): The prose of madness enters the play.…A strange mixture of verse, prose, and song…is all that makes the strength of these scenes [3.4, 3.6] and keeps them dramatically possible, citing Granville-Barker (1927, pp. 156–7): Their emotional strain might be intolerable without it. Vickers (1968, p. 352): Edgar, like Edmund and Kent, adopts prose for dissimulation as he feigns madness, and the disguise—stylistic and visual—is so real that Shakespeare has to periodically give him verse asides (III, vi, IV, iv [sic], vi) and verse soliloquies (with an added formalization of rhyme and language) to remind us that he is still Edgar (II, iii; end of III, vi, IV, i) the last of which comments explicitly on the man beneath the disguise: Yet…contemned. Like Kent, when Edgar begins to play a more positive part in tending the sufferers, he drops his disguise and speaks verse (IV, i), only falling back into prose again, and into a stage-rustic dialect for the fight with Oswald, presumably so that the servant will not recognize him and blurt out his name before he is ready to reveal it to Gloucester. Cf. 2018–19, 2056+5–+18, 2179–92, 2471–2, 2482–5, 2487–8, 2585–6, 2616–17, 2688 ff.

1827 Away]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Keep away from me! (OED, adv. 14).

1827 fiend]
Hunter (ed. 1972): The mad were often supposed to be possessed or followed by devils. Brown (ed. 1976): A Jacobean audience might have believed, with the fool, that a devil entered—though probably not for long, hearing him complain of a foul fiend. Theobald (ed. 1733): His whole Frenzy is Satire levell’d at a modern Fact, which made no little Noise at that Period of Time: and consequently, must have been a rapturous Entertainment to the Spectators, when it was first presented. The Secret is this: While the Spaniards were preparing their Armado against England, the Jesuits were here busily at Work to promote the Success by making Converts. One Method they used, to do this, was to dispossess pretended Demoniacks of their own Church.…This Transaction was so rife in every Body’s Mouth, upon the Accession of King James the 1st to the Crown; that our Poet thought proper to make his Court, by helping forward the Ridicule of it. I need only observe now, that Edgar thro’ all his Frenzy supposes himself possess’d by Fiends; and that the greatest Part of his dissembled Lunacy, the Names of his Devils, and the descriptive Circumstances he alludes to in his own Case, are all drawn from this Pamphlet [Harsnett’s Declaration, 1603, pp. 46 ff.]. See . The entertainment of Edgar’s sullen and assumed humor of Tom of Bedlam is advertised on the Q1 title page. Muir (1951, p. 16) compares Harsnett’s account (1603, p. 24) of Marwood’s night, or two, abroad in the fieldes,…scared with lightning, and thunder and thought to be possessed; see and n. 1258–67.

1827–8 thorough…wind]
Anticipating Capell (1783, 1.2:166), who suspected quotation…from some lost poem, Bishop Thomas Percy included this phrase in his own synthetic ballad The Friar of Orders Gray (Reliques, 1765, 1.2.18) made up of little fragments [dispersed through Shakspeare’s plays] of ancient ballads, the entire copies of which could not be recovered. Schmidt (ed. 1879), many succeeding eds., and even the OED (s.v. Cockle) quote Percy’s poem as if it were an actual ballad, not Percy’s own creation. Steevens (ed. 1773): I am very confident I have seen [this line] in an old ballad; but perhaps it was Percy’s. Kittredge (ed. 1940): This sounds like a line from some old song. Though no such song has been found, Long (1971, pp. 170–1) proposes a ballad tune: see . Hunter (ed. 1972): It would have most effect if derived from traditional material. The line is echoed at 1878–9.

1827 thorough]
Archaic form of through (OED, Thorough prep. and adv.).

1828 sharpe]
Refers to the haw’s thorns. Wilson (ed. 1960): Perh. alludes to the pins or thorns of his makeup, citing 1267.

1828 blowes…wind]
On F’s plural blow…windes see n. 1263.

1828–9 cold…cold]
F omits both words. Malone (ed. 1790): The editor of the folio 1623, I suppose, thinking the passage nonsense, omitted the [second] word cold.…That the quartos are right, appears from…[Shr. In. 1.10 (10–11)], where the same words occur. Wilson (ed. 1960): But Sh. had no metrical inducement to quote himself. Delius (ed. 1854): Sh. struck [the second cold] out in order to avoid the comic effect which it produced (Ger.). Dyce (ed. 1865): If so, why did not Shakespeare also strike out what Edgar presently says about eating…sallets? The fact is, the poet has studiously made the assumed madness of Edgar somewhat akin to the comic, that it might contrast the better with the real insanity of Lear. Clarkes (ed. 1868): The markedly frequent recurrence of the word cold during this scene has peculiar (and most likely intentional) effect; aiding to preserve in our minds the impression of its inclemency throughout. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 148): It seems very odd that F should erroneously omit two colds within two lines. Munro (ed. 1957): F’s omission of cold [1829] spoils the line: it not only destroys the antithesis; but cold bed in Tom’s mockery surely alludes to the grave, comparing 2043. Hunter (ed. 1972): The Q reading, cold wind, is supported by the same song-fragment below (line [1879]). Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 535): It seems likely that…the instruction to omit one led to unconscious omission of the other; Compositor E was particularly prone to omission between lines of prose (as here).…[It is] likely that an allusion to some lost play or poem is intended, a probability which reinforces the authority of Q’s adjective here.…The [later] repetition [1879] may have motivated F’s change. If Edgar is visibly half naked and shivering, the references here to cold may have been dropped in F as superfluous. They are kept at 1839, 1858, 1863, 1879, 1894, 1925, and 1954, however. Weis (ed. 1993) suspects a possibly taunting innuendo:…an unshared or sterile bed.

1828 Humh]
OED (int.): An inarticulate sound, more exactly h’mh (with aspirated m). = Humph int., giving only one ex., from Dekker, 1603. The word appears five other times in F, always set by Compositor B; perhaps here B influenced Compositor E, who set hum at Ham. 5.1.103 (3294). Cf. 390. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The interjection expresses his shivering with cold. Or simply a strong emotional reaction to it. Armstrong (1946. p. 45): Shakespeare uses the word [hum] in twenty contexts and in twelve of these there is death or sleep imagery. Armstrong is comparing different words having similar sound or spelling: the noun and verb hum as well as an interjection meaning variously ahem (Hem, v.2), hmm (Hum, v.1 2), and humph. Foakes (ed. 1997): Could indicate Edgar’s startled recognition of Lear.

1828–9 goe…thee]
This repeats the exhortation in Away (1827); the wind being cold, Tom urges the others to better shelter than his. Theobald (ed. 1733, 2:271–2) detects a humorous Banter upon Kyd’s Spanish Tragedy 2.5.1, What out-cries…naked bed. Staunton (ed. 1859) finds nothing risible here or in Kyd: To go to a cold bed meant only to go cold to bed; to rise from a naked bed signified to get up naked from bed. Clarkes (ed. 1868): An elliptical phrase…meaning bed to which one goes being cold, and bed feeling cold at first plunge into it. Craig (ed. 1901), followed by Dent (1981, B186.1): Probably proverbial; but no proverb has been found. Crook (ed. 1907): Cold refers to the person and not the bed, and is…transferred epithet, or hypallage.

1830–1 Hast…this]
Harrison (ed. 1937): I.e., nothing less than such sufferings could have reduced you to this misery. Craig (ed. 1931): Lear can interpret only in terms of his own great sorrow; the passage illustrates obsession.
Many commentators see this moment as a turning point in the play. Theobald (ed. 1733): Here Lear’s Madness first begins to break out. His Mind, long beating on his Afflictions, had laid a Preparation for his Frenzy: and nothing was wanting but such an Object as Edgar, to set it on Work, as it were by Sympathy. Moulton (1885, p. 215): This gives the final shock. So far he had not gone beyond ungovernable rage; he had not lost self-consciousness, and could say, My wits begin to turn; but the sight of Edgar completely unhinges his mind, and hallucinations set in; a moment after he has seen him the spirit of imitation begins to work, and Lear commences to strip off his clothes. Bradley (1904, p. 287 n.): What immediately follows…make[s] us think of Lear as pursued by a relentless fate. If he could go in and sleep after his prayer, as he intends, his mind, one feels, might be saved: so far there has been only the menace of madness. But from within the hovel [comes] Edgar—the last man who would have willingly injured Lear—…and, at the sight of Edgar, in a moment something gives way in Lear’s brain. Similarly Muir (1960, p. 35) and Bennett (1962, p. 140). Harbage (1963, p. 418): With his entrance, and Lear’s lapse into madness, which is triggered by it, the scene assumes the character of a grotesque charade. As the heavens rage, and the trio of Fool, mock-Bedlamite, and demented King enter into a fantastic intercourse, we stand on the verge of chaos, with allusions to the morality, religion, and philosophy of the world of order tossing about like bits of wreckage. Hargreaves (1970, p. 49): Gradually…the half-mad Lear sees that Edgar…is a living contradiction of the solution he has just broached. Here is a man whose inequities cannot be relieved by others, for who can share out to him the sanity that he lacks? For a different view see n. 1932. Rosenberg (1972, pp. 214–16): Though the exact point at which Lear breaks into madness has been vigorously debated, being located variously in 1.1, 2.4, 3.2, 3.4, 3.6, and 4.6, most critics and actors choose [this] fearful moment: Poor Tom’s apparition maddens Lear partly because Tom incarnates Lear’s most dreaded imaginings: to be houseless, naked, companion to the wolf and owl, to liberate the beast residing in man—…id, man naked, irrational, careless of social accommodations. Bratton (ed. 1987) records actors’ interpretations.

1830 Hast thou giuen…two daughters]
F’s Did’st thou giue and omission of two makes verse impossible. Bradley (1904, p. 288 n.): Surely verse. Lear has not yet spoken prose in this scene, and his next three speeches are in verse. The next is in prose, and, ending in his tearing off his clothes, shows the advance of insanity. Vickers (1968, p. 368): In Lear’s three mad-scenes (III, iv, III, vi, IV, vi) the King, As mad as the vexed sea, oscillates alarmingly and unpredictably between prose and verse…as Lear goes shooting off from one obsession to another: Justice, Revenge, Ingratitude, Lechery, Kingship, Humanity…the alternations corresponding (though not identically) to the flashes of reason in madness. Clarkes (ed. 1868): [Q’s] two lends additional point to Lear’s unsettled-witted question; it tends to make it more strictly arising out of his own personal sorrows, and more inapt to the stranger addressed. Edwards (ed. 1975): All wretchedness is now attributed to filial ingratitude. Weis (ed. 1993, p. 22): On seeing Poor Tom…[Lear] recognize[s] an image of his own self as shortly he will be.

1831 this]
Maclean (1952, pp. 608–14): In the speech—one of the great moments, in which Lear first recognizes his identity with unprotected nakedness scarred with self-inflicted wounds and suffers a complete change in his thoughts and feelings about the nature of man, beasts, the gods, and the universe, to the loss of his sanity, the crucial word is the monosyllable this: it is the one big word within this speech—the one right word…in the right place; it is the last word.…The right word should be irreplaceable and in some sense definite; only there are moments so tremendous that their exact size is without any definite boundary,…which have a size that is unmentionable, moments which cannot, at least in the instant, be fully faced or exactly spoken of by those who must endure them.

1832–41 Who…taking]
Vickers (1968, pp. 364–5): All of Edgar’s speeches as Poor Tom are—rightly—fragmented, hurried, as if pursued, and they all fall into the natural medium for this sort of utterance, the catalogue, and to a great moral and thematic effect. His first speech records the persecutions he has suffered but also reflects other parts of the play—Lear’s exile on the heath in the storm, his pride, Edmund’s treachery, Gloucester’s superstition—and are given the force and speed of a breakneck progress by the parallel structure. Cf. 1860–3, 1865–78.

1832 giues]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Edgar’s rambling speeches are started by some word of the previous speaker, comparing 1859–60. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Edgar, taking his cue from Lear’s word given, repeats the kind of petition expected of Bedlam beggars.

1833 through fire…Flame]
F’s addition of Flame seems redundant. Johnson (ed. 1765) apparently understands through to mean by means of: Alluding to the ignis fatuus, supposed to be lights kindled by mischievous beings to lead travellers into destruction. But through must refer to direction before foord, and whirli-poole. The fire and flame may be only hallucinations associated with the fiend and Hell, but just as likely the reference is to lightning: cf. 1659, 1669–70, 1698. Milward (1987, p. 178) compares the child in Mark 22 possessed by an evil spirit who oft times…casteth him into ye fyre, and into the water to destroye him (Geneva). Wells (ed. 2000) compares MND 3.1.106–7 (921–2).

1834 foord]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 178): Foord = ford. The F reading [Sword], with s for f, has the appearance of a misreading of handwriting; cf. n. 988. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 535): Sword is a period spelling of sward…but this hardly seems obstacle enough…for inclusion in Edgar’s list.

1834 whirli-poole]
Sh.’s only use of the word; it appears in Leir 2486 (see ); cf. n. 1840.

1835 that]
Page (ed. 1889): The antecedent is foul fiend. On the use of that for who see Abbott §258. Cf. Franz §339, and 2942.

1835 kniues…halters]
Steevens (ed. 1778): Infernal spirits are always represented as urging the wretched to self-destruction, citing Marlowe’s Doctor Faustus 2.2.572–4: swords and knives, | Gunnes, poyson, halters, and invenomb’d steele, | Are laid before me to dispatch my selfe. Suicide, being both murder and an act of despair, was a mortal sin that won a soul for Satan’s kingdom. Cf. nn. 2475, 2932, 3120, 3154, 3213, 3260. Malone (1790, 10:681) finds the same details in Harsnett (1603, p. 219): Ma: Mainy in his next fit said…that the deuil layd them in the Gallery, that some of those that were possessed, might either hang thẽselues with the halter, or kil themselues with the blades. See . Idem (in Boswell, ed. 1821): In Higgins’s Mirour Dispayre, after offering Both knyues, sharpe swordes, poyna[rde]s all bedyde | With bloud, and poysons prest, with a knife struck Cordila, who dyde, a damned creature like; see , . Kittredge (ed. 1940) finds in Greene & Lodge’s A Looking Glass for London (1594, sig. H4; 5.2.21) the SD The euill angell tempteth him, offering the knife and rope, and Brooke (ed. 1947) adds Spenser’s F.Q. 1.9.22 ff., where Despaire lends Sir Trevisan a rope and Sir Terwin a rusty knife. Craik (1958, p. 52) finds the suicide’s traditional rope and dagger offered by Despair in several moral interludes.

1836 pue]
Delius (ed. 1854): The fact that the devil pursued him even into his pew suggests even more strongly the danger to which he was exposed (Ger.). Deighton (ed. 1891): But pew was not always used for an enclosed seat in a church [OED, sb.1 2]; Pepys, for instance, in his Diary for 15th and 17th February, 1669, employs the word for seats in a theater [OED, 3]; and the word literally means only an elevated place (OED, Etymology: Late ME. puwe,…OF. puye,…L. podia, pl. of podium elevated place,…balcony). Tovey (ed. 1896): It may mean the box or cell in which poor Tom was confined in Bedlam. Pew-fellow, used by Shakespeare ([R3 4.4.58 (2829): Pue-fellow with others mone]) in the sense of companion in misery, is perhaps connected with this sense of prison-cell. More probably it refers to mourning in the same church pew; but see OED (3b): Transf. Station, situation; allotted place (cited by Horsman, ed. 1973). Kittredge (ed. 1940): A gallery in a house or outside a chamber window—not, a pew in church; Muir (1951, p. 17) agrees, citing Harsnett’s words Gallery (see prev. n.) and Pue-fellow (p. 77). Wilson (ed. 1960): But O.E.D. gives no support. The ord. meaning…w[oul]d make the temptation more sinister.

1836 ratsbane]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Not any specific poison, but anything destructive to rats. Hoeniger (1992, p. 260): Commonly white arsenic.

1836 pottage]
OED (sb. 1): Soup, esp. a thick soup. The word does not appear elsewhere in Sh. F’s Porredge, used 8 other times, is an altered form of the same word. Neither form means oatmeal until mid-17th. c.

1837 heart]
See n. 852.

1837 bay]
OED (adj.1 1): Reddish brown.

1837 trotting horse]
