Madden (1897, pp. 261–2): The foot-cloth horse served for show.…A great personage entering a town in state would exchange his ambling nag for a trotting-horse, called a clothsell horse or foot-cloth horse.…A trotting horse was associated with the idea of pride. Edwards (ed. 1975): A high-stepping horse. Weis (ed. 1993): A slow and stately horse. Wells (ed. 2000): Presumably…Tom is having illusions of greatness.

1837–8 foure incht]
Wells (ed. 2000): Four-inches-wide; OED’s first instance of inched in this sense. Wilson (ed. 1960): Cf. the half-witted tailor in The Magnetic Lady, v, i, 8 (Jonson, vi, 589), who speaks of running over two-inch bridges. Perh. proverbial; in any case <Lat. prov. ire per extentum funem, to walk the tight-rope, to perform a very difficult feat, as pointed out by Blunden (1934, p. 202). Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): Such riding would require diabolic help. Or might be inspired by diabolic malice.

1838 course…shadow]
Eccles (ed. 1792), course: Pursue (OED, v. 2); so all eds. Wilson (ed. 1960): I.e. like a cat chasing its tail. Cf. Tilley S281, To be afraid of one’s own shadow. Wilson’s readings seem oddly whimsical and anticlimactic. Tom’s career is more self-destructive; he rides at headlong speed, as if pursuing a traitor. Joseph (ed. 1966), fancifully: He regards his own shadow as a traitor because it slinks behind him—a reading that requires Edgar to chase what follows him. Elton (1966, p. 85 n.) suggests a pun on curse, citing Kökeritz (1953, pp. 100–1).

1838 for]
Abbott (§148): As being (OED, prep. 19: As equivalent to).

1838 traytor]
Campbell (1888, p. 501): Allusion to his recent danger and escapes, comparing 1252 ff.

1839–40 blesse…blesse]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): God bless. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 149) defends F’s Blisse…blisse, citing OED (v. 2): To give joy or gladness to.…(In 16–17th c. blended with bless.) Muir (ed. 1952): But see [2015],…and [1840] where bless [OED, v.1 3: To protect or guard, save, keep from (evil)] is more appropriate. Horsman (ed. 1973): Hallow by making the sign of the cross, and hence defend against evil. Cf. 2479.

1839 fiue wits]
The blessing is formulaic; cf. 2015, where Edgar repeats it. Following Bridge (1919–20, p. 16), Wilson (1960, p. 107) quotes from Orlando Gibbons’s The London Cry (B.L. Add. MS 17792, fol. 110) a cry to be heard in English town and country: Poor naked Bedlam, Tom’s a cold, a small cut of thy bacon or a piece of thy sow’s side, good Bess, God Almighty bless thy wits. So also Garton (1961, p. 904). Sternfeld (1963, pp. 177–80) reproduces Gibbons’s setting of this cry and discusses it and several other musical analogues. Several Bedlamite poems survive from the 17th c. in which Poor Tom, begging for bacon, blesses the five sound senses of his auditor: see Graves (1927, p. 23) and Wells (1961, p. 312), who prefer these latter lyrics as sources for Lr. Sternfeld provides musical settings (see ) for both sets of words, noting that it is uncertain whether Mad Tom sings or speaks them in the play. OED (Wit sb. 3b): Five wits: usually, the five (bodily) senses; often vaguely, the perceptions or mental faculties generally; see n. 682. The term occurs several times in Sh., in Son. 141.9 as distinct from the five senses (Malone, ed. 1790) and in TN 4.2.86 (2071) as the equivalent of full mental powers, or sanity. Johnson (ed. 1765, 2:256): The wits seem to have been reckoned five, by analogy to the five senses, or the five inlets of ideas. Malone (op. cit., 4:94): From Stephen Hawes’s poem called Graunde Amoure, ch. xxiv. edit. 1554 [sig. N2], it appears that the five wits were—common wit, imagination, fantasy, estimation, and memory. Collier (ed. 1843) quotes from the medieval interlude The Worlde and the Chylde, where Perseuerance describes first the .v. wyttes bodely, or the five senses, then other .v. wyttes: clere in mynde, imagynacyon, reason, understondynge, and compassyon. Tovey (ed. 1896): It does not appear that Shakespeare ever uses wits meaning senses, i.e., the physical faculties so called, though he often uses senses for the mental powers, or wits. Surely the blessing of a Bedlam, here to a mad king, refers to mental powers, not to the senses. Cf. 2247–8.

1839 a cold]
Abbott (§24): In a chill, treating a (or a-) as a worn-down proclitic form of OE preposition an, on; see n. 1147. OED (A prep.1 11): State: in; cf. 1976. OED lists Acold as an adj. dating from the 14th c., quoting this l. Cf. 1863, 1925, 1954, 2241. Tom’s a-cold seems to have been the habitual cry of Bedlam beggars: see prev. n. and n. 1265.

1839 O…do de]
Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxiii): Was this one of Shakespeare’s mature additions, on later revision? Stone (1980, p. 248) speculates whether a reviser has here been inventing nonsense gratuitously: having noticed the frequent irruptions of nonsense, chiefly in the part of Edgar, [has] he…enter[ed] into the spirit of the thing…, altering and embroidering as he felt disposed? Taylor (1983, pp. 407–8): The added syllables are dramatically sensible and defensible, by reference to the play’s preoccupation with both human bestiality and the unalterable insufficiency of human language. Cf. n. 1879. Eccles (ed. 1792): This seems intended to express the sound uttered by persons who shiver with extreme cold. Or, perhaps, it only marks some of those wild and fantastic noises which are oftentimes the indication of insanity. Many eds., for lack of any other explanation, accept the first of these suggestions; but such notions (or impressions) must not be urged too far (Campbell, 1888, p. 501). Furness (ed. 1880) and others adduce the verbs didder and dodder, but they refer to the action of trembling, not to a sound or interjection. Murphy (1984, p. 199): May be a prompter’s direction for the actor’s performance. The Harsnett material gives abundant testimony to the demonic cold, the chill wind of the demons, citing Harsnett (1603, p. 199): the devil aunswered in a trembling quivering voice…the poore devil chattered his teeth so sore.

1840 whirle-winds]
Muir (1951, p. 17): Harsnett [1603, pp. 140–1; see ]…refers to whirlwinds several times, describing the shapes taken by devils. Elton (1966, p. 153 n.): Whirlwinds were fairy eddies, thought to lift and abduct people in the air, citing contemporary fairy lore. OED attests only to natural kinds. The word also appears in Leir 2486 (see ), and several times earlier in Sh.

1840 starre-blusting]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 397): Misreading of a as u. See nn. 818 and 1451 on blast. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): This refers to the astrological belief in malign influences from the stars (OED, Star sb.1 20, quoting only this l.). Wright (ed. 1875) finds sparrow-blasting, or sprite-blasting of the deuil in Harsnett (1603, p. 80; cf. p. 136, and below); Muir (1951, p. 17) adds deuil-blasting (p. 107; see ) and Owle-blasted (p. 137; see ).

1840–1 taking]
See n. 1446. OED (vbl. sb. 2b): A seizure or attack of disease…; enchantment; blasting, quoting this l.

1841 charitie]
See n. 1271. Skillan (ed. 1967): Possibly he means that lear of his charity should pray for him against the fiend, referring to the following words. Or the beggar may be asking for any of the kinds of help he needs, esp. food and shelter.

1842–3 there…there.]
Moberly (ed. 1876): He catches at the fiend as he would at flies. Darton (ed. 1928, SD): Pointing in different directions at random. Sprague (1944, p. 291): Strikes on difft sides with his staff, a prompt note of George Frederick Cooke’s time. Soens (1968, p. 19): Edgar makes thrusts with an imaginary rapier and dagger at an unseen devil. Colman (ed. 1982): Tom lunges at an imagined fiend. Kittredge (ed. 1940), most probably: Edgar makes grabs at different parts of his body as if to catch vermin—or devils, comparing 2014+1. He clasps at the parts of his body where the devil is causing pain, or lice are biting.

1842 and and]
Halio (ed. 1994): The Q compositor obviously omitted a there after the first and.

1843 againe]
The comment of Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) on F’s ag ai ne surpasses their usual foliolatry: This spacing…is so regularly irregular that it suggests the intention to present the separation of the syllables meant to be howled out by the actor, as a climax of his crazy speech.

1844 What]
See n. 810. F’s substitution of Ha’s may have been an error. Doran (1931, p. 99): It is likely that Shakespeare wrote the line…just as it stands in Q1.…In the transcript [printer’s copy for F], has may have been added to smooth out the line. The printer may have then mistaken it for a replacement of What, or it may even have been so intended. Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 15–16): The line sounds clumsy in both Q and F.…There seems little doubt that Q accidentally omits the word has or haue.…The F editor, altering Q, inserted ha’s after What, and the compositor understood it as a substitution. On the possibility of Ha’s for have, see n. 204. Hogan (1962, p. 75): Perhaps the F compositor abbreviated because his measure was full.

1844 passe]
Schmidt (1875): Predicament (OED, sb.2 7). Only Soens (1968, p. 19): Fencing trick; see n. 1842–3.

1845 didst]
F’s Would’st gives a symmetry of sound, but perhaps implies more will and less helplessness than is consistent with Couldst.

1845 them]
On F’s ’em see n. 908.

1846–7 Nay…sham’d]
Kerrigan (1983, pp. 221, 237 n.): A joke directly addressed to the audience, comparing 1858–9. At least the Fool’s attempt at humor signals his recovery from his terror.

1846 reseru’d]
Wilson (ed. 1960): He recalls the reservation at [141, 1550]. The hundred knights had barely concealed Lear’s beggary.

1846 blanket]
Cf. 1262.

1847 sham’d]
Delius (ed. 1854): Embarrassed.

1848–9 plagues…faults]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Disease is poured down by planetary influence as a punishment on the wicked. Boswell (ed. 1821) finds the same idea in Tim. 4.3.109–11 (1722–4), and Kittredge (ed. 1940) in R2 1.3.284 (557+17) and 3.3.85–7 (1672–4); and see next n. The image of plague as divine punishment recurs at 2249 and 3132.

1848 pendulous]
Schmidt (1875): Impending (OED, a. 1b: Overhanging, quoting this l. and The Birth of Merlin 4.1.220–1 [ed. Brooke], what pendelous mischief roofs thy head, | How fatal, and how sudden; cf. 5.1.101, pendulous stones). Sh. does not use the word elsewhere. Page (ed. 1889): Refers (by hypallage) rather to the plagues than to the air. Chambers (ed. 1906): Heavy. Muir (ed. 1952) compares sensible accidents…made pendulous in the ayre in Harsnett (1603, p. 159). Lott (ed. 1974): But [here] it is transferred…to the air itself.

1849 fated]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Destined to fall. Crook (ed. 1907): As predestined punishments. Craig (ed. 1901) compares AWW 1.1.217 (224), fated skye. Gardner (ed. 1969): Invested with powers of fatal retribution.

1849 fall]
F’s light avoids a jingle with faults.

1851 traytor]
Skillan (ed. 1967): Because kent is opposing him (the king) in his belief.

1851 subdued]
OED (v. 2e): Bring to a low state, reduce, quoting only this l. and Ant 4.14.74 (2910). Hunter (ed. 1972): Accent…on the first syllable.

1851 nature]
See n. 441.

1852 vnkind]
See n. 132. Walker (1860, 1:87): First syllable accented. Kittredge (ed. 1940) compares 250, unchaste.

1853–4 Is…flesh]
Adelman (1992, p. 302): Three simultaneous and incompatible questions…: are fathers so cruel to their own bodies (= flesh)? are offspring (= flesh) so cruel to their fathers? are fathers so cruel to their offspring (= flesh)? Editors and directors usually foreground the first of these questions. Only the first answers Kent: Lear is arguing that Edgar/a discarded father would not mistreat his own body thus; therefore he must have cruel daughters who have done so.

1853 discarded]
Deighton (ed. 1891): A term at cards for getting rid of a worthless card (OED, ppl. a. 1). With the more general sense of rejected (OED, 2).

1854 haue…mercy]
Delius (ed. 1854): Refers to the sticking of pins in the mortified bare arms [1266–7] (Ger.). Clarkes (ed. 1868): Rather, the exposure of Poor Tom’s body to the severity of the weather. Craig (ed. 1901): Or to Edgar’s wickedness. Edwards (ed. 1975): Haue must mean receive, since Lear’s remark concerns rejected fathers being made to suffer physically. Furness (ed. 1880): Here Edwin Booth’s Lear Draws a thorn, or wooden spike, from Edgar’s arm, and tries to thrust it into his own. After line [1856]: Edgar seizes Lear’s hand and takes away the thorn.

1855 Iudicious]
Schmidt (1874): Discerning, wise (OED, a. 1). White (ed. 1883): Just, even-handed, retributive. Walker’s (1860, 1:64) Judicial is rightly considered doubtful here by OED (3). Carter (1905, p. 437) compares Wisd. 11:11, and Milward (1987, p. 178) Job 4:8, Wisd. 11:13. Lott (ed. 1974): The punishment is just since his own flesh was responsible for begetting such daughters. Edwards (ed. 1975): The idea that sexual desire is sinful, and that we therefore deserve any suffering our children bring us, occurs elsewhere in the play, esp. 3133–4.

1856 Pelicane]
Johnson (ed. 1765): The young pelican is fabled to suck the mother’s blood. OED (1b): In reference to the fable that the pelican revives or feeds her young with her own blood. This is given by Epiphanius and St. Augustine [Patrol. Lat. 37:1300]; it appears to be of Egyptian origin, and to have referred originally to another bird [see Horapollo, Hieroglyphics 1:11: Vulture]. Its appearance in medieval writers is documented by Marsh (1878, p. 445), Dyer (1884, p. 145), Murray (1904, p. 267), Dormer (1904, pp. 310–11), and B. W. (1904, p. 311), and among Sh.’s contemporaries by Steevens (ed. 1778: Dekker, Shirley), Green (1870, pp. 393–7: emblems), Wright (ed. 1875: Batman), Phipson (1883, pp. 285–90: Chester, Mirour for Magistrates), Verity (in Irving & Marshall, ed. 1889: Rowley, Middleton), Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905: Lyly), Muir (ed. 1952: Whitney, Edward III), Fraser (1962, pp. 91–2), and others. Stephen Batman’s version of Bartholomaeus Anglicus gives perhaps the more common Elizabethan form of the myth, that the mother bird wounds herself to revive, not feed her young: The Pellican loueth too much her children. For when the children bee haught, and begin to waxe hoare, they smite the father and mother in the face, wherfore the mother smiteth them againe and slaieth them. And the thirde daye the mother smiteth her selfe in her side that the bloud runneth out, and sheddeth that hot bloud vppon the bodies of her children. And by vertue of the bloud the birdes that were before dead, quicken againe (1582, fol. 186v). Hoeniger (ed. 1968) cites Greene, Quip for an Upstart Courtier [1592, sig. C]: like the yoong Pellican peckt at thy mothers brest with thy presumption. Sh. refers to the myth in R2 2.1.126–7 (770–1) and Ham. 4.5.147–8 (2896–7), and in his source, Leir 512–13, as Skottowe (1824, 2:105) points out, the King says, I am as kind as is the Pellican, That kils it selfe, to saue her young ones liues; see . The mother’s self-wounding is commonly taken as a symbol of parental love, piety, kingly care, or even Christ’s sacrifice. See Nameri (1976, pp. 101–5). The converse, that the young are symbols of impiety (Moberly, ed. 1876), rapacity (Verity, ed. 1897), cruelty (Craig, ed. 1901), or ingratitude (Brooke, ed. 1947), is questioned by Marsh and Phipson. Muir (op. cit.): Lear seems to go further [than the usual fable], and imply that the young pelicans strike at the breasts of the old ones, to drain their life out. Westerweel (1984, pp. 10–14), however, traces the unfavorable application to the child to the 3rd–4th c. Physiologus, widely used as a source of imagery in preaching manuals and religious textbooks of the later Middle Ages. There the story of the Pelican is associated with Isa. 1:2 as an emblem of Christ’s forgiveness. Hunter (ed. 1972): Lear sees Gonorill and Regan as assaulting him and also demanding that he sacrifice himself for them. Though the image has been applied to men (see above), Adelman (1992, p. 299) find’s Lear’s use of it grotesque and apparent gender confusion.

1857 Pilicock…hill]
Warner (1768, pp. 30–1): Perhaps the burthen of some song, which only Elson (1900, p. 244) thinks that Edgar sang. Verses found in J. Ritson, ed., Gammer Gurton’s Garland (1810), J. O. Halliwell, The Nursery Rhymes of England (3rd ed., 1843, p. 161), and the Opies (1951, p. 432), go Pillycock, Pillycock, sate on a hill; If he’s not gone, he sits there still. Kittredge (ed. 1940): But there is no evidence that this couplet is very old. Horsman (ed. 1973): Perhaps echoing an older rhyme. Hunter (ed. 1972, p. 341): Sounds like a ballad-refrain, but not otherwise known. Halliwell finds the word Pillycock in a 14th-c. MS, Harl. 913, fol. 54. Foakes (ed. 1997): [Edgar], not the Fool, now has rhyming jingles, comparing 1900–3, 1916–18, 1966–8.

1857 Pilicock]
Thirlby (MS notes, 1725–33): Introduced by Pelican in the previous line. Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:50, Gloss.): A fondling Term, signifying—little Cock, little Rogue [OED, 2: My pretty knave (Cotgrave)]: but in [Lr.]…it is (seemingly) the name of some minute spirit, such as Puck, or Robin Goodfellow. (Ibid., 3.1:2): Harsnett (1603, pp. 49, 141, 181; see , ) names a subordinate devil Killico, perhaps, the father of Shakespeare’s—Pillicock. Delius (ed. 1854): In his fear Edgar takes it for the name of an evil spirit (Ger.). Kemshead (ed. 1875): Dr. Latham…connects the word…with the name of one of the elves in the German and Slavonic mythologies. Malone (ed. 1790) first indicates, and Douce (1807, 2:160) supports with citations, a double entendre: Florio (1611), Piuiólo (also Pinco, Puga): A childs pillicocke, pricke or dildoe (OED, 1: Penis, citing this l.). Hunter (ed. 1869): A cant term of licentious familiarity, citing Rabelais, Gargantua 1.11 (tr. Urquhart, 1694, 1:44), where one of Gargantua’s nurses calls his penis her Pillicock,…her staff of Love. Partridge (1947, p. 165): Male generative organs (pill, testicle; i, euphony-convenient; cock, penis. So Williams (1994), s.v. pillie, pillock: Pillicock redoubles the sense. Wells (ed. 2000) records an obscene use, Piddecock bolt vpright, from 1639–40. Green (1987, p. 208), however, derives the word from piloke, a stuffed rod-shaped ball thrown in a game, which acquired sexual associations. Brooke (ed. 1947): Pelican suggests to Edgar this vulgar word, which he fancifully distorts into a bird of prey sitting on its hill. Wilson (ed. 1960): Alluding to this flesh begot, etc. Elton (1966, p. 317): Mad Tom interpolates the generative cause. Oppel (1980, p. 171): Edgar parodies the diction of the Psalms which Lear for a moment indulges in.

1857 pelicocks hill]
Partridge (1947, p. 165): The mount of Venus = the pudendum muliebre. Wilson (ed. 1960, p. 291), agreeing: Cf. Ven. 232. See prev. n. Colman (1974, p. 207): But perhaps Sugden [1925] (and others) may have been right in leaving Poor Tom’s nonsense as nonsense: A hill in the land of Nursery Rhymes. Murphy (1984, pp. 192, 199, 201) finds an analogy with the subjects of exorcism in Harsnett: I suggest that the voice speaking of the ribaldry of Pillicock is a demonic voice of lust, here issuing from the mad (possessed) Edgar. Edgar’s passages should establish clearly…three modes of speaking and vocalizing.…The responses of Lear, Kent, and the Fool should engage with the appropriately consistent voice.…Through defy the foul fiend, another rational voice of the prolocutor in a poetic catechism addressed to the public should be heard.

1857 a lo lo lo]
F’s alow: alow may be mere sophistication; it prevents reading the line in ballad meter. Furness (ed. 1880): Not unlikely…meant to imitate the crowing of a cock. I see no reason…[to] change alow into Halloo (see textual n.). So Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Pillicock suggests the cock-crowing sounds of the next line, which Theobald first spoiled. Zitner (1974, p. 15): If so, here is the reduction of paternity to barnyard pride. Sh.’s only unmistakable cock-crowing is cockadidle-dow (Tmp. 1.2.387 [528]). Campbell (1888, pp. 500–1): Loo, loo…was in Shropshire forty years ago…the customary cry in coursing to signal to the greyhound that a hare was in view.…It may well be that the same cry is here transformed by Edgar to his imaginary chase after the fiend. Craig (ed. 1901): A cry to excite dogs which I have heard in Cardigan, comparing Tro. 5.7.10 (3480), now dogge lowe, Paris lowe. OED (Loo int.): A cry to incite a dog to the chase; = halloo [under whose def. this l. is quoted]; (Hallow v.2): To shout, in order to urge on dogs to the chase, assist combined effort, or attract attention; cf. n. 1653. Cf. T. S[nodham], Jewell for Gentrie (1614, sig. G1): Now the hounds running in full Chase, the French-men vse to say…Swef, alieu, doute alieu, and we imitating them, say, there boys, there. The French original seems to be Suave[t], à lieu, douce à lieu; on the facing p. Snodham translates Sweft as Soft, the equivalent of the common cry Douce; it derives from Lat. suavis. In The Master of Game (ca. 1406–13; ed. Baillie-Grohman, 1909, p. 184) a call to slow the hounds pursuing a hare includes the sequence swef a la douce, a lui, a lui. Cf. n. 2031. Possibly Tom pretends to set the dogs on his tormenting fiend Pillicock. Bransom (1934, p. 102): Edgar is trying to attract a visionary dog, one of his persecutors (along with the foul fiend). Kittredge (ed. 1940): A wild halloo, as if he were calling a hawk, comparing Ham. 1.5.116 (803) Hillo. Perrett (1904, p. 260 n.): Not a shout, but the noise of the Bedlam’s horn. See T. S. (op. cit., sig. H2v): Where the Foxe is earthed blow for the Terriers after this manner. One long and two short. The second winde one long and two short. Muir (ed. 1952): Perhaps it is intended as the refrain of the song. Rosenberg (1972, p. 220): A Bedlam noise, or a song refrain, or an animal call…[or] sounds accompanying the sexual act, a suggestion defying comment. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 535): F’s Alow may mean below decks (cf. 1819) and Q may be simply a repeated imperative Lo! (Look, look, look!).

1858–9 This…madmen]
See n. 1846–7. The speech of course refers to Lear as well as to Edgar and himself, and could be a hint that he wants to enter the hovel again. Hunter (ed. 1972): As Edgar takes over the role of the broken, rhapsodic, song-singing madman, the Fool is reduced to the role of the balanced observer. Edwards (ed. 1975): It is rare to get a straight remark from the Fool. He is perhaps taken aback by the last sally of Edgar’s, which is so exactly his own brand of fooling.…He feels the air too full of non-reason to add his own quota, and during the rest of the scene he speaks only once.

1860–3 Take…cold]
See n. 1832. Armour (ed. 1930): To talk nonsense continuously is rather a strain on Edgar’s ingenuity, and he falls back upon the Ten Commandements of his childhood’s lessons. Noble (1935, p. 230): Edgar in his feigned madness quotes a number of Biblical injunctions. Eph. vi.1: Children, obey your parents; Deut. xxiii.23: But that which is once gone out of thy lips, thou must keep, and doe; Matt. v.34: Sweare not at al; Catechism: Thou shalt not commit adultery; 1 Tim. ii.9: Likewise also the women, that they aray themselues in comely apparell, with shamefastnesse and discreete behauiour, not in braided heare, either golde, or pearles, or costly aray. Wilson (ed. 1960): Injunctions by keeping which the foul fiend may be held at bay, adding Exod. 20:12 (5th Commandment); Catechism, Be true and just in all thy dealings; Exod. 20:7 (3rd Commandment); Exod. 20:14 (7th Commandment). Milward (1987, pp. 178–9) adds more. Vickers (1968, p. 365): A definite structure and a relevance to the action of the play…recur, in a symmetrical and oddly mad-sane decalogue which fits further elements—obviously the children’s disobedience, Edmund’s false speaking, Gloucester’s adultery, and pride; see n. 1832–41. Murphy (1984, p. 192) finds the influence of Harsnett: The catechetical injunctions…are either commands of the Christian exorcist or teachings remembered by the Christian penitent-possessed. Greenblatt (1985, p. 118): Edgar’s pretended demonic possession…is of the homiletic variety.

1860 at’h]
Q2’s and F’s of the. See nn. 669+10, 1105, 1613.

1860 foule]
Wilson (ed. 1960) detects a pun on fool, following 1858; Copley (1966, pp. 250–2), another on fowl, following 1856.

1861 words iustly]
Most eds. accept Pope’s emendation to word, since elsewhere Sh. uses the sing. noun in the expression keep one(s) word (OED, Word sb. 8: Promise, undertaking). Possibly the compositor misread the final e of worde (a spelling found often in the good quartos though not in F) as the abbreviation for -es, and set words. It is just possible that words here might mean commands (OED, 7) or even, in Edgar’s catechism, Ten Commandments (OED, 7b), making the sentence read obay thy parents, [in] keep[ing] thy commandments: sweare not, etc.; but Sh. never refers to the Commandments as the Ten Words, and keep seems to be parallel with obay, sweare, etc. Deighton (ed. 1891), justly: Honourably (OED, adv. 1: Righteously); Kittredge (ed. 1940): Exactly, scrupulously (OED, 5). A few eds. defend F’s words Iustice. The sense Justice (= Rightfulness [OED, sb. 3]) of thy words is possible, though Dyce (ed. 1865) finds it ridiculous. Schmidt’s (ed. 1879) Be as just in deeds as in words (Ger.) is even more strained. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 150): Speak justly and do not depart from justice in your word(s). Muir (ed. 1952): Perhaps in this passage, depending for its effect on echoes from the scriptures and the prayer-book [cf. n. 1860–3], the simpler reading [Q’s] is to be preferred. Wilson (ed. 1960): G. I. D[uthie] withdraws the defence of F.…F Iustice prob. = iustle [or iustlie] misread. Halio (ed. 1992): Keep the integrity of your utterances, i.e. do not lie or bear false witness. The parody of the Commandments strengthens the F reading.

1861 sweare not]
Jones (1970, p. 129) compares James 5:12 and Matt. 5:33–7, and Shaheen (1987, p. 150) the latter.

1861 commit]
OED (v. 6c): Absol. To commit an offence, offend; to commit adultery or fornication, quoting this l. as its second ex., after the Geneva Bible. Steevens (ed. 1778), Wright (ed. 1875), Craig (ed. 1901), and Williams (1994) give contemporary exx. Milward (1987, p. 179) cites the biblical injunctions in Exod. 20:14, Deut. 5:18, Prov. 6:32.

1862 sworne]
Horsman (ed. 1973): Taken by an oath.

1862 set…on]
Schmidt (1875): Make intent on (OED, v. 37).

1862 sweet heart]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 193): F [Sweet-heart] is definitely wrong. For heart see n. 852. Deighton (ed. 1891) makes sweet an adverb—Set not your heart sweetly upon—but it is probably an adj. meaning dear little (Wilson, ed. 1960); see n. 918. Gardner (ed. 1969): Delicate thoughts. Or it may (just) mean sweetheart?

1863 proud array]
See n. 1860–3. Hunter (ed. 1972): The idea of clothes leads Tom naturally to his next remark about the cold. Shaheen (1987, p. 150) and Milward (1987, p. 179) compare 1 Tim. 2:9 (see n. 1860–3), 1 Pet. 3:3–4.

1863 a cold]
See n. 1839.

1865–78 A…fiend]
Vickers (1968, pp. 365–7): Poor Tom’s third speech is the most elaborately constructed yet, beginning apparently with Oswald but widening to include the complete bestiality of man,…[using] anaphora, isocolon, parison, antithesis, and various types of rhyme.…The parallelism here reinforces the naif attitude…, and the sing-song rhythms suggest a viewpoint which, if not exactly complacent, seems somehow unconcerned…and therefore more shocking—as with the second and still more incongruous use of the Ten Commandments model at the end of the speech. See nn. 1832–41, 1860–3. Murphy (1984, p. 192): Drawn from the penitent-possessed victims in Harsnett: The full confessional mode…closes with a demonic salute to the Prince of Darkness. Carroll (1996, p. 200): Poor Tom’s self-description emphasizes the body in all ways—the vanity of physical appearance, the urgings of the sensual appetite, the bestial identification. Foakes (ed. 1997), comparing similar satire in Revenger’s Tragedy 1.3.5–6: Such attacks appear to reflect popular feeling about extravagance and corruption at the court of James I.

1865 Seruingman]
From the details of behavior in the following lines, Knight (ed. 1840) concludes, This is not a menial, but a servant [in love], comparing TGV 2.4.106 (756); cf. OED (Servant, n. 4b). Schmidt (1875) agrees that here it is a Term of gallantry…(cavaliere servente), but later (ed. 1879) he decides that though a gallant may be called a lady’s servant he is never called her serving-man, a word which here means only attendant (OED, 1, citing this l.). Verity (ed. 1897): A satirical but no doubt correct picture of the Elizabethan servant who aped the manners of his master. Craig (ed. 1901) cites Bartholomeus Cocles, Physiognomie (1556, sig. A7): The forhead ouer smal and narrowe through out declareth that man to be simple, sone styrred to Ire, lyghtly furious or cruel, a desyrer of bewtiful thinges [,] to be a courtyer or a seruinge man, foolyshe, vnapte to learnyng, a voluter, an ouer great feader and a glotõ. Bradley (1904, p. 448) will not hint that Edgar’s description of the servant doing the act of darkness with his mistress refers to Oswald and Goneril. Bransom (1934, p. 104): A masterly picture…of a rake’s progress. Muir (ed. 1952): Edgar’s account would fit either a fashionable lover or a servant who turned his good looks to account. Wilson (ed. 1960): Cf. [1914–16]. Abram-men often claimed to have been such; Harman [see n. 1265] writes of one Stradling who saith he was the Lord Stourton’s man (Judges, [Elizabethan Underworld, 1930,] p. 83). Cf. W. Stafford, Examination of Complaints (1581), p. 64, Now a dayes Seruingmen goe more costely in apparell…then their maisters were wont to doe in times past. Halio (ed. 1992): The description of a dandified servant as courtier fits Oswald as well.

1865 proud in heart]
For heart see n. 852. Traversi (1952–3, p. 134): Since he may be courtier and lover (see prev. n.), this phrase may indicate not only the satisfaction he feels in the position he has attained, but the intensity of passion in serving his mistress’ lust. Booth (1983, p. 164 n.): Also lustful (OED, Proud a. 8). Shaheen (1987, p. 150) compares Prov. 16:5, 21:4, 28:25, Psa. 101:5.

1866 curld my hair]
Rushton (1871, p. 47) compares Lyly, Euphues to Philautus (ed. Bond, 1:256): Be not curious to curlle thy haire. Furness (ed. 1880): This may, perhaps, refer to the love-locks that were worn by gallants. Verity (ed. 1897): Like a foppish gallant, citing Oth. 1.2.68 (286). Malone (ed. 1790) and Muir (1951, p. 17) find Maynie’s curled hair named as a sign of his pride in Harsnett (1603, p. 54).

1866 wore…cap]
Theobald (ed. 1733): As the Favour of a Mistress. Cf. R2 5.3.17–18 (2513–14), MV 4.1.426 (2347), Tro. 4.4.71 (2459). Wilson (ed. 1960): For contemp. references see Linthicum, [1936] p. 267.…The pl. suggests more than one mistress, comparing 1871–2. Weis (ed. 1993): If Tom was a servant in a great household, then mistress would mean both his lover and his master’s wife.

1866 serued]
OED (Serve v.1 10b): Gratify, furnish means for satisfying (desire), quoting this l.

1866 lust]
Main (ed. 1962): Apparently tormented by the sin of lust,…Edgar is actually describing the vices of his father and his brother.

1867 heart]
See nn. 75, 1029.

1867 act of darkenes]
Dent (1981, D184.1): Possibly proverbial: Deed(s) of darkness (1 murder; 2 fornication [the meaning here]; other). Shaheen (1987, pp. 150–1) compares deedes and workes of darkenesse from the homily Against Whoredome and Vncleannesse, part 2, and Rom. 13:12–14. Williams (1994), Darkness, cites numerous exx., including this.

1868 spake]
On the archaic form see n. 476.

1869 sweet]
See n. 918. Gardner (ed. 1969): Gracious.

1870 contriuing]
Craig (ed. 1901): Plotting (OED, Contrive v.1 1b). Muir (ed. 1952): Presumably in his sleep.

1870–1 wine…woman]
Muir (ed. 1952): Cf. Florio, Second Fruites [1591], p. 105: Shun wine, dice, and letchery, | Else will you come to beggery. From the same source Tilley and Dent (1981) quote Women, Wine, and Dice, will bring a man to Lice under the proverb Gaming (Play), women, and wine, while they laugh they make men pine (G27).

1871 deeply]
Schmidt (1874): In the inmost recesses of the heart, most feelingly. Wilson (ed. 1960): With obvious quibble (on drink deep), lost by F’s deerely. Halio (ed. 1992): F’s repetition [of deerely] appears intentional and emphatic. It could as well be an error of misreading, eyeskip, or anticipation.

1871 out paromord]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:47): Exceed in Number of Paramours.

1872 Turke]
Delius (ed. 1854): The Grand Turk, the Sultan (OED, Turk1 2b, citing this l.). Page (ed. 1889): Who is allowed, by the Mohammedan laws, to have a large harem. Wilson (ed. 1960): Prov[erbial] type of promiscuity. Colman (1974, p. 220): Type-figure of ambisexual lubricity.

1872 heart]
See n. 852.

1872 light of eare]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Credulous of evil, ready to receive malicious reports. Schmidt (1874): Foolishly credulous. Hudson (ed. 1879): Or greedy…of obscene talk. Verity (ed. 1897): Or (?) an eavesdropper. Craig (ed. 1901): Perhaps…incapable of retaining a secret. OED (Light adj. 23), light-eared: Ready to listen, credulous. Onions (1911): Frivolous. Harbage (ed. 1958): Attentive to flattery and slander, or to levity and falsehood (Kermode, in Evans, ed. 1974). Edwards (ed. 1975): Immoral in what he would listen to. Kittredge (ed. 1940) finds the phrase, supporting Johnson’s gloss, in The Schole house of Women (1572; in Early Popular Poetry, ed. W. C. Hazlitt, 1866, 4:107), and compares the disapproval of listening to slander in Stephano Guazzo’s Ciuile Conuersation (tr. Pettie, 1586, fol. 31v; ed. Sullivan, 1925, 1:74–5).

1873–4 Hog…Lyon]
Malone (ed. 1790): Harsnett (1603, pp. 141, 281; see ) describes the casting-forth from Maister Maynie of devils in animal shapes representing the Seven Deadly Sins: The spirit of Pride went out in the forme of a Peacocke (forsooth) the spirit of Sloth in the likenesse of an Asse: the spirit of Enuy in the similitude of a Dog: the spirit of Gluttony in the forme of a Woolfe. Wright (ed. 1875): Mr. Skeat has pointed out to me that in the Ancren Riwle [tr. Morton, 1907, pp. 148–56], the seven deadly sins are typified by seven wild animals; the lion being the type of pride, the serpent of envy, the unicorn of wrath, the bear of sloth, the fox of covetousess, the swine of greediness, and the scorpion of lust. Johnson (1905, pp. 530–1) finds similar representations in Chaucer’s tr. of Boethius 4. Prosa 3.112 ff. (ed. Robinson) and Spenser’s F.Q. 1.4.18–35.

1873 stealth]
OED (sb. 1d): Cunning thievishness, quoting only this l. Hunter (ed. 1972): And stealthiness. Cf. 345.

1874 madnes]
Hunter (ed. 1972): The dog represents madness because [of] the transmission of rabies to man.

1874 pray]
Schmidt (1875): The act of preying, of catching and devouring other creatures (OED, Prey sb. 4). Hunter (ed. 1972): Pillage, violence.

1874–6 let…women]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Do not give your heart to a woman as soon as you hear her shoes creak and her silk gown rustle. Houghton (ed. 1957): If you must have creaking shoes (accounted fashionable!) and rustling silks, to impress women, at any rate don’t trust them. To Edwards (ed. 1975) the details imply a midnight visitation. Brownlee (1960, p. 277) quotes Burton, Anatomy of Melancholy 3.2.2.4, on Artificial Allurements: She walks along, and with the ruffling of her clothes, makes men look at her, her shoes creak, an inaccurate translation of St. Jerome’s Epist. 117.7, which says nothing of Burton’s clamore vestium but does censure creaking shoes: Caliga…stridore iuvenes ad se vocat (ed. Wright, 1980, p. 386). Probably the creakings and rustlings are simply attention-getters, seductive because they are feminine rather than fashionable sounds; see the next n. Merchant (1960, p. 72): The speech anticipates Lear’s rejection of hide and silk in 1884. Like Davenport (1953, p. 21), Kermode (2000, p. 191) compares a couplet from Donne’s Elegy IV—I taught my silks their whistling to forbear, Even my opprest shoes dumb and silent were (to escape detection)—but admits it cannot be thought very likely that Shakespeare had read it in manuscript.

1874 creeking of shooes]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Shoes that creaked were fashionable, quoting A tunable heele and a Musicall creake from William Rowley’s A Shoo-maker a Gentleman, 2.1.70–9 (ed. Stork, p. 191). But in fact the lines cited are a gross joke: the creaking shoes, says the shoemaker, are designed to cover the sound of a lady’s farting. See prev. n.

1875 ruslings]
Jennens (ed. 1770) prefers the Q pl. to F’s rustling because the added sibilance echoes the sense better.

1875 heart]
See n. 122.

1875–7 women…booke]
F reverses singulars and plurals of five words (see textual nn.), all unnecessarily.

1877 placket]
OED (sb.2 2): An apron or petticoat: hence transf. the wearer of a petticoat, a woman; (3): The opening or slit at the top of a skirt or petticoat, for convenience in putting on and off, quoting this l. doubtfully; (3b): Also sensu obscæno. So Williams (1994), quoting this l. Partridge (1947, p. 166): Because it is placed in contiguity with the pudend, quoting LLL 3.1.184 (950). Other meanings suggested—stomacher (Singer, ed. 1826), covering for the breast (Hudson, ed. 1851), pocket or purse (White, 1886, pp. 342–50), and chastity belt (Adee, ed. 1890, pp. liv–lvi)—seem to be either related to the word placard (sp. plackat) or to be unattested in Sh.’s time. Furness (ed. 1880) mentions but does not quote the comment of the mischievous Steevens, who liked to attribute notes on bawdry to a guileless, dissenting clergyman settled not far from Steevens’s home at Hampstead (Furness), thus giving the impression that the Rev. Amner had a vast knowledge and obsessive interest in such matters. Thus Steevens (ed. 1778): It appeareth from the following passage in Any Thing for a quiet Life, a silly comedy, that placket doth not signify the petticoat in general, but only the aperture therein: —between which is discovered the open part which is now called the placket. Bayley in his Dictionary, giveth the same account of the word. Yet peradventure, our poet hath some deeper meaning in The Winter’s Tale, where Autolycus saith—You might have pinch’d a placket, it was senseless. Idem (ed. 1793) adds: —and, now I bethink me, sir Thomas Urquart, knight, in his translation of that wicked varlet Rabelais, styleth the instrument wherewith Gargantua played at carnal tennis, his placket-racket. See that work, Vol. I. p. 184, edit. 1750. Impartiality nevertheless compelleth me to observe, that Master Coles in his Dictionary hath rendered placket by sinus muliebris: and a pleasant commentator who signeth himself T. C. hath also produced instances in favour of that signification; for, saith he,—but hear we his own words: Peradventure a placket signified neither a petticoat nor any part of one; but a stomacher. See the word Torace in Florio’s Italian Dict. 1598. The brest or bulke of a man.—Also a placket or stomacher.—The word seems to be used in the same sense in The Wandering Whores, &c. a comedy, 1663: If I meet a cull in Morefields, I can give him leave to dive in my placket. So that, after all, this matter is enwrapped in much and painful uncertainty. Amner.

1877 pen…booke]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): The borrower was expected to sign an acknowledgment of receipt in the moneylender’s book of record. Contemporary allusions to or instances of the practice are cited by Steevens (ed. 1778), Douce (1807, 2:161), Harrison (ed. 1948), and Muir (ed. 1952).

1878–9 still…wind]
Hunter (ed. 1972): The same song-fragment as in line [1827–8]. Sternfeld (1963, p. 164): The refrain hey nonny nonny, also quoted by Ophelia in her mad scene, makes actual singing probable, presumably here and possibly in the earlier lines. For a possible musical setting, see . Murphy (1984, p. 201): The anguished voice of the suffering possessed person says, Still…wind. A markedly contrasting voice of the demon [possessing Tom] says, hey…trot by.

1879 Sayes…ny]
Q’s hay no on ny and F’s Sayes suum, mun, nonny are both obscure in meaning if not nonsensical. Though they are merged in modern eds., it is possible that one should replace the other, since the resemblance of the first and last words of each version suggests a common origin in a difficult-to-read MS. In Hand D of Thomas Moore many examples of the long s could be confused with an h whose looping tail was indistinct; however, the interjection is always spelled hey or heigh in F1 and good Qq, never hay. Moreover, Blayney reports that in some copies there are traces between no and on which could be the remains of a badly damaged n (Wells & Taylor, 1987, p. 517; cf. Blayney, 1982, p. 216); the familiar song refrain occurs in Ham. 4.5.166 (2918; F only) as Hey non nony, nony, hey nony, in Ado. 2.3.69 (906) as hey nony nony, and in AYL 5.3.17 (2548) as hey nonino, and so might have appeared here as hey no nonny, hey non nonny, or hey nonny nonny. Minim error could account for most of an F misreading of such a phrase except for the s of suum; since g and y are very similar, it is remotely possible that a blotted MS heigh was read Say s. Or possibly both Q and F are different misreadings of heigh ho, a phrase associated with cold wind in the songs of Amiens (AYL 2.7.180 [1162]), Feste (TN 5.1.390 [2561]), and Lear’s Fool (1730). Muir (ed. 1952): J. M. Nosworthy suggests, privately, that the Q reading may be the best a…compositor could do with Hay-ronomy or heyronomy (i.e. Jeronimy, Hieronimo), an allusion to Kyd’s Spanish Tragedy. These conjectures are all too doubtful for any confidence. The phrase in Q is at least recognizably like phrases elsewhere in Sh., whereas suum, mun F is both nonsensical and unknown, thus inviting the scorn of Capell (1783, 1.2:167): It must have been the issue of the proper brain of those [F] editors, or some one of their comrades, who was wise enough to think that stuff without meaning might suit a madman.…But Shakespeare was of another opinion; his real nor his counterfeit madman throw out nothing that has not vestige of sense, nothing quite unintelligible. Malone (MS notes, 1773–90, fols. 46r–v): Edgar mixes with his madness the jargon usually spoken by the fool or Vice in the old moralities; which it is a vain endeavour to reduce to sense, citing Nashe, Strange Newes (1592; ed. McKerrow, 1:275): in this Sonnet you haue counterfeited the stile of the olde Vice in the Morrals.…Tum diddy, tum da, falangtedo diddle; | Sol la me fa sol, conatus in fiddle. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Edgar is stringing gibberish together composed of scraps of old ballads. Deighton (ed. 1891): Edgar is probably merely humming such a refrain.
Eds. have risen to the challenge of finding sense or purpose in apparent nonsense. Johnson (ed. 1765): The mad-man, now counterfeiting a proud fit, supposes himself met on the road by some one that disputes the way, and cries Hey!—No—but altering his mind condescends to let him pass, and calls to his boy Dolphin (Rodolph) not to contend with him. On—Dolphin, my boy, cease. Let him trot by. Capell (loc. cit.) reads Ha! nenni, explaining, Edgar feigns himself one who is surveying his horses, and marking their paces; that his boy, whom he calls—dolphin (or dauphin) is about to stop one of them, and cries out to that boy in wild language,—Ha! no, leave to do it; let him trot by. Campbell (1888, p. 501): An attempt to express in writing, the effect of chattering teeth. Henley (in Reed, ed. 1785) notices a special comic use of the song refrain Hey, nonny nonny as a surprise substitute for an expected word of bawdry (OED, Nonny-nonny: Often used to cover indelicate allusions, as to the female pudendum); his examples and others are provided by Douce (1807, 2:162), OED, Muir (ed. 1952), and Seng (1967, pp. 58, 150–1); but Pye (1807, p. 289), Boswell (ed. 1821) and others deny that the phrase has such a use here or elsewhere in Sh. Assuming that F’s Sayes is correct, other eds. conclude that suum, mun, nonny is what Edgar hears the wind saying. Knight (ed. 1840): An imitation of the sound of the rushing wind. Craig (ed. 1901) compares sough, citing Holland, Cheshire Words (1885, p. 329): Soo, v. to moan as the wind does. Wilson (ed. 1960): Though perh. suum should be summ. Darton (ed. 1928): Nonsense words; but they may be garbled versions of [Lat.] suum (or teum and meum). Scott (1973): Ritual words addressed to the [hawthorn] plant invoking its aid. Wells & Taylor (op. cit., p. 535), having rejected sum (OED, v.2: To hum softly) because it is not recorded before or after 1440, explore other possibilities: Suum, too, is close to Latin sum (I am),…nonsensical in an onomatopoeic, teasing, recognizable way. But mun might be corrupt…and mum would be an attractive alternative. Weis (ed. 1993): F’s Says suum is probably a cry of incitement to accompany sessa.…i.e. Sessum…sessa.

1879–80 Dolphin…by]
Steevens (ed. 1773) quotes from a very old ballad about a French king who repeatedly dissuades his son from battle with the refrain Dolphin, my boy, my boy, Cease, let him trot by; It seemeth not that such a foe From me or you would fly. Furness (ed. 1880): Steevens’s black-letter volumes of unknown titles and dates, together with his ballads rehearsed from memory, are to be received with caution. No such ballad has been found, but the phrase Dauphin my boy is found by Farmer (in Steevens, ed. 1773, 10:2Q4r) in Jonson’s Bartholomew Fair 5.4.191–2, a play written after Lr.: Go my life! I am not allied to the Sculler, yet; hee shall be Dauphin my boy. Phelps (ed. 1854): There seems to be some allusion to the German legends of the Wild Huntsman. Campbell (1888, p. 501): Possibly the snatch…betrays a thought of Edmund, the accepted heir, and…let him trot by is equivalent to a despairing let him have his way. Tovey (ed. 1896) : Dolphin is supposed to be fretted by another horse coming up behind him; the snatch is suggested to Edgar by the rattling of the storm. So also Kittredge (ed. 1940), adding that the quote from Jonson seems to mean I’ll have nothing to do with him and, if so, tends to establish Dolphin…by as a cant phrase taken from some song or other. In such mad talk as Edgar’s we need not work out a logical connection. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Possibly Edgar calling on a dolphin to ride upon the floods. Lott (ed. 1974): An admonition to the devil to move away quickly; see next n. Brown (ed. 1976): Calling off his fiend, whom he now imagines in the shape of a dog. Colman (ed. 1982): Dolphin may be the name of an imaginary dog, urged on with sesey. Murphy (1984, p. 201): In Harsnett (1603, p. 262) Mainy deposes that when I rode to Denham…the horse I rid upon was a devil.

1879 Dolphin]
A sp. for both the sea-mammal and the Dauphin. Capell (1783, 1.2:167): He feigns himself Neptune; cf. prev. n. 1879. Lee (ed. 1908): The dolphin was often cited as a type of beauty; cf. OED (sb. 2). Muir (ed. 1952): J. Crow has called my attention to the Newcastle Play of Noah (The Non-Cycle Mystery Plays, ed. O. Waterhouse, 1909, p. 25 [ll. 204–5])…: I pray to Dolphin, prince of dead, | Scald you all in his lead.…Dolphin means Dauphin in this context, and he is identified with the devil because of the English hatred of the French. Edgar has just spoken of the fiend. So Wilson (ed. 1960): Poss. the name of a devil. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 535): No one has provided parallels…as the name of a dog or a horse. (Ibid., p. 517): This might be modernized to Dauphin,…but the animal seems more relevant here than the title. Only the King of France could call the Dauphin my boy. A madman could call an imaginary Dauphin that, and he in fact does so in the Oxford ed. (1986, F), which prints Dauphin in the belief that the italicized Sesey a few lines later may be French.

1880 caese]
F prints Sesey. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 535): F’s capital, combined with italics, suggests that Compositor B thought he was setting a proper name; no such name is known.…F’s odd use of italics would be explained by the switch to a foreign language…prompted by the preceding Dolphin. In fact neither the Q nor F word is familiar. Q2 and the occasional editor assume transposed letters and print cease; most eds. substitute a foreign word. Hanmer (ed. 1743–4, 6:Gloss. s.v. Sessa or Sessey): Peace, be quiet. Lat. Cessa. Johnson (ed. 1765), on 2031, sese: The French word cessez, pronounced cessey…be quiet, have done. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): But no Frenchman would say that to an animal, presumably because the form indicates courteous speech. Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:61): Corruption of—cessa (Ital.) and—cesser (Fre.)…leave, have done, let alone. Malone (ed. 1790) prints Sessa because that form appears in Shr. In.1.6 (8). Mackay (1887, p. 371): Keltic seise!…take it easy! Tovey (ed. 1896): An Italian word used in horsemanship…(cease, be quiet). This may have been part of the song. Verity (ed. 1897): Perhaps an interjection like so so, implying let be. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): An English hiss, perhaps, for Whoa! Chambers (ed. 1906): Get out! Budd (ed. 1935): Perhaps just a meaningless exlamation. Hotson (1954, p. 116): The Spanish ce ce, explained in Percivale’s dictionary as hola, hola…a soft calling unto one, that the rest about them may not hear. Skillan (ed. 1967): edg. is attended by devils throughout the scene and this may be one in the form of a dog or a horse to which he speaks with freakish coaxing and then bids it go away, bidding the others not to interfere with its passage. Wells & Taylor (op. cit., pp. 535–6): Since Q1 probably means cease…F here could so easily represent French cessez.…The syntax of the whole clause suggests an address to one party (Dolphin) concerning another (him); the second party is to be allowed to trot by, and it would be natural enough to interpret the imperative to the first party as an instruction to refrain from interfering. Cease (barking, or interfering). (Ibid., p. 535): Blayney argues convincingly that nonsense is unlikely here. Weis (ed. 1993): Perhaps an anglicized rendering of French çédez, i.e. yield passage.
An opposite interpretation begins with Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): [Cf.] Sylvester’s Du Bartas, ed. [1633]. Joshua urges on his troops; Sa, sa, my Hearts; turn, turn again upon-them…. The Captaines, p. 182; where the original has Cà, Cà, tournons visage, allons, &c.: Jezebel being killed, …Ses, ses, here Dogs, here Bitches, doe not spare…. The Decay, p. 229; where the original has Sus, lyces, deschirez. &c. For sa, sa, see nn. 2031, 2645. Campbell (1888, p. 500): Sessa…may be a corruption of (Fr.) C’est ça! and…Sa, sa, sa, sa, [2645] may be an adaptation of (Fr.) Ca, ça, ça, ça! Deighton (ed. 1891): For Sa, sa, exclamations of encouragement. Gollancz (ed. 1895): Onward! Herford (ed. 1899): A term of incitement to speed. MacCracken (ed. 1914): An exclamation, evidently intended to spur on a horse. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Here it would mean There he goes! or the like. Muir (ed. 1952): From the context and [2031], it would seem to mean…Off you go! Colman (ed. 1982): Cf. mod. Eng. seize ’im, comparing the use of sese again in doggy context at 2031. There can be no assurance that Sessa (Shr.), Sa, sa (2645), or sese (2031) are words at all similar in meaning to the very different forms caese and Sesey here; so OED (Sessa). Davidson (1998, p. 316), uniquely: Stenographic spelling of sayes he.

1880 Storme still]
See n. 1584.

1881–8 Why…art]
Bransom (1934, p. 105): The highest reach in the play of Lear’s intellect. Ribner (1958, p. 45; 1960, p. 127): The lowest point of [Lear’s] delusion.

1881 Why thou…thy]
F’s changes to Thou…a seem pointless and may have been accidental.

1881 thou wert better]
See n. 627. On the preferability of death Milward (1987, pp. 179–80) cites Job 3:11, Jer. 20:17, Matt. 26:24.

1881 answere]
Rann (ed. 1794): Encounter (OED, v. 26). So Hunter (ed. 1972), but his further finding of the microcosm/macrocosm analogy implies another meaning, correspond with (OED, 28).

1882 extremitie]
Schmidt (1874): Rigour, violence (OED, 4).

1882–8 is…art]
Hooker (1902, pp. 332, 364) compares a passage from Montaigne’s Apologie of Raymond Sebond remarking how alone among nature’s creatures naked man has nothing to cover and arme himselfe withall but the spoile of others (see ), and from the same essay Taylor (1925, pp. 9–10) and Anderson (1971–2, p. 275) quote another, beginning When I consider man all naked, about man’s borrowing…of wooll, of haire, of feathers, and of silke to shroud us (see ). Milward (1973, p. 48; 1987, p. 180) quotes a very similar passage from Robert Person’s Christian Directory (1585, II.iv.18). Taylor also quotes from Montaigne’s Of Phisiognomy another passage recommending that men should learne of beasts about nature, Wherewith men have done, as perfumers do with oyle, they have adulterated her, with so many argumentations, and sofisticated her with discourses, that she…hath lost her proper, constant, and universall visage (tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 3:305). Cf., from the first essay, wretched weake and miserable man: whom if you consider well, what is he, but a crawling, and ever-moving Ants-neast? (see ). Also from Sebond Reyher (1947, p. 504) compares Montaigne’s statement that to reveal his equality with other animals man must be stripped to his shirt (see ). Muir (ed. 1952, pp. 251–2) cites other similar passages from Montaigne’s Sebond; see . Elton (1966, pp. 190–7) discusses exhaustively the beast-in-man notion in the Renaissance, particularly Montaigne’s anticipation by Pliny, Plutarch, Erasmus, and others, and contemporary English treatments, including Thomas Fennes’s Fennes Fruites (1590) in which occurs an unnoted version of the Lear story. Hulme (1962, pp. 191–2) quotes Nicholas Udall [tr., Apophthegmes of Erasmus, 1542; 1564, p. 110]: Plato had thus diffined a man: A man is a liue thyng with twoo feete, hauyng no fethers.…Diogenes brought forth into the schole, a cocke pulled naked oute of all his fethers,…saiyng: Loe, here is Plato his manne. Donawerth (1977, pp. 10–14): The story is reported in Diogenes Laertius’s De vitis philosophorum. Carter (1905, p. 438) and Noble (1935, p. 230) compare Heb. 2:6: What is man, that thou shouldest be mindefull of him! or the sonne of man that thou wouldest consider him! (Geneva). Muir (op. cit., p. liv): This is the central moment of the play—a dramatic answer to the Psalmist’s question. Cf. Psa. 8:4. Colie (1974, p. 129) compares Job 7:17, and Milward (1987, p. 180) adds Psa. 22:6, Eccles. 3:18–19. Vickers (1968, p. 367): Lear catches up both this identification [of the human and the bestial] and the symmetrical structure (which he is given nowhere else in prose).

1883–6 thou…selfe]
Merchant (1960, p. 72): Rarely in Shakespeare has costume played so full a part either in direct stage business or in symbolic action.…[Here Lear’s] momentary insight into dereliction, in its pity for Edgar’s nakedness, is pointed by the contrast with the courtly costumes of the Fool, Kent, and Lear himself, who are all indebted to the worm and the beast. Elton (1966, p. 195 n.) cites contemporary English treatments of proud man’s theft of garments from lower creatures. Dent (1981, M218.1) suspects a proverb, Man borrows from the beasts. Greenblatt (1985, p. 121): When Lear thinks he has found in Tom-o-Bedlam the thing itself, unaccommodated man, he has in fact found a man playing a theatrical role.

1883 owest]
OED (v. 4): To be indebted or beholden for, quoting this l.

1884 beast]
OED (sb. 3): A domesticated animal…at first including sheep, goats, etc., but…gradually more or less restricted to the bovine kind.

1885 cat]
Delius (ed. 1854): The civet cat (OED, sb.1 4, quoting this l.). Foakes (ed. 1997): A perfume is derived from a gland in its anal pouch. Cf. 2572.

1885 her’s]
On the inflection see n. 204.

1885 ons]
See n. 632.

1885 are]
On the omission of the relative, see nn. 589, 1667.

1886 sophisticated]
Rann (ed. 1794): Adulterate, not genuine (OED, ppl. a. 1). Hudson (ed. 1856): Sophisticated out of nature in wearing clothes; cf. OED (2): Altered from, deprived of, primitive simplicity or naturalness. Taylor (1925, pp. 10, 65) thinks the word, not used elsewhere by Sh., came from Montaigne, Upon Some Verses of Virgil (tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 3:126); see also n. 1882–8. Doran (1933, p. 55) finds it also in Of Experience (3:332).

1886–7 vnaccomodated]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): Unfurnished with the conveniences of life (OED, ppl. a.: Unprovided, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Cf. 2528. Craig (ed. 1931): Also, Man without social modification. Hunter (ed. 1972): Unfurnished (with clothes etc.). Arguing that the many un- prefix words in the play provide a double perspective (see n. 46), Thomson (1993, p. 86): Edgar as Poor Tom is physically unaccommodated but not mentally so as Lear is, and this difference goes to the heart of the play.

1887 forked]
Hunter (ed. 1869): This refers to the human body terminating in legs like a fork (OED, ppl. a. 2, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Craig (ed. 1901) compares 2H4 3.2.311 (1839).

1888 off…leadings]
Moberly (ed. 1876): He longs to reduce himself, like [Edgar], to a state of absolute and unmitigated nature. Verity (ed. 1897): To tear off the clothes is a common feature of insanity. Goggin (ed. 1910): Lear, who has already imagined that Edgar’s destitute state sprang from the same source as his own, now tries to make the resemblance between them more complete. Muir (ed. 1952): Lear wishes to identify himself with the poor naked wretches, unaccommodated men. Whitaker (1953, p. 305): Lear’s first act of outright madness is also his first clear demonstration of moral sanity. Greenfield (1954, p. 285): Lear deliberately assumes the symbolic state of the nude figure, the emblem of naked truth and of the three theological meanings of the natural state of man conducive to humility;…the lack of earthly goods…; innocence. Similarly Fraser (1962, pp. 110–11) compares the iconographic convention of Nuda Veritas. Leggatt (1992, p. 184): In an age when clothing was expensive, and conveyed the wearer’s dignity and social position, there would be terrible impact in Lear’s attempt to imitate Tom by tearing his clothes off. For the Jacobean mind it was one of the most unsettling symptoms of madness that mad people showed no respect for their clothes, tearing them or even going naked. Foakes (1993, p. 197): The symbolism [is] of Lear shedding his royalty. He does not cast off his clothes in order to discover his humanity, as is sometimes claimed, for the finding of himself involves the restoration of proper clothing at 2773. Idem (ed. 1997): A strong stage tradition has Kent and the Fool prevent Lear from doing this, citing Rosenberg (1972, p. 223) and Bratton (ed. 1987). Ian Holm stripped himself naked in his 1997 performance.

1888 leadings]
Q1(c)’s lendings is a certainly correct emendation of a graphic error (Greg, 1940, p. 164). E. (1869, p. 467): Something lent [OED, vbl. sb.2 2a, quoting this l.]—lent indeed by the worm, the beast, the sheep, the cat. Florio (see n. 1882–8) refers to man’s borrowing from animals. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Clothes are not given to man by nature: they are lent him by art.

1888 come]
Generally assumed to be addressed to Kent and the Fool. Kelcy (1932, p. 367): Addressed to his clothes. Lear is unable to undo a button. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Lear instinctively uses the imperative, for he has never before taken off his clothes without a valet’s services. Wilson (ed. 1960): A command to an imaginary groom of his bedchamber. Only Weis (ed. 1993): Lear does not so much command his followers to undo his buttons as invite them to follow his example and strip with him.

1888–9 on bee true.]
Ridley (ed. 1935): The Q reading is defensible enough: Off with the lendings, the accidents, and then I shall be truly my self, my bare self. Wells (ed. 2000): Lear may speak to an imaginary attendant (true, loyal) or to himself. Possibly the Q corrector, not recognizing such senses, attempted some kind of emendation that eventuated in Q1(c)’s on with the following words and terminal punctuation omitted. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxiii): Finding a hopeless puzzle, the printer left it blank to be filled in on further advisement,—and forgot it. Greg (1940, pp. 164–5): Faced with nonsense and a copy he could not read the corrector threw up the sponge and merely deleted what obviously could not be right. F [vn-|button heere.] is undoubtedly correct, but the last word was evidently either wanting or wholly illegible in the quarto copy: for the rest, come on bee true is a fairly easy misreading of come vnbutton! Stone (1980, pp. 225–6): We must eliminate the reading in [Q1(c)] which is merely the result of an accident to the type. The full stop after bee true in [Q1(u)] having disappeared along with the words, it is unlikely that the compositor removed them deliberately. We should also probably discount heere in F as an interpolation. The remaining Come, vnbutton may easily represent a more accurate decipherment of the manuscript reading which yielded come on bee true in Q. The latter, however, makes sense. Werstine (apud Clayton, 1983, pp. 139–40, n. 11), contra Stone: If there is no evidence of the loosening of type in outer G…it seems most unlikely that two words could fall out at the same time without the whole page falling apart. Clayton (op. cit., pp. 126–8), rejecting Greg’s and Stone’s arguments, prefers to think that F is a genuine revision that intensifies a pattern of symbolic imagery of divesting; but clearly Lear is attempting to divest in both Q and F. Blayney (1982, p. 246): It is possible that the proof-reader indicated something a little closer to the presumed reading of his copy (which almost certainly agreed in substance with unbutton, although there is no evidence of heere in the uncorrected Q) but that the compositor somehow forgot to insert it. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 517): If vnbutton were the intended correction, then on should also have been deleted; the uncorrected reading makes local and contextual sense. Hammond (1988, p. 103): A possible contemporary spelling, unbotone, is a plausible and easy conjecture for on bee true.…The compositor…read un as on (under the influence of the preceding word come, quite reasonable); read bo as be (which he then set as bee); and read tone as true.…At line [2097] Q reads true where F has none, suggesting that Okes’ compositor B (who set both lines) was quite capable of reading one in his copy as rue.…As for heere, it could have been omitted by Q as redundant in the light of what it had made of the phrase, or it could have been added in F. On another possible misreading of on as ru, see n. 1786. Meyer (1994, pp. 134–5): G2v shows ample space at the end of the line for the compositor to insert type and complete the passage. This fact combined with the absence of terminal punctuation in Q[c]’s reading suggests a partially completed correction.…The presence or absence of heere has no substantive bearing on the sense or significance of F’s reading—which is the action of come unbutton and not the adverbial place of heere—and therefore does not support the decision to preserve Q[u]’s come on bee true.

1891 Prithe]
See n. 664.

1891 Nunckle]
See n. 634.

1891 content, this is]
F’s contented, ’tis is indifferent. Cf. 1530.

1891 naughty]
OED (a. 5): Of weather: Bad, nasty, quoting this l. as its latest ex. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Not a trivial or childish word, as in modern usage, comparing 1412, 2103.

1892 to swim in]
Tovey (ed. 1896): As if Lear were undressing himself to bathe. Hunter (ed. 1972): Also suggested…by the rain.

1892 fire]
Muir (ed. 1952): Presumably he sees Gloucester’s torch. Perhaps the sequence of thought would be improved if this sentence and the next were transposed.

1892 wild]
Dyce (ed. 1857): In the sense of—desert. Schmidt (1875): Uncultivated (OED, a. 4). Brooke (ed. 1947): Blustery, comparing 1612. Muir (ed. 1952): Wild suggested the lecher’s body, unfruitful, out of condition. It is just possible that Shakespeare wrote vilde. Walker (1860, 3:279), supporting wide (see textual n.), gives instances of wild misprinted for it.

1892 field]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Open country as opposed to woodland or town (see O.E.D. 1). The common sense: a piece of land, surrounded by hedges, not found in Sh.

1893 old leachers]
Bradley (1904, p. 294 n.) and Heilman (1948, p. 47): The Fool’s simile announces Gloucester’s entrance. See n. 1890 below.

1893 heart]
See n. 1029. Hunter (ed. 1972): Also the heart shown by his succouring of the King.

1894 in]
The preposition may here mean within, with the common omission of the article for that sense (OED, 1b); OED does not attest to a partitive use meaning of. For F’s on’s see n. 632.

1894 here comes]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Gloster’s torch advancing towards them. Muir (ed. 1952): The Fool does not know that he is speaking of Gloucester, though the audience, from the previous scene, expects his arrival.

1894 walking fire]
Halliwell (ed. 1865) quotes from A Helpe to Discourse (1633, p. 67): An Ignis fatuus, or a walking fire. Verity (ed. 1897): There was a class of spirits…who misled travellers by means of a false fire.…Hence Edgar’s explanation This is the foul fiend. Ribner (1958, p. 45): Gloucester’s torch is a light from the world of men who are not beasts, a sign of human kindness and self-sacrifice. Siemon (1985, p. 274): The staging reproduces a specific emblem…Cupid with a torch, identifying Gloucester with lechery.

1890 Enter]
On F’s earlier entrance see n. 1358. Even the Q placement seems too early for Furness (ed. 1880): The stage-directions are rather directions to the actors to be ready to go on than indications of their actual entrance. It is not easy to conceive, in the restricted space of the Shakespearian stage, how Gloucester could have remained unnoticed by Lear throughout Edgar’s speech from [1895] to [1904]. Bradley (1904, p. 294 n.) thinks Q pointedly has Gloucester enter just as the Fool finishes speaking of an old leachers heart, and that Pope destroyed the collocation by transferring the stage-direction to 1904. Dessen (1995, p. 75) prefers F: An onstage Gloucester would enrich 1892–4. Foakes (ed. 1997): Perhaps Lear, Kent, and the Fool are huddled together…hence Kent’s question at [1904]; meanwhile Edgar may keep Gloucester occupied until the latter becomes aware of the others. The F SD specifies the fire; torches are referred to also at 964 and F SD 970.

1895 This]
Wilson (ed. 1960): I.e. Glo. with the flickering torch.…Edg. prob. does not at once recognize him.

1895 foule]
F omits, though Edg. uses the epithet at 1827, 1833, 1841, 1860, 1878, 1910, 2006, 2248. Werstine (1983, p. 283): Probably…eyeskip.

1895 Sriberdegibit]
Q2’s Sirberdegibit obviously follows Q1(u); Q1(c)’s fliberdegibek is closer to both F’s Flibbertigibbet and Harsnett’s Fliberdigibbet and Fliberdigibet (1603, pp. 49, 119, 181; see ); cf. 2248+3 (Q only), Stiberdigebit. As Cauthen (1958, pp. 98–9) points out, the name occurs in The Castle of Perseverance (c. 1425; ed. Eccles, 1969) as Flepergebet (775), Flypyrgebet (1724), and Flepyrgebet (1733), referring to a minor devil who backbites and flatters. As Steevens (ed. 1773) notes, Hugh Latimer refers in his Second Sermon (1549, p. 69; ed. Chester, 1968, p. 84) to flatterers, and flibbergibs, and Thomas Heywood refers in his Epigrams (ed. Milligan, 1956, p. 239) to a wretch by that name, spelt flebergebit, flebergibet, and flebergebet. Wright (ed. 1875) cites Cotgrave (1611, s.v. Coquette): Tatling houswife; a titifill, a flebergebit. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 397): The copy for Q probably had fliberdegibet.…For confusion between t and k cf. [1248]. The name (or byword) was apparently common enough that the Q corrector may not have consulted copy in his attempt to correct it; probably the final -ek in Q1(c) is his error or the compositor’s misreading of his marginal correction. Muir (1951, pp. 17–18): In Harsnett (p. 49; cf. 119, 181) he is described as a dancing devil, without the attributes ascribed to him by Edgar. Lott (ed. 1974): A common name for a restless, unstable person. Perhaps Edgar is reminded of it by the spluttering flame of the torch.

1896 curphew]
Tovey (ed. 1896): In [Tmp. 5.1.40 (1990–1)], the elves reioyce | To heare the solemne Curfewe, i.e., they then have leave to move on earth. The couvre-feu (cover-fire) bell, at sound of which all fires and lights were to be extinguished, was rung, by the order of William I., who instituted it, at eight [or nine: OED] o’clock in the evening.

1896 till]
F’s at is apparently erroneous, a repetition [from] begins at… in the previous line (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 178). Weis (ed. 1993), however: First cock technically means midnight [see next n.], which makes good sense for F’s version. Schmidt’s (ed. 1879) attempt to justify F by taking walk in the sense of go away is scouted by Duthie (pp. 178–9): But in connection with ghosts, fiends, etc., there is no doubt that to walk usually means to be seen walking, appear (see N.E.D., walk v.1 9). To use walk in its meaning of go away…would be to court misunderstanding.

1896 first cocke]
Malone (ed. 1790): Spirits…were permitted to wander at large till the first cock-crowing, citing Ham. 1.1.150–5 (149–54) and 1.5.10 (695). Tovey (ed. 1896): Midnight, citing Thomas Tusser, Five Hundred Points of Good Husbandry (1557; ed. Grigson, 1984, p. 161): At midnight, at three and an hower ere day, | They utter their language as well as they may, cited also by Shirley (1963, p. 106). For second cock see Rom. 4.4.3 (2544), H5 4.pr. 15 (1804), Mac. 2.3.25 (766). In fact, Old Hamlet’s ghost walked until near dawn, and the term here may mean first cock-crow of the day (Lott, ed. 1974), at dawn.

1896 gins]
Q1(c)’s giues is the obvious correction. Though ’gins, begins, is remotely possible, it makes poor sense.

1896–7 web, the pin]
Q1(c)’s web, & the pin is closer to the usual name for this kind of cataract of the eye, the pin and web (OED, Pin sb.1 11); also called a pearl in the eye, it was a hardening and clouding of the lens. Moberly (ed. 1876): The pin was the bulls eye of a target; whence perhaps the application [i.e., hard center of the ulcer]. By the web is probably meant that the eye got webbed, or crusted round the central point.

1897 queues]
The proof-corrector or the compositor deciphering his marginal notes may have taken Q1(c)’s squemes to be a variant of the verb squeam (as squemish is a 16th-c. variant of squeamish), thinking it meant something like offend or make sick. F’s squints makes the obviously right sense but can not have been the word in the MS behind Q, and the verb appears nowhere else in Sh. (though see 3015). Greg (1933, p. 771): Squint, in the rare transitive sense, to cause to squint [OED, v. 5: To cause to look asquint or obliquely], is what is meant. Now, for squint Shakespeare uses at [2581] the form squiny (quarto and folio agreeing), and it is obvious that in the present passage the quarto squemes might easily be a misprint for squenies, or squinies, and the folio squints an emendation due to the unfamiliarity of the quarto reading.…[But] in view of the variant queues I suggest that it is a misprint…for squenes. As corroboration Greg notes the use of both squinny and squean (see quotations in OED) by Robert Armin two or three years after first playing Lear’s Fool. Taylor (1983, p. 448): F’s squints…too could arise from misreading (e/t). Q2’s pinqueuer is a helpless guess from Q1(u); Adee (ed. 1890, p. xvi) suspects the Q2 compositor of possibly conjecturing that the pinqueuer the eye might refer to one who, in the idiom of Shakespeare’s day, pinked the eye, that is, held the lids nearly closed (OED, Pink v.2 1). Possibly the Q1 compositor originally thought he was setting a variant of pinks, describing a peering or blinking resulting from the web.

1897 harte lip]
Q1(c)’s hare lip is obviously right; the compositor may have misread hart (Duthie, 1949, p. 51).

1898 white wheate]
Deighton (ed. 1891), doubtfully: Either the white variety of wheat as opposed to the red, or…proleptically for makes white with mildew. Craig (ed. 1901): Wheat no longer green, approaching ripeness, quoting John 4:35, fields…white already to harvest.

1898 hurts]
D’Avanzo (1977, p. 88), questionably: Blights men with ergot poisoning.

1898–9 creature of earth]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Composed of earth, or clay, i.e. mortal. Deighton (ed. 1891), questionably: The worm. Tovey (ed. 1896): May refer to the white wheat, but is better taken as a collective for creatures, here meaning produce. Foakes (ed. 1997): Animals and/or men.

1900–3 swithald…thee]
Q misprints as prose even a metrical charm. Tovey (ed. 1896): Feigning to see a fiend, Edgar utters the first ban or spell that he can think of. Kittredge (ed. 1940) quotes from Thomas Blundevill, The Fower chiefest offices belonging to Horsemanshippe (ca. 1570, ch. 23, sig. X4v) the following charm to protect a horse from nightmare, with obvious similarities to Edgar’s: Saint George our Ladyes Knyght, | He walked day so did he night, | Untill he hir founde, | He hir beate and he hir bounde, | Till truely hir trouthe she him plyght, | That she woulde not come within the night, | There as Saint George our Ladyes Knight, | Named was three tymes, Saint George. Kittredge adds, To recite how [the saint] encountered the demon…and subdued her, served as a charm against her power. Later versions of the charm have been found in Reginald Scot, Discoverie of Witchcraft 4.11 (1584, p. 87, where it is a cure for the incubus) by Upton (1748, p. 324), and in Beaumont & Fletcher’s Monsieur Thomas 5.1.37–42 (where it is a night spell) by Warburton (ed. 1747), who calls it a popular charm…against the Epialtes. For similar charms against nightspells, invoking other saints, see G. B. Evans, ed., Plays and Poems of William Cartwright, 1951, p. 637. Although almost no one believes that Edgar sings these verses (see textual n.), Long (1971, p. 171) proposes an early musical setting (see ), and Gooch & Thatcher (1991, 1:637) list a modern one. Hunter (ed. 1972, p. 341): Form and content suggest incantation rather than song.

1900 swithald]
The name is unknown. Theobald (ed. 1733) finds a Franciscan friar in The Troublesome Raigne of Iohn (1591, sig. E4v) invoking Sweete S. Withold for lenitie against extremitie; in his next speech he promises that Saint Fraunces…Shall shield thee from nightspells and dreaming of diuells. There is no Saint Withold, and Bullough (1962, 4:104) glosses Wittol, a cuckold or simpleton, often sp. wittold. Sh. might have remembered the scene and name from his source-play for Jn., and a bedlam beggar brought to ruin by lust might invoke such a saint instead of St. George. Following Theobald, many eds. (see textual n.) assume that S.Withold or possibly S’Withold in the MS was misread as swithald; this is possible, though Sh. almost never uses S. or S’ as abbreviation for Saint (Werstine, privately, points out an exception in F-only H5 3.1.34 [1117]), and the florid W in his signature would be hard to mistake for lower case. Greg (1928, p. 40): Read Swithald after Q, on the grounds that the change in F is probably accidental, that the form is slightly nearer its supposed source, and that it avoids the repetition of the syllable old in the line. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 398): But The Troublesome Raigne shows that the form with o existed; and I do not think we can be certain that the change of Q’s a to o in F was purely accidental. Kökeritz (1959, p. 8): We have evidence of a Continental-Germanic name Witold.…Dr. Olof von Feilitzen [finds]…the Old English name Swiδweald in the Liber Vitae (ca. 800).…In Middle English and early Modern English, Swiδweald would regularly appear as Swithold or Swithald. Such a name may well have survived in an ancient charm. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 518): F capitalizes the word simply because it begins a verse line, and italicizes it because it is clearly in context a name. Other names have been suggested. Tyrwhitt (in Steevens, ed. 1773) proposes St. Vitalis, and Nares (1822) identifies two saints by that name, a martyr under Nero at Ravenna ca. 62 A.D. and a slave who suffered with his master St. Agricola ca. 304, adding, Whether either was St. Withold, rests at present on mere conjecture. Wright (ed. 1875) and Craig (ed. 1901) assume him to be the second St. Vitalis, as do Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): St. Vitalis or Vitus. When but a child of twelve, according to Caxton’s Golden Legend (1483, [sig. x3v]), he cast out devils from Diocletian, son of the emperor. Like Wright and Craig, Porter and Clarke provide no evidence whatever for their conclusion: Hence he was the patron protector from witches and nightmare, and his name was invoked in such charms. Topsell, Four-footed Beasts (1607, p. 187) records a charm against the bite of wild dogs addressed to an obscure Saint (called Vithus). Wells & Taylor (op. cit.): It is impossible to believe that the written abbreviation S. for Saint led to the fusion of Saint Vitalis into Swithold. An altogether likelier identification was provided by, of all people, Nahum Tate, who in his adaptation [1681] altered the name to Swithin. Swithun (also spelled Swithin) was a popular early English saint, famous for healing, and prominently associated with rain; his appropriateness in Edgar’s rhyme is obvious. Caldecott (MS notes, 1813–33): Violent gales…in the western part of this country are called St Winnold’s storms. It remains unclear why any of these saints should be substituted for George in the traditional rhyme. The word sir could easily be misread sw, and it is remotely possible some other hero, named Sir Ithold or the like, was intended, even more obscure than Child Rowland at 1966 (see nn.).

1900 footed]
Verity (ed. 1897): Traversed (OED, Foot v. 3). On transitive verbs formed from nouns see n. 1197.

1900 thrice]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Magical number.

1900 old]
Farmer (in Steevens, ed. 1773, 10:2Q4r): The same word as wold. OED identifies the form as obsolete, Brook (1976, p. 154) as dialectal (from Northamptonshire), citing EDD. Hanmer (ed. 1743–4, 6:Gloss.), wold: A down, an open hilly country (OED, 3).

1901 a nellthu]
Q1(u)’s nonsense is replicated in Q2, set from an uncorrected copy of Q1. Q1(c)’s he met the could have been guessed at without recourse to copy: Q’s a means he (see n. 585), and the other two words are obvious substitutions. Greg (1940, p. 167): No doubt he is a sophistication.…The copy presumably had the spelling mett.

1901 night more]
Q1(c)’s night mare is the obvious correction. Steevens (ed. 1793): An incubus. OED (sb. 1): A female spirit or monster supposed to beset people and animals by night, settling upon them when they are asleep and producing a feeling of suffocation by its weight. Wilson (ed. 1960): But often (as perh. here) taken to be a demon female horse. Witch makes this unlikely; see n. 1903.

1901 nine fold]
F hyphenates. Budd (ed. 1935), nine: A mystic number. Tyrwhitt (apud Steevens, ed. 1773): Her nine fold is the same as her nine foals; i.e. her nine imps. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Familiar spirits in the likeness of foals. This imaginative reading, rising from the image of the nightmare as a horse (see prev. n.), has attracted many eds. OED (sb. 2) is somewhat less specific: An attendant set of nine, quoting only this l. and a probably imitative passage from Walter Scott.
