Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 536): Foals is supported by examples of excrescent final d elsewhere in Shakespeare (Cercignani, 318); alternatively, fold might refer to coils in a serpent’s body (sb.3 1e), appropriate enough for a devil. Neither interpretation permits F’s hyphen. Stone (1980, p. 209): But it is surely less arbitrary to suppose that nine fold is the adverb which it appears to be.…Unfortunately, if this be so, the verb modified by ninefold has been accidentally omitted. Not necessarily: it could easily be bid. If the first her is an error for he, the clause would read and he nine-fold Bid her alight. Alternatively, since line 1901 is hypermetrical, possibly the her is an accidental redundancy (being one of three in a line and a half), and the lines should read He met the night mare and ninefold Bid her alight. Even if the her is retained, a kind of awkward sense can be made if the second her is considered as a reflexive: He met the night mare, and [to] her ninefold Bid that she alight herself. The semicolon in F prevents such readings, but it may not be authorial; Q’s punctuation clearly implies a ninefold repetition, apparently of a charm. No entirely satisfactory meaning of fold as a substantive has been proposed.

1902 O light]
F corrects to a-light. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 398): An a has been misread as an o and misunderstood as an ejaculation. Warburton (ed. 1747): Alight from those persons whom she rides. Capell (1783, 1.2:168): Alight from your broom-staff.

1902 troth plight]
Warburton (ed. 1747): To do no more mischief; cf. n. 1900–3. Tovey (ed. 1896): To be gone. All eds. since Pope have considered F1’s hyphen erroneous.

1903 arint]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 398): Q’s arint is a pronunciation-spelling. F prints aroynt, the form in Mac. 1.3.6 (104). No other occurrences are known until Shn. imitations in the 19th c., though two post-Shn. analogues have been found. Halliwell-Phillipps (1887, 1:142): The Stratford town records report an altercation in which Goodie Bromlie said to a Mrs. Holder, arent the, wich. Hulme (1962, p. 17), identifying the document as Stratford presentment (Misc. I 160, ?1627), reads the text, Itm the wife of Anthrim holds or sayth goodie bromlie…arent the wich. The other is in a north country proverb quoted by Steevens (ed. 1773, 4:404): Rynt you Witch quoth Besse Locket to her mother. Ray (1674; 1691, p. 60) identifies this as Proverb, Cheshire, giving the term rynt ye the meaning By your leave, stand handsomly. Thoresby (1703) adduces as the same word Ryndta, used to cows [in Yorkshire] to make them give way, and stand in their stalls. Similarly an anonymous MS note in the Folger Copy 1 of Hanmer (ed. 1743–4, 6:Gloss.): From awry not thee—put yourself straight, get out of my way, said by a milk maid to a cow that stands athwart the stall. Wilbraham (1820, p. 55): Lan[cashire]…Rynty, to get out of the way. Rynt thee, is an expression used by milk-maids to a cow…to bid her get out of the way. Boucher (1832, s.v. Aroint) finds the same word spelled runt in Cheshire and areawt in Lancashire. OED (Aroint, aroynt v.), after noting that no etymology offered can be said to have even a prima facie probability, says of Ray’s and Thoresby’s term, The local nature, the meaning, and form of the phrase, seem all opposed to its identity with Shakspere’s Aroynt. Matthew’s (apud Anon., 1878, p. 601) suggestion that an obscure 15th-c. word is related to Shakespeare’s term is admitted as a possibility by OED (Arunt v.): To rail at, revile, scold, rate; or ? to drive away. (If the latter is the sense, cf. Shakspere’s Aroint. Matthew quotes from a Wycliffite tract (Trinity College, Dublin, MS C. v. 6, fol. 157v), And here schul men arunte þe feend, and takes the meaning to be avoid or shun. Hanmer (op. cit.) first gives the generally accepted meaning: Avaunt (OED).
In addition to these foregoing attempts, commentators have sought the origin and meaning of the word in several languages:
(1)Latin. Hanmer (op. cit.): Dii averruncent! Halliwell-Phillipps (1847; 1855, 1:86): From the Latin averrunco, the participle of which may have been formed into aroint, in the same way that punctum has become point; iunctum, joint, &c. He seems to derive this idea from B. Thorpe, apud Collier (ed. 1842–4, 7:103). C. (1874, p. 163): Averruncus being a deity supposed to avert evil.
(2)Greek and Gothic. Rodd (apud Knight, ed. 1840): Ar (or aer) go and hynt behind.
(3)Anglo-Norman. Becket (1787, p. 452): Royne, scab…Scab take thee! Tooke (1805, 2:241): A raynous (i.e. roynous, from ronger, rogner, royner; whence also aroynt) scall, is a separation or discontinuity of the skin or flesh, by a gnawing, eating, forward malady. Boucher (1832, loc. cit.): The words rogne Fr., rogna It.,…signify scab, leprosy, scurvy.…The plague take thee. Richardson (1838): Ronger. To gnaw, knap, or nible, off; to fret, eat, or weare away; (Cotgrave.) Aroynt thee—begnawed thee; be thou gnawed, eaten, consumed; similar to the common malediction—a plague take thee; a pock light upon thee. See Ronyon, Roynish, and Royne. Hunter (ed. 1869): Plague on thee, or the mange be on thee, from the Anglo-Norman roine, a scab. So Addis (1873, p. 321). Hulme (1962, p. 19; cf. 213, 216–17): Derived from the Anglo-French aloyner (from à to + loin far); cf. an English verb aloyn (OED: To remove far off, latest use 1464).
(4)French. Singer (ed. 1826, 4:216): Arry-avant, away there ho! Toone (1832, p. 53): A route, a word made use of by the French to urge their horses. V. (1873, p. 210): Éreinte-toi, break thy back or reins, used as an imprecation; (p. 321): Cf. errené,…ancient synonyme of éreinté.
(5)Gaelic. Mackay (1887, p. 9): Ath-roinnte…set apart.
(6)English. Johnson (ed. 1765, 6:378) rejects anoint, said of witches, who are related to perform many supernatural acts by the means of unguents, and particularly to fly through the air. Instead he refers to an ancient drawing reproduced in Thomas Hearne’s Ectypa Varia (1737) in which Satan addresses Christ, harrowing Hell, with the words Out out arongt. Others read the word arougt (see Boucher, 1832, loc. cit.; Jabez, 1874, p. 163). Halliwell-Phillipps (1847; 1855, 1:85), in support of Johnson’s first idea, quotes from Jonson’s Masque of Queenes 51, where the chief witch says anoynt, and come away, and Jonson’s note is When they are to be trãsported…they vse to anoynt them selues, and sometimes the things they ride on. H. (1784, p. 73): The Rauntree or Rantry is in the North considered as a preservation against Witches.…A Rauntree, witch! H. Rowe (ed. Mac., 1799): In Scotland, the rown-tree, in England, the witchen tree, or mountain ash.…A rown-tree! Carr (1824, p. 104): Royne-tree…Wigan, Witch Hazle: Mountain-ash.…a royn-tree! Cf. Entwisle (1874, p. 164), Rowan-tree or Roan-tree. Thomson (1826, sig. E2): A word of exprobation from Barbarous Latin aurina, to exorcise or allay, and Gothic run, runn, raun, which signified religion and sorcery. Douce (1807, 1:371): There is no doubt that aroint signifies away! run! and that it is of Saxon origin, comparing the 16th-c. form ryne for run and Icelandic runka, to agitate, to move. Wilbraham (1820, p. 56): Possibly it may owe its origin to the old adverb Arowne [OED, Aroom adv.: At a space or distance]…or from Ryman [OED, Rime v.4], or rumian [OED, Room v.1], A.S. to get out of the way. Crook (ed. 1907): Perhaps from Ice. ryma, to make room.

1903 with]
Q1(c)’s witch is certainly correct (Greg, 1940, p. 167). Swithald surely addresses the night mare. Wilson (ed. 1960), taking witch in its usual sense of sorceress: Addressed to the witch at whose orders the Incubus had visited its victim; but see OED (Witch sb. 2): The nightmare.

1904 Kent.]
Sisson (1956, 2:237) reassigns the speech: There is no reason why Kent at this moment should suddenly make this inquiry, but every reason why Gloucester should. Lear hears the strange voice (Kent’s is familiar) and asks, What’s he? Gloucester now hears voices, Lear’s and Kent’s, and naturally asks What…names? [1907]. Finally, Gloucester’s your Grace seems to be clearly distinguished from Kent’s my good lord as a mode of address to Lear. Stone (1980, p. 232) and Ogden (1994, p. 45) support this conjecture. Wilson (ed. 1960): But the words are in keeping with Kent’s tender solicitude throughout (e.g. [2014+14–+15]…). Glo. is still coming up and first addresses them in [1907]. Halio (ed. 1992): Since Lear, now subdued, has just undergone a vigorous struggle, the question by Kent is appropriate. The sequence in Q and F is logical: Kent may see that Lear, now partially undressed, is shivering from cold, or that he is staring apprehensively at the approaching flame. He asks Lear how he fares (1904); Lear’s first concern is with who or what approaches (1905); Kent therefore challenges the stranger (1906); and Gloucester answers in kind.

1904 your Grace]
See n. 218.

1905–7 Whats…What]
See n. 540.

1908–13 Poore…poole]
Vickers (1968, p. 367): The ultimate identification of man and beast again comes in a symmetrical form to emphasize its horror. Carroll (1992, p. 22): The often explicitly political dimension of Poor Tom’s language [is] an element which seems to have been Shakespeare’s own addition to the stereotype [of Poor Tom] in the sources.

1908 Poore Tom]
See n. 1271.

1908–14 that…who]
On the relative pronouns see Abbott (§259): That is used as a relative…in order to complete the description of the antecedent by adding some essential characteristic of it; §260: therefore, that comes generally nearer to the antecedent than who or which. Cf. 2165–7, 2305–2307+2.

1909 tode pold]
Q1(c)’s tod pole is certainly correct (Greg, 1940, p. 167). Wright (ed. 1875): The modern spelling was in use in Shakespeare’s time. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 518): The word’s first element was often spelled in the same ways as toad (which is what it means), and hence need not be corrected to tod (for which OED offers no parallels). The corrector presumably wanted the modern form tad, but only half of his alteration was carried out. But tod-pole is listed by OED as a 17th-c. spelling, and Q’s tod is repeated in all the Ff.

1909 wall-wort…water]
OED (Wall sb. 22c) lists more than a score of plants growing on or by walls, such as wall cabbage, wall spleenwort, etc.; though the term wallwort etymologically refers only to the inedible Daneweed (OED, Wallwort 1), it was applied erroneously to several other plants (OED, 2). The Q compositor may have known the term worts and water for pottage. Since Edgar is listing amphibious animals, however, Q1(c)’s wall-newt seems to make better sense in context, though OED (Wall 22b) defines the term doubtfully—? = wall-lizard—and gives no other ex. Wilson (ed. 1960): May be Sh.’s coinage to distinguish it from the water-newt (= newt or triton) (OED, Water sb. 30). Malone (ed. 1790), water: I.e. the water-newt. He cites similar constructions where the noun is not repeated, as does Schmidt (1875, p. 1419).

1910 furie…rages]
OED (v. 6a): To act with fury. Wilson (ed. 1960): Refers to the Abram-man’s fits of pretended madness, put on to terrify people. See n. 1265. Doran (1931, p. 31) explains Q2’s fruite: A word partly written will sometimes suggest another, which the hand produces.…When [the printer] had accidentally transposed the u and r, the shape of the word became altered in his mind.…The presence of the t is a bar…to the consideration of the error as a manuscript misreading. Cf. 2452, 3109.

1910 heart]
OED (sb. 12): The seat of the mental or intellectual faculties.

1911 sallets]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Combined sense of salads and of savoury morsels (OED, Salad 1, 1b).

1912 ditch dogge]
Delius (ed. 1854): The dead dog thrown into a ditch. Perrett (1904, p. 296): A scavenger dog, as referred to in the Ballad of Jane Shore (English and Scottish Ballads, ed. F. J. Child, 1860, 7:199: a ditch…Where carrion dogs do much frequent).

1912 greene mantle]
Kemshead (ed. 1875): The vegetable growth that collects on the surface of standing water (OED, Mantle 2c, quoting this l. as the second of two exx.). Deighton (ed. 1891): The scum, duck-weed. Tilley P465 compares the proverb Standing Pools gather filth.

1913 whipt…tithing,]
Steevens (in Reed, ed. 1785) cites Stat. 39 Eliz. (1598), quoted by Harrison (ed. 1937) and reproduced by Chambers (1923, 4:324): A Rogue Vagabonde or Sturdy Begger taken in a County Hundred Parish or Tything shall be stripped naked from the middle upwardes and shall be openly whipped untill his or her body be bloudye, and shalbe forthwith sent from Parish to Parish by the Officers of every the same, the nexte streighte way to the Parish where he was borne. Wilson (ed. 1960) cites the earlier Statute of 1572, An Acte for the punishement of Vacabondes (Chambers, 4:269–71), and Knight (ed. 1840) the later statute of 1 James (1604) (Chambers, 4:336–7). Furness (ed. 1880) refers to the account of such treatment in Harrison’s Description (in Holinshed, 1577, 3.5; 1587, 2.10; see n. 1265), and Craig (ed. 1901) compares 2H6 2.1.155–6 (909–10). Moberly (ed. 1876): As the tything is on the frank-pledge theory liable for the misdeeds of its sojourners, each would be glad to throw a Tom of Bedlam off on its neighbors by means however rough.

1913 tithing]
Clarke (ed. 1864): A tything is, strictly, a district consisting of a tenth part; the land, in ancient times, having been divided into hundreds and tythings. Hunter (ed. 1869): A neighborhood comprising ten households. OED (sb. 3): A company (originally) of ten householders in the system of Frank-pledge; now only as a rural division (originally regarded as one tenth of a hundred) to which this system gave its name.

1914 stock-punisht]
Craig (ed. 1901): Punished by being placed in the public stocks (OED, sb.1 65, quoting this l.). F’s stockt, punish’d is probably a scribal emendation or compositor’s error. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 194): In F, The general word punish’d sounds awkward between the two particular forms of punishment. Stone (1980, p. 220): F implies confusingly that being stocked is something other than being punished.

1914 hath had]
Verity (ed. 1897): In his better days, as a serving man. Schmidt (ed. 1879) tries to defend F’s hath: Q probably accords with the fact, but what have facts to do with madness? Tom hath three suits and six shirts;—where are they? who has taken them from him? Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 179): But note the word But in [1917]: surely in [1914–16] Tom is concerned with a contrast between his misery of the past seven years and prosperity before that. The F compositor [B] has presumably accidentally omitted a word.

1914 three sutes]
See nn. 1089, 1865.

1917–18 But…yeare]
Percy (in Johnson, ed. 1765, 8:2K5r) finds the original lines in the metrical romance of Bevis of Hampton, describing Bevis’s seven years in a dungeon. The romance was published in 1500 and went through nine eds. in the century, and Percy (in Steevens, ed. 1773, 10:2N5r) finds another allusion to the Bevis story in H8 1.1.38 (82). Capell (1783, 1.2:168) quotes the lines: Ratons & myse and soche smale dere, | That was hys mete that VII yere (ed. Kölbing, 1894, p. 74, ll. 85–6). Only Elson (1900, p. 244) thinks that Edgar sings the words. Hunter (ed. 1972, p. 341): The source in Bevis of Hampton makes music unlikely.

1917 Deere]
Johnson (ed. 1765): A general word for wild animals (OED, 3).

1918 Hath]
F regularizes to Haue. See n. 1636.

1918 seuen]
Dent (1981, Y25) cites the proverbial This seuen Years, meaning for a long period.

1918 yeare]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): An old form of the plural (OED: The normal OE. [flexionless] pl. géar is represented still in dialectal usage).

1919 Beware…fiend]
Murphy (1984, p. 202): Beware my follower could be addressed by the voice of the suffering possessed one to the company on stage. Peace Snulbug is a whining entreaty addressed to the demon. Peace, thou fiend is the exorcist’s voice to the same hallucinated presence.

1919 follower]
Delius (ed. 1854): The evil spirit that follows him. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Supposed to be one of those that possess him. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Then Edgar speaks to the fiend as if it were his dog.

1919 snulbug]
Apparently a confusion for the name of one of Harsnett’s devils, named Smolkin (1603, pp. 47, 140, 145, 181; see , ); F prints Smulkin. Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 398–9 ): Misreading in Q—n/m, b/k. Presumably there was minim confusion at the end of the word in the copy for Q: and if the g is not a pure guess by the compositor there must have been an accidental mark which looked to him like a tail. The compositor may have misread k as b at 1211 stobing/stocking. Stone (1980, p. 181): The spelling in Q copy evidently terminated in a hyper-correct -ing. Wilson (ed. 1960): The name was prob. suggested by mice [1917] since Smolkin is…reported [Harsnett, p. 140] as seen creeping out of a man’s ear in the form of a mouse; see . Stone and Taylor (1983, p. 369) consider F’s reading a half-correction; Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 518) imagine unconscious association with the noun smulkin. Nares (1822): Probably, as well as Malkin, a corruption of Moll. Mackay (1887, p. 383), fancifully: Probably a Keltic word compounded of smulc,…ferocious,…[or] smol,…a live coal,…with ceann, head. The word may signify only small size or value: OED (Smulkin): Obs. rare. [Irish?]…farthing. Brownlow (1993, p. 173): The suffix -kin is a diminutive suitable to this mouse devil. The first element of his name may be related to Smulk, meaning a dirty beast (Wright), or to a variously spelled Scottish word of Scandinavian origin with many derivatives, smule or smool meaning little pieces (Wright).

1920 What]
See n. 858.

1920 your Grace]
See n. 218.

1921–2 The…ma hu]
Reed (in Steevens, ed. 1793): In The Goblins [ca. 1638], by Sir John Suckling, a catch is introduced which concludes with these two lines: The Prince of darkness is a gentleman: Mahu, Mahu is his name [3.2.35, ed. Beaurline, 1971]. I am inclined to think this catch not to be the production of Suckling, but the original referred to by Edgar’s speech. Wright (ed. 1875): But as Suckling in other parts of his play is constantly alluding to Shakespeare, it is more likely that in this he is only quoting from Lear. Muir (1951, p. 15): Harsnett twice refers to the prince of darknes (1603, pp. 147, 168). Blunden (1929; 1936, pp. 331–2) thinks that Sh. had in mind four lines from Horace, Epist. 2.1.210–13, describing the tragic poet and containing the words extentum funem, falsis terroribus, magus, modo, Thebis, and Athenis. Supposedly the first phrase suggested foure incht bridges (see n. 1837–8), the last three or four words suggested Lear’s Theban and Athenian philosophers (1936, 1964), and the associative link with this passage was the idea of terrors and the common Latin word modo (now), coincidentally the name of Harsnett’s devil. Baldwin (1944, 2:520), recalling another possible allusion to the same ode (see n. 2037): Tom is…a philosopher in Persian attire.…Shakspere shows considerable familiarity with this first book of odes.…The magus of Horace is likely to have set off [this] train of thought. Muir (1951, p. 18), in support: Harsnett (1603, p. 137; see ) quotes and translates a passage from Horace’s next epistle (2.2.208–9), also mentioning terrors and magic, which may have reminded Sh. of the previous one. Wilson (ed. 1960): Since it is Horace’s description of the tragic poet…it is in fact the passage above all others in Horace we might expect Sh. to know, probably by heart, certainly to have in mind as he walked his own tragic tight-rope of King Lear. Thus, in hoc modo, a Latin homonym begets a suggestion which becomes a probability and then a certainty. Murphy (1984, p. 202): The speech should ring out with proud clarity in a most arrogant manner. The speaker is possessed by the demon of pride.

1921 Prince…Gentleman]
Steevens (ed. 1778): This is spoken in resentment of what Gloster had just said. Edgar answers that one can have no better company than a gentleman, and the prince of darkness, by virtue of being a prince, is such a one. Kittredge (ed. 1940): And therefore good enough company even for a king. Skillan (ed. 1967): Or for himself as one of the devil’s company. Dent (1981, D240.1) suspects a proverb, The Devil is a gentleman. OED (Darkness, 4a) records the epithet prince of darkness for the devil from 1526. Milward (1987, p. 181) cites the epithet in Matt. 9:34, 12:24; John 12:31, 14:30, 15:11; Eph. 2:2, 6:12.

1921–2 modo…ma hu]
The Q compositor failed to recognize the proper name, set in F as Mahu. Though Edgar seems to imply that these are both names for the same prince of darkness, in Harsnett (1603, pp. 54, 90; see also below and ) Modu and Maho are names for the devils of Master Mainy and Sara Williams respectively (p. 46; see ). Both of Harsnett’s demons are persons of rank if not indeed of nobility. Mainy identifies his devil Modu as the Prince of all other deuils (p. 268); Sara’s is Maho, the black Prince (p. 146), also called (pp. 50, 141; see , ) generall Dictator of hell and (p. 119) Prince of hel; Modu is described as Muster-maister ouer the Captaines of the seauen deadly sinnes (p. 48; see ) and the Generall of Styx (p. 54), and together they are Maho, and Modu (the two Generals of the infernal furies) (p. 148). Sara (p. 181) got her devil’s name from a book, for that she had heard before her vncle reade…a tale therein of Maho. Moberly (ed. 1876): Mahu is supposed to be the same as Mahound (ultimately Mohammed) (OED: Perh. suggested by Mahound, quoting only Sh. and Harsnett). Brownlow (1993, p. 173): A standard name for the devil, appearing in Scots English as auld Mahoun (OED [4]). Chew (1937, p. 396) documents the association. The names reappear in 2248+3.

1923–4 Our…it]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): One of Shakespeare’s subtle touches. Some tone, or inflection of tone, in Edgar’s voice has reached the father’s heart, and bitterly recalls his sense of supposed unfilial conduct of his elder son, causing him to blend that son’s tokens of unnatural hatred with those shown by Lear’s two daughters. Edgar, instinctively feeling this, perseveres with his Bedlam cry,…to drown the betrayed sound of his own voice, and maintain the impression of his assumed character. There is no reason to intuit such a response by Gloucester. Tovey (ed. 1896): Gloucester speaks to Lear as to a fellow-sufferer, believing that they both have met with filial ingratitude. Goggin (ed. 1910): Gloucester is of course thinking of Edgar as well as of Goneril and Regan, but there is no need to conclude…that he recognises something familiar in the tone of Edgar’s voice. Empson (1951, p. 139), followed by Olsen (1978, pp. 10–11): There is another idea for the audience: We have become so depraved that we hate the sexual process by which we are produced. Bevington (ed. 1992): Life is so wretched that it cries out against having been born.

1923 flesh and bloud]
See n. 1515. Moberly (ed. 1876): That is,…Gloucester’s son and Lear’s daughters, [who] all unnaturally hate their parents. Muir (ed. 1952), more widely: Humanity, our children. Milward (1987, p. 181): Human nature and blood ties, citing Matt. 16:17, John 1:13, 1 Cor. 15:50, Gal. 1:16. Wilson (ed. 1960), and Hoeniger (ed. 1968): No wonder Edg. shudders at this in 1925. See also the prev. n.

1923 is]
On the singular verb with two subjects see n. 754.

1924 vild]
See n. 1726.

1924 my Lord]
F’s transposition (see textual n.) is indifferent, especially in prose.

1924 gets]
See n. 349.

1925 Poore Toms]
See n. 1271.

1925 a cold]
See n. 1839.

1926 Go in]
Not into the hovel that Edgar has just emerged from, but into the better shelter that Gloucester has prepared (1931). See n. 1951.

1926–7 suffer to obay]
The general sense is clear enough, though the construction seems elliptical or archaic. Most eds. follow Mason (1785, p. 349) in supplying the accusative: That is, my duty will not suffer me, to obey (OED, Suffer v. 14: Const. acc. and inf.…To allow or permit a person…to do so-and-so.). Just as possibly the reflexive is understood: My duty will not suffer itself to obey (OED, 15b: To endure, consent…to do something). Wright (ed. 1875) takes suffer in the sense to be injured or impaired. Const. from, under (OED, 10) by understanding the infinitive to mean in, by, or from obeying, citing Abbott (§356), who gives many examples of the indefinite or gerundive use of the infinitive; Furness (ed. 1880) compares 1979–80. Cf. Franz §655, and 1189, 3168+2.

1927 in all]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Modifies commaunds. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Emphatic. Brooke (ed. 1947): In every respect—i.e., as an adverb modifying obay.

1929 tyranous]
See n. 1779.

1929 take…you]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Do what it likes with you. More precisely, act like a tyrant: OED (Take v. 69b): To get a person or thing into its (or one’s) hold or power.

1930 venter’d]
Venter was a common sp. variant of venture (OED); cf. 2723+1, Ven. 628, 1H4 5.1.101 (2738, F), AWW 2.1.170 (780), and both Q and F texts of 2H4 1.1.59 (116) and H5 1.2.192 (339).

1931 food and fire]
F’s inversion (see textual n.) is indifferent.

1931 is]
For the singular verb see n. 754. Verity (ed. 1897): In agreement with the single idea of provision contained in fire and food.

1932 Philosopher]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): It is here that Lear shows the first token of absolute insanity set in. His disordered judgment, his violent ravings, his wandering wits in the question, Didst…daughters? [1830], his snatching off his clothes to be like the base natural animal man, are all the symptoms of derangement and coming madness; but here is the actual madness itself, the fixed delusion, the conviction of unreason. The storm has told upon his physical condition, the flighty beggar-man’s appearance in naked unsophisticated truth of human individuality has struck his imagination, has caught his fancy, has engaged his belief in him as one who, because he abjures the vain adjuncts of clothing, must needs be a philosopher. Moberly (ed. 1876): Being so unsophisticated—having so completely reduced mankind to their elements, surely this man must have a spontaneous insight into the nature of things such as would as least tell him what is the cause of thunder. Deighton (ed. 1891): This stoic in caring nothing for external annoyance. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Man of science. Philosophy was the regular word for what we call science, citing Ham. 1.5.166–7 (863–4). Gordon (1944, pp. 126): Lear mistakes the Bedlam for a professional wise man such as various kings kept at court to answer philosophic questions; see n. 893–909. Traversi (1952–3, p. 137): It is Edgar’s persistence in grasping the unadorned truth about the human situation [Poor Tom’s a cold] that prompts Lear to hail him…as philosopher. Wilson (ed. 1960): Suggested by Edg.’s unaccommodated condition. Cf. the life philosophers commend in Lyly’s Campaspe (1.2.3)…[and] Diogenes’ entry from his tub in the same play.…Lear, we are to suppose, is now adding him to his mock court. Donovan (privately) compares Jonson, Every Man Out 1.1.11–12: I am no such pild Cinique, to beleeue | That beggery is the onely happinesse. That Sh. has Diogenes in mind is suggested by Boodle (1884, p. 217): Edgar is a philosopher because, like Diogenes, he owes as little as he can to others, citing 1883 ff.; so also Empson (1951, p. 139), Taylor (1955, p. 364), and Donawerth (1977; see n. 1882–8); see also n. 1936. Butler (1986, pp. 511–13) cites numerous Elizabethan and Jacobean references to Diogenes. Doloff (1991, p. 253): Here is a parody of the meeting of Alexander and Diogenes. Joseph (ed. 1966): Erasmus treats Diogenes as the man who had no little house or corner of his own in which to eat his food quietly, but who still found that he had superfluous property.…Udall’s translation of Erasmus, Apophthegms of Erasmus (1542) was widely read. Though Sh. never names Diogenes, he knew about both cynic and stoic schools, and represented them in Apemantus and Brutus. Tate (1681, p. 33) prefers Aristotle: his Lear addresses Edgar, Say, Stagirite. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Possibly Lear addresses Edgar this way because of his powers to charm. It might be noted that from line 1860 onwards Edgar urges moral advice and implies knowledge of powers of darkness, both of which might help suggest the philosopher to Lear. Foakes (ed. 1997): Perhaps Lear sees Poor Tom as an occult scientist in view of his acquaintance with devils.

1933 What…thunder?]
Wilson (ed. 1960): An apt question with the storm raging. Verity (ed. 1897): A stock subject of discussion, so that perhaps the question was a sort of joke, citing Chaucer’s Squire’s Tale 258. Kittredge (ed. 1940) cites the standard explanation discussed in Tourneur, Atheist’s Tragedy 2.4.[146–55; ed. Parfitt, 1978] and compares 1659–64, JC 1.3.49 (487), Tmp. 2.1.204, 2.2.108 (885, 1151). Gordon (1944; see n. 893–909) finds the question among the reasons of nature in Boccus and Sydrac (1537, no. 122), and Muir (ed. 1952) finds Ovid (Meta. 15.68 ff.) telling how Pythagoras taught whether Jove or else the wynds in breaking clowdes doo thunder (tr. Golding, 1567). Elton (1966, pp. 197 ff.) discusses a multitude of naturalist and skeptical Renaissance probings of the question, concluding (p. 212), In his attitudes to thunder Lear was…either (1) representing a pagan point of view, typified by the ancient skeptical tradition regarding the natural causation of that heavenly phenomenon, or (2) expressing an increasing doubt as to the reliability of the gods. In the first case, as heathen, Lear would have given no offense to his Elizabethan audience, while in the second case his developing distrust of ethnic deities could be construed as a fortunate change towards a theologically more enlightened position. Hunter (ed. 1972): The question is apposite both to the immediate weather and to the larger questions of God’s justice. Edwards (ed. 1975): In III.2 Lear interpreted the thunder in a number of ways.…He wants someone to tell him authoritatively what, if anything, the gods have to do with the turmoil he observes and suffers.

1934 My good Lord]
On F’s Good my Lord see n. 102.

1935 the house]
Verity (ed. 1897): The farm-house…where he has made provision for Lear. Perrett (1904, pp. 260–2): Gloucester’s house, not a farm-house.…They gain entry presumably by a side-door…to a room in the servants’ quarters.…Those knights of Lear’s…could not have met him at gate [2076], if the room in the preceding scene were anywhere but in the house itself, for after the plot had been discovered and the need for extreme caution urged…, Kent would have avoided passing the very gate with the litter, had the starting-point been anywhere else.…It is not till Lear is in the house, and Glou. goes in search of additional comforts ([1999]) that the latter overhears a plot of death ([2048]). If Lear is to be taken into any other than that same house, Kent’s [Glo.’s?] warning at the end of III, vi [2056+4? 2052–4?] loses its point, and Edgar’s Childe…came [1966] much of its magic. See n. 1996. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 194) finds F’s elision th’house awkward: The F compositor has probably unthinkingly substituted the contracted article.

1936 most]
F’s same cannot be intended to clarify, since Lear clearly means Edgar.

1936 learned Theban]
Lear’s epithet Athenian for his philosopher (1964) hardly requires comment, but here Theban is puzzling, since Thebes in Bœotia is not usually associated with philosophy or science. Steevens (ed. 1778) finds the phrase in Jonson’s masque Pan’s Anniversary [1620; ll. 96–7]: Then comes my learned Theban, the Tinker I told you of, and suspects that it is perhaps in ridicule of this passage in Lr. Craig (ed. 1901): This is very doubtful…; mention is made in the Masque before of a Tinker of Thebes [71]. See also Boyes of Bœotia; thinges of Thebes [85]; indeed, the phrase learned Theban may have been understood at the time. The idea that learned Theban was simply current slang for philosopher or Greek philosopher is repeated by Goggin (ed. 1910), Craig (ed. 1931), Harrison (ed. 1948), and Muir (ed. 1952). Still, why Theban? Deighton (ed. 1891) and others: Thebes was the first place in Western Europe into which the use of letters was introduced from Phoenicia. Tovey (ed. 1896): Thebes…and Athens were both centres of learning and culture in the ancient world. But Boodle (1884, p. 217): Lear calls his philosopher…in ridicule, a Theban, a name the very antithesis to an Athenian. Bœotia being famed for stupidity (Bœotum in crasso iurares aere natum, Hor[ace]. Epist. II, i, 244). So Lee (ed. 1908): An ironical incoherence. A Theban…commonly connotes stupidity. Wilson (ed. 1960): Here meaning members of ancient Greek universities, perh. hinting at Cambridge and Oxford. Similarly Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): Scholar; unattested in OED. Hulme (1962, p. 192): Of the extreme poverty of the Thebans Erasmus gives an instance, quoting Nicholas Udall, tr., Apophthegmes of Erasmus (1542; 1564, pp. 214–15): These poore soules [said Alexander of conquered Thebans]…haue [not] any thyng at all left vnto them, neither citee to dwel in, nor lande to tille. Skillan (ed. 1967): Perhaps, one with cultural reputation.…Thebes produced epic poems upon which some of the later Greek tragedies were based. Colman (ed. 1982): Perhaps suggested by Thessalian Hags in Harsnett (1603, p. 137). Weis (ed. 1993): Shakespeare’s references to Theban…and Athenian may derive from their collocation in Horace’s…the playwright…whisks me away—one day to Thebes, another to Athens (Epist. 2.1.[213], tr. Rudd., 1981); see n. 1921–2.
Allusions to particular Thebans have also been found. Moffatt (ed. 1889): Reference to the fact of [Thebes] being the birthplace of the famous soothsayer Tiresias. Gardner (ed. 1969): Who lived to a great age, was blind, and was represented as a Theban. Similarly Fleissner (1991, p. 182): A soothsayer could be called a philosopher, and Sh. could have known the Oedipus story through Alexander Nevile’s tr. (1560; rpt. 1581) of Seneca’s tragedy. Gloucester, not Edgar, he concedes, might be the more immediately obvious Tiresias-figure. Spilsbury & Marshall (ed. 1905): Thebes was the birthplace also of Pindar. Kranz (1938, p. 32), Sitwell (1948, pp. 51–2), Cutts (1963, pp. 478–9), and Hebert (1976) suggest Oedipus, solver of riddles; Cutts notes, Oedipus became a good Athenian—bringing a blessing to the land of his final rest. Butler (1986, p. 513): No Greek ever took him to be a philosopher. An allusion to Crates the Cynic, follower of Diogenes the Cynic, is detected by Petz (tr. 1839), Taylor (1955, pp. 364–5), and Butler, the latter citing his brief life in William Baldwin’s A Treatise of Morall Philosophie (facs. R. H. Bowers, 1967, pp. 38–41), which appeared in 18 eds. 1547–1605. An epigram by Crates was widely translated in the Renaissance (see Rollins, ed., Tottel’s Miscellany, 1928, 2:236–7) and others were included in collections of Apothegmata; and Diogenes Laertius’s (Lives, 6.87) anecdote about his throwing all his possessions into the sea so as not to be diverted by worldly goods from the study of philosophy, alluded to in Plutarch’s essay Against Usury (tr. P. Holland), is referred to in Erasmus’s De Ratione Studii (ed. Thompson, 1978, p. 676), in Baldwin’s life, in Nashe’s Anatomie of Absurditie (ed. McKerrow, 1:33–4), and twice in Lyly’s Euphues (ed. Bond, 1902, 1:268, 308) though never in Sh. Joseph (ed. 1966): Erasmus talks of the Thebans as poverty-stricken.…One particular learned Theban, named Epaminondas, is cited by Renaissance writers accessible to Shakespeare (with Plutarch among them) as an example of a man of noble birth whose family was poverty-stricken, but who did not allow lack of wealth to prevent his living a full life.…The thing itself can be an inspiration to fortitude. It is possible Sh. was thinking of a more widely known Theban philosopher, Plutarch, author of the Moralia, who lived and taught most of his life at Chæronea; the title page to North’s tr. of the Lives (1579) calls him that grave learned philosopher, and Amyot’s Address to the Readers (sig. *6) supposes him a royal tutor whose morall and naturall Philosophie had good effect on Trajan—as Lear hopes Tom’s philosophy will have on him. Viswanathan (1986, p. 362) proposes Cebes of Thebes, whose Tabula was occasionally read in Greek in the upper forms.

1937 what…studie?]
Deighton (ed. 1891): What is the problem engaging your mind? Kittredge (ed. 1940): What is your special department of scientific research? Edgar picks up the word study and applies it in another sense: That to which I give all my attention. Jorgensen (1967, p. 77): Stress on your, indicating that…his own specialty…happens to be unkind daughters.

1938 preuent]
See n. 50. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Forestall the assaults of the fiend. Muir (ed. 1952): Use preventative measures against, avoid. Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): I.e. avoid damnation. Bevington (ed. 1980): Thwart.

1938 vermine]
Presumably lice. Cf. 2014+1. Foakes (ed. 1997), however: Perhaps suggested by the devils in Harsnett, who frequently take the form of animals, like Smolkin the Mouse-devil (1603, p. 145; see n. 1919).

1939 word in priuate]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Lear speaks as if the learned philosopher had answered him sensibly, and as if, therefore, a private conference with him might be useful in the present crisis. Blunden (1929; 1936, p. 332): We can guess what the question would have been. How did he kill his daughters?

1940 importune]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Accented on the second syllable.

1940 him]
F’s him once more makes a pentameter. Doran (1931, p. 126): Q’s short line may be due to omission by the printer. Halio (ed. 1994): Blayney explains how these words, necessary to the metre if not to the sense, were probably omitted.…After the first twelve [letters] in [1939], one word follows; the copy may therefore have had two almost identical readings in [1939] and [1940] in nearly exact vertical alignment. If the compositor saw once more as the two words [one word] he had already set, he could have moved on to the next words.

1941 wits]
See n. 682.

1941 begin]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): This remark alone is enough to disprove the theory of those alienists who contend that Lear is suffering from senile dementia at the very beginning of the play.

1943 His…death]
Perrett (1904, p. 261): The conclusion which Glou. draws from the barbarous treatment and particularly the exposure…to which Lear has been subjected. Kittredge (ed. 1940) cites 1601 ff. Cf. 1755–7. Gloucester’s statement is apparently intuitive or hyperbolic. Soon his daughters will seek more directly: cf. 2048, 2128–30.

1944 He said]
Gloucester last saw Kent (as Kent) in the opening scene of the play. Furness (ed. 1880) thinks the reference here is to 159, Verity (ed. 1897) to 197–8, Smith (ed. 1902) to 166–8, Kittredge (ed. 1940) to Kent’s general apprehensions in 159–99. Bradley (1904, p. 447) imagines a scene not extant: see n. 6.

1947 out-lawed…bloud]
See n. 121. Deighton (ed. 1891): Disinherited and disowned as my son. Craig (ed. 1901): Condemned to outlawry (loss of estate, etc.), through corruption of blood. Those subject to attainder (stain or corruption of blood) formerly suffered such loss, citing 1H6 3.1.159, Let Richard be restored to his Blood—i.e., to his hereditary rights, by reversal of his attainder. See OED (Blood, sb. 13). Fraser (1962, p. 71): Not…a legalism only…but a physiological description: Edgar, now wasted, corrupted, diseased.

1947 sought my life]
Moulton (1885, p. 216): Edgar now learns how his father has been deceived; in his heart he is re-united to him, and from this point of re-union springs the devotion he lavishes upon his father in the affliction that presently falls upon him. On the other hand, that which brings Gloucester to this Hovel Scene, the attempt to save the King, is betrayed by Edmund, who becomes thereby the cause of the vengeance which puts out his father’s eyes. Thus from this meeting of the mad Edgar with the mad Lear there springs at once the final stroke in the misery Gloucester suffers from the son he has favoured, and the beginning of the forgiving love he is to experience from the son he has wronged: that meeting then is certainly the central climax to the double nemesis which makes up the Gloucester action.

1948 But]
See n. 235.

1948 late]
See n. 718.

1950 my]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Emphatic.

1950 craz’d]
Verity (ed. 1897): To impair (OED, v. 6, quoting this l.). Kittredge (ed. 1940): The literal meaning is cracked.

1950 wits]
See n. 682.

1951 beseech]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Here Gloster attempts to lead Lear towards the shelter he has provided in the farm-house adjoining the castle; but the king will not hear of quitting his philosopher. Gloster then [1955] induces the Bedlam-fellow to go into the hovel, that he may be out of Lear’s sight; but Lear proposes to follow him thither, saying Let’s in all. Kent endeavours to draw Lear away; but, finding him resolved to keep still with his philosopher, begs Gloster to humour the king and let him take the fellow with him. Gloster accedes, and bids Kent himself to take the fellow with them.…We point out the details…because, if it be not especially observed, the distinction between the hovel and the farm-house…would hardly be duly understood. On whether the new shelter is farm-house or something else, see n. 1996. Reynolds (1962, p. 93): There must be some way that Gloucester can show that he is bringing Lear and the others secretly to a different hiding-place. The gate of the castle is still closed as are also the curtains in front of it. The limit of three doors makes the problem more difficult.…We may suppose that Gloucester leads Lear, Kent, Edgar and the Fool from before the hovel across the Stage Right, and then goes between the curtain and the wall to enter the curtained space. There picking up the stools they need and the cushions [2014+15, +26]…they go before the curtains to give the scene supposed in some obscure place.

1951 your Grace]
See n. 218. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 194): Grace being here the title…the F compositor’s failure to supply an initial capital was an oversight.

1952 crie you mercie]
See n. 1711. Deighton (ed. 1891): Said in refusal to leave the company of his philosopher. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Lear is a little impatient at being interrupted in his conference. Budd (ed. 1935): Lear begs pardon for preferring the company of the Noble philosopher to that of Gloucester. F’s added Sir is hypermetrical.

1953 your]
Verity (ed. 1897): Emphatic.

1954 a cold]
See n. 1839.

1955 fellow]
See n. 557.

1955 in’t]
The form is not authorial; elsewhere in the Folio and good quartos it is always a contraction of in it. Here it is probably due to the Q compositor’s use of a short measure on this page. Q2’s into th’, followed by F1 and most eds., was an unauthorized correction and was less probably what lay in the MS behind Q1 than inth’ or ith’. The expansion to into makes the line hypermetrical, but not seriously enough, perhaps, to give the Q2 and F compositors pause if they independently substituted a more familiar form for the intended meaning here; Q2 did not necessarily influence F. Cf. n. 676.

1956 all]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Emphatic.

1957 This way]
Verity (ed. 1897): To the farm-house, not into the hovel.

1958 With him]
Ambiguous. In Q the phrase might modify keep; with F’s stop, it could mean either I will go with him (Edgar) or You go with him (Gloucester). Hunter (ed. 1972) upholds the former reading: Both words are heavily emphasized. Lear is impatient of the efforts to divert him from the conference with his philosopher.

1959 I…Philosopher]
Elton (1966, p. 95): While the king conducts the protagonist’s business, Edgar is left to voice its developing rationale, feeling. Ironically, only the mad beggar can give adequate expression to the disorder Lear experiences.

1959 stil]
Yet. Hunter (ed. 1972): Continuously; see n. 253.

1960 sooth]
Schmidt (1875): Humour (properly to say Yes [Sooth!] to what another says) (OED, v. 4).

1961 let him take]
Verity (ed. 1897): Hence it is through Lear that Edgar is brought near to Gloucester’s castle and is thus at hand when Gloucester needs his help ([2176+5–+7]). Spilsbury & Marshall (ed. 1905): This little incident is important as assisting the interweaving of the under plot into the main.

1961 fellow]
See n. 16.

1962 Take…on]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Gloucester assents: Very well. Do you take the fellow along to the farmhouse, and I will follow with the King. Hunter (ed. 1972): Kent should take ahead…Edgar so that Lear can be persuaded to follow. Foakes (ed. 1997): May refer to…the Fool.…Kent then goes off with the Fool…, followed by Gloucester, while Edgar brings up the rear with Lear.…Both Q and F have him you,…It seems likely that the words were accidentally transposed. But since both the Q printer and the scribe who prepared the F playbook apparently made the same awkward transposition, it was probably in Sh.’s MS.

1963 Sirah]
See n. 411.

1964 Athenian]
See n. 1936. Deighton (ed. 1891): Athens being the chief seat of learning in Greece. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): The home of Sokrates and Plato. Smith (ed. 1926): The strangeness of Poor Tom’s appearance suggests the cant term. Wilson (ed. 1960): Lear comes to think more highly of his philosopher as time goes on—i.e., at first he was a mere Theban. Joseph (ed. 1966, p. 39): It seems that now a memory of an Athenian philosopher consoles the suffering, tottering brain. (This Athenian is most likely to be Socrates whose fortitude not only coped with poverty but faced an undeserved death without despair.)

1965 No…hush]
Wilson (ed. 1960): A sign (to the audience) that they will be sheltering in a house near the castle, and therefore in danger of discovery. Skillan (ed. 1967): So as not to disturb the fantastic situation that is leading lear into shelter.

1966–8 Child…man]
Capell (1783, 1.2:169): Child Rowland, is he himself; the dark tower, his hovel; and the fie-foe-fum giant, his father Gloster; who, he fears, might still have the giant’s sagacity, and accost him. Edgar is not entering the hovel, but another house. Moberly (ed. 1876): The line seems to mean we must be as quiet as if we were coming into the house of the giant famed in story. Brooke (ed. 1947): Edgar’s mystical way of saying that he sees a dark adventure before him and smells a rat. Levin (1959, pp. 93–4): Edgar’s snatches of balladry and fairy-tale transform [the house] into a legendary dark tower, where a young squire is undergoing a ritual of knightly initiation while nameless giants objurgate: Fie, foh, and fum. Wilson (ed. 1960): Edg., warned by Glo.’s hush!, is himself the Childe venturing into a dark house where the unknown awaits him. He is also Jack invisible, of noble British blood, though outlawed from it ([1947]).…British Roland is entering the Giant’s Castle, where his blood (kinship) is in danger of being smelt (detected). Skillan (ed. 1967): edg. is simply creating an air of mystery and inventing a dark adventure as part of his act. Long (1971, p. 172): Gloucester’s castle…has become morally and symbolically a dark tower.…The blood of a British man will flow, when Gloucester’s eyes are so cruelly extinguished. Foakes (ed. 1997): The lines may…point to Edgar, who will turn into a hero and kill the giant Edmund. The audience does not know that he will, however, and so can detect no such meaning. Both Capell (op. cit.) and Staunton (ed. 1859) add a line of their invention to make a coherent ballad quatrain (see textual n.), to which Addis (1874, p. 476) objects that the stringing together of such disjointed snatches is quite in Edgar’s manner, under his assumed madness. Long (op. cit., pp. 172–3) speculatively sets the first line to a ballad, for Edgar to sing as exit song or bridge to the next scene: see . Hunter (ed. 1972, p. 342): But these do not sound like words for music.
These lines seem to derive from folk literature. Ritson (apud Steevens, ed. 1793): The first line derives from some French or Spanish ballad, the last two from some tale like Jack and the Giants. Dyce (1853, p. 146): The lines are from a ballad like the three Danish poems about Rosmer Hafmand from the Danske Viser (comp. Anders S. Vedel, Ribe, 1591) discovered and translated into Scots dialect by Jamieson (1806, 1:215–17, 2:202–9; 1814, pp. 411–19). The ballads concern the rescue of Lady Eline, daughter of the king of Iceland, from the mer-man Rosmer, through the efforts of her brother; in the second ballad he is called Young Roland (ungen Roland: Udvalgte Danske Viser, ed. W. Abrahamson, 1812, 1:224), and in all three the giant mer-man detects his presence by smelling a christen Mand. The ballad exists in Danish, Swedish, Norse, and Faroish versions, and Jamieson (1814, pp. 397–404) reconstructs from his own childhood memories a Scots version involving The Warluck Merlin—Child Rowland—and Burd Ellen and including the words fi, fi, fo, and fum, | I smell the blood of a Christian man spoken by the King of Elfland. On the hint of the name Merlin Jamieson makes Ellen and Rowland the children of King Arthur and Queen Gwenevra. Jamieson’s reconstruction is reprinted by Child (1860, 1:245–52), who thinks it is not impossible that Edgar quotes it but denies any connection with Arthurian legend because the name Merlin seems to have been given in Scotland to any sort of wizard or prophet. Later Child (1894, 5:201) came to doubt the version’s genuineness and did not reprint it. Lee (ed. 1908) suspects that it is partly based on Sh.’s lines; similarly Kittredge (ed. 1940): The Scottish fragments…are manifestly of modern composition, nor can any credit be given to the antiquity of the narrative in which they are embedded. But cf. Joseph Jacobs, [Childe Rowland] Folk-Lore, II (1891), 182–197, who accepts it uncritically. Prideaux (1885, pp. 133–4) and Yardley (1896, p. 423) suspect derivation from archetypes having many narrative forms in northern mythologies. Brie (1925) believes that Peele’s Old Wives Tale (1595), Christopher Middleton’s Chinon of England (1597), and Milton’s Comus all owe details to the same folktale of Childe Rowland, though the similarities he finds are common to many tales (and are unrelated to Lr.). Though Jamieson’s particular version is very doubtful, Sh. seems to have heard some version of the basic story. Hoeniger (1974, p. 101) finds suggestive analogies with the folk-tale versions of the Lear story collected by Cocchiara (1932) and esp. with primitive initiation rituals in which boys are led into a hovel where demons scream to possess them.

1966 Child]
Capell (1783, 1.2:168): A common appellative of the knight in romances, used by Spenser. Warburton (ed. 1747), more exactly: Noble youths who were candidates for knighthood (OED, sb. 5).

1966 Rowland]
Capell (1783, 1.2:168): A contraction of Orlando. Elizabethans knew this form of the name in the proverb To give one a Rowland for an Oliver (Tilley R195). Muir (ed. 1952): Charlemagne’s nephew, and the hero of The Song of Roland and other poems. Wilson (ed. 1960): The most famous figure in the retinue of Charlemagne. For the notion that Rowland here refers to a son of King Arthur, see n. 1966–8. Steevens (ed. 1773) finds a reference to childe Rowland in Fletcher’s The Woman’s Prize (ed. Bowers, 2.1.16), a work written later than Lr. (in 1611) and possibly echoing it.

1966 towne come]
F corrects to Tower came, followed by virtually all eds. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 399), towne: Doubtless an n/r misreading of copy towre, comparing 776 and/are. Ibid., come: Probably a misreading of a as o. Only Wells (ed. 2000) retains towne and (for rhyme) come, adding, Jowett suggests (privately) that town connects with Athenian, Athens being an enlightened city rather than a dark (British) town. Sitwell (1943, p. 125), uniquely: The dark towne is Death, its houses coffins.

1967 His word]
Verity (ed. 1897): I.e. the giant’s (inside the dark tower). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Edgar’s remark: His motto or watchword was always—, and then he completes the sentence with something that had nothing to do with Child Rowland and would be instantly recognized by the audience as the Giant’s speech in Jack the Giant-Killer, and therefore absurdly inappropriate for a knightly hero.…Compare the words on the shields of the knights in Per. 2.2.21 ff. (730): Lux tua vita mihi, etc. We may profitably contrast them with Edgar’s Fie, foh, and fum!. Anders (1904, p. 193): The earliest known edition of the Jack and the Giants story is 1711. Hunter (ed. 1972): Perhaps Edgar, returning to his home, remembers the story of another son’s triumphant return. The tower may have suggested the beanstalk.

1967 still]
See n. 253.

1967 fy fo and fum]
Steevens (ed. 1778) cites Nashe’s Have With You to Saffron Walden (1596): O, tis a precious apothegmaticall Pedant, who will finde matter inough to dilate a whole daye of the first inuention of Fy, fa, fum, I smell the bloud of an English-man (ed. McKerrow, 3:37). McKerrow finds Fee, Fa, Fum in Rowlands’s Knave of Clubs (1609; Hunterian ed., 2:31) as a mock conjuration to Beelzebub. Halliwell (ed. 1865): The original source of these popular words is unknown. They are alluded to in Peele’s Old Wives Tale, [ca. 1590; ed. Hook, 1970, 545–7],— Fee, fa, fum, Here is the Englishman, Conquer him that can.…The probability is that the distich…belongs to some early version of the tale of Jack and the Giants. Hook (op. cit., 3:335) quotes from the Oxfordshire St. George play (in Adams, Chief Pre-Shakespearean Dramas, 1924, p. 353): I am Giant Blunderbore, fee, fi, fum! | Ready to fight ye all,—so I says, Come!—but it is not known how much earlier than the 19th c. this play existed. Joseph (ed. 1966): The words are expressive of loathing and disgust. Garton (1993) compares variants in the formula, deriving Sh.’s sequence of vowels from the declension of the gerund in William Lily’s Latin Grammar (1549).

1968 British]
Wright (ed. 1875), following Malone (ed. 1790, 1:353): The substitution of British man for Englishman [in the popular saying; see prev. n.] points to the time when under James I the name of England was merged in the more general title of Great Britain, comparing 2703 (where the change from Q’s British to F’s English weakens this argument). Malone is more circumspect: Though a complete union of England and Scotland, which was projected in the first parliament that met after James’s accession to the English throne, was not carried into effect till a century afterwards, the two kingdoms were united in name, and he was proclaimed king of Great Britain, October 24, 1604. Chalmers (1799, pp. 417–18): The terms Britain and British for a united England and Scotland appear earlier, in a royal proclamation of 13 May 1603 and in verses upon James’s accession by Daniel and Drayton. Axton (1977, pp. 134, 136): During the Commons’ five years (1604–8) of debate on unification with Scotland, James addressed them personally three times, urging the names of Britain and Britons; the Commons steadfastly objected to the alteration of the ancient and honourable name England.…[The] final ratification of the Union of the two Crowns by Act of Parliament in 1608 [Wickham, 1973]…simply did not occur. James was defeated by his Commons and, despite the propaganda celebrating Union, his recourse to the Exchequer Chamber and high court judges in 1608 was a retreat. Cf. n. 7. Deighton (ed. 1891): Possibly [British] is a mere accident. Perrett (1904, p. 250): English is the solecism and British what would naturally be expected.…The change to British affords no criterion whatever for the dating of the play.…Even in [Leir], where Leir is a Christian, we always find Brittaine or Brittany, British, etc. Draper (1937, pp. 177 ff.): In October, 1604, James was proclaim’d King of Great Britain, France, and Ireland, that the Name of England might be extinct [quoting W. Camden, Annals of James I], though the union of England and Scotland under English Common Law did not occur until the reign of Queen Anne. According to Holinshed [see ], and obviously in Shakespeare, Lear is King of all Britain [citing this l., 2373, and 2703].…Perhaps [the play] was composed as direct propaganda to develop a public sentiment in favor of the Union, perhaps only as a courtly compliment to Shakespeare’s patron. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 159): Lear lived in pre-Anglo-Saxon times and was [also] King of Britain—i.e., British is used here to avoid an anachronism, not to compliment James. Budd (ed. 1935): The line in Child Rowland and Burd Ellen reads Christian; the change of this to British would be imperative, if Shakespeare had this ballad in mind. But he may not have; see n. 1966–8. Wittreich (1984, p. 20): Shakespeare emended his sources so that, instead of France defeating England, France is vanquished by Britain. But in all the sources the words England and English appear only thrice; Leir’s country is almost universally (and correctly) Britain and his people British.

1969 <Scena Quinta>]
Coleridge (MS notes, 1818–19, ed. Foakes, 1989, pp. 101–2): The scene <i.e. III.4> ends with the first symptoms of positive derangement—here [sc. 5] how judiciously interrupted in order to allow an interval for Lear in full madness to appear. Goggin (ed. 1910): The scene is adroitly interposed to lower the tragic tone; it prevents the growth of Lear’s madness from becoming too oppressive to the audience and too rapid. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The same stormy night as in iii, 2–3. Edmund is sent by Cornwall to seek Gloucester in order that he may be arrested. Reynolds (1962, p. 94), who assumes, questionably, that Sh.’s stage had a central door (gate) behind movable curtains hung on a removable frame: It has occurred to me that to keep the gate [cf. n. 1951] shut not only during the scenes when Lear and the Fool are stumbling in the dark, the wind and the rain, but also through the intervening scenes (Act III, v, and perhaps vii) would make the gate into…a recurring symbol. Where then should these intervening scenes be played? Adams, who as a matter of course, places the scenes at Gloucester’s castle in the Chamber (that is Hosley’s gallery), does so [see n. 333] with these three scenes, including scene vii, which J. W. Saunders’ helpful diagram I of the Globe, together with the argument of Richard Hosley’s Shakespeare’s Use of a Gallery over the Stage, shows to be quite impossible. I hesitate to put scenes iii and v there when nothing is going on below; but both are very short and can be played close to the railing; therefore to keep the doors closed I will. Scene vi must be on the main stage because of the number of people involved and the implied action. In any case there is no reason to leave the gate shut, for Lear is already on his way to Dover.

1971 reuenge]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Edmund has informed Cornwall of Gloucester’s intention to relieve Lear and to join the invading party in the King’s interest ([1760 ff.]).

1971 depart]
Regan and Cornwall went to Gloucester’s house to avoid Lear; now that he has left the house and is on his way to Dover, they may return home, where they would wish to be in any case to marshall resistance to the reported invasion.

1971 the]
F’s his makes explicit what is understood. Verity (ed. 1897): The fact that it is Gloucester’s house and that he will be having his revenge on his host does not trouble, or even occur to, Cornwall. Cf. Gloucester’s own protests, [2093, 2105]. Doubtless Cornwall considers treason (as he sees Gloucester’s actions) to be more important than etiquette.

1972 How…censured]
Craig (ed. 1901): What opinion people will hold me in. How probably means in what manner rather than how much. Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): Censure, to pass judgment or opinion on (OED, v. 1). Wright (ed. 1875): Did not necessarily imply blame or adverse judgment. Tovey (ed. 1896): Though Edmund apprehends blame.

1972 nature]
See n. 441.

1973 loyaltie]
Wilson (ed. 1960): To the crown, viz. you.

1973 some thing]
One word, as in F. Delius (ed. 1854): Somewhat (OED, adv. 1a).

1973 feares]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): To frighten (OED, v. 1). The subject is the noun clause How…censured.

1976 disposition]
See n. 329.

1976 made]
On the omission of the relative see n. 589.

1976 him seeke his]
I.e., Edgar seek Gloucester’s. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Such was the false information that Cornwall and Regan had received on arriving at Gloucester’s castle ([1025 ff.]). But many interpret it to mean Gloucester’s seeking Edgar’s arrest and dispatch (995) at the stake (999); see next n. The general sense of the speech is that Gloucester’s treachery shows that he as well as his son Edgar is culpable; but the phrasing and vague pronouns make the exact meaning obscure.

1977–8 prouoking…himselfe]
The meaning differs depending on whether the merit is attributed to (1) Edmund, (2) Edgar, or (3) Gloucester. The last is now the most usual interpretation.
(1) Edmund. Malone (ed. 1790): The merit of Edmund,…being noticed by Gloster, provoked or instigated Edgar to seek his father’s death—an attempt set a-work, presumably, by the reproueable badnes of Edgar’s jealousy. So Rann (ed. 1794): A sense of your merit, which naturally exasperated him that had none. Deighton (ed. 1891): A worthiness on your [Edmund’s] part, made more active by your horror of his [Edgar’s] badness,…urged him on [to seek Gloucester’s life].…Edmund’s merit is regarded as stimulated into fuller activity by the evidence of Edgar’s evil disposition, and this evil disposition as, in its turn, goaded on to desperate crime by the conspicuous proof of his illegitimate brother’s superiority of character. Such readings do not easily suggest themselves to an audience, since there is no scene in which Gloucester favors Edmund in Edgar’s presence, nor in which Edgar shows jealousy of such favor, or recognition or resentment of his brother’s supposed moral superiority.
(2) Edgar. Warburton (ed. 1747): A merit [in Edgar] which being neglected by the father, was provoked to an extravagant act. To the obvious objection that prouoking seems to mean the opposite of was provoked to, Hudson (ed. 1871) replies, A virtue apt to be provoked, or stirred into act; which virtue was set to work by some flagrant evil in Gloster himself.…Provoking for provocable; the active form with the passive sense. Mason (1785, p. 349): Provoking, here, means stimulating; a merit he felt in himself, which irritated him against a father that had none. Craig (ed. 1901): A merit, a virtue, in Edgar, provoking him, i.e. inciting him, in consideration of his father’s wickedness, to seek his life. A virtue which leads to parricide being a difficult concept, Mason gives merit the forced meaning of feeling of virtue, and in that he is followed by Delius (ed. 1854): Edgar…was incited by the knowledge of his own worth to practice against the life of his father, because of the detestable evil that he recognized in this father (Ger.). Again, such readings are not obvious to an audience, since in no scene does Edgar ever recognize such evil in Gloucester. Merit is similarly stretched to mean sense of justice (Hunter, ed. 1869), consciousness of his own worth (Wright, ed. 1875), an anticipative merit; that is, a meritorious forestalling of crime by its punishment (Moberly, ed. 1876), a feeling of his own worthiness and of Gloucester’s unworthiness (Verity, ed. 1897), meritorious incitement (Brooke, ed. 1947), evil justice incited by evil (a case of poison driving out poison) (Harbage, ed. 1958). Verity speaks for most in saying, I think that himself must refer, not to Edgar (as it should strictly), but to Gloucester, who is the he uppermost in Cornwall’s thoughts. An exception is Wilson (ed. 1960): Corn.’s main concern is not to find excuses for Edg., but to emphasize Glo.’s iniquity, which, he implies, is so black as to justify even patricide. Thus reprovable badness (= blameworthy depravity) is too mild a term for such iniquity and must refer to patricide, or rather to the wicked ambitions and designs which prompted (set awork) the idea of patricide. We paraphrase: I can see now that Edg. was provoked to seek Glo.’s death not merely by his own evil character but by a good impulse [merit] prompted by viciousness, in itself (>in himself) blameworthy.
Edgar’s virtue has also been seen as provoking (= irritating) to Gloucester. Boodle (1884, p. 217): It was not your brother’s evil disposition, but his good which provoked him (i.e., Gloucester) to seek his death (i.e., Edgar’s), and the goodness of Edgar was noticed owing to Gloucester’s badness. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): It was not Edgar’s badness that made his father want to kill him…but Edgar’s irritating goodness moving his father to do it because Gloucester was himself bad and deserved killing himself.
(3) Gloucester. The merit can be Gloucester’s if the term is understood in the neutral sense of desert (good or bad). OED (sb. 1): That which is deserved or has been earned, whether good or evil; due reward or punishment, quoting R2 1.3.156 (1153). Cf. 2987. Nichols (1862, No. 2, pp. 12–13): The provoking merit was in Gloucester himself.…a deserving on his part, set a-work…himselfe [i.e., Gloucester], that provoked your brother to the act. So Hudson (ed. 1879). Clarkes (ed. 1868): This probably refers to what the speaker considers the discovered turpitude of Gloster, which deserves punishment, and incites Edgar to seek his death, putting into activity the latter’s blamable badness of character. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Your father deserved to die. That fact, however, needed your brother’s evil nature to make it operate as a cause for his murderous plot.…Cornwall regards Gloucester as a traitor, and therefore as a complete villain. His character, he suggests, might tempt anyone to kill him. Gardner (ed. 1969) takes the sentence to refer to Gloucester’s seeking Edgar’s death by proclamation, and prouoking merit to refer to Gloucester’s touchiness or innate disposition to be easily roused; but the leap from merit = worth to merit = touchiness is a long one.

1977 a worke]
See nn. 1147, 1839.

1979–80 repent to bee]
On the infinitive used gerundially see n. 1926–7.

1980 iust]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Righteous, upright. Loyalty, Edmund implies, has forced him to reveal his father’s treason.

1980 letter]
Delius (ed. 1854): Cf. 1761. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Edmund has stolen the letter. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 179): F’s Letter which sounds hideous: probably the F compositor has anticipated the later which. Greg (1940, p. 437): The letter incidentally reveal[s] the urgency of the political situation.

1981 approues]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Proves (OED, v. 4). The Sokols (2000, p. 15): May carry connotations of accuse.

1981 intelligent]
See n. 1634.

1981 partie]
Delius (ed. 1854): Partisan (OED, sb. 12: A participator; an accessory).

1981 to]
Wright (ed. 1875), Furness (ed. 1880), and a few others make to depend on intelligent, citing Abbott §419a (cf. nn. 1707, 2181). But one would expect the idiom to be intelligent of something as at 1634, and intelligent to someone, as in WT 1.2.378 (484). Schmidt (ed. 1879) therefore prefers the usual idiom party to. It is also possible to make to a preposition governing aduantages: for the assistance (Muir, ed. 1952), on behalf of (Fraser, ed. 1963), in the interests (Brown, ed. 1976).

1981–2 aduantages]
This could mean the particular military advantages of landing an army at Dover: see OED (sb. 5): A favouring circumstance; anything which gives one the superiority or tends to improve one’s position. So Budd (ed. 1935): The advantages gained by the King of France in landing his forces in England. Most eds. take the word in the more general senses of The position, state, or circumstance of being in advance or ahead of another (OED, 1) or Benefit.…To one’s advantage (OED, 6; see prev. n.). Such interpretations usually assume plural for singular (Page, ed. 1889); but Delius (ed. 1854): Favorable opportunities (OED, 4), and Edwards (ed. 1975): Underhand gaining of superior positions.

1982 not]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 399): Q’s omission…makes nonsense. Weis (ed. 1993): Rather, a difficult sense: If only his treason…were the detector of his disloyalty. Wells (ed. 2000): This seems strained, especially as Q often omits words.

1985 matter]
See n. 398.

1986 mighty busines]
Delius (ed. 1854): Preparations for war against France.

1987 True or false]
McCann (ed. 1964): The letter itself is evidence enough; the exact facts do not matter. Evidence of Gloucester’s treason, presumably, as Edmund’s report of it is evidence of his loyalty. Edwards (ed. 1975): Even if the information of the French invasion is false, Gloucester is guilty of intriguing with a foreign power.

1987–8 made…Gloster]
Smith (ed. 1902): Edmund’s plans have succeeded, comparing 1773–4. Cf. 354–5. Rosenberg (1972, p. 230): The delighted Cornwall familiarly thees and thous the Bastard, offers himself paternally. Contra Rosenberg, Wells (ed. 2000) doubts an actual knighting here: This would slow the action, and the award is likely to be anticipative.

1989 readie]
OED (adj. 9): Immediately available.

1989 apprehension]
Delius (ed. 1854): Arrest. Cf. 412, 1049.

1990 comforting]
Johnson (ed. 1765): In the juridical sense for supporting, helping (OED, Comfort v. 2: Abet.…Formerly common in legal use). Campbell (1859, p. 101): The indictment against an accessory after the fact, for treason, charges that the accessory comforted the principal traitor after knowledge of the treason. Heard (1883, p. 95): But there are no accessories in treason, because of the extreme gravity of the crime.…All are principals, including those comforting and receiving a traitor. Since Lear is not treasonous, Gloucester can not technically be said to comfort a traitor; he does, of course, act contrary to Cornwall’s wishes; cf. 1756–7. Mason (1785, p. 349), contra Johnson: Means merely giving comfort or assistance, comparing 1999; OED (8): Allay physical discomfort. Wright (ed. 1875): The word retains its old meaning of strengthening and supporting, being derived from the Med. Latin confortare.

1990 stuffe]
Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Fill out and make more solid (OED, v.1 5). But the meaning may be the original military one of providing with supplies, reinforcements, etc. (OED, 1, 2). Page (ed. 1889): Furnish more matter (OED, 3). Weis (ed. 1993): Fill, feed.

1991 his suspition]
Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Suspicion of him; objective genitive.

1991 perseuere]
Wright (ed. 1875): Shakespeare has uniformly the accent on the second syllable.

1991 course]
See n. 201.

1993 bloud]
See n. 121. Wright (ed. 1875): Natural temperament, unattested. Rolfe (ed. 1880): Equivalent to nature. Deighton (ed. 1891): Natural feeling, unattested. Foakes (ed. 1997): Lineage.

1994 lay…thee]
Harbage (ed. 1958): Trust you (?) reward you with a place of trust (?).

1995 dearer]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 179): The Q reading is certainly superior. The F reading [deere] is probably a compositor’s slip.

1996 <Scena Sexta>]
Some eds. incorrectly locate this scene in the interior of the hovel (1715); but see nn. 1926, 1951. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The same stormy night as in Scenes i–v. Gloucester leaves Lear in the farmhouse ([1930 ff.]), returns to his own castle, and, learning of a plot of death against the King ([2048]), comes back to the farmhouse and arranges for Lear’s being taken to Dover. Perrett (1904): The scene is within Gloucester’s house; see n. 1935. Muir (ed. 1952): Perhaps Capell’s suggestion [see textual n.]…is better. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 177): The outhouse, all of his own castle that Gloucester dare offer. Greg (1940, p. 437 n.): Or some neighboring building—possibly Edmund’s lodging, since Gloucester has taken him into his confidence—possibly even the home of the tenant of [2193–4]—perhaps Theobald’s Farm-house. Idem (1940, pp. 300–1): The scene…demands some furniture.…But the joint-stool may be imaginary [see n. 2014+26]…and bench [2014+5, +18] and couch [2014+15, 2040] may be one. All that is needed is a narrow bench over which the arras could be let fall [2041–2]. Adams (1948, p. 325): Farmhouse will do for want of evidence. Clearly a simple room is intended. Reynolds (1962, p. 93), imagining a curtained space before a central stage door (see n. 1969): We may suppose Gloucester leads Lear, Kent, Edgar and the Fool from behind the hovel across the stage Right, and then goes between the curtain and the wall to enter the curtained space. There picking up the stools they need and the cushions,…they go before the curtains to give the scene supposed in some obscure place, i.e. some less public part of the castle reached less conspicuously than through the main gate. Campbell (ed. 1964): If at the end of Act III, Scene 4, we see them from the outside of a farm building going in, and now in Act III, Scene 6, we see them next (with no suggestion of lapse of time) from the inside of a farm building coming in, the building they are entering is the same one. Ringler (1981, p. 186): Scenes v, vi, and vii are all in the same place…within Gloucester’s house.…Lear’s mad arraignment of his daughters in an imagined legal trial in scene vi is held in the same place as the blinding of Gloucester without the form of justice in scene vii, and so gives emphasis to the questioning of legality and justice in Lear’s tortured world. Foakes (ed. 1997): Whether in or near Gloucester’s house, This explains why Gloucester can augment (piece out) comforts for Lear by making use of the resources of his own house, and convey him through the gates on his way to Dover at [2074–6]; it also explains why Edmund has no difficulty in finding his father comforting the King.
Hunter (ed. 1972): The antiphonally placed voices of the three madmen—lunatic King, court fool, feigned Bedlam—weave the obsessive themes of betrayal, demoniac possesson, and injustice into the most complex lyric structure in modern drama. Weis (ed. 1993, p. 23): This F scene, which is stripped of the trial and also of Edgar’s fourteen-line soliloquy, becomes primarily a transitional stretch in the play; and the scene’s centre-piece is Edgar’s invective against dogs. Brown (ed. 1996): This whole scene…is full of riddles, ironies, cross talk, fantasy, sudden piercing perceptions and equally perplexing attempts to hide true thoughts and feelings.…Actors will discover…that the crazy madness is founded on deep feelings and the words seem necessary to the experience of each individual.…Perhaps Shakespeare never trusted his actors so much as in this scene; clear speaking of the lines would here serve only to confuse and bore an audience.

1997 Enter…Tom]
In Q and F Gloucester leads the party in; F’s division into two entrances (see textual nn.) makes it clearer that Gloucester is talking to Kent, who answers him in both texts. Brooke (ed. 1947): Edgar has been holding back to avoid recognition by his father. Lear has kept with Edgar, and the Fool with Lear. Taylor (1983, p. 100): The Folio brings on Kent and Gloucester alone, beginning the scene with a moment of sanity and calm—and giving the trio of Lear, Poor Tom, and the Fool a separate, emblematic group entrance. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 108): The non-uniformity of Tom suggests that Q copy was not a prompt-book; in F, the name is Edgar in all entrances. Q names Tom here; at 2178, where Edgar is dressed as Tom but speaks as himself, he enters as Edgar; at 2430, at the beginning of a scene in which he plays Tom, a peasant, and at times himself, he enters as Edgar, erroneously printed Edmund; the SPs throughout Q are Edg. Werstine (privately): Theatrical books of Sh.’s time lack the uniformity in naming that Duthie presumes in them.

1998 better]
Tovey (ed. 1896): I.e., something better.

1998–9 take it thankfully]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Make the best of the change.

1999 peece out]
See n. 217.

1999 what]
OED (adj. 29): So much…as, quoting this l.

2000 Exit]
F’s SD marks the beginning of Gloucester’s exit, though he probably remains on stage long enough to hear Kent’s apologetic thanks. It is less certain that he remains long enough to hear Edgar’s speech (2004–5), which Capell (1783, 1.2:170) thinks is directed to his father as a memento of Gloucester’s cruelty. Campbell (1888, pp. 496–7): Kent accompanies Gloster to the outer door, and through his temporary absence the stage is left wholly to the three madmen.…The gentle words of Kent, How…amazed [2014+14] sufficiently indicate his surprise and concern at the state of matters which he finds on his return. Campbell’s conjecture is attractive: it would explain why Kent has no speech for twenty-three lines in Q, why Lear appoints only two judges initially [2014+5–+6], and why Kent is not appointed the third judge (apparently) until later [2014+18].

2001–2 All…kindnes]
Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Lear has not taken in Gloucester’s meaning, has not thanked him or come forward to answer him. Kent therefore speaks for him and says, Thank you.

2001 power…haue]
Jennens (ed. 1770), power: A noun of multitude (all the power of his wits signifying…all his wits) and consequently may be joined with a plural verb. Wright (ed. 1875): The verb [is] attracted to the number of the nearest substantive. Cf. Furness (ed. 1880), Franz §675, and n. 1176.

2001 wits]
See n. 682.

2001 giuen way to]
Craig (ed. 1901): Broken down…under.

2002 impatience]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Inability to endure his sufferings. Cf. 1571, 1689, 1798, 2016. Gardner (ed. 1969): A sick disposition, a testy irritability, that has broken his intellect. Lear is fully mad, and Kent sympathetically accounts for it. Edwards (ed. 1975): Were Lear able to tolerate his daughters’ behaviour, he would not be mad.

2002 deserue]
F’s reward replaces a less familiar meaning with an easier word. As Jackson (1963, p. 101) points out, comparing Oth. 1.1.183 (201), deserve could mean reward (OED, v. 6), the meaning obviously demanded by the context. So Weis (ed. 1993): Requite. Dent (1981, G211.1) suspects a proverb, God reward you for your kindness. Main (ed. 1962): This wish becomes a bitter irony, for Gloucester is horribly punished in the very next scene for this very kindness. On the emendation to discern (see textual n.), Halio (ed. 1994): Q’s deserue is a misprint for deserne; n/u inversions appear elsewhere in Q, comparing 1089 and deseruing at 2306.

2004 Fretereto]
F’s Fraterretto is closer to Harsnett’s Frateretto (1603, pp. 49, 119, 141, 181, 185; see , ). Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 518): Little brother seems more pertinent to Edgar and the play than little corrosive (OED fretter, sb.1), a derivation no one has proposed. Moberly (ed. 1876): With Hopdance [Hoberdidance] and Flibertigibbet are, according to Harsnet [p. 49; see ], devils presiding over the morrice-dance. Trotman (1919, p. 312): From Frater, a type of beggar like Abraham Man (OED, sb.2 2). Levin (1959, p. 92): A likely name for a diabolical brother. Musgrove (1981, p. 6): The thieves’ cant word frater means a brother in the fraternity of itinerant swindlers. Brownlow (1993, p. 172): Probably not little brother, an unlikely invention for Sara, but little flatterer, the substitution of r for l being easy.

2004 Nero]
Grey (1754, 2:112) points out the anachronism: the supposed time of Lear’s reign predated that of Nero’s; see n. 39.

2004–5 angler…darknes]
The lake of darkness is generally assumed to be in hell (Upton, 1746, p. 225) if not indeed Avernus (Armour, ed. 1930).
