Milward (1987, p. 182): In Rev. x.x.20 and xx.10 hell is described as a lake of fire, burning with brimstone; and in Matt. xxv.30 it is mentioned by Christ as a place of utter darkness. Muir (ed. 1952): Harsnett (1603) mentions the stygian lake (p. 45) and the bottomlesse pit (pp. 61, 116) as well as a Caesars humor (p. 47; see ), and Higgins (Mirour, rev. 1587, fol. 38r; not in 1574) has Cordila mention the darkesome Stygian lake. Sh. need not have used the 1587 ed. of Mirour: cf. his own (biblical) discend to Darknesse, and the burning Lake (2H6 1.4.39 [666]). Rabelais (Gargantua and Pantagruel, 2.30) describes Nero playing music (on a vielle—harsh fiddle or hurdy-gurdy) in hell, as well as Trajan angling for frogs. Upton, Ritson (in Steevens, ed. 1793), and Anders (1904, p. 57) detect an allusion to those descriptions even though no English translation of Rabelais yet existed (despite a S.R. entry for one on 4 Dec. 1594). Prescott (1993, p. 249), finding that the image suits the play’s terrible carnival of inversion, suspect[s] knowledge, direct or not, of Pantagruel, but proves none. Budd (1935, pp. 422 ff.): Chaucer’s The Monkes Tale *3665–76 (2475–86) is a more likely source: Suetonius’s detail of Nero’s costly fishing tackle (Nero 30.3: piscatus est rete aurato) is repeated by Chaucer (Nettes of gold threed), translated by Holland (1606, p. 193: Hee fished with a golden net), and referred to in Lydgate (Fall of Princes, ed. Bergen, 1923, 3:793: With nettis of gold fisshed), Higgins (Mirour, ed. Haslewood, 1815, 1:297: With golden nets…I woulde fishe), Grafton’s Chronicle (1569; ed. H. Ellis, 1809, 1:61: fishe with Nettes made of Golde), and Pedro Mexia (Historie, tr. Traheron, 1604, p. 96: nets…made of gold threed). Idem (ed. 1935): Edgar, pretending to have received his information from a fiend, might well have added in the lake of darkness. In Harsnett (1603, p. 49 [see ]) Frateretto is…immediately associated with the Fidler. To Shakespeare the Fidler suggests Nero.…The fact that the fiend Frateretto was Edgar’s informer would obviously necessitate the locating of Nero in hell, whereupon the Lake of Darknesse would immediately suggest itself…for his angling. Berryman (1946, p. 151): Nero had stood as a type of parent-murderer in King John and Hamlet, and it is Edgar, so accused, who is to speak. Edwards (ed. 1975): Nero is taken as the extreme example of those who commit crimes against their own family, for he murdered his mother. Such sinners will spend eternity in hell. Sitwell (1946, p. 55; 1948, p. 48) finds a reference to Pausanias’s Description of Greece 2.37, where Nero tries to sound the depth of the Alcyonian Lake, through which Dionysius went to Hell to fetch up Semele. Muir (op. cit.): It is unlikely that Shakespeare read Pausanias in the original, but it is possible that he read of Nero’s experiment elsewhere. Edgar’s gnomic statement may be merely a warning: even a world-emperor, if he is evil as Nero was, ends up in hell, therefore all men should beware the foule fiend. Frateretto’s motive would be different; perhaps in calling Edgar, presumably to hell, he offers the inducement that even emperors and princes inhabit there; cf. 1921. Musgrove (1981, pp. 6–7) detects a play on the thieves’ cant term angler meaning a thief using a hooked staff, concluding, The play consistently makes the point that evil in high and low places is of the same nature: ancient emperor and contemporary professional thief are therefore properly conjoined. Some commentators find deeper meanings. Sitwell (loc. cit.): The lake of darknesse—the bottomless depths of human nature, in which the mad Lear, the blinded Gloucester (in that world in which child turns against parent, Nature against Man) and the ghost of Nero the matricide, find blackness after blackness, depth beneath depth. Wittreich (1984, p. 102): Nero…is a type of Lear. MacIntyre (1962), comparing the bawdy Groping for Trowts in MM 1.2.90 (180), finds a reference to Nero’s relationship with his mother, Agrippina consistent with Lear’s preoccupation with the unnatural child and excursions into obscenity. Similarly Elton (1966, p. 176 n.) finds an allusion to the Neronic tradition of the depraved emperor’s curiosity concerning his birthplace that suggests the lust-ridden Edgar’s demonic underworld, comparing 2568–70 and 3133; cf. n. 762. Adelman (1992, p. 299): The female sexual place.

Steevens (ed. 1793): Perhaps he is here addressing the Fool. Fools were anciently called Innocents (OED, sb. 3b: A simpleton). Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Or innocent victim (perhaps both). Brown (ed. 1976): May be heartfelt, spoken for himself or, with some irony, in pity for his father. Capell (1783, 1.2:170) understands an adjective, not a vocative: Be innocent when you pray.

See n. 664.

2007 Nunckle]

2007–12 tell…him]
Delius (1876, p. 136): F’s 2010–12 were accidentally omitted from Q, since their absence makes an evident gap. Koppel (1877, p. 75): These lines and 54–5 are the only certain omissions from Q. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxiv) suspects censorship of the lines: An allusion…may have been well understood in relation to some Knights of James’ dubbing [in 1603–4]. If so, it is unlikely they would have remained in the playbook behind F. Since they interrupt a speech in Q, F’s lines 2010–12 seem more likely to have been a later addition than an accidental omission from Q due to eyeskip. Doran (1931, p. 67), however: In the quarto, Lear’s two speeches appear as one, with no break between them. Therefore, if the intervening speech of the Fool’s was omitted, it scarcely can have been accidentally. It may be that Lear’s exclamation, A King, a King, is to be considered a sufficient answer to the Fool’s question. The Fool’s own reply has no immediate bearing on Lear’s situation.…Still, the answer seems one anticipated in the question, not an afterthought. We can only suppose that the printer of Q1 had some difficulty with the passage and consciously left it out. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The fool expects no answer to his conundrum and of course rejects Lear’s passionate solution and furnishes the correct answer, which involves a wittily illogical inference from a bit of more or less proverbial worldly wisdom. Since the Fool would be unlikely to call Lear a madman, gentleman, or yeoman, presumably his initial question is occasioned by the raving of Poor Tom, though his remarks clearly apply indirectly to Lear. Traversi (1952–3, p. 137): As always the reproaches of the Fool are couched in terms of a cautious self-interest. Bratton (ed. 1987): In the 1982 BBC2 [television] production the Fool recognised Tom as Edgar, and delivered this line meaningfully at him, to show him he was discovered. The F lines may have been added to allow the clown to complete a routine cut short so abruptly by Lear’s answer. Stone (1980, p. 67): The F addition is the intrusion of fresh matter. Warren (1983, p. 49): With this addition and 2043 the intent in F is to give him a more effective final appearance. Kerrigan (1983, pp. 226–7): In both texts the Fool fights back, trying [with his question] to oust Edgar from the King’s favour.…In F it is rather the first half of a laboured and hard-headed jest, the contrast of whose worldly common sense with the madness of Lear’s next speech gives a sickening jolt. Weis (ed. 1993) prefers the absence of a reply in Q: The Fool’s easy banter with the King, when he would feed him trick questions, elicit a response and then provide the correct answer himself (cf. [660] ff.), is now no longer possible, because it was predicated on a form of rational discourse.
Collier (ed. 1843): Possibly proverbial. So also Boodle (1884, p. 217), comparing WT 5.2.139 (3147–8), I was a Gentleman borne before my Father: Can we find the origin of the proverbial expression in an allusion to the celebrated feudal right of lords with regard to the marriage of their yeoman tenantry? Though no proverb has been found, the subject was of topical interest. Harrison (ed. 1937): Many farmers who had become wealthy by war profits and enclosures sent their sons to London to learn to become gentlemen and to buy a coat from the heralds, citing Jonson, Every Man Out (1599) 2.3.10–11, I sir, he is a gentleman, though his father be but a yeoman. Tilley’s proverb G66 expresses scorn for a dunghill Gentleman, or a Gentleman of the first head. Davenport (1953, p. 21) compares Joseph Hall’s satire on the doting Lolio, a yeoman with an ungrateful child, in Virgidemiarum (1598, 4.2): Old driueling Lolio drudges all he can, | To make his eldest sonne a Gentleman. Wilson (ed. 1960): In that age of a rigid hierarchy of rank, it w[oul]d be exceedingly awkward, even disagreeable, for a son to become a gentleman first.…The Fool is as usual glancing at Lear who should be superior in rank and power to his daughters, but has become inferior to them as a result of his own mad folly. Bevington (ed. 1992): The Fool’s bitter jest…is that such a man might go mad to see his son advanced over him.
Eds. have also found a private allusion to Sh.’s own life. Hudson (ed. 1871): A rather curious commentary on some of the Poet’s own doings; who obtained from the Herald’s College [on 20 Oct. 1596] a coat-of-arms in his father’s name; thus getting his yeoman father dubbed a gentleman, in order, no doubt, that himself might inherit the rank. Smith (ed. 1917): His father, however, does not fall into the Fool’s category of mad yeoman; for the application was in John Shakespeare’s name, and consequently William was not made a gentleman before him. The details of the grant, and of a challenge to it and others in 1602 by the York Herald, are provided by Evans (ed. 1974, pp. 1829–31), who says, Apparently the original claim of John Shakespeare…was upheld…, since William Shakespeare…continued to sign himself as gentleman to the time of his death. MacCracken (ed. 1914) suspects this passage to be an indulgent reminder of this ludicrous episode. Doran (op. cit.) is skeptical: The event took place, however, a good while before King Lear was composed—almost a decade. Moreover, since John Shakespeare’s situation is the opposite of Lear’s and reference to it by Sh. would seem to have no point in the play except private self-congratulation, one may doubt that Sh. intended any autobiographical allusion. Tovey (ed. 1896) is willing to accept one if Shakespeare wrote this…passage [which] appears in no edition till 1623, after his death; Kerrigan (op. cit.) accepts it as confirmation that the F revision was by Sh.; but buying coats of arms was a common scandal.

2007 mad man]
Petz (tr. 1839) suggests a pun on a made man, a man assured of success in life (OED, ppl. a. 7). Similarly Joseph (ed. 1966) and Halio (ed. 1992); and see n. 2011. Kökeritz (1953, pp. 126–7) does not list this among his two exx. of a mad/made pun in Sh., both of which Cercignani (1981, pp. 236–7) thinks unreliable.

2008 Yeoman]
Hunter (ed. 1869): The Franklin or Yeoman of Elizabeth’s time was a freeholder, but not a gentleman [OED, 4]. In earlier times the yeoman was a person of higher dignity [OED, 1–3]. Edwards (ed. 1975): A gentleman had enough land to live off the income; a yeoman owned land but had to work for his living. Wells (ed. 2000): The yeoman was…not…arms-bearing. Foakes (ed. 1997): The gentleman may be Lear, and the yeoman, or freeholder of lower rank, Edgar, both qualifying as a madman.

Stone (1980, p. 67): It was evidently thought necessary that [in F] the Fool should supply the answer to his riddle…in the middle of Lear’s bitter outburst, thereby depriving its latter part not only of sense but also of grammatical structure. Honigmann (1982, p. 146): Lear’s mental state…sufficiently explains this discontinuity. Richman (1986, p. 382 n.): The Fool’s speech about madness is rewritten for the Folio. We used the grotesque, disjunctive reply in Q, rather than the topical joke in F. Most editors give both speeches, creating a redundancy. Warren (1983, p. 49): This is the last time we see the Fool.…Shakespeare wanted to give him [here and in 2043] a more effective final appearance. Foakes (ed. 1997): F’s addition compensates in some measure for the absence of his four speeches in [2014+1–+30].

Verity (ed. 1897): As, for; from the notion equivalent to. Cf. Abbott §189, OED (To prep. 11b).

Schmidt (ed. 1879) finds a pun here: A made yeoman, a yeoman whose luck is made, or,…a complete, thorough yeoman; but see n. 2007. Skillan (ed. 1967): Possibly distracted by the indignity of his son’s prior advancement. Mad may mean simply foolish or angry (OED, a. 2, 5), not necessarily insane (OED, 1).

2013–14 to…them]
Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Lear is always thinking of different forms of vengeance on his daughters. Deighton (ed. 1891): An anticipation of his daughters’ punishment in hell. Verity (ed. 1897): The Fool’s picture [in 2010–12] of a son taking precedence of his father (cf. before him) suggests to Lear his own case…and instantly the thought of revenge on his daughters (’em [from him]) flashes into words. But in Q, which lacks the Fool’s picture, as well as in F, Lear’s thought may be suggested by the images in 2004–6 of foul fiends, sinners, and the lake of darkness, as Goggin (ed. 1910), Wilson (ed. 1960), and others suspect.

Muir (1951, p. 19): Harsnett [1603, pp. 93–4; see ] mentions So many fiery needles…swords, darts, and speares of fire, pointed with grisly death…the Furies…fire in theyr hands…and a huge bunch of a thousand snakes. Lear’s thousand and hizzing seem to have been suggested by the thousand snakes, and the red burning spits were derived from the fiery needles, the speares of fire and the fire in the hands of the Furies. Edwards (ed. 1975), thousand: Devils?

OED (Hizz v.): To make a hissing or whizzing noise, quoting this l. Kittredge (ed. 1940): It suggests the whizzing sound of the redhot weapons as they are brandished by the thousand assailants.

2014+1–+30 The…scape]
The omission from F of these Q lines, containing the famous mock trial by Lear of his imagined daughters, is the most remarkable of the F cuts (and no one thinks it can be anything but a cut). Warren (1983), who has discussed the passage most extensively, thus describes this ensemble of madness (pp. 45–6): Shakespeare externalizes the chief preoccupation of Lear’s mad mind, the cruelty of his daughters and the injustice of those who wield power; it is appropriate to his vision of a world where accepted values are reversed that an apparent bedlam beggar should become a learned Iustice,…and that another man whose profession is folly should be his yokefellow of equity.…[But the trial] is sabotaged by the judges, who lapse from their judicial roles to the other roles which they habitually play—Edgar to the bedlam beggar obsessed by devils, the Fool to his songs and jibes which bring everything down to earth. It could be argued that this very state of confusion is in itself an appropriate image of Lear’s view of injustice, a tour de force of technical dexterity which combines various elements from the preceding scenes—Lear’s madness, the Fool’s professional folly, Edgar’s mock-possession—in an elaborate climax. Many commentators find the episode highly meaningful. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 178): Where Lear once sat in his majesty, there sit the Fool and the outcast Kent…while he, witless, musters his failing strength to beg justice upon a joint stool. Was there more justice done, asks the picture, when Lear himself sat there in majesty and sanity? Bransom (1934, pp. 110, 114): I regard [the episode] as necessary to the exposition of the king’s madness…and therefore as by no means to be cut. Muir (ed. 1952): The symbolic significance of the trial…is perfectly clear. He hath put down the mighty from their seat, and hath exalted the humble and meek. Quinn (ed. 1970): The majesty and ceremony of the opening scene are…parodied. Peacock (1946, p. 155): Lear, scarcely rescued from the fury of nature, his ideas scattered by suffering, conducts a trial of his daughters. It is an illumination that produces from the sub-conscious the effects of order. At the moment of greatest breakdown we are given a judgment that represents amidst chaos the memory of civilization. Moral assumptions are at the center of tragedy. Accordingly Kahn (1957, p. 324): There is something incredibly pathetic and sublime together…in this last desperate effort of a mind on the verge of complete disintegration to wrest meaning and truth from its predicament. Thus, the very idea of a trial…indicates a desire on Lear’s part to formulate his experiences according to some idea of justice. Oppel (1968): Henry Fuseli’s picture Fantasy on King Lear underlines the centrality of the mock-trial to the play’s principal problem of justice. Eure (1975, pp. 431–2): This combination of formal procedural correctness and insane babbling creates an extraordinary image of the impotence of human justice.…[But] the trial ends the long, wild sequence on the heath, and after it Lear, for the first time, is able to sleep.…For Lear the familiar forms of justice have allayed, at least temporarily, the demons that torture his soul.…In the midst of chaos, the use of legal process expresses the human need to attempt to deal with disorder. Axton (1977, p. 141): The trial scene…marks the turning away from an attempt to understand heavenly justice. When Lear asks, Is…hearts? he asks essentially the same question as, What is the cause of thunder? but he has now turned his eyes from the heavens to humanity. Moseley (1988, p. 65–6), seeing Lr. as structured around a series of trial scenes, declares this one essential to the thematic structure of the play and to Lear’s development. Leggatt (1992, p. 190): The mad trial itself has popular roots in the tradition of mock proclamations, mock trials, such as the trial of Carnival (or, in England), The whole trial and indictment of Sir John Barleycorn, quoting Peter Burke, Popular Culture in Early Modern Europe (1978, p. 122).
Though Pope (ed. 1725) considers the lines merely several speeches in the mad way, which probably were left out by the players, or by Shakespear himself, and restores some of them to leave ’em to the reader’s mercy, virtually all eds. since Theobald have restored them, arguing that Sh. could not have approved of the deleting of such remarkable if not essential matter. Capell (1783, 1.2:170): The critick…noting what [the scene] is reduc’d to, and the nothingness of the action in that state, he may not commend the reducers.…Among their other dismissions, are both the songs; put there for a very good purpose by Edgar, namely—to divert (were it possible) the stream of Lear’s thoughts at that time. Knight (ed. 1840) speculates that the physical exertions of the actor playing Lear (even Burbage) throughout Act 3 needed some relief at this point, or that his arraignment seemed too methodical for a man now fully mad. Delius (1876, p. 142): This un-authorial cut removes that essential part of Lear’s outbreak of madness, which alone justifies Kent’s following speech [2016–17].…If the audience saw nothing, or but little, of this outbreak, they would find it hard to comprehend the meaning of Kent’s words. Verity (ed. 1897, pp. xii, 183–4): The omission of the mock-trial in III.6 clearly bespeaks, to my mind, the hand of the actor, not author: the incident…almost defies representation.…I suppose that it was omitted in the acting-version of the play, the mock-trial being one of those daring pieces of imaginativeness which on the stage become perilously akin to the grotesque, or even comic.…The part of Lear here requires supreme capacity in the actor if the tragic effect is to be maintained. Herford (ed. 1899): It is hard to believe that Shakespeare could have cut out the trial of Goneril. Granville-Barker (op. cit., p. 227): One can only suppose that in acting it had proved ineffective. One cannot imagine Shakespeare regretting he had written it. Idem (rev. 1946, pp. 293 n., 331): This episode proves so admirable on the stage that it is hard to suppose Shakespeare’s actor failed to make it effective. But if it was a question of time and a choice between two scenes, doubtless his audience would be supposed to prefer the rhetoric of the storm.…It can hardly have proved ineffective, technically daring though it is. It certainly does not today. Chambers (1930, 1:467): A censor may have operated on [these and other lines]. But in the main we probably have to do with ordinary theatrical cutting. Doran (1931, p. 72): Proof that it is an omission lies in Kent’s remonstrance [2016–17].…In the folio, Lear has made only two remarks since he entered…which do not appear to justify Kent’s reproaching him with lack of patience. The imaginary trial, unlike…other omissions…is dramatic, and it is not easy to see how it would be sacrificed. Still, it is a good deal less weighty in philosophic import than Lear’s other mad scenes and could better be omitted than any portions of them. Hart (1942, p. 147): Crude clowning, omitted by an adapter; though madness was popular then as a dramatic theme and spectacle,…[this] was a trial with a phantom in the dock,…the audience knew that Edgar was shamming, and the fool was no clown. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 8): The absence…from F renders pointless the words Then…Regan which it retains at [2033]. Parrott (1949, p. 298): It is not unlikely that this scene overtaxed the restraint of an early audience and that the groundlings broke into guffaws at the catches of the Fool and the babble of the Bedlam. Muir (loc. cit., p. xlviii): Some members of every audience are inclined to laugh, and might have done so, since the Elizabethans were prepared to find madness entertaining. Stone (1980, p. 235): Undoubtedly a theatrical cut, the first of several in this part of the play, designed, it would seem, to hasten its pace towards the climax. Weis (ed. 1993, p. 23): A free-floating Then strongly points in the direction of a botched surgery. The Sokols (1999, pp. 436–9) argue that the lines were cut because of their possible application to the topical question (in 1610) of equity jurisdiction. The Court of Equity may not be alluded to: see n. 2014+18.
Justifying this extraordinary cut has required considerable effort from those who believe that F represents Sh.’s improvement on Q. Moriarty (1913, p. 459): The mock-trial, though dramatically effective, keeps the scene from running as directly to its needful end as it does in the folio. So also Urkowitz (1980, p. 17): Reasonable theatrical revision, designed to sustain the rapid sequence of actions in this part of the play rather than allowing the pace to slow down as in Q. Similarly Warren (op. cit., pp. 46 ff.) sees an attempt to streamline and speed up both scene and act by removing material at once unsuccessful and redundant. I think…that in rehearsal or performance it became clear that the focus of the scene had shifted from Lear’s mock-justice to eccentric individual detail—the Fool’s joint-stool joke, Edgar’s songs and devils—leading to a generalized sense of chaos,…[the audience] distracted (and perhaps bewildered) by the eccentricities, songs and jokes.…Although the Folio’s much shortened, speeded-up 3.6 omits the mad enactment of injustice, it rushes on instead to show us the thing itself [in the blinding of Gloucester].…[The cuts throughout the scene] bring closer together the crises of Lear’s and Gloucester’s ordeals, the cracking of Lear’s mind as he sees Poor Tom, and Gloucester’s realization of the truth about Edmund and Edgar.…This strengthens the dramatic structure of the play, and it also helps to prepare for the climactic meeting of the mad Lear and the blind Gloucester in 4.6.…[Indeed, the intent may be] to eliminate the less successful treatment of mock-justice in its dramatically weaker position in 3.6 in order to guarantee it maximum impact by concentrating it all in one place in 4.6…[and] making various additions to it there. Warren concedes that Perhaps Shakespeare originally intended the trial’s treatment of mock-justice to pave the way for that of the later scene, and that in one modern production, With this kind of preparation, 4.6 seemed the inevitable climax to which the earlier mad scenes had built; but Warren believes that such success with the Q scene is exceptional. The apparent redundancy of three mad scenes (3.4, 3.6, and 4.6) so far along in a lengthy play may indeed have been the reason for the cut, and it may have seemed easier to make here than in 4.6, which is both climactic and in many ways, as Warren argues, a greater scene. Taylor (1983, pp. 88 ff.): The motive for the cut was not censorship, since most of what has been omitted in the Folio contains no political or social comment whatsoever,…many contemporary plays satirize justices,…[and] an addition in 4.6 [2608–12]…directly and explicitly formulates the criticism of legal institutions only, at most, implicit here. Taylor speculates that Sh.’s self-censorship might even have prevented this scene from being more effectively satirical than it is in Q. (P. 97): But 3.6, as it stands in Q…, essentially gives us more of the same. The omitted passage…contains no new dramatic ingredients. Its omission improves the structure of the scene and the play. Idem (1983, pp. 418–19): The cut is authorial rather than vulgarly theatrical: Unauthorized theatrical adaptations regularly padded the role of a fool or clown; Folio Lear instead diminishes it, even though Tom’s role is advertised on the Q title page and madmen were enjoying a theatrical vogue. Of course, both the Fool and Tom have ample lines besides their 12 lines (net) lost between 2010 and 2015; and only as many of their lines are cut from this scene as are part of Lear’s trial (the final lines cut from the scene are spoken by Edgar, not mad Tom). Patterson (1984, pp. 62 ff.) argues, against Taylor and his assumption of great art as ahistorical, that political factors did shape the play and its folio changes. The Sokols (1999, pp. 436–9), finding that she gives no reasons for Shakespeare to self-censor the mock-trial, suggest one: that whereas in 1604–6 it was acceptable to show the separate equity and law jurisdictions as yokefellows on the same bench, by 1610 a political struggle had begun between these jurisdictions, hence reference to them was avoided in F. But such self-censorship need have eleminated only a few words, not the whole episode. Kerrigan (1983, pp. 227–8): One purpose of the cut is to change the Fool’s role: Whereas in [Q] 3.6 the Fool mimics Tom, in [F] he declines the gambit [i.e., his lines are cut]. As a result, he retains [his] marginal position.…His words seem far removed from the stormy center of the action.…Instead of joining Edgar and Lear in a crazy ritual judgement, the F jester stands apart, watching in silence.…If Kent finds this spectacle pitiful, the Fool finds it unendurable. He announces his intention of abandoning Lear (see n. 2043). McLeod (1983, p. 182), moreover, finds as motive for the cut a different characterization of Goneril: Q’s trial scene gives fantastic visions of Gonorill—as a ioyne stoole and as one who kickt…father.…F ignores Gonerill here to dwell on her sister, as if to give Regan her turn for Lear’s wrath.…F presents a relatively less extreme picture of Gonerill’s behaviour. In both texts, however, the daughters (with Cornwall) are reported a few lines later to be plotting their father’s death, than which no behavior could be more extreme. Foakes (ed. 1997): The mock-trial is too theatrically powerful in relation to the climax of this sequence of scenes in the blinding of Gloucester in 3.7.
To all this justification Halio (ed. 1992) replies: But these putative gains may not be worth the loss of what, in the theatre, is a most impressive piece of drama. The parallel with events in 3.7 is sharp: the madness in 3.6 contrasts with the diabolical cruelty in 3.7. Furthermore, the quarto version of 3.6 completes Lear’s descent into madness; the king does not appear again until much later in Act 4. Without appreciably shortening performance time (35 lines), removing the mock trial foreshortens a process that Lear has been struggling to contain since the end of Act 1. If Shakespeare was responsible for this cut, he may have had reason.…But authors—even Shakespeare—are not always the best judges of their own work, and theatre directors…seldom cut the mock trial in 3.6. Cantor (1996, p. 457 n. 16), agreeing: Just as one can always find reasons why a passage belongs in a work, one can always find reasons why it does not. The question is whether the reasons are on balance plausible. Richman (1986, p. 382): In our production, the mock trial achieved stunning effects. It was indeed an epicenter. Carroll (1988, pp. 230–6) challenges in detail the several unexamined assumptions which lead revisionist critics to denigration of the mock trial, e.g., that speed and simplicity are paramount values in Jacobean drama, that the scene failed to communicate a vision of political reality, that the uncut play proved too difficult for actors and audience. Honigmann (1996, p. 10): Isn’t this episode indispensable, as the geometric centre of the whole play? And if it can succeed in the modern theatre, why should it have failed at the Globe? Is there any evidence that it failed? Clare (1995, pp. 49–51): Most Lears would argue that the journey to 4.6 is only made possible by playing the mock trial first.…In F,…there is no basis for meaningful transition and development. Lear has hardly entered when he speaks of Regan, and then he falls asleep.…In Q, however, if the still, small voice [of clarity within madness] speaks thus clearly from the midst of chaos, we will be waiting for it to sound again from the moment that Lear next appears, in 4.6.…Lear actually begins to hallucinate here, thus leaving behind the familiar cynicism of the Fool and crossing over into the naked and more terrible world of the bedlam.…Edgar begins to think of others’ welfare as well as his own.…A note in passing: how long would Gloucester need to be offstage during 3.6? F barely gives him time to get out of the door, let alone to have overheard a plot against the king’s life, and to have organized a litter for his escape. Holland (1997, p. 40) similarly: in Nicholas Hytner’s F-based RSC production of 1990, the mock-trial was restored from Q; without it 3.6 seemed weak dramatically, and with it, a pivotal moment of transition and recapitulation, the mid-point of the play’s journey.

2014+1 bites]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Cf. 1842–3. Cf. 1938.

2014+2 He’s mad]
Eccles (ed. 1792): In his former speech he had been speaking of madmen, and the presence of Edgar may well be supposed to keep alive the idea of madness in his mind. Schmidt (ed. 1879): Does he wish merely to distract Lear, or to say that, in fact, the whole world is mad? (Ger.). Kittredge (ed. 1940): He continues his discourse on madmen with a further definition. Having named one form of madness (the yeoman’s), he lists several others, all having to do with misplaced trust.

2014+2–+3 trusts…oath]
The form is proverbial. Tilley H711: Trust not a Horse’s heel nor a dog’s tooth, citing from Ray’s Collection (1678, p. 158), as Ritson (in Steevens, ed. 1793) does: Till horsis fote thou never traist, | Till hondis toth, no woman’s faith. Douce (1807, 2:163) quotes from Simon Robson, Choice of Change (1585, sig. K2), Trust not three things. Dogs teeth. Horses Feete. Womens protestations, adding, The Italians say, Of a woman beware before, of a mule beware behind, and of a monk beware on all sides; the French, Beware of a bull’s front, of a mule’s hinder parts, and of all sides of a woman. These proverbs persuade some eds. to adopt Warburton’s emendation of health to heels (see textual n.), but most follow Johnson (ed. 1765): Shakespeare is here speaking not of things maliciously treacherous but of things uncertain and not durable. A horse is above all other animals subject to diseases. So also Edwards (1750, p. 42), adding, It is probable that he alludes to the tricks of jockeys in making up unsound horses for sale. So Horsman (ed. 1973): A horse’s health i.e., as reported by a horse dealer. Allusions to horses’ frailty have been found in Shr. 1.2.81, 3.2.50–6 (646–7, 1438–43) by Wright (ed. 1875) and Craig (ed. 1901) and in Yorkshire Tragedy 8.1–2 (ed. Brooke) by Tovey (ed. 1896). Madden (1897; 1907, pp. 293–5) lists many equine diseases, and Gervase Markham, How to chuse…Horses (1596) devotes 56 chapters to them.

2014+2 tamenes of a Wolfe]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Since the wolf can never be tamed. Koppel (1899, p. 92), comparing Woluish visage (827) and shee Foxes (2014+6): the Fool refers to Lear’s greedy daughter. Klinck (1977, pp. 113–14) finds in Robson (see prev. n.) a saying about three things whereof we may hope for no goodnesse, the first being a tamed wolfe (sig. K3r).

2014+3 boyes loue]
Proverbial: Tilley L526, Love of lads and fire of chats [chips] is soon in and soon out; Dent (1981, C318.1), Trust no Child. Wilson (1978, p. 149) detects an affinity between the discarded father Lear and Sh. betrayed by the young man of Son. Hammond (1997, p. 63) suspects that a perceived allusion to James I’s sexual inclinations may have led to censorship of this speech if not of the whole mock trial.
