Tilley T551 compares the saying No Trust is to be given to a woman’s word; Dent (1981) doubts that it is proverbial or relevant.

2014+4 arraigne]
The word could mean either, generally, to accuse of a crime, its usual meaning in Sh., or to summon before a court (Schmidt, 1874; OED, v.1 2). Bransom (1934, p. 112): The notion seems to have been spontaneous, for I see nothing that could have suggested it. Kittredge (ed. 1940): In his delirium Lear abandons the idea of attacking his daughters with an armed force and decides to bring them to trial. Skillan (ed. 1967): No more weeping under affliction, but presiding at the[ir] trial. Gardner (ed. 1969): The trial…is generated in Lear’s subconscious. A trial is essentially an expression of order, and an affirmation of civilized justice.…The decrepitude of senility is obsessed by, and hopelessly seeks to condemn, the unnatural agents which fashioned its state. Elton (1966, pp. 232 n., 282): Of eight occasions on which Shakespeare employs a form of arraign, most are in connection with treason, comparing 3117; Lear’s mad trial of the villains (III.vi) ironically introduces the villains’ trial (III.vii) of Gloucester.

2014+4 straight]
See n. 527.

2014+5 Iustice]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:36): Judge, Minister of Justice (OED, sb. 8). By analogy with 2014+30 and 2324 (Q1[c]) most eds. emend to Justicer, meaning the same (OED, 2, quoting this l.). Wilson (ed. 1960): Emendation metrically desirable. Like Rushton (1868, pp. 52–4), Heard (1883, p. 81): Most ancient law-books have justicers of the peace as frequently as justices, citing Lambard’s Eirenarcha (1582, p. 4): Contractly for Iusticiars. McElwaine (1911, p. 243), justicer: Used in the reign of Elizabeth for a High Court judge and also for a justice of the peace. Most eds. (see textual n.) assume that Lear addresses Tom because in 2014+17 the man of Iustice is robed, presumably in Tom’s blanket. But both Tom and the Fool have been appointed men of justice, and a fool’s gown might ironically suggest judicial robes. See next n.

2014+6 sapient]
Schmidt (ed. 1879): Not elsewhere used by Sh. Both this term and the respectful sir might suggest that the wise philosopher Tom is being addressed, though most eds. judge otherwise. See prev. n. Musgrove (1981, p. 10) detects a play on the thieves’ cant term Sapient meaning an itinerant medical quack.

2014+6 no]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 399): Q2’s now is obviously the required reading, citing the same Q/F variant at 2614. Halio (ed. 1992): There is nothing obvious about it. See textual n.

2014+6 Foxes]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Schmidt [1874] here, and in 2090, takes foxes as emblems of ingratitude; but the ordinary idea of cunning [OED, sb. 1b, 2] seems sufficient to the sense.

2014+7 he]
Rann (ed. 1794) and most eds.: The fiend. Hunter (ed. 1869): Lear. So Campbell (1888, p. 497): An aside of the true Edgar expressing his astonishment and grief at the sudden change in the appearance of the King. Foakes (ed. 1997), like Theobald (see textual n.) reading she: The emphasis here is on the imagined presences of Goneril and Regan.

2014+7–+8 wanst…madam]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Addressed to the visionary Gonerill,…Do you want to attract admiration, even while you stand at the bar of justice?. So Clarkes (ed. 1868), adding, The fiends are there to serve your purpose. Singer (ed. 1826): Addressed to some visionary spectator,…Do you want eyes…that you cannot see this spectre? Tieck (ed. 1833, 9:368): Possibly Kent covers his face for a moment to conceal his anguish or his tears, or the Fool does so (Ger.). Hunter (ed. 1869): Edgar…ask[s] the imagined madam if she will make trial with the king which can outstare the other. Tovey (ed. 1896): Can’t you look up and attend, when you are on your trial? So Skillan (ed. 1967): Possibly her eyes are downcast…in the presence of lear. Gildersleeve (ed. 1912): Edgar…asks whether she wishes to be stared at. Or…whether she lacks eyes to see the fiend. White (1913, p. 460): The accused may not want to be tried by the Blind Ey’d Goddess, Justice, but…may require eyes at her trial to see her innocence. Harrison (ed. 1937): Can’t you see who is present at the trial—but Edgar is talking deliberate nonsense. For emendations, see textual n. and . Rosenberg (1972, p. 233): Does she dare to be seen? Can she outstare the fiend—or Lear? Does vanity drive her to be admired even there? Or…is she, blind, finally ready to see?

2014+7 wanst]
Most eds. accept Q2’s wantst for want’st. On Upton’s anon. conj. (see textual n.) Eccles (ed. 1792) says, To wanton eyes is scarcely English. See . Ridley’s (ed. 1935) Wann’st, i.e. grows pale makes even poorer sense.

2014+7 eyes]
See n. 2014+7–+8. Harbage (ed. 1958): Such eyes (?) or spectators (?). Possibly witnesses. Bell (1852–64, 3:111), improbably: Oyez, the crier’s proclamation at the opening of court. If the comma after eyes is another of Q’s substitutes for stronger pointing, in this case a question mark, the line may mean simply Look…can’t you see him? See next n. Taylor (1983, p. 487): It could be addressed to Lear (staring as though he were blind), or to a joint-stool Gonorill…, or to Kent or the Fool. Gulstad (1994, p. 496): Edgar imagines her a witch, who could not look a man in the face.

2014+7–+8 at tral madam]
Most eds. follow Q2, making at triall modify eyes by removing the comma after the latter word. But the train of ideas is unclear, and it is possible that at tr[i]al madam is the beginning of a new sequence of ideas rather than the completion of a former one. Johnson (ed. 1765): Edgar, being supposed to be found by chance, and therefore to have no knowledge of the rest, connects not his ideas with those of Lear but pursues his own train of delirious or fantastick thought. Rann (ed. 1794), following Johnson’s suggestion (see textual n.) sees Edgar as turning his attention from his imagined demons to the imagined daughters, saying, At trial, madam!, i.e., Reflect, you are upon your trial, and behave with decency. Similarly Stone (1980, p. 197): A trial, [madam]…reproving one of the arraigned daughters. Taylor (1983, p. 487) defends an earlier conjecture (see textual n.): Are you playing troll-madam? or do you lack eyes with which to play troll-madam?. Though Sh. refers to the game of Troll-madam (OED: A game played by ladies, resembling bagatelle) in WT 4.3.87 (1755: Troll-my-dames), it seems to have no relevance to the daughters or the action of this scene, and the name in WT does not much resemble that in the Q text here.

2014+8 come…mee]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Edgar, with a beckoning gesture, addresses the imaginary Goneril and Regan in the words of an old song in which a lover calls upon his sweetheart to come to across the brook. McCann (ed. 1964): He beckons [them] to come closer to the place of trial. It is not clear that the words are sung; Long (1971, p. 173), however: The music is a symbol of a mad, torn world and is sung with great glee by the Fool and Tom o’Bedlam. The Clarkes (ed. 1868): The fool’s…supplying the remainder, indicate[s] that it was a generally-known song. Stevens (1961, p. 348): The song, in various forms, was widely current in the late xv and xvi centuries. Greer (1977, pp. 186–7) thinks the English song is based on a 15th-c. Spanish song. Anon. (1773, p. 4) finds a fragment, possibly of the original English love song, sung by the fool Moros in William Wager’s The longer thou liv’st [1569, sig. A3]. Steevens (ed. 1778) prints his words: Com ouer the Boorne Besse, | My little pretie Besse, | Com ouer the Boorne besse to me. All extant versions are moralizations, either calling Bessy as mankind to salvation, or Queen Elizabeth to be the dear lady of England, or the like. A version of the latter kind, written by William Birch, first entered in S. R. by W. Copland in 1558/9 under the title A Dyologe sett furthe by twene the quenes maiestie and Englonde (see Arber, 1:32b, 1:115b), was on 4 Sept. 1564 entered to W. Pickering as A saynge betwene the quene and Englonde Called comme ouer the browne Bessye to me and printed in an undated broadside (STC 3079). Murphy (1984, p. 179): The ballad is a bitter jibe at the Papists and the late Mary Tudor and a Protestant welcome to Elizabeth Tudor. Ritson (1783, p. 169) prints from a MS in his possession (now BM Add. MS 5665) a version of the song in which burn and burne appear instead of broome; the music and words are reproduced in facsimile by Halliwell (ed. 1865, 14:466), and the words are reproduced by Stevens (1961, p. 348), spelling burne throughout. Like the similar verses in manuscript versions at Oxford and Emmanuel College, they are a moralization, persuading Bessy as mankind to come to Christ. Greenhill (1889, pp. 10†–11†) and Stevens (op. cit.) list several MS versions, and Sternfeld (1963, pp. 167–71, 180–8) provides from extant MSS the various texts of the English lyrics and music for both lute and vocal performance (see ). In view of the striking conformity among the versions, he proposes that the Fool should sing all three lines of the refrain (or burden, holding, or foot), as quoted above from Wager. Like Chappell (1859, pp. 504–5), Simpson (1966, pp. 124–5) distinguishes the song from Come, Open the Door, Sweet Betty of the time of James II, and from the 18th-c. Scottish Blink over the Burn, Sweet Betty, the latter mentioned by Sternfeld as a later version of this song. Like Wooldridge (1893, 1:121–2), Hunter (ed. 1972, p. 343) prints the music from a later Cambridge lute manuscript without words (MS Dd.2.11; see ) whose rubric is Ouer the broom Bessy. Seng (1967, p. 210): Lacking the text of the original ballad, it is difficult to determine either the precise meaning of this fragment in Lear or its function in the episode where it occurs. But it seems likely that it may have been concerned with a lover and his leman who lived near to each other, but who were separated by a bourn running between them. The lover calls his mistress to come over to him, presumably to make love. Since the lost song was one of those prophane songs having to do with synne and harlotrie which pious ballad-makers like William Birche loved to moralize, Bessy very likely consented.

2014+8 broome]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 399): Q’s broome is doubtless a misreading by the compositor: boorne could easily be misread broom, citing the o/r misreading at 1785. White (ed. 1862) notes that in F Wiv. Brook is invariably printed Broome, which White thinks is a misreading of Bourne. Because some extant versions of the song lyric alluded to (see prev. n.) read bourn or burn(e), most eds. adopt Capell’s emendation (see textual n.); curiously, just before singing this song, Wager’s Moros sings another beginning Brome, brome on a hill. Hanmer (ed. 1743–4, 6:Gloss.), bourne: A brook or stream of water (OED, sb.1). A few defend Q. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): The broom or stick and flowers with which Bedlams and their women mates…made it their custom to make merry. Brooke (ed. 1947): Edgar may be intentionally misquoting, with a hint at witches and broomsticks. Colman (ed. 1982): Broom (moorland shrub)…makes poor sense, but it is what Q prints, and folk-songs have such vagaries. Broom might be short for broom-field (OED, sb. 5), and the Cambridge MS setting for lute (see prev. n.) is titled Ouer the broom Bessy.

2014+8 Bessy]
Malone (1780, 1:260): Bessy and poor Tom, it seems, usually travelled together, citing the description of rogue and harlot in Richard West, The Court of Conscience (1607, sig. F3): One calls her selfe poore Besse the other Tom. Musgrove (1981, p. 11): Francis Kirkman (The English Rogue Described, Pt. 2, 1668, p. 135) reports that the Abram-man hath but two names for all people whatsoever, and that is Tom and Bess. Williams (1994), Bess: Generic for wanton, not citing this l.

2014+9–+10 Her…thee]
Capell (1783, 1.2:170–1): The play that has this first line [Wager; see n. 2014+8] calls it—foot of a song, i.e. burden; so that what comes after it from the Fool, it is probable, has relation to some parts of the song itself, long since perished. Eccles (ed. 1792): An extemporaneous rhyme to Edgar’s quoted line, since as Ritson (1783, p. 169) remarks, The Fool’s reply does not seem to have been any part of the original song. Eccles takes nightingale (2014+11) to imply that the Fool likely sings his lines. Moore (1916, p. 81): It was expected that madmen would sing on the stage, and that the fool would cap Tom o’ Bedlam’s verse…to the infinite delight of the groundlings. Craig (ed. 1901) compares Tmp. 1.1.47 (55–6), leaky as an vnstanched wench. Partridge (1947, p. 76): Perhaps she is having her period [cf. p. 140], but probably she is suffering from gonorrhoea. Sternfeld (1963, p. 170): There is nothing delicate about the Fool’s improvisation but this is only the obverse side of the coin. Again the clowning scene and its song provide an oblique comment on the all-powerful emotion of love which ennobles the dying Lear and…softens the heart of the Macchiavellian Edmund as he lies dying. McCann (ed. 1964): The Fool…may be saying obscurely that the case of Goneril and Regan is not a sound one. Seng (1967, pp. 209–10): Since the original ballad survives only in a moralization, it is impossible to know whether the Fool’s [obscene] lyric is a quotation or improvisation.…The song may have been intended to echo the adultery theme of the play, or to elaborate on the sexual repugnance of speeches such as those assigned to Edgar and Lear ([1866–77, 2557–71]). Bevington (ed. 1980): The leaky boat suggests her easy virtue. Orgel (ed. 1999): The fool’s continuation is an obscene parody, punning on burn as the pain of venereal disease and because women are proverbially leaky vessels. Kerrigan (1983, p. 226) sees the Fool as interrupting rather than continuing or supplementing Edgar’s song: Not content with stealing Edgar’s idiom, he deprives him of his lines.

2014+11 foule]
Halio (ed. 1973) suggests that the word alludes to the Fool’s indecency in the previous lines. Rosenberg (1972, p. 233) detects a pun on fool.

2014+11 poore Tom]
See n. 1271.

2014+11 nightingale]
Wright (ed. 1875): Apparently suggested by the Fool’s singing, which Edgar pretends…is that of a fiend disguised as a nightingale. If so, the speech is uncharacteristically jocular for Edgar. Skillan (ed. 1967): Simply an inconsequential interjection made to preserve the notion of the phantasmal and devil-ridden substance of the scene. Brown (ed. 1976): When the fool mocks his pretense, he further pretends that his fiend is in the fool, possessing him and singing. Percy (in Steevens, ed. 1778) finds a reference in Harsnett (1603, p. 225) to a caged nightingale stolen by a devil and killed, but Wright doubts it has any connection to this passage.

2014+12 Hoppedance]
Percy (in Steevens, ed. 1778) quotes Harsnett, Declaration (1603, p. 49; see ): Frateretto, Fliberdigibbet, Hoberdidance, Tocobatto were foure deuils of the round, or Morrice; see n. 1895. The name is spelt Hobberdidaunce thrice on p. 180, and Haberdidance on p. 140 (see ). Furness (ed. 1880): This spelling may indicate the pronunciation, comparing Hobbididance at 2248+2. Wilson (ed. 1960): Q perh. corrupts Sh.’s spelling. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): It may be an appropriate name for the toad, supposed to croak like a familiar in Tom’s stomach; see n. 2014+13. Brownlow (1993, p. 172): In Harsnett (1603, p. 180), The name of a Rumpelstiltskinlike hero in a tale told to Sara by her mistress.

2014+12 white herring]
As opposed to a red (dried or smoked) herring. OED (Herring 1b): White h. (a) fresh herring; (b) herring salted but not smoked, quoting this l. Although Steevens’s (ed. 1778) pickled herring has been disputed by White or Loveday (1790, p. 402) and others, Craig (ed. 1901) finds the term used for pickled as well as fresh herring in Nashe, Lenten Stuff (ed. McKerrow, 3:222–3): embarreld white herrings, white pickled herring. Harbage (ed. 1958): Unsmoked (in contrast with black angel, i.e. smoked devil. Ridden (1998), imaginatively, refers the two herring to Goneril and Regan, who like Pickle Herring in the Revesby Play bring about the death of their father.

2014+13 Croke]
Cotgrave (1611): Gribouiller. To rumble, or croake (as the guts doe through windinesse) (OED, v. 3). Craig (ed. 1901): A sign of great hunger. Muir (ed. 1952): Cf. 1669. Steevens (ed. 1773) compares Harsnett (1603, p. 195; see ): If they [the priests] heard any croaking in her [Sara Williams’s] belly, (a thing whereunto many women are subiect, especially when they are fasting) then they would make a wonderful matter of that. One time…they said it was the deuill that was about the bedde, that spake with the voyce of a Toade. Muir (ed. 1951, p. 19): Shakespeare seems to have combined voyce of a Toade, nightingale, Hoberdidance [see prev. nn.], belly, and croak for Edgar’s speech.

2014+13 blacke Angell]
Fallen angel, or devil (OED, Angel 1b), commonly depicted as black. Harbage (ed. 1958) and Ribner (ed. 1967): Smoked devil. Hunter (ed. 1972): Black being the devil’s colour.

2014+14 amazd]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): In a maze. A very strong word, indicating a state of utter confusion (OED, ppl. a. 2). Deighton (ed. 1891): Terror-stricken (OED, 3). Possibly Lear has been distracted by the wild talk of Edgar and the Fool. Bransom (1934, p. 113), however: Here the king has an hallucination; he sees one of his daughters, or both of them.…At Kent’s kindly touch and tone it passes. Dent (ed. 1927): Throughout the mock trial Kent alone talks and acts like a sane man, and thus provides that contrast which makes the frenzy more shocking.

2014+15 cushings]
A common variant spelling of cushion (OED). Foakes (ed. 1997): May indicate Shakespeare’s pronunciation; compare javeling’s for javelins, [Ven.] 616. Eds. who misplace the scene in a hovel (see n. 1996) must account for such furnishings; thus Colman (ed. 1982): Brought to the hovel by Gloucester.

2014+16 bring in]
OED (Bring v. 18f): To introduce, quoting this l. as its first ex.

2014+16 their euidence]
Wright (ed. 1875): The witnesses, citing R3 1.4.183 (1015); so OED (sb. 7), quoting this l. and Luc. 1650 as its earliest exx. Furness (ed. 1880): Needlessly changed to the evidence (see textual n.). Abbott (§219): Your, our, their, &c. are often used…as genitives, where we should use of you,…from them, etc.; cf. Franz §322. Joseph (ed. 1966): Evidence concerning them. Furness’s misquotation of Wright—witnesses against them—has been followed uncritically by later eds.; the witnesses or their testimony could be for or against the daughters. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 518), rejecting the objective genitive here: The and their are often confused by scribes and compositors in this period, and in this case their could easily result from contamination by the preceding phrase.

2014+16–+18 thou…side]
Campbell (1859, pp. 101–2): This imaginary trial…is conducted in a manner showing a perfect familiarity with criminal procedure. Lear places the two judges on the bench, Mad Tom and the Fool.…But, although both were of the commission, I do not quite understand why the latter is called his yoke-fellow of equity, unless this might be supposed to be a special commission, like that which sat on Mary, Queen of Scots, including Lord Chancellor Audley. Lear causes Goneril to be arraigned first, and then proceeds as a witness.…But the trial could not be carried on with perfect regularity on account of Lear’s madness, and without waiting for the verdict, he himself sentences Regan to be anatomized. White (1913, pp. 461–2) also thinks the trial is a due and regular proceeding, with arraignment, question whether the defendant is guilty, and deposition of evidence, but Barton (1929, pp. 147–8), in view of its mad tribunal, two comic songs, the king’s acting as prosecutor, and his giving judgment without consulting the judges, calls it Gilbertian. Underhill (1916, 1:395): But for [this] passage, Shakespeare gives no hint that he knew of the existence of Courts of Equity as distinguished from Courts of Law. Wilson (ed. 1960): The Lord Chancellor presided at the one, the Lord Chief Justice at the other. As this was a trial of supreme importance in the mad King’s eyes, he seems to suppose the blanketed Bedlam as L.C.J. and his yoke-fellow the Fool as L.C. Similarly Merchant (1964, p. 122): It is a fully constituted commission in which two judges of Common Law are joined by a Chancery judge. Keeton (1967, p. 33): Campbell correctly surmises…a special commission, and obviously the Lord Chancellor was intended as yoke-fellow. Lear need not have the Court of Equity in mind: see n. 2014+18.

2014+17 robbed]
OED (Robe sb.) attests to the variant spelling robbe in the 16th c. Cf. nn. 1262, 1846, 2014+5. Muir (ed. 1952): Edgar’s blanket appears as judicial robes here, and later ([2037]) as the Persian attire of a Magus.

2014+17 yokefellow]
OED (sb. 1): Associate or partner, quoting H5 2.3.54 (873).

2014+18 equity]
Schmidt (1874): Justice (OED, 1). Horsman (ed. 1973): A system of precedents based on natural justice, supplementing common and statute law. Weis (ed. 1993): Equity (from Latin naturalis aequitas) in jurisprudence is a system of recourse to general principles of justice and was formally instituted in England in 1591 to supersede common and statute law where they conflicted with equity. As the thing itself Edgar seems uniquely qualified to adjudicate from general principles of natural justice. Keeton (1967, pp. 33–4): Too much should not be read into this sudden reference to the Court of Chancery. In the whole of his plays, Shakespeare refers to Equity only four times, and elsewhere it means simply justice, honest-dealing, or legal right. As it may here, rather than the Court of Equity. See n. 2014+16–+18.

2014+18 bench]
Delius (ed. 1854): To sit on the judges’ bench (OED, v. 3, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Wilson (ed. 1960): As in the Court of King’s Bench. On verbs formed from a substantive see n. 1197.

2014+18 you…too]
Since this directive would be redundant if addressed to Edgar or the Fool, both of whom have been benched, most eds. since Capell address it to Kent (see textual n.). Warren (1983, p. 72; cf. 1985, p. 28), however, argues that Lear’s change from thou to you does not indicate a change of address to Kent, since he usually uses thou to him, may be showing impatience with the Fool for not responding quickly enough, and is not in his right mind. He concludes, Kent does not participate in Lear’s fantasy as the others do; I believe that he stays separate from Lear’s court, acting as a commentator upon the mad action. In fact Kent does not comment until the trial is over (2016), nor participate in it; he may well be reluctant to encourage Lear’s fantasies, and in 2016 finally tries to restrain him (he is not a mere detached commentator). But at this point, having just failed to persuade Lear to rest, he might sit as directed rather than further aggravate the King’s distress by disobedience. Idem (1985, p. 28): Possibly Lear does not address anybody at all [in 2014+16–+18] since he is involved in fantasy; but since Edgar (2014+19) and the Fool (2014+24) immediately assume the role of judges, they clearly recognize that Lear has addressed them.

2014+18 ot’h]
More probably on the than of the; see textual n. and next n. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 518): The line is tightly justified in Q, with no possibility of turning up or down.

2014+18 commission]
OED (sb.1 2c): Commission of the peace: the authority given under the Great Seal empowering certain persons to act as Justices of the Peace in a specified district. Hence On the Commission: having the office of Justice of the Peace, quoting 2H4 3.2.88. Kittredge (ed. 1940): To whom the preservation of the king’s peace is entrusted. Harrison (ed. 1937): Persons of high rank or charged with extraordinary crimes were not tried before the ordinary courts but by commissioners specially appointed (OED, 6). Musgrove (1981, p. 9) detects a play on the thieves’ cant term commission meaning shirt: Kent is qualified to sit as a member of the court because he has a shirt to wear, as Tom has his robe—his blanket—and the Fool his long childish coat.

2014+19–+21 Let…gray]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Edgar assumes the air and manner of a dignified judge, but instantly breaks into song and follows his song with a mad exclamation, as if he saw a demon in the shape of a grey cat. Lott (ed. 1974): The song seems to have no particular relevance to the context, even ironically, and it is to be taken as a further display of Edgar’s feigned madness. Still, something must occasion these particular verses. Perhaps Lear is staring as if in a trance at his imaginary daughters; compare Lockhart (1975, pp. 470–1): Lear, the irresponsible shepherd who has abandoned his flock, will not be able to deal justly so long as his vision is darkened by his mental and physical anguish. Edwards (ed. 1975): The obvious inference is that if we are to deal justly with Goneril and Regan, we should note that the vigilance of Lear (the shepherd) could have stopped his daughters (the sheep) from having the kingdom (straying into the corn). Alternatively, Edgar may address one of his fellow-judges as a shepherd, whose function is to exercise authority and keep his flock from straying into harm; sleepest or wakest? would mean pay attention to your office, following logically on Let…iustly. Or possibly he pretends that he is arraigning an imaginary shepherd for dereliction: Are you sleeping, that you allow your sheep in the corn, etc.

2014+19–+21 sleepest…harme]
Johnson (ed. 1765): A stanza of some pastoral song. Steevens (ed. 1778): In [Rastell’s] Interlude of the Four Elements [l. 1399; ed. Axton, 1979],…1519, Ignorance sings a song composed of the scraps of several others. Among them is…Slepyst thou, wakyst thou, Geffery Coke? Halliwell (ed. 1865): Compare also the poem of King Arthur and the King of Cornwall [l. 196; in Syr Gawayne, ed. F. Madden, 1839, p. 283]:…sleepe you, wake yow, noble King Arthur? Staunton (ed. 1859): Edgar was surely intended by Shakespeare to sing these fragments of old ballads. Very few eds. agree: see textual n. For a possible early musical setting, see , and for modern ones see Gooch & Thatcher (1991, 1:637). Brooke (ed. 1947): Based on some version of the nursery rime of Little Boy Blue. Hunter (ed. 1972, p. 342): Form and content would make a ballad source quite plausible. Greer (1992): Item 31 in Thomas Ravenscroft’s anthology of old catches, Pammelia (1609) contains the couplet O sleep’st thou or wak’st thou, Jeffery Cooke? | The roast it burns; turn round about; another Ravenscroft catch has antecedents in the carol Jolly shepherd and upon a hill as he sate. Since all the analogues with Sh.’s line are musical ones, Greer believes that Edgar sings here. Duffin (2004, p. 233), doubting Greer’s proposed tune because Sh.’s words do not fit it, would substitute Pammelia Item 3. Foakes (ed. 1997): Nonsense verses, which have no obvious application.…He may be glancing at Lear as a ruler (shepherd) whose subjects have gone astray. He may be simply saying pay attention to a member of the bench who is showing fatigue.

2014+19 iolly]
Wells (ed. 2000): Had a wide range of meanings, including brave, amorous, arrogant, finely dressed, handsome; sometimes used ironically.

2014+20–+21 corne…harme]
A near-rhyme; Sh. often rhymes short ar and or. See Ellis (1869–89; 1871, p. 953), Kökeritz (1953, pp. 169, 226), Cercignani (1981, pp. 93, 114), and n. 1271–2.

2014+20 corne]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Wheatfield.

2014+20–+21 for…mouth]
Rann (ed. 1794): A single tune on thy pipe shall save them. Kittredge (ed. 1940): For the time it takes to play one strain on your shepherd’s pipe. Houghton (ed. 1957): While you turn aside to play us a tune. Brooke (ed. 1947): If you give me one kiss. Muir (ed. 1952): It may refer, ironically, to the shepherd’s shout, rather than to his pipe.

2014+20 minikin]
Steevens (ed. 1778): A term of endearment [OED, sb. 1: A playful or endearing term for a female.]…Handsome. Ritson (1783, p. 169): Little (and, therefor, perhaps, pretty) (OED, adj. 3: Tiny.…endearing diminutive). Nares (1822): Small, delicate [OED, adj. 1: Dainty, elegant).…Treble in music (OED, sb. 2). Bald (ed. 1949): Shrill (OED, adj. 2, quoting this l.). Wilson (ed. 1960): Doubtful whether this refers to the pipe or…voice. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): The shepherd’s delicate pipe. Horsman (ed. 1973): High-pitched treble.

2014+21 take no harme]
Most eds. understand take to mean incur or receive, a few to mean do. Johnson (in Steevens, ed. 1773): Impoundment for criminal trespass. Verity (ed. 1897): The punishment [the shepherd] deserves for letting his sheep stray. Muir (ed. 1952): But it is the corn, not the sheep, which will be harmed.…your precious sheep will leave the cornfield, whatever damage they have done. Or perhaps before they have done any real damage. Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): If you call back your sheep we will let them off without putting them in the pound (?) or we will consider a song from you compensation for the damage done by the sheep (?). Myers (1980, p. 63): If [sheep] break into a cornfield and eat for more than a few minutes they swell up and can easily die from it.…It is, therefore, to save his sheep that the shepherd must blow his horn.

2014+21 Pur]
Malone (ed. 1790): This may be only an imitation of the noise made by a cat. Purre is, however, one of the devils mentioned by Harsnet’s book [1603], p. 50; see . Craig (ed. 1901) compares the name Purson for a devil like a man with a lions face in Scot’s Discovery (1584, p. 379). Muir (ed. 1952): Edgar is referring to a demon or familiar in the shape of a grey cat, and this may be its noise, rather than its name. See next n.

2014+21 the cat is gray]
Hudson (ed. 1879): Too old to sing, hence purring. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Like Graymalkin, the Witch’s familiar spirit in Mac. 1.1.8 (11). Brooke (ed. 1947): Hinting that it is an old grey witch who is wheedling the jolly shepherd. Lear seizes the suggestion and identifies her with Goneril. Harbage (ed. 1958): Gray cats were among the forms supposedly assumed by devils. Bullough (1973, p. 301): Sara Williams was much haunted by [devilish] cats (Harsnett, p. 138 [see ]). Verity (ed. 1897): Moberly suggests that there was a proverb, If dun’s the mouse, the cat is gray—implying the mouse ought to remember that the cat is just as hard to see in the dark as the mouse herself. No such proverb has been found, but Tilley C50, When Candles be out (At night) all cats be gray, is cited by Dent (1981, C50) and others. Brown (1964) applies it to Lear’s situation: When all minds are in darkness, one action is as sensible as another. Similarly Lockhart (1975, p. 470): Where conditions for vision…are bad, no discrimination or judgment is possible. But the proverb is jocular, and means only that all women are attractive at night. Whatever their meaning, but especially if they refer to a demon or witch’s cat, Edgar’s closing words seem ominously to contradict his adjurations to deale iustly and take no harme.

2014+22–+23 Arraigne…father]
Kahn (1957, p. 317) sees this lapse from verse to prose as indicating his final passage into madness.

2014+23 kickt]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 400): Q2’s added she distinctly improves the sense. The Q1 compositor may have omitted it accidently. It may not be necessary: see textual n. The understatement of kickt is poignant.

2014+24 Come…Gonorill]
Hunter (ed. 1869): The fool says this to a joint-stool, as seeing nothing else where the king imagines Goneril to stand. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The Fool plays his part as if this were the good old time when he acted in plays as court.

2014+26 Cry…stoole]
Steevens (ed. 1778): Proverbial, citing Lyly, Mother Bombie (1594) 4.2.28. Tilley M897: A taunting apology for overlooking a person. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The Fool takes professional delight in this opportunity to give the worn-out phrase a point; for…the stool is there and Goneril is not. Wilson (ed. 1960): As usual, the Fool is aware of the true facts when Lear is not. Hulme (1962, p. 68): As proverb, the words imply injury without regard for the one who is hurt—Goneril’s attitude to her father. Lott (ed. 1974): The fool is making fun of the routine of the law courts, in which everyone appearing before the court is asked his name, without regard to whether he is well known or not. Bradbrook (1978, p. 192): A folk jest meaning kiss my arse. Only MacMichael (1904, p. 214): The saying is addressed to Lear rather than Goneril, reflecting on the senselessness of his remarks. Warren (1983, p. 46): The Fool’s joke reduces Lear’s imagined courtroom to the bathetic reality.…This leads Lear to imagine his court broken up in confusion at Regan’s escape. Possibly; but see n. 2014+30. Lear maintains his illusion for at least another two lines. Taylor (1983, pp. 94–5) dilates on the inadequacy of the joint-stool as an image of Goneril; but Lear may be only addressing a hallucination in the same direction as the stool; it is only the Fool who pretends facetiously to mistake the stool for her. Doloff (1989, p. 332): Witches might enchant items of furniture to resemble themselves, as stand-ins during their absence. Hart (1904, p. 66), citing Narcissus (1600, ed. Margaret Lee; 1893, p. 34), where the term is a metonymy for a judge: I took you for one of the bench (not a prisoner)—a joke without a clear point here, though anticipating 2597–8.

2014+26 Cry you mercy]
See n. 1711.

2014+26 ioyne stoole]
Mason (1785, p. 350): Part of the furniture of the…house, which Lear mistook for Goneril. Craig (ed. 1901), joint-stool: (More properly joyned stool…) a low stool, with three or four legs fitted into it. OED (sb.): A stool of parts joined or fitted together; a stool made by a joiner, as distinguished from one of more clumsy workmanship. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 400): Q’s ioyne for ioynt may be a misreading, giving exx. of other e/t misreadings in Q. But the term was spelt ioyne-, ioynt-, and ioynd- at the time.

2014+27 another]
Regan. Halio (ed. 1992): Lear points to or grasps another piece of furniture.…Note the pun on warped.

2014+27 warpt]
Schmidt (1875): Malignant, quoting only this l. Not supported by OED. Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Distorted (OED, ppl. a. 1), with dislike and hatred (Armour, ed. 1930), by evil passions (Kittredge, ed. 1940). Craig (ed. 1901): Perverse, unnatural (OED, v. 16). Kolve (1966, p. 189): Suggested by the warped joint stool he sees.

2014+27–+28 lookes…hart]
Possibly proverbial. Tilley F1: The Face is the index of the heart; Dent (1981) queries the allusion.

2014+28 store]
Rann (ed. 1794): Stuff, materials (OED, sb. 7: Stock <of anything material or immaterial>). Kinnear (1883, p. 421): Having, property…= what stuff her heart is stored with (OED, 5). Muir (ed. 1952): Treasure [OED, 6]; there may be an unintentional echo of Matt. vi.21. Wilson (ed. 1960): Such a sense goes ill with made on ( = composed of).…Some sort of substance seems required, favoring stone (see textual n.) in connection with hardnes (2035). But since warping does not easily proclaim or imply stone, perhaps the less specific sense of stuff is preferable. Foakes (ed. 1997): Abundance, plenty. Lear’s word is ironic. Wells (ed. 2000): The distorted material—or even warped wood, like that of a join-stool—of which her heart is made.

2014+28 an]
On, = of; see n. 331. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 400): Perhaps an o/a misreading. Very possibly; but see n. 669+10.

2014+29 fire]
Hunter (ed. 1972): It is not clear what fire is doing in this list.…There is no evidence that…in 1605 it could mean fire your muskets. Perhaps he is calling for torches; but in his excitement he may instead be including fire as a weapon of attack. Foakes (ed. 1997), improbably: The place of justice suddenly becomes hell in Lear’s imagination. Possibly a misreading of fie, the sp. at 1447, 1646, 2571.

2014+29 corruption]
Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Bribery.

2014+29 place]
Goggin (ed. 1910): I.e. the high place, the seat of justice.

2014+30 Iusticer]
See n. 2014+5. Presumably addressed to either Edgar, the Fool, or Kent. Only Taylor (1983, p. 93): Might be directed at Lear himself. But Lear is plaintiff (or counsel), not judge. Colman (ed. 1982): Edgar is the one most likely to be so accused: see [2018–19].

2014+30 her]
Since Lear has been talking of Regan, most eds. assume that she is referred to here. But Verity (ed. 1897): Meaning Goneril? Lear, I think, fancies that she has escaped while their attention has been directed to Regan, whom he seems later [2033–4] to consider still present.

2014+30 scape]
Bucknill (1859, p. 163): Kent or Edgar, seeing the bad effects which this vivid personification [of joint-stool as Goneril] was working, snatched away one of the stools; and this produced the passionate explosion on Regan’s supposed escape. Moberly (ed. 1876): Probably in Lear’s delirium the ideas succeed one another so rapidly that he cannot long hold the thought that he has Regan before him; consequently the vanishing of the image seems to him like an actual escape of his daughter. Kittredge (ed. 1940): In his delirium Lear sees Regan escaping. Cf. n. 2014+26. Halio (ed. 1992): The Fool may snatch the object away from Lear and hide it; or perhaps Lear drops it.…But the whole episode may be purely Lear’s hallucination. Gulstad (1994, p. 497): Lear must imagine her a witch, who could escape through locked doors.

2015 Blesse…wits]
See n. 1839. Clarkes (ed. 1868): This repetition…serves to mark the difficulty he has sustaining his character and inventing any more of the Bedlam beggar’s jargon. His next speech still more touchingly marks his inability.

2016 pity]
Apparently elliptical. OED (sb. 2c): In exclamatory phrases of adjuration, entreaty, etc.: for pity…for pity’s sake. Doran (1931, p. 72 n.): Better punctuated in F.

2016 patience]
See n. 774.

2018 take his part]
Harbage (ed. 1958): Fall on his behalf.

2019 Theile]
I.e., they will if I cannot control them and they are noticed as a sane man’s reaction. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 151) defends F’s They: Tears…which are spoiling, are interfering with.

2019 counterfeiting]
Craig (ed. 1931): Edgar’s counterfeiting has been so perfect that this is needed to remind the audience that it is counterfeit.

2020–1 dogs…me]
Steevens (ed. 1778) compares Plautus, Menaechmi 5.2.88–9 (tr. 1595), where a man pretending madness claims to see an old mastiff bitch…barking at me. Tilley D526 compares the proverb All Dogs bark not (No dogs shall bark) at him; Dent (1981) queries the allusion. Eccles (ed. 1792): The idea of the cruel injuries he has suffered is so predominant in the distracted imagination of Lear, that he fancies the very dogs are disposed to treat him with indignity. Moberly (ed. 1876): Because they spontaneously catch the hard-hearted temper of their masters. Verity (ed. 1897): How pathetic a touch it is that Lear thinks that even his old favourites have caught the infection of treachery and turned upon him. Orgel (ed. 1999): Even the lapdogs. Wilson (ed. 1960): I.e. he is utterly outcast—and they are his dogs. Cf. [2599] and the old nursery rhyme: Hark, hark, hark! | The dogs do bark | The beggars are coming to town.

2021 Trey…hart]
Cf. the similar familiar names for dogs in Shr. In. 1.17–26 (20–9), Wiv. 2.1.118 (661), TN 2.5.123 (1132), Tro. 5.1.91 (2965), Tmp. 4.1.255–7 (1932–4). Madden (1897, p. 51 n.) notes how many of these names have persisted into modern times, though he does not name the three in this l. Peacock (1895) and Ayeahr (1895) give instances of later uses of the name Trey, and H. (1895) supposes it to derive from Lat. traho and to be applied to a dog for vehicular traction. Muir (1951, p. 20): Possibly suggested by Trayford, often mentioned in Harsnett (1603, pp. 1 et passim; see , ). Hunter (ed. 1972): Lap-dogs (perhaps bitches, by their names). Weis (ed. 1993): Pampered lapdogs, unlike the strays and hunting dogs of Edgar’s address. McCombie (1981, pp. 132–3), followed by Taylor (1983, p. 99), applies the names to the three daughters: Tray [sic], a current diminutive of betray (OED entry for 1600–1 [int., Exclamatory use of OF. trai, tray, pa. pple of traïr, the only other ex. from 1440]), stands for Goneril,…Blanch stands for the fashion-conscious Regan (cf. [1567] ff.)…[referring to] cosmetic blanch…; and Sweetheart stands for Cordelia…[possibly] punning upon cor, cordis. But Regan never refers to cosmetics, nor does Sh.’s one use of the verb blanch refer to a fucus; doubtless the name refers to a white dog. Davidson (1998, p. 322), even more fantastically: T(rey)-gan, Goneril m. <Albe>[white]any, and the seeming cur, <Cur/Coeur>-delia, the Sweet-heart among the daug[dog]-ters. Foakes (ed. 1997): Trey could mean pain [OED, Tray sb.1, v.1], or betray ; Blanch make pale with fear [OED, v.1 4]. Trey, so spelt in Q and F, may have its usual and Shn. meaning of three in cards or dice, perhaps referring to the dog’s spots, or be a variant on True, another common name for a dog; Sh. never uses tray for betray. Wells (ed. 2000): Blanch could be the worn-down form of blandish (flatter).

2022 throw his head]
Delius (ed. 1854): As if it were a stone. Moberly (ed. 1876): Probably by jerking his head about as if it were loose, and then making a gesture of throwing with it, so as to alarm the dogs. Furness (ed. 1880): Edwin Booth’s SD is Throws straw crown. Sprague (1944, p. 292): Edgar used to throw either his hat or his straw head-dress. Bratton (ed. 1987): Likewise Kean, Macready. Muir (ed. 1952): In Gielgud’s 1950 production Edgar made as though to lift his head from his shoulders. Two other suggestions occur to me: (i)…As head means the antlers of a deer [OED, 6] it could be stretched to mean the ox’s horn of Poor Tom. (ii) Edgar might put his horn on his head, and pretend he is an ox attacking the dogs with it. Wilson (ed. 1960): Prob. = turn and face—the approved method with wild beasts. To throw one’s eyes is common in Sh.; cf. OED (Throw v.1 16). So Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): Stare them down (?). Doig (1981, pp. 141–4) supposes the head of a hobby horse property, inferred from 1837, 1880. Just possibly the phrase is metaphoric: Edgar hurls his mind (OED, Head 2a, 7a), viz. by throwing words (OED, Throw 15), in the chanted imprecation that follows. In A Declaration (1603, p. 48; see ) Harsnett describes vacant hell as having not a deuill to cast at a mad dogge, echoing the proverb He has not a Stone (bone) to cast (throw) at a dog (Tilley S880), which may be latent here.

2022–3 Tom…white]
Doran (1931, p. 107): The [F] printer had not sufficient room to complete his first line [correctly lined in Q]. In such a contingency he ordinarily either divided the line in two or printed the last word on the line above or below at the right-hand margin. But in several cases he has…printed two lines as prose, comparing 2111–12, 2405–6, 3174–5, all correctly printed in Q1.

2022–3 auant…curs]
Cotgrave (1611), devant: Vsed, as our, Auaunt, in the driuing away of a dog (OED, Avaunt int.).

2023–7 cur…trũdletaile]
Muir (1951, p. 20): Perhaps suggested by the devils in Harsnett who take the form of dogs [1603, pp. 97–8, 139, 249, 281; see , ].…Harsnett also mentions mad dogges, spaniel, hound, and various other dogs, and he uses the phrase, tag, and ragge, cut and long-tayle (pp. 50, 89, 174; see ). Hunter (ed. 1972, p. 343): These trochaic octosyllables suggest incantation rather than song. They are strongly reminiscent of the witches’ incantations in Macbeth.
Duffin (2004, p. 316): The opening strongly resembles many of the stanzas from Please One and Please All—e.g., st. 2: Be they white, be they black—and the eight lines of rhyming text would fit comfortably with the tune Tom Tinker (ca. 1605), which Duffin provides.

2023 blacke…white]
Steevens (ed. 1778): To have the roof of the mouth black is in some dogs a proof that their breed is genuine. Cf. Turberville, Arte of Venerie (1576, sig. D1): Suche [whelps] as haue the roofe of their mouthe blacke should be good, and suche as are redde there, should not be muche worth. Voss (tr. 1819, 3:638–9), black: Venom’d, comparing H8 1.1.120, 1.3.58 (188, 646). Cf. Turberville (op. cit., sig. Q4v): in the burning hote madnesse, their mouth will be very black, and will haue no fome nor froth in it.…All beastes which they shall byte…will doubtlesse runne madde also; cf. 2024. In another kind of madness, the dog driueleth and slauereth at the mouth (sig. Q5v)—possibly the white mouth Edgar refers to.

2024 poysons]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Through rabies. See prev. n.

2025–7 Mastife…trũdletaile]
Books on hunting, such as The Book of St. Albans, regularly contain such catalogues of dogs; the list attributed to Dame Juliana Barnes or Berners in 1486 (STC 3308) is reprinted substantially the same some fifteen eds. later in A Iewell for Gentrie (1614, sig. G3v): The names of diuers Hounds. First there is a Greyhound, a Hound, and a Spanyel, a Bastard, a Mungrell, a Mastiffe, a Lemor, Raches, Kenets, Terrours, Butchers Hounds, Dunghill doggs, Trindle tailes, and prick-eared Curres, and small Ladie Puppies. This list is also echoed in 2 Return from Parnassus (1602; ed. Leishman, 1949, 2.5.845–6). Cf. Mac. 3.1.92–3 (1093–4). Paul (1950, pp. 397–8): Added to both 1606 plays, Lr. and Mac., to appeal to King James’s love of hunting and dogs.

2025 mungril, grim-]
Ridley (ed. 1935): Both Q and F give the comma after mongrel which is usually omitted. Apart from the fact that there is no reason why a mongrel should be grim, the run of the lines seems to need four different types of hound in this line, followed by two pairs of the next line.…But I have to admit that I cannot find either meaning or emendation for grim. OED (Grim adj. 1): Of persons or animals: Fierce, cruel, savage.…Also, in weaker sense, daring, determined, bold. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 400): In putting a comma…Q and F have a common error. It looks as if Q understood grim-hoũd as the name of a kind of dog, and as if [the F] Scribe or the F compositor decided that Grim was the name of a kind of dog though Hound was a separate word. Muir (ed. 1952): But the comma may merely indicate that the adj. applies to all three kinds of dog. Wilson (ed. 1960): Greyhound and grim-hoũd [were apparently taken] as a pair.

2026 brach]
See n. 642.

2026 him]
F’s Hym is essentially the same reading, capitalized as are all the names in 2025–7. Hanmer’s emendation lym for the lymehound (OED, Lyam-hound) or leamer (OED, Limer; cf. lemor in n. 2025–7), the powerful bloodhound restrained by a lyam or leash, has been generally accepted until recently. Doran (1931, p. 98): Lym in Shakespeare’s manuscript must have looked like hym. The printer of the quarto thought it meant him and changed the spelling.…The transcriber [of the playbook], however, copied it just as it appeared to him, and the folio printer…capitalized it in conformity with…the other nouns parallel to it. One cause for doubt is that no ex. of lym, lime, etc. without the suffix hound has ever been found as name for the dog itself; it always refers to his leash. Blayney (apud Halio, ed. 1992): Hanmer’s claim that lyam, leash, also means leash-hound is about as plausible…as the analogous claim that fox means fox-hound or that cart means cart-horse. Mackay’s (1887, p. 245): Keltic leum, to leap…leaping dog is the merest conjecture. Ridley (ed. 1935): As both Q and F read him (F hym) I have left it so, the phrase thus meaning bitch or [male] dog. Brooke (ed. 1947): And a misreading of manuscript l as h is not likely. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 400): But the pronoun him sounds extremely odd in the midst of a list of kinds of dogs. The opposition of female and male seems quite likely because all the other dogs in 2026–7 are grouped as opposites: the fierce pursuing hound against the affectionate setting or retrieving spaniel, the bobtail against the dog with long curling tail. On the other hand, the pairing of brach and lymer was familiar, the lime-hound being the starter of the larger game of the chase, and the brach, led in traces by a braconnier, the hunter-up of smaller game. See The Master of Game, ed. W. & F. Baillie-Grohman (1904, N. Y., 1909, pp. 236, 246–7). Foakes (ed. 1997): Edgar could simply point to an imaginary him, or even to the Fool or Kent.…Shakespeare may have had a hard time finding a rhyme.

2027 Bobtaile tike]
Schmidt (1874), Bobtail: With a tail cut short (OED, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Steevens (ed. 1778), tike: A little, or worthless dog (OED, Tyke 1). Cf. H5 2.1.29 (534). Bobtaile-tike appears in John Taylor, The Sculler (1612, sig. B2r). F’s tight makes poor if any sense, and may be an expanded spelling of misread tite. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 179): For k misread as t see [1248].

2027 trũdletaile]
Nares (1822): A dog, with a curling tail (OED, 1, quoting this l.). Delius (ed. 1854) considers the word an attributive, modifying tike; most eds. take it as a noun. F’s Troudle is erroneous; since the spelling troundle is not recorded, F’s word probably is a misreading or misprinting of the variant trondle, n being misread as u (Stone, 1980, p. 60), or simply omitted (Taylor, 1985, p. 20). Cf. n. 2025–7. Sh. does not use the word elsewhere, and Tobin (1983, p. 119) suspects he got it from trundle-taile tike in Nashe’s Lenten Stuff (1599; ed. McKerrow, 3:182), though the word was common.

2028 them]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 151) defends F’s him, which may be supported by reference to the singular thy in [2023]. Most eds. find Q preferable, since them (2022), curs (2023), dogs, and all (2030) are plural; though Tom catalogues the individual breeds, he dispatches all of them.

2029 thus]
See n. 2022.

2030 leape]
Doran (1931, p. 94) considers F’s leapt a misreading: Perhaps the folio printer mistook e for d, but substituted the form of the past with t. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 151) defends F: The dogs have done it and are fled. Munro (ed. 1957): Leap seems the intended reading: Poor Tom, for Lear’s benefit, gets rid of the imaginary dogs; so, present tense.

2030 hatch]
Hunter (ed. 1869): A wicket or half-door (OED, sb.1 1). Joseph (ed. 1966) interprets the phrase metaphorically: Dashed out in confusion.

2031 loudla doodla]
Of F’s substitution Do, de, de, de Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 536) remark, The motives for exchanging one bit of nonsense for another remain obscure. Eccles (ed. 1792): Both readings bear some resemblance to the humming of a tune where words of a determinate signification are omitted, as Capell implies (see textual n.). Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 400): The actor presumably thought that the sounds of inarticulate snatches were in his own control. Walker (1953, p. 66): Q’s reading conceals, in all likelihood, a corruption (due to misreading) of loo, alo, doo, alo, a hunting cry appropriately evoked by the doggerel rhyme and in turn leading on to the mention of the Bedlam’s horn. Conflation of the quarto and Folio readings is…necessary. See n. 1857 for the cry alieu, douce, alieu. Weis (ed. 1993): May be a beggar’s rallying cry, or a cry to announce his presence at village wakes and fairs.…They carried an ox horn…and blew it (perhaps producing the Loudla, doodla sound?) to attract attention. Perhaps F substituted a hunting call on the trumpet. Cf. Thomas Snodham, A Iewell for Gentrie [Book of St. Albans] (1614, sig. H1v): To blow to the coupling of the Hounds at the Kennell doore, blow with one [wind], one long and three short—as represented in F by do, de, de, de, perhaps.

2031 sese]
Cf. nn. 1880, 2645. Johnson (ed. 1765): The French word cessez…be quiet, have done. F’s addition may reinforce the idea that in F the previous words were intended to suggest a hunting call. Alternatively, Verity (ed. 1897)—Stop—enough of that…used to introduce a fresh subject—and Hoepfner (1952, p. 502): Stop being afraid. Foakes (ed. 1997), reading Cessez: The dogs have fled, so that it seems more likely that Tom ceases to address imaginary dogs, and turns again to speak to Lear. Presumably then Cessez is directed at himself, not Lear; but the following words seem to be so too. Steevens (ed. 1773): Possibly Sessy (perhaps a female name corrupted from Cecilia)…[and] part of some old song. Collier (ed. 1843), printing See, see!: Directing attention to the supposed flight of the dogs. Duncan-Jones (1995, p. 265): Cf. OED Sess, used to call a dog to food. White or Loveday (1790) first suggests the now prevailing interpretation: a call to encourage dogs to attack or follow. So Moberly (ed. 1876): Probably like sa, sa below [2645], a word used in following the hunt; being the name for a note played on the horn. Rather, a vocal cry: see The Master of Game (ca. 1406–13; ed. Baillie-Grohman, 1909, p. 182), Sa say [sic] cy avaunt, and Berners, Book of St. Albans (1486, sig. d3v) and successive eds.: Sa sa cy auant, i.e., Ça, ça!, There, there!

2031 march]
Perhaps suggested by imaginary playing on his horn. See above. Hunter (ed. 1972): Tom addresses himself, to take his attention away from the painful scene before him. He resolves to set out for the places of resort most likely to yield good begging.

2031 wakes, and faires]
Delius (ed. 1854): Where Bedlam beggars went in order to beg. Cf. WT 4.3.102 (1770). Deighton (ed. 1891), wakes: Originally festivals held on the anniversary of the dedication of a church, then festivals generally, before which it had been customary to watch all night (OED, sb.1 4).

2032 poore…dry]
See textual n. Johnson (ed. 1765): Men that begged under the pretence of lunacy used formerly to carry a horn, and blow it through the streets. Cf. n. 1265; Furness (ed. 1880) gives further evidence of the Bedlam’s horn, and Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956) provide a woodcut showing it. If Edgar has been pretending to blow a horn in the previous line (see n.), that fact might lead to this remark. Steevens (ed. 1778): He says privately, —I can no more; all my materials for sustaining the character of Poor Tom are now exhausted.…Accordingly we have no more of his assumed madness till [2241]…[where he voices] the same dislike of it that he expresses here. Ritson (1783, p. 170): There is no necessity either for making him speak the words aside, or for giving them an allegorical signification.…The company, if they attended to him, would take the phrase in its most obvious and simple sense, i.e. that he had nothing to drink. Malone (in Boswell, ed. 1821): A horn was usually carried about by every Tom of Bedlam, to receive such drink as the charitable might afford him.…He merely means…to supplicate that it may be filled with drink. Sharma (1972): He hints his reason for marching off to wakes and fairs.

2032 poore Tom]
See n. 1271.

2033 Then]
Moberly (ed. 1876): After doing execution. Fraser (ed. 1963): I.e., if the Bedlam’s horn is dry, let Regan, whose heart has become as hard as horn, be dissected. Quinn (ed. 1970): To see if it serves the purpose. But Lear may mean simply, since Goneril has escaped, then let us turn our attention to Regan. Hunter (ed. 1972): Lear’s mind may have moved in this direction because of Edgar’s dry (line [2031]) and his reference to horn, which is formed by the process to which Lear alludes in 2034. Horsman (ed. 1973): In response to Edgar’s call for charity Lear thinks of Regan, who has no alms for beggars, or for her father. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 8) thinks Then is a non-sequitur in F: see n. 2014+1–+30. Halio (ed. 1992): An acceptable non-sequitur, given the context of mad speeches. Weis (ed. 1993): Awkward in the extreme [in F]…since [2014+22]: Arraign…Goneril to which Then refers back is absent. Meyer (1994, p. 139), arguing that F’s cut is not authorial: Then? Regan? Why not also anatomize Goneril? Without the context of the earlier passages from the mock trial, Lear’s exhortation creates a confusion—a stumble—that never occurs in Q.…He had already interrogated Goneril, yet Regan had escaped.…The King insists she be summoned for examination—or more correctly—anatomization.

2033 anotomize]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 400): An o/a misreading. Smith (1964, pp. 119–20): Not the literal meaning dissect (OED, v. 1), but the figurative analyze (OED, 3). Rosenberg (1972, p. 236): Most theatre Lears act out dissection: plunging the hand in the imaginary body, holding up the heart, striking it with the imagined knife. One particularly violent Lear, in 1982, accidentally killed the Fool in the process; see Bratton (ed. 1987).

2034 breeds…Hart]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): As if there were some stony growth about her heart. Muir (ed. 1952): As though her heart had become as hard as horn. It may be only coincidence that hunting manuals refer to a bone in the heart of the Hart: cf. Turberville, Arte of Venerie (1576, sig. E1), Markham, Gentlemans Academie [Book of St. Albans] (1595, fol. 35v), etc. Wilson (ed. 1960) makes her emphatic: Is Reg.’s heart as dry and bloodless as Gon.’s?…That and the cause in nature…are philosophical problems. Best, then, entertain this interesting philosopher. Gardner (ed. 1969): Like anatomise, a technical term from medicine, cf. to breed the plague, to breed bad blood (OED, v. 5).

2034 Hart]
See n. 1029.

2034–5 is…hardnes]
Traversi (1952–3, p. 138): It is this question…that indicates the true extent of Lear’s tragedy. A question less about the nature of justice or of its application to any particular situation than about human nature itself, it lies at the heart of both Lear’s madness and of his possible redemption.…[Since it is unanswerable,] the only possible transition from it is one into repose, sleep, quoting 2040.

2034 nature]
See n. 232. Edwards (ed. 1975): Natural reason (as opposed to divine).

2035 makes]
Schmidt (ed. 1879) defends F’s make, citing Abbott §367, Subjunctive used indefinitely after the relative; cf. Franz §648, subjunctive in relative clauses of rhetorical questions. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 536): But of only four examples Abbott cites…one is misquoted…two involve the idiom as please (object)…and MM 1.2.184 (277)…[is from] a scribal transcript…[and] may well be due to a false plural.…Given the ease with which compositors and scribes can omit terminal s, and Shakespeare’s overwhelming preference for the indicative in such circumstances, error seems probable here.

2035 this hardnes]
Q makes perfect sense—this hardness of heart—and can not have been a misreading of F’s these hard-hearts, which must be an intentional improvement. Taylor (1983, p. 117) imagines Lear in Q tapping on the joint-stool, identifying the phrase as a reference to the hardness of the stool, which he has equated with Regan. Richman (1986, p. 379): But perhaps Lear’s certainty about Regan’s escape would be unclear to the audience if he continued to associate her with a joint-stool. Eds. adopt F’s reading without the hyphen. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 536): But the compound was current as a verb and an adjective (OED), and…could easily have been understood as a substantive (persons with hard hearts). Elton (1966, p. 220): Hard hearts were caused…by falling from grace, by reprobation and sin,…[and represented] an ailment peculiarly theological, citing numerous Renaissance discussions. Hunter (ed. 1972): Despairing of supernatural causes, Lear asks for a natural, anatomical, reason. Biblical references to the metaphorical or moral hardening of wicked hearts are found by Milward (1987, p. 182) in Jer. 3:17, Exod. 7–14, Rom. 9:18, and by Foakes (ed. 1997) in Matt. 19:8, John 12:40, Rom. 2:5.

2035 entertaine]
Schmidt (1874): To take or keep in service (OED, v. 5). Bransom (1934, p. 114): He takes Edgar into his service because he drove away the yapping little curs. Most eds. direct the speech to Edgar. Only Orgel (ed. 1999): Perhaps addressed to Kent, who has, ironically, been in Lear’s service.

2035 you]
F’s omission may be accidental. Lear repeats you after You sir at 606.

2036 hundred]
I.e., his hundred knights, whom he imagines still attend upon him. Wilson (ed. 1960): Promotion indeed!

2036–7 garments]
Edgar’s blanket; cf. 1261, 1846.

2037 Persian attire]
F’s omission of the second word may or may not be accidental. Wright (ed. 1875): The allusion is to the gorgeous robes of the east, comparing Horace, Odes 1.38, Persicos…apparatus, and Cicero, De Senect. 59, ornatumque Persicum. Cf. n. 1921–2. Moberly (ed. 1876) suspects a topical glance at a Persian embassy to England early in the reign of James. Verity (ed. 1897): Note the earlier allusions to the Shah of Persia in [TN 2.5.181, 3.4.279 (1184, 1797)], due probably to the interest excited by the embassy, the first sent out from England to Persia,…in 1598 under the famous traveller Sir Roger Shirley and his brother Anthony. Chew (1937, p. 277 n.) is scathing: The only Persian mission reported in London before the arrival of Robert Sherley in 1611 is that…received by Queen Elizabeth in February 1601. This embassy is a very shadowy affair.…It does not seem likely that in 1605–6…a reference to an embassy of 1601 would have had much point to it. Nor was this embassy, if it ever came at all (which it almost certainly did not), an embassy to King James. As for the supposed embassy to Persia in 1598, It was not an embassy; it was not sent; it was not under Sir Robert Sherley; his name was not Roger; and he was not then knighted. Moberley’s further suggestion, repeated by Furness (ed. 1880), that the allusion was occasioned by the death of the secretary of the Persian ambassador is likewise impossible, since this death occurred a decade after Shakespeare died. Brooke (ed. 1947): The travels of the Sherley brothers had called attention to the opportunities of trade with Persia. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Edgar’s strange garb has suggested to Lear two distant nations already—Theban and Athenian ([1936, 1964]). Persian attire was proverbially gorgeous. Baldwin (1944, 2:520): His loosely flowing blanket makes of him a Persian philosopher, Horace’s magus; see above and n. 1921–2. The Souldan of Persia is mentioned in Leir 425 (see ). Henderson (1939, p. 225), followed by Salingar (1983, p. 166) suggests a source in Montaigne’s Sebond: Dionysius the tyrant offered Plato a robe made after the Persian fashion (see ). McKenzie (1956, p. 99) detects a pun on perishing—…because of the cold. Hulme (1962, pp. 192–3): The unacceptable excuse that a certain fashion is Persian is found in a story told of Socrates and Aristippus, quoting from Nicholas Udall, tr. Apophthegmes of Erasmus (1542; 1564, pp. 75–6); the fashion is perfume, not dress. Carter (1905, p. 438), chang’d: Cf. Dan. 6:8: not changed according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not [G]. Shaheen (1987, p. 151): The immutability of [their] laws…had become proverbial in Shakespeare’s day. In spite of the Persian nature of Poor Tom’s garments, Lear wants them changed. Colie (1974, p. 202): Evidently Lear’s retinue wore his colors.

2040 here]
Malone (ed. 1790): On the cushions; cf. 2014+15. Wells (ed. 2000): Possibly in the opening at the rear of the stage, as Gloucester does not immediately see him.

2040 and rest]
Perhaps added in F to make a pentameter.

2041–2 Make…morning]
Bransom (1934, p. 114): The appearance of childlikeness that ends the scene is in the next phase of his madness…very strongly marked; we are here prepared for 4.4 and 4.6.

2041–2 curtains]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): The splendid bed, with its curtains, is a part of his delirium. So Adams (1948, p. 326), adding, It may be that Kent covers him with his cloak. Foakes (ed. 1997): Or perhaps they are in a furnished room.

2042 so, so, so,]
Campbell (1888, pp. 501–2) cites several occasions in Sh. where these words accompany some business of a practical kind, here perhaps Kent’s arranging the pillows, while his master, perhaps, hands to him his girdle and outer garment. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Spoken as he settles down to rest: Ah! well and good! Harrison (ed. 1948): Lear imagines the bed curtains being drawn. Colman (ed. 1982): Probably yawning noises.

2042 Weele…morning]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): He suddenly remembers that he has had no supper—and remarks, madly, Never mind! We’ll have supper at breakfast time to-morrow. This sounds like a jest to the fool, who caps it [in F] with jester’s logic. Brooke (ed. 1947): Lear is hungry, but his weariness exceeds his hunger, and by royal decree (We’ll go) he postpones supper until the morning. Muir (ed. 1952): Since we have none to-night. Gloucester was to provide food, but Lear needs rest above all. Elton (1966, p. 322) finds a parallel in Eccles. 10:16–17: Woe to thee, O land, when…thy princes eate in the morning. Blessed…[when] thy princes eate in time.

2042 so, so, so,]
Perhaps cut from F so that there is no interval between Lear’s remark and the Fool’s joke on it.

2039 Enter Gloster]
On F’s earlier entrance see n. 1358. Taylor (1983, p. 117): Gloucester’s urgency makes it unlikely he would stand by silently during this interval [2039–44], and his first question makes it clear that he has not seen or heard Lear going to bed. Brown (ed. 1976): He sees only Kent standing on watch, not the three insensible and prostrated bodies. Dessen (1995, pp. 75–6), however: F’s early entrance may be designed to trouble or provoke us to see a Gloucester present but not really seeing or hearing what is going on around him.

2043 And…noone]
Though Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxiv) finds the jest a distressing anti-climax to Burbadge’s solemn profundity, and Stewart (1948, pp. 190–1) finds it simple fooling—His lying down then explains why he is urged not to stay behind at 2056+4—and Brooke (ed. 1947) ventures the possibility that these words may have been added by [the clown, Robert] Armin himself rather than Shakespeare, others find the line pregnant with meaning for the play as a whole. Capell (1783, 1.2:171): The facetious speech of the Fool…is meant as a preparation for losing him; for ’tis towards noon with the play, (that is towards the middle of it) when he does take his leave of us in that speech. Tieck (ed. 1833, 9:368): The purpose is to end this fearful scene with a half-joke. Hudson (ed. 1856): The poor dear fellow’s heart is breaking.…His beloved master’s wits are all shattered in pieces, so that he has no longer any thing to live for; he feels that he cannot survive to see the evening of the terrible day that has overtaken him. So also the Clarkes (ed. 1868): He has gone to his eternal rest even in the very noon of his existence. Moberly (ed. 1876): His fate…was sure to be hard, when he was separated from his master, under whose shelter he had offended so many powerful persons. White (ed. 1883): That is, [he will] do another foolish thing; a proverbial phrase adopted by S. as the Fool’s antiphonal response to the King’s supper in the morning. In Heywood’s Proverbs (1546) the phrase occurs in a wife’s complaint that her unfaithful husband would make an utter fool of her: And whan ye have made me a loute in all these [deceits], It seemeth ye wolde make me go to bed at noone. Tilley B197 gives only two other examples, both from John Grange’s Golden Aphrodite (1577) and both taking the form At noon I bid good night without any reference to going to bed; the first seems to be a pleasant apology that his defense to the reader has gone on so long that it concludes on the next day, and the second is a despairing lover’s complaint that his beloved has rejected him at the height of his hopes: My Lady…biddes my ioyes at noone good nighte. If there is a common thread of meaning, it is apparently that such behavior is irregular, perverse, or foolish. Craig (ed. 1901): The expression is not unusual in the Elizabethan drama; generally expressive of easy-going conduct. Vickers (1968, p. 363): The Elizabethans regarded as a peculiarly lustful practice, that of making love in the middle of the day, citing the lewd day-bed in R3 3.7.72 (2288); but the text there reads Loue-Bed. Andrews (1978, pp. 149–51) illustrates from three plays the sexual connotation of going to bed by day. Creighton (1913, pp. 70–5): Possibly an allusion to John Skelton, who died at noon 21 June 1529, the whole play being an allegory of the Reformation. Blunden (1929; 1936, p. 336): I do not wish to rhapsodize over these last seven words, but they impress me with their seven meanings: 1. They are a sort of tired ironical joke on Lear’s late hours. 2. They make a playful complaint that the Fool would like a little food before going to bed. 3. There is a pun on the people’s name for the scarlet pimpernel. The weak-bodied Fool with his coxcomb looks like that flower. 4. But, if so, he shuts late. Surely there has been storm enough during the night. 5. There will be a worse storm still; and at once. 6. It is the last time that the Fool speaks during the play. He presages his untimely death, with a secondary meaning in the word bed of grave. 7. He takes off his coxcomb for the last time to please his old friends the audience. Budd (ed. 1935): The actor would have to convey…the impression that the Fool was dying. Holland (1997, p. 49): In the National Theatre production of 1990, at the interval he was left dying, stretched out on the floor, shivering uncontrollably. Hulme (1962, p. 72), taking the proverb to refer to overcredulity: As it has hitherto been his [i.e., the Fool’s] office to voice Lear’s unacknowledged sense of the harsher realities, Shakespeare intends his last words here to indicate Lear’s decision—conscious or half-conscious—to withdraw from the actual world into a world of hallucination. Elton (1966, p. 322): His comment foreshadows also the sleep which descends at Lear’s crescendo point of madness and from which Lear later awakens to encounter death;…alludes further to the traditional topsy-turviness of fools;…[and] foreshadows metaphorically…Cordelia’s own leave-taking. Joseph (ed. 1966): The obscure meaning of the proverb seems to involve a reversal of truth and a refusal to recognize reality. Zitner (1974, p. 13): The remark is the Fool’s irony directed against Lear’s illusions. Colie (1974, pp. 131–2) compares Isa. 59:10, we stomble at noone day as in the twilight, and Job 5:14, They mete with darknes in the day time, and grope at noone day, as in the night. Jones (1975, pp. 135–6): Noon was the hour of the noon-day devil,…a time of dangerous, of death-like divorce between body and soul.…Noon [the zenith of the play] is the time of the estrangement of Lear’s mind.…When the play has reached this pitch, the Fool neither dies nor conspicuously exits, but slips quietly into irrelevance.…The [irrational] nature of the world…becomes more overt. Kinney (1976, p. 699) compares Eccles. 10:16, Wo to thee, ô land, when thy King is a childe, and thy princes eat in the morning (Geneva). Kavros (1981, pp. 305–6): The Fool…alludes to his Christ-like suffering and self-sacrifice…while serving Lear.…Christ…goes to the marriage bed of the cross, and of course he consummates his marriage [with mankind] at noon. Kerrigan (1983, pp. 228–9): The riposte…makes the audience keenly aware of the disorderliness of Lear’s life,…the world turned upside down.…[Moreover,] Goates beard or Go to bedde at noone…shutteth it selfe at twelue of the clocke [Gerard, Herball, 1597, pp. 594–5].…It cannot bear to see the kingly sun decline.…The Fool identifies himself with the flower, warning the audience that he can no longer follow the failing King. Similarly Doloff (1989). Brown (1985, p. 6): He folds up like the yellow goatsbeard. Taylor (1983, p. 405): The Folio’s added line…provid[es] the Fool with a much more prominent and enigmatic exit from the scene and the play; cf. Warren (1983) in n. 2010–12. Cope (1988, p. 278): He so avoids the destruction that wasteth at noonday (Psalms 91:6), the noonday devil of so many medieval and Renaissance commentaries. Halio (ed. 1992, p. 28): The remark heightens the nihilistic energies in the play. Foakes (1993, p. 197): It underlines the disorder in Lear’s mind and in the world around him.
Not all commentators have been convinced of the remark’s profundity. Lee (ed. 1908): It seems to lack recondite significance. Cunnington (1910, p. 451): An afterthought added to F, so that the Fool does not seem forgotten or thrown aside. Phelps (ed. 1917): Much sentimental nonsense has been gushed about this. Harrison (ed. 1948), simply: If it’s suppertime in the morning, it will be bedtime at noon. Wilson (ed. 1960): Critics have been mostly unaware of the proverbial relevance, which as a reply to Lear gives all the point required. Stone (1980, pp. 244–5): The proverb means: You are trying to deceive me, so that the Fool’s modification of it must mean: I shall, or am willing to, be deceived. But he has no motive at this juncture for saying any such thing. I suspect an interpolation, on the grounds that the reviser elsewhere interjects pointless or inappropriate quips.…[Deeper interpretations] are [not] warranted by anything but a sense that the Fool must surely say something important before departing finally from the scene—together, perhaps, with an impression that the line is oddly cryptic and must surely conceal more significance than it reveals. Weis (ed. 1993): For this entire scene Q offers a more integrated dramatic action with proper scope for the Fool (in F 3.6 the Fool speaks only three sentences altogether) and therefore does not require a valediction.…The Fool’s presence is in any case remembered by Kent in Q [2056+4].
As to the question why the Fool disappears so abruptly without explanation, there is some speculation. White (1880, p. 121): When Lear sinks from frenzy into forlorn imbecility, the Fool’s utterances would have jarred upon our ears. The situation becomes too grandly pathetic to admit the presence of a jester.…Even Shakespeare could not make sport with the great primal elements of woe.…Functus officio. Bradley (1904, pp. 258, 446) imagines an earlier explanation excised in revision: It seems doubtful whether his failure to give information about the fate of the Fool was due to anything more than carelessness or an impatient desire to reduce his overloaded material. Goggin (ed. 1910): There is nothing about his death in the play. He disappears suddenly from the action when his presence is no longer needed. Thaler (1929, pp. 37–8): To have made too much of the fool’s death—if, indeed, he does die—would have been to ignore essential human as well as dramatic distinctions.…The fool disappears…because he has done his work. He has outjested his master’s heartstruck injuries in the storm.…Cordelia brings true healing, and so the fool, his occupation gone, disappears.…Perhaps [Sh.] purposely allowed the fool to drop quietly out of sight because he also remembered that there was another person of the play who must go to bed at noon—Cordelia, a daughter and a queen. Welsford (1935, p. 164): His disappearance was a poetic necessity, for the King having lost everything, including his wits, has now himself become the Fool…so he now sees and speaks the truth. Brooke (ed. 1947): If Armin played only the Fool, it seems strange that so conspicuous an actor should have been allowed no appearance in the fourth or fifth act. The likelihood is that Armin, who was not very old [ca. 38 years in 1606], was obliged to take the part of Cordelia as well as his normal one, for Goneril and Regan made big demands on the available boys in the company. For this theory of double-casting see . Parrott (1949, p. 302): The rest of the action deals with what has been called the redemption of Lear; there was no place for this realistic humorous critic in the scene of reunion between father and daughter, even less in the tragic catastrophe which Shakespeare invented to bring this play to its tremendous close. Muir (ed. 1952): There is no particular reason, except novel-readers’ insatiable curiosity, why we should be told.…[The Fool] is no longer needed. (Ibid., p. lxiv): Since Lear can [now] act as his own Fool. Traversi (1952–3): At this moment, with Lear moved by the pressure of suffering to ask questions that transcend any conceivable particular situation, his function is complete. Felver (1961, p. 61): We may ask what part a Fool could play with a master whose wits have gone. Main (ed. 1962): It is not the sting of conscience that Lear will need when he regains his sanity, but the balm and tenderness of mercy.…In short,…Cordelia, not the Fool. Gardner (ed. 1969): The Fool’s function, to reflect Lear’s folly in his professional, particular mirror of truth, is finished. The King in his madness is now beyond the reach of the jester’s sharp sanity, and as Lear invited Poor Tom, the apparent Bedlam beggar, into service [i.e., as philosopher], the Fool sees his own service finished. Foakes (ed. 1997, pp. 57–8): I doubt if anyone watching a performance is troubled by it. Lear has gone mad, and can no longer relate to the wit of the Fool. The action takes a new direction with the blinding of Gloucester in 3.7, and Lear himself is offstage for roughly five hundred lines in the Quarto text.…When Lear returns in 4.6 he has become, in his madness, a kind of seer, with something of the Fool’s wisdom.…4.6 establishes a new cross-talk act in which Gloucester has become the feed to Lear, who effectively takes over something of the role of the Fool.…In Acts 2 and 3 the Fool’s comments are directed more to other characters such as Kent, or to everyone including the audience, and…usually have a generalizing force as expressing a kind of folk-wisdom. In Act 3 he is more concerned to persuade Lear to take shelter from the storm than to mock him. After 3.6 the Fool has no function, and it is understandable that Shakespeare should let him drop from sight. Webster (1942; 1955, p. 166) nonetheless: But he has also touched our hearts; quite simply, we want to know what happens to him. Shakespeare, perhaps, has no more need of him…, but we resent his disappearance.

Theobald (ed. 1733): These two concluding Speeches…which by no means ought to have been cut off, I have restored from the Old Quarto. The Soliloquy of Edgar is extreamly fine; and the Sentiments of it are drawn equally from Nature and the Subject. Besides, with Regard to the Stage it is absolutely necessary: For as Edgar is not design’d…to attend the King to Dover; how absurd would it look for a Character of his Importance to quit the Scene without one Word said, or the least Intimation what we are to expect from him? Delius (1876, pp. 142–3): Kent expressly asks the fool to help him carry out his master; as a result of F’s un-authorial cut, the Fool still helps to bear him out, but silently and unasked. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 227): [The cut of Kent’s speech] is probably due to a quick closing of the inner stage, which may have obviated the lifting of the sleeping Lear, and it has not the same validity [as the cut that follows]. Greg (1940, p. 301): Lear is picked up bodily and carried off by Kent and the Fool [citing 2047, 2056+4].…There is no hint that the traverse is used. Doran (1931, pp. 71–2): The lines give bibliographical evidence of having been deliberately removed and…yet, in themselves, show no reason for being undesirable.…[F 2056] is short unless each come is given a strong accent—as would be natural. Hart (1942, p. 147): Kent’s speech and Edgar’s platitudes were deservedly excised [by an adapter] as superfluous. Empson (1951, p. 141 n.): The speech is needed to give time to change the furniture on the inner stage; but see Greg above. Urkowitz (1980, p. 49): Because of the cuts, Q’s slower rhythms give way to those of F, unrelievedly urgent, compelling, and threatening.
