Idem (1983, p. 30): No canon of Renaissance stagecraft requires a sententious soliloquy for Edgar at this moment. Warren (1983, pp. 48–9): The Folio’s omission…helps to intensify the urgency of Gloucester’s point that even a half-hour’s delay could result in the death of Lear and his supporters.…[These cuts and 2014+1–+30] bring closer together the crises of Lear’s and Gloucester’s ordeals [1830, 2168].…This strengthens the dramatic structure of the play, and it also helps to prepare for the climactic meeting of the mad Lear and the blind Gloucester in 4.6. Muir (1983, p. 102): The soliloquy is…important to [Edgar] as a character. He plays so many parts…that we are liable to lose sight of the man behind the masks. The lines, moreover,…make the first verbal link between the two plots—He childed as I fathered—and they emphasize that the mental suffering of the King is harder to bear than the physical suffering of the Bedlam beggar. Whatever their effects, most probably the speeches were cut for the usual reason of shortening the scene and the play. The audience sees plainly enough without Edgar’s soliloquy that he does not accompany Lear because he has not been invited to do so (cf. 1955–63, 3168+5–+6), and that he is in mortal danger of discovery as long as he remains with Gloucester. See also n. 2056+5–+18. Weis (ed. 1993): Kent’s lines are not required to advance the narrative, but they function as a response to Gloucester’s urgings and spell out the bond which has gradually developed between Kent and the Fool; above all, Kent’s choric speech anticipates Lear’s madness. For these reasons Weis thinks (pp. 24–5) that the removal of Edgar’s soliloquy…is damaging to the F text and is not compensated for by F’s fleshing out of Edgar’s part by three and a half lines at [2184].

2056+1 Oppressed]
See n. 1384.

2056+2 balmed]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:5): Compose, heal as with Balm (OED, v. 3, Soothe, quoting this l.). On transitive verbs formed from nouns see n. 1197.

2056+2 broken]
OED (ppl. a. 5): Crushed or exhausted by labour, etc. Weis (ed. 1993): Broken by analogy with the rack.

2056+2 sinewes]
Malone (ed. 1790, 10:683) compares TN 2.5.75 (1089–90), we breake the sinewes of our plot; cf. OED (sb. 4): The main strength, mainstay, or chief supporting force, of something, the something in this case being the king’s whole frame (Malone, 1783, p. 50). Most eds. follow Delius (ed. 1854): Nerves (OED, 2); cf. Ven. 903. Theobald’s emendation senses (see textual n.), defended by many, is unnecessary. Wright (ed. 1875): Lear had received a great physical as well as mental shock. Gardner (ed. 1969): The thing least relevant is Lear’s body. But the physically violent imagery, applied to abstract considerations, is typical of the play, comparing 781–2, 1147.

2056+3 conuenience]
Schmidt (1874): Favourable circumstances (OED, sb. 7: Opportunity). Hudson (ed. 1881): Four syllables.

2056+3 hard cure]
Hudson (ed. 1881): Can hardly be cured. Cf. Oth. 2.1.51 (808), Stand in bold Cure.

2056+4 Come…behind]
Halio (ed. 1973): The Foole’s heart is evidently breaking; as he begins to sink from exhaustion, Kent…has to stir him to help bear Lear off to Dover.

–2056 Exit.]
Lear is not seen for almost another 500 lines, reappearing at 2526. The actor may rest after four strenuous scenes and before three more. Q’s singular SD includes Lear, Gloucester, Kent, and the Fool; F’s Exeunt includes Edgar as well.

2056+5–+18 Edg.…lurke.]
See n. 2056+1–+4, +5–+18. Though a few eds. share the suspicion of Clark & Wright (ed. 1866) and Hudson (ed. 1881), based on stylistic grounds, that the lines are spurious, most agree with Delius (1876, p. 143) that their presence in Q is a strong argument of their genuineness, and that the style is Shn. enough: We readily admit that the style…is not that of the rest of the drama; but…Shakspere is fond of introducing such rhyming lines [citing Oth. 1.3.201–19 (550–67), Cor. 2.3.113–24 (1503–15), Tro. 1.2.282–95 (440–53), Ham. 3.2.155 ff. (2024 ff.)], formed of a number of pointed, epigrammatic, antithetical sentences. They stand out from the surrounding blank verse, and point the moral which the audience should draw from the preceding situation, and the actions of the different characters.…[Also,] the poet lays great stress on the parallelism existing between the families of Lear and Gloster, and takes this opportunity of again impressing it upon his audience. A mere interpolator would hardly have known of this particular tendency of the poet, or have carried it out so thoroughly, and in so pregnant a manner, as in the few but completely Shakesperian words—He childed as I father’d. For the same reason, it is more than improbable that Shakspere should have cut out this passage, thereby thwarting his own purposes. Among those unpersuaded are Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxix), who finds the lines (and 3168+1–+18) if in reality…by Shakespeare,…among the most striking instances of degeneracy in rhyming passages which the plays present, and Deighton (ed. 1891): The passage comes upon one like a sudden gust of icy wind in warm weather. The language does not sound to me Shakespearean; I remember no play in which, in the midst of such intensely tragic interest, any similar moralizing intrudes itself; the progress of the action is not in any way furthered; while as to the parallelism between the families of Lear and Gloucester, it was not in Shakespeare’s way to write under a picture This is a house. Verity (ed. 1897) compares the rhyming lines 194–201, 3294–3301, etc., adding, In the latter part of Edgar’s words the rhyme produces the effect of leave-taking and conclusion to the situation. Cf. 279–86. Bradley (1904, pp. 452–3): Some words of soliloquy are wanted;…he is left to return to the hovel where he was first found.…He must be left behind, and surely would not go off without a word.…The lines are in spirit of one kind with Edgar’s fine lines at the beginning of Act IV. Granville-Barker (1927, pp. 150, 227): Edgar’s two soliloquies [i.e., this and 2179–92]…are somewhat redundant in mood if not in matter.…The Folio omission is of a speech ending a scene and moralising upon the event; it forms a considering point. Without it the catastrophe to Gloucester is linked more closely to Lear’s misfortunes, and the long due development of Edgar’s character then begins—and importantly—in the fourth Act.…[The present soliloquy] must lower the tension of the action. This may damage the scene of Gloucester’s blinding.…The chief purpose of the soliloquy, moreover, is to give Edgar a fresh start in his dramatic life. It is a quiet start, the effect of which the violent scene that follows must do much to obliterate. When the Folio, then, postpones it to the beginning of Act IV, it does Edgar a double service, as the Quarto doubles the disservice by making the second soliloquy, when it comes, seem dramatically redundant. Warren (1978, p. 103): The absence of Edgar’s moral meditation from the end of 3.6 brings the speech at 4.1.1 into sharp focus, isolating it more obviously between the blinding and the entrance of Gloucester.…Edgar gains in prominence, ironically enough, by the loss of a speech. Carroll (1988, pp. 240–2) rejects this less is really more paradox and gives several arguments for the speech’s retention, including its providing a full revelation of Edgar’s state of mind after the agonies of the mock-trial, comment on the Breughelesque spectacle we have just witnessed, and the powerful irony of He…fathered (2056+13). Doran (1931, p. 71): The omission is connected with the omission of several preceding lines belonging to Kent which are equally unobjectionable; cf. n. 2056+1–+4, +5–+18. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 8): Such sententious general observations drawn from what he has just witnessed…would be extremely likely to be cut in an abridgement. Crane (1952, pp. 164–5): There is great dramatic art in this conclusion, which brings forward the half-naked wretch to speak in sententious couplets whose orderly precision is at the farthest remove from his appearance and from his mad gabbling during the scene just past. Traversi (1952–3, p. 139): The first anticipation of a new spirit is finally confirmed at this point by Edgar. The rhyming sentences…express a new mood of acceptance which is to be characteristic of his future behaviour and of an attitude which comes, from now on, to play an increasing part in the development of the tragedy.…[The utterance’s] rhymed artificiality is clearly calculated to give it the value of a comment, isolating it, in a certain sense, from the surrounding action. Brown (ed. 1976): These stiff verses usefully effect a shift in the audience’s attention.…To the actor it is an opportunity to drop Edgar’s disguise and show a new thoughtfulness: the strange syntax and word order can suggest a tormented mind. Styan (1979, p. 138): The speech, carefully rhymed for impersonality, is pure choric commentary on Lear’s suffering, necessary for our understanding. Muir (1983, p. 102): The soliloquy is…important to him as a character. He plays so many parts in the course of the play that we are liable to lose sight of the man behind the masks. Weis (ed. 1993): Whereas in F Edgar leaves with the others, in Q he stays behind which better prepares us for his reappearance in 4.1.…F’s text fails to explain adequately how Edgar becomes separated from the others, and why he should have progressed…to the more sanguine verse of 4.1.

2056+5–+6 When…foes]
Inexplicably, Q misprints as prose the first of several rhyming couplets.

2056+5 our woes]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Woes of the same nature with our own. Skillan (ed. 1967): Cruelty of their own kin. Kittredge (ed. 1940) compares 2056+12–+13.

2056+5–+6 we…foes]
Harrison (ed. 1937): Our sufferings seem slight.

2056+6 our foes]
Harbage (ed. 1958): I.e. our peculiar foes (they seem rather a part of universal misery).

2056+7 alone suffers]
Hunter (ed. 1869) and most eds.: Has no fellow-sufferer. Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956) only: Has no example of the sufferings of others. Tovey (ed. 1896): The emphasis is on alone and most. Kittredge (ed. 1940): An elaboration of the familiar proverb: Misery loves company (Tilley C571, citing this l.). Cunliffe (1893, p. 86) compares Seneca’s Troas 1009–12, and Miola (1992, p. 150) adds his Ag. 664–7. Edwards (ed. 1975), however: The solitary sufferer…[is] excluded from the care-free life and happy scenes enjoyed by others. Doran (1931, p. 31): Q2’s omission of the second suffer may be deliberate, but…[is] ill-advised.

2056+8 Leauing…behind]
Rann (ed. 1794): Deriving no comfort from happier objects around him. Harrison (ed. 1937): As he contrasts the present misery with the happy past. Hunter (ed. 1972): Of carefree lives and joyful sights.

2056+8 free things]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Free, for undisturbed. Heath (1765, p. 341): Things free from suffering. Johnson (ed. 1765): States clear from distress. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Care-free, comparing 1791, 2525.

2056+8 happy showes]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Happy scenes. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Happy looks; all appearances of happiness. Traversi (1952–3, p. 140): In a certain sense as delusions.

2056+9 then]
Anticipating When in the next line. Eccles (ed. 1792): At such a juncture.

2056+9 sufferance]
Schmidt (1875): Distress, misery, suffering (OED, 4).

2056+9 or’e scip]
OED (Overskip v. 2): Fig. To skip over, pass over without notice, quoting this l.

2056+10 bearing fellowship]
Hunter (ed. 1869): When bearing, or suffering, hath fellowship. Moberly (ed. 1876), bearing: Endurance (OED, vbl. sb. 5). Verity (ed. 1897): More probably…a participle, thus: When grief hath mates and companionship which bear its (grief’s) troubles with it.

2056+11 portable]
Schmidt (1875): Sufferable (OED, a. 2: Bearable, quoting this l.).

2056+12 bow]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Here the stronger word, perhaps, implying that the king has broken down more completely than Edgar. But it may simply be synonymous with bend: cf. 2056+5, our woes. The words are often found together: see OED, and Tom a Lincoln 1445, 1606.

2056+13 He…fathered]
Delius (ed. 1854): He has just such children as I have father (Ger.). Hunter (ed. 1869): Or, he treated by his children as I by my father. Hunter (ed. 1972): Who seeks my life. Wales (1978, p. 402): Possibly He (being) made, turned into, a child as I (being) made, turned into, a father. Weis (ed. 1993, p. 25): F’s omission of this line removes the most explicit recognition by any character in the play of the extent to which the fates of Lear and Edgar interconnect. The lines acquire particular poignancy…because Lear is Edgar’s godfather. On passive verbs formed from nouns see n. 223. Childed, not found elsewhere in Sh., is the first ex. of the word cited by OED, and fathered is the second after JC 2.1.297 (939). Orgel (ed. 1999) would read He is childed.

2056+13 Tom away]
Generally taken to mean Tom, depart. Only Hunter (ed. 1869): Be no longer Tom.

2056+14 Marke…noyses]
Heath (1765, p. 341): Observe the event of those disturbances that are now on foot. Capell (1783, 1.2:171) takes high to mean among the high and the great; Steevens (ed. 1793), of high moment: The loud tumults of the approaching war. Malone (ed. 1790), alternatively: The proclamation…for bringing in Edgar. Tovey (ed. 1896): Rumours of great events. Quinn (ed. 1970): Evidence that events of great importance are about to take place. Horsman (ed. 1973): Rumors from high places, or about those in high estate. Most eds. understand that Edgar means to attend to the course of events, which will give him his cue when to bewray himself (Wilson, ed. 1960); only Delius (ed. 1854) thinks that Edgar finds solace in contrasting his own trivial concerns with those of the great.

2056+14 bewray]
See n. 1048. Here the meaning is discover (Heath, 1765, p. 341; OED, v. 4).

2056+15–+16 When…thee]
Heath (1765, p. 341): When the present false opinion entertained of thee, which stains thy reputation with a crime of which thou art innocent, being convicted by thy full proof, repeals thy present banishment from society, and reconciles thee to thy father. The expression is somewhat inexact, since false opinion can reconcile Edgar only when it ceases to be false. Delius (ed. 1854): The adj. false applies only when opinion is antecedent to whose…defiles thee, not when opinion is subject of repeals and reconciles (Ger.). Wells (ed. 2000), more simply: In this [second] line, the subject is understood to be true, not false, opinion.

2056+15 thoughts defile]
Furness (ed. 1880): For the sake of rhyme Theobald [see textual n.] changed this to thought defiles; but Walker [1860, 1:143], in his Article on occasional licenses of rhyme in Sh. and his contemporaries, shows, by many instances, how common such an imperfect rhyme, as this, is.

2056+16 In…proofe]
Delius (ed. 1854): When you are proven just.

2056+16 repeals]
Schmidt (1875): Restore[s] to honour or place (OED, v. 3a, 3d). Gardner (ed. 1969): The technical word for recall from banishment (OED, 3b).

2056+16 reconciles thee]
Most eds. take this to mean with thy father; only Harbage (ed. 1958) makes it reflexive: [Opinion] makes peace with you.

2056+17 What will hap]
Hunter (ed. 1869), what: Whatsoever. Cf. 3045. Most eds. understand Whatever else may happen; alternatively, Abbott (§254) would needlessly complicate the meaning by putting a comma after will and making hap optative: Happen what will, more to night—a construction that requires a fuller stop after night and thus weakens the connection with the following clause.

2056+17 safe scape]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): May the king escape safely.

2056+18 Lurke, lurke]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Remain in hiding. Brooke (ed. 1947): Edgar conceals himself as Cornwall et al. enter. Q lacks an Exit SD; in F Edgar has already exited, at –2056. Q’s omission and the mislining of Edgar’s first line might seem to hint at some irregularity in the MS—was the speech a later addition in Q or, alternatively, marked for omission?—but they are types of error too slight and common to prove anything here.

2057 <Scena Septima>]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): This scene takes place immediately after Scene vi, apparently on the next day—the day following the stormy night. Greg (1940, p. 437): For Cornwall is not the man to suffer delay either in the arrest of Gloucester or in preparations to meet the danger of invasion. Idem (1940, p. 301): [This] scene…requires a chair [citing 2098].…It may have been left over from iii.iv and be moved at the end along with the body of the servant. Adams (1948) assumes use of the upper stage; see nn. 333, 1969. Reynolds (1962, p. 94): The stage is as it was at the beginning of his series of scenes, the gate open or at least ajar, the place vaguely an outside court within Gloucester’s castle. Cornwall, the sisters, and Edmund enter Center; Oswald comes from the Right announcing Lear’s flight; Goneril, Edmund, and Oswald say goodbye and exeunt Left; Cornwall orders Gloucester’s arrest, and he is presently brought in Right, bound in a chair, just inside the gate, since after the blinding, Regan says Go…gate.

2058 Bastard]
F adds and Seruants. One is killed at 2155, and one or two also seem implied by the two commands at 2174–5. In Q two more are specified at 2176+1, +3.

2060–71 Post…Gloster]
Q misprints prose as if it were verse. Doran (1931, p. 129) suspects that the printer was confused by revisions in Sh.’s MS; Smidt (1990, p. 138) thinks these lines, with their redundant farewells (cf. 2081–2), were added in revision, to prepare for Albany’s participation in the war.

2060 Post]
Harrison (ed. 1948): Ride fast (OED, v. 2). Cf. 2393, n. 1306. Harbage (1963, p. 420): Goneril and Albany must unite to resist the invading French.

2061 letter]
See n. 1980.

2061 France]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): The French King.

2061 landed]
See n. 1764.

2062 vilaine]
Gloucester is called a villain again in 2099, 2164, 2174. For the word’s association with villein, peasant, thereby indicating low social and/or moral stature, see nn. 439, 444, 2152. F changes here to Traitor, the name used again in both Q and F at 2067, 2082, 2089, 2096, 2102. Since the terms are interchanged throughout the scene, probably the variant here is not highly significant, though Ioppolo (1991, p. 175) makes much of it. Kinney (1976, p. 700): Gloucester surely commits treason—he sends thirty-five or thirty-six men to join Lear. Main (ed. 1962): The real traitor [is] Cornwall, who would put Lear to death. Like Strier (1988, p. 119), Foakes (1993, p. 198): In supporting the French (Cordelia) Gloucester really is a traitor to his own country. There is no evidence that Gloucester supports the French in any way; he sends Lear to Dover to save him from a plot of murder (2048). At 2097 he denies being a traitor. His disloyalty is only to his arch and patron Cornwall, not to his country; and of course he remains loyal to Lear. Foakes (ed. 1997): Thus stressing the confusion of values in the play; to be loyal to Lear is to be a traitor to his daughters. Olson (1961, p. 215): If there was to be war the king had to be killed at once; Cornwall and Regan had already plotted his death; Gloucester had overheard and frustrated it. Mack (1965, p. 12): In Tate’s version Gloster is a traitor, sending letters to the Duke of Cambrai, urging help against the sisters (1681, p. 26), thereby giving Cornwall a motive. Tennenhouse (1986, pp. 138–9): He has polluted his class by declaring his bastard son legitimate: By undergoing ritual punishment, Gloucester purifies the aristocratic body. But the aristocrats who punish him both embrace Edmund, Cornwall as a father (1995), Regan as a lover (2417–19).
Sisson (1956, 2:237) questions the customary Exeunt here: Cornwall is as yet only laying out his plans. At [2082–3] he gives his order, and a stage-direction is necessary, Exeunt servants. There is no need to despatch two expeditions in search of Gloucester, who is in the castle.

2063 Hang]
Colie (1974, p. 204): Though noblemen could be, and were, put under attainder and executed for treason, they could not be hanged…and certainly could not be blinded. Neither were they properly subject to the summary justice meted out by Cornwall (who was himself uneasy about it <[2084–7]>).

2063 Plucke…eyes]
Foakes (ed. 1997): An appropriate punishment since it was sight that attracted men to commit adultery. Blinding had been a medieval penalty for rape. Cornwall is of course not punishing Gloucester for adultery, let alone rape. No one in the play defends the blinding as appropriate, nor would any audience think it so. Goneril proposes it, and Cornwall’s and Regan’s power simply does a courtesy to their wrath.

2064–6 company]
In Q(u) the final word (company) in line 2065–6, the last line on the page, is turned up after line 2064, as it must have been in the galley; when pages were made up, however, 2064 became the first line on the next page, and this turnover on the previous page was eventually removed in Q(c). Instead, the same final word was turned under the first line on the next page (turnovers not usually appearing above the first line of text). Blayney (1982, p. 118): The adjustment on the next page was assumedly made before presswork began.

2065 to my displeasure]
Cornwall is making a grim joke, the usual phrase being to (or at) one’s pleasure.

2065, 2066 company]
Delius (ed. 1854): On her journey back to her husband Albany (Ger.). The command is so natural as to be unnoticeable, but it begins the division between the sisters; cf. 2282–94. Rosenberg (1972, p. 240): Regan cares enough to notice and recall later how they are eyeing each other; cf. 2412, n. 2382. In Q1(u) the word company is turned both over and under sister. Greg (1940, p. 168): The compositor, when nearing the end of his page, set up in his stick more lines than were needed to complete it. He happened to turn up the end of one line. When he divided the page immediately before the line he remembered to set up the turned over word again below, but forgot to take out the original setting above.

2066, 2071 reuenge]
F’s plural reuenges had appeared earlier in 1579, where there were two objects of revenge. The change in F may have been made unconsciously, to even the prose rhythm.

2066, 2069 bound]
Craig (ed. 1901): Ready, prepared (OED, ppl. a.1 1). Muir (ed. 1952): Or possibly, obliged (OED, ppl. a.2 7).

2068 aduise]
F’s Aduice is a variant spelling.

2068 Duke]
Albany. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 401): The comma (absent from Q and F) must be added,…[lest] the reader might think that the where clause was the object of Aduice. The counterpart comma after going is added in F.

2068 where]
Mason (1785, p. 350): To whom. Kittredge (ed. 1940): To whose palace.

2068 To]
Wilson (ed. 1960): To make. Wells (ed. 2000) To expedite.

2069 festuant]
The correct festinate may have been intended in F1’s festiuate, and was achieved in F2’s festinat. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 401): The copy for Q probably had festinat. With an extra minim stroke ina could easily be misread uan. OED (Festinate adj.: Hasty) quotes this l. as its first ex.; Sh. had already used festinately in LLL 3.1.6 (776), and Schäfer (1980, p. 147) finds festinate as a verb in Nashe, Saffron Walden (ed. McKerrow, 3:91). Brook (1976, p. 30), festinate: Some Latin loan-words are used comically in some plays [i.e., LLL], but seriously in others [e.g. Lr.].…It may be that such words had come to be accepted between the date of the early play and that of the later play. Stone (1980, p. 182) proposes festinant, previously adopted by Ridley (see textual n.) but unattested in OED. Halio (ed. 1992): Either [F] Compositor B similarly misread copy, or more likely F festiuate is the result of a turned letter. See also .

2069 preparatiõ]
Craig (ed. 1901): For battle.

2069 the like]
Verity (ed. 1897): To make similar speedy…preparations.

2070 post]
See n. 1306. F’s plural Postes is not strictly necessary, and is more difficult to say before shall. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 519): Omission of the s would be particularly easy for a compositor carrying posts shall in his head, and it seems odd for Cornwall to imply that they have [will use?] only one messenger.

2070 intelligence]
Stone (1980, p. 220) understands Q’s word as a verb: Convey intelligence (OED, v. 1); Weis (ed. 1993), as a noun in an (elliptical) phrase: There will be…information traded between us. Since posts always convey intelligence, such readings may be more redundant than F’s intelligent if the latter means full of (rather than carrying) information (see n. 1634). Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 401): The [Q] compositor may have misread intelligent as intelligenc.

2071 Gloster]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Meaning Edmund, newly invested with his Father’s titles. The Steward, speaking immediately after, mentions the old Duke [sic] by the same title; by force of habit, Edmund’s claim to it being new and scarcely yet made known (Porter & Clarke, ed. 1905). Verity (ed. 1897): The title is pronounced with significant emphasis, indicating to Edmund that Cornwall has not forgotten his promise in 1987–8.

2072 Enter…]
On F’s anticipatory stage direction see n. 1358.

2073 How now]
See n. 361.

2073 whers the King]
See n. 2048.

2074 conueyd]
Schmidt (1874): Transport[ed] (OED, v. 4). Page (ed. 1889): Carried secretly (OED, 6).

2075 Some]
See n. 22.

2076 hot]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Rapid and eager (OED, adj. 6a).

2076 questrits]
Most eds. accept F’s Questrists, a nonce-word (OED) for questers (Capell, 1783 [1774], 1.1:54). Lott (ed. 1974): Associated with equestrian; Halio (ed. 1992) compares Latin equestris = equestrian. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 401): The compositor has accidentally omitted a single letter, an argument rejected by Taylor (1983, p. 488): The compositor would have needed an st ligature. Since F’s word amounts to a superfluous derivation from a noun, quester, of identical meaning (Stone, 1980, p. 50), and seems to imply the impossible verb to questrize (Tovey, ed. 1896), substitutes have been suggested. Among these are questist (Heath, 1765, p. 41), querist (Eccles, ed. 1792, from an ed. of Sh. pub. Dublin, 1771, 5.1:74), and questant (Rolfe, ed. 1880, from AWW 2.1.16 [613], another nonce-word; see textual n.). Whatever the word, eds. generally agree on the meaning: Seekers—ever since Lear left Albany’s house (Horsman, ed. 1973). Stone, however, recommends questrels, a variant sp. of custrel or coystril, groom, referring it to the squires accompanying Lear’s knights. But a custrel may not be a squire: Sh.’s only two known uses (TN 1.3.40 [156], Per. 4.6.166 [1935–6]) of the word have the pejorative sense knave (OED Coistrel 2, Custrel 2); a hot quest may be an easier sense than a hot custrel; and the further emendation of after him to after ’em is required. Porter (1986, p. 486) cites quistrell-scummes, clearly pejorative, in John Eliot’s Ortho-epia Gallica (1593, sig. s3r).

2076 at gate]
On omission of the definite article see n. 1285.

2077 other]
See n. 713.

2077 Lords dependants]
Hudson (ed. 1871): Dependant lords…of the King’s retinue. Furness (ed. 1880): Gloucester’s dependants.…We have heard of no lords who were dependant on the king. He had certain knights, and of these five or six and thirty had come to seek him, and, under the guidance of some of Gloucester’s followers, they had all hurried off to Dover, citing 2913–14. Cf. 2049, 2055–6. On no evidence whatever Schmidt (ed. 1879) imagines the lords to be vassals of Cornwall who had declared for Lear. Hudson (ed. 1879), like most subsequent eds., is persuaded by Furness’s arguments. Halio (ed. 1992): Some three dozen [knights] join with Gloucester’s men to form a suitable entourage for Lear’s trip to Dover, whence they seem to disappear or merge with the forces supporting the king.

2078 towards Douer]
How far and how long does Lear travel, if Cornwall’s house is in Gloucester (see n. 875) and Gloucester’s house, the present setting, is a night’s ride nearby (cf. 1040–3)? Greg (1940, pp. 431–2): Oswald goes from Cornwall’s [rather, from Gloucester’s; cf. 2400] to the neighbourhood of Dover [cf. 2431, 2675] while Lear is wandering distracted about the fields [cf. 2356–7, 2526].…All this vagueness is intentional and designed to prevent topographical difficulties impeding the rapidity of the action. On modern roads, the distance from Gloucester to Dover is about 180 miles. Hughes (1916, 1:201–2): Though on Elizabethan roads post riders might make 50 to 150 miles a day, For ordinary travel, English gentlemen rode…twenty or thirty miles. Whether transported by litter (2049) or wandering on foot, Lear would manage less. His journey would take several days, very likely a week or more.

2081 Exit…Bast.]
F omits the names; normally F has Exeunt without names (cf. 1586), making Exit plural as needed (e.g., 291, 598, etc.); here Exit seems to have been in the MS. The single form for plural departures is common; possibly the sense was understood to be Goneril goes out, with the Bastard. Greg (1940, p. 437): Oswald…posts on ahead and reaches home before them ([2269]).

2083 Pinion…theefe]
Houghton (ed. 1957): The language…provid[es] a parallel with Lear’s mock trial. Foakes (ed. 1997): A shocking way to treat an aristocrat.

2083 theefe]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): A robber. A stronger word than in modern usage. The point seems to be that Gloucester should be treated in a rough, undignified way, like a common criminal rather than an earl, not that he has stolen away Lear or anything else.

2084 we]
Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 519), on F’s well we: Though Q could easily have omitted well by eyeskip (as Blayney suggests), metrical emendation is unnecessary, since a defective initial foot is acceptable, especially (as here) where it could form a part of a line-divided foot (before us, | Though we may…).

2084 passe vpon]
Johnson (in Steevens, ed. 1773): Pass a judicial sentence (OED, v. 21c, quoting this l.). Steevens (ed. 1773): The original of the expression…may be traced from Magna Charta—hence, there is an anachronism here. Only Becket (1815, 1:162): From fencing…strike at (OED, 24). Bransom (1934, p. 85): He intended to put Gloster to death.…According to the political standards of Shakespeare’s time, this was the thing to do. Gloster was a powerful member of the king’s faction;…and in time of war forms of justice have sometimes to be suspended. In the event, Gloucester is blinded, not put to death.

2085 forme]
The term here probably implies both established legal procedure and mere outward ceremony (OED, sb. 11, 15); cf. 1351. Only Gardner (ed. 1969): The framing of a trial.

2085 power]
I.e., power to inflict penalties, legal authority (OED sb.1 5a).

2086 doe a courtesie to]
Johnson (in Steevens, ed. 1773): Comply with. The manner of compliance has been specified as bend to (as in doing a curtsy) (Steevens, ed. 1773), obey (Schmidt, 1874), yield to (Wright, ed. 1875), indulge (Moberly, ed. 1876), oblige (Tovey, ed. 1896), gratify (Johnson; Harrison, ed. 1937), serve (Gardner, ed. 1969), defer (Horsman, ed. 1973), etc. Cf. Kent’s anger has a priuiledge (1143).

2086 which]
Wright (ed. 1875): The antecedent is contained in the previous clause—i.e., the action…of condemning Glo. without a proper trial (Deighton, ed. 1891). Delius (ed. 1854): Though possibly wrath; cf. 1143. So Harrison (ed. 1937): Which will pass for a loss of temper.

2088 Enter…]
On F’s anticipatory stage direction see n. 1358.

2088 two or three]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 107): Too vague for a prompt-book. Werstine (privately): Prompt-book is anachronistic; such vagueness is common in actual theatrical MSS from Sh.’s time.

2090 Ingratfull]
See n. 1445. Hunter (ed. 1972): He has shown ingratitude by failing in loyalty to his arch and patron Cornwall.

2090 Fox]
See n. 2014+6. Hunter (ed. 1972): He has been foxy in his sly and secretive dealing with Lear and his friends. Foakes (ed. 1997): Proverbial for its craftiness, citing Tilley F629, F645.

2091 corkie]
Not elsewhere in Sh. Percy (in Steevens, ed. 1778): Probably suggested by an old corkie woman in Harsnett (1603, p. 23). Johnson (ed. 1765): Dry, withered, husky [like cork] (OED, a. 2: Sapless, quoting only this l. and Harsnett).

2092 meanes]
On the inflection see n. 204.

2093 good my friends]
On the transposed adjective see n. 102. Tovey (ed. 1896): Addressed to the servants, who are beginning to bind him. But the next words show that he is more probably addressing Cornwall and Regan. Foakes (ed. 1997): For friends to attack their host Gloucester in his own house is an especially brutal violation of hospitality, comparing 2105–7.

2094 foule play]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Not, as in modern usage, confined to the sense of murder,…[but suggesting] something that is out of acccord with law and justice.

2095 Bind…say]
Halio (ed. 1992): Cornwall has to order the reluctant servants twice.

2096 Hard]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Tight (OED, adv. 4).

2096 filthie]
Craig (ed. 1901): Odious, disgraceful (OED, a. 4). Cf. 1090.

2097 as]
Deighton (ed. 1891): That (OED, conj. 25, quoting this l.).

2097 true]
I.e., faithful (OED, adj. 1), not a traitor. F’s none substitutes a simple denial.

2098 To…him]
Wilson (ed. 1960): At [2095–6] his arms are bound to his body; here he is tied down to the chair. Leggatt (1992, pp. 182 f.): Anticipating Lucretia Borgia’s use of a chair in the murder of her husband in The Devil’s Charter—shortly thereafter [Feb. 1607], and in the same playhouse [the Globe]. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 103): This scene echoes the way the women subjected to exorcism in Harsnett were bound in a chair (1603, pp. 39, 42, 220, 243–4). Possibly; but prisoners are often so bound.

2100 kind Gods]
Warburton (1739, p. 194): Dii hospitales. Steevens (apud Johnson, ed. 1765) rejects any assistance from mythology, to furnish out a proper oath for Gloster. People always address the Gods as they would have them shew themselves at that time in their favour. So Davies (1783, 2:301): There is no occasion for any ostentation of learning or acuteness here. Cf. 2169, 2763.

2100 ignobly]
Schmidt (1874): Disgracefully. McCann (ed. 1964): Unworthy of the nobility, mean.

2101 pluck…beard]
Harrison (ed. 1937): The greatest indignity that could be offered. Cf. 2150–1 and Ham. 2.2.573 (1613). She probably scrutinizes the plucked hairs before her next speech.

2102 white]
McCann (ed. 1964): Symbolic of purity, said mockingly. Lott (ed. 1974): In contrast to…the blackness of his deed. Brown (ed. 1976): Venerable looking/cowardly.

2103 Naughty]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): Wicked (OED, adj. 3). Kittredge (ed. 1940): A strong adjective in Elizabethan English. Cf. 1412, 1890.

2104 rauish]
Schmidt (1875): Carry away by force (OED, v. 4).

2105 quicken]
Mason (1785, p. 350): Into life (OED, v. 6, 7).

2106 robbers]
Plural in most eds. Foakes (ed. 1997): Possibly Gloucester’s change from thou to you means hs is addressing both Regan and Cornwall.

2106 hospitable]
Wright (ed. 1875): Of me your host.

2106 fauours]
Steevens (ed. 1778) and most eds.: Features…of which a face is composed (OED, sb. 9c, quoting 1H4 3.2.136 [1956]). Wells (ed. 2000): Looks of welcome. Hunter (ed. 1972): Perhaps the indulgences of my hospitality is simpler.

2107 ruffell]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Roughly tear (OED, Ruffle v.2 5, quoting this l. as its first ex. of two). Deighton (ed. 1891): Disorder (OED, v.1 2, 3). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Treat with…violence (OED, v.2 4), comparing 1604. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 103): Incorporating a word associated by Harsnett with devils who ruffle and rage. See n. 1604.

2108–9 Come…France]
F’s division of one pentameter into two lines seems due to the insufficient width of the column.

2109 letters]
See n. 875. But Cornwall may suspect more than one letter.

2110 simple answerer]
Either Q’s reading or F’s simple-answer’d is good sense: simple means plain (Steevens, ed. 1773), straightforward(ly). In Elizabethan script d is easily confused with e or er; cf. 3136. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Answer’d is not a participle, but an adjective formed from the noun answer, citing similar exx. Cf. 2112. Weis (ed. 1993) makes Q’s reading a vocative: Be simple, answerer, which would be bathetic after filthie traytor and villaine.

2111–12 And…tratours]
F may fail to line as a pentameter because of the inadequate column width.

2111 confederacy]
Schmidt (1874): Alliance, conspiracy (OED, 2). Deighton (ed. 1891): Generally in Shakespeare…in a bad sense.

2111–12 tratours]
Ioppolo (1991, p. 175): Perhaps…refer[s] to Cordelia in the Quarto, and to the unidentified leader of the French troops in the Folio. It cannot refer to either, however, since neither owes allegiance to Britain. OED (sb. 2): One who is false to his allegiance to his sovereign or to the government of his country. Cornwall clearly refers to British who are gathering on the side of Cordelia, Lear, and Gloucester to oppose the dukes; cf. 2079, 2395–6, 2867–8. He is not thinking of an invasion from France, as at [2061], as Foakes (ed. 1997) claims. Only British residents disloyal to their leaders could be called traitors; the French are foreign-enemy invaders. The Britons loyal to Lear appear in the sources: see n. 2868+3–+4. Knowles (1999, p. 284): Cornwall and Regan first interrogate Gloucester about his connections with the French—What…France?—and then, to plumb the depth of his supposed treachery, ask him also about his connections with the British sympathizers at Dover, the well armed Friends of Lear’s knights—And <note the And> what confederacie…Lunaticke King.

2112 footed]
See n. 1764. On verbs formed from nouns see n. 1197. Kittredge (ed. 1940): An adjective, not a participle: see n. 2110.

2113 whose]
Eccles (ed. 1792): The relative to traitors, and not an interrogative: The words may, notwithstanding, be put interrogatively, i.e. as a continuation of Cornwall’s inquiry. Q2 inverts you haue to make an inquiry; Doran (1931, p. 33): this transposition is certainly for the better, although I do not believe that the order is necessarily wrong in Q1 and F. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 402): Regan may mean Tell us (speake) to whose hands…. If so,…the [Q1] inversion is harsh; but Shakespeare may have intended it to be so. Wilson (ed. 1960): Reg. need not ask, citing 2110, 2119. Foakes (ed. 1997): After all, Regan knows what Gloucester has done (see [2077–8]).

2114 lunatick]
Goggin (ed. 1910): How does Regan know that Lear is insane? Hunter (ed. 1972): A good example of Shakespearian foreshortening.

2114 King]
Wilson (ed. 1960): The F colon = a pause, wh. fills out the line.

2115 I…letter]
Colman (ed. 1982): Gloucester does not realize that Edmund stole it and gave it to Cornwall.

2115 gessingly]
OED (Guessing ppl. adv.): In a guessing manner; by guess-work or conjecture, quoting this l. as its first ex. Joseph (ed. 1966): Or evasively written, so that the significance must be guessed.

2116 heart]
See n. 852.

2122–3 Wherefore…that]
Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 222): Pysma is a figure which asks many questions requiring diverse answers.…If this figure is carried too far…it becomes the fallacy of many questions. Thus…Cornwall interrupts and checks [Regan’s] vehement impetuosity. For answers to Regan’s and Cornwall’s question, see n. 2256.

2123 at perill]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Under penalty (of death). In fact Cornwall warned only of displeasure (1756), but Gloucester understands it to be mortal: cf. 1768.

2124 first]
F’s omission may be metrical.

2125 tide…stake]
Muir (ed. 1952): Like a baited bear, comparing Mac. 5.7.2 (2396). Elton (1966, p. 234): When we recall the proximity of the bear pits to the Globe and the fact that sometimes the very theaters themselves were dismantled for bearbaiting, we recapture part of the powerful analogy in the spectators’ minds. Dent (1981, S813.1): A proverbial metaphor, citing JC 4.1.48 (1904). Willson (1989): The scene intentionally resembles a bear-baiting, to evoke special pity for Gloucester.

2126 stand]
OED (v. 52b): Withstand, quoting this l.

2126 course]
Johnson (ed. 1765): The running of the dogs upon me (OED, sb. 7). Tovey (ed. 1896): In bear-baiting, each attack was called a course (OED, 26b).

2127 sir]
F’s omission is possibly metrical.

2128–38 Because…children]
Pechter (1978, p. 196): The speech is unqualifiedly heroic, rich in alliteration, inversion, suspension of predication, Latinate and archaic diction—an assumption of the high style which, given [Gloucester’s] tendency…to short bursts of anxious declaration…is quite astonishing here, but completely convincing. Gloucester does not specifically name the plot of murder he has overheard; see 2048.

2128 nayles]
See n. 826.

2129 Pluck…eyes]
Verity (ed. 1897): By a stroke of terrible irony Gloucester suggests his own torture, comparing 2064. Koppel (1899, p. 93): He anticipates it. Olson (1961, pp. 214–15): The ensuing scene shows that Regan would be capable of doing this to Lear. Pauls (1984, p. 95) compares Leir 1906, where Ragan threatens to scratch out Cordella’s eyes.

2130 aurynted]
Q1(c)’s annoynted is certainly correct (Greg, 1940, p. 168). Apparently a misreading in Q1(u) of MS anoynted, and probably not influenced by arint (1903), set six pages earlier. Hunter (ed. 1869): An allusion to the Divine ordination of kings by the ceremony of unction, comparing 2 Sam. 1:16, 21; Shaheen (1987, p. 152) adds 1 Sam. 26:9, 2 Sam. 12:7, etc. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Thus a king was a consecrated personage, whom it was sacrilege to attack. Verity (ed. 1897) compares Leir 1696, the high anoynted of the Lord; see . Foakes (ed. 1997: The practice…since the Middle Ages…(another anachronism in the play).

2130 rash]
Steevens (ed. 1773): The old hunting term for the stroke made by a wild boar with his fangs [i.e., tusks]. Nares (1822) gives several exx. of this usage, in the sense of a headlong rush of wild beasts to butt horns or wound with tusks. The phrase Like unto wild boars rashing occurs in Deloney’s ballad of Sir Lancelot du Lac, whose first line is quoted in 2H4 2.4.32 (1062); see Simpson (1966, p. 98). OED (v.1 3): To dash…one thing against, in, or through another, quoting this l.; but possibly, as Nares suggests, the meaning of another verb is combined here: OED (Rash v.2 1): To cut, slash. Cf. the somewhat older Race (v.3 1, 2b): To cut or slash; ?with the tusks. Obs. Of F’s substitution sticke, Doran (1931, p. 42): Stick is a commonplace word which [the printer] might have substituted for one he did not understand. Taylor (1983, p. 374): There is no evidence that folio Compositor B deliberately made such changes. Greg (1942, p. xxxiv): Strike might have been better. But Q’s rash is so far more telling and vigorous…a reading that it is almost impossible to credit either to an actor or to a reporter, whose tendency is always to substitute a weaker and more commonplace word for a rarer and more individual one. (Ibid., pp. 99–100): In the prompt-book itself a difficult or obsolescent word appears now and again to have been altered on the occasion of some later production: or possibly these substitutions should be ascribed to the sophisticating editor of the folio.…[Rash] is I think certainly original. (Ibid., p. 182): Perhaps changed by prompter or press reader on account of the repeated sibilants in flesh rash boarish. Muir (ed. 1952): Possibly Sh. made the change for this last reason. Hunter (ed. 1972): The three sh sounds…imply a slow deliberate delivery. Foakes (ed. 1997): F’s change could have been made…by an actor. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 17): Rash could not possibly be a misreading of sticke and we must surely accept rash as the Shakespearean word—it is much more forceful and effective than the F reading. Munro (ed. 1957), rash: A more powerful word than stick. Hunter (op. cit.): Not only more picturesque but more accurate,…for the slashing sideways movement of the boar’s tusks.

2130 phangs]
Deighton (ed. 1891): A boar’s tusks (OED, sb. 4).

2131 of his lou’d]
Q1(c) emends to on his lowd, F to as his bare. Doran (1931, p. 41): Of his lou’d could be a manuscript misreading of as his bare. Greg (1940, pp. 168–9): We are bound to accept the folio reading as correct.…It is difficult to see how of and on could both be honest readings of the same original: on the other hand, lou’d and lowd are probably no more than alternative interpretations.…The compositor…must, if he thought at all, have assumed (rightly) that the lou’d head was Lear’s: the corrector on the contrary would appear to have taken lowd to apply to the head of the sea (perhaps the crests of the waves) [or cf. OED, Head sb. 17c: A high tidal wave], and this (with his reading on) does give sense of a sort [cf. OED, Endure v. 2: Continue].…The of in [Q1(u)] might conceivably be a misreading of as, if either a final secretary s or a tailed s were smudged. In that case lou’d would of course be a possible reading; or, if we assume [Q1(c)]’s w to have been in the copy, we might suppose lowd to be a misprint of bowd (i.e. bowed). Possibly, however, the simplest solution would be to regard both readings as graphic errors for bare in which every letter has been misread—a perfectly possible contingency! Though the Q corrector was probably not working from copy here, Ridley (ed. 1935) adopts his lowd as low’d (i.e. lowered, bent) [which] is at least as vivid as bare. Similarly Van Dam (1935, p. 64): Lowered, calmed; he takes head to mean surface, comparing 1H4 1.3.106 (428) and MV 2.7.44 (1017). Brooke (ed. 1947) defends Greg’s bow’d as accounting for both Q and F readings, and because a tragi-grotesque quibble with buoy’d in the next line is probably intentional. Wells (ed. 2000): Though OED’s first ex. is from 1848, the verbal sense was common much earlier. Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960) withdraws his previous reading (ed. 1949): Loved adds a touch of emotion, which is surely Sh.’s, in this speech of high passion, while the colourless bare looks like a careless substitution by the prompter (cf. bare-headed, [1714]) if it be not a simple…misreading of loud. Proudfoot (1973, p. 178): Q’s uncorr. lou’d may be a misreading of lone, and the correction lowd mistaken guesswork.

2132 hell blacke]
There is no reason to thinks that Sh. owes the epithet to Hakluyt (Navigations, 1599–1600, 3:849), as Capell (1783, 1.2:172) suggests, since Sh. had made the comparison frequently before, e.g. Luc. 764, Son. 147.14, TN 4.2.34–5 (2020–1), etc. Dent (1981, H397) compares the proverbial As black (dark) as Hell.

2132 layd]
Greg (1940, p. 169), more elaborately than Van Dam (1935, p. 64): The folio [buoy’d] is of course correct.…The compositor misread [Q copy boyd] as layd.…Evidently the [Q] reader deciphered bo all right, and presumably wrote these letters in the margin, striking out la in the text, but…the compositor…thought that the y had been deleted as well and reset [Q1(c)’s] bod. Weis (ed. 1993): F’s buoy’d phonically approximates bod. The modern passive idiom is buoyed has invited editorial doubt here. Heath (1765, p. 342): Used…as the middle form of the Greek verbs, to signify, buoy or lift itself up. Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:9): Rise as doth a buoy. Schmidt (ed. 1879): Transitive: The sea would have lifted up the fixed fires and extinguished them (Ger.; OED, v. 3b, fig., first ex. 1652). Moberly (ed. 1876): Swelled upward. OED (v. 1): To rise, swell (as the sea), quoting this l. as the earliest use of the verb. White (1880, pp. 832–3), rejecting Warburton’s emendation boil’d: Buoy, being unknown as a verb in Shakespeare’s time, buoyed could not have been put in type by a compositor, or written by a copyist, who had boiled before his eyes. Muir (ed. 1952): Boil’d…suggests the fury of the waves…but it should nevertheless be rejected, as buoy’d is so unusual a word that it is unlikely to be a guess.

2133 quencht…fires]
Wilson (ed. 1960) finds the same idea in Tmp. 1.2.4–5 (85–6). Hunter (ed. 1972): Here with the implication of formlessness overcoming the pattern of order. Miola (1992, p. 146): Gloucester recasts the Senecan image of extinguished stars in Thyestes 48–51. But extinguished stars are also biblical—cf. Rev. 6:13—and Seneca does not mention the sea as agent.

2133 steeled]
Since no good sense can be made of Q1(u), it is generally considered a misreading for Q1(c)’s stelled, whose meaning is disputed. Theobald (ed. 1733): An adjective coin’d from Stella (OED, a.: Starred, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Nares (1822): To fix, or place in a permanent manner (OED, Stell v. 2). Gardner (ed. 1969): As opposed to the wandering stars, the planets. Craig (ed. 1901): Perhaps,…with a play on the other sense (starry). Sh.’s two uses of the verb in Luc. 1444, Son. 24.1 may have the different meaning of portray, delineate (OED, 3). Smithers (1970, pp. 36–7): Consisting of stars; all the OED instances meaning fix are Scots.

2134 heart]
OED (sb. 16): As a term of compassion: Poor heart!, quoting H5 2.1.118 (616) as its first ex. Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 112): Synecdoche.

2134 holpt]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 402): Perhaps a misreading of e as t, corrected in F’s holpe. Doran (1931, pp. 41–2): The folio printer might himself have removed the excrescent t. Van Dam (1935, p. 64): Modernization. Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): The old past tense and participle of help. Moberly (ed. 1876): Encouraged. Wilson (ed. 1960): Aided, Sc. by his tears (in F; but see next n.). Sh. prefers holp to helped 17:6. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 519): Q’s form also occurs in Dekker and Middleton’s 1 Honest Whore 1.5.193 (holp’t).

2134 rage]
F has raine. Doran (1931, p. 42): The folio printer might have substituted raine for rage. Dace (1971, p. 98) and Clayton (1981, p. 361): Possibly Q’s rage is a misreading of copy rayn. That spelling does not occur in F or the good quartos, though rayne occurs in Mac. 3.3.16 (1241). Foakes (ed. 1997): Tears mark his reconciliation with Cordelia in 4.7. Q makes good sense but is less resonant. Q’s rage has many resonances, however. The word is used of the storm in 1622+1 and 1656, of Lear’s fury in 1598, and of his madness in 2370 and 2837. F’s raine implies weeping rather than fury, but Lear specifically abjures weeping in 1577–86 before the storm and again in 1797 during it, while he himself is seen Contending with the fretfull element (1619) and urging the winds to greater rage (1656 ff.).

2135 wolues]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Emphatic: even wolves—the outlaws among wild animals.

2135 heard]
Q could make sense only if an extrametrical subject thou were added to the line. Van Dam (1935, p. 65) understands herded, assembled (OED, v.1 1), but OED does not record such an apocopated past participle. All eds. accept F’s howl’d. Doran (1931, p. 41): Howl’d is…probably the original reading, although it is not easy to see how heard was misread from it. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 402) proposes a misreading in Q of MS hould, citing e/o misreading at 1329 and 2311+4, a/u at 644, and t/l at 867 etc. and r/t at 1415, the latter instances suggesting that in the copy for Q l and r were liable to look rather like each other.

2135 dearne]
On F’s substitution, sterne, see Greg’s comment on sticke in n. 2130. Doran (1931, p. 42): Stern appears to bear a somewhat unusual sense, not likely to have come from a printer. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 194): I agree with Greg.…Compositors do not generally substitute readings [i.e., Q’s] more satisfactory from the literary point of view than the genuine ones. McLeod (1983, p. 160): In the earliest known lay of the English case the compartment for the ligature in s and t is very near that of the d. Therefore, either reading…could easily be a typo for the other. The compartments are not adjacent, however. Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:18), dern: Dire, dreadful, Steevens (ed. 1778): Melancholy, and Nares (1822): Dark, are all supported by OED (Dern, adj. 4, 5) and make excellent sense here. The word occurs in Per. 3.ch.15. Stern can mean Of the weather: Severe, causing hardship (OED, adj. 6d, quoting this l.). Sisson (1956, 2:238) suggests somewhat timidly that it was substituted in rehearsal for the sake of euphony: Heard that dearne time slips over more easily with stern for dearne. Wilson (ed. 1960): Are not sibilants apt to the situation described? Proudfoot (1992, p. xxviii): The author of [Tom a Lincoln, ca. 1611] uses [derne] several times (ll. 1842, 2625), in contexts which identify it as belonging to the inflated language of rhetorical passion, hence perhaps its change in F: possibly derne had become a dangerous word to use in a context of serious emotion. Foakes (ed. 1997): In Per. dearn is used in a deliberately archaic context, the Chorus of Gower.…F corrects a lot of Q errors in this speech, and all the changes are likely to be revisions by the same hand, possibly the author’s, though this one might be an actor’s intervention. In fact there is no reason to think that many of the Q readings in this passage are errors at all or that the alterations in F are all by the same hand (or by Sh.); see the prev. nn.

2136 shouldst]
Gardner (ed. 1969): Were bound to. Horsman (ed. 1973): Wouldst certainly.

2136 turne the key]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Unlock the door. See n. 1323.

2137 All…subscrib’d]
Furness (ed. 1880) finds this the most puzzling phrase in this play, and Rolfe (ed. 1880) declares, The interpretations and emendations that have been proposed seem to us mere tricks of desperation. For conjectural emendations see . In F the verb form is subscribe, and the phrase is set off by colons before and after it; editors have of course made every possible combination of choices among these Q/F variants. For the commentators’ different interpretations of cruels, else, and subscribe(d) see the individual notes on those words below.
In the view of the present editor, the simplest interpretation requires that lines 2135–8 be read as two sentences, the first ending at key (as Q’s comma or F’s colon there might indicate). The first sentence would then express Gloucester’s disbelief at the sisters’ cruelty: You might have let in wolves from such a storm, yet you would not take in your own father! The second sentence expresses his defiant prediction that such cruelty as theirs must ultimately be punished: Let all other cruelties be approved (subscrib’d)—or Though one approve of (subscribe) all other cruelties—yet (but) Vengeance will still overtake you (who are guilty of the greatest cruelty of all).
Other interpretations have been legion. The following are grouped first according to whether the phrase all…subscribe(d) as a whole is taken as a remark by Gloucester to Regan, or a part of her imagined remark to the porter, or the first part of Gloucester’s subsequent prediction of vengeance; within each of these three groups they are subdivided according as the Q or F verb form (subscrib’d or subscribe) is chosen.
(1)As Gloucester’s remark to Regan:
(A)With Q’s subscrib’d. Johnson (ed. 1765): All cruels yielded, submitted to the necessity of the occasion— apparently meaning that all other cruel beings (besides the sisters) saw the need for mercy during the storm. This general idea is repeated with small variations: all cruels submitted their cruelty to the compassion they felt (Heath, 1765, p. 342), subscribed to pity…being exercis’d here (Capell, 1783, 1.2:172), yielded, submitted, or succumbed to the terrors of the storm (Hudson, ed. 1871), put off their savage natures (Page, ed. 1889), gave up for a time their cruel habits, their fierceness (Craig, ed. 1901), would have given in (Kelcy, 1932, p. 367), were on his side (Harrison, ed. 1937, ed. 1948). Seymour (1805, 2:120): All other cruelties yielding place or preeminence to that, presumably to that cruelty of shutting Lear out. Clarkes (ed. 1868): [All] cruelties…relinquished—apparently meaning all other conceivable cruelties; similarly Moberly (ed. 1876): All harshness otherwise natural being forborne or yielded. Cf. Tovey (ed. 1896): A nominative absolute.…You might have given wolves shelter; indeed, you might have suspended all other natural antipathies at such a time. Hunter (ed. 1869): Otherwise acknowledged thyself disposed to all sorts of cruelty—i.e., if you had acted otherwise than so instructing the porter, you would have acknowledged etc. Wright (ed. 1875): All their other cruelties being yielded or forgiven; cf. put out of consideration (Meiklejohn, ed. 1879), overlooked (Verity, in Irving & Marshall, ed. 1889), condoning or condoned (Herford, ed. 1899; Smith, ed. 1902). Crosby (1877, p. 13; essentially as 1879, p. 88): All thy feelings, no matter how cruel or inhuman else, i.e., at any other time, or under any other circumstances, having subscribed, i.e., succumbed, to the terrors of that storm, and yielded to the pity for the old King, thy father, comparing 1673. Leo (1880, p. 61): Even assuming (or conceding) every [other] cruelty on your part. Similarly Deighton (ed. 1891), reading cruelties: Though acknowledging, confessing to, any other acts of cruelty, however great. Dey (1900, p. 204; 1903, p. 150; 1909, p. 161): All cruels (cruel things, agents of cruelty) else (other than the cruelty of that stern time) subscrib’d (forgiven). Buck (ed. 1907): All acknowledged to be cruel beings otherwise, or at other times. Case (1927, p. 504; in Craig, ed. 1901, rev. 1927, p. 250): All other cruel creatures but the storm [being] yielded admittance, admitted by order; similarly Cuningham (1938, p. 188), reading cruelst: All the most cruel animals (as well as wolves) being admitted.
(B)With F’s subscribe. Eccles (ed. 1792): All cruels else assent to the justness of the sentiment which I now express. Schmidt (ed. 1879): Every [living] thing, which is at other times cruel, shows feeling or regard; you alone have not done so (Ger.); cf. yield their ferocity (Lee, ed. 1908), yield to feelings of compassion (Gildersleeve, ed. 1912), lay aside their cruelty (Bald, ed. 1949), would agree to give shelter (Munro, ed. 1957), give way at times to pity (Gardner, ed. 1969). White (1880, p. 830), taking F’s colon as equivalent to a comma, and but as meaning that: All other such cruelties attest that I shall see swift vengeance overtake such children. Spence (1900, p. 363): All other cruel things yield in cruelty to the cruelty of the storm—and are of no account in the comparison (Henley, ed. 1903); similarly Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): All other cruelties, such as the Wolves, yield allegiance to this master-cruelty of the storm. Dent (ed. 1927): All other cruelties are inferior to yours, a reading repeated by Van Dam (1935, p. 65), citing OED (v. 8c); but that rare usage, supported by only two exx. from Sh., means to submit or concur in admitting error, not to be inferior in some quality. Similarly Kelcy (1932, p. 367): All other cruel people acknowledge their inferiority to you in cruelty. Muir (ed. 1952), as a doubtful alternative: Leave on one side all other cruel creatures.
(2)As part of Regan’s imagined remark to the porter (good Porter…subscribe(d):
(A)With Q’s subscrib’d. Abbott (§433): All cruel acts to the contrary being yielded up, forgiven. Craig (ed. 1901): All cruels yielded, gave up for a time their cruel habits, their fierceness—the implication apparently being that the porter should do the same this once. Crook (ed. 1907): All thoughts of other acts of cruelty being put aside. Case (1927, p. 504), alternatively (see under 1A): Possibly Do at least this one act of mercy, even if all other cruelties are assented to.
(B)With F’s subscribe. Furness (ed. 1880): Acknowledge the claims [i.e., for mercy] of all creatures, however cruel they may be at other times, or Give up all cruel things else, i.e. forget that they are cruel,…surrender, yield, give up whatsoever was cruel in the poor beasts, and see only their claim to compassion. Similarly Verity (ed. 1897): Forgive the [wolves’] cruelties; alternatively, All things [but you, porter,] which at other times are cruel are now forgiving. Tupper (1902, pp. 58–9): Approve of or assent to all other cruelties I may command, but do not be guilty of…barring the door to any living creature, or to these poor creatures (Hunter, ed. 1972). Similarly Colman (ed. 1982): Whatever other cruelties you may do. Buck (ed. 1907): Acknowledge them at all other times to be cruel beings. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 153): Regan may be thought of as saying to the porter, Let the wolves in: all other cruel creatures yield to compassion…so let us yield to it now.…It may be objected that Regan would be unlikely to say to the porter that she—or he—or both of them—were cruel. But it is quite consonant with the mood of this speech of Gloucester’s that he should attribute to Regan such self-knowledge and such a cynical avowal of it. Edwards (ed. 1975): Otherwise, you countenance all cruelty (i.e., if you don’t pity even wolves and give them shelter, you are assenting to cruelty). Brown (ed. 1976): Aid any other cruelty you like. Following Stone (1980, p. 197), Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 519) read ile for else: All cruel creatures I will countenance, accept (Stone) or All cruel actions I surrender, give up, renounce. Foakes (ed. 1997): This is not much of an improvement. Weis (ed. 1993): All other cruelties I [Regan] will commit but not this one <I will needs to be supplied>.
(3)As introducing Gloucester’s prediction:
(A)With Q’s subscrib’d. Adee (ed. 1890, p. lii): Even though all other cruel beings be pardoned by the Gods, yet will their avenging minister punish such children as you. Quinn (ed. 1970): I am willing to undergo any torture if in return I may have the opportunity of seeing such vengeance.
(B)With F’s subscribe. Hudson (ed. 1879): Underwrite, guarantee, make good, all other deeds or instances of cruelty, if I do not see etc. White (ed. 1883): All other cruelties attest that I shall see etc. Perrett (1904, pp. 297–8): Never mind about your other cruel deeds, such as the harsh treatment of your subjects (cf. [2867–8]) and the violence you are offering me—subscribe them, let us leave them out of consideration—but for that impious act of shutting out your father in such a storm, such a night, I shall see etc.; cf. Disregard all your other cruelties: but I shall see (Wright & LaMar, ed. 1956), and the added implication since all are less diabolical (McCann, ed. 1964). Brooke (ed. 1947): The clause is concessive and general: Give sanction and formal allowance, if you like, to all other cruel creatures, yet I shall see, etc. Sisson (1956, 2:238): The Folio colon [after Key] is a period.…You will go on agreeing to all other cruelties (to Lear)—yet I shall see etc.
There is much to be said for this third class of readings. For one thing, it requires no stretching of the meaning of subscribe beyond Sh.’s usual meanings of allow or favor; see the following note on this word. Moreover, the conjunction but is most commonly adversative, and the meaning all other cruel people or deeds (allowed) makes a clear opposition with such children and their deeds (punished). Conversely, if Gloucester instead means All…subscrib’d to suggest great mercy in Regan, whether as a description of her imagined clemency to wolves (1) or as her imagined advice to the porter (2), the but and his ensuing prediction of vengeance make poor sense once he has attributed mercifulness to her.

2137 cruels]
Theobald (1726, p. 37): All Things of Cruelty. There has been wide disagreement whether these things are living creatures (human or otherwise), or acts, or feelings, or motives; see the prev. note. Schmidt (ed. 1879): The cruel, as a substantive, can only mean the cruel person or thing, not cruelty; as little can the old mean old age, or the young mean youth. All interpretations, therefore, which involve this abstract idea are inadmissible (Ger.). Perrett (1904, p. 297), however, adduces exx. from contemporary literature of the adjective used as abstract noun, including a unique substantive use of cruel ca. 1440 recorded by OED (sb.). Sh. does not elsewhere use the word in the plural, or as a substantive except in the vocative (Son. 149.2). Kittredge (ed. 1940) cites That young cruell from Lyly’s Love’s Metamorphosis (4.2.74), and Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 152–3) gives several Shn. examples of adjectives as personal nouns; cf. OED (adj. 1b): Absol. = Cruel one. Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 62): Anthimeria, the substitution of one part of speech for another…more than any other figure of grammar…gives vitality and power to Shakespeare’s language, through its packed meaning, liveliness, and stir.

2137 else]
As an adjective meaning other (OED, adv. 1b) the word has been referred to other cruel acts or feelings, to cruel beings or conditions other than the storm, to cruel animals other than wolves, and to cruel persons other than the sisters or the porter. As an adverb meaning otherwise (OED, 3, 4) it has been specified to mean either in other ways or at other times. For both kinds of readings see the previous long note. It may be possible to consider else as quasi-correlative with the conjunction but two words later: see (3) under the previous long note, and OED (1): Often…followed by but; (But adv. 5b): With [comparative; though normally negative and interrogative] sentences…esp. after else. On the substitution of I’ll, see above.

2137 subscrib’d]
F has subscribe; either word could easily have been misread for the other. The Q reading may be a past indicative or a past participle, and the F form either a present indicative or an imperative. All these possible variations are exemplified in the long note above, which also reveals how often and how far commentators have stretched the meaning of the word. In Sh. subscribe usually bears close relation to the meanings attest, assent to, or approve, viz. by underwriting (OED. v. 3, 4, 7), and eds. have suggested such senses here—admit to, confess, acknowledge (to be, or the claims of); accept, agree to; countenance, sanction, etc. Sh.’s occasional use in the sense submit oneself (OED, 8) is invoked here to support such readings as give in to, yield to, comply with, succumb to, be conquered by (Schmidt, ed. 1879) (the object of the preposition in all cases being compassion), as well as yield allegiance to (cf. n. 1673) and such related figurative senses as yield pre-eminence, be inferior to, etc.; while his unique usage at 359 (Sign away; OED, 6) is extrapolated here to mean transitively surrender, give up, relinquish, renounce, lay aside, forbear, suspend, etc. Such further extensions of meaning as forget, leave out of consideration, disregard, never mind, forgive, pardon, condone, and even cancel (Tovey, ed. 1896) seem to be wholly unattested.

2138 winged vengeance]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Swift. Porter & Clarke: Another pre-Christian allusion to the Erinyes or Furies. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The vengeance of the gods, sweeping down upon them like a bird of prey, comparing 1444–5, 2303+15–+16. Weis (ed. 1993): Or harpy. Muir (ed. 1952): He may be thinking of winged spirits, or of lightning, comparing Psa. 144.6. Munro (ed. 1957): ?Nemesis. Hunter (ed. 1972): An angel of divine wrath.

2139 Seet]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Emphatic. Verity (ed. 1897): For a similar, though less shocking, piece of jesting by Cornwall, cf. [1491–2].

2139 fellowes]
See n. 557.

2140 Vpon…foote]
To set one’s foot on the hand, neck, etc. of another person was to demonstrate outrageously his utter subjection; see OED (Foot sb. 28, 30c, 33), and cf. Shr. 5.2.177 (2735), TN 2.5.188 (1191), Tro. 3.3.140 (1992). Most probably Cornwall means that after gouging the traitor Gloucester’s eyes, or cutting them out with his dagger (Fripp, 1938, p. 661), he will tread triumphantly on them. In theatrical practice, however, the actor playing Cornwall sometimes enacts digging out the eyes with pointed toe or heel or spur (see Rosenberg, 1972, pp. 241–3, and Bratton, ed. 1987), to the considerable peril of the actor playing Gloucester, tied in a chair lowered to the floor. See the textual n. Dr. Tannenbaum (1931, p. 46; cf. 1933, pp. 89–90) insists that the whole action imagined by Sh. is impossible: Without the aid of cutting instruments the human eyeball cannot be extracted from its socket,…[being] attached to the skull by muscles below, above, and at the sides,…[and] held in position by the thick and strong optic nerve.…If the eyeball could possibly be pulled out, nothing but a hollow collapsed shell would remain in the person’s hand.…[More important,] such a violent tearing at the optic nerves would cause such a hemorrhage at the base of the brain as to cause instant death. Sh., who refers to the plucking out of eyes in Err. 4.4.104 (1392), Mac. 2.2.56 (720), and MM 4.3.119 (2209), took the incident from Sidney’s Arcadia 2.10.3 (see ), where the old king’s eyes are reported to have been put out by his bastard son. Shakespeare uses this incident [in Sidney] to serve his plot in a double way and binds the Lear and the Gloucester unfilialness more closely by making Cornwall the agent of Edmund’s double-dealing (Porter & Clarke, ed. 1905). Steevens (ed. 1778) cites a parallel from Selimus (ca. 1592; ed. Bang, 1908, ll. 1413–15), in which one of the sons of Bajazet jeers at a loyal Aga on stage, Puls out his eyes, and cuts off his hands; Steevens does not note that the play has a minor character named Regan, as does Ekeblad (1957, p. 193). Camden (1932, pp. 408–9) also cites Chapman, Bussy D’Ambois 4.1.78–9, you may have your…eyes thrust out, arguing, Shakespeare’s conception was accurate as far as Elizabethan knowledge went. Guilfoyle (1989; 1990, p. 118), seeing Gloucester as a Christ-figure, compares Caiaphas’s threat to blind Christ in the Towneley Coliphizacio, and links it typologically to the blinding of Samson.
Furness (ed. 1880) quotes a number of 18th- and 19th-c. critics who find the deed too horrible to be represented on the stage and who judge its inclusion by Sh. as an artistic mistake. See, e.g., Coleridge (MS notes, 1818–19, ed. Foakes, 1989, pp. 97, 102): In this one point the tragic has been urged beyond the outermost mark and ne plus ultra of the dramatic.…My reluctance to think Shakespeare wrong—and yet—. Such criticisms are repeated as late as Bradley (1904, p. 251): The mere physical horror of such a spectacle would in the theatre be a sensation so violent as to overpower the purely tragic emotions. Trewin (1978, p. 209): Lilian Baylis’s decision, at the Old Vic, [was] always to have the Blinding played immediately after the interval so that those who wished could come in later.
The act is performed in a variety of ways. Tieck (ed. 1833, 9:368) imagined a certain reticence on Sh.’s stage, believing that the deed was probably performed in an alcove at the rear, hidden by side-curtains and by servants holding Gloucester’s chair. For this there is no evidence, and audiences used to public hangings and eviscerations may not have been so squeamish as to require such devices. Bratton (ed. 1987): Tate retained the blinding scene on stage, but transferred the actual execution of the act to the servants. Garrick shifted the deed offstage, having Gloucester forced off and then brought back, and this was also Colman’s emendation.…Kemble did not even allow Gloucester to reappear. Macready, Phelps, Charles Kean, and Irving, cutting most of the scene, avoided an incident the Victorian audience would probably have been unable to accept; Phelps was the boldest, retaining the blinding itself, with Gloucester bound to a chair, facing upstage, and almost concealed by a pillar. Bridges-Adams played the scene as swiftly as possible.…The most common twentieth-century practice has been to repeat Phelps’s chair turned upstage. Darton (ed. 1928): Norman McKinnel…minimised it or had it done off. Mr. Bridges Adams, of the Stratford Memorial Theatre,…[has] Gloucester far up the stage in a chair, his back to the audience.…Cornwall bends over Gloucester from behind, half-hiding what he does.…Mr. Nugent Monck, of the Maddermarket Theatre, Norwich,…in 1926, put the crime under the balcony, with a crowd hiding the details. Davies (1783, 2:304): At the present, the sufferer is forced into some adjoining room; and the ears of the audience are more hurt by his cries than their eyes can be. Modern audiences, accustomed to Theatre of Cruelty and to the vivid violence of moving pictures and television, are often showed the deed as directly as possible. As Bratton (loc. cit.) reports, Less compunction is felt about the violence and blood since Brook’s 1962 production, where Cornwall used his golden spurs to do the deed.…[In Stratford, 1974, Regan] stabbed out his eye with a hairpin. Dessen (1978, pp. 60–1): If Gloucester’s head is placed under Cornwall’s foot, the audience will witness a powerful symbolic tableau that transcends verisimilitude, such as that in Stratford, Ont. in 1972, when Cornwall chose his gouging tool from a large rack of gleaming instruments. Brown (ed. 1996) also reports the use of a huge pin by Cornwall and Regan in the 1982 Stratford-upon-Avon production, after which they both collapsed in hysterical laughter [SQ rev.]. Cf. textual n.
The incident is defended on the grounds of audience expectations, dramatic purpose, and thematic import. Johnson (ed. 1765, 6:159): The extrusion of Gloucester’s eyes…seems an act too horrid to be endured in dramatick exhibition, and such as must always compel the mind to relieve its distress by incredulity. Yet let it be remembered that our author well knew what would please the audience for which he wrote. Bridges (in Bullen, ed. 1904–7, 10:322, 332): We may with all confidence…argue that certain scenes [such as this] which offend our feelings, so that we cannot endure to see them in representation…did not offend Shakespeare’s audience: and indeed if such exhibitions were comfortably tolerated, they were demanded of a dramatist who would fully arouse the feelings.…Shakespeare aimed at exciting his audience to the limit of their endurance. Byrne (1927, p. 200): Accustomed to a very considerable degree of cruelty in real life they needed something as violent as the blinding of Gloster if their sensibilities were to be penetrated at all, and an emotional reaction aroused. The men and women who watched Lear had perhaps watched Jesuit executions with the usual appurtenances of hanging, drawing and quartering. David (1935, p. 127): By the time that the scene…is reached, [Gloucester] should be firmly established as a comic character; so that the lamentings of the critics…are largely uncalled for. It seems to me much more likely that the Elizabethan audience received it with howls of encouragement and delight than with gasps even of gratified horror. The tortured Gloucester is much nearer to the long-suffering Pantaloon of Harlequinade, or the old horse disembowelled in the bull-fight, than to a tragic martyr. Fripp (op. cit., pp. 660–1): The grave and judicious spectators of 1606 could not so miss the point: Puritan feeling favoured extreme punishment [for adultery]—death as in the Mosaic law [citing Lev. 20:10], or blinding in according with [Matt. 5:28 f.]. The Reformers quoted with approval the punishment by death; but blinding, as among the Locrensians [citing several 16th-c. sources], was thought more Christian. Similarly Lyons (1974, p. 28): Blinding could be a Biblical and medieval punishment for lust (such as Gloucester’s). Cornwall is not acting as either Christian or puritan, of course, nor punishing Gloucester for adultery. Cf. n. 3131–4.
Others see the scene as a dramatic necessity. Heraud (1865, pp. 305–6): [Sh.] might have justified the act by the supposed barbarity of the legendary age whose manners he was tracing.…No such thing.…By inserting in the group a servant who did recognise its intrinsic horror, and compassioned the sufferer, he converted disgust into pity.…The other servants also compassionated the sufferer.…The entire current of feeling is turned in the direction of pity by the force of sympathy. Thus the horror of the horrid act is mitigated, and reduced to the level of terror; which feeling is enforced by the fearful looking-for of a coming vengeance, of which an instalment is secured even in the moment of crime. And this sentiment, too, is expressed by the servants. Smith (ed. 1902): It may be urged that a bold and direct treatment of this second case of barbarity was necessary after the terrible scene on the heath, as a bare narration of it would not in the circumstances have conveyed an adequate impression. Granville-Barker (ed. 1927, p. 150): Its dramatic justification [is] in the need to match in another sort—since he could not hope to match it in spiritual intensity—the catastrophe to Lear. David (op. cit., p. 128): There is something comic alike in the energy of his persecutors and in the pomposity of his defiance, pathetic as it is.…As the tragedy of Lear himself contains elements of the grotesque, it is imperative that Gloucester’s agony should be kept well under control, lest it should appear the more tragic of the two. Stewart (1945, p. 267): The scene serves as a means of intensification, a sort of crystallizing of [the] element of physical outrage [to the body] which the imagery holds so massively in suspension throughout the play…the oppressive atmosphere of the play here condensing in a ghastly dew. Watkins (1950, pp. 226–8): The visible action is illuminated by the dialogue so that we can feel its force more fully than…by the aid of the eye alone.…There is a ruthless insistence in the verbal presentation of Gloucester’s torment.…The terror is multiplied by the fact…that the poet not only states what we see but also prompts our feelings toward the action. Price (1952, p. 314): Shakespeare had to make the treatment of Gloucester by Cornwall and Regan…as fiendish as possible: anything less would not have moved First Servant to revolt, thus beginning the downfall of the anti-Lear faction (see n. 2145). Goodman (1954, p. 40): Lear is composed of many violent motions, and these prepare this other one of the blinding.
More recent defenders consider the scene’s thematic import. Prior (1951, pp. 120–1): It is one thing to maintain that conditions of the times made it possible for audiences to endure such a scene…but that is not the same thing as insisting that that is why it is there.…In a play in which it is necessary to display the behavior of characters who have wilfully abandoned the natural and conventional restraints that make possible humane action, this scene is a climactic presentation of their capacity for inhuman violence when they have authority and power and can excuse their conduct as expediency while they delight in their cruelty.…On this assumption [that the audience was insensitive to physical suffering] the play makes no sense at all. For the play depicts as unmistakably appalling the fact that the pitiable things which happen to Lear and Gloucester are unfelt by Regan, Goneril, and Cornwall; and in the characterization of Cordelia, Kent, and Edgar it represents as possible and laudable an order of sensitiveness to human suffering so acute as to be well-nigh unendurable. The play would be incomprehensible to any audience unable to perceive this contrast sympathetically.…One incident—when the anonymous servant, violating all traditional order and decorum, turns on Cornwall in disgust to check his master’s hideous purpose—indicates that Shakespeare felt the conduct of Cornwall to be almost intolerable to witness and that he expected his audience to feel the same way. Levin (1959, p. 89): Even that horrendous act has a certain propriety as a literal climax to a whole train of metaphors involving eyesight and suggesting moral perception, the lack of which is so fatal to Gloucester and Lear.
