Harbage (1963, p. 421): This is the most revolting scene in the whole range of poetic drama, but its artistic rightness cannot be challenged.…[It] belongs in the play as it is, projecting unshrinkingly a vision of evil absolute.…To gloze this action by treating it as a metaphor of Gloucester’s passage from moral to physical blindness is to mutilate the play. So Charney (1969, pp. 62–3). Cavell (1969, pp. 275, 281): This act of psychic cruelty literalizes evil’s ancient love of darkness; Regan imagines that she has just participated in blinding her father. Peat (1984–5, pp. 106–7): Because of the audience’s fascination and their resulting sense of complicity, the blinding forces us to acknowledge our capacity for cruelty. Tennenhouse (1986, p. 139): Gloucester is being punished for foisting a bastard upon the aristocracy; Cornwall purifies the aristocratic body. But see 1987; Cornwall should be punished. Halio (1992, pp. 221–3): It is a Freudian symbol for castration, and (cf. 3131–4) may be an appropriate punishment, having biblical precedent: the Homily Against Whoredom… reminds listeners that the Locrensians blinded adulterers. Wells (ed. 2000): Not the sin with which Gloucester’s tormenters are themselves concerned.

2140 those]
F’s these can hardly reflect a difference of staging. The variant is probably due to a common o/e misreading in Q or F.

2141–2 He…helpe]
Lott (ed. 1974): In their own interests they should stop Cornwall and Regan, whose ruthlessness will only grow worse, and who will certainly want to silence any witnesses. More probably than this complex thought, the agonized Gloucester utters the proverb Do as you would be done to (Tilley D395). Edwards (ed. 1975): But the servant who comes to his help does not live to be old.

2142 helpe,]
Wilson (ed. 1960): A long dash in F marks the moment of the deed—as does Q’s comma, less emphatically.

2143 mocke]
Schmidt (1875): Ridicule (OED, v. 1, 4). Wilson (ed. 1960): Make the other look ridiculous—i.e., by their disparity.

2143 another]
Abbott (§88): A is apparently put for the. Schmidt (1875) gives Shn. exx. meaning the other eye.

2143 tother to]
Regan’s ultimate improvement on others’ initiatives.

2145 Hold…Lord]
White (1880, p. 120): The voice of humanity, otherwise stifled there, is heard in the speech and embodied in the action of the serving-man, who, with words that recall those of Kent to Lear in the first scene, breaks in upon his master, fights him, and is himself slain by the hand of Regan,—an outburst of manhood which is a great relief. Although Shakespeare found the incident of the loss of Gloucester’s eyes in the old story, and used it in a way which illustrated at once the savage manners of the time in which his tragedy was supposed to be acted and the cruelty of Cornwall and Regan, he intuitively shrank from leaving the scene in its otherwise bare and brutal hideousness. Brooke (ed. 1947; cf. 1912, p. 62): The intervention of the servant…is not in Sidney’s Arcadia…. It is taken from…A Yorkshire Tragedy [ed. Brooke, 5.36], produced by Shakespeare’s company in the late summer or autumn of 1605. Price (1952, p. 313): The capture of Gloucester marks the peak of the success of the anti-Lear faction, and their blinding of him is probably the most intense representation of their cruelty. Yet a few seconds after this Cornwall receives a mortal wound and their cause begins to decline.…[He was] the only person strong enough to hold them together and lead them. With his removal the conflicting interests of the others become active.…In addition Cornwall’s death puts the control of the forces of Goneril and Regan into the hands of Albany, and the news of the blinding of Gloucester…impels him to oppose his wife…and to resolve to do all he can to forward peace and justice. Harbage (1963, p. 421): The Servant…has a just claim upon us as the most cherishable of Shakespeare’s heroes, defender of our human faith. Myrick (1964, p. 69): In the sudden intervention by his servant we have one of the most stunning reversals in all drama, and one of the most momentous in its consequences. At the time, the servant seems to fail entirely. He is treacherously slain, and Gloucester loses both his eyes. But the wound the servant gives his master will lead to the death of Cornwall and the destruction of the other four villainous characters. The death of Cornwall will make Regan the rival of Goneril in their common passion for Edmund. Goneril will entrust a message for Regan and a letter for Edmund to the trusty scoundrel Oswald. Regan…will promise [him] a handsome reward for killing Gloucester. The result will be Oswald’s death at Edgar’s hands, and Oswald’s last act of fidelity will place the letter in the hands first of Edmund’s wronged brother, and then of Goneril’s wronged husband. Hence Edmund will die by Edgar’s hand, Regan by her sister’s, and Goneril by her own.…Albany’s This…justicers [2323–4] makes the poet’s meaning clear. The fact that, to us and to Gloucester, the servant is an anonymous stranger deepens the impression that his sole function is to be Heaven’s instrument. Elton (1966, pp. 294–5) sees the event symbolically, prefiguring the final rebellion of Lear, first servant of the state, against the arbitrary cruelty of the cosmos and microcosmic to the play. Gardner (1967): Gloucester’s cry for winged vengeance has been answered, swiftly and unexpectedly. Gardner (ed. 1969): As so often in Shakespeare, the reaction is more important than the action. Here the First Servant’s challenge itself justifies the incident. The active, immediate, self-denying intervention of the commoner would be more remarkable to Shakespeare’s audience than the commonplace insensitivity of power.…This instinctive revulsion, and the transcendent assertion of human kindness is something exceptional, and essential to the meaning. Strier (1988, pp. 104 ff.): Here Sh. dramatized a Protestant ideology of political resistance, justifying the servant’s petty treason (p. 119). Taylor (1994, p. 294 n.): But the only English sources Strier can cite are texts published half a century before by Marian exiles. The Sokols (2000, p. 400): The servant kills his master without committing petty treason, for the master is guilty of greater treason.

2146 seru’d]
Q1’s omission of you is probably due to the compositor’s failure of memory, and Q2’s and F1’s correction is such as we should expect to find in a reprint (Doran, 1931, p. 21). F’s you implies that the First Servant [is] not one of Gloucester’s retainers, but one of Cornwall’s (Weis, ed. 1993); cf. My villaine (2152) and his great maister (2319).

2149 How now]
See n. 361.

2150 If…chin]
Eccles (ed. 1792): There seems to be some room for doubt whether this be addressed to Cornwall or to Regan. There is no evidence whether Cornwall is bearded. Tovey (ed. 1896), assuming Regan is addressed: If you were a man.

2150 you]
Verity (ed. 1897): I.e. like poor Gloucester. you: emphatic.

2151 id’e…it]
Edwards (ed. 1975): I would do to you what you did to Gloucester; cf. 2100–1. Foakes (ed. 1997): Fight with you.

2151 this quarrell]
OED (sb.3 2): A ground or occasion of complaint against a person, leading to hostile…action. Cf. 2997+2.

2151 what…meane]
Moberly (ed. 1876), apparently following Delius (ed. 1854: auf Grund solcher Sache): What do you mean by calling me dog (Ger.). Furness (ed. 1880) speculatively assigns the question to Cornwall, and Craig (ed. 1901) to Regan; see textual n. Goggin (ed. 1910): These words seem inappropriate in the Servant’s mouth. Harbage (ed. 1958): They are no more unservantlike than those that precede them. More probably the servant, taking such drastic action as to oppose his master, directs his anger at Cornwall for blinding Gloucester rather than at Regan for name-calling; and Cornwall, not Regan, responds in the next speech. Addressed by the servant to Cornwall, the words would mean, What in heaven’s name are you doing? Hoeniger (ed. 1968): How dare you? Halio (ed. 1992): Some stage business, unrecorded in Q or F, may prompt the servant’s query. Thus, after quarrel Hunter [ed. 1972] inserts sd Cornwall draws his sword.

2152 villaine]
Steevens (ed. 1778): Here perhaps used in its original sense. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Bondman, serf, feudal retainer [OED, Villein sb. 1].…Regan’s words, A peasant… show this to be the sense. Moberly (ed. 1876): That one should raise his sword against his master would be unheard-of presumption, for which any punishment would be admissible. Deighton (ed. 1891): Do you, my slave, dare to challenge my actions. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Regan in…[2164] implies that Gloucester was bound to submit to their overlordship, as if he also were no better. The word in this play usually has the modern sense of scoundrel (OED, Villain sb. 1), cf. 2699. Kittredge (ed. 1940) finds only the modern meaning here, Harbage (ed. 1958) both. Perrett (1904, p. 228): Ragan twice insults inferiors by calling them peasants; compare Leir 1972, 2362 (see , ).

2153 chance of anger]
Craig (ed. 1901): Risk of fighting while angry. Crook (ed. 1907): What may result from your meeting an angry man. Foakes (ed. 1997): As to who is hurt or killed.

2154 Giue…sword]
Verity (ed. 1897): Apparently Cornwall is getting the worst of the fight (cf. [2173]), so Regan intervenes. Collier (ed. 1843): She may…have seized the weapon which her husband had drawn in vain; Idem (ed. 1858): May have been addressed to the wounded Cornwall. Just as probably Delius (ed. 1854): Addressed to a bystander.

2154 stand vp]
OED (v. 103n): To hold oneself boldly erect to confront an opponent; to make a stand against, quoting this l. as its second ex., after JC 2.1.167 (800). Mahood (1992, p. 167): It is a high-energy verb. The man is not only upstanding by nature, and ready…to stand up and be counted. He is also the one who rises, as man by his erect posture was assumed to rise, above the animal savagery of the scene.

2154 thus]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Question marks in F may often = exclam. marks.…But Corn. and Reg. are incredulous—can a menial be so bold?

2155 Shee…behind]
Hudson (ed. 1856) compares the contradictory account at 2319–20. Possibly after Regan incapacitates the servant Cornwall also wounds him. Bratton (ed. 1987): The SD suggest[s] a direct report of a performance witnessed. It could as easily be an author’s descriptive SD; so Greg (1942, p. 99), who thinks F’s Killes him preserves the terse orders of the prompter.

2156 yet haue you]
F changes to you haue to make smoother meter, but even so its line 2156 is too long and 2157 too short. If the Q line is divided after one, no other alteration is needed. Q did not set verse, and F’s change does not seem authorial.

2157 mischiefe on him]
Delius (ed. 1854): The injury that the servant has just inflicted on Cornwall (Ger.). Moberly (ed. 1876): Some vengeance fall on my murderer.

2157 oh!]
A dying groan. In the Oxford eds. (1986; Wells, 2000) it is occasioned by Regan’s stabbing him again; see textual n.

2158 more]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): I.e., more harm than you have already done me.

2158 preuent]
See n. 50.

2158 vild]
See n. 1726.

2159 luster]
Quinn (ed. 1970) alone: A pun on Gloucester.

2161–7 wher’s…thee]
Law (1958, p. 121): The lines may owe some suggestion to the attempted murder of Leir. For Gloucester, like Leir, declares that the offspring he has so favored may help in his need, only to learn that the betrayer of his secret was his ungrateful illegitimate son. See Leir 1606–30 ().

2162 vnbridle]
Since Q’s image—unbridling sparks—seems nonsensical, virtually all eds. adopt F’s enkindle. Only Weis (ed. 1993) finds Q’s reading apocalyptic and F’s a narrowing sophistication. Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 357–8) gives exx. of u/e and b/k misreadings. Harrison (ed. 1948): Blow into flame—perhaps suggesting hot anger, but not necessarily: cf. 280. Edmund’s surviving sparks of filial feeling would need to be enkindled after Gloucester had done so much to damp them.

2162 sparks of nature]
See n. 441. Joseph (ed. 1966): (i) all the sources of light in the universe; (ii) all the fires of natural piety. In each case the image replaces the light of Gloucester’s sight with light of a fire.

2162 nature]
See n. 441 and prev. n.

2163 quit]
Singer (ed. 1826): Requite, repay with revenge (OED, v. 11b).

2164–6 Out…vs]
Verity (ed. 1897): This is the finishing stroke, and she, as we should expect, deals it. The old man’s agony, mental and physical, being now complete, it only remains to thrust him out of his own castle; and she gives the order [2170].

2164 Out]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Out upon thee! An interjection of cursing (OED, int. 2).

2164 villaine]
F’s treacherous Villaine makes more regular meter, though Q’s line, with two stresses, serves well enough.

2165–7 that…that…who]
On the alternation of the pronouns see n. 1908–14.

2166 ouerture]
Malone (ed. 1790): Opening or discovery (OED, sb. 2: Disclosure, quoting this l.). A few eds. would accent the second syllable, a pronunciation not attested by OED.

2168 O]
Abbott (§§481–2): Monosyllabic exclamations…often take the place of a whole foot, quoting this l. and 2295.

2168 abus’d]
See n. 1226.

2169 that]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): My treatment of my son.

2170 out at gates]
See nn. 655, 1285.

2170–1 smell…Douer]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Contemptuous: His joining the band of traitors there will be small harm. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) compare the treatment of the Paphlagonian king by his son in Sidney’s Arcadia (see ). See also n. 2256.

2171 Exit with Glouster]
Halio (ed. 1992): Although Cornwall repeats Regan’s command two lines later, F is probably right in placing the sd here; Cornwall’s repetition [2174] is for emphasis.

2172 How looke you]
Jennens (ed. 1770): She could never ask how he look’d; she saw that. Eccles (ed. 1792): How you look! Deighton (ed. 1891): Why do you look in that strange way? Kittredge (ed. 1940): How do you seem to be (well or ill)? Harbage (ed. 1958): How looks it with you, what is your condition.

2174 Turne…villaine]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Preoccupied with his wound, he does not notice that Glo. has gone. Wells (ed. 2000): Gloucester may still be present: either a servant may still be untying him, or the servants are too shocked to have begun untying him.

2174–5 throw…dungell]
Bevington (ed. 1980): At some point the body of the slain First Servant must be removed. Eds. do not usually mark this exit.

2175 dungell]
OED (Dunghill sb. 3d) records the sp. dunglecocks in 1580.

2175 apace]
Schmidt (1874): Fast (OED, adv. b).

2176 vntimely]
Deighton (ed. 1891): At an unfortunate moment. Tovey (ed. 1896): When I am wanted at the wars.

2176+1–+9 Seruant.…him]
Theobald (ed. 1733): This short Dialogue I have inserted from the Old Quarto because I think it full of nature. Servants, in any House, could hardly see such a Barbarity committed on their Master, without Reflections of Pity; and the Vengeance that they presume must overtake the Actors of it, is Sentiment and Doctrine well worthy of the Stage. Johnson (ed. 1765): It is not necessary to suppose them servants of Glo’ster; for Cornwall was opposed to extremity by his own servant. Verity (ed. 1897, p. xiii and ad loc.): The consideration of stage-effect seems to have dictated the omission [from F].…[The] passage adds a touch of naturalness and is effective in its way, but that way is not the stage-way, for each [i.e., this passage and 2843+1–+11] marks a pause after the obvious climax, and the climax is the point where the actor, caring primarily for a striking effect, will always wish the scene to close.…[This passage was] omitted in the Folio, probably because merely an after-comment on the situation.…Cornwall’s exit marks the real close of the situation, which is the point where the ordinary playwright and actor will always bring down the curtain, so as to avoid the risk of anticlimax.…There is a tendency to revert to Shakespeare’s method of quieter endings, because it is both monotonous and essentially artificial that every act should close with a striking climax. Goggin (ed. 1910): The Q passage is in accordance with Shakespeare’s practice: the lines furnish a practical comment on the wickedness and barbarity of Cornwall and Regan and on the speedy punishment of crime, while at the same time they give the highly-wrought feelings of the spectators time to calm by showing first what will happen to Edgar and, secondly, that Gloucester’s trial is over and that he is going into safe hands. Granville-Barker (1927, pp. 227–8): I cannot pretend to say why [the cut was made in F], if it was not that when this text was settled, the actors to speak the lines were lacking. No one need abide by this cut. Doran (1931, p. 71): The two Servants…agree to get mad Tom to lead [Gloucester].…We hear nothing more of them, and they may as well be dispensed with here. In the next scene Gloucester, being led by an Old Man, meets Edgar by chance, and he himself hits upon the plan of having the mad beggar lead him. [The omissions of these lines and 2843+1–+11]…make possible the performance of the play with two minor actors instead of with three. (Ibid., p. 77): Only two servants need be present during this scene, one to be slain by Regan and one to be addressed by Cornwall as he leaves the stage. Only the first has to speak. Muir (1957, p. 166): How much the scene would lose by the omission of this choric comment by ordinary humanity on the cruelty of Regan and Cornwall, how necessary it is to end the scene and the act quietly rather than violently, and how desirable it is to prepare the way for Poor Tom’s meeting with Gloucester! Urkowitz (1980, p. 51) finds two justifications for cutting the Q lines: The First Servant’s plan is at odds with how the meeting between Gloucester and Edgar occurs in the next scene, and it removes the theatrical element of surprise.…The meeting in 4.1 should be a surprise to the Old Man who is leading Gloucester, to Gloucester himself, to Edgar, and especially to the audience. Muir (1983, p. 104): But the upsetting of the servants’ plan is itself a surprise,…Shakespeare, often, even usually, writes scenes which happen differently from what he has led us to expect, [and] the real poignancy of the scene depends on the meeting of the son with the father who cannot see him. Mahood (1992, pp. 169, 171): The fact that both [servants and Old Man] remain in the Quarto…[reflects] a manuscript from which Shakespeare had not eliminated unwanted lines.…[The First Servant’s] intervention is overwhelming, not just as a coup de théâtre but in the shock it gave to Elizabethan social assumptions and the lift it gave to the moral sense of the audience. To try to maintain that moral response by means of a choric exchange between the Second and Third Servants was to risk its attenuation…[and] detract from [the] theme of stark retribution. Accordingly, their grief and solicitude and their willingness…to endanger themselves by acting upon them, were transferred to the Old Man. On Sh.’s reasons for inventing the Old Man see n. 2178. Brown (ed. 1996): Did Shakespeare or the actors’ bookkeeper judge that such heroism was unbelievable or that it weakened the contrast of Edgar’s following soliloquy? Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 8): Reduces the number of speaking parts in the scene by two. Taylor (1983, p. 411): But in fact [?] these variants do not affect the number of actors which the King’s Men would have needed to perform Lear, because…the affected roles could easily be doubled…[and] the two characters are probably required on stage whether or not they speak. Edwards (1982, p. 696): The moment of stillness provided by the shock and compassion of the servants in Q is a theatrical experience of the highest order. Whoever cut the scene failed to grasp its theatrical imaginativeness as well as its thematic importance, and he could hardly have been Shakespeare. Warren (1983, p. 64): For a moment the ferocious movement of the play halts and a moral insight is presented; characters comment upon the event in a way that reflects common human feeling confronting enormity; the audience is reminded of the existence of pity and kindness by hearing moral outrage and charitable sentiments expressed. Muir (op. cit., p. 105), speaking from his own experience in acting the part: Gloucester ha[s] very little time between his exit in 3.7 and his reappearance in 4.1 to change his clothes or put on a cloak, and to have his eyes bandaged. Even with the additional 2½ [F] lines in Edgar’s opening soliloquy, Gloucester has only 14 lines in the wings if we stick to the Folio text. It is not enough. Apart from its dramatic value, the dialogue between the servants is a theatrical necessity. Either the cut was made accidentally by the Folio compositor, or the cut was not Shakespeare’s. Anyone who saw the Peter Brook [1962] production of the play will remember the dire effect of the omission of this scene; and this was the Director’s aim. He wanted to eliminate this trace of humanity, so that he could enrol Shakespeare as a forerunner of the Theatre of Cruelty. In omitting these lines Brook was anticipated by Komisarjevsky (Stratford, 1936), who continued the scene into 4.1 by giving Q’s sympathetic Alack sir, you cannot see your way (2198) to the Second Servant instead of the Old Man. Leech (1957, p. 260): If ever an interval was needed at the Globe, it was surely here. Taylor & Jowett (1993, pp. 48–9): The F cut was made possible by an Act-pause between Acts 3 and 4, which gave Gloucester time to change. See . Peat (1984–5, p. 108): F leaves the audience with a feeling of unrelieved hopelessness. The irony of the sententious comments with which Edgar opens the following scene is then immense—an effect usually lost in modern productions, which take an interval after the blinding. Richman (1986, p. 382), on his experience in performance: After Gloucester’s blinding, the chair to which he had been bound and the swords used by Cornwall, Regan, and the slain servant had to be cleared away. Words of pity for Gloucester and horror at his abusers provided an appropriate accompaniment to the servants’ cleaning the mess, and did not slow the action. Weis (ed. 1993): Q (but not F) ends on a choric note which also clarifies the movement of the plot. Here we learn that Edgar’s…presence at Gloucester’s castle is known and that the servants hope to entrust Gloucester to him. (Ibid., p. 25): This cut…is damaging to the F text.

2176+1 Seruant]
Capell named this character 2. S., the first servant having just died.

2176+1–+2 Ile…good]
Tovey (ed. 1896): It will be a proof that there are no avenging gods.

2176+3 old course]
Malone (1780, 1:260): A natural death. Clarkes (ed. 1868), old: Usual, ordinary; Herford (ed. 1899): Familiar. OED (Course sb. 19): Ordinary manner. Edwards (ed. 1975): As against a divinely sent vengeance. Wordsworth (1864, p. 72) compares Num. 16:29, die the common death of all men.

2176+4 women…monsters]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Because [from her ex.] they will lose all fear of vengeance from the gods, comparing 2311+2.

2176+5–+9 2 Seruant, 1 Ser.]
Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): The source for these servants is Sidney’s Arcadia 2.10.3 (see ). Mahood (1992, pp. 170–1): Why then do they make no attempt to defend their master?…They are too few in number,…they are unarmed,…[and] they come under the control of Cornwall as overlord.

2176+5 bedlom]
See nn. 464–5, 1265. Eccles (ed. 1792) first notes the inconsistencies that the servants speak of the Bedlam as a well-known person though Edgar had assumed his disguise only the previous evening, and that in fact an old man subsequently leads Gloucester until, meeting Edgar by accident (2206), he hands Gloucester over to him only with reluctance (2233). He assumes either that the servants here refer to a genuine Bedlam known to them (of whom there is no other trace in the play) or that they have seen Edgar in Gloucester’s company (for which there is no evidence, though such an event is not impossible). Horsman (ed. 1973): Perhaps [these lines represent] Shakespeare’s earlier intention. See n. 2178.

2176+6 he]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Gloucester.

2176+6 his]
Wilson (ed. 1960): The Bedlam’s.

2176+6 rogish]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Vagrant (OED, a. 1, quoting this l.). Greg (1940, p. 169): The word…is required by the metre and in any case is too appropriate to have been invented by the compositor. Its removal in [Q1(c)] must be an accident. Possibly the corrector, intending to alter the spelling, crossed the word out and forgot to write in his emendation. Stone (1980, p. 213): There is no sign of typographical disturbance in [Q1(c)]. Blayney (1982, 1:250): The proofreader’s substitution ed intruding from an adjacent margin of the forme (opposite body/bed in 2297) may have been misread as the delete symbol in this margin.

2176+7 Allows]
Heath (1765, p. 342): Carries its excuse with it—presumably, for aiding a traitor. So Weis (ed. 1993): No one who is sane now dares oppose the wills of Cornwall and Regan, but the bedlam cannot be called to account. Kemshead (ed. 1875): Lends (OED, v. 9, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Budd (ed. 1935): Accommodates itself to any suggestion. Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956): Is available for. Wilson (ed. 1960): Can be persuaded to do. Joseph (ed. 1966): This may mean he is not afraid to do. Only Gardner (ed. 1969): There is no knowing what might happen to him in his vagrant madness; but the servants’ main concern must be for Gloucester, not Tom. Halio (ed. 1973): A vagabond Bedlam, or madman, would be a suitable enough guide, not having any other responsibilities, and the blind man might aid his begging of alms.

2176+8 flaxe…egges]
This common emollient dressing for staunching blood and assuaging the pain of wounds (Clarkes, ed. 1868) is referred to in Jonson’s The Case is Altered (1597) 2.7.141 and is recommended in many medical treatises of the time. Bucknill (1860, p. 268) finds it in John Banister, Chyrurgerie [1575, fols. 48v f.], Craig (ed. 1901) in Philip Barrough, Phisicke ([1583]; 1601, 1.61) and Walter Bailey, Preseruation of eie-sight ([1586]; 1616, p. 53). Cf. William Clowes, Prooued Practise (1588, sigs. D2, P3, P5, et passim). Hoeniger (1992, p. 258) adds Felix Platter’s Praxis Medica (1602–8, 2:col. 270) and Celsus’s De Medicina (6.6.1H–I). Bergeron (1972, p. 207): A treatment recorded as practiced by Shakespeare’s son-in-law, John Hall, physician; Wells (ed. 2000) cites Joan Lane, John Hall and his Patients (Stratford, 1996), pp. 8–10, adding that the flax could be either woven linen or raw fibers.

2177 <Actus Quartus>]
Gentleman (ed. 1773): The Fourth Act…is, in the whole, rather languid, compared to the Third. Baker (1907, pp. 267–8): [Having] just brought the story of Lear…to a fine climax in Act III, [Sh.] must necessarily give immediate attention in Act IV to…Edmund and Edgar. It is much easier to get climax, a swift and unbroken movement, in manipulating a plot of a single interest than with a complicated plot. Leech (1957, p. 260): In Act IV Gloucester and Lear, blind in eyes and in mind respectively, come together; Cordelia arrives in the kingdom; Gloucester and Lear both come to terms with life, both realise their guilt and find a deeper vision and a precarious happiness.…Act IV will remind us of the counter-actions in Macbeth and Titus and Julius Caesar,…a precarious and transient rise, and then a descent to death. Goldberg (1974, p. 97): As a whole, this fourth Act…seems to me to illustrate Shakespeare’s capacity to think about life so powerfully that the energy of the thinking cannot be distinguished from the most powerful capacity to create its object: swiftly, incisively, cumulatively, and in the most searching and disciplined particularity. There is an astonishing and beautiful economy not merely in the way each scene is built, but in the way they are so tellingly juxtaposed. Bullough (1973, p. 294): To intensify the action Shakespeare now makes his most considerable omissions from the old play [Leir]: Cordella’s envoy sent to invite her father to France (Sc. 16 [1229 ff.]); her journey with her husband in disguise, Leir’s crossing and exchange of clothes with the seamen (Sc. 23 [1991 ff.]); and, later, the embarcation of the Gallian forces, the beacon-watchers (Sc. 27 [2388 ff.], 29 [2476 ff.]), the landing and the capture of Dover. Shakespeare wished to have Lear meet his daughter on British soil, to avoid emphasizing the French invasion and to bring all his characters together for the catastrophe.

2177 <Scena Prima>]
Eccles (ed. 1792) reasons from last nights storme (2216) that the time is the same morning as in 3.6, and from 2193–4 that the scene lies at no great distance from the castle of Gloster…somewhere near the road…to Dover. Kittredge (ed. 1940): It follows [3.7] almost immediately.

2178 Edgar]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): The servants,…not finding the supposed beggar, have left the blind nobleman in charge of his faithful tenant. See nn. 2176+1–+9, 2176+5. Sh. included both sets of characters for an obvious reason: the two servants who help Gloucester within the house cannot leave their household service to guide the earl for any distance on the road towards Dover, whereas a tenant farmer might do so. Having imagined the reunion of Gloucester and Edgar as taking place in the blasts of the open air (2185–6), perhaps so that Tom’s shivering (2241) can occasion Gloucester’s charity, Sh. has the Old Man carry out by proxy the two servants’ purposes: to start Gloucester towards Dover and to enlist Tom to lead him. Halio (ed. 1992): Edgar has become detached from Lear and his entourage, left behind deliberately, perhaps, since he is ignored at the end of 3.6.

2179–87 Yet…blasts]
Bradley (1904, p. 306), following Koppel (1899, pp. 96–7), sees this speech as a key to Edgar’s character: The inextinguishable spirit of youth has blown him to the worst; for him the worst returns to laughter. Styan (1979, p. 138), seeing Edgar as a commentator without a defined character: This, another chorus speech, points to the existence of hope at a time when the audience has been desolated by the madness of Lear and the blinding of Gloucester. Wilson (ed. 1960): Deeply ironical in view of what immediately follows.

2179–80 Yet…worst]
Both the Q (see text) and the F punctuation (a comma after flattered, colon after worst) make each line one half of a comparison: Better to be thus (openly scorned) [2179] than to be in the worst condition (secretly scorned though flattered) [2180]. So Reynolds (in Malone, ed. 1790): Better to be thus, in this fixed and acknowledged contemptible state, than, living in affluence, to be flattered and despised at the same time. Cf. Duke Senior’s preference of honest discomfort to flattered pomp in AYL 2.1.2–11 (608–17). Beginning with Pope (see textual n.), the period put after flattered makes to be worst the subject of stands and liues two lines later; though followed by most eds., this construction is awkward in itself and inferior to Q and F, whose thing of Fortune is the easier and more natural subject for those verbs. So Perrett (1904, p. 298): Modern editions which follow Pope…make the passage unintelligible.…The colon after worst [in F] does not denote that what follows is an equivalent of to be worst, but on the contrary denotes that the sentence is complete.…The curious antithesis of better and worst draws the attention to the word which is so much dwelt on in Edgar’s subsequent meditations ([2184, 2186, 2207–11]).…Clearly the subject to lives is thing, not the infinitive, which belongs to the preceding sentence. Similarly Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Better be in this known scorn (i.e., a Bedlam openly despised by everybody) than in unknown scorn, falsely seeming to be esteemed, to be the worst off possible (i.e., a legitimate son apparently held in the highest honor, actually as much underrated as if he were an outlaw). This state he had been in was the worst. He holds it better to be as he is now. Pope’s change makes him contradict himself, by putting in the next sentence, which further unfolds this idea, what does not belong there. Though following Q, Muir (ed. 1952) thinks Perrett’s objection not insuperable, because Shakespeare often changes the construction in the middle of a sentence, and thing is the real subject of stands. Cf. Leir, 2077–8: Why, say the worst, the worst can be but death, And death is better then for to despaire; see . Greg (1940, p. 395) also compares Leir 1470, For fear of death is worse than death itself; see . Rosenberg (1972, p. 245) finds a meaningful ambiguity in Q: Worst is to feel flattered at being worst. Edgar has preened himself on degradation, not citing any evidence. Pope’s change is most vigorously defended by Horsman (ed. 1973): Clearly the occurrences of worst in lines [2180, 2184, and 2186] must all correspond, in opposition to best in line [2183]. It seems too confusing to follow the F and Q punctuation…, for it is not this state [i.e., of being scorned while flattered] which can change only for the better, but rather the state of beggary itself. Traversi (1953, pp. 206–7): The speech has, in fact, a definite positive content. More clearly than ever before, it lays stress upon the advantages of the self-knowledge to be gained from adversity, and so confers universal relevance upon the process of moral illumination we have seen taking place in Lear himself. Kermode (2000, p. 193): This might be the motto of the play, an unrelenting study in protraction; patience, which is continually recommended, is defeated by fortune, by nature, by the indifference of heaven to justice.

2179 Yet]
Collier (1852, pp. 441–2) prefers Yes: Edgar enters, moralising with himself, and giving his assent to some proposition that he had stated before he comes upon the stage.

2179 thus]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Thus contemned. Kittredge (ed. 1940): In this beggarly condition.

2179 knowne]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Known to yourself. Schmidt (ed. 1879): Conscious of, and familiar with. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Emphatic. Johnson (loc. cit.) defends his emendation unknown: a man incognito feels no pain from contempt, because he supposes it incurred only by a voluntary disguise. Lee (ed. 1908): Unknown…conflicts with the context.

2180 contemn’d]
Schmidt (1874): Despise[d] (OED, v. 1). Cf. 2303+1. Halio’s (ed. 1992) substitute condemned is a word with a different meaning and etymology. To contemn is to treat with contempt, not condemnation.

2180 flattered]
F’s comma makes clearer sense if its counterpart is added after Then. Wilson (ed. 1960): Sc. as at court.

2181–2 The…feare]
Theobald (ed. 1733): Copied from Ovid, Ex Ponto 2.2.31–2: Fortuna miserrima tuta est; nam timor eventus deterioris abest (Utter misery is safe, because lacking fear of an outcome still worse). Brower (1971, pp. 126–7) compares Ovid’s Meta. 14.480 and Arthur Golding’s translation of those lines (1567; ed. W. H. D. Rouse, 1961, pp. 285–6, ll. 552–7), ending But when the woorst is past of things, then feare is under foote. And when that bale is hyghest growne, then boote must next ensew. Steevens (ed. 1778) compares Milton, PR 3.206, For where no hope is left, is left no fear. Cf. Vergil, Aen. 2.354, Una salus victis, nullam sperare salutem (One safety the vanquished have, to hope for none). Cunliffe (1893, p. 86): Cf. Seneca, Thebais [Phoenissae] 198–9 and Oedipus 855 [834]. Wilson (ed. 1960): Cf. Bunyan’s He that is down needs fear no fall. Cf. Tilley G464: He that lies upon the Ground can fall no lower. Mrs. Griffith (1775, p. 364): A poetical paraphrase on the flattering old English proverb, that when things are at the worst, they’ll mend (Tilley T216, not citing these lines, though Dent, 1981, does). Elton (1966, p. 98 n.) cites also Tilley B59, D84, W892, adding, Edgar’s choral exposition at his nadir is preliminary to the momentary hopefulness of the same act’s close. Bradbrook (1978, p. 191) compares Malevole in Marston’s Malcontent (1604; ed. G. K. Hunter, 1975, 1.4.43): He’s resolute who can no lower sink; later (4.5.143) he says, He needs must rise who can no lower fall.

2181 deiected]
Schmidt (1874): Humbled (OED, ppl. a. 2, quoting this l. as its first ex.).

2181 thing]
Craig (ed. 1901): In contempt, comparing Cym. 1.1.16, 125, 1.5.62 (23, 149, 562). Joseph (ed. 1966), questionably: Condition, state. But a condition cannot live in fear. More probably, creature or plaything.

2181 of Fortune]
Delius (ed. 1854): Modifies dejected, not thing. On the transposed participle see n. 1707. Wright (ed. 1875), of: By. Craig (ed. 1901): At the hands of, comparing AWW 1.1.6 (11). Tovey (ed. 1896): Or, In the scale of.

2182 Stands…in]
See n. 337.

2182 still]
OED (adv. 6): Even then.

2182 experience]
F corrects to esperance, hope, a word found three other times in Sh. and very likely the word in Q’s copy. Delius (ed. 1854): The rarity of the word caused the Q error (Ger.). Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 403): Alternatively, the copy may have had esperence,…so that the compositor thought he saw esperience. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 519): But this spelling is not recorded; it seems likelier that the compositor misinterpreted his copy as experiance (which is recorded). Only Weis (ed. 1993) attempts to construe Q: The absence of fear results from being numb and arrested (Stands still) in the experience of utter desolation; but still hardly means numb and desolate.

2184 returnes to laughter]
Hudson (ed. 1871): There can be no further change but for the better. See n. 2181–2. Verity (ed. 1897): I.e. to a happy state of things, when laughter is possible. Brooke (ed. 1947) detects the familiar image of Fortune’s wheel, constantly revolving. Those on its bottom live in the element of tears, those on the top in the element of laughter. See n. 1250. Traversi (1953, p. 207): The worst, in other words, is at least as much a turning-point as an end. Empson (1951, pp. 139–40): The notion that there will be happy laughter at any future change…is too absurd.…The point…is that if mad beggars like himself are the worst they are only a form of clown; they can laugh as well as be laughed at. Colman (ed. 1982): Desperation brings its own kind of cheerfulness.

2184–7 Welcome…blasts]
Delius (1876, pp. 136–7): These lines must have been in the original text, for in them [Edgar] applies to his own circumstances comforting reflections on experience in general. The [Q] editor, when he cut them out, certainly was not aware how indispensable they were. He perceived, however, that the omission of them disturbed the metre, and accordingly altered the But…here of the Folio into Who is here; Delius concedes, however, that Q is not usually so careful about meter. Though in Q the next lines are erroneously set as prose, their first two words Who’s here would have completed verse line Q2184 (pace Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 39). The present lines seem therefore just as likely to have been intentionally added to F with metrical adjustment, as to have been accidentally or intentionally omitted from Q. For the idea that this four-line sentence was added to compensate for an earlier cut of fourteen redundant lines in Edgar’s part, see Granville-Barker in n. 2056+5–+18 and Warren (1978, p. 103): In F Edgar speaks still more facilely courageous lines of resolution against fortune just prior to having the inadequacy of his vision exposed by the terrible entrance of his father.…The additional lines at this point emphasize the hollowness of Edgar’s assertions.…Edgar gains in prominence…by the loss of a speech [in 3.6], and the audience becomes more sharply aware of his character. Kerrigan (1983, p. 224): F emphasises his optimism. Halio (ed. 1992, p. 285): The lines make Edgar more vulnerable to the shock of seeing his newly blinded father. The difference made by the added sentence is of degree, since in both texts Edgar resolves to endure present misfortune in the hope of better times; in F he defiantly embraces the worst that the open air can offer, since (then) it is prelude to improvement. So Stone (1980, p. 245): The lines, though more histrionic in tone than those which have preceded, merely echo—somewhat indistinctly at that—the same meaning. There seems no motive for introducing them except to prolong Edgar’s speech and to raise it from the level of introspective musing to that of brave declamation.

2184–7 Welcome]
Brown (ed. 1976): I.e., by my nakedness.

2185 vnsubstantiall]
OED (a. 2 ): Having no…material substance, quoting this l. as its second ex., after Rom. 5.3.103 (2956). Hunter (ed. 1972): Lacking in substance, in wealth, in gifts, in comforts.

2186 The Wretch]
The third-person generalization refers of course to himself. Foakes (ed. 1997), however: Refers to Lear as much.

2187 Owes nothing to]
Eds. have been puzzled by the apparent non-sequitur: having embraced the air, Edgar seems to reject its power upon him. Hudson (ed. 1871): They have done their worst upon him, and so absolved him from all obligations of gratitude. Idem (ed. 1881): He is not indebted to thy blasts for any favour shown him. Moberly (ed. 1876): He need not care for them. Empson (1951, p. 140): He has no feudal duties towards Nature, who is an evil lord. Gardner (ed. 1969): He is entitled to owe neither good nor ill will…to elements that are indifferent. Verity (ed. 1897): Is no debtor to; so has nothing to fear from. Kittredge (ed. 1940): When a man’s debts are paid, he fears no creditor. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): The insubstantiall winds that have done their worst to him, and are empty of everything, these he embraces: they can owe him nothing more (but it is Edgar who owes nothing, not the winds). Joseph (ed. 1966): The wretch…has nothing that thy blasts can claim from him (has been stripped of everything by them). Hunter (ed. 1972): Because the wind’s help led only to the worst, Edgar is free of obligation, and therefore can embrace his creditor without fear—creditor here being apparently ironical. Horsman (ed. 1973): Having paid all he can, he owes it no more—or owes it no deference (as the courtier would to his flatterers. Bevington (ed. 1980): Can pay no more, adding (ed. 1988) is free of obligation. Halio (ed. 1992): Has nothing left to be swept away and therefore can embrace you freely. Most of these readings take owes in the sense of is indebted or obliged to pay and result in strained sense: why, after all, should one owe or have to render anything to harsh blasts of wind? For that reason Moberly and Gardner may be right, taking owes (apparently) in the different sense of cherish a feeling, owe good or ill will (OED, v. 3). Edgar cares nothing for, owes no ill will to, the harsh winds, since they bring him to the point of return to good fortunes; for their doing that he can even embrace them. Perhaps Hudson’s meaning is present as well: Edgar owes the winds no good will either, considering the pain they have caused him.

2188 Enter…]
Adams (1948, p. 327): Does Edgar slip behind a Tree, i.e., a stage post? Perrett (1904, pp. 211–12) compares Leir 2140–78 (see ), where Cordella only gradually recognizes her father in his mariner-disguise, and addresses him as father before discarding her peasant-dress disguise.

2189 poorlie,leed]
Q1(c)’s parti,eyd has only recently been seriously considered; most eds. have adopted Q2’s and F’s poorely led because it makes obvious sense and seems reinforced by the graphically similar though incorrect Q1(u) reading. It may mean either led like a poor man or beggar, not attended as usual by his liveried retainers (Frost, ed. 1909), or led by some poor man (Crook, ed. 1907). Either circumstance would have been a very unaccustomed thing…[and] bespeaks deep humiliation of Gloucester (Skillan, ed. 1967). Doran (1931, p. 103 n.): Although no such word as parti-eyed is known to exist, it does convey a kind of sense as an exclamation…, and it may be a revision. It is probable, however, on account of the form of the words, that in this case the [Q] corrector…was himself misled. Greg (1940, p. 170) finds the F reading exceedingly feeble, and questions why, if it was approximately the reading in Q copy (as Q1[u] suggests), the Q corrector made any alteration. He therefore believes that Q1(c), which is too obscure to be a guess and doubtless incorrect, is an emendation gone wrong (perhaps a perversion by the printer) made from illegible copy whose intended reading is now irrecoverable. Brooke (ed. 1947): Edgar has not yet noticed his father’s blindness.…[Q1(u)] is probably a misreading of poorlie-ledd and…parti,eyd a mere guess. Muir (1949, p. 365): Perhaps Q copy read poorely ’rayed, since the Paphlagonian king in Sh.’s source is so described (Sidney, Arcadia 2.10.1; see ). Idem (ed. 1952): Miss Janet Leeper suggested to me…[that] the initial a deleted by a vertical stroke [presumably for meter]…might have been read as the l of leed. On the other hand, Mr. Wilson Knight points out that Edgar would notice that his father was being led before he noticed his clothes, and R. Flatter (TLS, 22 July 1949 [p. 473]) points out that -ly represents like (cf. Abbott §447 [and Franz §123]). (Ibid., rev. 1957, p. 258): Cf. Tottel, [ed. Arber, 1870, p. 108], poorly rayd, suggested by Maxwell. Davenport (1953, p. 21) defends parti-eyed as meaning displaying contrasted colours at the eyes, a reference to the bloodstained flax and egg-whites, or to blood on the bandages (Orgel, ed. 2000). Evans (1961, p. 325): Possibly a Shakespearean coinage…meaning motley-eyed, comparing LLL Q 5.2.766 (2724), partie coted (F: partie-coated). Sh.’s only other cognate form is party-colourd, MV Q 1.3.88 (415). Similarly Hunter (ed. 1972): Having his eyes looking like a fool’s coat in the red of blood and the white of eggs,…a grotesque image, adding, In F a comma is often a substitute for a hyphen, and may be so here [i.e., in Q1(c)]. Sisson (1956, 2:239): The [Q] corrector misread porely (or porly) [or porlie?] ledd as parti,eied, the y read as i plus the usual straight comma.…He would not see Gloucester’s eyes at first, and his subsequent words refer to effects of age. He learns that Gloucester is blind at [2205] (or [2199?]). The phrase and the situation hark back to Lear’s condition in [1920].…Now Gloucester is in the same condition, poorly accompanied and led. Wells (ed. 2000): With eyesockets of varied colours—bruised and bloody. Blayney (1982, p. 172): The corrector’s decision to change poorlie, leed to parti, eyd was no doubt as mystifying to [Q1 Compositor] B as to everyone else. It is mystifying why Edgar would remark on the eyes’ variegation, not on their being apparently wounded or blinded. Wilson (ed. 1960) explains his poorly eyed: With something wrong with his sight! Cf. Spenser, F.Q. IV.iii.7, watchfull and well eyde. The modern coll. poorly…. [I] first conj. pearly (<sp. parli) = with cataracts, cf. [TGV 5.2.13 (2054)],…too definite for the context. So Horsman (ed. 1973), hyphenating in order to explain why the corrector of Q should need to rewrite the word (and so lead to the compositor’s misreading parti,)—i.e., not only to cut out the comma between the two words but to make them into one compound adjective. Like Greg and Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 403), Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 519) think that a copy of Q with this page in the uncorrected state influenced F (but there is no need to think that Q1 influenced F1; see ), and hence they dismiss the Q-F similarity as insignificant: Q[c] offers the difficilior lectio, and must result from consultation of copy. Q[u]’s poorlie, leed could have arisen from misreading of partie, eyd as porlie, led, followed by dittography of e in the second word. Commas as hyphens occur elsewhere in Shakespearian foul-paper texts. (Ibid., p. 536): Some of the Q[u] readings may occur in F because of a failure to correct Q2 (which derives from Q[u] here). Q2’s influence on F is yet unclear; see . Watt (1997, p. 54): Gory-eyed. Foakes (ed. 1997): But it is not easy to confuse g and p in secretary hand. David Ward, apud Watt: Poor eyes bleed.

2191–2 But…age]
Pope (ed. 1728): The world is so unhappy by its various mutations, that we grow to hate it: otherwise none would endure to live to old age, but in expectation of the period that will put [end] to life, and all its miseries. Malone (ed. 1790) makes the application more immediate and personal: If reverses of fortune and changes such as I now see and feel, from ease and affluence to poverty and misery, did not shew us the little value of life, we should never submit with any kind of resignation to the weight of years, and its necessary consequence, infirmity and death. Muir (ed. 1952) and Anderson (1971–2, p. 270) find a similar idea (and the word mutations) in Montaigne; see . None of the emendations proposed (see textual nn. and ) seems necessary, and many interpretations seem to strain the letter. Clarkes (ed. 1868): We should never be willing to surrender life even in old age—but this converts yeeld to to yeeld in, as does Gardner (ed. 1969), omitting only the Clarkes’ even. Craig (ed. 1901): Being detached from the world, hating it, we can bear its mutations with a certain stoical equanimity—but this converts not yeeld to age to its opposite: we could not endure the stress and strain of life, and so would yield or succumb. Similarly Phelps (ed. 1917): Otherwise we would kill ourselves; no one would grow old. Lee (ed. 1908), embroidering: It is a trifling matter whether we are young or old, strong or weak. Perrett (1904, p. 299), comparing Mac. 3.1.107–10 (1109–12): He would take his life but that the vile buffets of the world which reduce him to such misery also inspire him with hatred for the world and the desire to be avenged on it. There is no hint of revenge in Edgar’s speech. The idea may derive from Nichols (1862, p. 6), who thinks Sh. no mean psychologist in recognizing that hatred…supplies us with powers of endurance little short of those supplied by piety itself; cf. Harrison (ed. 1937): One would not trouble to live but to spite the hated world, and Colman (ed. 1982): Only our vindictive hatred of the world’s unreliability makes us cling to life. Dent (ed. 1927): It is the strange vicissitudes of life that make us grow old—a statement not literally true, though Brooke (ed. 1947) repeats it. Flatter (1948, p. 7): The strange mutations are the transformations that happen to us when we die or are dead. Empson (1951, p. 140): Yield may be…allow authority to old persons, the normal process whose failure has made all this chaos. The chaos has many causes besides age, however, and But that does not mean because. Joseph (ed. 1966): Edgar may be separated from Gloucester and the Old Man by a considerable space. It is highly unlikely that at this point Edgar is commenting on anything more than the change in his father’s fortunes. The fact that Gloucester is blind does not seem to strike Edgar before [2207]. His first reference to his father’s injuries comes only in [2244].

2188 Enter…]
On F’s earlier entrance see n. 1358.

2193–4 O…forescore]
F sets Q’s prose as two rather unsatisfactory pentameters. There is no reason to think that the Old Man speaks verse, and some of his other lines resist metrical linking: cf. 2198, 2205, 2214, 2233.

2193 tenant]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Supposedly the occupant of the farm-house in which Gloster placed Lear for shelter. Since the farmhouse may be an editorial invention (see n. 1996), Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) propose an old retainer of Gloucester, i.e., tenant under him in feudal tenure, not a tenant of a house. So Schmidt (1875): Vassal; servant. In any case, the action takes place near Gloucester’s dwelling (Wells, ed. 2000). Perrett (1904, pp. 210–11) derives the character from Perillus: Sh. was unwilling to lose entirely the pathos…of one old man in utter distress being led and comforted by another, a faithful vassal of no less age and infirmity, comparing Leir 872–87 (see ). Horsman (ed. 1973): An important dramatic contrast to the treatment of Gloucester and Lear by their dependants in III.

2194 forescore—]
On F’s fourescore yeares., Halio (ed. 1992) says, Compositor B…appears guilty of sophistication, completing a sentence meant to be interrupted, as Q indicates. The change could be scribal. The number is biblical for great age: see Psa. 90:10.

2195–7 Away…hurt]
Elton (1966, p. 61) compares the exhortation of the blind Paphlagonian king to his son (Sidney, Arcadia 2.10.1; see ).

2196 comforts]
Schmidt (1874): Assistance. OED (sb. 5): Relief or support in mental distress or affliction, quoting this l. Cf. 2924, 3269, n. 1990.

2197 hurt]
Deighton (ed. 1891): I.e. if his help comes to the knowledge of Cornwall. Harbage (ed. 1958): Since they [i.e., comforts] are forbidden. Edwards (ed. 1975): As assisting an alleged traitor.

2198 Alack sir]
F apparently omits these words to make a pentameter with 2197; but see n. 2193–4.

2199 I…way]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): There is no path in life for me to follow. Skillan (ed. 1967): I.e., life has lost its purpose.

2199 want]
Schmidt (1875): Need;…hence = to wish for.

2200 I…saw]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Walked blindly into trouble. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Gloucester refers to the terrible blunder that he made in believing Edmund’s lies about Edgar, which, he thinks, ought to have been obvious to any clear-sighted judgment. Caldecott (MS notes, 1813–33): How many volumes of declamation are these five words worth? Heilman (1948, pp. 41–64): These words express one of the central paradoxes of the play; moreover (p. 44), Gloucester here summarizes his whole career. Carter (1905, p. 439) compares Matt. 13:13, The seeing see not, and Isa. 59:10, we stomble at noone day. Colie (1974, pp. 131–2) adds Job 5:14, They…grope at noone day. Delasanta (1987, p. 27) finds a despairng parody of John 11:9–10: If a man walke in the day, he stombleth not, because he seeth the light of this worlde (Geneva), i.e. Jesus. Following Henderson (1940, pp. 41–2), Atkinson (1949, pp. 356–8) notes in Montaigne a detail that queerly connects with the blinding of Gloucester: Therefore was it, that a worthy Philosopher pulled out his eyes, that so he might…the better and more freely apply himselfe unto Philosophy; see . Henderson cites also Montaigne’s Sebond: The weaknesse of our judgement, helps us more than our strength to compass the same [viz., religious faith], and our blindnesse more than our cleare-sighted eies; see . Muir (ed. 1952, p. 252), followed by Salingar (1986, p. 138), also compares another passage from the same essay: We must be besotted ere we can become wise, and dazled before we can be led; see .

2201 meanes secure vs]
Knight (ed. 1840), means: Resources, powers, capacities (OED, Mean sb.2 12). Wordsworth (1864, pp. 248–9): In Gloster’s case, his sight. OED (Secure v. 1): To make free from care or apprehension; also, to make careless or overconfident, quoting Oth. 1.3.10 (336) and this l. as its first exx.; cf. Tim. 2.2.176 (852), and the common use of the adjective in Sh. to mean over-secure. The unusual verb long puzzled commentators and led to tortured interpretations and many emendations (see textual nn. and ). Rankin (1841, p. 178) first gives the most likely interpretation here—Our abilities and powers make us rash and unwary. J. (1853, p. 4) gives examples of the verb and a Biblical analogue (2 Cor. 12:9–10), and Stylites (1855, p. 153) adds Judges 8:11. The idea is proverbial: Tilley W152, The Way to be safe is never to be secure. The Clarkes (ed. 1868) support the reading as a parallel to Gloucester’s previous sentence I stumbled when I saw, and Moberly (ed. 1876) and Verity (ed. 1897) point out the antithesis of two paradoxes, harmful advantages (means) and saving defects. Elton (1964, p. 226) gives means the theological meaning of good works, quoting the opinion of Gulielmus Bucanus (Institutions, 1606, p. 150) that God’s providence is abused by them who being preposterously secure neglect all mænes, and adding, In Gloucester’s bewildering universe, good works seem paradoxical or inconsequential,…[bringing] false complacency.
The following are mostly earlier and less successful interpretations. Warburton (ed. 1747), reading mean secures: Moderate, mediocre condition. Capell (1783, 1.2:173): Had [Gloucester] been a man in that station, he had ’scap’d these calamities; his defects (his want of fortune and title) had screen’d him from the machinations of wickedness, and so prov’d his commodities. Malone (ed. 1790), retaining means: A plural, when the subject spoken of related to more persons than one.…In a moderate or middle state of life, we are secure from those temptations to which the more prosperous and affluent are exposed. Rann (ed. 1794): A moderate fortune is most secure. Caldecott (MS notes, 1813–33): Golden mean. Schmidt (ed. 1879) denies that means = moderate condition occurs in Sh. or elsewhere, and OED does not support such a sense. Jennens (ed. 1770): Mean things…i.e. adversae res. Arrowsmith (1855, pp. 97–8): Gloucester’s means are straitened by the loss of his eyes, and thereby Providence keeps him safe from further excesses…ruinous to himself, as well as hurtful to others. Halliwell (ed. 1856), means: Want of means, the low state of our means. Wright (ed. 1875): Things we think meanly of, our mean or moderate condition. Lee (ed. 1908), followng Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Our…weaknesses cause us to employ such care as to make them of advantage to us.…Now that [Gloucester] is blind…he is likely to avoid stumbling.

2201 and]
Most eds. now take this to mean and on the other hand. Harrison (ed. 1948): And then.

2201 meare]
Hudson (1881): Very (OED, a.1 4: Absolute). Cf. 3108.

2201 defects]
Rann (ed. 1794): Wants. Muir (ed. 1952): Disadvantages. Bevington (ed. 1980): Afflictions. Only Elton (1966, p. 82): Deficiency of good works; see n. 2201.

2202 Proue]
Prove to be. Moberly (ed. 1876): We are saved by something that seemed a weak point. Verity (ed. 1897): Leads us to be circumspect and take heed lest we fall. Darton (ed. 1928): Tests our ability. Kittredge (ed. 1940): It forces us to recognize the facts of life.

2202 comodities]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Advantages. Meiklejohn (ed. 1879) compares 2H4 1.2.248 (496–7), turne diseases to commoditie.

2203 food]
Schmidt (1874): Nourishment. Craig (ed. 1901): Object for. Wells (ed. 2000): Victim of, or food for.

2203 abused]
See n. 1611. Rosenberg (1972, p. 246): Also literally.

2204–5 Might…againe]
Whalley (1748, p. 59) compares blind Oedipus’s similar wish for his daughters, OT 1469–70. Bradley (1904, p. 258): Why does Edgar not reveal himself to his blind father, as he truly says [3155] he ought to have done? Hazen (1943): Had Edgar revealed his identity, he might have been able to save Gloucester in some other way, but the method he chose would have been impossible.…[Secondly,] what audience wants to be delayed by a tearful reconciliation?…Surely it is better to compress the recognition and reconciliation…in the subplot to the great recognition scene when Lear finds Cordelia.…[Moreover,] the change of heart that is true forgiveness requires the healing power of time.…[Finally, perhaps] Edgar does not hear the two significant remarks of Gloucester in lines [2202] and [2217], or at least he fails to grasp their significance. Muir (ed. 1952): He had wished, we may suppose, not only to overcome his father’s desire for suicide, but also to convince him that the gods were not spiteful. He may have delayed the revelation of his identity in order to impose a penance on his father, and to guarantee the genuineness and permanence of his repentance.…There is, too, a suggestion [2056+14–+16?] that Edgar wished to rehabilitate himself in the eyes of the world, and punish Edmund, before revealing himself. Cavell (1969, pp. 282–5): This [first explanation] seems to me psychologically fantastic; it suggests that the first thing which occurs to Edgar on seeing his father blinded is to exact some further punishment.…What Edgar does is most directly described as avoiding recognition.…He is himself ashamed and guilty.…He failed to confront his father, to trust his love.…He is as responsible for his father’s blinding as his father is.…He cannot bear the fact that his father is incapable, impotent, maimed. He wants his father still to be a father, powerful, so that he can remain a child—a motive he never expresses. To remain a dependent child Edgar would have to be one; instead, having fled from Gloucester, he now becomes his father’s guard, and will shortly risk his life twice in personal combat to save both Gloucester and Albany—hardly infantile behavior. He is of course not trying to punish Gloucester but to cure him of the mortal sin of despair. As far as Edgar knows at this moment, his father is still scarce friendes with him, is obviously suffering the anguish of wounds, blindness, betrayal, and rejection, and is in suicidal despair; and Edgar may wish to avoid recognition by yet other enemies such as Edmund and the sisters. Edgar first tends to Gloucester’s immediate needs—protection, guidance, comfort; his own self-discovery, with its complex of explanation and further extreames of passion (3161), can wait. Foakes (1993, p. 199): In maintaining his disguise he always remains in control of himself, aloof from, and when necessary able to manipulate, the feelings of Lear and Gloucester, and so is able to become an agent of their recovery. (Ibid., p. 48), like Hazen: Shakespeare may simply have wanted to avoid a recognition scene that might undercut the effect of awakening of Lear in 4.7. See also n. 2224–5.

2204 see…tuch]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): The poetically expressed aspiration of a blind man. Eds. have worried the metaphor unnecessarily. Steevens (ed. 1793) compares 2593, but there feelingly means emotionally, not palpably. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Hold thee in my embrace. Alpers (1962, p. 144): What is important for Gloucester is not insight but a relationship.

2205 I…againe]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): It would be as great a blessing as the restoration of eyesight.

2206 How now]
See n. 361. Wells (ed. 2000): Presumably a response to some movement or sound from Edgar.

2207 say]
Deighton (ed. 1891): As I presumptuously did just now [2180]. Barton (1971, pp. 25–6): Edgar too discovers the limits of language.…Situations overwhelm words, comparing 2585. Hunter (ed. 1972): The scene up to this point may be taken as an illustration of the folly of Edgar’s initial confidence.

2208 worse]
Moberly (ed. 1876): By my father’s misery. Armour (ed. 1930): Because he cannot reveal himself to his stricken old father.

2209 poore mad Tom]
See n. 1271.

2210–11 worst…worst]
Warburton (ed. 1747): While we live; for while we yet continue to have a sense of feeling, something worse than the present may still happen; a retraction of 2180–6, as Skillan (ed. 1967) notes. Moberly (ed. 1876): There is always in lowest depth a lower deep of possible suffering. Hudson (ed. 1879): He concludes death to be the worst. Kittredge (ed. 1940), following Kelcy (1932, p. 368): For so long as we can take comfort in assuring ourselves,…we are not hopeless and so not actually at the worst. Joseph (ed. 1966): What seems to us the worst may not truly be so. It may be followed by worse still. Only when things have improved can we see what was worst. Rosenberg (1972, p. 247): Also, in this context, things will be [worse]. Bullough (1973, p. 388 n.) compares Leir 2077: Why, say the worst, the worst can be but death; see .

2212 Fellow]
See n. 557.

2212 goest]
On omission of the pronoun see n. 562.

2213 begger man]
OED (sb. 7a): Earliest ex. of the compound.

2215 has some reason]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Is not wholly madman. Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956): Has enough sense to be aware of his physical needs.

2217 a worme]
I.e., the lowliest of creatures. Page (ed. 1889): On account of his nakedness [and filth]: cf. 1258–62. Elton (1966, pp. 62, 192, 195) cites contemporary instances of the comparison in Sidney, Montaigne, and others. Like Jean Calvin’s reference to man as a worme of five feete long (Institutes, 1.5.4, tr. T. Norton, 1587), Gloucester’s comparison may derive from Job 25:6 (Krauth, apud Furness, ed. 1880) or 17:14 (Holloway, 1961, p. 85; Aberbach, 1979, p. 130). Horsman (ed. 1973) compares Psa. 22:6: I am a worme, & not a man, and Colie (1974, p. 129) adds Job 17:14, and Milward (1987, p. 185), Isa. 41:14. OED (sb. 10a) records exx. of the metaphor from ca. 825.

2217–18 sonne…my mind,]
Eccles (ed. 1792): The appearance of the supposed madman…suggested to his mind the hardship to which his son might hereafter be exposed in consequence of his displeasure. Moberly (ed. 1876) compares Orlando’s thoughts of Rosalind in the presence of Ganymede, AYL 5.4.28–9 (2604–5), and Hudson (ed. 1879), Cymbeline’s remembrance without recognition of Imogen in Cym. 5.5.92–3 (3357–8). Cf. 1946–9.

2220 heard more]
Crook (ed. 1907): Of his merits. Cf. 2165–8.

2221–2 As…sport]
The topos of Mankind as sport for, or tossed by, the gods is documented fully by Elton (1966, pp. 164–7). Of his many examples, Plautus’s Captivi, Prol. 22, and Sidney’s Arcadia 2.12.2 (see : Balles to the starres) are first adduced by Steevens (ed. 1773; MS notes, 1793–1803); the latter passage is proposed as Sh.’s immediate source by Muir & Danby (1950, p. 50). Elton also finds men as the devils’ tennis balls in Harsnett’s Declaration (1603, p. 153). Armstrong (1949, p. 665) and Bullough (1973, p. 412 n.) cite Arcadia 3.10.4 (see ), where Cecropia argues that the gods are no more moved by men than men by flies. Like Robertson (1909, p. 110), Muir (ed. 1952) quotes from Florio Montaigne’s tr. of Plautus’s lines; see . In Upon Some Verses of Virgil Montaigne also ascribes to Plato the idea that man was made by the Gods for them to toy and play withall (tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 3:105). This speech of Gloucester is usually quoted in discussions of the play’s import, often to quite opposite effects. Mrs. Griffith (1775, p. 365): This is a most impious and unphilosophic reflection…better not spoken at all. Swinburne (1880, pp. 171–2): Tragic fatalism; The words…strike the keynote of the whole poem…. There is no…light of heavenly harmony or of heavenly wisdom. Chambers (1940, p. 30): The gods are giving Gloucester his wish, and, if he can but be saved from despair, he will live to know it. Shakespeare’s irony runs deep. Heilman (1948, p. 111): What the reader already knows is that…Edgar and his love for his father have both survived, so that the main cause for Gloucester’s despair no longer exists. Rosenberg (1972, p. 247): He is blaming the Gods now for all that man the worm does to his kind.…This is not insight. Edwards (ed. 1975): Gloucester pauses to ask what reason there can be in what he and Edgar have suffered.…He may be excused his bitterness, but he perhaps forgets his own complicity in Edgar’s misfortunes. See .

2221 are toth’]
F’s are to may indeed correct confusion here with the second part of the same line (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 404), though Q’s line is clear and metrical enough despite the unidiomatic article (Wells & Taylor, 1987, p. 519).

2221 wanton]
Schmidt (1875): Playful, sportive (OED, adj. 3); cf. 1400. OED (1, 1d): Naughty, unruly; Said of boys, with mixture of sense 4 [spoiled]; often…with reference to childish cruelty, quoting this l. as its first ex. Ridley (ed. 1935): Thoughtless (OED, 5: Reckless…merciless). Satin (1966, p. 464): Cf. Leir 210 (see ).

2222 bitt]
An apparent misreading of F’s kill. Like Greg (1940, p. 159), Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 358) cites a b/k error at 1211 and l/t errors at 867, 1786, etc. Only Weis (ed. 1993): Q’s bitt…could mean bit: to put the bit into the mouth…[or] to bite.

2223 this]
Moberly (ed. 1876): His father’s aphorism, whose truth Edgar is questioning. Furness (ed. 1880): His father’s blindness. Verity (ed. 1897): And present plight—perhaps including his loss of faith. Tovey (ed. 1896): That his father’s mind has changed towards him. Wilson (ed. 1960): A cry of anguished astonishment [at several changes].…What was the meaning of it all? Joseph (ed. 1966): What is happening here? Hunter (ed. 1972): How can the mental even more than the physical condition of Gloucester have changed so radically?

2224–5 bad…others]
Rann (ed. 1794): ’Tis an irksome task to attempt the relief of another’s sorrow by forced follies, which are at once both disgusting to ourselves, and [to] those we mean to amuse. Perrett (1904, p. 299): Is there not an expression of Sh.’s own dislike, in certain moods, for the actor’s profession? Empson (1951, p. 141): Edmund rejects Gloucester’s accusation that the gods are malicious mockers: This is the trade Edgar has adopted, and he feels it is too bad a trade for the gods—a reading which makes play the fool mean be the deceiver, not the foolish victim. Wilson (ed. 1960): An apology <by Sh. to his audience> for the strange part Edg. is now to play in company with his sorrowing and suffering father…though it is never explained why he must, comparing 2243 and 3155. Rosenberg (1972, p. 248): Bad indeed—…unpleasant, difficult, but also cruel, teasing, deceiving, even evil…wanton…masochistic as well as sadistic, citing 3155. Horsman (ed. 1973): The only reason…is that the parallelism of plot and subplot must be continued into Act V. Mack (1965, p. 12): Tate’s Edgar tells us immediately [1681, p. 42; 4.2]…it is for fear the old man’s heart will break of extremes of grief and joy. See also n. 2204–5.

2224 trade]
Schmidt (1875): Occupation (OED, sb. 5). Craig (ed. 1901): Path [OED, 1].…Some [Dyce, ed. 1866–7, 9:457] explain trade as course [OED, 3].

2224 the foole]
F omits the article, apparently to smooth meter. Hudson (ed. 1871): The Fool’s part, to divert off distressing thoughts, or to turn grief into laughter. Foakes (ed. 1997): Possibly a comment on the Fool and Poor Tom, as well as on his immediate role.

2225 angring]
Heath (1765, p. 342): Displeases (OED, Anger v. 1: To distress, trouble, vex, latest ex. 1440). Capell (1783, 1.2:174): Term for a sore’s fretting (OED, 3: Irritate). Hudson (ed. 1871): Grieving, a sense denied by Rolfe (ed. 1880) and unsupported by OED. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Perhaps…anguishing. Foakes (ed. 1997): Because he feels forced to conceal his real identity?

2225 it selfe]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Grammatically refers to the trade, but logically to the man.

2225 others]
Budd (ed. 1935): E.g. Gloucester, referring to 2216–19. But Edgar may be speaking generally.

2225 blesse thee]
Wells (ed. 2000): Probably a begging cry, comparing 2015.

2225 maister]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Sir.

2226 fellow]
See n. 16.

2228 Then…gon]
Q’s line is metrically complete; F’s omission of the first two words and substitution of away results in an imperfect line and one that is difficult to link metrically with 2227, if such was the intent. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 180): Q’s first two words improve the sequence. Gloucester says…Is…fellow? He is answered in the affirmative, and goes on—in effect—In that case (Then) please go away.…F seems to me disconcertingly abrupt. The F compositor may well be guilty of a careless omission. Werstine (1983, p. 283) cites other instances where Compositor B omitted the first word or two of a speech. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 536), defending F: It seems excessive to attribute three variants in five words to the compositor. F’s tetrameter is acceptable.

2228 prethee]
See n. 664.

2229 here]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 404): The compositor may have misread…as heere F’s hence.

2230 ancient loue]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Good will you have…[long] borne me; cf. 2193–4. Harbage (ed. 1958): Such love as formerly bound master and man; cf. AYL 2.3.56 ff. (760 ff.). Fraser (ed. 1963) finds both meanings, as does Edwards (ed. 1975): Of long standing (and hence old-fashioned).

2231 bring some couering]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): This request…serves the dramatic purpose of accounting for Edgar’s subsequent appearance in better clothing than his Bedlam beggar’s blanket; and also serves the moral purpose of showing Gloster’s thought for the unfortunate, elicited by his own misfortunes. Ringler (1981, p. 191): As naked Bedlam he could neither fight Oswald in 4.6 nor advise Albany in 5.1. Lott (ed. 1974): An important dramatic device. The stage is now left clear for Gloucester and Edgar to be alone together, and for the revelation of Edgar to his father to begin. Milward (1987, p. 185) finds echoes of Isa. 48:7 and Matt. 25:36.

2231 soule]
Mahood (1957, p. 46): Both person [OED, sb. 12] and the immortal part, the understanding spirit [OED, 2, 9].

2232 Who]
Crook (ed. 1907): Nominative by position (instead of whom). On F’s Which see n. 744+4.

2232 leade me]
Fraser (1962, p. 67): Edgar enacts the familiar emblem of Aeneas bearing Anchises, comparing 2H6 5.2.62 (3284).

2234 times]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Time (= the world [OED, sb. 5: state of affairs at a particular period]) is generally sing. elsewh. in Sh.; but the meaning could be the age now…present (OED, 3d), expressed in both sing. and pl. in Sh. Edwards (ed. 1975): Characteristic…of the times. Dyce (ed. 1865) gives Shn. exx. of the plural, Rolfe (ed. 1880) of the singular.

2234 plague]
See n. 337.

2235 when…blind]
Proverbial: Dent (1981, B452), If the Blind lead the blind they both fall into the ditch (Luke 6.39). Carter (1905, p. 439): Cf. Matt. 15:14. Eccles (ed. 1792): The observation appears to have had a political origin, and to be expressive of the consequence of the ignorant and short-sighted multitude being led away by the indiscreet zeal of rash and misjudging enthusiasts. Moberly (ed. 1876): The elements were already working in England which produced the Fifth Monarchy and the Blackfriars’ fanatics, Naylor, General Harrison, and the like. As for the proverb’s application here, Deighton (ed. 1891): When the times are under a curse. Tovey (ed. 1896): A common misfortune therefore, to which I will submit. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Gloucester makes a kind of parable out of his own situation. Reibetanz (1977, p. 43): Paradox leaps to life when Edgar, supposedly mad but really the sanest man in the play, leads out a blind Gloucester who has finally gained a clearer vision of himelf. No iconographer could portray it more concisely. Butler (1984, pp. 228 ff.) compares an emblem in Thomas Combe’s tr. of Guillaume de la Perrière’s The Theater of Fine Devices (1614) depicting a blindfolded Lady Fortune leading a blindfolded man over an uneven field. He argues that Edgar is analogously a providential agent leading Gloucester; but neither the emblem’s details, motto, nor verse, warning against following Fortune’s guidance, is very apposite.

2236 doe thy pleasure]
Armour (ed. 1930): Gloucester remembers that he has no longer the power to order.

2237 Aboue the rest]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Above all other things (OED, Rest sb.2 5c: Especially, quoting only this l.).

2237 be gon]
See n. 2195–7.

2238 parrell]
OED (Parel sb.): Aphetic form of…Apparel. Abbott §460 and Craig (ed. 1901) list other such forms in Sh., though no other instance of this one occurs. Mahood (1992, pp. 173–4): He succeeds, for Edgar is dressed as a countryman when Oswald encounters him near Dover.…The gift…has a bearing on the play as a whole. It represents a first step in the restoration of man from the level of a poor, bare, forked animal.…[It is also] a reverberation of the theme of charity so clearly sounded in the third act.…[It] prepares us for Edgar’s rescue of his father from despair and Cordelia’s rescue of her father from madness.

2239 Come…will]
Tilley C529 compares the proverb Come (Hap) what come (hap) may.

2240 Sirrah]
See n. 411.

2240, 2242 fellow]
See n. 16.

2241 Poore Toms]
See n. 1271.

2241 a cold]
See n. 1839.

2241 dance it]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 404): Perhaps a misreading: (i) u/n: (ii) a badly written b might conceivably be taken as a long s plus e. The Q compositor may have misread [F’s daub] as danse and set up dance. Stone (1980, p. 221): Possibly Tom has been dancing his way along, like the clown Kempe. Weis (ed. 1993): Q’s reading is dramatically stronger. It does not require the line to be spoken aside (as in F), since Gloucester will dismiss it as nonsense or as a statement about his being rigid with cold and therefore unable to proceed (dance). Eds. generally follow F. Hanmer (ed. 1743–4, 6:Gloss. s.v. Parget): To daub or plaister over; cf. 1139. Hence Warburton (ed. 1747): Disguise. Rann (ed. 1794): Carry on the farce. OED (v. 7b): To put on a false show; to dissemble, quoting this l. as its first ex. Joseph (ed. 1966): (Literally) paint it white. Deighton (ed. 1891): In daub there is the idea of doing a thing clumsily (OED, 5). For the indefinite use of it see n. 435.

2241 farther]
Weis (ed. 1993) imagines a pun on father, precluded by F’s further.

2243 And…must:]
F’s addition is a continuation of Edgar’s aside in 2241. Stone (1980, p. 220): Since Edgar none the less continues to put on a false show the [F] reviser felt it necessary to add these words here. Halio (ed. 1992): Edgar’s half-line completes the sense of I…further and regularises the line metrically. Its omission in Q may be accidental, or its appearance in F may be a consequence of the correction daub for dance. It is possible that 2243 was intended to make a pentameter with 2244, despite a line break after the colon to show change of address. Metrical regularization, however, was not necessary, since in Q 2242 and 2244 make a pentameter. Foakes (ed. 1997): It is hard to see why he still must conceal himself from his father, except in terms of the needs of the plot. See nn. 2204–5, 2224–5.

2244 Blesse…bleed]
Wilson (ed. 1960): He now sees the full horror of it. See n. 2189. Wells (1961, pp. 311–13): The title Blesse thy faire eyes from the foule fiend affixed to a version of Tom o’ Bedlam’s song in Bishop Bancroft’s commonplace book in the Bodleian Library may allude either to Sh.’s line or to a conventional formula. Sh.’s line would surely gain in poignancy if it were seen to begin as a conventional begging phrase, followed by a breakdown into personal emotion.

2246–2248+5 Both…maister]
] Obviously false verse in Q.

2246 horse-way, and foot-path]
I.e. both highways for horse and cart traffic, and smaller paths for foot-passengers only (OED, quoting this l. for both terms). Hunter (ed. 1972): Each kind of path has its appropriate obstacle—the stile for the footpath, the gate for the horse-way (bridle-path).

2247 Poore…wits]
Hunter (ed. 1972) attempts to find consecutive thoughts: The landscape is for Tom a series of places to be scared in, where the foul fiend has appeared. But Edgar may be simply resuming from 2241 his Poor Tom routine, to re-identify himself to the blind Gloucester. Murphy (1984, p. 211): Good is emphatic.

2247, 2248+1 Poore Tom]
See n. 1271.

2247 wits]
OED (Wit sb. 4b): = Sense sb. 10. See n. 2765.

2248 the]
Probably a variant spelling or misreading of F’s thee; cf. 196, 817. Edgar uses the formula blesse thee at 1840, 2225, and 2248+5, and blesse thy at 2015 and 2244. It is evident from 2248+5 that the good man being blessed is Gloucester rather than himself.

2248 good man]
F’s change to good mans sonne is puzzling, since the added sonne is not clearly necessary; Sh. does use the F phrase elsewhere. Wilson (ed. 1960): Poss. goodman’s son, i.e. son of the old tenant (l. [2193]) who has just left him. Good-man = a man of substance, not of gentle birth (O.E.D. [4]). Foakes (ed. 1997), on F: Addressing his father as if he were the son of a yeoman or innkeeper, but also a good man.

2248+1–+5 Fiue…maister]
