Theobald (ed. 1733) restores the passage, cut from F, as it came from our Author, by the Help of Bishop Harsenet’s Pamphlet [see n. 1827].…We find there, all these Devils were in Sarah and Friswood Williams, Mrs. Peckham’s two Chambermaids; and particularly Flibbertigibbet, who made them mop and mow like Apes, says that author. And to their suppos’d Possession, our Poet is here satirically alluding. Sara had within her all the deuils in hell, not just five; see . Johnson (ed. 1765): Omitted in the folio, because I suppose as the story [i.e., of the Jesuits’ dealing with demoniacs] was forgotten, the jest was lost. Capell (1783, 1.2:172): It had previously been [left out] in the representation;…the matters alluded to being then stale with the publick.…The only purpose it serves…is—shewing how much the speaker is straiten’d for materials to carry on his deception. Bratton (ed. 1987): Tom’s fiends were cut by eighteenth- and nineteenth-century actor-editors. Like Moriarty (1913, pp. 458–9), Granville-Barker (1927, p. 228): The cut is, I think, to the good. A few lines before he says: I cannot daub it further. And in any case the effect of the mad lingo will have been exhausted in the scenes with Lear. Doran (1931, p. 76): Obscurity of meaning may explain the omission. Edgar may intend the speech to remind or reassure the blind Gloucester that he is the same mad Tom of the previous scenes. Hart (1942, p. 148): Edgar’s catalogue of fiends…may have been preserved in Q1 out of compliment to King James whose Daemonologie had been reissued in London during the plague year, 1603. Stone (1980, p. 272): The reviser very probably felt that there was more in this speech than was dramatically justified. Halio (ed. 1992): Edgar’s identity as Poor Tom is by now well established and does not require further ravings. Gloucester has earlier heard Edgar talk of Modo, Mahu, and the prince of darkness (1921–2, 2014+12) but not of lust, stealing, or other sins (1861–77) or of Fliberdegibit (1895), Hoppedance (2014+12), or Obidicut. Foakes (1993, p. 200): F omits lines which distract from the pathos of the scene. Idem (ed. 1997): They are perhaps too much like repetition of 3.4.

2248+1 at once]
Percy (in Steevens, ed. 1778) finds the idea of simultaneous possession by several fiends in Harsnett’s Declaration (1603, pp. 278, 281): The deuill in Ma: Mainy confessed his name to be Modu, and that he had besides himselfe seaven other spirits.…[281] [The exorcist Edmunds and those present cried out] so as both that wicked Prince Modu, and all his company might be cast out. Halliwell (ed. 1865): Percy is not helpful, since Harsnett refers to seven devils, which, emanating from priests, ha[ve] no doubt reference to the seven devils of Scripture. Perhaps those of Edgar have more allusion to the five senses, or wits, as he has called them, each of which is troubled by a separate devil. The correlation is not obvious. Muir (ed. 1952) also cites Harsnett (p. 50): These were all in poore Sara at a chop.…Shee poore wench had ALL hell in her belly; see . Harbage (ed. 1958): Shakespeare identifies each devil with some form of possession. Lott (ed. 1974): The devils are associated with particular evils in the way that patron saints are looked to for particular kinds of help.

2248+2 Of]
Halio (ed. 1992): I.e. prince of lust (syllepsis). Or fiend of.

2248+2 as]
Walker (1860, 2:249): Namely, to wit. OED (adv. B.26): Introducing instances in exemplification or illustration of a general designation: Like and including, such as. Lott (ed. 1974): In the person of (OED, 11b). For a suspected inversion, see textual n.

2248+2 Obidicut]
Craig (ed. 1901): An evident corruption of the word Hoberdicut, named in Harsnett (1603, pp. 119; spelt Haberdicut, p. 181). Muir (1951, p. 20): The only [fiend] not mentioned earlier. Only Kittredge (ed. 1940) cites Tocobetto (see n. 2014+12). Wells (ed. 2000): Hudson’s re-ordering…seems unnecessary (see textual n.).

2248+2 Hobbididence]
Presumably the same as Hoberdidance; see n. 2014+12. OED, citing only Harsnett and this l.: The first element seems to be Hobby…the rest seems to be F. de danse of the dance sc. Morris. The name of a malevolent sprite or fiend, one of those introduced in the morris-dance. In Harsnett (1603, p. 180), he also vsed his cunning, to make a Lady laugh.

2248+2 dumbnes]
Though most eds. accept Q’s reading, it makes poor sense, since dumbness is not a sin like lust, stealing, murder, etc., and in Harsnett (1603, p. 140) Haberdidance has a voyce was heard by a Cooke. Wilson (ed. 1960): A fiend of dumbness is intelligible; but what is a Prince of Dumbness? Possibly Sh. forgot that Maho, not Hoberdidance, is called The Prince of hel and the black Prince in Harsnett (pp. 119, 146), as Modu is Prince of all other devils (p. 268–70, 278); or perhaps the epithet prince of darkness may be applied to more than one devil: see n. 1921–2. Since u/a and b/k misreadings occur elsewhere in the play (644, 1840; 1211, 2222) and a final upward stroke of an a (of which there are several exx. in Hand D of Thomas Moore) could easily be misread as a minim, a misreading of darknes as dumbnes is very likely. Foakes (ed. 1997): An obvious error, since this passage recalls [1921–2]…. In Harsnett [1603, p. 140] Hobbididance appears like a whirlwind, turning round like a flame of fire; see .

2248+3 Mahu…Modo]
See n. 1921–2.

2248+3 Stiberdigebit]
See n. 1895. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 404): Fliberdigebit must have been the reading of the copy for Q. Perhaps the horizontal stroke crossed the l rather than the f, so that the f appeared a long s and the l a t. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 519): The error suggests that the initial capital is compositorial.

2248+4 Mobing]
Most eds. accept Theobald’s emendation to mopping, though a few have adopted Duthie’s mocking; see textual n. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 404): As regards Mobing—the b does not look to me like a turned p: straightforward misreading of p as b seems hardly likely; and taking graphic considerations into account Mobing might be more easily supposed to be an error for moking, i.e. mocking, than for moping, i.e. mopping [comparing 1211].…Mocking and mowing go quite well together (to mow is to grimace derisively [see next n.]). On the other hand, mopping and mowing go perhaps even better together (mop = grimace [OED, sb.3: Chiefly in phrase mops and mows]), comparing Tmp. 4.1.47 (1702), Sh.’s only other use of the word. Manuscript b and p may look quite similar despite their different heights within the line. Ingham (1967, p. 84): Possibly an example of voiceless stops in intervocalic positions. Whalley (in Reed, ed. 1785), Nares (1822), and Halliwell (ed. 1856) give several contemporary instances of mops and mows. Malone (ed. 1790): The words are paired in Harsnett (1603, p. 136; see )—to…make anticke faces,…mow, and mop like an Ape; they reappear on pp. 38, 158, and 166 (Muir, 1951, pp. 20–1), as does mouthes and mops (p. 30). The phrase mock and mow, also proverbial (Tilley M1030), was apparently older (OED, Mop v.1); it appears in Tmp. 3.3.82 SD (1617). There is little difference in meaning, though mock (OED, sb.1 1: A derisive or contemptuous action or speech) may include words and gestures as well as grimaces.

2248+4 Mohing]
Error for mowing, making moues. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 519): This error suggests that the initial capitals and italics in the preceding names are all compositorial. Rann (ed. 1794): Making mouths (Mow, OED, v.3 1; cf. sb.2 1: A derisive grimace). Nares (1822): Particularly attributed to apes. Craig (ed. 1901) adds to Nares’s exx.; cf. Tmp. 2.2.9 (1048) and see prev. n. Moberly (ed. 1876) understands chambermaids’ antics before their mistress’ dressing-glass, and Kittredge (ed. 1940) adds in support, A flibbertigibbet is a flirt, a frivolous creature. Hence this is a good name for the demon that prompts affected airs and graces; cf. 1686–7. But the word suggests rather the mockery of others, a more serious sin like lust, stealing, etc. So Wilson (ed. 1960): A general ref. to serving-women who make derisive grimaces at their mistresses behind their backs.

2248+4 since]
Wilson (ed. 1960): I.e. since he left Tom. Joseph (ed. 1966), less probably: Therefore.

2248+4 chambermaids]
Furness (ed. 1880): This is generally supposed [since Theobald, ed. 1733, and Warburton, ed. 1747] to have been suggested by the three chambermaids in the family of Mr Edmund Peckham, mentioned in Harsnet’s Declaration [1603, p. 1]. Sarah and Frideswide (Friswood, Fid) Williams had been in service at Denham, and Anne Smith was a recent arrival from London (Brownlow, 1993, p. 24). Wells (ed. 2000): Presumably thought of as mocking their mistresses behind their backs. Greenblatt (1985, p. 113): Humorous anachronism; like Merlin’s prophecy in 3.2, a reminder of the play’s conspicuous doubleness, its simultaneous distance and contemporaneity.

2248+5 so]
Though most eds. punctuate as if this were a conjunctive adverb modifying blesse—i.e., to prevent such possession as I have suffered, bless thee—it may equally well modify possesses—i.e., possesses them in this manner, inducing such behavior as mopping and mowing.

2249 purse]
Lott (ed. 1974): Beggars expected alms in return for the blessings they gave.

2249 thou]
Foakes (ed. 1997): F has yu in a crowded line where abbreviation was necessary. The context suggests that thou is preferable to you.

2249 heauens plagues]
See n. 1848–9.

2249 plagues]
Schmidt (1875): Vexation, torment, calamity (OED, sb. 2b). Deighton (ed. 1891): Blows of adversity (OED, 1: A blow, a stroke).

2250 humbled…strokes]
Crook (ed. 1907): Cowed into taking all ills humbly. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Brought so low that thou sufferest every kind of misery. Harrison (ed. 1948): Made so humble that you can endure anything.

2250–1 that…happier]
Wordsworth (1864, p. 216): My wretchedness now teaches me to compassionate those who are in distress; by the similarity and sympathy of condition (Deighton, ed. 1891). Verity (ed. 1897): A thought developed in what follows. Budd (ed. 1935): I.e. by receiving the purse. Wilson (ed. 1960): But prob. there is another meaning, as at [2056+7]—i.e., misery likes company.

2251 heauens]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Your in [2253–4] suggests a vocative here. Joseph (ed. 1966): Either a wish or an invocation.

2251 deale so]
Rann (ed. 1794): Go on levelling. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Make his sufferings a common experience of the great and high when…they have abused their prosperity. Joseph (ed. 1966): Share out in this way (possibly with…the secondary sense of handle) (OED, v. 3, 16). Hunter (ed. 1972): So that one man’s misery should be comforted by another’s (see n. 2250–1).

2251 still]
See n. 253.

2252 superfluous]
Mrs. Griffith (1775, p. 365): Superabundant; see n. 1565. Johnson (ed. 1765): Lear has before uttered the same sentiment; cf. 1814–17. Verity (ed. 1897): Misfortune has taught Lear and Gloucester the same lesson, and the fact is intentionally emphasised by the similarity of their language. Elton (1966, pp. 227–8) cites contemporary legal and homiletic injunctions against superfluity.

2252 lust-dieted]
Craig (ed. 1901): A very greedy or gluttonous man, one whose dieter is Lust, citing Cym. 3.5.141–2, 4.2.50–1 (2058, 2311–12). So apparently Wilson (ed. 1960): Whose appetite (of all kinds) is ruled solely by his lusts or desires. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Whose lusts (i.e., desires of every kind) are fed to the full, citing Oth. 2.1.294 (1077). Horsman (ed. 1973): Dieted does not mean fed to the full and…lust in such compounds is commonly objective or instrumental, citing Oth. 5.1.36 (3123). Partridge (1947, p. 147): Fed on lust. Heilman (1948, p. 45): Gloucester is describing himself. A range of meanings is possible: lust could mean pleasure, desire, appetite, one’s wish, sensuous appetite, and sexual appetite (OED, sb. 1, 2, 2c, 3, 4), and diet could mean feed or regulate the food of (OED, v. 1, 2). Such a man is as over-indulged in his appetites as he is superfluous in his possessions. Blythe (1980) compares the metabolic causality between gula and luxuria in 2566, but no such causality is suggested in his other ex., 753, or here. Henderson (1940, pp. 44–5) compares Montaigne’s discussion in Sebond of men’s lustfull desires which are neither natural nor necessary, but superfluous; see . Salingar (1986, p. 127): Gloucester’s striking epithet…concentrates Montaigne’s argument about man’s lustfull desires…with a sharp recall of the speaker’s personal history, i.e. his adultery.

2253 stands]
Most eds. believe that F’s slaues corrects a triple misreading—t/l, n/u, d/e (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 405). Malone (ed. 1790): Stands may mean abides, apparently in the sense of endures, is subject to, the criminality appearing only in the subsequent words, that…not feele. Perring (1885, p. 328): Withstands (OED, Stand v. 55, quoting this l. as the first of only two exx.), and Stone (1980, p. 56): For ’stands. So Weis (ed. 1993): Resists your decrees of destiny. Wells (ed. 2000): Stands against, defies. F’s slaues in turn has seemed difficult and has invited emendation: see textual nn. and . Upton (1748, p. 332): That makes a slave of your ordinance; that makes it subservient to his superfluities and lust (OED, v.1 1: Trans.…to enslave; to bring into subjection, quoting this l. as its first ex.) Heath (1765, p. 343): Making it subservient to his views of pleasure or interest. Johnson (ed. 1765): To slight or ridicule it; so Harrison (ed. 1937): Treats…like a slave, i.e. contemptuously. Capell (1783, 1.2:174): Apply to uses unworthy. Steevens (ed. 1773): Make it subject to us, instead of acting in obedience to it. Moberly (ed. 1876): Crushes it down. Herford (ed. 1899): Tramples on, overrides. Elton (1966, p. 227): Implying that the highest possible law or ordinance has been inverted and made slave to the lowest. Nicholson (MS notes, –1892): Causal-reflexive.…He enslaves himself to the arrangements of your providence which have ordained him rich. Sledd (1940, pp. 595–6): Tear away or split (OED, v.2, from OE slæfan). Muir (ed. 1952): [Sledd] does not give any Elizabethan parallels. Shakespeare uses sliver in the next scene, [2303+3], and it is just possible that he was quibbling here. Edwards (ed. 1975): Treats…contemptuously. Sh. does not elsewhere use the word as a transitive verb.

2253 ordinance]
Capell (1783, 1.2:174), followed by Rann (ed. 1794): The things of your ordinance;…the accommodations of life, throughout all it’s allotments. Similarly Verity (ed. 1897): Your dispensation that there should be inequalities of rank and wealth in the world. The rich man who studies only his own pleasure treats this general law as if it were laid down by Providence merely for his special interest and benefit. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Divine ordinations. Schmidt (ed. 1879): The established order of things, law of nature. Wordsworth (1864, p. 217) compares St. Paul’s exhortation (2 Cor. 8:14) that your abundance supplieth their lacke,…that there may be equality (Geneva). Moberly (ed. 1876): The ordinance meant is probably what the parable of Dives and Lazarus expresses, that ignorance of the sufferings of those near us is itself a crime; see Luke 16:19–31. Craig (ed. 1901): Gloucester, made here, though a pagan, to speak like a Christian, is thinking of the commands, do good and distribute, etc., and to give one’s goods to the poor. [Cf. Mark 10:21.] Ordinance is used in the sense of divine will [in Cym. 4.2.145 (2432), R3 4.4.184 (2963)]. Brooke (ed. 1947): To love one’s neighbor as oneself. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The gods…have ordained that one man shall be rich and another poor. Thus they have imposed upon the man who has a superfluity the obligation to use his riches for the relief of his needy fellow-creatures. But he treats this ordinance of the gods as if it were his slave—as if it were not an obligation but an unlimited privilege. Kittredge seems to be speaking of two related ordinances, one a state of things and the other an injunction. Wilson (ed. 1960): Arrangement in…proper relative position (O.E.D. 2), hence = rank (cf. Cor. 3.2.12 [2097]). Lott (ed. 1974): The system you have ordained.

2253–4 not see…not feele]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Who refuses to see the miseries around him because he does not feel them in his own person. Craig (ed. 1901), feel: Feel the effects of, suffer pain. Muir (ed. 1952): But it may mean rather feel sympathy. The man is blind and without wisdom because he does not put himself in the place of his poor neighbours. McCann (ed. 1964): Who will not see the truth because he is insensitive. Hunter (ed. 1972): Also, like Gloucester, see how things are…by touch.

2254 quickly]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Perh. a triple pun—(a) very soon; (b) while he is still alive; (c) sharply, piercingly (cf. Per. 4.1.24 [1544]). See OED (Quick adj. 24, 2, 18c: Of air or light). Possibly (Quickly adv. 1): With strong feeling, sensitively, as Horsman (ed. 1973) suggests.

2255 So…should]
Should is better interpreted as would than as ought to. Quinn (ed. 1970): Then an equalizing principle would operate in the world.

2255 distribution]
Thaler (1955, p. 38) compares Luke 18:22: distribute vnto the poore, and thou shalt haue treasure in heauen (Geneva). Wilson (ed. 1960): Quibble;…(a) administration (of justice; cf. Cor. 3.3.99 [2384]), (b) sharing out. Following Empson (1951, p. 142), Elton (1966, p. 226): Ironical reminder that it is Lear’s distribution which has itself created excess. Joseph (ed. 1966): Perhaps also the legal meaning of distribute, to hand over a case to investigators for reliable investigation (not attested in OED). Edwards (ed. 1975): Gloucester means both the sharing out of misery and the obvious corollary, that wealth should be shared out too.

2255 vnder]
Doubtless an error for F’s vndoo. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 405): Misreading: (i) e/o, (ii) r/o or r/e. Eds. generally take the meaning annul, cancel (OED, v. 7a). Schmidt (1875) and a few others: Hinder from coming into existence (OED, v. 7b: To reverse the…making of <some…effect>).

2256 Douer]
Moberly (ed. 1876): It is remarkable that Gloucester goes to Dover…simply that he may throw himself from the cliff in utter despair. Moberly attributes this certain sacrifice of probability to Sh.’s following Sidney’s Arcadia 2.10.2 (see ). Still, Bradley (1904, p. 257) asks, Why in the world should Gloster…wander all the way to Dover simply in order to destroy himself? Phelps (ed. 1917): If Gloucester is in Dorset, as seems generally to be supposed, Gloucester has a long walk ahead of him. Budd (ed. 1935): It has, however, this convenience for the plot, that it enables him and Edgar to come into contact with Lear and the French forces. Bransom (1934, p. 117): Dover was the obvious place for Gloster to seek [cf. 2170–1].…The king’s friends were gathering at Dover. He was not a resolute man, and his desire for death to end his misery did not amount to a resolve to commit suicide.…Shakespeare has effected the meeting of Lear and Gloster with a good deal of naturalness. Muir (ed. 1952, p. xlix): It may be argued that the reiterated question, Wherefore to Dover?, recalls the cliff to Gloucester’s mind, and in his half-crazed state he has an irrational urge to end his life there. Muir (p. xlii) compares Marston’s Malcontent (1604) 4.[1.138–45], where Pietro, in disguise, describes his own feigned suicide by leaping from a cliff into the sea. Liebermann (1923, p. 101): Pushing a condemned man from Dover cliff was customary capital punishment. Cavell (1969, p. 281): He sets out for Dover because he is sent there: by himself, in sending Lear…; and by the thrust of Regan’s evil and confusion. But he has no reason to go there, not even some inexplicable wish to commit suicide there.

2258 high]
Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): It is still about 350 feet high from ebb-tide mark.

2258 bending]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Brow overhanging its base.

2259 firmely]
Stone (1980, p. 221): Fixedly, steadily. Weis (ed. 1993): Undaunted. F’s fearfully, adopted by virtually all eds., provides good sense and the necessary trisyllable; it has been taken to mean either inspiring or exhibiting fear. Pye (1807, p. 292): The cliff is represented not as looking at itself in [the deep]…but rather as looking tremendous when reflected in it. Schmidt (1874): Terribly (OED, adv. 1: So as to cause fear; dreadfully; terribly, quoting this l.). Moberly (ed. 1876), fearfully: The cliff seems to be looking down with alarm over the sea which it hems in. Deighton (ed. 1891): Looks down with dreadful menace. Kittredge (ed. 1940): So as to inspire terror in one who looks over the edge. Muir (ed. 1952): But the cliff is personified. If fearfully stood in Q copy, Q’s misreading of it is not easy to explain. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 405): Conceivably the compositor’s eye caught brimme [2260] too soon, and…under the influence of brimme he changed fearfully to firmely as he was carrying line [2259] in his head.…[Alternatively, he] may have misread the first five letters as firme,…[then] may have been able to read the suffix ly correctly, but the ful may have been totally illegible. Since what he had managed to read, or misread, viz. firme plus ly, gave him a word, he may have decided to be content with that. Taylor (1983, p. 457) proposes sawcely, insolently, but a saucy cliff is a whimsical image not likely to occur to a man describing the place of his intended death. Halio (ed. 1994): Blayney conjectures fiercely, but accepts F’s fearfully. Although sternly does not correct the metre, it seems more plausible that it stood in the copy (st/f and minim misreadings) than saucely, and in context makes better sense.

2259 in]
Malone (ed. 1790): Shakspeare considered the sea as a mirror. Singer (ed. 1826): In is here put for on. Anon. (in Knight, ed. 1840): Situated in the bays on each side of it. Wright (ed. 1875) and most eds.: In, into; Abbott §159 and Franz §506 cite Shn. exx. of the usage; cf. 2993.

2259 confined]
Capell (1783, 1.2:174): Pent in straits. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The Strait of Dover. Tovey (ed. 1896): Restrained by the cliff. Craig (ed. 1901): Kept back, i.e. (the deep) to which it acts as an effectual barrier.

2261 repaire]
Schmidt (1875): Restore. OED (v.2 5): To remedy, citing this l.

2265 poore Tom]
See n. 1271.

2266 <Scena Secunda>]
Dent (ed. 1927): The crisis of the play is past; the catastrophe has not yet come. To introduce it now would spoil the balance of the play; our sense of proportion would reject it as inartistic. Shakespeare therefore introduces a new thread into the plot—the intrigues between Edmund and the two sisters. From these intrigues spring the deaths of all three. Albany now comes into the limelight, and the way is prepared for the prominent part he plays in the catastrophe. Bransom (1934, p. 150): This scene between Albany and his wife has the strongest and profoundest dramatic significance. Neither of them is ever the same again. Quinn (ed. 1970): The two closely related plots are here interlocked even more firmly as Edmund becomes Goneril’s lover. Lott (ed. 1974): Edmund now takes Gloucester’s place as the link between the two plots. Edwards (ed. 1975): Albany dissociates himself from Goneril and the anti-Lear party. With the news of Cornwall’s death, both sisters are without their husbands’ help, and Edmund comes into a position of new importance. Daniel (1877–9, p. 220): A separate day [from 4.1], in consideration of the distance which Goneril and Edmund must have travelled between Gloucester’s Castle and Albany’s Palace. Kittredge (ed. 1940): This scene follows Scene i almost immediately—perhaps on the next day. Houghton (ed. 1957): Albany’s [castle], wherever that may be.

2267 Enter…]
F’s entrance direction includes the Steward here, not after 2269. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 536): If Oswald enters now…it is presumably from another direction. Tovey (ed. 1896): Goneril and Edmund have gone to the Duke of Albany’s castle, in accordance with the advice of Cornwall ([2060–81]); they come from Gloucestershire (Bevington, ed. 1980). Goggin (ed. 1910): Apparently they have been making love on the way, and Goneril, who has already shown [in 830–72] that she despises her husband, has conceived a violent adulterous passion for Edmund. This new interest in the action suggests how the dénouement is to be brought about: the wicked are to become the instruments of their own punishment. Wilson (ed. 1960): Gon. has sent Osw. to find Alb., and proceeds to welcome Edm. to her dwelling.…It is significant of Osw.’s intimacy with Gon. that she appears to let him hear all that follows.

2268 Welcome]
Delius (ed. 1854): She welcomes him to her house after she has reached it in his company (Ger.). Tovey (ed. 1896): Goneril bids Edmund Welcome as his hostess. Budd (ed. 1935): A formal welcome.

2268 our]
Wells (ed. 2000): Goneril appears to be adopting the royal plural.

2268 mild]
Johnson (ed. 1765): It must be remembered that Albany…disliked, in the end of the first act, the scheme of oppression and ingratitude. Verity (ed. 1897): Said scornfully. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Cf. 865–8.

2269 Not met]
On the transposition see n. 1012.

–2267 Enter…]
On F’s earlier entrance see n. 1358.

–2267 on the way]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): On the way from Gloucester’s castle. Goneril probably does not expect to meet Albany following her to Gloucester’s house (see n. 1470), but has sent advance notice of her return and expects to be met. Albany’s failure to welcome her home is a suggestive sign of his growing alienation from her, confirmed in the Steward’s following speech.

2270 chang’d]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): That is, from the approval and affectionate admiration of his haughty wife…and also from blind partisanship, and belief in the steward’s representations of what is going forward. Brooke (ed. 1947): One of the most successful minor touches in the play is the development of Albany, who is evidently young and honest, and at the opening stands in confused awe of his majestic wife. Goneril’s misjudgment of him is a large factor in her downfall. Foakes (ed. 1997) apparently connects the change in Albany to friction between him and Cornwall, citing 938–9, 1628–30, and says, His moral rejection of Goneril makes her pursuit of Edmund more plausible. But Goneril has already begun her pursuit wholeheartedly. How Albany has learned of Lear’s rejection by both sisters in 2.4 (see 2303+8–+14) is unclear; Oswald does not report informing him of it.

2274 loyall seruice]
Verity (ed. 1897): I.e. in betraying Gloucester to Cornwall.

2275 sott]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): Fool. Schmidt (1875): Dolt, blockhead (OED, sb.1 1).

2276 turnd…out]
Though OED (Turn v. 75m) quotes this l. as its only ex., the phrase appears elsewhere in Sh. and other writers: see Dent (1981, S431.1). The wrong side is the inner side of a fabric (OED, Wrong adj. 10a, quoting this l.). Eccles (ed. 1792): Espoused the worst cause; placed what was evil in the most advantageous point of view, and considered it as most deserving of regard. Crook (ed. 1907): Meaning that he ought to have said Gloucester’s loyalty and Edmund’s treachery.

2277 desire]
As a misreading for F’s dislike, desire may be somewhat unlikely. Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 405–6): The compositor may have been misled by pleasant both here and at 3131. Stone (1980, p. 183): Desire is more probably a misreading of defie (= set at nought, reject; OED, v.1 5), comparing AYL Ep. 20 (2794). So Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 519): Substitution of antonyms is a rare compositorial error, and desire is not the most obvious antonym to dislike. Neither however is F’s dislike an obvious misreading of Q’s desire, though it is the obvious antonym of like in 2278.

2278 like offensiue]
Abbott (§395): Antithetical sentences frequently do not repeat pronouns, verbs, &c. Cf. 2713–14, 2750.

2279 goe no further]
Deighton (ed. 1891): I.e. not accompany her in doors, lest the result should be a quarrel between him and her husband. Armour (ed. 1930): It would merely delay things if Edmund entered the house and met Albany in his present mood. McCann (ed. 1964): You will not accompany me at this point towards Gloucester’s castle but return to Cornwall, comparing 2283.

2280 cowish]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:16): Soon cow’d, dastardly (OED, adj. 2: Cowardly, quoting this l. as the later of two exx.). Because the word is rare and not used elsewhere by Sh., Wright (ed. 1875) proposes currish, an epithet far less appropriate to the mild Alb. (Wilson, ed. 1960) but related to the following word; see next n. Craig (ed. 1901) cites instances of cow = coward (see OED, sb.1 4), though finding currish in both Sh. and Harsnett (1603, p. 98). Muir (ed. 1952): If the copy had read cowish terrer, with a marginal correction curr, the compositor might easily have substituted curr for terrer instead of for cow. The corrector, seeing that something was wrong, might have restored terrer without realizing the intentions of the writer. Bransom (1934, p. 139): Instead of offering a sufficient excuse she reiterates her old estimation of her husband’s character. The reiteration betrays the hidden fear that the estimation is no longer true. Clayton (1981, p. 351 n.): One of the reasons Albany is said by Goneril to have a cowish spirit and to be milk-livered [2304] is that albus is Latin for white and is a (false) root of Albany; see n. 5. There is no evidence that Goneril makes such a connection.

2280 curre]
Greg (1940, p. 170): The emendation [F’s terrer] is certainly correct in intention, but the spelling was bungled, perhaps by the printer. See the prev. n. Stone (1980, p. 183) finds terror both too strong and pleonastic: see . Wells & Taylor (1987, pp. 519–20): But Gonoril is not given to understatement…[and] terrer is an easier emendation of curre than is Stone’s tenner, a spelling and sense not found elsewhere in Sh. Weis (ed. 1993): Q’s degrading image of Albany as a craven mongrel is consistent with Q’s several dehumanizing animal references and the alliterative structure of the phrase.

2280 spirit]
OED (sb. 8): A particular character, disposition, or temper existing in, pervading, or animating, a person; (11): The immaterial intelligent or sentient element of part of a person.

2281 vndertake]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): To venture, to hazard (Johnson’s Dict. [1755]). OED (v. 8): To enter upon, commit oneself to, an enterprise. Colman (ed. 1982): (a) take charge, (b) show initiative. Foakes (ed. 1997): Take responsibility.

2281 not feele]
Hudson (ed. 1879): Ignore. OED (Feel v. 8): Become aware of; (13): Be emotionally affected by.

2281 wrongs]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Specifically, the French invasion.

2282 answere]
Schmidt (1874): Retaliation. Rolfe (ed. 1880): That is, a manly answer to a challenge. OED (sb. 7): A practical reply; anything done in return. Cf. also 1881.

2282 our wishes]
Rann (ed. 1794): Relative, probably, to the disposal of her husband, and future junction with Edmund. Only Craig (ed. 1931) takes our to be the royal we: My wishes.

2282 on the way]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Either before our march is at an end or by the by. Most eds. follow Mason (1785, p. 351): On our journey, meaning which we discussed on the way here.

2283 proue effects]
Mason (1785, p. 351): Be carried into effect—on the presumption of Albany’s cowardice, apparently. See n. 472. Horsman (ed. 1973): I.e., Edmund may supplant my husband (perhaps by murder, as may be hinted in [2288]).

2283 backe]
Greg (1940, p. 438): Goneril, foreseeing trouble with her mild husband, sends Edmund straight back to Cornwall—out of harm’s way.…Albany asks what has happened to Edmund, and is told [2337, 2339]. Goneril, who parted from Cornwall at 2081, cannot know that he is dead and that she is sending Edmund unchaperoned to his widow, to whom also he will make love (cf. 2417, 2902). Edmund next appears at 2845 in Regan’s company, presumably having joined her in leading Cornwall’s troops, under the commander-in-chief Albany.

2283 Edgar]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 406): Possibly a wrong expansion of a contraction (Ed.) in the copy. Q2 and F correct to Edmund. Cf. 2430.

2283 my brother]
Schmidt (1874): Brother-in-law (OED, sb. 1a). Cf. 2303+13, 2384, 2858.

2284 musters]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Enrolment of troops.

2284 conduct]
Schmidt (1874): Lead as a commander (OED, v. 4, quoting this l.). But Goneril is certainly not directing Edmund to supplant Albany as commander. Halio (ed. 1992): Escort, guide, accompany (OED, 1). Thirlby (MS notes, 1725–33): A fault of Shakespear’s I suppose. How cd she know yt Cornwall cd not do it himself, & to suppose she knew he wd not, being able, is I think very odd, especially considering the character of Cornwall, hot, fiery, active. Neither the audience nor (apparently) Goneril hears of Cornwall’s death until later in this scene (2313).

2284 powers]
See n. 1638+1.

2285 armes]
Most eds. consider F’s names inferior; it is probably a misreading from MS copy. Jackson (1983, p. 328): Conceivably the Folio compositor…set rames, and this was subsequently miscorrected; though no such press variant is recorded. Though a distaff, a staff used in spinning, is not literally arms, it is a symbol of women’s occupation and authority (OED, 3, quoting this l.; 4), and it might be wielded as a weapon, as in WT 1.2.37 (94): Wee’l thwack him hence with Distaffes. Thus Craig (ed. 1901): The insignia of my sex. I must take the sword out of my weak husband’s hands, resigning to him the distaff. Compare the old terms for husband and wife, the spear side and the spindle side [OED, 4], and Cym. 5.3.33–4 (2961–2), turn’d A Distaffe, to a Lance. Cf. R2 3.2.118 (1476), distaffe women mannage rustie bils. Budd (1935, p. 427) compares Chaucer, Prologue of the Monkes Tale *3096–7: I wol have thy knyf, And thou shalt have my distaf and go spynne. Idem (ed. 1935): Armorial bearings. Brownlee (1960, p. 281) compares Burton, Anatomy of Melancholy 1.2.4.4, reporting a scoff by Sophia, Justinian’s empress, at a eunuch: He was fitter for a distaff…than to wield a sword. Joseph (ed. 1966): The distaff in heraldry stands for the female side [OED, 4].…She means literally what is expressed metaphorically. Hunter (ed. 1972): (1) I must change into military accoutrements; (2) my husband and I must exchange the work we do with our arms. Weis (ed. 1993): The story of Omphale forcing Hercules to use the distaff to indicate his subjugation (cf. Ovid, Fasti II.318–25) was a famous motif in the Renaissance.…But change arms can also mean…Change embraces, i.e., discontinue intimacy with my husband.
F has been defended, however. Delius (ed. 1854): I must take the name of Albany, my husband, and give him the name Goneril (Ger.). White (ed. 1862): Be master instead of mistress. Sisson (1956, 2:240): Change the name of woman for that of a man. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 537): Shakespeare might have altered Q because the corporeal sense of armes was ludicrously encouraged by hands;…see also [MM 1.4.47 (397), as schoole-maids change their names], where as here change = exchange. Foakes (ed. 1997): Perhaps changed in F to avoid a confusion between literal and figurative arms. In Q Goneril must be speaking figuratively: she will not exchange limbs or armor, but authority.

2287 passe betweene]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Convey letters between. Cf. 2391.

2287 like]
See n. 325.

2288 venture]
Craig (ed. 1901): Be bold or adventurous. Cf. n. 2283.

2288 owne behalfe]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Thinking of yourself (and not of your loyalty to the cause). Like Moulton (1903, p. 142), Hudson & Black (ed. 1911, p. lvi): The success of Edmund’s intrigue is entangling him in a relation which will be the nemesis to punish him. The adulterous love of Goneril for Edmund is resented by Albany—and by Regan.

2289 mistresses]
Delius (ed. 1854): With the double meaning of Lady and lover (Ger.).

2289 coward…this]
Q1(c)’s change to command…this, is certainly correct (Greg, 1940, p. 170). Duthie (1949, p. 51): The copy read comand.

2289 coward]
Muir (ed. 1952), command: She is presumably going to ask Edmund to murder Albany. Cf. 2715–20. Harrison (ed. 1948): Edmund, having disposed of his brother and father, now looks higher; he will through Goneril become possessed of her half of the kingdom of Lear.

2289 weare this]
Deighton (ed. 1891): A ribbon or other token of her love. Goggin (ed. 1910): Such as a glove or jewel to be worn, comparing 1866. Bransom (1934, p. 140): A Flower. Rosenberg (1972, p. 252): In the theatre, a ring, scarf, or even her extended necklace. Halio (ed. 1973): She may simply refer to a kiss.

2289 spare speech]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Say nothing in reply.

2290 Decline your head]
Steevens (ed. 1773): That she might give him a kiss (the steward being present) and that it might appear only to him as a whisper. Wright (ed. 1875): This gives Goneril credit for too much delicacy, and Oswald was a serviceable villain. Tovey (ed. 1896): But if…speake seems to imply that Goneril does not say all her mind before Oswald. Delius (ed. 1854): Perhaps she wishes to put a chain around his neck (Ger.). Bradley (1904, p. 461): Edmund is a good deal taller than Goneril, and must stoop to be kissed. Dowden (1875; 1877, p. 264): To complete the horror they produce in us, these monsters are amorous. Their love is even more hideous than their hate. Brown (ed. 1996): Rarely in Shakespeare’s plays are lovers required by the text to kiss: but here they are, and it is the woman who leads. Perhaps it is a formal kiss, but the words accompanying it are provocative.…The sexual overtones…[may] have been underplayed (as Jacobean decorum, military dress and the practice of using male actors in female roles would all seem to imply).

2290–1 your…thy]
Abbott (§235): A kiss induces the speaker to pass from [formal] your to [intimate] thy.

2290 durst]
See n. 398.

2291 stretch thy spirits]
Heilman (1948, p. 314): These lines contain several kinds of sexual innuendo. Muir (ed. 1952): Goneril puns on spirits and conceive, and Edmund puns on death, as Lear does [2460–1], often used as a metaphor for orgasm (Hunter, ed. 1972). Williams (1997), spirit: Penis. Not all such puns are universally accepted. Presumably a kiss would be the more sexually arousing if it durst speake not simply promises of his advancement but also the extent of her lust. For spirits see n. 989.

2292 Conceaue]
Seymour (1805, 2:101): Conceive what I would say. Delius (ed. 1854): That which I dare not speak aloud (Ger.). Deighton (ed. 1891): Imagine to yourself all that this kiss means. Budd (ed. 1935): Imagine what this kiss would say if it dared speak. Harbage (ed. 1958): (1) Understand (2) quicken (with the seed I have planted in you). Cf. 15. Foakes (ed. 1997): Imagine (what we may do).

2292 you]
On F’s thee, Blake (2002, p. 54): Thee and thou especially after verbs in the imperative, though these may be taken as reflexive forms.

2293 Yours…death]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Through all time and in all circumstances. Tovey (ed. 1896): He speaks as her soldier, who would join a forlorn hope in her service. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 153): The regal impudency of the woman, the falsely chivalrous flourish of the man’s response—pages of dialogue might not tell us more of their relations. Bransom (1934, p. 140): There is a ring of sincerity about the words. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Spoken with a flourishing gesture of devotion. Fraser (1962, p. 66): Goneril and Edmund play at chivalric romance. Main (ed. 1962) sees an ironic prophecy, comparing 3179–80. Stone (1980, p. 221): Both a vassal’s profession of fealty and a courtly lover’s vow. See also n. 2291.

2293 Exit.]
Halio (ed. 1992): Since Q does not supply this SD, Gonerill’s entire speech is thus directed in Q to her lover, not to herself as in F. But Edmund could have gone off at the same time in Q, and his speech sounds like an exit line.

2295 Oh…and man]
Stone (1980, p. 245): F’s added line serves to clarify the sense of the two succeeding lines.…We should be puzzled by the abrupt reference to my fool unless we realised that Goneril was comparing one man with another.…[But if] Qa’s reading My foote is the correct one…the additional line stands exposed as irrelevant. Halio (ed. 1992): In Q, Gonerill’s line is unnecessary, since she apparently addresses Edmond (whose exit is missing); but in F, Edmond leaves, and Gonerill comments to herself. But the staging in Q and F could be the same: see n. 2293. Foakes (ed. 1997): Probably an addition designed to enhance Goneril’s moment of rapture. Craig (ed. 1901) compares TNK 2.1.53–4, Lord, the Diffrence of men. Taylor (1983, pp. 379, 436) compares North’s Plutarch (1579, p. 798), there is a difference betwext manhood & manhood (as betwext wisedom & wisedom and iustice & iustice—qualities, not persons), and Tilley D332, There is a Difference between Peter and Peter, not found in Sh. The idea that men are distinct, sheep from goats, wheat from chaff, fools from wise, etc., is of course too much a commonplace to derive from a particular source; cf. 619, 667. Rosenberg (1972, p. 253): Her tribute…is heartfelt, and often evokes sympathetic audience laughter. The naive spectator does not yet know of…Edmund’s attachment to Regan.

2295 Oh]
For the word’s iambic value see n. 2168.

2296 womans]
Q1(c)’s added a is certainly correct: the verse requires it even though the sense is not much affected (Greg, 1940, p. 170). McKenzie (1973, p. 128): The omission is the result of the compositor’s indenting the stick to a narrower measure.

2296 seruices]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Wifely offices. The word refers to purely sexual activity as distinct from romantic devotion or domestic duties in, e.g., AWW 4.2.17–18, 4.5.24–31 (2039–41, 2505–12). See Williams (1994).

2296 dew]
Due. Wilson (ed. 1960): Emphatic. Antithetical to usurps in [2297].

2297 My foote]
Though White (ed. 1862) inclines to foote and Wright (ed. 1875) compares My foote my Tutor? in Tmp. 1.2.470 (629), only three eds. adopt the reading: Brooke (ed. 1947): Albany in the rôle of husband is as if the foot presumed to control the whole body; Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 520): In its slang sexual sense foot (= French foutre…) suggests that Gonoril has allowed her sexual organs to dominate her body entirely; and Halio (ed. 1994). Stone (1980, p. 221): Foote may make sense if Edmund, contrary to the F exit at 2293, is still present and, kneeling, kisses his hand and places it on her foot: She replies to his act of homage by insinuating that the relationship he is dramatising should be reversed. Clayton (1981, pp. 350–1) adduces biblical commonplaces (1 Cor. 11:3, Eph. 5:23–4; cf. Shr. 5.2.146–7 [2704–5]) about the husband as head in a marriage, thus to explicate Q1(u): My so-called husband—my sometime head, now my foot—usurps my body.…Since Albany has not exercised his authority and manliness and acted as a proper husband, he has in effect abdicated his right, ceased to be Goneril’s head, and sunk to her foot; as such an inferior member, he usurps the body over which a proper man and head would have a legitimate claim of rule and all rights of service. But (to use St. Paul’s analogies) as the prince is head of the body politic of which he is a member, and Christ the head of the church which is his body (Eph. 1:22–3), so the husband is head of the body matrimonial, in which he and his wife are both members, and not simply head of his wife’s person (Goneril’s my body), as Clayton’s argument seems to require. Fleissner (1991, p. 176) compares Tilley F562, Do not make the foot the head; neither Tilley nor Dent (1981) cites this line. Virtually all others, following F, accept the second element of Q1(c)’s A foole, and only a few the first (see textual n.). Goneril calls Albany a fool or foolish four more times in the scene (2303+6, 2307+1, 2307+5, 2311). Doran (1931, p. 102): My…could not be a misreading of A, and its presence in both uncorrected Q1 and in F suggests that it was in the manuscript.…Perhaps [Sh.] afterward substituted A for My and bed for body. But the original readings were not crossed out, and both the playhouse transcriber [producing the playbook] and the printer of Q1 were led to follow them; the proofreader, who was paying close attention to his copy in this place (he had just altered curre to terrer and coward to command)…made out Shakespeare’s substitutions. Greg (1940, p. 171): I see no possibility of the compositor having misread A (or a) as My (or my) nor any reason why he should have substituted the latter for the former. The corrector, on the contrary, may have been puzzled to know what the lady meant by her fool, and have at a guess substituted the non-committal A. Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 156–7): It is not impossible that, influenced by my body, [the compositor] unconsciously substituted My foote for A foote—he may even have made the change consciously, thinking it more likely that, speaking of her own body, the lady would speak of her own foot than that she would speak indefinitely of a foot!…But My Foole seems to me a superior reading to A foole. Using the phrase A foole Goneril directs attention only to the foolishness of her husband: using the phrase My Foole she implies not only that he is foolish but also that she is duping him (one’s fool can mean one’s dupe, a person that one fools).…I have little doubt that My Foole, more pregnant with meaning, is the true reading. Walker (1953, p. 57) defends A: My might have been the Q1 compositor’s anticipation of the pronoun later in the line or might have been picked up from [2294].…The possessive pronoun loses the detachment of the indefinite A, which gives to Goneril’s description of Albany the depreciation and indifference she felt. So Wilson (ed. 1960): In Gon.’s eyes, Alb. is just a fool who has no business to be sharing her bed. Kittredge (ed. 1940), fool: One who should rather be the court fool than my husband. Gardner (ed. 1969): She sees her husband as her jester, an object of ridicule—her puppet.

2297 vsurps]
OED (v. 3): To take or hold possession of (something belonging to another), quoting this l. as an ex. of figurative use. Delius (ed. 1854): Emphasized in contrast to is due (Ger.). Now that Goneril admires another, she rejects her husband’s rights to her womans seruices (see n. 2296). Quinn (ed. 1970): My husband is my legal, not my true, lord. For the usurpation of a person rather than a place or possession, see TN 1.5.186–7 (481–2), and cf. 3292.

2297 body]
Q1(c)’s bed, accepted by some eds., may be unauthoritative; Q2’s head can have no authority, and is merely a desperate attempt to make some sense of [Q1(u)], which here served as copy (Greg, 1940, p. 171). F agrees with the uncorrected Q reading and may like it derive from the original in Sh.’s MS. Agreeing with Daniel (facs. 1885) in preferring bed, Adee (ed. 1890. p. liii) cites 2719–20; but see below. Doran (1931, p. 102): Body is a less likely misreading of bed than bed of body. If body were the original word, the y might have been indefinitely trailed off…[or] blotted out.…But if the original word were bed, the only way to explain body as a misreading of it is to suppose that the printer, taking the e for an o, added the y to give a satisfactory reading; see n. on My foote for Doran’s theory of the provenance of bed. A confusion of bodie and bedde is conceivable; both spellings occur repeatedly in F and the good quartos. Though Greg (op. cit.) finds no essential difference to the meaning whether we read body or bed, he prefers the latter on the score of rhythm and urges quite a possibility of misreading. The letters e and o are frequently confused; while, if the final d had a tail to it, as was not uncommon in secretary script, this might conceivably be taken for a y. It is, I think, more likely that the compositor should have misread bed as body, than that the reader should have mis-corrected body to bed. Contra Greg, Clayton (1981, pp. 352 n., 355–6) argues that the rhythm and meter are ambiguous…[and] not a consideration of much weight here, and that dy/d confusion is unsubstantiated elsewhere. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 157): Body seems to me more forceful. Strictly speaking, the bed would be Albany’s already, granted to him by Lear with the rest of his property, and Goneril in fact refers to it as his bed at 2719–20; he could not usurp what is his by law, whereas in rejecting him as husband and lover Goneril would naturally claim her body for her own. Kittredge (ed. 1940), body: Emphatic. Edmund has her heart. McManaway (1967, p. 139), body, citing Marlowe’s Massacre at Paris 15.3–4 and Arden of Feversham 1.98–100, where wives complain of husbands who usurp their hearts. Hunter (ed. 1972), comparing 2719: Bed seems better…since it is the connubial possession of her she objects to rather than sexual possession of her body—perhaps an overnice distinction, since she wishes Edmund to replace Albany in both ways, and body…is here a synecdoche for the whole person (Clayton, op. cit., p. 352). Foakes (ed. 1997): The sense is much the same, for both words extend the meaning of services to include the bedchamber.

2298 Madam…Lord]
Frost (ed. 1909): Oswald is a serviceable villain, and here is part of his service in the cause of anything but virtue. Clayton (1981, p. 352 n.): With either body. Ma’am or bed. Madam the line [2297–8] would be a hexameter, and it is just possible that [2298]…was not conceived as part of a verse-line.

2298–9 Exit…Albany]
Most eds. retain Q’s SD. Wilson (ed. 1960): Presumably F comp. took…[the] addition for a substitution. This assumes that F was printed from a copy of Q, with the entrance noted in the margin; but the assumption is doubtful, and the oversight may have been scribal: see . The obviously needed SD for Albany’s entrance is supplied in both Q2 and F, possibly independently. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 537): Oswald’s exit, marked in Q but not in F, is not strictly necessary, and his presence increases the indecorum of the quarrel, and (perhaps) confirms his inseparability from his mistress. They mark his exit at 2334 in their F text. It is unlikely he would stand silent on stage for the most of the scene.

2300 worth the whistle]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Proverbial, citing Heywood’s It is…A poore dogge that is not worth the whystlyng; see Tilley D488, who gives nine exx. 1546–1675. Dent (1981) finds most relevant Tilley’s second ex., from Breton (1602): There are more maids then Maulkin, and I count my selfe worth the whistling after. Tilley interprets whistle in his W311, Not worth a Whistle, to mean small wind instrument, not the act of whistling, and gives only three exx. of the proverb, 1525–1565; Sh. says the not a whistle, and clearly alludes to the former proverb, not this one. It may be that Sh. conflated the older and the more recent proverbs, or used an otherwise unrecorded variant of the older, and that the Q corrector changed to the more recent and familiar whistling, as Greg (1940, p. 172) and Muir suspect. Harsnett (1603, p. 89) says that for efficacy against devils the priest’s vestments are worth the whistling out of the Popes kennel. Doran (1931, pp. 102–3): It is hard to see how a termination so apparent to the eye could have been twice missed and finally discovered.…It is possible, however, that both whistling and shewes [2309] are substitutions by Shakespeare, perhaps made in the margin so they were missed by both the playhouse transcriber [preparing the playbook] and the printer of Q1. The proverb’s application here is clear enough: Goneril has remarked peevishly in 2268–9 that her husband has not troubled to meet her despite Oswald’s announcement of her approach (2272), and now she reproaches him with a sarcasm for his belated appearance. So Hudson (ed. 1879): Goneril thinks that her husband…ought to have sallied forth, with a retinue, to meet her, and to give her a grand welcome home. Wilson (ed. 1960): She says, in effect, Here have I been whistling for [OED, v. 9: Await…in vain] you, but there was a time when you thought me worth whistling [v. 7: Summon…by or as by whistling; fig. to entice, allure] for. Cf. (sb. 3b): Fig. or in figurative phrases: Call, summons, quoting this l. Bevington (ed. 1980): Worth the attentions of men. Stone (1980, p. 205): The proverb means You cannot much value what you take no pains to get.…We may accordingly gloss Goneril’s speech…: So you have thought me worth some effort after all! Johnson (in Steevens, ed. 1773; ed. 1778) substitutes one unlikely interpretation for another: according to the first, Goneril is alluding to Edmund’s love for her: I have found one that thinks me worth calling; according to the second, she is reproaching him for not having summon’d her to consult with on the present critical occasion. Rann ed. 1794, adopting the latter interpretation, adds over-literally, I have been…worth a welcome of music.

2302 dust…wind]
Proverbial: Dent (1981, D648.1), Like Dust (powder) in the wind, comparing Psa. 1:4. Idem (1984, D646.11): Not worth (As cheap as) (the) dust. Holloway (1961, p. 85) compares Job 7:21, 10:9, 21:23–6, 34:15.

2302 rude]
Schmidt (1875): Rough (OED, adj. 6, quoting this l.). Halio (ed. 1992): Also uncivil.

2302 wind]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Even the wind that cares nothing for you whistles as it throws dust at you…; that’s how much whistling you are worth. Lott (ed. 1974): An immense transformation of Goneril’s ironically joking whistle.

2303–2303+17 I…deepe]
Pope (ed. 1725) restores the lines omitted from F as being necessary to explain the reasons of the detestation which Albany expresses here to his wife. Capell (1783, 1.2:174), agreeing: Omitted…in the folio’s for the sole purpose of short’ning. Knight (ed. 1840, p. 393), disagreeing: In its amplified state [the passage] does not advance the progress of the action, nor contribute to the development of the characters. Delius (1876, pp. 143–4): Little or nothing remains of Goneril’s dispute with her husband, in which the clashing division between them is so powerfully exhibited. This is especially important for the delineation of Albany’s character, so significant of the rôle he was afterwards to perform. Also, there is no connection, either by sense or metre, in the poor remainder of the conversation.…Goneril answers, as if he had spoken the whole rebuke which exists in the Quartos, especially referring to particular points of it.…Also we miss in Goneril’s speech the so essential reference to the impending danger from France, and to Albany’s sluggish inactivity.…Only the actors, without the concurrence and knowledge of the poet, could so have treated his text. Verity (ed. 1897): The curtailment [by the actors] of the interview…, though it sacrifices a fine piece of characterisation and contrast, does not prejudice the plot-development. Herford (1899, p. 5): The lines are necessary…for the consistency of the context, for without them Goneril’s Milke liuerd man (2304) appears unprovoked. Moriarty (1913, pp. 459–60): Albany’s and Goneril’s bombastic interchange, with its melodramatic excess, needlessly interfer[es] with the rapid development of plot and is [460] old-fashioned threat motivation. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 228): Here we have some ruthless cutting of Albany by the Folio. Shakespeare may have yielded here to the exigencies of bad acting or to a wish to knit the action more closely. But he is taking some pains at this juncture to develop Albany, and we shall be on the safe side in keeping to the fuller text. Doran (1931, p. 73): The reason for [the cut] is not obvious. The effect is to remove the sermonizing element from Albany’s part and to make the quarrel between him and Goneril a series of quick retorts. Her one long reply to him has likewise been shortened. Bransom (1934, p. 143): The dialogue so cut is almost meaningless.…Albany’s behaviour is difficult enough to understand with the full Quarto text; in the curtailed Folio it is inexplicable altogether. Hart (1942, p. 148): James and his queen agreed little better than Albany and Goneril; the quarrel [here, 2307+1–+6, and 2311+1–+8] between the latter may have been a politic omission [by an adapter] because Albany bore a Scottish title. Perhaps, too, some members of the audience may have had their enjoyment spoilt by such recollections of their domestic life. Taylor (1983, p. 114, n. 24): But the play makes nothing of Albany’s Scottishness, and his name never appears in the dialogue after 3.1.…The passages not present in F contain no discernible links with James, while those retained include gibes at Albany’s…pacifist nature…more likely to offend anyone alert to parallels between Albany and James.…The Folio also retains the adultery of Albany’s wife, her plot to poison her husband, and her retort the Lawes…for’t [3116–17]—all more objectionable, if a link with Queen Anne were suspected, than the omitted lines. Albany meant Scotland, of course, and the title Duke of Albany belonged at various times to James, his father, and his son; see DP n. 6. Warren (1978, p. 100): The reduction of Albany’s part…severely reduces his theatrical impact.…In Q the succeeding lines of moral outrage [2316 ff.]…present Albany as a man of righteous wrath, outraged by injustice; the same sequence in F presents Albany as equally outraged, but because of the brevity of his previous rebukes he appears more futile in context, less obviously a man capable of action. The cutting diminishes his stature. If that is the intent, it is hard to see why F inconsistently omits Goneril’s scathing criticisms of Albany’s inaction in 2307+1–+6. Urkowitz (1980, pp. 89–93), followed by McLeod (1983, pp. 183–5), argues rather that the F cut, removing Albany’s references to wisdom, goodness, grace, reverence, and the obligation of gratitude, results not in vaguer characterization or diminished stature but in moral ambiguity: Albany in the Folio seems to espouse no positively defined ethical standards. Taylor (1980, p. 30): Albany need not go on at such length in iv, ii in order to motivate his eventual repudiation of his wife in v, iii; so horrendous are the events of acts ii and iii that we will easily infer that Albany’s feelings are similar to our own. If Albany speaks so vehemently and at such length as he does in the Quarto, we may rightly object that his delay in changing sides becomes inexplicable. Muir (1983, pp. 102–4): Warren gives not a single dramatic, or even theatrical, reason for spoiling Albany’s part. Perhaps the company found that the actor was not adequate for the part.…As two moral speeches are retained, it is absurd [for Urkowitz] to pretend that Albany is deprived of defined ethical standards. Presumably the cuts in 4.2 were made because the play was thought to be too long—possibly for a provincial tour.…[Contra Taylor,] the point of Albany’s speeches is not to motivate his later repudiation of Goneril—obviously he repudiates her in 4.2. The various comments by the good characters on the deeds of the evil ones are felt by the audience to be a necessary expression of our sense of outrage. The multiple choric effects of the speeches of sympathetic characters are an essential part of Shakespeare’s method. To cut them out will leave us feeling deprived, if not in a moral vacuum. Richman (1986, pp. 381–2), who restored the lines in performance: Our audience’s attention was always engaged by this scene, and their understanding of the devolution of the wicked daughters was enhanced and clarified by Albany’s speeches. Weis (ed. 1993): F fails to legitimize the tensions and irreconcilable differences between Albany and Goneril, which are presented in Q as a conflict between good and evil.…Q’s text also here launches Albany in the role of avenging agent which he will occupy during the second half of the play. Clare (1995, pp. 44–5): If we agree that Albany is indeed weakened by F’s cuts in 4.2, it is arguable…that Goneril is diminished too. Strength is determined by its testing.…If we lose Q’s lines, we lose, above all, the potential for Goneril and Albany’s encounter actually to develop our apprehension of their characters and relationship, so that they are more compellingly realized on leaving the scene than they were when they entered it.…If Albany does not confront Goneril in 4.2., then it is actually a playable option that he finally confronts her in Act 5 only because he has learned by then that she has made him a cuckold. Such moral ambiguity…would almost certainly constitute an unhelpful sideshow. In Q there is no danger of this: Albany confronts Goneril on properly disinterested grounds.

2303 feare]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Fear the consequences that may follow from (OED, v. 5). Hudson (ed. 1856): Albany’s reasoning is, that if she will take her father’s life, whose life will she spare? Schmidt (1874) and Wright (ed. 1875): Fear for (OED, 8a). So Craig (ed. 1901), Have fears concerning, and Kittredge (ed. 1940), Be worried about. Skillan (ed. 1967): Not for himself, but for herself and others. Cf. 2863.

2303 disposition]
See n. 329. Only Davies (1783, 2:307) and Rann (ed. 1794): [How] heaven should dispose of you…to make you a terrible example of its vengeance.

2303+1–+2 nature…selfe]
Dent (1981) compares the proverb Like will to like (L286).

2303+1 contemnes]
See n. 2180.

2303+1 it]
Greg (1940, pp. 172–3) declares Q1(c)’s ith clearly wrong, adding, But it is difficult to imagine what the reader’s intention can have been. One’s natural impulse is to suppose that ith is somehow a misprint for its, but this form was only just beginning to replace the earlier it (or his) as the possessive, and is not found in any of the original quartos of Sh.’s plays. The reader may somehow have got a confused notion that the construction was condemned i’th’ origin, and made a partial alteration before discovering his mistake. The reading ith is not likely to have arisen through an accident to the type, since it involves the addition of a letter. See n. 727. Hunter (ed. 1972): It would be easy to mistake s for h in the manuscript.

2303+1 origin]
Hudson (ed. 1871): Parents (OED, sb. 1b: Parentage, quoting this l.).

2303+2 Cannot…selfe]
Heath (1765, p. 343): Cannot from thenceforth be restrained within any certain bounds whatever, but is prepared to break out into most monstrous excesses every way, as occasion or temptation may offer. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Cannot comprise reliable component substance in itself. Tovey (ed. 1896): Cannot be fixed within limits, such as a settled character of its own would determine for it, comparing 2724. Verity (ed. 1897): Restrained surely, with certainty, i.e. so that one can depend on its not breaking out into monstrous excesses. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Can have no sure boundaries of conduct in its own character. In it selfe is also specified as within the bounds that nature prescribes (Warburton, ed. 1747), within the bounds of decency or humanity (Rann, ed. 1794), within the bounds of right and truth (Moberly, ed. 1876), Within any fixed bounds (of law and order) (Lee, ed. 1908), within the moral code (Wilson, ed. 1960).

2303+2 bordered]
OED (v. 2b): Confine, quoting only this l.

2303+2 certaine]
Schmidt (1874): Fixed. Harbage (ed. 1958): Safely…predictably.

2303+3 sliuer]
Rann (ed. 1794): Tear off (OED, v. 1, quoting this l. and Mac. 4.1.28 [1555] as its first exx.).

2303+3 disbranch]
OED (v. 2): To cut or break off, as a branch, quoting this l. as its first ex. Sh. uses the term nowhere else. See n. 1364. Traversi (1953, p. 211): She has herself been disbranched by the passionate following of self-interest from the family tree. Shn. imagery of the tree as emblem of natural health and mutual interdependence of parts, central to Lear, is discussed by Fraser (1962, pp. 33–9); he compares Leir 224–7, where Leir’s daughters are florishing branches of a Kingly stocke; see . Perrett (1904, p. 275): The emblem is thoroughly common in Euphuistic literature.

2303+4 materiall]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Whereby a branch is nourished, and increases in bulk by fresh accession of matter. Jennens (ed. 1770): Which supplies it with the very identical matter by which it (the branch) lives, and of which it is composed (OED, sb. 3b, quoting only this l.). White (ed. 1883): Essential. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Figuratively, her own parental blood.…Materia, in Latin, besides signifying material, matter, substance, signifying also timber, wood, the trunk of a tree. It also means nutritive matter and natural disposition or character. McCann (ed. 1964): The characteristics Goneril should have received from Lear. On Warburton’s conjecture maternal, Steevens (ed. 1793) points out that Sh. never uses the word.

2303+4 wither]
Perrett (1904, pp. 274–5) compares Leir 1242–6 (see ), where Cordella laments her rejection by Leir—If so the stocke be dryed with disdayne, Withered and sere the branch must needes remaine—and the Gallian King comforts her—But thou art now graft in another stock;…And from my root continuall sap shall flow—but thinks the similarity derives from a commonplace of Euphuistic literature. Muir (ed. 1952) finds the same idea in R3 2.2.41–2 (1315–16) and Oth. 5.1.13–15 (3253–5). Elton (1966, p. 299): Albany is committed to the bond of humanity on its various levels, organically sustaining each other. The symbolic tree is analogous to the Renaissance exemplum of the body and its members. Coursen (1976, p. 273) compares John 15:4, 6 and Mark 2:20–1.

2303+5 deadly vse]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Such a use as a dead or withered branch is capable of being applied to. In such an interpretation deadly means relating or subject to death (Schmidt, 1874; OED, adj. 1) or death-like (OED, 7; cf. 3258), and use means either employment or possibly usefulness, utility (OED, 20). Hunter (ed. 1869): Alluding to the Scripture text [Heb. 6:8] respecting withered branches being consigned to the fire. Carter (1905, p. 440) and Shaheen (1987, p. 152) compare John 15:6. Wilson (ed. 1960): Perh. a hint of Hell-fire. Joseph (ed. 1966): Destruction. A well-known Renaissance emblem likens the malefactor being executed by the sword to a withered branch being cut from the tree by the gardener’s pruning hook. In Albany’s image, however, Goneril…is cutting herself off. Other eds. take deadly in the sense of Causing death, mortal (OED, 4). Warburton (ed. 1747): Alluding to the use that witches and inchanters are said to make of wither’d branches in their charms, an idea that Delius (ed. 1854) supports by citing Mac. 4.1.28 (1555). Hudson (ed. 1879), more vaguely: As being good only for the Devil to make an instrument of. Brooke (ed. 1947): Poisonous. Traversi (1953, p. 211): The nature of this deadly use, indeed, and its relationship to the entire tragic process, are not long in declaring themselves. Skillan (ed. 1967): Deadly practices, e.g. murder. Foakes (ed. 1997): Of herself and Regan.

2303+6 text]
Capell (1783, 1.2:175): Goneril derides Albany’s speech as a preachment. Delius (ed. 1854): The text of your moralizing sermon (Ger.). OED (sb. 4): A short passage from the Scriptures, esp. one quoted…as the subject of an exposition or sermon. Deighton (ed. 1891): If the sermon you are about to preach is as foolish as its text, it will not be worth hearing. McCann (ed. 1964): She recognizes Heb. 6:8 as Albany’s text. Foakes (ed. 1997): Alluding to the biblical injunctions to children to honour their parents, as in the First Commandment in Exodus, 20.12, repeated in the Gospels, e.g. at Matthew, 15.4, and by St. Paul, Ephesians, 6.2–3. The term, however, has a wider figurative sense: The theme or subject on which any one speaks; the starting-point of a discussion (OED, 4c, quoting this l. as its first ex.).

2303+7 Wisedome…vild,]
French (1959, p. 525) compares 1 Cor. 2:14: But the natural man perceiueth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishnes vnto him (Geneva).

2303+7 vild]
See n. 1726. Muir (ed. 1952) suspects a pun on wild after tame.

2303+8 Filths…themselues]
Carter (1905, p. 440) compares Tit. 1:15: Unto them that are defiled…is nothing pure (Geneva). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Proverbial: To the filthy all things taste filthy [Tilley F219, quoting this l.]. Camden (1957, p. 253), however: Filthy persons like only filth, citing Palingenius’s Zodiake of Life (1576, p. 234): Things filthy, filthy folkes doe loue, and villaines villanie. Similarly Dent (1981) prefers an allusion to the proverb Like will to like (Tilley L286).

2303+8 Filths]
OED (sb. 4): Vile creature[s], quoting this l. The sense whore applies in Tim. 4.1.6 (1509) but not apparently here.

2303+8 sauor]
The sense depends on the proverb: see prev. n. Capell (1783, 1.2:175) and most eds.: Relish (OED, v. 11). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Get the taste of (OED, 10, quoting this l.).

2303+9 What…perform’d]
Albany’s rhetorical question serves as reminder that he was not present when Lear was shut out in 2.4. Perhaps he has received an account of the incident from Oswald, though Oswald does not say so (2271 ff.); cf. n. 2303+12.

2303+10 father…aged]
Watson (1960, p. 374): The daughters completely defy the ethical canons of their age.…Shakespeare interweaves the two [Elizabethan] themes of respect for the parent and respect for the elder.

2303+10 gracious]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Kindly (OED, adj. 4). Perhaps, as Brown (ed. 1996) suggests, Albany knows more of this side of Lear than the play shows, or else, like Kent (cf. 1637), he may exaggerate.

2303+11 reuerence]
Reverend form (Moberly, ed. 1876), face (Deighton, ed. 1891), hand (Kittredge, ed. 1940), or person (Horsman, ed. 1973). Only Crook (ed. 1907): Whom from reverence. Reverence is an example of metonymy. Cf. 2779.

2303+11 head-lugd]
Nares (1822): Pulled by the head. Wright (ed. 1875) compares Harsnett (1603, p. 106; see ), as men leade Beares by the nose, and 1H4 1.2.74 (185), a lugd beare. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) compare 1283. A more specific sense is more likely: To tease, worry, bait (a bear, bull, etc.) (OED, Lug v. 1). So Craig (ed. 1901): Dragged by the head, and ears, and so infuriated by the attacks of the dogs.

2303+12 madded]
Schmidt (1874), mad: To make mad, to madden (OED, v. 1). Kemshead (1875) mistakes a question—Have you gone mad?—that leaves the sense of the previous two and a half lines incomplete. It is unclear how Albany has learned of Lear’s madness; see n. 2303+9. Oswald may have known of it: cf. 2074–8.

2303+12 lick]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Do homage by licking. Harbage (ed. 1958): Treat with affection.

2303+13 good brother]
Smith (1974, p. 284): When good-brother appears as a hyphenated word in Elizabethan English, it means brother-in-law (OED: Scots). As did the word brother alone: see n. 2283. Skillan (ed. 1967): A courtesy title.…We have already heard of the divisions between them; but as yet he does not realize corn.’s…support of his wife’s cruelty towards her father.

2303+14 A…beniflicted]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Three reasons why Cornwall should not have acted thus: (1) he was a human being; (2)…a prince, one with moral standards higher than those of mere humanity; (3)…greatly in Lear’s debt.

2303+14 beniflicted]
Q1(c) changes this obvious nonsense to benifited, adopted by most eds. Greg (1940, p. 173): The compositor must somehow have confused the word with afflicted. Taylor (1982, pp. 121–2) thinks beniflicted an unlikely misreading of benifited and so proposes the stronger word, the rarer word benefacted, recorded only once before 1898 and never in Sh. But if the Q copy read benifitted the misreading would have been easy, l/i and c/t being common errors.
Warburton (ed. 1747) imagined the omission of a line or two which upbraids her for her sister’s cruelty to Glo’ster, which Warburton supposed alluded to in 2307+1–+2. Like Johnson (ed. 1765), Heath (1765, pp. 343–4) finds this conjecture erroneous: If Gonerill knew of the cruelty exercised on Glo’ster, Albany at least was as yet utterly ignorant of it, which is sufficiently testified by his surprize at the first mention of it [2316], and the enquiries he makes into the circumstances attending it [2325–6, 2335, 2340].

2303+15–+17 If…deepe]
Hudson (ed. 1871): If the gods do not avenge these crimes, the crimes will avenge themselves by turning men into devourers of one another, or by inspiring humanity with a rage of self-destruction. The meaning may be more general: that if punishments do not uphold the laws, men will be emboldened to ignore them. Cf. 2176+1–+2. Greg (1940, p. 394) compares Leir 1651–2: How canst thou suffer such outragious acts To be committed without iust reuenge?; see .

2303+15 visible spirits]
For spirits see n. 1820, 1823. Tovey (ed. 1896): Spiritual beings becoming visible avengers. Kittredge (ed. 1940), visible: Emphatic, comparing Mac. 1.7.21–3 (495–7). Wilson (ed. 1960): Lightning and thunderbolt, or at least some form of physical intervention and retribution (Skillan, ed. 1967). Lloyd (1960, p. 324) and Elton (1966, p. 253) find an allusion to Plutarch’s avenging daemons. Hunter (ed. 1972): Manifest interventions, like those which will precede the Last Judgement. Lott (ed. 1974): Being visible, therefore the more convincing and terrible. Edwards (ed. 1975) takes spirits in some such sense as inspiring influence (OED, 6): Albany hopes to see in the actions of men evidence that God is shaping human history, comparing 2323–5.

2303+16 quickly]
Wilson (ed. 1960) detects a quibble as at 2254.

2303+16 tame]
Schmidt (ed. 1879): A suspicious word on account of its weakness. After visible spirits we should expect rather to doom or to damn (Ger.). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Subdue, put down (OED, v.1 2). Joseph (ed. 1966): Chasten, check, quell.

2303+16 the]
Greg (1940, p. 173): If [Q1(c) this] is correct offences should have been altered to offence, but that would have upset the metre and called for further emendation.…It seems most likely that the corrector wrote thes (for these) and that this is a misprint. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 520): But the corrector need only have added s to [Q1(u)]; the preceding e need not have been touched, by corrector or compositor.…Since this is a recorded 15th–17th-c. spelling of these,…it seems safest to accept [Q1(c)] as a restoration of the manuscript. Contrary to Greg, altering to offence improves the meter, removing a feminine ending to a line; and in fact Albany has accused Goneril of only one offense, madding the king. It seems most likely that the corrector intended the more pointed this and that the change to offence was overlooked.

2303+16 vild]
See n. 1726. Muir (ed. 1952): There may be a quibble intended on…wild, the opposite of tame. See textual n.

2303+16 offences]
Craig (ed. 1901) and others: Offenders; the abstract for the concrete. But this is not necessary; see prev. nn.

2303+16 it will come]
Though eds. attempt to specify it as consequent punishment (Crook, ed. 1907), chaos (Harbage, ed. 1958), etc., it is more probably indefinite, as Greg (1940, p. 173) understands: It will come to this that. Some editors prevent the latter syntax by putting a heavy stop after come (see textual n.), as Daalder (2000–1, pp. 63–4) notes. Bethell (1944, p. 53): An irregular line of three monosyllables introduces with particular solemnity the doom upon humanity. Muir (ed. 1952): It allows room for a dramatic pause before the climax of Albany’s speech. Wilson (ed. 1960): Possibly something has been lost or the words may be an actor’s addition. These latter comments are based on Malone’s lineation (see textual n.), which is by no means certainly correct; Collier’s lineation, treating it…perforce as one line, may well be preferable, since it makes full regular lines throughout, without two part-lines.

2303+17 Humanly…deepe]
Greg (1940, p. 173): Q1(c)’s Humanity is no doubt correct. Van Dam (1935, p. 12) imagines that Sh. had written the word without the i. Chambers (1939, pp. 224–8) finds the idea of this line in Tro. 1.3.119–24 (578–83) and in Sir Thomas More (Add. II, ll. 84–7): for other ruffians…| woold shark on you and men lyke ravenous fishes | woold feed on on another. Wilson (1949, pp. 19–20) finds parallels in Cor. 1.1.186–8 (197–9), the medieval moralities Everyman [47–50] (anticipating Salter, 1954, p. 110) and Pride of Life [361–2], and John Poynet’s Short Treatise of Political Power (1556, p. 10): As Theodoretus sayeth, the great fish eat up the small. Muir (ed. 1952): The idea goes back even beyond Theodoretus. See Hesiod, Works and Days, in a passage thus translated by George Chapman, [Georgics] i. 434–7: Fish, fowl, and savage beasts (whose law is power), | Jove lets each other mutually devour, | Because they lack the equity he gives | To govern men, as far best for their lives. The following references may be added: Bestiary in Arundel MS. 292, ed. R. Morris, 1872, 505–16; Whitney, Emblems, p. 52: The mightie fishe deuowres the little frie; Christopher Dawson, The Making of Europe, 1939, p. 267 (citing an example from A.D. 909); and the well known drawing by Pieter Bruegel. But it should be noted that whereas most of these writers compare the rich to big fish and the poor to little fish, Shakespeare suggests that the violation of order would lead to actual cannibalism. The more commonplace comparison is to be found in a doubtful scene in Pericles, II. i. 29–34 [578–84]. Similar exx. of the commonplace may be found in H. N. Hillebrand, ed., Variorum Tro. (1954, pp. 57–8). Elton (1966, p. 299): Recalling one of the traditional signs before doomsday. Gardner (ed. 1969) cites Pliny’s account (tr. Holland, 1601, pp. 236–7) of whales and Orcae attacking their dams and young, adding, Albany’s thought…is not only the destruction of order and degree, but the reversal of man’s nature. Cf. 773.

2304–2307+2 Milke…drum]
The lineation of Q and F agree for the first line and a half and not thereafter, where Q is clearly wrong. It may be noted that Q makes fairly regular pentameter if lined so as to end bloes,…browes…suffering,…pitty…mischiefe, with Wher’s thy drum? as a short line (perhaps followed by a dramatic pause during which Albany declines to answer). F’s lineation is such as to accommodate its cuts, so that its agreement with Q in 2304–5 may be coincidental. Q’s initial short line was not intended by the compositor to link metrically with a previous part-line, and though it may reflect copy, it may also be simply the consequence of the Q compositor’s setting 2303+17 as a turned-over line, with the deepe occupying the end of typographical line 2304 and so preventing a full line of verse even if the Q compositor had recognized one. Such a hypothetical lining of the passage results in greater coincidence between the rhetorical units and the verse lines than if restored Q lines are re-divided to agree with later F lineation made in a shortened text. See n. 2303+16.

2304 Milke liuerd]
See n. 1090. Hunter (ed. 1972): In his liver, a substitution of female Milk for male blood. Weis (ed. 1993): Milk is a symbol of gentleness, citing Mac. 1.5.17 (363). More probably it means simply white (= bloodless): cf. MV 3.2.86 (1432), lyuers white as milke. The image is proverbial: see Dent (1981, M931, F180). Bransom (1934, p. 144): There was nothing very milk-livered in [his] rebuke…[and] as a matter of fact her servant had only brought him the news of the French landing a few hours before.

2305–2307+2 That…Who]
On the alternating pronouns see n. 1908–14.

2305 bearest]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Have (as a part of oneself). Poss. bar’st—an echo of Luke vi. 29—upbraiding him for Christian long-suffering—an allusion detected by Carter (1905, p. 440) and Noble (1935, p. 232), who cite also Matt. 5:39.

2305 head for wrongs]
