Hunter (ed. 1972): An object for other people to rain their wrongful blows on. Adee (ed. 1890, p. liii): An unnoticed allusion to the horns of the cuckold.

2306–7 Who…suffering]
Capell (1783, 1.2:175–6): He wanted sense to distinguish between wrongs that might be overlook’d, and wrongs that might not; intimating—that the wrong expected from Lear, was a wrong of the latter sort, in which his honour was interested. Verity (ed. 1897): I.e. he is so ready to suffer and put up with things, that he does not see when he is doing so at the expense of his honour. Cf. 2281–2.

2306–2311+6 thy]
Horsman (ed. 1973, p. 225) notes the shift in the quarrel from the more distant you to the less respectful thou. In his reply Albany also uses the pronoun, the only occasion in the play in which he does so (Bransom (1934, p. 147).

2306 deseruing]
All eds. adopt F’s discerning without its erroneous hyphen. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 406): Probably a misreading—e/i, u/n. The copy for Q may have had diserning. Halio (ed. 1994) compares 2002.

2307+1–+6 that…so?]
Theobald (ed. 1733): This I have retriev’d from the first Quarto. It seems first to have been retrench’d by the Players, for Brevity’s sake: but, besides that the Lines are fine, they admirably display the taunting termagent Disposition of Gonerill, and paint out her Contempt of her Husband’s mild pacifick Spirit. Hart (1942, p. 148) thinks fear of royal disfavor caused the cut; see n. 2303–2303+17. Doran (1931, p. 73): Perhaps the hand of the censor is to be detected here; the direct reference to France might be considered likely to give offense to the French…The notable fact that the references to invasion by a foreign power remain untouched when the power is unnamed and when the circumstances of the invasion are shrouded in a certain vagueness ([1759–70, 2050–1, 2271, 2870–2, 2984–5]), but that they are generally missing from the folio when France is directly named, is good evidence of their having been deleted by the censor. The Master of the Revels [Sir George Buc] was on guard to catch any matter in plays which might be offensive to the court or to the foreign ambassadors.…France is twice named without being directly connected with the invading forces: [1980–2, 2109]. One direct reference [2061] to the French invasion is allowed to stand…but it is short and may have been missed by the censor. It could not be overlooked by an audience, since it is the grounds for Cornwall’s interrogation of Gloucester as a traitor. For arguments against such censorship see n. 1638+1–+12. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 8): Certain passages which are cut concern the French landing in England—[1638+1–+12], [2307+1–+6], [2868+1–+5]. One of these, [2307+1–+6], is a passage of recrimination addressed by Goneril to Albany; other such passages of abuse between them are omitted from the same scene at [2303+1–+16] and [2311+1–+8]. Taylor (1980, p. 31): F systematically remov[es] verbal and visual reminders of the French presence, thereby deliberately excising an extraneous political complication and removing even the ghost of a reason for Cordelia’s military defeat. Since four references to France (1638+1, 2307+3, 2347+2, +9) occur admidst much longer passages cut from F—1638+1–+12, 2307+1–+6 (amidst some 34 lines cut overall from the episode, as Duthie notes), 2347+1–+56, and 2868–2868+4—their deletion from F is most probably incidental to those larger cuts, not specific and systematic. Besides, F retains many other references to France (1982, 2061, 2109, 2377, 2834) and adds yet one more (1633), besides keeping the five allusions to invasion by a foreign power listed by Doran; and two additional visual emblems of France are specified in the F stage directions: see nn. 2349 and 2918. None of this suggests systematic revision to diminish the presence of France; the foreign invaders are consistently and unmistakably French. For further argument against different Q and F invasions, see Knowles (1999, pp. 270–7). Halio (ed. 1992): In Q, Gonerill’s speech…comes to a proper conclusion.…In F, Albany abruptly and vehemently breaks into…her speech.

2307+1 not know’st]
On the transposition see n. 1012.

2307+1 know’st fools,]
On Q1(c)’s know’st,fools Greg (1940, pp. 173–4) says, The shifting of the comma [in F] is certainly an improvement, but it might have been removed altogether. It is redundant grammatically, and if there is a pause it is metrical, due to the line-ending. The line ending may occur elsewhere; see n. 2304–2307+2.

2307+1–+2 fools…mischiefe]
Horsman (ed. 1973), fools: Only fools. The general sense is clear: It is foolish to object to punishment which precedes crimes (Hunter, ed. 1972). Edwards (ed. 1975): I.e., pre-emptive punishment. (The common specious justification for aggression: that you are preventing aggression from the other side.) More particularly, eds. have identified the vilain as (1) Gloucester, (2) Lear, (3) Goneril, (4) the King of France, (5) Albany, (6) Cordelia, or (7) no one in particular.
(1)Gloucester. Warburton (ed. 1747): see n. 2303+14. Hunter (op. cit.): Gloucester’s case must also [i.e., with Lear’s] be in the mind of Gonerill and of the audience, though Albany has not yet heard of his punishment.
(2)Lear. Capell (1783, 1.2:175): Gloster had done the harm he was punish’d for.…Horrid as it may seem, her father is the villain…; he, indeed, is punish’d ere any mischief is done by him. Singer (ed. 1826): She refers to the pity for his sufferings expressed by Albany, whom she means indirectly to call a fool for expressing it. Deighton (ed. 1891): Fools, like yourself, pity villains, like my father, when they are punished before they can accomplish their wicked purposes, such as…bringing the French army down upon us. Dey (1900, p. 204), comparing 314–32: Consequently they do something, and i’ th’ heat, to make it impossible for him to carry authority…bears. This is the mischief which, in Goneril’s opinion, has been prevented.
(3)Goneril. Eccles (ed. 1792): Persons who harbor evil intentions, but, through irresolution, or dread of consequences, delay the execution of them till disappointment overtake them and they meet their punishment, obtain pity from none but fools.…We have mischief in hand, which it is expedient to effect: if so, the more speedily it is accomplished the better…even if our proceeding merited such an imputation as villainy. Verity (ed. 1897): Only fools (observe its emphatic position) pity the villain who bungles in his crime and gets punished. She cynically admits the evil of her treatment of Lear, speaks as if Albany were as much responsible for it as she herself and they were both villains, and tries to taunt him into action. Reference to Lear is just possible, since their mischief might conceivably allude to Lear’s intention of resuming his power [828], a danger that has become serious through the intervention of the French king.
(4)France. Malone (ed. 1790): If her words are considered as connected with what follows in the next lines. Tovey (ed. 1896): Though Albany has spoken only of Lear, Goneril…has Lear, Gloucester, and France in mind.
(5)Albany. Furness (ed. 1880): May it not be that she refers to Albany himself? She has told him that his preachment about her father was foolish, and that he should drop the subject. Is it likely that she would resume it? On the contrary, she wishes, as soon as possible, to turn the tables, and put him to his defence, therefore she launches into bitter railing against his supineness;…none but fools will have any pity for villains, like himself, who are punished before they have struck a blow. Crook (ed. 1907): Even fools pity those villains whose fear of consequences gives them the punishment of dread before the offence they contemplate is performed. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Albany’s inaction, she implies, will be his ruin, and nobody will ever pity him. Brooke (ed. 1947): Grant that we are all villains, Goneril seems to mean; yet you are involved with the rest of us, and only fools pity the sort of villain you are, who will allow yourself to be punished for treason before you have done any act.
(6)Unspecified. Mrs. Griffith (1775, p. 367): She means…that it is necessary to guard against foreseen evils, as well as to defend against those that press us; but fools being too short-sighted to see the prevention in the punishment, are apt to bewail the sufferer. Delius (ed. 1854): Goneril means to justify the course of action of herself, her sister, and her brother-in-law in a general way, without dealing with particulars.
Most eds. agree with Capell (2) that Goneril is spurning Albany’s condemnation of her treatment of Lear. Thus Muir (ed. 1952): The implication is that Lear is a villain because he is in league with France. The French invasion is the wrong Albany is suffering meekly; and Goneril returns to the subject after referring to Lear’s punishment.…[Furness’s] interpretation seems to me highly unlikely, since Goneril harps on Albany’s feebleness and foolishness, not on his villainy; and she regards the repelling of the invader not as mischief but as a patriotic duty. I think villains can scarcely apply to the King of France, since he has not been punished, though it might conceivably mean that he is about to be defeated.

2307+3 Wher’s thy drum]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Why are you not rallying your forces? Weis (ed. 1993): With the martial drum of war; but also, tauntingly, the tabor that a fool beats.

2307+3 France]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): The King of France. As represented by his army; the king himself is not present, of course. See n. 2868–2868+4.

2307+3 noystles]
Noiseless. Delius (ed. 1854): Making no commotion [OED, adj., quoting this l.] at the invasion of the French (Ger.). Wright (ed. 1875): With no sound of preparation for war. Tovey (ed. 1896): With no sound of drum or trumpet on our side. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Quiet—i.e., passive and unresisting. Q1(c) corrects to noyseles, Q2 to noiselesse. Greg (1940, p. 174): The previous drum makes this emendation practically certain. The confusion of st and se is very easy in many secretary hands. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 520): Since Q1(u) uses an st ligature, noystles cannot be a typographical error for noyseles. It could, however, be a foul-case error for noysles.

2307+4 helme,]
Sisson (1956, 2:240): A full stop after helm. Thy state begins to threaten with plumed helm will not serve…for Goneril’s complaint is precisely the opposite, that Albany is not fighting. But most eds. agree with Verity (ed. 1897): France is the subject of begins, and state the object of threat. Hunter (ed. 1972): A new grammatical subject…could only weaken the antithesis between France and thou. Plumed helm is simple metonymy for the army of France in battle dress.

2307+4 thy slayer]
Though Q1(c)’s thy state—thy government; thy dominions (Kittredge, ed. 1940)—is now accepted by virtually all eds., Q’s uncorrected slayer—would-be slayer (Houghton, ed. 1857)—enjoyed long life. Greg (1940, p. 174) suggests his for thy because in the absence of an And joining this line to the preceding, I think it requires a new subject. Though Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 407) accepted this emendation, he later (in Wilson, ed. 1960) came to agree with Walker (1953, p. 52) that it made unnecessarily heavy weather of difficulties in the text, since no new subject is required: see prev. n. Muir (ed. 1952): And state would be awkwardly applied to the French army. Taylor’s (1983, p. 488) single easy emendation to thy flaxen requires the change of as many letters as Q1(c): see next n.

2307+4 begin threats]
Neither this nor Q1(c)’s begins thereat makes sense with either slayer or state. Colman’s (ed. 1982) unique defense of the latter—Your prosperity could begin, with war upon the French—seems desperate, since Albany is already prosperous. Weis (ed. 1993) in turn broadly expands the meaning of state: The true exercise of your political power starts (i.e. should properly start) with this situation (and not with lecturing me). Foakes (ed. 1997): This seems to me to be wrenching the meaning of state. The reading favored by many eds. before this century—thy slayer begins threats—has the virtue of simplicity (requiring the change of a single letter of Q1[u]) and the disadvantages of somewhat inferior sense and meter. Greg (1940, p. 174) doubts the emendation usual today, Jennens’s thy state begins to threat: [Q1(c)’s] thereat makes no sense, but it proves that threats cannot be right, though the graphic outline is similar. The letters reat are common to both…but what reading may be concealed in [them] I am at a loss to imagine. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 406): To threat does not agree sufficiently closely with the graphic outline of either threat or thereat—there would certainly appear to have been no to in the copy. Muir (ed. 1952): Possibly a line has dropped out. But threat could easily be misread or miswritten as thereat and the word to may have been omitted. Walker (1953, p. 52): Jennens’s emendation…satisfies the textual conditions. Bad handwriting started the trouble and bad spelling (thereat for threat) led the painstaking proof-reader astray. State begins to threat makes perfectly good sense and presupposes no more complicated error than the omission of to. Hulme (1962, p. 317): Syllabic r is occasionally found in the Shakespearean text, citing also Garace (Tit. 2.3.182 [929]) and several words in regional dialects. Taylor (1983, p. 488) accepts Stone’s (1980, p. 184) biggin (cap or hood) and proposes thy flaxen begin threats, and Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 520) cite examples of biggin used in a derisive way—as might be expected of a word usually meaning child’s cap or night-cap (OED, 1, 2). Though OED records the rare spelling begin it does not instance it, and in Sh.’s only use of the word (2H4 4.5.27 [2549]) it is spelled biggen (Q, F). Halio (ed. 1992): The emendation, which makes sense and is paleographically sound, alters Q uncorr. minimally. The comparison between the King of France with his plumèd helm and Albany in his nightcap is deliberately ludicrous. Foakes (ed. 1997): Biggen is an ingenious emendation…[but] an implausible association with an aristocrat like Albany. Of the many proposed conjectures (see ) Perring’s thy slayer, big in threats, requires the least change to Q, but results in a static sentence of one parenthetical modifier after another.

2307+5 Whil’s]
Q’s uncorrected form is less probably an elision of Whiles (found in F at 1256) than an error for Q’s corrected form Whil’st, found also at 3168+4. Cf. Q’s whilst at 179 and 1717. All mean the same.

2307+5 morall]
Delius (ed. 1854): Moralizing. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Arguing about the rights and wrongs of the matter instead of opposing the invader, in reference to 2303+7 ff. Fraser (ed. 1963): With the implication that morality and folly are one.

2307+5 sits]
Wright (ed. 1875) cites Abbott (§340): In verbs ending with -t, -test final in the second person sing. often becomes -ts for euphony. Cf. Franz §152, and 2605.

2307+5 still]
Probably in the sense of motionless, not constantly. Weis (ed. 1993), however: (1) stands by passively; (2) continues sitting.

2308 See…deuill]
Verity (ed. 1897): Instead of judging him. thyself: emphatic. Capell (1783, 1.2:176) suggests that the whole speech may be an apostrophe: He first apostrophizes the devil to come and see his own picture [i.e., in Goneril]: but, on second thoughts, thinks the picture outré; for that the wickedness of such a woman as Goneril, has more deformity in it than that of the very father of wickedness. Halio (ed. 1992): Holding up to her, perhaps, the mirror she carries by her side. There is no evidence that she carries such a mirror, though Meagher (1972, p. 253) imagines one. Mazzon (1992, p. 129): Albany’s shift from you to thy as the situation deteriorates is the first of five such switches here and in 5.3, reflecting his progressively mixed feelings towards his wife.

2309 proper]
Numerous eds. have adhered to each of five possible meanings for the word: (1) one’s own, (2) attractive, (3) appropriate, (4) thorough, and (5) real:
(1)One’s own—either the devil’s own, or Goneril’s. Warburton (ed. 1747): Diabolic qualities appear not so horrid in the devil, to whom they belong, as in woman who unnaturally assumes them. White (ed. 1862): Deformity which…be-monsters the feature or peculiar personal traits—viz., of Goneril. Herford (ed. 1899): Innate. OED (adj. 1): Belonging to oneself;…intrinsic, inherent.
(2)Attractive. Delius (ed. 1854): Deformity which conceals itself under a pleasing, fair outside (Ger.). OED (8): Of goodly appearance. Though Wright (ed. 1875) says, This interpretation would require some such word as specious instead of horrid in the next line, and Furness (ed. 1880) declares it ingenious, and one which none but a Shakespeare-scholar would have made, Harbage (ed. 1958: fair-surfaced) and Fraser (ed. 1963) repeat it. In his next speech Albany talks to Goneril as a fiendish thing covered with an attractive womans shape. Possibly he means here that while fiends often adopt attractive disguises, it is more horrid for a real, beautiful woman to hide an inner demon. Black (1980, p. 36): An oxymoron.
(3)Appropriate. Schmidt (1875): Deformity conformable to the character (OED, 9: Fit, apt). Hudson (ed. 1881), crediting Crosby [1876, p. 225]: The deformity, or depravity, of the fiend is proper to him, is his own, and in keeping with the rest of his being, so that the inside and outside agree together; and therefore is less horrid than when it is covered with a woman’s shape: for to have the shape of a woman and the heart of a fiend, or to transfuse the inside of the one into the outside of the other, is in the fullest sense unnatural and monstrous; and she who so translates her inner self literally be-monsters her proper make-up, her womanhood. Tovey (ed. 1896): Perhaps an instance of confused expression, proper really belonging to deformity in the fiend, not in woman;…in the fiend deformity is to be expected, and therefore in keeping, but in the woman it is all the more horrible because it is against nature. Else we must explain proper as innate [(1) above] without any difference, however, in the general drift. Craig (ed. 1901): Which is the proper attribute of, and only to be expected from it (the fiend), comparing 2H4 4.1.37 (1904). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Appropriate to his character, and therefore not so repulsive.
(4)Thorough. White (ed. 1883): Thorough, complete deformity. OED (6): Complete, perfect, out-and-out. This makes an excellent but not a particularly Shn. sense.
(5)Real. Moberly (ed. 1876): Wickedness showing its real colour and shape. So Meiklejohn (ed. 1879). OED (5): Genuine, true.

2309 deformity]
Most eds. understand moral deformity or depravity (see prev. n.). Muir (ed. 1952), alternatively: Albany may be referring…to Goneril’s face distorted by evil passion. Wilson (ed. 1960): Moral and physical deformity.

2309 seemes]
Like Q1(c)’s shewes this means appears. Doran (1931, pp. 102–3): Seemes…does not immediately appear to be a manuscript misreading of shewes…. The sh ligature [in script], however, took a variety of shapes, in some cases looking not very different from a single s. If shewes was the original word, then seemes is a misreading of it common to both uncorrected Q1 and F. See also n. 2300. Greg (1940, pp. 174–5): Seemes makes perfectly good sense, and there is therefore no reason why the reader should have altered it if it stood in the copy; moreover shewes is a reading so greatly superior as to possess intrinsic probability. I have no doubt that F took over the reading of [Q1(u)] inadvertently. Stone (1980, p. 184): The copy-spelling was doubtless sewes, misread as semes. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 520): But the [Q1(u)] error could easily result from compositorial substitution rather than misreading. All other occurrences of the word in Shakespeare texts are spelt sh-. It is also possible that the Q compositor and the scribe preparing the playbook both read seemes in their difficult copy, and that the corrector, reading shewes, replaced what seemed to him an easy misreading.

2309–10 fiend…woman]
Verity (ed. 1897) compares Perillus’s rebuke of Gonorill in Leir 2581–2: Nay, peace thou monster, shame vnto thy sexe: Thou fiend in likenesse of a humane creature; see . Muir (ed. 1952, pp. xxxi f.) points out the echoes in 2309–2311+2 of shame, fiend, monster, and woman. Idem (1957, p. 142): The similarities are sufficient to show that Shakespeare knew the old play.

2311 vaine]
Schmidt (1875): Silly (OED, adj. 3). Gardner (ed. 1969): Ineffectual. Halio (ed. 1992): The epithet may reflect back upon Gonerill ironically, citing 1109.

2311+1–+8 Alb.…newes]
See nn. 2303–2303+17, 2307+1–+6. Urkowitz (1980, p. 29): These cuts make the Folio version more vigorous and theatrical…fierce and quick, the one here supplanting the urgency of the messenger’s entrance found in the Quarto (interrupting Goneril’s speech at 2311+7) with the power of Albany’s crushing interruption of Goneril in the Folio. Foakes (1993, p. 200): F removes these lines, apparently, because Albany has already called her devil and fiend.

2311+1 changed]
Crosby (1876, p. 225): Metamorphosed into a fiend in shape (feature), and disposition, and conduct. Idem (1879, p. 385): Bewitched, be-devilled. Deighton (ed. 1891): In whom the real self is changed and hidden by fury. Bransom (1934, p. 146): Possibly blushing. These interpretations are somewhat off the mark. It is clear from 2311+6 that she retains her outer womans shape, which Albany warns her not to Be-monster; it is her inner nature that has become a fiendish thing. See the next n. and .

2311+1 selfe-couerd thing]
When not emended (see textual n. and ) this enigmatic phrase is interpreted to mean (1) that Goneril’s natural self is now hidden by a fiendish one, (2) that her inner fiendishness is now revealed in her features, (3) that her inner fiendishness is covered by a womanly exterior, or (4) that she is completely selfish:
(1)Fiendish covering. Johnson (ed. 1765): Thou that hast disguised nature by wickedness; thou that hast hid the woman under the fiend. Malone (ed. 1790): Thou who hast put a covering on thyself, which nature did not give thee…the semblance and appearance of a fiend. Steevens (in Boswell, ed. 1821): Perhaps…said in allusion to the envelope which the maggots of some insects furnish to themselves. Or…to the operation of the silk-worm. Hudson (ed. 1871): Covered or lost thy proper self under an usurped monstrosity. Quinn (ed. 1970): Deceitful. Brower (1971, p. 389): Goneril will in time look the monster she is.
(2)Fiendish features. Henley (apud Eccles, ed. 1792): Goneril, having thrown off the convenient seeming of female gentleness, now no longer played the hypocrite, but exhibited in her face the self-same passions she had covered in her heart. Seymour (1805, 2:122): Thou thing, whose exterior exhibits…thy inward and essential wickedness. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Who hast covered thyself with the hideousness only proper to a fiend. Schmidt (1875): Goneril must be supposed to have, by changing countenance, betrayed all her wickedness. Furness (ed. 1880): Is it over-refinement to suppose that this revelation to Albany of his wife’s fiendlike character transforms, in his eyes, even her person? Verity (ed. 1897): He tells Goneril warningly that she is becoming externally in appearance—cf. changed—the monster that she is inwardly in character.…Self-cover’d might be taken quite literally = covered with thy self, i.e. thy [fiendish] character.
(3)Womanly covering. Crosby (1876, p. 225), reading sex-cover’d: Covered…in the sense of shielded, comparing 2311+6. Kinnear (1883, p. 424): Hidden from thyself. Tovey (ed. 1896), as alternative to (2): Hitherto disguised by thyself, i.e., thy plausible outside, thy woman’s shape. Craig (ed. 1901): The self, the essence of Goneril, is fiend, but that essence is outwardly changed and covered by the shape of woman. Bradley (1904, p. 461): Really he is addressing her as a fiend which has changed its own shape and assumed that of a woman; and I suggest that self-covered means either which hast cover’d or concealed thyself, or whose self is covered, not (what of course it ought to mean) which hast been covered by thyself. Tamblyn (1922, p. 348): Fiend still disguised in so fair a shape. Gardner (ed. 1969): But if she continues, her whole aspect…will undergo a hideous metamorphosis. This was the ultimate peril of demonic possession.
(4)Covering of selfishness. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): A woman unsexed, sufficient to herself, the opposite of the married woman, or femme couverte, as she was termed in law. This, to her husband, was abhorrence of her as a masculine monster whose woman’s semblance alone restrained him from utterly destroying. Crook (ed. 1907): Clothed in selfishness. Major (1958): Cover = to impregnate or engender; Like a fiend or some monstrous beast out of fable, she must have begotten herself upon herself: conduct so inhuman could not proceed from any creature born of man and woman. Elton (1966, p. 120): Albany’s reply…suggests self-generation and self-creation, monstering nature. In addition, since cover, in a relevant sense, is used mainly of horses, it suggests a link with the Ixion-centaur motif.
Of these four kinds of interpretation the third, most often accepted by eds., seems to make most consistent sense with the rest of Albany’s speech. Delius (ed. 1854): Since only your woman’s appearance keeps me from doing violence to the fiend you are, do not bemonster your countenance (Ger.). Furness (loc. cit.): Goneril’s feature is quivering and her face distorted with passion. Then it is that Albany tells her not to let her evil self, hitherto covered and concealed, betray itself in all its hideousness in her outward shape.
It is possible, however, that self appears here in its common Shn. adjectival sense of same (OED, a. 1–3) or pronominal sense of same person. Albany may be simply saying that though her inner nature is changed, the thing that she has become retains the self-same covering, the person or appearance of the old Goneril. This seems to be Bald’s (ed. 1949) understanding: Still the same in outward appearance.

2311+1 thing]
Tamblyn (1922, p. 349): For thing as fiend see [2511, 2522]. Wells (ed. 2000): She has become a thing rather than a person.

2311+2 Be-monster]
See nn. 760, 2309–10. OED (v. 1): To make monstrous or hideous; to deform, quoting this l. as its first ex. Verity (ed. 1897): Do not make thyself look like a monster—i.e., by angry scowls and hostile carriage. Hunter (ed. 1972): Show in your external appearance the monster that lives within you. Smith (ed. 1917), less probably: Take on the outward form of a woman, unnatural to a devil. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Albany knows that Goneril is a woman; yet she seems to be changing to a fiend before his eyes. Brownlow (1993, p. 117): Cf. Harsnett (1603, p. 128): To disguise, difforme, and monster-like to mishape. See prev. two nn., and n. 2309–10 for a similar image in Leir.

2311+2 feature]
Malone (ed. 1790): The general cast of countenance, and often beauty (OED, sb. 3). Clarkes (ed. 1868): General aspect or personal appearance. Schmidt (1874): Always in Sh., The shape, make, exterior, the whole turn or cast of the body (OED, 1), not the lineaments of the face. Wright (ed. 1875): Thy natural form of woman. OED gives no warrant for Crosby’s (1879, p. 385) womanhood or Hudson’s (ed. 1881) selfhood. Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): (Human) appearance.

2311+2 wer’t my fitnes]
Rann (ed. 1794): Did it become my manhood. Smith (ed. 1902): Were it fit for me. Page (ed. 1889) adds, as thy husband. Skillan (ed. 1967), rather: Consistent with his nature.

2311+3 To…bloud]
Dyce (ed. 1865): A mutilated line. Wilson (ed. 1960): Perh. through accidental omission. Abbott (§508): A foot…can be omitted where there is any marked pause…arising from emotion. More probably Albany puts strong stress on each word of let these hands, giving the effect of a pentameter line.

2311+3 bloud]
Singer (ed. 1826): My passion, my inclination (OED, sb. 5: Temper, mood, disposition,…anger). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Passionate impulse.

2311+4–+5 dislecate…bones]
Clarkes (ed. 1868) find an intervolved construction or kind of chiasmus, meaning To dislocate thy bones and tear thy flesh. Craig (ed. 1901): For a similar threat as a punishment for infidelity, compare Ado. 4.1.184 (1847), Oth. 3.3.431 (2080), Cym. 2.4.147 (1329); but Albany has charged Goneril with unfilial cruelty, not infidelity.

2311+4 dislecate]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 407): O/e misreading. OED (Dislocate v. 2b) quotes this l. as its first ex.

2311+5 how ere]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): However much (OED, However adv. 1c, quoting this l.). Wright (ed. 1875): Although, notwithstanding; so Franz §574.

2311+7 Marry]
See n. 1692. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Here used as a slight interjection, dismissing the subject: Well, well. Only Weis (ed. 1993) construes it as a verb: Why then don’t you marry your gentlemanly (i.e. effeminate) self (rather than the fiend-like unnatural woman you claim I have become)? But Goneril’s evil, not Albany’s marriage, is at issue.

2311+7 now]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Oh! now you give proofs of your manhood in forbearing to treat with merited violence…one of the softer sex. Delius (ed. 1854): Now, says Goneril sarcastically, your manhood appears, against a woman (Ger.). Moberly (ed. 1876): A nice notion you have of manhood! Verity (ed. 1897): It seems to be a sarcastic withdrawal of her former charge of want of courage. Kelcy (1932, p. 368): You get one vain and crazy notion in your head after another. Now it’s your manhood. Campbell (ed. 1964): What a fine specimen of manhood you now are. Defenders of Q1(c)’s mew as a bona fide correction from copy (Halio, ed. 1992, ed. 1994) treat it as either interjection or verb. Wright (ed. 1875): Keep it in, restrain it (OED, v.2 1–3). Cummins (1968): Following 2304 ff., meant sarcastically: Oh, your great, terrible manhood! Restrain that dreadful force! Daniel (facs. 1885, p. xv): Mew here…is merely an interjection of contempt. Point it thus, Marry, your manhood—Mew! To Daniel’s exx. of such a use in contemporary drama Craig (ed. 1901) adds more; most appear in OED (v.3 b; int. and sb.3 2). Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): The naked fierceness of this marital quarrel suggests that Gonerill may have really mewed like a cat at Albany here, in her taunting scorn of his feebleness. Brooke (ed. 1947): The cat-call employed by an Elizabethan audience to hiss a bad actor. Stone (1980, p. 213): Such a reading makes…Goneril’s reaction to Albany’s outburst too crudely dismissive. Joseph (ed. 1966): Albany has talked of her false womanliness…. She sneers back at his alleged manliness in threatening her, implying that the threat does not even frighten her. Quinn (ed. 1970): A scornful dismissal of Albany as effeminate. Edwards (ed. 1975): Who are you to talk of what is fit for man or woman? Brown (ed. 1976): Shut up. Greg (1940, p. 175): The [Q1] reader should have deleted the hyphens which the compositor had inserted under the impression that the speech was broken off. It makes little difference whether we punctuate: …manhood—mew! or manhood! mew! Halio (ed. 1994): The entrance of the messenger may indicate that Gonorill’s speech is, in fact, broken off. Ridley (ed. 1935): Goneril surely means, if all that is troubling you is the difference in sex, put off your manhood (mew = moult, shed [OED, v.1 1]) and I shall be happy to meet you on equal terms. Similarly Fraser (ed. 1963): Molt or shed it, if that is what is supposed to shield me from you. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Your valour seems to be feeble—in need of nursing and tender care to restore it to vigour. Shut it up in the mews awhile, as we confine an ailing falcon that requires dieting and medicine. The mews was a building in which hawks were caged (OED, sb.2 1, 2). Weis (ed. 1993): Either parodying Albany’s Tigers [2303+9—29 lines earlier]…(i.e. I had rather be a kitten, and cry mew) or likening his role as husband to that of a self-appointed falconer.

2312 Gentleman]
See n. 1615. On F’s Messenger and the SP Mes. throughout the scene Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 83) says, These are doubtless just different appellations for the same small-part actors. Mahood (1992, p. 169): Several directors have identified him with Curan,…intimate with Edmund.…Curan’s awareness of animosity between the dukes would make him the more eager to tell Albany of Cornwall’s savagery.

2314 going]
For the participle without a noun see n. 1195. Deighton (ed. 1891): As he was about to.

2317 bred]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Brought up in his household. See n. 2152.

2317 thrald]
Doubtless a misreading for F’s thrill’d, though Doran (1931, pp. 95, 103) thinks the opposite may be the case, and Wells (ed. 2000) glosses in thrall to the passion of pity. Weis (ed. 1993) proposes repunctuating Q: bred thrald, with remorse Oppos’d. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 407): The il may have looked something like an open a…[or] the copy may have had…an extra minim stroke between the r and the l. Crook (ed. 1907): Pierced.…incited by. OED (v.1 5): To affect or move with a sudden wave of emotion, quoting this l. as its first ex. Harrison (ed. 1937): Trembling with (OED, 6). Mahood (1992, p. 168): Remorse drills [OED 1] agonisingly into the Servant’s heart.

2317 remorse]
Davies (1783, 2:308): Pity, not compunction (OED, sb. 3).

2318 Oppos’d]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Made opposition. Rolfe (ed. 1880): Opposed himself. Cf. 2868+4.

2318 bending]
See n. 982.

2319 To]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Against, a meaning suggested at 355. Cf. OED (prep. 25), Franz §527.

2319–20 who…dead]
Cf. the apparent inconsistency with 2155, which eds. are at pains to explain away. Malone (ed. 1790): I.e. they (Cornwall and his other servants) amongst them fell’d him dead. Delius (ed. 1854): They (Cornwall and Regan together) is the understood subject of fell’d (Ger.). Lott (ed. 1974): The…subject comes from amongst them. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Regan having snatched a sword…and helped her husband to dispatch the one who turned upon him. Hudson (ed. 1871), more fancifully: Although Regan thrust the servant with a sword, a wound before received from Cornwall may have caused his death. Verity (ed. 1897): Apparently the Messenger does not know what really occurred. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Regan’s part in this death is shielded, the messenger not daring to tell it or not knowing more than his instructed message. For amongst them = between them Craig (ed. 1901) compares 2H4 5.4.17 (3187–9). Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 520) also compare Ado 5.1.191 (2275) and add, The referent for them depends less on grammar than on an audience’s knowledge. Conceivably something has dropped out, but the agreement of Q and F, and their metrical regularity, argue against this. See also n. 2320.

2319 thereat inraged]
Collier (ed. 1843) comments on F’s threat-enrag’d: A striking compound word, which might be right, if the quartos did not contradict it, and if the verse were not thereby injured. Stone (1980, p. 221): It shows [a] reviser sorrily misapplying his ingenuity. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 537): F1 could as easily result from Compositor B omitting a single type as from misreading of, or in, the manuscript. Doran (1931, pp. 94, 103) disagrees, preferring a misreading from MS: The hyphen indicates that the folio reading represents what the printer understood the words in the manuscript to be and not that there has been merely an accidental loss of an e. Cf. the similar confusion at 2307+4 (begin threats).

2320 amongst them]
Moberly (ed. 1876): The blow came from Regan’s hand. Eds. therefore interpret amongst them to mean with others he or amongst themselves they (see next n.) or out of their number. Horsman (ed. 1973): Between them Cornwall and Regan killed him. Clarkes (1879, p. 655), however: [Amongst] those present, and Skillan (ed. 1967): Before everybody [he]. Bevington (ed. 1980): Together with others (?) in their midst (?) out of their number(?). The Gentleman’s account need not be erroneous: see n. 2155.

2320 feld]
Wright (ed. 1875) suspects omission of the obvious nominative they; see n. 230.

2322 pluckt]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): The regular Elizabethan verb for to pull; used six times in Lr. Cf. 2992.

2322 him after]
Kittredge (ed. 1940), him: Cornwall. The object of the adverbial preposition after is understood: Tovey (ed. 1896): After the servant. Bevington (ed. 1980): Along (to death). Harbage (1963, p. 423): Albany becomes de facto ruler of Britain.

2323–6 This…eye]
Hubler (1935, p. 435): In Q1, A speech which begins and ends in a half line has both the beginning and the end compressed. This mislining affects 2327–9 as well. F’s lining is clearly correct.

2323–5 This…venge]
Verity (ed. 1897): Albany is thinking of what he had said, [2303+15–+17]. Bullough (1973, p. 384 n.) compares Leir 1909–10 (see ) and Lr. 3131. Carter (1905, p. 440) and Shaheen (1987, p. 153) compare Luke 18:7–8.

2324 your]
Q1(c)’s you is certainly correct (Greg, 1940, p. 175).

2324 Iustices]
Most eds. have preferred Q1(c)’s Iustisers to the Q1(u)-F reading. Doran (1931, p. 102): An r made hastily and joined to the following s might be missed by [F] scribe and [Q] printer and discovered on a closer scrutiny by a proof-corrector. The line was probably corrected because of the erroneous your, and its extraneous r type may have been added (acceptably) to the manuscript’s Iustices to avoid re-justifying the line with a space type. Greg (1940, p. 147) finds Iustices slightly ludicrous; the reader altered it to Iustisers, which has the support of [2014+30]. Jackson (1983, p. 344): Editors repeat Greg’s pronouncement…, but gloss [Q1(c)’s] Iustisers as judges, which Iustices also means. Is Greg’s point that Iustices is the more concrete word, evoking wig and gown? Only Crook (ed. 1907) understands not the gods but the visible spirits of 2303+15.

2324 nether]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Committed on earth (opposed to above [2323]) (OED, a. 5, quoting this l.).

2324 crimes]
See n. 511.

2325 venge]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Not to be printed ’venge, as in many eds. (OED, v.).

2325–31 Gloster…Gloster]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Albany calls the father by his title of Gloster, while Goneril calls the son my Gloster. The old earl is wholly in the thoughts of the husband, while the new-made earl possesses those of his wife.

2328 letter…answer]
Bransom (1934, p. 148): Regan’s letter probably contained a summary of what had happened to Cornwall and what plans she was making. The answer to it…cannot have contained much that was important. The two sisters were already rivals for Edmund’s affection, and I do not think either confided to the other the secrets of her heart.

2330 One…well]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Gonerill is well pleased that Cornwall is destroyed, who was preparing war against her and her husband, but is afraid of losing Edmund to the widow. Ritson (1783, p. 171): It does not appear that Cornwall was making any hostile preparations against Albany. On the contrary, in act III. scene [vii] Goneril is on a visit to Cornwall, who dispatches her with amicable letters to her husband. She is glad to hear of Cornwall’s death, because, by her sisters, now rendered less difficult to compass, she could possess the whole kingdom. Mason (1785, p. 351): Goneril’s plan was to poison her sister—to marry Edmond—to murder Albany—and to get possession of the whole of the kingdom; as the death of Cornwall facilitated the last part of her scheme she was pleased at it. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Regan, being widowed, was defenceless against her sister’s ambition, unless she married and, finding a still stronger man than Cornwall in Edmund, turned the tables against Gonerill. So Brown (ed. 1976): Her rival is now less able to rule in Britain. In support of Mason’s interpretation Kittredge (ed. 1940) compares 2715 ff., 2906–12, 3027 ff.; but except that Goneril has adulterous intentions towards Edmund, the extent of her plans is unclear at this point. Skillan (ed. 1967): The cause for satisfaction is the fact that reg. will be incriminated as joint perpetrator of the outrage upon glo. In fact that outrage was punishment of a traitor according to the forme of Iustice, an act which men may blame But not controule (2085–7); possibly since Goneril does not know the circumstances, she may have the expectations that Skillan imagines. Bevington (ed. 1980): She is pleased because Edmund is now Duke of Gloucester, and Cornwall, a dangerous rival for the throne, is dead. Whatever her motive to like this well, it is not made explicit.

2331 being]
The pronoun she or her is understood; see n. 1195.

2332 building on my fancie]
Steevens (ed. 1793) compares Cor. 2.1.200 (1113), the Buildings of my Fancie. Collier (ed. 1843): Probably, on in the quartos is to be understood of; see n. 331. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 407): Perhaps the [Q] compositor has anticipated the on in Vpon in the next line. Doran (1931, p. 95) finds on preferable, but only White and Weis retain it: Weis (ed. 1993): The edifice erected on my dreams (of marrying Edmund); White (ed. 1862): F’s substitution of in may be a mere misprint. Or possibly F simply substitutes by analogy with such common idioms as in my mind, in my imagination, etc. The meaning is essentially the same: the building that my fancy has been rearing (Moberly, ed. 1876), my castles in the air (Deighton, ed. 1891). Hunter (ed. 1972) takes fancy to mean not simply fantasy, imagination, but amorous inclinations (OED, sb. 8b).

2332–3 plucke…life]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): If Regan wins Edmund as a husband, Goneril’s plan will obviously fail and she will probably lose her own half of Britain. Munro (ed. 1957): There seems also a reminiscence of Samson’s exploit in the house of the Philistines (Judges xvi, 29, 30). Reminiscence of Judges occurs also at [2964–5]; and the blinding of Gloucester is like that of Samson.

2333 hatefull life]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Future life, made abhorrent…filled with hate (Becket, 1815, 1:167). So Schmidt (ed. 1879), A prolepsis, and Crook (ed. 1907): Proleptically…my life which will afterwards be hateful. Delius apud Koppel (1899, p. 109): Hated by her sister. Brown (ed. 1976): I.e., her married life. Turner (1988, p. 108): Her life is hateful to her now…—odious to her because filled with hatred.

2333 another way]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Really the same as the One way in [2330]. Tovey (ed. 1896): The removal of a rival in power, by the death of Cornwall, is a boon, Cornwall being an obstacle to sole reign with Edmund (Harbage, ed. 1958). Skillan (ed. 1967): The idea of poisoning her sister comes into her mind; if so, the audience could not possibly know it.

2334 tooke]
Virtually all eds. accept F’s tart. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 407): Triple misreading: o/a, o/r, k/t. Schmidt (1875): Sour, harsh. OED (a. 1): Painful, grievous, quoting this l. Only Joseph (ed. 1966) gives an apparently positive sense, Piquant, unattested by OED. Wells (ed. 2000), tooke: Perceived, interpreted.

2334 answer]
See n. 2391.

2334 Exit.]
Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 537): If Oswald does not leave earlier (see [2298]), and if Goneril exits here, then Oswald must go with her. However, the absence of an exit direction in F may be correct: her presence, and her reaction to the Messenger’s next revelation, could be dramatically effective. Most eds. take 2334 to be an exit line, and Albany would not be likely to ignore Goneril completely, or she to remain silent, were she present through his exit at 2347.

2335 Where…sonne]
Bransom (1934, p. 150): Albany could not know of Goneril’s intrigue with Edmund; He did not even know they had made a journey together until [now].…The discreet Oswald had not mentioned this detail.

2337 Come]
Elliptical. Hunter (ed. 1869): He was come.

2339 backe againe]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Upon his return. Wright (ed. 1875): On his way back. Kittredge (ed. 1940): To Gloucester’s castle.

2340 Knowes…wickednesse]
Weis (ed. 1993, p. 11): Albany either knows about Edmund’s treachery or he does not.…He hears the news of it from Oswald and then, shortly after,…he seems to have forgotten that Edmund betrayed his father. But there is no inconsistency. Albany has learned (2273–4) only that Edmund impeached his father for treason, a capital crime. Oswald knows that reuenge (2066) of several kinds was threatened but can not have reported the blinding of Gloucester because he was not present for it. That blinding is the wickednesse that Albany is inquiring about here, not having heard of it before now.

2341 informd]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): See [1969–95, 2065–7].

2343 course]
OED (sb. 9): Opportunity of…moving.

2344–6 Gloster…eyes]
Jennens (ed. 1770) approves Johnson’s marking the speech as an aside: It was not proper the messenger should know his intention of revenging the ill usage of Glo’ster.

2344 I liue]
Deighton (ed. 1891): My object in living shall be.

2345 loue…King]
Albany has heard this much from Oswald; see 2273–6.

2346 reuenge]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Avenge (OED, v. 2).

2347+1–+56 Enter…Exit]
The whole of 4.3 is omitted from F. Pope (ed. 1725): This Scene…is restor’d from the old edition [Q1]; it being manifestly of Shakespear’s writing, and necessary to continue the story of Cordelia, whose behaviour here is most beautifully painted. Johnson (ed. 1765): This scene seems to have been left out only to shorten the play, and is necessary to continue the action. Capell (1783, 1.2:174): The scene…contains many particulars necessary for a right introducing of the actions ensuing. Tieck (ed. 1833, 9:371): The scene contains inconsequential details—the King of France’s landing at Dover and immediate return to France, the mention of Marshal la Far who is never named again—and raises many questions—how Lear has gotten to Dover, why Kent is not with him, how Lear is situated in the town, how he is first seen in Cordelia’s vicinity but later running madly in the fields, etc. To remove these questions and doubts, Sh. himself removed the scene from the play. Knight (ed. 1840, p. 393): The greater part of the scene is purely descriptive; and, exquisite as the description is, particularly in those parts which make us better understand the surpassing loveliness of Cordelia’s character, we cannot avoid believing that the poet sternly resolved to let the effect of this wonderful drama entirely depend upon its action. Delius (1875–6, pp. 144–5): The scene was omitted by the actors because in it nothing is done, but something only talked of. And yet…it must be explained why the King of France, Cordelia’s husband, who would only have been an encumbrance to the farther intentions of the poet, disappears, so to speak, from the play.…It probably appeared right to the poet, to prepare the audience for the re-appearance on the stage of [Cordelia].…The nobleman, whom Kent…had sent to Cordelia, is expected to give an account of the Queen’s reception of himself.…Lastly, the poet [reveals]…a new condition of Lear’s disturbed mind. The madness which begins to wane, is succeeded not by clear consciousness, but a lucid interval, seen in his shame and avoidance of his formerly misunderstood and ill-treated daughter. Idem (1875–6, pp. 215–17): By reporting this information as well as Cordelia’s learning the heart-rending news of her beloved father’s sorrows, Sh. does away with the necessity for several scenes which would else have been requisite for the plot, thereby preserving the swiftness of the dramatic action. Moreover, The attention of the public is throughout concentrated on old Lear himself, and is not disturbed and diverted by the sight of the troubles of others. Koppel (1870, pp. 89–90): Since Cordelia will soon be seen, she does not need to be described here. Hudson (ed. 1879): As it is, both poetically and physiognomically, one of the best in the play, the purpose of the omission could hardly have been other that to shorten the time of representation. Fleay (1891, 2:202): The omission of the scene was probably accidental. Verity (ed. 1897): The extreme beauty of the scene almost forbids the thought that the hand which wrote it erased it.…[It] adds little to the development of the plot. Moriarty (1913, p. 458): Describing Cordelia’s grief here weakens its actual presentation in 4.7. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 228): It is a carpentered scene if ever there was one. It begins with a lame explanation of the non-appearance of the King of France; it goes on to a preparation for the reappearance of Cordelia and it ends with some unconvincing talk about Lear’s shame and Kent’s disguise. I could better believe that Shakespeare cut it than wrote it. There is, certainly, a little life in the description of Cordelia, and a case can be made for so heralding her return to the play. The rest is explanation of what is better left unexplained; and whoever…discovered this—Shakespeare or another—did the play a good service. Dent (ed. 1927): The dramatic tension continues to relax and there is a tendency for the action to drag. Cordelia has not been on the stage since the opening scene of the play. To bring her on without any introduction would have been abrupt. We naturally wish to know how she has received the news of Lear’s ill-treatment.…It is not Shakespeare’s purpose to dwell on Cordelia’s grief; the play concerns itself chiefly with the agony of Lear.…But is is significant that she makes her reappearance just when her sisters are busy with their vile intrigues. We cannot miss the contrast of Sc. iv with Sc. v. Doran (1931, p. 166): The abridgement made in the theater…does not impair the conduct of this portion of the plot and reduces the play by the length of fifty-six lines.…Since, in Act IV, Scene iv, Cordelia herself takes active steps to find her father, the long report of the Gentleman to Kent in the preceding scene of how she received his news can be dispensed with.…Since there has been no previous mention of France’s coming with his troops and since he and his general are never spoken of again, it is unnecessary to say anything about them here. Brooke (ed. 1947): This sentimental and undramatic scene is certainly Shakespeare’s. Its purpose is to reawaken the audience’s sympathy for Cordelia, who…is now about to reappear. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 8): F omits two other passages in which characters describe in highly poetic terms the previous behaviour of other characters who are not on the stage—[1622+1–+8] and [3168+1–+18]. Danby (1949, pp. 132–6, 229) sees the scene, in which Cordelia is described as no one else is in the play, as particularly important for a full understanding of Cordelia as the play’s representative of ideal humanity and beneficent Nature. Walker (1953, p. 52): The scene is intended to cool the air after the emotional tension of the Third Act and Albany’s vehement denunciation of Goneril in iv.ii. Houghton (ed. 1957): May have been dropped in revision perhaps because it proved too sentimental in presentation. Muir (1957, p. 166): At first sight it seems to be a passage which could be omitted without loss. But Cordelia’s part is so very short that her next appearance requires a preparation and build-up. The ineffectiveness of the Cordelia in many modern productions is largely due to the omission of this preparatory scene. Apart from that, the audience needs to be informed of the reason why Lear refuses to see Cordelia. Stroup (1961, pp. 130–1). The scene is exactly parallel in purpose to the build-up for the Fool’s first entrance. Just as the Fool had been characterized and the inception of Lear’s remorse indicated in that scene, so in this one Cordelia is characterized and Lear’s final remorse described. The commingling of Cordelia’s smiles and tears in anticipation of the reconciliation with her father matches the Fool’s wit and grief as described before he comes on. The scene emphasizes the affinity of the two roles and yet, if the two were played by the same actor [see ], the audience must dissociate the person now appearing as Cordelia from the person recently appearing as the Fool. The scene provides just such dissociation.…It is also possible that Shakespeare wrote the scene chiefly to provide for the change of roles. Its intrusion allowed additional time for the change of costume and make-up.…Later, when the two roles were no longer played by one actor but given to two, the scene was no longer necessary either for time or for the introduction of the changed Cordelia. Mack (1965, pp. 8–9): Kent and a Gentleman…wrap Cordelia in a mantle of emblematic speech that is usually lost on a modern audience’s ear and difficult for a modern actor to speak with conviction. We cannot assume that the Elizabethan actor and audience had our kinds of difficulty with the scene. Taylor (1980, p. 30): The narrative prelude…is hardly necessary; it is much more immediately satisfying to hear and see Cordelia than to be told about her. Urkowitz (1980, p. 53): The F cut of 4.3 improves the play by removing a major anomaly: Kent describes how Lear’s soueraigne shame (2347+43) prevents his meeting Cordelia, but in 4.6 and 4.7 Lear mentions neither shame nor previous awareness of Cordelia’s presence in England. Muir (1983, p. 109): [Taylor] does not appreciate the serious disadvantage of omitting the account of Cordelia in this scene. She has been absent from the stage for 2000 lines—the length of some of Shakespeare’s entire plays—and she will have a difficult entrance in the next scene unless the audience has been reminded of her. She is presumably dressed as a soldier and some who have not read the play will wonder who is she? or even who is he? Cordelia’s part, moreover, is the tiniest of any major Shakespearian character—just over 100 lines, and she often speaks in monosyllables. The account of her weeping and Kent’s comment on it help to build up her importance in the scheme of the play.…Urkowitz’s complaints seem to me to be frivolous. It is made clear that it is only in his lucid moments (his better t[une] [2347+40]) that Lear remembers the situation.…His kneeling to Cordelia is the expression of his sovereign shame. Clare (1995, p. 40): May not the very fact that Lear is wandering at large in 4.6 be a consequence in itself of the burning shame that detaines him from his daughter? And might not that shame inform his every action, and much of what he says, when he is at last brought face to face with her in the next scene? Warren (1983, p. 67) infers that one intent of the omission of 4.3 is to alter characterization: This scene is representative of Kent’s function in the Quarto as spokesman for deep human feeling and profound moral concern. The absence of this scene from the Folio diminishes our awareness of Kent and removes this function; the Folio text is not only more rapid and more vigorous, but also more objective and more challenging, because less overtly moral.…The Folio presentation of Cordelia maintains her virtuous qualities but, without Monsieur la Far as general, she is presented as a commander;…she is neither sentimentalized nor glorified in advance by the hyperbolic static imagery of the Gentleman. Though Cordelia, as nominal head of the forces of France, can order a military search party (2356–8), she is never shown as actual commander of the army; see nn. 2347+2–+7, 2349. Mahood (1992, p. 165): Once the unknown boy actor who played Cordelia had said, with simple fervour, All…tears! ([2366–8]), the Gentleman’s metaphors of rain and diamonds and holy water showed themselves to be superfluous to the great moment of Be your tears wet? ([2827]). Bratton (ed. 1987): Many productions…have omitted this scene. Jones (1995, p. 211): [It] is dramatic in the wrong way. Removing it constitutes the most striking single step in the process of purging Lear of romance elements. Brown (ed. 1996): Both style and matter provide a complete contrast to the turbulence of the previous scene.…The lowering of dramatic tension allows a sensitivity in performance and response, and this can reassure or recuperate an audience after so much violence, and before still more follows.
It may be noted that 4.3 provides other information without which the action is somewhat less clear in F. Since Lear was accompanied by Kent when last seen (2056) and was soon joined by some thirty-five knights (2075), an audience may wonder how he comes to be unattended, running and singing madly according to Cordelia’s description in the next scene, and appearing solus in 4.6. The preparatory scene 4.3 explains the absence of such a solicitous and vigilant guardian as Kent. We learn that Lear, out of shame, has declined to be reunited with Cordelia; Kent, thus denied immediate access to the French army, has gone scouting to find news of the present state of things (2347+2, +8, +49). Evidently Lear somehow eludes his knights—easier to do in Kent’s absence. Perhaps one or more of them, among the centurie sent out by Cordelia (see n. 2356), catches up with him in 4.6 (2630). So Clare (1995, p. 42): Without this scene, the audience cannot properly appreciate what Kent is trying to do: that is, to continue what he began at the start of Act 3, using the agency of the Gentleman to reunite Lear and Cordelia. Kent must be certain of Cordelia’s feelings towards her father before he delivers him into her hands.…The need to meet his agent again in 4.3 to confirm that Lear will be safe with his daughter at least, is the only conceivable reason for Kent to have left the king unattended. What he does not anticipate, is that Lear will meanwhile go off again on his own.…Without 4.3, the audience must wonder why Kent should have abandoned Lear, since he exited from 3.6 with the king in his care.
Secondly, the audience here learns that Cordelia has been informed of her sisters’ cruelty, a fact never made explicit except in 4.3, and that she has the means to learn (from Kent) of Lear’s madness and guilt before she sends out a search party for him in 4.4. Finally, Kent here prepares (in 2347+51–+53) for his own appearance and Lear’s reunion with Cordelia in 4.7; whether or not the Gentleman who finds Lear at 2630 is the very Gentleman whom Kent here appoints his proxy attendant (2347+52), obviously the deere cause that will keep Kent yet absent from Lear is his intent to bring about the reunion that we see in 4.7. Without this scene of preparation the audience may wonder why Lear is alone in 4.4 and 4.6, how Cordelia knows that he needs aid, and how Kent, Lear, and Cordelia suddenly appear together in 4.7.
Taylor (op. cit., p. 31) sees the excision of 4.3 as part of a pattern in F of systematically removing verbal and visual reminders of the French presence [cf. n. 2307+1–+6], so that Cordelia seems to lead not an invasion but a rebellion, like Bolingbroke’s or Richmond’s. There is no mention of such a rebellion in the text, and no one has ever before imagined it (though Tate invented one in his adaptation of the play). Nor can there be any doubt that Cordelia, the Queen of France, is leading French forces. We hear of French spies (1633, F), of Gloucester being apprised of French aduantages (1981–2) and receiving letters from France (2109), and of a French army that has landed (2060, 2271), among other clues; and cf. n. 2918. Foakes (1993, pp. 245–6): Taylor’s arguments that the Folio changes a French invasion into a civil war…[are] not borne out either by the text, which in F, in spite of omissions, still emphasizes that Cordelia leads a French army, or by the stage directions calling for the colours of what must be a French army; cf. n. 2349. Foakes nonetheless thinks that references to France have been removed systematically, for another purpose; see . A foreign invasion being of the utmost seriousness, 4.3 shows that this invasion has the full sanction of the King of France, whose moral authority was firmly established in 1.1. Since his presence hereafter is unnecessary and would indeed be a complication in the last Act, he returns without our seeing him, leaving his moral and political sanction behind in his general la Far. Sh. repeats the fact of France’s approval and the purity of his and Cordelia’s motives in 2377–80; rather than hide the French presence, both Q and F emphasize its justness. Halio (ed. 1992, p. 28) restates Taylor’s argument in different terms: References to a French invasion are almost all cut in the Folio so that Cordelia’s appearance in Act 4 seems more like an attempt to restore rightful authority and forestall an inevitable and overwhelming anarchy than mere political aggrandisement. But neither text suggests impending anarchy (despite rumors of friction between the dukes) or a motive of political aggrandizement in France or Cordelia. Knowles (1999, p. 274): Both Q and F repeatedly emphasize that Cordelia’s forces are made up of both French invaders and British sympathizers; the latter include not only Lear’s knights, who join her, and possibly sympathizers with Gloucester whose hearts are moved against Regan and Goneril ([2395–6]), but also the old king’s well armed Friends at Dover (2079), the Traitors, late footed [i.e., afoot] ([2111–12]), and others, whom the rigour of our State | Forc’d to cry out ([2867–8]).…Clearly the forces are of mixed nationality in both texts, and essentially so, since the presence of British supporters in Cordelia’s army allows the audience to sympathize with her efforts more than if she led only a French invasion.
Eccles’s (ed. 1792) reasons for transposing this and the next scene to follow scene 5—to bring together the scenes (4.3, 4.4, 4.6) near Dover, to avoid the supposition that Lear passes a night in the open fields, etc.—are fully represented in Furness (ed. 1880). By Eccles’s reckoning, such an arrangement would make the time of this scene the fourth morning since Lear left Gloucester’s house for Dover. Bransom (1934, p. 152) tentatively approves: Then scenes iii and iv might well open the final movement of the play. This takes place entirely in Kent and is dominated by the battle. Daniel (1877–9, pp. 220–1), on the original sequence of scenes: Some short interval between…[4.2 and 4.3] should probably be supposed; as the news now is that the forces of Albany and Cornwall are afoot ([2347+49–+50)], which was not the case [in 4.2]. Kittredge (ed. 1940): In the interval between this scene and Scene ii Lear has reached Dover ([2347+39]). The interval cannot be long; for Gloucester was being led toward Dover Cliff in iv, 1, and he reaches the cliff in iv, 6. Scenes iv, v, and vi of this Act all occur on one and the same day. On the time for travel to Dover see n. 2078.

2347+1 Gentleman]
Johnson (ed. 1765): The Gentleman whom he had sent in the foregoing act [3.1] with letters to Cordelia; cf. 2347+10. See n. 874. Eccles (ed. 1792): From…their conversation we are led to conclude that this meeting has but a very little while before taken place: Kent appears to be but newly arrived: The Gentleman, though he could not have set out many hours before the king and his party, yet, having travelled…with much greater expedition, may reasonably be thought to have been long enough arrived to have had an opportunity for that conference with Cordelia, of which he here gives an account.

2347+2–+7 reason…necessarie]
Steevens (ed. 1793): The king of France being no longer a necessary personage, it was fit that some pretext for getting rid of him should be formed, before the play was too near advanced towards a conclusion. Decency required that a Monarch should not be silently shuffled into the pack of insignificant characters; and therefore his dismission (which could be effected only by a sudden recall to his own dominions) was to be accounted for before the audience. For this purpose, among others, the present scene was introduced. It is difficult indeed to say what use could have been made of the king, had he appeared at the head of his own armament, and survived the murder of his queen. His conjugal concern on the occasion, might have weakened the effect of Lear’s parental sorrow; and, being an object of respect as well as pity, he would naturally have divided the spectator’s attention, and thereby diminished the consequence of Albany, Edgar, and Kent, whose exemplary virtues deserved to be ultimately placed in the most conspicuous point of view. Moberly (ed. 1876): He would have been a dramatic embarrassment in that defeat of his forces which English patriotism and the stern development of the plot rendered necessary. Verity (ed. 1897): Dramatically, his withdrawal from the action was advisable on several grounds, one being that it adds greatly to the pathos of the situation that Cordelia is left thus alone to do the best she and her army can for Lear. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Did Shakespeare choose to send France back to avoid even the appearance for Lear’s side of any but a disinterested invasion of England by French arms?…Shakespeare’s ending of the play being different from any previous account of Lear, there were difficulties to obviate in his version. Goggin (ed. 1910): The departure of the King of France is due to Shakespeare’s desire to make Cordelia the chief figure in the struggle on behalf of Lear. This could not have been the case had the King remained. Granville-Barker (1927, pp. 148–9 n.): The King of France comes armed with Cordelia to Lear’s rescue, as is natural. Then, by virtue of the clumsiest few lines in the play, he is sent back again. Did Shakespeare originally mean Cordelia to restore her father to his throne as in the old play; but would a French victory in England not have done? It may be; but I cannot think he ever intended Lear to survive.…This decided on…, he would certainly have to get rid of France.…The Folio cuts the clumsy explanation, as if on the principle—and it is an excellent one in the theatre—of: Never explain, never apologise. Thaler (1929, p. 34) Sh. wished to avoid the awkwardness of stressing the appearance of the pelican daughters as the champions of England against the foreigner. Bransom (1934, p. 199) finds France’s conduct both ignominious and unchivalrous, assuming that he abandoned his army and Cordelia when, faced with a united British force, he saw the game was up [and] left the field. Greg (1940, pp. 444–5): There was less shock to patriotism in an invading army led by a British princess than by a French King. But Shakespeare need never have brought France over at all. Besides, the excuse given for his return is childish. France left his kingdom in such a hurry that he altogether forgot about some pressing danger, and had to scurry back to meet it.…We can hardly be intended to take [the public explanation] at its face value. The real reason…was that Cordelia succeeded in persuading her husband to abandon his purpose of wresting a portion of the kingdom for himself and retire to his own land, thus leaving her free to use his army in defence of her father, should the occasion arise. Cordelia is of course not just a British princess but a French Queen, there is no hint of haste or forgetfulness on the part of France (he has thought further on Something left imperfect), and no evidence at all that he wished to wrest a portion of Britain for himself and needed to be dissuaded from that by Cordelia. Levin (1959, p. 96): The King of France had discreetly withdrawn so that his rescue party would not be mistaken for a foreign invasion. Gardner (ed. 1969): The presence of the King of France would be a distraction and a nuisance as the theme develops between Cordelia and Lear. Shakespeare dismisses him. Commentators have…absurdly discuss[ed] Cordelia’s real reason in persuading her husband to return home, leaving her free to use his army in defence of her father. See also n. 2347+1–+56. Perrett (1904, pp. 215–16): In Mirour France stays home, in the 1574 version committing The soldiers to her fathers aged hand but in the 1587 version vnto captaynes euery band (see ). In Holinshed he is an afterthought—Cordeilla with hir husband…fought with their enimies (see ), and in Faerie Queene (see ) he is not mentioned. In Leir 2399 (see ) he takes the lead. Bullough (1973, p. 294): His sudden removal…helps to explain the defeat of his army, and allows Cordelia to devote herself entirely to her father henceforth. Goldring (1983, pp. 148–9): By removing mention of La Far, the Folio place[s] Cordelia at the head of the invading army, rather than in its company. In both Q and F Cordelia as queen of France would, in the absence of her husband, be the nominal leader of an invading French force; she is not, however, its commander in battle. Perrett (1904, p. 217): Cordelia…is at the head of the expedition ([2375–9]) though not in actual command of the troops, citing 2660–1 (Q and F), where an unnamed commander must be leading her army to battle without her, a fact unmentioned by all those who would make her her army’s general. As Edmund is the general of Regan’s forces in battle, and as Mountford was the Gallian king’s lieutenant commander in Leir (see n. 2347+9), so this unnamed commander—presumably La Far in Q, he or his equivalent in F—is general of Cordelia’s powers. Though Cordelia appears (naturally) with some of her troops in 4.4 and 5.2, there is no evidence that she leads and marshals them in battle. See n. 2349. Mahood (1992, p. 159): Perhaps France never reappears because the part was intended for a capable and experienced player who was destined to act another character in later scenes, e.g. (p. 164) the Gentleman; cf. n. 874. Knowles (1999, pp. 279–80): Obviously the King of France has given his moral sanction to the invasion, as both Q and F make clear ([2377–8]), and one would normally expect that as king he would lead the French army into Britain, as happens in Shakespeare’s source, the old King Leir play. [These] few lines in Q…explain his surprising absence, a useful bit of information that is sacrificed when F cuts the whole scene.

2347+4 imperfect]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Incomplete; Bevington (ed. 1980): Unsettled. Only Harbage (ed. 1958): Rift in affairs of state.

2347+5 imports]
Schmidt (1874): To carry with it,…to imply (OED, v. 5a). Craig (ed. 1901): Portends (OED, 5e).

2347+6 feare]
Harbage (ed. 1958): Uneasiness. Just as probably OED (sb. 5a): Ground or reason for alarm.

2347+8 Who]
On the lack of inflection see n. 555.

2347+9 Marshall]
Trisyllabic if the line is verse, as Pope (ed. 1725) indicates by the spelling Mareschal. Contemporary spellings such as mareshall suggest that it was often so pronounced. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 520): Q could easily have omitted a single e, or have adopted its own preferred spelling of a word in what the compositor regarded as prose. OED (sb. 2): One of the chief functionaries of a royal household or court; in the middle ages usually entrusted with the military affairs of his sovereign; (4): A commander, general.

2347+9 la Far]
Steevens (ed. 1793): It is a sign of Sh.’s poverty in French names that here the mareschal of France is given the same name as the soldier (le Fer) in H5 4.4.26 (2407). Perrett (1904, p. 216): Lord Mumford is the Gallian king’s lieutenant, put in command of the fighting in Leir 2403 (see ). So in Lr. the French king is naturally the titular leader of a foreign invasion, but his lieutenant or general commands the army and marshals its movements on the field, even (in both Q and F) in the absence of the king. See n. 2347+2–+7.

2347+10 letters]
On the pl. form for a single letter see n. 875. Like Koppel (1870, p. 90), Bradley (1904, p. 445): But in III. i [1638+5 ff.] he had given to the Gentleman not a letter but a message. Thirlby (MS notes, 1733–47): He might write afterwards. But yt is a poor excuse. Muir (ed. 1952): He may have sent a letter as well as a verbal message, or Shakespeare may have forgotten, or hoped that his audience had. Hunter (ed. 1972): The inconsistency would allow Shakespeare to make better dramatic effects at both points. The written letters may have been in the purse that Kent gave the Gentleman to carry to Cordelia; see n. 1643.

2347+10 pierce]
Schmidt (1875): Transferred sense: To affect, to touch, to move deeply. Craig (ed. 1901) compares 2317 thrild, meaning pierced. Crook (ed. 1907): Prick, provoke; so Harbage (ed. 1958): Goad.

2347+10 to]
OED (prep. 14b): So far…as to cause. Cf. Franz 524.

2347+11 say]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 408): The compositor may have misread sir as sai and set up say.

2347+12–+31 And…eyes]
Traversi (1953, pp. 212–13): His account of Cordelia’s grief is…a remarkable example of the way in which great mastery of verse and language lends significance to dramatic action.…One is struck at once by the tremendous range of imagery at the poet’s disposal. Cordelia’s sorrow is expressed in a whole series of comparisons, few of which have a plain factual connection with the scene and emotions described; sunshine and rain, ripe lip, guests, pearls and diamonds are all connected with one another and with Cordelia less on account of any visual image than because of the sense of value, of richness and fertility which they impart.…Last of all…Cordelia’s tears become holy water dropping from her heavenly eyes and the poetical transformation of natural human emotion into its spiritual distillation is complete. On the contrary, Bransom (1934, p. 153) thinks the Gentleman comically affects a poetic diction of which he is absurdly incapable and that tries Kent’s patience, Mason (1970, p. 215) speaks of the insufferable conceits of the passage, and Rosenberg (1972, p. 257) finds the speech cloying, ornamented with elegant redundancies and artificial antinomies, earnest, sentimental, and a motive for cutting the scene. Goldberg (1974, pp. 98–9), while admiring the beauty and moral power of the passage, concedes that it is rather too sweet: What is left out…[is] her human need (and capacity) to act at all. This patience and sorrow explicitly avoid rage; she is notably still, an image to be contemplated, not the leader of an army. Brown (ed. 1976): The gentleman seems to lose himself in the pleasure of elaborating his story or else tries to defend himself from too much sympathetic feeling by concentrating on artifice. Milward (1985; 1987, p. 188): The description hints a pietà, of the Virgin Mary, mourning the death of Christ. Cf. n. 3216. Adelman (1992, p. 120): A virtual icon of the mater dolorosa.…Only thus redefined as the holy mother can Cordelia safely return to love her father all. The scene mentions no mother, nor identifies Cordelia as one. Jones (1995, p. 209): Static.…Apprehension of life and flux has been trapped in a slightly contorted ingenuity. The stylization is very conscious and just a touch weary, the style of the Late Romances. Lee (1909, p. xli): Possibly Sh. took the cue for this splendid outcry from Ragan’s angry outburst of unfilial heartlessness in Leir 1172 ff. (see ).

2347+12 ample]
See n. 86. Skillan (ed. 1967), less probably: As large as the grief it expressed (OED, a. 4).

2347+12 trild]
Schmidt (1875): To trickle (OED, v.2 1: with a more continuous motion than is expressed by trickle; to purl). Sh.’s only use of the word; Taylor (1925, p. 66) thinks he got it from Florio’s tr. of Montaigne (ed. 1910, 3:128).

2347+13 delicate]
Schmidt (1874): Tender (OED, a. 8). Craig (ed. 1901): Lovely, delightful (OED, 1). Cf. OED (6): Exquisitely or beautifully fine in texture, make, or finish.

2347+13 passion]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Emotion, sorrow.

2347+14 rebell-like]
OED (Rebel sb.1 3) quotes this l. as its first ex. of the compound. Kittredge (ed. 1940): As rebelling against one’s reason or self-control, citing several Shn. analogues. Perrett (1904, p. 242): The rebellion of the nephews [of Cordelia, in several sources]…perhaps supplied the figure, a suggestion Muir (ed. 1952) finds fanciful.

2347+15 it]
Wilson (ed. 1960): I.e. the letter.

2347+16 rage]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): A violent outburst of grief—not, wrath (OED, sb. 6c). Cf. 2370.

2347+16 patience]
See n. 774. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Self-control, comparing 2016. Cf. TN 2.4.114–15 (1003–4): She sate like Patience on a Monument, | Smiling at greefe. The description was a commonplace: see Samuel S. Chew, The Pilgrimage of Life (1962, pp. 120–1). Moberly (ed. 1876): No poet ever ventures, as Shakspere does here, to imagine a grief, the most powerful of which human nature is capable, thus controlled by the tranquil graciousness of a calm nature, which cannot do otherwise than hold its own amid all disturbance, and is incapable of losing its balance; the inward perfection thus giving lovely mildness to the accidental and temporary emotion which still remains entire and undestroyed. Foakes (ed. 1997): Patience and sorrow are personified as female figures.

2347+16 streme]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 408): Misreading of stroue (e for o; m for u—minim error. OED (Strive v. 6): To contend in rivalry, quoting this l. as its first ex. of figurative use.

2347+17 expresse her goodliest]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Lend her the greatest charm. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Give her the most beautiful expression. McCann (ed. 1964): Give her the most appropriate expression. Hunter (ed. 1972): Each seeming to make her more lovely than the other. Lott (ed. 1974): Express her emotion more fittingly…[thus] appear paramount.

2347+18 Sun…teares]
Verity (in Irving & Marshall, ed. 1889) compares AWW 5.3.33–4 (2737–8), For thou maist see a sun-shine, and a haile | In me at once. Steevens (ed. 1778) compares Sidney’s description of the weeping of Philoclea in Arcadia 3.5.1 (see ) as raine in Sunshine; Malone (ed. 1790) cites a similar description in 3.23.1, where Philoclea’s tears amidst smiles are like whẽ a few Aprill drops are scattered by a gentle Zephyrus among fine coloured flowers (ed. Feuillerat, 1:490); and Coyle (1980, p. 140) cites a description of Urania in 1.1.1 (ed. Feuillerat, 1:6), whose eyes combine cherefulnesse with sorrow (but not tears). Sh.’s comparison was proverbial: Tilley L92a, To Laugh and cry at once (like rain in sunshine). Wilson (1970, p. 444) gives exx. antedating Sidney, the earliest of which was cited by Steevens in Reed (ed. 1803). Gardner (ed. 1969): The image was a poetic commonplace. Indeed the whole account of Cordelia’s reaction to the letter is given by the Gentleman in terms of literary and courtly conventions quite different from Shakespeare’s usual style. Lott (ed. 1974): The speeches of the courtly Gentleman are suitable for the use of this style, and their wide range of imagery introduce it newly to the play.

2347+19 like…way]
The ingenuity exercised in emending this phrase is represented in the textual n., in the appendix (), and in the rationales recorded by Furness (ed. 1880). The text as it stands was given an explanation by Boaden (apud Singer, ed. 1826) that most eds. now accept: Cordelia’s smiles and tears were like the conjunction of sunshine and rain, in a better way or manner. Eds. disagree, however, in what this better way consists. Boaden’s answer is, Why simply in the smiles seeming unconscious of the tears; whereas the sunshine has a watery look through the falling drops of rain.…The better way of charity is that the right hand should not know what the left hand giveth. White (ed. 1862) takes a better way as absolute rather than comparative, as an epithet implying eminence…to which, in kind, her emotional struggle is likened.
