Hudson (ed. 1871) keeps the same words but puts a stop after like; the rest of the phrase then introduces a new thought: to express it…in better words, those happy smilets, &c.; likewise Jespersen (1937, p. 271), and thus Brisman (1972, p. 206): The better way is one of organized innocence described in the following lines, not the strife and contraries implied by the previous one. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Her mingled smiles and tears expressed her feelings in a better way than either patience or sorrow could do separately.…[Moreover], her emotion vented itself in nothing like rage, but (a better way) in gentle smiles and tears. Moberly (ed. 1876): The meaning here may be a better course of nature, something better than nature knows. Perring (1885, pp. 331–2): Her smiles and tears were simultaneous, but they were not intermingled, as in the natural phenomenon.…There was no cloud, no shade, no dampness in her beautiful sunshine. Similarly Verity (ed. 1897): Only in a better, more beautiful manner, because the smiles were not marred by the tears as the sunshine by the rain. Lee (ed. 1908): Had an effect of greater beauty than even the concurrence of sunshine and rain could produce. Hunter (ed. 1972): Like may mean were like one another (each resembled the other and in this relationship revealed a better way), or perhaps were like a vision of a way to Heaven. Halio (ed. 1973): Were like a better way of expressing conflicting attitudes. Foakes (ed. 1997): To cry with one eye and laugh with the other was proverbially associated with dissimulation…; Cordelia’s little smiles (smilets) and tears were like sunshine and rain, but in a better sense, neither being aware of the other, and both being good. There is no hint here, of course, of dissimulation, or of crying and laughing with separate eyes.
As for the emendations, Steevens (ed. 1778) explains better day as the best day,…most favourable to the productions of the earth…[because] there is a due admixture of rain and sunshine. Hunter (ed. 1869): Scil. in prospect, or breaking through. Tollet (in Steevens, ed. 1778): Whether better day or May, sunshine prevailed over rain.

2347+19 smilets]
Jennens (ed. 1770): As the smiles are to play, he personifies them by infants, calling them smilets, or young smiles. Clarkes (ed. 1868): To denote the but slight smiles that patience could struggle to muster (OED, quoting this l. as its second ex.).

2347+20 ripe]
Schmidt (1875): Brought to perfection in growth, mature. Craig (ed. 1901): Probably red. We might compare [VA 1103], ripe-red cherries,…also [MND 3.2.139–40 (1164), AYL 3.5.120–1 (1894–5)]. But could it mean weeping-ripe, ready to weep? Compare [LLL 5.2.274 (2193)]; if so, it points to the appearance of a lip struggling against tears. Onions (1911): Red and full. Sidney’s descriptions of both Philoclea (in 3.5; see n. 2347+18 and ) and Urania (1.1.1; ed. Feuillerat, 1:6) compare lips to cherries, a commonplace: see Tilley C277. Houghton (ed. 1957): Probably sunshine and rain, suggesting good crops, prompted the adjective ripe.

2347+20 seeme]
Craig (ed. 1901), on Pope’s seem’d (see textual n.): Coming after play’d [and before were and parted], it is most probably right. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 409): Q may have a misreading of d as e. Muir (ed. 1952): Though Shakespeare elsewhere drops into the historic present.

2347+21 which]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Who—i.e., the guests in her eyes, the tears. See n. 744+4, and cf. Abbott (§266): When the antecedent is personal and plural, which is generally preferred to who.

2347+21 parted]
Lott (ed. 1974): Departed, continuing the idea of…guests.

2347+22–+25 As…question]
Though many eds. follow Q’s line division, it results in a short first line and a long last one (2347+24–+25) and may be here, as often elsewhere, incorrect. Steevens’s (ed. 1793) suggestion, emending dropt to dropping, hardly improves the meter of the first line. Capell’s simple adjustment (see textual n.) makes three regular lines if, as Guest (1882, p. 287) proposes, a cesura after briefe serves as an unaccented syllable.

2347+22 pearles…dropt]
Steevens (ed. 1793): The idea might have been taken from the ornaments of the ancient carcanet or necklace, which frequently consisted of table diamonds with pearls appended to them, or, in the jewelers’ phrase, dropping from them. Pendants for the ear are still called—drops [OED, sb. 10a]. So Hunter (ed. 1869), dropp’d: Suspended; the sense is figurative, not attested by OED. Steevens (ed. 1778) finds the comparison of tears with pearls in Middleton’s Game at Chess 1.1.78–80, and Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) in Sidney’s description of Philoclea in Bk. 4 of the Arcadia (ed. Feuillerat, 2:111): her teares…followed still one another like a precious rope of pearle. Kittredge (ed. 1940): We should remember that it is a courtly gentleman who is speaking, and that elegant language was expected of courtiers. Shakespeare often calls tears pearls, as in Lucrece, 1213, 1553; Two Gentlemen, [3.1.226 (1294)]. Constance styles Prince Arthur’s tears heaven-moving pearls and crystal beads (King John, [2.1.169, 171 (471, 473)]). Diamonds for eyes, however, is (fortunately) less common; but Falstaff protests to Mistress Ford, I see how thine eye would emulate the diamond (Merry Wives, [3.3.55 (1398)]). Cf. also [Glapthorne’s?] Revenge for Honour [ca. 1640; in Chapman’s Tragedies, ed. Parrott, 5.2.58–60]: In tears those eyes cast forth a greater lustre, | Then sparkling rocks of Diamonds inclos’d | In swelling seas of Pearl.

2347+23 raritie]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Something choice and excellent (OED, 4). Cf. Son. 60.11. Hunter (ed. 1972): Precious as pearls and diamonds—or the beauty of Cordelia in her patience.

2347+24 If…it]
Crook (ed. 1907): If everyone could make it so becoming. Muir & Danby (1950, p. 50): In Sidney’s Arcadia 3.5.2 (see ) Philoclea’s eies are able to make tears comely.

2347+25 verball]
Warburton (ed. 1747), justifying his emendation quest: Why, what kind of question could she make but verbal? Johnson (ed. 1765): Such pleonasms are common. Steevens (ed. 1773): By words as well as by the foregoing external testimonies of sorrow, viz. her tears and looks. Gardner (ed. 1969): Kent’s stilted language in this scene is abnormal, and reflects the official, courtly relationship between the two speakers.…[It] changes as he comes to speak of Lear, 2347+39 ff.

2347+25 question]
Heath (1765, p. 345): Not…enquiry, but comment or reflection (OED, sb. 2: Talk, discourse). Warburton’s (ed. 1747) Quest = complaint is not attested in OED.

2347+26 heau’d]
Craig (ed. 1901): Uttered with effort (OED, v. 8, quoting AYL 2.1.36 [643] and this l. as its first two exx.). Joseph (ed. 1966): The name, like the sigh, must be heaved up because it presses on the heart causing physical and psychological malaise. Hunter (ed. 1972): With heart in the next line, should remind us of [97–8].…Cordelia is throughout the play characterized by a lack of fluent rhetoric.

2347+28 shame of Ladies]
Greg (1940, p. 396) compares Perillus’s reproof to Gonerill in Leir 2581: shame vnto thy sexe; see .

2347+29 Kent]
Capell (1783, 1.2.177) considered this word a speech prefix and the next two words a sarcasm, believing Any mention of Kent…was not probable…and most unfit for this place. But Cordelia is reacting to a message from Kent and remarking on his continuing care for Lear.

2347+30 Let…shooke]
The line, says Greg (1940, p. 75), is apparently indented, but actually some letters probably dropped out of the line (most likely after be where there is a rather wide gap) and the first four words shifted to the right, leaving a gap at the beginning, into which the K from the line above and the T from the line below partially shifted. Turner (1987, privately): If a space quad to the right of the line of type got pulled or dropped, I can see how the whole might shift to the right, but I don’t understand how part of it could and the gap still be present at the beginning.…Could Greg be right that letters were pulled? What letters? Does the inking to the right of the line mean anything? Since speech prefixes were usually written in the margin, the compositor almost certainly did not originally set Kent as a prefix, as the comma after it also indicates; but possibly in setting up the page he momentarily was misled to think so by all the other Kent prefixes nearby, started to indent it and/or the line below, realized his error, and pushed the line back to the margin but not quite tightly enough, hanging this line up on the initial letters above and below it which he had disturbed in first moving the line(s). The raised quads or furniture at the end of the line may be a consequence of such temporary shifting of the line.

2347+30 Let…beleeft]
OED (Believe v.) records the participle beleft. Steevens (ed. 1773): Let not such a thing as pity be supposed to exist. Clarkes (ed. 1868): In or to exist is here elliptically understood after believ’d. Some eds. find such a sentiment inappropriate to Cordelia, especially after hearing of Kent’s services to Lear, and propose other senses or else emendations. The reason is not compelling, since believe may mean not believe to exist but rather trust in, rely on or expect (OED, 1b, 4), making acceptable sense. So Tovey (ed. 1896): May mean either, (1) If there was no pity for him, then pity must not be trusted any more; or, (2) So sad a tale is beyond belief. Kelcy (1932, p. 369): Let not such a pitiful thing as my father’s being shut out in the tempest be believed; possibly th between Let and pity is absorbed in the final sound of Let. Lott (ed. 1974): Let the pity <of the bringer of this report> not be believed (because he must surely have been exaggerating). Harbage (ed. 1958), followed by others: Let it for pity (?)—a sense not clearly implied; but Hoeniger (ed. 1968) so emends (see textual n.). Pope (ed. 1725) and Jennens (ed. 1770) (see textual n.) assume that beleeft is a contraction of believe it. Brooke (ed. 1947), agreeing: The repetition of be is probably accidental. Wilson (ed. 1960): Pope’s text gives better verse and a meaning apter to the context. Poss. Q copy read not beleeft (= not believe it) and the be was added in proof. Wells & Taylor (1987, pp. 520–1) defend their emendation pietie (= filial duty) on the grounds that a type may have been pulled (see prev. n.) or pietie may have been misread as pittie; they also propose that the phrase may be a question rather than an exclamation—What, not to let piety be heeded?; but believe does not mean heed.

2347+30 there]
Muir (ed. 1952): Pope’s emendation, then, is open to the objection that it weakens the force of the same word two lines later. There means at that point. The Q compositor or the MS he was working from omitted a stop before the word, while adding an unneeded one at the end of the line.

2347+30 shooke]
Dey (1903, p. 151): The word will have a peculiar significance for those familiar with the ceremony of Asperges at High Mass, in which the priest sprinkles members of the congregation with holy water. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 521): This could mean that she sprinkled tears from her eyes; or that she brusquely dislodged or removed or cast out the tears from them…by shaking her head, or wiping her eyes, preferring the latter. See the next n.

2347+31 holy water]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Water blessed by a priest for use in Catholic ritual. Fripp (1938, p. 666): A touch of the Old Faith amid the New. Elton (1966, p. 84 n.), comparing 1655, suspects that many in the audience would react ambivalently to this mention of a Catholic superstition often alluded to disparagingly in the source, Harsnett’s Declaration (e.g., 1603, ch. 18, Of the dreadfull power of holy water…, pp. 98–104). But Muir (ed. 1952): The sprinkling of the holy water seems to consecrate the clamour. Foakes (1993, p. 201): F omits the elaborate establishment of a quasi-religious aura about Cordelia, though she echoes Christ’s words at 2376–7.

2347+31 heauenly eyes]
Andrews (1984, p. 205) compares a description of Philoclea in Sidney’s Arcadia 3.3.4 (ed. Feuillerat, 1:369): her teares rained downe from her heauenly eyes.

2347+32 clamour…her]
Since her is extrametrical and requires clamour to mean tears, most eds. assume it is erroneous. Malone (ed. 1790): I have no doubt that the word her was inserted by the compositor’s eye glancing on the middle of the preceding line.…It may be observed that the metre is complete without [it]. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 521): It might also result from misreading: her and then are readily confused. It is also possible that the word was transposed, the MS reading her clamour. Halio (ed. 1994): Blayney retains her, rejecting a trivial metrical regularisation for the sake of greater clarity. If her is retained as in Q, clamour must be the subject of moystened; if her is omitted, clamour is either part of an absolute or adjectival phrase or the object of moystened. The following readings have been proposed in each case:
(1)As subject. Johnson (ed. 1765): That is, her outcries were accompanied with tears. Delius (ed. 1854) takes moystened as intransitive and justifies her as an ethical dative. Page (ed. 1889) accepts a literal meaning: Her tears…fell on her and bedewed her person. Similarly Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Her outcry having relieved her, i.e. clamour having moystened her, away she started. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 409) finds such readings too crude to be Shakespearian, and rightly points out that clamour refers not to Cordelia’s tears but to her outcries (expostulations, or outbursts of grief; cf. 3168+4) in 2347+28–+30. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 521) also object to an unfortunately ridiculous image. Skillan (ed. 1967) takes moystened metaphorically and omits her: Clamour thereby became softened, modified, (perhaps) melted away,…yielded to tears. Similarly Gardner (ed. 1969): Her anguish dissolved in tears.
(2)As part of a phrase. Heath (1765, p. 345) understands an ablative absolute, clamour being moystened: Cordelia had at first broke out into exclamations;…then followed the tears, with which when she had moistened these exclamations…she retired to the farther indulgence of her grief in private. Walker (1860, 1:156–7), followed by Leo (1880, p. 62), hyphenates to make a compound adjective modifying eyes: heavenly,…And clamour-moisten’d. Sisson (1956, 2:240): The original [word] order is common enough in such highly-wrought poetic language as that of the Gentleman here. White (ed. 1862) adopts the hyphen but applies the compound to she in she started (which requires a change of punctuation: And, clamour-moisten’d, then): And with her cheeks wet with her outburst of sorrow, away she started. Hudson (ed. 1871), adopting White’s text: Meaning…her voice being smothered with weeping [ed. 1879: meaning, apparently, that she wept aloud], or her crying drenched with tears. Wright (ed. 1875) objects that clamour is the outcry and not the tears, conceding that perhaps the clamour is the indirect cause of the tears. Similarly Verity (ed. 1897): Like the original Q reading, this makes clamour (the expression of grief) equivalent to grief itself. Bevington (ed. 1980): Her outcry of grief assuaged by tears.
(3)As object. Capell (1783, 1.2:177): Cordelia [may] be said…to moisten them [i.e., her previous exclamations] with tears that follow’d them instantly; or…a grief ready to burst out into clamour…she moisten’d, allay’d by moist’ning, with the tears that then broke from her, as winds are by rain. The idea here that tears succeeded clamor is emphasized by Moberly (ed. 1876), Verity (ed. 1897), Kittredge (ed. 1940), and Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 409), among others. Kittredge says, The Gentleman outdoes himself in this phrase, but the meaning is clear enough, comparing Tmp. 2.1.127–8 (799–800), your eye, | Who hath cause to wet the greefe on’t. More usually the idea here that tears qualify the clamor is adopted: for Capell’s clamour…allay’d other eds. substitute Gave to her outcries a weeping or tearful tone (Hunter, ed. 1869), her voice…became softer Evans (ed. 1898), her emotion calmed by a flood of tears (Craig, ed. 1901; Muir, ed. 1952), soothed her cries of grief in tears (Crook, ed. 1907), allayed her utterance (Lee, ed. 1908), drowned her voice (Darton, ed. 1928), mixed, and thus muted, lamentation with tears (Harbage, ed. 1958), and even sanctified her resentment by moistening the clamour with…holy water (Dey, 1903, p. 151).
As for emendations: Warburton (ed. 1747) explains clamour-motion’d: Provok’d to a loud expression of her sorrow, which drives her from company. Brooke (ed. 1947), on clamor-moisten’d hair: In Shakespeare ladies’ tresses suffer remarkably when they weep, citing Jn. 3.4.61 ff. (1445 ff.). Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 521), averring that moistened is unfortunately ridiculous and grotesquely suggests spitting, prefer Stone’s (1980, p. 184) paleographically plausible maystered as indicating an energetic effort followed by what they imagine to be her equally energetic departure, comparing Ado 3.2.28 (1234), master a griefe. Both the Oxford eds. (1986 Q; Wells, ed. 2000) and Foakes (ed. 1997) adopt the emendation.

2347+33 It is]
Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) justify their interrogative Is it as making Kent’s speech tall[y] particularly well with Lear’s query concerning the cause in Nature [2034–5].

2347+34 stars]
Hudson (ed. 1879): As Cordelia and her sisters had the same father and mother, Kent can only account for the difference in them by the astrological effects of spherical predominance. Verity (ed. 1897): Kent, old-fashioned like Gloucester, believes in their influence. Cf. 433 ff., 451, 1182. Elton (1966, p. 291) cites a discussion of the question in Palingenius’s Zodiake of Life (1576, p. 92).

2347+34 gouerne]
On the omission of the relative see n. 589.

2347+34 conditions]
See n. 322. Joseph (ed. 1966, p. 55): Our physical make-up, the physical humours which determine temperament, which incline, but do not determine, the will. Foakes (ed. 1997): Personal qualities, natures.

2347+35 selfe]
See n. 74.

2347+35 mate and make]
Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Husband and wife; an old turn of phrase, spoiled by the reading of the Second Quarto [mate and mate], perpetuated in the text ever since Pope adopted it. OED (Make sb.1 5): Husband or wife.

2347+36 spoke]
Abbott (§347): Simple past [is used] for complete present with since, &c. Cf. Franz §635.

2347+37 King]
Thirlby (MS notes, 1733–47): Of France.

2347+37 No, since]
Thirlby (MS notes, 1733–47): Why is this mention’d?—a question no commentator has ever addressed. The line establishes that France returned before Cordelia was moved to weep at the Gentleman’s news of Lear’s mistreatment; but in the next scene we hear that he was (previously) swayed by her mourning…teares (2378) to approve her British campaign. What could have occasioned those tears, and when? On this question the text is silent.

2347+39 towne]
From their silence it appears that most eds. assume the town to be Dover; but Cordelia sends a search party for Lear into the fields (2356–7). Horsman (ed. 1973): A group of farm buildings or a hamlet.…Lear is found in the fields, between the two armies. Brown (ed. 1976): Village, estate.

2347+40 some time]
On the form see n. 1270.

2347+40 better tune]
Craig (ed. 1901): Saner intervals, comparing 2765 and Ham. 3.1.158 (1814), iangled out of time [F: tune]. OED (sb. 5): Frame of mind, quoting this l. The metaphor is of a well-tuned instrument.

2347+43–+47 A…Cordelia]
Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): The superior grandeur and appeal to honor and sympathy of Shakespeare’s Lear over all preceding Lears are here obvious. Other Lears sought Cordelia. Bullough (1973, p. 295), however: As in Leir [1991 ff.] (Sc. 23), the old King feels a sovereign shame. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 149 n.): A dramatically feeble…excuse for the delay in handing Lear over to his daughter’s care and none for the devoted Kent letting the distracted old man out of his sight to roam the fields crowned with wild flowers. But Kent is on a scouting expedition: see n. 2347+1–+56. Lott (ed. 1974): The mood in common between Kent and the Gentleman is mirrored in the similarity of their poetic styles. Warren (1983, p. 66): Kent is the means by which the audience of the Quarto learns of the state of Lear’s mind in what must be a brief moment of lucidity upon arrival at Dover; he presents a Lear…grappling with the moral consequences of those earlier acts of his that sting his mind. See n. 2347+1–+56 for other views.

2347+43 A…vnkindnes]
Guest (1882, p. 243) considers the line a loose and slovenly pentameter, in which -bows him his is elided without accent.

2347+43 soueraigne]
Schmidt (1875): Supreme, paramount. Page (ed. 1889): Over-ruling, o’er-mastering. Tovey (ed. 1896): Prevailing over every other emotion, comparing Ant. 5.1.41 (3158). Joseph (ed. 1966): Also curative, medicinal (OED, adj. 3).

2347+43 elbows]
The most general meaning of restrains (Rann, ed. 1794) is clear enough, but whether the figurative meaning implies nudging, or thrusting, or standing close, is not clear. Badham (1856, p. 282): A more incongruous figure of speech…it would be difficult to imagine. Sovereigns elbow no one. Delius (ed. 1854): Allows him no rest. Schmidt (1874): To haunt, to harass. Idem (ed. 1879): Perhaps…pushes him aside. Wright (ed. 1875): Stands at his elbow and reminds him of the past. Moberly (ed. 1876): Seems to buffet him. Hudson (ed. 1881): Digs him in the side. Verity (ed. 1897): Perhaps urges him on, i.e. in his obstinate course…of not seeing Cordelia. OED (v. 1): To thrust with the elbow; to jostle; also fig., quoting this l. as its first ex. Craig (ed. 1901): Forcibly thrusts him back from her breast. Lee (ed. 1908): Thrusts him aside (from a reconciliation), comparing 2347+47. Kittredge (ed. 1940) compares Marlowe’s Edward II 5.1.33, sorrow at my elbow still attends.

2347+43 vnkindnes]
See n. 132.

2347+44 stript]
Schmidt (1875): Metaphorically…to take away (OED, v.1 2a, quoting this l.).

2347+44 benediction]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Cf. 289–90.

2347+44 turnd]
Craig (ed. 1901): Turned out, expelled (OED, v. 25).

2347+45 forraine casualties]
Moberly (ed. 1876): The chances of foreign life.

2347+45 deare rights]
See n. 785. Deighton (ed. 1891): The inheritance which was justly hers, was precious to her.

2347+46 dog-harted]
Schmidt (1874): Unfeeling, inhuman; pitiless. Craig (ed. 1901): Probably referring to the wild savage dog.…Shakespeare rarely, if ever, says anything good of the dog. Joseph (ed. 1966): A reference to the way in which Goneril and Regan flattered Lear till he gave them what they wanted, whereupon they bit the hand that fed them and fell to snarling among themselves.

2347+47 burning shame]
OED (Burning ppl. a. 1d): Fig. In burning shame…the prevailing idea is now perhaps flagrant, flaming, conspicuous; but there is often a mixture of notions derived from other senses, such as these of branding, stigmatizing; torturing as an inward fire; causing the cheeks to glow, etc., quoting this l. as its first ex.

2347+49 powers]
See n. 1638+1. Here as at 2374 it is not immediately clear if the armies are joint or separate. Greg (1940, p. 438 n.), however: Regan has not yet set out in [4.5; see 2401].

2347+50 Tis so]
Since the idiom seems nonsensically to confirm the negative in Kent’s question, eds. are at pains to explain it otherwise. Johnson (ed. 1765): So it is that they are on foot. Malone (ed. 1790): I have heard of them; they do not exist in report only; they are actually on foot. So Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Yes indeed (affirmative following a negative). Eccles (ed. 1792): So as you have heard; so as was reported. Clarkes (ed. 1868): As was rumoured, it is just as we expected. Harbage (ed. 1958): I have to this extent. Neither speaker has heard of Cornwall’s death.

2347+50 a foote]
Schmidt (1874): In motion, in action. Craig (ed. 1901): In arms, out in the field.

2347+52 deere cause]
See n. 1628. Malone (ed. 1790): Important business. Budd (ed. 1935): Never revealed. Edwards (ed. 1975): The reconciliation of Lear and Cordelia; he will reveal himself to Lear only when the work is done. Since Kent is still under sentence of exile he may think that he must maintain his disguise, at least awhile. Later he is equally vague about a different intent; see n. 2757. Hunter (ed. 1972): The real reason is Shakespeare’s desire to keep the revelation of Kent’s identity till the last scene. Smidt (1990, p. 132) imagines an earlier version in which Edgar, not Kent, is the unknown challenger of Edmund. Foakes (ed. 1997): Kent thus parallels Edgar.

2347+53 concealement]
OED (sb. 4b) quotes this l. as its first ex.

2347+54 When…knowne]
Eccles (ed. 1792) notes that Cordelia must not have revealed Kent’s true identity to the Gentleman, as in 1644–6 Kent had expected she would do. Cf. 2843+6, where the Gentleman is still in the dark.

2347+54 aright]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): In my true character.

2347+55 Lending…acquaintance]
Muir (ed. 1952): For having been acquainted with me. Joseph (ed. 1966): Becoming temporarily acquainted with me (but not in my real person).

2348 <Scena Tertia>]
The fourth scene in Q and most eds., the third in F because the previous Q scene is omitted. Grey (1754, 2:112–13): This scene should have been lain in France, as in Geoffrey of Monmouth 2.12 (see ), Milton’s History of England [ed. Krapp, 1932, 10:20] 1.19–20, etc. Adams (1948, p. 329): This brief scene [is] not specifically localized but by clear implication [is] placed near Dover. See n. 2374. Daniel (1877–9, p. 221): Possibly the day after 4.3: Lear has been met in the fields…and Cordelia sends out in search of him. The news is that The British…hitherward [2374]. See also n. 2347+1–+56. Smith (ed. 1902): This scene…does not help on the action of the drama; but it reintroduces Cordelia, who has not appeared since the very first scene. Goggin (ed. 1910): Impressing on us her anxiety for Lear’s recovery,…Shakespeare continues to show himself tender of patriotic sentiment, citing 2376–80. Bransom (1934, p. 153): I suggest…that in an acting version we drop the scene, which is in Shakespeare’s worst manner. Besides the fact that all the information about Lear and the armies is perfectly conveyed to us in scenes vi and vii, The great dramatic mistake is to introduce Cordelia here, and to stuff her mouth with such third-rate lines and sentiments. It takes away from the tremendous effect of her reappearance in scene vii, and We no longer need her apology to-day for invading her native land. Hunter (ed. 1972): The fertile English landscape is used to evoke both the ungoverned wildness of the King (in preparation for IV.6) and the natural powers of restoration that Cordelia can call up. Wells (ed. 2000): An abrupt shift from wintry night to high summer (observed by Sohmer, 1999, §13) has sometimes been reflected in the staging, with ironical effect.

2349 Enter]
F adds with Drum and Colours. Doran (1931, pp. 83–4): Evidently particular properties which the prompter has ready to be carried in whenever the soldiers go across the stage. Just as probably they mean (what amounts in an entrance to the same thing) A drummer and a soldier carrying a flag (Harrison, ed. 1948). Dessen & Thomson (1999): These items indicate readiness for battle and are part of a show of power. Adams (1948, p. 329): In the Globe, Drum-and-colors processions always enter the platform. Bratton (ed. 1987): The change is part of the folio text’s clarification of the conduct of the war, stressing the fact that Cordelia heads these troops. The F addition does not necessarily suggest a different staging from that originally intended in Q. These are kinds of explicit detail added to stage directions in playhouse manuscripts so that the book-holder might adequately prepare his actors for their entrances. Cf. 2845, 2864, 2918, 2938–9. To Doran their addition in F where they are never mentioned in Q indicates the hand of the prompter. Nor does the presence of a color-guard necessarily imply that Cordelia heads these troops as their military commander; see n. 2347+2–+7. Indeed, Bratton records performances in which she appears here as Queen of France and escorted by French knights (Charles Kean, 1858), in a brilliantly white gown and rich blue surcote (Byam Shaw, 1959), in contrast to her less successful appearance in forbidding battledress (in Stratford, 1976). Rosenberg (1972, p. 259): Her tenderness in the midst of steel is one of the bittersweet dialectics here. Though some critics assert that F systematically removes signs that the invaders are French (see nn. 2307+1–+6, 2347+1–+56), here and at 2918 F adds specific evidence of their nationality, as Honigmann (1990, p. 59) points out. So Foakes (1993, p. 107): The Colours shown…would presumably be those of France, perhaps echoing a display of a French coat of arms or banner when the King of France enters in the opening scene. Cf. Leir 2465, Now march our ensignes on the Brittish earth, and cf. 2307+3 (Q), France spreds his banners in our noystles land. Banners were used to identify and rally troops in battle; here and at 2918 an army led by a French queen would show a French flag or insignia, while at 2938 Edmund’s Colours would be British. Hodges (1999, p. 82): The playhouse property room would in time have built up a collection of such heraldic devices…of possibly frequent use, such as the lions of England or the lilies of France—with some other ordinary flags. Foakes (ed. 1997): She enters in soldierly fashion. From the evidence of the SD, however, one can say only that she enters with soldiers.

2349 Cordelia]
Since in F the reference to Marshall la Far (2347+9) is omitted, and the King of France is not present, Cordelia is presumptive leader of the French party, though not its commander in battle; see n. 2347+2–+7. Urkowitz (1980, p. 94) finds this a significant difference from Q: Whether indeed she is the leader is immaterial. According to the Folio text only Cordelia acts like a leader. Since la Far never appears in either text, and as Queen of France Cordelia would be his superior in any case, there is no practical difference.

2349–50 Doctor and others]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 107): The last two words seem too vague for a prompt-book. (Ibid., p. 409): In F the Doctor is cut out and his part given to a Gentleman. Cf. IV vii [2744]. F’s Gentlemen in this S.D. may be an error for Gentleman. Though the others in Q would almost certainly be members of Cordelia’s forces, Taylor (1980, pp. 29–30), like Urkowitz (1980, pp. 40–1, 94), lists F’s Souldiours among significant differences from Q: Nothing in the Quarto text suggests that Cordelia’s others are an army; the speeches decidedly suggest a more intimate scene.…The Quarto text thus seems to envision Cordelia in IV.iv in the company of several nondescript attendants; in the Folio she enters at the head of an army. Knowles (1999, pp. 272–3): The others attending Cordelia in or near the camp of her invading army would certainly be soldiers, officers, or other attendants [including perhaps some of Lear’s knights who have joined her army] suitable for military duty. Evidently at least one of them is an officer, since within a few lines Cordelia directs him to issue a military order that a hundred soldiers be sent to search for Lear. Moreover, the Q and F scenes must be equally intimate, since the number of speaking parts is identical and their spoken lines are substantially the same, and there is no indication anywhere that there are fewer of Q’s others on stage than of F’s Souldiers. Both texts could equally indicate an army.…There is no reason to think that the Q and F scenes are different in any essential way; Q’s stage direction is simply that of an author’s draft, F’s is that of a theatrical prompt-book. Taylor adds, Nor does the Doctor’s presence fit a military scene, for though we easily associate surgeons with armies, Shakespeare and his contemporaries did not, usually restricting their doctors [distinguished on stage by…conventional red costume: Philip C. Kolin, The Elizabethan Stage Doctor (Salzburg, 1975 [p. 12])] to attendance upon royalty. Perhaps partly or wholly for this reason, the Folio throughout turns the Quarto’s Doctor into the vaguer, less anomalous Gentleman. C. G. Cruickshank, Elizabeth’s Army (1946; 2nd ed. 1966, p. 174), cited by Taylor, in fact records that historically English armies travelled with both physicians (for the king) and surgeons (for the soldiers). In 2 Tamburlaine 2.4 and 5.3, Zenocrate and Tamburlaine are attended by several Physitians (i.e., doctors, not surgeons), as is the title character in Fletcher’s The Humorous Lieutenant (1619), 3.5. In Q the Doctor does undeniably attend on royalty, Cordelia and Lear, in a military scene; Sh. clearly saw no anomaly in that, and the change in F may have been made for other reasons: see n. 2744 and .

2351 euen now]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Only a short time ago.

2352 vent sea]
Virtually all eds. accept F’s vext Sea. Craig (ed. 1901): Agitated by the wind. The comparison is proverbial: Tilley S170 and Dent (1981) cite other Shn. uses of it. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 409): The Q reading does not make sense and it is not likely to be an actor’s or compositor’s substitution.…A misreading of x as n hardly seems likely. We may have to do with foul case. Taylor (1983, p. 458): But ract (= racked) presumes an easy misreading in Q, makes good sense, and continues the imagery of tortured bodies. OED does not recognize such a participle, and Cordelia’s empathy is with Lear, not the sea.

2352 singing aloud]
Sternfeld (1963, pp. 166–7): Lear’s Fool sang for him; now in madness arrogant Lear has become wise enough to play the fool, with wise laughter, gaiety and humanity. Butler (1989, p. 397 n.): This singing of mad folks is one of the more terrifying sound effects of Jacobean drama. Proudfoot (1992, pp. xxiii, xxviii) detects echoes of both Ophelia’s and Lear’s in Tom a Lincoln 2647–55.

2353–5 ranke…weedes]
Steevens (ed. 1773) compares the description of weeds in untilled France in H5 5.2.44–53, in which several of the same rank weeds are named. Prothero (1916, 1:358–60) takes both passages to reflect the deterioration of English farming in the early part of the 16th c. Farren (1833, p. 74): These plants are all wild and uncultivated; of bitter, biting, poisonous, pungent, lurid, distracting properties. Thus Lear’s crown is admirably descriptive or emblematic of the sources and variety of the disease under which he labours. Blunden (1929; 1936, p. 334): They carry a meaning beyond that of mere picturesque detail of madness. They are his crown of thorns. Knights (1956, p. 214) compares the medicinal plants (2364–8) to illustrate Cordelia’s and Sh.’s balanced attitude towards Nature. Gardner (ed. 1969): Plants…with narcotic properties, and used in the main in the treatment of mental disorder. The description gives Lear an identity typical of madness on the contemporary stage. Righter (1962, p. 133): Lear assumes the traditional crown of flowers worn by the Whitsun ruler, the mock king, and in this guise delivers to an imaginary kingdom fantastic edicts and commands in 4.6. Lott (ed. 1974): A travesty of the wreath of flowers or laurel…[of] the hero or leader. McCombie (1981, p. 133): He has been searching the ditches for remedies for his pains and sickness (see following nn.). Murphy (1984, p. 201): A ghastly parody of the festival-king and the associations of harvest, fullness, and abundance. Butler (1989, pp. 396 ff.), having cited exx. from contemporary theater of parodic crowns of paper, thorns, garlic, nettles, willow, feathers, and wheat, concludes (pp. 399–402) that Lear has made the crown from plants chosen by himself, and crowned himself with them. It is an action of affirmation, of triumph over his enemies; rejecting sustaining corn in favor of poisonous weeds, Lear is symbolically rejecting fruitfulness, marriage, family, and civilization. None of the obvious herbs used in curing insanity is present, such as hellebore and borage.…[Moreover,] the mere wearing of them would achieve nothing. They have to be seethed or concocted or steeped in wine, and taken internally. Webb (1991, p. 19): Idle weeds…are a common sign of neglected husbandry and the malaise of failed authority, comparing H5 (above), adding (p. 93), The listed flowers show the extent of Lear’s unhappy wanderings.…Furrow-weeds…spring up in ploughed fields; Darnel flourishes in corn; the Lady’s Smock in damp meadows. Proudfoot (1992, p. xxviii) compares the distracted queen Bellamy’s crown of cockle, fearne-lock tares in Tom a Lincoln (ca. 1611) 2649, supposing an echo of Lr. Satin (1966, p. 510) compares Leir 2050–62 (see ), and Milward (1987, p. 188) and Shaheen (1987, p. 153) find further analogies in the homily Of the Misery of All Mankinde: We…bring foorth but weedes, netles, brambles, briers, cockle, and darnel. Foakes (ed. 1997): Lear wears this crown when he enters in 4.6…All the weeds and flowers mentioned here belong to the summer season in Britain and provide the only indication of a time of year in the play.
Sprague (1944, p. 293): On stage, Like Ophelia’s flowers, the idle weeds…become straws. Lear’s straw-made crown was already, by Garrick’s time, a famous property.…Kemble, too, had a Sceptre of Straw, as well as a straw crown as large, massive, and elaborately constructed as a bee-hive. Cooke accomplished much with the straw in his hand, paying money with it [2533–4] and presenting it as the challenge which he would have Gloster read [2582].…Forrest…pointed with a straw at [2610]. Phelps’s delivery of—Every inch a King [2554 ff.] was superb; at each word he rises his form higher, and waves the straw around his head. Booth, too, is praised for the fashion in which he played with his straw sceptre, and (Idem, 1954, p. 29) he represented justice and the thief by two straws [2595–8]…and changed them about handy-dandy.

2353 ranke]
Schmidt (1875): Too luxuriant. OED (a. 5, quoting this l.): In rank weed also with implication of sense 15: Of a strongly marked, violent, or virulent type. Craig (ed. 1901): Some explain heavy-scented [OED, 12], comparing TN 2.5.124 (1133); the meaning may fit fumiter but not all of the weeds named. Hunter (ed. 1972): Of bitter, pungent, or poisonous kinds and therefore an appropriate crown of thorns. Rydén (1978): The fumitory…is aptly rendered by rank.…The plant often forms dense tufts, staying green and lush throughout the winter.

2353 femiter]
Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 181–2): Modern editors generally accept Theobald’s reading fumiter. The F n [in Fenitar] is certainly an error, possibly foul-case, since n and m are…adjacent in the type-case (Taylor 1985, p. 20). The form fumiter is etymologically correct (O.Fr. fumeterre, med. Lat. fumus terrae).…Cf. [H5 5.2.45 (3032)], F [ranke] Femetary. Doran (1931, p. 93): Evidently a minim misreading; cf. n. 988. OED (Fumitory): A plant of the genus Fumaria (or the related Corydalis), usually F. officinalis, recording both femiter and femitar, and explaining the name: So called because it spryngeth…out of the erthe in grete quantyte as smoke… (Trevisa, tr. Barth. De P. R. xvii.lxix). Crook (ed. 1907) and Savage (1923, p. 30) give the popular etymology—So named from its strong or rank smell—and Webb (1991, p. 105) thinks it therefore alludes to Goneril and Regan. Ellacombe (1878, p. 75): Of Fumitories we have five species in England, all of them weeds. Pott (1885, p. 251): Bacon, Sylva Sylvarum 7 lists it among flowers which seldom come but amongst corn. Farren (1833, p. 73): The leaves are of bitter taste, and the juice was formerly employed for its bitterness, in hypochondrism and black jaundice. McCombie (1981, p. 133): Fumiter was principally useful in curing scabs or any other filth growing on the skin (Gerard, A), the foul scurffe, and rebellious olde sores (Lyte, B), and it purifieth the bloud (Gerard, B). See next n.

2353 furrow weedes]
Weeds that grow on fresh-plowed land. McCombie (1981, p. 133): Healeth greene wounds (Gerard [Herball, 1597, p. 234], [s.v.] A; Lyte [Herball, 1578, p. 504], [s.v.] B.

2354 hor-docks]
F reads Hardokes. OED (Hardock): Some coarse weedy plant: probably burdock, quoting only this l. and offering no certainty that burdock is meant; see below. Steevens (ed. 1793): The hoar-dock, is the dock with whitish woolly leaves. OED does not record the name, but cf. Hoar (sb. 2): Grey, greyish white, and (3b): Canescent hairiness, an herbalist’s term. OED (Dock sb.1 1b) records White Dock (Rumex salicifolius), but Steevens may be describing Velvet Dock, or mullein (Verbascum thapsus). Rydén (1978, pp. 55–7; cf. 1984, p. 160): Q’s ho(a)r-dock is correct whether a local name or Shn. coinage from familiar plant-name elements, comparing Ham. 4.7.166–7 (3158–9), a Willow…| That showes his horry leaues (hore, F1), where hoar[y?] refers to the silver-grey underside of the leaves, as in horehound and horewort it refers to leaves hoary with white down. Salicifolius, the specific name for White Dock, means willow-leaved. As for F’s reading, Since F1 dokes can hardly be anything else but a corrupt form of docks, it is only natural to assume that Har is a corrupt form, too; it may be just an ex. of an a:o misprint…, but when choosing har, the printer may have had in mind hare, a common Elizabethan plant-name element. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 521) object that doke is not a recorded spelling of dock. Poussa (1989): Grey dock; an invented name, punning on whore. Doran (1931, p. 98): F’s Hardokes was not copied from hor-docks of the quarto; the folio reading has an earlier, less formalized spelling, and it must be an independent reading from the manuscript. Thus the Q and F variants would each represent unsuccessful attempts, by the Q compositor and the scribe preparing the playbook, to decipher an unclear word in Sh.’s rough draft. Halio (ed. 1994): F’s Hardokes probably represents the same word as q’s hordocks, the result of a compositorial misreading of burdocks. It is possible that the F scribe or compositor, seeing the unfamiliar hor-dock (or hordock) misinterpreted it as hard-oke or hard-ook, since oak leaves were used as head-garlands (OED, Oak 5, quoting Cor. 1.3.15 [375]). Oak was regularly spelt oke and ook, and oakum was spelt ockam. Since the words in Q and F are otherwise unknown, several substitutes have been proposed:
(1)Jennens (ed. 1770), supporting Hanmer’s burdocks (see textual n.): Burdock frequently grows among corn, and is most likely to be what Shakespeare means. Steevens (ed. 1773) compares a line in H5, 5.2.52 (3039), that mentions both Docks and Burres. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Burdocks could not be intended.…They bear leaves too large to mingle in Lear’s crown,…[and] they do not grow among corn. Prior’s (1879, p. 102) ingenious argument that the burrs of burdock are the hards of hardock is rejected by Skeat (see below) as a wild guess without foundation, though it may have influenced OED (see above). Stone (1980, p. 209) finds a b/h misreading or foul-case error unlikely. McCombie (1981, p. 133) argues that the herb would be appropriate (see n. 2353–5) because it was a cure for spitting blood and the bites of mad dogs and serpents.
(2)Farmer (in Steevens, ed. 1773, 10:2Q4r): Harlocks, citing a unique occurrence of the word in Drayton, Eighth Eclogue 156. OED: Some flower not identified, but neither hardock or charlock. Rydén (op. cit.) objects that Drayton’s word occurs in a list of sweet flowers, a significantly different context from Sh.’s. Sprinkle-Jackson (1989, p. 18): Another British name for Charlock.
(3)Steevens (ed. 1778) mentions but does not propose charlock. Laertes (1786, p. 214) thinks it probable: Charlock…grows in great quantity amongst the barley. Corn charlock (Raphanus Raphanistrum of Linnaeus). White or yellow flowered charlock (Raphanus sylvestris).—Gerard. [Herball, 1597, pp. 179–80]. Gerard lists Corn charlock (Rapistrum aruorum), which grows among corn, and Water charlock (Rapistrum aquaticum), which grows along marshes and swamps. OED: Popular name of Sinapis arvensis or Field Mustard…; but applied also to other gregarious field-weeds of the same order, listing the forms carlok(e and chadlock(e. Farren (1833, p. 73), Beisly (1864, p. 143), and Savage (1923, p. 283) think charlock = harlock. Sprinkle-Jackson (1989): Corruption from either charlock or harlock is likely.
(4)Nicholson (apud Clark & Wright, ed. 1866): Hediokes. The term is not explained nor recorded by OED.
(5)Wright (ed. 1875) finds in a MS herbal the unique word hardhake used as the equivalent of knapweed (Jacea nigra), and in John Russell’s Boke of Nurture (ca. 1460; ed. 1868, p. 183) the unique yardehok. Of the latter OED (Yardhove) says, (?error for yardehof), ground ivy; the former word is listed with Hardhead as a variant of Hardhaw, Knapweed. Kittredge (ed. 1940) refers to the New England weed (or rather shrub) hardhack, but the name is American and not recorded before 1851.
(6)Skeat (ed. John Fitzherbert, The Book of Husbandry, 1534; 1882, pp. 29–30) finds the name haudoddes or hawdod in a list of weeds that includes darnel, charlock, and dock. From Fitzherbert’s description of it—a blewe floure, and a fewe lyttell leues…and groweth comonly in rye—Skeat identifies it (p. xxx) as corn blue-bottles…(Centaurea Cyanus) and proposes it as the word meant here: It is…one of the idle weeds that grow in corn, and…its bright colour would be particularly attractive to the gatherer of a wild garland. He suggests that there may be some relationship to the name hardewes (var. of Hardhewe) for wild succory (Cichorium intybus) in Turner’s Names of Herbes (1548; ed. 1881, p. 44). Craig (ed. 1901) says of hawdod, Only for its ugly name this might be Shakespeare’s word here.

2354 hemlocke]
Beisly (1864, p. 142): Noticed by the prophet Hosea, chap. x. verse 4, as springing up in the furrows of the field (Authorized; wormewood in Geneva). Prior (1879): A name originally applied to any of the Umbelliferae, at present confined to two poisonous species, Common-, Conium maculatum, L., Water-, Cicuta virosa, L. The root of one of these is an ingredient in the weird sisters’ cauldron in Mac. 4.1.25 (1552) (Rolfe, ed. 1880) and the witches’ broth in Jonson’s Masque of Queens 188 (Ellacombe, 1878, p. 91). Muir (ed. 1952): Used as a poison and a narcotic. Savage (1923, pp. 38–9), however, thinks that here Sh. means not the poisonous root in Mac. but one of the Umbelliferae plants popularly called hemlock: Wild Carrot, Hogweed, Parsley, Gout, Chervil, and Fool’s Parsley.…The Hemlock (Conium) I have never yet seen growing in cultivated fields among corn or other crops.…The places it likes best are shady situations and in woods. Sprinkle-Jackson (1989, p. 22): Being deadly, it serves as imagery for Goneril and Regan.

2354 netles]
Farren (1833, p. 73): Suitable (see n. 2353–5) for its well-known irritating power of stinging and burning; analogous to the continuous spiteful pin-pricks and stabs inflicted by Lear’s daughters (Armstrong, 1946, pp. 80–1). Ellacombe (1878, p. 136), on 12 Shn. references to the term: We have two native species (Urtica urens and U. dioica) with sufficiently strong qualities, but we have a third (U. pilulifera)…which is far more virulent. Blunden (1929; 1936, p. 334): Throngs about graves. McCombie (1981, p. 133): The herbalists record its aphrodisiac properties, power to cleanse the breast of phlegm and other humors, and efficacy as a counterpoison for henbane, serpents, and scorpions and as a dressing for the bites of mad dogs and for ulcerous sores; see n. 2353–5. Sprinkle-Jackson (1989, p. 22): As a remedy against the poison of Hemlock, [it] could function as imagery for Cordelia. Savage (1923, pp. 52–3), however, thinks that neither Ophelia (Ham. 4.7.169 [3161]) nor Lear would put stinging nettles into their crowns, but rather pretty White Dead-nettles (Lamium album), [which] grow on poorly cultivated land, and are found in almost every hedge-row.

2354 cookow flowers]
OED (Cuckoo-flower): A name given to various wild flowers which are in bloom when the cuckoo is heard, among them Lady’s Smock or lesser (wild, meadow) watercress (Cardamine pratensis), Ragged Robin (crowflower, wild gilliflower) (Lychnis flos-cuculi), and several other varieties to which the name is applied locally, quoting this l. as its first ex. of the latter category. Farren (1833, p. 73) identifies the Lady’s Smock as employed among the Greeks and Romans for almost all affections of the head…[and at present] as a remedy for convulsions, epilepsy, and other diseases of the brain or intellect; Grigson (1955, p. 66) says that in some parts of England picking it was unlucky. McCombie (1981, pp. 133–4): According to Gerard’s Herball (1597), the wild water-cress was a treatment for scurvy and skin blemishes. Beisly (1864, p. 143): Ragged robin, a well-known meadow and marsh plant, with rose-coloured flowers. Ellacombe (1878, pp. 53–4) considers cookow flowers to be the same as the Cuckow-budds of yellow hew in LLL 5.2.896 (2861); since in the next line these are distinguished from Ladi-smockes all siluer white (5.2.895 [2862]), Ellacombe denies their identification with watercress (nor does it grow among Corn), entertains Jervis’s (1861) [and Schmidt’s (1874)] suggestion of yellow cowslips, but prefers Prior’s identification with the Buttercup (see below). Rydén (1978, pp. 43–4) denies that cuckoo-buds and cuckoo-flowers are the same, and adds: The cuckoo-flowers, says Gerard, flower for the most part in Aprill and Maie, when the Cuckowe doth begin to sing her pleasant notes without stammering. However, as appears from the context (in the high-grown field [2351]), the season in Shakespeare’s text is…the late summer. Evidently, the contextual significance of Lear’s cuckoo-flowers is not that of calendar or habitat—neither the lady-smock nor the ragged robin is a cornfield weed. The plants…are all unpleasant and repellent, consonant with the mental state of the king. He therefore inclines to the lady-smock, which had unpleasant associations with madness and bad luck. Craig (ed. 1901) inclines to the cowslip, and Muir (ed. 1952), though preferring Lady’s Smock, concedes, The Bedlam Cowslip…would be an apt flower for the mad Lear. Armstrong (1946, p. 81): Shakespeare’s cuckoo is frequently…associated with foolishness.…The cuckoo-flower is therefore appropriate…in a crown for a crazy king.…Buttercups were called cuckoo-buds [citing Prior, who does not say this at all].…Thus it was with crazies—buttercups—that the crazy king crowned himself. Prior (1879, p. 57): Crazy, or Craisey, in Wiltshire and the adjoining counties, the buttercup, apparently a corruption of Christ’s eye,…the medieval name of the marigold, which…has been transferred to the marsh marigold, and thence to other ranunculaceae; (p. 59): Cuckoo buds…are probably the buds of the crowfoot.…Cuckoo flower, a name given in old works to the ragged robin,…but now more generally to the lady’s smock. Savage (1923, pp. 18–20) suspects that cuckoo-buds is a general term for any yellow field flower, attests that the term crazies is applied to both buttercups and (less frequently) to lady-smocks, and thinks that cuckoo-flowers are Creeping Buttercups (Ranunculus repens), all too common in the fields…[and] in the borders of ploughed fields. Rydén (1984, p. 157): Cuckoo is suggestive of fool and hence of Lear’s madness. Butler (1989, p. 405) suspects a significant wordplay on cuckoo: Man prepares the field—a nest for the corn. But the tares are planted in it by the enemy, ousting the rightful inheritors, just as the cuckow does.

2355 Darnell]
OED (1): A deleterious grass, Lolium temulentum, which in some countries grows as a weed among corn…The grass is now rare in England, but appears to have been much more common formerly when seed-corn was largely imported from the Mediterranean regions, where the weed abounds. Steevens (ed. 1778): According to Gerard [Herball, 1597, p. 71],…the most hurtful of weeds among corn. Farren (1833, p. 73): Called temulentum from its intoxicating or narcotic powers,…whence our own vulgar name for it of wray-grass [or ray-grass] or drunkard-grass. Beisly (1864, p. 114) cites other witnesses to the power of its seeds to produce drunkenness, giddiness, bad dreams, and impaired vision. Ellacombe (1878, p. 59): Wild rye grass. But in Shakespeare’s time Darnel, like Cockle…, was the general name for any hurtful weed, citing Newton’s tr. of Lemnius’s Herbal for the Bible (1587, p. 226), as does Prior (1879, p. 64). Verity (ed. 1897): The tares…of the parable, Matthew xiii.25; so William Smith, Dictionary of the Bible, 1860–3. Wilson (ed. 1960): Prob tares…though in Drayton (Poly-Olb. xv, 166) the crimson darnell flower seems to be the common poppy. Blunden (1929; 1936, p. 335): It represents Lear’s affliction, being sickly and usurping. King (1968, p. 141), finding evidence in Thomas Cooper’s Thesaurus that it was believed to make the head giddy, and in Ovid’s Fasti 2.691–2 and Plautus’s Miles Gloriosus 2.321–3 that it impairs the vision, concludes, Thus Cordelia’s mention of darnel may serve to reinforce the themes of madness and blindness. McCombie (1981, p. 134): The herbalists thought it could treat tumors, ulcers, and skin diseases. Adelman (1992, p. 307): May…be taken from the lolium in Ovid’s account [Meta. 5:485] of Ceres’s revenge on Sicily for the loss of her daughter.…Cordelia combines in herself aspects of both Ceres and Proserpina: she is simultaneously the mother who searches for her child and the child who is lost then found. Cf. n. 2368.

2355 idle weedes]
Delius (ed. 1854): Unproductive, unprofitable, worthless weed, in opposition to sustaining corn (Ger.). Sh. uses the phrase in R3 3.1.103 (1685). OED (Idle a. 3): Serving no useful purpose, useless, quoting Err. 2.2.178 (572), idle Mosse. Cf. 2456.

2356 sustayning]
Eccles (ed. 1792): That nourishes and supports life (OED, ppl. a., quoting this l. as its first ex.). Empson (1951, p. 143), improbably: The corn appears to sustain also the idle weeds.

2356 corne]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Wheat.

2356 a centurie is sent]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 410): Q’s is sent does not agree, as F’s [send] does, with the imperatives Search and bring in lines [2357–8]. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 521), reading the centuries: Blayney plausibly suggests that Q’s centurie is results from a misreading of centuries. None the less, it seems unlikely that the compositor interpolated a (apart from the fact that this produces a less metrical line than Q). But substitution of a for the, and vice versa, is common. Halio (ed. 1994): Clayton suggests (privately)…a nominative absolute…written A centuri e sent.…[F] is both metrically better and consistent with the indirect allusion to Lear’s hundred knights. A compositor holding a centurie send in his memory might easily confuse it with a centurie’s and unconsciously change send to the requisite sent. F is clearly right. Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:11): An Hundred: also,—a Command or Party of Men consisting of that Number (OED, 1, 3, not recording F’s sp. Centery). Cor. 1.7.3 (716) is Sh.’s only other use of the word. Collier (ed. 1858): Cordelia was anxious that search should be made for her father in every direction. Craig (ed. 1901): I take it that centery of the Folio as well as the Quarto word Centurie, Century, is only an older form of sentry [citing OED, Century: Obs. var. of Sentry, supported by two exx., 1649 and 1759].…Century, a division of a Roman army, is quite out of place in Britain before the Romans. Perrett (1904, p. 201): But surely sentry makes no sense. Cor. is in great anxiety.…Under such circumstances it would be strange to send forth a sentry to search every acre… [2357]. Century is to be taken…rather as a hundred knights…of whom the five and six or thirty hot questrists [2076]…form the nucleus. Who the searchers are is not specified, though obviously they are members of Cordelia’s forces, and Lear is found in 4.6 by one or more Gentlemen, possibly knights, one of whom speaks of Cordelia as if from near acquaintance (your most deere…who redeemes nature). Perrett’s unprovable guess that the searchers include some of Lear’s knights is defensible, since they would be more likely to recognize Lear than her French or English common soldiers; cf. nn. 2347+1–+56, 2349–50, 2630. Ridley (ed. 1935): There is no evidence that sentry ever meant anything but a single man on a fixed post of guard, and in any case one man is inadequate for the search. So that the meaning is,…anachronism or no anachronism, simply a body of soldiers. Kittredge (ed. 1940) compares 473+4, Cohorts. Elton (1966, p. 123): Cordelia’s healing restoration ([2776]) extends even to the balance between the loss of his knights and the company of soldiers she issues to seek him. Butler (1989, pp. 402–3) detects a quibble on the bitter-sweet herb centaury, anticipating Lear’s bitter-sweet experience of repentance and reconciliation. Foakes (ed. 1997): The word may have been prompted by its echo of centaury,…linked by Turner in his New Herball (1551), Iir, with marjoram (see [2540]), and said by him to heal the ake of the mother. In his Herbal (1597), 437, Gerard…notes that it grows especially well on the chalkie cliffes of Greenehith in Kent. Pauls (1984, p. 99): In Leir 1884 Cambria sends light-horse to search for Leir (see ).

2357 hie growne]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Standing corn which might…conceal the king. Harrison (ed. 1937): The season is late summer; but cf. n. 2354 s.v. cookow flowers. Edwards (ed. 1975): The weather is more notable than the seasons in King Lear, and the storm…could belong to any season.

2358 bring]
Wells & Taylor (1987, pp. 521–2): Since Cordelia later says seeke…him ([2369]), it is possible that no one leaves yet.

2358–9 what…sence]
Most eds. now interpret this as a question rather than as an introduction (what = in doing what) to the next clause.

2358 can]
Delius (ed. 1854): Be able to do. A few eds. adopt Q2’s added do, unnecessarily (see textual n.). Abbott (§307): Can means …have knowledge or skill. This, the original meaning of can [OED v1 1; cf. 8], is found, though very rarely, in Shakespeare.…A trace of this emphatic use of can is found in this line. Schmidt (1874) lists 7 Shn. exx. of can followed by (here, preceded by—what) an accusative.

2358 wisdome]
Craig (ed. 1901): Science, medical knowledge. Cf. n. 434.

2359 bereued]
OED (ppl. a.): Deprived or robbed; taken away by force, quoting this l.

2359 sence]
OED (sb. 10a): Pl. The mental faculties in their normal condition of sanity; one’s reason or wits; (10b): Sing. (with the same meaning), quoting this l. Cf. 2528.

2359–60 he…worth]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 410): F takes over faulty lineation from Q. Or from Q2, or from an original MS common to Q and F. The line is somewhat hypermetrical, and so may have seemed to more than one compositor or scribe to need division.

2359 the restoring]
On the article before the verbal, and the absence of of, see nn. 348, 973.

2359 can helpe]
F’s helpes may have been substituted on metrical grounds (see prev. n.) or because the typographical line was full. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 410), however, suspects an unintended repetition in Q of can in 2358. Schmidt (1874), help: Cure (OED, v. 9).

2360 outward worth]
Delius (ed. 1854): The valuables I bear upon (or with) me (Ger.). Page (ed. 1889) and most eds.: Worldly possessions, wealth. Joseph (ed. 1966): As distinct from her internal, spiritual worth.

2361 Doct.]
On F’s Gent. see n. 2349–50.

2361 meanes]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Used as a noun singular (OED, sb.2 10c).

2362 foster nurse]
Sh. apparently coins the phrase in AYL 2.3.40 (744). Harbage (ed. 1958), foster: Fostering (OED, sb.1 4). Schmidt (1875), nurse: Metaphorically, that which…nourishes (OED, sb.1 1d). Joseph (ed. 1966): Who continues what the mother has started.

2362 nature]
If nature here means the recipient of the nourishment, see nn. 1427, 1566. If (less probably) of nature means in nature, natural, see n. 232 and OED (sb. 11c): Contrasted with medical skill or treatment in the cure of…diseases. In the latter case the Doctor proposes to use herbal art to bring about sleep, nature’s cure. Orgel (ed. 1999): What naturally cares for us.

2363 prouoke]
Schmidt (1875): To call forth,…to cause (OED v. 6b: Transf.…induce, bring about).

2364 simples]
Hudson (ed. 1871): Medicinal herbs (OED sb. 6). Kittredge (ed. 1940): So called in contradistinction to compounds.

2364 operatiue]
Schmidt (1875): Effective (OED a. 2).

2365 close the eye]
Deighton (ed. 1891), literally: In closing the sufferer’s eyes. Verity (ed. 1897) compares the metaphor in MND 3.2.435 (1483): sleepe, that sometimes shuts vp sorrowes eye.

2365 anguish]
Schmidt (1874): Excessive pain, either of body or of mind. Wright (ed. 1875): Generally used in Shakespeare of physical pain, comparing 2438. Lear’s mental anguish is evident; his physical pain is supposedly exhaustion.

2366–7 All…earth]
Doran (1931, p. 130) suspects that a characteristic of Shakespeare’s manuscript…is the printing as one line of a half-line beginning a speech with the full line following. Cf. 129–30, 2103–4, 2301–2, 2327–8, 2344–5, 2373–4, 2745–7, 2763–4, 3014–15, 3189–90.

2366 secrets]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): In old times every distinguished physician claimed knowledge of secrets—special remedies, unknown to the majority. The next line repeats the sense with elaboration of phrase.

2367 vnpublisht]
Schmidt (1875): Unknown, secret (OED ppl. a.: Not divulged or disclosed, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Gardner (ed. 1969): Concealed in (the plants of) the earth.

2367 vertues]
Schmidt (1875): Power, efficacy (OED sb. 9b, specifically: Strengthening, sustaining, or healing properties). Gerard’s Herball (1597) etc. list the vertues of various herbs. Elton (1966, p. 81) cites contemporary attributions of these secret virtues to divine providence. Kittredge (ed. 1940) and others take the word to refer to the plants themselves, which Spring (2368); so Wilson (ed. 1960): Abstract for concrete.

2367 of the earth]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): That grow in the earth (see prev. n.). More exactly, virtues (in the plants) that derive from the earth.

2368 Spring…teares]
Eccles (ed. 1792) finds a double meaning: Spring from the ground and be discovered,…be brought to light. Deighton (ed. 1891) finds a similar idea in Ant. 4.2.38 (2459). Hunter (ed. 1972): As the herbs themselves do after a spring shower. Wells (ed. 2000): Be germinated by. Lott (ed. 1974): The concept…is of classical origin and common in literature, giving no exx. Adelman (1992, p. 306): A seasonal reference linking Cordelia with Ceres and Proserpina.

2368 aydant]
Wright (ed. 1875): Helping (OED Aidant), comparing 3090, Conspirant, for the Romantic form of the participle (Tovey, ed. 1896), or the French present participial suffix (Brook, 1976, p. 133).

2368 remediat]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:56): Remediative, strong to remedy (OED, a.: Remedial. Perh. an error for remedial or remediant, quoting only this l.). Wright (ed. 1875): A word of Shakespeare’s coinage, which he seems to have formed on the model of immediate. Muir (ed. 1952): Perhaps to avoid the jingle that would be caused by remediant. Hunter (ed. 1972): With aydant, Rare words…to fit into the remote and incantatory atmosphere of Cordelia’s prayer. The a may lack a tilde.

2369 good mans]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 195): The reference is to Lear, and F’s [Goodmans] is entirely improper, citing Onions (1911), who defines goodman as husband, yeoman, or farmer. Delius (ed. 1854): F makes only a forced sense, in that one understands good man generally, without reference to Lear (Ger.).

2369 distresse]
Most eds. consider F’s desires a MS misreading, though Werstine (1983, p. 286) finds it atypical of F Compositor B, most of whose non-literal substitutions affect…connectives and minor modifiers. The misreading could have been a scribe’s, however, as Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 182) suggests. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 537): Alternatively, a simple ligature error (producing disires in place of distres) might have been miscorrected in foul proofs.

2370 vngouernd]
Delius (ed. 1854): Ungovernable, wild; see n. 284. Schmidt (1875): Unbridled.

2370 rage]
The word may mean furious passion and action (see n. 1598) or insanity (OED, 1); cf. 2837. Joseph (ed. 1966): Mania…by too great abundance of hot blood intoxicating the head. Halio (ed. 1992): Cordelia is afraid that in his madness Lear will kill himself.

2370 dissolue]
Foakes (ed. 1997): A proper use in relation to dying, citing OED (v. 6).

2371 wants]
Harbage (ed. 1958): Lacks.

2371 meanes]
Johnson (ed. 1765): The reason which should guide it. Joseph (ed. 1966): There is a play upon means in the senses of (i) moderation, (ii) measure, way in which.

2371 lead]
Harbage (ed. 1958): Govern.

2374 hitherward]
I.e., towards Dover, for the final battle.

2375 preparation]
Schmidt (1875): A force ready for combat (OED, sb. 3).

2376–81 ô…him]
Hudson (ed. 1881) marks the lines as spurious. Verity (ed. 1897): Said by Shakespeare with a view to reconciling an Elizabethan audience to the presence of French troops on English soil. In fact that presence is never adequately explained; see n. 1638+1. Bransom (1934, p. 195), speculating beyond evidence, imagines that France’s original motive has changed to that now voiced by Cordelia: The king’s friends were flocking to the invaders, drawn by the presence of Cordelia in the French army, and the invasion did eventually become little more than a half-hearted, ill directed attempt to reinstate the king.…[But probably] the French king’s [original] object was to take advantage of the British factions and seize his wife’s dower. The nominal restoration of the old king might have followed victory, and beyond that France might have seen for himself the prize of the succession. Snider (1887, p. 200): Lear had resigned his power and divided his kingdom; he had no longer any just claim to the crown.…She did wrong—she violated the majesty of the State. Danby (1949, p. 133): Cordelia’s invasion of Britain is simply right. It is of a piece with the rest of her conduct—firm, unconfused, quietly assured.…Cordelia’s speech itself has the force of prayer. Cf. next n. Rosenberg (1972, p. 261): Spoken probably kneeling. Joseph (ed. 1966): Critics have seen in this speech a justification for interpreting Cordelia as representing a saviour-figure, even a Christ-figure.…Nevertheless, it should not be overlooked that Cordelia’s words are occasioned by the news that her countrymen are approaching, that her soldiers will shed British blood. She reminds herself that no other way is open to her if she is to rescue her father. She does not know that Albany is determined to re-instate him, and that the sole fact which makes the duke oppose her is the presence of her force of French invaders on British soil. Bullough (1973, p. 274): Apparently Sh. wishes to refute Holinshed’s implication (after Caxton) that Cordelia in invading Britain wanted to take possession of the land. Her immediate end, however, is to see him againe restored to his kingdome; see .

2376–7 father…about]
Fraser (1962, p. 68): Like the kind son of Sidney’s unfortunate king (in Arcadia 2.10.1; see ). Bethell (1944, p. 60) compares Luke 2:49: knewe ye not that I must go about my fathers busines? (Geneva). Milward (1987, p. 188), citing also Luke 15:20: Cordelia goes forth to meet and welcome back her prodigal father. Weis (ed. 1993): The echo of the Gospel helps further mitigate the political awkwardness of having a good character (Cordelia) leading a foreign invasion. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 32): This most direct Christian reference in the play is deeply ironic, for Cordelia’s business is to fight to restore Lear’s right ([2380]), whereas Christ’s was to leave his parents to attend to God’s affairs in the Temple. Kermode (2000, p. 195): The echo is very bold, but probably without the allegorical significance sometimes attributed to it, for Lear is not God, and Cordelia could not save him, even if, absurdly, he would in that case have needed to be saved. Dundes (1976, p. 361), inferring incestuous desire: Cordelia is primarily concerned with her father, not her husband, who therefore cannot appear in the final act.

2377 It…France]
Though Ioppolo (1991, p. 178) imagines that the mislining may indicate a marginal addition, the difficulty is not mislining but extrametrical material. Most eds. make therfore great France a part-line (see textual n.); alternatively, Tis…before might be the part-line.

2377 therfore]
Deighton (ed. 1891): For that reason; viz. that she was seeking to help her father. Her motives are anything but clear: see nn. 1638+1, 2347+37, 2376–81.

2377 France]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Her husband.

2378 mourning]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): A noun, not an adjective.

2378 important]
Hanmer (ed. 1743–4, 6:Gloss.): Importunate (OED, a. 3, quoting Err. 5.1.138 [1610] and Ado 2.1.71 [479] as its first of three exx.); cf. AWW 3.7.21 (1880). Since Sh. repeatedly uses the word in this sense, there is no reason to agree with Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 410) that it may be a misreading of importund or importand, or an actor’s substitution, nor to prefer F’s importun’d, which may be a mere sophistication and can make sense only if treated as a passive participle with the active sense importuning; see Abbott (§374) and Franz (§661), who do not cite this l. Schmidt (1874) so treats it, defining it importunate, urgently soliciting. Smithers (1970, pp. 36–7) compares 2133 stelled = stellate, but there the meaning remains passive, starred, formed into stars, not starring. Muir (ed. 1952): The epithet [importun’d] is transferred from the King of France to Cordelia’s tears. The Q reading does not require such contortions. Importunate tears could conceivably mean that they were too pressing for Cordelia to deny their appearance in her eyes, but more probably that they were solicitous of France’s aid. Perrett (1904, p. 215) compares Higgins, Mirour (1574 only; rev. in 1587): Then I besought my king with teares vpõ my knee, | That he would aide my father (see ).

2379 blowne]
Johnson (ed. 1765): No inflated, no swelling pride (OED ppl. a.1 5b, quoting this l.). Craig (ed. 1901): With the pride of conquest. Muir (ed. 1952) compares 1 Cor. 13:4: Loue suffereth long:…it is not puffed vp (Geneva).

2379 our armes]
Foakes (ed. 1997): As if she is in charge of the army. As Queen of France she is of course in charge, though she is not the army’s general during battle. See n. 2347+2–+7. Our, however, may here mean no more than it does at 2375 in Our preparation, referring to the French army.

2379 in sight]
An aural error for F’s incite (Q2’s insite), perhaps resulting from the compositor’s carrying the word in his memory. OED records neither insight nor insite as variant sp. of incite. Ingham (1967, p. 83): The normal pronunciation of sight was with [χ]. Urkowitz (1980, p. 134): Eye-rhyming with right [2380] by poet or compositor. So Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 121): Apparently the compositors were more concerned with the look of the final words in a rhyming couplet…; in Q in sight rhymes with right (the correct word), while in F incite (the correct word) rhymes with Rite, an odd spelling for right.

2380 deere loue]
Jackson (1983, p. 339) detects an echo of 89 (Q) and the source play Leir; but see n. 89.

2380 right]
Only Kirschbaum (1945, p. 55) defends F’s Rite: The formal duties owing to Lear as both king and Cordelia’s father. Of course, Shakespeare may have intended a pun. Such a meaning (duty) is not supported by OED, nor is rite as a variant sp. of right later than the 15th c. Most probably a compositor or scribe carried the word in his head and substituted the homophone. Greg (1946): The spelling being attracted to that of the rime-word incite. Cf. Leir 2561: And we are come in iustice of his right; see . In Leir Cordella seeks both iust reuengement (2557) for attempted murder, and Leir’s right (2634) to rule Britain again. It is unclear exactly what right Cordelia hopes to restore—the throne, or something less such as protection, respect, love, and care.

2382 <Scena Quarta>]
The fifth scene in Q and most eds.; see n. 2348. For the time when the scene takes place see n. 2347+1–+56, end. Daniel (1877–9, p. 221), however, thinks that it is misplaced between 4.4 and 4.6 and belongs earlier, before 4.3: The news as to the movement of the troops favours the notion that it represents an earlier date; moreover, if it is allowed to retain its present place, we are called on to believe that Oswald, who again makes his appearance in sc. vi., is present with Regan, and is at Dover on one and the same day. On Eccles’s (ed. 1792) transposition of this scene before Scene 3, see n. 2347+1. Greg (1940, p. 438 n.) offers and rejects reasons to place it before Scene 4: Since the distracted Lear is already wandering about the fields in iv.iv…, he has to continue doing so throughout Oswald’s journey from Cornwall’s to Dover in search of Edmund (announced in v), before they can both reappear in the course of vi.…[But] it may be [Albany’s powers, not Regan’s] that are reported nearing Dover in iv; and…we really have no idea how long it would take Oswald to reach the neighborhood of Dover, or…there is no reason why Lear should not continue his wanderings during the night. Greg also questions the more usual editorial location, Gloucester’s house: Regan must have returned to her own palace to muster her troops. Similarly Brooke (ed. 1947): There is no reason to suppose that Regan would continue to live in Gloucester’s castle (which she complained of as little, [1588]). When she speaks of Goneril’s late being here in line [2411] she means in this part of the country, in the South; or else it is a dramatic license which in Shakespeare’s theatre would never be detected. Similarly Rosenberg (1972, p. 261): The scene may open on Regan in the field, her own armed men on the march. But as Perrett (1904, p. 263) points out, the last occasion when Regan could have observed here…strange aliads (2411–12) between Edmund and Goneril was in 3.7, at Gloucester’s house.
Eccles (ed. 1792) deduces the action between scenes: Edmund had departed from Regan upon the business which she here mentions [2393–9].…It appears that the steward, not finding Edmund as he expected [cf. 2283, 2286–7], sets out towards Dover without loss of time in pursuit of him.…I suppose the troops of Albany to have begun their march towards Dover, but in another direction, and headed by the duke, about the time of the steward’s departure from home [i.e., Albany’s house] charged with the execution of Goneril’s commission. On Oswald’s letter(s) see n. 2391. Smith (ed. 1902): This scene…does not advance the plot; but it prepares us for the dénouement by showing the increasing jealousy of Goneril and Regan. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Oswald’s fidelity to Goneril comes out clearly in this scene. Regan does not succeed in getting a sight of Goneril’s letter. Hunter (ed. 1972): The self-seeking wickedness of Gonerill and Regan has found out its own punishment in the desire that both feel for the person of Edmund. General destructive hate here is in strong contrast to the love and protectiveness that was the keynote of the preceding scene.

2384 brothers]
See n. 2283.

2384 powers]
See n. 1638+1.

2387 much ado]
Schmidt (1874): Pains, difficulty (OED, sb. 4). Gardner (ed. 1969): A great deal of fuss. More specifically, Moberly (ed. 1876): It was hard to get him into the field; so Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): After much persuasion. Craig (ed. 1901): It would appear that Albany at first hesitated to serve against an army, though it was composed of foreign invaders, which was fighting in the interests of Lear. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Albany’s reluctance is made clear in iv, 2. Hunter (ed. 1972): The term reflects Gonerill’s view of Albany’s moral scruples. Lott (ed. 1974): Implies he is less powerful in military affairs than his wife.

2388 soldier]
Abbott (§479): Trisyllabic.

2389 Lord…home]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): We do not hear the whole of the conversation between Regan and Oswald. He has apparently already given her that information, and she then recalls his words and asks for confirmation.

2389 spake]
On the archaic preterite see n. 476.

2389 Lady]
Most eds. adopt F’s Lord. Ritson (1783, p. 171): Goneril not only converses with lord Edmund, in the steward’s presence [2269 ff.], but prevents him from speaking to, or even seeing her husband [2279]. Capell (1783, 1.2:178): For what imported it Regan to know if Goneril was spoke with at home? the matter that she dreaded might as well pass by the way, and in that she knew that Edmund accompany’d her: this question’s answer, which (perhaps) she expected, encreases her jealousy; his [i.e., Edmund’s] abrupt sending-off without doing what he [actually, Goneril: see 2060–1] had in commission, (settling matters with Albany) has the appearance of hiding him, and of something private between him and his lady: Which lady she is bent on anticipating, on being beforehand with her, and therefore speaks and acts openly; sending…by the Steward…a ring [2420] to Edmund; with licence [2421] to tell all to his mistress, as well what she [Regan] had done as what said. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 411), following Malone (ed. 1790): Q is perhaps a wrong expansion of a contraction (.L.) in the copy. Weis (ed. 1993): If Q’s reading is correct, then Oswald tells Regan a straight lie.

2391 import]
Schmidt (1874): Purport (OED, v. 5c: Convey as information).

2391 letters]
On Q2’s and F’s singular letter see n. 875. Malone (ed. 1790): The meaning is the same in either case. Cf. 2286–9. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Regan is justly suspicious as to its contents. See [2715] ff. Hunter (ed. 1972): Oswald has delivered to Regan the letter that Gonerill promised to send at [2334]; and he has mentioned, it appears, that he is carrying another letter, from Gonerill to Edmund.

2393 Faith]
See n. 669+9. Hunter (ed. 1972): Regan’s uncharacteristic oath is presumably designed to make palatable what may seem to Oswald to be a mere evasion.

2393 posted]
See n. 2060.

2393 serious matter]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Important business. Edwards (ed. 1975): I.e. he is not to be bothered by letters from Goneril.

2394–6 It…vs]
Muir & Danby (1950, p. 49) compare Sidney’s Arcadia 2.10.1; see .

2394 ignorance]
Schmidt (1875): Stupidity, silliness, a sense unattested by OED but frequent in Sh. Here it means simple-minded or ill-considered ignorance of probable consequences, leading to thoughtless bad judgment. So Caldecott (MS notes, 1813–33): Want of foresight. Regan here judges herself, not Cornwall (see 2170–1), though originally she had urged Gloucester’s instant death (2063). Joseph (ed. 1966): Blindness of wit. Hunter (ed. 1972): Lack of (political) understanding. Horsman (ed. 1973): Lack of skill.

2396 harts]
See n. 1029.

2396 and now]
F’s Edmund is preferred by virtually all eds. Greg (1933, p. 256), whimsically: Q repeats an actor’s anticipation of Gloucester’s attempted suicide in 4.6. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 411): Q makes nonsense. It may represent a desperate guess by the compositor trying to decipher a very badly written edmond. There is little graphic similarity. Van Dam (1935, p. 105): It is only a pair of brackets that the Q lacks. Put one before It [2394] and one after vs [2396]. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 522): Blayney interprets Q’s and now as a continuation of [2393], enclosing It was…vs in parentheses.
