Neither the construction nor the ambiguity is attractive, and mund could have been misread nowe. Quite possibly Van Dam and Blayney are right: commas often set off parenthetical remarks, and this one may even have been an aside in both Q and F, since in the next line Regan gives Oswald a quite different motive (pitie, not fear of resentment). F may have been revised to simplify the construction.

2397 pitie]
Muir (ed. 1952): Presumably ironical. But see the prev. n. Wilson (ed. 1960): A thin cloak for parricide.

2397 dispatch]
See n. 995.

2398 nighted]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Made dark as night by the loss of his eyes (OED, ppl. a. 1, quoting Ham. 1.2.68 [248] and this l. as its first exx.). On the verb see n. 223 and Smithers (1970, p. 31). Wells (ed. 2000) prints ’nighted to indicate a shortened form of benighted.

2398 discrie]
Schmidt (1874): To espy, to discover (OED, v.1 6, 7).

2399 at’h]
For F’s of the, see nn. 669+10, 1105, 1613.

2399 army]
All eds. prefer F’s Enemy. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 411): Q might be a misreading of enmy. Q, however, makes perfectly good sense, since the only army Edmund would be interested in was the enemy army (cf. 2384); F is simply more explicit.

2400 must]
On the omission of the verb of motion see n. 312.

2400 needs]
See n. 634.

2400 him]
Following Taylor (1985, p. 26), Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 537) rightly find F’s him, Madam, a metrical emendation, but wish to improve on it: Madam could have been intended…to replace rather than…to follow Q’s him; in Q they omit him and place Madam at the end of the line, reasoning, All Oswald’s other speeches in this scene address Regan as Madam or Lady, and the omitted punctuation is also suspicious. There is no reason to think the F line unmetrical or a bungled correction, however; it is a passable pentameter with a feminine ending.

2400 letters]
On Q’s plural for F’s Letter see n. 875. Cf. 2408.

2401 troope sets]
Though most eds. prefer F’s troopes set, and OED (sb. 2) quotes this l. for its second ex. of the sense pl. Armed forces collectively, Q may be more accurate, since Regan refers to her (or Cornwall’s) forces (led by Edmund) rather than to the British forces collectively. Albany’s powers have already set forth (2384). In 1H6 1.1.112 (124) Talbot’s troupe (OED, 1: A body of soldiers), almost six thousand strong, is, like Regan’s power, one lord’s troop that is part of the British troops collectively.

2401 stay]
Deighton (ed. 1891): She wishes to delay his taking the letter, and perhaps to take measures to get it from him. Skillan (ed. 1967): Or counteract its effects.

2402 dangerous]
Armour (ed. 1930): With the country thus disturbed, the roads are perilous for the solitary traveler.

2404 charg’d my dutie]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Insisted upon the exact performance of it [i.e., this busines]; such as strict duty demanded of me. OED (Charge v. 14): To command,…exhort authoritatively; OED (sb. 4b): Moral obligation. Some eds. emphasize the action due rather than the motive of duteousness; thus Muir (ed. 1952) revises Craig’s (ed. 1901) gloss enjoined me, to be…duteous to enjoined me to carry out her instructions. Lott (ed. 1974): Gave me particular instructions. Bald (ed. 1949), interpreting in as with, interprets charg’d to mean burdened with (OED, v. 13).

2405–6 Why…belike]
On F’s mislined verse see n. 2022–3.

2405 Why…Edmund]
Skillan (ed. 1967): gon. has replied to edm. and not to reg. Cf. 2328.

2406 Transport her purposes]
Harbage (ed. 1958): Convey her intentions.

2406 by word]
Wright (ed. 1875): By word of mouth.

2406 belike]
At root this word means it is likely (Moberly, ed. 1876), and like this modern phrase its nuances may range (see OED, adv.) from perhaps (Wright, ed. 1875) through as it seems,…I suppose (Schmidt, 1874) to probably (Kittredge, ed. 1940).

2407–8 Some…letter]
Verity (ed. 1897): The disjointed style marks her hesitation in making the request that follows. Hunter (ed. 1972): It betokens her attempt to think how she can overcome her sister’s advantage with Edmund and Oswald’s unco-operativeness. Greg (1940, p. 392) compares Goneril’s similar request of a reluctant Messenger in Leir 995–1005 (see ).

2407 thing…what]
Muir (ed. 1952): Obviously she suspects that Edmund and Goneril are lovers (cf. 2331–3). Q’s implied meaning seems to be, Something is going on privately between them, exactly what or to what extent I can only guess. Some eds. defend F’s things: Perhaps she begins to say that some things are not to be trusted even to Oswald’s discretion (Brooke, ed. 1947) or would be advisable for me to learn (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 157).

2407 ile…much]
As Hawkes (1959, pp. 178–81) points out, the verb love could mean either hold dear (OED, v.1 1) or estimate the price or value of (OED, v.2 2; cf. Crook, ed. 1907: Value thee highly). In either case eds. have recognized a bribe: [I’ll] give you great proofs of my regard (Deighton, ed. 1891), I’ll make it well worth your while (Wilson, ed. 1960, comparing Jn. 3.3.67 [1371]). Flatter (1948, p. 133): An unequivocal proposal from a harlot princess. Rosenberg (1972, p. 261): She sets out to seduce Oswald to her party.…Often, in the theatre, it is accompanied by physical imagery: she comes close, may caress, even kiss him, as she reaches for the paper, perhaps searches him for it. Mahood (1992, p. 172): A promise of advancement.…Though her sister’s dealings with her steward can be played in such a way that she can be seen to be exploiting his infatuation, the love that Regan offers him is monetary, not sexual. So Foakes (ed. 1997). Cf. 2677–8.

2409 rather]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Presumably elliptical for something like I had rather die than disobey my lady. Johnson (ed. 1765): I know not well why Shakespeare gives the Steward, who is a mere factor of wickedness, so much fidelity here and at 2701–3. Pye (1807, p. 293): Dr. Johnson…did not recollect the character Edgar gives of this steward after he is dead:—[quotes 2705–6]. Fidelity in agents of wickedness is, I fear, not so uncommon as to be unfit for the general probability of dramatic manners. Verplanck (ed. 1844): Zealous, honourable, even self-sacrificing fidelity…appears to be so little dependent on any principle of virtuous duty, that it is often found strongest among those who have thrown off the common restraints of morality.…The most abandoned mind…as it loses sight of nobler and truer duties becomes, like the Steward, more and more duteous to the vices of its self-chosen masters. Buck (ed. 1907): As far as we know, this unreasoning fidelity is the only good trait in Oswald’s character. It was probably owing to this that Goneril reposed so much confidence in him. Joseph (ed. 1966, p. 31) seems to infer that Oswald is acting upon instruction, with ironic results: The double game of the two sisters has meant that the younger must be kept out of the plot to remove Albany. As a result Oswald must not let her know the contents of the letter which he is unable to give to Edmund. And ironically, Edmund is not there to receive it, not only because he has gone to descry | The strength o’th’enemy, but to stop Gloucester moving all hearts against us.…Edmund’s absence costs him throne, queen, and life. Regan’s assurance that Preferment…off leads Oswald to make the mistake of trying to attack the blind traitor. With Oswald’s death, Edgar finds himself at last quite unexpectedly in a position to make a real move against Edmund. Mahood (1992, p. 238): Oswald’s words at 2676–8 confirm that Oswald’s fidelity…is mercenary. In a similar scene in Leir 990 ff. the Messenger fears punishment if Gonorill opens the king’s letters; see n. 2407–8.

2411 late]
See n. 718. The occasion referred to cannot be later than 3.7. Therefore here is apparently Gloucester’s house. See nn. 2065, 2066, and 2382.

2412 aliads]
This and F’s Eliads are variant spellings of Oeillade, A glance of the eye, esp. an amorous glance (OED). In Wiv. 1.3.61 (351) it appears as illiads.

2412 speaking]
Schmidt (1875): Expressive (OED, ppl. a. 2b). Muir (ed. 1952): Montaigne calls the lookes and rowling of [lovers’] eyes one kind of speaking (tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 2:144–5).

2413 of her bosome]
See n. 125. Delius (ed. 1854): In her confidence. OED (Bosom sb. 6a): To be of (a person’s) bosom: to be entrusted with his secrets, quoting this l. Adee (ed. 1890, p. lx) finds here a hint at Goneril’s…infidelity with her Steward Oswald (of which we have a broader glimpse in the old chronicle play of Leir). There is no such glimpse; the fauour that Gonorill promises (Leir 1044–5) is preferment, not sex; see . Perrett (1904, p. 207): There is much against Adee’s idea. Would such a woman kill herself for love of Edmund? Colie (1974, p. 192): Why was he so willing to act as go-between for his mistress and Edmund? Cf. 2859+2–+3.

2414 Madam.]
Most eds., adopting F’s question mark or converting it to an exclamation point, imply that Oswald expresses surprise—sometimes played as an easy joke for a frankly effeminate Oswald (Rosenberg, 1972, p. 261). But it is probably not necessary to assume with Wilson (ed. 1960) that Osw. misinterprets bosom…at first. Regan should not expect, Oswald may mean to suggest, that a duchess would make a confidant of her steward. Regan, however, knows that Goneril has done so, having received from her a private letter composed and embroidered upon by Oswald (cf. 858–63).

2415 vnderstanding]
Schmidt (1875): Knowledge (OED, vbl. sb. 4).

2415 for]
Most eds. prefer F’s Y’are, though Q makes sense. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 411): The copy may have had yar…; if so, the y was presumably completely illegible (for y can hardly have been misread as f) and the compositor presumably guessed for. Wilson (ed. 1960) finds Y’are awkward in a mod. text. Evans (1961, p. 326) objects to editors’ expansion to you are, and to you’re at 2442 and 2444: Y’are is a shortened form of ye are not of you are (see NED) and indicates a different emphasis and pronunciation. Cf. n. 2799.

2416–23 take…farewell]
Lott (ed. 1974): Regan…snaps out short clauses in a peremptory style, designed to scare Oswald into conniving with her.

2416 this note]
Most eds. do not think that note means a short letter, as it does at 2970. Regan would not have written a note to Goneril warning her away from a relationship that she has begun to suspect only a moment before, nor has she an evident reason to send a note to Edmund, who must return that day from his reconnoitering if he is to lead her troop on the morrow. Smith (in Grey, 1754, 2:114) also objects that no letter from Regan is found on Oswald in the next scene [2709 ff.], for Had there been one of Regan’s too, the audience no doubt should have heard of it. Smidt (1990, p. 130): What becomes of that letter? The plural letters at 2701 and 2709 does not necessarily indicate more than one letter; see n. 875. Jennens (ed. 1770): The words give him this [2420]…explain it to be a letter; but see n. 2420. Campbell (1888, p. 496; 1904, pp. 251–2) holds for a letter as a way of revealing Regan’s passion, but thinks that Sh. suppresses it at 2709 so as not to load unnecessarily (and so to weaken) that later scene. Perrett (1904, p. 209): It appears that Reg. wished to substitute her note for Gon.’s letter; but she does not say so. Gardner (ed. 1969): Either a letter or some token is handed to Oswald four lines later. It is effective dramatically for take this note to refer to the letter, which Regan holds on to, pinning his attention, till she hands it over at [2420]. Smith (op. cit.) would emend to take note of this, whereas she only desired him to give, or deliver so much by word of mouth. Johnson (ed. 1765) and many followers give the same interpretation without emending: Not letter, but a remark. Therefore observe what I am saying. But the idiom is not quite right: when Sh. uses the sense notice, regard, or attention (OED, sb.2 20) in the phrase to take note (OED, 20b), he uses of, which is absent here. Collier (ed. 1843) seems more probably correct: This knowledge, or information, comparing 1627; cf. Hunter (ed. 1869): This notice. This sense of note is rare (OED, 20c), though Sh. uses it in Tro. 4.1.44 (2216); more common is the phrase take a note meaning fix in the mind or memory (OED, 13b, quoting TGV 2.7.84 [1059]). The latter makes ideal sense here: Regan says Now get this straight, proceeds to give Oswald a succinct account of what the true situation is, tells him he may infer the rest, and concludes by demonstrating her closeness to Edmund in sending some token. Only Brooke (ed. 1947), questionably, detects a musical metaphor: Speak to her in this key. One other meaning is remotely possible—note = Office; employment (OED, sb.1 2)—but the sense is not recorded after 1513.

2417 My…dead]
Skillan (ed. 1967): This is news to osw. and puts him more in the persuasive power of reg.

2417 talkt]
Delius (ed. 1854): Come to a mutual agreement. Craig (ed. 1901): Are affianced to one another. Cf. 2902. Rosenberg (1972, pp. 263–4): Regan now fills in a blank…[and] provides them a history—of unseen events anticipated by Goneril in 2330–3. Foakes (ed. 1997): There has been no chance for them to speak about love or marriage in the play so far; Shakespeare again short-cuts the action. Not necessarily. Goneril sent Edmund to Cornwall (thinking him still alive) at 2283; instead he met Regan, whom he has recently left (2393); the interim was theirs for love-making.

2418 conuenient]
See n. 1709.

2419 gather more]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Infer more than I have directly told you. Harbage (ed. 1958): Draw your own conclusions. Quinn (ed. 1970): Become more informed. McCann (ed. 1964): That we are already lovers. Eds. put a stop after more, making the next line a separate statement that Hunter (ed. 1869) calls parenthetic. Weis (ed. 1993) puts a stop before more: She is being curt here.…The placing of more at the end of the line…conveys the necessary emphasis and the speaker’s feeling of urgency. But Wells (ed. 2000) defends Q’s pointing: The cryptic quality…is in keeping with the rest of the speech.

2420 this]
Eds. are divided whether this is a letter (see n. 2416) or a love-token (first suggested by Capell, 1783, 1.2:178) to demonstrate to Oswald her intimacy with Edmund. In either case, Oswald, who Kent had predicted could pander for his master (1095, 1146–52), now assents to pander for his mistress’s rival. Quinn (ed. 1970) alone: This account of the situation.

2421 thus much]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): I.e., what I have told you. And perhaps shown, in sending a token to Edmund.

2422–3 I…farewell]
Hubler (1935, p. 435): The [Q1] compositor has combined a fraction of a line with the preceding line.

2422 desire…her]
Hudson (ed. 1881): Tell her to do her worst, and help herself, if she can. But clearly the phrase means, Tell her to come to her senses. Moberly (ed. 1876): And give up all thoughts of Edmund. Edwards (ed. 1975), call: Recall. On the infinitive without to see Franz §650.

2425 Preferment]
Schmidt (1875): Advancement, promotion (OED, 2). Skillan (ed. 1967): Since osw. is gon.’s servant, [this] implies an open but subtly made attempt to win him away from her so that there can be no more messages. Van Dam (1935, p. 104), most improbably: I prefer you [Oswald] to him [Edmund] if you kill Gloucester.

2426 him]
F’s omission is a kind of error to be expected from Compositor B (Werstine, 1983, p. 283).

2426–7 I…follow]
Perrett (1904, p. 209): In [Leir 1211, 1318–24; see , ], the Messenger is bribed by Ragan, with a purse of gold for each, to murder both Leir and Perillus.…The idea of having Leir murdered originates with Gonorill [Leir 1053–5].…That of murdering Perillus, on the contrary, belongs entirely to Ragan. See , , . Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905), of Ragan’s Messenger: The bolder nature of his readiness appears in his answer to Ragan.…I weigh no more the murdring of a man, Then I respect the cracking of a Flea [Leir 1214–15].

2427 Lady]
I.e., in this case he follows Regan (rather than Cordelia). But he is in Goneril’s employ, and has been steadfastly loyal to her, and talk up to now has been about Regan’s competition with her. Greg (1933, p. 255), improbably assuming a text reported from performance: An actor’s confusion. Van Dam (1935, p. 104), imagining absurdly (see 2417–19) that Oswald intends to marry Regan: Lady is genuine, and party is slip-slop. F’s party may be intended to avoid ambiguity about what lady Oswald means: he follows the home party, not the invaders as Gloucester does. So Hunter (ed. 1972): Like a good politician Oswald…express[es] the solidarity of Gonerill and Regan. Colman (ed. 1982): A nicely ambiguous statement of loyalty, since there are now several opposed parties.

2429 <Scena Quinta>]
The sixth scene in Q and most eds.; see n. 2348. For the time when the scene takes place see n. 2347+1–+56, end. Kittredge (ed. 1940): This scene must take place on the same day as in Scene v. The interval between the present scene and Scene iii cannot be more than one day. Adams (1948, p. 329) imagines (unnecessarily) that the Globe stage had painted curtains over the central discovery space and property trees at either end, perhaps even a cave-mouth entrance at the rear. Johnson (ed. 1765): This scene and the stratagem by which Glou’ster is cured of his desperation, are wholly borrowed from Sidney’s Arcadia (2.10.1–2; see ). Hunter (ed. 1845, 2:273): But this is a mistake. It is true we have a blind king, who seeks the brow of a rock with the intention of throwing himself headlong. He asks his son to conduct him thither.…[But] the son in the Arcadia…refuses to conduct his father to the spot. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Shakespeare’s Edgar, on the contrary, obeys, guessing what his father intends without discussing it with him, and saves him by the ruse here enacted, which also cleverly serves the dramatic purpose of the author by enabling Edgar to drop his Bedlam disguise. Muir (1955, p. 15): in Holinshed, two pages before the story of Lear, the cliff over which Corineus threw the giant Gogmagog is called the fall or leape of Gogmagog, but afterwards…the fall of Douer: It is possible that Edgar’s description of the imaginary fiend with eyes like two full moons was influenced by Holinshed’s account. Dutton (1986, pp. 142–3): An allusion to Brute, who caused Corineus to wrestle the giant Gogmagog, would be consistent with Jacobean use of British mythology to support the efforts of James, the new Brute, to unify England. Since Gloucester is no Gogmagog, however, such an allusion might not have been recognized by an audience nor its point understood. Coyle (1984, p. 206), anticipated by Maxwell (in Wilson, ed. 1960), also compares Malbecco’s attempted suicide in F.Q. 3.10.56–7, in which Spenser stresses the terror of looking over the edge of the cliff, and Malbecco is blind in one eye, driven to madness and despair by womankind [by Hellenore], and cheated of death as Gloucester is by surviving a fall.
Smith (ed. 1902): This important scene is divided roughly into three parts. The first…is a direct continuation of the opening scene of this act; the second brings into comparison Lear and Gloucester in the height of their suffering; and the third, unlike the others, is devoted mainly to the unravelling of the plot. Hunter (ed. 1972): In this stupendous scene the stories of the blind Gloucester and the mad Lear…cross and reach a common climax.…The broken reverence of Gloucester, never far from despair, and the free-wheeling phantasmagoric energy of Lear point up two opposite ways of reacting to oppression and impotence.…The denouement of the Gloucester plot is prepared for by the time-honoured device of an intercepted letter. Edwards (ed. 1975): Lear’s manic patter, conveying a profound and painful assessment of man’s life, is one of the most brilliant things Shakespeare does in this play. Warren (1983, p. 50) stresses the superiority of the middle section of this scene to the mock trial in 3.6, which he believes was cut to throw this one into greater prominence: The mock trial presents an arraignment of the daughters and of false justice in terms of an ensemble of madness, whereas 4.6 does so by concentrating on Lear’s mad mind alone. This scene provides the most effective presentation of the way his mind works, of the logical connections which underlie the mad remarks.…These connections help to provide a concentration, a focus, upon the mad remarks which the eccentric digressions of the mock trial tend to dissipate.…Lear’s verbal arraignment of women and justice arises out of the details of their dramatic relationship, rather than through the elaborate creation of an imaginary courtroom. The reunion of Lear and Gloucester in 4.6 is a much simpler, more human scene. One reason that the Lear section here is more prominent and affecting, of course, is that it is four times as long as the mock trial. Foakes (1993, p. 204): The scene begins with a mock-death, goes on to the encounter of two old men conscious of ruin and mortality, with Lear imagining killing his sons-in-law…, and running off to die bravely, and then ends with the violent death on stage of Oswald.…Edgar grows in power and stature, mentally in manipulating his father, physically in defeating and killing Oswald. At the same time this scene registers a sense of reconciliation between Gloucester and Edgar…and between Lear and Gloucester. The power of the scene lies in its extension of the sense of confusion, in its extraordinary combination of violence and pathos, cruelty and pity, hostility and reconciliation, and its visual and verbal reminders that Lear and Gloucester have death on their minds. He describes how staging and costumes in modern productions suggest an apocalyptic vision (ibid., p. 33).

2430 Edmund]
Error for F’s Edgar. See n. 2283. Wilson (ed. 1960): Edg. has received the best ’parel promised by the Old Man at [2238]. See textual n. Martey (1952): Edgar assumes different disguises of increasing social stature, which point the way to and symbolically aid in Gloucester’s conversion from despairing subservience. Foakes (ed. 1997): He looks like a peasant to Oswald at [2683], and no longer speaks like Poor Tom.

2431–44 When…spoken]
Foakes (ed. 1997): Shakespeare seems anxious to dispel illusion and make us conscious of the trick being played on Gloucester, as he draws the attention of the audience to Edgar’s deception of his father.…In leading his father to suicide, Edgar is playing the traditional role of the devil, citing 1835–6, 2517.

2431 we]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 157): F’s I accords with Edgar’s You in 2432. But cf. we in the same line. Hogan (1962, p. 75): F just fits [the column]; with we it would not fit. Werstine (privately): Other, less intrusive space-saving devices could have been employed: cutting hill down to hil, or omitting space after the SP. It hardly seems likely therefore that the variant is compositorial as Hogan suggests. Blake (1996, p. 161): By the change Edgar’s answer is made more specific.…The wish to be more literal is perhaps evident here.

2431 same hill]
Delius (ed. 1854): Dover cliff, described by Gloucester, 2256–9. Chambers (1940, p. 48): Symbolically, the mountain of Purgatory. Guilfoyle (1989; 1990, p. 119): Rather, the pinnacle of the temple at Jerusalem where Christ was tempted. The text does not make such allusions evident.

2432 it vp now]
Wright (ed. 1875) provides contemporary exx. of this inversion of the preposition with climb up and go up. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 522) think Q’s order unmetrical, adding, Blayney notes that Q’s spacing error [vpnow] suggests that vp was omitted in foul proofs, and then inserted in the wrong place.

2433 euen]
Schmidt (1874): Level (OED, a. 1, quoting this l.).

2434 Horrible]
Abbott (§1): Adjectives are freely used as Adverbs, as this one is in TN 3.4.179 (1695), 1H4 2.4.366 (1322); §2: Hence two adverbs were freely combined together, the first being a kind of adverb qualifying the second. So OED (adv., quoting this l.); cf. Franz §241. Collier (ed. 1858): It might be meant that Edgar should not speak with strict propriety.

2435–6 harke…truly]
The line is a syllable short but may be read with five accents. James (1960, pp. 60 ff.) shows how Edgar’s question haunted and influenced Keats.

2437–8 other…anguish]
See nn. 1791–4, 2365. Muir (ed. 1952): Probably means the physical pain Gloucester is suffering, rather than his grief at the loss of his eyes.

2437 imperfect]
Schmidt (1874): Defective (OED, a. 2, quoting this l.). Evans (ed. 1898): In [2457] Edgar has another reason ready.

2440 altered]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Edgar alters his voice in order to pass afterwards for a malignant spirit—who presumably would sound as Poor Tom had previously. Kelcy (1932, p. 369), answering Johnson: I cannot see how that would help Edgar to pass for a malignant spirit. I think there are two possible explanations: (1) Shakespeare thought that Gloucester’s remark would have some dramatic effect on the audience, who know that the beggar is really Edgar. From a psychological standpoint Shakespeare would justify the change in Edgar’s voice and language by his being tired of his assumed character. (2) Edgar speaks in better phrase and matter than he did so as to prepare his father for his magnificent description of Dover Cliff. Or has Edgar unconsciously changed his speech with his change of clothes? See n. 2443. Muir (ed. 1952): Shakespeare marks the change by making him speak in verse. Houghton (ed. 1957): Whereas in iv. i. he spoke [to Gloucester] in prose.

2441 With]
F’s In makes no better sense with phrase and worse with matter.

2441 phrase]
See n. 2467–9. Wells (ed. 2000): Edgar now speaks verse.

2441 matter]
See n. 398 and OED (sb. 11b): Sense, substance (as opposed to nonsense or trifling). Cf. 2616.

2442, 2444 much deceaued]
Mooney (1985, p. 162): Gloucester is right in saying the ground is level, that he does not hear the sea, and that Edgar’s speech is altered. But…his son is duping him as to his real identity, is duping Gloucester’s ability to feel and hear, and is drawing attention to Gloucester’s defective ways of perceiving the world.

2443 garments]
Joseph (ed. 1966): The clothes brought for him by the old servant to Gloucester [see 2238]. They provide Edgar with a more substantial disguise than the near nakedness of a Bedlam. He can now speak like a peasant; there is no need to feign the madman.

2444 better spoken]
Delius (ed. 1854): Comparative of well-spoken. Franz (§661, spoken): Past participle with active sense. Craig (ed. 1901): You speak with better accent, propriety, grace.

2446–59 her’s…headlong]
This passage has been much discussed both for its own merits and as an example of the literary sublime. Lessing (1762–6; ed. Barner, 1990, 5.2.306) compares Edgar’s lines with Milton’s description of the prospect of Chaos in PL 7.210–215: This depth is far greater than Dover Cliff, and yet the description of it produces no effect, because there is nothing visible to make it real to us, whereas in Shakespeare this is so admirably managed by the gradual lessening of the various objects (Furness’s tr.). Johnson (ed. 1765), who put a premium on the grandeur of generality, finds it too particular for sublimity: Addison [Tatler, No. 117, 7 Jan. 1710]…remarked, with a poor attempt at pleasantry, that he who can read it without being giddy has a very good head, or a very bad one. The description is certainly not mean, but I am far from thinking it wrought to the utmost excellence of poetry. He that looks from a precipice finds himself assailed by one great and dreadful image of irresistible destruction. But this overwhelming idea is dissipated and enfeebled from the instant the mind can restore itself to the observation of particulars, and diffuse its attention to distinct objects. The enumeration of the choughs and crows, the samphire-man and the fishers, counteracts the great effect of the prospect, as it peoples the desert of intermediate vacuity, and stops the mind in the rapidity of its descent through emptiness and horror. Mason (1785, p. 353): Edgar is describing an imaginary precipice, and is not therefore to be supposed to be impressed so strongly with the dreadful prospect of inevitable destruction, as a person would be who really found himself on the brink of one. Eccles (ed. 1792): The purpose of Edgar’s enumeration of particulars was not…to excite in the mind of the reader, or spectator, the most sublime and awful affections, but, by a minute and faithful detail of…circumstances…, to give the highest possible air of probability to the imposition which he designed to practice on…his father. Knight (ed. 1840) sees the dislike of the observation of particulars as typical of neoclassic criticism and of Johnson, and quotes a passage from Boswell’s Life [Hill-Powell ed., 1934, 2:85–7] preferring a passage from Congreve to this one on these same grounds. Knight argues that a more general description would have had less dramatic propriety, failing to provide the blind man an imaginary standard by which Gloster can measure the altitude of the cliff.…The very defects which Johnson imputes to Shakspere’s description constitute its dramatic merit…[and] surpassing poetical beauty. Saintsbury (1908, 2:45) admires the regular, cunningly jointed, but swiftly moving verse, a sort of under-the-breath of apprehension, as if boisterous speaking might bring danger. Rolfe (1895, p. 180): It has been generally agreed…that this cliff is the one just outside of Dover to the southwest, now known as Shakespeare’s Cliff.…Some critics have questioned whether Shakespeare had ever seen the cliff.…As the chalk is only about 350 feet high at this point, objects below do not seem so small as one would infer from the passage.…But the critics seem to have forgotten that Edgar is not describing what he sees. They are not standing on the edge of the cliff,…but at a safe distance from it…on the Road to Dover. Verity (ed. 1897): It may be that the lack of scenery…on the Elizabethan stage had something to do with the introduction of long passages of description. Smith (ed. 1902), preferring romantic to neoclassic description: A generalized description could present only a vague image of altitude. It would never make us feel the giddy height. Buck (ed. 1907): Its height is exaggerated to increase the effect of the supposed miracle wrought in Gloucester’s favor. Goggin (ed. 1910) agrees, adding a second reason: The dramatist wished to emphasise to the audience the tragic character of the Scene and the horror of Gloucester’s meditated act.…It may be added that Shakespeare is obviously describing what he had himself seen, and that the whole speech is out of accord with Edgar’s assumed character. Ewbank (1971, p. 18): It creates and makes real to us a scene which yet our eyes tell us does not exist. McLuhan (1962, pp. 15, 17): The first…piece of verbal three-dimensional perspective in any literature.…What Shakespeare does here is to place five flat panels of two dimensions one behind the other. By giving these flat panels a diagonal twist they succeed each other, as it were, in a perspective from the stand-still point. Hunter (ed. 1972): The set-piece description built up, layer by layer, by accumulation of small details is designed to convey to the blind Gloucester the standards of measurement he should apply to the precipice and to convey to the audience the powerful and coherent nature of poetic illusion, by which Gloucester’s cure is to be effected. Kott (tr. 1964, p. 145): The non-existent cliff is not meant just to deceive the blind man. For a short while we, too, [believe] in this landscape. Halio (ed. 1992): We do and we don’t.…The trick Edgar plays on his father’s imagination is also the trick Shakespeare plays on ours—except that here he means us to be conscious of everything that is happening, including the way in which our imagination is being made to work. States (1982, p. 422): Sh. achieves the illusion of spatial depth by employing Breughel’s technique of articulating distant detail more clearly than the eye would actually see it. Goldberg (1988, p. 247): Edgar’s lines describing Dover Cliff establish themselves as illusion by illusionistic rhetoric, including (pp. 250 ff.) Albertian perspective leading the eye towards (p. 256) the nothing of the vanishing point. Watkins (1950, p. 205): Even the rhythm of his words suggests vertigo and the holding of the breath. Darras (1994, p. 162): A profound meditation on space. Toliver (1985, pp. 175–7): The vertiginous danger described is a metaphor for the personal situations of both Gloucester and Lear.
Taylor (1925, p. 11), Henderson (1940, pp. 42–3), and Anderson (1971–2, p. 280) suggest a source in Montaigne, who describes in Sebond how a man’s sight of…exceeding height must needs dazle his sight, and amaze or turne his senses, and who records his own dreade and giddinesse in the Alps; see and cf. n. 2949. Perhaps on a hint in Murray (1910, 2:264 n.), however, Harrison (ed. 1937): This vivid description seems based on observation. The King’s Players visited Dover in September 1606 [actually 30 Aug.; see Gibson, 2002, p. 495 and Gurr, 1996, p. 305], an idea repeated by Fripp (1938, p. 655), who says that Sh. had been there before in Feb. 1588 and Sept. 1597. The Chamberlain’s company was there at least some time prior to 3 Sept. 1597, when payment was made (Gibson, p. 484). See Chambers (1930, 2:321, 333), and n. 2775+1–+2. Muir (ed. 1952, p. xxiv) adds 4 Oct. 1605. The latter date is unattested, but Gibson (p. 602) and Gurr (p. 304) record the company’s presence nearby in Fordwich, Kent, on 6 Oct. 1605. Gibson (pp. 484, 562) and Gurr (pp. 303–5) also list Dover and Faversham visits in 1596–7. Following Armstrong (1946, pp. 18–19), Wilson (ed. 1960) compares Ham. 1.4.69–78 (658–663+4). Kaula (1979), improbably, finds Biblical associations between the samphire-gatherer and Christ, the cock-boat and the Church, etc., designed to reinforce [Gloucester’s] despair by demonic temptation.

2447 dizi]
Schmidt (1874): Causing giddiness (OED, a. 4, quoting only this l.).

2448 choghes]
Commentators are divided whether the word refers to the common jackdaw, Corvus monedula (OED, Chough 1, quoting MND 3.2.21 [1043], russet pated choughes), or to the Red-legged Crow (Fregillus Graculus), which frequents the sea-cliffs in many parts of Britain, being particularly abundant in Cornwall; whence distinguished as the Cornish Chough. <This may have been Shakspere’s chough in Lear; the bird, now rare at Beachey Head, was abundant on all the Sussex cliffs a century ago, and may well have been common on the Kentish coast at an earlier date.> Kittredge (ed. 1940): Pronounced chuffs.

2448 wing]
OED (v. 3a): Fly through, quoting this l. as its first ex.

2448 midway]
Delius (ed. 1854): Halfway between the top and foot (OED, adj. 1, quoting this l. as its first ex.).

2449 grosse]
Schmidt (1874): Big (OED, adj. 1, quoting this l.).

2450 sampire]
Samphire (F. herbe de Saint Pierre). OED: Possibly the attribution to St. Peter may have been suggested by Late L. petra (F. pierre) rock. 1. The plant Crithmum maritimum (growing on rocks by the sea). Prior (1879, p. 206): From its love of sea-cliffs, dedicated to the fisherman saint. Tollet (in Steevens, ed. 1778), quotes from Smith’s History of Waterford (1774, p. 315): It is terrible to see how people gather it, hanging by a rope several fathom from the top of the impending rocks as it were in the air. Malone (ed. 1790): The gathering of samphire was literally a trade…, it being carried and cried about the streets, and much used as a pickle. Idem (in Boswell, ed. 1821): Dover Cliff was particularly resorted to for this plant, citing Drayton, Poly-olbion 18.763–4 (ed. Hebel); Gerard, Herball (1597, p. 428) says the same (Wright, ed. 1875), and Rydén (1978, p. 62) cites other contemporary references to the fact, adding, The collection is not always as dramatic as described by Shakespeare. The plant may grow within easy reach. Beisly (1864, p. 144): The plants do not grow on any place which the sea covers; and Shakspere noticed this fact in describing it as growing half-way down the cliff at Dover. Moberly (ed. 1876): This [account of samphire-gathering] is the realizing touch in the description, as it seems a thing that could not be imagined.

2452 walke]
F’s walk’d shows the confusion of final e and d (Walker, 1860, 2:65).

2452 beach]
Doran (1931, p. 31): If Q2’s beake is a purely mechanical misprint, due to foul case or faulty muscular co-ordination, it is a double one, k being misprinted for c, and e for h. It does not appear to be a manuscript misreading, beach mistaken for beack, for instance, because neither the English nor the Italian h resembles an Elizabethan k. Possibly, then, it represents confusion: see n. 1910.

2453 yon]
Though the spelling is indifferent, F changes to yond four times: cf. 2563, 2596. All instances were set by Compositor B. Hunter (ed. 1972): A recurrent Folio mannerism, spread across several plays, and seems to reflect its modernizing tendencies…rather than its concern for accuracy. Franz (§319), however, thinks yond was archaic, not modern. In fact both forms had been used for centuries and are still used (OED, Yon a. 1, Yond a. 2).

2453 anchoring]
Deighton (ed. 1891): At anchor (OED, ppl. a. a, quoting this l. as its first ex.).

2453–4 barke…boui]
A bark is a small ship. Hunt (1990) finds sexual puns on bark (female body), cock, and boy (passive homosexual) that indicate Goneril’s and Regan’s unnatural and self-destructive hermaphroditic sexuality. The speech does not refer to them, however, and Edgar is concentrating on his suicidal father, not the sexuality of Lear’s daughters.

2454 cock]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Cock-boat (OED, sb.3, quoting this l.). Knight (ed. 1840): A small boat towing. Whall (1910, pp. 9, 31): The second boat of a ship; Large ships of that day had three boats. The boat, the cock and the skiff.

2454 boui]
Whall (1910, p. 32): The anchor buoy. Blayney (1982, p. 172): Q1 Compositor B would probably have changed to buoy if he had understood the word, which probably follows copy.

2455 surge]
OED (sb. 2a): A high rolling swell of water; (2b): Such waves or billows collectively. Falconer (1965, p. 83): Especially…which beat and break upon the shores.

2456 vnnumbred]
Delius (ed. 1854): Innumerable. See n. 284.

2456 idle]
Glosses such as barren, uncultivated (Warburton, ed. 1747), trifling, insignificant (Eccles, ed. 1792), unprofitable (Deighton, ed. 1891), etc. are extensions of the basic meaning useless; see n. 2355. Skillan (ed. 1967): Motionless, in contrast with…the surf. Edwards (ed. 1975): Shifting about like a crowd of people with nothing to do.

2456 peeble]
Eds. unnecessarily alter to a plural, producing harsh sibilants (Furness, ed. 1880). Verity (ed. 1897): In a collective sense, like the sand (OED, sb. 1b).

2456 chaffes]
OED (Chafe v. 9): To rub; to press or strike with friction (on), quoting this l. and comparing (10c): Of the sea, etc.: To fret, rage, or fume.

2457 its so hie]
Though virtually all eds. follow F (see textual n.) in making so high adverbial, modifying heard, the Q punctuation indicates that its so hie introduces the next clause: it’s so high I’ll look no more. Q makes perfectly good sense, and can hardly be objected to on the grounds of an extra unaccented syllable its, whose removal in F makes strictly regular meter. The punctuation of Q2 has no authority, and it is possible that F’s similarity to it means that a scribe or compositor either adopted it or arrived at it independently to remove ambiguity from a MS having commas after both heard and high.

2458 turne]
See n. 1722.

2458 deficient]
Delius (ed. 1854): Refers to a defect of the senses; cf. Oth. 1.3.63 (400). Schmidt (1874): Failing, fainting (OED, a. 4, quoting this l. as its first of two exx.). Hunter (ed. 1869): Losing…discernment. Deighton (ed. 1891): Unable long to look down such a dizzy height.

2458 sight]
Seymour (1805, 2:127) first points out the metonymy: The person defective of sight. Kittredge (ed. 1940) glosses as an absolute construction: I, my sight failing me. Harbage (ed. 1958): My dizziness.

2459 topple]
Most eds. treat the verb as intransitive. Harbage (ed. 1958), however: Topple me.

2461–3 Giue…vpright]
Q’s lineation makes regular verse, F’s results in two short lines and two irregular ones. Doran (1931, p. 109): The misalignment in F indicates that the F printer was not using Q1 copy but a manuscript.

2462 th’extreame verge]
Crook (ed. 1907): Edgar, of course, places his father well out of danger from falling. Wells (ed. 2000): Not spoken close to the edge of the stage. For the accent on the first syllable of extreame, see n. 250. For verge see n. 1427.

2463 vpright]
Schmidt (1875): Straight up (OED, adv. 2, quoting this l.). Warburton (ed. 1747): But what danger in leaping upright or upwards? He who leaps thus must needs fall again on his feet upon the place whence he rose. Malone (ed. 1790): If [Warburton] had tried such a leap within a foot of the edge of a precipice, before he undertook the revision of these plays, the world would, I fear, have been deprived of his labours. Heath (1765, p. 346): Even upright. Harbage (ed. 1958) adds, Let alone forward.

2465 another pursse]
Delius (ed. 1854): See [2249]. Tovey (ed. 1896): Well-to-do persons sorted the money and valuables they carried about with them in separate purses. The extravagance with which characters in the Elizabethan drama part with their purses is apparent rather than real.

2466 Fairies]
The exact role of the fairies depends on the referent of it (see next n.). Some eds. refer it to Gloucester’s jewel. Delius (ed. 1854): Gold acquired with the help of fairies brought especially good luck (Ger.), comparing WT 3.3.123 (1562), Faiery Gold. The idea seems not relevant here. Kittredge (ed. 1940): There are two superstitious notions about fairy gold. One is that it merely seems to be gold, and resumes its real nature as rubbish when the finder has stored it away. The other is that hidden treasure is guarded by fairies and that they make it multiply miraculously in the possession of the discoverer. The latter notion could apply here. Other eds. take it as an impersonal pronoun, referring to Edgar’s future luck. Edwards (ed. 1975): May fairies and gods make the jewel bring good to you. Foakes (ed. 1997): Gloucester may also be asking for secrecy, since Fairies treasure…but reveal’d, brings on the blabbers ruine (Philip Massinger and Nathan Field, Fatal Dowry, ?1617–19, 4.1.191–2); see also WT 3.3.123–6 [1562–5]. Armour (ed. 1930): The credulous nature of Gloucester has been referred to already. Harrison (ed. 1948): As this tale is pre-Christian, it is natural for the characters to call on the gods of the elder world. Elton (1966, p. 152): Gloucester’s reference here implies a paganism leaning toward superstition. Already, in the Daemonologie (1597), King James had condemned such beliefs as deluded paganism.

2467 Prosper it]
Probably the it is impersonal. Joseph (ed. 1966): Give thee prosperity. (But it may refer to the purse and the jewel; make it increase with you and bring happiness with it.)

2467–9 thee…you]
F changes you to ye. Abbott (§232): Thou is generally used by a master to a servant.…It may seem an exception that in sc. iv. i [2244], Edgar uses thou to Gloucester, but this is only because he is in the height of his assumed madness.…Afterwards, in sc. vi., he invariably uses you—a change which, together with other changes in his language, makes Gloucester say: Thou…thou didst. [2440–1]. It may be partly this increased respect for Edgar, and partly euphony, which makes Gloucester use you in [2444, 2460]. But Gloucester probably says ye at 2444; see n. 2415. Cf. n. 490.

2470 heart]
See n. 402. Hunter (ed. 1972): I endorse heartily what you have said; I am going to fare well where I am going (to my death).

2471–2525 Why…thoughts]
Stewart (1914, p. 112): There is not in all literature—there could not be—a scene so beautiful as this cliff episode when we understand it. The son, with deep insight of the state of affairs, contrives to heal his father’s maimed soul. He has given him back his faith. Craig (ed. 1931): This passage has important moral and theological import. Its plain teaching is against suicide; in that, as in other matters, the play is Christian in spite of its pagan setting. Gardner (1967, p. 9 n.): To our taste the deception of a blind man is not matter for laughter; but Shakespeare exploited it for comic purpose in The Merchant of Venice, and…[the episode here] has a parallel in the cruel trick that Lazarillo de Tormes plays on the blind beggar, his master, telling him to jump across a non-existent stream when he is actually standing face to face with a stone pillar. The incident is referred to in [Ado 2.1.198–200 (604–5)]. But the motive there is revenge. Foakes (ed. 1997): Edgar may be seen as playing a game with his father, one that has an element of cruelty, since it leads Gloucester to expect, and then denies him, the one thing he wants, death (see [2489]). It is often said that Gloucester in his despair is brought to accept his lot [Hunter, ed. 1972], but although he does so for the moment, [2520–2], his encounter with Oswald later in the scene leads him again to desire death, [2681–2], and he is in ill thoughts again at [2931]. No wonder that there has been much debate about the nature of this episode, which may be seen as grotesque, comic, absurd, tragic, or a combination of these, comparing Bratton (ed. 1987). Edgar says that he is being cruel in order to be kind. Psychoanalytic critics find less admirable motives of guilt, shame, and denial. See n. 2204–5.

2471–2 Why…it]
Verity (ed. 1897): Edgar sees that the only way to keep his father from suicide is to make him believe that heaven has interposed miraculously to prevent his self-destruction. Kittredge (ed. 1940): A very necessary aside for the enlightenment of the audience. Edgar is trying a dangerous experiment, for the agitation may be too great for Gloucester’s strength; but the experiment succeeds. Brooke (ed. 1947): Edgar’s purpose is to give Gloucester a sense of the value of his life by persuading him that the evil powers have attempted to destroy him and the good have preserved him. Joseph (ed. 1966): Edgar stands away from his father, who must hear him remove himself. This is not a direct speech to the audience, out of character.…Here, almost weakened in his resolution by pity, Edgar wishes he did not have to continue. Kernan (1966, p. 61): The point of Edgar’s brief morality play is clear. The last sight that Gloucester saw was the diabolic face and the hands of a man reaching to tear out his eyes, and he staggered away from this total denial of human-kind,…despairing of any value in life.…Edgar…arranges a lesson to persuade his father that life itself, under any conditions, is a miracle to be valued and cherished. Schleiner (1985, p. 338): His actions are not only curative but consistent with the psychiatric theory and practice of the period,—that the therapist pretend to believe the patient’s delusions while inventing ingenious subterfuges to restore him to reason.

2471–2 Why…cure]
Though the meaning is clear enough the syntax is illogical because Why is elliptical for (the reason) why (Page, ed. 1889; OED, adv. 5d, quoting this l. as its first ex.) and done is redundant (Harbage, ed. 1958). Abbott (§411): The sentence combines Why I trifle is to cure and My trifling is done to cure. Cf. 2914–15. Muir (ed. 1952): Such a confusion is, of course, common in colloquial speech.

2473–9 O…him]
Knight (1930, p. 187): A prayer of noble resignation—breathing that stoicism which permeates the suffering philosophy of this play; (ibid., p. 215): Gloucester moves beyond self-interest, through suffering, to the nobility and grandeur of his prayer. But see n. 2475. Milward (1987, p. 189) detects echoes of the ceremony of baptism and of 1 John 2:15–16. Leggatt (1992, p. 186): There is irony for a Christian audience: Gloucester kneels in a traditional act of prayer just before attempting suicide. Dodd (1752, 2:130) compares the Chorus’s speech on acceptance of heaven’s will in Sophocles’ Oed. Col. 1692–3.

2474 sights]
On the plural see n. 9.

2475 Shake…off]
Edwards (ed. 1975): He will end his life in resignation, not hot anger. The line reflects Gloucester’s ambivalence throughout the speech. To be patient means to bear, to endure, the opposite of shake off by suicide, an act which for Christians is a mortal sin caused by despair. See nn. 774, 1835, 2932, 3120, 3154, 3213, 3260. He seems to mean that he is presently resigned enough to accept the gods’ will to afflict him, but renounces life now rather than let the affliction continue until it is unbearable and he begins to quarrel with their will. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Gloucester implies that such rebellion would be a greater sin than suicide.

2476–7 fall to]
Craig (ed. 1901): Start…begin (OED, v. 99c).

2477 quarel]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Come to a state of rebellion against. Harbage (ed. 1958): Irreligiously.

2477 opposles]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:46): Not to be opposed, resistless (OED, a., quoting this l. as its first ex.). Clarkes (ed. 1868): Also ought not to be opposed.

2478 snurff]
Q’s sp., for F’s snuffe, is otherwise unrecorded, and may be due to a minim error in the copy Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 412) or to unconscious assimilation to a related word. OED (Snur v.), To snort, quotes from Skelton (1523) to snurre and snuf. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The meaning here is explained by the phrase that follows. Muir (ed. 1952): His brief candle is nearly burnt out. The image, occurring elsewhere in Sh., is proverbial (Dent, 1981, C49). OED (sb.1 1) quotes many exx. comparing the end of life to the guttering of a candle; in such cases snuff may either refer to a candle-end (Wilson, ed. 1960; cf. Cym. 1.6.87 [696]) or to a smoldering (and stinking) wick (Craig, ed. 1901; cf. AWW 1.2.59 [306]), implying either way what is faint, feeble, or on the point of extinction (OED, 1b), a useless residue (Bevington, ed. 1980). Chaplin (1969, p. 40), unnecessarily: Phallic, signifying his own sexuality. Greg (1940, p. 400) and Bullough (1973, p. 276), on a hint from Perrett (1904, p. 273): It may derive from Spenser; see n. 728–9.

2478 part of nature]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Remnant of life. See n. 1566.

2479 Burne…out]
Delius (ed. 1854): Burn out by itself. Tovey (ed. 1896): I.e., I would not seek death.

2479 blesse]
See n. 1839–40. Since the verb usually takes an object, eds. generally adopt F’s extrametrical him.

2480 fellow]
See n. 557.

2480 thee]
See n. 194.

2480 He fals]
F’s omission of the SD is probably due to oversight. There has been much comment on the staging of Gloucester’s fall, and on its effect on an audience. Lennox (1754, 3:300): The Adventure of the Rock is heightened by Shakespear; perhaps with too little Attention to Probability. Gloster, though deprived of Sight, might easily be sensible of the Difference between walking on a level Plain, and ascending a steep and craggy Rock; nor could he possibly suppose, when he fell gently on that Plain, that he had precipitated himself from an immense Height to the Margin of the Sea. Bratton (ed. 1987): In 1773 [apud Steevens, ed.] it struck one critic at least as a despicable farce to see Gloster taking a jump upon the boards.…Edmund Kean had his Edgar advance and catch Gloucester as he prepared to fall, and this became the accepted practice.…Charles Kean had Edgar interpose verbally instead of physically, shouting out Hold—who comes here?…The usual twentieth-century practice has been to require Gloucester to make the jump. Foakes (ed. 1997): In Peter Brook’s 1962 production he fainted as he fell. Bradley (1904, p. 249): Contrary to expectation, it is not, if properly acted, in the least absurd on the stage. The imagination and the feelings have been worked upon with such effect by the description of the cliff, and by the portrayal of the old man’s despair and his son’s courageous and loving wisdom, that we are unconscious of the grotesqueness of the incident for common sense. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 151): This inspired scene is a cunning set-off to the actual horror of his blinding. Knight (1930, pp. 187–8): Gloucester has planned a spectacular end for himself…a noble, tragic sacrifice. And what happens? The old man falls from his kneeling position a few inches, flat, face foremost…—just this. The grotesque merged into the ridiculous reaches a consummation in this bathos of tragedy: it is the furthest, most exaggerated, reach of the poet’s towering fantasticality. We have a sublimely daring stroke of technique, unjustifiable…on the plane of plot-logic.…The stroke is audacious, unashamed, and magical of effect. Kott (1964, p. 105): The scene is a philosophical buffoonery. Harrison (ed. 1937) thinks that the actor leaps from the upper gallery (though he does not explain how the blind Gloucester gets over the railing): While Gloucester is praying Edgar comes down from the gallery and reappears on the main stage as Gloucester falls from above. Idem (ed. 1948): To be effective this episode needs an actor who is not afraid of hurting himself, for unless Gloucester’s fall is heavy it is quite unconvincing. After his fall, he lies stunned for a few moments. A fall from a height of some eight to twelve feet would of course be convincing, but actors have understandably sought other expedients. Sprinchorn (1992, p. 93): What would the engrossed viewer think of a son who would lead his blind, not-so-spry father to the edge of a seven or eight foot drop, and then let him jump? Gloucester cannot in all reason be put in peril of so great a fall. Sprague (1944, p. 293): A discreet compromise was usually made, in nineteenth century performances, with the plain implications of Shakespeare’s lines. It involved, to be sure, a good deal of cutting. Gloster plunges forward, or is about to plunge forward, when Edgar catches him, and at the same time Lear enters to interrupt them. Adams (1948, pp. 330–1) imagines that a ramp, the oft-used mossbank, up which Edgar has helped his father, would supply a rim for the blind man’s toe to feel out—a verge evident to the audience as well as to Gloucester’s limited senses. The bank was apparently not oft-used; Dessen & Thomson (1999) find only five instances in SDs. Sprinchorn (loc. cit.) thinks such a lumpish hill would be theatrical flim-flam and inconsistent with the ground is euen (2224). He proposes instead a somewhat raised rear platform across the stage; see n. 2918. Levin (1959, pp. 98–100), seeing the scene as Gloucester’s descent to his nadir—a symbolic gesture of expiation, re-enacting his own original sin, as well as the fall of man and his consequent progression toward self-knowledge—discusses its impossibility on a modern representational stage, for, depending on realistic scenery, we should be fully aware whether Gloucester was or was not at the top of a hill.…On occasions, the Dover Cliffs have been painted upon the backdrop; it was to be inferred that Edgar had taken Gloucester directly to the beach, where he should not have had any trouble hearing the waves.…He falls, at all events, but not far. Not so far as from the upper stage,…inasmuch as Romeo needed a rope and—lacking one—Prince Arthur lost his life. There may be a single step or a simple platform; or, again, the business may be enough…the motions of an ineffectual jump. Similarly Kernan (1966, pp. 60–3; cf. 1979, pp. 122–3), seeing the leap as summariz[ing] the experiences of Lear and Gloucester and Edgar to this point in the play, supposes that the awkwardness, i.e., the stylization of having Gloucester fall off some sort of low step, though a shabby theatrical device, is part of the point: While Edgar’s miracle may be a trick, it is a trick devised to stage and state a truth in such a powerful way that Gloucester can understand that truth feelingly. McNeir (1962, pp. 97–9), after reporting the use of an onstage ramp in modern productions, proposes that Sh.’s company used instead a special Booth Stage erected against the rear wall; Gloucester and Edgar appeared on the gallery, climbed onto the roof of this stage, wherefrom first Gloucester and then Edgar leaped only seven or eight feet to the main stage. Peat (1973, p. 198): The working of the scene depends on our remaining confused on the very point of whether or not the cliff and sea exist. Idem (1980, p. 48): Perhaps the spectators are…terrified by the possibility that Gloucester has actually fallen from a cliff. It is only…after the event that Edgar reveals it is all an illusion. Dessen (1975, pp. 303–5) prefers no attempt at realism: Gloucester’s fall would be from a kneeling position to the ground on a perfectly flat stage.…This pious fraud [Levin’s term] perpetrated by Edgar (and Shakespeare) places the audience in a curious position. In questioning (or rejecting) the miracle and the moralization, the viewer is simultaneously questioning Albany’s confident assertions of iv.ii and the accompanying assumptions about heavenly intervention in man’s affairs. The obvious fiction created by Edgar and accepted by Gloucester prevents the audience from sharing that comforting illusion. Schleiner (1985, p. 341): It would enhance the believability of Edgar’s curative invention if Gloucester took his fall from an elevation, be it ever so slight. For after all, would the therapist, already once tripped up by the shrewd old man [at 2433–6]…, have risked blatantly challenging the physical perceptions of even a thoroughly disoriented Gloucester? Hattaway (2000, p. 210 [cf. Idem, 1992, ed. F. Laroque, 2:217–33]): Gloucester’s leap may be a visualization of the central metaphor of a tragic fall. We may read it as a penance that Edgar forces upon his father, and we may think it cruel.
The germ of the idea of Gloucester’s attempted suicide comes from Sidney’s Arcadia, and further analogues have been found in Spenser and Holinshed; see n. 2429. Muir (1957, p. 147): [Sh.] may have remembered, too, Seneca’s Thebais,…in which the blinded Oedipus asks Antigone to let him fall over a precipice, and…in Marston’s Malcontent [1604; 4.1.111–47] in which Pietro, in disguise, describes his own feigned suicide by leaping over a cliff into the sea. Livermore (1965, p. 188) finds a doubtful parallel with the un-Christian suicide of the Roman Curtius in St. Augustine, CD 5.18. Mueller (1994, p. 217): Details…come from Ariosto’s story of Ariodante (Orlando Furioso 5.58 ff.). Idem (1994, pp. 309): The similarities are Ariodante’s peasant guide, who is aghast at the height and steepness of the cliff, Ariodante’s putative happiness to die Had he bene blind, and a subsequent duel between brothers: see n. 3037–42.

2481 Gon sir]
Knight (ed. 1840): Not a question, as if Edgar asked Gloster if he had gone, but an assurance that his instruction in 2467 has been obeyed. Dyce (1844, p. 230): Gloster certainly does not leap, till after Edgar has said this line. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Edgar…goes, and lets him hear him going.…The distance is convenient both for his aside and for the pretext of approaching him again, as if he were another person.

2482 And yet]
Deighton (ed. 1891): And yet perhaps I ought not to pretend to leave him, for etc.

2482–4 I…theft]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Imagination may rob life’s treasury, when life seeks and expects its own destruction. Many instances have realized the saying, Imagination kills and cures. Goggin (ed. 1910): Edgar debates whether the belief that he is dead may actually have the effect of killing Gloucester. Wilson (ed. 1960): Since he has no desire to stay alive. Skillan (ed. 1967): edg. is genuinely alarmed. Holmes (1929, p. 61): This allusion to auto-suggestion is one of Shakespeare’s flashes of insight, his sharp human guesses, which science has since justified. Verity (ed. 1897) cites Montaigne’s anecdote in Of the Force of Imagination (tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 1:92–3) of a man on the scaffold killed without hanging, wounded only by the stroke of imagination. Schleiner (1985, p. 341; 1991, p. 283): As some Renaissance physicians reported, imagination can kill, citing one famous example often referred to in medical works.

2482 how]
Hudson (ed. 1871): Has about the force of whether or but that. Wells (ed. 2000): To what degree, citing Schmidt (1874, 4), who does not cite this line. Verity (ed. 1897): Elliptical…= I know not how it is, but it is a fact that. No ed. treats I…how as a parenthesis.

2482 conceit]
Schmidt (1874): Conception, idea, image in the mind (OED, sb. 1; cf. 2, The faculty of conceiving, and 3: The process or action of conceiving). Craig (ed. 1901): Imagination, wrong belief (OED, 7: A fanciful notion).

2482 my]
Simple error for Q2’s may.

2483 treasurie]
Deighton (ed. 1891) compares Jn. 5.1.40–1 (2208–9), An empty Casket, where the Iewell of life |…was rob’d. Only Brown (ed. 1976): Treasure (OED, sb. 5).

2484 yealds]
Schmidt (1875): To assent (OED, v. 17).

2485 this]
Abbott (§145): This time. Cf. Franz §313.

2486 ho]
Verity (ed. 1897): Edgar assumes another character, i.e., another voice (Goggin, ed. 1910).

2486 heare]
F’s Friend, heare, perhaps intended to make regular meter, provides neither ten syllables nor regular accent. Q’s lines are set as prose, though evidently verse.

2487 thus…indeed]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Thus he might die in reality. I.e., were he really to die, he would look thus. Only Hunter (ed. 1869): In this way, i.e., through fancying that he has leaped…he might pass from life indeed. Cf. 3287.

2488 what]
See n. 540.

2490–6 Hadst…fell]
Biggins (1979, pp. 27–8) finds an only partly successful attempt by Sh. at a special kind of decorum: Edgar’s comically strained or exaggerated language and behavior are used to suggest a situation that is unreal or falsely based. Coyle (1984, p. 206) derives the details of airy lightness and harmless fall from Spenser’s account of Malbecco: see n. 2429. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 62): The conventional stage device of having a character die and return to life…is basically comic, but Shakespeare transforms the convention.

2491 gosmore]
Gossamer. F’s Gozemore is otherwise unrecorded. Grey (1754, 2:116): The white, and cobweb-like exhalations that fly about in hot sunny weather (OED, sb. 1). The image is proverbial: Dent (1981, G380.2), As light as any Gossamer. Hunter (ed. 1972): The Q and F spellings…indicate…two-syllable pronunciation.

2491 feathers ayre]
Proverbial comparisons: Dent (1981, F150, A90).

2492 fadome]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): S. uses both fathom and fathoms in the plural; see OED (sb. 3b), and cf. Franz §190.

2492 precipitating]
Schmidt (1875), precipitate: To fall headlong (OED, v. 2, quoting this l. as its first ex.); Sh.’s only use of the verb. Taylor (1925, p. 63) thinks he got it from Florio’s tr. of Montaigne.

2493 Thou hadst]
F’s Thou’dst simply makes explicit the elision required to say the Q line is a pentameter.

2493 shiuerd]
Rann (ed. 1794): Flown to pieces (OED, v. 2, quoting this l.).

2494 Hast…substance]
Deighton (ed. 1891): I.e. are not mere gossamer. Hunter (ed. 1972): Are made of flesh, are not a ghost.

2495 at each]
Though Qq and Ff accept the reading, the apparent uniqueness of the idiom has invited emendation (see textual n. and ). The intended meaning is clearly each to each (Wright, ed. 1875), end to end or on end (Johnson, ed. 1765), at the extremity of each other (Theobald, ed. 1733), by each, one after the other (Porter & Clarke, ed. 1905), one on top of another (Kittredge, ed. 1940), and at easily allows such a meaning. OED (At prep. 1): Determining a point or object with which a thing…is practically in contact…when the exact relation…is not more particularly expressed by the prepositions…near, by,…on,…over,…etc., all of which may at times be covered by at. Hulme (1962, p. 333 n.) compares Eche (OED, sb.1, A piece added (e.g. to a bellrope)).

2496 fell]
Abbott (§344) lists this among irregular participial formations (OED, Fall v.); cf. n. 103. Rolfe (ed. 1880) compares Tit. 2.4.50 (1123), Tim. 4.3.265 (1892).

2497 miracle]
Deighton (ed. 1891): That you still live. Elton (1966, p. 92–3): Both miracles and demonic possession were current topics of royal as well as popular interest,…joined with Catholicism in James’s and the popular mind.…Shakespeare avoided direct verbal attack and yet seemed to demonstrate a method of such trickery. Cf. n. 243. Greenblatt (1985, p. 115): Edgar’s miracle-minting is Sh.’s disenchanted analysis of religious and theatrical illusions. Demonic possession is responsibly marked out for the audience as a theatrical fraud, as in Harsnett. Siemon (1985, p. 273): If this ordering of existence works for poor, befuddled Gloucester, the play makes certain that we remain distanced from his solution. The low comedy of the fall should assure that much as least. Not everyone detects low comedy: see n. 2480. Foakes (ed. 1997): The play no more supports the idea that miracles happen…than it does the existence of the gods, citing Goldberg (1974, pp. 151–[8]). McAlindon (1991, p. 194): What has preserved him is the miracle of his son’s love. On the meaning of miracle see nn. 243, 1242.

2498 no]
In Q the letter l follows mistakenly instead of a question mark. Though Greg (1940, p. 101) identifies the letter as not an I, Weis (ed. 1993) prints no, I?

2499 sommons]
Daniel (facs. 1885, p. xix) thinks that F’s Somnet is the result of a blundered correction of Q, but the word appears in Q2 of Ham. at 1.4.70 (659) and 3.3.18 (2291). Greg (1928, pp. 68–9): There can be no doubt, therefore, that somnet was Shakespeare’s spelling. The N.E.D. gives it as a recognized though erroneous form. Wilson (1934, 1:107), however: A minim error; the Sh. sp. is sommet. Brooke (ed. 1947): A rather rare word in the seventeenth century, often spelled somnet as in French. Duthie (1949, p. 67): Possibly the Q compositor, able to make out only the beginning of the word, guessed sommons. Stone (1980, p. 185): In the copy the tittle representing m or n was misplaced, so that the compositor found not somtatets (= somnets) but somẽts (= soments), which either he or the press-corrector then further corrupted into sommons. Presumably F’s Shn. form derives from the playbook.

2499 chalkie borne]
Steevens (ed. 1793): Chalky boundary of England, towards France. Wells (ed. 2000): Between land and sea.

2500 a hight]
For a as worn-down on see n. 1147 and OED (A prep.1 5): In the direction of, towards. Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:2): Aloft, on high (OED, A-height: The full on height is equally common, quoting this l. as its first ex.).

2501 shrill gorg’d]
Rann (ed. 1794): Shrill throated. Hudson (ed. 1871): Loud. Schmidt (1875): Singing in a high tone. Hunter (ed. 1972): Even with…its shrill, penetrating voice.

2501 seene or heard]
Hoeniger (ed. 1968): That a rising skylark cannot be seen is common; that it cannot be heard suggests a much greater distance.

2504 yet]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): The emphatic yet: after all, when things were at the very worst. See n. 245.

2505–6 beguile…will]
Taylor (1925, p. 10) suspects an echo of Montaigne’s anecdote of the mutual suicide by Ignatius the Father and the Sonne…[to] frustrate the Tyrant’s cruelty (tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 1:237).

2505 beguile]
See n. 1186–7. Here, cheat (Schmidt, 1874) or outwit (Bevington, ed. 1980) and so foil (Page, ed. 1889), i.e., by suicide (Kittredge, ed. 1940).

2505 tyrants]
Perhaps of Cornwall, whose death is unknown to Gloucester. Hunter (ed. 1972), however: Gloucester is thinking not of his own particular case, but of the traditional defence of suicide as it appeared among the Romans, and especially the Roman stoics under the tyranny of such emperors as Nero and Domitian. Wells (ed. 2000): Or Cleopatra’s.

2505 rage]
See n. 1598.

2508 Vp, so]
Foakes (ed. 1997): Has Gloucester been prostrate for twenty lines?…Honigmann [Myriad-minded Shakespeare, 1989, p. 87] suggests that he may struggle first into a kneeling position, providing a visual parallel with [2812].

2508 how…legges]
Q’s punctuation suggests this phrase as one question: How do your legs feel to you? (OED, Feel v. 6b: To perceive…; to have a sensation of…the condition of any part of the body). This reading allows a line with five stresses, on vp, so, feele, legges, and stand. Conceivably the phrase could be read as two questions: How? Feel you your legs? (OED, How adv. 4: Ellipt. for How is it? or How say you?), but such a reading requires six stresses in the line. F does make two questions, changing how to How is’t? If the F line is not to be extrametrical, Vp, so must be spoken quickly as an iamb rather than naturally as two spaced (and stressed) interjections marking two steps in getting Gloucester on his feet. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 522): There is no reason is’t should have been omitted here; now, on the other hand, is a word frequently omitted. Craig (ed. 1901) takes F’s second question to mean Can you use your legs?, but the idiom is not recorded before the late 19th c., and OED’s (v. 6d) only other ex. (from Spenser, S.C., Ep. Ded., 1579, quoted by Craig—not yet well feeling his winges) may not be analogous. Muir (ed. 1952): Possibly, have you any feeling in? Harbage (ed. 1958) takes feel to mean Test (OED, 4), as at 420.

2509 Too…well]
Delius (ed. 1854) believes that this answers Edgar’s question, but it follows pertinently his closing remark: I stand too well for a man who sought death. Skillan (ed. 1967): Still resenting being alive.

2510 aboue all strangenes]
Kelcy (1932, p. 369): The phrase may mean more strange than all strange things.…Or it may mean above all mere strangeness, i.e. miraculous. Some critics concur with the first. Hunter (1845, 2:273): The incident of the cliff is so extravagantly improbable that there is no defending it.…[It] is too improbable to give as an incident any degree of pleasure. Hudson (ed. 1856): The incident…has always struck me as a very notable case of inherent improbability overcome in effect by opulence of description. Idem (ed. 1871): It is authenticated to our feelings, though not to our reason, by the array of vivid and truthful imagery that induces it. Dent (ed. 1927): The whole business trembles dangerously on the brink of absurdity. Cf. n. 2480.

2511 cliffe]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 182): The full stop [in F] is obviously wrong. Doran (1931, p. 105): It might result as easily if the printer were setting from a lightly punctuated manuscript as if he were following Q1. Since the lines could not have been spoken in the theater according to such pointing, possibly in the prompt-book there were at best commas after strangenes and cliffe, and a scribe making F copy from the prompt-book converted the wrong one to a period.

2513 bagger]
Obvious error for F’s Beggar. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 412): Misreading—a/e. The copy may have had begger. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 522): Perhaps results from metathesis (though begger is the usual spelling in this text).

2514–19 As…thee]
Bradley (1904, p. 296): This passage is odd in its collocation of the thousand noses and the clearest gods, of grotesque absurdity and extreme seriousness. Edgar knew that the fiend was really Gloster’s worser spirit, and that the gods were himself. Doubtless, however—for he is the most religious person in the play—he thought that it was the gods who, through him, had preserved his father; but he knew that the truth could only enter this superstitious mind in a superstitious form. Carroll (1996, p. 199), to the contrary: Edgar describes to his father the figure he was.…As a paradigm of a demonized beggar, Poor Tom was the body of a nightmare. Stauffer (1949, p. 197): Edgar zealously proceeds as a physician of souls. Heilman (1948, p. 260): The episode is very strongly reminiscent of the temptation of Christ [Matt. 4:1–11, Luke 4:1–14] (just as Lear, who enters ten lines later with his crown of nettles and weeds, is reminiscent of Christ in another way). Peat (1980, p. 48): In the Bible, the Devil promises that Christ will be unharmed if he jumps, but the whole point of the story is that Christ refuses the temptation.…For the contemporary audience, the sight of a man damning his soul with a blessing on his lips must have had an impact it is hard for us to imagine.

2514 me thoughts]
See n. 704. OED (Methinks): The curious form methoughts, used in the 17th and the first half of the 18th c., prob. owes its s to the analogy of the present tense methinks. It occurs five more times in Shn. texts.

2514–17 eyes…fiend]
Tovey (ed. 1896) compares Ham. 1.4.72 (661), And there assume some other horrable forme, etc., and Burton, Anatomy of Melancholy (1621, p. 63): Fiery Diuels…likewise they counterfeit Sunnes & Moones, etc. Craik (1958, pp. 52, 95): Suggestive of the ugly masks of the grotesque devils in the moral interludes. Bullough (1973, p. 301): Based on the folk-devil in Harsnett ([1603], p. 134) with ougly hornes on his head,…eyes like a bason; see . Cf. n. 2431–44. Greenblatt (1985, p. 114): Thus Harsnett’s priests describe the demons departing from their subjects.

2516 welk’t]
F’s wealk’d is simply a sp. variant. Pope (ed. 1725): Twisted. Malone (ed. 1790): A welk or whilk is a small shell-fish. OED (Whelked ppl. a. 1): Twisted, convoluted, or ridged like the shell of a whelk, quoting this l. Hanmer (ed. 1743–4, 6:Gloss.) and others attempt derivation from another word, whelk = pustule (wheal) or welt (weal), but a participle having the first meaning is unattested, and that having the second does not appear until the 18th c. Both Skeat (1908, pp. 282–3) and Williams (1911, p. 88) find the phrase welked horns repeatedly in Golding’s tr. (1567) of Ovid, Meta. 5.327, 9.85, 10.222. Bate (1989; 1993, p. 193) therefore thinks Sh. has in mind Ovid’s Libyan god Ammon from Bk. 5.

2516 waued]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:77): Rising in Waves or Ridges.

2516 enridged]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:22): Lying in Ridges (OED, ppl. a., quoting only this l.). Abbott (§440) on the prefix en-: Sh. likes some kind of prefix as a substitute for the old participial prefix; cf. 847. Craig (ed. 1901): Furrowed. Malone (1783, p. 50) compares Ven. 819–20, the wild waues…VVhose ridges with the meeting cloudes contend. Most eds. find Q superior to F’s enraged, either as being a more apt word to describe horns or on the score of pictorial beauty (Furness, ed. 1880). Kittredge (ed. 1940): The Folios read enraged; but Edgar is not thinking of huge billows, but of the normal appearance of the surface of the ocean, comparing Luc. 1438–9, VVhose waues to imitate the battaile sought | VVith swelling ridges. Weis (ed. 1993): F’s enraged sits awkwardly with waved which does not suggest a storming sea. Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 182–3) ascribes F’s word either to manuscript misreading or to the F compositor’s carrying words in his head and unconsciously substitut[ing] the more common enraged for the less common enridged owing to the similarity in sound between the two words. Hunter (ed. 1972): F’s enraged is an obvious vulgarization. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 537), who print enridged in Q, apparently think that Sh. emended to enraged in F: Shakespeare describes the sea as enraged 11 times elsewhere; he also associates fiends with rage, citing 1910 and R3 1.4.223 (1054).

2517 happy]
Harbage (ed. 1958): Lucky (OED, a. 2).

2517 father]
OED (sb. 8): A respectful title given to an old and venerable man. White (ed. 1883): Without implying relationship. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Throughout this scene Edgar [avails] himself of the customary style…in order that he may indulge himself with using the title really due to Gloster from his son. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Edgar’s use of the term, therefore, does not reveal his identity ([3155–6]), but he takes comfort in thus addressing Gloucester. Cf. 2666, 2708, 2742, 2921. Muir (ed. 1952): Edgar uses the term ambiguously. Verity (ed. 1897) compares Leir 2218–21, where the disguised Cordella so calls Leir, and he calls her daughter without recognizing her; see .

2518 cleerest]
Theobald (ed. 1733): Righteous, comparing Tim. 4.3.28 (1630), you cleere Heauens; Johnson (ed. 1765): Purest; the most free from evil. This sense (OED, adj. 15: Unspotted, unsullied) is usually applied to humans, not gods, as in Mac. 1.7.18 (492). Capell (1783, 1.2:179): Clear-sighted…with some reference to the imposition on Gloster, his weak belief of his bastard (?OED, 8, 10). Similarly Frost (ed. 1909): Who see the clearest into the ways and the hearts of men and therefore know what is best for them. Schmidt (1874): Beautiful, magnificent, glorious (OED, 5: Illustrious, quoting this l. as its latest ex.), adding opposed to some fiend; so Kittredge (ed. 1940), Glorious, clarissimi, and Hunter (apud Muir, ed. rev. 1957), an anglicisation of candidissimi dei. Tovey (ed. 1896): Most manifest in their intervention (OED, 9), by performing a miracle such as they just have done for Gloucester (Stewart, 1914, p. 110). Lott (ed. 1974): Evident, apparent to all. Verity (ed. 1897) converts the word to an adverb: It is the gods beyond all question—most clearly—who have been your preservers. Brooke (ed. 1947): Most serene (OED, 2d: Of unclouded spirit), usually applied to humans. Neilson & Thorndike (ed. 1909): Combines the ideas of purity and brightness; so Reyher (1947, p. 500): Expresses the pure and luminous essence of divinity.

2518 made their]
Weis (ed. 1993): Q seems to refer to the gods’ mythic deeds in the past, as…in Ovid’s Metamorphoses. F’s present tense make is clearly superior, since Edgar is arguing that the gods’ miracles continue even now; F’s them seems also superior because, without further qualification, their honours appears to imply all their honors, making an untenable statement. Though Greg (1940, p. 153) doubts k would be misread as d, Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 413) finds the same error twice in Q (see n. 865), and surmises that the Q compositor may have misread them as ther; cf. n. 1713.

2518 honours]
Deighton (ed. 1891): In the gratitude paid to them. Kittredge (ed. 1940): By helping men who cannot help themselves; such is the gods’ glory (Harbage ed. 1958).

2519 mens impossibilities]
Capell (1783, 1.2:179): Doing things which [man] reckons impossible. Seymour (1805, 2:128): By performing miracles. Hunter (ed. 1869) compares Luke 18:27: The things which are vnpossible with mẽ, are possible with God (Geneva), and Houghton (ed. 1957) compares Matt. 19:26, With men this is vnpossible, but with God all things are possible (Geneva). Cf. Tilley M471, Man’s extremity is God’s opportunity, quoting this l. though Dent (1981, p. 280) excludes it as dissimilar, and N300: Nothing is impossible to God, not quoting this l.

2520 remember]
Tovey (ed. 1896): He calls to mind the utterances of the supposed fiend, i.e., strange action and speech on the part of the supposed Bedlam beggar (Kittredge, ed. 1940). Hunter (ed. 1972): Perhaps he remembers the morality of endurance proper to a religious man.

2520–1 henceforth…Affliction]
Verity (ed. 1897): After the miracle Gloucester feels that the gods have pronounced so clearly against his suicide that he must continue to live and bear his affliction.

2521–2 till…die]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Till affliction itself is tired of afflicting and dies of its own accord or asks to die (Crook, ed. 1907, perhaps following Delius, ed. 1854, in thinking die an imperative); or till Affliction recognizes that I have been afflicted enough and itself dies (Muir, ed. 1952). In any case affliction dies, rather than Gloucester.
