Muir offers the alternative, till Affliction…allows me to die a natural death, but the subject of die is more likely it than the more remote I of ile.

2522–3 thing…it]
On the redundant pronoun see n. 1066.

2523 would it]
F’s ’twould makes more regular meter. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 522): The compositor might have transposed would and it,…or he might have substituted often for copy oft.

2525 Bare]
Perhaps an error resulting from scribe or compositor carrying the homophone in memory, though bare was a sp. variant for bear (OED), and its vowel would have been pronounced as [æ:] (Ingham, p. 83). Doran (1931, p. 25): The spelling…evidently misled the [Q2] printer into taking the word for an adjective parallel to free and patient (see textual n.).

2525 free]
See n. 1791. Bransom (1934, p. 209): Generous or magnanimous. Empson (1951, p. 144): Free from a fixation on his wrongs and on the horror of the world. Craig & Bevington (ed. 1973): Probably, free from despair. Gardner (ed. 1969): Guiltless. Gloucester’s conscience is clear if he was tempted to destruction by a fiend. Hunter (ed. 1972): Typically, the moral poise that Edgar achieves here is immediately subverted by the entry of Lear. Dent (1981) rightly excludes Tilley T244, Thought is free, where free means untrammeled.

2525 patient]
See n. 774.

2528–9 safer…thus]
Virtually all think Edgar means that Lear’s attire confirms his madness. Hulme (1962, p. 276), however, followed by Edwards (ed. 1975), thinks the safer sense is here still Gloucester’s, whose precarious mental balance…will never be able to maintain itself against the shock and horror of encountering Lear as he now is. Hunter (ed. 1972): Sights like this cannot be accommodated inside a sane view of the world, i.e. Gloucester’s.

2528 safer sence]
For sense = (sane) mental faculties, reason, see n. 2359. Capell (1783, 1.2:179): Sounder. The adjective may mean sounder, saner (Johnson, ed. 1765; OED, adj. 4, quoting Oth. 4.1.269 [2669]: Are his wits safe?) or sounder, surer (Clarkes, ed. 1868; OED, 11: Trustworthy, quoting Oth. 2.3.205 [1325], My blood begins my safer Guides to rule). If the first, the comparison means, wits saner than his seem to be; if the second, it means, reason, which is a surer guide than passion. Less probable is Blakeway’s (in Boswell, ed. 1821) interpretation: The eye-sight, which, says Edgar, will never more serve the unfortunate Lear so well, as those senses which Gloster has remaining will serve him. See also prev. n. The underlying metaphor is of a personal servant dressing his maister.

2528 neare]
Like F’s ne’re, a variant of ne’er (OED).

2528 accõmodate…thus]
Furnish thus; see n. 1886–7. Warburton (ed. 1747) and most eds.: Alluding to Lear’s extravagant dress. Harrison (ed. 1948): Edgar with unconscious irony repeats Lear’s accommodated. Hulme (1957, pp. 127–8; 1962, p. 276): Adapt itself to [OED, v. 2, 3], maintain itself when confronted by (see n. 2528–9), the latter sense not attested by OED or found in Sh. Cf. prev. n. Joseph (ed. 1966): Humour, obey the whim of.

2529 his]
For his as its see n. 727.

2526–2665 Enter…]
On F’s earlier entrance see n. 1358. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 151): This inspired scene of the meeting of the mad Lear and blind Gloucester is detached and—as far as the mere march of the action is concerned—wholly unjustifiable.…[It] is, of course, most germane to the play’s idea—a more important thing to Shakespeare than the mere story—but it does check the march of the story. Doran (1933, p. 49) speculates that since the plot is in no way furthered by this episode, and since its misprinting of blank verse as prose may reflect a difficult revised manuscript, it is probably a later insertion in the text of Q. Granville-Barker (1946, p. 295 n.): There are signs…that this…encounter is a second thought on Shakespeare’s part. Apart from its redundance to the action, the Gloucester-Edgar scene is complete without it; and originally, one would guess,…[2522, die] was followed directly by [2666]. Hargreaves (1970, p. 494) sees Lear’s entrance as a visual contradiction of Edgar’s divine faith during the foregoing lines.
Crane (1952, pp. 165–6), on Lear’s wavering between verse and prose: This speech may serve as a symbolic representation of Lear’s breakdown, the verse becoming increasingly irregular and finally turning into prose; a listing of words and mere ejaculations of revulsion; lastly, an attempt to recover.…Lear summons up dignity and verse to remind Cordelia’s man that he is king; then shouts two lines of prose and runs out. Kahn (1957, pp. 325–8) contrasts the style of this scene, which exhibits reason in madness, with that of 3.6, which exhibits madness encroaching on reason: here most of Lear’s speeches are in prose; they are his most incoherent, least logical speeches, related by free association of ideas and obscure psychological significances; they repeat not only words, phrases, and disgusting sexual and animal images but also obsessive references to earlier experiences and themes, esp. justice, secret sins, and guilty feelings.

2526 mad]
Kahn (1957, p. 323) sees F’s omission of this word as part of a pattern of cuts by an actor or editor intent on giving less prominence to Lear’s madness; see n. 2618–45. Dessen & Thomson (1999): Few of the plentiful mad scenes provide specific signals. Concerning the plants that Lear is usually bedecked with as sign of his madness (see textual n.), Furness (ed. 1880) says, We must remember that these flowers are an addition by Theobald, who was undoubtedly induced to add them from Cordelia’s description in IV, iv [see n. 2353–5], and also, as suggests Schmidt [ed. 1879], from Edgar’s speech, [2528–9]. Sisson (1956, 1:32), who believes that Lear must be wearing a hat at 2625 (see n.): Cordelia is our authority.…We may not ignore the word crowned [2353]. Such a garland of weeds on a bare white old head might well be ludicrous rather than pitiful. But there would be deep dramatic significance in decking of a King’s hat with weeds instead of royal plumes. Wilson (ed. 1960): Is not Sh. thinking of Christ’s crown of thorns, wh[ich] w[oul]d necessitate a bare head? Holloway (1961, p. 97): The figure Crown’d…corn [2353–6] whose first words are I am the King himself, who jests and preaches ([2622]), who is filled with a conviction that he is soon to be killed…, and [can] run away dressed in his flowers and pursued by the attendants;—this figure is easily recognizable. He is a Jack-a-Green, at once hero and victim of a popular ceremony. Rosenberg (1972, p. 267): Before Garrick, Lear often carried a straw scepter, might wield as sword a sapling, or a straw as Forrest did, might lean on a tree branch as did Kistov and Gielgud—who also wore round his neck a chain of flowers.…Lear might brandish Fool’s bauble. Bratton (ed. 1987) records other ways in which productions have indicated Lear’s madness: handfuls of straw or wildflowers, wild looks and gestures, incoherent speech, etc. Edwards (ed. 1975): Probably he is festooned with weeds.…His appearance is enough to shock Edgar, who was with the King in the early stages of his madness. Aberbach (1979, p. 131) suspects a visual allusion to the comparison of life to a flower in Job 14:2; but even were such an allusion not doubtful on several grounds, the comparison is a commonplace. Murphy (1984, p. 212): Rather than Capell’s wild flowers, Cordelia’s lines (2353–6) suggest wild plants that are sinister and even death-dealing. Uniquely, he adds, Lear is neither mad nor philosophic; he is possessed.…Then kill, kill, kill, kill, kill, is murderous language; it is morally damnable; it is the voice of one who is possessed by the Prince of Darkness. Lear must be extricated from this spiritual state. Brownlow (1993, p. 116): It is surely essential for the structure of the play’s action that Lear be sick of a natural madness, and not possessed. Halio (ed. 1992): Obviously, to have the Fool accompany him in this state would be both superfluous and distracting: another reason to terminate his role in Act 3. Foakes (ed. 1997): Cordelia reports at [2351–6] that Lear has been seen crowned with flowering weeds.…The mock-crown…curiously helps to restore regality to him even in madness.

2530 cannot touch]
Schmidt (1875), touch: Hurt, injure (OED, v. 12b: Spec. To lay hands on or meddle with so as to harm). Since Lear is probably thinking of the hand of the law, cf. OED (19): To take to task, rebuke, reprove, censure; to charge, accuse. Deighton (ed. 1891): Lay hands upon me in order to punish. Clarkes (ed. 1868): The ancient and fundamental principle of the English constitution, that the king can do no wrong. So Rushton (1907, p. 37): Rex non potest peccare (2 Roll. R. 304), comparing 3116. Rushton (1872, p. 246): The right of coining is comprehended in those royal rights, which never leave the kingly sceptre. Hudson (ed. 1881): He, being a king by nature or by birth, is not subject to legal or artificial control touching the matter in question. Edwards (ed. 1975): Being the true king, my coinage is the true coinage (i.e. it is the others who are the false rulers). Hunter (ed. 1972): Touch—…test gold [OED, 8]—leads to coining. So Fischer (1985), adding, and to try (bring to trial) as a punning extension of to test.

2530–9 coyning…clout]
Capell (1783, 1.2:179): Lear’s ravings…rise chiefly from…the exercises that he as king had been us’d to, namely—war, and war’s appendages then; in some he is listing, engag’d in battle, in others training his bowmen and seeing them exercise. Delius (ed. 1854): Through Lear’s mad speeches runs a ruling idea, that he is at the head of a military force that will revenge the injustice done to him. The preparations under way for that purpose occupy him in several ways. Thus he thinks of the gold that by virtue of his royal right he may have coined,…[which] then serve as press-money for enlisting his soldiers; the latter he then subjects to a further test…and arranges an archery practice (Ger.). Verity (ed. 1897): Lear has seen some of the British or French troops assembled near Dover, and the sight has given this military turn to his thoughts. Stewart (1914, pp. 84–5): From the impressment of soldiers for war his mind jumps to the opposite of war in peace, peace, whose sound leads him to piece and the unmilitary activity of catching a mouse; reacting to war again, he refers to bills, which remind him of birds, falconry, and the flight of a feathered arrow. Blunden (1929; 1936, pp. 332–3): Some details—the bird-boy, the mouse—are actually present in the scene, not Lear’s fantasies: We have from him a picture both of the country circumstances and his life and times; see the following nn. Muir (ed. 1952): Although he leaps from one subject to another it is often possible to see that there is a subconscious connection between them. Coining, which was a royal prerogative, leads to the thought of press-money. This suggests watching recruits at target practice and war. War suggests peace, which in turn suggests piece, and also a challenge and brown bills. Bills suggests bird, bird suggests an arrow in flight, and its target.

2530 coyning]
Since Q makes such excellent sense in context (see prev. n.), few eds. prefer F’s crying, and it is easier to imagine that the latter is due to misreading (cf. n. 988) than that someone intentionally altered Q to make inferior sense. Tieck (ed. 1833, 9:371) takes crying to mean bewailing his fate. Schmidt (ed. 1879), who usually prefers F readings, repels this possibility: Lear rejects tears as unworthy of a king (Ger.), citing 820–1, 1577–8, 1583–6, 2966–7. Kings do weep, and are not arrested (touched) for doing so. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Crying suggests that those Cordelia sent to find him had called to him but not been able to get near enough to lay hands upon him—a sense from which the rest of the speech does not easily follow. Rosenberg (1972, p. 267): Lear, whose recent offstage anguish has been dominated by shame, may now be struggling against tears as he comes on. But the manic energy, almost gaiety, of Lear’s opening lines, with their confident authority and even boastfulness, do not suggest shame or sorrow. Taylor (1983, p. 483): The deliberate alteration of Q may have resulted from censorship, since the verb coin in its senses counterfeit, dissemble, and beget children might have been perceived…as a jibe at the King himself, and a debasement of the coinage was proclaimed on 16 July 1605…[and] 23 November 1611. But obviously the meaning of Q is that Lear is the real king, not a pretender; the right of the British king to coin was not an issue for Lear or James (see M. Judson, The Crisis of the Constitution, 1949; 1988, pp. 24–6, 145), and coin does not mean devalue.
Warren (1984, p. 320): OED touch vb. 2.b refers to the practice of monarchs touching for the king’s evil.…Lear enters complaining that he cannot be cured of his weeping as people are cured of the evil, because he…should himself be the curer.…The Folio reading does not provide any transition to the rest of the speech,…[but] the scene contains numerous instances of rapid shifts in Lear’s mind. The supposed analogy between weeping and scrofula is far-fetched; kings do not touch for weeping. Doran (1931, p. 94): The sign of abbreviation for the n in coyning [coỹing] must not have been distinguishable to the folio printer. Greg (1933, p. 261 n.): Probably the compositor accidentally set up coying and the proof-reader guessed crying. Williams (ed. Rom., 1964, p. 116), finding coyning misread as coying in Q2, proposes that compositors of both plays missed a tilde over the y and that in Lr. the compositor also made the common misreading of r for o (cf. Kellner, 1925, §142, citing Lr. 1063, 1627, 1786, 2657, and this l.). A scribe might have made the same misreading.
Many eds. think that Lear enters with either real or imaginary press-money in his hand (see nn. 2530, 2530–9), others that the remark refers metaphorically to himself. Knight (ed. 1840): It is his prerogative to coin money.…New levies are brought to him at 2533–4. Bransom (1934, p. 119): He has in his hand something he regards as money, pebbles perhaps.…He is the king himself and may therefore issue any coinage he chooses. Houghton (ed. 1957): Mr. Norrington suggests to me that Lear comes in fingering his flowers and fancying them money. Nature, above art [2533] might then mean these natural coins are better than the coiner’s counterfeits. Metaphorically, Moberly (ed. 1876): My adopting the king’s image is…a truth, and I cannot be punished for it. Sitwell (1943, p. 106), considering the play largely a diatribe against procreation: The coyning [is]…the procreation of his daughters, that base metal. Muir (ed. 1952): Coining often had a sexual significance. Though Sh. describes the begetting of bastards in terms of counterfeiting in MM 2.4.45 (1049–50) and Cym. 2.5.5–6 (1342–3), neither Muir’s other exx. nor OED supports the usage coin = beget children or bastards, nor does such a meaning sort well with Lear’s following speech. Hulme (1962, p. 182): Sh. may have remembered that Diogenes is believed to have been banished for the coining of money; the relevance here is unclear. Weis (ed. 1993), however: Lear protests that, unlike Gloucester, he cannot be charged with adultery. Quinn (ed. 1970): Lear is apparently alluding in a disjointed manner to the fact that as king his face would be represented on a coin. Oppel (1981, p. 346), comparing Lyly’s Euphues and his England (ed. Bond, 2:95), al coynes are not…golde that are coyned with the kinges stampe: Lear deludes himself that he may still command royal privileges that he long ago gave away.

2532 side pearcing]
Schmidt (1875): Heart-rending; OED (Side sb.1 25) quotes this l. as its first ex. Tovey (ed. 1896): Like a knife thrust through the side to the heart. Caldecott (MS notes, 1813–33) and Wilson (ed. 1960) detect an echo of John 19:34, describing Christ’s suffering on the cross. Joseph (ed. 1966): Agonizing. Parrott (1949, p. 298): Shakespeare guarded against [audience laughter] by comments he put into the mouths of the actors on the stage with Lear, here and at 2646–7. Styan (1979, pp. 138–9): Edgar reinforc[es] our appropriate responses throughout the scene, citing also 2616–17.

2533 Nature…respect]
Muir (ed. 1952): The relative importance of art and nature was often discussed in Shakespeare’s day, citing Puttenham’s Arte of English Poesie (1589) 3.25 [pp. 253–7], WT 4.4.[esp. 87–97 (1897–1908)], and AWW 2.1.118 (727). Harbage (ed. 1958): Cf. the coeval debate on the relative merits of poets of nature, i.e. born, and poets of art, i.e. made by self-effort. See Edward W. Tayler, Nature and Art in Renaissance Literature (1964); Elton (1966, p. 125 n.) provides other citations. A crown of plants on Lear (see n. 2526) would visually emphasize the preference for Nature in this speech. What the respect is depends on whether the coining of money or a king or both is at issue (see n. 2530). Eccles (ed. 1792): He, possibly, considers his title to those immunities attendant upon royalty as derived from nature, while to that policy of government which inflicts a punishment upon delinquents, he ascribes the appellation of art. Schmidt (ed. 1879): A born king can never lose his natural rights (Ger.). Schmidt means the right to mint coins; Kelcy (1932, pp. 369–71) argues elaborately against his own misunderstanding, that Schmidt means that Lear is thinking of his having given his regal power away to Albany and Cornwall, and says that he has a right to assume the government again if he can, because a king cannot give away his right to govern. Page (ed. 1889): I am a real, born king, not a mere imitation. Tovey (ed. 1896): The king himself, the original of the effigy [on a coin], is nature’s product and is free to coin; above the sons of art, therefore, in that respect. Kittredge (ed. 1940): A madly philosophical reflection: Art is said to improve nature; but that does not hold true in the case of kingship, for a king’s authority comes by nature and nothing can abrogate it. Brooke (ed. 1947): A king cannot be arrested for issuing false currency, for the currency is all the king’s and bears his image. Therefore nature (royal birth) is better than the counterfeiter’s art. Harbage (op. cit.): A born king is above a made king in legal immunity. Wilson (ed. 1960): A king who coins by divine right standing for Nature & a forger for Art. Fraser (ed. 1963): A born king is superior to legal (and hence artificial) inhibition. Hunter (ed. 1972): It is better to be the king who creates the coinage than the image of the king that the coin bears, for only the latter can be counterfeited. Brown (ed. 1976): What I am is more important than what I have accomplished. Halio (ed. 1992), who adopts crying: Lear may…allude to the natural propensity for emotional outlet.

2533 Nature]
OED (sb. 11d): The creative and regulative physical power…operating in the material world…contrasted with art. Cf. n. 232.

2534 presse money]
Douce (in Steevens, ed. 1793): The money…paid to soldiers when they were retained in the King’s service (OED, Press-money, prest-money 3: the acceptance of which was the legal proof of his engagement: the King’s [or Queen’s] shilling). The phrase derives from Prest, meaning an advance of money; many eds. erroneously derive it from impressment (enlistment) or from the adj. prest = ready. Goggin (ed. 1910): Presumably Lear offers money to Gloucester or Edgar. On stage he sometimes offers straw; see n. 2353–5.

2534 fellow]
See nn. 16, 577. Rosenberg (1972, p. 269): Edgar with his staff? Gloster, his hands helpless? Any poor houseless wretches [bystanders]….? Some unseen presence?

2534–5 crow-keeper]
Theobald (ed. 1733) takes the word to mean Scare-crow, citing Rom. 1.4.6 (461), a sense attested by OED (Crow sb.1 11), but a better sense is given by Heath (1765, p. 507): A fellow placed to keep off crows, rooks, and other birds, from grounds newly sown…with a bow and arrows (OED: = crow-herd). Steevens (ed. 1778) finds both the term and a description of the practice in Drayton’s 48th Idea [ed. Hebel, 1932, 2:334], Nares (1822) cites Tusser, A hundreth good pointes of Husbandry (1570, sig. C1v): Set a boy to kepe crowes, and Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956) reproduce a contemporary illustration. A rustic civilian, probably a boy, would be much less skilled than a military archer, and Croft (1810, pp. 19–20) suspects that crow-keeper was a proverbial term of contempt, quoting Ascham, Toxophilus (1545; ed. Wright, 1904, p. 102): An other [awkward archer] coureth downe, and layeth out his buttockes, as though he shoulde shoote at crowes. Tieck (ed. 1833, 9:372) thinks that Lear refers to Edgar and his cudgel; cf. 2694.

2535 me]
Muir (ed. 1952): For me; ethical dative.

2535 clothiers yard]
Steevens (ed. 1773) quotes from the 15th-c. ballad Chevy Chase 93: An arow, that a cloth yarde was lange, and Craig (ed. 1901) from Drayton’s Polyolbion, Song 26, l. 328: They not an Arrow drew, but was a cloth-yard long. This length was by statute the 36-inch yard plus one inch (Butt, 1892, pp. 451–2; OED, Cloth-yard, quoting this l.)—making a far longer arrow, Butt asserts, than could be drawn its full length to the head. Wilson (ed. 1960): Yet the imaginary recruit…is supposed to bring it off.

2536 mowse]
Moberly (ed. 1876): He probably sees a mouse run across, and in his humour of destruction thinks how to kill it. Blunden (1929, 1936, p. 333): Apparently a reminiscence of the classical proverb, certainly a Falstaffian comment on a supposed recruit’s usefulness, and clearly a remark brought on by his spying a field-mouse in the corn. Presumably the proverb that Blunden means is Horace’s The mountain labored and brought forth a mouse; see Tilley M1215. Elze (1876, p. 298), however, thinks the mouse is simply a figment of Lear’s delirium. Muir (ed. 1952): Possibly as imaginary as the dogs in III.iv. Bevington (ed. 1980): An imagined enemy. Halio (ed. 1992): Perhaps imagined, through association with crow-keeper. Murphy (1984, pp. 212–13): In Harsnett (1603, pp. 67, 140) possessing devils, including Edgar’s Smolkin, leave the body in the form of a mouse. Lear is neither mad nor philosophic; he is possessed. Brownlow (1993, p. 116): It is surely essential for the structure of the play’s action that Lear be sick of a natural madness, and not possessed.

2536 peace, peace]
Dent (1981, M1240) compares the proverb Whist (Peace), and catch a Mouse; the exx. postdate the play. Halio (ed. 1992): Addressed to the soldiers Lear imagines are startled into action.

2537 do it]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Catch the mouse.

2537 gauntlet]
Craig (ed. 1901): A leather glove plaited with steel (OED, 1, 1c, citing the mediaeval custom of throwing down a glove or gauntlet in challenging an opponent). Cf. 3040. Bransom (1934, p. 120): In stooping to give the mouse something he passes off as toasted cheese he drops his glove.…He regards it, however, as thrown down in challenge, and calls it his gauntlet. Or perhaps he confuses tossing a morsel of cheese to a mouse, or throwing down the imaginary mouse that he has caught, with hurling down his gauntlet.

2537 proue it]
Schmidt (1875), prove: To establish as a truth, to demonstrate;…With on in the same sense (OED, v. 5). The means of proof is trial by combat. Cf. 2887, 3038, 3040, 3095. Tovey (ed. 1896): I.e., my cause, or make my challenge good. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Put my cause…to the test of combat. Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956): Test my prowess.

2537 on]
Bald (ed. 1949): Against (OED, prep. 20, 21).

2538 browne-billes]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Either a sort of halberd (OED, Bill sb.1 2) or the soldiers who bore them, the bill-men: a division of infantry (OED, 3). The weapons, half pike, half battle axe, were either painted brown (OED) or varnished (Harrison, ed. 1948) to keep them from rusting. Foakes (ed. 1997): An anachronism, as these weapons were developed in the late fifteenth century. The chemical process of browning gun barrels did not come into use until the 19th c.

2538 well flowne bird]
Warburton (apud Theobald, ed. 1733): Lear is here raving of Archery, and shooting at Buts, as is plain by the Words i’th’ Clout. Warton (1754, p. 308): He suddenly thinks himself in the field…and that he has shot his arrow successfully. Steevens (ed. 1778): But…well-flown bird was the falconer’s expression when the hawk was successful in her flight, citing Heywood, A Woman Killed with Kindness (1603; 1607, sig. B2v); Douce (1807, 2:166) finds O well flown addressed repeatedly to a hawk in a song by Thomas Ravencroft. Capell (1783, 1.2:179): It was once thought, that falconry…had a place in these ravings, and that bird was meant of the hawk; but tis better understood of the arrow, which he calls well-flown from it’s being lay’d in the clout (in F). Malone (MS notes, [1773]): I.e., bird-bolt. Eccles (ed. 1792): Well-flown [may] be understood as a compound epithet to bird. Most eds. take it as an exclamation and bird as a vocative. Rolfe (ed. 1880): The phrase is taken from falconry. Lear uses it figuratively of the arrow. Goggin (ed. 1910): On account of its feathers. Blunden (1929; 1936, p. 333), followed by Budd (ed. 1935): His enthusiasm for falconry [is] bursting forth as he sees the hawk drop on that mouse. Cf. n. 2530–9.

2538–9 bird in the ayre]
F’s Bird: i’th’clout, generally preferred by eds., makes specific reference to target practice; but this may be simply a sophistication of Q, which makes perfectly good if different sense. The words immediately preceding and following suggest that Lear imagines himself on the battlefield, and in Q he could indeed be there, admiring a shot from the long bow, not still inspecting recruits as in F. The change in F must be intentional, since ayre could hardly be a misreading of clout. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 413), assuming that F gives the true reading, can only imagine that the Q reading represents a confusion of words held in the memory. Budd (ed. 1935), taking bird literally (see prev. n.): Lear praises the bird’s swoop in terms of archery, not falconry.

2539 clout]
Nares (1822): The mark, fixed in the centre of the butts, at which archers shot for practice (OED, sb.1 6). Only Rosenberg (1972, pp. 269–70): It may also mean a kind of loin cloth.

2539 hagh]
A variant sp. of Ha (OED: A natural exclamation). OED records both it and Heugh (17th.-c. sp. heuk) as exclamations of surprise, relating the latter word to both Whew (used in 1H4 2.2.28 [764]) and F’s Hewgh. Q’s word seems to indicate merely an expulsion of breath; F’s word, like its two homonyms, may imitate the sound of whistling, though OED gives no other ex. than this l. to support either the form or its definition. Craig (ed. 1901): An imitation either of a supposed arrow whizzing through the air or of the whistling of the wind. Wilson (ed. 1960): Or a cry of astonishment at the success of the shot—substantially the same meaning as Q. Weis (ed. 1993), however: In Q Ha!…indicates Lear’s startled realization of the presence of Gloucester and Edgar—i.e., up to now he has been talking to imaginary auditors, not to Edgar and Gloucester. Foakes (ed. 1997): F may mean the same as Q.

2539 word]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Watch-word (OED, sb. 2e, quoting this l.). Lear supposes himself in a garrison (Johnson)—or an encampment.

2540 Sweet Margerum]
The herb is not mentioned in 2353–5 among those worn by Lear, but may still make allusion to the latter (Verity, ed. 1897). Savage (1923, p. 278): All about Dover the flower is most plentiful.…How likely the walk towards the cliff would be to suggest it. Blunden (1929; 1936, p. 333): Sweet marjoram was accounted, according to Culpeper, a blessed remedy for diseases of the brain. Edgar was clearly a friend. Foakes (ed. 1997): Sweet Marierome is a remedie against cold diseases of the braine and head, according to John Gerard’s Herball (1597), 540, so Edgar’s password relates to Lear’s madness, and is not merely fanciful. Brown (ed. 1976): An herb, used as a tranquilizer and charm against witchcraft.

2541 Passe]
Bratton (ed. 1987): Edmund Kean and Macready both had their Edgars respond to this order, crossing the stage.

2543–72 Ha…imagination]
Hart (1954, p. 8): The effect of incoherence is produced in part by the use of both verse and prose.

2543 Ha…Regan]
See n. 2539. No one explains the Q text. Apparently as Gloucester and Edgar, having given the password, approach Lear, he mistakes them for his two daughters and expresses astonishment at seeing them. He must not have so recognized them when he spoke to Edgar in 2539 and 2541, perhaps because they were still at some distance from him. After recognizing them he must speak his remaining lines about them to one of his imaginary soldiers, or to himself. In F, where he recognizes only Goneril, he could speak the remaining lines to Edgar. Q makes for better continuity, since he goes on to talk about both daughters, not just Goneril. To account for the discontinuity in F, Wilson (ed. 1960), followed by Halio (ed. 1973), takes they to refer to the world in general; but Goneril and Regan are the obvious flatterers. Hunter (ed. 1972): It seems as if something in Gloucester’s action or tone of voice suggests flattery.…[Perhaps Gloucester] falls to his knees like a loyal servant.

2543 with…beard]
Capell (1783, 1.2:179) approves of F’s addition because it leads on to Lear’s remarks about his own beard. Delius (1876, p. 137) even thinks that the sense is destroyed without it, hence that it must have been mistakenly omitted from Q. Such explicit connections are hardly necessary in mad talk; possibly in F Lear simply strokes Goneril’s chin as he recognizes her. Besides, the train of ideas that follows is already familiar: Lear has earlier been reminded that he has age without wisdom (749, 916–17), has mentioned his white head (1661, 1679), and has struck it for its folly. Buck (ed. 1907) speaks for many eds.: It seems hardly possible that Lear mistakes Gloucester for Goneril. Halliwell (ed. 1865) even prefers to believe that Lear refers to his own beard: To be so unfilial to a father with a white beard. Moberly (ed. 1876): I suppose you are Goneril, though your white beard seems against it. Leo (1885, p. 113): Perhaps the band over Gloucester’s eyes reminds Lear of Goneril’s frontlet (703–4); but Goneril’s band is metaphorical. Granville-Barker (1927, rev. 1946, p. 296), followed by Wilson (ed. 1960): Goneril, disguised, pursuing him still! Rosenberg (1972, p. 270): The line may be a cry of fear, or a horrified exclamation.…The image…suggests transexuality, the distaff side turned threatening man,…the hag daughter as mother (and father?). Foakes (ed. 1997): This is to press the text very hard; Lear at once shifts to a concern with himself and flattery in general. Lear’s uninterrupted flow of observations does not suggest fear or horror so much as wonder.

2544 like a dogge]
Johnson (ed. 1765): They played the spaniel to me. Seymour (1805, 2:128–9): By fawning. Clarkes (ed. 1868) find a double signification: And They smoothly humoured my whims as one strokes a dog. Proverbial: Dent (1984, S704): As flattering (fawning) as a spaniel.

2544–5 tould…there]
Capell (1783, 1.2:179): Told [him] he had the wisdom of age before he had reach’d to that of a youth. To emphasize that the idea was prompted by the sight of Gloucester’s beard (Muir, ed. 1952), Wilson (ed. 1960) would make my emphatic.

2544 white]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 183): F’s the white sounds clumsy and unnatural. Presumably the F compositor has anticipated—cf. the blacke ones in the next line.

2545–7 to say…diuinitie]
In Q1 these words form one complete sentence, the comma after saide introducing (as commonly) quotation or indirect discourse; in Q2 and F, the colon after saide divides the lines into an exclamation and a comment upon it. Crook (ed. 1907): In either case Lear means that they were too flatteringly subservient to be good counsellors. Though most eds. have preferred F, Q arguably makes better sense, and F’s punctuation and alteration of toe to too may simply derive from Q2’s unauthoritative interpretation of Q1 (see ).
The word diuinitie suggests a Biblical text. Verplanck (ed. 1847), Wordsworth (1864, p. 99), and Sims (1966, pp. 74–5) propose 2 Cor. 1:18: our worde towarde you was not Yea, and Nay (Geneva), where Paul avows his consistency in preaching God’s word without making ambiguous concessions to his audience; the text is apposite here. Two other texts, James 5:12 and Matt. 5:37, are not so applicable because they enjoin against swearing oaths; but like Jones (1970, p. 129), Hunter (ed. 1972) points out that the verse in Matthew is preceded by Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black, which might seem to have suggested [2544–5], and Candido (1986, pp. 17–18), that as in Lear’s speech it is close to remarks upon adultery. Eds. also cite several literary texts in which flatterers are explicitly said to agree with or hold up another’s ay and nay: Terence, Eunuchus 252 (Tovey, ed. 1896); Udall, Ralph Roister Doister (ca. 1552) 1.1.49, and Hall, Satires 6.1 (ed. Singer, p. 149) (Kittredge, ed. 1940); Palsgrave, Acolastus (1540, sig. B4), and Cooper, Thesaurus (1565, s.v. assentor) (Maxwell, apud Wilson, ed. 1960). Elton (1966, p. 230) provides other instances of both religious and secular uses of the phrase, as does Dent (1981, A411.1; 1984, Y4.11). Q1’s text here says clearly and explicitly that the daughters have matched their ays and nos to Lear’s; the F text says only that they spoke ay and no to euery thing, not necessarily implying flattery as the context demands. Pye (1807, p. 295): It does not appear how it could be flattery to dissent from, as well as to assent to, every thing he said. Singer (ed. 1856): It may, however, mean…that they had double thoughts, and said ay to flatter him, when they said no to themselves, and vice versa. Page (ed. 1889): It is not necessary to show any considerable amount of coherence in Lear’s successive utterances. Q1, however, shows such coherence, and its reading has been offered as independent conjecture by Pye, Anon. (1875, p. 103), and others. Stewart (1914, pp. 83–6) suggests that Lear picks up ay, no from the sound of Gloucester’s I know in 2542.

2546, 2550 toe]
A variant of either to or too (OED).

2546–7 no good diuinitie]
I.e., sinfully dishonest; see n. 2545. Hudson (ed. 1879): The extreme of sycophancy…may well be called no good divinity. Bald (ed. 1949): False religion. Wilson (ed. 1960): Not good theology. Foakes (ed. 1997): Suggesting they treated him as a god, and perhaps alluding to the divine right of kings, claimed by James, citing Works (ed. McIlwaine, 1918, p. 307). But the bad theology is the daughters’ dishonesty; no one ever pretends to think that Lear is divine.

2547–51 when…argue-proofe]
Steevens (ed. 1773): This seems to be an allusion to king Canute’s behaviour when his courtiers flattered him as lord of the sea. Moberly (ed. 1876) finds the same idea in AYL 2.1.5–11 (611–17). It is proverbial: Tilley E137, An Enemy (Adversity) makes a man to know himself.

2548 chatter]
OED (v. 3a): Of the teeth, quoting this l. Weis (ed. 1993) also thinks it refers to rapid talk, and Foakes (ed. 1997), to talking nonsense; but Lear is descibing the ague.

2549 peace]
Wright (ed. 1875): A verb formed from an interjection. Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 64): Anthimeria; see n. 2137. OED (v. 2): Keep silence, quoting this l. Lear never gives such an order.

2549 smelt]
Dent (1981, S558): Proverbial. See n. 897.

2549 them]
On F’s ’em see n. 908.

2550 goe toe]
Partridge (1947, p. 122): Copulate. See n. 100.

2550 men]
Though Lear uses a proverbial phrase (see OED, Word sb. 8; Tilley M184; Dent, 1981, M395.2), there may be unconscious humor in his applying the generic noun to his daughters; see . Dodd (1752, 2:131), however: It is plain, he runs off from the thought of his daughters, to those who flatter’d him, and all through the speech speaks of them only. Weis (ed. 1993): Lear uses a specifically masculine idiom implying a subjective misogynism; but men after a negative may refer to both sexes (OED, sb.1 1b).

2550 words]
On the plural see n. 9.

2551 argue-proofe]
F’s Agu-proofe corrects an obvious error, perhaps a misreading (too many minims in the copy) (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 413). Harbage (ed. 1958): Proof against chills and fever (OED, Ague 4, quoting this l.; a dissyllable). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Lear is shivering and has, in fact, taken a severe chill. Rosenberg (1972, p. 271): But the [involuntary] shiver…is psychic too. Doran (1933, p. 52 n.), anticipating Wilson (ed. 1960): The ague (gout, etc.) as a refutation of false flattery of a king is an example given by Montaigne in Of the Inequalitie That Is Betweene Us (tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 1.297, 299). Cf. AYL 2.1.6–11 (612–17), WT 1.2.12–14 (63–5).

2552 tricke]
Hanmer (ed. 1743–4, 6:Gloss.): Pecularity in a face, voice or gesture (OED, sb. 8b, quoting Jn. 1.1.85 (93) and this l. as its first exx.). Law (1934, p. 42) compares Leir 2140–1; see .

2554–73 I…thee]
F sets Q’s prose as metrically clumsy verse through 2562; eds. disagree about lineation of the whole (see textual nn.). Malone (ed. 1790) prints 2562–9 (through inherit) as verse but adds, I doubt much whether any part of it was intended for metre. Singer (ed. 1856), on the same section: It is too rhythmical to be left as mere prose, yet is rather lyric than heroic metre. White (ed. 1862): Not improbably the remainder of this speech [i.e., 2569 ff.] is mutilated blank verse. Abbott (§511): Single lines with two or three accents are frequently interspersed amid the ordinary verses of five accents.…These lines are often found…where passion is at its height [citing 2557–69].…The highest passion of all expresses itself in prose, citing 2569 ff. and Oth. 4.1.34–44 (2412–20). Craig (ed. 1931): Gloucester’s words bring Lear back to the recollection of his kingly state, and he begins to speak in blank verse, irregular to correspond to his wandering sanity. Doran (1931, p. 106): In F the speech is wrongly aligned [verse], and the rest, as though the transcriber or printer had given up the attempt to divide it, is printed as prose.…It seems probable that Shakespeare wrote [the lines] out as prose, even when they contain several distinct lines of verse. Brooke (ed. 1947): After a line and a half of blank verse matching Gloucester’s, Lear reverts to undoubted prose. The Folio made a half-hearted attempt to divide it as poetry and modern editors have gone further, with sad results. Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 413–14) finds the speech nearer verse than rhythmic prose: It contains quite a number of pentameters and what sound like fragments of pentameters.…Either what we have is a roughed out version of the speech which Shakespeare meant to revise: or—perhaps more probably—the verse was made purposely irregular…to accord with Lear’s state of mind. Houghton (ed. 1957): If it be intended as verse there are a quite unusual number of incomplete lines. More probably it is prose, as are Lear’s previous and following speeches. Brown (ed. 1976): Short verse-lines suggest pauses for stage business.

2554 euer…King]
F’s euery corrects an obvious error. Proverbial: Tilley, M161, He is a Man, every inch of him. For stage business see n. 2353–5. Following Coghill (1964, pp. 25–6), Foakes (ed. 1997): Apparently Gloucester kneels here rather than at [2543; see textual n.], his homage being taken by Lear as the sign of a guilty criminal begging for mercy. Thomson (1988, p. 187): Not necessarily.

2555 stare]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Look angry (OED, v. 3). Skillan (ed. 1967): Merely with the fixed look of authority.

2555 subiect]
I.e., any subject; he imagines a particular one in the next line. Some eds., however, agree with Walker (1860, 1:246) that it is a collective noun for subjects. Coghill (1964, pp. 25–6) thinks Lear refers to Gloucester, whose kneeling before him suggests a culprit begging for mercy. Rosenberg (1972, p. 272): Or possibly one of Lear’s hallucinations, or Edgar.

2556 pardon]
Schmidt (1875): Release (from a penalty) (OED, v. 1: Remit, citing this l.).

2556 cause]
OED (sb. 9): Charge, accusation, quoting this l. as its latest ex.

2557–71 adultery…pah]
Vickers (1968, p. 369): The precariousness of [Lear’s] hold over verse and dignity is shown as his tortured imagination forces out more details of what is below the girdle, and he collapses into prose. Foakes (ed. 1997): The exact point at which verse gives way to prose is indeterminate. See textual n. Hunter (ed. 1972): The speech contrasts progressively more violent forms of illegal sexuality with legal propriety; its process mimics the collapse of these legal safeguards into the horror of animal sexuality. Taylor (1925, pp. 11–12): Montaigne notes how an adulterous judge will condemn an adulterer, a licentious woman will raile and scold…bitterly against the same fault in her neighbour, and some condemne men to die for crimes, that themselves esteeme no faults; see . Bratton (ed. 1987) records the various bowdlerizations of these lines in 18th- and 19th-c. performances; see also .

2557 adultery]
Bransom (1934, p. 122): We may infer that Lear recognized Gloster, who suggests to him th[is] sin. Unconsciously perhaps; but in 2560 Lear refers to Gloucester as if he were absent, and does not explicitly recognize him until 2619. Bradbrook (1978, p. 192): Lear acts as the mad King of Summer, crowned with weeds; in a wild mixture of the sacred power to absolve sin, and total licence of midsummer revelry, he pardons Gloucester’s adultery. Wreen (1984, p. 41): Lear is confusing adultery with copulation. Animals do not commit adultery.

2557 die]
Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 522) find F’s dye: dye metrically preferable, but metrical emendation of Lear’s uncertain verse seems unsafe here. Edwards (ed. 1975): Adultery was not a capital offense in Elizabethan times nor (as we gather from Gloucester’s history) in the imagined period of the play. Noble (1935, p. 231): Doubtless in allusion to the penalty prescribed for adultery in Lev. xx. 10, also John viii. 5. Since Puritans had proposed the death penalty for adultery, Elton (1966, p. 118 n.) suspects an implication of Puritan hypocrisy here.

2559 letcher]
Schmidt (1874): To indulge lust (OED, v.: To play the lecher, quoting this l.). Foakes (ed. 1997): Copulate.

2560 kinder]
Presumably in denouncing Edgar. Though we are not shown how Lear has learned of the accusation against Edgar and of Edgar’s presumed unkindness, Cornwall heard of it instantly (1025–6), Gloucester has spoken of it to acquaintances (1048–9; 1946–8, apparently unheard by Lear) and may have done so to the King during their journey to Dover, and Edgar has been proclaim’d (1252). See n. 132. Granville-Barker (1927; rev. 1946, p. 296): A slight unconscious turn of the sightless eyes toward him, a simple gesture—unseen—in response from Edgar, patiently biding his time, will illuminate the irony and the pathos.

2561 got]
See n. 349.

2562 wren]
Wreen (1984, p. 42 n.) Baseless calumny of a noble bird.

2562 toot]
I.e., go to it (OED, To prep. 1c). Williams (1997): Copulate. Cf. 2566.

2562 luxurie]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): Lasciviousness (OED, 1).

2562 pell, mell]
Craig (ed. 1901): Promiscuously, confusedly (OED, adv. 1). Hunter (ed. 1972): As if in headlong, indiscriminate, and confused battle. Wells (ed. 2000): Q’s italics suggest that the French was not yet fully anglicized.

2562 lacke souldiers]
Fraser (ed. 1963): Whom copulation will supply. Q2’s synonymous want is simply a printer’s substitution (Doran, 1931, p. 33).

2563–71 behold…pah]
Edwards (ed. 1975): Having authorised promiscuity, Lear now argues that chastity in women is only a façade, anyway. Tilley M553 compares the proverb Men (Women) may blush to hear what they were not ashamed to act (do); Dent (1981) finds it dissimilar. The idea is in Montaigne: see n. 2565.

2563 simpring]
Schmidt (1875): Smiling in an affected manner (OED, ppl. a. 1). Maxwell (apud Wilson, ed. 1960) compares Hall, Virgidemiarum (1598) 4.1.156–7: sits shee simpring in her [p]ew | Like some chast dame, a shrined saynt—in shew.

2563 dame]
Though Bradley (1904, p. 448) will not hint that this refers to Goneril, Heilman (1948, p. 101) and others make the identification: Lear’s word drama about sex is an excellent metaphor for the general corruption of his daughters.…The sisterly alliance breaks down in sexual rivalry. Lott (ed. 1974): His concern with women’s hypocrisy springs from his daughters’ behaviour. As Donnelly (1955, p. 155) suggests, Rosenberg (1972, p. 273): Lear may be looking at Gloster.

2563–4 between her forkes]
Edwards (1750, p. 74): The construction is not whose face between her forks, &c. but, whose face presages snow, &c., the phrase meaning therefore between her legs (Schmidt, 1875; OED, Fork sb. 12b, quoting this l. as its first ex.); cf. 1887. Williams (1994): The crutch. The idea continues in the next sentence: down frõ the wast etc. Failure to recognize (or accept) this construction has led eds. to ingenious interpretations of the phrase: Her hand held before her face in sign of modesty, with the fingers spread out, forky (Warburton, ed. 1747; cf. Jourdain, 1857, open fingers); The forks were two prominences of the ruff rising on each side of the face (Johnson, ed. 1765); Forks here may mean instruments then worn by women for keeping up their hair (Hart, apud Craig, ed. 1901). Dyce (ed. 1867) wryly remarks that such readings require the next words to mean presages a fall of snow. Gardner (ed. 1969): Perhaps one of Shakespeare’s most violent quibbles. Snow typified chastity, by contrast with the fire of lust. The fork of the throat (or breast) is an obsolete term in anatomy for the breast and collar bones, which support the face as if between forks [OED, sb. 8, of inexact meaning and used only in the sing.]. On the other hand, face could mean front side or appearance, and forks could mean legs. Halio (ed. 1992): The pudendum. Dorfman (1994, p. 32): Ideas clustering around Sh.’s 12 different uses of fork—mortality, cuckoldry, nakedness, banishment—may support a genital reference here.

2564 snow]
An emblem of coldest chastity (Hunter, ed. 1869). Edwards (1750, p. 74) compares Tim. 4.3.385–6 (2025–6), the consecrated Snow | That lyes on Dians lap, in light of which quotation Hunter’s (ed. 1972) reading seems even more questionable: Indicates that the other face between her forks [legs] is frigid or chaste.

2564 minces vertue]
Capell (1783, 1.2:182): That affects a shew of virtue and modesty in her mincing and soft pace. OED (v. 6): To show…affected delicacy in manner of gait; (6b): Trans. To perform or enact mincingly, quoting this l. Edwards (ed. 1975): Primly parades her virtue. Kittredge (ed. 1940) understands mincing airs, not gait; cf. OED (5b): To speak with affected elegance. The figurative construction, in which vertue is a kind of adverbial objective, proved sufficiently difficult that Collier (1852, p. 443) proposed mimics virtue. Rosenberg (1972, p. 273) detects a quibble, mangles, not exactly attested by OED (but cf. v. 1c, 1d).

2564 do]
F’s do’s corrects an obvious error.

2564–5 shake the head]
Hunter (ed. 1972): In disapproval. Lott (ed. 1974): In shocked surprise.

2565 heare…to]
F corrects to to heare…The. The omission in Q of a necessary to and an erroneous appearance of the same word later in the line suggests to Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 414) some kind of printing-house accident, though he admits the possibility of compositorial neglect, misreading, or forgetfulness.

2565 pleasures]
Harbage (ed. 1958): Of sexual indulgence.

2565 name]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Emphatic. It shocks her to hear even the word mentioned. Muir (ed. 1952, p. 253) compares Montaigne (tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 2:355–5): Wee have taught Ladies to blush, onely by hearing that named, which they nothing feare to doe. Wee dare not call our members by their proper names, and feare not to employ them in all kinds of dissolutenesse.

2565 fichew]
Pope (ed. 1725): A kind of Polecat. Nares (1822): This animal was supposed to be very amorous; and Mr. Steevens tells us, that its name was often applied to ladies of easy or no virtue. Colman (1974, p. 194): Type of lechery. This relative of the weasel emits a fetid smell. Cf. Tilley P461. OED (Fitchew 1b): Used as a term of contempt, quoting only Oth. 4.1.146 (2532). Williams (1994), s.v. polecat: Whore, giving many exx.

2566 soyled horse]
Grey (1754, 2:117): A horse that has been fed long with hay and corn in the stable, and in spring has fresh green carried to him thither, upon which he feeds greedily. Heath (1765, p. 348): Which both cleanses him, and fills him with blood. See OED (Soil v.4 1; Soiled ppl. a.2, quoting this l. as its first of two exx.). Craig (ed. 1901): I.e. the horse wanton with rich feeding, citing among several exx. Montaigne (tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 2:335): I have heretofore put forth an old stalion to soile, who…was so lusty, that no man could rule him. Wilson (ed. 1960): In mod. slang full of beans. Blythe (1980, p. 87), citing Vergil’s Georgics 3.214: Being soiled brings a horse to an unmanageable sensual excitement, and no other image in either classical or modern literature so typifies aroused sexuality as that of a pent-up and ruttish stallion. Rosenberg (1972, p. 273): Also the sense of moral and sexual licentiousness, perhaps recognized by Colman (1974, p. 214): There could also be a quibble on soil. Though in all exx. cited by eds. the horse is male, Wells (ed. 2000) cites Williams (1997): Equated with woman.

2566 goes toot]
See n. 2562. Foakes (ed. 1997) cites the unwed mother Joan Go-to’t in The Birth of Merlin (1608?; ed. J. Udall, 1991, p. 131).

2567–71 down…consumation]
Muir (1951, p. 21), seconded by Brownlow (1993, p. 116): The passage…has been thought by some critics to reflect Shakespeare’s own revulsion against sexuality; but it may well have been suggested by Harsnett’s account [1603, pp. 122, 141, 202; see , ] of the way the exorcists pretended that Sara Williams, at a time of menstruation, was possessed with a devil in a peculiar part of the body, applied reliques vnto that place, and burned sulphur under her nose. Muir quotes other passages (pp. 61–3, 94–5, 109) filled with the imagery of darknesse,…burning, scalding, stench; see . Bransom (1934, p. 122): Disgust at woman’s sexual nature, and, almost at her anatomy too, is expressed with peculiar force and vividness. Until he utters these lines the subject matter of them does not appear to have exercised Lear’s mind, though they may intimate a dark place in Lear’s experience, perhaps (pp. 221–2) an old, repressed, incestuous passion for one of his daughters, most likely Goneril or Cordelia. Empson (1951, p. 138) finds the elderly Lear’s obsession with sex here ridiculous and rather sordid. Mack (1965, p. 69) therefore insists on a psychic distance between speaker and speech: If we overstress by gestures and facial movements the pyschic authenticity of Lear’s lament, we lose altogether its emblematic and Morality-based dimension as a meditation or oration in the tradition of De Comtemptu Mundi. Rosenberg (1972, p. 274): Of course we lose this. The speech is nothing of that kind.…His very preaching is discolored by…madness. Jorgensen (1967, pp. 125 ff.): The supposition of a period of sexual nausea in Sh.’s life rests on the supposedly gratuitous nature of the sexual passages.…The vileness of sex seems to have little to do with either the reason for [Lear’s] tragedy or the nature of his ordeal. But it is the culmination of his own self-discovery: He had discovered part of himself through unaccommodated man. But with woman he reaches one step further and sees not just the weakness but the vileness of humanity. It is perhaps this that leads him, when Gloucester asks to kiss his hand after the speech about woman, to say, Let…mortality. Edwards (ed. 1975): Lear turns away in disgust from his own invocation of sexual license. Women’s sexuality destroys man physically and spiritually.

2567 centaures]
Lee (ed. 1908): The type of sensuality. The Centaurs, according to Ovid, Metam., xii, 210, seq., were given up to lust and violence. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Shakespeare is thinking of the attempt of the Centaurs to carry off the bride of Pirithous…mentioned in [MND 5.1.44 (1841)], [told in Ovid, and]…summarized in the Life of Theseus in North’s Plutarch. Colman (1974, pp. 187, 205) compares Nessus, who tried to rape Deianira. Brooke (ed. 1947): Ben Jonson had the same idea, if not this line, in mind when he called one of the ladies in The Silent Woman (1609) Madam Centaur. Heilman (1948, p. 100): The Centaur is exactly the right image here, for it admits the possibility of high intellectual and spiritual attainment and yet connotes primarily the proneness to violence and disorder which the play exhibits throughout. It exhibits man as a rational animal. In its embodiment of sexual license, also, the Centaur figure is especially effective as a sharp focusing of the sex motif that constantly appears in the play. Starnes & Talbert (1955, p. 115): Lear has in mind the description of Centaurs in Cooper’s Thesaurus (1565), which emphasizes their lustfulness and adultery: As Lear thought of his daughters as Centaurs, he did not forget that his role was that of Ixion, the father of the Centaurs; see n. 2795–6. Fraser (1962, p. 86): The image, horse and rider indivisible, signifies reason armoured in grace astride ebullient will. Elton (1966, p. 121): Ironically indicative of the daughters’ monstrosity, the centaurs being male, notoriously addicted to rape. Lear is describing all women, not just his daughters. Hunter (ed. 1972): They are bestial like…soilèd horses…below the waist. Hoover (1989, p. 350): Lear radically alters the pagan Centaur myth by transforming it from male to female and then…proceeds to combine it with a second image based on the Christian belief that it is the sexuality of woman which leads to the damnation of man. Bate (1989; 1993, p. 194): Their duplex natura ([Meta. 12.503]) was the perfect image for mankind’s double nature as both beast and rational creature.

2568–9 but…fiends]
Collins (in Steevens, ed. 1778): According to Grecian superstition, every limb of us was consign’d to the charge of some particular deity, citing Gower’s Confessio [5.1493–6], where the lower parts are assigned to Venus. Warren (in Boswell, ed. 1821, 3:460) identifies as a heresy known to Augustine the belief that the lower parts of the human body originated from an evil principle (a diabolo factas); Anders (1904, p. 287) quotes the Latin text (De Haerisibus 85). Ingleby (in Furness, ed. 1880) finds the idea in England’s Vanity (1683, pp. 59–60), and Danby (1949, p. 34), identifying it as Manichaean, finds it in a sermon of Launcelot Andrewes. Contemporary belief that the lower part of man’s body is evil is documented by Elton (1966, p. 269 n.). Craig (ed. 1901) cites Beaumont & Fletcher, Love’s Cure 2.1.28–31 (perhaps an imitation of these lines), and Tilley W520 compares the proverb There is no Wisdom (law) below the girdle, for which Dent (1981, p. 31 n.) provides a pre-Lr. ex. Muir (ed. 1952): The priests who were exposed by Harsnett tried to exorcise the devils from the lower parts of the body; see n. 2567–71. Bradbrook (1978, p. 196): A martyr’s girdle confine[d] the chief fiend to the lower part of the woman’s body, her hell; but see next n.

2568–9 inherit]
See n. 1092.

2569 hell]
Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): Traditional slang for the female genitals. Though the usage is not attested by OED, and Colman’s (1974, p. 167) two Shn. citations refer only to venereal infection, Williams (1994) gives many exx. Hoover (1989, pp. 351, 354): Lear invokes the Christian belief that devils possess women through their genitals. He is attempting to avoid responsibility for the results of his own sexuality, i.e. his ungrateful daughters, whom he suspects of bastardy (764, 1409–10).

2570 burning, scalding]
Colman (1974, pp. 186, 213) refers both words to venereal infection. See n. 1739.

2570 sulphury]
OED (Sulphurous a. 3a): Pertaining to sulphur or brimstone as an adjunct of hell, quoting Ham. 1.5.3 (686) and this l. (F: sulphurous) as its first exx.

2570 pit]
Both Hell and, in common slang, vagina (Williams, 1994).

2571 consumation]
The action of consuming, destruction (OED, 1, not quoting this l.); The disease consumption (OED 2). It is etymologically a different word from consummation, whose root meaning completion, perfection is quite different from the meaning consuming, destruction (by fire or disease) that is required here. Rosenberg (1972, p. 273), however, finds a sexual sense in Q, which he takes to mean consummation, as does Foakes (ed. 1997): Both fulfilment of the sex act and the end or death of things [OED, Consummation 1a, 2].…Here…is glimpsed an apocalyptic vision of the end of the world. Virtually all eds. prefer F’s more common word consumption, meaning the same as Q’s word: Schmidt (1874): Decay of the body (OED 4: Wasting of the body by disease; a wasting disease). Colman (1974, p. 189): With allusion to gonorrhoea, possibly though not supported by OED. Since Q makes perfect sense, there is no need to agree with Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 414) that in Q copy, either the p in consumption looked as if it had no tail (cf. 463) or copy’s consumtion had too many minim strokes. Still, since Sh. nowhere else uses the form consumation, but uses consumption twice in the near-contemporary Timon, it may well be the word intended here.

2571 ounce]
Sigismund (1882, p. 15): A great quantity.

2572 Ciuet]
See n. 1885. Wilson (ed. 1960): Prob. ironical, since the perfume was made from the very uncleanly flux of a cat [AYL 3.2.70 (1265)].

2572 Apothocarie]
Bucknill (1860, p. 268): An apothecary…was the recognised perfumer as well as the drug-vendor. Brown (ed. 1976): Often spoken to Gloucester.

2572 to]
On F’s omission, Kirschbaum (1945, p. 57): F’s imperative is much the stronger reading; after the specific appeal for Ciuet, there is a general appeal to the Apothecary…[having] great pathos. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 157): The semicolon after Ciuet in F is against the compositor having simply omitted to accidentally. If to had been omitted earlier by a scribe, a later corrector or compositor might have added the semicolon to rectify matters. Muir (ed. 1952): The F reading…is perfectly possible, but seems rather awkward in rhythm.

2572 sweeten my imagination]
Hunter (ed. 1972): The imagination that has just conjured up stench and consumption. Craig (ed. 1901): This expression is found in Marston’s play Parasitaster [Or The Fawne (1606) 2.1.91–2]. Muir (ed. 1952): Th[e] juxtaposition of satire on women with the phrase quoted suggests that Marston was imitating Shakespeare…[or] the other way around. Wells (ed. 2000): Civet was used to alleviate melancholy, citing Hoeniger (1992, p. 257).

2575 Here]
F’s Let me could reflect the same stage business.

2576 mortalitie]
Schmidt (1875): Subjection to death, necessity of dying (OED, sb. 1). Bransom (1934, p. 123): He had been picking flowers and perhaps handling dirty pebbles. His hands were of the earth, earthy, and smelt of the grave. Harbage (ed. 1958): Death (OED, 2c). Fraser (ed. 1963): Or existence. McCann (ed. 1964): The bitter experience of life. Joseph (ed. 1966): Either (i) rot, murrein; or (ii) frailty, subjection to death. Since smels must mean smells offensively, Lear probably is speaking by metonymy of the corruptions associated with the mortal condition (OED, 1b: Mortals collectively), such as he has just been contemplating. Colie (1974, p. 139) compares Psa. 38:3, 5. Adelman (1992, p. 113): Traditionally derivative from the woman’s part in conception…the mark of…female corruption.

2577 ruind]
OED (ppl. a. 3) quotes this l. as its first ex.

2577 peece]
Schmidt (ed. 1879): Sh. often uses piece with of where we should expect some such word as model or master-piece (Ger.), citing Ant. 3.2.28 (1570), 5.2.99 (3319). Rolfe (ed. 1880) adds Tmp. 1.2.56 (148), WT 4.4.32 (1832), etc. See OED (sb. 8): Exemplification, specimen, or example; (17): A production,…work of art. But the word may mean simply part of the whole (OED, 2); thus Harbage (ed. 1958): I.e. the universe (macrocosm [great world]) will decay like this man (microcosm; cf. [1622+3]). So Brown (ed. 1976): Fragment/instance/product.

2577 nature]
See n. 435.

2577 great world]
Muir (ed. 1952): The universe. See prev. n. Holloway (1961, pp. 75–9) finds several allusions in the play to the world’s inevitable dissolution, culminating in Doomsday, as does Wittreich (1984), and quotes contemporary statements of the idea, including, from Donne’s First Anniversary, So did the world from the first houre decay.

2578 should]
In Q Gloucester expresses hopeless dismay; F’s shall reduces his statement to a simple prediction.

2578 so]
Verity (ed. 1897): Even as Lear’s little world of man [1622+3] has worn out.

2578 weare…naught]
Elton (1966, pp. 247–8) gives instances of the Renaissance idea of the decay of the universe. Andresen (1974, pp. 159–60) finds the commonplace of Time the Destroyer pervasive in the play.

2579 do you]
Brooke (ed. 1947), of F’s Do’st thou: There seems no reason for Gloucester to speak familiarly to his king at this point. Blake (1996, p. 160): The reading in Q which is neutral and formal would appear to be the right one.

2580 remember thy eyes]
F substitutes thine for euphony. Wilson (ed. 1960): Clearly Glo.’s eyes were not bandaged. They were to have been bandaged (see 2176+8–+9); would they have healed sufficiently in the two or three intervening days to be unprotected now? The analogy with Blind Cupid can offer no certainty: see n. 2581–2. Edgar has earlier remarked in 4.1 (2244) that Gloucester’s eyes bleed and only a few moments before now has urged him to Looke vp (2500), and here Lear seems to see eyes squinting half-shut and at 2612–13 recommends glasse eyes, all of which suggest absence of a bandage. Edwards (ed. 1975): Lear is aware (at some level and in some fashion) who Gloucester is and what must have happened to him. This powerful phrase includes the sense of remembering him as a man who had eyes and of asking himself why he should now be eyeless.

2581 squiny]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:64): A comic Alteration of—squint. See n. 1897. Halliwell (ed. 1865): Looking askance, or under the eyelids (OED, v.1 1, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Craig (ed. 1901): With side glances. Harrison (ed. 1937): Like a prostitute.

2581 on]
By analogy with look on, a frequent Shn. idiom. F’s at is an unnecessary change.

2581–2 no…loue]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Lear…fancies Gloucester to be the blind Cupid, and says, you may try all your artifices upon me, but they will be of no effect, you will not be able to make me fall in love. Bransom (1934, p. 123): Perhaps the notion…is to lovers’ quarrels followed by a challenge to a duel [with a rival]. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Lear’s mind jumps back to the idea of defying an enemy ([2537]); but now that enemy is blind Cupid. Gloucester does not know that the written challenge exists in Lear’s mad fancy. Brooke (ed. 1947) compares Benedick’s challenge to Cupid in Ado 1.1.40 (40), and Muir (ed. 1952) compares Titus’s imaginary petition in Tit. 4.3.109 (1976). Wilson (ed. 1960) thinks the challenge is Cupid’s, wh. he has just rejected. The phrase do thy worst is proverbial (Dent, 1981, W914).

2581–2 blind Cupid]
Proverbial: Tilley L506, Love is blind; neither he nor Dent (1981) quotes this l. Verity (ed. 1897): This notion of Cupid’s blindness is mediæval rather than classical. Wilson (ed. 1960): Cupid is sometimes in Sh. hoodwinked with a scarf (Rom. 1.4.4 [459]), sometimes without eyes ([AYL 4.1.214 (2120)]). Muir (ed. 1952): Sidney, Arcadia, ii. xiv [.3], contains a poem about blind Cupid, and Miso is warned not to love (ed. Feuillerat, 1:239–40); but both the image and the idea are commonplace. Harrison (ed. 1937): The sign over a brothel; cf. Ado 1.1.252–4 (242–4). Traversi (1953, p. 219): The symbol of the brothel…at once refers to Gloucester’s own past sin, from which Edmund was born, and leads to Lear’s own passionate rejection of sexual love…caused in him by its observed consequences through the play. Elton (1966, pp. 317–18 n.): Also an allusion to the blind Eros which befuddles man’s intellect by exciting Voluptas unguided by reason, citing contemporary sources and modern studies. Vickers (1968, p. 353): Lear’s description of Gloucester as a blind Cupid (both amorous and sightless) is perfectly accurate. Weis (ed. 1993) compares 3133–4.

2582 challenge]
Eds. differ whether Lear refers to his former challenge (2537) or a new one (see n. 2581–2). Staunton (ed. 1859): Perhaps…the poor King exhibits the proclamation for the killing of Gloucester. For stage business see n. 2353–5.

2582 penning]
Schmidt (1875): Style (OED, vbl. sb.2). Or handwriting (Foakes, ed. 1997).

2584 sunnes…see]
Adee (ed. 1890, p. xliv) compares Sidney’s Arcadia 2.10.3; see .

2584 one]
F’s omission, perhaps metrical, changes the meaning slightly.

2585 take]
Schmidt (1875): Receive into the mind. OED (v. 41b): To accept as true, quoting this l.

2585 this]
Verity (ed. 1897): Not merely Lear’s state nor Gloucester’s blindness, but the terror and pity of the whole scene between them. Hunter (ed. 1972): An oblique Shakespearian defence of the non-realism of what is before us.

2585 from report]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): I.e., without witnessing such pathos. Dent (1981, E266.1) compares the proverb To see with one’s own Eyes.

2586 it is]
Wright (ed. 1875): Is is emphatic. Ewbank (1971, p. 18): Apparently, we are faced with a reality so overpowering that language is utterly defeated. Edgar can speak only what he feels, and what he feels needs no other expression than the most ultimate stage direction: it is. In many ways, this it is is the greatest line of Shakespeare, the theatre poet.

2586 heart breakes]
See n. 1585.

2588 case]
Jennens (ed. 1770): The sockets (OED, sb.2 2: Receptacle, quoting this l.). Malone (ed. 1790) finds the figure of eyes as jewels in cases in Per. 3.2.98 (1299) and 5.1.110 (2091). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Emphatic. Foakes (ed. 1997): Also plight, condition.

2589 there with me]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Even with me; cf. OED (There adv. 6b): In that respect, quoting this l. Such a reading would be only metaphorically true, perhaps glancing at a common proverb. Tilley F452: A Fool and his money are soon parted; cf. M1042, He that has Money in his purse cannot want a head for his shoulders. Neither Tilley nor Dent (1981) cites this l. Rosenberg (1972, p. 275): Are we blind together? Halio (ed. 1992): I.e., are we both victims of imperceptiveness? Wright’s (ed. 1875) Is that what you mean? would indicate that only at this moment Lear realizes that Gloucester is truly eyeless. So Horsman (ed. 1973): Is that what I am to understand? Compare [2H6 2.1.48 (770)]: I am with you = I understand. Dent (1981, W295.1) compares the proverb I know Where you are (he, she is). The Clarkes (1879, p. 399) infer a challenge: Are you on the tack of trying to delude me, are you trying to catch me with that plea? Crook’s (ed. 1907) Is that how you answer me?, Lee’s (ed. 1908) Do you understand me?, and Harrison’s (ed. 1937) Do you agree with me? all make inferior sense.

2590 nor no]
On the double negative see n. 427+1.

2590–5 your…eares]
Vickers (1968, p. 354): Lear’s horrifying puns (see the following notes) and the hypallage of looke with thy eares are not a sign of a limited intellect but of a powerful and increasingly perceptive mind hovering between prose and verse, madness and reason, paradox and truth. Cavell (1969, p. 280), grotesquely and without evidence: Lear is picking at Gloucester’s eyes, as if to make sure they are really gone.…This picking spiritually relates Lear to Cornwall’s and Regan’s act in first blinding Gloucester.

2590–1 heauie case…light]
Puns on all three words. Schmidt (1874), heavy: Sad (OED, a.1 25). Delius (ed. 1854), case: Both a covering and a situation. Craig (ed. 1901), light: Merry…[and] empty. Weis (ed. 1993): Dark/light, i.e. blind/seeing; but heavy does not mean without light or sight, nor can a purse see. Muir (ed. 1952): There is a reference to the proverb: A heavy purse makes a light heart; so Dent (1981, P655), who also cites In (a) heavy Case as proverbial (C112.1).

2591–2 how…goes]
Proverbial: Dent (1981, W884.1), Thus (How) goes (fares) the World.

2593 feelingly]
Eds. have detected four meanings: 1) By the sense of feeling, touch, as I have no eyes (Moberly, ed. 1876); 2) by experience (Craig, ed. 1901; OED, adv. 4, esp. of pain); 3) in an inward and heartfelt way (Moberly, ed. 1876), with the keenest feeling—in a way that pierces me to the heart (Kittredge, ed. 1940; OED, 3: With emotion); and 4) with just perception, understandingly, sensibly; appropriately (OED, 2, cited by Spevack, 1958).

2594 art mad]
On omission of the pronoun see n. 562. Deighton (ed. 1891): Lear takes Gloucester’s feelingly in a literal sense as though he had said he had no perception except through the sense of touch.

2594–5 see…no eyes]
For similar ideas see n. 2200.

2595–2612 see…lips]
Parker (1955, p. 138): The most passionate attack upon human justice ever made. Walton (1960, p. 12): The last time we saw Lear he had attempted to obtain justice, but he had sensed its inadequacy. In this scene he is able to proceed to an analysis of justice and authority which includes in its scope his own exercise of them in the initial action of the play. Foakes (ed. 1997): This passage marks the great shift that has taken place in Lear, comparing 561, 611. Elton (1966, pp. 231–2) cites many contemporary statements about judicial bias, corruption, and ineffectiveness.

2596 yon]
On F’s yond see n. 2453.

2596 simple]
Schmidt (1875): Witless (OED, adj. 10). Craig (ed. 1901): Of low estate (OED, 4). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Ordinary, mere (OED, 5). Wells (ed. 2000): Humble, wretched. There may be a hint of innocent (OED, 1).

2596–7 harke…eare]
Probably Lear confides the following wisdom to Gloucester, demonstrating how to looke…eares. Hunter (ed. 1972), however: A whisper to the justice of the peace bribes him.

2597 Change places, and]
Not needed, but added to F1 for greater clarity (Delius, ed. 1854). Delius later (1876, p. 137) decides that the whole sentence becomes meaningless without it, hence that it must have been mistakenly omitted from Q. Dane (1995, p. 326) suspects that a proofreader’s direction to transpose theefe and Iustice in F has found its way into the text. There is no evidence that this page was proofread, though its forme-mate was.

2597 handy, dandy]
Malone (ed. 1790): A play among children, in which something is shaken between two hands, and then a guess is made in which hand it is retained. Halliwell (ed. 1865) and Kittredge (ed. 1940) illustrate the game’s antiquity and popularity. OED (Handy-dandy adv. phrase 1c): The words used, as in the game, in offering a choice, or when it is indifferent which of two things is chosen; = Choose which you please, quoting this l. Hunter (apud Muir, ed. 1952; rev. 1957, p. 259): In Langland [Piers Plowman] (B. iv. 75) this is a term for bribery.

2597–8 which…Iustice]
F inverts to repeat the order of 2596; Q changes places. Verity (ed. 1897): The leading idea in Measure for Measure. Brownlee (1960, p. 284) compares Burton, Anatomy of Melancholy: Magistrates make laws against thieves, and are the veriest thieves themselves (ed. Holbrooke Jackson, 1932, 1:51). Hulme (1962, p. 193) quotes from Nicholas Udall, tr., Apophthegmes of Erasmus (1542; 1564, p. 117): See, see (quoth Diogenes) the graund theues leden the petie theef to ward. Elton (1966, p. 86 n.) compares Thomas Powell, The Attorneys Academy (1623, p. 217): To play at handy-dandy, which is the Guardian, or which is the foole? For stage business see n. 2353–5.

2599 dogge…begger]
See n. 2020–1. Tutt (1964, p. 22): Truth and justice do not exist in a world where humans may be ruled by beasts.

2601 And…cur,]
Most eds. follow Q2 (see textual n.) in pointing this as a question. Sisson (1956, 2:241–2) is doubtful: It does not seem necessary for Lear to pursue his question, to which Gloucester had answered, Ay sir. There is no question mark here in the Folio, though they are numerous on this page.…Lear is drawing conclusions here from what Gloucester agrees he has seen. And…frequently has the sense of if [see n. 630].

2601 creature]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Human being (OED, 3). Hunter (ed. 1972): Man in his lowest state…nearest to the animal. Lott (ed. 1974): One of God’s creatures.

2602 great image]
Schmidt (1874), image: That…in which an idea is embodied (OED, sb. 4b: Emblem, representation; 4c: Type, typical example, embodiment). Deighton (ed. 1891): Perhaps great belongs rather to authority than to image. Harbage (ed. 1958): Universal symbol. Muir (ed. 1952, p. 252) compares Montaigne (tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 3:20), The guide striketh the blinde man he leadeth. A horrible image of justice.

2602 dogge]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Emphatic: even a dog. Muir (ed. 1952, p. 252): Montaigne mentions [Sebond] that there are Nations, who receive and admit a Dogge to be their King; see . Doran (1933, p. 52 n.): Lear’s observation that the office, not the man in it, commands respect occurs in Montaigne’s Of the Inequalitie That Is betweene Us (Hieron complains, Such respects are rather due to royaltie, to majesty, than to me) and Of the Art of Conferring (We judge of him, not according to his worth; but…according to the prerogative of his ranke) (tr. Florio, 1:303, 3:173). Harbage (ed. 1958): I.e. man bows to authority regardless of who exercises it.

2602–3 dogge, so bade]
Often taken as some kind of phonetic error (see ) for F’s obviously correct Dogg’s obey’d; Q2’s dogge, so bad barely makes sense. Doran (1931, p. 125): The printer may have occasionally set from dictation, or here unconsciously substituted words similar in sound. Ingham (1967, p. 83): If so, he used an advanced monophthongal pronunciation [ε:] for M. E. ai in obey’d. Greg (1933, p. 254): A reporter’s mistake of hearing. Though Greg (1942, p. 94) concedes that the mental substitutions of a compositor may sometimes have the appearance of mishearings, neither he nor Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 81) can accept such an explanation here; Greg notes, The punctuation has been accommodated to the false sense in Q. Brooke (ed. 1947): A subconscious association with a dog so bayed may have put him off the track. Recent eds. suspect rather a graphic confusion. Owen (1949, p. 142): If [Q copy] read a dogges obaide in office, then bade is a minim misreading; or if it read a dogges obeide in office, then bade is an a/e and minim misreading; and in either case the rest of the error is due to misdivision. Urkowitz (1980, p. 126): I offer that the manuscript copy had something like a dogges o bade in office. The compositor may have joined the detached o to the preceding rather than to the following letter grouping…and then a comma was inserted after dogge. Blayney (apud Wells & Taylor, 1987, p. 522; Halio, ed. 1994) also believes graphical, rather than auditory, confusion misled the compositor. Of the 105 occurrences in Sh. of obey and its inflected forms, 19 are spelt with an a in F, the good quartos (including those of the poems), and (if Shn.) Sir Thomas Moore. The form obayed occurs only in Ven. 111; obade, obaid(e), or obayd do not occur; obeyd occurs twice, obey’d 8 times, and obeide never.

2603–45 thou…sa]
Vickers (1968, p. 370): Out of prose his dignity and moral perception…gradually climb up to verse.…Lear remains at this majestic level for a long time…to the final collapse into prose [at 2644–5].

2603 beadle]
Craig (ed. 1901): A parish constable (OED, sb. 4). Kittredge (ed. 1940): One of whose duties was to punish offenders by whipping. Weis (ed. 1993): In London whores were commonly whipped in public at Bridewell.

2604–5 strip…backe]
Houghton (ed. 1957): Cf. He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her and the whole story of Christ’s treatment of the woman taken in adultery, John. viii. 1–11. Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960, p. xxxvi) adds Rom. 2:1, and Foakes (ed. 1997), Matt. 7:1–5. Weimann (1967, 1978, p. 220): Perhaps addressed to an individual in the audience singled out by an icy stare or accusing finger.

2604–5 thine]
On F’s thy see n. 1804.

2605 thy bloud]
OED (Blood sb. 6): The supposed seat of…sensual appetite; hence, the fleshly nature of man. Though F, like Q, prints the speech as prose, Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 41) and others assume that F shortens to thou for metrical regularity; but perhaps it was done to avoid repeating thy bloudy (2603) with a different meaning. Greg (1942, p. 93), considering Q a reported text, thinks that Q here is an actor’s recollection of 2603. It could have been an authorial play on words. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 522) elaborately defend emendation to Thy bloud as, thereby insisting that QF prose is verse and adding a quantitative comparison without an expressed correlative, implying either as hers does or as to whip her.

2605 lusts]
In Q the verb presents no problem; in F, after thou, one would expect lust’st. Walker (1860, 2:129) suspects shortening for euphony; see n. 2307+5.

2605 kind]
Schmidt (1874): Way, particular manner (OED, sb. 8).

2606 vsurer…cosioner]
Tovey (ed. 1896): The cheat on the great scale hangs the poor and petty cheat. Craig (ed. 1901): A magistrate who secretly practises usury, though illegal, passes sentence on one only guilty of petty cheating. Wilson (ed. 1960): Usury [was] a respectable way of defrauding others.…Cf. Meas. 3.2.6–10 (1495–9), which voices the same complaint, viz. that usurers, allowed by law (i.e. the Act of 1571), became wealthy citizens and sat on the magistrate’s bench. Foakes (ed. 1997) cites plays associating usury with greed and lechery. Hunter (ed. 1972): Against the protests of preachers and poets. Elton (1966, p. 314) and Dent (1981) compare Tilley T119, The great Thieves hang the little ones. Muir (ed. 1952) quotes from Barclay, The Mirrour of good Maners (ed. 1885, p. 34): What difference betwene a great thiefe and a small, | Forsooth no more but this to speake I dare be bolde, | The great sitteth on bench in costly furres of pall, | The small thiefe at barre standeth trembling for colde, | The great thieues are laded with great chaynes of golde, | The small thiefe with yron chayned from all refuge, | The small thiefe is iudged, oft time the great is Iudge. Blayney (1982, p. 187 n.): The rare spelling cosioner may be compositorial, since it appears in another Okes book of 1607.

2606–10 through…it]
Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 137): The lines are structured by a form of antithesis called syncresis, which compares contrary things in contrasting clauses.

2606–8 through…all]
Jourdain (MS notes, ca. 1859?) compares Greene’s Pandosto: Though Kings sonnes daunce in nettes, they may not be seene: but poore mens faultes are spied at a little hole: Well, it is a hard case where kinges lustes are lawes, and that they should binde poore men to that, which they themselues wilfully breake (ed. Grosart, 4:293). Elton (1966, p. 232 n.) compares Tilley L116, Laws catch flies (little flies) but let the hornets (great flies) go free; neither Tilley nor Dent (1981) cites this l.
