The idea that justice favors the rich is old and commonplace; Rushton (1867, p. 62) finds it in Demosthenes, Trierarch Cor. 11 (tr. A. T. Murray, 1939, 6:60–1).

2606–7 through]
Those who think QF prose is really verse are troubled by F’s Thorough, since Q is metrically rather smoother (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 158). Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 537) suspect the o was added to justify the line.

2607 tottered]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 414): Doubtless a misreading of a. But totter(ed) was a 17th-c. variant (OED).

2607 raggs]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 41) finds F’s cloathes preferable: If we read rags…its effect at [2610]…is much weakened.

2607 smal]
Most eds. prefer Q to F’s great, probably because small makes a better antithesis to all. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Shakespeare allows the word even to be elliptically understood…even small vices. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Even trivial faults are visible when a man’s clothes are full of holes and cannot hide his real self. Small is emphatic. Furness (ed. 1880), defending F: When looked at through tattered clothes, all vices are great. Dey (1900, p. 205): It is not a question as to whether the vices appear great or small, but whether they appear at all. Kirschbaum (1945, p. 59), as usual assuming Q to be corrupt: The vices of the poor are not only always noticed but also magnified. Brooke (ed. 1947): F’s great is cold-blooded perversion by somebody who thought he could improve the text. The meaning is that the smallest vices are seen (and punished) in the poor, but the privileged classes can conceal even the greatest. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 183): A scribe may have misunderstood the passage and conjectured great himself. Muir (ed. 1952): F would mean that all vices are great when looked at through tattered clothes; but it would be difficult to convey that meaning in a theatre. It would be easier if great were printed after do. Maxwell (in Wilson, ed. 1960): In Q, Lear makes the commonplace remark.…But in F the whole drift of the speech is that we are all in the same boat, all offenders, Theft, whoredom, cozenage, etc. are not small vices but sin. But the phrase smal vices does not necessarily refer to those previously named. Hoeniger (ed. 1968), by great, apparently understands number, not magnitude: I.e. all vices—nothing can be hidden. Hunter (ed. 1972): The antithesis is somewhat muffled by great; he prints it anyway. Weis (ed. 1993): All humankind is guilty of great vices.…F offers a tougher and more pessimistic view of human nature. Or an untrue one; but the lines do not say that all humankind is guilty of vice and crime, only that some of the guilty escape punishment.

2607 appeare]
Harbage (ed. 1958): Show plainly (OED, v. 3).

2607–8 robes…all]
Malone (ed. 1790) compares Luc. 93: Hiding base sin in pleats of Maiestie. Spence (1900, p. 363) compares MM 2.2.127–8 (885–6). Tilley A284: Handsome Apparel makes fools pass for wise men (hides much deformity); Dent (1981) finds the proverb dissimilar and irrelevant.

2608 furd-gownes]
Verity (ed. 1897): Such as ermine-trimmed robes of judges, peers. See Underhill (1916, 1:397): The judge’s cape is furred with minever. Craig (ed. 1901): Gowns worn by aldermen. Hunter (ed. 1972): Perhaps also…usurers, citing MM 3.2.7 (1497). So Fischer (1985): The traditional garb for a stage usurer was austere clothing with a lining or trim of fur.

2608 hides]
F’s alteration to hide is unnecessary: see n. 1697.

2608–12 Place…lips]
Delius (1876, p. 137) thinks these lines were mistakenly omitted from Q, since their absence destroy[s] the evidently personal bearing of the following words, Get…eyes, on the blind Gloster. Doran (1931, p. 68) and Stone (1980, pp. 68, 122) make the reverse argument, that the lines are interpolated because their focus on the immunity of the rich interrupts a consecutive line of thought from Gloucester’s blindness, appeare, and hide all to get thee glasse eyes. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxv), followed by Chambers (1930, 1:467), suspects suppression by a censor, James having restocked the bench in 1603 and 1604 with his own following, and hints of venality were more than whispered. Censorship would not have occurred in the rough draft apparently behind Q. Greg (1955, p. 387) doubts claims of political censorship of earlier passages when this one was allowed to stand. Stone (op. cit., pp. 123–5) thinks the F lines date from 1616 or later because they refer to the Overbury case, concerning which the King’s suspected preferential treatment of some of the accused and his suppression of evidence was widely rumored. Taylor (1983, p. 403) rejects this particular topical reference because the ideas were commonplace, comparing Ham. 3.3.57–60 (2333–6). Hankins (1953, p. 160) quotes from Palingenius’s Zodiake (tr. Googe, 1576, pp. 73, 95) GOLD guides the lawes and With money lawes corrupted are, and compares Cym. 2.3.70–1 (1036–7), ’tis Gold | Which…saues the Theefe.

2608–10 Place…it]
Stone (1980, p. 68): The new lines form a curious digression.…In Q the idea of factitious visibility or invisibility (through…all) leads directly to the idea of factitious vision (get…eyes); in F no such connection is apparent.…It would be strange if the more natural succession of ideas in Q had been achieved by the omission of these lines. It is much less improbable that the new matter in F constitutes an interpolation. Honigmann (1982, p. 146): Both Q and F pick up Lear’s earlier thought, A man…eares.…Lear’s straying from the point, in F, merely continues his established mental zigzagging.…What is remarkable is that [F’s added lines] fit in so well. Warren (1983, p. 52) speculates that F may have added this passage in compensation for omitting the mock trial’s statement of this idea; by this idea he refers to Lear’s treating the naked Tom as a robbed (i.e. robed) man of Iustice (2014+15–+16) and thereby signifying that the justice is as guilty as the ragged offender. In fact the point of this passage is the different one that justice is corruptible by gold. Weis (ed. 1993, p. 24): The fact that F expands Q’s text [here]…cannot convincingly be taken to compensate for its omission in 3.6, since the F extra lines…qualify and expand a train of thought already fairly explicit in the passage which immediately precedes the added text.

2608 Place]
Pope’s emendation Plate (see textual n.) is obviously right, since what is needed is a parallel to Arme (2609), and c/t misreadings are easy and common. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Shakespeare uses the word plated elsewhere [e.g., R2 1.3.28 (325)] to express clad in plate armour (OED, Plate sb. 3; v. 1). Craig (ed. 1901): Perhaps there is a quibble with the sense of plate, a coin [OED, sb. 13], citing Ant. 5.2.138 (3366). Lott (ed. 1974): The gold…offers sufficient protection against the strong weapon of the law. Foakes (ed. 1997): Ironic: Gold is a soft metal. Heilman (1947) defends QF: Place can have the second meaning listed in NED: To appoint (a person) to a place or post…. That is, Purchase an evil person…official position with gold, and he becomes immune to justice, comparing Tim. 4.3.36 (1638), where gold is said to be able to place Theeues. Such a reading requires sinnes to mean sinners, and contrasts the poor with corrupt judges only, not with all the rich and powerful. Colman (ed. 1982) takes Place as a noun = someone of high status: Someone highly-placed commits sin through bribery or usury; but for parallelism both Place/Plate and Arme need to be verbs. Foakes (1993, p. 204) thinks it a verb: Put in office.

2608 sinnes]
Theobald’s emendation sin (see textual n.) seems required by it (2609–10). Perhaps in Sh.’s MS the terminal e looked like the similar es symbol, or (Foakes, ed. 1997) a tail on the final e…[was misread] as s. Colman (ed. 1982), who makes sinnes a verb, refers it to Place (see prev. n.), thus making very odd sense: high place is armed by being dressed in rags which allow it to be pierced.

2609 hurtlesse]
Schmidt (1874): Doing no harm (OED, a. 2).

2610 Pigmies straw]
Sh. several times refers to pigmies, e.g., in Jn. 5.2.135 (2389), Pigmy Armes. Theobald (1909, p. 311): Pigmies…are described by Pliny [Nat. Hist. 7.2.26] as only three spans or 27 inches high, whose weapons therefore were figuratively but straws. Hunter (ed. 1972): The frogs in the pseudo-Homeric Battle of the Frogs and Mice carried rushes for spears. The parallel mock-battle of the cranes and pygmies was also well known in Shakespeare’s age. For stage business see n. 2353–5.

2610–11 None…say none]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): In the interest of justice Lear—as king—issues a royal edict: I abolish all punishment. Nobody shall be regarded as guilty of any offence against the law. I will give everybody a license to act as he pleases. Skillan (ed. 1967): I.e., none of the poor [will be punished], because their judges are spuriously more righteous than they who are thus comparatively innocent. Muir (ed. 1952, p. 252) compares Montaigne (tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 3:167): I say not, that none should accuse, except hee bee spotlesse in himselfe: For then none might accuse. Several eds. detect a Biblical allusion: see n. 2604–5. Danby (1949, p. 192): The Pauline All have offended [Rom. 3:23: sinned] becomes Lear’s None…none. Delaney (1977, p. 436): A Christian view of political corruption…that where all offend, none offends. Foakes (ed. 1997): Rather, Lear is ridding himself of his own compulsion to punish, citing (as does Halio) Rosenberg (1972, p. 277): Lear needs to forgive so as to forgive himself, too. Lear may rather be saying that he will provide means to evade judgment: see the next n.

2611 able]
Since Lear has been talking of the power of money in the previous lines, and seems immediately to give bribe money to an imaginary defendant, the best reading is that of Verity (ed. 1897): Give them the means, i.e. money…to set things straight (OED, Able 3: Endow with fitting power or strength; Enable 3c: To supply with the requisite means). See the next n. But there are many alternative readings. Warburton (ed. 1747): Qualify, or uphold (OED, Enable v. 4: To regard as qualified or competent, a rare usage; Able v. 4c: To warrant, vouch for, quoting only this l.). The reading does not fit the context particularly well, and its weak support in OED makes it doubtful. Heath (1765, p. 348): I will take off all legal disabilities which they may have incurred by their crimes. OED does not directly support this reading, but provides another legal sense perhaps suitable to the context here (Able v. 4b: To empower legally, to make competent). Skillan (ed. 1967) adopts this sense, explaining: Warrant (able)…[by] turn[ing] a charge into an accusation of the judge. Rosenberg (1972, p. 277): This is no Christian forgiveness for all stone-casters:…he empowers sinners to sin, he emancipates the id-world.

2611 take that]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Lear imagines that Gloucester is a criminal, and makes a gesture as if he were handing him a pardon signed and sealed. Muir (ed. 1952): Or piece of information. Horsman (ed. 1973): What I have just said. Foakes (ed. 1997): Learn that, citing OED (v. 34c) and Shr. 2.1.190–4 (1061–5). Wilson (ed. 1960): Lear having money (i.e. the power…lips) offers it to the penniless Glo. (see [2590]) to…enable him to win his case or to escape a verdict. The money is, of course, illusory, like the press-money of [2534]. Lear’s thought-processes change abruptly; and the next moment he seems to suggest that Glo. [should] use the money to buy spectacles. On how gold Buyes out the lawe (Ham. 3.3.60 [2336]) see n. 2608–12. Hunter (ed. 1972): Either bribe money or, if he is concerned with his kingship,…some document of the royal prerogative.…In either case his flowers would seem the only things he can give.

2612 who haue]
The subject is apparently the I implied in me, not that.

2613 glasse eyes]
OED (sb. 1): Spectacles, quoting this l. as its first ex. Doran (1931, p. 68): Though the preceding F lines add a new metaphor, Get thee glasse-eyes… perhaps follows more logically upon the [Q] statement of circumstances under which vices are seen or not seen than upon the [F] description of the power of bribery. Hunter (ed. 1972): Conceal your blindness behind…spectacles. Sigismund (1883, pp. 37–8): Artificial eyes. So Edwards (ed. 1975): False eyes, rather than spectacles. But Foakes (ed. 1997): False eyes made of glass were first mentioned in the late seventeenth century.

2613 scuruy]
Schmidt (1875): Vile, contemptible (OED, a. 2). Foakes (ed. 1997): Because scabby.

2613 polititian]
Verity (ed. 1897): In Shakespeare always a depreciatory word, implying intriguer, schemer (OED, 1). Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Opportunist. Orgel (ed. 1999): Vile Machiavel.

2613–14 seeme…not]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Lawyers who make themselves blind by poring over old deeds to discover imaginary points. Hunter (ed. 1972): Politicians discovering, for example, imaginary plots so as to justify repression. Or more generally, all hypocrites and deceivers. The train of thought is elliptical and obscure. Lear seems to be advising Gloucester, as a victim of corrupt justice, to adopt the ways of the world and, as by bribing a justice, to put expediency and duplicity above morality and truth. Halio (ed. 1992): Lear’s fierce attack sets Gloucester weeping. Or perhaps his references to eyes and seeing.

2614 no now]
Q makes adequate sense: having directed Gloucester to buy spectacles, Lear says, No, now pull off my bootes. Halio (ed. 1994) so punctuates. Since F substitutes Now, now, now, now, it is quite possible that the MS behind Q read now now and the compositor accidentally omitted a letter; see n. 2014+6. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 399): In both cases the final w may have been indistinct in the copy for Q1. F’s doubling of the number of nows may simply reflect the stage time Lear needed to get to a sitting position; those who think the lines are verse suspect the change was made for metrical reasons. Strings of two, three, or four nows are found at TN 2.5.57 (1071), Tro. 5.2.65 (3048), and TNK 3.4.7 (1574). Skillan (ed. 1967) hyphenates—Now-now, now-now—to form the modern expletive of admonition or reproof: lear reproves him sharply for weeping; but this usage of now, now was not contemporary. Brown (ed. 1996): May be spoken in compassion, not command, or for alerting himself for a major new effort; cf. n. 2629. Blayney (apud Wells & Taylor, 1987, p. 522) suspects a lacuna on metrical grounds, proposing No grief now, weep not now, or no tears now, the last adopted by the Oxford eds. (see textual n.).

2614–15 pull off my bootes]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Lear imagines that he has just come back from hunting or from a journey. Empson (1952, p. 837): He tells an imaginary servant to do it, and needs on the stage to do it himself because the symbolism needs to be made vivid. This sets him free to recognize Gloucester and preach patience to him, waving his boots about.…[At 2645] he runs away gleefully, still waving his boots so not likely to get far. Muir (1953, p. 73): The removal of the boots is a figment of Lear’s imagination, like the drawing of the bed-curtains in III, vi. We ought to be spared the spectacle of Lear waving his boots as he runs away. Hunter (ed. 1972): Exhausted by his speech, Lear sinks down and gives the command that might accompany such a feeling in ordinary life. Weimann (1967; 1978, p. 219): A remarkably profound piece of stage business.…He abandon[s] all the accoutrements of royal prestige. Lear’s stockinged feet might suggest his stratagem; see n. 2627.

2615 so]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Ah, well and good! My boots are off at last. Cf. [2042]. Halio (ed. 1992): Relief at being rid of the uncomfortable gear.

2616 O…mixt]
Eds. have found many Shn. parallels, e.g., Ham. 2.2.205–6 (1243), 4.5.174–9 (2926–30), etc.

2616 matter]
See nn. 398, 2441.

2616 impertinencie]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:34): Matter not pertinent (OED, 1: Irrelevancy, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Bransom (1934, p. 124): I quite fail to see where Edgar discovered any impertinency in the words.

2618–45 If…that]
Kahn (1957, p. 328): Though we find the various attempts to versify Lear’s mad prose to have been superfluous and even impertinent, we agree with the Folio editor that his final speeches in this scene should be read as verse. Shakespeare realized that the madness had spent itself, had done its dramatic work, and that the exalted mood of tragedy required a poetic conclusion.

2619 I…inough]
Proverbial: Dent (1981, K171.1), though spoken to supposed knaves, villains. Foakes (ed. 1997): His trial for adultery…suggests that Lear has had some idea of the identity of Gloucester all along.

2620 patient]
See n. 774. Welsford (1935, p. 266): Patience, here [and at 2933–5], seems to imply an unflinching, clear-sighted recognition of the fact of pain, and the complete abandonment of any claim to justice or gratitude either from Gods or men. Foakes (ed. 1997): Lear can now preach patience, comparing 1571.

2620–2 we…cry]
Proverbial and widely known: Tilley W889, We weeping come into the World and weeping hence we go, quotes many exx. cited by other commentators. Tilley D82, I wept when I was born and every Day shows why, is a later proverb that Dent (1981) rejects as dissimilar. Muir & Danby (1950, p. 50) compare Sidney’s Arcadia 2.12.[2] (see ), where Plangus laments, the man that feeling knowes, | With cries first borne, the presage of his life. Muir (ed. 1952) compares a passage in Montaigne; see . Mack (1965, pp. 87, 111–12): The play’s dominant tragic theme, comparing George Gascoigne’s tr. of Innocent III’s De Contemptu Mundi: We are all born crying that we may thereby expresse our misery (Works, ed. Cunliffe, 1910, 2:220). Among classical precedents are Pliny, Nat. Hist. 7.1.2, Lucretius, De rerum nat. 5.222–7 (Steevens, ed. 1773; Martin, 1945, p. 179), and Seneca, Ad Polyb. de Consolat. 4.3 (C., 1855, p. 348). Robertson (1909, pp. 321–2) finds the lines from Lucretius in Montaigne’s Sebond; see . Carter (1905, p. 441) and Noble (1935, p. 231) compare Wisd. 7:3, 6, and Colie (1974, p. 134) adds Eccles. 5:14.

2622 wayl]
Synonymous with both cry and F’s wawle (OED, Waul). On other y/w variants see n. 2710. Philemon Holland’s tr. (1601 [p. 152]) of Pliny (see prev. n.) has men cry and wraule from birth (Anders, 1904, p. 37; Porter & Clarke, ed. 1905).

2622 me]
F omits, presumably to make a decasyllable, but the improvement is dubious.

2625 this great stage]
Proverbial: Tilley W882, This World is a stage and every man plays his part, listing Sh.’s several uses of the topos. Elton (1966, pp. 167–70, 259 n.) details its use from Plato through the mid-17th c. See also Hankins (1953, pp. 20–6), Fraser (1962, pp. 120–2), Christian (1969, pp. 160–4), and the Variorum ed. of AYL (1977, p. 130). Muir & Danby (1950, p. 50) find it in Plangus’s lament (see n. 2620–2) just before the phrase blockish braine (cf. good blocke), and Muir (ed. 1952; rev. 1985, p. 245) in William Fulbecke’s A Booke of Christian Ethicks (1587, sigs. E7r–v) in connection with a child’s weeping when born. Dent (1981, W896) cites also The World is full of fools (knaves).

2625 of fooles]
Welsford (1935, p. 264): He sees…the whole of human life as a vast sottie. Milward (1987, p. 192) compares Eccles. 1:15, according to the Latin Vulgate: Stultorum infinitus est numerus—a verse on which Erasmus laid emphasis in his Praise of Folly.

2625 this]
Walker (1854, p. 80): This is is not infrequently,—like that is, &c. contracted into a monosyllable. Abbott (§461) supplies Shn. exx.; cf. Franz §55a. Smith (ed. 1902): The reason in Lear’s madness is but fitful. He has no sooner begun to moralize to Gloucester on the folly of this world than his thoughts again wander. Most eds. refer this to stratagem, not to stage.

2625 blocke]
The word has proved enigmatic; Kittredge (ed. 1940) says, The action here is left to the discretion of the actor. Proposed meanings include 1) a hat or hat-block; 2) a block of wood; 3) a head; 4) a plot; 5) a boot-block or boot; 6) a quintain.
(1)Hat or hat-block. Preceded by S. W. (1765, p. 234), Steevens (ed. 1773): Upon the king’s saying, I will preach to thee, the poet seems to have meant him to pull off his hat, and keep turning it and feeling it, in the attitude of one of the preachers of those times…till the idea of felt, which the good hat or block was made of, raises the stratagem in his brain of shoeing a troop of horse with a substance soft as that.…This makes him start from his preachment. Steevens attempts to show that the hat itself might be called after the block it was made on, but OED does not support the usage, and Steevens’s quotations seem rather to refer to the style or fashion of a hat (OED, sb. 4b). Bransom (1934, p. 127): The block was a wooden mould on which felt hats were made, and therefore would stand for the shape or fashion of the hat, or possibly the hat itself. Gloster’s bald head might suggest it. Eds. frequently note that Lear himself seems to be wearing no hat (cf. 1622+7 vnbonneted, 1714 bare headed, 2783+4 With this thin helme). In Edwin Booth’s prompt-book Lear takes Curan’s [i.e., Gentleman’s] hat (Furness, ed. 1880), and other Lears have taken Gloucester’s or Edgar’s (Sprague, 1944, p. 294). Brooke (ed. 1947): Lear (or Gloucester) is wearing one of the flamboyant hats that current fashion prescribed, either the copintank or sugarloaf, or more probably one of the newer type with broad drooping brims. Lear suggests, there would be enough felt in a few of these to shoe a troop of horse. Sisson (1956, 2:242): Every man praying, or prophesying, says St. Paul, having his head covered, dishonoureth his head (1. Cor. xi. 4). The custom indeed survives, though the Puritans rejected it, as did Cranmer (Confutations of Unwritten Verities, 1582). Lear therefore takes off his hat, looks at it, and his mind wanders from the preaching he has barely begun, in consideration of the block and of the material, felt, into a crazed logic of strategy for revenge; see nn. 1622+7, 2526. Wilson (ed. 1960): The mad king has a hat—a royal one, the crown of flowers.…This he takes off, and before putting it down to begin his sermon, turns it round in his fingers admiringly—had he not made it himself?—and says This…block! Skillan (ed. 1967): He turns the hat upside down with his fist…in it, which suggests to him the covering of a horse’s hoof. Oppel (1981, pp. 342, 345): The hat could be imaginary, but the phrase is figurative: this sermon is old-hat or conventional wisdom. Colman (ed. 1982): Possibly an actual hat fell off Gloucester’s head during the suicide attempt.
(2)A wooden block. Johnson (ed. 1765): Though possibly Lear picks up a flock of wool and so thinks of felt, Yet block may stand, if we suppose that the sight of a block put him in mind of mounting his horse. Furness (ed. 1880): Possibly block is used in its ordinary sense, and…Lear mounts one to deliver his preachment from, citing evidence from Tieck (1811, 3:241) that German actors mounted the stump of a tree. Craig (ed. 1901): Some have supposed that Lear mistakes a block of wood or the stump of a tree for the mounting block which was in every market town, and then quibbles on the word. Muir (ed. 1952): The word was probably suggested by stage, since the stage was often called a scaffold. Idem (1953, p. 73): It looks as though the word stage suggested, by way of unworthy scaffold, the executioner’s block, and this recalled to Lear’s (or Shakespeare’s) mind the other three kinds of block—the book block [see 5 below], the mounting block and the hat block. Lott (ed. 1974): An execution block…might lead his thoughts to…judicial murder [2629]. Weis (ed. 1993): He sits down…for his boots to be pulled off.…The block is a rock or a tree-stump. Porter (1986, p. 487): A speaker in John Eliot’s Ortho-epia Gallica, 1593, sig. s5r) sits upon a blocke, not further specified, under a shade tree.
(3)A head. Seymour (1805, 2:130): I believe Lear now alludes to the eyeless head of Gloster, to which succeeds the idea of hat and felt. Williams (1978, p. 421): The stage of fools suggests to the King his own role as fool.…His foolishness suggests the gate that let his folly in—his head.…Finally, his head suggests…his crown, the King’s hat.…Taking off his headdress, he inspects his handiwork and approves of what he sees: a headdress fit for a King who has created by his own actions his own suffering and folly. Good (1982, p. 47): [Ustinov] accompanies [this speech] with a confident tapping of his leonine head with one finger. It’s a wonderful discovery. He congratulates himself (as Lear) that he’s not only still all there, but even more so than before his recent rough time out on the heath. Brown (ed. 1996): Or he strikes approvingly on Gloucester’s head.
(4)A plot. Collier (1852, p. 444), emending (see textual n.): He does not advert to his hat as a good block at all, but to the excellent stratagem he has in his mind, of shoeing a troop of horse with felt. Frazer (1977, p. 355): One meaning of block listed in the OED [sb. 17] is a scheme, contrivance; generally used in a bad sense.…Examples quoted from Shakespeare’s time generally have a slightly different implication—bargain, bartering, exchange [OED, 18].…Moreover, if block and ransom were associated ideas in Shakespeare’s time,…Lear’s next speech, You…ransom ([2635]), fits neatly into the context. Both usages are Scots. King James twice uses the verb to block = To sketch out, plan (OED, 9); see Works, ed. Craigie, 1955–8, 1:17, 68; 2:292. Stone (1980, p. 209) judges that the problem would be solved if a convincing emendation of a good were forthcoming; that, notwithstanding, an association between blocke…and stratagem was probably also intended. Klawitter (1989), assuming that block follows from stage and refers to stage blocking or layout: He could be congratulating himself for blocking a fine judgment: that life is meaningless on this great stage of fools. This specifically theatrical usage is not attested by OED.
(5)A boot-block. Empson (1952, p. 837): I do not see why the word should not mean a boot as well as a hat, since both are sewn round a wooden form.…[Lear] takes his boots off.…[After preaching to Gloucester,] one of the boots catches his eye, and as soon as he reflects that it is strong his mind is hurled back into its craving for revenge. Muir (1953, p. 73): I have since noticed—what may be thought to support Mr. Empson’s interpretation—that in the first scene of Julius Caesar we get the following sequence: cobbler, surgeon, shoes, blocks, shout, weep. This may be compared with the sequence in the Lear passage: boots, weep, cry, block, shoe, surgeons.…I am informed that block is now used…in saddlery to signify the wooden form over which the damp leather is stretched, and in boot-making it is the form round which the leather is moulded.…[But] I have not yet found any proof that block could be used in Shakespeare’s day in any of these senses—Deloney’s meaning [A Heel-blocke, Gentle Craft, ed. Mann, 1912, p. 89] is rather different.
(6)A quintain. Fraser (ed. 1963): The quintain, whose function is to bear blows,…an object shaped like a man and used for tilting practice, comparing AYL 1.2.251 (417), a quintine, a meere liuelesse blocke. But apposition is not definition, and OED does not attest the meaning.

2626 delicate]
Schmidt (1874): Fine, ingenious (OED, a. 11b, quoting this l.).

2626 shoot]
F shoo. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 415): Perhaps a t/e misreading—the copy may have had shooe. Stone (1980, p. 89), improbably assuming a reported text in Q: Shoot…fell…an actor’s spoonerism.

2627 fell]
It is as possible that Lear, handling his boots, conceives the notion of shoeing horses with fell, leather, a word used at 2966, as that, handling a real or imagined hat (see n. 2625), he thinks of shoeing them with F’s Felt. Either way the other word is probably an l/t misreading (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 415). If Felt is right, it need not have been suggested by a supposed hat, since shoes and cloaks were also made of felt; conceivably Lear’s boots or his stockinged feet could have suggested felt shoes, or his walking noiselessly in woollen stockings could have suggested covering horses’ hooves similarly with fell (OED, 3: A covering of hair, wool, etc., esp. when thick and matted). Johnson (ed. 1765): A practice I believe sometimes used in former ages, for it is mentioned in Ariosto [Orlando Furioso 14.130]: —fece nel cadar strepito quanto | Avesse avuto sotto i piedi il feltro. The line, however, may simply mean that Rodomonte landed as softly as if he landed upon felt, and in any case the detail is omitted from John Harington’s tr. of 1591 where Sh. would most likely have found it. Nicholson (MS notes, Wright Shakespeariana, –1892): A favourite practice of the Hussites. Malone (ed. 1790): This delicate stratagem had been put in practice about fifty years before Shakspeare was born, quoting Lord Herbert’s Life of Henry the Eighth (1649, p. 41): The Lady Margaret…caused there a Jousts to be held in an extraordinary manner; the place being a large Roome, raised high from the ground, by many steps, and paved with black Square Stones like Marble; while the Horses to prevent sliding and noyse, were shod with felt or flocks. Kemshead (ed. 1875) dates this exhibition 13 Oct. 1513, at Lisle. Steevens (in Reed, ed. 1785) compares Geoffrey Fenton’s Tragicall Discourses (1567, p. 58), where a man wears shoes of felte in order to walk stealthily.

2627 Ile…proofe]
Since these words are not necessary to Lear’s train of thought, but simply make it more explicit, they may have been added to make F verse. See n. 2618–45. If they were accidentally omitted from Q, possibly the printer’s eye skipped over proofe, misreading it as a word he had just set, troupe or shoot.

2627 proofe]
Schmidt (1875): Trial, experiment, test (OED, sb. 4).

2628 stole]
F’s stolne may be an unnecessary refinement, since the curtailed participle stole occurs in JC 2.1.238 (879) and Mac. 2.3.68 (821). See n. 103.

2628 sonne in lawes]
Doran (1931, p. 97): A possible colloquial plural, giving analogous forms from OED.

2629 kill]
Lear repeats the word once too often to make verse with five stresses. Malone (ed. 1790): Formerly the word given in the English army when an onset was made, citing Ven. 562 and Mirrour for Magistrates (1610, p. 315), to which Craig (ed. 1901) adds North, Plutarch’s Lives, Scylla (1595, p. 505), Leggatt (1992, p. 198) A Larum for London (1602, E2) and Knight of the Burning Pestle (ca. 1607, 5.60–1), and Moore (1994, pp. 19–20) exx. from recent military history. The Clarkes (1879, p. 467) compare Cor. 5.6.130 (3804), and Dessen & Thomson (1999) cite several SDs. Muir (ed. 1952): Meaning No quarter! Rosenberg (1972, p. 279) records stage business, mostly predictable; see also the textual n. Goldman (1981, p. 42; 1985, pp. 88–9) discusses the histrionic problem set by such use of intensifying repetition, comparing 2614, 3217, 3280: In performance [the lines] act out a tension between the desire for absoluteness of response and the need for renewal, between the thrill of letting go, of crying out, and the labor of concentration, of finding a precise image for each exclamation in the series. Such lines long to be only a cry, but they must have a content or they go dead.…They too demand, and make possible, that regular renewal of sensation crucial to the role.

2630 three]
Three, presumably, because two will be needed to pursue and restrain Lear while the third stays to talk for a few moments with Edgar. Brooke (ed. 1947): In the Folio text the frugality of the stage manager has reduced them to one. Taylor (1983, p. 447) denies that such a cut would have reduced the number of actors: The two gentlemen affected could double anyone except Gloucester, Lear, Edgar, and Oswald. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 195): In Q, lay…him in line [2631] is addressed to the other two Gentlemen who enter with the speaker. In F, where only one Gentleman enters, lay…him is left in mid air. Urkowitz (1980, p. 25) even argues for an intentional difference in dramatic effect: In the Quarto, the two mute players may chase after Lear immediately. But in the Folio the king runs, unpursued, while the solitary Gentleman thinks and talks. This does seem strange, but the Gentleman’s revery and his elaborately courteous conversation with Edgar appear to agree with the other bizarre actions, entrances, transformations, and surprises out on the heath. The Quarto certainly permits the more practical action, while the Folio underscores the fantastic or dreamlike pattern of events in the scene. As Edwards (1982, pp. 695–6) points out, it would be absurd if a sole member of the centurie sent by Cordelia to rescue Lear allowed him to escape immediately on finding him, in order to stay and talk first to himself (2646–9) and then to strangers (2650–62). In all likelihood the single Gentleman (possibly one of Lear’s knights; see nn. 2347+1–+56, 2356) in F enters in the company of one or more unnamed attendants (probably soldiers, perhaps other knights; see n. 2349–50); mute supernumerary characters are often omitted from stage directions. He announces his discovery to them (O here he is), directs at least one of them to arrest the king, and begins to explain to Lear his reasons for their actions (2632). It is altogether unlikely that he would order strange commoners to seize a king or that Edgar would instantly comply with such an order from a stranger; in fact, Edgar’s later Haile (2650) implies that he remains separate from the action, not even speaking to the Gentleman until it is over. In talking of ransom and his need for seconds Lear seems to be addressing an organized party rather than a single stranger attempting to seize him, and both his plural my maisters (2642) and the Gentleman’s we (2643), noted by Edwards, reinforce the impression of a party of several, too large for Edgar to challenge as he challenges Oswald a few minutes later. When Lear runs off, the Gentleman trusts his men to pursue and catch him, and follows them unhurriedly. Taylor (op. cit.), agreeing that more than one Gentleman is indicated: I therefore assume that arabic 2, or roman ii or iii, was misread as a, and as a consequence either Gentlemen was misread Gentleman, or Gent. mis-expanded to Gentleman. In fact if the manuscript read (ambiguously) Enter Gent., the compositor might easily have assumed that the singular was meant, and supplied a himself, citing parallels elsewhere in Sh. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 516) assume that the Gentleman who speaks and who stays behind and talks with Edgar is the same one who appears at 1615 (see n.) and 2744. Halio (ed. 1992): They hold him so gently that he easily breaks free, or they release their hold momentarily to kneel when he says I am a king ([2641]).

2631 sirs]
Q’s vocative, if it is correct, is apparently directed by one member of the entering party to the others (see prev. n.). F’s singular Sir could be addressed to one of them. Most eds., however, assume that the word was made singular in F in order to refer to the King, without a corresponding change in punctuation, and so follow Rowe in putting a full stop after him. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 415): It is most unlikely that the Gentleman would begin to speak to Lear without some vocative.

2632 Daughter]
F’s word seems necessary if the audience is to guess the drift of the Gentleman’s interrupted speech. The fact that Q1’s line ends at the right margin suggests accidental omission of the one remaining word. Q2, unable to make sense of the incomplete your most deere in its Q1 copy, omitted the phrase; F apparently restored the original complete phrase. Blayney (apud Wells & Taylor, 1987, p. 523): Q’s Daughter should have been turned up or down but was omitted. Urkowitz (1980, p. 24) finds instead a change in dramatic conception: The physical threat…[of] the two other gentlemen in the Quarto is replaced in the Folio by a mental terror, the idea of Daughter, an explanation that Edwards (1982, p. 695) rejects as frankly incredible. Mahood (1992, p. 166), oddly, thinks that the Gentleman refers to either Goneril or Regan, not to Cordelia, who has sent him and whom he praises in 2647 ff.

2633–42 No…that]
From Q’s prose F makes very clumsy (and therefore suspect) verse; even with a good deal of cutting and adding, the result is still a short line at 2638, hypermetric lines at 2640, 2642, and 2645, and a very awkward 2644. It is entirely likely that the verse of Lear’s preachment begins to dissolve at 2629, and that the sudden appearance of his captors causes him to drop completely into less measured, more irregular speech as he seeks to elude them.

2633 no reskue]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Does no one come to my rescue? Am I to be allowed to be taken prisoner without anyone stirring to save me?

2633 what]
See n. 810.

2634 naturall]
Walker (1860, 2:309): Born to be the (OED, Natural-born). Deighton (ed. 1891): With an allusion to natural in the sense of idiotic (OED, Natural adj. 14). Empson (1951, p. 145) finds other senses as well: It surely means something good, at any rate in Lear’s intention; the wicked are unnatural, but Lear has found his way back to unsophisticated nature, like the fool.…Since Lear now feels that death would be welcome he feels he is a toy of fortune because he can no longer be hurt.

2634 foole of Fortune]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Because just recently leading a charge against the sons-in-law, and now a prisoner. Cf. Rom. 3.1.136 (1574): O I am fortunes foole (Steevens, ed. 1778). Proverbial: Dent (1981, F617.1).

2635 ransome]
Harrison (ed. 1948): Prisoners of good family could buy their freedom from their captors, comparing H5 4.3.79–125 (2325–73). Wilson (ed. 1960): A royal prisoner was worth a great sum; would be well tended and his wounds carefully dressed.

2635 let…churgion]
Brooke (ed. 1947): He imagines himself on the battlefield and wounded. Wilson (ed. 1960): He imagines the attack he led at l. [2629]…has ended in his capture.

2635 a churgion]
F’s Surgeons may be pronounced as a trisyllable (Abbott §479), but here the accent falls awkwardly on the middle syllable. Q would make preferable verse.

2636 cut to the braines]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): One of the most powerfully, yet briefly expressed, utterances of mingled bodily pain and consciousness of mental infirmity ever penned. Tovey (ed. 1896): Lear fancies that he has been taken prisoner in battle, and the oppression of his brain makes him think he has received a wound in his head. Craig (ed. 1901): Irritated, vexed to madness, comparing Acts 5:33, cut to the heart (AV; Geneva says brast for anger; Bishops 1568 [like Tyndale 1535 and Great 1539] reads clave asunder; Rheims 1582 has it cut them to the hart). Muir (ed. 1952): Used literally and figuratively; he is vexed to madness, but requires a surgeon for an imaginary wound to the head. Skillan (ed. 1967): Refers to the wounds and pain inflicted by his daughters.

2638 No…selfe]
Moberly (ed. 1876) misunderstands Lear to mean that he will haue any thing all to himself, without sharing it with a second person; but this would not make him weep. Page (ed. 1889), correctly: No one to aid me or take up my cause? Tovey (ed. 1896): By myself, unaided, comparing 2633. Goggin (ed. 1910): He will face his captors single-handed. Joseph (ed. 1966): No one to act as my second? Lear has thrown down his gauntlet with the boast to prove it on a giant. This makes him use the term appropriate to a duellist.

2639 man…of salt]
F’s unnecessarily added a man seems designed to eke out a verse line; see n. 2633–42. Johnson (ed. 1765): Would make a man melt away like salt in hot weather. Margery the Cookmaid (1765, p. 4): Salt melts away in cold, damp Weather, not in hot. Malone (ed. 1790): A man made up of tears. Delius (ed. 1854): The following two lines make it clear that salty tears are meant (Ger.). Skillan (ed. 1967): I.e., tears of humiliation. Tovey (ed. 1896): Like salt, melting away in tears. Houghton (ed. 1957) suspects an allusion to Lot’s wife (Gen. 19:26), but its point is unclear. Edwards (ed. 1975): A man must be made of salt to weep so many tears. Weis (ed. 1993), taking Q’s make as the auxiliary of to vse: A man who cries easily…i.e. a man of tears.

2640–2640+1 to…dust]
I.e., to weep copiously. Cf. TN 1.1.28–9 (35–6): And water once a day her Chamber round | With eye-offending brine. Possibly a proverbial image: Dent (1981, D650.1).

2640+1 I…dust]
Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 183, 416): These words go well with the Garden water-pots of the previous line: and they seem to me to be too good to be an [inauthentic] interpolation.…Omission from F may be due simply to carelessness in the compositor. Their sense being inessential and somewhat repetitive, and the syntax loose (a second for is lacking), they may have been sacrificed to F’s attempt to make verse from Q’s prose; see n. 2633–42. Hunter (ed. 1972): Compositorial eyeskip in F from I and laying to I will die. Stone (1980, p. 236): Omitted very probably by the reviser on grounds of obscurity.

2640+1 laying]
Hoeniger (ed. 1968): (i) settling, (ii) perhaps, allaying.

–2640 Lear.]
Either 2639–2640+1 should have been assigned to another speaker or the Q1 compositor erroneously supplied this speech prefix (both improbable suppositions), or a speech dropped out of Q between these two speeches by Lear. F solves the difficulty by removing this prefix (and previous part-line) and running the speeches together; Q2, by adding an intervening speech of doubtful authority (see textual n.) which could also complete a pentameter. Doran (1931, p. 35): It is possible that the printer of Q2, noticing two speeches of Lear’s coming together…inserted a colorless remark by the Gentleman. Contrary to [his] general practice…the short additional speech is not set up on a separate line to the left but fills out another short line. This circumstance may indicate that the printer or press-reader inserted the speech after the proof for this sheet had been made. On the other hand, the more significant circumstance that the addition…improves the meter, combined with the observation that the deficiency of the verse, printed as prose in Q1, would not have been readily apparent to the printer’s eye or even to his ear because of the omission of a man, strongly suggests that he was not here making an improvement on his own, but that he had recourse to some source other than the printed text of Q1.…But we have seen that none of the other variant readings prove such a source for Q2. Daniel (facs. 1885, p. xiv): Q2’s added speech might have existed in a corrected state of the Q1 page no longer extant. Greg (1940, pp. 189–90) doubts the survival in Q2 of a lost Q1 press-correction: There is greater likelihood that the corrected rather than the uncorrected state of the sheet would have survived, that Q1 erroneously divided one speech into two, and that so simple an added speech could have been supplied in Q2 by anyone who noticed the error in Q1 and thus can have no authority. In a postcript (pp. 191–2), however, Greg gives reason to think that in later sheets proof correction was progressively delayed, so that if there ever were two states of [this sheet]…, the proportion of corrected to uncorrected pulls may have been very low indeed, and very likely the sheet was invariant. Evans (1961, p. 326): The Q2 addition deserves consideration for several reasons. (1) The fact that there are two distinct speeches given to Lear in Q1 should carry more weight than has been allowed it. (2) The verse arrangement in F1 which telescopes Lear’s two speeches in Q1 (omitting five words which all editors receive as genuine Shakespeare) is very irregular metrically. (3) The Gentleman’s Good sir of Q2 is not (pace Greg) the sort of speech which a proofreader or compositor would be likely to invent; the natural thing would have been to run Lear’s speeches together as F1 does. (4) The fact that the Q2 reading appears on the same type-line as the conclusion of Lear’s first speech (thus giving it the appearance of an insertion) carries little weight, for, although Q2 generally begins each speech on a separate line (unlike Q1), it does not always do so, but sometimes follows the arrangement found in Q1 (e.g., sigs. B4v, C1v, C4r, L3v, and L4r). (5). Q2’s interruption by the Gentleman is perfectly in tone with his earlier and later speeches of solicitous concern for Lear and serves as a dramatic break in Lear’s speech, the sudden I will die bravely answering a movement toward him as the Gentleman says Good sir, a movement which Lear interprets as a threatening gesture. Taylor (1983, p. 432): Blayney in vol. 2 provides further evidence that Q2’s added speech may well derive from a press-correction in Q1. (Ibid., p. 364): If we accept the authority of Q2’s addition, then the manuscript [behind F] must have been contaminated by Q1, because [Compositor] B was at this point either working directly from that manuscript, or from a copy of Q2 (in which the addition must have been deliberately struck out). But there is no reason to think that F was set from Q1 or Q2 copy; see . The line could have been missing from the playbook, possibly because of the same obscurity in rough draft that caused it (initially?) to be missing from Q1. The F text, descended from that playbook, could represent the playbook scribe’s or the company’s solution to the difficulty; see n. 2640+1. Halio (ed. 1992): F was not here influenced by Q2. Working on an exemplar of Q with uncorrected sheet I, the F reviser or collator solved the problem of Lear’s consecutive speeches by fusing them, but left the lines metrically irregular. Foakes (ed. 1997): Q2’s speech, the only addition made there to the Q text, fills a gap. The interruption…turns Lear’s attention from weeping to fighting.

2640–1 die…bridegroome]
Deighton (ed. 1891) compares Ant. 4.14.99–101 (2941–3: I will bee | A Bride-groome in my death, and run intoo’t | As to a Louers bed). Craig (ed. 1901) compares the similar MM 3.1.83 (1298). Harrison (ed. 1937) finds the comparison in a contemporary account of the execution of Sir Charles Danvers in 1600, and again (ed. 1948) of the approach to supposed execution of Lord Grey of Wilton on 9 Dec. 1603. Harbage (ed. 1958): The image [is] suggested by the secondary meaning of bravely, i.e. handsomely, and the sexual suggestion of will die. See next n. Dundes (1976, p. 361): Lear has in mind incest with Cordelia. But of course Lear is running from Cordelia, and is being facetious. The comparison was proverbial: Dent (1981, B664.1), Fresh as a Bridegroom.

–2640 die brauely]
Schmidt (1874), bravely: Valiantly. Kittredge (ed. 1940): In fine attire [OED, adv. 2].…Lear is thinking of his floral adornments. Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956): An ironic reference to his weed-ornamented rags. Skillan (ed. 1967): In high spirits; as a bridegroom puts on his very best clothes and is at the height of happiness. A few suspect a bawdy quibble on die. Partridge (1947, p. 101): To experience a sexual orgasm. Colman (1974, p. 191): (a) loss of life, (b) detumescence following orgasm. Edwards (ed. 1975): Perform the sexual act well. Lear’s mad remarks usually grow somehow out of the context; here a supposed joke about his own sexual performance as he is being arrested by pursuers would seem to be gratuitous bawdry, more characteristic of the Fool than of Lear.

2641 smugge]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): Neat, spruce, trim OED (a. 1). Verity (ed. 1897): Not necessarily contemptuous then as now. Weis (ed. 1993): Finely arrayed, perhaps recalling Lear’s crown of flowers. If the word was added in F to eke out a verse line (see n. 2633–42), it is apt enough, repeating the idea of brauely (Kittredge, ed. 1940).

2641 what]
See n. 858.

2641 Iouiall]
Schmidt (1874): Merry OED (a. 6). OED (5): Having the qualities imparted by the planet Jupiter, which as a natal planet was regarded as the source of joy and happiness. Gardner (ed. 1969): Majestic,…like Jove (OED 1). Wells (ed. 2000): Perhaps…glancing at Jove’s many sexual conquests.

2642 I am a King]
Lear leaves the scene as he entered upon it, asserting his regality—meaning here, apparently, kingly courage. Foakes (ed. 1997): Possibly the attendants back off, or even kneel, as in several recent productions, so allowing him to make his exit running.

2642 my maisters]
Deighton (ed. 1891): My fine fellows; a familiar title, sometimes implying respect, sometimes used ironically. F’s omission of my may possibly imply slightly less familiarity.

2643 You…you]
Mahood (1992, p. 166): The Gentleman’s reply…is pivotal. It initiates that counterflow in the action by which Lear, seemingly mad beyond recovery, will be restored to humanity’s rightful kingdom. The importance of the moment…is confirmed by Lear’s reply. Wells (ed. 2000): They may bow or kneel, dropping their guard in a way that makes it easier for Lear to escape.

2644 theres life int]
Proverbial: Tilley L265 and Dent (1981). Johnson (ed. 1765): The case is not yet desperate. Steevens (ed. 1773) compares Ant. 3.13.191 (2379), There’s sap in’t yet. Hunter (ed. 1972): Hearing them say that they obey him, he realizes that captivity is not…absolute. Horsman (ed. 1973): Come, if you are to get the ransom ([2635]). Foakes (ed. 1997): There is no need to die bravely.

2644 and]
See n. 630.

2644 it]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Your object. Tovey (ed. 1896): My person, or what you want with me. Wilson (ed. 1960): The ransom.

2645 you…running]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): A defiant challenge: Catch me if you want me! Holloway (1961, p. 97): He is a Jack-a-Green, at once hero and victim of a popular ceremony.

2645 Sa…sa.]
Of F’s addition Adee (ed. 1890) asks ironically, Another ripe addition in the poet’s Stratford retirement? It might be actor’s gag, or an attempt to make a pentameter from Q’s prose. Though eds. have often considered the words nonsense—Lear’s panting as he runs (Hudson, ed. 1871), Lear skips away carolling (Ger.) (Stark, 1871, p. 80), meaningless babble (White, ed. 1883), sounds…of running away in a certain child’s play (van Dam, 1935, p. 102)—other eds. since Deighton (ed. 1891) have recognized an incitement to them to pursue him taken from the old hunting cry used to urge dogs on in the chase: see n. 2031. Brown (ed. 1996): Or perhaps to follow in chase of those sons-in-law. Both Craig (ed. 1901) and Kittredge (ed. 1940) supply many contemporary exx. of sa, sa! (Fr. ça, ça!) as a defiant call inciting pursuit or attack; Porter (1986, p. 487) adds John Eliot’s Ortho-epia Gallica (1593, sigs. s3r, t1r), and Leggatt (1992, p. 198) adds A Larum for London (1602, sig. E2).

2645 King running]
F may omit these words, which express the obvious, because the line lacks room for them.

2646–9 A…to]
Apparently an aside. Cf. 2650 and see n. 2630. The Gentleman’s train of thought is not entirely clear. Possibly he is now completing the statement he began in 2632; perhaps the idea of ransom suggests the idea of general redemption. On the speech’s possible dramatic purpose, see n. 2533; on its possible Christian meaning, see n. 2649. Mahood (1992, p. 166): The plain sense of these words is much more powerful, in dramatic terms, than the message of paradise lost and paradise regained which has been read into them by redemptionist critics. In Lear’s elder daughters Nature has appeared as universal rapine; but Cordelia, though she cannot efface the vision of humanity preying upon itself, will transcend it in the ensuing scene of Lear’s awakening and restoration.

2647 past…of]
Deighton (ed. 1891): No words can describe. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 523): the of is hypermetrical, an easy compositorial interpolation.

2647 one]
Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 183–4): More than F’s a, Q’s one forms an effective antithesis to twaine in line [2649]. The F compositor may have substituted a for one owing to his having set up a King earlier in the same line.

2648 nature]
Usually understood as human nature (see n. 441), but the pronoun her (2649) implies the goddess Nature (see n. 232) and hence perhaps the world in general (see n. 435). Milward (1987, p. 192), less probably: The nature of Lear.

2648 generall curse]
Kittredge (ed. 1940), general: Universal (OED, a. 1). Cf. 3294. Tovey (ed. 1896): The wickedness of Regan and Goneril taints the whole world. Hunter (ed. 1972): The current state of Britain, with brother against brother etc. ([436–41]). Some identify it as the original sin of Adam and Eve; see the next n. Shaheen (1987, p. 154) compares Leir 908–9; see .

2649 twaine]
Delius (ed. 1854): Goneril and Regan. Danby (1949, p. 125): Not Goneril and Regan. Quite obviously Shakespeare is referring here to Adam and Eve. Though Muir (ed. 1952) finds this idea fanciful, others accept at least an allusion to the Biblical parents. Houghton (ed. 1957): Although the primary reference is to the evil sisters a Christian hearer could hardly avoid thinking of the original sin. Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960): Gon. and Reg. have, like Adam and Eve, by their sin brought all humanity under a curse; Cord. is the Christ-like redeemer. See also Milward (1973, p. 101; 1987, p. 193), Coursen (1976, p. 287), Hills (1977), and , .

2649 her]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Human nature. See n. 2648.

2650 gentle]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Noble, honourable (OED, a. 2). Horsman (ed. 1973): Well-born.

2651 speed]
Delius (ed. 1854): I.e., God speed you (OED, v. 6b; 6: Cause to succeed or prosper); cf. 353. Deighton (ed. 1891): Make haste; I have no time to loiter (OED, 12b)—a less likely reading, since the Gentleman seems in no hurry; see n. 2630.

2652 toward]
See n. 938.

2653–4 Most…sence]
Doran (1931, p. 109): The misalignment in F indicates that the F printer was not using Q1 copy but a manuscript. Less plausibly, Taylor (1985, p. 27) attributes it to Q2 copy for F; but since F replaces Q2’s omitted word with another (see n. 2654), it could have retained (or restored) the more correct Q alignment.

2653 sure]
Deighton (ed. 1891): That rumour is most certain.

2653 vulgar]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Commonly or generally known, publicly reported (OED, a. 6).

2654 here’s that]
Possibly the Q1 compositor carried the word (Q2’s heares) in memory. Q2’s omission of that seems occasioned by Q1’s immediate repetition of the same word, and may indicate another memorial error or simple misunderstanding.

2654 That]
On F’s which see n. 235, and OED (pron. 9b): Introducing a defining clause, quoting this l. Doran (1931, p. 45): It was probably euphony which dictated the change from that to which.…However, the change to which instead of to who conforms to Shakespeare’s distinction between which to indicate a kind of person (qualis) and who to indicate an individual (qui).

2654 sence]
OED (sb. 20c): The gist, upshot, or general purport of words spoken or written. Though most eds. prefer F’s sound, Q’s meaning is more exact and Shn. OED (Distinguish v. 5): To perceive distinctly or clearly (by…hearing…); to make out by…listening, quoting Luc. 1785 and this l. (F) as its first exx. The line in Lucrece means No man could distinguish the sense of what he said, his speech being thick (rapid), as all could hear. Likewise the Gentleman refers here not to one who can hear the sound of speech, but one who can make sense of it, and heare (understand, perceive, distinguish) from it the intelligence of a battle toward. Duthie’s (ed. 1949, p. 416) proposal of a quadruple misreading is less likely than an intentional alteration, perhaps by a literal-minded person who found hearing sound easier to imagine than hearing sense. Weis (ed. 1993): Who has any understanding (Q); or who has ears to hear (F). Foakes (ed. 1997): Possibly referring to drums.

2655 by your fauour]
Schmidt (1874): By your leave, good will, pardon (OED, sb. 3). Tovey (ed. 1896): An apology for detaining him with another question. Gardner (ed. 1969): Polite deference. The contrast of tone with what has gone before is marked.

2657 on speed fort]
Q2’s on speed for’t makes a possible sense of Q1. Ridley (ed. 1935): I.e. for it, the battle. Weis (ed. 1993): Eager to get into the fray. But F1’s on speedy foot perhaps better fits the context and is accepted by most eds. Duthie (ed. 1949) suspects an o/r misreading of foot, and Halio (ed. 1994) compares the missing -y at 2554. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 523): Besides being unmetrical, the phrase on speed has no Shakespearian parallels…. There are several o/r misreadings in Q, and since Compositor C apparently preferred the spelling speed…he might well have normalized what he saw as speede—either by overlooking a penultimate i, or misreading -y as -e. Craig (ed. 1901) compares Mac. 2.3.125 (893), Vpon the foot of Motion, and 1H4 5.3.20 (3157), Vpon the foot of feare.

2657 maine descryes…thoughts]
Q’s erroneous descryes is corrected by F’s descry, but leaving maine as an adjective when it ought to be the object of descry results, as many eds. since Johnson have said, in an expression that is harsh, perhaps exhibiting courtierly finicalness (Clarkes, 1879, p. 6). Emending to the maine’s descry would solve the problem; possibly an error of metathesis in the MS was reproduced in Q and only partly corrected in F. Johnson (ed. 1765): The main body is expected to be descried every hour. McCann (ed. 1964): The main body of troops (as distinguished from the reconnoitring troops sent out ahead). Presumably sightings of the advance troops are the reason that the Gentleman expects the main body to be descried imminently. Wright (ed. 1875) makes adjectival maine refer ambiguously to both the troops and their descry: The full view of the main body is hourly expected. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 523) propose an attractive alternative: Q1’s punctuation is almost certainly wrong: as often elsewhere, Compositor C has simply placed a comma at the end of the line, and no punctuation elsewhere, even though the sense-break occurs somewhere in the middle.…F follows Q2 in breaking the line before the maine.…If the break were placed after the maine, the Gentleman could be understood to say the main part <of the other army> is near and on speedy foot.

2657 descryes]
The verb descry occurs at 2398, but here the word must be a noun. OED (sb. 2): Discovery of that which is distant or obscure; perception from a distance, quoting this l. as its first ex. of two. Cf. also Daborne, A Christian Turned Turk 1.2 (1612). Since the word is a neologism and does not agree with the following verb, it has aroused suspicion. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 523) emend to descryers (in Q only) to produce the meaning, (their) scouts and spies (already) demand our hourly attention. Since the Q compositor clearly had trouble understanding this line, he may have misunderstood descrye as a verb completing the clause (hence the comma after it) and either simply made it agree with the singular subject maine or misinterpreted the final e as the -es symbol. Halio (ed. 1994): A flourish on the tail of the y in descry might have led [the compositor] to print descryes. Another possibility is that Sh. wrote a different neologism, descryal, which was misread as descryes; OED (Descrial) lists a single instance of the word from 1605.

2658 Standst]
Clearly the second-person ending is incorrect. Halio (ed. 1994): A not uncommon s/st error could have resulted in Standst. Wells & Taylor (1987, pp. 523–4): Even if a question were possible here, the Gentleman elsewhere addresses Edgar as you.…The error is probably due to aural assimilation (stands[t] on). F’s Stands agrees with F’s singular subject descry; it could also agree with Q’s plural descryes: see n. 1697.

2658 Standst on…thoughts]
Virtually all eds. prefer F’s generalized singular thought though Q also makes acceptable sense. The source of the real difficulty in this line is the expression stand on, used also at 2916 in a different sense. Since Johnson (see n. 2657) it has often been taken here to mean is awaited or expected from hour to hour—i.e., in men’s thoughts every hour. Though stand may connote waiting in such senses as standing watch or standing in attandance, OED does not clearly support Johnson’s interpretation; certainly the definitions (73, 98) of the phrase stand on are all inappropriate to the context. More basically, Johnson glosses the verb as passive when it is active; if stand on = await, the line says that descry awaits hourly thoughts, the reverse of Johnson’s reading. Verity (ed. 1897) attempts a more fanciful metaphorical gloss, to be on the tip-toe of expectation—not a Shn. phrase. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Literally, to rest on, to depend on (OED, 78d, defining the phrase stand upon). It is remotely possible that the sense concerns, affects, involves (OED, stand upon, 78p, quoting Err. 4.1.68 [1055]) could apply here: the descrial is on our minds from one hour to the next. Schmidt (1875) glosses stand here as to be (on), a sense supported by OED (15, 38; see n. 337), but to be or remain on the thought is not a Shn. (if it is an English) idiom. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 524) are the first to suggest, plausibly, that on is here a misreading of in; though they prefer in Q a sense of stand on (= insist on) that suits their emendation descryers (see n. 2657), the QF text makes perfect sense if on is altered to in: the descrial remains in our thoughts hourly—or as Wells & Taylor freely read in F, is what is hourly expected, essentially Schmidt’s paraphrase.

2660 that]
See n. 273.

2660 speciall cause]
Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Her waiting upon her father’s movements and illness.

2661 army…on]
From pitched camp to battlefield. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): This made the taking of Lear and Cordelia easier. But they join their fighting forces later, in 5.2, before being taken. Foakes (ed. 1997): The clash is postponed while she searches for Lear—i.e., the army has moved on elusively or in retreat to avoid battle, leaving Cordelia unprotected? Rather, in all probability, her army is moving on towards the battlefield, necessarily under the direction of a marshal, because The powers of the kingdome are expected howerly (2658), their drums are heard by 2741, leading Edgar to attempt to bestow his father safely during the oncoming battle (2742, 2921–2), they approach apace at 2843+9, and appear on stage at 2845–6, having Cordelia’s forces in vew (2897). In the interim Cordelia stays in camp to await and care for Lear, both of them joining her army before fighting and being captured in battle.

2663–5 You…please]
Gloucester renounces the idea of another attempt at suicide, leaving it to the merciful gods to fix for me the hour of my death (Crook, ed. 1907), when the appointed time comes (Kittredge, ed. 1940). Verity (ed. 1897): Gloucester’s thought is prompted by the feeling that after all there is some one (Lear) worse off than himself. Or perhaps by now the lesson that Edgar wished him to learn has sunk in. Maxwell (1950, p. 146): Gloucester’s religious feeling here is both genuine and profound, yet he is contemplating an act that is by Christian standards a mortal sin.…Shakespeare is careful to avoid putting any words that suggest Christianity into his mouth.

2664 worser spirit]
See n. 1820, 1823. Steevens (ed. 1793): My evil genius. Delius (ed. 1854): The supposed evil spirit who pursued him on Dover Cliff in the disguise of a possessed beggar (Ger.); cf. 2513–24. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The evil side of my nature; or, perhaps, my evil genius. There is at least an allusion to the old idea that every man is attended by two spirits, one good and one bad. So Horsman (ed. 1973): bad angel, comparing Son. 144:2–4. Hunter (ed. 1972): Perhaps only my ill thoughts.

2666 father]
See n. 2517.

2667 what are you]
On what = who see n. 540. Tovey (ed. 1896): The appearance of Lear has postponed this question hitherto; or we may suppose that Edgar comes forward in a new character. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): During Edgar’s talk with the Gentleman his normal speech has recurred enough to make his father wonder. Brown (ed. 1976): He does not risk a true reply: either he fears for his father’s sanity or fears his own ability to endure. The question is answered offstage (see 3155–6); The present matter is full enough without such a revelation (Skillan, ed. 1967).

2668 lame by]
Both Q and F’s tame to make good sense, and either adjective could be a misreading of the other; the same variant occurs at 1576. Whichever printer or scribe misread his MS substituted, intentionally or unconsciously, the preposition appropriate to the adjective he saw. Malone (ed. 1790) preferred Q because of parallelism with Son. 37:3, So I, made lame by Fortunes dearest spight. F’s tame, meaning subdued (Schmidt, 1875), without resentment (Crook, ed. 1907), humbly submissive, parallels Gloucester’s humbled to all strokes (2250). Carroll (1988, p. 237): In some sense Edgar has been made tame by his experience, yet in the next few lines he will confront Oswald and kill him in a fight. I find Q’s lame by more appropriate to the dramatic context, and truer to the intensely physical suffering Edgar has experienced. Idem (1996, p. 199 n.): Q’s lame by reinforces the subplot’s emphasis on the physical body, and…the poor man who is lame is a standard beggar type. Foakes (ed. 1997), for F: Habituated to.…Edgar is anything but lame in fighting Oswald.

2669 Art]
Most eds. understand this term to mean knowledge or skill acquired by experience; see n. 1725–6 and OED (1). A number, however, take it to mean instruction (Delius, ed. 1854), a sense not supported by OED.

2669 feeling sorrowes]
Not simply familiar (knowne) but deeply felt, as at WT 4.2.7–8 (1620). Upton (1746, p. 310): He uses the active participle passively.…feeling, i.e. causing themselves to be felt. So Abbott (§372): Realized. OED (ppl. a. 3): In quasi-passive sense: That is deeply or sensibly felt or realized, heart-felt, acute, vivid, citing this l. Hunter (ed. 1972): Sorrows that I have both felt in myself and known in others. Eccles (ed. 1792) urges a more active meaning: Awakening sympathetic sensibility…[for] others. So Wright (ed. 1875): Sorrows that move compassion.

2670 pregnant]
Disposed to (Rann, ed. 1794), susceptible to (Delius, ed. 1854), both attested by OED (a.2 3d). Foakes (ed. 1997): Or, like a pregnant woman, big with.

2671 biding]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Place of abode, or shelter (OED, vbl. sb. 2b, quoting this l.).

2673 bornet and beniz]
Q1(c)’s bounty and the benizon is reproduced in F1 and all later eds., seeming certainly correct, except for the unnecessary final comma [after heauen]. Only Stone (1980, p. 210): Though…beniz is intelligible as a mistake for benizon, it is less easy to regard bornet as a misreading of bounty or even bountie.

2673 beniz]
OED (Benison sb. 1a): That blessing which God gives, quoting this l. Cf. 290.

2674 to saue thee]
Q1(c)’s to boot, to boot, altered in F and most eds. to To boot, and boot, has raised doubts because Q1(u) cannot be a misreading of it. Greg (1940. p. 176): The compositor’s reading is difficult to account for: he must have been guessing at the sense of a passage he could not decipher. There is, indeed, some resemblance of graphic outline, and the confusion of e and t is not unknown, but the [long] s and h can hardly have been suggested by the ductus literarum. The absence of the second to, in conjunction with the discrepancy between [Q1(c)] and F, is significant. If, as seems likely, the copy read to boot boot, the insertion of a comma and a to would be the natural correction for the reader to make in order to restore both the sense and the verse. At first sight, indeed, it looks as though he were right and the folio somehow corrupt; but in fact…there is a sort of play on the double meaning of the phrase—to boot, in addition (to my thanks) [Clarkes, ed. 1868; OED, sb.1 1], and boot, and to your behoof [Tovey, ed. 1896; OED, 3]. Stone (1980, p. 210): Q[1(c)] supplies a good reading, but comparison with Q[1(u)] raises serious doubt whether it is the true reading. The phrase to saue thee (to-save thee?…), which must have stood in the copy, has entirely disappeared. Blayney (1982, pp. 251–2): If it is the first to boot which means in addition, the construction of the speech is atrocious, with the last two words attempting to express a tautologous afterthought by means of an all-but-incomprehensible ellipsis.…Had the words boot, to boot been in copy it is quite possible that the compositor omitted what he failed to understand, but if so those words probably followed what he read as saue thee. Blayney conjectures an original line to send thee boot, to boot, of which send was first misprinted as saue and the last three words were omitted as making no sense. The proof-reader would have struck out aue and written…end/ boot, to boot in the margin—a phrase describing what the compositor made the speech do. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 537): It would…seem most economical to suppose that F differs from Q2 because the [F] manuscript did.…However, the annotator or the compositor might have substituted and for the wrong to: And boot to boot would be more intelligible. In Q it looks as if the proof-reader must have consulted copy (in order to make sense of an obviously garbled speech) but the compositor, in the process of altering several words, adding others, and relining, for some reason (perhaps Blayney’s) overlooked or omitted saue thee. There is no sure accounting for F; whatever difficulties in Q’s MS caused the original garbling of the line must have been resolved somehow in the playbook; possibly the line was trimmed to make continuous F verse, though as Blayney points out (p. 251), part-lines separated by an entrance are neither always nor necessarly complementary in Shakespeare, and (if Blayney’s reconstruction is right) verse could have been made by striking out the last two words, yielding To send thee boot and a simpler meaning without Greg’s apparent corruption. F is sometimes interpreted one benefit after another (Delius, ed. 1854), over and over again (Deighton, ed. 1891), to the fullest possible extent (Lee, ed. 1908), in addition, and more on top of that (Joseph, ed. 1966), as well, as well (Colman, ed. 1982). Possibly the two boots refer respectively to the two kinds of heavenly gift, bounty and blessing; so Hoeniger (ed. 1968) may intend in his puzzling gloss: In addition, and may heaven’s bounty help you also. It is possible to distinguish between heaven’s bounty, meaning kindness or generosity (OED, 3, 4), and boot, meaning material profit or active help (OED, 3, 7).

2676–2703 Enter…]
Bullough (1973, p. 406 n.) finds an analogue in Sidney’s Arcadia 2.10.4; see .

2676 proclamed prize]
Delius (ed. 1854): Oswald refers to [Regan]’s promise in 4.5 [2424–5]. Deighton (ed. 1891): One who has been proclaimed as a traitor and on whose head a price has been put. Cf. 1252, and 2684, publisht. Perhaps Oswald interprets his private instructions from Regan as a proclamation; there is none other concerning Gloucester in the play. For the accent see n. 250. Crane (1952, p. 166): Oswald’s verse denotes his pride in his station.

2676 happy,]
See n. 1253. Doran (1931, pp. 105–6): F’s omission of the comma reveals a misunderstanding of the sense on the part of the folio printer that could not have arisen if he had been printing from Q1. Taylor (1985, p. 69): It could easily be an unintended by-product of its division of [Qq] prose into verse. Joseph (ed. 1966) finds multiple ironies: Edmund’s successes have actually brought Gloucester and Edgar together; and Edgar’s presence, when Oswald makes a bid for a reward which he expects to win easily, leads to the revelation of the plot against Albany.

2677–8 that…fortunes]
Mahood (1992, p. 172): The play’s most horrific expression of self-interest. Cf. 2425.

2677 framed]
Made. Q1(c)’s first framed improves meter, and since the proof-reader had apparently consulted copy in correcting the previous speech, there is great likelihood that the inserted word here is correct: it had no doubt been accidentally omitted by the compositor (Greg, 1940, p. 176).

2678 most]
F’s old is both supererogatory and less emphatic.

2678 vnhappy]
Brown (ed. 1976): Miserable/doomed.

2679 briefly…remember]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Quickly recollect the past offences of thy life, and recommend thy self to heaven. Wright (ed. 1875): Remember thy sins and confess them before death. Tovey (ed. 1896): He gives him short shrift. OED (Remember v. 5): Reflect upon (oneself), quoting this l. Dent (1981, R72.1): Possibly proverbial. Milward (1987, p. 193): Repeated biblical advice: Ecclus. 7:36, 8:7, 28:6.

2681–2 friendly…to’t]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): He calls upon Edgar to defend him. Furness (ed. 1880) and most eds.: Addressed to Oswald, begging him to put strength enough to his destroying sword to make sure work with it. Stauffer (1949, p. 198): His despair has not been cured. Again Edgar’s hand saves him. Greg (1940, p. 394) compares Leir 1659–60: My friend, I am prepared for the stroke: Strike when thou wilt, and I forgiue thee here; see .

2681 friendly]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Since I long for death. Harbage (ed. 1958): Unconsciously befriending.

2682 to’t]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Either into itself or to the work.

2683 pesant]
He so infers from Edgar’s dress; cf. 2238, 2443. Like Crane (1952, p. 166), Hunter (ed. 1972): Oswald’s words here, as well as the general affectation of his language, give Edgar the idea of the vocabulary and the identity he can assume to answer him. See n. 2688–97. Parrott (1949, p. 300): This is no doubt a comic touch. There was no reason for Edgar to play the peasant, but Shakespeare’s audience must have been amused and pleased to see a country fellow armed only with a cudgel…knock down and kill the overweening retainer of a great lord, a type heartily disliked by London citizens.

2684 durst]
See n. 398. Q2’s darst changes the verb from conditional to present indicative, but durst could also have that meaning.

2684 support]
Foakes (ed. 1997): Edgar may here threaten with his staff (see [2694]), thrust himself in front of his father, or make some other gesture of support.

2684 publisht]
OED (ppl. a. 1): Publicly announced, quoting this l. as its first ex.

2684 hence]
See n. 132.

2685–6 least…thee]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Lest you suffer the same misfortune with him, i.e. die by my sword. OED (Take v. 69b), take hold: Of…a disease, etc.: to seize and affect forcibly and more or less permanently, quoting this l. Weis (ed. 1993): Ironically, of course, Edgar is already himself proclaimed.

2685 least]
F’s added that is superfluous to both meter and sense; see n. 273.

2688–97 Chill…Chill]
That Edgar’s rustic dialect, found in Sh. only here, was based on a familiar convention of stage speech is seen in the various improvements to it that Q2 and F add to Q1 (see textual nn.). Q1 includes the proclitic remnant of the Teutonic ich (= I) in chill, chud, and cheuore; Q2 and F supply z for s in zir, zwaggar’d, and zo; Q1(c) and F supplement Q1(u)’s voke with vortnight, vor, and vurther; and F replaces Q’s ile with ice while changing Q’s cagion and voke to the seemingly less genuine ’casion and volke. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 537): Such elaborations of dialect in Q2 and F are in a manner typical of Jaggard’s shop, comparing Q3 of H5. Furness’s (ed. 1880) note gives many instances of such contemporary pronunciations in southwestern dialects especially, and Bradley (1916, 2:570–1) discusses some of the inaccuracies of their manifestations in literature. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Edgar assumes the lingo that, from the Elizabethan time to the end of the eighteenth century, served as the stage dialect of rusticity. It accords well enough with the dialect of Somersetshire, but the dramatists were not finical. Kittredge cites virtually every instance cited by other eds. of its appearance in plays and poems of the period; one such play, The London Prodigal (1603–5), had just been performed by Sh.’s company and published under his name. Kökeritz (1951, p. 17; 1953, p. 39): From a dialectal point of view this passage from King Lear is…nothing but a patchwork of current colloquialisms and conventional stage dialect. A more indulgent view would be to interpret it as a fairly realistic representation of a Bedlam beggar’s jargon, with linguistic odds and ends from many quarters added to this stage idiom of rusticity. Trewin (1978, p. 211 n.): Similar Mummerset occurs in the Elizabethan ballad Plain Truth and Blind Ignorance. Blake (1989, p. 64): F’s changes of have to ha’ and of it would to ’twould, and its addition of ’tis for it is run the risk of confusing colloquial speech with dialect speech.
Tovey (ed. 1896): Edgar assumes the language proper to his dress as a peasant.…[Otherwise] Oswald would have detected the discrepancy, and recognized him as Gloucester’s son and another publish’d traitor. Bradley (1904, p. 257): Is it not extraordinary that, after Gloster’s attempted suicide, Edgar should first talk to him in the language of a gentleman, then to Oswald in his presence in broad peasant dialect, then again to Gloster in gentle language, and yet that Gloster should not manifest the least surprise? Muir (ed. 1952, p. xlix): Either he could appear surprised without words, or he could assume that his other senses had become imperfect with the loss of his sight. Shakespeare had prepared the way by making Gloucester comment, earlier in the scene, on the improvement in Poor Tom’s speech. Reibetanz (1977, p. 40): Edgar represents and champions the peasants with whom Lear and Gloucester have been brought to sympathize. Carroll (1996, p. 199; cf. 1987, p. 438): He has risen on the social scale above the level of beast and beggar, but he remains a most poor man.

2688 cagion]
Occasion; see n. 1063. F substitutes the more familiar ’casion and adds vurther apparently to fill out a pentameter (i.e., so that ’casion need not be pronounced as a trisyllable); but then it mislines as two verses. The first change is someone’s intentional improvement, the mislineation is probably a compositor’s error. Hunter (ed. 1972): ’Cagion is stage rustic…; casion has some advantage for the mere reader, but the Q form may well preserve the noise made on Shakespeare’s stage. Blake (1989, p. 64): F’s ’casion is an aphetic form of occasion. It is not dialectal any more; it is simply colloquial.

2690 goe your gate]
Nares (1822): In country language, to pass along (OED, Gate sb.2 1, 2: Way). A Scots and northern expression misplaced in Edgar’s southern dialect.

2691 voke]
Kökeritz (1953, p. 38) suspects that this is closer to the dialect pronunciation than Q2 and F’s volke, which Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 537) consider to be probably an unintentional normalization. Blake (1989, p. 65): The spelling with the l was now regular in print.

2691 and]
See n. 630.

2691 chud]
Hunter (ed. 1869): I could. More probably I should, as in The London Prodigal (1603–5) 3.3.7 (Muir, ed. 1952).

2691 swaggar’d]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Frightened…by mere bluster (OED, Swagger v. 1c, quoting Tro. 5.2.136 [3133] and this l. as its first exx.). Blake (1989, p. 65): Possibly spelt with ar to suggest dialect or colloquial pronunciation.

2692 long]
F adds as ’tis apparently to make the meaning more explicit.

2692 fortnight]
Greg (1940, p. 176) thinks Q1(c)’s vortnight no doubt correct: but the dialect is in any case not very consistent in the quarto, and probably was no more so in the copy. Skillan (ed. 1967), questionably: The time that he has been treated as poor Tom. Edgar may be speaking only with jocular vagueness. Foakes (ed. 1997): It would have been shorter by a fortnight.
