Halio (ed. 1992): I would not have lasted a fortnight.

2693 out,]
Greg (1940, p. 176) finds Q1(c)’s omission of the correct comma curious and probably accidental.

2693 cheuore]
Johnson (ed. 1765): I warn you, in western dialect. Halliwell (ed. 1865): This, in the old West country dialect, was equivalent to,—I warrant ye. The latter is surely right: Alexander Gill, in Logonomia Anglica (1621, p. 17) so defines the term, identifying it as of a southern dialect, and the instances quoted by Capell (1783, 3.1:68, 271) and Muir (ed. 1952) from The Contention between Liberality and Prodigality (1601) 2.3.4 and The London Prodigal (1603–5) 2.4.80, 3.3.43, 5.1.355 support this sense. Though OED defines che as a southwestern dialectal word for I, and quotes both this l. and another instance of che(e) vor, neither it nor Wright’s Dialect Dictionary defines vor(e) or lists the term as a variant of warrant. Kökeritz (1942, pp. 98–103) assumes that it is a worn-down form of warrant and gives further instances of its use. Horsman (ed. 1973): A mere expression of strong belief or emphasis. Blake (1989, p. 65), on F’s che vor’ye: The apostrophe was probably added because the compositor did not know what the word was but thought an apostrophe would add the appropriate impression of colloquial or dialectal speech.

2693 ye]
On the objective form see n. 490.

2693 ile]
F’s ice is a reduced enclitic form of I shall (Abbott §§315, 461; OED, Shall A.5, quoting this l.), from the southwestern provinces (Wright, ed. 1875; Kökeritz, 1953, pp. 279–80). Blake (1989, p. 62): Possibly ile misread as ise and set as ice.

2694 coster]
Q1(c)’s costerd provides the usual spelling; the d was dropped only in compounds such as coster-monger. Greg (1940, p. 176): The inferior spelling may or may not have been that of the copy. This name of an apple was applied humourously or derisively to the head (OED, Costard 2, quoting this l.).

2694 bat-|tero]
In Q1(c) when press-corrections were made elsewhere in the two lines shared by this word, bat- became bat, a word that made sense in itself, and tero disappeared. Blayney (1982, p. 246 n.): A false emendation, not an accident, since the dividing hyphen was also removed. F substitutes ballow, a word of dubious authenticity. Blake (1989, p. 67): If [battero] is original, it would imply an instrument for battering, which would be comic rather than dialect. It could even be intended as a substandard variation of battery. The form bat is surely a simplification of battero, because that word was not understood. There is no other record of such a word. Bland (privately): Possibly foul-case error for battery, o and y being adjacent in the case. But some kind of weapon (instrument) seems called for, and the only contemporary uses of battery in such sense have to do with gunnery. Eds. agree that Q1(c) erroneously shortened Q1(u)’s word but disagree whether Q’s original word was a misreading of that in F, or vice versa. Greg (1940, pp. 176–7) gives the older view: There can be little doubt that [Q1(u)] is a misreading of the word in the folio, and consequently that the [Q] reader, when he cut out what seemed superfluous letters, was merely guessing. NED treats Ballow as probably a ghost word, perhaps an error for batton. This is not very likely, seeing that the folio editor must have made the error deliberately. Duthie (1949, p. 60): The Q compositor misread l as t twice, and o as e. A badly formed w might be misread as ro—making four literal errors in a six-letter word. Brooke (ed. 1947), printing batoon, represents a view recently gaining favor: The older English form of the French baton. The word made trouble. The Quarto printed it battero, reduced in some copies to bat. The Folio printed Ballow, a word not otherwise known and probably, like battero, a misreading of battoon. So also Stone (1980, p. 185), Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 538). Skillan (ed. 1967): Or a nonce word for baton, giving no reason for its creation. The debate turns on the genuineness of the word ballow, whose uniqueness may have been over-emphasized; unless it was a word created accidentally in the preparation of F, it must have made sense to someone, and has been allowed to stand by the great majority of eds.; even granting that, one may suppose that bat(t)oon stood in the Q MS. The arguments for each word are as follows:
(1)Ballow. The word appears in Nathan Bailey’s An Universal Etymological Dictionary (1740; not in eds. 1721–1736), where its definition is a Pole, a long Stick, a Quarter-Staff, &c. Shakesp.—apparently a contextual definition from this play without independent support. Francis Grose, A Provincial Glossary (2nd ed., 1790), quite possibly here dependent on Bailey, defines it as A pole. North., without support. Collier (ed. 1843): Balo means a beam in Norfolk. Page (ed. 1889): It may be connected with A.S. balca, a balk, beam. Moberly (ed. 1876): Properly an adjective meaning thin; (as on a ballow nag) hence a thin piece of wood, a cudgel. Moberly apparently has in mind Drayton’s Poly-Olbion, 3.24, the ballow Nag out-strips the winds, whose marginal gloss on ballow is Gant, presumably = gaunt, as Nares (1822) thinks. Halliwell, A Dictionary of Archaic and Provincial Words (1847) defines an adj. (Bony, thin), a verb (To select or bespeak), and a noun (A pole; a stick; a cudgel, citing only this l.); so does Thomas Wright, A Dictionary of Obsolete and Provincial English (1857), adding to the Shn. ref. a definition of an unidentified word from Richard Huloet, Abecedarium (1552 or 1572), A baller, malleus ligneus quo glebae franguntur, evidently a club for breaking up balls or clods of earth; OED does not record it, but s.v. Balled quotes the phrase clods of earth broken, balled ground, or rolled ground from 1591. Hall (1885, p. 274) fancifully imagines ballo to be a truncation of Fr. ballon, bundle, referring to a stick and bundle carried by Edgar. W. D. Parish & W. F. Shaw, A Dictionary of the Kentish Dialect (1887) cite only Lr. Swithin (1885, p. 431) finds the word baleys, defined by the Lat. virga, in Promptorium Parvulorum (ca. 1440; ed. A. L. Mayhew, 1908, cols. 31, 442, 454, and p. 562, n. 135); though virga may mean either a thin whipping-rod or a staff for walking, baleys meant the first (OED: A rod;…a scourge, citing exx. 13th–16th c.). Stevenson (1889, p. 76) quotes from his own ed. of the Records of the Borough of Nottingham (1889) two uses of ballow: from 13 Aug. 1621 the memorandum paid to dyuers for kyddes and ballow wood; and for 1503–4, entry for an action of assault against a cobbler who assaulted another man cum uno baculo [small staff] cum ferro rostrato [either hooked or pointed with iron] uocato a ballowe staffe. The latter may conceivably have been a cobbler’s implement; Stevenson explains that kyddes are faggots, and guesses that ballow wood is wood of larger growth—not underwood, which is described in the Nottingham records as tinsil or trowse, but perhaps young trees and saplings. OED (Balgh 1: Round, rounded) quotes a possibly misapplied ex. from the 15th c.—balowe tymbre & bygge—which may refer to wood of a certain size. Wright, EDD, repeats Halliwell’s definition, citing Bailey, Grose, Parrish & Shaw, Stevenson, and Lr. Mayhew (op. cit., n. 136) on Prompt. Parv. Balhow, or pleyn: planus (1499 ed., Balwe or playne), explains the meaning to be smooth (OED, Balgh 2), takes Stevenson’s first ex. to mean smooth wood without bark (i.e., too small and young to have developed a rough bark?), and explains the word in Lr. to mean a quarter-staff made from ballow wood—an idea repeated in W. W. Skeat & A. L Mayhew, A Glossary of Tudor and Stuart Words (1914). Brooke (op. cit.): This last sense…has very scanty support; Idem (1948, p. 106): The Folio’s ballow is a possibly poetic, but quite unknown, weapon that shows that someone was improving on the old poet long before the Restoration adapters took up the task.
(2)Battoon. Murray (1885, p. 167) asks whether ballow is anything but a ghost word and, receiving no assurance, concludes in OED in 1888 (Ballow, sb.1), before some of the above evidence has appeared, that no such word seems to exist, or to have any etymological justification. On the suggestion of Buckley (1885, p. 216) that F’s word is a misreading of baston (OED, 1: Cudgel, club, bat, truncheon; = baton 1, Batoon 1), Murray writes (1885, p. 431): Ballow, in one quarto battero, is an obvious misprint for one of the many current spellings of baton, e.g. batton, battoon, battone, all found about 1600, citing Cotton, Scoffer Scoft (1675, p. 44), With my Battoon Ile bang his sconce, and adding, It is evident that battone, badly written, might easily be read battero or ballow. Halio (ed. 1994): Clayton (privately) suggests that copy may have had battõ and that the tittle above or near the o was mistaken as an abbreviation for -er-; hence Q uncorr. battero. Soens (1969, pp. 149–50): Bat, batoon, and baston are synonymous for waster and cudgel in fencing contexts. Wasters, bats, or cudgels were the training substitutes for the dangerous rapier and sword in Elizabethan fencing schools.…Since the audience had seen prizes [i.e., public fencing examinations] fought with cudgels,…when Edgar opposed his cudgel to Oswald’s rapier, the audience settled back to enjoy a display of technique and skill with which they were enthusiastically familiar.…Shakespeare makes Edgar into a popular champion by arming him with the plebeian cudgel, and pitting his English techniques against the aristocratic rapier and Italian technique of Oswald. See n. 2698. Edelman (1992, p. 159) prefers the staff, citing George Silver’s Paradoxes of Defence (1599, pp. 36–8) on its effectiveness against even two swords or rapiers. Oswald could be stunned, then stabbed. Foakes (ed. 1997): The blind Gloucester might more naturally have a staff, and, if so, Edgar borrows it to defend himself, citing Spenser’s F.Q. 6.7.46. yron batton.

2696, 2703 they fight, He dies]
Perhaps the SDs were omitted from F as being obvious.

2696 Out dunghill]
See n. 2164. Wright (ed. 1875) finds the same phrase in Jn. 4.3.87 (2097). Craig (ed. 1901): Applied to a person of very base station or strain, citing 2H6 1.3.193 (590) and A. Parker, Supplement to the Glossary of Words Used in Oxfordshire (1881, p. 80): Dunggul bred,…low-bred, or low-born.

2697 pick your teeth]
Dent (1981, T424.1): A proverbial threat in duelling or battle. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 212 n.): This suggests that he stabs him, either with a knife he wears, or, possibly, with Oswald’s own dagger, wrested after a tussle. No knife is mentioned in the text; in Forrest’s performance Edgar closes with Oswald & wrests his sword from him—(throwing his Staff up Stage—) & stabs him (Sprague, 1944, p. 295). More likely Edgar, with grim humor, refers to his stick as an oversize toothpick as he strikes at Oswald’s head. So Harbage (ed. 1958), Fraser (ed. 1963), Edwards (ed. 1975), and Dessen (1978, p. 55): I’ll knock out your teeth, implying a blow to the head with a cudgel. Foakes (ed. 1997): In some modern productions Edgar has brutally driven a staff or dagger into the body of Oswald. Wells (ed. 2000), quoting from George Silver’s Paradoxes of Defence (1599; ed. 1933, p. 38): Against a sworder, the staff-man never striketh but at the head, and thrusteth presently under at the body,…to cause the opponent to protect his head and then swiftly to attack his body before he can bring his arms down.

2698 foyns]
Hanmer (ed. 1743–4, 6:Gloss.): Push in fencing (OED, Foin sb.2 1). Wilson (ed. 1960): The foppish Osw. follows the fashionable thrusting style of fighting; Edg., the good old English downstroke, albeit with a cudgel.

2699 villaine]
See n. 2152.

2701 letters]
Smith (in Grey, 1754, 2:115) would read letter since only one is produced and read at 2715. The plural form could refer to only one letter (see n. 875) and is so understood by most eds. This would be the letter referred to at 2391 and 2408, from Goneril. A few eds. think that Oswald is also carrying a note from Regan: see n. 2416. So Verity (ed. 1897), and Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): The contents of but one, Gonerill’s, are later made known to us; but this is all that is needed to be known to Albany.

2702 Earle of Gloster]
Verity (ed. 1897): The title would bring home to Gloucester and his legitimate son the extreme treachery of the bastard Edmund; and their feelings should be indicated…by some gesture from them as the words are spoken.

2702 out]
Greg (1940, p. 177): [Q1(c)] alone inserts a comma after out. It is quite uncalled for: the reader must have felt that there was a pause without realizing that this was metrical, and that what required correction was the line-division.

2703 vpon]
OED (prep. 5): Within, quoting this l. Kittredge (ed. 1940): On the side of the British.

2703 British]
Of Q1(c)’s Brittish Greg (1940, p. 177) says, The reader presumably thought he was improving the spelling: he may have been conforming to the copy, though why he should have troubled to make the alteration it is difficult to imagine. Perhaps at first the compositor confused the mark for an inserted space after the word (#) with the note for an inserted t (t/). Those who find great significance in an apparent change from proverbial English to British at 1968 (see n.) are hard put to explain the reverse change to F’s anachronistic English here. Knight (ed. 1840): Perhaps the distinction between British and English, which was meant as a mark of compliment to James, had ceased to be regarded. White (ed. 1862): English is a sophistication, doubtless. Shakespeare must have known well enough that in Lear’s time there were no more Englishmen in Britain than in America. Verity (ed. 1897): The line is obviously far less significant than [1968], since the latter was a well-known quotation. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 159): He may have written English through inadvertence.…That English…is anachronistic by no means necessitates the view that it is un-Shakespearian. Stone (1980, p. 116 n.): Due to a reviser’s fastidiousness: Lear was not King of Scotland. But his realm included Albany. Weis (ed. 1993): Perhaps F’s use of English may reflect a strategic Jacobean/Stuart change, as if it intended to remove Albany (Scotland) from the war against King Lear. It does not do so.

2703 death! death.]
Possibly a separate line; see textual n. 2702–3. Foakes (ed. 1997): Perhaps…muttered as Edgar speaks.

2704 seruiceable]
Schmidt (1875): Officious; in a good as well as a bad sense (OED, a. 1: Ready to do service;…diligent, quoting this l.). Cf. 1091.

2705 dutious]
Schmidt (ed. 1879): Always in Sh. = obsequious, obedient (OED, a.: Subservient, quoting this l.).

2707 What]
See n. 858.

2708 father]
See n. 2517.

2708–9 you…of]
Greg (1940, p. 177): [Q1(c)]’s insertion of a comma after you is an improvement, if hardly adequate: F has a full stop. The similar insertion after of is unnecessary, and is not in F; there is, however, a slight natural pause, and it marks in fact the end of a line.

2709 his…These]
F’s these…the has raised suspicions of accidental error, viz. these having been caught, I think, from the next clause (White, ed. 1862).

2709 pockets]
Schmidt (1875): Bag[s] inserted in a garment. But cf. pursse…about me (2699–2701); hence Joseph (ed. 1966): Pouches, wallets. OED (sb. 2) supports both senses.

2709 letters]
See n. 2701.

2710 sorrow]
Q2 and F’s sorry seems to correct an error, but may not. Abbott (§230) finds Cym. 5.5.297 (3597), I am sorrow for thee, a survival of an ancient usage analogous to the frequent Shn. I am woe, and Wells (ed. 2000) cites Webster’s White Devil 5.1.45. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 417), however, notices four w/y variants in Q Lr.—cf. 1237, 1728, 2622—and wonders if in the copy for Q Lear y and w were liable to look somewhat similar.

2711 deathsmã]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): Executioner (OED, quoting this l.). Schmidt (ed. 1879): Edgar is sorry that he anticipated the hangman (Ger.). Budd (ed. 1935): Edgar implies that Oswald would sooner or later have met his death at the hangman’s hand.

2712 leaue]
Wright (ed. 1875): Give me leave, or by your leave, comparing Cym. 3.2.35 (1504), Good Wax, thy leaue; cf. TN 2.5.92 (1105), By your leaue wax. Harbage (ed. 1958): Formula used in opening documents. Tilley B637: The Breaking open of letters is the basest kind of burglary, citing this speech; Dent (1981) doubts the saying is proverbial.

2712 gentle]
Weis (ed. 1993): Sealed with a noble crest or coat of arms. Or it may mean mild, forgiving.

2712 manners…not]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 184): It may be that the [erroneous] F colon after manners should come after not. and that it has been carelessly misplaced by [a scribe] or the F compositor.

2713–14 To…lawfull]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Our enemies are put upon the rack, and torn in pieces to extort confession of their secrets; to tear open their letters is more lawful. Heath (1765, p. 348): In order to discover our enemies’ designs against us, we should make no scruple even of ripping up their hearts, if we were assured they were legible there.…Hearts are never ripped on the rack. Hunter (ed. 1869) compares Cym. 3.5.86–7 (1995–6), Ile haue this secret from thy heart, or rip | Thy heart to finde it. Malone (ed. 1790): The construction is,—To rip their papers, is more lawful. On omissions in antithesis see n. 2278.

2713 wee’d]
Many eds. favor F’s we, though Q’s conditional better suits a hypothetical case; F’s faulty punctuation, putting the condition To…minds with the previous clause, may have blurred the fact.

2713 hearts]
See n. 75. Foakes (ed. 1997), however: By killing them (the obvious meaning), or torturing them?

2714 more lawfull]
Deighton (ed. 1891): A less offence.

2715 <A letter.>]
Greg (1940, p. 177): Whether there was any direction in the quarto copy may be doubted, but the addition may be allowed to count as a correction. McKenzie (1973, p. 128): The omission is a result of the compositor’s indenting the stick to a narrower measure. He failed to alter the spacing quads to take in the extra words within the 3-em space to the right; they were later added within the shorter line-length, probably in place of a 3-em pica quad to which they are exactly equivalent as set, and without disturbing the larger, indenting quad.

2716–21 Let…labour]
Q2, oddly, sets the letter as verse. Doran (1931, pp. 35–6) notes that the new compositor who set this and successive formes takes more liberties with his Q1 copy, including realigning faulty verse and prose. He may have thought these lines to be verse; or he may have been setting prose as verse to stretch the text to fill out the last page of this forme (Io).

2716 your]
Stone (1980, p. 222): F [reading our] assumes the meaning mutual for reciprocal [OED, a. 4a: Corresponding or answering to each other, quoting this l. as its first ex.], Q the meaning given in return [OED, 2]. For the vows see 2287–94. Taylor (1925, p. 64) suggests that Sh. found reciprocal in Florio’s Montaigne.

2717 him]
Wilson (ed. 1960): I.e. Alb[any].

2717 if…not]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): If your will be not wanting, (if you have the will). Harrison (ed. 1948): Will means both willingness and lust (OED, sb. 2, 1).

2718 fruitfully]
Delius (ed. 1854): Abundantly (OED, adv. 2, quoting this l. and AWW 2.2.70 [890] as its first exx.). Joseph (ed. 1966): To good effect, not fruitlessly. Foakes (ed. 1997): Also suggesting sexual fulfilment.

2718 done,]
The sense is, We shall be no nearer our desire (Deighton, ed. 1891), The victory will be meaningless (Hunter, ed. 1972). Q2’s colon and F’s period do not make good sense. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 184): There is no suggestion that she is reproaching Edmund for being dilatory.…We must read done, if.…The source of the corruption in F is probably Q’s initial capital in If, which may just be an aberration on the part of the Q compositor. Taylor (1985, p. 29) argues that error is progressive from Q1 to Q2 to F and shows F’s dependence on Q2 copy. Halio (ed. 1992): But Q’s majuscule If may have independently influenced the Q2 compositor and the F collator to introduce heavier punctuation.

2720–1 supply]
Schmidt (1875): Fill (OED, v.1 9: As a substitute).

2721 for your labour]
Deighton (ed. 1891): As a reward for the trouble you will have taken. Hunter (ed. 1972): Also, as a place for your (amorous) labours.

2723 seruant]
Herford (ed. 1899): Lover. Hunter (ed. 1972): It may be nothing more than conventional politeness.

2723+1 and…Venter]
Brooke (ed. 1947): The second Quarto and Folio omitted the words entirely (rather than print foolishness, presumably). Stone (1980, p. 132 n.): It is not at all unlikely that the editors of Q2 and F would omit it independently for that reason.…In both Q2 and F the omission has prompted a doctoring of the syntax…and F’s method here is, significantly, quite different from that of Q2. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 418): It may be that [the words] were so indistinct in the playhouse MS that [a scribe] contented himself with excising [them]. But it is at least equally likely that they were not present in the playhouse MS at all. They may have been thought redundant, repeating her offer of herself in 2721–2. Since the whole letter refers to their exchange of vows in 2287–94, eds. have reasonably found an allusion here to Goneril’s invitation in 2288, If you dare venture (Q2 venter) in your owne behalfe; but if that is the case, one would expect this line to read [I am] your owne for venter, i.e., your own if you dare venture for me (Muir, ed. 1952). Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960) does in fact conjecture that this was the MS reading: The first for in Q is compositor’s anticipation of the second, and…you her may be a [confusion; Duthie says mishearing, but it could be an error of aural memory by the compositor] of your. Mitford (1844, p. 469) had earlier suspected a misreading of and youre owne for euer. Craig (ed. 1901): It is just possible that the nonsense of Q1 may point to some such meaning as this: and one who holds you her own for venturing, for your hardihood and courage on her behalf. Ridley (ed. 1935): The fact that it makes no sense as it stands seems to be no excuse for omitting it. We may suspect either for venture or fore-venter: but the italicisation raises difficulties. But Duthie compares the equally meaningless capitalization and italicization of Mohing in 2248+4. It is not clear what Ridley means by fore-venter; the word venter meant One or other of two or more wives (OED, sb.1 1) or A mother in relation to her children (OED, 2) (the sense a woman’s first or second marriage [OED, 1b], facetiously suggested by White [ed. 1862], does not appear until the 18th c.); but neither fore-wife nor fore-mother is very good sense. Brooke (op. cit.) proposes her own tormenter, one who torments herself with thoughts of you; Wilson (op. cit.) proposes and you own Goneril for venture, a phrase not graphically close to Q’s line. Halio (ed. 1973): The original reading may stand if life or service is understood after her owne. Bevington (ed. 1992): One ready to venture her own fortunes for your sake. Halio (ed. 1994): Blayney believes that…the only changes needed are a comma after you and a typographic alteration from Venter to venter (= venture). The sense of for venture, he says, is either (1) to bestow on you at her own venture, or (2) to be won by your venture. Stone (1980, p. 198): Emend: forfender (forfend = secure or protect by precautionary measures) (OED, v. 3); the participle with a different sense occurs in 2859, but the noun here proposed is unknown to OED. Foakes (ed. 1997): Richard Proudfoot suggests emending to for you her own to venture, meaning, ready to take responsibility for herself in the venture of love for you.

2724 Edg.]
Q’s speech prefix is redundant; see textual n.

2724 Indistinguisht]
F’s indinguish’d is clearly an erroneous contraction. Most eds. take the -ed as equivalent to -able; see n. 284. So Dyce (ed. 1857): Whose limits are not to be distinguished, hence unbounded (Rann, ed. 1794), unlimited (Meiklejohn, ed. 1879), undefinable (Craig, ed. 1901), beyond the range of sight (Kittredge, ed. 1940). Tovey (ed. 1896) compares 2303+2, Cannot be bordered certaine in it selfe. Steevens (ed. 1793) would make the passive participle active in effect—undistinguishing. So apparently Staunton (ed. 1859: Indiscriminate) and, with a different meaning, Deighton (ed. 1891): That sets no limits to its own range area. Singer (ed. 1856), questionably, tries to have both meanings—Undistinguishing and unlimited—as do the Clarkes (ed. 1868): Edgar exclaims against the wide license which Goneril permits herself…and against the want of discrimination that can induce her to prefer the vicious Edmund to the virtuous Albany. Possibly the word means simply not comprehended, implying incomprehensible: this may be what is meant by OED (a): Not distinguished; undistinguished, quoting this l. as its first ex.; it is certainly what Schmidt (1875) means—Incalculable, unaccountable—and Wright (ed. 1875): Its workings cannot be discovered.

2724 space]
Most eds. accept Theobald’s (1730; in Nichols, 1817, 2:382) hesitant interpretation: Scope. So Hunter (ed. 1869) and many others: Extent (OED, sb.1 9b, quoting JC 4.3.25 [1995] and this l. as its first exx. of this figurative use). Lettsom (1853, p. 464): Depth. There is little support for Theobald (ed. 1733): ’Tis not the Extravagance, but the Mutability, of a Woman’s Will that is here satiriz’d. The Change of which…is so speedy, that there is no Space of time, no Distance, between the present Will and the next; but it is an undistinguish’d Space. Moberly (ed. 1876): A woman’s will knows no limits between good and evil.

2724 wit]
Most eds. prefer F’s will, probably because Goneril’s desire seems more remarkable than her cleverness. Wit could have been mistaken for wil, or vice versa. Most eds. take will to mean lustful appetites (Davies, 1783, 2:314; OED, sb.1 2), but some to mean faculty of willing (Theobald, ed. 1733; OED, 6) or wilfulness (Staunton, ed. 1859: caprice; OED, 9, 9b) or inclinations (Steevens, ed. 1793; OED, 1) or the object of her desire (Clarkes, ed. 1868: Vicious preference; OED, 3). Foakes (ed. 1997) cites the proverb Women will have their wills (Tilley W723).

2726 exchange]
Deighton (ed. 1891): What she hopes to gain in exchange (OED, sb. 7, quoting this l. and 3045).

2726 sands]
Perrett (1904, p. 299): What sands were these? Edgar is not speaking for Gloucester’s ears, who alone believes himself on the sea-shore. Muir (ed. 1952): Either Edgar is speaking for his father’s benefit, or Shakespeare forgot. Wilson (ed. 1960): The sands were convenient to the context and Sh. prob. felt he might risk the inconsistency. But how was the body disposed of on the stage? Does Edg. drag it off at l. [2731], leaving Glo. talking, and then return at l. [2740]? Hunter (ed. 1972): Or at the end of the scene. Adams (1948, p. 332): Closed behind the rear-stage curtains. Horsman (ed. 1973): Or disposed of through a trap. Brown (ed. 1976): Hurriedly starts to bury Oswald with his own hands. See n. 2731, and textual nn.

2727 rake vp]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Cover (OED, v.1 4b: or bury…as with a rake).

2727 post]
See n. 1306.

2727 vnsanctified]
Chedworth (1805, p. 325): Wicked. Steevens (ed. 1793): Refers to his want of burial in consecrated ground. Wilson (ed. 1960): Perhaps = unsanctifiable.

2728 mature]
Abbott (§492) would accent the first syllable. Deighton (ed. 1891): When the time is ripe (OED, a. 5, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Maclean (1960, p. 52): He understands the need to use his disguise, for some time, comparing 2893–4. Smidt (1990, p. 130): The fairy-tale plot requires an unknown champion, which may be one reason why Edgar retains his disguise for so long.

2729 vngratious]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Wicked (OED, a. 1b).

2729 strike]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Blast (OED, v. 43: Trans. Of lightning, thunder, a thunderbolt). Skillan (ed. 1967): Stun. Joseph (ed. 1966): (i) show to his sight; (ii) weaken the sight, affront the sight. The meaning To impress or arrest (the eye, view, sight) (OED, 65) is not recorded before the 18th c., but it occurs in Jonson’s Epicœne 1.1.101–2: all th’adulteries of art. | They strike mine eyes, but not my heart.

2730 death practis’d]
Johnson (ed. 1765): The Duke of Albany, whose death is machinated by practice, i.e. planned by stratagem (Dyce, ed. 1867, Gloss.). On verbs formed from nouns see n. 223.

2731 tell]
Capell (see textual n.) marks Edgar’s exit here and re-entrance at 2739, evidently to remove Oswald’s body. Urkowitz (1980, pp. 158–9): He has a rhyming couplet, a usual signal for an exit.…Two gross improbabilities arise if this removal isn’t managed here. First, since Edgar has to get Oswald out at the end of the scene, he’ll be leading his blind father with one hand and tugging the corpse with the other. A very clumsy exit, at best. Second, Edgar’s last speech in the scene…becomes a totally uncharacteristic response by Edgar to his father’s morose yearning for insanity. Sprague (1944, p. 295): Gloucester’s lines [2732–9]…become a covering soliloquy during Edgar’s absence. Rosenberg (1972, p. 282): Edgar’s two actions have been combined in the theatre: thus, Brook’s Edgar handed his staff and Oswald’s sword to Gloster…[and] slung Oswald over his shoulder. So the procession went out, Gloster holding on to Edgar, his sword, and his stick. See n. 2726 and textual nn. for other possibilities.

2733 stiffe]
Clarkes (1879, p. 594): Stubborn. Craig (ed. 1901): Obstinately unbending.

2733 vild sence]
See n. 1726. Empson (1951, p. 146): Chiefly for sanity [see n. 2359], vile because it seems disloyal to outlast the king’s.…He might [also] be regretting the past sensualities [OED, Sense sb. 4?] which have coarsened his sensibility [OED, 8, 9]. Muir (ed. 1952): This is too ingenious. Gloucester calls his senses vile because they still allow him to be fully conscious of his sorrows, and do not give him the relief of insanity. Harbage (ed. 1958): Hateful consciousness. Hunter (ed. 1972): Vile (basely physical) in this very incapacity to give way before huge sorrows. Foakes (ed. 1997): Power of sensation (the senses as a single faculty, OED, sb. 3).

2734 stand vp]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Do not bend, and therefore suffer more. Budd (ed. 1935): Am not bowed down by madness.

2734 ingenious]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Exquisite; Clarkes (ed. 1868): Acutely perceptive, keenly appreciative; Wright (ed. 1875): Delicately sensitive. The meaning of acute sensitivity fits the context, but is not attested by OED. Singer (ed. 1826): Witty,…acute (OED, a. 1a)—a sense not apt to huge sorowes. Schmidt (1874): Dwelling in the mind,…conscious; Page (ed. 1889): As distinguished from corporeal; but the sense is not attested by OED. Clarkes (op. cit.): Intelligent (OED, 2: Discerning, sensible). Joseph (ed. 1966): Normally sane. Ingenuity has the sense, normal condition of mental faculties (OED, sb. 5; not recorded before 1651). Rosenberg (1972, p. 282): The word already meant inventive, skillful, and suggests a clever destructive inner force (OED, 3a: Having an aptitude for invention…; clever at contriving…; skilful).

2734 feeling]
Schmidt (1874): Perception (OED, vbl. sb. 6: Pleasurable or painful consciousness, quoting this l.).

2735–9 better…themselues]
Cunliffe (1893, p. 86): Cf. Seneca, Hercules Furens 1100–5 [ed. Putnam, 1917, 1094–9].

2735 distract]
Abbott (§342): Some verbs ending in -te, -t, and -d, on account of their already resembling participles in their terminations, do not add -ed in the participle. Cf. Franz §159. Craig (ed. 1901): Out of his senses (OED, ppl. a. 4: Deranged).

2736 fenced]
Q’s word is similar enough in graphic outline to F’s seuer’d so that either could be a misreading of the other. Doran (1931, p. 48): Although most editors prefer the folio reading, fenced is, I think, just as good. Brooke (ed. 1947): Here the Quarto keeps the Shakespearean word, the Folio…being an easy but trite misreading. If Gloucester were distract, he would still have both thoughts and griefs, but they would be fenced or railed off from each other, so that, as he says in the next lines, the griefs (woes) would no longer be interpreted by thought and would lose the knowledge of themselves.

2738 wrong imaginations]
Hudson (ed. 1871): Imaginary felicities. Deighton (ed. 1891): Hallucinations.

2741 me thinks]
See n. 704.

2741 drum]
Empson (1961, p. 67): The sound should continue ominously, growing louder through the next scene.

2742 father]
See n. 2517.

2742 bestow]
See n. 1589.

2742 friend]
Muir (ed. 1952): We are not told how the fugitive Edgar has got in touch with a friend. Rosenberg (1972, p. 282): The friend does not appear. Another pretense? Bhattacharya (1980–1, p. 103): A person who would be friendly. Perhaps Edgar only expects to meet Albany and his friendly troops.

2743 <Scæna Septima>]
Doran (1931, p. 70): Evidently Scene iii had been marked out in the transcript [i.e., playbook], but the headings to the scenes were left as they had been first made. The printer of the folio corrected the fourth, fifth, and sixth to third, fourth, and fifth in his text. Either he forgot to alter the heading of the seventh or, as is suggested by the different spelling, scæna, another printer was at work here who knew nothing about the preceding irregularities of the manuscript. The latter shrewd guess is in part correct: F Compositor E set this scene heading, Compositor B the previous three. Halio (ed. 1992): The F compositors suspended work on Lear at precisely the page on which this scene begins (signature ss), and did not resume composition until the last pages of Rom.…and all of Tim. were set. Conceivably, when he returned to King Lear, Compositor E forgot to continue altering scene numbers which Compositor B had begun. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 418): The play must have been divided into acts and scenes before IV iii was cut in the abridgement given in F. Greg (1955, p. 388): The collator when preparing the [marked-up Q] copy for F…apparently began by dividing Act IV in Q correctly into seven scenes, then deleted Scene iii since it was not in the prompt-book, and corrected the numbering of iv–vi to agree, but overlooked Scene vii. The use of Q copy for F is doubtful: see . Taylor (1983, p. 417), citing other plays: Numerical errors of this kind (vi/vii) are easy enough to make, by misreading or memorial substitution; such a Folio error could have been made either by Compositor E, or by the printing-house scribe…or by the theatrical scribe.…Prompt-books usually or at least very often did not contain scene numbers at all. If the Act-divisions were introduced into the prompt-book to mark the observation of act-intervals in the Blackfriars Theater, they would not have been inserted before the King’s Men began to use that theater in 1608–9. Scene-divisions may or may not have been marked and numbered at the same time. Since scene numbers (as distinct from scene divisions) had little practical use in the theater, such an error as vi/vii might have been overlooked or ignored.
Daniel (1877–9, p. 222): This must be a separate day…for Regan’s troops which [in 4.5] were to set forth on the morrow [2401] are now present, led by Edmund. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Perhaps on the day after Scene vi. Lear has been found by the searchers sent out in Scene iv. He has been brought to Cordelia’s camp and put to bed. The counterpart reunion in Leir occurs in 2140–2355 (see ). Skottowe (1824, pp. 103–4): Holinshed, the old play, and the ballad, agree in sending Lear to France [for this reunion].…Shakespeare’s arrangement [has] the advantage of considerably simplifying the action, and is more probable than the old play’s chance meeting in disguise. See , .
Bradley (1904, p. 453): It is evident from the text that the scene shows the first meeting of Cordelia and Kent, and the first meeting of Cordelia and Lear, since they parted in I.i.…Cordelia has not seen her father at all until [2776].…Hence the tone of the first part of the scene, that between Cordelia and Kent, is kept low, in order that the latter part, between Cordelia and Lear, may have its full effect. Buck (ed. 1907): This scene is like a glimpse of bright sunlight in the interval of a terrible storm. Dramatically it may be called the final suspense before the inevitable catastrophe. As we read we feel that this mutual happiness is too ethereal to endure. Traversi (1953, p. 221): The way is at least open for a restoration of natural harmony. The scene in which this takes place (IV, vii) is, from the point of view of Shakespeare’s capacity to unite the dramatic and poetic elements with which he is working, the most advanced in the play. It is full of the symbolism of the last period.…Sleep we have already found to be part of a symbolic effect of this kind; and Shakespeare now adds music, with its associations of harmony, and fresh garments, suggesting the purification accomplished in Lear. Levin (1959, p. 89): Even that horrendous act has a certain propriety as a literal climax to a whole train of metaphors involving eyesight and suggesting moral perception, the lack of which is so fatal for Gloucester and Lear. Milward (1973, p. 256): This reunion of Lear with Cordelia is the turning-point not only of King Lear, but of Shakespeare’s whole dramatic career…from the inferno of the tragedies to the paradiso of the last plays. Fraser (1962, p. 132): I.e., to put off the old man, to put on the new, citing Eph. 4:22–4. Kernan (1966, p. 65): Where Gloucester’s miraculous survival was put to him in the realistic terms of the harmless fall from the cliff, Lear’s is manifested in the less realistic but more real terms of sleep, a change of garments, music, and Cordelia. Collins (1903, p. 121): Reminiscent of Euripides’ Orestes 132–240. Wittreich (1984, p. 98): The garments here signify man’s victory over his troubles, his enemies, and…the royal estate which he has attained.…The Book of Revelation is but one of many possible sources of the imagery.
The staging of the scene in Q and F can be inferred, from small bits of evidence in those texts, to have been significantly different. Q’s Doctor disappears from F and his lines are given to a Gentleman with medical knowledge, who exists as an attendant in Q, his entrance not marked. The scene is shortened in F by the omission of Kent’s conversation with this Gentleman (2843+1–+11) and of a few other lines. F adds a stage direction that Lear be carried on in a chair, and a spoken reference to stage music is cut, suggesting that the music is dispensed with in the F version. See notes 2744, 2761, 2765, 2768, 2770, 2771, 2772–5, 2775+1–+2, 2843+1–+11 for discussion of particular changes. Since the textual changes are all cuts of Q material, they and the added SD suggest to most commentators purely theatrical alteration, possibly in part to adapt to a change of venue; those arguing that F is Shakespeare’s revision attribute them to his new conception of the scene (see ). Winterton (1970, pp. 133–4), anticipated by Koppel (1899; see n. 2761), notices a dramatic incongruity resulting from clumsy conflation of the Q and F versions in modern eds.: The Gentleman at the end of the scene shows clearly he does not know who Kent is.…Yet at the beginning of the scene he is placed on stage when Cordelia openly addresses the Duke, instead of entering with the King at 2771. Edwards (ed. 1975): It is important that at the beginning of the scene the Gentleman should be talking to the Doctor well away from the conversation in which Kent talks to Cordelia in his own person. Halio (ed. 1994): In Q, The Gentleman does not hear Cordelia identify Kent…but follows after them with the Doctor.
In both Q and F several of Cordelia’s remarks indicate that Lear is not visible to her before she draw[s] neere him (2775+2); nonetheless many eds. since Capell (see textual n.) have a sleeping Lear visible to the audience from the beginning of the scene. Bradley (op. cit., p. 454), objecting to this arrangement: The reader at once assumes that Cordelia has already seen her father; for otherwise it is inconceivable that she would quietly talk with Kent while he was within a few yards of her. The edge of the later passage where she addresses him is therefore blunted. In the second place, through Lear’s presence the reader’s interest in Lear and his meeting with Cordelia is at once excited so strongly that he hardly attends at all to the conversation of Cordelia and Kent; and so this effect is blunted too. Accordingly, eds. who do not accept F’s later entry in a chair place Lear behind curtains at the rear of the stage. Tate (ed. 1681) has Lear a Sleep on a Couch rather than in a bed. Sprague (1944, p. 295): In later stage performances, Tate’s way prevailed. Dyce (ed. 1857): Cordelia has evidently come with Kent into the chamber where her father is asleep on a bed, the curtains of which conceal him from view. A bed or couch would not have been carried onto the stage, of course, but could have been placed in (or represented by) a curtained alcove at the rear of the stage. Rhodes (1922, pp. 34–5), after discussing such use of curtains in Elizabethan drama, finds such staging preferable to F’s: Now, it is rather strange that while an obsequious gentleman is desiring permission to awaken the King [2767–8], the old man is being carried about by servants [2771].…From [2775+1–+2, Q only] it is clear that they moved towards his bed, and drew apart the curtains, the action taking place on the after-stage. Greg (1940, p. 301) finds such staging the natural way to present [the scene].…There is nothing in the text to contradict this, and so editors and producers have generally conceived it. But the Folio is quite explicit with the direction Enter Lear in a chaire carried by Seruants—rather a clumsy way to bring on a sleeping patient, but the only one if the use of the traverse be denied.…Bradley [op. cit., p. 454] protested against the absurdity of representing Lear in bed. Of course he is not in bed, nor is he in his night gown: he is arrayed ([2770]). Bratton (ed. 1987): Discovery on a bed or couch underlines the pathos of the scene, and was normally preferred in the nineteenth century. Some modern productions follow the F SD, which ensures that this scene is visually an echo of the first, over which Lear presided from his throne—an uncertain assumption: see n. 39. Sisson (1956, 2:242): The scene is Before a tent in the French camp, the tent being the inner stage. The tent is Capell’s invention (see textual n.) and is rejected by Adams (1948, p. 332): There was insufficient time…to change the study [i.e., inner stage] setting from a glade to a tent. The upper stage was never used for tent scenes, and the outer stage rarely (and never, to my knowledge, after 1594). Rosenberg (1972, p. 283): The scene is often played indoors, sometimes in a tent.

2744 Enter…Doctor]
Malone (ed. 1790): In the quartos the direction is, Enter…Doctor, omitting by negligence the Gentleman, who yet in those copies is a speaker in the course of the scene, and remains with Kent, when the rest go out. In the folio, the direction is, Enter…Gentleman; to the latter of whom all the speeches are given, which in the original copies are divided between the physician and the gentleman. I suppose, from a penury of actors, it was found convenient to unite the two characters, which, we see, were originally distinct. Cordelia’s words, however, might have taught the editor of the folio to have given the gentleman whom he retained the appellation of Doctor, quoting 2769–70. The Doctor is also replaced by the Gentleman in an earlier scene (4.4) in F: see n. 2349–50. Duthie (in Wilson, ed. 1960): In F there are indications of adaptation to the needs of a cast smaller than that required by Q1, adding that when Cordelia speaks to the Gentleman in F she is clearly speaking to a person with medical training. Urkowitz (1980, p. 41): One of the changes in F to suppress the importance of the Doctor-Gentleman as master of healing, leaving instead only Cordelia and Lear as the centers of attention. The merging of parts, however, results in the loss of only one line (2777) before Lear and Cordelia exit. Taylor (1983, p. 411) denies that the merging of two roles into one would affect the number of actors which the King’s Men would have needed to perform Lear, because in each case the affected roles could easily be doubled by a number of other available actors.…Moreover, if the Doctor and the Gentleman were conflated solely to save an actor, then the role sacrificed would surely have been the Gentleman rather than the more dramatic and identifiable Doctor. Taylor adds that the carrying on of Lear in a chair in F requires at least two extra actors; but of course these mute actors could have been mere stage hands, such as rolled the cannon balls in the storm scenes or carried on and off the stocks, dressed in minimal costume here. It is quite possible that the disappearance of the Doctor, whose eight speeches in all of Q hardly establish him as a dramatic character, was the result of the cut at the end of this scene. When the Gentleman’s dialogue with Kent was cut as being inessential, he had only two lines left in the scene (2774–5), and no other apparent function there; for dramatic economy his lines were understandably merged with those of the Doctor. However, in terms of number of appearances and of lines in the play, the Doctor is far minor to the Gentleman, who appears in at least four and perhaps seven scenes in Q (see n. 1615). It would easily have seemed economical (even without a saving in personnel), for the larger role to absorb the lesser here and in 4.4. Knowles (1999, pp. 272): F thereby merges a minor character, the Doctor, who in Q appears in only two scenes and has only eight speeches, with a larger and more essential character, the Gentleman. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 524): Unless the Quarto compositor accidentally omitted Gentleman from this stage direction, it must be assumed that Shakespeare had not fully worked out the detail of the scene when he wrote this direction. If the Doctor does enter here, he must stand apart silent while Kent and Cordelia converse, ignoring him; it seems more likely that Cordelia would turn to him as soon as he entered. Q’s entrance direction thus looks like an authorial anticipation of the format of a scene, rather than a precise instruction for the character to enter now. The interval of ignoring the Doctor would be only some thirty seconds; possibly he goes and looks behind the curtain drawn before Lear’s couch (see n. 2743) to learn what he then reports in 2762. It would be natural for the Doctor to inspect his patient before allowing visitors, who would accordingly pause behind him. Wells (ed. 2000) nonetheless has him enter 11 lines later, at 1460. Mahood (1992, pp. 166–70): This change…can have been deliberate and dramatic, rather than enforced and theatrical. It is in keeping with his previous role…of nurse-companion to the ageing Lear that Cordelia should rely on the Gentleman’s wisdom for treatment which was within the competence of a layman with some knowledge of mental disorders. Above all, she relies on his being a familiar presence. Weis (ed. 1993): F’s use of the Gentleman instead of the Doctor may reflect…[that he] has now become a confidant of the royal pair.…In Q he is cast as an onlooker, waiting for his cue to talk to Kent.

2745–9 O…me]
Hubler (1935, p. 432): The Folio compositor found the lines…too long for his double column. But they are not too long. Greg (1936, p. 181): This speech in fact consists of one half-line followed by two whole lines [and is so lined by Q2 and Capell; see textual n.].…No doubt the compositor liked occasional fat. Taylor (1985, pp. 25–6): The Folio’s inane arrangement is exactly what would have happened if E had—in his usual literal fashion—ended a verse line both where Q2 did and where the annotation told him to. His arrangement can hardly have come from a manuscript or from Q1, nor is it easily explained as a normal compositorial error. Halio (ed. 1992, p. 65): Compositor E, however, as Taylor acknowledges in a footnote,…might have been deliberately stretching his copy,…the result of inaccurate casting-off of copy.
Pauls (1984, p. 99) finds a parallel in Cordella’s thanks to Perillus in Leir 2335–6.

2747 match]
Schmidt (1875): To equal, to rival. Deighton (ed. 1891): Adequately reward.

2749 measure]
Johnson (ed. 1765) and most eds.: All good which I shall allot thee, or measure out to thee (OED, sb. 14)—i.e., any amount of recompense made in gratitude. Becket (1787, p. 239): Effort, endeavour (OED, 21). Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): Attempt to measure out an adequate recompense; in quantifiable terms (Weis, ed. 1993). Schmidt (1875): That by which extent or quantity is ascertained (OED, 4–7). Page (ed. 1889): Proportion (of the return to the benefit conferred) (OED, 11). Gardner (ed. 1969): I.e. in living up to Kent’s example in loyalty. Lott (ed. 1974), taking match to mean rival: Comparison with your [goodness]. Wells (ed. 2000): Plan or course of action (OED sb. 21, not recorded before 1698).

2749 faile me]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Be scanty. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Since thy goodness is unmeasurable.

2750 To be acknowlegd]
Foakes (ed. 1997): To have recognition (for my service).

2750 is ore payd]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Elliptical: i.e., Is to be overpaid. For omissions in antithesis, see n. 2278. Skillan (ed. 1967): A courtly and kind extravagance simply implying that no thanks are due. Edwards (ed. 1975): I.e. reward would be understandable if more had been claimed, or if more had been done.

2751 reports]
Muir (ed. 1952): I.e. about Lear, and his own service as Caius. Hunter (ed. 1972), followed by Halio (ed. 1992): What you say of me. See next n.

2751 go]
Schmidt (1874): Accord (OED, v. 5, 16). Brown (ed. 1976): Let…accord. Halio (ed. 1992): Indicative or volitive: Either (1) Everything I have said…is accurate and unadorned, or (2) may everything said about me be told simply and accurately.

2751 modest]
See n. 1300.

2752 Nor…so]
Lee (ed. 1908): Neither exaggerated nor curtailed, but just the truth.

2752 clipt]
Theobald (1726, p. 31): To Clip, is illegally to cut or maim the coin (OED, v.2 4). Figuratively, Curtail, diminish (Schmidt, 1874; OED, 5). Gardner (ed. 1969): Spoilt by omissions. Brown (ed. 1976): Pun on paid in 2750.

2752 so]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Just as things happened. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Emphatic. Muir (ed. 1952): As I have described them.

2753 better]
Brooke (ed. 1947): More suitably to your rank. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Kent is still disguised as a servingman; see nn. 531, 534.

2753 suited]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Drest (OED, ppl. a. 2).

2754 weeds]
Schmidt (1875): Garments (OED, sb. 2 5b: distinctive of a person’s…profession). They are Kent’s disguise as a servant.

2754 memories]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Memorials (OED, sb. 10: Memento, quoting this l.).

2755 prithe]
See n. 664.

2756–9 Pardon…meete]
Bradley (1904, p. 258): Why does Kent so carefully preserve his incognito till the last scene? He says he does it for an important purpose, but what the purpose is we have to guess. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 196): But Shakespeare’s own purpose here is clear enough; not to spoil Lear’s recognition with Cordelia, by adding to it a recognition of Kent.…We might suppose…that Kent is counting, if Lear is defeated, on serving him still in disguise, when known he could not. But he does not appear in the battle or the defeat.…The simple explanation is that Shakespeare finds he has no more dramatic use for Kent till…[3189–90]. So he must just keep him in being meanwhile. Muir (ed. 1952): The dramatist is bound to explain only those things that would otherwise seem incredible. Indeed, a certain mystery in the characters prevents them from seeming mechanical. Maclean (1960, p. 53), questionably: The subsequent refusal to abandon his disguise at the request of Cordelia, although it can hardly benefit Lear at this stage, merely confirms earlier hints that Kent has somehow lost control…[and] become the baffled prisoner of his own game. Hunter (ed. 1972): Sh. regularly delays the penetration of disguise till the final denouement.

2756 me]
F omits to make smoother meter.

2757 Yet]
Schmidt (1875): Already (OED, adv. 5b: So soon as this). Cf. Franz §423.

2757 shortens]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Would make me come short of. Deighton (ed. 1891): Interferes with. OED (v. 38): To render (an intention) ineffectual, quoting only this l. Ridley (ed. 1935): Leaves inadequate time for. Brooke (ed. 1947): Limit[s] the scope.

2757 made intent]
Warburton (ed. 1747), misunderstanding this to mean a thing done, substitutes laid intent; i.e. projected. Heath (1765, p. 349): Will any one deny it to be good English to say, I made it my intent to do such or such a thing? So Johnson (ed. 1765): An intent formed. Wright (ed. 1875): The plan I had formed. Hudson & Black (ed. 1911): Namely, a full restoration of things to the state they were in at the opening of the play. Kent speaks similarly in 4.3 of an obscure deere cause; see n. 2347+52. Smidt (1990, p. 131): All apparent reason for secrecy has vanished. Only Orgel (ed. 1999): Plan (for Lear to recognize him as Kent).

2758 my boone]
Hunter (ed. 1869): I make it a boon to me that you will seem not to know me; Schmidt (1874): Favour begged or granted (OED, sb. 3, 4). More probably, Kittredge (ed. 1940): I ask it of you as a special favour; OED (1b): A request addressed to a human being; esp. the asking of a favour.

2760–3 Then…Gods]
Q and F each misline the passage: Q runs together 2763–4; F divides 2760–1, perhaps both because of change of address and because there is not sufficient room for 2761 on the same line with 2760 (though the line could have been turned over).

2760 good]
Q2 omits, apparently to make a regular pentameter. That F’s Compositor E does not follow Q2 in the omission here (as he does at 1227) argues against his use of Q2 as copy; he would not have restored Q1’s unnecessary and hypermetric word had he not found it in his manuscript.

2761 how]
Koppel (1899, pp. 118–21) argues that the Doctor should enter here since Kent, wishing to remain yet unknown, would not have spoken with Cordelia as he did had another person been present. Bradley (1904, p. 455 n.): This change however is not necessary, for the Doctor might naturally stand out of hearing till he was addressed; and it is better not to go against the stage-direction without necessity. See n. 2744.

2762 sleepes]
For the omitted nominative see n. 230.

2763 kind Gods]
Elton (1966, p. 76): To her, a believer in providence and divine justice, the gods are kind Gods…; and it is to them she prays. Pauls (1984, pp. 98–9) finds a parallel in Cordella’s wish for Leir’s renewal in Leir 2188–95.

2764 cure…breach]
Elton (1966, p. 77): Like Shakespeare’s royal patron, who had recently united Scotland and England, Cordelia is devoted to curing division…[through her] healing and restoring forgiveness.

2764 breach]
OED (sb. 7d): Injury, quoting this l. as its first ex. of figurative use.

2764 abused]
See n. 1611.

2764 nature]
See n. 185.

2765 vntund…wind vp]
Delius (ed. 1854): A musical image, from turning up untuned and discordant strings of a musical instrument (Ger.) (OED, Wind v.1 22e, quoting this l. as its first ex. of this figurative use). Wright (ed. 1875) compares Ham. 3.1.158 (1814), Like sweet bells iangled out of time [F: tune]. Elton (1966, p. 78): Cordelia takes up, antithetically, the discordant musical image announced by Edmund in 466.

2765 hurrying]
Generally considered a misreading of F’s word iarring. Only Rook (in Wolfit, ed. 1956), hurrying: In a state of commotion, and Wells (ed. 2000): Confused?

2765 sences]
See n. 2359, and cf. n. 2247.

2766 child changed]
Eds. divide on whether the phrase means changed to a child by his years and wrongs (Steevens, ed. 1773), changed by his children (Malone, ed. 1790), or both (Brooke, ed. 1947). OED (Child sb. 22, quoting only this l.) is non-commital. Henley (in Reed, ed. 1785): Lear is become insane, and…insanity is not the property of second childhood, but dotage. Delius (ed. 1854) alone: He has exchanged children;…has left Regan and Goneril and come to Cordelia (Ger.). Harbage (ed. 1958) alone: Suggesting changeling, wherein mental defect is associated with the malignity of witches. Joseph (ed. 1966), alternatively: Who has changed places with his children.

2767–8 So…king]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Evidently interrogative, though in Q2, which omits that [perhaps to improve meter: Doran, 1931, p. 26], the sense may be—if it so please, &c. Deighton (ed. 1891): May your majesty be pleased to give us permission.

2768 slept long]
I.e., long enough for recovery. Gardner (ed. 1969), however, quotes Burton’s claim (Anatomy of Melancholy 1.2.2.7) that immoderate sleep fills the head full of gross humours.

2769 your knowledge]
Clearly medical knowledge is referred to even if the speech is said to F’s Gentleman, who has such knowledge: see 2361–5, and n. 2744.

2770 sway]
Schmidt (1875): Direction, management, government OED (sb. 5, 6); cf. gouernd, 2769.

2770 is he arayd]
Delius (ed. 1854): Apparently Lear is not on the stage. Furness (ed. 1880): If Lear be represented on or in a bed, Cordelia’s question is not inappropriate, or, if he be asleep, in a chair, swathed round with robes, the question might still be asked. Since she cannot know that he will wake or rise, the question whether, under his robes, he is dressed would seem to be pointless curiosity. Deighton (ed. 1891): Have you put fresh clothes on him?—not quite what the question asks. Wilson (ed. 1960): Is he in his royal robes?—an improbability whether he is in bed or seated wrapped in outer robes. Delius is probably right, but not in his further conclusion that the F staging is the correct one, since Lear may be behind a curtain in Q: see n. 2743. Mack (1965, p. 59): Cf. the new clothing brought to Skelton’s Magnificence, after his repentance, by Redress, Magnificence (ca. 1515), 2402–6.

2771 Enter…chaire]
See n. 2743. Bradley (1904, pp. 455–6), preferring this staging to the modern convention of a bed: The moment of this entrance…is doubtless too soon. It should probably come at the words Please you, draw near.…But that the stage-direction is otherwise right there cannot be a doubt.…This arrangement (1) allows Kent his proper place in the scene, (2) makes it clear that Cordelia has not seen her father before, (3) makes her first sight of him a theatrical crisis in the best sense, (4) makes it quite natural that he should kneel [which he could not easily do if abed], (5) makes it obvious why he should leave the stage again.…Of course the chair arrangement is primitive, but the Elizabethans did not care about such things. All of the first four reasons apply as well to a Q staging if Lear is discovered on a couch (not a bed) behind a curtain. As for the fifth reason, neither Q nor F offers a motive, nor does F suggest why he should not be carried off in the chair again. Presumably he walks to further sustenance, or even for restorative exercise; in Q he exits to allow private conversation between Kent and the Gentleman. Rhodes (1922, p. 35): For the change [from Q to F staging here] there are two possible reasons, the first being that the after-stage was not available [1924, p. 114: perhaps because the after-stage was occupied by properties for another scene], the second being the desire of the actors that this pathetic scene…should be played as close as possible to the audience, the latter reason suggested by Albright (1909, p. 145). Rhodes (1923, p. 109): The change in F is a sign that the text was revised for a special revival—not on the stage of the Globe. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 182): There is reason in the Folio’s stage direction.…For when he comes to himself it is to find that he is royally attired and as if seated on his throne again. It is from this throne that he totters to kneel at Cordelia’s feet. (Ibid., p. 221): The great chair with the unconscious Lear in it may be…carried from an inner stage. Greg (1940, p. 301 n.): This is picturesque, but…strikes me rather as illustrating Shakespeare’s masterly way of extracting dramatic effect from theatrical necessity than as itself conditioning the arrangement. It is not clear that Lear is seated on a throne at the beginning of the play; see n. 39. Sisson (1956, 2:242): This may have been an additional direction inserted upon performance on a stage without a study. Edwards (ed. 1975): It seems clear that originally Lear was revealed in the recess at the back of the stage, and that in later years the staging was changed to that indicated in the Folio. Hunter (ed. 1972), lest the entrance seem too early: When Lear is carried on, Cordelia falls to her knees.…The Gentleman says Be by and prepares to wake him; Cordelia’s Very well is not, however, followed by any immediate movement. The Doctor repeats the request…and only now does Cordelia move forward. Taylor (1983, p. 412) names other Shn. plays in which beds are called for (though none is here) and people are carried on stage in chairs. He suspects a visual reminder of 1.1 (where Lear may not be seated) and of Gloucester, bound and tortured in a chair (though Lear is neither bound nor being tortured here). Dessen (1995, pp. 114, 245) cites numerous sick-chairs in contemporary SDs, and Dessen & Thomson (1999, sleep) show that they were either carried on or discovered.

2772–5 Doct.…temperance]
Though a few eds. have followed Q2’s assignment of the second speech to Kent., it is probably an error; Kent seems a newcomer to the scene (still explaining his purposes to Cordelia), there is no evidence that he has taken part in Lear’s medical treatment, and Cordelia asks the Doctor, not Kent, about that treatment. On F’s merging of the two speeches and assigning them both to the Doctor see nn. 2743, 2744. Many eds. agree with Capell (1783, 1.2:181): The quarto’s were right in making a seperation [of the two speeches]; but not right in those speeches’ assignment, which they should have inverted. He gives no reason, but presumably expects that one of Lear’s knights (see n. 1615) would attend to his dressing, and that the Doctor would speak of his temperance.

2772 his]
F omits, making regular meter. Furness (ed. 1880) prints of ’ sleep to indicate the absorption of his.

2773 fresh garments]
On possible symbolism, see n. 2743. Redemptionist critics find religious meaning, e.g. Milward (1987, p. 194): This recalls not only…Luke xv.22: Bring forth the best robe, and put it on him, but also the Pauline image of putting on the new man (in terms of clothing) in Eph.iv and Col.iii. More literally, Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): In the Gesta Romanorum (ed. Herrtage, 1879, p. 51) Cordell sends money to her father by a knight, to araye hym richely of riall clothing. Cordeilla does the same in Holinshed (see )—probably coincidentally, since the Gesta seems to have had no influence on later versions (Perrett, 1904, p. 70). Teague (1991, p. 135): From this point (4.7) onward, Lear undoubtedly wears a gentleman’s hat. It signals not only his return to sanity, but also the loss of his kingdom. In addition, the hat may gain importance in the play’s closing moments.…He may refer to the feather in his hat when [at 3227]…he hopes Cordelia breathes. But perhaps a plumed hat sorts oddly with an unconscious invalid and Cordelia’s these white flakes (2781). Foakes (ed. 1997): Though in many productions Lear is dressed in white to signify humility, now he is properly clothed once more, and possibly in early performances was visibly a king again.

2774 Gent.]
Doran (1931, p. 28): Q2 alters to Kent. apparently under the mistaken impression that Gent. was an error; the Gentleman had not been named among the characters at the beginning of the scene and had not…[spoken] up to this point, yet is clearly present: see 2843.

2774 Good…by]
F’s inversion makes more regular meter.

2775 not]
Q’s word, needed to make a full line with 2775+1, seems to have been omitted from F by accident. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 538): F1 might be defended: the Gentleman wanting Cordelia’s help in case Lear were not temperate. However, this seems unlikely. Halio (ed. 1992): Compositor E apparently omitted not accidentally, as at [315].

2775 temperance]
See n. 919.

2775+1–+2 Cord.…there.]
Doran (1931, p. 69): F’s omission may have been accidental. But there seem to be two reasons why these lines might have been purposely dropped from F: if spoken to Cordelia, the words Please you draw neere make little sense if Lear’s chair is being carried to her, and the scene may have lacked music. See the next two nn. Capell (1783, 1.2:181): [The Folios’] mode of bringing in Lear, was a meer stage convenience; and for that conveniency too, those folio’s sink the speech at line [2775+2], and (in that) a noble thought of the Poet’s,…that a soft musick should be heard at the scene’s opening, and behind the bed which is distant; that this musick had been Lear’s composer, and…his cure; that it is now call’d-to by the Doctor for the purpose of waking him, by such strains as were proper, rising gradually; which is not a noble thought only, but just, and of good effect in the scene. Collier (ed. 1843): Music, whether soft or loud, is not mentioned in the old stage directions, but it is to be understood—at least in Q. White (ed. 1862): Shakespeare caused Lear to be roused from his convalescent slumber, not by words or touch, which, however gentle, might have stirred up anew the subsiding tumult of his faculties, but by the music, soft at first, and gradually swelling louder. Thus the Physician steps aside to order as soon as he has asked and received, as a matter of form, Cordelia’s permission to waken her father. Not till then…does he permit her to approach the bedside, lest the old man should be startled from his sleep by her mere propinquity; and as she approaches, he directs the music to be louder, that the sleeper’s senses may still be controlled by the influence least calculated to disturb them. Sternfeld (1963, p. 244): [Sh.’s] introduction of music at this stage is the more remarkable, since it is lacking in both the Chronicle and the ballad: it is a dramatic stroke of considerable pathos and originality. The transition from chaos to cosmos, from untuned and jarring senses to recognition and self-knowledge is one of the great instrumental passages in verse tragedy. Wilson (ed. 1960): Perh.…the music was cut out of the prompt-book, which may account for the displacement of the entry from 2775+2 to 2771. Taylor (1983, pp. 413, 425), preferring to think that F’s changes are authorial improvement, not theatrical adaptation, depreciates Q’s semi-magical, harmony-wielding Doctor, moody musicality, and generalised ready-made emotion: Excising the music…leaves the silences truly silent, filled only with the deep specific emotions of the three characters. He concedes (pp. 447–8, nn. 131–2) that virtually all eds. prefer Q’s music and that F’s apparent elimination of music clearly goes against the theatrical fashion of the period. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 538) similarly oppose the idea that the music’s presumed excision reflects the reduction of personnel for a provincial tour, arguing that no such tour is known, that musicians regularly toured, that the play requires musicians elsewhere, and that such changes should not have affected the prompt-book presumably lying behind F. Werstine (privately): Lack of documentary evidence about repertoire and company make-up for touring, as well as about the nature of the manuscripts that touring actors customarily bore with them, makes arguments of this sort futile. At best one can suggest possibilities. Records of provincial performance usually do not name the plays performed, but Sh.’s company made several tours to Dover, where this play would have been a natural choice—see n. 2446–59. The music required in this play is mainly drums and trumpets and might have been provided by the touring actors themselves, while extra musicians (such as a consort of viols or recorders suitable for this scene) might have been dispensed with on tour. Gurr (1999, p. 71) intimates that the playbook would regularly travel with the touring company; one reason would be that it bore the Master of the Revels’ license, which would satisfy provincial officials that performance could be allowed (though it might not be). If the tour were extensive and the number of plays performed during it was large, staging changes might have been marked in the playbooks. One can not be entirely certain, of course, that music was absent from F during this scene, only that it is not specifically called for here to wake Lear. Mahood (1992, p. 167) imagines that despite the lack of specific reference in F to music, the Gentleman can himself provide lute music as the accompaniment to Cordelia’s words. But in this case the music would occur as public (instead of offstage) performance, and the medical Gentleman might seem too much like a strolling minstrel. Dessen & Thomson (1999, music): Typically music is played within, though (s.v. play, playing) occasionally SDs specify musicians on stage. Long (1971, pp. 178–9) gives music for a consort of recorders playing within (offstage), possibly with a sackbut to sound the lower bass notes: see . Taylor & Jowett (1993, p. 50): In F, what appears to be a cut was probably, in fact, merely a relocation to the end of the scene to form a soothingly musical fourth interval—soothing to the audience, not to Lear. Jones (1995, p. 215): Its removal from F is part of a shift from romantic artifice to tragic naturalism. Foakes (ed. 1997): Music was the best comforter / To an unsettled fancy ([Tmp.] 5.1.58–9 [2014–15]), and so is appropriate here, and may always have been played. The main purpose of the omission from F is probably to get rid of an unnecessary part, the Doctor.

2775+2 Please…neere]
In Q this remark would have been addressed to Cordelia, summoning her to her father, perhaps after he is disclosed behind a curtain at the rear of the stage. In F it could have been spoken to the bearers of the chair, as Koppel (1899, p. 121) suggests; but F omits it.

2775+2 louder]
Malone (ed. 1790) finds soft music used to encourage sleep in 2H4 4.5.3–4 (2521–2) and louder music used to awaken a sleeper in Per. 3.2.88–103 (1288–1303) and WT 5.3.98 (3306). Sternfeld (1963, p. 243): The aristocratic strings were easily audible at the Blackfriars Theatre or in a covered hall, but at the Globe Playhouse their softness constituted an acoustical hazard.

2775+2 musicke]
Granville-Barker (1927, p. 222): Consort of viols,…one presumes. Or conceivably of recorders, or a mixture; a lute alone might not have the volume to waken Lear. Manifold (1956, p. 93): Wherever instruments are mentioned in such a context, they are stringed instruments. Brown (ed. 1976): Soft and formal music. The use of music to treat the insane is, as Bucknill (1860, p. 222) notes, at least as old as David’s calming of Saul (1 Sam. 16). Fripp (1938, p. 664): And playing on [one’s] nervos (strings), as Apollo and Orpheus do in Ovid: Met. i.588, x.40. The practice is alluded to in R2 5.5.62 (2728) and Tmp. 5.1.58–9 (2014–15); the latter passage exemplifies its efficacy, as does Per. 5.1.80–4 (2063–7). Kittredge (ed. 1940) cites several other contemporary allusions to the idea, and Gardner (ed. 1969) adds Burton, Anatomy of Melancholy 2.2.6.3. Hoeniger (1984, pp. 55 ff.; 1992, pp. 261–9) traces the theory and practice from classical times to the present. For other Shn. references to the curative powers of music see 2H4 4.5.3 (2521), Per. 3.2.91 (1291), Tmp. 1.2.392–3 (534–5) and 5.1.58–9 (2014–15), and H8 3.1.12–13 (1630–1). Zenocrate calls (unsuccessfully) for curative music in 2 Tamburlaine 2.4.77, it is invoked to restore Pasquil’s wits in Marston’s Jack Drum’s Entertainment 5.1 (1600), and Dr. Corax uses it to treat Meleander in Ford’s Lover’s Melancholy 5.1 (1628), probably echoing this scene in Lr. Provost (1961, p. 56): The music has a symbolic function, in addition to its medical function: it represents Lear’s new-found harmony of mind. Ingram (1964, p. 171): This drama makes greater and more violent demands upon the emotions than any other play.…The necessary restorative of the audience comes with this music of Cordelia for her father.…For the first time there is a moment of true repose in the action. After sustained drains on the audience’s capacity to respond this music is, literally, blessed and quiet, the instrument perfectly adapted to cure…sences [2763–4]. The music is the immediately intelligible aural symbol of order, clearly defining itself by its own harmony after the chaotic roar of the storm.…It is to such music, amid such harmony, that Lear would retire with Cordelia, even if it were only to prison to sing…pray, and sing [2949–52]. Lott (ed. 1974): The stage music has both a therapeutic effect and dramatic significance in emphasising this climax in the play.

2776 restoratiõ]
Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 538): Editors…comment on the peculiarity of F’s spelling [restauratian], which is not recorded in OED; but it recurs in Dekker’s Whore of Babylon 3.2.142; Compositor E set the word nowhere else, and this might be his preferred spelling. The peculiarity is only in the -ian ending, a common enough variant for many words ending in -ion and thus perhaps an unconscious substitution here; Dekker’s word in fact ends -ion. It is Q’s spelling with an o rather than Latinate au that is peculiar (OED does not record it before 1660) and that suggests alteration by scribe or compositor. The fact that Sh. does not use the word elsewhere contributes to editorial doubt about its meaning here. Warburton (ed. 1747): She invokes the goddess of health, Hygieia, under the name of Restoration. Steevens (apud Johnson, ed. 1765, 8:2K6v): Restoration means no more than recovery personified. Delius (ed. 1854): The construction is Let restoration hang (Ger.). Moberly (ed. 1876): Recovering power. Deighton (ed. 1891), oddly: May my life be the medicine which shall bring to you the restoration of your senses. Though the context seems to demand the meaning power of restoration, all of OED’s definitions for restauration refer to the action or fact of restoration to a proper or former condition. Perhaps Cordelia means, Let the fact that you have been restored to me be the means of your cure. But see the next n.

2776–7 hang…on]
The verb may mean either (transitively) attach to, furnish (OED, v. 1, 5), or (intransitively) rest upon, depend on (OED, 13) or be attached to as an adjunct (OED, 16). Most eds. interpret it either as an imperative addressed to a personified Restoration or as a volitive subjunctive: let restoration hang on my lips; in either case restoration is the assumed subject and the meaning is transitive. See Warburton and Delius in the prev. n. An alternative reading is possible with an intransitive meaning. Having exclaimed O…father, Cordelia apostrophizes: Restoration (i.e., of my father to his senses), let thy medicine (means of cure, or effectual cure: OED sb.1 2a, 2d) hang on (depend on, rest on) this kiss; the difference is that medicine rather than restoration is the subject of hang. Such inversions in statements of volition are common in Sh.: cf. 133, be my graue my peace.

2777 thy]
Eds. disagree whether the reference is to a personified Restoration or to Lear. Thus Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): The medicine of Restoration, with whose efficacy she is besought to empower Cordelia’s kiss. Delius (ed. 1854): Thy medicine is Lear’s medicine, the medicine which is to restore him (Ger.); anticipated by Thirlby (MS notes, 1725–33): The cure of thee. See prev. two nn.

2779 thy reuerence]
Rann (ed. 1794): So venerable a person. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Thee, to whom all reverence is due. Joseph (ed. 1966): Thy state of being reverenced. Cf. 2303+11. Skillan (ed. 1967): I.e., inflicted on the weaknesses of his old age, a period of life that should be revered. Horsman (ed. 1973): The respect due to you.

2780 Kind]
See n. 132.

2781–90 Had…all]
Armour (ed. 1930): The exigencies of the dramatic situation demand a pause of some length, since the old king must be awakened gently and with care; the genius of Shakespeare fills it with splendid poetry worthy of the great lady who speaks the lines. In F, where Lear may be waked by Cordelia’s touching or kissing his face rather than by a gradual swelling of music in the background (see n. 2775+2), the speech is truncated. Cordelia has doubtless learned from Kent its details of Lear’s suffering. See also n. 2783+1–+4.

2781 Had…father]
Mrs. Griffith (1775, p. 371): Had you been even an alien, or a stranger. Kittredge (ed. 1940) makes bene emphatic.

2781 white flakes]
Craig (ed. 1901): Snowy locks (OED, Flake sb.2 8; the word is related to flocks). Houghton (ed. 1957): And beard. Wells (ed. 2000): With perhaps a hint of snowflakes.

2782 Had challengd]
See n. 58. F’s needless change to Did challenge replaces a regular tense sequence with an irregular one. Abbott (§317) provides other exx.

2782–3 was…winds]
Brooke (ed. 1947): There is a reminiscence, as elsewhere in Shakespeare, of Marlowe’s great line, Was this the face that launch’d a thousand ships?

2783 exposd]
An easy misreading of F’s oppos’d. Q makes inferior sense with against; Sh. always says exposed to, never exposed against. OED (Oppose v. 4c) gives the questionable sense Expose, citing only one other ex. The metaphor here is of meeting an adversary head-on; cf. warring, stand against (2783+1), Per du (2783+3), and helme (2783+4).

2783 warring]
Most eds. find F’s iarring inferior and suspect misreading or erroneous substitution. Delius (ed. 1854): Derives from jarring senses above [2765]. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 185): Perhaps a recollection of that word by scribe or compositor. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 538): Compositor E could have substituted iarring from above [2765] (where it would have been written in the margin of his copy). Sisson (1956, 2:243) argues for a misreading of warring: Shakespeare uses an a with a preliminary ascender. OED (Warring ppl. a. 2): Contending; (2a) Of the elements, quoting this l. as its first ex.

2783+1–+4 To…helme]
Doran (1931, p. 76): Perhaps omitted because of obscurity of meaning; see also n. 1622–1622+8. Stone (1980, p. 118 n.): Cut by a reviser who evidently failed to notice that the…cut had left a short line in the middle of Cordelia’s speech.…It was very likely the copyist who…made matters worse by redistributing the two following lines in order to disguise the gap. Halio (ed. 1992): The lines are inessential though eloquent. Weis (ed. 1993): F avoids Q’s expanding apposition which duplicates the storm scenes. For other explanations see n. 2781–90.

2783+1 deepe]
Schmidt (1874): Loud. Muir (ed. 1952): Bass. OED (a. 14): Low in pitch, grave; full-toned, resonant. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Rumbling. Halio (ed. 1992), alternatively: Deeply dreaded.

2783+1 dread bolted]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Charged with dreadful bolts, noting the many compound words in this play. See n. 1660.

2783+3 crosse]
Schmidt (1874): Zigzag (not attested by OED). Deighton (ed. 1891): Forked (not attested). OED (a. 1): Transverse; passing from side to side, quoting JC 1.3.50 (488), crosse blew Lightning. Craig (ed. 1901) suggests hyphenating as quick-cross, darting quickly across the sky.

2783+3 lightning]
Walker (1854, p. 17) suggests a trisyllable.

2783+3 watch]
