Schmidt (1875): To act as sentinel (OED, v. 6). Halio (ed. 1992): Also, Go without sleep (OED, 1).

2783+3 poore Per du]
Warburton (ed. 1747): The allusion is to the forlorn-hope in an army, which are put upon desperate adventures and called in French, enfans perdus. Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:49): An Out-sentinel in a Camp; so call’d from the Danger he is expos’d to; Tovey (ed. 1896): From sentinelle perdue. OED (Perdu sb. 2) supports both senses (dangerous action, outlying sentry duty), quoting this l. as its first ex. Moberly (1876): The meaning may be simply poor lost one. Probably both the general and special meanings are intended. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905), fancifully: A natural employment of the new language which her…marriage must have made dear to her. Eds. provide numerous exx. of the term’s use in contemporary English: see Furness (ed. 1880) and Kittredge (ed. 1940). Wells (ed. 2000), however: In italics, indicating that the word, first recorded in 1591, could still be thought of as French. Walker (1854, p. 17) would accent the first syllable, and that was one possibility (OED). Milward (1987, p. 195): Lear is like the Prodigal: see Luke 15:24, 31. Cf. n. 2786–8.

2783+4 thin helme]
Thin helmet, metaphorical for Lear’s thin hairs (Capell, 1783, 1.2:181), or possibly his bare skull (Brooke, ed. 1947).

2784–6 mine…father]
F’s excision has resulted in some imperfect verse in the following lines. Cf. n. 2783+1–+4.

2784 iniurious]
Deighton (ed. 1891) compares Lear’s complaint against his unkind dogs at 2020–1 and Edgar’s details of injuries they might do (2023–4). Stone (1980, p. 226), followed by Weis (ed. 1993): Wilfully inflicting injury. There is little choice metrically between Q’s word and F’s Enemies. If one word is a misreading of the other, as Doran (1935, p. 141 n.) and Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 419) suggest (misreading of enemies), it is quite as extraordinary as that of runaways for enemies in [Rom. 3.2.6 (1650)] (Collier, ed. 1858). Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 524), finding that Q adds nothing to the following line (Though he had bit me) but believing that F’s Enemies is unlikely to be what stood in Q’s copy, accept Capell’s injurors, which emphasizes the injury done to Cordelia herself, rather than presupposing a state of mutual hostility. To make a regular line they add a word; see textual n.

2784 bit]
On the participial form see n. 103.

2785 Against]
Schmidt (1874): Before (OED, prep. 1b: Exposed to, quoting the same phrase in Jn. 5.4.25 [2486]).

2786–8 faine…straw]
Schmidt (1874), fain: Obliged (OED, adj. 2b). Muir (ed. 1952): In Higgins’s Mirour the emprisoned Cordelia was forced From deinty beddes of downe, to be of strawe full fayne; see . Following Wright’s (ed. 1875) and James’s (1951, p. 120) recognition of an inverse allusion to Luke 15:16, Wilson (ed. 1960, p. xxi): Surely [Sh.] also has in mind the story of the Prodigal Son who…wolde faine have filled his bellie with ye huskes, that the swine ate. [Geneva]…The parent and child roles are reversed. The Prodigal’s father symbolizes the Divine. Once more Shakespeare invests Cordelia with an aura of Christian purity. Snyder (1966, pp. 361 ff.) detects many links between play and parable, seeing Lear and Gloucester as like the Prodigal and Cordelia and Edgar as like the forgiving parent. Similarly Battenhouse (1964, p. 207), and Milward (1973, p. 100; 1987, p. 195), who understands Son and Father typologically. Fisch (1999, pp. 118–19): Cordelia too has come a long way from her stoic immobility in Act I.…She too is a kind of returning prodigal, bountiful now in her expressions of love and honour.

2787 houill]
OED (Hovel v.1): To shelter as in a hovel or shed, quoting this l. as one of two exx. In fact Lear does not seem to avail himself of the hovel and straw first offered him (see nn. 1715, 1724, 1807–8) but rather of a nearby house (see nn. 1935, 1951).

2787 rogues]
Walker (1860, 2:308): Like slave and villain,…not originally an opprobrious term, signifying properly vagrant (OED, sb. 1, quoting this l.). Cf. 2176+6.

2788 short]
Earlier eds. understand as insufficient (Moberly, ed. 1876), scanty (Tovey, ed. 1896), etc.; more recent ones follow White (ed. 1883): The fresh, unbroken straw was used for the beds of decent folk; when broken and soiled it went to barns and stables and sties. Thus Craig (ed. 1901): Chopped, cut short for litter; Kittredge (ed. 1940): Broken up into short lengths by constant use as bedding. In either case, giving no warmth (Wilson, ed. 1960).

2789 wonder]
Wright (ed. 1875) takes this to mean wonderful (OED, a.); Rolfe (ed. 1880) suspects that an a was omitted.

2789 wits]
See n. 682.

2790 wakes]
Rosenberg (1972, p. 284): Rossi took a full minute.

2790 speake]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Cordelia’s sense of shame and guilt, together with her temperament…prompts her to retreat behind the Doctor. But she may be simply deferring to his expertise.

2792–3 royall…maiestie]
One verse line is set as two. Edwards (ed. 1975): While Lear was asleep, Cordelia addressed him as my dear father ([2776]); when he is awake, he is her sovereign king. Brown (ed. 1996): Cordelia addresses him reverently, as a subject rather than as a child. Perhaps, like Edgar, she is afraid to reveal herself to her father too soon. Foakes (ed. 1997): Cordelia addresses her father…as restored to the right she has invaded England to reclaim for him. If so, she speaks prematurely; and her motive for invasion is never made clear: see n. 1638+1. (Ibid., p. 8): Cordelia addresses her father as thou only while he is asleep, but when he wakes she relates to him formally.

2794 wrong]
Though conceivably Lear refers to the crime and sacrilege of opening a grave, his main meaning is the wrong of restoring him to painful consciousness. Nowottny (1960, p. 55): This is precisely the most unexpected thing Lear could have said…mounted on the immediate background of Cordelia’s prayerful concern and pity.…Lear astonishes us. Nevo (1972, p. 301): In fact, he is taken out of the grave to suffer a still greater loss. Halio (ed. 1992) specifies the painful awareness of shame and consciousness of the afterlife.

2794 take…graue]
Coursen (1976, p. 289): The lines recall the story of Lazarus (Luke 16:19–26). Milward (1987, pp. 195–6): And Psa. 30:3.

2795 blisse]
Crook (ed. 1907): The happiness of heaven. Elton (1966, p. 258): May indicate as well the happy state of the virtuous soul.

2795–6 bound…fire]
Davies (1783, 2:317): Though Lear is a heathen, he speaks the words of one in purgatory. Armour (ed. 1930): Shakespeare was perhaps thinking of Ixion’s punishment. Muir (ed. 1952): Harsnett (1603, p. 73) refers to Ixion with his wheele; see . Braden (1993, p. 259): In Seneca’s Hercules Furens, possibly a source for this scene (see n. 2801), Hercules waking from madness compares himself to Ixion (ll. 1297–8). Fraser (1962, Pl. XXX) reproduces a contemporary emblem-book engraving of Ixion. Muir (ed. 1952): H. W. Crundell has pointed out to me that the torment of the wheel of fire, although not scriptural, is traditional in the medieval legends and visions of Hell and Purgatory. They all draw upon the New Testament Apocrypha. In The Apocalypse of Peter, the Sibylline Oracles, and The Acts of Thomas, the wheel of fire is the punishment inflicted upon the damned. Cf. M. R. James, Apoc. N. T., pp. 517, 525, 390.…Holinshed discusses the authenticity of the stories of St. Patrick’s Purgatory, so we can assume that they were known to Shakespeare’s contemporaries. Hankins (1978, pp. 56–7): In the Vision of Owen (1153), who visited St. Patrick’s purgatory, some souls are whirled on a great wheel of fire, while others are scalded with molten lead. Here, he believes, the fiery wheel of Ixion in Hades is also merged with the wheel of Fortune, as in Macrobius, Somnium Scipionis 1.10.14. Starnes & Talbert (1955, p. 116): Lear was father of the lustful daughters as Ixion was of the lecherous Centaurs [cf. n. 2567]…[and] like Ixion, was bound to a wheel—though in Cooper’s Thesaurus (1565) it is a wheel full of Serpentes. Rosenberg (1972, p. 287): Ixion was bound on his wheel for an overt act—boasting of adultery with Juno—quite unlike Lear’s.…Ovid’s description of him as both pursuing and flying from himself [is] a tremendous, fertile image implicit in Lear’s—in human—action. Hardison (1975, pp. 228, 237): During the Renaissance the Ixion myth was interpreted as an allegory of irresponsible rule…and familial ingratitude is an important part of the myth.…[Also,] Ixion’s wheel was interpreted as the wheel of fortune on which man is bound when he allows violent passion to override reason. Bate (1989; 1993, p. 195) cites George Sandys’s Ovid’s Metamorphosis Englished (1632, p. 163): Ixion’s wheel is allegorically referred to…the desperate remembrance of perpetrated crimes. Sh. never mentions Ixion by name. Kirsch (1966, p. 285): Lear’s horoscope,…his fundamental constitution; his Self is set on fire. Elton (1966, pp. 237–8): The wheel-of-fire allusion…is syncretic, citing Renaissance iconography of burning wheels of the sun, Fortune’s wheel, the wheel of birth, fiery wheels in hell, and the wheel upon which prisoners were punished. Lascelles (1973, p. 78): A common cut, used in The Kalender of Shepherdes [ed. H. O. Sommer, 1892, p. 68], shows the torture of the wheel as punishment [in hell] for pride. Soellner (1984, p. 282 n.) adds the flaming wheel symbolic of Donar’s (or Thor’s) lightning.

2796 that]
Seymour (1805, 2:132): So that. Abbott (§283): So before that is very frequently omitted.

2797 scald]
With F’s erroneous scal’d Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 195) compares F’s wil’d for wild at 1322 and 1612—all set by Compositor E. Skillan (ed. 1967): I.e., scald his cheeks. Cf. 816 hot teares, and Jn. 5.7.45 (2654), Ham. 4.5.155–6 (2908–9). Halio (ed. 1992): His tears…are heated by the fire. Wells (ed. 2000): And scald what they fall on.

2798 know]
A second question from Cordelia seems more natural than a directive here, and both Q2’s know ye and F’s do you know make one explicit. Doran (1931, p. 24): Q2’s bold and remarkable change both amend[s] the meter and chang[es] a somewhat brusque, even if beseeching, imperative into a more natural question. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 419): Q’s omission of do you is probably a slip by the compositor. Only Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 525): Q1 makes sense and is metrically acceptable, either forming a feminine tetrameter with [2797], or a hexameter with [2799].

2799 Yar]
Doran (1931, p. 51): F’s expansion You are makes the line more regular. But see n. 2415.

2799 spirit]
I.e., soule in blisse (OED, sb. 2). Elton (1966, p. 258): Here, pagan, as much as Christian, doctrine may suggest the happy ascent of Cordelia’s spiritus…, as his own manes descends to the torment of his wheel of fire.

2799 where]
Most eds. adopt Q2’s when, on the grounds that Wher is a possible misreading of when (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 419) and that Where is all but nonsense (Dyce, 1844, p. 231). But Q has its defenders. Collier (ed. 1858): It may appear…no greater nonsense to ask a spirit, Where did you die? than When did you die? Munro (ed. 1957): Lear’s mind is perplexed about place. He first thinks Cordelia a soul in bliss but imagines he’s in hell…; then perceives fair daylight and asks where he is. Wilson (ed. 1960): Coll[ier]’s argument is more specious than cogent. Lear, restored to sanity, is still wide, still bewildered, being scarce awake, but now quite rational. Remembering that he has been in hell, he thinks at first that he must be in the next world and Cord. a soul in bliss. The question when did you die? is therefore perfectly natural and affecting. The geographical question, where, w[oul]d be irrational because pointless,…the question of a madman…[and] a mere puzzle to the reader or spectator, citing when/where confusion in Qq 2H4 Ind. 36 (39) and Ham. 2.2.447 (1490). Wilson had earlier (1923, p. 117) cited exx. of the same confusion in Oth. and 2H4.

2800 wide]
Nares (ed. 1822): With allusion to archery,…when the arrow flew…on one side or the other, of the mark. Delius (ed. 1854): Widely separated from reason. Craig (ed. 1901): Astray, wandering, not coherent in talk. OED (a. 10b): Astray in opinion or belief, mistaken, adding about this line, perh. Wandering in mind, delirious.

2801–4 Hees…light]
Two verse lines are set as four.

2801 scarce awake]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): We should observe that Lear is no longer delirious. He merely needs a few minutes to adjust himself to the present situation, for he has no memory of what has happened in the interval. His confusion is well understood by the Doctor. Miola (1992, pp. 165–6): Seneca’s Hercules Furens 1138–40 provides the model for this awakening into painful self-consciousness, as for similar scenes in Legge’s Ricardus Tertius (1580, Part 3, 5.3.14–15), Marston’s Jack Drum’s Entertainment (1600, 3.217), and Greville’s Alaham (1600, 5.3.99–102). Braden (1993, pp. 259–60): Hercules wonders if he has returned to hell, Lear finds Christian grace and forgiveness absent from Seneca’s fundamentally malevolent cosmos.

2804 faire day light]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Is this then actually fair day-light? Deighton (ed. 1891): Am I alive? Joseph (ed. 1966): Honest daylight. Rather, broad daylight (OED, a. 12b, quoting this l.).

2805 abusd]
See n. 1611. Eds. disagree slightly whether Lear means that he is confused, in a strange mist of uncertainty (Johnson, ed. 1765), that his senses deceive him (Craig, ed. 1901), or that he thinks Cordelia must be an hallucination (Muir, ed. 1952). Lott (ed. 1974): With some element of ill-used also. Halio (ed. 1992) adds the further meanings of taken advantage of and misrepresented (OED, v. 2, 3). Bevington (ed. 1992): Perhaps Lear feels hurt by the reminder of his having divided the kingdom.

2805 ene]
Foakes (ed. 1997): Indeed, to be sure (OED [Even] adv. 8b).

2805 pitie]
Muir (ed. 1952): This is not to be taken as indulgence in self-pity, but as an objective statement to guide the audience in their emotional reactions.

2806 To…say]
A hexameter, though it may be read naturally as a pentameter if the first three syllables are elided.

2806 thus]
Delius (ed. 1854): Thus abused.

2808 pin]
Skillan (ed. 1967): Of his big brooch which pins his cloak together. Wells (ed. 2000): Or a jewel or fastening on…Cordelia’s garments.

2811 your hands]
F1(u) prints yours hand, F1(c) your hand. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 538): F[(u)] looks like compositorial metathesis, followed by (in F[(c)]) correction without reference to copy.

2811 benediction]
Hudson (ed. 1871): Cordelia longs first of all to have her father revoke the curse he pronounced upon her in the opening of the play [see 116–27]. Bullough (1973, p. 394 n.) compares 2950–1 and Leir 2323–4, where Cordella asks of Leir your blessing, and your pardon Of all my faults committed any way; see .

2812 no sir]
Necessary if 2812–13 are a verse line; F’s omission may be accidental; but see n. 2813.

2812 kneele]
Steevens (ed. 1766, 1:16): The incident seems borrowed from Leir 2298–2353 (see ), since the father kneeling to his daughter…[is] a circumstance two poets were not very likely to have hit on separately. Idem (ed. 1773) is less certain whether the similarity is accidental or the result of imitation. White (ed. 1862, 11:202): It might have been fortuitous, as it was most natural, that in both Cordelia should kneel to her father…; but that in both the father should manifest an inclination to kneel to the daughter must be due…to a reminiscence. In Leir the constant rising and falling verges on the comical. Brandes (1896; tr. 1898, 2:139): On the stage…two persons kneeling to each other cannot but produce a comic effect.…[Sh. imitated the incident] in such a manner that only its delicacy remains, while its external awkwardness disappears. Cf. 2950 and n. 1436. Byrne (1960, p. 201): In Byam Shaw’s 1959 production, for a brief moment they kne[lt] together, like effigies on a tomb that face each other with hands uplifted in perpetual prayer.…They held it for one brief instant and conveyed an eternity. Foakes (ed. 1997): This is the supreme moment for Cordelia and Lear. Fisch (1999, p. 118): The ritual of kneeling…suggests atonement and consecration.…It is a moment inconceivable in ancient tragedy. It gives us a true dialogue of soul and soul, a true mutual offering of unconstrained love which redeems the language of sale and barter in 1.1.

2813–32 Pray…not]
Hussey (1982, p. 166): When Lear finally achieves true knowledge of himself and of events, the exaggerated simplicity of his diction—too simple, surely, for any real speech—with its predominantly monosyllabic cast, and of his syntax, with its short, coordinate clauses, incorporates the change.

2813 mocke]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Having been so long accustomed to cruel treatment, he is inclined to suspect every expression of kindness and regard of proceeding from an intention to deride his credulity. Halio (ed. 1992) suggests the additional meaning defy (OED v. 1c). F agrees with Q2 in adding me, perhaps indicating that an F scribe or Compositor E was influenced by Q2 here. Doran (1931, p. 118–19) notes that in 2819–43 there is greater agreement in punctuation between Q2 and F than anywhere in the play. Just possibly F’s me was added by an F scribe or reviser independently of Q2, as a final stressed syllable to compensate metrically for F’s omission of no sir in 2812; in Q2, however, where there is no such omission, the added me gives the line a feminine ending, so that it must have been added either by eyeskip from 2811 or because mocke seemed to invite a personal pronoun object here—a possible reason in F as well. Like Q2 also, F replaces Q1’s comma with a colon, confirming the impression of Q2 influence, though it may simply reflect the tendency towards heavier punctuation by Jaggard’s compositors in both books. Although there is no reason why a scribe or the F compositor needed to consult Q2 to clarify punctuation here, the breakdown of meter and sense caused by F’s added 2816 may have led to such consultation, with the result that he picked up Q2’s me: unconsciously. Werstine (privately): This is to imagine improbable coincidences.

2814 fond]
See n. 384–5. Craig (ed. 1901): Perhaps we should read foolish-fond, i.e. foolish, silly from dotage.

2816 Not…lesse]
Reed (ed. 1785): Probably the interpolation of some player, and is better omitted, both in regard to sense and versification. So Horsman (ed. 1973): Q would make a complete, although not a very good, line. Malone (ed. 1790) finds the added phrase absurd since it means not an hour more or less than an indeterminate number, for such is—fourscore and upward. Knight (ed. 1840) and many followers: Why, who is speaking? One who speaks logically and collectedly? No!…It was the half-consciousness of the foolish, fond old man which Shakspere meant to express. Delius (1876, p. 137): These words were not intended to define the time more exactly, but as an indication of Lear’s slowly and partially returning reason. Stone (1980, p. 70; cf. p. 246) objects: His madness should not appear as idiocy; nowhere else in the text is it allowed to do so. Wilson (ed. 1960) attempts to reduce the nonsense by reinterpreting the prev. line: Prob. = over eighty but not yet eighty-one. So Hankins (1978, p. 63), fancifully: The climacteric of his life, which has progressed according to nines [e.g., 9 x 9]. Thompson (1987, pp. 135–6) compares Justice Shallow in Wiv. 3.1.56 (1206), who has lived foure-score yeeres, and upward; here in Lr. the combination of the vague and the precise, while odd, is strangely effective. Bratton (ed. 1987): F’s troublesome phrase was cut by Colman, Macready, and Charles Kean.
Pace Honigmann (1965, p. 123), this F addition need hardly represent Shn. revision. Halio (ed. 1973): F at this point is obviously stretching (and adding to?) copy, comparing 2826 and 3175. In fact this page (309, fol. ss1) was the last page of Lr. to be set, long after rr6v (see Hinman, 1963, 2:280, 293), and the compositor seems indeed to have been stretching his copy to fill the remaining space, as is apparent not only from the generous space-leading but also from several verse lines (2745–9, 2760–1, 2792–3, 2801–4, 2815–17, 2827–8, 2842–3) that are set as two part-lines rather than as full or turned lines. Blayney (apud Jones, 1995, p. 156): A compositorial stopgap, set as a single short line, like the preceding line. Halio (ed. 1992): Lear’s nonsense line seems more like an interpolation than an accidental omission from Q.

2818 perfect]
OED (a. 3d): Sound;…sane, quoting this l.

2819 Mee thinks]
See n. 704.

2820 mainly]
Schmidt (1875): Mightily. Wright (ed. 1875): Greatly (OED, adv. 2, quoting this l.). Franz (§383): Perfectly. Only Tovey (ed. 1896): Which is the main thing I might be expected to know.

2821 skill]
Delius (ed. 1854): Practical knowledge based on experience (OED, sb.1 6). Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.) and most eds.: Reason (OED, 1).

2822 nor…not]
On the double negative see n. 427+1.

2823 laugh]
Halio (ed. 1992): Lear misinterprets the smiles of Cordelia, Kent, and the Gentleman; they are smiles of compassion and understanding, not derision. But there is little to smile at, and Cordelia is weeping. More likely he is anticipating derision for what he says.

2824 as]
In asseveration (Franz §578f).

2824–5 think…to be]
On the accusative and infinitive construction after verbs of thinking or desiring, see Franz §656.

2824–5 Ladie…child]
Muir (ed. 1952): The contrast between these two words indicates Lear’s return to sanity.

2826 I…am]
The effectiveness of F’s repetition has often been admired; nonetheless, it may not be authorial. In Q 2825–6 form a regular verse; the added foot in F leads to a hypermetric 2826–7 and a short 2828. Stone (1980, pp. 62–3): Cordelia’s half-line has apparently been padded out to join with the succeeding half-line [2827].…In Q this speech of Lear’s begins correctly with a complete line [2827–8]. Halio (ed. 1992): Moreover, throughout this column of printing in F, Compositor E seems to be stretching copy [and adding to lines?]. Ruskin (1855; ed. E. T. Cook & A. Wedderburn, 1903–12, 14:17): All Cordelia is poured forth in that infinite I am of fulfilled love. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Never surely was the passionate weeping of a reticent woman more perfectly expressed in brief written words than these and the No cause, no cause that follow. They so admirably portray the suppressed weeping natural to such a character as Cordelia’s; concentrated and undemonstrative, yet intensely loving and earnest. Charney (1973, p. 200): Cordelia’s line is the ecstatic high point of her own quest for identity as the child Cordelia.…Cordelia’s exuberant assertion uses no metaphor, simile, imagery, or any rhetorical device except repetition.…But in context it is one of the most remarkable examples of Shakespeare’s unpoetic poetry.

2827–8 Be…not]
One line of verse set as two.

2827 Be…wet]
Davies (1783, 2:318): Can you really feel grief for one who so cruelly treated you? Delius (ed. 1854) and most eds.: The wetness of the tears…must persuade him of the reality of that which still appears to him to be a dream (Ger.). So Moberly (ed. 1876): Are you real, or only a dream or shadow? Lott (ed. 1974): I.e. not the scalding leaden tears of hell [2796–7]. Sprague (1944, p. 296) records performances in which Lear touches Cordelia’s wet cheeks, and responds with tears of his own.

2828 yes faith]
See n. 669+9. Wilson (ed. 1960): He touches her cheek.

2829–32 If…not]
Perrett (1904, p. 277) finds the germ of this in Leir 1577–85 (see ), where Leir greets Ragan’s messenger, sent to murder him, as if he came from Cordella in France, and offers to resigne my life, A sacrifice to mittigate her ire; see . Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 181): A chain of reasoning [sorites] underlies the words. Lothian (1949, p. 26), of the first line: The humblest of all words in the play.

2830 I…me]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Said partly in consciousness that his behaviour to her has been such as to warrant no love from her, partly in remembrance of her former speeches [93 ff.]…[which] seemed to him so cold, so untender.

2834 France]
Rosenberg (1972, p. 283): The question may be occasioned by some hint of France in the scene: Cordelia’s attendants—or…she herself—may wear martial costume, French blue. Halio (ed. 1992): Lear recalls that the King of France married Cordelia. In all the sources Lear and Cordelia are reunited in France.

2835 your owne]
Hunter (ed. 1972): (Still) yours.

2836 abuse]
See n. 1611. Gardner (ed. 1969): He thinks Kent is simply consoling him. Colman (ed. 1982): He reflects that he has no kingdom.

2837 Be comforted]
Halio (ed. 1992): Cordelia is overcome momentarily with emotion. Or the physician, satisfied with Lear’s progress, simply wants to terminate the interview, and does so with this reassurance.

2837 rage]
See n. 2370.

2838 cured]
F’s odd substitution kill’d replaces one word with another of opposite meaning, and a natural expression (cf. 2764) with a forced one: to kill madness. Kirschbaum (1945, p. 60), however, defends F as Shakespearean, Q as hackneyed.

2838+1–+2 and…lost]
Possibly omitted from F because Trouble him no more repeats the same general idea. Still, the resulting line is such clumsy and hypermetrical verse that eds. suspect accidental omission. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 419) suggests eyeskip, or omission by a Folio scribe who did not understand euen ore. Stone (ed. 1980, p. 236): The reviser may have been, as modern editors are, puzzled by the reading euen ore.

2838+1 danger]
See n. 2789. Here is probably an ellipsis of an a, since danger as an adjective is doubtful (OED, a. B). Wright (ed. 1875): The danger consisted rather in allowing Lear’s mind to exert itself in recalling the past, than in telling him what happened. Budd (ed. 1935): The danger would lie in the shock that the memory of his wrongs might give him. Greg (1940, p. 395) compares Gallia’s warning to Cordella in Leir 2196–8 to Forbeare…Lest being ouer-ioyed with seeing thee, His poore weake sences should forsake their office; see . Cf. 3159–62.

2838+1 euen ore the time]
Conceivably the phrase may be either adjectival, referring to him, or verbal. Delius (ed. 1854) and a few others assume the former: it is a danger to make him clear, correct, and complete [in his mind] regarding the time lost in madness (Ger.). Except for the sense exact, precise (OED, adj. 7), no recorded sense of the adjective supports this reading. Steevens (ed. 1793) seems to mean something similar: It is dangerous to render all…even (i.e. plain or level [OED, 1, metaphorically]) to his understanding, while it continues in its present state of uncertainty—but this requires even to refer to a nonexistent substantive all. Most eds. take even here as a verb. Capell (1783, 1.2:182) guesses that it means run over, a sense unattested in OED but accepted by many eds.: thus trace or reckon over (Hunter, ed. 1869), pass wholly over (White, ed. 1883), pass over in his mind and memory, as on a smooth and even track (Page, ed. 1889). Eccles (ed. 1792): To recollect, and regulate in his fancy, the order and relation of the several circumstances and events; the recorded sense closest to put in order is OED (v. 4): To make (accounts, etc.) even. A few eds. in fact base their readings on this latter sense: thus Hudson (ed. 1871): Account for the time, or to make the last day of his remembering tally…with the present, and Craig (ed. 1901): To score up to, to give full information about…from the language of accountants. Most eds. follow Wright (ed. 1875): Smooth over [OED, 1a, fig.], render what had passed unbroken in his recollection. The metaphor is of filling in gaps or holes; so Harbage (ed. 1958): Fill in. Sh. elsewhere uses the image of a gap of time: cf. Ant. 1.5.5 (527), Cym. 3.2.62 (1530–1), WT 5.3.154 (3368), etc.

–2838 goe in]
Wilson (ed. 1960): In theatrical terms, go off-stage.

2839 trouble…more]
Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) compare the Gallian King’s cautions to Cordella not to overtax her father’s poore weake sences in Leir 2196–9; see prev. n.

2839 setling]
Hunter (ed. 1869): Scil. of his mind. Schmidt (1875), settle: To become calm (OED, vbl. sb. 5, quoting this l. as its first ex.).

2840 walke]
Schmidt (1875): Withdraw; or possibly OED (v.1 5h): to take a walk. Joseph (ed. 1966): Walk (or be carried)? See n. 2771.

2841 beare]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Presumably he leans on her as he leaves, so that the verb has both a physical and a mental reference.

2842–3 pray…foolish]
In Q these words can be read as a verse line and were probably intended as such; the addition in F of you makes that more difficult, and F (like Q2 and many later eds.; see textual n.) sets as two lines. Of these, 2843 is clearly a short line, but 2842 might be read as a pentameter with a medial pause. Most likely Compositor E was stretching his copy, since nine lines are divided and set as eighteen on this page; the fact that 2843 is just too long to set in the same line as 2842 without some marginal adjustment probably encouraged the line-division here. Taylor (1983, p. 61 n.) suspects, unnecessarily, that F1 derives the lineation from Q2. Munro (ed. 1957), questionably, finds the division intentional, expressing Lear’s failing and tired speech. Hankins (1953, p. 29) detects an echo of Eccles. 4:13: Better is a poor and wise child, than an old and foolish king, which will no more be admonished (Geneva).

2842 forget and forgiue]
Proverbial: Tilley F597. Coleridge (MS notes, 1818–19, ed. Foakes, 1989, p. 102) remarks on the affecting return of Lear to reason, and the mild pathos preparing the mind for the last sad yet sweet consolation of his death. Foakes (1993, p. 205): The open syntax allows the meaning forget and forgive all wrongs, and it is especially poignant that Cordelia cannot do as he would: In seeking to restore him to his right…she ends by inflicting on him yet more suffering.…Why does Cordelia not simply take him back with her to France? The play does not raise this question, but it does show her determination to seek conflict, to restore Lear to power, and, apparently, to revenge herself on her sisters. Cordelia never speaks of revenge, pointedly disavows any selfish motive (2379), and explicitly seeks restoration of her fathers right (2380); and Lear apparently approves of the effort, becoming its figurehead: see 2929.

2843 Exeunt]
Granville-Barker (1927, p. 182): Lear must pass from the scene with all the ceremony due to royalty; not mothered—please!—by Cordelia.

2843+1–+11 Gent.…Exit.]
Starting with Theobald (ed. 1733), most eds. believe that F’s omission of these lines represents stage abridgement. Theobald defends restoring the passage: The Matter of it is natural and easie; and tho’ the Language be not pompous, it is to the Subject: and the Uncertainty of common Report, with Regard to Kent and Edgar, must be very pleasing to the Audience, who knew how Rumour was mistaken in representing them to be abroad. Johnson (ed. 1765) considers the lines at least proper, if not necessary, and omitted by the authour, I suppose, for no other reason than to shorten the representation. Malone (ed. 1790), like Theobald: It is much more probable, that it was omitted by the players, after the authour’s departure from the stage, without consulting him. The Clarkes (ed. 1868): One of those brief comment-scenes upon passing occurrences…judiciously introduced by our dramatist. Delius (1876, p. 145): The lines prepare us for…the impending bloody fight, and…its doubtful issue. Verity (ed. 1897; cf. n. 2176+1–+9) sees the passage as an intentional pause after a climax, omitted by the actors so as to end the scene on a striking effect, in this case, the exit of Lear and Cordelia. Doran (1931, p. 71): The passage contains only a report of circumstances known to the audience…and an unfounded rumor not made use of in the plot. Hart (1942, p. 148): A small gossiping episode…is well left out by the adapter; it spoils the natural close of this scene which should end on the reconciliation of father and daughter. Empson (1951, p. 147): A brief dull conversation on the apronstage, while the inner set is altered (no doubt coats of arms were the important objects, to show which camp one is in). But the carried colours would do that: see 2845, n. 2349. Crane (1952, p. 166): The episode contains the last significant prose in the play.…From this point on, the play, except for [3060–3], resolves itself into verse. Following Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 8), Wilson (ed. 1960): Though the matter is nec. to the plot, the cut is prob. theatrical, as the talk is between minor characters at the end of a full intense sc. Urkowitz (1980, p. 54): This passage has no relationship to any action or event in the play. As a result of the cutting, a pair of closely related stage-pictures in different scenes are brought closer together.…This gentle pageant of physical and familial restoration is followed abruptly in the Folio by a martial display. Muir (1983, p. 110): This comment is…lacking in theatrical understanding. The audience needs a moment to wipe away their tears; they also need to be told that Edmund is leading Regan’s forces. Halio (ed. 1992): If an interval were inserted between the acts, this effect would be lost.…The deletion, however, obviates a potential inconsistency, the Gentleman’s not recognizing Kent: see nn. 2743, 2744. Halio (ibid., p. 30) argues instead that the cut in F gives the audience a false optimism: Without these lines, and without the gradual but consistent upturn of events in Act 4, the outcome in Act 5 appears more promising. Mahood (1992, p. 165): Besides preparing us for Edmund having taken Cornwall’s place in the battle…it brings a moment’s welcome relaxation.…But the play’s momentum is now such as to leave no time for explanatory or discursive pauses. Taylor & Jowett (1993, pp. 48–50): The cut, ending Act 4 on the peak of emotion and meaning, was made possible by, and capitalized on, the act-pauses introduced in the Blackfriars Th. after 1609. Weis (ed. 1993): This passage of choric dialogue…serves to remind the audience…of the political situation as it has shaped up since 4.2, when Goneril instructed Edmund to take a leading role in Albany’s preparation for war. Clare (1995, p. 43): The Gentleman makes it clear that [Edgar and Kent] are yoked together in the general consciousness.…The rumour suggests that the whereabouts of Edgar and Kent are a matter of real concern to at least some of the population, implying that their presence would make a significant difference. For the audience, who know that they are actually on hand, they may be seen as twin pillars of hope. Brown (ed. 1996): It is not strictly necessary for establishing the progress of the action and not easy to perform after the intensity of the previous moments. On the other hand, it may have been written to heighten a sense of danger, not to clarify the narrative.

2843+1 Holds it true]
Craig (ed. 1901): Is it still credited? Kittredge (ed. 1940): Is the report confirmed?

2843+3 conductor]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Leader of his forces.

2843+5 banisht]
Breen (1994, p. 494): But Edgar was not expelled; see 994, 1254–6.

2843+6 Kent in Germanie]
Smith (ed. 1902): It will be remembered that Kent had declared his intention to shape…countrie new. Bradley (1904, p. 445): In III.i [1644–6]…[Kent] says Cordelia will inform the Gentleman who the sender of the message was; but from IV.iii [2347+54–+55] it is evident that she has done no such thing, nor does the Gentleman show any curiosity on the subject. Muir (ed. 1952): Perhaps Shakespeare changed his mind. On confusion resulting from the conflation of the Q and F versions of this scene, see n. 2743.

2843+7 Report is changeable]
Harrison (ed. 1937): Rumors are not reliable.

2843+7 looke about]
Schmidt (1874): Be on your guard (OED, v. 11: To be watchful or apprehensive). Dent (1981, T305.1): Proverbial.

2843+8 powers]
See nn. 1638+1, 2347+9. From 2897 it is evident that two armies are separately led by Edmund and Albany.

2843+8 kingdome]
I.e., Britain.

2843+9 arbiterment]
Valpy (ed. 1833): Decision (OED, Arbitrament 3b). Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 420): The compositor doubtless transposed the r and e accidentally.

2843+9 like]
See n. 325.

2843+10 poynt and period]
The terms are synonymous. OED (Point sb. 28): Aim, object, end; (Period sb. 9): Fig. The end to be attained, the goal. Lott (ed. 1974): Seems to look forward to further action in the disguise he would not abandon; but nothing comes of it. He refers generally to his intent to vindicate and restore Lear. A few eds., however, follow Eccles (ed. 1792) in thinking he may mean the conclusion of his mortal existence (OED, Point 29, Period 5), and with it his entire future of life and fortune (Skillan, ed. 1967). Brown (ed. 1976) alone: Summit and conclusion/punctuation mark and whole sentence, accordingly making wrought ambiguous: Formed/written.

2843+10 throughly]
Hudson (ed. 1879): Throughly and thoroughly…were used interchangeably (OED). Cf. Franz §393.

2843+10–+11 wrought…fought]
Crook (ed. 1907): Rimes to end the scene.

2843+11 Or…or]
Foakes (ed. 1997): Either…or; a common usage. See Abbott §136, Franz §586.

2844 <Actus Quintus>]
Bullough (1973, p. 296): Shakespeare omits the conventional altercation between army leaders in Leir [2548–2613], Sc. 30; but as in Leir [2614–30], Sc. 31, the battle is merely sketched in V.2; see . Goldberg (1974, pp. 86–7 n.): As has often been pointed out, a good deal of the writing…in Act V before Cordelia’s death is (to say the least) not Shakespeare at his best. It is neither imaginatively intense nor even very attentive; and although it may be dramatically necessary that, while we are being prepared for the final catastrophe, we are not prematurely overawed by anything before it, it does rather look as if Shakespeare’s own attention was so intent on the final scene that he did not bother very much with what had to be spelled out first. Foakes (1993, p. 207): Entries of marching armies and the battle set the tone for most of Act v, which is full of stage action, and foregrounds a series of events and discoveries that have been seen as more appropriate to romance than to tragedy, but which deliberately engage the audience’s immediate attention, and allow the matter of Lear and Gloucester to fade into the background.

2844 <Scena Prima>]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Manifestly the same day as iv, 7. Cf. [2741] with the first stage direction in the present scene. The battle mentioned as this day’s battle in [2843+11] occurs in v, 2. Lott (ed. 1974): One of the summary scenes packed with information for the furtherance of the plots, all of it treated perfunctorily. Foakes (1993, p. 206): Here the vivid presentation of forces gathering for war, the reminders of discord between brothers (Edmund and Edgar), sisters (Goneril and Regan), and partners in battle (Edmund and Albany), brings also a threat to the lives of Lear and Cordelia. Idem (ed. 1997): The location is somewhere near Dover.

2845 Enter]
On F’s added with Drumme and Colours see n. 2349. Foakes (ed. 1997): However the badges of Goneril and Albany might be distinguished from those of Edmund and Regan, both presumably would include some indication that they are British, as distinct from the French forces who enter in 5.2.

2846 powers]
See n. 1638+1. Again (see n. 2349) F’s Gentlemen, and Souldiers probably simply makes more specific for playhouse purposes the makeup of the powers—both officers and common soldiers. Wilson (ed. 1960): Gentlemen is what officers were called in Sh.’s day. Rather, some officers were so called: see OED (sb. 1c, exx.). The powers would of course be represented on stage by only a small handful of men; cf. H5 4.pr.50 (1839), With foure or fiue most vile and ragged foyles. Dessen & Thomson (1999, power): As a term used in SDs, most of the examples are from the Shakespeare canon.

2847 Know]
Schmidt (1874): Learn (OED, v. 8).

2847 Duke]
Albany, the only living duke. Lott (ed. 1974): Ostensibly Edmund and Albany are to take joint command of the British forces. More precisely, Edmund will command Regan’s forces, and Albany, the noble of highest rank, will be commander-in-chief. Cf. 2909–10, 2999–3000.

2847 last purpose]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): I.e., to join us in the battle against Cordelia’s forces. See [2384–8]. Weis (ed. 1993): Or merely perhaps his most recent directive as commander-in-chief.

2848 since]
In the meantime.

2848 aduis’d]
Schmidt (1874): Persuaded (OED, v. 9b, quoting 2068).

2849 course]
See n. 201.

2849 abdication]
Virtually all eds. agree that Q1(c)’s alteration, the reading of Q2 and F1, is correct. Greg (1940, p. 177): One would suppose that the copy must have been rather confused to allow of such a misreading, if misreading it was. Q1(u) has its rare defenders. Rosenberg (1972, p. 292): Abdication has more energy, and is curiously prophetic. So Stone (1980, p. 251), seconded by Taylor (1983, p. 459): Q1(c)–F is both easier and less pointed than the original. But alteration makes superior sense. Edmund means that Albany is wavering, vacillating, from attacks of conscience such as we hear described in 2271–82 and 2304–2307+6 and observe directly in 2865–74. One may be full of such an attitude but not (except figuratively) full of an action, and Albany shows no inclination to abdicate or renounce children, property, or legal rights or offices—the only contemporary meanings of the word (OED, sb. 1, 3; v. 1, 3–5). On the dubious notion that Albany does eventually abdicate, see n. 3295.

2850 selfe reprouing]
Hudson (ed. 1879): His second order appears to reprove his first. Joseph (ed. 1966): He keeps changing his mind and disapproves the next moment of what he has done the moment before. But the phrase is self-reproving. More probably, Muir (ed. 1952): Self reproach, conscientious scruples (OED, Self-reproof, quoting this l.).

2850 constant pleasure]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Settled resolution. Cf. n. 48. Delius (ed. 1854): In contradistinction to alteration…reprouing (Ger.). Kittredge (ed. 1940), constant: Emphatic.…What he has finally determined as his course of action. Joseph (ed. 1966): Sarcasm.…What he wants without changing his mind the moment he has made it up.

2851 Our]
Colman (ed. 1982): Regan now affects the royal plural. Or perhaps she is already thinking of Edmund as her proper mate, as the following lines reveal, and so includes him in the plural Our.

2851 man]
Servant; cf. 1467. Delius (ed. 1854): Oswald, who was to return from Regan to Goneril (Ger.), comparing 2421.

2851 miscaried]
Lost, killed (Rolfe, ed. 1880), Come to some harm (Deighton, ed. 1891), both supported by OED (v. 1b, quoting this l.). Cf. 2888. In Leir 2361–5 (see ) Ragan wonders why her messenger has not returned; and see n. 1274–5.

2852 doubted]
Delius (ed. 1854): Feared (OED, v. 5). Cf. 2859+2.

2854 intend vpon]
Wright (ed. 1875): That is, intend to confer upon—a dukedom, by marriage. Although we do not see this promise made, between the time when Edmund returns to Regan (cf. 2283, 2331) and leaves her again (2393) she and Edmund haue talkt (2417), and she sends him a love token or letter at 2420.

2855 but then]
The meaning seems to be but even then. Craig (ed. 1901): But if, in case what I suspect is true. Muir (ed. 1952): Even if the truth is unpalatable to me.

2857 I]
Virtually all eds. accept F’s In. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 420): The copy may have had i with a stroke [ = macron or tilde] over it, and the compositor may not have noticed the stroke.

2857 honor’d]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Either honorable or respected. Most eds. agree with the former; thus Deighton (ed. 1891): As far as I may do so consistently with honour. Only Joseph (ed. 1966): Love which goes hand in hand with holding another person in honour.

2858 brothers]
See n. 2283.

2859 forfended]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:26): Forbidden (OED, v. 1). Hoeniger (ed. 1968): By the commandment against adultery.

2859 place]
Muir (ed. 1952): Goneril’s bed…forbidden by the commandment against adultery. Partridge (1947, p. 115): Pudend. So Williams (1994). Cf. her next speech.

2859+1–+3 Bast.…hirs.]
Doran (1931, p. 69): F’s omission may have been accidental. Possibly the lines were cut because they repeat Regan’s suspicion in 2858–9 and Edmund’s denial in 2860. Halio (ed. 1992): This cut and 2864+1–+2 remove some slackness and gratuitous comment. Weis (ed. 1993): The extra lines [mostly] amplify the train of thought. Foakes (1993, p. 205): The jealousy of Regan is well established by now.

2859+1 abuses]
Starting with Malone (ed. 1790), many eds. interpret as deceives (see n. 1611). But the word may also mean wrongs (Harrison, ed. 1948), dishonours (Wilson, ed. 1960), is unworthy of (McCann, ed. 1964); cf. OED (v. 5–7). Lott (ed. 1974): But he does not answer the question.

2859+2 doubtfull]
Fearful; see n. 2852.

2859+2–+3 coniunct and bosom’d]
On coniunct see n. 1194; here the word may mean conjoined not in purpose but in body. Though some eds., comparing 2413, give bosom’d the relatively innocent meaning admitted to her confidence, Steevens (eds. 1773, 1778) gives contemporary exx. of the sense take[n] to the bosom, embrace[d] (OED, v. 3, quoting this l. as its first ex.), breast to breast (Muir, ed. 1952), sexually intimate (Hoeniger, ed. 1968). Partridge (1947, p. 77): Lap-joined. Cf. n. 2413. Kermode (in Evans, ed. 1974): Regan uses words that might be used of a traitor—in league with her and admitted to her private counsel—but intends them in their primary physical sense, as her following words show.

2859+3 as…hirs]
A few eds. follow Delius’s (ed. 1854) mistaken So far, that we can call you hers (Ger.); none follows Page’s (ed. 1889) equally wrong As far as (him) we call hers; i.e. her husband. Hunter (ed. 1869): Hers in the full sense of the word; Hudson (ed. 1881): As far as she has any favours to bestow. Harrison (ed. 1948): United in intimacy with her in every way; Harbage (ed. 1958): In mind and body.

2861 I…hir]
Delius (ed. 1854): I shall never suffer her to be so intimate with you (Ger.). Deighton (ed. 1891): I shall never bear the sight of her, if you are too friendly with her. Lee (ed. 1908): I shall never submit to her capture of you. Lott (ed. 1974): A cry of hatred and jealousy at the thought. Wilson (ed. 1960): I never can bring myself to [endure her]. An indirect advance to Edm. Muir (ed. 1952): I could never endure her to loosen you and me, parallel to Goneril’s next speech; alternatively, as Lloyd (1892, p. 471) suggests, this speech is a continuation of Edmund’s, and deere…her is a verse line of Regan’s.

2863 Feare…not]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Fear not for me, comparing 2303+1. Deighton (ed. 1891): Of me being too intimate with her. Craig (ed. 1901): Doubt, distrust.

2863 me]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 186) suspects accidental omission in F, since the Q line is metrically perfect, that of F is not.

2863 shee…husband]
Dyce (1844, p. 231): I.e. Here she comes, and the duke her husband. Only Weis (ed. 1993): Or an expression of contempt to convince Regan of the absurdity of a relationship with the married (as opposed to the safely widowed) sister. Some eds. (see textual n.) think the speech is interrupted by the entrance.

2864 Enter…troupes]
On the more detailed F direction see n. 2349. Hogan (1962, p. 80), comparing the parallel entrance direction at 2845: Here it is got into one line by shortening the spelling of Drumme, Souldiers, and omitting Gentlemen and and. Foakes (ed. 1997), on F’s Colours: Flags presumably showing British insignia, such as heraldic lions.

2864+1–+2 Gono.…mee.]
Theobald (ed. 1733): This I have restor’d from the old 4to; and, considering the Jealousy of the Princesses on each side, it comes very naturally from Gonerill, upon her seeing Regan and Edmund together: as well as helps mark the Business going on, to the Reader. Doran (1931, p. 69): F’s omission may have been accidental. But if Albany and Goneril enter together at the head of their troops, surely an aside from Goneril as she enters is very unusual and may have been hard to manage; perhaps that is why it was cut from F, Goneril’s intentions towards Edmund being already well established. But it would have been more natural as an aside from Regan as Edmund turned to acknowledge the arrival of the party, and perhaps the speech was misassigned in Q; misattributions of speeches to characters named in immediately prior entrance directions are fairly common. If such was the case, the lines may have been cut as redundant, since they mainly reiterate the thought of 2861–2. Bransom (1934, p. 156) provides a reason for the aside: Goneril catches sight of her sister in Edmund’s embrace. Urkowitz (1980, p. 98): The cut concentrates the attention of the audience immediately upon Albany rather than on romantic intrigue. McLeod (1983, p. 186): The lines’ absence from F, removing evidence of Goneril’s continuing inner turmoil and anxiety, confirms her stronger character in F. Foakes (ed. 1997): May have been cut in order to enhance the immediate dramatic irony of Albany addressing Regan as loving after what she has just been saying.

2864+1–+2 loose…loosen]
Muir (ed. 1952): The Q spelling loose brings out the quibble. OED (Loosen v. 3b): Fig. To detach in affection, make a breach between, quoting only this l. Foakes (ed. 1997) compares 822.

2864+1 that]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Either a conjunction or an emphatic demonstrative, that sister. Possibly a second that or a this was overlooked because of two previous words beginning in th.

2865 very louing]
Weis (ed. 1993): Probably ironic, comparing 2320; but Regan’s cruelty is not there named.

2865 sister]
See n. 1219.

2865 be-met]
Abbott (§438): In participles…[the prefix be] is often redundant, and seems to indicate an unconscious want of some substitute for the old participial prefix; cf. Franz §662. Schmidt (ed. 1879): The word is only found here, and perhaps was coined by Sh. OED (Bemeet v.) quotes this l. as its first of only two exx. Wright (ed. 1875): The prefix here has apparently no force whatever. Page (ed. 1889): Used here simply for metrical reasons. But Crook (ed. 1907) thinks it has here an intensive force, and OED (Be- prefix 2) agrees.

2866 For]
Q’s word follows naturally enough from well bemet: For I wish you to know that the King and others have joined with the foreign invaders. In Q Albany goes on to discuss how that news concerns him; in F, he simply reports it. To most eds., F’s Sir seems preferable; Albany addresses Edmund as well as Regan before beginning his remarks. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 420): The copy may have had sir (with long s), which if carelessly written could be misread for. Weis (ed. 1993) finds Q more effective than F, which acknowledges Edmund’s presence and his legitimate interest.

2866 heare]
Wilson (ed. 1960): F [heard] is poss. but Q is better, and e:d misreadings common.

2867 rigour…state]
Rann (ed. 1794): Our oppressive government. Schmidt (1875), rigour: Relentless severity, hard-heartedness (OED, sb. 1). There is no evidence in the play of mistreatment of the populace; in Leir 2525 (see ) they are said to have been greatly tax’d. See also n. 1246.

2868 crie out]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Complain loudly (OED, v. 21b).

2868–2868+4 where…oppose]
Warburton (ed. 1747): This speech…[is] very necessary; for otherwise, Albany, who is characteris’d as a man of honour and observer of justice, gives no reason for going to war with those, who, he owns, had been much injured under the countenance of his power. Delius (1876, p. 145): Cut by the actors; but they have naïvely retained Regan’s reply…which refers solely to Albany’s words.…It is not Shakspere’s nature to destroy a feature so essential to the comprehension of Albany’s character, and to the development of the plot. Verity (ed. 1897): The lines seem to be a kind of apology and explanation, showing that Albany does not wish to appear as the willing associate of Goneril and Regan in their conduct towards Lear, and defining his (Albany’s) position in the whole affair.…The lines serve—perhaps were intended by Shakespeare—to reconcile the audience to the invidious part which the circumstances force the moderate Albany to play. Goggin (ed. 1910): Omitted in the Folio, for what reason is not clear: they exactly explain Albany’s position. Doran (1931, p. 73), followed by Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 8): The lines are one of several passages cut because they name a French invasion. See nn. 1638+1–+12 and 2307+1–+6 for counter-arguments. Similarly Foakes (ed. 1997, pp. 401–2): France must mean the King of France, and the speech survives in Q from an earlier version of the play that brought on the King of France at the head of his troops, a notion that Foakes admits is speculative. F omits the reference to France here and at 2307+3, he believes, lest the audience think the King of France himself is in Britain. Knowles (1999, p. 273): The lines might have…seemed redundant. Albany…intimat[es] a moral scruple: he cannot attack Cordelia’s invading forces without also attacking the old King and some of his own native countrymen. The[se] next five lines may have been cut because they repeat the same scruple: he says that he can honestly fight against a foreign invasion, but is not touched by (or moved to fight against) the King and other Britons. There is no real likelihood of any ambiguity or mystery about the meaning of Q’s France here or in 2307+3, necessitating the F cuts of these allusions. (Ibid., pp. 280): They clearly refer to the country’s army, acting in their king’s name and in the second case clearly not in his presence. Though he is at home in both Q and F, the King of France might still be said to invade our land, since the French army was levied, mobilized, and embarked under his authority and with his approval. But there would be no reason for an audience of either a Q or F Lear to think that in V.i he himself was present in Britain and personally leading the combined French and British forces. He had not been seen since returning to his own country at the end of I.i, and no allusion after I.i in F (and only IV.iii.1–2 in Q) ever places him in Britain. Urkowitz (1980, p. 99): By omitting mention of a French invasion, Albany’s speech now in no way justifies his participation in the war. Instead he raises a strong objection to fighting against the opposing army…[which] implies that he sees a real conflict in his loyalties. Both Albany and the audience, of course, know that the invaders are French, Albany never objects to fighting them, indeed agrees readily to do so five lines later; and the F cut also removes material—with…oppose—which would make Albany’s supposed objection here even stronger. He sees a conflict in his loyalties in both Q and F, but says so more fully in Q. Foakes (1993, p. 206): The relationship between [Albany] and Edmund [is left] uncertain, perhaps in preparation for the breach between them in the next [sic] scene. Brown (ed. 1996): With strangely shifting emphases and rhythms, and with some prevarication, [Albany] declares his political allegiance, speaking now to Edmund as head of Regan’s army.
The difficult style of the speech leads Clark & Wright (ed. 1866) and others to suspect that the Q lines are corrupt, perhaps representing two shots in Sh.’s foul papers (Wilson, op. cit.). Theobald’s (ed. 1733) paraphrase, which is far wide, confirms the difficulty: Before We fight this Battle, Sir, it concerns me, (tho’ not the King, and the discontented Party;) to question about your Interest in our Sister, and the Event of the War. Warburton (op. cit.) does better: As France invades our land I am concerned to repel him, but as he holds, entertains and supports the king, and others…make, or compel, as it were, to oppose us, I esteem it unjust to engage against them. Capell (1783, 1.2:182) would make with others (in conjunction with the others) refer to France. Steevens (ed. 1778) would make busines, not France, the subject of bolds, an idea rejected by Wright (ed. 1875): France is the subject of bolds as well as of invades. Clark & Wright (op. cit.), suspecting a line omitted before Not bolds: Albany ought to say something of this kind: I should be ready to resist any mere invader, but the presence in the invader’s camp of the king and other Britons, who have a just cause of enmity to us, dashes my courage. Munro (ed. 1957): It does not appear, however, that Albany’s courage is in question. He implies that honour compels him to fight. France is an invader and must be opposed for that reason. Skillan (ed. 1967): The speech does not make the king or his fellow countrymen appear to be traitorously bold, because they are answering unjust and grievous wrongs. Clarkes (ed. 1868): The diction is condensed and cramped here; and very characteristically so, in a man who has just before been described as full of alteration and self-reproving. Wilson (op. cit.): Yet the general sense is fairly clear: I could never fight except in a cause I believed in. As regards the present affair, France is our enemy as an invader, not as a supporter of King Lear. Joseph (ed. 1966), questionably: It is possible that Albany means that France gives aid to others as well as the King.

2868–2868+1 where…valiant]
Smith (ed. 1902): Albany gives [here] the explanation of his weakness at the beginning of the play.

2868 where]
Craig (ed. 1901): In a case, in a position where.

2868 honest]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Honourable (OED, a. 3).

2868+2 touches]
Muir (ed. 1952): Concerns (OED, v. 20). Brown (ed. 1976) alone: Injures (OED, v. 25).

2868+3 Not bolds]
Steevens (ed. 1778): Not as it…emboldens him to assert his former title. Foakes (ed. 1997): Or encourages him to oppose British forces. OED (Bold v. 2): Encourage, quoting this l. as its latest ex. On the formation of verbs from adjectives, see n. 1197; Sh. nowhere else uses this verb. Edwards (ed. 1975): If bolds is correct, it must mean give support to—the implication being that Albany does not think that supporting the King is treasonable. Pope (see textual n.) emends to holds, for obliges or binds; Warburton (ed. 1747) glosses that word as entertains and supports, and Hanmer (Letter to Warburton, 11 Sept. 1736) explains his holds to (see textual n.) as applies to. The Oxford eds. (1986 Q; Wells, 2000) make a quadruple emendation, reading Yet bold’s (= bold is) and ending the line with a sentence period after fear, thus making separate sentences of this and the following line. See textual nn., and .

2868+3–+4 with…oppose]
Singer (ed. 1856) considers these words as just a mere paraphrase of words occurring just before and so omits them. Brooke (ed. 1947): The similarity of meaning as well as form between the two clauses beginning with others whom [cf. 2867] is very suspicious. Horsman (ed. 1973): One or the other should perhaps be deleted. Cf. Clarke & Wright and Wilson in n. 2868–2868+4. Wells (ed. 2000), declaring the syntax is difficult, makes 2868+4 a separate sentence meaning Fair and serious causes are driven into opposition—a vague generalization requiring an unattested use of oppose as a noun. Q’s original punctuation gives the clause its full force as a specific (and syntactically clear) explanation of why some British should choose to fight against a British army: they are others whom…most iust and heauy causes [i.e., the rigour of our state] make [to] oppose [us].

2868+3–+4 others]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Others besides the king. Warburton (ed. 1747) understands Albany to include Gloucester. Bullough (1973, p. 328 n.): In Mirour (1574; see ) subiectes sword and might fight on the side of Leire; in 1587 (fol. 35v) this is expanded: And of our Britaynes came to aide like wise his right | Full many subiects, good and stout that were. Similarly in Leir 2524–8 British citizens are eager to support the former king, and do revolt (Leir 2616–17) against their new rulers; see , .

2868+4 heauy causes]
Craig (ed. 1901): Weighty reasons. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Albany implies that the government of Britain has been tyrannical of late. In Leir 2524–6 a nobleman tells Leir, all the Country…since your absence haue bin greatly tax’d, For to maintayne their ouerswelling pride; see .

2868+4 make oppose]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Cause or compel to fight against us. Cf. 2318.

2868+5 Bast.…nobly.]
Urkowitz (1980, p. 99): Edmund’s speech would serve no purpose in the Folio.…The duke has not delivered a noble rationalization for a questionable moral decision. He has only questioned the decision. Capell (1783, 1.2:1): Edmund’s reply is irony. Pye (1807, p. 298): Rather say, hypocritical. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): But Regan’s impatient query and Gonerill’s rejoinder, urging action on the pressing subject which Albany has admitted does concern him, combine to show that his reply was politic. Rosenberg (1972, p. 293): Might be satirical; but…as easily a romantic response to seem to match Albany’s in sincerity. Edwards (ed. 1975): Heavy sarcasm from Edmund. If so, Edmund is mocking Albany’s assertions of honesty, valor, and justice despite his reluctance to fight. Possibly speak is emphatic.

2869 reason’d]
See n. 1564. Deighton (ed. 1891): What is the use of this discussion? Kittredge (ed. 1940): Why do you waste time thus in arguing with yourself about the justice of our cause? Joseph (ed. 1966): Why split hairs this way? Edwards (ed. 1975): How can you reason thus (i.e. make a distinction between opposing the French army and not opposing Lear and his allies)? Urkowitz (1980, p. 99): As a result of the F cut, Regan’s question…takes on a new meaning:…Why are you raising this embarrassing new issue?…She perceives his speech as threat to their entire enterprise. But that threat is in both Q and F. F’s cut weakens the continuity, leaving less motive for Goneril’s question.

2871 domestique]
Often taken in the root sense of pertaining to the home (OED, a. 2). Steevens (ed. 1793): Door particulars, signify, I believe, particulars at our very doors, close to us, and consequently fitter to be settled at home. Jackson (1819, p. 337): Domestic door particulars (their family quarrels). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Family (OED, 2). Halio (ed. 1994): Blayney (privately)…analogous to kitchen door. According to Schmidt (1874), however, here and generally in Sh. the word means pertaining to a person’s own country or nation (OED, 3: internal; not foreign). So Delius (ed. 1854): Affairs that should be dealt with indoors,…refer[ring] to the latter part of Albany’s speech, to civil as opposed to foreign enemies (Ger.). Not internal unrest but foreign invasion from France should be our main concern, Goneril insists. This interpretation is clearly right, since Albany has said nothing of family matters.

2871 dore particulars]
Though a kind of sense can be wrenched from Q, most eds. either accept F’s and particurlar broiles or emend Q’s dore. Malone (ed. 1790) suggests dear, important, possibly from MS spelling dere; Quinn (ed. 1970), adopting this reading, glosses it intimate, a sense unattested by OED. Mitford (1844, p. 469) finds a few followers for poore, possibly from MS spelling pore. See also . F is widely glossed as family quarrels (Jackson, 1819, p. 337), private dissensions (Verity, ed. 1897), private quarrels (Harbage, ed. 1958), etc. Brooke (ed. 1947): F is easy but not very convincing. Shakespeare uses broils to describe tumults of a more violent character than the bickerings Goneril wishes to suggest, and particular broils is a muddy phrase not used elsewhere by Shakespeare. It took quite a number of people to make a broil. If the Folio text were original there would be no accounting for that of the Quarto; but if both rest on a manuscript in which the scribe had carelessly repeated the d of domestic in the next word, making door out of poor, the compositor or editor of the Folio may have felt justified in rewriting the line according to his own lights. Similarly Muir (ed. 1952) suspects that F is a sophistication, but inclines to Malone’s dere. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 525), defending pore: Goneril’s dismissive attitude is unlikely to describe these domestic…particulars as dear.…The error made the middle word alliterate with the preceding, rather than the following word. Wells (ed. 2000): Insignificant details.…We assume foul case or a turned letter in emending dore to pore. Davidson (1998, p. 316): A stenographer omitted a w from dowre; but Cordelia’s loss of dowry is not at issue here. Perhaps because it leaves the origin of F’s reading unexplained, no one has suggested lowe, which makes passable sense and might easily have been misread by Compositor E (who uses both forms) as dore. Alternatively, it is just possible that F’s broiles was in the MS behind Q, but so awkwardly (these domestic-broil particulars) that the line was recast in F. Written badly enough, broil (or broyl) could conceivably have been misread by the Q compositor as doore, and the number of compounds in this play is high. The phrase Domesticke broyles occurs in R3 2.4.60 (1552). By broiles Goneril does not refer simply to household bickerings (pace Brooke) but to the dissension and strife—the word’s common meaning in Sh.—within the country, that are alluded to by Albany.

2871 particulars]
For F’s adjective see n. 861. Joseph (ed. 1966): As distinct from common. Q’s noun may mean particular details, circumstances (OED, sb. 2b) as distinct from the large general threat of invasion led from abroad; less probably, it could mean personal concerns (OED, 6), viz. Albany’s personal moral scruples, or private quarrels (Brown, ed. 1976), possibly Regan’s willingness to take issue with him. In either case Goneril wishes to emphasize Cordelia’s army as their main concern, and to discuss nothing else.

2872 to question]
Q may mean to be questioned; see n. 378. Schmidt (1875): To examine (2) or To consider (4) (OED, v. 4). Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 420) suspects that Q’s to is a misreading from F’s the question. Schmidt (op. cit.): Subject, matter, cause (OED, sb. 4).

2873–4 Let…proceedings]
Though Q prints this speech as prose, the fact that the speeches before and after it are verse makes it likely that this speech should have been printed in Q as verse dividing after determine. F, which omits 2874+1, divides so that 2874–5 make a verse line, but at the cost of a clumsily hypermetric 2873. Wright (ed. 1875): The line is metrically defective and may be corrupt.

2873 Let vs then]
Albany abandons his objections, whether persuaded by Goneril’s arguments or by his three allies’ lack of sympathy with his scruples. Exactly who he means by vs is tied to the staging of the following lines (see n. 2875). Perhaps he means that the ranking nobility present—himself, Goneril, and Regan—whose armies are assembled need to consult the advice of more purely military leaders. Whether he understands that Edmund is the military leader under Regan and so includes him in the council of war is unclear; if not, Edmund invites himself in Q (2874+1). Danby (1949, p. 80): Albany, of course,…does intend a full pardon to Lear and Cordelia once he has scattered their army [see 2912–13].…[Yet] there can be no doubt that his decision is wrong. Cordelia’s cause is just, the invading army a righteous one, rebellion necessary. Joseph (ed. 1966, pp. 31–2) finds this moment decisive: Albany’s self-reproving and his disapproval of the others almost bring them into conflict.…[But] Albany controls himself and there is immediate agreement upon a council of war. Although he does not know it, his decision has determined the murder of Cordelia. This one scene also decides the fate of Edmund.…If Cordelia wins, then…machination ceases. But if she loses, Albany and Edmund must each move swiftly.…Albany must destroy Edmund and confound Goneril to save his own life; justice and mercy for Lear must wait for the threat to his would-be protector to be dealt with. Unfortunately, Edmund is forced by circumstances to put Lear and Cordelia in front of Albany in his timetable. In his ignorance he thinks he can deal with Albany later. In this situation each plays unintentionally into his opponent’s hands, and so Cordelia dies as well as Edmund.

2873 auntient of warre]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Such as are grown old in the practice of the military art; Clarkes (ed. 1868): The experienced in war. Tovey (ed. 1896): Probably meant as a check to the presumption of Edmund, and a hint at his inexperience. Brown (ed. 1996): His words may be a diplomatic way of delaying the battle. The battle is not delayed, however. The Clarkes’ suggestion that a single officer only may be meant, the enseign or standard-bearer (Hunter, ed. 1869; OED, Ancient sb.2 2), is accepted by a couple of eds. but rejected by Verity (ed. 1897) as obviously not appropriate here. Fortescue (1916, 1:117–18): In frequently making an ancient or ensign a general’s third-in-command, Sh. displayed no very profound acquaintance with the art of war. To avoid the (allowable) pronunciation of ancient as a trisyllable (Abbott §479), some commentators would add a syllable to the line: see .

2874 proceedings]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 160): F’s proceeding is quite possible. It means line of action, course of conduct.

2874+1 Bast.…tent.]
Doran (1931, p. 69): F’s omission may be accidental. Stone (1980, p. 237): Inadvertently dropped by copyist or compositor. The omission is odd, since the Q line makes clear (1) that Edmund intends to be present at the council of war even though he has not been explicitly invited and (2) that his arrival there will be delayed for a few moments, either while he leads off Regan’s forces or (as Wilson, ed. 1960, thinks that Edmund hints he wishes to do) while he stays for a private conversation with Goneril. Without this line Edmund may seem about to absent himself from Albany’s council of war without explanation, leaving Regan, who will certainly not be leading her forces, to attend it (see n. 2875). Weis (ed. 1993): F’s omission may reflect a stricter sense of decorum since Edmund is not a member of Albany’s general staff. But Edmund is clearly Regan’s lieutenant and leader of Cornwall’s forces (see 2398–2401, 2843+3–+4, 2845, 2938, 2984–5, etc.), and must consult with Albany if they are to combine together (2870) in battle. Most eds. restore the line.

2874+1 presently]
See n. 431. Horsman (ed. 1973), however: Perhaps taken by Goneril to carry a hint of private conversation first.

2875 vs]
There is no reason to imagine a royal plural, as does Foakes (ed. 1997). The us may mean Regan and her forces, but may include Albany with his forces as well; in either case Goneril seems not inclined to leave with the others. Like Koppel (1899, p. 128), Bradley (1904, pp. 462–3) imagines the first scenario: The Council will consist of Albany, Edmund, and the ancient of war. Regan, accordingly, is going away with her soldiers; but she observes that Goneril shows no sign of moving with her soldiers [who are being led off, presumably, by Albany before Edgar intercepts him]; and she at once suspects that Goneril means to attend the Council in order to be with Edmund. Full of jealousy, she invites Goneril to go with her. Tamblyn (1922, pp. 346–9) imagines a more elaborate variation with the same outcome: Edmund starts to go in the direction of Regan’s tent, Regan turning to go with him and taking his arm. Reflecting, however, that Goneril left with Albany may be present at the Council of War and perhaps gain a tactical advantage over her,…[Regan suggests] that during the Council of War about to meet, Goneril will have more of feminine privacy in Regan’s quarters. Then it rushes over Goneril’s mind not only that her sister is jealous, but that complying with her invitation she will have a chance on her own of watching Regan and poisoning her.…[At Regan’s quarters, Edmund] gets a paper, which he brings to Albany [2898].…He also perhaps has Goneril put her signature to a warrant for the execution of Lear and Cordelia. Unfortunately, the play does not suggest, nor could an audience divine, all of these thoughts supposedly going through the minds of both Goneril and Regan. Brooke (ed. 1947): Regan most surprisingly invites her sister to join Edmund and herself…as chaperon. This attributes great delicacy to Regan, who in any case has arrived with Edmund without chaperon or need for one if he is her general. Harbage (ed. 1958): Regan invites Goneril to exit with her rather than Edmund as each leads an army from the stage; but Edmund would be leading Regan’s army, not Albany’s; he would leave with Regan, and Goneril with Albany if with anyone. Much more probable than any of these is the alternate scenario. Albany starts to leave with his forces, expecting Regan to join him since she, as duchess, has ultimate authority over her army, and Edmund, at best her subaltern (see n. 2873), seems not likely to join them immediately (in Q) if at all (in F). Since Goneril seems about to stay behind her husband, perhaps leaving military matters in his hands (as would be natural and as everyone in the scene seems to assume), the jealously vigilant Regan asks her pointedly to join the council of war so that she can have not even the briefest opportunity of being alone with Edmund while it is in progress.

2877 conuenient]
See n. 1709. Bransom (1934, p. 156): Regan suggests it ill becomes a woman to attend the council of war. Joseph (ed. 1966): Expedient.

2877 you]
Perhaps omitted from F to make a verse line with 2876; in Q, 2877 is metrically perfect by itself.

2878 I…riddle]
Hunter (ed. 1869): I see what is hid under that. Moberly (ed. 1876): You want me with you only that you may keep watch over all my dealings with Edmund. Tovey (ed. 1896): Or, I can see through your pretence of propriety; or…both meanings. Muir (ed. 1952): Or, You don’t want me to attend the council of war, where I shall be close to Edmund. Brooke (ed. 1947), fancifully: The riddle Goneril reads is apparently Regan’s secret intention to take advantage of her sister’s visit to poison her. When we next see them, we find it is Goneril who has poisoned Regan. On the stage the words would be delivered with a sort of wink to the audience, inviting them to watch developments. There is no way an audience, even if winked at, could guess such thoughts in Goneril; Regan has no need to poison Goneril, who is safely married to Albany. Wilson (ed. 1960): Gon. had intended to stay behind for a conversation with Edmund,…but changes her mind, seeing Reg., had noticed what was up. See n. 2875.

2880 Edgar]
Brown (ed. 1976): Few generals would stop for an unknown poor man. Halio (ed. 1992): Edgar is still dressed as a peasant, though his speech is correct.

2881 your Grace]
See n. 218.

2881 had speech]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Condescended to speak.

2879 Exeunt]
Q2’s Exit and F’s Exeunt both the Armies are both moved up to precede Edgar’s entrance (see textual n.). Doran (1931, p. 27): The position of Exeunt in Q1 is better, because Albany’s remark in the line following [2883] is evidently addressed to the sisters and perhaps to the soldiers as they go out. But armies were not mentioned in the copy [i.e., Q1] from which the printer of Q2 was setting. He perhaps assumed that the Exeunt after Edgar’s speech was misplaced, and removed it to the place where it appeared to belong, changing it at the same time to the singular, because Goneril’s I will goe seemed to make it refer to her. Why the direction is also moved up in the folio is not immediately apparent. It is doubtful if the printer was influenced by Q2, because the folio direction is an exact one; it may be that the prompter placed the direction after Goneril’s speech because he wished the soldiers to begin to move off at that cue—Albany could call after them, even if they had all got outside. Werstine (privately): As evidenced from their extant work, prompters were not meticulous about the placement or even the presence of exits, e.g. in The Captives MS.

2883 you]
Crook (ed. 1907): Those who are leaving.

2884 letter]
Wilson (ed. 1960): I.e. Gon.’s to Edm. taken from Osw. by Edg. and read aloud at [2715–23].

2886 For him]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): To summon him.

2887 champion]
Schmidt (1874): A man who undertakes a cause in single combat (OED, sb.1 2: on behalf of another).

2887 proue]
See n. 2537.

2888 auowched]
See n. 1533.

2888 miscary]
See n. 2851.

2889 of]
Furness (ed. 1880) cites Abbott (§173): In the sense of as regards. Cf. 1053.

2890 And…ceases]
Delius (1876, p. 137): It is evident from considerations of metre, that the words…were in the original text, for they are almost indispensable as a conclusion to the whole passage. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxv): Crowded out, I think, by the Quarto printer, who crammed in Albany’s Stay…letter on the same line, to finish his stickful. Or added in F perhaps to eke out a full line of verse. As Honigmann (1965, p. 123) points out, in Q lines 2890–4 may be read as full verse lines if lines 2892–4, which were set as prose, are divided after but. F instead fills out 2890 and redivides 2892–4, in so doing ending the speech with an incomplete line.

2890 machination]
See n. 442. Steevens (ed. 1793): All designs against your life—which Albany will read of in the letter.

2890 loue]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 186): The sense shows that Q is right, not F’s loues. The same good wish occurs in Cor. 1.5.21–2 (593–4). Foakes (ed. 1997): Another case perhaps of a long tail in a manuscript being read as s.

2892 forbid]
On the curtailed form see n. 103. Deighton (ed. 1891): Edgar is afraid of having questions put him which would lead to his discovery. Hunter (ed. 1972): Forbid by Shakespeare, who does not wish any anticipation here of the denouement in V.3.

2892 it]
Tovey (ed. 1896): To stay.

2893 Herald]
Skillan (ed. 1967): The heralds superintended tournaments and trials by combat.…This is an anachronism.…Shakespeare is speaking in terms of his own day and the elaborate organizations of the College of Arms. See n. 3037–42.

2895 ore-looke]
See n. 373–4.

2897 in vew]
OED (View sb. 15b) quotes this l. as its first ex.

2897 draw vp]
Schmidt (1874): Assemble (OED, v. 89f, quoting this l. as its first ex.).

2897 powers]
See n. 1638+1.

2898 Hard]
Malone (ed. 1790): The most diligent inquiry does not enable me to form a conjecture concerning the true strength of the enemy. Doran (1931, p. 94): Hard…would seem to fit the context better. If hard is correct, heere must be a misreading; cf. n. 988. Most eds., however, think Q is a misreading of F’s Heere, spelled Here in the copy. Collier (ed. 1843): Edmund hands to Albany some paper. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 525): Alternatively, there might be a line missing after forces. On the difference between Hard and Heere, supposedly reflecting the difference between an oral and a written report, Urkowitz (1980, pp. 101–2) infers radically different conceptions of Albany and of the scene in Q and F: In F Albany holds two letters. The one handed him by Edgar perhaps may lead him to forego or postpone the battle. The one from Edmund will aid him in pursuing the engagement.…At the crucial moment he turns and rushes out to greet the time. He’ll fight. The systematic difference between the versions is the presentation of Albany carefully weighing his choices with clearly defined and articulated moral certainty in the Quarto and…in the Folio, where he repeatedly [as here] makes hasty and ill-considered decisions in a state of moral ambiguity strongly influenced by Goneril, Regan, and Edmund.
