Thomas (1984, pp. 509–10): Hard is simply a mistake for here.…The words by diligent discovery…can only mean that the estimate has already been made.…Both versions, therefore, imply the delivery of a written report, and there is no real difference here between the two texts. Wells & Taylor (ibid.): Whether Albany takes the paper immediately, or at all, is debatable. Or whether he reads it offstage. Edgar’s revelations and Edmund’s advice are identical in both texts, and Albany neither exits nor decides more hastily in one than in the other; indeed, he has already decided to fight (2872–3, both texts) on the grounds that a foreign invasion by an enemy cannot be tolerated whatever the domestique issues are, and the true estimate of enemy strength he receives in F is no more likely to dissuade him than Q’s report that it is great.

2898 quesse]
Error for F’s guesse, probably from misreading or foul case, but possibly from unconscious associaton with quest. Rann (ed. 1794): An estimate (OED, Guess sb. 1, quoting this l.).

2898 great]
The point of F’s change to the more neutral true is unclear; see above in this n.

2899 discouery]
Inquiry, investigation (Eccles, ed. 1792), espying (Schmidt, 1874), reconnoitring (Wright, ed. 1875), all supported by OED (sb. 3b, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Brooke (ed. 1947): Edmund has been engaged on a reconnaissance. See [2398–9].

2899–2900 your…you]
Heath (1765, p. 349): The urgency of the present exigence will allow you but a short time for the perusal of it. Schmidt (ed. 1879): The need, that you be not dilatory now falls to you. Hitherto you have let me do everything (witness the reconnoitring just finished), now you yourself must act (Ger.). Verity (ed. 1897), agreeing: Your…you; emphatic. Deighton (ed. 1891), your haste: The haste which you must make. OED (Urge v. 2b): To press with importunity.…With impersonal subject, quoting this l.

2901 Wee]
Foakes (ed. 1997): Royal plural, perhaps as a deliberate snub to Edmund. But Albany may simply mean himself and his powers.

2901 greet]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Be ready to meet. Deighton (ed. 1891): Welcome…as a guest (OED, v.1 4, quoting this l. as its first ex.).

2901 time]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Occasion. Craig (ed. 1901): Emergency. Wilson (ed. 1960): (First) opportunity.

2902–16 To…debate]
Dent (ed. 1927): Edmund’s soliloquy with which the scene closes is one of those rapid pieces of summary by which Shakespeare prevents the confusion of a complicated plot from spreading from the stage to the auditorium. Harrison (ed. 1948): Edmund has now reached the crisis in his fortunes. Both sisters are in love with him, he can have either, or he can aim higher and, with Lear and Cordelia out of the way, achieve the whole kingdom for himself. Muir (ed. 1952): Edmund hopes that Goneril will kill Albany, and kill, or be killed by, Regan, leaving him free to marry the survivor. The survival of Lear and Cordelia would prejudice his chances of becoming king of the united kingdom.

2902 sister]
Q2’s sisters corrects an obvious error.

2903 iealous]
Delius (ed. 1854): Both envious and suspicious (OED, a. 4, 6). Cf. 598.

2903 sting]
Doubtless a misreading for F’s stung.

2904–5 Which…inioy’d]
Doran (1931, p. 29): Q2’s inadequate relining (see textual n.) shows that the printer is himself responsible for it, working without the aid of a correctly aligned manuscript.

2904–5 take]
Partridge (1947, p. 200): Copulate with.

2907 Gonorill]
On the scansion see n. 47.

2908 hardly]
Schmidt (1874): Not likely (OED, adv. 7). Harbage (ed. 1958): With difficulty (OED, 6).

2908 cary…side]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Bring my purpose to a successful issue, to completion. Side seems here to have the sense of the French word partie. So Malone (ed. 1790): To maintain my cause. OED (sb.1 1): The action…of one person, or set of persons, in relation to another or others, quoting this l. Mason (1785, pp. 355–6) shows from several contemporary exx. that the phrase was used in card play; Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.) and White (ed. 1862) refer the term to any game or contest in earnest in which people take sides. Joseph (ed. 1966): Win my game, attain my goal. Edwards (ed. 1975): Play out my part in the game (with Goneril). Edmund’s purpose is apparently to become a great power in England (Harbage, ed. 1958), or even to win the crown (Wilson, ed. 1960). Muir (ed. 1952): Another explanation is possible, i.e., fulfil my side of the bargain with Goneril—satisfy her lust in return for advancement. Houghton (ed. 1957): Possibly deliberate double entendre.

2909 now then]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Let me see, let me think it out.

2910 countenance]
Delius (ed. 1854): Protection, support (OED, sb. 8b). Schmidt (1874): Authority, credit, patronage (OED, 8a).

2911–12 Let…off]
Verity (ed. 1897): It is characteristic of his selfishness that he leaves the risk to Goneril. Edwards (ed. 1975): In her undelivered letter, Goneril had suggested Edmund should murder Albany; cf. 2716–20. Bransom (1934, p. 160) imagines that Edmund had vowed to do so during the battle.

2911 that]
On F’s who see n. 235.

2912 taking off]
Delius (ed. 1854): Murder; cf. Mac. 1.7.20 (494).

2912 his]
Though Q is not wrong, most eds. prefer F’s the, which removes the redundancy of two restrictive modifiers of mercy.

2913 entends]
On Q2’s extends, Doran (1931, p. 34): The words are similar in appearance, and the second syllable is the same in sound. Extends might be a misprint; but…it might also be a substitution which was made unconsciously by the printer. Halio (ed. 1992): Albany has nowhere explicitly mentioned his intention regarding Lear and Cordelia, let alone revealed it to Edmund. Shakespeare introduces the information here partly to develop Albany’s character and to prepare for Edmond’s treachery after the battle.

2914–15 and…Shall]
As Capell (1783, 1.2:183) and Delius (ed. 1854) point out, the construction is elliptical: being…they are not repeated from earlier in the sentence but are understood from context: and they being within our power, they shall. On such omission of the nominative see n. 230. Other explanations are more difficult. Abbott (§411): A confusion of let the battle be done, and they and the battle (being) done, they. Cf. 989, 2471–2. Moberly (ed. 1876), followed by Verity (ed. 1897): The time when the battle is done shall never see his pardon. Tovey (ed. 1896): We should perhaps remove the comma after power; and will then mean and then, and the idiom is the familiar one,…And then they (being) within our power shall never, etc.

2915 for my state]
Eds. differ whether for means as for (see n. 1054) or because; F’s comma after state implies the former, Q allows either meaning. Johnson (ed. 1765): As for my state, it. Capell (1783, 1.2:183): For my state is such that it. Most eds. take state in the sense of situation, position, condition of affairs. Delius (ed. 1854): My high position requires me (or depends on me) to defend, not debate (Ger.). Edwards (ed. 1975): Position as Earl of Gloucester and potential husband of one of the rulers of England.

2916 Stands on me]
Most eds. assume that the impersonal subject it must be supplied to make the common idiom: (It) behoves, is incumbent on;…concerns,…is the duty of, is to the interest of, is urgent or necessary for (a person);…one ought, one must needs (OED, Stand v. 74l, 78q, quoting this l.); cf. Abbott §204, Franz §293 (for the dative), and n. 2658. Muir (ed. 1952) compares Err. 4.1.68 (1055) and Ham. 5.2.63 (3567). The sense it requires (Johnson, ed. 1765, and others) seems to be an extension of such meanings. Wright (ed. 1875) and a few others allow the possibility that state, not an understood it, is the subject of stands: For my state makes it incumbent on me &c. Similarly Tovey (ed. 1896): For my position concerns me as a thing to maintain, and not to make a question of; he would give the active infinitives to defend,…to debate the passive meanings to be defended,…to be debated; cf. n. 2872. If state is the subject, the sense of stand on = depend on, is contingent on (OED, 74c, 78d), first suggested by Delius (see prev. n.), may make easier sense. So Harbage (ed. 1958): My status depends upon my strength, not my arguments.

2916 defend]
virtually all eds. take this to mean actively protect; only Rushton (1870, p. 77): To command (OED, v. 3: Forbid).

2916 to debate]
Some eds. understand a reference to his present debate with himself about possible outcomes: deliberation (Johnson, ed. 1765), talk (Lee, ed. 1908), my arguments (Harbage, ed. 1958). More eds. refer it to any imminent or future moral debates about killing Lear and Cordelia: scruple (Tovey, ed. 1896), questions of right and wrong (Frost, ed. 1909), etc.

2917 <Scena Secunda>]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): This scene takes place on the same day as Scene 1—the day of the battle. Adams (1948, p. 333): Though technically a new scene because the stage is cleared, this and the next are parts of one long scene beginning with the arrival of the armies.
Furness (ed. 1880) reports at length Spedding’s (1877–9 [1877], pp. 15–20) reasons for thinking that Act IV should end after 2925 of this scene. In brief they are that Lr. lacks a strong crisis after Act III, so that the audience’s hopes and interest flag, and that the momentous battle in Act V is so carelessly hurried over during four lines of speech (2921–5) that it is disappointing and incredible. Spedding’s remedy would end Act IV with suspense at its highest pitch pending the outcome of the battle, and the Act interval, perhaps to be filled with some great battle-piece of Handel, would allow a more believable period of time in which to imagine the battle was decided. Perrett (1904, p. 257): The effect would be paralyzing. Bayne (1880–6 [1881], pp. 222–3): [Spedding’s] alteration is proposed as a means of assisting the audience to realize that the battle is a final crisis in the fortunes of Lear. This I deny. Lear could have been perfectly happy with Cordelia, and the final crisis in his fortunes occurred, not when the battle was lost, but when she was dead.…The drama of Lear, whatever else it may be, is first and foremost and supremely a domestic and personal tragedy. And if this is so, Shakespeare will interest his audience in the battle as little as he reasonably can. Bradley (1904, pp. 457–8): The pause at the end of the present Fourth Act is far from faulty…; that Act ends with the most melting scene Shakespeare ever wrote; and a pause after it, and before the business of battle, was perfectly right. (2) The Fourth Act is already much longer than the Fifth.…(3) Spedding’s proposal requires…the disappearance and re-entrance of the blind Gloster. Gloster, as the text stands, is alone on the stage while the battle is being fought at a distance, and the reference to the tree shows that he was on the main or lower stage. The main stage had no front curtain; and therefore, if Act IV. is to end where Spedding wished it to end, Gloster must go off unaided at its close, and come on again unaided for Act V. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): The exigencies of Shakespeare’s stage required an alternation of back-stage and fore-stage scenes and of both together, and a clearing of the whole at each act-end. At the close of Act IV the back- and fore-stage have been in use, Lear and Cordelia and their retinue retiring into the back-stage, a curtained compartment supposed to be Cordelia’s tent, while Kent and the Gentleman remain in the fore-stage for their dialogue, whereupon the entire space is cleared, as is needful, for the close of the act. Furthermore, Act V requires the back-stage for the opposite royal party. First, the entire fore-stage is needed for the entrance and meeting of the two allied English armies, and second, the back-stage for the retiring-place now supposed to be Albany’s tent. Thither Goneril and Regan retire, also Albany who is only detained from retiring with the queens long enough to talk with Edgar. Fore-stage scenes follow, before the tournament and closing scenes take place, which require the entire resources of Shakespeare’s stage-space at once. Albany’s tent remains at the back meanwhile, while Regan being conveyed thither ([3056]), Gonerill going thither ([3117]), and both bodies being brought thence ([3194]). The natural division in view of all these exigencies seems to corroborate the Folio division of acts. Muir (ed. 1952): This would make Act IV extremely long, and the shortness of this scene may be rather explained as an example of dramatic economy, since the battle itself is not important. We are only interested in the result of the battle. In Macbeth and Antony and Cleopatra the battles are important since the heroes of both plays are soldiers.
Though Spedding’s theatrical imagination was that of a Victorian—the Elizabethans were untroubled if decades of history passed in a few minutes on stage, and Lr. was almost certainly written to be performed without intervals—his critical censures on this scene have occasioned much further comment and so deserve some quotation: The army so long looked for, and on which everything depends, passes over the stage, and all our hopes and sympathies go with it. Four lines are spoken. The scene does not change; but alarums are heard, and afterwards a retreat, and on the same field over which that great army has this moment passed…reappears, with tidings that all is lost, the same man who last left the stage to follow and fight in it. That Shakspere meant the Scene to stand thus, no one who has the true faith will believe. Still less will he believe that, as it stands, it can admit of any reasonable defence. When Mr. Macready brought out the play at Covent Garden in 1839, he endeavoured to soften the harshness of the effect by two deviations from the text. The French army did not pass over the stage, and so some room was left for imagining the battle already begun; and during the absence of Edgar five or six lines transferred from a former scene were put into the mouth of Gloster, by which some time was given for its disastrous issue. Verity (ed. 1897): The fact that all our hopes and sympathies go with the army which is beaten seems a reason why the contest should be passed over lightly. Moreover, the great length of the play may have weighed with the dramatist. Smith (ed. 1902): A fuller description of the battle would have tended to direct the attention from the main interest of the story. Indeed the dramatic purpose would have been as adequately fulfilled by a bare narration of the result of the battle. Moreover, the circumstances of the play demand the sympathy of the audience for the French army rather than the British, and the sturdy Elizabethan patriotism probably weighed with Shakespeare in making the description so meagre. Bradley (1904, p. 225): There is something almost ludicrous in the insignificance of this battle.…The main [reason for its insignificance] is simply that there was no room to give it its due effect among such a host of competing interests. Even if Cordelia had won the battle, Shakespeare would probably have hesitated to concentrate interest on it, for her victory would have been a British defeat. Perrett (1904, p. 257): Neither Lear, Cordelia, Edgar, nor Gloucester take part in the actual fighting, and There are reasons why Albany and Kent should not be shown fighting on opposite sides. Although the result is so important, the battle in itself is of no importance whatever, unless it is spectacle we want.…Lear and Cordelia have to be on the losing side and to be taken prisoners. Why prolong the agony? Granville-Barker (1927, p. 182): Shakespeare…has transported [Lear] spiritually altogether beyond such issues as defeat, disgrace, and disillusion. This is, perhaps, why the action of the battle which will seemingly defeat his fortunes is minimised.…He has passed [in the last scene] beyond care for revenge or for victory, beyond the questioning of rights and wrongs. Munro (ed. 1957, 6:894): The din and scurry of a vigorous stage-battle…would have diminished the dramatic stature of the characters and reduced the beauty and pathos of the words and actions which move us at the conclusion of this tremendous drama. Shirley (1963, p. 66): A battle is necessary to the story, but it is not part of an important military atmosphere. Shakespeare…relied entirely on off-stage sound.…It would be a mistake to show the actual combat between the bad British led by Edmund and the good French led by Cordelia and her enfeebled father. Alarum and retreat within ([2926]) consumes only an instant, but it symbolizes the defeat of the French forces and explains the capture of Cordelia and Lear. In 1959, the battle was staged at Stratford-upon-Avon. It was done elaborately, took a great while, and was so fascinating to watch, with arrow- and stone-throwing machines, that it made one lose track of the mood and almost of the thread of the story. Hunter (ed. 1972): Shakespeare is interested in motives and results, but the actual process of the battle is unimportant to him. The real battle between good and evil must be fought out elsewhere. Lott (ed. 1974): The cursory treatment of the battle is in proportion to its own small significance.…[It] is the first of the play’s apparent approaches to resolution which come to nothing. Taylor (1980, pp. 27–8): The anticlimax…must be deliberate. Everything takes place offstage; the audience sees nothing.…The promised apocalypse does not materialize. Any attempt to minimize this anticlimax—like Spedding’s proposal…, or Glen Byam Shaw’s interporated battle scene, or Macready’s interpolated soliloquy…, or Kozintsev’s expansive cinematography,…or the Royal Shakespeare Company’s allusions in 1976 to World War I…—any such attempt seems to me fundamentally misguided. The battle…must work…as an aggressive disappointment: the author’s defiant and conscious refusal to give us what we want. Halio (ed. 1992): Having shown the British side, Shakespeare now has Cordelia’s army march with her father. Mahood (1992, p. 175): Onstage skirmishes full of exciting swordplay would weaken, by anticipation, the effect upon us of the single combat of Edmund and Edgar.…Shakespeare therefore keeps the battle offstage, but ensures our emotional engagement by keeping onstage the blinded Gloucester who must, like us, strive through hearing alone to interpret the outcome. Foakes (1993, p. 208): He wanted to highlight the fight between these two, in which the forces of evil are overcome symbolically by the forces of good. Kermode (2000, p. 11), on the eloquence of silence: Gloucester says nothing at all. How long this silence continues depends on the director’s skill or nerve.…[In] Peter Brook’s 1962 production, Gloucester, horribly blinded, sat sniffing the air for an intolerably long time, in a silence only emphasized by the distant noise of battle…a silence probably much longer than the speeches—a silence at the very heart of Shakespeare.

2918, 2926 Alarum]
A variant sp. of Alarm. Originally a cry (It. all’arme), later any substitute such as a trumpet call, drums, bell, or a combination of these (OED, Alarm sb. 3, 4)—at 2918, perhaps a trumpet call, though Naylor (1896, pp. 165–6) thinks that here, as in 70 of the 72 occurrences in the canon, it means drums. Horsman (ed. 1973): Call to arms; cf. 3107. It also could mean a loud noise in general (Schmidt, 1874; OED, 10), esp. the sounds of warning and danger in battle (OED, 5, 8), and that is perhaps the kind of sound indicated at 2926. Stevens (1964, p. 15): Usually when alarums are a mere symptom of battle…drums seem to be required, but they might be joined with trumpets, and clashing of armour (Manifold, 1956, p. 176). See Dessen & Thomson (1999).

2918 Enter]
on F’s added with Drumme and Colours see n. 2349 and the next n. Horsman (ed. 1973): Probably a march from the level of the yard…up and across the stage, and out by one of the doors at the back of it, beyond which the battle is taken to occur. Gurr (1992, p. 189): It has been conjectured [A. Nicoll, ShS, 1959] that passing over the stage meant…climbing onto the stage from the yard and descending to the yard again on the other. I find this doubtful, if only because the stage doors leading straight from the tiring-house were already in existence, and because there is no evidence that steps ever existed from the yard up to the stage. Sprinchorn (1992, p. 90): Ouer the stage may mean above the stage, on a raised platform at the rear. He notes (p. 80) that Enter over occurs also in JC 1.1.0.1–2 (1–2) and Mac. 1.7.0.1–2 (473–4), and that pass over, meaning simply traverse, is common (see OED, Pass, v. 57, quoting AYL 5.3.19 [2549]). Like Sprinchorn, Dessen & Thomson (1999, pp. 158–9) cite countless instances of pass(ing) over the stage in SDs, including 2H4 5.5.4.1 (Q, 3209+1), Cor. 5.5.0.2 (3639), and H8 4.1.36.26 (2445), few of which would suggest the need for a raised platform. The direction most commonly describes the action of crossing the stage from one door to another. The SD here, Enter…ouer, may simply be a short version of Enter…passing over in Cor. 5.5 and other exx. provided by Sprinchorn (pp. 78–9). Foakes (ed. 1997): How they crossed the stage is not known—whether, for instance, they came in by one door and out the other, or marched round the perimeter, or did it in some other way.

2918 powers of France]
See n. 1638+1. Taylor (1980, p. 30–1) sees F’s mere Souldiers as a fundamental change, part of a pattern in F to remove explicit mention of France; see n. 2347+1–+56, end. There is of course no doubt that the army is French, and its colours, the same ones flown here as at 2349 and 2845, would have been (or at least included) the flag of France. Foakes (1993, p. 206): Are the colours those of Lear…or those of France? The logic of the play would suggest the latter.…Enough indications remain in the text that Cordelia is at the head of a French invading force moving against British powers ([2374]). Knowles (1999, p. 274): Possibly when F added Colours in the entrance direction…it dropped Q’s powers of France as unnecessary, since the colors showed whose the powers were.

2919 her…hand]
An authorial rather than a theatrical direction. Brooke (ed. 1947): His hand clasped in hers.…The Folio version is drier and more technical. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 108): We should probably expect a prompt-book to read Lear instead of her father. Some, esp. revisionist textual critics, think the Q and F SDs here indicate significantly different concepts of the scene, characters, and play. Rosenberg (1972, p. 295): The Lear party may already be losing the battle in the Quarto stage direction…: the old man only a bystander, led along by his daughter…, a defeated Joan of Arc. One could imagine the same of the Folio direction, or something quite different of both. Leaving nothing to chance, the Oxford eds. (1986; see textual n.) have Lear enter with Cordelia and others in F but led by her in Q (1986; Wells, 2000). Thus Ioppolo (1991, p. 180): Cordelia, accompanied by her father, enters as the head of the French powers in the Quarto…, while Lear, accompanied by Cordelia, enters as the head of a group of soldiers in the Folio.…The focus of Cordelia and her father in the Quarto shifts to Lear and his daughter in the Folio. Naturally Lear and Cordelia would enter together as a pair in either text, and it is impossible to say from the SD whether either enters in advance (as the head) of a handful of soldiers (see n. 2846), or together with them, or preceded by those who are named first in each SD. The F direction may list Lear first according to his rank, not because the manner of F’s entry is different from Q’s. Halio (ed. 1992) also thinks that F’s entrance is significantly altered from Q: Lear’s strength and defiance are suggested, not his weakness and infirmity; regally attired, he may also carry a sword. There is no textual evidence that the aged Lear has so quickly recovered from days of mental and physical exhaustion, and his speeches before and after this entrance, in 4.7 and 5.3 (2948–68), are pacific. Foakes (1993, p. 107): In Q it seems that Cordelia…follows on after her powers…whereas in F Lear and Cordelia are at the head of their Soldiers. But there is no reason to think the two entries are different (see above), and whether or not Lear and Cordelia are at the head in sequence, they are at the head in authority: in both Q and F at 2929, King Lear hath lost, he and his daughter taine. That is, the soldiers (even the French) fight in Lear’s name, and Lear and Cordelia apparently remain together until they are taken. Idem (ed. 1997): In Q Cordelia holds her father by the hand, and appears to be following the French forces; it is not clear who leads the powers of France, and the SD in Q may be left over from an earlier draft in which the King of France led the invasion. On this imaginary early draft, see n. 2868–2868+4. In both Q and F, though Cordelia heads the army as queen, she is not the military commander; see n. 2347+2–+7.

2921 father]
See n. 2517.

2921 bush]
F changes to Tree. Brooke (ed. 1947): But a bush would be better cover for the old man in battle. Adams (1948, p. 333): One of the two stage posts; so Dessen (1995, p. 61). Brown (ed. 1996): Or the back [wall] of the stage. Foakes (ed. 1997): Property trees were in use, and one could have been brought on stage for this scene, or painted on a hanging; see Gurr [1992], 187–9. Gurr (1992, p. 189), however: The three trees listed in Henslowe’s inventory are all designed for specific purposes: one of golden apples, one for Tantalus and one bay-tree. There is no hint that he bothered at all about undifferentiated trees for forest scenes, and he might not even have supplied rose bushes for the rose garden scenes in Shakespeare’s history plays.

2922 hoast]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Here used for protection, shelter, a host being one who shelters and protects his guests.

2922 pray]
Skottowe (1824, p. 113): In Leir [2539–44; see ] it is Leir [along with Cordella and Perillus] who prays for victory; The arrangement did not, apparently, fall in with Shakspeare’s views.

2923–4 If…comfort]
Greg (1940, p. 440 n.): Since the speech suggests that he is about to enter the battle, which he does not do, this speech from an earlier draft may have been left standing. But of course one may be endangered near a field of battle without being a participant. Muir (ed. 1952): Dramatic irony. Cf. [2928].

2924 comfort]
See n. 2196.

2924 Exit]
See n. 2917.

2925 Grace]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): The favour of the gods (OED, sb. 6b).

2926 Alarum]
Rosenberg (1972, p. 296), after describing how producers have sometimes staged…battles here, adds, The text suggests no sight of battle, only sound: Alarum and retreat. This absorbs the war quickly into the flow of the action, an admirable restraint. Foakes (ed. 1997): The emphasis is to be on the fight between Edgar and Edmund in the next scene. Bratton (ed. 1987) describes other stagings.

2926 retreat]
Dessen & Thomson (1999): A frequent direction for sound…from a trumpet or drum played within to mark a particular stage in battle, sometimes called for alone, more often with alarum and other sounds, as Naylor (1896, p. 172) says. See n. 2918, 2926. F’s added within means behind the scenes (Kittredge, ed. 1940).

2927 Edgar]
Bradley (1904, p. 457 n.) questions Spedding’s (see n. 2917) statement that Edgar returns from the fighting: Where did Spedding find this? I find no trace of it, and surely Edgar would not have risked his life in the battle, when he had, in case of defeat, to appear and fight Edmund. He does not appear armed, according to the Folio, till [3067].

2929 King Lear]
Edgar thinks of Lear, not Cordelia, as the titular leader of the army; his is the cause (busines 2377) her army fights for, to restore him to an unspecified right (2380). But in all probability neither the ancient, weakened king nor his inexperienced youngest daughter is the active leader of the troops: see nn. 2347+1–+56, 2347+2–+7, 2349, and 2661.

2929 taine]
Elliptical; either are (Clarkes, ed. 1868) or being (Page, ed. 1889) is to be understood.

2931 rot]
Deighton (ed. 1891): For dying. Andresen (1974, p. 148): Gloucester, the old man, is by no means the wise man impervious to the vicissitudes of fortune. On the contrary, he explicitly connects his age and state of mind to rottenness.…Edgar, the young man, is the wiser; ripe in wisdom despite his youth, he personifies his own aphorism, that ripeness is all.

2932–3 What…indure]
Perhaps F’s mislining reflects its MS copy, since with a little squeezing the compositor could have set one line.

2932 ill thoughts]
Many eds. agree with Deighton (ed. 1891) that Edgar refers to thoughts of suicide. So Houghton (ed. 1957): This is the force of the famous lines that follow, not…that men must put up with death as with birth. But just as probably Edgar refers to despairing inaction; the sin of despair was mortal to the soul, and its practical effects on the body here—allowing oneself to be captured as a traitor by British forces—would be self-sacrifice if not suicide. Edgar may simply be urging him on to persevere, enduring existence rather than giving up. Bullough (1973, p. 388 n.) compares Leir 2078: death is better then for to despaire; see , and cf. nn. 1835, 2475, 3120, 3154, 3213, 3260.

2932–4 men…hither]
Robertson (1897, p. 66), Hooker (1902, pp. 319, 364), and Reyher (1947, p. 498) compare Florio’s Montaigne, That to philosophie, is to learne how to die: Depart (saith she [i.e., Nature]) out of this world, even as you came into it…without passion or amazement; see . Craig (ed. 1931): A stern utterance of the doctrine of fortitude, repeatedly applied to poor Gloucester. It must be said, however, that fortitude is the crowning quality of Edgar’s character. Stauffer (1949, p. 198): Endurance is not the equivalent of supine despair. Edgar answers again with the lesson of true patience in action. Elton (1966, p. 103): Edgar’s speech, containing one of the oldest of human commonplaces, is in the tradition of ancient consolatory oratory (e.g., all men must resign themselves to age and the coming of death) and was in the Renaissance proverbial (e.g., He that is once born once must die. etc.), giving citations. Hunter (ed. 1972): Just as childbirth involves pain and trouble, so death…is a painful process that has to be struggled through till it be granted from above. Milward (1987, p. 197): Recalls Job 1:21, Eccles. 5:14, 1 Tim. 6:7, and the Homily Of the Misery of All Mankind. Foakes (ed. 1997): Endure seems to imply the necessity of suffering, and his assumption of the moral high ground leaves many readers uncomfortable.

2935 Ripeness is al]
Steevens (ed. 1773), ripeness: To be ready, prepared, comparing Ham. 5.2.222 (3671), the readines is all. Malone (MS notes, 1773–90): Maturity is all—Men must not put an end to their lives till they are ripe for death—till they drop off of themselves, comparing Mac. 4.3.238 (2089), ripe for shaking. Fisch (1999, p. 128): Hamlet anticipates death, Edgar the direct opposite…an ongoing and undetermined course of trial and endeavour, like Job’s. Eds. differ whether the advice is atheistic, stoical, fatalistic, or Christian. Birch (1848, p. 425): Full of material meaning, likening man to fruit which must fall. Delius (ed. 1854): Readiness (ripeness, maturity) to patiently endure both birth and death, without anxiety (Ger.). Moberly (ed. 1876): The due time for death, like the due time for birth, should decide our fate. Tovey (ed. 1896): One must have the maturity of mind which is prepared to encounter death. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905) compare some lines from Florio’s tr. of Montaigne’s essay That to philosophie, is to learne how to die (see ): There is no more inconvenience to feare [all kinds of death] than to endure one: what matter is it when it commeth, since it is unavoidable?…Moreover, no man dies before his houre. Like Hooker (1902, pp. 319, 364; cf. prev. n.), Muir (ed. 1952) quotes other lines from the same passage (e.g., It consists not in number of yeeres, but in your will, that you have lived long enough), and from Elyot’s definition in The Gouernour 1:xxii that Maturity is a mean between two extremities. Pancoast (1925, pp. 406–8): He is not telling him that he must endure death, but that, longing to die, he must be patient to endure life.…[In Ham.] emphasis is laid on the thought that a man should hold himself ready to die; in [Lr.]…on the fact that tragic as life may be, a man should wait patiently until the great forces that rule over life bring his death to an end. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The only thing that is important in life is to be ready for death when it comes. Cunningham (1951, pp. 12, 14): The metaphor shifts our point of view from a man’s attitude toward death [readiness, endure]…to the absoluteness of the external process of Providence.…Man dies when God is ready. Harbage (ed. 1958): The time decreed by the gods for the fruit to fall from the branch. Levin (1959, p. 101), calling it the most positive statement of the play: The manner of one’s death and the moment of it were ultimate concerns to Elizabethans. Joseph (ed. 1966): By the sixteenth century this sentence had become associated with the motto festina lente.…Ripeness is achieved by a slow growth of the strength in which speed and steadiness are equal. When mature, the concealed power is suddenly released with devastating effect.…Edgar says Ripeness is all not only to reconcile his father to the snuff and loathed part of nature, but because his opportunity has come; he is about to move swiftly after a long and patient wait for events to mature in his favour. Elton (1966, pp. 100–4): The play syncretically includes both biblical Christian and pagan Stoic versions of the ideas that men must endure suffering, recognize the brevity of life, and accept the inevitability of death when providence determines the moment of ripeness for it. Elton cites numerous Renaissance exx. of both viewpoints, including Eccles. 3:1–8; others are provided by Rossiter-Smith (1965, p. 97), Schoff (1965, p. 353), Godshalk (1967, p. 145), and Stanley (1967, p. 228). Skillan (ed. 1967): All that is required, [is] a readiness but not a haste. Hunter (ed. 1972): Man’s duty is not to wait to rot [2931], but to await the time of Ripeness, which is the time appointed for death. Andresen (1974, p. 147): The familiar content of commonplace truth draws us in.…At the same time, the deliberately artificial form works in the other direction to create an esthetic and psychological distance that permits our momentary detachment from and reflectiveness about the crowded, confusing situation.…Even Edgar’s vocabulary works to this end: he says to his father, not you nor we, but Men must endure. Edwards (ed. 1975): This phrase has behind it a whole philosophy of decorum, which is the desire that all one’s actions should be wholly suited to and worthy of the time and the occasion. Bonnefoy (1988, pp. 203–5): Hamlet’s sentence implies a bleak, joyless world, Edgar’s one in which order and meaning persist. Foakes (ed. 1997): Edgar’s moralizing seems hardly adequate to the nature of the action, and is undercut by the next scene; and yet the phrase has great evocative power, and the ring of a conclusive cadence [Brooke, 1963, p. 49], behind it the shadow of the proverb Soon ripe, soon rotten (Tilley R133), as suggested by Ormerod (1996, pp. 662–5).

2936 And…too]
F’s addition may have been intended to end the scene on a full line of verse. Adee (ed. 1890): It may distract attention from Edgar’s adage. Van Dam (1935, p. 66): This quasi-addition belonged to the original text and restores the blank verse truncated in Q. Stone (1980, pp. 69–70) cites this l. among metrical expansions in F that do not contribute to the sense, adding, The vacuousness of these stopgaps descends on occasion to fatuity. Blayney (apud Jones, 1995, p. 156): A compositorial stopgap, invented to stretch copy to fill the page. Stauffer (1949, p. 198): The little scene of eleven lines is a comment on the entire play. Gloucester accepts Edgar’s truth…but only as a partial truth. Urkowitz (1980, p. 44): A speech of extraordinary simplicity and depth, balancing his attitude (2931) in equal validity with Edgar’s (2935). So Peat (1980, p. 44) also thinks. Weis (ed. 1993): [It] may indicate that at last he is reconciled to his fate. Or that his newly regained faith is shaky, and he is weak and passively led. Thus Foakes (ed. 1997): To Gloucester, who has endured so much, all moral sayings now sound equally true; but the phrase could also be taken…to suggest that Gloucester is finally cured of ill thoughts. Since with or without the addition Gloucester accedes to Edgar’s exhortation, it makes no practical difference.

2937 <Scena Tertia>]
Smith (ed. 1902): All the chief characters…reappear in this last scene to taste the wages of their virtue and the cup of their deservings. The dénouement, as in so many of Shakespeare’s plays, is rapidly achieved, and somewhat resembles, with its bustle and wealth of incident, the closing scene of Hamlet; and, as in Hamlet, the guiltless fall with the guilty. Lott (ed. 1974): This final scene…is a series of advances and repudiations of visions of hope, a see-saw of comfort and disaster.…There is also a reversion to the expository and summary modes of the first scene of the play and a few other scenes; there is much ground to cover, and many threads need to be caught up.…The treatment of the Gloucester plot…retains in language and method of exposition the characteristics of allegory and the Morality play.…Such treatment exposes the naturalness of the Lear plot, its calculated refusal to fit into some grand order of things ruled by a just supernature. Kinney (1976, pp. 706–7): The play’s final scene holds the first scene in delicate equipoise. Now, for the second time in the play, the entire court has assembled; again Edmund’s eyes are on the throne; again Goneril and Regan compete against each other, their ambition overriding even their lust. The ceremonial duel between Edgar and Edmund carries the same prize as the initial love-test.…Edmund, who first betrayed his half-brother with a conspiratorial letter, now finds his last letter from Goneril undoes them all.…Cordelia’s fateful silence in the opening scene is duplicated in Edmund’s reticence here regarding his warrant on the murders of Cordelia and Lear—the first silence had divided them; this kills them both. Reibetanz (1977, p. 115): The audience are suspended between hope and despair because Shakespeare invites a kind of double perspective: we follow the action as it progresses towards both its actual and its possible conclusions. Peat (1980, pp. 49–50): From this point, Shakespeare creates tension between an awareness of impending catastrophe and the possibility of a happy resolution.…No audience in the theatre remains…detached: during this scene of mounting suspense, their emotion is intense. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The scene takes place on the same day as Scenes i and ii.

2938–9 Enter…prisoners]
Brooke (ed. 1947): The Folio stage direction [was] probably composed by the stage-manager. Shakespeare may have written the simpler (and insufficient) version of the Quarto. See nn. 2349, 2846. As at 2349–50, Taylor (1980, pp. 32–3) here imagines in Q a secluded, secretive scene with a few guards, but no more, in F a crowded stage and public scene: We imagine from its fuller stage direction that in F Edmund demands a much larger share of our attention before Albany enters. Edmund here has reached the summit of his pyramid; by implication, he alone has won the battle. The opening lines in Q and F are identical, however, the staging in both texts require several officers (2940), a Captaine (2969), and the two royal captives, and in each text Edmund refers to Albany and Goneril as greater. Edmund has no more reached the summit in one text than in the other. Knowles (1999, pp. 274): Neither is there any hint that he has done so single-handedly (even his soldiers, we are soon reminded, are levied in Albany’s name).…Whether or not Drums and Colours formed part of the Q entrance (in performance it might well have), in all essential details the entrances in the two texts are the same.
Rosenberg (1972, pp. 298–9) recounts how variously critics and actors have imagined Lear upon his entrance: helpless, enfeebled, childish, sane, dignified, proud, serene, genial, joyful, even jubilant. In both Q and F Lear and Cordelia are specified to be prisoners, possibly implying chains or fetters; see Dessen & Thompson (1999, prisoners).

2940 good guard]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Keep, or let there be, is elliptically understood before good.

2941–2 their…That]
Abbott (§218): Genitives…may stand as the antecedent of a relative. Cf. Franz §321, and 2993–4, 3148.

2941 greater pleasures]
Delius (ed. 1854): Greater than Edmund’s own subordinate decision: the higher pleasure of those who have authority to pass judgment on the prisoners, i.e. Goneril, Regan, and Albany (Ger.). Hunter (ed. 1972): More explicit decisions. Hudson (ed. 1871) and most eds.: The pleasure of greater persons. Foakes (ed. 1997): In public, and in front of Albany’s soldiers…Edmund defers to…[those] who will pronounce sentence on (censure) the prisoners. His private intentions emerge at [2969].

2941 best]
Most eds. prefer F’s first, though Deighton (ed. 1891) finds it redundant and Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 421) suspects that Q is correct and that F anticipates first in 2943.

2942 That]
On that for who see n. 1835. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The antecedent is their (i.e., of them).

2942 censure]
Steevens (ed. 1793): Pass sentence or judgement on (OED, v. 4); cf. 1972. Verity (ed. 1897) compares Leir 505–6: sue not to reuerse Our censure; see .

2943 not the first]
Tilley F295 and Dent (1981) compare the proverb I am not the First and shall not be the last.

2943–6 first…frowne]
On the rhymes see n. 194–201. Houghton (ed. 1957): Gives a kind of formality to Cordelia’s words, as if she dared not let herself go.

2944 worst]
Malone (ed. 1790): The worst that fortune can inflict.

2945–50 thee…thou]
Johnson (1975, pp. 154–5): Lear does not address Cordelia as thou until he is sure that she is his daughter and not a spirit; she drops her usual formal you to reveal her deep feelings.

2945–6 for…frowne]
Hudson (ed. 1881) marks the lines as spurious. Raleigh (1907; 1925, p. 170): Shakespeare often [as here] makes his most cherished characters do the menial explanatory work of a chorus. Chambers (1940, pp. 23–4): There is reason,…expressly to show that the poet’s conception is different from that of [his sources, where Cordelia commits suicide].…Shakespeare makes his point still clearer [at 3211–14].

2945 oppressed]
See n. 1384. Joseph (ed. 1966): Deprived of one’s own and burdened with wrongs and griefs.

2945 am I]
F’s inversion, preferred by a few eds., is inferior in symmetry and meter.

2945 cast downe]
OED (Cast v. 76d): Downcast, quoting this l. Hudson (ed. 1879) misunderstands the term to mean reduced in fortunes: It is not rightly in character for Cordelia to be prating thus of the self-sacrifice she is making. Similarly Halio (ed. 1992): I.e. by Fortune; humbled.

2946 outfrowne…frowne]
Schmidt (1875), outfrown: To frown down, to overbear by frowning (OED, v., quoting this l. as its first ex.). Gardner (ed. 1969): Look my fortune in the face. Delius (ed. 1854) cites parallel constructions in Ham. 3.2.14 (1861), AWW 4.3.273 (2374), and R2 5.3.109 (2610). Perrett (1904, p. 275) finds fortune’s frown in Nevile’s free tr. (1563) of Seneca, Oedipus 86–7. He discounts the casual resemblance with Leir 704 (see ), Ile mock fortune; cf. AYL 1.2.34 (200–1).

2947 these…sisters]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): A bitter sarcasm in simplest words, thoroughly characteristic in the woman of quiet expression with intense feeling. Crook (ed. 1907): Those who call themselves. Bevington (ed. 1988): Aren’t we even allowed to speak to Goneril and Regan before they order to prison their own father and sister?

2948–59 No…Moone]
White (1880, p. 118): The tone of his mind has gone; he has passed even the pride of manliness, and…can look upon the remnants of his former self without anger, and even with a gentle pity. Of all the creations of dramatic art this is the most marvelous. Bradley (1904, p. 290) sees rather the pathetic blindness of Lear’s enfeebled mind: Cordelia knows well what mercy her father is likely to receive from her sisters; that is the reason of her weeping. But he does not understand her tears; it never crosses his mind that they have anything more than imprisonment to fear. And what is that to them?…This blindness is most affecting to us, who know in what manner they will be parted; but it is also comforting. Walton (1960, p. 14) disagrees: He is not speaking literally.…Lear has always been conscious of his age, and he can hardly be here taken as actually expecting a further long lease of life. His mind is now raised far above the immediate events by which he is assailed, because of the knowledge he has acquired.…What unites him for ever to Cordelia is their active interest in truth. Harbage (1963, p. 429): Lear appears momentarily as comforter of his daughter, firm in his redemption and indifferent to all things but their love. Munro (1964, p. 242): Lear is not wholly concerned with transmutation to a higher state, rather his eyes are turned the other way so that he can contemplate the scandals and machinations of the court at a safe distance. Barber (1980, p. 199): His vision of prison amounts, almost literally, to a conception of heaven on earth—his heaven, the kind nursery after all, having infantile residues: Lear’s vision of prison [is] a regressive wish demanding that Cordelia join in it. Lear of course does not say that he has a wish to be emprisoned, only that he wishes to avoid seeing Goneril and Regan first; better to accept the inevitable right away. Neither does his vision include nursery by Cordelia; what he describes is mutual love and companionship. Following Maxwell (in Muir, ed. 1952), Anderson (1987, p. 13): The description of the holy old hermit’s dwelling in Spenser’s [F.Q. 6.6.4.9] distinctly and significantly informs the content and imagery of Lear’s lyric speech to Cordelia. Like Pauls (1984, p. 97), Miola (1992, p. 169 n.) compares Cordella’s avowal of love for her future husband in Leir 698–706; see . Linville (1990, pp. 312–14) finds in the speech the absolutely contradictory implications of the emblematic and the psychological. Lear envisages a tableau vivant of Cordelia as an allegorical or emblematic figure of absolute goodness, truth, and, above all, love, and their future life in prison as atemporal, a perpetual reenactment of reciprocal requests for a father’s blessing and a daughter’s forgiveness. This denial of time and death is also a denial that Cordelia is a character existing within a real or natural or biological time frame, and it is soon destroyed by the actual experience of life. Foakes (ed. 1997): Cordelia alone seems to exist for Lear. He insulates himself against reality in a vision that is at once self-centred, absurd, pathetic, and a renunciation of power. As the end approaches, he seems to retreat into himself, no longer conscious of other sufferers, or concerned with justice, or able to feel what wretches feel. At the same time, a number of biblical allusions in his lines, and in a play that is overtly pagan, add a special dimension to what are the last words he speaks to Cordelia while she is alive. (Ibid., pp. 28–9): The ending was designed perhaps to avoid giving offence to James I when he saw the play in 1606, citing Patterson (1989, p. 115): If the play retreats finally into the domestic and familial, as a shelter from sociopolitical awareness, one of Shakespeare’s motives may well have been the need for moving delicately among the enemy, and with ambiguous signals, to baffle the eluded sentinel. For modern musical settings see Gooch & Thatcher (1991, 1:635, 637).

2948 No…no:]
Q’s line makes good meter if the first two words are read naturally with stress on and a pause after each; F ekes out a more regular line. Capell (1783, 1.2:183), questionably, finds Lear here making allusion with contempt and levity to the burden of Sidney’s Certain Sonnets 26 (ed. Ringler, 1962, p. 155). Mack (1965, p. 113): He puts aside Goneril and Regan forever; he does not even want to see them. Joseph (ed. 1966, p. 21) finds this speech an ironic turning point: Cordelia is ready to make a scene, to stay and see These daughters and these sisters.…Albany intends to set them free. But Edmund…is determined that they Shall never see his pardon. Unless he can get them away before they see Goneril and Regan, and with them Albany, Edmund’s whole plan will be ruined. Lear does Edmund’s work for him by persuading Cordelia not to stay.

2949 We two alone]
Some feminist and psychoanalytic critics find here evidence of a suppressed incestuous desire: see, e.g., Donnelly (1955, p. 153), Boose (1982, pp. 325–47) and Stockholder (1987, pp. 118–47). The vision that follows, however, with its many religious overtones, does not include anything that sounds like incest.

2949 birds]
Proverbial; see next n. Dundes (1976, p. 359): Lovebirds, hinting daughter-father incest. Lear’s and Sh.’s metaphor, however, is songbirds, followed soon by Gods spies.

2949 cage]
Craig (ed. 1901) finds a quibble on the meaning prison (OED, sb. 2). Maxwell apud Muir (ed. 1952) compares the carelesse bird in a cage in Spenser, F.Q. 6.6.4.9. Elton (1966, pp. 196 n., 240 n.) gives contemporary exx. of the image; Dent (1981, B387.1) considers it proverbial. Brownlow (1987, p. 27): In Epistle of Comfort (1604; ed. Margaret Waugh, p. 119) Robert Southwell compares the free soul imprisoned to a bird singing in a cage. Doloff (1994, p. 312) finds an emblem of a singing caged bird, exemplifying patience, in Thomas Combe’s Theater of Fine Devices (ca. 1593, emblem 38), and compares Ado 1.3.4.5 (373–4), Cym. 3.3.42–4 (1599–1600). Ellrodt (1975, p. 39 n.): A passage in Montaigne’s Sebond, adduced by Henderson (1940, pp. 53–4), is not parallel: the Philosopher in a wire cage is not experiencing paradise in prison but fear and dizziness (see and cf. n. 2446–59).

2950 aske me blessing]
See n. 1711.

2950 kneele downe]
Muir (ed. 1952) finds the source in Leir; see nn. 2811, 2812. Wilson (ed. 1960): In the old play, a ridiculous stage-trick out of which Sh. makes the lovely game Lear proposes here. Cf. n. 1436.

2952 old tales]
Craig (ed. 1901): Improbable fictions of bygone times. McCann (ed. 1964): Talk over old times. In Tit. 3.2.81–3 [1535–7, F1 only] the grief-stricken Titus invites the maimed Lavinia to her closet to read Sad stories, chanced in the times of old.

2953 guilded]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Gay coloured (OED, v. 5: Fig. To adorn with a fair appearance). Crook (ed. 1907), by extension to men: Richly dressed. Brown (ed. 1976): Attired in gold. Cf. 3029.

2953 butterflies]
Craig (ed. 1901): Gay courtiers. Crook (ed. 1907): Popinjays. OED (sb. 2): Fig. A vain, gaudily attired person (e.g. a courtier who flutters about the court), quoting this l. as its first ex. Muir (ed. 1952), perhaps over-literally: Actual butterflies, the other meaning merely suggesting the court news in the following line; Idem (1952, p. 555): Harsnett (1603, p. 47) refers in one sentence to the new Court cut and an vrchin butterflie boy; see .

2953 heare poore rogues]
F’s heere (poore Rogues), making Talke a noun, is obviously wrong; rogues must mean not Lear and Cordelia (as Schmidt, ed. 1879, believes) but the persons they will talk with, the necessary referent for them in the next l., as Furness (ed. 1880) points out. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Wretched creatures. Muir (ed. 1952): Their fellow-prisoners or jailers. Wilson (ed. 1960): Visitors, who are interested in such things, poor wretches. Gardner (ed. 1969): Also a term of endearment, and this seems to suit the reconciliation now possessing Lear’s mind. Edwards (ed. 1975): Courtiers…thought of by Lear as mere idlers and wastrels, doing nothing more useful than vagabonds (rogues).

2955 in…out]
Wright (ed. 1875): Of office, of favour (OED, In adv. 6c; Out 19b; for both, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Taylor (1925, p. 54) compares Montaigne’s praise of household books recording who came, who went, changing or removing of household officers, taking of new, etc. (tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 1:238); the parallel is not close. Wenzel (1984, p. 3) suspects allusion to a medieval game (in which fingers in a noose of string are suddenly released) and to its moralization in sermons, concerning the deceptions of the world.

2956 take vpon’s]
Schmidt (1875): To pretend to…a knowledge, to profess. Schmidt supports this interpretation by several Shn. exx. which are followed by an infinitive, as is not the case here; cf. OED (v. 18d): To affect, feign, pretend, make believe, to do something. The meaning is possible here if one supplies an understood infinitive, as do Craig (ed. 1901) and many followers: profess to understand; cf. Wilson (ed. 1960): A playful hit at the philosophers he had thought so much of when mad. A less pejorative sense is OED (v. 18a): To charge oneself with, undertake (an office, duty, or responsibility); to make oneself responsible for, again with some action understood: thus undertake inquiry into (Lee, ed. 1908), undertake to explain (Goggin, ed. 1910). Or possibly OED (v. 18b): Presume, make bold, again with an understood verb: cf. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Assume…that we can explain. Similarly Elton (1966, pp. 249–50) suggests that the term has presumptuous or blasphemous overtones when applied to human attempts to plumb divine mysteries, giving many contemporary exx.; cf. OED (v. 18c): To profess, claim to do something; to assume, presume that…(with implication that the claim or assumption is unwarranted). Just possibly it means OED (v. 16): To assume…[an] attribute,…part, or character, or in this case an occupation or profession: see the next n.

2956 mistery of things]
Craig (ed. 1901) and most eds.: Mysterious course of worldly events, comparing, for things, 1622; cf. OED (Mystery sb.1 6): Mysteriousness. Also, mysteries collectively, citing as its first ex. AWW 5.3.103 (2815), Hath not in natures mysterie more science. Many eds. emphasize worldly secrets. Thus Johnson (ed. 1765): The original motives of action and the mysteries of conduct. Rann (ed. 1794)—Public affairs—and Moberly (ed. 1876)—The mainsprings of all politic events—may have in mind the sense recommended by Parrott (1953, p. 431): The practices of the state secret service [OED, 5c: A secret of state]…[shedding] a new light on the phrase Gods spies. Harrison (ed. 1948), more generally: Deep secrets. Noble (1935, pp. 231–2): A knowledge of events to come, citing Dan. 2:29 and Psa. 139:2–3. Others emphasize the other-worldly. Brooke (ed. 1947): The mysterious ways of providence. Harbage (ed. 1958): [Let us] contemplate the wonder of existence as if with divine insight, seek eternal rather than temporal truths; cf. OED (2): A religous truth known only from divine revelation. Following Robertson (1897, p. 66; 1909, p. 107), Hooker (1902, pp. 324, 364) compares Montaigne’s censures on seers (tr. Florio, ed. 1910, 1:230), a rable of men, that are ordinarie interpreters and controulers of Gods secret desseignes, presuming to finde out the causes of every accident, and to prie into the secrets of Gods divine will, the incomprehensible motives of his works. Though Montaigne’s attitude is the opposite of Lear’s, this and similar passages are cited by Elton (1966; see prev. n.), who detects a rebuke of human presumption. The text does say mistery, not mysteries, and just possibly mystery here has its most common Shn. meaning of art, skill, profession (OED, sb.2 2): We shall practice the art of studying things—whether human or divine. Brownlow (1987, p. 27): In Epistle of Comfort (1604; ed. Margaret Waugh, p. 126) Robert Southwell says Prison is a school of divine and hidden mysteries to God’s friends, i.e. recusants. Foakes (ed. 1997) compares 2 Thess. 2:7, the mysterie of iniquitie, citing OED (Mystery, sb. 1, 5e).

2957 Gods]
Q and F agree in the capital, not surprisingly, since Q capitalizes gods everywhere but at 2568 and 2663, and F capitalizes throughout. An apostrophe, lacking in both Q and F, has been added after God by virtually every editor since Rowe, making this the only mention of God in the play. Fripp (1938, p. 664): Shakespeare forgets the Act of Parliament [An Act to Restrain Abuses of Players, 3 Jac. I, ch. 21 (27 May 1606), forbidding use of the name of the deity on stage], and writes out of his heart, God. Perrett (1904, pp. 250–1) argues that this anomaly is erroneous and that the punctuation should be gods’: Throughout the play, which is placed entirely in pagan times,…there are some nineteen passages in which gods or the gods are mentioned.…Five lines later Lear speaks of the gods again…and it is difficult to see why he should become a sudden and momentary convert to monotheism. Wilson (ed. 1960) responds: Pedantry. Parrott (1953, pp. 427–9): One would expect, if the word referred to heathen deities, to find the [before it] here, as in line [2962]. This is a plausible but not a convincing argument. Abbott [§89]…states that Shakespeare often omits the before a noun qualified by another noun.…Considerations of meter, and probably of haste, dictated the terse Gods spies. Thaler (1955, p. 34) rightly objects that Sh. repeatedly has…incongruous juxtapositions of God and the gods, giving exx., but his further argument, that in more than a thousand passages about God and the gods there is not a single instance…of a genitive plural without the article the, is utterly without force, since there is only a single genitive plural gods’ in the whole canon, in Tro. 5.2.140 (3137), If sanctimonie be the gods delight, where the meter requires the article. Houghton (ed. 1957): God in the singular…would seem to be dictated by the atmosphere of the speech, which breathes forgiveness and trust—but those qualities are not at issue in this sentence. Horsman (ed. 1973): In the theatre it is not clear whether this is God’s or gods’, though it is perhaps most commonly heard as God’s. If audiences discern a monotheistic God in a polytheistic world, that fact shows their predispositions, not Sh.’s intent.

2957 Gods spies]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Spies over God Almighty, to watch his motions—an objective genitive. Heath (1765, p. 349) and most others: Spies commissioned and enabled by God himself (or by the gods; see prev. n.)—a subjective genitive. Johnson (ed. 1765): As if we were angels commissioned to survey and report on the lives of men. Kittredge (ed. 1940): As if God had endowed us with the power to understand everything. Parrott (1953, pp. 431–2), recommending the sense political spies: The omniscient God of Christian theology needs no spies.…The heathen deities, on the contrary, at times need human informers. Lloyd (1960, p. 324) identifies the gods’ espies as pagan Daemons…who aid the living in their pursuit of virtue, described by Plutarch (tr. Holland, 1603, p. 1329) as ministers of the gods…Daemons which are their espies and escouts and which monitor and punish humans. Elton (1966, pp. 252–3) also suggests a syncretic or pagan reference to daemons, known also as spirits, geniuses, and angels, citing several references to their roles as divine intelligencers, ministers, or secretaries,…privy to providence and the mystery of things, comparing 2303+15. Edwards (ed. 1975): Lear sees himself and Cordelia, with the knowledge he has so terrifyingly earned in madness and suffering, as in a special relationship with God as compared with worldly men still preoccupied with externals. They will not be spying on men, but they will be like soldiers in enemy country, with secret knowledge entrusted to them by God. Coursen (1976, p. 295) compares the injunction in the Homily on Rogation Week: Let us be found watchers of [our] times and tides.

2957 weare out]
Some such meaning as out-stay (Clarkes, ed. 1868), outlive (Deighton, ed. 1891), or outlast (Harbage, ed. 1958) is intended. Wilson (ed. 1960) cites OED (v. 9): To waste…by use or attrition; perhaps more pertinently, cf. OED (11): Fig. To efface, destroy, exhaust…by lapse of time. Lott (ed. 1974): With perhaps a nuance of the sense weary.

2958 packs and sects]
The terms are roughly synonymous, meaning party combinations and factious confederations (Clarkes, ed. 1868), political rings (Hudson, ed. 1881), parties, sets (Kittredge, ed. 1940). Cf. packings (1635) and sectary (473+6). Onions (1911), pack: Conspiring gang.…Apparently a blending of pack = bundle…[and] pack = plot, conspiracy, intrigue (OED, sb.1 1, sb.2). OED (Sect sb.1 6): A school of opinion in politics, science, or the like, quoting this l. as its first ex. Brooke (ed. 1947): Flocks and flocks of office-holders. The distinguishing thing about all these is that they have no personal existence, but are all mere units in a transient crowd. The lowest ones are grouped in packs, like dogs or wolves; the most intelligent in sects, like philosophers. Skillan (ed. 1967): Men in power contending in their conspiracies and rivalries.

2959 ebbe…Moone]
Clarkes (ed. 1868): Are in place and out of place, as often as the moon changes, every month. Deighton (ed. 1891): Have no more stability than the tides. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The moon is not only the mistress of tides…but also the emblem of change, citing MND 2.1.103 (478) and Rom. 2.2.109 (907).

2961–8 Vpon…come]
In this speech Carter (1905, p. 442) finds references to Samson and the foxes, to the famine in Egypt, and to Pharaoh’s dream of the kine, citing Jud. 15:4, Gen. 41:20–6; cf. n. 2332–3. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): The spirit of the Lord…came upon [Samson] when he loosed the foxes with firebrands to destroy the fields and vineyards. So Lear, if any more wrong by parting them is done himself and Cordelia, speaks of…ravag[ing] the good fortunes of their enemies. The idea that Heaven can scourge wrong even by means of the prosperity of the wicked comforts him, and makes him bid Cordelia wipe her eyes. Muir (ed. 1952) finds additional allusions to Jephtha’s daughter, who was sacrificed, and of the destruction of Sodom by a brand from heaven, Jud. 11:31–9 and Gen. 19:24. Cf. the following nn.

2961 sacrifices]
Verity (ed. 1897): Lear seems to have a premonition of what is coming. So Muir (ed. 1952): There seems…to be an underlying suggestion of human sacrifice, which looks forward to the murder of Cordelia. But a more immediate sacrifice must be meant, at the least. Bradley (1904, pp. 289–90): That serene renunciation of the world…which is at the same time a sacrifice offered to the gods. Chambers (1940, p. 38) compares Wisdom 3:2, 5–6: In the sight of the vnwise thei appeared to dye, and their end was thought grieuous.…They are punished, but in a fewe things, yet in many things shal they be wel rewarded: for God proueth them…. He tryeth them as the golde in the fornace, and receiueth them as a perfect frute offring (Geneva). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Such sacrifices as thou hast made for my sake. Brooke (ed. 1947): Of liberty. A paganized echo of two well-known Scriptural passages: The sacrifice of God is a troubled spirit: a broken and contrite heart, O God, shalt thou not despise (Psalm 51.17), and for with such sacrifices [as doing good] God is well pleased (Hebrews 13.16). Milward (1987, p. 199) adds Rom. 12:1, Eph. 5:2, Psa. 141:2. Wells (ed. 2000): As in the story of Abraham and Isaac (Genesis 22:1–19). Houghton (ed. 1957): Imprisonment.…But Cordelia has already made sacrifice of her freedom in trying to vindicate her father. So Lott (ed. 1974): Referring to Cordelia’s return to Britain, by which she has deliberately put her life in danger. Harbage (ed. 1958): Such sacrificial offerings to love as we are. Gardner (ed. 1969): Their acceptance of adversity in patience. Edwards (ed. 1975): The offering up their lives in prison to the service of the gods.

2961 Cordelia]
On the scansion see n. 47.

2962 Gods…incense]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Show their approval; consecrate as the priest consecrated the victim by sprinkling him with incense. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The gods themselves attend as priests. Wilson (ed. 1960) equates incense with the message of the gospel itself. Gardner (ed. 1969): Incense evokes the idea of ritual. This is a formal blessing…[that is] part of the reaffirmation of order.

2963 haue…thee]
Muir (ed. 1952), following Capell (1783, 1.2:183): Cf. [Wiv. 3.3.43 (1387): Haue I caught thee, my heauenly Iewell?]. Falstaff is quoting from the second song in Sidney’s Astrophel and Stella (ed. Ringler, 1962, p. 203). Brockbank (1976, p. 16) proposes that Lear carry Cordelia off live in his arms, before returning with her dead at 3216.

2964 shall]
Abbott (§315): Must (OED, v. 3b, quoting this l.). Cf. n. 40.

2964 brand from heauen]
Capell (1783, 1.2:184): This implies…that parting them should be a work of no mortal. Deighton (ed. 1891): Nothing less than the will of heaven shall be sufficient. Tovey (ed. 1896): Nothing earthly could avail. Mack (1965, p. 59): In two surviving early plays…the Vice is driven offstage by fire from heaven, citing Bale’s Three Laws (1538) and the anonymous King Darius (1565).

2965 fire…Foxes]
Schmidt (1874): To drive by fire (OED, v.1 8, quoting this l.). Heath (1765, p. 350): An allusion to the practice of forcing foxes out of their holds by fire; cf. Son. 144.14 (Delius, ed. 1854). Eds. have cited many refs. to the practice; the most immediate is Harsnett (1603, p. 97): Fire him out of his hold, as men smoke out a Foxe out of his burrow (Muir, 1951, p. 21); see . Turberville, Arte of Venerie (1576, sig, O5v) describes the method. Upton (1746, p. 218) and Grey (1754, 2:117–18) are the first of many to find an allusion to Samson’s foxes (Jud. 15:4). But Steevens (ed. 1793): The brands employed by Sampson were not brought from heaven. In fact they were used for his revenge on the Philistines. Furness (ed. 1880): I believe no one since Upton’s time has discovered the point of similarity. See n. 2961–8. Brooke (ed. 1947): At Judgment Day the whole world will be subjected to the same treatment. Cordelia and Lear will dwell in their prison secure and united as foxes in their earths, and nothing shall drive them hence but the angel of judgment with his fiery brand. Patterson (1984, pp. 69–70): In a pro-Union tract of 1605, Bishop John Thornborough compared a people disjointed with Sampsons Foxes running divers and contrary waies, with fire-brands of dissention. More extravagantly, Wittreich (1984, p. 79): In Shakespeare’s play, Samson is made to figure the tragic impulses that had earlier devastated the Lear universe and that will continue to threaten the history of the world, as well as the self-consuming nature of evil and the rending to pieces of Great Britain. Lear is not referring to universal or national division, of course, and Samson is not named in this line.

2966 good]
F’s good yeares, making better meter and a kind of sense, is accepted by most eds. Theobald (see textual n.) prints good-jers. Taylor (1983, p. 489): The Q MS might have had the sp. goodier; cf. Wiv. 1.4.122 (509) good-ier: The Q compositor might have regarded goodier as nonsense, and so set good, the only part of the word he could make sense of. Dissatisfied with all interpretations of F’s plural (see below), Taylor goes on: All Shakespeare’s other uses of the word (goodyere), and all other examples cited by OED and editors, are in the singular.…This Folio page was set by Compositor E, who is notorious for adding terminal s to words in his copy. F’s plural is thus doubly suspicious. All other eds. follow F’s plural.
Commentators have imagined good yeares to mean 1) a venereal disease, 2) famine or pestilence, 3) eye-gougers, 4) the devil or other evil force, 5) times of prosperity, and 6) the passage of time:
(1)The pox. Hanmer (ed. 1743–4, 6:Gloss.): The French disease (lues venerea) from the French word Gouje, which signifies a common Camp-Trull.…The first name of the disease was the Goujeres. Hudson (ed. 1871): A disease noted for its effects of eating away certain parts of the body, thus suiting deuoure. Mackay (1887, p. 194): Gaelic guitear, a running. OED (Goodyear): So far as the sense is concerned, this explanation is curiously plausible, as it seems to be applicable without any violence to all the examples of the word (cf. what the pox, etc.). But there is no evidence that the definite meaning of pox was really intended by any of the writers who used the word; and the alleged etymology is utterly inadmissible. Hanmer’s spurious form goujeres or goujeers has, however, found its way into many editions of Shakspere, and was adopted as the standard form in Johnson’s Dict. 1755, and hence in every later Dict. which contains the word. Rubinstein (1989, p. 71 n.): The explicitness of devour almost demands recognition of a wasting disease. She attempts to prove that the term’s vicinity to bawdy lines in Sh. implies such a meaning.
(2)Bad years. Farmer (in Steevens, ed. 1773, 10:2Q4): Florio (Second Fruites, 1591, p. 7) translates With a good-yeare to thee as Il mal’anno che Dio ti dia. Tieck (apud Knight, ed. 1840): Used ironically for the bad year—the year of pestilence, citing Florio. Clarkes (ed. 1868): The English imprecation…perhaps grew out of the bad years of pestilence, scanty harvest, etc. Henley (ed. 1903): The plague—an ironical sense given to an old greeting.
(3)Gougers. So Croft (1810, p. 20), citing the Indian torture of gouging eyes. But Muir (ed. 1952): There is no evidence that Lear had heard of Cornwall’s brutality to Gloucester, though he knew Gloucester had lost his eyes.
(4)Devil. Morwenstow (1852, p. 607): The old Cornish name of the Fiend, or the Devil. Davies (1876, p. 202): The goujeres referred to by King Lear are neither the morbus Gallicus nor years of pestilence, but hellish demons, often represented in mediæval drawings as preying on the flesh of their unhappy victims. OED (loc. cit.): a. Used as a meaningless expletive, chiefly in the interrogative phrase What a (or the) goodyear [from a Dutch idiom, an elliptical use of good year as an exclamation, = as I hope for a good year.]. b. App. from the equivalence of this phrase with What the devil, What the plague, What the pox, etc., the word came to be used in imprecatory phrases as denoting some undefined malefic power or agency. Maxwell (1971, p. 149) cites a historical document in whose Scots version the devil sinter us replaces the goodyeere untye us in the English version. Chambers (ed. 1906): Evil influences. Lee (ed. 1908): The bad powers. Harrison (ed. 1937): Bogey-man. Cordelia, in Lear’s imagination, is once more his little girl and he talks baby language to her. Wilson (ed. 1960): Supernatural powers of evil. Skillan (ed. 1967): Their own evil will destroy them.
(5)Prosperity. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): The grimmest of grim puns,…in its primary sense referring to the idea that the prosperity even of the wicked was a pitfall, as in the Samson story [cf. n. 2961–8], the good yeares were pitfalls that made the corn grow occasioning their destruction. Ridley (ed. 1935): Here there is a very clear reversed allusion to the devouring of the good kine-years by the lean ones in Genesis xli.18–21. Muir (ed. 1952): In Pharaoh’s dream [Gen. 41:22–7—an allusion detected by Carter, 1905, p. 442]…the thin ears that devoured the seven good ears symbolized seven years of famine; and the words devour…and starv’d…suggest that the story of Joseph was, vaguely, at the back of Shakespeare’s mind. Lear may mean that Goneril and Regan will be destroyed not by misfortunes but by their evil prosperity, and till the day of their ruin he and Cordelia will not deign to weep. Taylor (loc. cit.): But there the good ears which symbolized good years were themselves devoured by the lean ears; they did not devour anything. Biblical allusion seems most unlikely. Elton (1964, p. 178): In a sequence such as Lear’s and Cordelia’s, devoted to a contemptus mundi renunciation of false fortune’s frown ([2946]), commentary on the transitoriness of worldly goods is appropriate. The text is therefore James v.2–3, against the worldly evil and prosperous: 2 Your riches are corrupt, and your garments motheaten. 3 Your gold and silver is cankered, and the rust of them shall be a witnesse agaynst you, and shall eate your flesh as it were fire (Geneva version, 1603). Brady (1970, pp. 496–7): There seems, in Lear’s mind at least, to be an almost Hegelian process in time.…The good years (ears [of Pharaoh’s dream]) have been devoured by the evil years, which are to be devoured in turn by the good years to come.…We shall see these daughters and these sisters (or their evil times) dead (from lack of food) before they shall make us weep. Foakes (ed. 1997): As long as Lear can be with Cordelia, the years, as he imagines them, will be good.
(6)Time. Joseph (ed. 1966): I.e. they shall fall prey to time (it will take longer than they have to live). Gardner (ed. 1969): In good time they will die.

2966–8 em…vm]
On F’s change to them…e’m see n. 908. Tovey (ed. 1896): Our enemies. Verity (ed. 1897): Their captors, whom he scorns to name.

2967–8 Ere…come]
Probably the lineations in both Q (hypermetrical verse line ) and F (two short lines) are wrong; most eds. follow Pope (see textual n.) in making come a separate line. Exits in Sh. are often preceded by a full line and an added directive like Come, and Ere…first makes a satisfactory enough verse line.

2967 fleach and fell]
Grey (1754, 2:118): Flesh and skin. Verity (ed. 1897): One of those proverbial phrases due to alliteration (OED, Fell sb.1 2). Craig (ed. 1901), with exx.: Used to express the whole body (OED, Flesh sb. 1c, quoting this l.). Muir (ed. 1952): I.e., altogether. Wilson (ed. 1960): Perh. suggests that they are animals.

2968 starue]
Q’s starue elides easily with first; F’s staru’d is a little harder to pronounce. Either word could be the result of e/d confusion. Edwards (ed. 1975): Perished (not specifically with hunger) (OED, v. 1); Colman (ed. 1982): Dead from cold. Other eds. do not comment, apparently taking the more modern meaning (OED, 4).

2968 Exit.]
Q2’s added SD makes explicit the obvious. Though the Q1 page is crowded, and the compositor was evidently indenting his stick (as the turned-under come shows), room could have been made in Q for the Exit direction, suggesting that it may have been missing from the Q MS. Taylor (1980, p. 33 n.): It might be thought that, since Folio [and Q; see nn. 2846, 2938–9] brings on the semblance of an army, some of it might remain onstage after the prisoners leave, but this possibility is denied by the necessary intimacy of the interview with the Captain, and more specifically by [3052–4],…lines ludicrous if part of Edmund’s army still stood onstage. Halio (ed. 1992): It is not necessary to clear the stage entirely for Edmond and the Captain to talk apart, and the drummer is needed later for the concluding dead march. It is unlikely the drummer would stand idly onstage through the whole scene. See nn. 2982, 3120, 3052–4.

2970 note]
Malone (ed. 1790): A warrant, signed by the Bastard and Goneril, for the execution of Lear and Cordelia, citing 3202–3, 3211, where Edmund refers to my writ, but also to Commission from thy wife [Goneril] and me. Kittredge (ed. 1940), perhaps to explain how Edmund could order the execution of a king: He has special authority as Regan’s commissioned substitute in the campaign, citing 3003–4. Presumably at some time after 2878 Edmund and Goneril, or Regan and Goneril, or all three have agreed on this course of action.

2971 And]
Greg (1940, p. 178): Q1(c)’s One is certainly correct. The copy would have a minuscule; and the error, of course, was a graphic one. (The alteration of the [sig. 4r] catchword [from And to One] is from our point of view irrelevant.)

2971 step]
Crook (ed. 1907): Upward in promotion.

2972 make thy way]
OED (Way sb.1): To make progress in one’s career…by one’s own efforts, quoting this l. as its first ex.

2973 noble fortunes]
Like Hunter (ed. 1972)—become a nobleman—Mahood (1992, p. 175) takes the phrase literally: Nothing less than a peerage. But noble need mean only splendid, high (OED, a. 6–8). Foakes (ed. 1997): Great wealth.

2973 men]
Crook (ed. 1907): Men who are really men.

2974 Are…is]
Page (ed. 1889): Are to be bold, resolute, and merciless, like the times in which we live. Kittredge (ed. 1940): May be merciful in time of peace but must be savage in war, comparing Rom. 5.3.37 (2890), H5 3.1.3–17 (1086–1100). Hunter (ed. 1972): Moral principles change according to the circumstances. Lott (ed. 1974): Edmund’s view of life is Machiavellian. Dent (1981, T343) cites the proverb Times change and we with them.

2975 sword]
Craig (ed. 1901): A sworder, a soldier, comparing 2993 launces.

2975 imployment]
See n. 2970.

2976 beare]
Malone (ed. 1790): Admit of (OED, v.1 13, quoting this l.). Gardner (ed. 1969): Wait [for].

2976 question]
Theobald (ed. 1733): Thy sufficient warrant…will secure thee from being questioned about the business. Most eds, however, think the question is by, not about, the captain, defining it as doubtfulness (Roderick, in Edwards, 1758, p. 234), debate (Malone, ed. 1790), scrupulous inquiry (Hudson, ed. 1879), scruples of conscience (Tovey, ed. 1896), discussion (Gardner, ed. 1969), etc. OED (sb. 1a): Investigaton…inquiry…discussion…doubt. Cf. 520, 946. Fraser (1962, p. 83) compares Per. 4.1.82–3 (1499–1500). Craig (ed. 1901): This either means, it must be carried out promptly or it is too delicate a matter to be spoken of, comparing Leir 1310, when Ragan, bribing the messenger to murder her father, says well I cannot utter it in words; see .

2977 other meanes]
Delius (ed. 1854): There is an implied threat of discharge (Ger.).

2979 About it]
Elliptical for Be about it. OED (About adv. 9): Astir,…in action; (prep. 6): Occupied with. McCann (ed. 1964): Go to it, then!

2979 write happy]
Seymour (1805, 2:134) and most eds.: Subscribe yourself a happy man, for your fortune will be made. Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): To write or style oneself (OED, v. 8b). Craig (ed. 1901): But it may possibly mean, write down terms which will make you happy to receive; these I will grant. Perhaps OED (3a) so understands in quoting this l. for the first ex. of to pen…in fig. context. Only Weis (ed. 1993): Don’t consider yourself fortunate until.

2979 thou hast]
F’s th’hast makes explicit the necessary elision.

2980 instantly]
Verity (ed. 1897): So as to forestall the mercy which Albany intends [cf. 2912–13].

2980 carie]
Schmidt (1874): To manage, to execute (OED, v. 22).

2980 so]
Moberly (ed. 1876): That is, so that it may appear that Cordelia slew herself. Cf. 3213–14. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): As the Cordella of Spenser and the Mirour did. Shakespeare…takes the reproach of suicide from Cordelia and puts it upon Goneril. See , .

2981+1–+2 Cap.…do’t]
Capell (1783, 1.2:184): A speech wholly impertinent, and foolish besides…which all editors since have very rightly agreed in rejecting. But virtually all eds. since Capell have restored the Quarto lines, and many have defended them.
