Deighton (ed. 1891): I am not a mere beast of burden, like a horse; referring to the word carry in a literal sense, comparing Macbeth’s distinction between man and beast, Mac. 1.7.46–7 (523–6). Tovey (ed. 1896): A soldier’s jest on carry. Craig (ed. 1901): Shakespeare may have had here in his mind the messenger or murtherer in [Leir], who…displays a similar eagerness for his work, as a man not a horse, quoting Leir 1210–15; see . Bullough (1973, p. 369 n.): This villain [in Leir] resembles Lightborn in Marlowe’s Edward II, V.4. Kittredge (ed. 1940): A bit of rough humour based on the proverbial contrast between a man and a horse (thought of as a stupid animal and a beast of burden), citing exx. Brooke (ed. 1947): I cannot live like a beast of burden: I must better my condition. Muir (ed. 1952): I’m not a horse. I don’t want to be driven by necessity after the war to become an agricultural labourer. (Ibid., rev. 1957, p. 258): G. K. Hunter suggests that the contrast is between man as a moral being and a horse as amoral. Wilson (ed. 1960): The crude form suggests a crude nature, apt for the deed. Stone (1980, p. 237): An amusing touch of characterisation which was perhaps thought superfluous or out of place. Urkowitz (1980, p. 47): Although the Q text gives us a Captain vividly realized in only a dozen or so words, the line seems to have been cut in order to allow Edmund to be shown, at his most villainous moment, against a neutral rather than against a lively background. Further (p. 104), F’s cut removes a reminder of Albany’s analogous questionable moral choice in 5.1 to fight the invading army. The analogy is not easily recognizable. Muir (1983, pp. 110–11): An audience would never want to sacrifice such a condensed biography and such a revelation of character. The cut is too silly even for those who perpetrated the others: it must have been accidental. Mahood (1992, p. 238), contra Muir: Farm hands do not munch dry oats. She offers (p. 176) an explanation for the cut: If in rehearsal the original actor of the Captain’s part, in an action perhaps not anticipated by the dramatist, unfolded and opened Edmund’s note as soon as it was handed to him, and then, after a silence in which the contents would become apparent to the audience, looked up and said I’ll do’t, my lord, the effect would be of clear-sighted and totally evil moral choice, an effect which Shakespeare could have felt to be weakened by lines which would then seem to offer a mere rationalisation. But with or without these lines, both audience and Captain can guess why Edmund’s un-tender-minded intentions towards them in prison are unspeakable, and the Captain accepts the totally evil moral choice immediately without question. Evans (1961, pp. 326–7): The omission of these surely genuine lines from F1 may perhaps be connected with the switch from Q2 copy-text to Q1 copy-text.…The lines omitted in F1 occur at the top of sig. K4v in Q2, which Cairncross (1955, p. 256) thinks was F1 printer’s copy here. But it is doubtful that either Q1 or Q2 was printer’s copy; see . Foakes (1993, p. 210): Omitted perhaps to avoid any distraction from the ruthless order Edmund gives for their deaths instantly or (p. 145) from the immediate entry of Albany to demand Edmund’s prisoners.

2982 Enter…]
On F’s added Flourish see n. 202. Hogan (1962, p. 80), comparing the parallel F entry at 2938–9: Here, no conquest, drum, colours. Has Albany then done no fighting? It cannot mean this; [2997+1–+5] imply that he has fought. The omissions may mean that Albany has chosen not to celebrate Lear’s defeat as a triumph—but they may only mean that F was determined to have a single-line stage direction.

2982 Duke]
On F’s Albany, Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 108): We should expect that in a prompt-book the two Dukes would each be clearly designated and distinguished from the other. Brooke (ed. 1947): Shakespeare’s more casual way of dealing with such details probably appears in the Quarto version. There is no ambiguity here in Q, of course, since only one duke is now alive.

2982 others]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 421) adds another Captain, citing 3058+1. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 525): It would be natural for Albany’s entourage to include a Captain, and less logical to assume that he enters as an appendage to a herald at 3050. Knowles (1999, p. 275): The others in Q would be some kind of military personnel, whether officers or common soldiers, who will soon arrest Edmund. F’s SD reads Soldiers. Halio (ed. 1992): Oxford [ed. 1986] has the drummer re-enter…accompanied by a trumpeter, although F calls only for a Flourish. Knowles (ibid.): Neither drum nor trumpet is any more called for in F’s direction or spoken lines than in Q’s. There is no need for the drummer before 3293, and several places in the scene (3050, 3184, 3216, 3264, 3293) where he might conveniently enter. See n. 2968. Foakes (ed. 1997): The trumpeter is…required later, citing 3037, 3063–5.

2983 strain]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Character, disposition, possibly…hereditary (OED, sb.1 8, quoting this l.). White (ed. 1862): Lineage (OED, 5). Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): But would Albany here compliment on his lineage the man whom he soon after calls half-blooded fellow? Kittredge (ed. 1940): Albany implies that Edmund has shown himself worthy of being a legitimate son of Gloucester.

2984 Fortune…well]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Fortune gave you a good opportunity of showing your spirit. Greg (1940, p. 178): The insertion in [Q1(c)] of a comma after well is quite necessary.

2985 opposites]
Schmidt (1875): Adversar[ies] (OED, sb. 3).

2986 We]
Brooke (ed. 1947), preferring F’s I: The Quarto, doubtless misled by the next line, has We. Albany does not until much later (line [3270] below) assume the royal We, as Regan does in line [3001]. In line [2987] we…our means all of us in our council and our general safety. But in using We Albany may simply be speaking generally for all the leaders of the war, who are Edmund’s superiors in rank and title—himself, Goneril, and Regan.

2986 require]
See n. 208.

2986 then]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 421): An n/m misreading of F’s them.

2987 find]
Hoeniger (ed. 1968): I.e. find that.

2987 merits]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Deserts (OED, sb. 2, quoting this l.). Cf. 1977. Bransom (1934, p. 198), without evidence: His policy was to offer an amnesty to all British subjects who had joined the invaders, and redress their wrongs.

2988 equally]
Schmidt (1874): In the same manner, at the same time. Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): Equitably (OED, adv. 3: According to one and the same rule or measure, quoting this l.). Tovey (ed. 1896): On a just balance: when we balance what mercy suggests with what safety requires.

2989 Sir]
On this hypermetric vocative see n. 60.

2990 saue]
Greg (1940, p. 178): Q1(c)’s send is certainly correct.

2990 retention]
Delius (ed. 1854): Confinement, custody (OED, 4a: Detention, quoting this l.). A few eds., among them Crook (ed. 1907) and Kittredge (ed. 1940), understand a place of confinement.

2990+1 and…guard]
Q1(c) adds this phrase as a turnunder, there being no room on the page to allow the setting of to some…guard as a separate line, the form it takes in Q2 and most modern eds. The omission of the phrase from both Q1(u) and F has occasioned much comment. To Daniel (facs. 1885, p. xix) the congruence suggests that a copy of Q1 containing…uncorrected…[sheet] K was made use of in preparing the Fo. edition. Doran (1931, p. 101): The phrase…may have been an afterthought by Shakespeare written in the margin, where it was missed by both the playhouse scribe [in preparing the playbook] and the printer of F [who used the playbook as copy]. Greg (1933, p. 259): And by the author revising the playbook—yet another improbability. Idem (1940, p. 178), following Daniel: It is impossible to credit the [Q] corrector with the invention of this half-line, which is necessary to the verse if not to the sense and is accepted by all modern editors; and we are bound therefore to suppose that it stood in the copy (having been accidentally overlooked by the compositor) and came ultimately from Shakespeare’s autograph. It must…have also stood in the playhouse manuscript, though it may, of course, have been obscured. Its absence from F consequently proves…that in this sheet the folio editor had before him the uncorrected state of the quarto. To that sheet the Folio collator did not restore the phrase from the playhouse manuscript (though he corrected saue to send in that same line) very likely because he allowed his attention to wander (p. 141). So also Greg (1942, p. 98). Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 10): The Q compositor must have originally overlooked [these words], and the press reader must have got them from copy.…Here F depends on a copy of Q in which the outer forme of sheet K was in its uncorrected state. Idem (in Wilson, ed. 1960): Unless we assume that someone involved in the transmission of F independently overlooked the same words as the Q1 compositor has originally overlooked, and independently produced the same anomalous lineations—and such coincidence is surely incredible. Walker (1953, p. 39): The Folio text can neither have been printed [by Jaggard] from the same copy of Q1 as Q2 nor from Q2 itself. Halio (ed. 1973): Possibly this line should precede [2990]. McKenzie (1973, p. 128): The omission from Q(u) is the result of indenting the stick to a narrower measure for verse passages. In the uncorrected forme the long line ends exactly 3-ems short of the full [23-em] measure and…justified itself nicely within the 20-ems. With his stick already indented [to 20-ems] for the next line or two, the compositor failed [by oversight] to alter the quads to take in the extra words. This explanation does not account for the similar omission from F. Stone (1980, p. 237), assuming non-Shn. deletion from F: The phrase appears to produce a false relation between guard and [Whose].…The reviser may well have thought it advisable to remove the temptation to understand appointed not as the participial adjective it is evidently intended to be but as a second main verb, parallel to thought and sharing its subject I.…The reviser’s procedures elsewhere do not always leave the meter intact. It might seem, perhaps, a little too markedly coincidental that he should delete the same phrase that Q[(u)] has accidentally omitted. But…the words in question spill over the edge of a very long line in the Q[(c)] version…[and] would have positively invited the pen of an editor who happened to be dissatisfied with them on other grounds. Taylor (1983, pp. 361–2), finding this variant crucial to his theory that F was a Shn. revision, rejects as improbable both Doran’s supposition that both an Okes compositor and a [Folio] scribe were identically misled and Stone’s that the adapter deliberately excised the same three sensible and metrically necessary words that had been accidentally omitted by a [Q] compositor in order to remove an ambiguity more apparent than real. He argues instead that the most economical and plausible explanation…is that the process of rewriting was actually begun on or from a copy of Q1 with the outer forme of sheet K in the uncorrected state. Presumably Sh. did not notice Q’s uncorrected error here (or, less probably, allowed it to stand in his revision).
A growing number of recent commentators accept Doran’s argument that the agreement of Q1(u) and F is most easily traceable to common copy—Sh.’s rough draft—behind both Q and F. Craig (1961, p. 16; 1962, p. 61) asserts the idea generally. Smidt (1964, p. 158), on 2990+1 in particular: I find Greg’s evidence of Quarto copy for this passage quite unacceptable. A common manuscript source seems a simpler and more reasonable solution. The words and appointed guard may have appeared in that manuscript either as a marginal insertion or as part of a deletion, or they may for a number of other reasons have been written in such a way as to make them easily missed. Howard-Hill (1986, pp. 427 ff.; cf. 1985, pp. 171–3) strongly questions’s Greg’s argument for somewhat different reasons, doubting that the agreement of Q1(u) and F here is any grounds, let alone the one strong piece of evidence to involve Q1 [specifically, Q1(u) here] in the preparation of copy for the Folio compositors. Assuming that this page of F was set from marked-up Q2 copy (see ), he explains the omission of this phrase (which was printed in Q2) by adducing evidence that underlining of words in copy could signify either omission or emphatic insistence on inclusion. He hypothesizes that a marginal or interlinear addition of these words to the foul-paper MS behind Q was overlooked by the Q compositor but inserted by the Q corrector; that the same thing (i.e., initial omission, later restoration of the phrase) happened in preparing prompt copy—i.e., the scribe preparing prompt copy from the foul papers overlooked the same marginal or interlinear phrase there, and it was later added marginally, with underlining to make the addition more obvious; and that something similar happened a third time when a collator marking a copy of Q2 to serve as printer’s copy for F struck out these words printed in Q2 because he found them as an underlined addition in the promptbook and misinterpreted them as marked for omission.
Parts of Howard-Hill’s argument suggest an even simpler explanation that does not depend, as his does, on repeated omissions and restorations of the phrase. He notes (p. 433): The similarity of lineation between Q1[u] and F does not prove a direct connection; the respective compositors reproduced similarly lined copy; and he concedes (pp. 431–2 n.) that the only reason for thinking that the phrase was restored to the promptbook was the fact that it improves the metre.…It is not impossible that Shakespeare could have approved its omission and made some other adjustment to the verse in Edmund’s part which was not entered in the promptbook.
On these hints, the simplest explanation of all is that the phrase had never appeared in the promptbook; it had been struck out in rough draft—perhaps, as Howard-Hill suggests, by underlining—probably because it was redundant with send to retention and because it made Whose awkwardly remote from its antecedent King. Working from that same rough MS at different times, the scribe preparing fair copy for the playbook, and subsequently the compositor setting the Q page, both correctly interpreted the marking of this phrase for deletion. Years later the F compositor simply and correctly reproduced what he found in his copy; whether that was a transcript from the playbook, or (less probably) a copy of Q2 corrected according to the playbook, in either case it lacked these words because they had never been part of the playhouse manuscript. Both the scribe initially preparing the playbook and the compositor later seting Q had needed to decide what to do with the surviving phrase to some retention, and had decided from its disposition in the MS (as a fragment, but apparently completing the sense) that it should end verse line 2990 rather than stand as an orphaned part-line. As for survival in F of the resulting hypermetric line 2990, there would have been no practical need to reline the playhouse scribe’s erroneous lineation of it in the playbook. If lines 2989–90 are divided at old, they begin Edmund’s speech with two perfect pentameters (ending old…retention,), as was perhaps intended after and appointed guard was struck out; an actor could have spoken them so without any further adjustment of the verse in Edmund’s part or any written change in the playbook. The underlying regularity of the meter despite mislineation in Q1(u) and F was first suggested by Doran (loc. cit.) with this explanation: The passage may be aligned correctly without [2990+1].…[2988] is left as a half-line, but it is at the end of a speech, where half-lines frequently occur. Moreover, if [2988] is combined with…[2989], as is necessary in the corrected passage in Q1, the result is an Alexandrine. All the later editorial confusion was caused by the Q corrector, who, noticing in Q1(u) a long and hypermetrical line that made no sense (because of its erroneous reading saue), checked his much-revised manuscript copy; apparently misunderstanding its alterations, he decided to restore 2990+1 so as to complete the original verse line, even though the crowded page could accommodate this lengthened line only by the turning under of the added words. The Q1 proof-corrector made the only error of interpretation in the whole process. Q2 correctly replicated Q1’s (erroneous) restoration, making the obvious relineation to form two regular verse lines (as they may have existed in Sh.’s manuscript before and appointed guard was struck out). The original scribe correctly interpreted his manuscript, producing the playbook lines correctly reproduced in F1. Howard-Hill (Letter, 16 May 1993): It would be a lot simpler [than my 1986 explanation] if you could get the phrase out of the [playbook] in the first place.…The simplicity of your solution is great commendation of its correctness, it seems to me.

2990+1 appointed]
Probably not accoutred, equipped (Dyce, ed. 1867, Gloss.; Brown, ed. 1976), but expressly ordered to keep him (Schmidt, 1874), duly appointed (Edwards, ed. 1975). Conceivably appointed could be read not as a participle but as a second main verb, parallel to thought and sharing its subject I (Stone, 1980, p. 237): and so I appointed; but that would make an awkward sentence.

2991 has]
Though most eds. prefer Q’s present verb as implying a continuing danger, F’s had is defended as indicating a danger ended. Thus Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 161): Of course Lear in prison is of the same age and has the same title: but I think Edmund implies that the danger lay in Lear’s being seen by the people and by our imprest Launces.…Since they cannot see him, they will presumably remain true to their employers.

2991 title]
Hunter (ed. 1972): (1) kingship; (2) legal right to the possession of the land.

2991 more]
Greg (1940, p. 178): Q1(c)’s comma is correct, since…whose title more is parenthetical.

2992 pluck]
See n. 2322.

2992 coren bossom]
Greg (1940, p. 178): Q1(c)’s common bossome is certainly correct in intention: the copy probably read comon bossom. But the spelling bossome is a very imperfect correction,…sufficiently misleading…to induce the second quarto to print blossomes. Capell (1783, 1.2:184): The affection of all men generally. Delius (ed. 1854) and Schmidt (1874) cite many Shn. instances of common = common people’s. Bosom here combines the senses of the seat of the emotions (see n. 125), the emotions of love (OED, sb. 6b), and the persons feeling that emotion (OED, 7).

2992 of]
F’s substitution of on is unnecessary. See n. 896.

2993 our…our]
Verity (ed. 1897): It is to be supposed that Albany here manifests some surprise at Edmund’s assumption of equality.

2993 imprest]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Press’d into our service (OED, ppl. a.2: Enlisted, quoting this l. as its first ex.). Cf. 2534.

2993 launces]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Launce-men; cf. 2538 browne-billes. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Both the weapons and…those who bear them. Hunter (ed. 1972) insists on the strongly physical side of the image:…press their points into [our] very eyeballs.

2993 in]
Abbott (§159): Into; see n. 2259. Wilson (ed. 1960): So as to wound. Quinn (ed. 1970): Against us.

2993–4 our eyes Which]
On the construction see n. 2941–2. Delius (ed. 1854): The eyes of us which.

2994 queen]
Bullough (1973, p. 276): In Higgins’s Mirour (1574, fol. 56r) Morgan, son of Gonerell, imprisoned Cordila fearing lest she should recouer ayde.

2997 session]
Schmidt (1875): The sitting of a council, particularly of a court of justice (OED, 2, 4). Lott (ed. 1974): To try Lear and Cordelia for treason.

2997+1–+5 at…place]
Theobald (ed. 1733): These very necessary Lines I have restor’d from the Old 4to. and they were, certainly, first left out by the Indiscretion of the Players, merely for the sake of shortening. But without them, as Edmund’s Speech is made to end, ’tis plain, he does not pretend to advise, but submits the whole Process to Albany. How absurdly then does the other reply, that he holds Edmund but a Subject of the War? Perhaps Albany resents Edmund’s presumption in placing a king and queen under arrest, thus disposing of royal hostages without consulting him, the commander-in-chief, and then in seeming to deny Albany’s request to have them now rather than tomorrow. Doran (1931, p. 76): Obscurity of meaning may explain F’s omission. Urkowitz (1980, p. 107): The excision makes a substantive difference: Authority is the sole issue of Albany’s reply in the Folio, not [his] justice, the question in the Quarto. But Edmund is questioning, not Albany’s justice, but anyone’s disposition to question at such a time. Stone (1980, p. 238): It is not strictly necessary for Edmund to advance his specious arguments for delay. Brown (1988, p. 159): The lines are rejected by modern directors, who are less willing than Shakespeare to spend time on being aware of time, to identify and draw attention to physical suffering, and to recognize the complexity of events. In the full text Edmund transcends his immediate concerns…and may have a premonition of his own danger. Halio (ed. 1992): Edmond’s speech in F…is sufficient to justify his action; in Q, the speech continues beyond the point of impertinence. Albany’s response is appropriate with or without the deleted lines, which are largely reflective and sententious.

2997+1 mee]
Q1(c)’s wee is doubtless correct.

2997+2 best quarrels]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Noblest causes. Foakes (ed. 1997): In war and in law. See n. 2151, and the next n.

2997+3 In the heat]
Craig (ed. 1901): When the blood is hot, excited, before passion has cooled. Cf. 332, 483. Brooke (ed. 1947), perhaps over-ingeniously: Edmund is saying that we are in no mood to judge dispassionately while suffering personal discomfort. He illustrates by a figure from an archery contest, heat meaning bout (as in horse-races). A man who has been accidentally struck by one of the quarrels (cross-bow arrows) is more likely to curse it than to praise its extraordinary length of flight. Of course there is a quibble on the other sense of quarrel. Men do not ordinarily shoot at each other in archery contests. Hunter (ed. 1972): Edmund stalls for time to get Lear and Cordelia killed, pretending that they would not, at the moment, get a fair hearing at their trial. Lott (ed. 1974): Immediate trial is another way in which Lear and Cordelia may win over the public to their side.

2997+3 that]
Abbott (§260): That is generally used after he, all, aught, &c. where a class is denoted. Cf. Franz §339.

2997+3 sharpes]
Most eds. accept Q1(c)’s sharpnes, though Greg (1940, p. 179) is suspicious of it: It is, of course, to quarrels that their refers, and it might be argued that what Shakespeare has in mind is not so much their sharpness, that is their bitterness, as the wounds and losses they inflict. Horsman (ed. 1973): Q’s sharpes makes this even clearer and may well be right. So Stone (1980, p. 213): Sharp edges…wounds. Most eds. prefer the more general sharpness: Painful effects (Harbage, ed. 1958), in the loss of friends, or perhaps in their own wounds (Hudson, ed. 1871).

2997+4 question]
Steevens (ed. 1773): The determination of the question, what shall be done with.

2997+5 fitter place]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Greater privacy. Kelcy (1932, p. 372): Place merely to avoid repeating time. Kittredge (ed. 1940): A fitter place than the camp.

2998–3000 Sir…brother]
Fatally, Albany does not pursue the question of Lear’s and Cordelia’s retention; instead, he upbraids Edmund for presumption and then becomes involved in argument with Regan. Joseph (ed. 1966, p. 34) explains Albany’s mistake: He assumes that Cordelia and Lear are safely guarded by soldiers all levied in his name, who owe no duty to Edmund. Indeed, he has discharged Edmund’s troops; see 3052–4.

2998 by your patience]
Delius (ed. 1854): If you please. Deighton (ed. 1891): If you will pardon my saying so. OED (Patience sb. 3): Sufferance; indulgence; leave, permission; chiefly in by or with your patience, quoting Tmp. 3.3.3 (1518). Kittredge (ed. 1940): A phrase of courteous apology…for plain language. McCann (ed. 1964): I beg your pardon—you do not understand my meaning. Lott (ed. 1974): Said with ironic deference.

2999 subject]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Subordinate to my command. Harrison (ed. 1948): I.e., not one who gives orders.

3000 brother]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Equal in authority. Verity (ed. 1897): Perhaps too with a hint that Edmund has not taken the place of Albany’s brother-in-law Cornwall.

3001 That’s…him]
Schmidt (1874), list: To please, to choose (OED, v.1 2). Deighton (ed. 1891): [That] depends upon the position I choose to give him. Kittredge (ed. 1940): That question…depends upon my will to do him honor. Regan uses the royal we, speaking as a sovereign. McCann (ed. 1964), followed by Lott (ed. 1974), refers That to brother: That is the manner in which we wish to regard him; i.e., as an equal. Most eds. take grace to mean to confer honour or dignity upon (OED, v. 5); only Quinn (ed. 1970): Style.

3002 Me thinkes]
See n. 704.

3002 our pleasure…demanded]
Deighton (ed. 1891): My will…asked. She probably means that Albany should have inquired what her intentions were for Edmund, not that he should have asked her permission to rebuke him.

3003 spoke so farre]
Craig (ed. 1901): Said so much, made such heavy charges, comparing H8 3.1.64–5 (1689–90).

3003 powers]
See n. 1638+1.

3004 commission]
Most eds. understand generally, as Warburton (ed. 1747): Authority (OED, sb.1 2). More particularly, Harrison (ed. 1948): Commission appointing him commander as my deputy (OED, 3b).

3004 place]
Wright (ed. 1875): Rank. Horsman (ed. 1973): As daughter of the King and widow of Cornwall. Page (ed. 1889): Royal office. Lott (ed. 1974): Place…in command.

3004 person]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Me personally.

3005 imediate]
Probably a misreading for F’s immediacie. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 421): The copy may have had imediacie: the compositor may have misread the c as a t…and the third i may have been crowded out of sight. Capell (1783, 1.2:1): Immediateness; Honours in immediate—i.e. present—Possession. Johnson (ed. 1765): Supremacy, lacking quiddam medium between itself and power. Malone (ed. 1790): Close and immediate connexion with me, and direct authority from me. So Wells (ed. 2000), though reading as Q. Delius (ed. 1854): Place immediately next to the throne (Ger.). Clarkes (ed. 1868): Regan wishes to state that Edmund has his position immediately from herself, and not intermediately through any one else; therefore that it is equal in rank and power to that of Albany himself, who is her brother or brother-in-law. OED (sb. 1): Freedom from intermediate or intervening agency; direct relation or connexion, quoting this l. as its first ex.; Sh.’s word is possibly a coinage, since it is not recorded again until 1658. Hudson (ed. 1856): That is, he is her lieutenant, not Albany’s. More accurately, Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): He represented our place and person in the closest possible manner. He is therefore your peer. Deighton (ed. 1891): Oneness with me. Skillan (ed. 1967): A hint of intended marriage.

3005 stand vp]
Schmidt (1875): To rise in order to make a declaration or put in a claim. Tovey (ed. 1896): Hold itself erect, and as an equal, not bow as an inferior.

3007 Not so hot]
Craig (ed. 1901): It is unnecessary you should urge it so excitedly. Crook (ed. 1907): Not so much hot haste, please.

3008 grace]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Accomplishments, or honours. Rann (ed. 1794): Merit. OED (sb. 11e, 13b): Virtue. Verity (ed. 1897): A sarcastic glance at Regan’s words in [3001].

3008 exalt]
Schmidt (1874): Elevate. OED (v. 2b), surely wrongly: Elate with pride, joy, etc., citing this l.

3009 aduancement]
Goneril means that Edmund alone raises himself higher in honors than Regan can raise him by promotion; F’s addition makes the speech mean that Edmund’s own honor cannot be enhanced by any titles that Regan can bestow (see n. 144). There is no practical difference. Doran (1931, p. 47) would hesitate to attribute to a printer the striking F variant.

3010–11 In…best]
Regan retorts that Edmund’s honors could not possibly be higher than those she delegates. Horsman (ed. 1973): Clothed with authority by me, he equals the best.

3011 com-peers]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:14): Equal[s] (OED, v., quoting this l. as its first ex.). Rolfe (ed. 1880): The verb is not found elsewhere in S., and the noun occurs only in Sonn. 86.7. Muir (ed. 1952, p. 250) finds it in Florio’s Montaigne, citing Taylor (1925).

3012 Gon.]
There is no reason to doubt Q’s attribution; F’s reattribution to Alb. may have been done accidentally or in order to avoid leaving Albany silent for twenty lines. Capell (1783, 1.2:184–5): This speech suits Goneril, who might want to know the whole of her sister’s intention; and Albany’s standing by, and enjoying their wrangling, seems better than mixing with it. Goggin (ed. 1910): It seems more natural in Goneril’s mouth, while Albany’s intervention…would not at this point be very effective. Doran (1931, p. 81): The reassignment is insignificant. Kirschbaum (1945, p. 62): The line suits Albany, who is caste-conscious here as in 2998–3000. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 161): Albany interposes in the squabble at lines [3023 and 3025]: I cannot see why he should not be allowed to do so here also. It is not clear why he should. Weis (ed. 1993): [F] produces an odd and somewhat unseemly intervention by the commander-in-chief. The speech is intentionally provocative; as Capell notes, Goneril has the motive (jealousy) to goad Regan; Albany’s main concern is rather to confound Goneril and Edmund—his motive for finally intervening in 3023.

3012 That…you]
Malone (ed. 1790): If he were married to you, you could not say more than this, nor could he enjoy greater power. So most editors, paraphrasing the sense but missing the point. Goneril is mocking her sister’s claim that Regan’s commission and Edmund’s immediacie in fact make him compeer of the best; he is after all not a duke, and thus is not the equal of Goneril and Albany. Were he to husband Regan, she could then make such a claim; is that what Regan intends, Goneril sneers, knowing that she herself has already taken means to prevent it. Were should be emphatic.

3012 most]
Most eds. understand utmost, i.e. that could be said or done. Edwards (ed. 1975): Most clearly shown, and Wells (ed. 2000): Most true.

3012 husband]
OED (v. 5) quotes AWW 5.3.126 (2840) and this l. as its first exx. of the sense to marry. Partridge (1947, p. 132): With especial reference to sexual intercourse.

3013 Iesters…Prophets]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): A form of the proverb, There’s many a true word spoken in jest (Tilley W772). Dent (1981, F526.1) cites another proverb, Fools and children prophesy.

3014 Hola, hola]
OED (Holla int. 1): An exclamation meaning Stop! cease!, quoting AYL 3.2.244 (1438). Only McCann (ed. 1964): Feigned surprise: Well, well! (?OED, 2: A shout to excite attention). Skillan (ed. 1967): A cry of glee; she is toying with the poisoned Regan.

3015 that eye]
Delius (ed. 1854): Regan’s own eye. Or the prophet’s eye.

3015 a squint]
Steevens (ed. 1778): Proverbial: Love being jealous makes a good eye look asquint (Tilley L498; OED, adv. 2a: (to look)…jealously). Eccles (ed. 1792): Giving but an imperfect view of the matter (OED, 4c). Houghton (ed. 1957): Goneril says you must be in love with him. Hoeniger (ed. 1968): Cross-eyed (OED, 4a); Quinn (ed. 1970): Crookedly. Horsman (ed. 1973): With…prejudice (OED, 2b). Weis (ed. 1993): I.e. you are wrong…(because Goneril has already poisoned Regan, and because she and Edmund have pledged their faiths to each other). Sh.’s only use of the word. It is found in Harsnett (1603, p. 96) (Muir, 1952, p. 555).

3017 full flowing]
Schmidt (1874): Freely venting its passion. Muir (ed. 1952): With a flood of angry words. Skillan (ed. 1967): Full-spiritedly.

3017 stomack]
Tovey (ed. 1896): The seat of pride and anger (OED, sb. 6). By extension, those passions (OED, 8b, 8c). Horsman (ed. 1973): Resentment. Colman (ed. 1982): Courage. Rolfe (ed. 1880) notes the quibble on the primary meaning.

3018 patrimonie]
The half-kingdom she inherited from Lear. She here declares her intention to make Edmund duke.

3019 Dispose…thine]
Delius (1876, pp. 138–9) thinks the sense incomplete without these words, which he believes the Q editor omitted because he did not understand them: When Regan yields not only all her possessions, but her own person also to Edmund, it was necessary that the poet should speak clearly at first, and not have afterwards added [these words] to the Folio text. Similarly Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxvi): Perhaps the…[Q] printer may have found this saying as hard as the commentators since. Stone (1980, p. 246): Very possibly an accidental omission. The absence of this troublesome line from Q is, however, no more puzzling than its inclusion in F, where it seems simply to repeat information from the lines before and after it. It looks like several other additions of a line or more in F to clarify or amplify existing Q text; see .

3019 Dispose]
The word must mean order, control, direct (OED, v. 2; so Schmidt, 1874) rather than deal out, distribute (OED 3).

3019 the walls is thine]
For a singular verb with plural subject see n. 1697. Literal-minded critics have had great trouble with the phrase. Theobald (in Nichols, 1817, 2:384): The walls of what? Of her soldiers, her prisoners, and her patrimony? Besides, Regan is here in an open camp; had she been in an house, and given the Bastard the keys of the fore and back gate, she might with some propriety have told him, the walls were his. Wright (ed. 1875): The words refer to Regan’s castle mentioned below in [3202]. Tovey (ed. 1896): The point…is not merely that the castle is hers, and she gives it to Edmund…but that he is in possession as well as right, and may keep the prisoners and hold the fort in defiance of Albany. Taylor (1983, p. 377): As no walls appear in this part of the play, or in its treatment of the battle, the allusion to them here is surprising. The expression is of course figurative. Warburton (ed. 1747): A metaphorical phrase taken from the camp, and signifying, to surrender at discretion—meaning here, presumably, that she surrenders to Edmund, at her own discretion, the responsibility for her possessions and herself, as her new lord and master. Delius (ed. 1854): Regan surrenders herself to him as a beleaguered city surrends its walls to the besieger (Ger.). Schmidt (ed. 1879): A very common metaphor in Sh.; cf. Luc. 464, Cym. 2.1.63 (899). Page (ed. 1889), more domestically: Meaning herself; as an unoccupied dwelling ready to receive its lord and master [3021]. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxvi), less kindly: Regan’s immaculate fortress [is] surrendered at discretion. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The metaphor by which a woman or a woman’s heart is identified with a castle or walled town defending itself against besiegers was common in the Middle Ages and had become conventional long before Shakespeare’s time, citing several exx. Harrison (ed. 1948): You have won the outer defenses. Gardner (ed. 1969) compares H5 5.2.322–3 (3312–13), gyrdled with Maiden Walls, that Warre hath [neuer] entred. Stone (1980, p. 246) would emend to wall as in the common expressions to give or take the wall, as the cleaner and safer side of a pavement.…Regan…cedes him the position of superiority which till now has been hers. There have been many other attempts at emendation: see textual n. and .

3020–1 Witnes…maister]
The Sokols (2000, p. 363): This declaration seems to be one half of a valid spousal, although her words in the present tense still need to be matched by Edmund’s words or gestures of present consent. Before this happens, the marriage is objected to by Albany.

3022 inioy]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Have him for your husband. Schmidt (1874): Possess with pleasure. See Williams (1994). Verity (ed. 1897): A dreadful piece of sarcasm in view of what she has done.

3022 then]
F omits, apparently to make more regular meter, without great success. Q reads easily if you to in- are elided without accent; F must be read as a line with a weak ending.

3023 let alone]
The only possible meaning of let as a substantive is something that hinders, an impediment (OED, sb.1 1). Thus Ritson (1783, p. 173): The power…to prevent the match. Malone (ed. 1790): To obstruct their union lies not in your good pleasure: your veto will avail nothing. A positive sense of let, implying permission, is asserted by some eds. but is recorded only in the sense a letting for hire or rent (OED, sb.2), not certainly attested before the 19th c. Delius (ed. 1854): Your is emphatic: not she, but he, will prevent Regan’s marriage. Edmund’s response shows that he so understands the line. Capell (ed. 1768), followed by many eds. (see textual n.), hyphenates to make the compound noun let-alone, by analogy with the verb phrase (OED, v.1 18), a command not to do something (Kittredge, ed. 1940). Hoeniger (ed. 1968): The (power of saying) don’t interfere. Kelcy (1932, p. 373) reverses the meaning: Your letting them alone, and the Clarkes (1879, p. 519) change the agent: The [i.e., our] relinquishment of the match. Brooke (ed. 1947) detects a legalism: Quit-claim.…Waiver of one’s claim, promise to pursue a laissez-faire policy; used of land with a clouded title. Goneril, Albany says, has no property in Edmund, no legal position in regard to him. Unfortunately, no other instance of the substantive in such a sense is recorded, nor any such adjectival use before the 19th c. (OED, 18f).

3023 good will]
Verity (ed. 1897): I.e., Goneril’s. Albany means that the time has come when he is going to assert himself and expose Goneril and Edmund. Kelcy (1932, p. 373): Good will means favorable disposition, not choice or pleasure. If let means hindrance, the phrasing is elliptical: The only obstacle is not the impossibility of gaining your approval.

3024–5 thine]
Bransom (1934, p. 161): The use of the insolent thine to his superior, amounts to an insult. So Albany takes it, for he answers back in kind and henceforth always addresses Edmund by the singular pronoun. Cf. n. 3114.

3025 Halfe blouded]
Delius (ed. 1854) correctly interprets: Who is only half from royal blood, since his mother was of inferior birth (OED, 3, quoting this l. as its first of two exx.), but then adds more questionably, for that reason he may not marry Regan (Ger.). Deighton (ed. 1891): Bastard. Cf. OED (Blood, sb. 9).

3025 fellow]
See n. 577.

3026 Bast.…good]
The obscure sense may have caused F’s alteration to Reg.…thine; neither version of the line has ever been satisfactorily explained. Capell (1783, 1.2:185), preferring F: Edmund’s passions are not rais’d so high, nor he so fix’d in his title that he should want to prove it by arms; ’tis the enflam’d Regan, who is ignorant of her forces’ dismission, that is for pushing him to it, and to an exit for that purpose, which is prevented by Albany. Furness (ed. 1880): It is doubtful whether Stay, in the next line, refers to Regan’s departure, as Hanmer and Capell evidently supposed; it may refer to Regan’s order to the drum to strike. Deighton (ed. 1891): Give the order for the drums to beat and thus show that you wield my authority—a feeble proof, since as general Edmund can already give such an order. Tovey (ed. 1896): To call together Regan’s soldiers under Edmund’s command: then Regan and Edmund are going off to join them; unless Albany’s Stay yet means Wait, before you give that order. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): On Albany’s insult to Edmund, Regan takes Edmund’s side wholly and precipitates the open break and resort of force to which this quarrel has been tending; but Albany stops her, proceeding against all three of them. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Prove. I.e., by combat, if necessary. Greg (1942, pp. 94–5): Regan urges Edmund to use her army to make good his claim to her land…; whereas in Q it is Edmund himself who says: …prove my title good which is nonsense—a drum can prove nothing but its capacity for noise. Edmund could be threatening to use the army of which he is general. So Edelman (1992, p. 154): To strike up the drum…is invariably an order (or offer) to prepare for battle, and in Q, Edmund is daring Albany to decide their differences…by renewing the civil war.…In F, the meaning of the line is the same.…There is no challenge until Albany throws down his glove at 3040. Greg (1949, p. 397), believing Q a reported text: The substitution of Edmund’s nonsense [in Q]…I believe to have occurred on the stage; a robustious Bastard filching boy-Regan’s line. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 88): Proue is an imperative addressed by Regan to Edmund. Harbage (ed. 1958): Fight and win for yourself my rights in the kingdom. Sisson (1956, 2:243): Regan has a title, Edmund none. The Quarto reading suggests editorial incomprehension. Title need not refer to noble rank, but may mean the title to property (OED, sb. 7), as Greg takes it, or to an appellation in virtue of function, office, or attainment, such as Generall (3017) or Lord and maister (3021). Brown (ed. 1976): Prove by combat your right to be my lord—and thus, presumably, to receive from Regan the title of Duke. Urkowitz (1980, p. 109): Her speech is another step in Regan’s ceremonial investment of dignity upon her beloved Edmund. Jackson (1984, p. 210): Restored to Regan, Q’s line, addressed to Edmund, makes the same sense as F’s. So thine may be Shakespeare’s change to avoid ambiguity. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 525), supporting Q against Greg and Jackson: In itself a drum can prove neither that Edmund’s title is good, nor that Regan’s is Edmund’s; but let the drum strike is here probably a challenge to battle, seen as the ultimate test of legitimacy of power.…In Q Regan’s last three speeches are all concerned with her sickness (a pattern F disrupts). And why need Regan prove that her own title is good? While Albany’s Stay does not necessarily imply Edmund’s intent to exit, the order to strike the drum—commonly a signal to march (see the next n.)—certainly reinforces that idea. But it would be astonishing if Edmund and Regan intended to commit their army, instantly and without any discussion, to civil war against Albany’s forces simply because he speaks a fact tauntingly (Halfe blouded fellow); as Capell says, there is no evidence that Edmund’s passions are raised so high, nor Regan’s either. Nor is it clear why, if he is immediately intent on making war against Albany, Edmund should allow himself to be arrested on (or diverted by) a charge of treason against Albany; he does not yet know that his army has been dispersed. Rather, he may merely mean contemptuously to turn on his heel and ignore Albany, marching away with Regan, who will prove good by marriage his title to everything that is hers. In the line before, Albany has taunted him with being base-born; Edmund’s response is that (by marching off, defying any let) he will both show his equality with Albany and prove his noble title—not Generall, a title not in doubt, but Lord and maister of Regan, and in effect the new Duke of Cornwall. It is even possible that Edmund is reverting to the initial cause of this quarrel: the control of the prisoners (2986). By simply marching away and retaining possession Edmund and Regan will prove good his title to them. Bevington (ed. 1980) suggests alternatively, Let there be a public announcement (?), and subsequently specifies (ed. 1992) i.e., to announce our banns (?). While this may be possible, the connection between military drums and marriage might not be clear to an audience; and Regan has already cried her own banns (3020–1), as Albany notes (3032). Halio (ed. 1992) thinks the intent is first to get attention—Regan orders the drum to beat, so that the world will witness her action—and then to [put] the matter to trial by combat if necessary.

3026 strike]
OED (v. 29c): To beat or sound (a drum, etc.), esp.…as a signal to march;…said also of the drum.

3026 title]
Stone (1980, p. 229): Used by Edmund [as in Q], must mean my title to Regan; used by Regan [as in F], my title to soldiers, prisoners, patrimony, powers made over to Edmund.

3027 heare reason]
Wilson (ed. 1960): A delicious understatement. With all the cards in his hand Alb. begins to enjoy himself. Hunter (ed. 1972): Not…talk rather than action, since almost immediately he calls for the trumpet to sound. His speech contains the details of the complex situation, the reasons which will be needed to prove title.

3028 treason]
Surprisingly, there is almost no discussion of what Edmund’s treason is. Perhaps on the strength of Goneril’s letter and its ambiguous phrase our reciprocal vows (2715) Albany is convinced that Edmund has conspired and consented to assassinate him, though Edmund himself says that it will be up to the sisters to arrange that if they wish it (2910–11). Even if such treachery is what Albany has in mind, that charge can make little or no sense to Edmund, who does not know that Albany has intercepted Goneril’s letter, or what that letter says, or even that it exists. Buckley (1972, pp. 87 ff.), noting that there is hardly any crime in the English code so severely limited by statute as capital treason, doubts that Edmund could be convicted under any of its provisions. Only the line Conspirant…prince [3090] could possibly refer to a strictly treasonous act—though firm evidence for either such conspiracy by Edmund or of actual adultery with Goneril (the other possible ground for his conviction) is lacking (in fact her letter mentioned the death of Albany as a necessary preliminary to the desired event). Moreover, since Cornwall had created Edmund earl of Gloucester, Edmund’s fealty would (after Cornwall’s death) have been due to Regan, not to Albany. The escape from this dilemma is no doubt simply to allow that as commander of the united forces of the two realms Albany was entitled to Edmund’s subjection and obedience. Buckley does not suggest that what could be construed (and denied) by Edmund as being criminal disobedience, if not actual treason, is the very act he is now committing: a refusal to turn over to the duke who leads the British forces those nobility taken in battle. Cf. 1H4 1.3, where King Henry warns Hotspur on pain of severe reprisal not to withhold his prisoners. That Albany, despite his earlier reluctance, is in fact supreme commander is evident from 3052–4. Colie (1974, p. 208): Edmund is arrested…on a charge familiar enough in sixteenth-century England, adultery with the Queen.

3028 attaint]
Because it is an easier, less technical term, and repeats a word from the previous line, F’s arrest has been suspected of being a sophistication or compositorial or scribal error. Wright (ed. 1875) explains Q: In convicting thee—presumably making the line mean in convicting thee, I also convict this gilded serpent. Schmidt (ed. 1879) demurs: Sh. does not use the noun attaint in the sense of accusation, and the verb in his plays is equivalent to convict of high treason, not to accuse of it. There can be no reference to a conviction in the present passage (Ger.). Furness (ed. 1880) similarly questions Wright: This interpretation is doubtful; it seems to defer the checking of Goneril until after the result of the combat has proved Edmund’s treason; whereas Albany’s object was to unmask his wife on the spot.…The argument is wearisome that Sh. never could have used the same word twice within the compass of a few lines…unlike any writer that ever lived in the tide of time.…In arresting Edmund, Albany arrests Goneril, not on capital treason, but in her matrimonial plans. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 187): Admittedly, Shakespeare does not use the verb attaint in the sense of accuse: but it can bear that meaning [citing OED, v. 7], and it is possible that Shakespeare does here use the noun in the sense of accusation.…Goneril’s statement You…off [2716–17] amounts to incitement. Hunter (ed. 1972): I also arrest Gonerill who has provided the attaint or accusation against you. Deighton (ed. 1891) considers attaint not in its technical but its more literal sense, that of disgrace, i.e. as being tainted by her connection with you in your foul plots—assuming that plots rather than disobedience are the issue (see prev. n.). So Kittredge (ed. 1940): As a sharer in the treason of which thou art guilty. Verity (ed. 1897) disagrees: Impeachment.…The verb attaint, whence attainted, convicted of treason, is formed from the p. p. of attain, to reach, hence to detect in, convict…[and is] not connected etymologically with taint…a stain (OED, v. 2; ppl. a. 1). Nonetheless, attaint (OED sb. 5, 6, quoting Son. 82.2) meant the same as attainder both in its legal sense of conviction of treason and consequent corruption of the blood line, and in its figurative senses of a dishonouring accusation or stain of dishonour (OED, Attainder sb. 2a, 2b, giving Shn. exx.). Pace Furness, Albany did not need to wait for the conviction of Edmund before arresting Goneril; the dishonorable accusation of treason against Edmund is enough to throw suspicion on Regan, his lover and would-be wife; Goneril’s letter to Edmund has revealed an actual plot against Albany. So Crook (ed. 1907): Tainted or charged with the same crime as thyself; Brooke (ed. 1947): In conjunction with your attainder or accusation of dishonor. Joseph (ed. 1966): (i) convicted in your guilt; (ii) infected by you. If attaint is right, arrest (3027) has two objects: I arrest thee and, in consequence of your impeachment, this serpent as well. The Sokols (2000, p. 374): An accusation of treason or the taint of treason often provokes challenges to a trial by battle in Shakespeare, citing 1H6 2.4.96–8 (1027–9), 2H6 2.3.47–50 (1103–6), R2 1.1 and 1.3, and Per. 2.5.56–64 (1007–15). Munro (ed. 1957), alternatively: Both readings involve an ellipsis: and in thy arrest (or attaint) <I include> This gilded serpent. Though other eds. invoke the verb attaint, only Weis (ed. 1993) considers it a possibility here, thine referring back to treason.

3029 gilded]
The same literal image appears in AYL 4.3.108 (2259). Deighton (ed. 1891): Decked out in her splendour. Muir (ed. 1952): Superficially beautiful. Skillan (ed. 1967): Gilt with rank and position and looks. Lott (ed. 1974): Not pure gold. Halio (ed. 1973) compares 1569.

3029 Serpent]
OED (sb. 3b): A treacherous, deceitful, or malicious person, quoting this l.

3029 sister]
F’s erroneous plural Sisters is typical of Compositor E’s habit of adding -s.

3029–31 for…Lord]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Elaborate irony. As for your claim to Edmund, sister Regan, I bar it, acting in my wife’s interest. It is she that is contracted to marry this lord, and I—as a husband asserting my wife’s rights—forbid your marriage. Critics who argue that Albany is a weak character ignore the humor and assurance of this remarkable statement. He displays great poise amid trying circumstances. Cf. n. 3034.

3029–31 sister]
See n. 1219. On F’s erroneous Sisters see n. 3033.

3030 bare]
A common spelling (OED, Bar v.).

3031 subcontracted]
Johnson (1755): Contracted after a former contract. Eccles (ed. 1792): Goneril’s first contract was her marriage with himself, after which she made a sub-contract with Edmund (Tovey, ed. 1896). Skillan (ed. 1967): I.e., contracted to marry edm. after alb.’s assassination. OED (v. 1), weakly: To be betrothed for the second time, quoting only this l. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Bound by a contract which depends for its validity on the fulfilment or abrogation of a previous contract.…A pre-contract with another party was enough to bar or invalidate a match. Harbage (ed. 1958): Sarcastic play on precontracted, a legal term applied to one facing an impediment to marriage because previously engaged. The Sokols (2000, pp. 263–4): Albany’s notion of a subcontract, a spousal contract for the betrothal to Edmund of the already married Goneril, is of course a deliberate absurdity. Yet, under that absurd premise, Albany properly contradicts the banns of Goneril’s sister with Edmund on grounds of affinity (see impediments). To cap his mock-argument, Albany suggests that his sister-in-law Regan approach him for marriage, which of course would be bigamous as well as incestuous (because of affinity). He then sarcastically offers a pseudo-logical justification for this suggestion, My lady is bespoke.

3032 banes]
A common spelling (OED). Kittredge (ed. 1940): The banes (or banns) were the notice of intended marriage given out in church in order that any one who knew of a legal impediment (such as a contract of intended marriage with another person) might protest.

3033 make…me]
Crook (ed. 1907): Woo me (OED, Love sb. 7g, quoting this l.). Tovey (ed. 1896): I am free, by reason of this subcontract. Hoeniger (ed. 1968), questionably: Make known your love.

3033 loue]
Halio (ed. 1992), on F’s loues: Faulty plurals [are] characteristic of Compositor E, comparing 3029.

3034 bespoke]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Promised; betrothed; engaged to be married (OED, v. 5; ppl. a. 2: Arrange for…; to order <goods>). Joseph (ed. 1966): She is merchandise no longer for sale. Foakes (ed. 1997): Albany’s humour in this scene adds a new dimension to his character, as he sees the absurdity of his own situation. On the participial form see n. 103.

3035, 3037 An enterlude…Let…sound]
Johnson (ed. 1765): This short exclamation [3035] of Gonerill is added in the folio edition, I suppose, only to break the speech of Albany, that the exhibition on the stage might be more distinct and intelligible. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxvi): Two interruptions to a bit of solid declamation. Cunnington (1910, p. 451): The latter [phrase] restores the verse broken by An interlude, thereby suggesting insertion [in F, not omission from Q]. In the quarto Albany’s speech runs on without interruption; it is very unlikely that the interruption and the half line then required to keep the verse should both have been accidentally dropped. Righter (1962, p. 152): When Albany threatens unnecessarily to increase the formality of the verse with his involved irony, Goneril’s contemptuous judgment…recognizes the absurdity and artificiality of his speech. Her remark returns the scene to a more naturalistic plane. Honigmann (1965, p. 127): The added lines give edge to the dialogue—and, if we are to regard them as deliberately cut in Q would save very little time. They cannot be accidental omissions in Q, for…[Q] yields perfect blank verse without F’s two half-lines. Stone (1980, p. 246): Albany’s half-line seems likely to have been introduced to fill the metrical gap occasioned by Goneril’s [added] interruption (An enterlude) and the intrusion of the latter is probably explained by the fact that Albany’s speech in Q changes direction very abruptly.…The Q line is not only perfectly intelligible in its context, but also metrically acceptable. Weis (ed. 1993): Q’s omission of this half-line may be an oversight, as the dialogue requires it to make sense (notwithstanding the verbatim repetition of the line at [3057]). There seems to be no real need for adding Let…sound except to eke out a verse line; it does, however, provide an antecedent for Edmund’s thy trumpet (3047). Since the trumpet evidently does not sound until 3058, Albany’s statement here is apparently conditional rather than imperative. Urkowitz (1980, p. 110), however, sees it as symptomatic of an Albany changed from Q: [He] eagerly presses for a confrontation. But Albany has already arrested Edmund, and is about to challenge him, in either text.

3035 An enterlude]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Spoken…in contempt and derision of Albany’s taunting speech. Hudson (ed. 1871): Sarcastically; as if Albany had got up a play or a scene for the entertainment of the company. Schmidt (1874): A play performed in the intervals of a festivity (OED, sb. 1: Hence…a comedy, a farce). Moberly (ed. 1876): Our play has plot within a plot. Verity (ed. 1897): Here used with something of its radical sense…, since Albany’s intervention interrupts Regan’s love affair. Tovey (ed. 1896): Quite a little comedy! Craig (ed. 1901): The plot thickens. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Goneril’s contempt for her husband’s elaborate irony seems well deserved. McLeod (1983, pp. 185–6) sees a different Goneril in F: She tries to laugh off the allegation of adultery.…By contrast, Gonorill’s silence in the Quarto…eloquently points up her vulnerability.

3036 arm’d]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Edmund still wears the armour that he wore in the battle. Tovey (ed. 1896): Ready, therefore, to fight at once.

3037–42 Let…thee]
Keeton (1930, pp. 176–7; 1967, p. 216): An appeal of treason…[not] as it survived in English law until 1819, and as Shakespeare may himself seen it in operation, but the appeal according to the forms prescribed by the laws of chivalry. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Albany is acting in accordance with the instructions that he has received from Edgar in the letter mentioned in [2884]. Fripp (1938, p. 663 n.): The tournament is the weak spot of the play, and its result is not determined by moral considerations. Edmund might just as well have won, and then—? The strange thing is that Shakespeare, in his dark view of the world, did not make Edmund the winner. Arms (1944) queries why Lear, after his brief poignant appearance, is supplanted onstage by this violent and mechanical intervention, unnecessary to the denouement because Albany already has proof of Edmund’s guilty communication with Goneril and has dismissed Edmund’s soldiers. Perhaps Sh. regarded it as an effective bit of theatrical business, one sanctioned by dramatic convention and by popular approval,…[one of the] natural accoutrements of a romantic story with a medieval background [such as the duels of Mowbray and Bolingbroke (not enacted) in R2 and of Hector and Ajax in Tro.].…Perhaps also he was conscious of the prolonged strain of tragic tension in the play and felt that this device would provide a spectacular diversion before the final breaking of Lear’s mind and heart. Hankins (1945), however: The duel completes the subplot. The fates of Gloucester, Edgar, Edmund, Goneril, and Regan are all…precipitated or revealed by the duel, while the climactic deaths of Lear and Cordelia are reserved for the end of the play. The divinely-judged trial-by-combat also confirms Albany’s authority and the control of divine providence. James (1951, p. 113): A piece of hollow stage trumpery. Main (ed. 1962): This medieval ritual emphasizes the scrupulous justice of Edgar’s cause. Elton (1966, pp. 132–3) cites contemporary statements that a bastarde shall not be admitted to the honour of combate. The Sokols (2000, p. 216): But otherwise…there was no bar to judicial combat between near relatives. McNeir (1966, p. 111): The anachronism of such a trial in prehistoric Britain disturbed Shakespeare no more than it did his audience. It is one more feature contributing to the remote atmosphere of the play. The formal aspects of this climactic trial are fairly prominent—a challenge and a reply, an exchange of pledges, trumpets sounding, a herald reading the charge against Edmund…— but they are not usually emphasized in modern productions. Gardner (ed. 1969): As the frame of social order is restored we move from primeval, instinctive passions and reactions to the old-fashioned, noble, simple resolution of the tournament. Marks (1967–8, p. 166): Only apparently: Then Lear enters bearing Cordelia dead, and order once again is overturned, our expectation frustrated. Epperson (1976, pp. xxvi f.): The challenge is…framed in the ceremonious language of the law.…Edmund’s answer is characteristically contemptuous of custom and rule.…The lawless Edmund is therefore checked by the law, by the ritual forms and customary procedures he held in such contempt. The irony of his death, equal to that of Cornwall’s, Goneril’s, and Regan’s, reminds us of the biblical injunction: They that take the sword shall perish with the sword. Brown (1981, p. 73): The analogy of the brothers’ physical duel here with their duel of wits in Acts 1 and 2 is part of a pattern of symmetrical pairings throughout the play. Edelman (1992, p. 146): Sh. follows with surprising fidelity the tenets of the High Court of Chivalry, an Anglo-French institution established in the reign of Edward III. Brown (ed. 1976): The formal challenge and trumpet calls give the persons onstage time to regroup as onlookers for the trial and give Edmund time to prepare sword and armor.
Verplanck (ed. 1844) attributes the presence of anachronistic ceremonies of chivalry in pre-Christian England to the influence of Geoffrey of Monmouth’s romanticized history. Pyle (1948, p. 453): The introduction (though not the conduct) of the duel governed by rule of knighthood (so little in keeping with the manners and atmosphere of the play) may surely be traced to preoccupation with the chivalric Arcadia, where there are battles [2.10.4; see ] between Plexirtus and Leonatus (the prototypes of Edmund and Edgar) and others (2.22.5, 3.18; ed. Feuillerat 1:292, 1:454). Cairncross (1976, p. 180) finds similarities in Ariosto (OF, canto 5): The combat of two brothers [Ariodante and Lurcanio], one a villain, the other unknown; the third sound of the trumpet; the defeat, confession, and death of the villain; and the revelation of identity. Further, the unknown challenger in Ariosto gives the impression of nobility by his bearing, as Edmund attributes nobility to Edgar. Polynesso, like Goneril’s husband, is Duke of Albany; and Ariodante’s (intended) suicide is reminiscent of Gloucester’s. Mueller (1994, pp. 307–9) draws the same analogy, including the previous false suicide: see n. 2480. Edelman (1992, pp. 151–3) doubts that Sh. got from Ariosto details which are ubiquitous in romantic literature; and the third call of the trumpet was statutory, summoning the defendant to appear to honor his pledge. Mueller also suspects (pp. 304–8) that, having the name of Brian Annesley in mind (see ), Sh. was reminded of one John Anneslie’s trial in Holinshed’s account of the reign of Richard II; but that combat was almost comic, degenerating into a wrestling match, fainting, madness, and death from despair. Carroll (1987, p. 439; 1996, p. 200): As in any doppelgänger tale, one must be vanquished. Leggatt (1992, p. 197): The Bedlamite ballad [From the Hag and the Hungry Goblin; see ] gives a context, putting in its own eerie terms the play’s image of the hero whose wilderness journey is both an excursion into madness and a preparation for a final, mysterious combat:…By a knight of ghosts and shadows | I summon’d am to tourney.

3037 Let…sound]
The F phrase may be borrowed from 3057 to fill out a line of verse, since F’s addition of 3035 (making a verse line with 3034) left 3036 as a part-line. There is no reason to think that the trumpet sounds here, interrupting Albany’s speech, since at 3047 Edmund still anticipates its sounding, and it is ultimately called for at 3057 when the proceedings begin. Here the direction seems to be anticipatory, as Albany initiates events. Halio (ed. 1992): Neither Q nor F…provide[s] an entrance for the trumpeter who sounds the calls at [3063–5], and who must enter with either Albany ([2982]) or the Herald ([3050]). Like Battenhouse (1969, p. 275), Wittreich (1984, pp. 95–6), in accordance with his interpretation of the play, finds the five ensuing trumpet calls a signature of the Apocalypse, and Edgar’s combat an emblem of Armageddon. Naylor (1896, p. 168) lists more ordinary uses for the 51 directions for trumpets in 22 plays: Trumpets divides the honours with Flourish as the mark of Royalty; 13 times it figures as part of the proceedings in Duels.

3038, 3040 proue]
See n. 2537. F’s ma ke (3040) has been explained as elliptical for make proof (Delius, ed. 1854; Wright, ed. 1875) or make it good (Hunter, ed. 1972), as marke with a letter pulled in printing (Brooke, ed. 1947), and as equivalent to show (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 161, citing OED, Make v.1 56b).

3038–40 head…heart]
The conventional pair, head and heart, here refer literally to points of attack in combat; they are alluded to again at 3102–3 and 3104–6 as the objects of attack first by words and then by sword. Tovey (ed. 1896), heart: Stronger than head…implying that he will certainly take his life’s blood. F’s substitution of the less specific person for head breaks both parallelism and meter.

3040 pledge]
Schmidt (1875): A pawn, a gage (OED, sb. 2c). Apparently he throws down his gauntlet. Cf. 2537. Lott (ed. 1974): According to the code of chivalric warfare, contestants in a quarrel, especially if they were nobles, would appoint or permit champions to fight in single combat on their behalf. Albany here says he will fight Edmund…himself if no champion comes forward to fight on his behalf.…The glove is the symbol of a challenge to fight, with the aim of deciding the truth or otherwise of the accusation. The overriding implication is that if the contestant loses, he is guilty. So also Edelman (1992, pp. 146–7).

3041 Ere…bread]
Dent (1981, B627.2): A proverbial oath.

3041 in nothing]
Deighton (ed. 1891): In no respect.

3044 poyson]
Heath (1765, p. 350): For, poison, some editions give us [F’s medicine], which, as it is not likely to be an alteration of the transcriber or printer, though it was natural enough for either of them to substitute, poison, in its place, bids fair for being the true reading. Kirschbaum (1945, p. 63) considers F unusual, Q vulgar. F’s reading doubtless represents an intentional change, and is generally assumed to be an ironic euphemism, somewhat more sinister than Q’s word, perhaps suggesting that Goneril is curing herself of the disease that is her sister. However, in Sh. and elsewhere the word commonly meant drugs used for other than remedial purposes: e.g.…poisons (OED, sb.1 3); cf. Schmidt (1875). McLeod (1983, p. 187): An ironic echo of 2777.

3045 Ther’s…is]
Flatter (1948, p. 17): Edmund is not supposed to have heard [Goneril’s aside]; he, therefore, starts a new line.

3045 exchange]
See n. 2726. Rann (ed. 1794): Pledge in exchange. Craig (ed. 1901): Glove thrown down in exchange; the technical term. Crook (ed. 1907): As a sign that the challenge was accepted. Joseph (ed. 1966), perhaps over-ingeniously: The word can also mean substitute, in which case Edmund could be sneering that he does his own fighting, he is his own substitute, while Albany is expecting a champion.

3045 what]
Abbott (§254): Whoever. Cf. nn. 540, 2056+17. Brown (ed. 1976): Whatever rank.

3045 he is]
F’s hes makes the line impossibly awkward (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 188). Doran (1931, p. 51): There is sufficient room on the right-hand margin for the printer to have used the full form; his habit of contraction here may have betrayed him into the blunder. Werstine (1983, p. 293): Had Compositor E intended the contraction, he would almost certainly have included the apostrophe (of which he was fond).

3046 villain-like he lies]
Harrison (ed. 1948): This is the lie direct,…a direct challenge to mortal combat, comparing AYL 5.4.82–97 (2656–71). Joseph (ed. 1966): He lies like a fellow of no nobility.

3047 trumpet]
Either the instrument or the trumpeter; cf. 3057, 3066.

3048 who not]
Delius (ed. 1854): Elliptical for on whom not. Abbott (§254): On everybody. Deighton (ed. 1891): On any.

3048 maintaine]
Schmidt (1874): To support, to defend, to vindicate, to justify (OED, v. 11).

3050 Herald]
OED (sb. 1b): An officer…employed in the tourney to make proclamations, convey challenges, and marshal the combatants. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 525): The trumpeter might enter as a part of Albany’s entourage…, but he would be a natural attendant for a herald. Wells (ed. 2000) quotes C. W. Scott-Giles, Shakespeare’s Heraldry (1950, p. 120): The heralds wore tabards emblazoned on back and front, and on the elbow-length sleeves, with their Sovereign’s arms. They were thus clearly recognizable.

3051+1 Bast.…Herald.]
Capell (1783, 1.2:185): The spirit of Edmund’s character is kept up…by means of two little speeches…from the quarto’s: in the first, he meets Albany’s forwardness; cf. n. 3064–5. Greg (1946, p. 233), assuming a reported text: Q may represent a performance in which the actor of Edmund was of the robustious sort, who breaks in…and steals the speeches of others. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 102): Q makes the line metrically complete. But the words may nevertheless be an actor’s interpolation. On the other hand, 3049 and 3051 may also make a complete verse line, without 3051+1, which may have been cut as an inessential duplication. Munro (ed. 1957): The speeches may have been purposely omitted in F for simplification, as also the similar [3058+1]; but they serve a dramatic purpose. Though a villain, Edmund is no coward: in the vaunting and challenging which occur, he displays, Goneril standing by, eagerness for the fight: witness his speech to Edgar, [3097–3106], at the end of which he cries Trumpets, speak! an assertive repetition of [3051+1, 3063].…It seems advisable to retain the two speeches. Urkowitz (1980, p. 110): F leaves Albany asserting his control more personally. Though Edmund says less, Albany says no more. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 402): In F the role of Albany is diminished by the omission of substantial passages in [2303–12], and some lines in [2868–9], and the changes here in 5.3 may be designed to confirm the restoration of Albany’s authority. He is in charge in both texts. Edmund is presumably summoning a herald from his own ranks in addition to the one Albany is calling, and so the speech may provide the occasion for Albany’s reply; see next n. (Ibid., p. 145), contradicting Taylor (1980, pp. 32–4): In Q Edmund behaves with confidence as though he expects to win, whereas in F Albany is in control, and Edmund seems trapped and at bay.

3052–4 Trust…discharge]
Albany cannot suspect that Edmund is going to summon troops to aid himself; his remark is probably only in response to Edmund’s calling on any of his men. So Deighton (ed. 1891): It is no use your summoning a herald. Foakes (ed. 1997): How and when the soldiers who entered with Edmund at [2939] melt away from him is not indicated. Possibly they drift away during the quarrel between Goneril and Regan, [3001–35]. Stage movements are usually more definite. Some soldiers have a direction to leave at 2960, and all may do so, since Edmund’s plotting with the Captain (2969 ff.) seems to be a private conference. See n. 2968.

3052 single]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Unaided. Only Brown (ed. 1976): Weak.

3052 vertue]
Steevens (ed. 1793): Valour (OED, sb. 7). Delius (ed. 1854): Strength or ability (OED, 5, 6).

3053 in my name]
Under my authority.

3054 tooke]
On the curtailed form of the participle see n. 103.

3054 discharge]
Eccles (ed. 1792): This must be supposed to have been done immediately after the battle by a secret order from Albany. Foakes (ed. 1997): Compare 2H4 4.2, where Prince John tricks rebels into discharging their army while keeping his own intact. Taylor (1980, p. 34): By making Edmund the victim of a trick…the Folio makes him more sympathetic. But the trick is the same in Q and F.

3055 growes vpon]
Schmidt (1874): To gain on, to get the better, the upper hand of (OED, v. 9).

3057 trumpet]
See n. 3047. Kirschbaum (1945, p. 64) considers F’s Trumper an obsolete form of trumpeter rather than a misprint, but OED (sb.1) does not record it after the 15th c.

3058– out]
OED (adv. 11): So as to be heard, quoting this l.

3058+1 Cap.…trumpet?]
Doran (1931, pp. 78–9) assumes improbably that this is the same captain who in 2969 was commissioned by Edmund to kill Lear and Cordelia and has presumably gone about that business, but who (she thinks) nonetheless appears here to order the sounding of a trumpet and (without provision for his exit) reappears at 3239 to second Lear’s account of Cordelia’s hanging. She intimates that he disappears from F in order to remove this improbability: In the folio…the term Captain is restricted to the man who hangs Cordelia; after he has himself been slain by Lear [cf. 3211–12, 3238] he does not make the mistake of coming back on the stage. His command to Sound trumpet? has been converted [here] into a stage direction in the folio.…The announcement that Edmund is dead [3266] is given to a Messenger. But surely there may be more than one captain in the combined armies of England, and Sh. intended two different characters. Cf. n. 3208–10. Thirlby (MS notes, 1733–47): Perhaps the same player acted the Captain [2969] & the herald. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 188): The absence of this Captain from F may be due to abridgement. Only Sisson (1956, 2:243): I take [Q’s speech] to be a stage-direction, eked out in error with a speaker. Skillan (ed. 1967) alone: It is the her[ald] who gives the orders such as these, changing his text accordingly; cf. n. 3063–5.

–3058 A…sounds]
From 3057–8–, it is apparent that this trumpet is prelude to the herald’s proclamation, as distinct from the three further trumpet calls ordered by the herald (3062) to summon any challengers. See n. 3063–5.

3060 qualitie or degree]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Birth or rank. Edmund may be challenged by a gentleman-officer, not by a common soldier. OED (Quality sb. 3): Rank or position; (4): Nobility, high birth or rank. Cf. 3071. OED (Degree sb. 4): Relative social or official rank.

3060 hoast]
Though preferred by most eds., F’s lists may merely replace an obscure word with a more obvious one; there is enough graphic similarity to suggest, however, that one word may be a misreading of the other. Hoast, in its familiar Shn. meaning of army (OED, Host sb.1 1), would be redundant, but in its meaning of great company, multitude, large number (OED, 2) it makes excellent sense. Lists makes acceptable sense if it means bounds, limits (Chambers, ed. 1906; Kittredge, ed. 1940; OED, sb.3 8), but perhaps it more obviously means rosters (Harrison, ed. 1948; OED, sb.6: A catalogue of the soldiers of an army).

3061 maintaine]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Maintain by combat. OED (v. 14b): Assert or contend.

3061 supposed]
Wright (ed. 1875): In opposition to the true Earl. As far as Albany knows, Gloucester is still alive.

3062 manifold]
OED (a. 1b): Entitled to the name on many grounds, quoting this l.

3063 he…defence]
Deighton (ed. 1891): He is ready boldly to defend himself; a formal conclusion to proclamation of this nature.

3063–5 1…3 Trumpet]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 188): In the proclamation the Herald makes it known that the trumpet is going to be sounded three times [see n. –3058]. He specifically directs the second and third blasts in F: it seems desirable that the first should be similarly directed…[and] he is the most natural person to call for the first. The F compositor may have accidentally omitted the word Sound from the Herald’s speech. Or…deletion of the speech-heading Bast.…may have accidentally included part of the Sound. Cf. n. 3058+1. Sisson (1956, 2:243): The signal for the trumpet’s first sounding is the end of the Herald’s challenge, and possibly a gesture. But he must notify the second and the third sounding with [in F] Again, and Again. There would be an interval between trumpet calls to allow a challenger time to appear; Q sets 3064 and 3065 in the same line but separates them by almost an inch of space, possibly to indicate such an interval. The Oxford eds. (1986; Wells, 2000) of Q, as if to indicate a different staging from F, marks only one trumpet call, after 3064; presumably that after 3065 is too obvious to need a SD, but the third trumpet named by the herald (unless one is supposed to be sounded though unmarked after 3063) would then have to be that before the Herald’s proclamation, at –3058. Such an arrangement (if intended) could not be right; it would be illogical for the Herald to lay down conditions for a challenge after one of them had already been met, and there seems no reason (except the wish to spare the trumpeter the effort of one more blast) to reduce in Q the formulaic three summonses. Long (1971, p. 180): We are witnesses to a legalistic ritual, and the music augments the ceremony with brassy color.…I would guess that the Herald’s trumpeter sounded a parley three times. Edgar’s answering call was probably a tucket. For the music of these standard trumpet calls see .

3064–5 Bast.…Againe]
F gives the speeches to Her. and changes Sound to Againe. Jennens (ed. 1770) thinks the Q assignment is wrong: It was the Herald’s business. Capell (1783, 1.2:185): Edmund anticipates [Albany], and the Herald too, whose office he discharges himself; see n. 3051+1. Sisson (1956, 2:243): Bast. Sound? is again [see n. 3058+1] a stage-direction, Sound, with a prefix.…Certainly for Edmund to give the order for the trumpet would be unthinkable to Shakespeare or his audience, as against all laws of chivalry. Gardner (ed. 1969): With typical spirit Edmund forestalls the herald. Colman (ed. 1982): Edmund’s ill-bred intervention in the Herald’s business has point. If Bast. is an erroneous prefix, the word is hard to explain. It is not a likely misreading of Her. Possibly through eyeskip the compositor confused this call for a trumpet with Edmund’s earlier call for a Herald in 3051+1, the last time that Bast. had appeared in the MS.

3066–7 Trumpet…before him]
See n. 3047. In Q, possibly Edgar’s trumpeter precedes him on stage in order to play a response, even though like the calls of Albany’s trumpeter it is unmarked by SD in the text; otherwise there is no need to bring the trumpeter onstage, unless according to some ritual of combat he is expected to play along with Albany’s trumpeter at 3106. John Selden’s The Duello (1610, p. 43) notes no such custom, only that Vppon the sound of the alarme the battell begins. In F the trumpeter remains off (3066), producing an effect sometimes admired. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 223): The triple sounding by the herald, to be answered, when our suspense is keenest, by Edgar’s trumpet without, is a most carefully calculated dramatic effect, comparing Beethoven’s Fidelio. Siegel (1957, p. 168): It is as the trumpet announcing the last judgement. Sternfeld (1963, p. 214): The final trumpet, answering off-stage, comes as a surprise both to Edmund and the audience. Its mere sound signifies the arrival of justice.…The function…is not musical, it is dramatic. Taylor (1983, p. 411): The Folio leaves Edgar’s dramatic entry uncluttered by supernumeraries, emphasizing instead his self-reliance. Foakes (ed. 1997): F maintains suspense by a delay as an answering trumpet is heard offstage before [Edgar] comes on. The delay, if there is one, can last only a few seconds. It is possible that Q’s a trumpet before him means that a trumpet call precedes his entrance, and that F’s Trumpet answer within is simply a more precise theatrical direction for the same effect more vaguely indicated in the rough draft behind Q.

3067 Edgar]
F’s added armed makes explicit what would be required. Dessen & Thomson (1999): Typically armed means wearing armor rather than carrying a weapon. Harrison (ed. 1948): Edgar is wearing full armor, his face concealed by his closed helmet. Halio (ed. 1973): Hence he is not recognised, comparing 3097–8. Foakes (ed. 1997): His name is lost ([3073]), so he has no coat of arms, or identifying marks.
