Edelman (1992, p. 154) surmises that Edgar would have had to borrow armour or strip it from a body on the field, hence that it would have to be without a covering gown or other colourful insignia…[and] look drab. The audience is never invited to wonder how the fugitive Edgar might have acquired his armor, which need be only a sword and helmet, possibly augmented by breastplate and target. He is usually dressed in bright metal, but in some productions has been in black, a white mask, or even in peasant dress; see Foakes, Rosenberg (1972, p. 304), and Bratton (ed. 1987). Critics often comment on the stage effect and symbolism of his armor; Edgar has come full circle, from young nobleman to outlaw and beggar to knightly champion. To Lings (1966, p. 62) his appearance at the third sound of the trumpet is unmistakeably Messianic.

3068 Aske…appeares]
Blakeway (in Boswell, ed. 1821): This is according to the ceremonials of the trial by combat in cases criminal. The Appellant and his procurator first come to the gate.…The constable and marshall demaund by voyce of Herehault what hee is and why hee comes so arrayed. Selden’s Duello [1610, p. 42]. Hudson (ed. 1879): The same ceremonial is followed in detail in R2 1.3. Hawley (1998, p. 70) quotes from Coke’s 2 Institutes 247 the common-law requirements of the ceremony of duellum.

3069–70 Vpon…you]
Since Albany speaks less than two verse lines, and 3069 is short in both Q and F, F relines to divide the Herald’s opening pentameter, and this in turn results in some trimming of 3073 and 3076 and rewriting of 3075. The F relining would be unnecessary if these lines were divided after purposes, giving Albany a short introductory question and then a full verse line.

3070–1 What…qualitie]
Warburton (ed. 1747): If one who was no knight accused another who was, that other was under no obligation to accept the challenge. On this account it was necessary as Edgar came disguised, to tell the Bastard he was a Knight. Elton (1966, p. 85 n.) quotes such a rule from John Ferne, Blazon of Gentry (1586, p. 322). Cf. 3109–10.

3070 What]
On what for who see n. 540.

3071–2 your…summons]
Abbott (§382): Elliptical: (I ask) Your name etc. Cf. n. 2053. Deighton (ed. 1891): Otherwise we must understand do after why.

3071 qualitie]
See n. 3060.

3073–6 Edg.…cope]
Werstine (privately) finds it striking that everyone indulges Edgar’s shattering of the forms of the duel, without comment until Edmund’s in 3097 ff.

3073 O]
F’s omission makes more regular meter.

3074 tooth.]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 422): F inherits erroneous punctuation [tooth:] from Q. But that is Q2’s punctuation, and may differ from Q1’s in implying lost…: that is, Bare-gnawn etc. So Doran (1931, pp. 110–11)—an appositive phrase—adding, It is not certain that Q2 and F are actually mispunctuated.…If the printer of the folio referred to a copy of Q2 here, he did not desert his manuscript. The alignment of F does not disrupt the meter of the lines that precede and follow as does the alignment of the quartos. Moreover, in the next line the folio provides a good reading for an unintelligible reading of Q1 which has been omitted from Q2; cf. n. 3075. Possibly the agreement of Q2 and F here is coincidental and meaningless; any alert scribe or compositor might see that Q1’s full stop in mid-sentence is wrong and substitute a lighter one.

3074 Bare-gnawne]
Moberly (ed. 1876): Like a tree which has lost its bark by goats or rabbits. Houghton (ed. 1907): I.e., by Edmund’s deceit and lying.

3074 canker-bitte]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Eaten away as by the canker-worm…that preys upon blossoms. Craig (ed. 1901): The canker is the caterpillar (OED, sb. 4: or any insect larva, which destroys the buds and leaves of plants). Kittredge (ed. 1940): The figure is here particularly appropriate because of Edmund’s duplicity, or treacherous undermining of his reputation (Wright & LaMar (ed. 1956).

3075 are I mou’t]
Steevens (ed. 1778): A corruption of—ere I move it. OED (Ere conj.) records the variant sp. are 13th–16th c. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 525), accepting ere, report erroneously that the same modernization was made in BL2, i.e. in 17th-c. MS notes in a copy of Q1 in the British Library; in fact the annotator emends to am (see Greg, 1940, p. 124), making little if any sense. Pace Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 422), Q’s phrase is not likely to be a misreading of am I nobl, requiring the misreading of five letters out of seven. Possibly Edgar refers to his name, meaning before I utter it (OED, Move v. 4); if so, he never does utter it, since to do so could result in his immediate arrest as a proclaimed criminal. Perhaps he means rather before I put it (the challenge) in motion (OED, 2) or bring it (the action at law) forward (OED, 15a), as he does immediately Edmund steps forward. Possibly Q2 omitted the phrase as unintelligible. F’s am I Noble, and its consequent change of Q Where is to as, makes good sense and is preferred by virtually all eds., but cannot have been the original in Q’s MS. Perhaps the ambiguity of the pronoun referent in Q led to the substitution that more nearly answers the Herald’s question without disclosing Edgar’s identity.

3076 cope]
Schmidt (1874): Encounter…as an adversary (OED, v.2 2). F’s verb, lacking with, means the same (OED, 1).

3076 with all]
The original spelling of withal, a word substituted for With prep. in post-position, esp. at the end of a relative clause or…question. F continues trimming Q words in order to reline (see nn. 3069–70, 3073), here to make a verse line with 3077. If Q 3075–6 had been divided after come (as perhaps it should have been) the effect would have been the same.

3077 Which…aduersarie]
Albany knows the answer, but is following the formalities of the challenge.

3078 What’s]
See n. 540.

3078 speakes for]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Answers for when he is challenged.

3079–3136 thou…heere]
Horsman (ed. 1973, p. 225) notes the enmity in thou between social equals. Foakes (ed. 1997): The usage slides readily into the intimacy of brothers.

3081 offend]
Schmidt (1875): Affront (OED, v. 7). More probably, Crook (ed. 1907): Do injustice to (OED, 3: Wrong).

3081 hart]
See n. 75.

3082 arme]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Weapon, sword. Just as probably, the arm wielding it.

3083 it]
Capell (1783, 1.2:185): His sword. More probably, Harbage (ed. 1958): Wielding this sword, against a traitor (Edwards, ed. 1975).

3083–5 Behold…protest]
Q makes perfect sense and meter; in substituting Honours for tongue F garbles the lines, producing two metrically short verses, needless redundancy, and possibly an erroneous period after profession. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxvi): The Folio printer…probably repeated the priuiledge, and the proofreader corrected the first the to my. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 422): In F it looks as if the compositor had blundered, setting up my priuiledge instead of the priuiledge, and then setting up the correct reading in addition. As it stands the F version sounds extremely clumsy, and I do not think it can be right. Munro (ed. 1957) defends the redundancy: It forms part of the rhetoric of a highly rhetorical speech.…He emphasises by iteration. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 538): Since the page was set by Compositor E, it was probably proof-read more carefully than usual, and—though errors do slip through—something so blatant as this shouldn’t have. If the proposed duplication occurred in the manuscript, however, the annotator [or scribe] might well have transferred it to the printer’s copy, since it makes acceptable sense. Compositor E would then have split the line because it would not fit his column.
Interpretations of the lines vary accordingly as it is taken to refer to (1) Edgar’s charge, (2) his sword, (3) the right of bringing the charge, or (4) the act of doing so:
(1)The charge. Warburton (ed. 1747): The charge he is here going to bring against the Bastard, he calls the privilege &c.…The old Rites of Knighthood are here alluded to; whose oath and profession required him to discover all treasons, and whose privilege it was to have his challenge accepted, or else to have his charge taken pro confesso.
(2)His sword. Jennens (ed. 1770): Privilege refers to his sword…as a privilege, granted at…being knighted, for the vindicating betrayed innocence, and punishing the traitor. Capell (1783, 1.2:185): His sword.…He took authority from it to call a traitor a traitor, and bring him to such account for his treasons as he was bound to by his oath, and his profession as knight. Capell does not explain how the sword gives authority—by might, by the soldier’s honor it represents, by a knight’s oath, or what. Moberly (ed. 1876): I hold here my sword, to which I am entitled by honourable birth, as well as by oath and profession of knighthood.
(3)The right to challenge. Johnson (ed. 1765): The privilege gained by taking the oath administered in the regular initiation of a knight professed. Malone (ed. 1790): It is the privilege or right of my profession to draw [my sword] against a traitor.
(4)The act of challenging. Wilson (ed. 1960): The drawing of a sword against an adversary, and the challenging of him to single combat. Possibly Q’s comma after profession is correct, and that is understood after it: It is my right to accuse, and my sworn duty and profession as knight, that lead me to protest…thou art a traitor.
Most eds. assume that priuiledge of refers to all three nouns following. The difficulty of the assumption, however, as Stone (1980, p. 211) recognizes, is that of must change its meaning in mid-phrase: privilege granted to my tongue, but in consequence of my oath and profession. Perhaps that is why Q’s tongue was changed to Honours, making the three nouns parallel. Thus Eccles (ed. 1792): In consequence of the honours he had obtained, of his oath, and of his profession. But of may govern only tongue— see the paraphrase in (4) above—in which case the lines suggest three different motives for the challenge: my prerogative to speak, my sworn duty, and my way of life. Edelman (1992, p. 153): The language is as ceremonial as anything to be found in Shakespeare, and in identifying Edgar with such ritual, Shakespeare makes Edgar a symbol of order and legality.

3083 priuiledge]
Schmidt (1875): A particular right (OED, sb. 4).

3084 of my tongue]
Stone (1980, p. 211): The license or sanction for what I am about to say. Or more generally, my privilege to speak, to make such an accusation. Weis (ed. 1993), less probably: Reputation, or well-bred accent. For a motive for F’s substitution of Honours, see n. 3083–5, and Foakes (ed. 1997): Tongue…seems unrelated to Edgar’s act of drawing his sword. Wells (ed. 2000): Perhaps it means my native tongue; Weis [ed. 1993] suggests report, reputation, or well-bred accent. Capell (1783, 1.2:185): Honours, the arbitrary word of some player who was blind to the place’s meaning, which has it’s obscurity. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 538), questioning F’s plural: All the other nouns in the four following lines are singular, as is Q’s variant here; Compositor E is notoriously apt to add terminal s; and integrity or good name or high rank (singular) seems more appropriate here than honours won, marks of esteem earned (plural). Other eds., however, take the plural to mean my rank and title as a gentleman (Clarkes, ed. 1868), the honours pertaining to his rank (White, ed. 1883), the noble rank I may rightly claim (Tovey, ed. 1896), the state of knighthood (Weis, ed. 1993), etc.

3085 oath]
Most eds. since Warburton (see n. 3083–5) take this to mean his oath of knighthood. Stone (1980, p. 211) alone denies this, since Edgar could not intelligibly be seeking to justify his knightly status. It is just possible that we should infer an allusion to the oath, accompanying a declaration of profession of the justice of his cause, which each of the participants in a trial by combat was required to swear before entering the lists (cf. R2 I.iii).…There is no trace, it must be admitted, of an oath in Edgar’s speech.

3085 profession]
Most eds. understand profession as knight. Hunter (ed. 1972): My religious vows.

3085 protest]
This verb apparently introduces the dependent clause beginning in 3088: I protest…[that] thou art. Schmidt (1875): Declare with solemnity (OED, v. 1).

3086 Maugure]
An otherwise unknown variant of F’s Maugre, or an error for it. Schmidt (1875): In spite of (OED, prep. 1).

3086 youth, place]
Most eds. prefer Q, and probably F’s inversion is accidental. Furness (ed. 1880), however: The immediate recurrence of the similar sounds [in Q] is somewhat harsh: strength, youth, place, eminence. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 162): Those who prefer Q here may defend it by pointing out that strength and youth on the one hand, and place and eminence on the other, form pairs of words, the two members of each pair being similar in sense. Thus, there is a single contrast—strength and youth on the one hand, place and eminence on the other. But why should Shakespeare not have given us parallel contrasts strength—place, youth—eminence? McCann (ed. 1964), place: High command; Brown (ed. 1976): Office of state.

3086 eminence]
McCann (ed. 1964): As newly appointed Earl of Gloucester. Edgar would have heard him so called in 3061.

3087 Despight]
Doran (1931, p. 94): Probably spelled despite in folio manuscript. Q’s spelling, reproduced in Q2 and appearing again at 3201, is doubtless Sh.’s; either it or (rarely) dispight appears 49 times in F and 13 times in the good quartos; despite occurs only twice in F and never in the good quartos. F’s Despise is an obvious error. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 538): F can hardly result from misreading…; even in manuscript, [long] s and t are not easily confused; F’s error presumably results from substitution. Always elsewhere E spelled despight (as in Q). A few of the ts are graphically close to s, however, in Hand D of Thomas Moore, a fairly typical secretary hand; and cf. 1575. If F’s error is a misreading of the copy’s Despite, as seems more likely than that Compositor E substituted a form he never used elsewhere, F’s copy here was manuscript, not either quarto.

3087 victor,]
F’s hyphen is preferable to Q’s erroneous comma. The noun is used attributively to mean victorious (OED, sb. 2a, quoting this l.).

3087 fire new]
Nares (1822): Newly come from the fire; said originally of things manufactured in metal. Afterwards applied to all things new, as we now say…brand-new, the same metaphor (OED, Fire-new, quoting R3 1.3.256 [727] as its first ex.). Cf. LLL 1.1.178 (189), TN 3.2.23 (1402). Delius (ed. 1854): Just forged. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Newly-coined or smelted metal being especially bright. Dent (1981) cites the proverbial New out of the Mint (M985).

3087 fortun’d]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 422): Presumably e has been misread as d. F corrects to Fortune. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Edgar refers to Edmund’s recent elevation to the rank of Earl of Gloucester. Cf. n. 3086. Foakes (ed. 1997): Success in battle, and promotion as leader of an army. Edgar cannot know of Edmund’s questionable fortune in love, but the audience does.

3088 heart]
Schmidt (1874): Courage (OED, sb. 11). Cf. n. 1364 on the play’s use of close synonyms.

3089 False…Gods]
Houghton (ed. 1957): By his perjury in the plot against Edgar and his father. Or by his general amorality.

3090 Conspicuate]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 422): The compositor doubtless misread [F’s Conspirant] as conspicuat. OED (Conspirant): A. adj. Conspiring. B. sb. A conspirator, quoting Harsnett (1603, p. 19, as a noun) and this l. (as an adjective) as its only 17th-c. exx.

3090 illustrious]
Schmidt (1874): Excellent, glorious. OED (a. 3a): Possessing lustre by reason of high birth or rank, noble or lofty action or qualities, quoting LLL 1.1.177 (188) and this l. as its first exx.

3091–2 from…feet]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Traceable to the practice of scanning an adversary from head to foot, which was imitated on the tragic stage until it became ridiculous. Kittredge (ed. 1940): An elaboration of the familiar from head to foot or from top to toe. Wilson (ed. 1960): Bombastic. Shaheen (1987, p. 155) compares 2 Sam. 14:25.

3091 vpward]
Schmidt (1875): Top (OED, sb. 1, quoting only this l.). Cf. the substantives backward (Tmp. 1.2.50 [140]) and inward (Cym. 3.4.6 [1676]).

3092 descent]
Schmidt (1874): Extremest downward (OED, 2c, quoting only this l.). Deighton (ed. 1891): Very lowest part of your body; Kittredge (ed. 1940): Sole. Brooke (ed. 1947) unnecessarily takes descent and dust to be a hendiadys: Dusty depth.

3092 beneath]
OED cites F’s below as its earliest ex. meaning beneath.

3093 toad-spotted]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Your soul spotted with treason as thickly as the body of a toad is with blotches of colour; with the further notion of the poisonousness formerly ascribed to toads. OED (Spotted a. 2b): Fig. Morally stained or blemished.

3093 say thou]
Deighton (ed. 1891): If thou should say.

3093 best spirits]
See n. 989.

3094 As]
Q2’s Is is an unauthoritative guess, F’s are is probably right. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 423): The copy may have had ar. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 525): There are no certain as/is errors elsewhere in the canon, and Q1 are is unanimously emended to Q3 as at Venus 1031.

3094 bent]
Schmidt (1874): Intent (OED, ppl. a. 3). Harbage (ed. 1958): Directed (OED, 2). Cf. 982.

3095 proue vpon]
See n. 2537.

3095 whereto]
Delius (ed. 1854): Refers to prove, not to heart. Deighton (ed. 1891): To heart, to which my words will reach. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Edgar’s accusation comes from the heart and is addressed to the heart and conscience of Edmund.

3097 wisdome]
See n. 3070–1, and cf. 3109–10.

3098–9 since…that]
See n. 981.

3099 being]
Universally considered an error for F’s tongue, probably spelt tong in the MS. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 423): O may be misread as e; and there may have been an extra minim stroke making the n look like in. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 525): Q’s being essentially repeats outside ([3098]), and is aurally awkward in this line; say and breathes strongly suggest that F is right.

3099 some say]
Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 195–6) explains F’s nonsensical parenthesis: The word [say] is certainly a noun here. It looks as if [a scribe] or the F compositor did not know this aphetic form, assumed that the verb say was intended, took some say as = some people say, and inserted brackets. Edmund has heard no one say anything about Edgar’s breeding; Harbage (ed. 1958), however: One might say (?), and Hunter (ed. 1972): Perhaps F’s say only means speech. Pope (ed. 1725): For essay, some shew or probability; similarly Hunter (ed. 1869): Proof. These senses are unattested in OED; but see Assay (sb. 18): Approved quality, proof. Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:59): Assay, specimen (OED, sb.2 9: = Assay, sb. 17). Jennens (ed. 1770): Perhaps…discourse (OED, sb.4 1: What a person says). So Meiklejohn (ed. 1879), by extension: Tone and accent; unattested. Steevens (ed. 1778): A sample, a taste (OED, sb.2 7b). Craig (ed. 1901), by extension: Smack, flavour. Most eds. agree with Capell or Steevens. Cf. n. 381.

3099 breeding]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): A gentleman’s education.

3099 breathes]
Schmidt (1874): To speak, to utter (OED, v. 12).

3100–1 What…spurne]
Malone (ed. 1790) on 3100: A whole line is sometimes omitted at the press. The subsequent line without this is nonsense. As Delius (1876, p. 138) says, the line provides the needed object for the verbs disdaine and spurne. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxvi): Probably the Quarto printer’s careless omission.…There are three eye-blunders in these four lines,—being…hatedly…oreturnd. Stone (1980, p. 69): In F the misprint By [for My; see ] is overlooked and preserved.…[Consequently] the verbs disdain and spurn must be supplied with an object. An extra line comes in aid, and…results in confusion.…What must refer to the coming combat, yet that is not the object of Edmund’s disdain. Honigmann (1982, p. 147): It remains possible that Q accidentally omitted [3100] and changed rule to right. Perhaps several revisions in consecutive lines reduced their legibility; the meaning of these two lines remains obscure as they stand. Eccles (ed. 1792): What was that but the combat? And how can he be said to disdain and spurn that which, without delay, he determines to undertake? But Capell (1783, 1.2:185): Must mean—the delay I might use. Malone (op. cit.): That delay which by the laws of knighthood I might make, I scorn to make. Clarkes (ed. 1868): The diction here is purposely confused in expression; like that of a man enraged at finding himself denounced as a villain, and conscious that he is one.…I disdain to avoid that trial by battle which…I might safely delay. Muir (ed. 1952): Edmund changes the construction in the middle of the sentence. Page (ed. 1889): The construction is rather according to the sense than the exact words of the passage. I disdain and spurn that consideration; viz. that I might delay. Verity (ed. 1897): The objection which I might raise very properly, or the reluctance which I might show. Weis (ed. 1993): Q is intelligible if In…name (3097) is understood as the object of disdaine and spurne. Brooke (ed. 1947): For the sake of the record, Edmund makes the most of the fact that knights accepted challenges only from opponents of proper rank; but his action, like all his actions, is practical and self-interested. Deprived of military power, arrested as a traitor, and challenged by Albany, he has little to lose in encountering the unknown and a good deal perhaps to gain, since victory in trial by combat cleared the victor of charges against him. Colie (1974, p. 208): Edmund is attracted…to the idea of himself as a real aristocrat. Edwards (ed. 1975): Having been dubbed Earl of Gloucester, Edmund has become very attentive to the niceties of rank and blood.

3100–1 safe and nicely]
Verity (ed. 1897), safe: Cautiously (cf. in wisdom). Craig (ed. 1901): Safely, without any fear, of clear legal justification. Houghton (ed. 1957): Safely (from the point of view of honour). For nicely = punctiliously see n. 1179. Hunter (ed. 1869): According to strict ceremony. Abbott (§1): Adjectives are freely used as Adverbs. Adams (in Irving & Marshall, ed. 1889): Probably one of those cases in which the adverbial ending does double duty, comparing JC 2.1.224 (862), looke fresh and merrily. Franz §244a gives other exx. of such pairs.

3100–1 delay]
Schmidt (1874): Refuse; not attested. All other eds. understand the usual meaning postpone. Deighton (ed. 1891): Sc. till it had been proved that you were my equal in rank.

3101 By right]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 423): The copy may have had rule, and the compositor may have misread it as rite and set up right. If so, we have i/u and t/l misreadings. Alternatively, rule may have been corrupted to right by the…compositor owing to the influence of the next word but one—Knight-hood. Stone (1980, p. 69): As a consequence of F’s added line 3100, By right, being unidiomatic, must be modified, as it was to F’s By rule. But the phrase is perfectly idiomatic: see OED (Right sb. 7c; cf. 8c). Weis (ed. 1993): Right rather than rule would seem the apter phrase for Edmund to use, because he proudly arrogates to himself the code of honour of a nobleman.

3102 Heere…head]
Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 538), believing that Q2 served as copy for F1: Q2 omits the whole line, which therefore must have been reintroduced by the [F1] annotator. More probably, a transcript for the F printers made from the playbook would have included the line, and its absence from Q2 is evidence against that text’s use as F1 copy; see .

3102 those]
Either Q (those treasons you have named) or F’s these (these that I am now accused of) makes good sense, and either might be a misreading for the other.

3102 treasons]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Accusations of treason.

3102 to thy head]
Craig (ed. 1901): In thy teeth. But see also n. 3038–40.

3103 With]
Wells (ed. 2000): Perhaps at the same time as rather than by means of.

3103 hell hated]
Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:32): Hated equal with Hell (OED, Hell sb. 12, quoting this l.). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Since treason is the most odious of all crimes. Only McCann (ed. 1964): Hated even in hell.

3103 ly]
I.e., your false accusations.

3103 oreturnd]
If, as Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 423) suggests, Q’s word represents a d/e misreading for oreturne, Q means the same as F’s ore-whelme: Destroy, overwhelm, bring to ruin (OED, Overturn v. 3). Of Sh.’s four other uses of Q’s word, three refer to military action and the fourth (2H4 5.2.19 [2903]) to misrule; F’s substitution may make a somewhat easier sense with heart. Stone’s (1980, p. 189) proposed emendation return’d makes good sense (OED, v. 17b: To retort [a charge, argument, etc.] to or upon a person; cf. 21), and his explanation—that a final e on lye was misread as an initial o—is possible, though his added word to is extrametrical, and its omission by ellipsis, though conceivable (see Abbott §§198, 201), results in an awkward construction. Taylor (1983, p. 460): Oreturn produces the same construction as in F, with minimal emendation. Wells & Taylor (1987, pp. 525–6): Both Stone and Blayney assume that With is here instrumental (by means of), a sense they find unsatisfactory; but it could as easily be associative (at the same time). F, and the simplest emendation of Q, both have Edmund declare that he intends to overwhelm or overturn both the lie and Edgar himself.

3104 Which]
Capell (1783, 1.2:185): The proper word had been—But. Eccles (ed. 1792): Which heart. Clarkes (ed. 1868): Here to is elliptically understood before which; signifying to which heart. Furness (ed. 1880): As to which, citing Abbott §272; cf. Franz §347. Most eds. follow Moberly (ed. 1876) in referring Which to treasons and ly. Deighton (ed. 1891): Since these charges of treason and falsehood are scarcely felt by you, my sword shall quickly make a passage for them to your heart. Verity (ed. 1897): When the speaker began he intended to use some word like drive, thrust. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Them (in [3105]) is superfluous in grammar: it repeats the object of the verb (which). Wilson (ed. 1960): Left without predicate by change of construction. Hunter (ed. 1972): Which probably refers back both to treasons and to heart (into which).

3104 for]
Because. See n. 246.

3104 glance by]
Schmidt (1874): Dart aside and miss the aim (OED, v.1 1b). Moberly (ed. 1876) elaborates: My reply has little weight as yet against your assertion. Deighton (ed. 1891): Are scarcely felt by you. Crook (ed. 1907): Being merely words.

3105 instant way]
Crook (ed. 1907): Immediate entrance. Harbage (ed. 1958): Routed into you with my sword-thrust. Gardner (ed. 1969): I.e. to Edgar’s heart.

3106 Where]
Capell (1783, 1.2:186): To where.

3106 rest for euer]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Be heard of no more. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Remain [with you] forever, for the combat will prove that thou art the traitor.

3106 trumpets]
Stone (1980, p. 199) thinks the plural erroneous: Only one trumpeter has so far appeared. But it is clear in both Q and F that both Albany and Edgar have trumpeters: see 3037, 3047, 3057, 3058+1, –3058, 3066, 3067.

3107 Alb.…him,]
Q and F give the speech to Albany. Johnson (ed. 1765): He desired that Edmund’s life might be spar’d at present, only to obtain his confession, and to convict him openly by his own letter. Rann (ed. 1794): To reserve him for a fate better suited to his crimes. Budd (ed. 1935): I.e., a less honourable death. Lee (ed. 1908), alternatively: Illustrates Albany’s humanity. Gardner (ed. 1969): Albany is in charge, and Edmund’s survival is still a dramatic necessity. Horsman (ed. 1973): Does Albany wish Edmund…merely to be saved from falling, and escorted to a bench whence he may take his important part in the dialogue which follows? Muir (ed. 1952): In some productions…spoken of Edgar, when he is temporarily disarmed. Halio (ed. 1992): Edgar [may be] momentarily in danger, as Gonerill with murder in her eyes accuses him of practice. Other eds. reassign the speech. Theobald (in Nichols, 1817, 2:384): Certainly a corruption either from amb. or lad., to signify both the women, or ladies; Idem (ed. 1733), assigning to Goneril: ’Tis absurd that Albany, who knew Edmund’s Treasons, and his own Wife’s Passion for him, should be so sollicitous to have his Life sav’d. Edelman (1992, p. 156) agrees: If Edmund has fallen, his guilt…has already been proved…in trial by battle; moreover, no one may interfere with a battle of chivalry, though Goneril’s passion for Edmund might lead her to do so. Halliwell (ed. 1865): The exclamations…are too passionate to be spoken by any but Goneril. Van Dam (1935, p. 100): All.…It does not mean all persons on the stage but, especially, the bystanders. The emendation is adopted by the Oxford (1986; Wells, 2000) eds. (see textual n.), citing Van Dam and Blayney. Foakes (ed. 1997): Unnecessary.
On F’s Alarums see n. 2918, 2920. Brown (ed. 1996): Suggests a prolonged and varied fight; the word is used usually of battles rather than a single combat. But it may refer only to the trumpet flourish(es) beginning the duel. See n. 3066–7.
On F’s Fights, Foakes (ed. 1997): The s perhaps [is] a compositor’s error.…This bare direction does not mean that the fight is perfunctory; there is a stage tradition of making it a strenuous and extended encounter between two strong adversaries, Edgar winning with difficulty. See Rosenberg (1972, p. 305), Bratton (ed. 1987).

3108 meere]
F’s omission makes more regular verse. See n. 2201.

3108 practise]
See nn. 502, 1010.

3109 armes]
Blayney (apud Wells & Taylor, 1987, p. 539), rejecting F’s Warre: What governs trial by combat is the law of arms, and even if a law of Warre were supposed to exist it would be irrelevant.

3109 art]
Q’s present verb states a generality independent of time; F’s wast applies that rule to the incident that just transpired. Van Dam (1935, p. 101): Q gives a very possible misprint for wert.

3109 answere]
Doran (1931, p. 31): Q2’s offer may be a printer’s substitution; yet it is a strange one: The letters of the one word…[could] resemble those of the other; an abbreviation mark might be used for the n. But the w is a letter which could not well be overlooked. See n. 1910.

3110 opposite]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): Adversary (OED, sb. 3).

3110–11 Thou…beguild]
Halliwell (ed. 1865): [She] tells him that he is not to consider this a legal victory—i.e., his treasons have not been proven.

3111 cousned and beguild]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Synonyms (OED, Cozen v. 1); cf. 1186–7, 2505.

3112–13 Stop…stople it,]
F’s substitution of Shut…stop it: seems to be stylistic, and its addition of hold Sir seems to be metrical (Muir, ed. 1952). Ridley (ed. 1935, p. x): Q is a perfectly good line, but the Folio, presumably to avoid the somewhat colloquial though vigorous word stople, reads the awkward Or…Sir. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 43) prefers F’s Shut, since Stop here spoils the effect of stop or stople in the next line. Van Dam (1935, p. 101): Rather, its anticipation of stople leaves…little doubt that Stop is genuine. Horsman (ed. 1973): The change of person addressed is clearly indicated by F punctuation; but the typically lighter Q punctuation could mean the same.

3113 paper]
Craig (ed. 1901): The love-letter; see 2715, 2884.

3113 stople]
Brooke (ed. 1947): Close as with a bung or cork (OED, Stopple v.; sb.1 1). Sh. does not use the verb elsewhere, and it is unrecorded by OED before 1795; a noun meaning plug or action of plugging was common, however. In all the exx. cited by Tilley M1264 and Dent (1981), the phrase is stop [one’s] mouth. Van Dam (1935, p. 101): F [after Q2] has changed the unusual word, and…the Q[1] word is undoubtedly genuine. Muir (ed. 1952): F’s stop may be a sophistication. Hunter (ed. 1972): It is not clear if the stopping is to be physical or mental. Stone (1980, p. 222): F’s reading was derived from Q2 copy; but both eds. may have substituted the known for the nonce word. Their common substitution of a colon after it, where some kind of stronger stop is obviously required, may also be coincidental; it was often used by Jaggard’s compositors, as here, for change of address.

3113 hold Sir]
Brooke (ed. 1947): It looks as if the Folio editor added the words Hold, sir to complete his metrically deficient line, under the erroneous impression that line [3114] is addressed to Edmund. Houghton (ed. 1957): Without them, Albany speaks to Goneril right down to her frantic exit. Eds. disagree as to the words’ meaning and intent. Capell (1783, 1.2:186): Albany sees Edgar’s resentments carrying him to a present dispatch; which it behov’d him to hinder, as well for punishing Edmund with a death of more infamy, as for getting out of him by torture or otherwise the whole iniquitous business in which he had been an actor. Dyce (ed. 1857): Spoken to Edmund,—Hold being formerly a word commonly used when any one presented any thing [here, the letter] to another, giving exx. also cited among others by Schmidt (1874), who also (ed. 1879) equates it with Fr. tenez, a word used to get attention. Deighton (ed. 1891), over-literally: Take this paper in your hands; said to Edmund. Verity (ed. 1897), more correctly: A form of address, like There! used in handing something—to Edmund, he thinks; cf. OED (v. 15b: Here Take it!). Tovey (ed. 1896): Edgar is to hold the paper lest Goneril should tear it. Kittredge (ed. 1940): A mere interjectional phrase, like the modern Just a moment! Before he can show the paper to Edmund he must give attention to Goneril. Harbage (ed. 1958): If addressed to Edmund,…Albany hopes to obtain a confession. Wilson (ed. 1960): Yet Alb. could not give Edm. what he was just about to make Gon. look at; and why give away at all, least of all to Edm., a vital piece of evidence in settling the account with his treacherous wife, which must come to the State trial he is clearly preparing for in the double arrest.…At the moment what he clearly wishes is to confront her with the damning document while keeping a tight hold of it himself.…All he shows, as l. [3114] tells us, is her name subscribed. Cf. the next n. Foakes (ed. 1997): Edmund…perhaps tries to grab the letter. Lott (ed. 1974): Probably addressed to one of the men around Goneril who are ready to support her.

3114 thou…thine]
In Q these words probably refer to Goneril, who is addressed as dame before and Lady after this line; F’s preceding word Sir leads some eds. to direct the line to Edmund. On the your/thine alternations see n. 2308. Hudson (ed. 1879), to Goneril: I hardly think Albany would say to him read thine own evil, when that evil was properly Goneril’s. Schmidt (ed. 1879): From the manner in which the letter came into Albany’s hands, Albany could not know whether Edmund was acquainted with its contents or not (Ger.). Kirschbaum (1945, pp. 67–8): Albany holds it out to Edmund with the injunction that the latter read it.…(It will be remembered that Edmund’s treason is revealed in Goneril’s letter…; that Albany arrests Edmund On capital Treason…; and that Albany’s Saue him, saue him…can only refer to Albany’s desire to have Edmund…admit his guilt.…However, one cannot be cocksure that [this speech] is not spoken to Goneril.) Muir (ed. 1952): The letter was never delivered; and we are not told whether Regan’s letter was also found on Oswald’s body. Edmund could have seen neither, though Albany would not know this for certain. [Cf. n. 3028]…Bransom, [1934; see n. 3024–5] p. 161, argues that the pronoun [thou] would not have been used of Goneril by Albany [who addresses her by your and you in this speech]. But cf. [2311+1]. Cf. n. 3118. Munro (ed. 1957): Edmund’s guilt is manifest [from 2715]. Line [3114] appears to be addressed, like Hold, sir. to Edmund. Goneril now intervenes, and attempts to seize the letter; and l. [3115] is addressed to her.

3114 any thing]
Like Van Dam (1935, p. 101) and Kirschbaum (1945, p. 67), Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 43): Infinitely weaker than F’s [any name]—a commonplace reading…for an unusual one. A deliberate change in F, not a restoration. Page (ed. 1889), name: Any evil thing that can be named.

3115 nay]
F’s omission makes a regular verse line.

3115 tearing]
Steevens (ed. 1773) compares Leir 2586: Knowest thou these letters? She snatches them & teares them; see . Muir (ed. 1952, pp. xxxi f.) compares the speech with 3117: Know’st thou [is] common to both passages…and these letters [is] echoed in…this paper. Taylor (1983, pp. 370–2) takes the congruence as one of several instances showing that Q is closer to the acknowledged sources than F, in which Edmund rather than Goneril answers (3119).

3115 you]
Bransom (1934, p. 164): Emphatic. She recognized the letter, for she had written it.…[Edmund] did not…, for it had never reached him.

3116 Say if]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Suppose (OED, v.1 10). The usual conjunction would be that; here if = in the case that, redundantly emphasizing the conditional meaning of the verb.

3117 mine not thine]
Tovey (ed. 1896): Albany’s powers in Goneril’s patrimony are deputed, she contends; she is sovereign. Houghton (ed. 1957): Goneril means that she is the King’s daughter, and…Albany only her consort.

3117 who…me]
Crook (ed. 1907): As Goneril is queen in her own right she claims to be above trial. Kittredge (ed. 1940): For a sovereign cannot be brought to trial. See also n. 2530.

3117 shal]
Van Dam (1935, p. 101) thinks F’s can an elucidatory change.

3118 Most…paper?]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 423): F takes over faulty lineation from Q. But it may derive from a common MS, and may not even be faulty, since the usual editorial relining of QF 3117–19 (see textual n.) to make two lines produces fairly rough if not hypermetrical verse. Still, short lines before and after a full 3118 would be unusual, though they might suggest Goneril’s desperate agitation.

3118 monstrous]
F’s added O ekes out a verse line, either within 3118 or in combination with 3117. Furness (ed. 1880): The groan that breaks from Albany…at the revelation of his wife’s abandoned effrontery, should not be omitted; it is as needful to the character as it is to the rhythm. F’s punctuation, however, indicates that O introduces Albany’s following question, in F apparently addressed to Edmund. If, as most eds. agree, the line should be divided after monstrous, F’s added O is extrametrical and clumsy; instead of accepting it, most eds. treat monstrous as trisyllabic. OED (Monstrous a. 7): Astounding, quoting this l.; see also n. 238. Greg (1940, p. 396) compares Leir 2581, where Perillus addresses Gonorill as thou monster; see .

3118 thou]
Addressed to whoever responds. See the next n.

3119 Gon.]
The counterpart speech in Leir is addressed by Leir to his daughter Ragan; see n. 3115. Q’s attribution makes sense on several grounds: it makes 3112–19 a continuous confrontation between Albany and his wife without involving a man lying mortally wounded, it gives Goneril a good exit line, and it avoids the apparent inconsistency of Edmund obstinately refusing any comment here and then volunteering a confession one speech later. Besides, Albany’s question makes little sense if addressed to Edmund, who cannot know an obviously intercepted letter he has never seen. Collier (ed. 1843): Albany again appeals to Goneril whether she knows the paper, and in all the quartos the answer is assigned to her, who then goes out. The folio, having erroneously fixed her exit earlier, transfers [3119] to [Bast.]. Clarkes (ed. 1868): We think that Albany’s words, Go…desperate, show that he is intended to say them immediately upon Goneril’s uttering this refusal to be questioned, and then rushing out. So Van Dam (1935, p. 101): The Q place [of exit] is a little more probable because, then, immediately after Goneril’s exit Albany orders: Go after her. So Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 190): It seems odd that Albany should, after Goneril’s exit, question Edmund and receive an answer from him and then say Go…gouerne her. These words sound urgent.…And if Goneril goes out, desperate, at the end of [3119], it is obviously suitable that she should speak [3119]. Muir (ed. 1952): Goneril needs an hysterical, not a defiant, exit line. Stone (1980, p. 57): Without 3119, Goneril is left with scarcely enough to establish that she is desperate. The main objection against the Q attribution is expressed by Knight (ed. 1840): Why should Albany address this question [3118] to Goneril, when he had previously said to her—No tearing, lady; I perceive you know it?—an objection Furness (ed. 1880) finds unanswerable. Albany’s first remark, however, could be spoken as a question or rhetorical question or exclamation, and Kittredge (ed. 1940) sees this line as a follow-up to it: Albany insists on a direct answer, though the evidence is clear enough. Similarly Duthie (op. cit.): Albany tells her that he perceives she knows it: Goneril replies Say if I do,…, horrifying Albany: but she has only implied a confession: Albany, bent on securing a definite confession, asks her point blank Know’st…paper?: and she goes out refusing to answer: she goes out obviously desperate, and Albany sends attendants after her, to gouerne her. I think that this is a perfectly coherent sequence, much better than that of F. [A scribe] may have made an alteration on his own responsibility, thinking Albany’s question to Goneril in [3118] inconsistent with his statement to her in [3115]. Bradley (1904, p. 464) adds another objection: When Albany is undoubtedly speaking to his wife [in 3112, 3115], he uses the plural pronoun [you].…When he asks Know’st thou this paper? he is probably not speaking to her. But see n. 3114. Leo (1880, p. 62) sees Edmund’s response as prelude to a voluntary disclosure: Do not trouble you with asking me, I shall tell you all. A higher motive is given by Hudson (ed. 1856): Edmund, with some spirit of manhood, refuses to make any answers that will criminate or blacken a woman by whom he is beloved; and then proceeds, consistently, to answer Edgar’s charges. Similarly Furness (op. cit.): Edmund…refuses to know anything of the letter, but confesses that what he has been openly charged with, that he has done. So Bradley (op. cit.): Edmund…refuses to answer…from chivalry towards Goneril. Not all find the argument convincing. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 230): It is at least a question whether the Folio’s change is not erroneous. For Edmund’s so sudden change of front is not easily explicable. Bransom (1934, p. 172): There is no trace of chivalry in [3211]. So Duthie (op. cit.): It should be noted that Edmund says not only What…done but also And more…out. This last line ([3123]) seems to me inconsistent with assigning [3119] to Edmund. From [3121–3] I think we can say that Edmund does not wish to keep any of his crimes secret—he is near death, he has not time to spend making a full confession, and he declares that his full guilt will be revealed in time. Halio (ed. 1973): In Q Gonorill’s name after Exit…would be also redundant if the speech were hers. But Q has such redundant exits at 291, 309, 498, 2081, 2298, and 2645. Urkowitz (1980, p. 113), having declared (p. 38) either Q or F Shakespearean, purposeful, and theatrically intelligible, argues that the F reassignment implies more divided attention and a pattern of delay on the part of Albany; McLeod (1983, pp. 187–8) thinks that it allows Goneril to exit in a position of strength rather than defeated and shamefaced as in Q. Brown (ed. 1996): Edmund’s refusal to speak can be impatient, as he struggles with pain; or it can be a resolute refusal to treat Albany as his judge or better.…[He may be] determined to finish his life in his own way.…[If given to Goneril,] the words can hardly express stoicism, but rather a wild, ungovernable panic.

3120 Go after]
At least one of the officers on stage needs to exit; actually, the several who are onstage might exit here to provide a more intimate setting for the reconciliation between the brothers, the account of Gloucester’s death, and the reappearance of Kent. They would reappear after 3184 and at 3216. Halio (ed. 1992), following Urkowitz (1980, p. 113; cf. prev. n.): Somewhat belatedly, Albany recognises Gonerill’s despair and shows justified concern; this is consistent with his emerging pattern of delayed response. There is no delay at all if Goneril speaks 3119 as in Q, and no more than a few seconds if she does not. If such a delay is a real concern, it may be yet one more argument that 3119 is misassigned in F. Foakes (ed. 1997): The slight delay hardly justifies the perception…of an emerging pattern of delay in Albany.

3120 desperate]
Hunter (ed. 1972): In the state of despair, theologically defined as having lost any sense of Divine Grace, and therefore liable to commit suicide (OED, adj. 1); cf. 2471, nn. 1835, 2475, 2932, 3154, 3213, 3260. Brown (ed. 1976), however: Merely reckless or violent (OED, 4); see 1609 and the next n.

3120 gouerne]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Restrain, control (OED, v. 9, quoting this l.). Kittredge (ed. 1940): Albany fears that she may kill herself. Cf. [3175–8, 3259]. This may be merely critical hindsight. As an arraigned criminal who has just declared herself above the law and has rushed out in a rage, she might attempt any of several desperate measures including escape or violent attack on others (including Albany). Neither Albany nor the audience need expect attempted suicide. Brown (ed. 1976), nonetheless: There is probably a scream from offstage: Goneril is killing herself.

3121–4 you…thou]
Bradley (1904, p. 464): He goes on to admit the charges brought against himself previously by Albany ([3027 ff.]) and Edgar ([3088 ff.]). I should explain the change from you to thou…by supposing that at first he is speaking to Albany and Edgar together.

3123 And…more]
Some commentators think that this must refer to his orders to kill Lear and Cordelia; see n. 3164. In fact, however, Albany has charged him only with many treasons and attempted adultery, and Edgar (unrecognized by Edmund) further with being generally False to the Gods thy brother and thy Father. Edmund alone, as far as he knows at this point, is fully aware of all the particular betrayals of Edgar, Gloucester, Goneril, Regan, Albany, Lear, and Cordelia that are past, and that time will bring out. He may be thinking of his whole career, not just of his most recent device.

3123 bring it out]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Make it clear (OED, v. 21d, quoting this l. as its first ex.).

3124 what]
See n. 540.

3125 on]
Upon (Wright, ed. 1875), over (Page, ed. 1889). OED (prep. 23): After verbs of winning, gaining, taking (by force), quoting this l.

3127 charity]
Johnson (ed. 1765): Our authour by negligence gives his heathens the sentiments and practices of christianity. Ritson (1783, p. 173), however, denies that benevolence, or a forgiveness of injuries could not subsist without a belief in christianity, or that heathens could not act like men, especially since the first Christians borrowed (or, rather, stole…) all their morality from the possessors of Paganism. Muir (ed. 1952): Let me forgive you for your crimes against me, as you have forgiven me for killing you. Joseph (ed. 1966): Love without conditions. Edmund says he will forgive his opponent if he is noble.…Edgar insists forgiveness must come from each other without talk of merit.

3129 If more]
Harbage (ed. 1958): If greater (since legitimate). Halio (ed. 1992): Edmond is half-blooded ([3025]).

3129 the more…wrongd]
Abbott (§480): Both dissyllables. Various other expedients have been proposed to fill out the line metrically: see textual n. and . Kittredge (ed. 1940), more: Since Edmund is only half-blooded [3025].

3131–4 The Gods…eies]
Coleridge (MS notes, 1818–19, ed. Foakes, 1989, p. 97): As the fittest means for reconciling the feelings of the spectators to the horrors of Gloucester’s after-sufferings—at least, of rendering them somewhat less unendurable…—Shakespeare has precluded all excuse and palliation of the guilt incurred by both the parents of the base-born Edmund; by Gloucester’s confession, that he was at the time a married man, and already blessed with a lawful heir to his fortunes. Wordsworth (1864, p. 113) compares Wisdom 11:13: Wherewith a man sinneth, by the same also shal he be punished [Geneva]. Carter (1905, p. 443) and Noble (1935, p. 232) compare Wisdom 12:23: Wherefore, whereas men haue liued dissolutely and vnrighteously, thou hast punished them sore with their owne abominations [Geneva: by their owne imaginations], and Jer. 2:19: Thine owne wickednes shal correct thee, and thy turnings backe shal reproue thee [Geneva]. Milward (1987, p. 200) adds Job 4:8. Fripp (1938, p. 663 n.): The occasion of Gloucester’s loss of his eyes was not vice but virtue, an heroic defence of the poor old King. Yet the cause was the Bastard’s treachery, and behind the treachery was the bastardy; cf. n. 2140. Empson (1951, p. 150) compares 1855–6, where the punishment seems to be for an entirely legitimate sexual act. Muir (ed. 1952) compares Leir 1909: The heauens are iust, and hate impiety; see . Dent (1984, H348.11) compares the proverbial Heaven (God) is (The heavens, gods are) just. R. W. David (apud Wilson, ed. 1960): Lear, intemperate in mind, is betrayed by unfilial daughters, and loses the light of his mind; Gloucester, intemperate in body, is betrayed by his bastard son and loses the light of his body. Watson (1960, p. 332): The judgment is severely Hebraic and self-righteous: Gods who will punish mere lust with blindness shock our sense of justice. Maxwell (1950, p. 146): Unlike the invocations frequently uttered by other characters, His mood for dealing with the divine is the indicative. Myrick (1964, pp. 67–8): The lines…seem self-righteous and cruel as coming from a man to his dying brother, even though the brother be a traitor to their father. Yet Edgar is in reality both humble and gentle. Only as a general comment, voicing the spontaneous feeling of the audience, are his words truly appropriate and dramatic. For on occasions like Edmund’s fall, it was second nature for both the common man and the philosopher to see the hand of God. So Leggatt (1992, pp. 198–9): The brothers agree on a moral analysis of the whole action.…The satisfaction of the moment [for the audience] comes not just from the event itself but from the commentary that finds a meaning in it. Mack (1965, p. 61): Edgar’s views reflect his Morality backgrounds, and are less…characteristics of the solicitous and patient guide of Gloucester and the pitying observer of Lear than necessities of his role as presenter of legitimacy and polar opposite to his brother’s Appetite. McAlindon (1991, p. 167): Usually interpreted nowadays as an unacceptably harsh piece of moralising which the drama itself does not endorse; but that, I think, is to ignore its philosophic status as part of a continuing emphasis on fidelity as the only alternative to social chaos. Fidelity to wife, parent, and master, and indeed to every personal commitment, are all one in the ethic of this play [quoting 1860–2 obay…spouse]. Elton (1966, pp. 107 ff.) discusses contemporary attitudes towards retributive justice, and in particular towards blinding as a punishment for adultery: When…the dying brother confesses and repents, Edgar eases his last moments by offering extenuating comfort in the only terms Edmund is able to comprehend, through the latter’s own lex talionis formula.…The Bastard predictably concurs.…[But] in a world where distributive justice is not evident, retributive justice seems bitterly awry.…Since Edmund’s harsh lex talionis is the precise opposite to Edgar’s frequently expressed pity,…it seems unlikely to represent Edgar’s outlook. To mistake these views, by ignoring dramatic context and exigencies, for those of Edgar or the tragedy itself, would thus seem to involve a misinterpretation. Advocated by Puritans, who were both inimical to the stage and displeasing to James, such retribution would, furthermore, hardly have been applauded by many in Shakespeare’s audience. Halio (1992, p. 223), however, finds biblical precedent for the blinding of adulterers cited in one of the Homilies (1547) that Elizabeth appointed to be read; see n. 2140. Joseph (ed. 1966, p. 57): Are we to agree that he has caused his own sufferings only by the act of lust, and not by his much more recent loyalty and determined self-sacrifice? The immediate cause for Gloucester’s punishment is of course Cornwall’s conviction that he was a traitor. Orgel (ed. 1999, p. xli): As a summation of Gloucester’s tragedy, the lines seem singularly obtuse; Gloucester dies blaming his gullibility and imperceptiveness; he never gives any sign of regret for his youthful adultery.

3131 iust]
See n. 1817. Elton (1966, p. 109 n.): Edgar’s just may also ambiguously imply ironically appropriate or precise, as in Lear’s Judicious punishment ([1855]), but Edmund seizes upon it for his own vindictive justification.

3131 pleasant]
Schmidt (1875): Delightful. Quinn’s (ed. 1970) Pleasure-loving and Colman’s (ed. 1982) Pleasure-seeking are unattested in OED.

3131 vertues]
Few defend vertues; Stone (1980, pp. 116, 222), calling F’s revision rather literal-minded, proposes accomplishments, powers, capacities, specified by Orgel (ed. 2000) as sexual prowess. Carroll (1988, p. 238) prefers Q: The paradox that we suffer because of our virtues—our powers and the forms of our goodness—is truer to the tragic experience in Lear than the far more moralistic and finally untrue, or at least incomplete, maxim about our vices. For the theory that vertues may be an unconscious substitution for its antonym, F’s vices, see n. 2277, and Kopff (1975, pp. 117–20). Hunter (ed. 1869), pleasant vices: Sinful pleasures. Verity (ed. 1918): Gloucester’s sin…was a transgression against the vows of wedlock.

3132 scourge]
Both Q’s word and F’s plague are conventional and Shn. terms for punish (Schmidt, 1875; cf. 435). On the latter image see n. 1848–9.

3133 darke]
Like Heilman (1948, pp. 44–5), Halio (ed. 1992): (1) dim, unlit, (2) morally benighted.

3133 vitious]
Schmidt (1875): Devoted to vice (OED, a. 1). Cf. 249.

3133 place]
Muir (ed. 1952): The adulterous bed, and so the act of adultery. Hankins (1953, p. 106): The womb of Edmund’s mother, where his evil character was determined before he was born, citing Pangenius’s theory of heredity. Wells (ed. 2000): The vagina or the brothel.

3133 gotte]
See n. 349.

3135 truth]
F’s substitution right and redundant addition tis true leave the meaning unchanged; they may simply be metrical adjustments, the consequence of eliding Q’s Thou hast in F. Hunter (ed. 1972): Edmund picks up Edgar’s point about the poetic justice of Destiny…and applies it to himself. Brown (ed. 1976): Denying all that he has lived by.…Huge issues are involved here, but the audience is given little time to ponder them.

3136 wheele…heere]
Delius (ed. 1854): The Wheel of Fortune, that lifted me so high, has, in turning, brought me back to the lowly place that I originally occupied (Ger.). Cf. 1249–50. Many eds. extend the image beyond Fortune’s wheel to other cyclical patterns of time or providence or nemesis. Hunter (ed. 1869): The round of my destiny is completed, comparing JC 5.3.23–5 (2503–5): Time is come round, | And where I did begin, there shall I end. | My life is run his compasse. Wright (ed. 1875) compares TN 5.1.376–7 (2546–7), and thus the whirlegigge of time, brings in his reuenges. Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): The wheel of events…the absolute justice of Providence. Moulton (1885, p. 208): The position which Edmund has gained involves him in intrigues, which by the development of the play are made to result in a nemesis upon his original intrigue. And it is a nemesis of exquisite exactness: for he meets his death in the very moment of his success, at the hands of a brother whom he has maligned and robbed, while the father he has deceived and sought to destroy is the means by which the avenger has been brought to the scene. Bransom (1934, p. 171): He seems to mean The gods have punished our father for his adultery, and they have punished me. Hankins (1953, p. 19): Not Fortune’s wheel, but the complete revolution of one’s fate from birth to death, the Aristotelian cycle of generation and corruption, comparing a 15th-c. drawing which imposes the Seven Ages of Man upon a wheel, perhaps originally suggested to the artist by the wheel of nativity (rota nativitatis) in the Vulgate reading of James 3:6, a reading not retained in the English translations. Similarly Soellner (1984, p. 283): Wheels of life…were common in iconography from the Middle Ages to the Renaissance. Munro (ed. 1957): Fortune’s wheel may be to some extent implied; but more direct reference to Edgar’s last preceding sentences is intended. As though by inexorable law time has brought about for Edmund the full accomplishment of those results which were inherent in his origin and his own way of life. Wells (ed. 2000): I am punished for the events that I set in train. Elton (1966, p. 109) documents the historical evolution and interrelation of the ideas of the wheels of retributive Justice (Dike), Destiny (Moira), Time, and Fortune. Soellner (op. cit., p. 286 n.): The divinely sanctioned Wheel of Fortune was sometimes identified with Ezekiel’s wheel in Ezekiel i.4–21, as it was by King James in the Basilicon Doron. Hunter (ed. 1972), more concretely: He embraced force and deceit as methods; and now the disguised Edgar has conquered him by force.…He alleged that Edgar’s sword had wounded him in II.i. Now he is killed by that means. Edwards (ed. 1975): Edmund not only accepts Edgar’s grim belief in divine punishment, but extends it. He is the fruit of the adultery, and in his destruction the sin is fully repaid. Bate (1989; 1993, p. 195): Ixion’s wheel is a powerful symbol for this process of crime catching up with the perpetrator; see n. 2795–6.

3136 full circled]
Virtually all eds. adopt F’s full circle. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 423): Probably the compositor misread circle as circld. The opposite happens at Rom. 2.2.110 (Q2). F’s construction is a kind of adverbial objective, like run his compasse (see prev. n.) or Carowse full measure (Shr. 3.2.225 [1611]). Since OED (Circle sb. 17c) quotes no other ex. of the phrase before 1878, and since in Sh. full often precedes a participle but virtually never a noun, Q’s reading is possibly right. Circled occurs elsewhere in Sh. five times. Wells (ed. 2000): Come may easily mean become (OED v. 24a), and OED records circled as Rounded; circular.

3137 gate]
Schmidt (1874): Manner of walking (OED, Gait sb.1). Craig (ed. 1901) and Baldwin (1944, 2:481): Perhaps echoes Vergil, Aen. 1.405: Et vera incessu patuit dea.

3137 prophecie]
OED (Prophesy v. 2c): To indicate beforehand, foreshow, quoting only this l.

3138 royall]
Though Edgar is Lear’s godson (1030) he is not of royalty. Albany’s term must mean kinglike, noble, majestic (OED, Royal a. 9). Foakes (ed. 1997): But perhaps anticipating Albany’s invitation to Edgar…to share the rule of the realm at [3294–5]. Albany can hardly anticipate that offer, since it is not yet his to make, Lear and Cordelia being (so far as he knows) still alive.

3139 split]
A variant of break the heart (cf. n. 1029) unrecorded before Sh. (OED, v. 3a). Gardner (ed. 1969): Not merely rhetorical. Physicians emphasized the physical damage which sorrow could do to the heart.

3141 Worthy]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Noble, honourable.

3144 List]
Abbott (§199): The preposition is…sometimes omitted before the thing heard after verbs of hearing (OED, List v.2 2). Cf. n. 174.

3144 tale]
Skottowe (1824, p. 130): All which the audience were…well acquainted with.…But Shakespeare found the story twice narrated in [Sidney’s] the Arcadia [2.10.2, 3; see ], and he was seduced, on this occasion, to the commission of tautology.

3145 O…burst]
Halio (ed. 1992): Emotionally overtaxed by now, Edgar uncharacteristically…yearns for death. Foakes (ed. 1997): If he means [in 3145] that he would wish to die, he might seem to repudiate all that he did to persuade his father to stay alive.…His compassion here also seems unrelated to his oddly objective moral condemnation of his father’s sin at [3131–4].…It is odd that he begins a speech wishing his own heart would burst, and end it describing how his father’s heart did burst, citing Rosenberg (1972, pp. 306–8) on Edgar’s inconsistencies. The image of a heart broken by sorrow was of course a rhetorical commonplace, and should not be taken too literally. It occurs at 1029, 1283, 2586 (spoken by Edgar), and 3160, and such a fracture is anticipated or even invoked at 1585, 1624, 1711, 3139, and 3285, as well as here. See also n. 3168+12. Edgar, having just risked his life and killed his brother, is unburdening himself of almost intolerable sorrows at his father’s death, his own possible guilt in causing that death, Lear’s piteous tale, and Kent’s grief which threatens the strings of life…to crack. He may be allowed a conventional hyperbole.

3146–62 The…smillingly]
Baker (1907, p. 263): Edgar tells Albany much that is already well known to us [because] Shakespeare felt that the public so loved story for its own sake that it would take great pleasure in seeing how all the unhappy strokes of fate seemed working to a happier ending. Hunter (ed. 1972): The narrative of important and moving events off-stage, told by a messenger, traditionally makes its effect by a more rhetorical, more statuesque mode than is usual in dramatic poetry. The example here (properly called a period—a classical paragraph—in line [3168+1]) involves continuously suspended syntax carrying the narration forward without a single full-stop. Brown (ed. 1996): Only the end of Edgar’s narrative contains news for the audience, and so the speech is often cut greatly for performance. But it is printed in both the Quarto and Folio texts and its length can be justified if the actor shows how great a struggle it is for Edgar to speak: he reveals life’s sweetness and accepts his own fault. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 64): Shakespeare thus avoids another recognition scene that might have undermined that between Lear and Cordelia, and provides a suggestive verbal image that anticipates the death of Lear.

3146 To escape]
Malone (ed. 1790): A wish to escape the bloody proclamation, taught me, &c. Deighton (ed. 1891): To escape the consequences of the proclamation, which consequences followed. Brooke (ed. 1947): In order to escape.…When this sentence resumes after the parenthesis, the construction is altered. Instead of taught me…one would expect something like I was obliged.

3147–9 O…once]
Muir & Danby (1950, p. 50) compare Plangus’s lament in Sidney’s Arcadia 2.12.[2] (see ), that death is feard, and life is held with paine. Elton (1966, p. 99 n.) cites Tilley L254—Life is sweet—and other instances of the proverb. Neither Tilley nor Dent (1981) cites this l.

3147 liues]
Maxwell (apud Wilson, ed. 1960): Rather the sweetness that life has for us than the sweetness of our (several) lives.

3148 that]
Kittredge (ed. 1940), following Delius (ed. 1854): Who. The antecedent is implied in our (= of us) (Ger.). See n. 2941–2. Or conceivably the antecedent could be liues: Our lives would die (OED, v.1 7: Suffer pains identified with those of death) hourly rather than die (OED, 10: Come to an end) at once. Only Weis (ed. 1993) makes sweetnes the antecedent. If F is followed (see next n.), that is a conjunction introducing an exclamatory clause (OED, conj. 1e).

3148 with…Would]
Q makes sense as it stands (see prev. n.), but many eds. follow Jennens in improving it by emending Would to we’d (see textual n.). Malone (ed. 1790), would: A misprint…for w’ould, i.e. we would. Most eds. follow F’s substitution of we for with. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 424): The compositor may have misread this as wt (t/e) and taken it as an abbreviation of with. Stone (1980, p. 200) considers with a phonetic error; it could have been made by a compositor carrying the line in his head. Halio (ed. 1994): Reading from copy, the compositor might easily have assimilated and then erroneously redivided we the to with the, as Blayney says. F’s die the pain of death has seemed to some to be harsh language (Bailey, 1866, 2:99) in need of explanation. Capell (1783, 1.2:186): Die the death is a hebraism. Boswell (ed. 1821): Does not seem to me a very harsh ellipsis for, To die suffering the pains of death. Deighton (ed. 1891): A kind of cognate accusative construction. Craig (ed. 1901) finds parallels of idea in 1 Cor. 15:31, I die daily, and Cym. 5.1.26–7 (2883–4), my life | Is euery breath, a death. Quinn (ed. 1970), freely: Die, i.e., endure.

3149 at once]
Lee (ed. 1908): Once for all.

3149 shift]
Craig (ed. 1901): Change (OED, v. 9d, quoting this l. as its first ex.).

3151 habit]
Schmidt (1874): Dress (OED, sb. 1).

3152 rings]
Rolfe (ed. 1880): Sockets; the case of [2588]. Malone (ed. 1790) finds a similar image in Per. 3.2.98 (1299), Craig (ed. 1901) in Revenger’s Tragedy 1.1.20, and Elton (1966, p. 112 n.) and Saner (1968, pp. 163–4) in Dante’s Purgatorio 23.31. Budd (ed. 1935): With a play on the normal meaning of rings set with precious stones. Adelman (1992, p. 297) detects puns on stones = testicles and rings = female genitals, citing Partridge (1961), and thereby finds in the line an image of castration, as does Halio (1992, p. 222; cf. n. 2140); neither Partridge nor Williams (1994) cites this l. for either quibble.

3154 dispaire]
On despair as a sin mortal to the soul, see nn. 1835, 2475, 2932, 3120, 3213, 3260. Foakes (ed. 1997): Shakespeare was also well aware of the Stoic defence of suicide in the Senecan tradition of accepting it as proof of having the ultimate power over oneself,…and the two attitudes overlap disturbingly in King Lear. See nn. 2473–9, 2505.

3155 Father]
Though Q makes acceptable sense, F substitutes fault. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 424), proposing l/t and t/r misreadings: The Q compositor may have misread falt as fatr which he would naturally take as a contraction of father. Stone (1980, p. 200): Q makes an unconvincing melodramatic aside, as the [F] reviser apparently felt. Weis (ed. 1993): Q’s [reading] is more poignant, since Edgar…imagines himself back with his father. Delius (ed. 1854), fault: Misfortune; unattested. Rolfe (ed. 1880): But possibly Edgar now blames himself for not making himself known to his father sooner. So Kittredge (ed. 1940): Error in judgement; mistake (OED, sb. 5). Or OED (7): Culpability. Horsman (ed. 1973) compares Edgar’s similar deprecation of his own role in 2224–5. Skillan (ed. 1967): Tragic fault, error, because it might have saved his father’s life—i.e., had the recognition taken place when Gloucester was stronger. Budd (ed. 1935): Edgar’s reasons for not revealing himself are nowhere suggested. Joseph (ed. 1966, p. 57): The fact that Edgar leaves his father ignorant for so long…is no less hard whether we ascribe it to the son’s inability to forgive completely or to the circumstances which force him to continue to hide his true identity. Foakes (ed. 1997): It was necessary for the structure of the play that Edgar should maintain his anonymity, but the fault he acknowledges here is part of his character too, for it is appropriate that he should be morally perceptive about himself.

3156 some]
See n. 22–3.

3156 armed]
Cavell (1969, p. 285): Armed, and with the old man all but seeped away, he feels safe enough to give his father vision again and bear his recognition. As sons fear, and half wish, it is fatal. Edgar himself names a less squalid motive: see n. 3158.

3157 successe]
Schmidt (1875): Issue, result. See n. 472.

3158 blessing]
Hudson (ed. 1879): Edgar, apprehensive that he might fall, had piously craved his father’s benediction on the undertaking.

3159 my]
F’s inferior our may be an accidental compositorial substitution (Duthie, ed. 1949, p. 191). Withdrawn in Wilson (ed. 1960); see next n.

3159 pilgrimage]
Schmidt (1875): Any long and weary journey:…Used of human life (OED, sb. 1c). See Samuel C. Chew, The Pilgrimage of Life (New Haven, 1962). Wilson (ed. 1960): Perh. with a Christian significance—by the end of the journey Glo.’s soul is saved <G. I. Duthie>. Fraser (ed. 1963): (Purgatorial) journey.

3159–62 his…smillingly]
Mrs. Lennox (1754, 3:300–1) finds the source in Sidney’s Arcadia 2.10.7; see , and cf. nn. 2838+1, 3283.

3159 flawd]
Schmidt (1874): Damage[d] by a fissure (OED, ppl. a., quoting this l. as its first ex.). Cf. n. 1585. Rolfe (ed. 1880): Broken. Cf. 1029, 3139, n. 3283. Kittredge (ed. 1940): On account of what it had already suffered. Hoeniger (1992, p. 172): Weakened by his grief. Horsman (ed. 1973) finds a cross-association with the noun flaw = squall, outburst of feeling (OED, sb.2 2).

3160 conflict]
Explained in the next l.

3160 support]
Schmidt (1875): Endure (OED, v. 1b, quoting Oth. 1.3.258 [608] and this l. as its first exx.). As Walker (1860, 3:284) points out, there should be no punctuation after support.

3161 ioy and griefe]
McCann (ed. 1964): Sadness at the suffering he had inflicted upon Edgar and the joy of knowing him to be a loving, faithful son. Edwards (ed. 1975): It was the grief that had cracked his heart;…but it was with his new happiness that he died. Foakes (ed. 1997): Joy at knowing Edgar to be alive…; also, a kind of happiness in dying at such a moment. Perhaps also joy at reunion, grief at Lear and Cordelia’s defeat and capture. Elton (1966, p. 271) cites Tilley J86—Sudden Joy kills sooner than excessive grief—and contemporary discussions of the idea. Neither Tilley nor Dent (1981) cites this l.

3163–5 This…say]
Granville-Barker (1927, p. 156) calls these lines flatter than a pancake: Edmund may be dying, but surely Shakespeare might rouse him, if he would, to something livelier.…I challenge any actor to give colour to that last line.

3164 perchance do good]
Bradley (1904, p. 253 n.): No sufficiently clear reason is supplied for Edmund’s delay in attempting to save Cordelia and Lear.…He despatches a captain with secret orders to put them both to death instantly [2980].…As he lies dying, he says to Edgar (at line [3122], more than a hundred lines after he gave that commission to the captain): [quotes 3122–4]. In more, much more he seems to be thinking of the order for the deaths of Lear and Cordelia (what else remains undisclosed?); yet he says nothing about it.…Then he hears the story of his father’s death, says that it has moved him and shall perchance do good (what good except saving his victims?); yet he still says nothing. It is only when directly questioned about Lear and Cordelia that he tries to save the victims who were to be killed instantly [2980]. How can we explain his delay? Perhaps, thinking the deaths of Lear and Cordelia would be of use to Goneril and Regan, he will not speak till he is sure that both the sisters are dead. Or perhaps…he is still too self-absorbed to rise to the active effort.…[But] the real cause lies outside the dramatic nexus. It is Shakespeare’s wish to deliver a sudden and crushing blow to the hopes which he has excited. In fact many particular things remain undisclosed; see n. 3123. Thaler (1929, p. 47): Perhaps Edmund hesitated in the first place lest his confession embarrass Regan or Goneril, and perhaps he delays finally because he is sunk in dreamy reflections on his past [Bradley, p. 303] (Yet Edmund was beloved). In any case he is a dying man; he listens to Edgar, but he speaks few words of any sort.…[He] has behind him a life-long habit of putting himself first, and no experience in the luxury of yielding quickly to unselfish impulses. So Muir (ed. 1952): Edmund’s delay…may be explained by his loyalty to Goneril, or by the gradual workings of repentance. At 3168 Edmund is prevented by the rest of Edgar’s long narration from immediately disclosing his orders for Lear and Cordelia; still, he evidently believes later that there is time to do some good (3200) if ’twere done quickly (3201).

3166 more…wofull]
Deighton (ed. 1891): More, and that of a more woeful nature.

3167 dissolue]
Delius (ed. 1854): Either dissolve in tears, or die, as in Ant. 3.13.162 (2345) [cf. Lr. 2370] (Ger.). He and other eds. prefer the former, Wilson (ed. 1960) citing Ant. 5.2.298–9 (3550–1). OED (v. 15): In various fig. applications of prec. senses: To become faint, faint away; to become softened in feeling, to melt (into tears, etc.), quoting this l. as its first ex.

3168 hearing]
Abbott (§178): Hear of does not mean, as with us, hear about.…The verbal means in the act of. Cf. nn. 508, 973.

3168+1–+18 Edg.…slaue.]
Like Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 8), most eds. think F’s omission of these lines represents a theatrical cut that leaves a lacuna. Theobald (ed. 1733), blaming the players for another of their judicious Retrenchments: This fine and necessary Description I have thought fit to restore from the Old 4to; as it artfully opens to Albany the Concealment of Kent at home, during his Banishment; and gives a beautiful Picture of the Emotions that good Old Man felt for the Death of his friend Glo’ster, and the Piety of Edgar towards his distrest Father. Capell (1783, 1.2:186): Left out by the folio editors; a more ill-judg’d omission is not to be found in their work. For Adee’s different evaluation see n. 2056+5–+18. Delius (1876, pp. 145–6): The play opens with a conversation between these friends; and certainly their chance meeting, after having been separated so long, lay very near the heart of the author. The plan of his play prevents his allowing the audience to witness their reëncounter, but at least he paints it for them in the strongest colours. The actors cut out this passage; but…they retained Edmund’s previous words, which lead up to it.…Could Shakspere have either omitted or retained so clumsily? Verity (ed. 1897), agreeing that it is an actors’ abridgement: As Knight observed [see n. 2347+1–+56], it is mainly descriptive and adds little to the development of the plot.…Its omission makes the entrance of Kent and Edgar’s words Here comes Kent [3181] a little abrupt; but the abruptness would escape notice in the dramatic stress and excitement.…Some corruption of the text seems probable; and the great obscurity is probably the cause of the omission of the speech from the Folio. Doran (1931, p. 72): Edgar’s speech was evidently introduced as preparation for Kent’s entrance a few lines farther on…and explains why Albany evinces no surprise at seeing him. Still, the speech was not absolutely necessary and could be spared. The fact that 3179 was altered to make a verse line with the remaining 3168 she takes as evidence of Sh.’s hand in the abridgement, but any reviser might have added O helpe to 3179. Bransom (1934, p. 169): Albany is occupied with other thoughts. Hart (1942, p. 148): Struck out by the actors without much loss: Were the Jacobean actors and audiences becoming too sophisticated to accept the dramatic convention of a double disguise? Rosenberg (1972, p. 308): The lines are wisely cut, since they diminish both the tension of the moment, and Edmund’s plot against Lear and Cordelia, The language…has no sustaining poetic energy, The reported Edgar-Kent meeting seems…to detract from Kent’s touching appearance later, and Important only is the clue to Kent’s deterioration. Horsman (ed. 1973): The sentence comments (like [1622+1–+8], also omitted from F) upon the action, in its continued intensification of suffering. Warren (1978, p. 104), arguing for Shn. revision: F’s cut diminishes the sense of Edgar as the immature, indulgent man displaying his heroic tale of woe.…In so doing F develops Edgar into a man worthy to stand with the dukes [sic] at the close of the play, capable of assuming power. Edgar is not displaying his heroic tale of woe, but Kent’s, preparing Albany for his entrance. Stone (1980, p. 238): An obviously dispensable messenger-speech, though its omission leaves unexplained Kent’s premonition of approaching death at the end of the play. Brown (1988, p. 160), on the basis of theatrical experience, recommends inclusion of the lines: although by this cut directors ensure that the play becomes much simpler dynamically, and the focus is held more securely by outward behavior and spoken reactions, they remove words that emphasize the complexity and extremity of events…as these three men slowly begin to comprehend some great force that they are powerless to contradict or to avoid, and manifest strenuous torment, both inward and outward, both individual and shared. Williams (1985, p. 100), on the 1984–5 Folger Th. experiment with a Folio-only text: [Dramaturg Genie] Barton emerged skeptical of doing the pure Folio text, pointing to the absence of passages necessary for both their information and their emotional valence—such as Edgar’s First Quarto speech describing Kent just before Kent’s final entrance to Lear. Clayton (1983, p. 137): Deletion of these lines has notable accelerating and other effects:…to defer reference to the King…, to give special prominence…to the burst[ing] smilingly of Gloucester’s heart, and to precipitate the movement from Gloucester’s death to Lear’s and explicitly prepare for it. Similarly Warren (1983, pp. 69–70): And without it also Edgar appears a stronger, more commanding figure; but Kent is left with his heroic career uncelebrated.…The Folio focusses on Edgar as the youth of the realm, not, as does the Quarto, on Albany and the generation that has already known power. Halio (ed. 1992): As if taking a cue from Albany, F cuts seventeen lines; (ibid., pp. 276–7): F’s omission…reduce[s] the inexplicable delay between Edmond’s announced intention to do some good and the actual attempt to save Lear and Cordelia.…Moreover, [it] more sharply juxtaposes the pathos of Gloucester’s death with the deaths of Gonerill and Regan. The inexplicable delay, if there were one, would include not only Edgar’s lines but almost twice that many more (3169–3201) retained in F; but though Edmund says vaguely in 3163–4 that Edgar’s speech shall perchance do good (he might be understood to refer to himself, moued by Edgar’s words), he does not in fact announce an intention to do some good until 3200, and acts on that intention without any delay whatsoever. Weis (ed. 1993): Edgar’s account of meeting Kent is necessary if his recognition of Kent at [3181] is to be credible. F is prepared to sacrifice such narrative credibility in order to secure the theatrical counterpoint between Albany’s wish to be spared more suffering and the entry of the Gentleman with the bloody knife. Foakes (ed. 1997): It seems more likely that Kent has there shed his disguise and appears in court dress. Still, Albany is remarkably unsurprised by Kent’s presence. Brown (ed. 1996): By this cut the play loses an impression of people pressing, painfully and powerfully, to a halt or to self-destruction…[and] the implied criticism of a world founded on authority, precedence and service.

3168+1–+3 This…extreamitie]
Of this difficult passage the Clarkes (ed. 1868) rightly note, The interpretation depends upon the sense that is to be ascribed to another, either taking it to mean [1] another man, other persons, or [2] another period, another ceasing point.
(1)Another man.
