Dodd (1752, 2:134) makes the speech a reproach to Edmund, who is another kind of man than Albany: The bastard, whose savage nature is well display’d by it, desires to hear more: the gentle Albany, touch’d at the sad tale, begs him no more to melt his heart: upon which, Edgar observes, sensibly affected by Edmund’s inhumanity, One should have imagined, this would have seem’d a period, a sufficient end of woe, to such as love not sorrow,…: but another <a person of another and more cruel temper> to amplify too much, <to augment and aggravate that which is already too great> would still make much more <would still increase it>, and top extremity itself. Heath (1765, p. 351), followed by Hunter (ed. 1869) and others, makes the speech rather an apology to Albany for continuing with the story of another wretched man: But another (meaning Kent…) to amplify what was already too much, would make that much still more. Hudson (ed. 1856) apparently refers to the teller of the story rather than to its audience or subject: Another man, or another sort of men, to amplify what is already too much, would make the tale much worse, and so pass beyond the extreme of suffering.
(2)Another period. Capell (1783, 1.2:186–7) takes the speech as a proper reproof of Edmund’s unfeelingness, the reproof expressed directly in a parenthesis following Edgar’s announcement of yet another account of personal suffering: Since you will put me upon amplifying what is already too much, upon making much more, and topping extremity, take another relation—i.e., the stories of Kent and Lear. Similarly Steevens (ed. 1773), without following Capell’s emendation of Would make to to make: but,—another; i.e. but I must add another, i.e. another period, another kind of conclusion to my story, such as will increase the horrors what has already been told. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Another woe. With varying shades of emphasis this general interpretation is followed by Malone (ed. 1790), Collier (ed. 1858), and with minor alterations (see the following nn.) by most recent eds. Verity (ed. 1897): Another is meant to prepare, as it were, apologetically, for the story about Kent that follows.

3168+1 periode]
Malone (ed. 1790): An end or conclusion…the utmost completion of woe; see n. 2843+10. Wright (ed. 1875): A termination of the narrative. Tovey (ed. 1896): Climax (OED, sb. 6: Highest point,…acme). Crook (ed. 1907): The limit, the utmost extent. Hunter (ed. 1972): A complete sentence, with its own consummation and final point of punctuation; see also n. 3146–62.

3168+2 but…much]
Most eds. take but as a conjunction, but Wright (ed. 1875), followed by Furness (ed. 1880), Rolfe (ed. 1880), Deighton (ed. 1891), and others take it as an adjective (= only) modifying another, considering to amplifie as an infinitive used gerundially (= in or by amplifying); see n. 1926–7. So Tovey (ed. 1896): Perhaps here only another (circumstance); one other and no more. Many eds. since Capell (1783, 1.2:186–7) take too much as a substantive meaning what is already too much; thus Hunter (ed. 1869): The too-much of my sorrow. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 526), believing that the construction as it stands leaves would make without an object, put the end-of-line comma after amplifie, assuming that too much belongs with what follows rather than what precedes. Edgar is then saying: This would have seemed the conclusion; but to amplify another (sorrow, or tale of sorrow) would turn what-is-already-too-much into much more (than too-much), and top extremity.…The Q compositor, dealing with virtually unpunctuated copy, has as elsewhere simply put a comma at the end of what he set and/or saw as the end of a verse line. But many eds. since Capell, however, think that would make does have an object, namely the substantive too much. Thus Hunter (op. cit.): Would have the much made more.

3168+2 amplifie]
Most eds. agree with Warner (1768, pp. 101–2): To exaggerate, to encrease, to enlarge. Craig (ed. 1901): Enlarging too much on another circumstance. Muir (ed. 1952): To describe it in detail. Shakespeare is using the terms of rhetoric, citing Baldwin (1944, 2:228–9: amplifying by increment). Joseph (ed. 1966): Give too many alternative ways of treating the theme—repeat it too often, in other words. Hunter (ed. 1972): The first period was an amplification (in the language of rhetoric) of one sorrow (Gloucester’s); to amplify another sorrow (Kent’s) in the same way would take one beyond the period (limit) of what one can stand. Kent’s period is in fact shorter than Gloucester’s.

3168+3 Would]
It may be significant that Edgar does not use the indicative Will. He may be giving deference to Albany’s hold it in, by speaking hypothetically: Yes, this would have seemed the endurable limit; but another circumstance, if you would let me relate it, would (or bids fair to) surpass it. He then ventures to speak of Kent, Lear, and Gloucester, without objection.

3168+3 much more]
Tovey (ed. 1896): (That which is) much, more (still). See n. 3168+2.

3168+3 extreamitie]
Dyce (ed. 1867, Gloss.): The utmost of calamity. Tovey (ed. 1896): What seemed the extreme of sorrow. Craig (ed. 1901): The extreme limit of anything, comparing Cym. 3.2.56 (1524), beyond, beyond.

3168+4 big]
Wells (ed. 2000): Loud (OED a. 6).

3168+5–+6 hauing…society]
Tovey (ed. 1896): When he saw me; i.e., when I was disguised as a lunatic, Kent avoided me; as is noticeable in III., scenes 4 and 6, where Kent only addresses Edgar when compelled.

3168+5 estate]
Schmidt (1874): Condition (OED, sb. 1). I.e., as Poor Tom.

3168+6 abhord society]
Brooke (ed. 1947): Abhorrent company.

3168+9 me]
Malone (ed. 1790): Kent in his transport of joy, at meeting Edgar, embraced him with such violence, as to throw him on the dead body of Gloster. White (ed. 1862): Does Edgar mean, Threw himself on my father? the expression being like Ascends me into the brain. But most eds. agree with Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 424): Theobald’s reading, him, is obviously required. Steevens (ed. 1793): There is tragick propriety in Kent’s throwing himself on the body of a deceased friend; but this propriety is lost in the act of clumsily tumbling a son over the lifeless remains of his father. Dyce (1844, p. 232): An incident more suited to a comic pantomime than to a serious narrative in a tragedy. The progress of the error here is plain;—him—’em…—me.

3168+12 puissant]
Schmidt (1875): Powerful (OED, a.).

3168+12 strings of life]
Schmidt (1874), heart-strings: The tendons supposed to brace and sustain the heart (OED, sb. pl.). Cf. n. 1029. Hoeniger (1992, pp. 145–6): The heart’s fibrous bands or stretching strings, described by Galen; extreme grief makes the heart-strings crack. Bayley (1908, pp. 241–2) and Kittredge (ed. 1940) provide many allusions to powerful emotions cracking the vital strings. Wilson (ed. 1960): Thus he enters (l. [3182]) a dying man. Or perhaps just weakened. Hunter (ed. 1972), questionably: Also vocal cords.…[cracked by] the violence of his outcry.

3168+13 twice…trumpets]
Capell (1783, 1.2:187) defends a singular, trumpet: That trumpet which call’d the speaker to combat. So Malone (ed. 1790): For one trumpet only had sounded. In fact the trumpet sounds several times between 3058 and 3065; perhaps Edgar means that he stayed with Kent until the second sound but then left him lest he not appear at the third sound (3067).

3168+14 traunst]
Entranced. Schmidt (1875): Seemingly dead; insensible (OED, Tranced ppl. a., quoting this l. as its first ex.).

3168+17 enemie]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Used as an adjective. Harrison (ed. 1948): Who had declared him an enemy. Muir (ed. 1952): Hostile.

3169 one]
F specifies a Gentleman.

3170–8 Helpe…it]
Q makes passable meter if lines 3177–8 are divided after the second Lady, or if 3176 is taken as a short line and poysoned is trisyllabic; F’s additions and repetitions result in the somewhat awkward 3174–6. Doran (1931, p. 54): With the omission from the folio of Edgar’s speeches, lines [3168+1–+18]…it became necessary to recast the verse of the following passage. Helpe, helpe, two monosyllabic exclamations, each with the value of a foot, had been used in the quarto to complete the half-line of Edgar’s speech. The reviser…gave Albany’s first line to Edgar, divided it, inserted an exhortation by Albany to Speake man, and also added to the Gentleman’s speech a third exclamation, O helpe, which would not have been necessary, but which furnished the new line with the required number of syllables. This new division of lines necessitated the addition of the words O she’s dead, which was done in such a way that the printer mistook the Gentleman’s speech…for prose. Albany’s next speech…was revised, evidently with the intention of increasing its effectiveness by the repetition of dead and Speake man. It was then left as a half-line, and she hath confest it altered to she confesses it in order to repair the meter. Doran’s division of Q 3177 at Lady, results in regular verse, if the extra unaccented syllables in the next line are elided. Van Dam (1935, pp. 68–9) proposes a clumsier relineation of Q, dividing of helpe,…smokes,…speake?; this gives 3170–1 four consecutive stressed syllables. David (1935, p. 107): The stuttering horror of the gentleman keeps the audience in greater suspense. Like Albany, they are desperate to know who actually is dead. They fear for Cordelia; their relief, at hearing that it is only Gonerill gone, is correspondingly great, and they are thus raised to a pitch of security which makes the final disaster all the more unexpected and terrible.

3170–3 Helpe…knife]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 87): It is conceivable that in the copy for Q [3171, 3173] were correctly assigned to Edgar: the headings in the copy for Q may have run: Gent. | Edg. | Gent. | Alb. | Gent. The compositor may have altered the first alternation from Gent./Edg. to Gent./Alb. owing to his eye having caught the next alternation (Gent./Alb.) too soon. Kirschbaum (1951, p. 171): It looks to me as though Q combined [3171] with [3173] because of telescoping, omitting 3172 because the single reporter of the Q text remembered it as occurring at 3176. On the unlikelihood that Q is a reported text, see . Halio (ed. 1992): F gives Edgar two speeches. By sharing the interrogation with Albany, he begins taking over responsibility for events. Surely in aiding his father, killing Oswald, seeking out Albany, volunteering to be his champion, and mortally wounding Edmund, Edgar has long since begun to take responsibility for events. So Foakes (ed. 1997): The text does not seem to me to justify such an interpretation, despite this slight strengthening of Edgar’s role in F. Weis (ed. 1993): Q’s version is dramatically more satisfactory because (1) it observes the proper decorum of the commander-in-chief (and not Edgar) questioning the Gentleman, and (2) Q eschews the repetition of Speak, man.

3170–3 Helpe]
Booth (1978, p. 101): Note that the gentleman…has no practical use for the help he asks.

3174–5 Its…dead]
On F’s lineation see nn. 2022–3, 3170–8.

3174 smokes]
Muir (ed. 1952): Steams. Wilson (ed. 1960): Fresh blood commonly smokes in Sh.

3175 O…dead.]
Steevens (ed. 1793): Added in F in defiance of metre and propriety. Rather, added to make a verse line with 3176; see n. 3170–8. Van Dam (1935, p. 69): This…insertion is laughable.…When one reads that a bloudy knife…comes from somebody’s heart, no reader needs the extra assurance that the sufferer is dead. Halio (ed. 1973): Looks like an interpolation, i.e. non-Shn.; cf. n. 2816. Hunter (ed. 1972): The failure to complete the statement allows the coup de théâtre of suggesting for a moment that it is Cordelia who is killed. Mahood (1992, p. 177): It has been suggested that the original audience would have taken [these words]…to refer to Cordelia, whose story, as they would have read it in The Faerie Queene, ends in suicide. But most of them would have been more familiar with the happy ending of King Leir than with Spenser’s aristocratic romance, and must have felt, as they learnt that Goneril and Regan had got their deserts, that a morally comforting conclusion was imminent. Weis (ed. 1993): With its almost pedantic extra half-line, F arguably weakens the pregnant dramatic pause.

3176 Alb.…speake?]
Delius (1876, p. 138): F’s Who dead? Speake, man., mutilated in Q, is necessary to introduce Albany’s Who dead? But Albany needs only 3174. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxvi) thinks that the Q line quicken[s] the action more than F’s.

3178 hath confest]
F’s confesses makes more regular meter. Boswell (ed. 1821): It is surely more proper to say that a person who is already dead hath confessed. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 163): The present tense is effective, emphasizing the Gentleman’s agitation. Weis (ed. 1993): [It] does not imply that Goneril is still alive.

3179–80 I…instant]
Gardner (1967, p. 18): His old sardonic wit flashes out. Possibly the lines should be divided after both, making two verse lines if the first two words of each are stressed.

3179 contracted]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Betrothed. Elton (1966, p. 134): A term possessing not only a physical but an ethical, legal, and metaphysical significance.

3180 marie]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Are united in death. Cf. 2293. Foakes (ed. 1997): The hint of sexual consummation provides a bitter irony.

3181–2 Edg.…Kent]
Collier (ed. 1843): In the folio the entrance of Kent is marked too early, and Here comes Kent, is erroneously placed before Produce the bodies, &c. The folio also places the bringing out of the bodies of Goneril and Regan too early. The quartos are right in this respect. Kirschbaum (1945, p. 73): In F Kent enters while Albany is concerned with the corpses. To have Kent enter, reminding us of Lear, at the very moment when we are already keyed up by the sisters’ deaths, is tremendous art. Brooke (ed. 1947): The Quarto…would seem to be more effective; but the metrical dove-tailing of speeches indicates that the Folio order was intentional. Weis (ed. 1993): Whereas Q’s timing fluidly interleaves the various strands of the dramatic action, F’s positioning of Edgar’s view of Kent ([3181]), immediately before Albany’s command to produce the bodies, results in a dialogue which awkwardly alternates between a recognition of Kent and a proper response to the deaths, and the appearance of the bodies on the stage. F’s decision earlier to dispense with Edgar’s account of meeting Kent renders Kent’s appearance here and F’s placing of it in the text unsatisfactory. Since Kent is in a weakened condition (see 3168+12–+14), the earlier entrance in F may be to allow him a slow advance, at cost of Albany’s ignoring him for three lines. So Muir (ed. 1952): He comes slowly down the stage while Albany is speaking. Brown (ed. 1976): Albany is so awed by events that…he does not see Kent until 3185. F’s lines scan well, whereas in Q 3189–90 is an extrametrical verse. Still, Q would scan perfectly if 3186 were left as a short line, and the following Q lines (3186–90) were divided as in F.

3181 sir]
F’s omission avoids a feminine ending. For Warren (1978, p. 104) it is evidence of the elevation of Edgar…and relative reduction of Albany in F. Thomas (1995, p. 574), however, points to Edgar’s deferential address to Albany at 3141, 3144, and 3090.

3183 Produce…bodies]
Granville-Barker (1927, p. 155) sees this direction, the removal of Edmund’s body at 3215, and Lear’s entrance with Cordelia as designed to repeat as in parody the opening scene of the play: The same company are here, or all but the same, and they await his pleasure. Rosenberg (1972, p. 309): But a personal motive insists, too; Albany will see the dead woman for whom he had his great love. Main (ed. 1962): A significant difference…is revealed visually on stage. The bodies of Goneril and Regan are brought in and deposited on stage; no one, not even Edmund, cares to touch these cadaverous demons.…Lear enters with Cordelia dead in his arms. Foakes (1993, p. 209): It is rare for bodies to be brought on. So it is an unusual and powerful theatrical moment.

3184 The bodies…in]
Doran (1931, p. 84): The F direction appears eight lines before the corresponding direction in the quarto so as to alert the prompter, who was responsible for the bodies’ appearance on stage; cf. n. 1358. Muir (ed. 1952): According to F the bodies are brought in here; it seems more natural to leave a short time, as Q does, for Albany’s order to be obeyed. Kirschbaum [1945, p. 72], who argues for the F arrangement, says that it is significant that Kent makes no comment on the bodies; but he does later ([3195]). Foakes (ed. 1997): Albany’s This judgement… ([3185]) becomes stronger if he can point to them. Hunter (ed. 1972): Q’s brought in reflects a literary copy not used for stage purposes, and F’s change from in to out implies a theatrical origin for the copy behind it; cf. 1217. Brown (ed. 1976): This entry takes time and tact if it is to be managed without raising unwanted laughs. Often it is cut entirely, with the loss of a significant echo of the first scene…[as Lear] will again stand surrounded by his three daughters. Halio (ed. 1992, p. 42 n.): F’s SD may suggest a litter or bier for each one, or perhaps dummies, if the actors were now needed as supers. Hodges (1999, pp. 165–7): It is impossible to suppose that they are simply brought on manhandled as bodies: they must be carried in on litters.…The drama has now entered its formal last phase, that is of tragic ceremonial. The two royal sisters have been brought back to set the scene,…making a proper tragic setting for the death of Lear with the dead Cordelia.

3185–6 This…pity]
Tyrwhitt (in Steevens, ed. 1778): If Shakespeare had studied Aristotle all his life, he would not perhaps have been able to mark with more precision the distinct operations of terror and pity. Delius (ed. 1854): Albany explains why he does not avoid bringing the bodies of Regan and Goneril into the view of the spectators (Ger.). Moberly (ed. 1876): We can calmly accept it [the judgment of the heavens] as true and righteous without wishing to alter or mitigate it. Halio (ed. 1992): This divine retribution is terrible (in swiftness and finality), but it does not evoke sorrow or compassion (since the victims deserved their fate).

3185 tremble]
F’s erroneous full stop is probably only a misprint (Doran, 1931, p. 105).

3186 tis]
F’s inversion is this makes no practical difference.

3187–8 time…vrges]
Hudson (ed. 1879): There is no time now for the interchange of courtesies which mere good-breeding requires, to say nothing of old friendship and affection.

3187 complement]
See n. 327–8.

3188 that]
On F’s Which see n. 235.

3188 very]
Hudson (ed. 1879): Mere.

3188 manners]
Schmidt (1875): Good breeding (OED, sb.1 7, quoting this l.).

3190 ay]
Valpy (ed. 1833): For ever (OED, adv. 1a). Wilson (ed. 1960): I.e. with his last breath. He c[oul]d not know that Lear w[oul]d himself be dying. Bransom (1934, p. 170): No doubt he expected and was prepared to be treated as a prisoner himself, for there was no further service he could render. Skillan (ed. 1967), comparing 2843+10–+11: The day is lost and he is ready for death. Hunter (ed. 1972): Whether [or not] Kent has a premonition of Lear’s death or assumes that his own death is imminent,…his dramatic task is done.

3192–3215 Great…awhile]
Brown (1988, pp. 161–2): To improve forward drive and sharpen focus on the main action, modern directors commonly cut most of these lines, particularly the short phrases that give an impression of a shared and dazed urgency—the brief questions, imperatives, affirmations, and exclamations, each one wrung out of need and forceful as an attempt to cope with and hold back disaster.…The strongest defense of Shakespeare’s full text would be to argue that a confused and urgent sense of crisis should be established before the king enters with Cordelia in his arms; men should be seen to be doing their ineffectual best.…Shakespeare seems to have found means to accentuate the passage of time and the increase of complexity. The entry of the dead bodies and the bearing off of Edmund…provide a slow visual augmentation of what urgent words might deal with too quickly for full comprehension.

3192 Duke.]
In Q, so called when he entered at 2982, but Alb. since then. There seems to be no significant reason why he is once again Duke for the rest of the play. Blayney (1982, p. 142): The change may be a simple expedient adopted because the A box [in the compositor’s case] was empty. Taylor (1983, pp. 326, 485) notes a larger pattern: Duke is used in 1.4, 2.1, 2.2, 2.4, and 5.3; but…Cornwall and Albany are used in 3.5, 3.7, 4.2, and 5.1.

3192 forgot]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): This amnesia on everybody’s part is necessary for the climax that follows, but—though the audience thinks little of it—the reader always feels a shock. Orgel (ed. 1999, p. xlii): Cordelia and Lear are killed as much by passive forgetfulness as by active villainy. Muir (ed. 1952): But, after all, there is no reason why Albany should expect that Lear and Cordelia were in danger; and he had had plenty to occupy his mind during the wasted ten minutes. Foakes (ed. 1997): I have heard members of an audience titter with nervous laughter on this line.

3194 obiect]
See n. 1268. Muir (ed. 1952): Kirschbaum [1945, p. 73], defending the Folio through thick and thin, takes this to refer to Edmund, lying wounded. It is more natural for it to refer to the bodies of Goneril and Regan, especially when one takes Edmund’s next speech into consideration. He is really answering Kent’s question. The bodies are brought on to the stage so that Lear can be confronted with his three daughters, as in the first scene of the play. Nonetheless Urkowitz (1980, pp. 119–21), insisting that The bodies have been onstage for ten lines, prefers to believe that Albany momentarily turns away from the issue of Lear and Cordelia…prompted [only] by some eruption of concern within himself.…He does not try to help them and then fail; he simply does not try. This disjointed timing in F, Urkowitz argues, dramatizes Albany’s growing irresolution and ineffectiveness in the last Act (though as commander-in-chief he has defeated the invading army), a change in characterization resulting from authorial revision. Similarly Halio (ed. 1992): Albany reveals an inability from here on in to take effective and timely action. The bodies cannot have been on stage for ten lines (since 3184) if Albany’s order to bring them in occurs the instant before (3183). Attendants would have to exit, lift the bodies, and then carry them across the stage to Albany and Kent—a process that would take up the twenty seconds needed to speak the intervening lines before the present one. Foakes (ed. 1997): It is understandable that for Albany the death of his wife and Regan, and their bodies on stage, the horrible object or spectacle that confronts him, absorbs his immediate attention. His reaction, it seems to me, hardly justifies the claim of ineffectiveness. Senes (1997, p. 65) imagines that the whole line is spoken by Edmund, desirous for some reason to demonstrate to Kent that he was eventually more loved (i.e., by Goneril and Regan) than he seemed when introduced by his embarrassed father in 1.1—an odd concern for a dying man who has not seen Kent (as far as he knows in F) since that brief introduction.

3196 Yet]
See n. 245. Moberly (ed. 1876): Yet even this sight shows that I, baseborn as I was, had some to love me. Harrison (ed. 1948): The bastard’s last grim triumph—two women died for his love. Muir (ed. 1952): Heilman [1948], p. 244, remarks that Edmund’s sole thought is of himself. But it is a brilliant stroke to reveal here that Edmund’s career of crime was caused by his feeling that he was not loved. Gardner (ed. 1969): With a touch of irony he asserts his fulfilment. And the good deed…follows upon the surprised recognition, as if from outside his nature.…It is one of Shakespeare’s moments of revelation, when the vicious and the sordid becomes a grace. The fleeting effect is heightened by the emotionally worn, enigmatic agreement of Albany. Conceivably Yet is a misreading of Yt = That, which makes an answer to Kent’s question; cf. n. 3214. Halio (ed. 1992): Edmond’s boast…deeply wounds Albany, who utters a terse Even so.

3198 after]
Wright (ed. 1875): Afterwards (OED, adv. 2).

3199 Euen so]
Bransom (1934, p. 170): Not an answer to Edmund’s remark, but a humble acquiescence in the judgment of heaven. Cf. n. 1396. Foakes (ed. 1997): May mark a pause as he looks at the bodies; the phrase extends the line into a hexameter.

3199 couer their faces]
Hodges (1999, p. 165): The coverings [a rich ceremonious pall, of black or purple, embroidered and fringed with gold] are drawn up fully over their heads. Darton (ed. 1928) here directs, The biers are borne out again; but see n. 3194.

3200 pant for life]
Deighton (ed. 1891): To be allowed sufficient time to save Lear and Cordelia. More probably, simply gasp for life (Herford, ed. 1899).

3200–1 good…nature]
Elton (1966, p. 146): Although Edmund’s last-minute prise de conscience anticipates the Restoration libertine conversions, also notable for their improbability, Shakespeare employs the conventional repentance device for his own ironical purposes. Edmund’s contrition…arrives too late to save his victim. Thompson (1971, p. 132): This may be the Vice-like Edmund’s last mischievous act, ironically designed to fail and thereby increase the agony of the others present. But he cannot know it will fail. Murphy (1984, pp. 214–16) is instead inclined to believe the deathbed language of the ars moriendi: At least here is a drama of redemption. Dent (1981) compares the proverb Bastards by chance are good, by nature bad (B104).

3201 nature]
See n. 185.

3202 brief, int]
Wright (ed. 1875): Be quick about it. Q1’s comma has been misplaced before int. Doran (1931, p. 23) notes the clever way in which the [Q1] passage has been made intelligible in Q2: Q1’s int toth’ castle…Tis becomes into the Castle…tis.

3202 castle]
Delius (ed. 1854): Dover castle, whither he has sent the prisoners. Perrett (1904, p. 262): Believed in Sh.’s days to date from pre-Roman times, citing Lyly, Euphues and his England (ed. Bond, 2:35).

3202 writ]
Cf. 2970. Foakes (ed. 1997): The proper legal term.

3203 is on]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Has been issued against.

3203 Cordelia]
On the scansion see n. 47.

3204 Nay]
See n. 630.

3205–7 Runne…repreeue]
Brown (ed. 1976): Albany panics, giving a wild order to the nearest soldier. Edgar is equally urgent but more collected.

3206–8 To…Captaine]
Anticipating Taylor (1983, p. 51), Doran (1931, p. 111) finds it striking that Q2 and F differ from Q1 in mislining 3206 and omitting the Captaine from 3208, though she then notes that F and Q2 immediately differ in the division of 3208–9 and the assignment of 3210. The double agreement of Q2 and F may, however, be mere coincidence. A passable verse line might naturally end with a question mark, thereby making both 3206 and 3207 coincide with complete sentences; such a pattern is so common that the change may have been made unconsciously or automatically; and the phrase the Captaine has seemed redundant and dispensable to almost all eds. Evans (1976, p. 54), however: The two words (the Captaine) complete metrically what is otherwise a four-stress line; and…pointed with a period after sword and a dash after Captaine, they help through dramatic broken syntax to stress Edmund’s exhausted state of mind, speculating further that Q2 may reflect an unknown state of Q1 that omitted the words.

3206 To who]
On the lack of inflection see n. 555.

3206 Lord]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Spoken to Alb.; Edg. never calls Edm. my lord. But the rest of the speech must be addressed to Edmund, who alone knows the answer to the question and can authoritatively countermand his own order.

3206 office]
Schmidt (1875): Who is on duty? See n. 1046. More precisely, Deighton (ed. 1891): Who has been commissioned to carry out your order? (OED, sb. 2b: Task to be performed). Wilson (ed. 1960): Sc. of killing them.

3208–10 take…Duke.]
Given the complete lack of exit and entrance directions here in Q and F, and the fact that F’s reassignment of Albany’s speech to Edg. at 3210 requires Edgar to remain on stage, there is much disagreement about who takes Edmund’s sword, who runs off to save Lear and Cordelia, and who if anyone returns with Lear at his entrance at 3216. Earlier eds., following Theobald (see textual n.), who follows F at 3210, send a messenger or soldier to the castle; those assuming that Edgar is the proper agent give him an exit at 3210, maintaining that F’s reassignment of 3210 to Albany was erroneous. Capell (1783, 1.2:187) scorns Theobald’s arrangement because it makes Edgar inconsistent: Edgar, whom we see [3206–7]…so feelingly alert about Lear, becomes quite another thing…within the space of a line or two; and, instead of flying himself to preserve him,…sends a simple attendant, a messenger. Similarly Sisson (1956, 2:244): This was no task for an Officer, and Edgar shows that it was he whom Albany ordered to run. He re-enters with Lear and Cordelia at l. [3216]. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 191): Edgar’s words at lines [3206–7] suggest that it is to him that Albany has said run, run, O run; and in lines [3209–10] it appears to be Edgar that Edmund instructs to take his sword and give it to the Captain. Obviously if it is Edgar who goes to the castle he cannot speak [3210]. Malone (ed. 1790): In the folio this speech [3210] is improperly assigned to Edgar, who had the moment before received the token of reprieve, which Edmund enjoined him to give the officer in whose custody Lear was. So Collier (ed. 1843): All [Qq] assign Haste…life to Albany, and not to Edgar as in the folio: Edgar was the person dispatched, and the words are, therefore, addressed to him. Not all agree. Munro (ed. 1957): Edgar, who has interrogated Edmund, receives the sword from him and is bidden hand it to the attendant Captain.…Note that in Q (l. [3239]) it is the Captain, who reports what has happened within. Rather, it is a Captain (Gent. in F), who presumably enters before or with or behind Lear having witnessed Lear kill the hangman; but there is nothing to indicate that this is the same person sent off to the castle with Edmund’s sword only five lines before Lear enters. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 526): The only character other than Lear who later shows knowledge of what went on off stage is the Cap. [Gent. in F] who speaks at [3239]; this cannot be Edmund’s Captain [2969] (presumably the slaue that was a hanging thee), and one would expect the person dispatched to save Lear to be the one who re-enters with him and reports on off-stage events. Edgar could exit with this Captain, but there is no need for him to do so, and he reacts to Lear’s entrance—just as Albany and Kent do. Moreover, one does not want Lear’s most important entrance to be cluttered with attendants: one is necessary, but two (including a major character) would be superfluous and unfortunate. Mahood (1992, pp. 177–8): For one thing, Edgar is weighed down with armour. For another, it is preferable for him to be prominent among the stage audience of Lear’s entry, rather than to slink back in Lear’s wake as modern stage directions imply he does. Edgar needs to be near Albany and Kent so that all three may speak almost chorically in response to Lear’s outcry. One minimal character, however, seems made for this messenger role: Curan, the political busybody.…If the speaker [of 3239] is identical with the Messenger, the short time he has been offstage makes his testimony implausible, unless some silent action has been inserted, such as Albany intervening to prevent Kent from killing Edmund when he confesses to his plot upon Cordelia’s life. An attractive possibility is for these words to be spoken by the faithful Gentleman who helped Lear’s recovery in Act 4 and who can be thought of as sharing his master’s captivity.
For so much speculation there is little supporting fact. Edgar urges Edmund to send a token but does not necessarily give it to him. We do not know to whom Albany says Runne…runne; he may say it a captain, gentleman, or other messenger whose exit Edgar alertly forestalled until Edmund provided the necessary information and an identifying token. Either Albany or Edgar might urge that person Hast…life. Edgar may wish to remain with the dying brother whose mortal wound he is responsible for. It is unclear who if anyone enters with Lear. Edgar seems to react to the sight of Lear as Kent and Albany do at 3224–6, and perhaps all three nobles are on stage and react together in horror and dismay as Lear enters alone with Cordelia; but possibly Edgar is only confirming the reactions of the other two as he re-enters with Lear. If the Captain/Gentleman who speaks at 3239 is the messenger sent out at 3210, and if he re-enters with or after Lear at 3216, he has apparently run to Dover castle, witnessed Lear’s execution of the hangman, and returned alongside Lear within the time taken to speak five lines. Since that is impossible, he may be another of Albany’s men who has witnessed the events in Dover Castle before accompanying or following Lear to Albany. The most that the evidence allows one to say is that at 3205 Albany urges someone to run; that Edgar insists that that messenger (himself or another) be properly instructed and carry a token of reprieve; that Edmund complies; that either Albany (in Q) urges that messenger (Edgar or another) to hurry, or (in F) Edgar urges haste to someone besides himself; that Lear enters at 3216 either alone or with one or more others; that if he is not alone he may be accompanied by Edgar, and/or the messenger sent to save him, or by someone else who witnessed Lear’s execution of the hangman; and that eventually this latter person confirms that act at 3239. It is entirely possible that except for the reassignment of 3210, the staging of F is exactly the same as that of Q, and that Edgar remains on stage throughout, reacting along with Albany and Kent to Lear’s entrance.

3208 sword]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): As proof that you are the bearer of orders from me.

3208–9 take…Captaine?]
Most eds. consider the repetition of the Captaine in Q1 an error; thus Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 424): The compositor has set up the two last words of the speech…too soon, and has repeated them in their proper place. Furness (ed. 1880), however: Noteworthy is the dramatic reading of Q1, followed by Jennens [ed. 1770]: Take my sword, The captain—give it the captain. Noteworthy also is that in Q1 Edgar’s lines 3208–10 make two complete and fairly regular verse lines; in F 3207 and 3208 are both metrically short. Halio (ed. 1992): [F] Compositor E was [likely] influenced by Q2, whose compositor tried to correct the syntax, save space (making [3209–10] one line), and avoid what seemed to him an awkward and unnecessary repetition. Edmond’s gasping repetition [in Q], however, is dramatically effective and helps make the next line [3209–10] metrically complete, though half an iamb in [3208] is sacrificed.

3209 Giue…Captaine]
Nielson (1993, pp. 16–17): A villainously indeterminate line, meaning either to hand over or to make an attack. If the Gentleman hands the sword to Edmund’s hired murderer, he will probably be slain; if Edmund miraculously survives, he can claim he meant the murderer to be attacked. Nielson does not believe in Edmund’s conversion or redemption, nor, apparently, in the truth of deathbed statements.

3210 Duke.]
The speech seems more consistent with Albany’s urgent haste in 3205 than with Edgar’s cool presence of mind in 3206–7; for other reasons to suspect that F’s Edg. is a misassignment, see n. 3208–10. Doran (1931, p. 81) finds the reassignment insignificant. Critics holding that F is revised to elevate Edgar and reduce Albany (cf. n. 3194) find the reassignment of great significance. Warren (1978, p. 104): The transfer of the command…gives Edgar a more active role in the urgent events. Urkowitz (1980, p. 121): The Folio variant serves again to leave Albany only the speech [3205] indicating his inner turmoil, removing the speech [3210] that in the Quarto indicates some degree of effective participation in the rescue effort. Rejecting such significance, Thomas (1995, p. 575): It is Albany who gives the first decisive command [3205].…Edgar’s words merely echo Albany’s. Moreover, throughout v.3 it is always Albany who is in command, and directs the necessary action, citing 2984–9, 2997–9, 3027–34, 3035–41. In F this speech may simply have been assigned the wrong prefix, a common error. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 191): At lines [3206] and [3208] two consecutive speeches are assigned to Edg. and Bast.: the next two speeches (lines [3210] and [3211]) should be assigned to Alb. and Bast.: but the F compositor may carelessly have repeated the Edg./Bast. alternation (a compositor’s memorial error). Hunter (ed. 1972): Edgar must be placed on the stage beside Edmund; he takes the sword from him and gives it, with his instructions, to the Officer. But he might give the sword silently as Albany urges haste.

3210 Hast thee]
Abbott (§212): Verbs followed by thee instead of thou have been called reflexive.…Haste thee, and some other phrases with verbs of motion, may be thus explained; cf. Franz §§283, 307, 628. See also n. 194.

3210 for thy life]
Deighton (ed. 1891) interprets this as a threat: If you value your life (OED, sb. 3c); but it may be a mere asseveration (OED, 3d).

3211 thy wife]
The commission has seemed to be Edmund’s alone: see 2912–15, 2981, 3202. Bransom (1934, p. 172) finds this detail very ugly.

3212–14 hang…selfe]
Perrett (1904, pp. 92, 240 ff.) finds the origin of Cordelia’s manner of death in Spenser (see ); p. 242: Wherever, outside FQ, the manner of suicide is specified, it is by the steel. Muir (ed. 1952, p. xxxiv; 1957, p. 143): Perhaps suggested to Spenser by his need for a rhyme (long-hong).

3213 vpon]
See n. 960.

3213 despaire]
Suicide is the sin of despair. Muir (ed. 1952, p. xxxv) compares Despair’s inciting Cordila to suicide in Higgins’s Mirour; see . Bullough (1973, p. 298): In Leir the theme appears only briefly, citing 1656–7 (where Leir voices only resignation) and 2073–82, and adding, Shakespeare shifts the condition to Gloucester; see , . Cf. nn. 1835, 2475, 2932, 3120, 3154, 3260.

3214 That]
Tovey (ed. 1896): (And say) that she, etc.; or it may be an amplification of despair—(which caused) that, etc. As probably it introduces an adverbial clause modifying lay the blame: OED (conj. 2b): Introducing a clause expressing the cause, ground, or reason of what is stated in the principal clause.

3214 fordid]
Steevens (ed. 1773): Foredo, signifies to destroy (OED, v. 1). As Malone (ed. 1790) points out, Cordelia committed suicide in Geoffrey of Monmouth; so she did in Polydore Vergil, Holinshed, Higgins, and Spenser (see Perrett, 1904, pp. 240–6, and , , , ). Skottowe (1824, p. 119): The poet judiciously evaded the termination of Cordelia’s life by such revolting means as suicide. Chambers (1940, p. 24): Logically the words should surely be their own despair, that they for did themselves.…So intent is [Sh.] on contradicting this current story that he allows Lear (for the moment) to slip out of the memory of his audience. Muir (ed. 1952, p. xxxvii): The suicide of Cordelia would have been intolerable to a sensitive audience [as a mortal sin of despair; see n. 3213], and her murder necessitated the punishment of the guilty: Goneril and Regan could not be suffered to escape, if Cordelia were to die; and Lear could not, without anticlimax, be restored to the throne.

3215 defend]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Forbid (OED, v. 3), thinking that her refers to Goneril. Almost certainly it refers to Cordelia, the sole subject of the previous three lines. Bradley (1904, p. 326): I might almost say that the moral of King Lear is presented in the irony of this collocation of Albany’s wish and Lear’s immediate entrance with the dead Cordelia. Muir & Danby (1950, p. 50): Plangus’s repeated question, Must Erona dye? and his complaint that the gods fail to answer prayers [Sidney, Arcadia, 2.12.[2]; see ]…may be compared with the juxtaposition of Albany’s prayer for the safety of Lear and Cordelia and Lear’s entrance with her dead body.

3215 beare him hence]
Craik (1984, p. 49): It was perhaps to emphasize this visual effect [of Lear reunited with his daughters] that Shakespeare had Edmund borne off stage to die. He may also have considered that four bodies were quite enough to remove at the close. Furthermore, since it was Edmund’s remorse that had prompted the attempt to save Lear and Cordelia, Lear’s entry with Cordelia’s body would demand an emotional response of some kind…an unwelcome distraction of the audience’s attention.

3216 Enter…]
Rosenberg (1972, pp. 310–12) recounts actors’ various manners of entrance here—passionate, solemn, nervously energetic, exhausted, etc. Macaulay (1907, p. 29): There is nothing like this last scene in the world. [Dr.] Johnson [who found Lear’s and Cordelia’s deaths unbearable] talks nonsense. Torn to pieces as Lear’s heart had been, was he to live happily ever after…? Wonderful as the whole play is, this last passage is the triumph of Shakespeare’s genius. Bradley (1904, pp. 252–3, 271): Such a tragic catastrophe as this should seem inevitable. But this catastrophe, unlike those of all the other mature tragedies, does not seem at all inevitable. It is not even satisfactorily motived.…It is as if Shakespeare said to us: Did you think weakness and innocence have any chance here? Were you beginning to dream that? I will show you it is not so. Lewis (1927, p. 180): [Bradley] implies that in this irony there is no ultimate despair, but rather that it is to be referred to a christian optimism. That does not seem likely.…But the punctual arrival of Cordelia…cannot be anything but what it forces us at once to see it as: an expression of the poet’s mockery at the vanity of human supplications, and notions of benevolent powers. Granville-Barker (1927, p. 183): The main tragic truth about life, to the Shakespeare that wrote King Lear, was its capricious cruelty. And what meeter sacrifice to this than Cordelia? Empson (1951, p. 150): With Lear and Cordelia the whole movement of necessity is finished and we last saw him planning a life of mystical gaiety. The death[’s]…shock and senselessness (…essential to the effect) are as far as Chehov from normal tragedy. Harbage (1963, p. 429): Without it, the victory of right would seem fortuitous and false, and the emotions we have felt exorbitant and irrelevant; indeed the work would soon fade from our minds as a grotesque curiosity. The play ends as it has to end. Elton (1966, p. 254): The ritual aspect of Lear’s dead march, his entrance carrying Cordelia in his arms, is matched by the verbal accompaniment of his blasphemous defiance of the gods.…Shakespeare seems deliberately striving for fidelity to heathen life and experience as the Renaissance could have understood them. Vitale (1968, pp. 142–4): Cordelia’s martyrdom and Edgar’s succession [which is doubtful; see n. 3295] are predetermined necessities: Her desire to help her father is irrelevant since he is technically no longer king, he has not appealed to her for help, and…she cannot plead a usurped crown as a justification for the invasion. However, with Goneril and Regan dead, she becomes, by right of birth, the next in line to the throne. This creates an intolerable situation. The wife of the King of France has brought a foreign army on to British soil, has in fact committed a treasonable act, however loyal her motives: she cannot be allowed to live to reign over the land. She does in all the sources, however. Holloway (1961, pp. 86–8): By the middle of Act IV…something of an ordinary tragic action has been completed.…If we ask what extends the play further, the Book of Job reveals the answer. Adelman (1973, pp. 9–10): Lear begins with a dramatic logic so taut that the end in illogic is almost intolerably disturbing. Old men who do not have faith in their good children and who trust instead to the aural and ocular evidence of their evil children will cast out the good children and be badly treated by the evil ones. The plot is shocking but inexorable: there is nothing accidental or gratuitous here. But suddenly this logical rigor of plot collapses.…Lear enters with the dead body of Cordelia in his arms; and our sense of order is forever shattered. There is neither narrative nor moral necessity for her death.…We have been caught up in the working out of a providential scheme when a perfectly gratuitous act destroys this scheme.…It is no wonder that Dr. Johnson found the death of Cordelia too shocking to watch; it shatters our sense of a coherent universe in a way that no conceptual assertion can repair. Booth (1978, pp. 101–2): The most terrifying five minutes in literature have begun for the audience.…Shakespeare has presented an action that is serious, of undoubted magnitude, and complete; he now…presents the culminating events of his story after his play is over.

3216 Cordelia…armes]
For many commentators, symbolic. Freud (1913; 1925, p. 256): Cordelia is Death.…Eternal wisdom, in the garb of primitive myth, bids the old man renounce love, choose death and make friends with the necessity of dying.…It is in vain that the old man yearns after the love of woman as once he had it from his mother; the third of the Fates alone, the silent goddess of Death, will take him in her arms. Nowottny (1960, p. 56): Visual language reaches sublimity here…bringing the whole plot to its point.…We see in an instant of time Lear’s sin and its retribution, the wider evil that has struck both, the full fatherhood of Lear bearing his child in his arms whilst at the same time the natural course of life is seen reversed (Lear senile, so lately cared for by Cordelia), the world’s destruction of the love and forgiveness that had transcended it.…Those suggestions of a saviour’s death [in 4.6]…now make it inescapable that Cordelia dead in her father’s arms and displayed by him to the world should strike deeply into responses that lie midway between religion and art. Gardner (1967, p. 28): A secular Pietà. Battenhouse (1969, p. 288): Reminiscent of many a medieval painting of the Deposition from the Cross. So also Mack (1965, p. 116), Reibetanz (1974, p. 43), who compares the endings of Marston’s Sophonisba (1605) and Chapman’s Bussy D’Ambois (1604), and Milward (1973, p. 101). Brockbank (1976, p. 120), however: We do not see Cordelia’s death as a prefiguration, we experience it as a representative event of human history. Kinney (1980, p. 25): Inverse Pieta. Linville (1990, p. 317): Cordelia finds her ultimate bridegroom in Death, as Lear’s act of carrying her onstage in his arms—the ritual of the bridegroom and his bride—figures forth, in an ultimate tableau of vanitas.…Freud’s association of Cordelia both with the Hours and with Death is replaced by an identification of Lear as [devouring] Time and Death. The identification must be imperfect if Death claims Lear a few moments later. Peat (1980, p. 51): The tension created by the reverse Pietà stems from an emblem of death that contains a promise of rebirth.…Throughout the remainder of the scene, the possibility that Cordelia lives remains open and the audience continue to alternate between hope and despair. Honigmann (1984, pp. 57, 59–60; 1989, pp. 90–2): [Sh.] stops short of identifying Cordelia as a Christ figure.…The word dead was first inserted by Nicholas Rowe in 1709…and Rowe could not have followed a stage-tradition here, since Tate’s adaptation was the only version of the play acted in the theatre from 1681, and in Tate’s version Cordelia did not die.…Cordelia…may equally be alive when Lear carries her on in his arms.…She is unable to speak.…Perhaps her neck is broken.…[The ensuing scene] recapitulates the father’s and daughter’s earlier attempts to get through to one another, and repeats the tragic message that we are all locked away within ourselves. The first clue the audience hears, however—Lear’s unambiguous shees gone for euer…Shees dead as earth does not prepare the audience to continue to alternate between hope and despair for her life (Peat, 1980, p. 51); and clearly none of the bystanders on the stage thinks that she is alive. For most of the next fifty lines Lear ignores her body completely, as if his hopes were small or none, and apparently imagines signs of life only in F’s added final phrases. Nonetheless Williamson (1983, pp. 414–17): Cordelia’s hanging, which is not in the majority of the sources, adds the horror of indignity, but its interruption by Lear also allows the possibility that she was still (if barely) alive, though strangulated. It is at least arguable that Shakespeare decides on the manner of Cordelia’s death precisely because it would allow uncertainty as to the outcome.…Shakespeare may have intended us to feel that Lear is right…not to give up hope. Foakes (1993, p. 210): The symbolism of the scene requires that she must be [dead],…as the presence on stage of all three of [Lear’s] children shows what he has brought upon himself.…Kent, Albany and Edgar see his entrance carrying her as an image of…the end of the world, for they and we know she is dead. Idem (ed. 1997): But all that follows depends upon a measure of uncertainty, both in Lear and in the audience, who may hope against hope until the very end that Cordelia will revive. As for her being alive but unable to speak, Would an audience spot this?

3216 in his armes]
Sprague (1944, p. 296): Kean…knelt on his right knee…, laying her on the ground, and kneeling on both knees.…Morley speaks of his nursing and rocking of the body of Cordelia and the tenderness with which he lays her down.…Salvini…entered dragging her …as a weak old man. Wilson (ed. 1960): Lear, I think, lays the body down on the front stage, and then speaks, standing over her. See also Rosenberg (1972, pp. 311–12), Bratton (ed. 1987). In Ronald Harwood’s The Dresser (1981), the actor (modeled on Donald Wolfit) playing Lear auditions his Cordelia by seeing if he can lift her. In his television performance of 1983 a weakened Olivier needed to have her flown on wires.

3217 Howle…stones]
Usually performed as an extended cry of anguish, but it could be a last command that others howl out their grief (Foakes, ed. 1997), as in the National Theatre production in 1990, where Brian Cox went quietly up to a number of the people on stage, quietly urging them to howl, speaking the word as if in some perplexity as to why they were not howling (Holland, 1997, p. 45). Rosenberg (1972, p. 312): Howl is not articulated usually as a word; rather, as a voiced pain, often an animal ululation,…an anguished cry,…a quiet sobbing,…a deep baying,…the wail of a wolf,…of a mourning dog. See also n. 2629. Black (1980, p. 40): Unaccommodated language. Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 88) identifies the repetition as epizeuxis; cf. 3280. Q’s line is decasyllabic; F’s omission of one howle does little to make it more regular, unless O your are was to be read as one unaccented syllable. The F line is crowded, but since there is room for a turnunder the omission need not be from compositorial choice. Hogan (1962, p. 76): F [i.e., Compositor E] saw that he could not fit another howle into his line, even if he wanted to. Shortening the heading to Le., setting it further out, and correcting your to you would not have sufficed. He could of course have tucked down stones, but this is a procedure he does not care for.…Metrical considerations surely prove that Q is right. Werstine (1983, p. 285): There is double warrant for adopting the Quarto Lear reading into the Folio text: the shortness of space in the line and the parallel omission [also by Compositor E] from Romeo [3.2.37 (1684)] of the second repetition of hees dead.

3217 you]
On F’s obvious error your see n. 867.

3217 stones]
Walker (1860, 1:237–41) cites many exx. of the addition of final s in Sh., supposing that, if it is an error at all, it is due to some peculiarity of Shakespeare’s handwriting. Cf. esp. MV 4.1.31 (1936), harts of flints [Q, F], and R3 3.7.224 (2444), I am not made of Stones. Muir & Danby (1950, p. 50) compare Sidney’s Arcadia 2.12.[2] (see ): Griefe is the stone which finest iudgement proues: | For who grieues not hath but a blockish braine. Muir (ed. 1952, p. xl f. and ad loc.): Shakespeare may have been thinking of the story of Deucalion as told by Ovid in Meta. 1.[381–416]. Bate (1989; 1993, pp. 191, 236) compares Niobe (Meta. 6.[273–312]). Elton (1966, p. 275) cites Tilley M172—He that cannot be angry is no Man (a fool)—and, showing how often the image is used in contemporary criticisms of stoicism, concludes, As Edgar has been shown…to provide indications contrary to Stoicism, so Lear, whom he parallels, repudiates such unfeeling impassiveness. Neither Tilley nor Dent (1981) cites this l. Hunter (ed. 1972): The primary idea here is of statues, silent, frozen (in horror) and impermeable by grief; see the next n. Cf. R3 3.7.25 (2238): like dumbe Statues, or breathing Stones. Anderson (1987, p. 14 n.) compares Spenser, F.Q. 5.Pro.2, men…transformed into hardest stone. In Tom a Lincoln (ca. 1611) 2000 the grieving Caelia accuses her ladies of lack of feeling: O yow are made of stone. Proudfoot (1992, p. xxviii) suspects she echoes this line.

3218 eyes]
Hunter (ed. 1972): It is not clear how they could use their eyes to make heaven’s vault crack, except that tongues used for outcry and eyes used for weeping come irresistibly together. Perhaps the only point made is that Lear’s eyes are failing him. Edwards (ed. 1975): Eyes here are for seeing as well as weeping. If I were in your place, seeing what you see, my tongue would lament and my eyes would weep, so that, etc. Halio (ed. 1992): Perhaps for lightning looks.

3219 vault…cracke]
The same image as at 3168+8–+9. OED (Vault sb.1 1c): The apparent concave surface formed by the sky, quoting this l. Hunter (ed. 1972) alone: The over-all image…may be that of a funerary chapel or pantheon with statues and a vault: but as this is heaven’s vault an intentional confusion between the living and the dead is created.

3221 lend…glasse]
Heilman (1948, p. 55): His words…recall the joke of the Fool in 1686–7. Halio (ed. 1992): Someone may actually give Lear a glass (perhaps one that Gonerill wears [see nn. 2308, 3227]), or he hallucinates having one about him. If he has a glass, why does he refer to a feather four lines later? Shickman (1991, pp. 85–6) less convincingly associates this mirror with the Fool (Foakes, ed. 1997).

3222 If that]
On added that see n. 273 and OED (If conj. 5, quoting this l.).

3222 mist]
On transitive verbs formed from nouns see n. 1197. OED (v.1 2): To cover…as with mist, quoting this l.

3222 staine]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Blur with moisture.

3222 stone]
Delius (ed. 1854): Metal mirror. Idem (ed. 1872): Crystal mirror. Deighton (ed. 1891): Stone, of which formerly mirrors were often made. Craig (ed. 1901): A mirror of polished stone or crystal. OED (sb. 2f): A mirror, quoting only this l., but referring to specular stone, OED (Specular a. 1): A transparent or semi-transparent substance formerly used as glass…; a species of mica, selenite, or talc; (1b): A piece of this used as a mirror. Steevens (ed. 1778) first notes the use of a mirror or feather (both are named) to detect living breath in Webster’s White Devil [1612] 5.2.38–9. Like Frost (1968, pp. 149–50), Halio (ed. 1992): Webster doubtless recalled Shakespeare’s scene. Whalley (in Reed, ed. 1785) notes the test of a feather in 2H4 4.5.31–4 (2554–7). Turner (privately): Such use of both mirrors and feathers is referred to in Helkiah Crooke, Mikrokosmographia (1631, p. 253). See also n. 3227.

3224–5 promist end…horror]
According to an unknown 18th-c. author, Says Kent,…Is this the end promis’d to filial obedience?…Edg. goes on,…pointing to the bodies of Gonerill and Regan,…where horror is put for death. Steevens (ed. 1773): Is this the conclusion…such as the present turn of affairs seemed to promise? Or is it only, replies Edgar, a representation of that horror which we suppose to be real? Davies (1783, 2:325): Do all my hopes of Lear’s restoration end in his distraction and the death of Cordelia? Similarly Halliwell (ed. 1865): The reference…is to the unexpected catastrophe, so unlooked for just at the moment when everything seemed to promise a happy termination to the innocent and injured parties. Empson (1951, p. 151): Kent…might mean the death in religious peace which Lear had aimed at by renouncing the kingdom. Foakes (ed. 1997): Or his own anticipated death, citing 3190. But most eds. think Kent and Edgar refer to the same thing: The horror of which this sight was an image, according to Edgar, is—the horror of the last day, or day of judgment, call’d emphatically—that horror (Capell, 1783, 1.2:188). Although an allusion to the Christian idea of Judgment would be anachronistic, Wordsworth (1864, p. 303) remembers that the heathen had their Sibylline verses and prophetical books, and that both Lucan and Ovid foretell of prodigies, and of the conflagration of the world, at the last day. Mason (1785, pp. 357–8): In St. Mark’s Gospel [Mark 13], when Christ foretells to his disciples the end of the world, and is describing to them the signs that were to precede,…he says, For in those days shall be affliction such as was not from the beginning of creation…[and] Now the brother shall betray the brother to death, and the father the son; and children shall rise up against their parents, and shall cause them to be put to death. For previous apocalyptic imagery in the play see nn. 441–2, 1661–4, and cf. 2577–8. Henley (apud Eccles, ed. 1792): Does not the exclamation [from Kent]…refer to the confidence expressed in her letter to himself…[paraphrasing 1245–7]? As the words…were not addressed to Edgar, there is no necessity for considering them as understood by him in their proper sense: his resumption, therefore, or rather adaptation of them, may not only admit, but even require, a different interpretation.…Though the passage of St. Mark…does not refer to the end of the world…but to the destruction of Jerusalem and the Jewish state, yet the prediction itself is vulgarly received in the sense in which [Mason] applies it. Moberly (ed. 1876) compares Young Clifford’s expostulation on finding the body of his father, 2H6 5.2.40–3 (3262–5). Wordsworth (1864, p. 232) and Noble (1935, p. 232) cite Matt. 24:6–13 and 1 Pet. 4:7; Foakes (ed. 1997) adds Luke 21. Munro (ed. 1957) compares 2 Pet. 3:10: The heavẽs shal passe away with a noyce.…The earth with the workes, that are therein, shalbe burnt vp (Geneva). Fraser (1962, p. 80): Chaos is the absence of the justice which is order.…The emblem of that confusion is Doomsday. Elton (1966, pp. 291–2): May carry overtones not only of the Last Judgment but perhaps also of the well-known Stoic notion concerning the anticipated periodical consumption (ecpyrosis) of the entire world, citing contemporary discussions. Hunter (ed. 1972): Kent may also mean the end that Lear promised himself when he divided the kingdom. Apparently Edgar does not so understand the line, since the horror of the present scene is much more than an image of that in the play’s opening scene. Rosenberg (1972, p. 313): Hope [that Cordelia lives] is dashed against the dismay of Kent, Edgar, Albany.…No mistaking this implication: her certain death, Lear’s fool’s hope, reflect the final dissolution of the world, chaos, the Last Judgment. Miola (1992, p. 170): Perhaps echoing Mary of the Wakefield/Towneley pageant as she beholds her son crucified, Is this the promised sight (Crucifixion, 440).

3225 image]
Malone (ed. 1790): Delineation or representation. Tovey (ed. 1896): A strong word = counterpart. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Exact likeness, comparing 1364, 2602. Mason (1785, p. 358) compares The great Doomes Image in Mac. 2.3.78 (833).

3226 Fall and cease]
Johnson (ed. 1765), on this and the prev. line: These two exclamations are given to Edgar and Albany…to animate the dialogue, and employ all the persons on the stage, but they are very obscure. The eds. verify this judgment. Steevens (ed. 1773): Albany is looking with attention on the pains employed by Lear to recover his child, and knows to what miseries he must survive, when he finds them to be ineffectual.…He [accordingly] cries out [to Lear], Rather fall, and cease to be, at once, than continue in existence only to be wretched. Capell (1783, 1.2:188): The wide display of his hands, and the lifting-up of his eye, both directed towards the heavens, would shew plain enough that it is they who are call’d upon, to fall, and crush a world that is such a scene of calamity.…Fall, Heaven! and let things cease! According to an unknown 18th-c. author, Albany remonstrates with a pious injunction: Prostrate yourselves before the throne of heaven, and cease your impertinent enquiries into what is above. Davies (1783, 2:326): Perhaps [to Edgar]…Lower your voice, and cease all exclamation, lest you interrupt the dying King. Mason (1785, p. 358): This possibly might be an allusion to the theatre;…Let fall the curtain, and end the horrid scene. Sh.’s theater had no curtain. Becket (1815, 1:175): Yes [agreeing with Edgar],…the overthrow and the extinction of all things…is near at hand. Likewise Delius (ed. 1854), considering fall and cease to be substantives: Albany continues Kent’s train of thought.…Kent asks: Is this the promised end of the world? Or the image of that horror? asks Edgar. Of that fall and cease? continues Albany (Ger.). Clarkes (ed. 1868): Nay, let it [the true end of the world, not just events that are its image] befall at once, and cause these terrible events to cease. Furness (ed. 1880): Is it likely that Albany’s attention would be so far diverted from the sight [of Lear and Cordelia] as to reply to Edgar’s question, which really needed no answer? If Fall and cease be addressed to Lear, there is a curt harshness in the words which is scarcely in keeping with Albany’s character. I have tried in vain to find authority for interpreting Fall in the sense of Fall back, Give way. Then the sentence might be addressed to Kent and Edgar, and equivalent to Make room, hush. After all, Capell’s interpretation may be the true one; and yet, an address to the Heavens, unaccompanied by any invocation, is unusual, to say the least. Perhaps for the last reason most eds. now take the statement not as an imprecation to heaven but simply as a personal expression of utter dismay: i.e., if such a horror as this can happen, then Let the world fall to ruin (White, ed. 1883). Verity (ed. 1897): Apostrophising the end, he says, fall and have done. Cease implies that it should no longer be held in suspense over mankind (cf. promised).…It is just possible that the gentle Albany means himself, as if he were overcome by the whole scene. Similarly Kittredge (ed. 1940): Addressed to the universe: Let the end of all things come! Brooke (ed. 1947): Fall, heavens! Cease, earth; similarly Harrison (ed. 1948): Let Doomsday come and the world end. Hoeniger (ed. 1968), alternatively: perhaps fall on your knees and be reverently quiet, addressed to Kent and Edgar. Warren (1982, p. 179): Also…commanding that they kneel before their rightful king.

3227 This…liues]
Since Capell (see textual n.) most eds. have punctuated the two phrases as affirmations. Brown (ed. 1976): A Jacobean audience who knew the history of Lear would believe he was right. Halio (ed. 1992), however: The line…carries an implied if at the beginning, reporting (ed. 1994) Blayney’s agreement.

3227 feather]
Cf. n. 3222. Lear may actually be consecutively applying both of the standard tests for life or, more probably, in his state of shock, is merely imagining that he is doing so. Since it is impossible that a feather, if there is one, actually stirs with a dead Cordelia’s breath, he may be hallucinating the feather itself. Sprague (1944, p. 297) records performances in which the feather was either imaginary or plucked from Kent’s cap. Rosenberg (1972, p. 314): Salvini plucked an actual plume from a soldier’s helmet, Redgrave used a wisp of his hair, Forrest a strand of Cordelia’s. An old Lear whose hand shook might indeed see a stirring. Meagher (1972, pp. 256–7), with needless literality, supposes that Lear mistakes for a feather a mirror fetched from offstage or from the body of Goneril (see n. 2308). Teague (1991) imagines that Lear wears a plumed hat; see n. 2773. Halio (ed. 1992): He may…pluck a feather from his garment.

3228 chance]
Schmidt (1874): Fortune (OED, sb. 1: Happening of events).

3228 redeeme]
Schmidt (1875): Atone for (OED, v. 10: Compensate for).

3231 Prethe]
See n. 664.

3233 your]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 424): The compositor [or a scribe] may have misread [you, F] as yor, comparing 2324. Manuscript you and yor may be confused in Hand D of Sir Thomas Moore, a fairly typical secretary hand. But it is possible that Q is right, and that your is used indefinitely for all murderous traitors, as often in Sh.: not with reference to the person addressed, but to what is known and common (Schmidt, 1875; cf. OED 5b: Often expressing contempt). Lear might speak indefinitely of murderous traitors in general, since there is no evidence that he knows who in particular gave the order for Cordelia’s death, or why anyone did so. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 8): The pathos of Lear’s address to the body of Cordelia is enhanced by his use of the affectionate thou to her, and the common you to everyone else.

3233 murderous]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 424), assuming that F’s Murderors is right: Perhaps a u/r misreading. But several eds. prefer Q (see textual n.). Foakes (ed. 1997): Lear seems to denounce everyone as if all are to blame for Cordelia’s death. Moberly’s (ed. 1876) n. could apply to either form: They have distracted his attention for a moment, and in that moment he might have saved his child. But perhaps he is cursing generally whoever killed his child (see prev. n.), or else he means simply that he can trust no man, if any man has killed Cordelia.

3234 I…her]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): We are not to suppose that Cordelia was alive when Lear brought her in. He was deluded by his desperate hope. Cf. n. 3216.

3235 Cordelia]
Nowottny (1960, p. 57): Pronounced differently [i.e., as a trisyllable] the second time. This is exactly what we all do in calling a name again after getting no answer. One can hear the increasing urgency. But see below.

3235 stay a little]
Hunter (ed. 1972): Ironic, Lear having exiled her. Halio (ed. 1992): The eloquence and poignancy of this simple utterance are unsurpassed.

3235 ha]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Eh?…He thinks he hears her speak and bends down to listen. Halio (1998, p. 106): She may give some last fleeting indication of life. Howard (1984, p. 84): Definite silences must punctuate Lear’s speech after these words and sayest, agonizing because they signal the final rupture between father and daughter. Nowottny’s (1960, p. 57) scansion improbably leaves this word unaccented.

3237 gentle…low]
Synonyms of soft: OED (Gentle a. 6c; Low a. 10b; quoting this l. as the first and second exx. resp.). Bradley (1904, p. 317 n.) compares 163. Wilson (ed. 1960): He explains to himself why he cannot hear her now. Granville-Barker (1927, pp. 154–5): Dumb and dead, she that was never apt of speech—what fitter finish for her could there be? What fitter ending to the history of the two of them, which began for us with Lear on his throne, conscious of all eyes upon him, while she shamed and angered him by her silence? The same company are here, or all but the same, and they await his pleasure. And this must not be counted as chance, for the bodies of Goneril and Regan are brought on—why else?—and the dying Edmund…is removed.

3237 excellent…women]
Moberly (ed. 1876) sees this as the perfecting touch of Sh.’s type of the ideal Englishwoman: Her voice was the outward signature of her graciously tempered nature. Analogous ideas have been found in Euripides, Troades 656 by C. (1855, p. 348) and in Eccles. 36:23 by Abend (1950, pp. 554–8). Milward (1987, pp. 201–2) recalls Ecclus. 26:14–5, 1 Pet. 3:4.

3238 slaue]
Hunter (ed. 1972): So much for the noble fortunes (2973).

3238 a hanging]
On a- compounds see n. 1147. OED (A prep.1 13a): Engaged in. On the source for this mode of Cordelia’s death see n. 3214.

3239 Cap.]
On F’s change to Gent. see n. 3058+1.

3240–77 Did…see]
Bradley (1904, p. 292 n.): An interval during which he has absolutely forgotten Cordelia.…To make Lear during this interval turn continually in anguish to the corpse, is to act the passage in a manner irreconcilable with the text, and insufferable in its effect.…I have seen the passage acted thus, and my sympathies were so exhausted long before Lear’s death that his last speech, the most pathetic speech ever written, left me disappointed and weary.

3240 fellow]
See n. 557.

3241–2 I…skippe]
Muir (ed. 1952) cites parallel passages from Sh. and elsewhere. Dent (1981, D81.1) considers I have seen the day proverbial.

3241 biting]
Schmidt (1874): Cutting.

3241 Fauchon]
Schmidt (1874), falchion: Scimitar (OED, sb.: A broad sword more or less curved with the edge on the convex side). Hunter (ed. 1972): An old-fashioned word…appropriate to the memory of Lear’s youth.

3242 them]
F sophisticates to him. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 191): Q gives the better sense. Lear is surely speaking of people indefinitely or of his enemies indefinitely—not of the executioner of Cordelia whom he has actually killed. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 539): Compositor E commits the same error at [Tit. 2.3.256 (1011)]. Possibly the change is the result of an accidental sequence of associations in the mind of scribe or compositor: them-’em-him.

3243 crosses]
Schmidt (1874): Any thing that thwarts, vexation, hinderance, mischance (OED, sb. 10b). Skillan (ed. 1967): Afflictions. Hunter (ed. 1972): Of my old age. Soens (1968, p. 22) detects a fencing pun on the sense parries, as does Jackson (1980, pp. 387–90), citing George Silver’s Paradoxes of Defence (1599); the sense does not appear elsewhere and is unattested in OED. Fischer (1985), oddly, detects yet a third sense, coins.

3243 spoyle]
Schmidt (1875): Damage. Tovey (ed. 1896): For a fighter. Foakes (ed. 1997): He refers generally to all his afflictions,…not merely as a swordsman.

3243–89 who…longer]
Lamb (1834, p. 414): So ends King Lear, the most stupendous of the Shakespearian dramas; and Kent, the noblest feature of the conception of his divine mind.…What a pudder would a common dramatist have raised here of a reconciliation scene.…The old dying king partially catching at the truth, and immediately lapsing into obliviousness, with the high-minded carelessness of the other to have his services appreciated…are among the most judicious, not to say heart-touching, strokes in Shakspeare.

3244 Mine…best]
Hoeniger (1992, p. 96): In persons close to death, the spirit of the eye grows weak, so that the sight becomes dim or fuzzy.

3244 tell]
OED (v. 6): Recognize. Wilson (ed. 1960): Tell you…who you are. Craig & Bevington (ed. 1973): Or, I’ll admit to you, qualifying the first half of the line; see textual n.

3244, 3253 straight]
See n. 527.

3245 bragd]
Though eds. all prefer F’s present subjunctive brag (= ever do brag), Q’s conditional use of the past in the antecedent clause (= were ever to brag) makes virtually the same sense. If Q is in error and F right, Q’s MS may have had bragge, which the compositor misread as braggd and set as bragd.

3245–6 two…One]
All eds. reject Q’s or as making little or no sense and accept F’s and; having done so, they propose the following referents for one and Two with these divers meanings of the phrase loued and hated:
(1)Both Kent and Lear have been both loved and hated. Capell (1783, 1.2:188): The two objects of fortune’s love and her hate are—himself, and his master; they had both felt them, and both in extremity…: of these two, says the speaker, you…behold one, and I another. Clarkes (ed. 1868): We here means Lear and himself; each beholding in the other a man highly favoured and cruelly used by fortune. So Tovey (ed. 1896), Verity (ed. 1897), Dnargel (1890, p. 202: two men she loved and hated by turns), Spence (1890, p. 202: One of them we (each) behold), Wilson (ed. 1960: Kent and Lear are gazing into each other’s eyes), and others. Weis (ed. 1993): But Kent does not strike me as likely to compare his suffering to his master’s. It is more in keeping with Kent’s self-sacrificing character to think of Lear only. Cf. Joseph under (5).
(2)Kent is the hated man, the loved man is not named. Eccles (ed. 1792): Kent speaks of the object of her love indefinitely, without intending any particular person, but considers himself as the object of her hate.
(3)Lear is the hated man, the loved man is not named. Malone (ed. 1790): Kent may…be only thinking of Lear, the object of her hate. Probably Mason (1797, p. 59–60): If fortune, to display the plenitude of her power, should brag of two persons, one of whom she had highly elevated, and the other she had wofully depressed, we now behold the latter. Verplanck (ed. 1844): Of two persons who had in turn received her highest favours and injuries, Lear is one of them.…There can be but one besides Lear who has suffered such reverses. Nicholson (1890, p. 305): It is doubtless difficult not to suppose that the second person is Kent himself. But…Kent [is] too modest…to allow of his associating himself with Lear. Deighton (ed. 1891): It does not seem to me that the one loved by fortune is indicated at all, or that Kent’s speech has any reference to himself. So Delius (ed. 1854), Moberly (ed. 1876), Bradley (1904, p. 465), Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905), Brooke (ed. 1947: Understand the word respectively before lov’d), and others. Budd (ed. 1935): The play can produce no darling of fortune.
(4)Kent is the loved and hated man. Hudson (ed. 1879), substituting ye for we: This is said, apparently, in answer to Lear’s question…[3243]. By two, Kent means…himself and the King; by one, himself. In former days, Fortune had indeed seemed to love them both; but, of late, her persecutions have been as bitter as her smiles were sweet before. So Furness (ed. 1880), Rolfe (ed. 1880), Lee (ed. 1908), and others.
(5)Lear is a loved and hated man. Muir (ed. 1952): We may here have an example of a change of thought in the middle of a sentence, Kent meaning: If Fortune brag of two people, one of whom she loved and one hated—but no, Lear, who was thrown down from great prosperity, can serve as an example of both. Harbage (ed. 1958): Lear, and a hypothetical second extreme example of Fortune’s cruelty [i.e., favored, then victimized] with whom he may be equated. Joseph (ed. 1966): It is not in the nature of the speaker to regard his own troubles as approaching those of his master. Lear has been loved and hated by Fortune. Has enjoyed the best, has lost it, has regained it, to lose it again. This is more than Fortune usually does. Lear has undergone two complete turns of the wheel.…Nobody else has ever been so treated that Fortune would always cite him as an example of her perfection in dealing with human beings. Colman (ed. 1982): The second person is ?Cordelia ?Kent; so also Orgel (ed. 1999), Wells (ed. 2000).

3245–6 or]
See prev. n. Only Stone (1980, p. 200): Emend ere. Q makes no sense, and F no point. The point, I think, is the fickleness of Fortune who changes her mind with a turn of the wheel. That usage permitted the ellipsis after ere of repetitions now strictly required (two she loved ere [she] hated [them]) is confirmed by Abbott §386.

3247 This…sight,]
Delius (1876, p. 138) thinks that the Q editor (N. Butter) omitted this line because he did not understand it. As Honigmann (1965, p. 124) notes, without F’s addition, Q’s 3246–7 make a regular verse; with it, 3246 remains short. Both Q and F seem to misdivide 3248–9, which all modern eds. divide after same; without the F addition, such a division would in Q make a passable two verse lines of 3246–9. Capell (1783, 1.2:188) attempts to fill out 3247 by adding This sight of mine (see textual n.); Walker (1854, p. 80), Wright (ed. 1875), Schmidt (ed. 1879), and Furness (ed. 1880) try to make a scannable line out of newly-formed 3246–7 One…sight by eliding Q’s This is to This’, a change adopted by few eds., though Wells & Taylor (ed. 1986; 1987, p. 539) adopt and support it. Halio (ed. 1992): The Q compositor, nearing the end of his copy and obviously crowding his text…may have omitted the speech deliberately.
Besides causing metrical difficulties, the F addition has proved difficult to interpret, since sight may refer either to Lear’s powers of sight or to what he sees. Steevens (ed. 1793) compares Mac. 2.2.18 (675), This is a sorry sight; Craig (ed. 1901): rather, a melancholy. Blakeway (in Boswell, ed. 1821): His eyesight was bedimmed: either by excess of grief, or, as is usual, by the approach of death. Hoeniger (1992, p. 96): As Hippocrates noted, in persons close to death, the spirit of the eye grows weak, so that the sight becomes dim or fuzzy. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxvii): Perhaps Burbadge tried pointing to Cordelia’s body as a dull sight. Deighton (ed. 1891): These eyes of mine are very dull. Tovey (ed. 1896): Lear puts or passes his hand over his eyes to shade or clear them. Harbage (ed. 1958): Instinctively Lear shuns the admission that he is dazed and weeping. Wilson (ed. 1960): He cannot believe his eyes which, not o’th’best, he thinks must be deceiving him. Are you not Kent? he asks in astonishment. Many take this as referring to the dead Cord. Stone (1980, p. 247): Serves merely to emphasise what Lear has said three lines earlier. Booth (1983, pp. 30–1) finds no clear referent but all of these meanings.

3249 where…Caius]
Granville-Barker (1927, pp. 230–1): I cannot discover that any editor has commented upon the strangeness of Kent—Kent of all people, and at this moment of all others—asking Lear a kind of conundrum. The Pied Bull Quarto [Q1] at least gives no note of interrogation. And if the line can be spoken as if it meant Your servant Kent, who was your servant Caius [see ], it will at least not jar. Leave it as a question and Lear’s answer seems to apply to Caius, whereas Kent’s next line makes it clearly a reference to Kent. But in Kent’s mind they are the same. As for the apparent conundrum, the possibly dying Kent, who is still under Lear’s banishment, wants Lear to know that he is not a traitor but the very man who has served him loyally through many difficulties. Cf. Bradley (1904, p. 309): He cannot but yearn for recognition, cannot but beg for it even when Lear is bending over the body of Cordelia; and even in that scene of unmatched pathos we feel a sharp pang at his failure to receive it. Skillan (ed. 1967): A resourceful attempt to rouse some warmth of feeling in lear. Brown (1985, p. 9 n.): This is quite unlike Shakespeare’s usual practice: first to tell the audience that the character is going to adopt a disguise, then to adopt the disguise and a name…, and at the end to explain. Kent says he is going to adopt a disguise, then does, but anonymously, and at the end cannot explain who Caius was, since poor Lear is too far gone to understand. Kent’s speech at 3252 gives the audience as much clarification as it needs.
