Darton (ed. 1928): The name has not been mentioned before, but is evidently that adopted by Kent when he served the wandering king. See n. 570. Rosenberg (1972, p. 316 n.): Sh., having improvised the name [here, in rehearsal]…may well have told the actors to use the name in the earlier acts, without bothering to write it into the manuscript.

3249 Caius]
Kent’s Roman alias is a name appearing in Tit., Wiv., JC, Ant., Cor., and Cym., and in previous plays by other playwrights. Perhaps Sh. wished to suggest that Kent, like the stoic Horatio, was something of an antique Roman in strength. Musgrove (1956, p. 296) suggests that the name may have caught Sh.’s eye from a reference in Camden’s Remaines (1605, p. 52; see DP n. 9–10) to Dr. Caius of Cambridge. Elton (1966, p. 290 n.): Caius is…used by Renaissance writers in the sense of John Doe, citing John Ferne, The Blazon of Gentrie (1586, pp. 301–2). Dramatic characters so named, however, are always Romans, except for the French doctor in Wiv. and the Florentine judge in Sharpham’s The Fleer (1606). Duncan-Jones (1978, pp. 151–3) derives Kent’s alias from the name of a hypothetical quarreler in Saviolo’s Practise (1595, sigs. R3v–4); this may be an ex. of its common use noted by Elton. Perera (ca. 1987) suggests that it derives from King Arthur’s Seneschal Sir Kay, whose name is Latinized by Geoffrey and Malory as Kaius or Kay(y)us.

3250–1 Hees…rotten]
Capell (1783, 1.2:189): He knows Caius is living, and speaks of him as living at first; his speaking contrary afterwards, is no other than a way of expressing his own perfect abandonment to all the outrage of fortune; who, he thinks, could never admit of that person’s living who was either useful or dear to him. Wright (ed. 1875): But Lear’s mind is again off its balance, He knows not what he says.

3250 fellow]
See n. 16.

3250 tell]
F’s tell you, accepted by virtually all eds., seems necessary to fill out the verse line.

3251 strike]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Sc. in defence of his master. Delius (ed. 1854): Lear must be remembering 616 [and possibly 1318].

3251 dead and rotten]
Dent (1981, D126.1): Possibly proverbial.

3252–7 No…else]
With the exception of Lear’s short line 3253, 3252–8 make regular meter in Q. Cartwright (in Deighton, ed. 1900, p. 251), accepts F’s erroneous division of 3257–8 (see n.) so as to give Kent 3255 + 3257 as a full line, and considers Lear’s short muttered interpolations 3253 and 3256 as extrametrical lines, not interfering with the regular pattern of Kent’s verse. Flatter (1948, p. 57) goes even further: Lear does not listen to Kent or does not grasp what he is told.…The passage is…[an] instance of simultaneous speaking. The regular verse in Q makes both ideas unlikely.

3253 Ile…straight]
Moberly (ed. 1876) gives the most probable and poignant reading: The effort to identify Caius with Kent is too much for the king’s weakened perceptions. Followed by several recent eds., Kittredge (ed. 1940): I’ll attend to that in a moment. Lear’s mind is wandering, not from insanity, but merely at the approach of death. So Wilson (ed. 1960), adding, The mind returns to Cord.; Caius-Kent has ceased to interest him. Weis (ed. 1993): He does not wish now to be disturbed while he is ministering to Cordelia. Lear continues to speak to Kent nonetheless, though obviously abstractedly. Brooke (ed. 1947), uniquely: You must prove that to me at once.

3254–5 That…steps]
Like the Clarkes (ed. 1868), Deighton (ed. 1891): Kent continues his speech without noticing Lear’s remark. It is true that Kent’s further remark here grammatically depends on and completes his previous one, but such a pattern is common in speech and hardly implies that Kent ignores or speaks over (see n. 3252–7) Lear’s response. More probably, in his urgent desire to reestablish his bona fides with Lear (as Kent, not Caius; see n. 3249), he is distressed by Lear’s failure even to recognize him and continues (pathetically and unsuccessfully) his attempt to get Lear to do so. After Lear’s next inconsequence (3256) he gives up.

3254 from]
In both Q and F the word may mean indicating…the beginning of a period (OED, prep. 3); in Q alone it might mean because of (OED, 14). Stone (1980, p. 223) understands something like moving from: Difference and decay refers surely to the loss of worldly standing, and Lear’s life has improved in this one respect at least: he has been restored to honour and dignity, if nothing else. See next n.

3254 life]
Q’s reading, which must mean Lear’s recent particular manner or course of living (OED, sb. 12c), seemed preferable to Pope (see textual n.), who imported it into his F-based text; all other eds. prefer F’s first, meaning beginning (OED, absol. 5c). Schmidt (ed. 1879), first, cites similar quasi-substantive uses in Tim. 1.1.118 (147) and Mac. 5.2.11 (2187). The words are graphically similar enough that one may be a misreading of the other, as Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 424–5) suggests, but enough unlike that F’s word may be an intentional substitution. Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 526), believing Q wrong: The error might be in Q’s preposition: perhaps from was substituted for in…or through. Halio (ed. 1994): Blayney ingeniously explains how [Q] Compositor C might have been led to substitute life (the last word in L3v1, just below the headline) for first (in L4r1).

3254 difference]
Rann (ed. 1794): Misfortunes; Schmidt (1874): Turn of fortune. Only Brooke (ed. 1947): Friction, i.e. with his daughters, and Bevington (ed. 1992): Beginning of your quarrel (with Cordelia).

3254 decay]
Warburton (ed. 1747): Misfortune. Schmidt (1874): Decline from a better to a worse state. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Synonymous with difference; see n. 1364.

3256 You’r…hither]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Polite indifference.

3256 You’r]
On F’s Your are see n. 867.

3257–8 Nor…deadly]
F falsely divides this pentameter instead of turning over a long line.

3257 Nor…else]
Theobald (1726, p. 141): I.e. Neither I, nor any Man, can be said to be welcome hither, where the Scene is all Calamity. Perrett (1904, p. 300): The omission of the correlative neither was common, citing 2565. Capell (1783, 1.2:189): Here’s no welcome for me or anyone. Meiklejohn (ed. 1879): No stranger would be welcome to such a collection of horrible sights. Bransom (1934, p. 177): He plays on the word-formation of welcome.…Nor any one else is well come here. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): I who loved him am no more to him than anybody. Kittredge (ed. 1940): This is no occasion for the courtesies of normal life.
A sizable minority of eds., however, take Kent’s statement not as a reply to Lear but as a continuation of 3255 that ignores Lear’s intervening remark. Delius (ed. 1854): Kent proceeds in his speech without heeding Lear’s interruptions (Ger.). Furness (ed. 1880): Kent says, in effect, I am the very man, and no one else, that has followed your sad steps. Ulrici (in Schmidt, ed. 1871) objects that this interpretation leaves Nor and else unaccounted for, and is untrue besides because the Fool also followed Lear. Deighton (ed. 1891): But perhaps the Fool’s services are hardly to be construed as material; and the very man, in l. [3252], looks as if Kent left them out of account. Verity (ed. 1897): But it makes Kent dwell too much on his loyalty. Moreover, if Kent is still emphasizing his own services, there is no transition to als…deadly, as there is if Theobald’s reading is right. Edwards (ed. 1975) combines both readings: In completing what he was saying before, Kent’s words come to have a second meaning as an answer to Lear’s welcome: no one is welcome at such a scene as this.

3257 Nor no]
On the double negative see n. 427+1.

3258 deadly]
OED (a. 7c): Death-like in darkness, gloom, dullness, silence, etc., quoting this l.

3259–60 Your…dead]
Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Having failed to make Lear recognize him, Kent seeks to rouse his numbed consciousness with mention of his eldest Daughters. Rosenberg (1972, p. 326): Has anyone observed that in all Shakespeare’s major tragedies, no women are left alive to keep life going? In Lear this is particularly meaningful—nature’s own organs of increase have dried up.

3259 daughters]
Collier (ed. 1843): Only Goneril had, in fact, fordone herself.

3259 foredoome]
Q’s word could easily be a misreading of foredoomd (Halio, ed. 1992). Capell (1783, 1.2:188): The propriety of [Q2’s] fore-doom’d strikes at first thought; the sense of F’s fore-done is imply’d in the words of next line, and therefore useless in this. OED (Foredoom v. 1a): To condemn beforehand, quoting this l. as its first ex. Q’s meaning is that the sisters doomed themselves before Lear could; F’s meaning is simply that they destroyed themselves (see n. 3214). Wells (ed. 2000): But Regan has not committed suicide. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 425), preferring F: The [Q] copy may have had foredoone, and the n may have had an extra minim stroke.

3260 desperatly]
Schmidt (1874): In despair (OED, adv. 1, quoting this l.). Idem (ed. 1879): So that their souls are lost; see n. 3213. Lott (ed. 1974): From despair. Horsman (ed. 1973): (a) in despair (Goneril); (b) wretchedly (Regan), citing for the latter OED (adv. 2, giving a unique ex. from 1630). Just as probably the word refers not to their feelings but to the manner of their deaths. OED (Desperate adj. 5): Applied esp. to actions done or means resorted to in the last extremity;…hence often connoting extreme violence.

3260 are dead]
Have died (OED, Dead a. 1d, quoting this l.).

3262 sees]
There is no need to agree with Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 425): Q probably has misreading—e/a, e/i: the copy probably had sais. Though most eds. have preferred F’s saies, Q makes good sense and has had many defenders. Jennens (ed. 1770), sees: He won’t even know us when he sees us. Deighton (ed. 1891): It is vain for us to try to make him recognize us. Hudson (ed. 1856): Either may be right; says agreeing better with what precedes, and sees with what follows. And the latter may have some countenance from what Lear says a little before, This is a dull sight.…Nevertheless, on the whole, the folio reading seems the better. Hunter (ed. 1972): Lear’s sight, rather than his utterance, has become imperfect. Stone (1980, p. 223): Q’s is by far the apter in the context.…The point is that Lear has failed to recognise Kent, and pays no heed even to the bodies of his elder daughters when Kent attempts to draw his attention to them. Foakes (ed. 1997): But saies points up the incoherence of Lear’s words.…OED lists seis or ses as possible variant spellings of says (v.1 2[c]). But seis is a 14th–15th c. variant, ses is 19th-c. dialectal, and neither is a known Shn. spelling.

3264–6 Captaine…Capt.]
On F’s anticipatory entrance see n. 1358. On F’s change to Messenger…Mess. see n. 3058+1. But Duthie (ed. 1949, pp. 163–4): It may be suggested that when the Captain of line [3058+1] was cut, someone else (the Herald? the Gentleman who entered at line [3169]?) was made to go out at line [3215] and—renamed Messenger—to return with the news of Edmund’s death at line [3264]. But even if in the unabridged play the actor who played the Captain of line [3058+1] re-entered as line [3264], he may have re-entered as a Messenger, so marked in the playbook.

3267–81 Thats…sir]
Doran (1931, p. 129) suspects that Q misprints these lines as prose because they were additional or revisional matter written in the margin without clear line divisions. But Q elsewhere misprints much verse as prose.

3268 our intent]
Brooke (ed. 1947): Albany, as the last survivor of those to whom Lear had transferred his absolute power, now assumes the royal prerogative and language [i.e., the royal we] in order to return to him what he had resigned. Wilson (ed. 1960): The play ends as it began, with resignation of the throne—but of a very different sort. Or rather, Albany intends such an ending; but, Lear dying almost immediately, there is no evidence that Albany offers to resign his power to anyone else, or does so: see n. 3295. Walton (1960, p. 17) and others compare the similar speech by Malcolm in Mac. 5.9.26–41 (2513–28), ending the play with a ceremonial promise of restoration of order: It is Lear himself who in his last speech and death demonstrates its inadequacy. Shaw (1966, pp. 261 ff.): Unlike all his other great dramas, this play’s last speech is not spoken [in F] by the highest ranking character left alive; it is not a eulogy for the dead…; nor is it a reassertion of the principles of order and justice.…What we have, in a sense, are two endings to the drama, the earlier being [this, which]…has all the characteristics of a ceremonial closing address.…Certainly Albany’s naive hopes are shared by at least a portion of the audience.…[But after] the agonising death speech of King Lear…his very last speech is in an entirely different tone…subdued, almost numbed.…[Sh.] has written for Albany an interrupted cadence as a means of throwing into sharp relief the discrepancy between the superficial view of Lear’s universe and the reality of it. See n. 3298. Similarly Robbins (1969, p. 82): The ethical edifice of Albany’s reasoned idealism and hope for poetical justice collapses utterly before the tragic reality of Lear’s entrance. Foakes (ed. 1997): The presence of the dead Cordelia renders almost absurd the idea of virtue rewarded.

3269 comfort]
See n. 2196.

3269 great]
Wells & Taylor (1987, p. 526): The metre suggests that a monosyllable had dropped out here, and F’s solution echoes the Homilies…(II.x.Pt.i). But there is no particular reason why great should have dropped out of Q here, suggesting instead darke.

3269 decay]
OED (sb. 3b): Ruined remains, quoting this l. as its first of two exx. of this fig. use. Eds. disagree whether Albany refers to the state of things or to Lear. Warburton (ed. 1747): Desolation. Steevens (ed. 1773): Lear, as if he had said, this piece of decay’d royalty. Capell (1783, 1.2:189): Decay’d person or thing, by the same figure that makes majesty the person of majesty. Malone (1783, p. 51), supporting Steevens, compares 2577, O ruind peece of nature. Furness (ed. 1880): Delius [ed. 1854]…is right in referring it not to Lear, of whom Albany speaks afterwards as this old majesty, but to the collective misfortunes which the scene reveals. Deighton (ed. 1891): The terrible disorder of the realm. Verity (ed. 1897): Like maiesty in 3271, the abstract for the concrete, Lear being meant in each case. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): Lear and all that was his, state and life and line. All that can be restored to him he gives, physical care and the empty title, and to his loyal friends the honors deprived them. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Cf. [MND 4.1.173 (1698)]: like a sickness, i.e., like one who is sick. Bald (ed. 1949): This great man in decay. Wilson (ed. 1960) compares Ant. 3.10.18 (1999), The Noble ruine. In support of Furness’s more general reading one may note that Albany attempts to apply comfort not just to Lear (by temporarily restoring his kingship) but to Edgar and Kent (by permanently restoring them to their rights, and more) and to all friends.

3269 may]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): Can.

3269 come]
Perhaps be brought. Bevington (ed. 1980), however: Present themselves.

3270 for]
See n. 228.

3270 vs we]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): The royal we, since Albany is to all intents and purposes King of Britain. Cf. n. 3268.

3270–2 resigne…power]
Chambers (1940, p. 42): Lear, then, dies a king, as in the sources. Actually Albany says he will resign, but the transfer of power to Lear does not occur. Chambers continues, But he could not have continued to live a king. After what he has suffered, and…learnt, it would be, as Charles Lamb [1811; 1812, p. 309] has said, a childish pleasure to get his gilt robes and sceptre again. Foakes (1993, p. 211): After all that Lear has done to abuse his power, it would be sentimental in the extreme to give it back to him, but Albany is making a fitting gesture to an aged man. If Albany’s intent is sentimental or unwise, so is Cordelia’s, being apparently identical—to restore our ag’d fathers right (2380). Presumably neither could have realistically expected Lear, in his weakened state, to be much more than titular ruler. Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 99): In the old play, Leir ends by resigning his power to the King of Gallia (2638). This is simply wrong: Leir offers to reward France for the meanes and his owne persons scathe by which he enabled Leir to be againe possessed of his kingly title; Leir, like Albany, makes the offer in the future tense—if it please you to accept…I will resigne to you. But France clearly declines the offer—Thank heavens, not me,…Commaund my utmost—and Cordella approves: He…Will not be to [my] father unkind seene. See . In both plays the offer to abdicate is never realized.

3271 old maiesty]
Deighton (ed. 1891): Our venerable king.

3271 our absolute power]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): All the sovereign power that is in my hands.

3272 you…rights]
Deighton (ed. 1891) takes this as a directive: Do you return to the exercise of your rights. Tovey (ed. 1896): Supply we will restore from we will resign, which also implied restoration. Brooke (ed. 1947): I wish you a happy return to the rightful dignities you have been deprived of. Weis (ed. 1993): Their true station in life. See the next n.

3273 with boote]
Johnson (ed. 1765): With advantage, with increase. Colman (ed. 1982): Extra (wealth or titles). Cf. n. 2674. Meiklejohn (ed. 1879) alone: Amends (OED, sb.1 2).

3273 addition]
Since Capell (1783 [1774], 1.1:8), many eds. consider the word as synonymous with boote. Delius (ed. 1854), however: Boote refers to an enlargement of former rights of Kent and Edgar, while addition refers to new honors of rank and dignity that they will receive as rewards. So Muir (ed. 1952): With such additional titles and rights. Cf. n. 144. Murphy (1984, p. 9): I take the rights of Kent and Edgar as the full restoration of their titles, Earl of Kent and Earl of Gloucester. The boot is land and money; the honours suggest advancement in titles of honour. Their Earldoms would be raised to a Marquisate or to a Dukedom.

3273 honor]
The plural haue suggests that Q2’s and F’s Honours is correct. Mason (1785, p. 358): These lines are addressed to Kent as well as Edgar, else the word honours would not have been in the plural number.—By honours is meant, honourable conduct. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Noble deeds. Wells (ed. 2000): In battle.

3275 tast]
See n. 1591.

3276 cup]
Deighton (ed. 1891): The bitter cup. OED (sb. 9): Fig. Chiefly in the sense (derived from various passages of Scripture): Something to be partaken of, endured, or enjoyed; an experience, portion, lot (painful or pleasurable, more commonly the former), quoting this l. Lott (ed. 1974) compares Matt. 20:22, 26:39.

3276 O…see]
Capell (1783, 1.2:189): Occasion’d by seeing Lear exert himself to embrace the body he lay upon once more, and pour his agonies over it. Anon. (1833, p. 197): Some sudden physical alteration, made dreadfully visible, urges Albany to cry out. Harrison (ed. 1948): There is a sudden change in Lear. Hunter (ed. 1972): Some new posture…as he cradles Cordelia in his arms, or picks her up again, or kneels at her side. See Rosenberg (1972, p. 317) for other business.

3277–83 And…o.]
One would expect Lear’s death scene to be in verse, and all eds. since F reset Q’s prose accordingly, but can do so only by a good deal of adjustment—adding another no in 3277, omitting O (and eliding to Thou’lt in 3279), adding neuer, neuer in 3280, and replacing the quadruple O…o. with a new line and a half (3282–3; see n.). Warren (1990, p. 56) thinks that never, never, never, pray you vndo is not bad verse; if so, the rest of Lear’s words make another pentameter, and the whole speech is metrically regular. Assuming that the lines should be verse, either it was (perhaps intentionally) rough in the Q MS, or else the Q compositor made a number of errors or even perhaps intentional omissions in order to fit the speech onto this last very crowded page. Meyer (1994, p. 143): It is altogether conceivable that [because of drastic crowding] the [Q] compositor omitted one no [3277], two nevers [3280], and inserted a simple O,o,o,o for Lear’s last words, Do…there. Too much remaining text had to be crowded onto L2r because the outer forme, including its final blank page, had already been printed off: see Blayney (1980, pp. 217–18). Foakes (ed. 1997, p. 122): Because of crowding on the final page,…some verse is set as prose. Bradley (1904, p. 292): In the simplicity of its language, which consists almost wholly of monosyllables of native origin, composed in very brief sentences of the plainest structure, it presents an extraordinary contrast to the dying speech of Hamlet and the last words of Othello.…The language is more than simple, it is familiar.

3277 And…hangd]
Gurr (1988, p. 116): This is Lear’s rejection of Albany’s well-intentioned statement [as] a nonsense.…The connective And…[implies] How can you say such a thing when Cordelia is dead? For other interpretations see below.

3277 poore foole]
Commentators disagree whether Lear means (1) his Fool, (2) Cordelia, or (3) both.
(1) The Fool. Reynolds (in Reed, ed. 1785) gives an extended defense of this identification: Lear’s affectionate remembrance of the Fool in this place…was one of those strokes of genius, or of nature, which are so often found in Shakspeare, and in him only. Lear appears to have a particular affection for this Fool…[and shows concern for him] in the midst of the thunder-storm.…It does not therefore appear to me, to be allowing too much consequence to the Fool, in making Lear bestow a thought on him, even when in still greater distress.…As there was a necessity, the necessity of propriety at least, that this Fool, the favourite of the author, of Lear, and consequently of the audience, should not be lost or forgot, it ought to be known what became of him.…The words poor fool are undoubtedly expressive of endearment,…[but properly only towards] some very inferior object, which may be loved, without much esteem or respect. Sitwell (1948, pp. 77–8) imagines that the Fool’s reference to a halter for Goneril in 841 foreshadows his own means of death. Speaight (1955, p. 100): When they hanged the Fool they killed Reason;…when they strangled Cordelia they murdered Love. Fleissner (1963, p. 426): The initial conjunction And might easily suggest ellipsis, i.e. Cordelia is hanged and my poor fool is hanged. Idem (1991, pp. 175 ff.) offers further arguments. Meagher (1984, p. 18): Lear means the Fool, being momentarily confused.
Objections are numerous. Steevens in Reed (ed. 1785): The Fool of Lear was long ago forgotten. Having filled the space allotted him in the arrangement of the play, he appears to have been silently withdrawn in [3.6].—That the thoughts of a father, in the bitterest of all moments,…should recur to the antic who had formerly diverted him, has somewhat in it that I cannot reconcile to the idea of genuine sorrow and despair. Besides this, Cordelia was recently hanged; but we know not that the Fool had suffered in the same manner, nor can imagine why he should. The party adverse to Lear, was little interested in the fate of his jester. The only use of him was to contrast and alleviate the sorrows of his master; and, that purpose being fully answered, the poet’s solicitude about him was at an end. Collier (ed. 1843): As Cordelia had been hanged, the poet would probably have chosen some other death for the Fool.…On the other hand, if Shakespeare did not mean to revert to the Fool, he has certainly omitted to account for a prominent and important character. Clarkes (ed. 1868): We do not believe that Shakespeare would have made the bereaved father recur for even one moment to any thought of other loss than the one before him—his murdered Cordelia. Furthermore, if Shakespeare had intended to denote a tender reminiscence of the fool on the part of his old master, and to take an opportunity of definitely stating the mode of the fool’s death, we do not think that he would have made this the opportunity, or have made hanging the means by which the lad came to his end; he would not have reserved Lear’s mention of the faithful jester until a time when the father’s whole soul is engrossed with but one idea, nor would he have committed the dramatic tautology, as well as the dramatic injury to tragic effect, of making the fool as well as Cordelia hang’d. Moberly (ed. 1876): He means Cordelia, as the next words plainly show. Thaler (1929, p. 38): Lear’s fool has no more right to these words than Touchstone has to the tears which Jacques [sic] weeps for his poor…fools of the forest. The end must belong to Cordelia. The fool disappears long before because he has done his work. Wilson (ed. 1960): Surely the Fool, like Kent, is forgotten. Only Eastman (1964, p. 534) gives as reasons why the Fool could have been hanged, that Goneril has shown her animosity to him as early as the first act; that hanging was a fine undignified death to visit on one’s enemies and traitors; that the Fool, as adherent to Lear, was automatically a traitor to the perverted minds of Goneril, Regan, and Edmund; that none of these was either temperate or legalistically precise in the meting out of punishment.
(2) Cordelia. Steevens (ed. 1773): This is an expression of tenderness for his dead Cordelia (not his fool…) on whose lips he is still intent. Idem (in Malone, 1780, 2:261): Poor fool was an expression of tenderness in the age of Shakspeare. The term—poor fool…has no impropriety when used by a weak, old, distracted king; in whose mind the distinctions of nature only survive, while he is uttering his last frantic exclamations over a murdered daughter. OED (sb.1 1c): Used as a term of endearment or pity, citing a few exx., which Empson (1951, p. 116) questions. Malone (1780, 1:261; 1783, p. 51) cites several Shn. exx. of this usage; Idem (ed. 1790), after elaborating on Steevens’s arguments: [Sh.] certainly has applied this term in another place [Ven. 578] to the young, the beautiful, and innocent, Adonis.…In the passage before us, Lear, I conceive, means by it, dear, tender, helpless, innocence. Many other non-Shn. instances of fool as a term of endearment have been supplied by Verplanck (ed. 1844), Halliwell (ed. 1856), Craig (ed. 1901), Rollins (ed. A gorgious Gallery, of gallant Inventions [1578], 1926, p. 199: Means practically poor soul), and Kittredge (ed. 1940). Davidson (1963, pp. 58–60): Cordelia is a fool for not accepting her sisters’ doctrine of prudence, and it is a foolishness which we tend to approve.…The critic must accept imprudent Cordelia as a soul in bliss…and as a type of the Christian saint [citing St. Paul’s use of the term moros in 1 Cor.].…Fool here denotes one who renounces his own selfish understanding and will. Lott (ed. 1974): There is a train of logic in citing Cordelia as an instance to disprove what has just been said: Cordelia, though a friend, has not tasted the wages of her virtue. It is clear from the speech which follows that he cannot be referring to the Fool.
(3) Both Fool and Cordelia. Forster (Dickens) (1838, p. 69): Lear, bending over the dead body of all he had left to love upon the earth, connects with her the memory of that other gentle, faithful, and loving being who had passed from his side—unites, in that moment of final agony, the two hearts that had been broken in his service. Knight (ed. 1840): Shakspere, in this place, meant to express a peculiar tenderness, derived from Lear’s confused recollection of his regard for his poor follower, the Fool.…In the depth of his distress, during the storm, Lear says—Poor fool and knave,…sorry yet for thee [1727–8]. And now, when the last and deepest calamity has fallen upon him, his expressions shape themselves out of the indistinctness with which he views the present and the past, and Cordelia is his poor fool. Lloyd (in Singer, ed. 1856, 9:527): No more may be meant than that in his wandering state he confuses the image of the fool with that of his daughter in his arms. Halliwell (ed. 1856): I do not think that it is even necessary to allow for the broken thought and incoherent expression of a madman, and imagine that his ideas of who is the victim, his daughter or his fool, are confused in his crushed intellect. Verity (ed. 1897): Though this view [that Cordelia alone is meant] is most probable, I think that many of us would like to believe that there had flashed through the old man’s wandering, dying thoughts a momentary recollection of his faithful follower, a recollection instantly lost in the night of grief over his child. Perhaps indeed he does think of both. Bradley (1904, p. 314): Even if it is intended to show a confused association in Lear’s mind between his child and the Fool who so loved her (as a very old man may confuse two of his children), still it tells us nothing of the Fool’s fate. Perrett (1904, pp. 302–3): When Cordelia is away, her place as the representative of utter truthfulness is taken by the Fool. In this respect the two characters are one. When Cordelia suffers death, the Fool, who on her going into France did much pine away ([602–3]), dies with her. Empson (1951, p. 152): Lear is now thrown back into something like the storm phase of his madness, the effect of immediate shock, and the Fool seems to him part of it. The only affectionate dependent he had recently has been hanged, and the only one he had then was the Fool.…He must be utterly crazy to call one by the name of the other. Gard (1964, p. 209): Fool acquires a generalised sense in King Lear.…Against the inhumane reason…of Goneril, Regan, and Edmund, foolishness of various kinds becomes the chief bulwark.…The word has become a kind of compliment. Elton (1966, pp. 323–6) lists as ways in which the Fool resembles or substitutes for Cordelia that they are both beloved, devoted, child-like, truth-telling dependents who become victims and hapless instruments of higher powers. Eastman (op. cit., pp. 539–40): There is a rightness in Lear’s meaning his daughter, a rightness in his meaning the Fool, a rightness in his meaning both at once, but rational prudence compels us to admit we cannot know what he means. We cannot know what happened to the Fool. We can know, however, what Shakespeare is doing here.…He achieves, as in the greatest of his late plays, a double vision that fuses past and present. He overcomes the limitations of time, the necessarily linear sequence of perceptions an audience has, and provides instead a simultaneous vision of cause and effect, of what has gone before and what exists now.…By the superb ambiguity of poor fool, which connotes at once the Fool and the daughter, the removal of both from the bounds of reason, the innocence and purity both share, the suffering both endure, the love Lear has for both, Shakespeare achieves such a simultaneous vision here. Edwards (ed. 1975): There is something inexpressibly poignant in Lear’s using this endearment for Cordelia at this point. His tenderness seems all the greater for gently using a disparaging term like this. And she is a fool, fooled by fortune, or the gods. He also brings back to our minds the Fool,…who is the only other person he has seemed to love. Booth (1978, p. 104): One sentence…makes two distinct and yet inseparable statements. Some commentators have supported Lear’s supposed confusion of the Fool and Cordelia by invoking Brandl’s (1894, p. 32) questionable theory that both roles were played by the same actor; see . Stringer (1897, pp. 5 ff.), preposterously, claims that the Fool is Cordelia in disguise.

3277 no…life]
Reynolds (in Reed, ed. 1785): Spoken not tenderly, but with passion: Let nothing now live—let there be universal destruction. Most eds., however, consider it a comment on the body of Cordelia, not an imprecation.

3278–9 why…all]
Elton (1966, p. 105) compares Pyrocles’ lament in Sidney’s Arcadia 3.22.8 (ed. Feuillerat, 1:485): Philoclea is dead, and yet Life is not ashamed to cõtinue vpon the earth.

3278 of]
Q2 corrects to haue. An aural error; perhaps the Q1 compositor carried the phrase in his memory.

3279 O…more]
Elton (1966, p. 256), perceiving a pagan sorrow devoid of hope of immortality or resurrection: Similar Old Testament instances of grief…[2 Sam. 12:23, Job 7:9–10] could be explained, like [Lear’s], in the light of their pre-Christian paganism.

3280 neuer…]
F’s two more neuers make up a trochaic pentameter, and may have been added for that purpose; or Q may have omitted two of the five words because of crowding: see n. 3277–83. Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 88) identifies F’s repetition as the figure as epizeuxis; cf. n. 3217. The effect has been much admired. Bradley (1904, p. 293): To make a verse out of this one word required the boldness as well as the inspiration which came infallibly to Shakespeare at the greatest moments.…The Quartos give the Never only thrice (surely wrongly), and all the actors I have heard have preferred this easier task. Saintsbury (1908, 2:45) admires the incomparable audacity and the more incomparable success of the five-times repeated troche. Barton (1971, p. 26): The last two acts are filled with frenzied repetitions, some of them hammered upon as many as six times in the course of a single line: Kill [2629], Now [2614], Howl [3217], Never, the monosyllable No [3277]. One comes to feel that these words are being broken on the anvil in an effort to determine whether or not there is anything inside.…So, Lear’s five-times-repeated Never in the last scene is like an assault on the irrevocable nature of death, an assault in which the word itself seems to crack and bend under the strain. Cf. n. 2629. Rosenberg (1972, p. 319): The five death-knell nevers seal her end, and prepare for his. The words have been moaned, almost sung, whispered, cried. Simplicity has seemed essential. Orkin (1979, p. 68): What is simply couched is also artfully couched…with the rhetorical devices of Brachylogia and Epizeuxis—the repetition of a single word. John Hoskyns, in his Direccions for Speech and Style, [Harley MS 4604, ca. 1600] describes Anaphora as a figure that beates vppon one thinge to cause the quicker feeling in the audience, and the comment is relevant to other figures of repetition as well. The word Shakespeare beats upon is never and it points not only to the irrevocability of death but to the cessation of the one life Lear values most. In this cessation he finds a truly terrible meaning to the word nothing. Here, again, the art is utterly integrated and the artifice appears to be natural. Sh. had parodied the figure in MND 5.1.306 (2099). Clayton (1983, p. 135): In context perhaps the profoundest expression of human grief and loss in all literature. Foakes (ed. 1997): Perhaps the most extraordinary blank verse line in English poetry.…[It] recalls the repetition of nothing in the opening scene. Tobin (1978, p. 40) thinks that Sh. had in mind a passage in Apuleius’s Golden Ass, Bk. 7 (tr. Adlington, 1566) where Lucius, accused of committing robbery, says Never, never, never with hanging lips; but the parallels are weak and inapposite. On the possibility that Sh. wrote only three nevers, see n. 3277–83.

3281 pray…sir]
Bradley (1904, p. 293): The familiarity, boldness and inspiration [of 3280] are surpassed (if that may be) by the next line, which shows the bodily oppression asking for bodily relief. The imagination that produced Lear’s curse or his defiance of the storm may be paralleled in its kind, but where else are we to seek the imagination that could venture to follow that cry of Never with such a phrase as undo this button, and yet could leave us on the topmost peaks of poetry? Kirschbaum (1949, p. 154): The difference between 1888–9, said without any humility and consciousness of others, and this speech said with humbleness [and] gratitude, measures accurately the difference between what Lear was and what he has become through his great spiritual purge. The speech is sometimes addressed to Kent or an attendant (see the next n.). Matchett (1979, pp. 202–3): Or it could be addressed to Edgar, who seems to be closest at hand, or to Albany, the highest ranking survivor, or, demonstrating Lear’s new-found humility, to the lowliest anonymous servant or soldier within reach, an idea repeated by Foakes (ed. 1997). Warren (1985, p. 30): Who is asked…and does he actually do it? Is there a button? Is there a sir?

3281 vndo this button]
Most commentators think that this request, and Lear’s subsequent thanks, refer to the loosening of his own dress; a few argue that it may refer to Cordelia’s. Steevens (ed. 1773): The Rev. Dr. J. Warton judiciously observes, that the swelling and heaving of the heart is described by this most expressive circumstance. Idem (ed. 1778) provides other exx. of the swelling heart threatening to burst the constraining buttons or lace: R3 4.1.33–5 (2512–14), WT 3.2.173–4 (1359–60), S. S.’s Honest Lawyer [1616, sig. B3v], Nathan Fields’s A Woman’s a Weathercock (1609, ed. Peery, 1950), 1.2.389; cf. Ant. 1.3.71 (385). Anon. (1833, pp. 197–8): The intense excitement which Lear has undergone…gives place to the exhaustion of despair.…Shakspeare contrives to indicate by a gesture the very train of internal physical changes which are causing death. The blood gathering about the heart can no longer be propelled by its enfeebled impulse. Lear, too weak to relieve the impediments of his dress, which he imagines cause the sense of suffocation, asks a bystander to undo this button. Similarly Muir (1952, p. 761): His heart becomes less able to pump blood to his head and other extremities.…He has less oxygen, and he gets a sense of suffocation.…His fingers, moreover,…cannot undo his buttons. Dr. Eickhoff (1952, p. 19) supports this explanation. Wilson (ed. 1960): Kent, I think, loosens the button—his last service. The symptoms recall 1328; the request, 1888–9. Some see the gesture as symbolic. Deighton (ed. 1891): As though he were suffering from a suffocation which prevented his soul from taking its flight. Greenfield (1954, p. 285) compares Man in Medwall’s morality Nature (c. 1495), who prepared for his heavenly salvation by casting off his garments. Like Heilman (1948, pp. 82–3), Rosenberg (1972, p. 319): The release from his last garment—symbolically, from life—recalls visually his first divestment, and both visually and verbally the culmination of that undressing before Edgar in the storm. Charney (1973, p. 201): The speech is a sudden shift to the practicalities of daily life. Lear feels himself suffocating in his new garments, and he needs once more to be released from the imprisonment of clothes, and the constricting mortality they represent. Like Battenhouse (1957, p. 62), Milward (1987, p. 203), as elsewhere, sees a Pauline symbolism of putting off the old man (Eph. 4:22, Col. 3:9).
Harvey (1952, p. 743): The button is Cordelia’s. He thinks he sees her lips move, his feeble old fingers fumble at the gown at her throat and he gasps out for help…and dies in an ecstasy of hope triumphant. Is there any place whatever here for a sudden switch of that tremendously concentrated attention to his own physical comfort? If he were choking, he would have fallen dead rather than ask for any assistance for himself.…We do not want to be even for a moment distracted while some attendant fiddles with Lear’s buttons. Williamson (1983, p. 417), arguing that Lear may not be deluding himself (see n. 3277): In cases of strangulation, it is in fact possible that when the ligature is removed or the air passages freed by the loosening of any restriction such as clothing, air trapped in the lungs will be exhaled, causing a slight tremor of the lips, although the victim is already dead. Such a phenomenon may be behind Lear’s final words. Several commentators confute Harvey. Muir (op. cit., p. 761): That the button is Lear’s own is supported by stage tradition, by editorial unanimity, by the medical evidence [see above], by the evidence of the imagery [of clothing, citing Heilman, 1948], and by its greater effectiveness.…It would be appropriate for him to use another clothing image when he comes to divest himself of this muddy vesture of decay.…Lear’s sudden switch of attention from Cordelia to his own sense of suffocation switches also the eyes of the audience from Cordelia’s face. When Lear cries Do you see this? we look again at Cordelia, prepared, against our better judgment, to believe that her lips have really moved.…There is no need for a nameless attendant to fiddle with Lear’s button. Kent, as in many stage productions, can perform this last service for his master.…A dying man may be excused some concern about his own symptoms. Harvey (op. cit., p. 797): Lear would not have interrupted his passionate concentration upon Cordelia at this supreme moment.…The switch of attention…is rather a distraction than an enhancement. Eickhoff (op. cit.): To read Lear’s button prepares us subtly for Lear’s end which otherwise would come with the suddenness of a schoolboy’s creation. Peat (1980, p. 45): If…Cordelia’s…it may open to reveal the lacerations of the noose. Perhaps her mouth…falls open and utters nothing…as an enduring silence. To McGuire’s (1985, p. 105) suggestion that possibly no one acts in response to Lear’s words, no button is undone, and Lear is in a world of his own imagining, Thomson (1993, p. 81) sensibly replies, That Lear not only asks for an action to be performed but also thanks the performer is persuasive evidence that one actor is cueing another. She thinks that the gesture also cues the audience to release Lear from life with final sympathy.

3282–3 Do…there.]
On F’s substitution for Q’s O…o. see n. 3277–83. Adee (ed. 1890, p. xxxvii): That accursed Quarto printer was evidently crowding to avoid overrunning, and to get room on this last page for the welcome Finis. Could this have led him to substitute O, o, o, o, so as to make room on the same line for Edgar’s He…Lord? Doran (1931, p. 68): The F substitution may be a brilliant afterthought of Shakespeare’s. Stone (1980, p. 247): It is difficult to see these [F] lines as anything more than an attempt on the reviser’s [perhaps Massinger’s, he thinks; see ] part to provide Lear’s speech with a more dramatic ending. His final words in Q…certainly reach the limit of dramatic understatement (but are all the more effective for that…). The reviser, however, unable to supply anything original, reverts weakly to an idea that has already been exploited to moving effect ([3227–9, 3235–6]), viz. that Lear fancies Cordelia may still be alive. There is even reason to argue that, in doing this, he has misunderstood the drift of the scene. It appears from Q that Lear, as his vitality ebbs, loses his grasp of the reality outside him.…The additional lines in F…are, of course, inconsistent with this. Clayton (1983, p. 129): The evident superiority of the Folio reading is attested by the consensus of adopting editors and the declared or implicit agreement of critics.…[Q, however] must be regarded as substantially Shakespeare’s earlier version.…[It is] coherent and conclusive, and in fact it better accords with the gloomier interpretations of the play and of Lear’s passing than the Folio conclusion.
The F addition has allowed critics to argue (see prev. n. and , ) that Lear dies in joy, however illusory, thinking that Cordelia is alive after all, and even that F’s ending is optimistic. Bradley (1904, p. 291): To us, perhaps, the knowledge that he is deceived may bring a culmination of pain: but…any actor is false to the text who does not attempt to express, in Lear’s last accents and gestures and look, an unbearable joy. Raven (1921): The self-deception is possible because Lear is going blind. Chambers (1940, p. 47): Lear’s desolation over Cordelia dead gave [Sh.] the symbolic truth he wanted. Yet the moving of Cordelia’s lips is the last thing seen by Lear’s dying eyes. That also gave Shakespeare the symbolic truth he wanted. Greg (1946, p. 233), however: Q may have omitted the lines because the suggestion that Lear dies of joy in the belief that Cordelia lives, may have proved too subtle to put across in performance. Weis (ed. 1993, p. 13): F’s version would seem to anticipate Dr Johnson’s censure [see ] in its inability to accept the finalities of Cordelia’s death. Everyone else on the stage, however, clearly accepts them, and Joseph (ed. 1966, pp. 35–6) finds this kind of argument wishful thinking: There are strong grounds for insisting that Lear dies admitting to himself that the movement of her lips was not real. Throughout the scene he has alternated between admitting she is dead and trying to convince himself that she is not,…[citing 3291–21, 3221–3, 3227, 3234, 3235–6, 3277–80]. Lear is not arguing with other people but with himself, he is fighting his own unwillingness to accept reality. He cannot face her death, he would like to be able to will her back to life. But he knows the truth, there is no hope.…There is recognition of the truth in his if it be so [3227].…This is the pattern: his admission of her death gives way to an attempt to convince himself that she is alive, which is itself followed by the recognition of the truth.…We may therefore be justified in imagining him killed, not by the joy of thinking her alive, but by…reality [that] is too much to bear. Marks (1967–8, p. 166 n.): If Lear dies deluded, surely the onlookers would make some pitying remark. Walton (1960, pp. 11, 17): If he dies from joy thinking that Cordelia still lives he dies, unlike all other tragic heroes, not aware that any tragedy has taken place, for the other deaths are not to be thought of as tragic.…[Rather,] Lear dies with the effort of realizing to the full the implications of her silence. That, and not merely despair, brings about his death. Edwards (ed. 1975): It is a crueller play if Lear is shown dying in a misapprehension that her lips have moved, and that she is alive. It is a greater play, perhaps, if we accept…that Lear dies in full recognition of what has happened. Bradbrook (1978, p. 192): It is idle to ask what is this he points to at the end, on the Threshold.…He is in death’s dream kingdom, talking to himself or to her. Beckerman, 1985, pp. 94–5): F’s addition makes the ending equivocal.…Instead of closure in Lear’s death, there is uncertainty, and bewilderment, consistent with Albany’s failure to offer a convincing provision for the future. Foakes (ed. 1997): These lines complicate the ending by their very ambiguity. Lear’s death is at once painful and a welcome release.…Even if he is deluded, he dies with all his attention focused on Cordelia, not any longer on himself.

3282 lips]
Capell (1783, 1.2:189): His expressions about her lips…might proceed from an imagination of motion in them; or else from some actual convulsive appearance. Eccles (ed. 1792): Perhaps he points to the pale colour of the lips in death. Elton (1966, p. 258 n.): May suggest not only breath, but also…the passage through her mouth of Cordelia’s soul.

3283 there]
Usually taken to mean Cordelia’s lips. In productions having a redemptionist slant, Lears have pointed towards heaven. Peat (1980, p. 45): In Peter Brook’s production [Stratford, 1962], Paul Scofield sat staring out blankly into the auditorium. Miola (1992, p. 172): An anguished invitation to behold the unaccommodated figure of death? Butler (1992, pp. 14, 19), believing that Cordelia, Edgar, Kent, Gloucester, and Lear are dying into life by separating the flesh from the spirit: possibly he sees Cordelia’s soul leaving her body and ascending into bliss. The action is pre-Messiah, however. Holland (1997, p. 171): In the 1993 RSC production, Robert Stephens focused his eyes on a vacancy at the edge of the stage…which the audience could only find unbearably empty.

3283 O…o.]
Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 44): In Q we have a truly horrible quadruple O, expressing dying groans to the utterance of which Burbadge seems to have been addicted at moments like these—they occur also at the end of the folio Hamlet [5.2.358 (3847): O, o, o, o. Dyes.]. Surely neither here nor there are they Shakespearian. Walton (1960, p. 17): Presumably an actor’s interpolation. Or possibly a compositor’s substitution: see nn. 3277–83, 3282–3. Werstine (privately): Honigmann’s collection of examples [see below] from several plays casts strong suspicion on the idea that these are a compositorial interpolation. Lear being the first play ever printed in Okes’s shop, what is the chance that his compositor would hit on a theatrical formula as a stop-gap. Small, if people should fall into so deepe an O (Rom. 3.3.90 [1906]) only on the stage. Rosenberg (1972, p. 319): Quarto follows [3281] with four heartbreaking O’s—a more human equivalent to the howls [in 3217]—and leaves him to die there; Folio includes the two lines that have been seized upon by redemptionists as casting a warm and hopeful glow over the dark and deadly scene. Charney (1978, p. 111): They [Q’s O’s] have a brute force very apt for the old king’s final burst of energy before he dies. Clayton (1983, pp. 133, 141): O…o’ expresses an ineluctable nullity as darkly and as deeply as the most pessimistic could wish. Hawkes (1986, p. 88): The similar O’s in Ham. exhibit an involving and implicating musical power beyond ordinary words that is unmistakably Shn. Honigmann (1976, p. 123; 1989, p. 183), however, giving several exx. of O’s and O, o’s from contemporary plays, designates these mere crypto-directions, each amounting to no more than a conventional shorthand which directed the actor to make whatever noise was locally appropriate. It could tell him to sigh, groan, gasp, roar, weep. Hussey (1982, p. 7): Are there Lear’s own dying groans or a realisation that Cordelia is in fact dead?

3283 He dies]
In F the SD may be suitably placed, after Lear’s last speech (but see n. 3290); in Q, where there is no SD, Lear faints here but speaks one more dying line. See nn. 3284, 3285. Meyer (1994, p. 144) suspects that the Q compositor omitted the SD for lack of room; see n. 3277–83. Honigmann (1989, p. 175): Although Lear may indeed die at the point indicated, the crucial fact is that we are left in uncertainty for a while, in the theatre: the moment of death is not obvious. It seems not obvious to the onlookers on stage until 3290.
Daniel (ed. 1824, p. 7): The death of Lear realizes all that can be imagined of human woe. Any future poet who shall carry distress beyond this, may claim even a prouder laurel than Shakspeare. Bradley (1904, p. 291) imagines that Lear dies in unbearable joy (see n. 3282–3): Though he is killed by an agony of pain, the agony in which he actually dies is not one of pain but of ecstasy.…This interpretation may be condemned as fantastic, but the text…will bear no other. The text that Bradley refers to is F, not Q, where there is neither hope nor joy. Chambers (1940, pp. 44–5): That Bradley’s interpretation is not fantastic…can be proved, I think, when we examine Shakespeare’s sources.…It is precisely such an ecstasy of joy, succeeding affliction, which Sidney depicts as killing his old king.…Shakespeare reproduces this in the death of Gloucester:…then gives the same death to Lear, citing Arcadia 2.10.7 (see ). Cf. 3159–62. So also Davenport (1949, p. 555) and Duncan-Jones (1997, pp. 15–16). Moore (1997, pp. 484–90) is unable to find any precedent for Bradley’s view that Lear dies in joy. In reading pre-Bradleyan commentary on Lear, one is struck with how little attention is, in fact, paid to the last scene.…When the ending is alluded to, the assumption is that he dies in despair.…[Yet] no twentieth-century critic, until very recently, thought [Bradley’s] reading fantastic, even when Bradley was most unfashionable in some critical circles. His reading, in fact,…became the standard interpretation. Smith (1955, pp. 403–4) documents contemporary belief in death caused by joy. Walton (1960, p. 17): If we take it that Lear finally believes that Cordelia is alive, we alter the direction of the whole movement which has been taking place throughout the play, a movement by which he attains an ever greater consciousness.…There is, in fact, nothing in his speech…which indicates a transition from grief to joy.…As at the beginning of the play [Cordelia] says nothing, but this time Lear dies with the effort of realizing to the full the implications of her silence. That, and not merely despair, brings about his death.…The view proposed by William Empson [1951, pp. 151 ff.], who regards Lear in the last scene as mad again, and, as, finally, the eternal fool and scapegoat who has experienced everything and learned nothing,…makes it difficult to regard King Lear as a tragedy at all. Stampfer (1960, p. 10): With Lear’s death each audience…shares and releases the most private and constricting fear to which mankind is subject, the fear that penance is impossible, that the covenant, once broken, can never be re-established, because its partner has no charity, resilience, or harmony—the fear, in other words, that we inhabit an imbecile universe. Mack (1965, pp. 114, 117): We are offered two ways of being sentimental about this conclusion [i.e., asserting transfiguration or meaninglessness], both of which we must make an effort to eschew.…The victory and the defeat are simultaneous and inseparable. Meagher (1972, p. 259): Despite the way in which Lear’s final lines are usually understood, it is not really self-evident that they are to be spoken in a tone of joy, particularly in the quarto version…and we perhaps ought not to assume that Burbage was necessarily pointing to Cordelia’s lips as he said Do…there. Rosenberg (1972, p. 319): Though the facts of the text are that Cordelia is physically dead, and that all about her—except possibly Lear—see nothing to alleviate a sense of absolute woe, yet a wide variety of possible modes of Lear’s dying, from ecstasy through dread…has been suggested by actors as well as critics: so Gielgud, dying grandly in joy at his perception of apotheosis in Cordelia; Forrest, frankly hallucinating her reviving, staring vacantly into space; Carnovsky, shocked to death at the horror of Cordelia’s stillness. Hennedy (1974, p. 375): Lear dies neither deluded nor mad but happy in his knowledge that Cordelia, having died, lives. See further , .

3284 faints]
In Sh. faint often means not to swoon but to grow weak (Schmidt, 1874; OED, v. 2). See next n.

3285 Lear.]
F and virtually all eds. reassign to Kent. Collier (ed. 1843): This line is in the quartos erroneously given to Lear, whose death is not there marked in the stage directions. White (ed. 1862): I am not sure that [this] does not belong to [Lear]. The stage direction, He dies, at the end of Lear’s foregoing speech, may be only a timely warning to the prompter.…Possibly Lear was supposed to expire during Kent’s next speech. Ridley (ed. 1935): Q gives far better effect. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 85), assuming that Q is wrong: This may be a repetition of the preceding alternation (Lear./Edg., lines [3277, 3284]). Muir (ed. 1952): Q, impossibly, gives the words to Lear who is already beyond speech. But there is no impossibility at all in Q, which lacks a SD fixing death at 3283. In Q, Lear, groaning in anguish, could perceptibly falter (see prev. n.) in 3283, and a moment later, looking for final release from his pain, speak 3285 with his dying breath. If so, does he speak of Cordelia’s heart or his own? (Foakes, ed. 1997, p. 75). Clayton (1983, pp. 133–4): We may think that O,o,o,o, looks and sounds final enough, but it need not be so. Othello’s two last-scene O,o,o,o’s [Oth. 5.2.198, 281 (3484, 3581)] could represent heart-breaking terminal cries, but they do not.…Lear may well implore his heart to break and render him deliverance. Assuming that the F revisions are Sh.’s, he continues (p. 135): What Shakespeare has done in revising is to transfer Lear’s ultimate Quarto line [3285]…to Kent, thus utterly altering action, character, context, and significance. Weis (ed. 1993): F needs to attribute [3285] to a speaker other than Lear (Kent) since Lear dies on there; but he seems only to faint, and Edgar, who is apparently closest to him, repeatedly speaks to him as if he might still be alive. The transfer of a man’s dying words to a bystander would seem to be so extraordinary as to suggest error; wrong speech prefixes are a common scribal or compositorial mistake, and may sometimes even represent corrections made from misapprehension—e.g., from the misperception that Lear could not speak here if he seemed to die at 3283. Just possibly the speech was intentionally reassigned to Kent in F in consequence of F’s adding lines 3282–3, since after such a sudden hopeful turn as they indicate Lear would have little reason to say Breake hart; but just as probably one would have expected 3285 to be deleted altogether. Werstine (privately): If John a Kent is of Munday’s composition as well as his inscription, then it offers examples of speeches misassigned by a play’s own author.
Whereas the speech is entirely suitable for Lear dying in agony in Q, it seems in F (if directed to the King) somewhat out of character for the solicitous Kent, who, just after hearing Lear restored to his kingship and seeing him momentarily rally before becoming faint, would seem to have no clear reason to wish him straightway to die. Meyer (1994, p. 144), however, believing that the compositor accidentally assigned Kent’s line to Lear: Kent’s characteristic sympathy is expressed in his wish for his master’s death.…death brings peace at last. Kent does say Vex not his ghost; but that is after Edgar’s failed attempt at revival shows Kent that Lear is in fact at his life’s end; and mercifully wishing not to prolong Lear’s dying agony is quite different from exhorting him to die prematurely. Eds. cannot agree what Kent would mean by such a remark. Bradley (1904, p. 309): It is of himself [Kent] is speaking, perhaps. Wilson (ed. 1960): But at this point is not Kent’s whole soul intent upon Lear? McCann (ed. 1964): Probably [Kent] is expressing a prayer, which is continued in his next speech, for mercy on Lear. Or Kent, whose strings of life, Began to cracke a few moments earlier, does not now hope to live beyond his master, as he says (3296–7), and here is prepared to die from the agony of watching Lear die. Rosenberg (1972, p. 321), and similarly Foakes (ed. 1997): Perhaps speaking…to himself as well as his master. In Webster’s Duchess of Malfi (ca. 1614), 4.4.82, Bosola says sympathetically to the dying Antonio, Breake heart! On the other hand, Charmian’s O breake! O breake! (Ant. 5.2.313 [3564]; see Spevack, ed. 1990) seems addressed to herself a few lines before she dies, rather than to her mistress; Clayton (op. cit., pp. 132–3, 137) discusses the parallel. Both Juliet (Rom. 3.2.53 [1706]) and Hamlet (Ham. 1.2.159 [343]) say break(e) my hart, and Macduff’s grief Whispers the o’re-fraught heart, and bids it breake (Mac. 4.3.210 [2057]).

3285 prethe]
See n. 664.

3286 Look vp]
Proverbial exhortation: Dent (1984, L431.1), citing the same Shn. exx. as OED (Look, v. 45c): Take courage, be cheerful.

3287 Vex not]
Quinn (ed. 1970): Let him die in peace.

3287 ghost]
Kittredge (ed. 1940): His departing spirit (OED, sb. 1). Elton (1966, p. 258): The word does not require an exclusively Christian interpretation…perhaps suggesting also, as in Ovid, the pagan ghost, or umbra.

3287 passe]
OED (v. 11b): To depart from this life, quoting this l. Cf. 2487.

3287 him]
Doran (1931, p. 26): Q2’s added much makes a line scan which does not, in Q1, only because the divisions in the passage come at the wrong places, not as in F.

3288 wracke]
Variant sp. of rack, the instrument of torture (OED, sb.3). Wilson (ed. 1960), finds the same image in Sidney; see n. 3283 and . Hunter (ed. 1972): Here the tough suggests that it is the body that is referred to, as the rack of the spirit. Bevington (ed. 1980): With suggestion, in F and Q spelling wracke, of shipwreck, disaster.

3288 tough]
Pope and a few followers (see textual n.) print rough; Furness (ed. 1880): In Capell’s copy of Q2 the t resembles an r. Collier (ed. 1858): Tough does not so much apply to the world as to the rack.…To apply the poor and trite epithet of rough to the world would be very unlike Shakespeare. White (ed. 1883): Racks are tough rather than rough. Schmidt (1875): Not easily worn or broken. Clarkes (1879, p. 599): Inexorable, pitiless, unrelenting, unyielding. Deighton (ed. 1891): So hard to struggle against. Crook (ed. 1907): Hard-hearted. Muir (ed. 1952): Obdurate, rigid, referring perhaps to the rack as well as to the world.

3289 longer]
Following Miriam Joseph (1947, p. 170), Muir (ed. 1952) detects a grotesque syllepsis: (a) for a longer time, (b) with his body extended further by the rack.

3290 O]
F omits, avoiding a weak echo of [3287] (Jones, 1995, p. 232 n.).

3290 gone]
Craig (ed. 1901): Dead. Wilson (ed. 1960), like Bradley (1904, p. 292 n.), thinks that the F SD at 3283 comes a few lines too soon, and that this line was intended to mark the moment, though the audience c[oul]d prob. see no difference between fainting and dying.

3291 The wonder is]
OED (Wonder sb. 6f) quotes this l. as its first ex. of the phrase.

3292 vsurpt]
Eccles (ed. 1792): Held it by…force and violence, in opposition to so many assaults. Deighton (ed. 1891): His hold upon life was but a factitious one, the strength of excitement and despair. Crook (ed. 1907): He had really no right to be alive, lives in spite of what should have killed him. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Emphatic: He lived beyond the rightful (allotted) term of mortality. Lear’s uncommon vigour is more than once emphasized. Brooke (ed. 1947): Retained against natural law. Rosenberg (1972, p. 321): Illictly commandeered Lear’s identity, drove out the rightful self. Lott (ed. 1974), most simply: He was merely holding on to life when it was no longer his.

3293 Beare…hence]
Wilson (ed. 1960): Here Sh. had no curtain…to hide the dead at the end of the play. Foakes (ed. 1997): A signal within the text for the soldiers and attendants in the scene to begin to take up the bodies…in preparation for a processional ending. Hodges (1999, p. 167): Two other litters are quietly brought in at the back, and the old king and Cordelia are laid upon them and covered with their palls. I imagine that Cordelia’s will be black…but Lear’s would be of royal purple.

3293–4 busines…to]
On busines as trisyllabic, see n. 1070. Though F omits to, Q makes sense if business is taken in the sense solicitude, care, attention (OED, sb. 5, 6). In F it has the more modern meaning matter demanding attention (OED, 15).

3294–3301 friends…long]
White (ed. 1883): Were it not that S. always falls into feebleness with rhyme, I should believe that these words…were a tag added to please the players and the vulgar among the audience.…Indeed, I am at every reading of them nearer being sure that they are not from the hand that wrote the rest of this tragedy. They and 3290–3 were cut by Charles Kean, Macready, Phelps, and Irving (Bratton, ed. 1987). Verity (ed. 1897): The rhyme shows that the end is at hand. Houghton (ed. 1957): The couplets give a kind of proverbial ring which prelude[s] the end and make[s] it unnecessary to attach too precise a meaning to [3299]. Marks (1967–8, pp. 164–5): Modest Albany and [in F] self-effacing Edgar, bowed with respect and grief for Lear, recognize that they must speak briefly.…There is not, then, that strong concluding reassertion of order in the kingdom that is customary at the end of Shakespeare’s plays. Zitner (1974, p. 4): All the theatrical oughts: apostrophe, lament, sentence, the grand futurity, even simple aesthetic closure, are rejected in a monosyllabic flatness that rebukes the shallowness of their big rhetoric, rejected in favour of speaking what one feels. Booth (1978, p. 102): The three final speeches, a reprise of the division of the kingdom in I. i, leave us in new doubt about who will rule.

3294 generall]
See n. 2648. Skillan (ed. 1967): National distress.

3295 Rule in]
The many critics who would have Albany here offer to give up his sovereign power permanently to Edgar and Kent as he has already offered to relinquish it temporarily to Lear do not distinguish between the meaning of this word, which may mean to govern by wielding any of several kinds of administrative or executive power or authority (OED, v. 3, 4), and reign, which in Sh. always refers to exercise of royal authority (Schmidt, 1875; OED, v. 1). Moreover, in both Q and F Albany says clearly Rule in the kingdome or Realme, not rule or rule o’er it. The most that can be said with certainty is that Albany is, as he promised would happen (see 3272–3), reinstating Edgar and Kent, who at this moment are still legal outcasts, to some kind of title—at least, one would expect, the earldoms that they rightfully should possess. They will sustaine the state, or kingdome—both singular, not plural nouns. There is not the slightest hint that they will jointly reign over it. That this northern duke, now sovereign authority in Britain, might be making them dukes of their home regions, southwest and southeast Britain, where they now have claims only to earldoms, there is at least a hint (see n. 3273). That in addition he himself is abdicating, without giving any motive for such an astounding act, and is offering his sovereign power to two men of inferior rank, thereby once again dividing authority within the kingdom as soon as it was reunited under him, is hardly credible. Were he to do so, he would have learned nothing from the tragic error of Lear’s division; and not even Lear was foolish enough to appoint two sovereigns in the same kingdom: Nor can one England brooke a double raigne (1H4 5.4.66 [3028]). Even less believably, once Kent had declined to rule in the realm, would Albany leave his sovereign power by default to Edgar alone, who despite his success in man-to-man combat shows no evidence whatever of experience or ability in political or military leadership—who has not yet, in fact, even inherited his father’s earldom? For a victorious warrior-duke suddenly to submit himself to an untried and untitled youth would demand explanation; the play offers none because Albany proposes no such surrender of power. Bradley (1904, p. 298) is uneasy at the idea of abdication: If this means that he wishes to hand over his absolute power to them, Shakespeare’s intention is certainly to mark the feebleness of a well-meaning but weak man. But possibly he means by this realm only that half of Britain which had belonged to Cornwall and Regan. Boddy (1968, pp. 431–2) rejects the supposed abdication: The earliest editors (e.g. Theobald) in comments on this passage apparently assume Albany’s position as ruler and discuss the propriety of allowing the ruler to make the final speech of the play…or the breach of decorum which would be involved if Edgar made no response to Albany’s gracious invitation.…Some similar language was used…by John [who was not abdicating] to Falconbridge: Have thou the ordering of this present time (Jn. 5.1.77 [2246])].…[Albany’s lines] are perhaps closer to [this] than to any speeches of abdication of power in any of the plays.…[The righteous Albany’s proper assumption of power might have] the flavour of a compliment to the new king. The title of Duke of Albany had been borne by James I until he bestowed it on his son Charles at his birth in 1600. Flahiff (1974, pp. 233–5): The (presumed) succession of Edgar, whose historical namesake was a model for James I (see DP n. 9–10), adds a hopeful note to the ending. Bradbrook (1978, p. 200): Albany asks Kent and Edgar to serve as his counsellors (he is not, surely, after what has happened, proposing a division of the crown). Urkowitz (1980, p. 124): We cannot be sure why Albany disqualifies himself from further rule in the kingdom. We are not told. But certainly we should ask. Perhaps he perceives at Lear’s death the ultimate consequences of his rigid code of justice, untempered by mercy, humility, or kindness, and the consequence of his failure to act with moral responsibility when he held the reins of power. Lake (1983, pp. 9–10), also believing that Albany declines rule, thinks he lacks perception: The exchange…reveals one of the play’s most salient themes, that vicarious experience may not engender knowledge. Murphy (1984, pp. 8–9): I believe we can take Albany’s absolute power as remaining with Albany.…I take [rule]…to mean be the chief officers of the King’s Council.…The King reigned in his realm; he ruled in and with his Council and Parliament. Edgar, earl of Gloucester, would surely have been startled had a transfer of royal power descended to his rank. Edgar in the final act of the quarto constantly and continuously identifies himself as the loyal subject of Albany. Dutton (1986, pp. 146–7): There are two historical problems…: one is that Edgar has no obvious right to the throne (other than as a gift from Albany which is, to say the least, an unusual means of succession); the second is that this goes far beyond creative adaptation of the matter of Britain—the apparently arbitrary creation of a totally fictitious king based on a fictional character derived from Sidney’s romance Arcadia. For Edgar to be vaulted from Poor Tom to sovereign, from Beggar to King, would be the stuff of romance, not history or tragedy. Mahood (1992, p. 238): Not…an abdication. He has said that he will resign his power to Lear, but now that the King is dead Albany, as ruler of the north, welcomes Gloucester’s heir as the successor to Cornwall’s western duchy and Kent as the successor to that south-east portion which was intended as Cordelia’s. Knowles (1997, p. 72): This is conceivable, but Shakespeare surely would have known that his audience, having watched the tragedy caused by division, would prefer unification under the absolute power of the Scots ruler, such as James I was then attempting to bring about. James had formerly held the title Duke of Albany; see DP n. 6. Arguing that Albany may be inviting the other two to govern jointly with him, Foakes (ed. 1997) embroiders on Rosenberg’s (1972, p. 322) completely improbable suggestion that at this point Albany and Edgar lay hands together on King Lear’s crown to indicate their sharing of power. Rosenberg imagines that Albany took Lear’s crown from Edmund, who had taken it from Lear when arresting him. For this fantasy there is not a shred of evidence, while to the contrary we do know that Lear resigned his power and gave away a small crown in 1.1, was chided that thou gauest thy golden one away (677–8), has been seen vnbonneted (1622+7) and bare headed (1714), and has worn an improvised crown of weeds (2353) during his wanderings. McGuire (1985, p. 170) similarly sees a possible agreement of Albany and Edgar to rule together as both optimistic, emphasizing the moral goodness of the future rulers, and pessimistic, recalling the original sharing of power by Albany and Cornwall. His only reason to think that such a sharing of power is intimated is the use of we, which may be…in the royal sense; but there is no reason to think so (cf. n. 3298–3000), and one would expect a less oblique hint of such a momentous division of power. Berry (1999, p. 116): The proposed relationship between Albany and Edgar is that of Chairman to CEO. The reassignment of the final lines to Edgar…would certainly give Jacobeans problems.

3295 kingdome]
Doran (1931, p. 47): Since F’s synonymous Realme disturbs the meter, it may with reasonable assurance be attributed to the printer. Or to a scribe. Van Dam (1935, p. 45), however, finds F’s line metrically right, presumably for having one fewer extra syllables.

3295 goard]
Schmidt (1874), gore: Metaphorically, to wound or hurt deeply (OED, ppl. a.1, quoting this l.). Foakes (ed. 1997): Bleeding. Doran (1931, p. 34): Q2’s good is probably a [printer’s] emendation of a word which was not understood.

3295 sustaine]
Jennens (ed. 1770), followed by Rolfe (ed. 1880): The play would best end here.

3296–7 I…no]
Most eds. reject F2’s unauthoritative SD (see textual n.). Jennens (ed. 1770): Kent only declines the share in the government offered him by Albany, on account of his age: how unexpectedly and aukwardly would he die, after saying only, he had a journey shortly to go, and without bidding farewel, or discovering any symptoms of death. Steevens (ed. 1773): The speech rather appears to be meant for a despairing than a dying man; and…the old editions give no marginal direction for his death. Malone (ed. 1790): Kent on his entrance in this scene says, I…good night [3189–90];—but this, like the speech before us, only marks the despondency of the speaker. The word shortly decisively proves, that the poet did not mean to make him die on the scene. He merely says, that he will not live long, and therefore cannot undertake the office assigned to him. Halliwell (ed. 1865): Albany’s next speech appears to be intended as a gentle reproof to Kent’s despairing speech, telling him that the weight…obey. Had Kent died, some sensation would have been created, and his death not passed over as a piece of stage show that is expected; and the speech of Albany would have lost its pertinence. Hudson (ed. 1881): He means…that all the treasure he had in life is now gone; that the death of his revered and beloved master, and of his kind and dear Princess, must needs pluck him after. This reminds me of Coleridge’s judgment, that Kent is perhaps the nearest to perfect goodness in all Shakespeare’s characters. His passionate affection for, and fidelity to, Lear act on our feelings in Lear’s own favour: virtue itself seems to be in company with him (Coleridge, MS notes 1818–19, ed. Foakes, 1989, p. 99). Goggin (ed. 1910): It is to be remembered that Edgar has said of Kent that The strings of life begin to crack. Kittredge (ed. 1940): Kent feels unable to survive the death of the master to whom he was so devoted. We are not to take his words literally—as if he were soon to die. Wilson (ed. 1960): To die on the scene w[oul]d indeed be theatrically a disservice to Kent’s master. Mahood (1992, p. 179): The figure we are most aware of in this concluding moment is that of Kent, who has twice [3168+12, 3190] spoken of being close to his own death. These statements come so unexpectedly from the pugnacious Caius that signs of his having been wounded in the battle are perhaps needed to render them plausible. But they do ensure that all eyes follow his final exit…among the bearers of the King’s body. Bate (1991, p. 118): Kent gracefully withdraws, presumably to commit suicide. No one else seems to have presumed that.

3296 iourney]
Moberly (ed. 1876): To another world. Craig (ed. 1901) cites other instances of the metaphor in Sh. and Marlowe.

3297 maister]
Schmidt (ed. 1879): I.e., Lear, not, as some understand, God. It would be hard to find in Shakespeare a reference to God as master.

3298 Duke.]
Whether Q’s assignment, or F’s Edg., or both, is correct, has been much discussed. Theobald (ed. 1733): In the Edition by the Players [F1] it is given to Edgar, by whom, I doubt not, it was of Custom spoken. And the Case was this: He who play’d Edgar, being a more favourite Actor, than he who personated Albany; in Spight of Decorum, it was thought proper he should have the last Word. Wells (1983, p. 7): Theobald knew no more than we do about the relative popularity of the original impersonators. Delius (ed. 1854): The speech is Edgar’s, to whom it falls to answer on his part the request that Albany has directed to him and Kent (who has just declined) (Ger.). Halliwell (ed. 1865): Rightly assigned in the quartos to Albany, not to Edgar, as in the folio, Albany being the person of greatest authority in the scene. Schmidt (ed. 1879), agreeing with Delius, adds, Moreover, the substance of what he says, viz. that for the moment he is incapable of saying what he ought, by no means befits Albany, who, during this last tragic scene, has not for a moment lost sight of public interests. On the other hand, the two last lines are in character if spoken by the Duke, to whom dramatic etiquette gives the last word. Perhaps the true order might be restored by dividing these last few lines between them. McNeir (1966–7, pp. 183–4) would reverse Schmidt, giving The waight…say to Albany, who as the senior member of this new partnership, can more appropriately express the approval and reluctant acceptance of Kent’s decision, and the last two lines to Edgar, the yong. Craig (ed. 1901): The words we that are young come somewhat more naturally, I think, from [Edgar’s] mouth than from that of Albany. Bradley (1904, p.465): The gentle reproof of Kent’s despondency…is like Edgar; and, although we have no reason to suppose that Albany was not young, there is nothing to prove his youth. Porter & Clarke (ed. 1905): To Edgar, who is Shakespeare’s man of thought and fortitude and philosophy, he gives the last word of excuse and caution on the woe threatening to master Kent and drive him to follow Lear. He implies that he has said what he ought not to say, yet what is is excusable to feel, and he joins in the feeling although he is younger. Budd (ed. 1935): Since [Edgar] does not otherwise reply to Albany’s remarks in ll. [3294–5], [the speech] may be his. Its matter would be appropriate to either of them. Kirschbaum (1945, p. 78): Edgar, who has so often been Shakespeare’s Chorus in the play, should speak the last lines. Kittredge (ed. 1940): The Quartos are correct, for such a concluding speech (serving as an epilogue) would, in a tragedy, regularly be assigned to the person of highest rank who survives. Greg (1946, p. 233): The actors are…likely to have insisted on the normal theatrical ritual. Brooke (ed. 1947): Albany…might be expected to close the play, but the Folio is right. It is Edgar’s reply to Albany’s commission.…He accepts. But that is not what the speech says. The speaker accepts the need to speak what we feel, not a commission. Duthie (ed. 1949, p. 85): The Q compositor may have repeated the preceding alternation (Kent./Duke., lines [3291, 3293). Hoepfner (1954, p. 110), believing that Albany has abdicated, argues that Edgar therefore is the person of highest rank and so should speak the lines; moreover, since Albany is the husband of Lear’s eldest daughter [and] should be at least middle aged, he is not among we that are yong. On the likelihood, or lack thereof, of Albany’s abdication, see n. 3295. Shaw (1966, p. 266): Boldly and deliberately defying the decorous pattern of the usual ending, Shakespeare is implying that any return to routine after the events of this tragedy would constitute an outrage to one’s sense of moral justice as well as to one’s sense of artistic rightness; see n. 3268. Hunter (ed. 1972): There may be in [not…say] an element of apology for taking the last speech from Albany; but those words appear in Q, where Albany is the speaker. Horsman (ed. 1973), questionably: Albany…has resigned the throne to Kent and Edgar, each of whom should make a reply. Edgar’s is sad and submissive, in contrast to Albany’s more hopeful lines, [3268–76]. Trewin (1978, p. 210): The tone is Edgar’s. Mack (1965, p. 63): If so, Edgar has changed: The words ring no longer with high conviction; their form has little of the sententiousness that has characterized him earlier. See also the next n.
