Taylor (1983, p. 451, n. 162): Sh. first gave the speech to Albany in Q perhaps because Albany represented Scotland, and so may have been intended to compliment King James, who besides being a Scot had a son who was the current Duke of Albany; Edgar may have been intended for an actor (Armin [see ]) whose talents best suited its eccentric and mutable, rather than its heroic and moral, aspects; Edgar’s historical associations were, though potent, chronologically impossible [see DP n. 9–10]. Taylor believes that in F Albany’s part is reduced and Edgar’s strengthened, as by the reassignment to him of this speech. Beckerman (1985, p. 94): The transfer accent[s] the utter disruption of order and the leaderless condition of the state. As the ranking nobleman and victorious military leader, however, Albany is in charge and is attempting to restore order. Trousdale (1986, p. 222): Since the names Albany and Edgar were both historically associated with King James (see DP nn. 6, 9–10), the difference between Albany and Edgar as signifiers at the ends of these plays [Q, F] may be less than we imagine. Nonetheless Foakes (ed. 1997, pp. 78–9): Perhaps Shakespeare decided that to leave Albany in charge might be taken as suggesting that he would like to see Prince Charles, Duke of Albany, succeed James. Idem (1993, p. 254), citing McGuire (1985, [pp. 109–18]), argues that the silence of either Edgar (Q) or Albany (F) may show their refusal to take on power after Lear dies. This argument is another way of destabilizing the play, and the silences of Edgar and Albany here are invented by the critic: the absence of a speech becomes a presence, pregnant with meanings. (Ibid., p. 218): It does not much matter which of them has the closing lines. At Stratford in 1936 and 1937 Komisarjevsky gave the first two lines (3298–9) to Edgar and the last two (3300–1) to Albany; in the RSC productions of 1950 and 1953, these assignments were reversed; cf. textual n. McGuire (op. cit., p. 169): Nothing dictates that Edgar has to reply [Muir, ed. 1952] to Albany, and Edgar’s reply does not have to be verbal. Knowles (1997, p. 72): Edgar, of course, might acknowledge Albany’s wishes silently by bowing or kneeling, without needing to speak at all. Stallybrass (2000, p. 131): Speeches could be reassigned by a scribe,…. by another dramatist, or by the acting company, or by a particular actor,…by a compositor,…[or] by the dramatist who wrote the play. In the context of the lines that precede and follow it, the speech comes best from Albany: see n. 3298–9.

3298–3000 we]
Following the suggestion of McGuire (1985, p. 170), Foakes (ed. 1997) takes all the we’s to be the royal plural, and debates whether Albany or Edgar more properly speaks them. But they need only be simple plurals.

3298–9 The…say]
The meaning is obscure. The waight means burden and pressure, sad means sorrowful (and heavy, hence waight—Hoeniger, ed. 1968), and obey means submit to (Kittredge, ed. 1940), accept (Quinn, ed. 1970). In the other uses of the phrase obey the time cited by Dent (1981, T340.2) the sense is to accept as inevitable the imperatives of the moment. Beyond these meanings, the sense here depends on who is meant by we. Brooke (ed. 1947): Edgar replies that the young must accept the burden of the time and answer its demands by the dictates of their hearts rather than their heads: Speak what we feel, not what we ought (prudentially) to say. He accepts Albany’s commission. But if Albany is in fact offering to restore Edgar’s lands and titles and much more (see n. 3295), Edgar’s head and heart both ought to tell him prudentially to accept, and thus such a reply would seem nonsensical. If Albany speaks the lines, however, they are a sympathetic and tactful acceptance of Kent’s demur that he will not be able to provide much or long service of the kind that Albany expects. Perhaps, says Albany, Kent ought to express courageous, stoical sentiments of duteous resolve, but the burden of the time being so heavy, Albany understands why he cannot do so but instead speaks what he feels, despondence; besides, since the oldest (Kent and Lear) have borne more than we that are young (Albany and Edgar), we can hardly pass judgment on them, or reproach Kent for his diffidence. Knowles (1997, p. 73): The lines may best be read as Albany’s response to Kent, accepting his refusal in an understanding way. Joseph (ed. 1966): The conventional thing would be to make a speech of dedication consoling his new subjects, promising them better times. But Edgar [or Albany] insists this is no time for promise and rejoicing. He will speak what he feels; that is, grief for Lear, and a sense of emptiness. Lear has gone, his place can never be filled. Skillan (ed. 1967): They must face the grim facts. Robbins (1969, p. 81): A striking statement on the inadequacy of the concept of poetical justice. Matchett (1979, pp. 204–6) thinks that these and the following lines, which he thinks are Edgar’s, are intentionally made curiously vapid…flat generalizations to frustrate any audience sense that order has been restored. Similarly Leggatt (1992, p. 199): Albany’s final injunction…leads nowhere, as there seems to be nothing to say. Hunter (ed. 1972): The word [weight] may imply that Edgar is already carrying Lear (or Cordelia) from the stage; but this is no occasion for a pun. Bhattacharya (1981, p. 3), comparing Seneca, Epist. 75.4 (ed. Gummere, 1920, p. 138), Quod sentimus loquamur, quod loquimur sentiamus: The speech sums up and rounds off the play by referring to Cordelia’s initial predicament (see n. 93), and Such a summing-up could come only from Edgar—who has lived through storm and thunder under threat of death…and has emerged as the champion victorious over evil. But Albany, also a victor, feels as well as Edgar the weight of this sad time, having lost wife, king, and friends. Cf. the next n. Foakes (ed. 1997): It would seem that for Edgar and Albany the overwhelming events have freed them to speak feelingly…so they will not need to suffer in order to see properly.

3300–1 The…long]
Probably the obscurity of the previous two lines, to which these are logically related, is responsible for much of the disagreement about the meaning here. Jennens (ed. 1770): The two last lines…are silly and false. Capell (1783, 1.2:189): Albany intimates that his life would be shorten’d by the terrible scenes he has lived through. Moberly (ed. 1876): [Lear’s] life has been prolonged into times so dark…that even if we live as long as he has (which will hardly be), our existence will never light on days as evil as those which he has seen. Deighton (ed. 1891): If it were not that the play would end abruptly with Kent’s speech, these last lines would look like a player’s tag. Tovey (ed. 1896): Albany lays a feeble comfort to his soul: In these events the oldest has had the most to bear; we cannot expect to live so long, and therefore may see less sorrow. Bradley (1904, p. 465): A poor conclusion to such a play.…The oldest is not Lear, but the oldest of us, viz., Kent, the one survivor of the old generation [see the next n.]: and this is the more probable if there is a reference to him in the preceding lines. The last words seem to mean, We that are young [i.e., Albany and Edgar?] shall never see so much and yet live so long: i.e. if we suffer so much, we shall not bear it as he has. Duthie (apud Wilson, ed. 1960): It is possible to see in these lines an element of sombre optimism. Lear has lived long and had suffered dreadfully; but such appalling suffering will never occur again. Elton (1966, p. 249), more pessimistically: The final couplet brings the wheel full circle, remirrors the protagonists, and appropriately prophesies the decline. Skillan (ed. 1967): Consistent with the style of the play, this is a final hyperbole to describe the enormous events that have gone to its making. The rhyme provides unforced emphasis. Lindheim (1974, p. 183), comparing 2253–4, 2593: See has little to do with moral perception here, but is another form of endurance or experience, parallel in meaning with borne and live. Oppel (1976, p. 28) proposes three possible, not mutually exclusive, complements for so long: as fools of time, in the world’s report, and as compared with Lear’s vitality. For the most probable interpretation (because most relevant to the preceding lines), see the prev. n. Knowles (1997, p. 73): In Q the lines naturally follow [Albany’s acceptance of Kent’s refusal to help rule in the realm] as justification to his new lieutenant Edgar why they, the young and energetic, must sustain the gor’d state without the help of older men such as Kent. In F the change (which may or may not be authorial or even deliberate) to the singular verb—The oldest hath borne most—changes the speech to an elegiac generality about Lear’s life, which Albany could pronounce as well as Edgar. Bullough (1973, p. 378 n.) compares Leir 1672, where the king says, Dispatch, I pray thee, I haue liued too long; see .

3300–1 haue]
Bradley (1904, p. 466): If Q’s plural verb is right, the reference is to Lear, Gloster and Kent. F’s singular hath could refer to the oldest of the three men present, Kent (see prev. n.). Kittredge (ed. 1940), however: The oldest are Lear and Gloucester.…The Folios read hath, thus confining the reference to Lear.

3300–1 we]
Regardless of whether Albany or Edgar speaks the lines, this pronoun probably refers to both of them. Compared to the generation of Lear, Gloucester, and the forty-eight-year-old (or older; see n. 570) Kent, Albany is surely still young. He is of the generation of Lear’s and Gloucester’s children—i.e., of Edgar’s generation—, and since Lear in the first scene is just arranging his daughters’ dowries (cf. 48–9), Albany must have only recently married. Rosenberg (1972, p. 323): The we may signal [Edgar’s] prompt assumption of the royal plural, as he puts on the crown; it may too, though, include Albany, whose design of uncertainty perhaps involves…his presence in the ranks of the young. It may be recalled that Hamlet, who on the testimony of the First Gravedigger or sexton is thirty years old, is consistently and repeatedly called youth and young. Knowles (1997, pp. 72–3): In F, Edgar clearly would include Albany in the we of the previous two lines, and could do so in we that are yong. Whatever Albany’s exact age, the contrast intended in these words is clearly with Lear or Kent or both, the only two representatives of older generations present in the scene.

3302 dead March]
Like Naylor (1896, pp. 172, 175), Cowling (1913, p. 35): Would be played on the drums alone. Long (1971, p. 181): Probably muffled. For musical notation see . Booth (1978, p. 103): This is the only one of the tragedies where the last lines do not point to an immediate off-stage destination and invite the remaining characters to repair to it. The last lines…leave the survivors just to walk off the stage. Mahood (1992, p. 178): This direction reminds us that on the Jacobean stage the tragic effect of the play’s last moments was a responsibility shared between the actors of Albany, Kent and Edgar as the triumvirate who now (another reprise of the opening scene) rule Britain, and the attendants who had four bodies to remove from the stage.…The two men who have borne [Edmund] out [at 3215] return, so that one of them, as Messenger, can announce his death—a trifle here ([3267]).…They can then drag the sisters off through the same door, while the remaining attendants carry Lear and Cordelia out in high state through the other. Hodges (1999, p. 167), however, thinks that all four bodies are carried off in tragic ceremonial (cf. n. 3184): While the last funerary speeches of the play are spoken by Kent and Edgar [or Albany]…, two other litters are quietly brought in at the back, and the old king and Cordelia are laid upon them and covered with their palls. Leggatt (1992, pp. 199–200) imagines the funeral march giving a sense of formality and order that may be some comfort to the Jacobean audience, but the actors perhaps adding still further customary entertainment—a clown’s song and dance, a graceful dance by the principals—creating in the remaining spectators a more sharply upbeat mood…a recoil from the play they have just seen.
